## Volume front matter

### Series title page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the Apostolic Age down to the time of Innocent III;** a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived from the Church’s first twelve centuries, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with certain manuscripts, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all the works discovered after the extensive editions owed to the last three centuries had been completed; furnished with particular analytical indexes accompanying each volume or each author of some importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject treated; augmented with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: the first, of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the second, of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be learned which Fathers commented on the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture, and in which passages of their works they did so.

A most accurate edition, and one easily preferable to all others if the following features are taken into consideration: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the whole work, the low price, and especially this collection, the first methodical and chronological gathering of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but now assembled for the first time in our library from works concerning every age, place, language, and form.

**FIRST SERIES, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Gregory the Great.** Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

# List of the works contained in this second volume

## Four classes of letters

**First class.** Letters written while Augustine was not yet a bishop (from A.D. 386 to 395). | p. 1 |

**Class II.** Letters written by Augustine as bishop before the conference held at Carthage with the Donatists and before the Pelagian heresy was detected in Africa (from A.D. 396 to 410). | 121 |

**Class III.** Letters written during the remainder of his life (from A.D. 411 to 430). | 471 |

**Class IV.** Letters written to Augustine, even while he was bishop, whose date is less certain. | 1025 |

## Contents of the appendix

Several letters formerly, but falsely, attributed under Augustine’s name. | 1093 |

# Preface to the second volume

Just as the eyes surpass the other bodily senses, so the letters of illustrious men everywhere surpass their other writings. In them, as in a double mirror of the eyes, the qualities, affections, virtues, and vices of their authors shine forth, so that no one can express them more vividly, and nowhere else can one observe them more clearly than in letters. If this is true of anyone, it is certainly true of Augustine’s letters, in which the genius of the most holy Doctor, his unadorned eloquence, prudence, zeal, firmness of spirit, devotion to truth and piety, humanity, modesty, and other virtues shine forth.

Augustine had already expressed himself brilliantly in the books of the *Confessions*; yet, if one may say so, not as genuinely as in the Letters. For it happens that when holy men write about themselves, they either exaggerate their faults immoderately, if they are bad, or diminish their virtues more than is proper, if they are good. If someone else writes about them, he may be unable to penetrate sufficiently into their inmost character; or, even if he can do so, he may not be able to explain it with suitable precision. But in various letters authors spontaneously reveal themselves, and paint themselves in natural colors—colors which nature, place, occasion, persons, and the subject matter of the writing bring out even in those who are not thinking about it. Thus any careful judge of human affairs can, in epistolary writings, observe the author’s face and spirit at close range.

Augustine’s Letters are given an additional dignity by the fact that, since the most holy bishop was occupied with the gravest affairs of the Church, his collection of letters embraces not merely his private history but almost the whole ecclesiastical history of his age. Therefore, if anyone wishes to investigate carefully and understand fully the history of the Donatists and Pelagians—the two heresies that most grievously afflicted the Church during that period—let him read and diligently turn over Augustine’s Letters, and he will at last bring his desires to the outcome he seeks.

In earlier editions, however, the order of Augustine’s Letters was so confused that no one could easily grasp their arrangement without lengthy and frequently repeated reading and reflection. Letters belonging to the same period and subject had been scattered here and there throughout the whole collection; earlier letters had been placed after later ones and relegated to the end; and, finally—a confusion that was intolerable—Augustine’s replies were sometimes placed at a great distance from the questions and consultations to which they responded. Indeed, the replies were often placed far before the consultations, so that, for example, the letters of Evodius the consulter received Augustine’s answer only after many intervening letters.

It was therefore desirable that Augustine’s Letters be arranged in proper chronological order. Augustine himself would doubtless have undertaken this task if he had been able to complete the recension he had begun. For in the preface to his *Retractations* he states that he wishes his works to be read in the order in which they were written, and that he would devote himself to this task so that readers might finally understand how he advanced through writing.

Several considerations nevertheless prevented us from attempting this. There was the practice of earlier times; the order accepted for approximately one hundred and seventy years; and the customary citations, which it seemed wrong to violate or finally to overturn, lest this change cause excessive difficulty for students. In addition, there were serious difficulties in establishing an order of the Letters that everyone would approve, since scholars dispute the date of some of them. This consideration in particular held us back, because we had resolved above all not rashly to oppose or favor either side in this work of ours. These considerations therefore deterred us from changing the order, and it did not seem easy for us to undertake such a change against the earlier editions.

On the other hand, we were persuaded not only by the various examples furnished by learned men in the Letters of Saint Cyprian, Saint Leo, and others, but also by the authority of men distinguished no less by learning than by rank, who wished to provide for posterity through this new edition. Moved altogether by these examples and authorities, we finally agreed to restore Augustine’s Letters, as far as possible, to an accurate chronological sequence. And lest we seem to have established this sequence on a slight foundation, we took care to investigate it not only through our own studies and judgments but also through those of others. The reasons supporting the order we have established will be presented somewhat later, after we have first prefaced this new edition of the Letters with a few remarks.

Once the Letters had been arranged chronologically, we divided them into four classes. The first presents those written by Augustine while he was not yet a bishop. In this we followed Augustine himself, taking as our guide the first book of the *Retractations*, where he reviewed only those minor works that he had published before becoming a bishop.

The second class contains the Letters that he issued from the beginning of his episcopate until the conference held with the Donatists at Carthage and the introduction of the Pelagian heresy into Africa. These letters are concerned for the most part with exposing or eradicating these two errors, and they accurately describe their beginnings, progress, and condemnation.

The third class contains the Letters that the holy Doctor wrote from that time until the end of his life, namely those to which a definite date can be assigned.

Finally, we placed in the fourth class the remaining letters of Augustine that he wrote as bishop but to which no other indication of time or circumstances is prefixed that would establish a definite date. This fourfold division will have the advantage that we noted earlier: the diligent reader will be able to grasp, almost at a single glance and in a continuous sequence, those matters that concern the heresies of the Donatists and Pelagians.

The reader must next be warned that we have not moved certain treatises that have hitherto been included in the order of the Letters, although reasons of no small importance seemed to recommend doing so. Among these is the public document by which Augustine designated Heraclius as his future successor, besides several more extensive works that Augustine himself counts among books in the *Retractations*. We have left these where they were in order to serve the convenience of readers as far as was permissible.

We did, however, consider it necessary to remove to the Appendix the commonly circulated *Debate with Pascentius*, which had been numbered 178 among Augustine’s Letters. Its spurious character is established by manifest arguments, which we set forth in the Notice prefixed to that *Debate*.

Moreover, we thought we would do students a favor and provide them with something useful if we restored certain letters—not only those that Augustine sent to others under his own name, but also some of those addressed to him by many persons. Thus we have inserted in their proper places the letters of Timasius and James; of Honorius and the Emperor Theodosius; of Quodvultdeus, Prosper, Hilary, and an Anonymous writer to Augustine; and the letters sent by Augustine to Pelagius, to Simplicianus concerning the work dedicated to him, to Aurelius, to Valerius, to Claudius, and to Quodvultdeus concerning books bearing their names, which had previously been absent here.

We have likewise inserted the replies of Catholic bishops to the tribune Marcellinus on the occasion of the conference at Carthage, as well as the Letter sent to the Gallic bishops Proculus and Cylinnius on behalf of Leporius. These writings should certainly be regarded as no less true and genuine offspring of Augustine than those Letters addressed to Innocent in the name of the Councils of Carthage and Milevis, which everyone accepts, together with Augustine’s other Letters, as dictated by the holy Doctor.

The treatise *On the Good of Widowhood* should also have been restored here, had not long-established usage prevented it. That usage assigns it the title of a book, although it is truly Augustine’s Letter to Juliana and is not mentioned separately under that name in the books of the *Retractations*.

The same is true of the Letter that the holy Doctor wrote to the faithful entrusted to his pastoral administration against Petilian. From Augustine’s own time, as he testifies in Book 2 of the *Retractations*, chapter 25, it took the place of the first book written against that heretic’s letters.

There was also the Letter of Secundinus the Manichaean to Augustine. Since it contains nothing worthy of observation that should properly be submitted to learned readers, it has been left in the sixth volume of Augustine’s works, for the sole purpose that it may be read so that the arguments Augustine makes there against Secundinus’s errors may be more fully understood.

We have not merely reprinted published Letters; we are also bringing several new ones to light for the first time. Among them is the notable Letter of Augustine, then a presbyter, to Alypius, bishop of Thagaste, whose subject is exceptionally excellent.

For some time Augustine had been striving to abolish the Christian banquets and drinking parties that were customarily held in the basilicas on the feast days of the saints. His words on this matter in Letter 22 to Aurelius, section 5, are:

> “The evil must be removed not harshly, but—as it is written—in a spirit of gentleness and meekness. These things are not removed harshly or in an imperious manner, but more by admonishing than by threatening. For this is how one must deal with a multitude of sinners.”

Here he relates how, over three days, and specifically on the feast of Leontius, he insisted during a solemn sermon, using authorities drawn from divine Scripture and also prayers, weeping, and tears, that this disgraceful custom be eliminated from the Church. When he realized that this had moved only a few people, he immediately added further exhortations with more intense zeal and secured the support of the devout through the recitation of prescribed prayers. Thus, by God’s gift, the drinking parties eventually ceased.

Among the other records of ecclesiastical discipline reported here, the rites then practiced at celebrations of the saints deserve notice: a sermon delivered to the people; sacred readings and the singing of psalms repeated in alternating turns; and the sacred evening offices, which were customarily celebrated daily.

Two other letters likewise emerge from darkness. They complete the number of Augustine’s Letters to Paulinus of Nola recorded in Possidius’s catalogue. They are shorter, but full of Christian piety and benevolence. In them Augustine declares that he ardently desires Paulinus’s letters and the little work against the pagans that Augustine had learned Paulinus was preparing.

Longer and more important is the Letter to Mercator. It was formerly presented only in part in the book addressed to Dulcitius, but here it is given in full for the first time. It reveals Mercator’s sharp intelligence and Augustine’s singular modesty: Augustine receives with the greatest gratitude Mercator’s resentment that he had not written back.

The state of the controversies between Catholics and Pelagians is clearly explained in this letter, especially as it concerns the question of the baptism of infants and the death imposed as recompense for sin. The date of Augustine’s Letters to Sixtus and to the deacon Caelestinus is also established here.

Most worthy of notice, however, is the fact that from this same letter we learn that Catholic writers living outside Africa were accustomed to send Augustine the works they were publishing against the Pelagians. This could already be conjectured from the shorter Letter to Sixtus, section 1; but it is much more certain from Augustine’s words to Mercator:

> “Therefore, my dearest son, when you write to me or send me your writings for my consideration, far be it from me to receive them negligently,” and so forth.

In this edition we retain the chapter divisions that had previously been introduced into a few of the Letters. We have established new divisions in others wherever this seemed convenient. In all of them we have also marked frequent sections with numerical references, as had already begun to be done in the minor works of the first volume, so that Augustine’s writings might thereafter be easier to use and passages might be found more readily.

We have also taken care to correct the summaries of the Letters, which learned men had observed to be full of serious errors and contrary to history. Although it is by no means our intention to force our opinions and thoughts upon scholars, we could not refrain from adding a few brief notes, both on the principal corrections made in the received text and on passages that seemed suitable for establishing the dates of the Letters.

It would be unnecessary to list here all the errors that we have removed with the help of countless manuscript copies. The reason why it was not possible to remove every error is that several of the holy Doctor’s Letters were preserved in only one manuscript, and that manuscript was not sufficiently corrected, as will be evident to anyone who consults the catalogue of the codices we used, appended at the end of the volume.

Finally, so that nothing properly belonging to us would be lacking in this edition of the Letters, we have attached four indexes. The first presents this new order of the Letters in comparison with the order previously published. The second contains the former order, insofar as it can be reduced to the new one. The third consists of the names of those to whom Augustine sent Letters or from whom he in turn received them, arranged alphabetically. The last distributes the Letters according to the principal subjects treated in them.

At one time we had also decided to insert a fifth series of the Letters corresponding to the order more commonly found in manuscript codices. But the labor proved fruitless and wholly useless, both because of the great variety among the manuscript codices—indeed, we do not know whether one could find two or three that agree with one another on this point—and especially because very few manuscripts contain even half of the holy Doctor’s Letters. Consequently, no certain, fixed, or ordered arrangement can be established from them, except in the case of some codices approximately six hundred years old, which present the first six or seven Letters in the sequence represented by the published editions, while the others are woven together in a very different and entirely illegitimate order.

Finally, as with the other volumes, this volume too will receive an index of the subjects and passages of Scripture that are explained, prepared as honestly and carefully as we were able.

It remains, therefore, to present here, as we previously promised, the reasons for the new order of the Letters.

[Col. 0013]

# The chronological order of the Letters demonstrated by arguments

## Letters of the first class

### Letters written by Augustine while he was not yet a bishop, from A.D. 386 to 395

## I. Written near the end of A.D. 386

Just as the books *Against the Academics*, written by Augustine in the estate at Cassiciacum shortly after his conversion, occupy the first place in the *Retractations*, so the Letter written to Hermogenianus on the occasion of those same books rightly precedes Augustine’s other Letters here.

The year in which this Letter—or those books—appeared is investigated as follows. Augustine had begun the work some time before his birthday, which fell on 13 November, as is stated in Book 1 of the *Retractations*, chapter 2. When he completed the work, he was in his thirty-third year, as he testifies near the end of that work, Book 3, chapter 20, section 43.

Possidius, chapter 31, assures us that Augustine lived seventy-six years. No one has so far called into question that he died on 28 August A.D. 430, according to Prosper’s chronicle. He must therefore have been born on 13 November A.D. 354, converted and withdrawn from the world in A.D. 386, and published the books *Against the Academics* during that same year, approximately four months before the baptism that he received in the following year.

Although this chronological calculation may appear easy and straightforward, it is nevertheless necessary to linger somewhat over its establishment. For from Book 3 *Against Petilian’s Letters*, chapter 25, it is clear that Augustine did not return to Africa until after the death of the tyrant Maximus, which occurred at the end of July or in August A.D. 388. At the same time, from Book 9 of the *Confessions*, chapters 8, 10, and 11, it is equally certain that Monica died at Ostia on the Tiber, in the thirty-third year of Augustine’s life, when Augustine was returning to Africa after receiving baptism at Milan during the Easter solemnity, while they were preparing together to resume their voyage.

As a result, learned men have adopted different opinions. Some wish to count Possidius’s statement that Augustine lived seventy-six years from the consular registers, and to regard as his first year the very brief period from 13 November, the day on which Augustine was born, to 1 January; then to count as his seventy-sixth year the period extending from 1 January to 28 August. On this calculation Augustine was born on 13 November A.D. 355, converted in A.D. 387, baptized in A.D. 388, and in reality lived not seventy-six years but seventy-four years and nine or ten months.

Others say that Augustine, both in the passage cited above from Book 3 of *Against the Academics* and in chapter 10 of Book 1 of the *Soliloquies*—a work that he also completed before his baptism—when he says that he is in his thirty-third year, means not a year begun or currently running but a year fully completed and elapsed.

They suppose that Augustine was accustomed to count his years in this way from Book 6 of the *Confessions*, chapter 11, where he says that he was thirty years old. In the preceding chapter 6 he mentions that he had recited praises of the emperor. They take this to refer to the same panegyric that he delivered to Bauto when Bauto entered the consulship on the Kalends of January A.D. 385, according to Book 3 *Against Petilian’s Letters*, chapter 25, although it is more probable that this was another panegyric, which Augustine calls a praise of the emperor.

According to this calculation, Augustine’s birth belongs to A.D. 354, while his conversion and withdrawal belong to A.D. 387; his baptism is then assigned to A.D. 388, by which time Augustine, having completed his thirty-third year, was passing through his thirty-fourth.

But these two opinions forcibly distort the words of Augustine and Possidius from their genuine meaning, without any necessity requiring it. What prevents us from understanding that some circumstance caused a delay to Augustine when, after his mother’s death, he was preparing to sail to his homeland? What compels us to believe that he sailed for Africa immediately after his mother’s death, when he says nothing of the kind?

On the contrary, in Book 1 of the *Retractations*, chapters 7, 8, and 9, he reviews minor works that he composed at Rome after his baptism. He certainly could not have completed these in the very short time he spent in the city before his mother’s death, especially since he had not yet recovered from the fatigue of the journey that he and his companions had endured on their return from Milan when they arrived at Ostia on the Tiber. “There,” he says, “after the labor of the long journey, we were restoring ourselves for the voyage.”

Therefore his stay at Rome should be placed not before Monica’s death but after it, and we must believe that something prevented him from returning to Africa so quickly.

For the history of that period shows that the tyrant Maximus descended into Italy with a hostile army in this very year, A.D. 387, around the month of August, and, after driving Valentinian from Italy, occupied Africa as well. It may therefore have happened that Augustine, informed of these events while he was detained at Ostia on the Tiber by his mother’s illness—there is no reason to place her death later than August—changed his plan and decided to await the outcome of the upheaval at Rome, where he could live more safely than at Thagaste from the disasters of civil war.

Moreover, if Augustine’s conversion is assigned to A.D. 387, one is forced to say that he rested in the country retreat near Milan at the very time when all Italy was being disturbed by Maximus’s invasion and the Emperor Valentinian was being expelled from it. This was the middle of the turmoil of war, which raged especially around Milan, since the imperial court generally resided in that city. Baronius believes that from Ambrose’s words it may be understood that the citizens of Milan were thinking of flight at that time.

## II. Written around the same time

Next comes the Letter to Zenobius, who, as it seems to us, was the same man to whom the books *On Order*, published toward the end of A.D. 386, were dedicated. Compare this Letter with Book 2 of *On Order*, chapter 7, section 20, where Augustine says that he had often discussed the order of things with Zenobius and indicates that Zenobius was then away from home.

In this Letter Augustine misses the absent Zenobius and wishes that they might complete together the discussion they had begun.

## III. Written in A.D. 387

The third Letter in this order, addressed to Nebridius, appeared not long after the work of the *Soliloquies*, which was completed at the beginning of A.D. 387. Augustine implies that this work had just been published, section 1:

> “What if Nebridius had read the *Soliloquies*? He would have rejoiced much more abundantly, yet he would not have found anything more to call me than blessed.”

And in section 4:

> “The *Soliloquies* already contain all this.”

From these words we understand that the books *Against the Academics*, *On the Blessed Life*, and others, composed toward the end of A.D. 386 and at the beginning of 387, before the *Soliloquies*, had pleased Nebridius when he read them. Carried away, as it were, by the movement of his joyful spirit, he could not restrain himself from calling Augustine blessed.

This Letter must therefore be numbered among those about which Augustine says in Book 9 of the *Confessions*, chapter 4:

> “There, that is, at Cassiciacum, what I did in literary work … while Nebridius was absent, the Letters bear witness.”

Nebridius had not followed Augustine when he withdrew there. “He had yielded to our friendship,” Augustine says in Book 8 of the *Confessions*, chapter 6, “in order to assist our most intimate friend, Verecundus, a citizen and grammarian of Milan, in teaching.” This is why, in the final part of the Letter, Augustine proposes to him several small questions about the conjugation of verbs.

## IV. Written around the same time

From the same estate at Cassiciacum Augustine sent the fourth Letter here, addressed to Nebridius, in which he answered Nebridius’s inquiry about how much progress he had made during his withdrawal.

The other Letters dictated by Augustine to Nebridius during that period of leisure have disappeared. From the passage cited above in Book 9 of the *Confessions*, we infer that they were written in greater number and with greater effort.

## V. Written near the end of A.D. 388

The fifth Letter is the one Augustine received from Nebridius while he was at Thagaste in Africa. Augustine had returned there from Italy after the death of the tyrant Maximus, which occurred in July or August A.D. 388.

Nebridius marvels that Augustine bears patiently the interruptions caused by the affairs of the citizens of Thagaste. He is sorry that Augustine has not yet obtained the retreat from worldly cares that he so ardently desired.

This Letter therefore seems to belong at the end of the same year, or at the beginning of the following year. For after Augustine returned to Thagaste, he did not delay in carrying out as soon as possible the plan he had conceived after his baptism: to withdraw with his friends to the estates they possessed near Thagaste.

In fact, he spent nearly three years there in retreat, having already detached himself from secular concerns, according to Possidius, chapter 3. Then, having gone to Hippo on a particular occasion, he was ordained a presbyter there, which occurred at the beginning of A.D. 391.

Nevertheless, it may be said that even during his retreat he sometimes took charge of more serious matters brought to him, since he was excessively loved by his fellow citizens and loved them in return with equal affection.

## VI and VII. Written around the beginning of A.D. 389

The date of the sixth Letter can be determined to some extent from Augustine’s immediately following reply, where, in section 4, he calls Verecundus his former friend. Augustine, when he was at Milan, would not have spoken of Verecundus in this way if Verecundus were still alive there; still less would he have done so at Cassiciacum, where Augustine himself was staying at Verecundus’s villa.

Nor does it seem that both Letters should be assigned to the period when Augustine was staying at Rome, although Verecundus had died by then: first, because this does not agree with the expression “former”; and second, because we have no evidence of any such literary exchange between Augustine and Nebridius at that time.

We therefore conclude that the sixth Letter of Nebridius and the seventh Letter of Augustine to Nebridius were written when both men were already in Africa.

## VIII–XIV. Written around the same time

The same is much clearer concerning the remaining Letters that they sent to one another in turn—that is, the eighth, ninth, tenth, eleventh, twelfth, thirteenth, and fourteenth.

Although it is not easy to assign precisely the point in time at which each was written, the order that they occupy here among themselves is readily established from their mutual relations.

At the very least, it is absolutely certain that all the Letters to Nebridius were written before A.D. 391. Augustine writes of Nebridius’s death in Book 9 of the *Confessions*, chapter 3, section 6:

> “You released him from the flesh not long after our conversion and rebirth through baptism.”

These words clearly teach us that Nebridius died before Augustine was promoted to the presbyterate.

According to the observation of learned men, Augustine was promoted to that office in A.D. 391. Their conclusion rests on two testimonies of Possidius. First, in chapter 3, Possidius assures us that after Augustine returned from Italy to Africa, he spent nearly three years in retreat at Thagaste and was then ordained a presbyter at Hippo. As stated above, Augustine returned in A.D. 388, after the death of Maximus.

Then, in chapter 31, Possidius testifies that Augustine lived in the clerical or episcopal office for approximately forty years, that is, until 28 August A.D. 430.

Some think that his ordination occurred at the beginning of Lent; we think it took place somewhat earlier, with an interval of several days. For in Letter 21 Augustine implies that, after undertaking the presbyterate, he tested his strength in that office and in preaching the divine word. For this reason he says that he begged Bishop Valerius for a few days’ delay and permission to withdraw until Easter, so that he might devote himself to the sacred Scriptures, in which he already understood that he was less well instructed.

## XV. Written around A.D. 390

Baronius believed that the Letter to Romanianus, which is fifteenth in this order, was written by Augustine after he had become a bishop. On this basis, and from the Letter itself, he observed that bishops were accustomed to write letters on ivory tablets or paper, but rarely on parchment, and then only when paper was unavailable.

But since the holy Doctor reports in this Letter that the book *On True Religion*, which was especially dedicated to Romanianus, had been completed and would soon be sent to him, it unquestionably belongs to the period immediately preceding Augustine’s presbyterate.

In the *Retractations* Augustine lists this book last among those that he published while not yet a presbyter. Certainly this same book was one of the five that Alypius sent as a gift to Paulinus before A.D. 395, and therefore before Augustine’s episcopate, as is stated in Letters 24 and 27.

## XVI and XVII. Written around A.D. 390

The seventeenth Letter, addressed to Maximus of Madaura, from whom Augustine had previously received a letter, appears to have been written from his retreat at Thagaste.

We infer this not only from the indication that Augustine had some association with that pagan—perhaps because they lived not far from one another, since Madaura bordered Thagaste—but especially from the fact that the Letter contains no trace of his episcopal or priestly office.

Moreover, the worship of idols—which was prohibited by imperial law at the beginning of A.D. 391—was still public, as Augustine repeatedly implies here. It may therefore be inferred that the Letter was written in A.D. 390.

## XVIII–XX. Written around the same time

The next Letters—to Caelestinus, Gaius, and Antoninus—appear to have been written by Augustine while he was still a layman, since in their headings he does not attach any title of rank to his name.

This is also confirmed by their style, which, as in his earliest writings, is somewhat more elegant, and by the order in which they are found in ancient codices. They are placed alongside the first fifteen Letters, and there are even manuscripts that contain nothing at all besides those Letters. A very ancient book of this kind is preserved in the library of Saint-Germain.

## XXI. Written at the beginning of A.D. 391

The twenty-first Letter is nothing other than the supplicatory petition that Augustine presented to Bishop Valerius some time after his ordination. He requested that, since he had discovered that his strength was inadequate for the office he had undertaken, he be granted a short period—approximately until Easter—during which he could devote himself wholly to the study of the sacred Scriptures.

This Letter must therefore be placed at the beginning of A.D. 391, the year in which we have established that Augustine was ordained a presbyter.

## XXII. Written around A.D. 392
Many days had elapsed since his ordination when the presbyter Augustine wrote Letter 22 to Aurelius. By then, as is evident from §1, a community of brothers had begun to grow around the monastery established at Hippo. In this letter he replies to a certain letter, now no longer extant, received from Aurelius; Augustine indicates that the administration of the Church of Carthage had recently been entrusted to him, when he mentions the hope which all good men had conceived with him—that God, having conferred authority upon him, would at last apply a remedy to the ailments of the African churches. He writes to him with such complete familiarity that one can easily believe that Aurelius had earnestly asked him by letter to assist him, laboring under his new burden, now with suitable advice, now with prayers offered to God. Accordingly, it is permissible to suppose that Aurelius—who in 388, when Augustine saw him near Carthage on his return from Italy, was performing the office of Carthaginian deacon, as Augustine records in *The City of God* 22.8—was not raised to episcopal dignity before 391. In fact, his predecessor Genethlius presided over the Second Council of Carthage on 19 May 390. Thereafter, that is, in 393, the Council of Hippo on 8 October, and other African councils of the following years, are recorded as having been held under Aurelius.

Moreover, we believe that Aurelius was moved by this very letter, of which we are speaking, to convene the Council of Hippo, so that by his authority he might prohibit the banquets in which Africans indulged in the churches under the pretext of piety. So great, Augustine writes in §4, was the pestilence of this evil that it could not be healed except by the authority of a council.

### XXIII.—Written at about the same time.

Letter 23, addressed to Maximinus, is understood even from its heading to have been written by Augustine while he was still a presbyter; but in what year is entirely uncertain.

### XXIV, XXV.—Written toward the end of 394, before winter.

The two following letters belong to Paulinus and were sent by him from the city of Nola to Africa in 394. One was addressed to Alypius, “the father,” that is, the bishop. He had undoubtedly learned that this dignity belonged to Alypius from the letter which he says he had received from him. The other was addressed to Augustine, “the brother,” whom he had heard was still serving as a presbyter and with whom, as he says in §4, he was associated in office—or, according to the Cistercian manuscript, was equal in the office of the senate.

From the earlier letter, §2, we learn that this letter was sent together with the other. From the beginning of Letter 30, which Paulinus certainly wrote to Augustine at the beginning of 395, we learn with certainty that this same letter to Augustine—namely Letter 25—and also the other letter to Alypius, here Letter 24, were sent before the preceding winter, that is, in the autumn of 394.

### XXVI.—Perhaps written at the beginning of 395 and sent with the following letter.

Letter 26 is Augustine’s letter to his former disciple Licentius. In §5 he praises Paulinus as a man then extremely well known to him. He may therefore have written it after receiving Paulinus’s earlier letters and after seeing the man whom Paulinus had sent to greet him. In the immediately following letter, §6, Augustine recalls this letter written to Licentius and sends it—or at least a copy of it—to Paulinus himself to read on the same occasion.

### XXVII.—Written at the beginning of 395.

We place Letter 27 to Paulinus at the beginning of 395. After receiving Paulinus’s letters written before winter, Augustine entrusted this letter for delivery to Romanianus, as he indicates in §4. Romanianus, the father of the Licentius mentioned above, was sailing to Italy on family and domestic business, perhaps in the spring of that year, and certainly while Augustine was not yet a bishop, as is clear from Letters 31 and 32.

### XXVIII.—Written in 394 or 395.

At the beginning of Letter 28 to Jerome, Alypius is praised as having already attained episcopal dignity after his return from Jerome. Baronius assigns Alypius’s journey to Palestine to 393 and his promotion to the episcopate to 394. This letter, then, was written in 394 or certainly in 395; no later, since Augustine wrote it while he was not yet a bishop, as is clear from Letter 71, chapter 1, §2. This is supported by the fact that Augustine here attacks Jerome’s judgment concerning Peter rebuked by Paul, while omitting the author’s name; Augustine likewise attacks it in *On Lying*, chapters 5 and 20. In the *Retractations*, Book 1, he places that short work last among those he wrote while not yet a bishop.

### XXIX.—Written in 395.

It has seemed appropriate to assign to the same year, 395, that outstanding letter addressed to Alypius which is now published for the first time from a very old manuscript of the Cistercian Fathers of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem at Rome. It could not be placed later, since Augustine wrote it while he was still serving as a presbyter; indeed, during this very year he was raised to the episcopal office. Nor could it be earlier, since no evidence appears that the dignity of the episcopate had been conferred before 394 upon Alypius, who here is called bishop of Thagaste.

Alypius had not assumed this office only recently, as is sufficiently clear from Augustine’s words in §12: “For in great part we rest with you in the joyful ardor of our zeal, since such frequent gifts from the spiritual Church of Thagaste are announced to us.” It is also indicated by what is said in §2 of the same letter: Alypius had very recently departed for Hippo, where certainly, had he been a newly appointed bishop, he would not have left his own church as a stranger; and this had occurred not long after the beginning of the year, if the letter is assigned to the beginning of Lent and if the copyist has not erred in the manuscript, where we read: “But after the days of Lent had dawned.” Something is noted about this reading in its proper place.

### XXX.—Written in 395.

Paulinus wrote Letter 30 before he had received from Romanianus Augustine’s reply, namely Letter 27 above. That holy man, inflamed by an extraordinary longing for Augustine through reading Augustine’s letter, saw that the messenger whom he had sent to Africa before winter was delayed on the journey and was uncertain whether his own letters had arrived. He could not suspend his duty any longer; instead, he gave a second letter to Romanus and Agilis for delivery to Augustine, so that his devotion and respect for Augustine, together with his most ardent desire to see him, might remain evident.

## LETTERS OF THE SECOND CLASS

Those which Augustine wrote as bishop, before the conference held at Carthage with the Donatists and before the discovery of Pelagius’s heresy in Africa, from the year of Christ 396 to 410.

### XXXI.—Written at the beginning of 396.

Augustine, now a bishop, at last returned Letter 31 to Paulinus after receiving Paulinus’s later letters, sending it to him immediately by Romanus and Agilis. In this letter he informed Paulinus of his promotion to the episcopate, so that Paulinus might understand that Augustine could not consider traveling to Italy to visit him; and Augustine invited Paulinus—who was not yet a bishop and therefore was freer from ecclesiastical cares—to cross over to Africa.

Augustine’s promotion occurred shortly before the Lord’s Nativity, as is clear from Homily 25 among the fifty, chapter 3, and certainly before 397. In that year, the Third Council of Carthage, celebrated on 1 September or 28 August, decreed that the decisions of the councils should be read aloud to those being ordained bishops or clergy. This decree was established at Augustine’s request, and Augustine himself subscribed to that council.

Yet we have not sufficiently determined whether 395 or 396 was the year marked by Augustine’s ordination. The inclination of the mind would easily favor 396, since the first two of the books which, as he says in *Retractations* 2.1, he composed as bishop are addressed to Simplicianus. In the dedicatory letter and at the beginning of Book 1 he honors Simplicianus with the title “Father.” This title seems to indicate that Simplicianus had already succeeded blessed Ambrose, whose death, however, occurred only in 397, on 4 April.

But let us grant that, out of his exceptional respect for so distinguished a man, Augustine would not have given him any other title even if Simplicianus were only a presbyter, since Augustine himself calls him the spiritual father of Saint Ambrose in *Confessions* 8.2. What then of the fact that, when speaking of these books, Augustine consistently says that he wrote them now to Simplicianus, bishop of the Church of Milan, now to Simplicianus, the successor of Saint Ambrose, as in *Retractations* 2.1, *On the Predestination of the Saints* 4, and *On the Gift of Perseverance* 20? He even says that he discussed what Simplicianus, bishop of Milan, had once asked him, as in *Letter to Dulcitius*, Question 6.

For this reason John Rivius assigns the same books to 397, clearly certain that Simplicianus was already bishop at that time; in this matter he seems to have followed Baronius’s view. If, then, we place Augustine’s ordination before 396, we must admit that he refrained from writing for nearly two years. This can scarcely be believed of that holy teacher, who placed the cares he owed to his brothers principally in this: that he might serve their praiseworthy studies in Christ with his tongue and his pen, by which, as he himself says in *On the Trinity* 3.1, the two-horse chariot of love drove him.

Add to this that he testifies in *On the Predestination of the Saints* 4 that the books mentioned above were written by him at the very beginning of his episcopate. Nevertheless, Prosper, under the consulship of Olbrius and Probinus—that is, in the year of Christ 395—writes: “Augustine, a disciple of blessed Ambrose, outstanding in remarkable eloquence and learning, was ordained bishop at Hippo Regius in Africa.” And all who have written Augustine’s acts have regarded this authority as so clear, like a chronological epoch, that they have considered it established, fixed, and entirely beyond doubt. Thus, however strong the conjecture may seem in our judgment, we hesitate to depart from it.

Accordingly, this letter to Paulinus, given by Augustine as a newly appointed bishop, had to be assigned to the beginning of 396. Hence, as you can readily understand, the dates of several preceding and following letters also had to be set one year earlier than might otherwise appear.

### XXXII.—Written shortly after the preceding letter.

When Romanus and Agilis returned from Africa, Paulinus could not refrain from immediately sharing with Romanianus the most welcome news he had received concerning the holy men, and especially Augustine’s advancement to the episcopate. On the following day he gave Romanianus Letter 32 concerning this very matter, congratulating him on it, as it was fitting that a holy man of God should rejoice.

### XXXIII.—Written at the beginning of Augustine’s episcopate.

Whether Augustine wrote Letter 33 to Proculeianus, the Donatist bishop at Hippo, while he was still a presbyter or when he was already a bishop cannot be determined with sufficiently clear evidence. It is easier, however, to believe that he was already a bishop, chiefly because of what he writes in §5 concerning the honors which people bestowed upon them when, as he says, they wished to settle their secular cases before us, “whenever we were necessary to them . . . and for which matters we are daily greeted with bowed heads.”

We do not think it can be established that those who were merely priests either ought or were able to settle the affairs and lawsuits of the people, unless perhaps this responsibility had been entrusted to them because of some serious circumstance. That later happened in Augustine’s own case with the presbyter Heraclius, but only after the consent of the people had first been requested, and with Heraclius already designated as Augustine’s successor in the episcopate.

In any event, Augustine gave this letter no later than the beginning of his episcopate, since Valerius was still alive and, in the immediately following letter, which he wrote later, Augustine admits that he was still a novice in the episcopate.

### XXXIV.—Written after the preceding letter.

Thus in Letter 34 to Eusebius, §6, Augustine says: “Although I do not sufficiently understand what this man, who says that he has been a bishop for so many years, fears in me, a novice, so that he is unwilling to confer with me in conversation.”

These words mark the first period of his episcopate. They show that Proculeianus’s attitude had changed: he now favored something different from what, according to Augustine’s report in the preceding letter, §2, had been announced to him—that he wished to confer with Augustine while good men were sitting as witnesses. From this the order and date of the present letter are established.

### XXXV.—Written after the preceding letter.

Letter 35, addressed to the same Eusebius shortly after the preceding one, belongs to the same period.

### XXXVI.—Perhaps written in 396 or at the beginning of 397.

Others will judge whether we have correctly determined the date of Letter 36 to Casulanus from these words in chapter 14, §32: “I shall tell you what the venerable Ambrose, by whom I was baptized, bishop of Milan, answered me when I asked him about this.”

These words may lead one to believe that Augustine wrote the letter before Ambrose’s death, which occurred on the day before Easter in 397. Since nothing in the letter anywhere contradicts this view, it seemed appropriate to place it among the letters dictated at the beginning of Augustine’s episcopate.

### XXXVII.—Written at about 397.

Letter 37 is usually prefixed to the books of *Questions to Simplicianus*, on whose occasion it was written. It is commonly believed that these books belong approximately to 397. We have already said enough about them above, in connection with Letter 31.

### XXXVIII.—Written around the middle of 397.

Letter 38 was written almost exactly a month after the death of Megalius, primate of Numidia, as is clear from §2. Megalius had died shortly before the Council of Carthage held in 397 on 28 August. At that council Aurelius testifies that he had received a letter from Crescentianus, in which Crescentianus implied that he himself was primate of Numidia.

We therefore place this letter around the middle of 397. Its date can also easily be established from another consideration. The letter was delivered to Profuturus by Victor, who had warned Augustine about him because Victor was going to Constantina, as §3 shows. It cannot be doubted, therefore, that this Profuturus was the bishop of Cirta, or Constantina, who is said in chapter 16 of *On the Singular Baptism against Petilianus*, published around 400, to have died a few years earlier and to have been the predecessor of Fortunatus, who then occupied that see.

Profuturus was ordained bishop in 394 or 395 and died not long afterward, as can be understood by comparing Letters 28.1 and 71.1.2 with Letter 72.1.1. Profuturus, moreover, must have survived Megalius by only a very short time, since his successor Fortunatus was ordained before Megalius’s supposed immediate successor, Possidius. Henry de Noris correctly infers this in *History of Pelagianism* 2.8 from the fact that at the Carthaginian Conference of 411, and in the letter of the Council of Milevis of 416, Fortunatus is named before Possidius.

Among the African Fathers this order was religiously maintained, according to the episcopal office each person had assumed. The importance of preserving this custom consistently was addressed at the Council of Milevis held on 27 August 402.

### XXXIX.—Perhaps written in 397.

Jerome entrusted Letter 39 to Praesidius, who was sailing to the West. These are Jerome’s second letters to Augustine, for he had sent the first, now lost, through the deacon Asterius, who promptly returned the courtesy of a greeting, as Jerome says here in §1—not in response to letters previously received from Augustine, but, as Augustine replies in the following letter, §1, in response to the greeting appended to another letter.

In this letter, §2, Jerome sends greetings to Pope Alypius and gives Augustine the same title. From this we understand that it was not written before 396. Since Jerome does not congratulate Augustine in it on his elevation to the episcopate, we believe that he had already done so in the letters sent through Asterius during the preceding year.

Jerome also indicates that he was established in a monastery but nevertheless tossed about by various disturbances from every direction. We therefore think that the letter was written no later than 397, but before Jerome had been reconciled with John of Jerusalem. We do not find that, from that reconciliation until the persecutions stirred up against Jerome by the Pelagians, he had occasion to complain in this manner.

If anyone believes that this letter came after Letter 68 and that it is the very letter in which Jerome, as is read in Letter 82.1, recalled having sent Letter 68 through Asterius, we hope that no one will take it amiss that we have assigned its position differently on the basis of other conjectures, with which most of the evidence fits reasonably well.

### XL.—Written at about the same time.

At approximately the same time Augustine also sent from Africa his second letter to Jerome, namely Letter 40. In chapter 5, §8, he indicates that he had previously written to Jerome and that the letters had not arrived. At the beginning he expresses gratitude that, in response to the appended greeting, Jerome had returned a complete letter, though a shorter one.

By these words Augustine does not refer to the preceding Letter 39, but to another letter that has so far been missing, in which Jerome criticized Origen. This can be seen here in chapter 6, §9. Augustine may have mentioned Origen when, by appending a greeting to another man’s letter, he courteously sent greetings to Jerome.

This, we think, is the letter which Jerome sent through Asterius, perhaps in 396, in order to return Augustine’s courtesy of greeting. As for Letter 40, which we are discussing, Paulus, who had received it for delivery, changed his plan of sailing, as is clear from Letter 72.1.1, but did not return it to Augustine, according to Letter 73.5. Consequently, this letter was circulated through Italy before it reached Jerome. That could have sown the seeds of discord between them, had not Augustine’s humility and the charity of both men suppressed the seeds of offense.

Something similar had happened with another letter written to Jerome before this one: its bearer, Profuturus, was made a bishop as soon as he prepared to set out and therefore did not cross over to Palestine, as is clear from Letter 72.1.1 and also from Letter 71.1.2. There Augustine explains that he had prepared those first letters while still a presbyter, so that the second and later letters must be understood as having been dictated after he had become a bishop.

### XLI.—Written at the beginning of Augustine’s episcopate.

We assign Letter 41 to the earlier years of Augustine’s episcopate. It was written in the name of Alypius and Augustine, who congratulate Aurelius of Carthage chiefly because he was now beginning to permit presbyters, in his presence, to expound the word of God to the people.

A different practice had prevailed, one universally established throughout the African churches. Valerius had been criticized for having granted the presbyter Augustine authority to preach the Gospel in the presence of the bishop himself. But Possidius observes in chapter 5 that, when the fame of Augustine’s sacred sermons to the people of Hippo spread far and wide, the other bishops thought it wiser to imitate Valerius’s example.

It is proper to believe that Aurelius led the way in this matter; indeed, this is sufficiently clear from the present letter itself. It therefore should not be assigned to later years.

### XLII.—Written toward the end of the summer of 397.

Letter 42 to Paulinus, now published for the first time from the Phimarcon manuscript, belongs to 397. It was written during the second summer after Paulinus’s last letters of 395 had been received. Compare this letter with Letter 31, §8.

### XLIII, XLIV.—Written around the end of 397 or the beginning of 398.

The two following letters, addressed to Glorius, Eleusius, and Felix, may reasonably be thought to have been written at one and the same time, namely toward the end of 397 or the beginning of 398.

In Letter 43, which we suspect to be the earlier of the two, Augustine recalls Optatus of Thamugadi’s tyranny with complete freedom of speech, chapter 8, §24, but in words that imply that the tyranny had not yet ended. It did end in 398, as we note in the commentary on Letter 53, §6. He also says there that the Donatists unjustly refused to have their sacrileges corrected by the temporal punishments imposed through ordinary human authorities. This refers most suitably to the period they called the Macarian period, about which the Donatist bishop Fortunius complained in the conference at Tibursicum, as is clear from the following Letter 44, chapter 2, §4.

It is appropriate to establish when Augustine attended that conference with Fortunius. We commonly see learned men who follow Baronius’s annals assign it to the year of Christ 412. The following considerations lead us away from their opinion.

When Augustine was traveling from Tibursicum to Cirta, as Letter 44.1 states, he was making the journey not, as Baronius thought, on the occasion of a synod—which the Louvain edition calls the Cirtense Synod, while the earlier editions and ancient manuscripts consistently call it the Zertense, both in *Retractations* 2.40 and in Letter 141—but because he had been summoned there for the ordination of a bishop, as Augustine himself expressly testifies in Letter 44, chapter 6, §13.

A successor had to be appointed, either for Fortunatus himself—who still governed the Church of Cirta in 416 and was named before Possidius among the Fathers of the Council of Milevis—or, certainly, for Profuturus, who had attained the episcopate in 394 or 395 and died shortly afterward. But Fortunatus himself succeeded Profuturus, and from what was said above concerning Letter 38 it is scarcely possible to place his ordination later than the beginning of 398.

It is also established from another source that Augustine’s meeting with Fortunius occurred before 411. This can be understood even from Augustine’s own attitude, which was still opposed to persecuting heretics, here in chapters 4 and 5. It is completely clear that the Donatists were enjoying peace at that time, and the entire letter presents them as enjoying complete freedom. Nothing of the sort ever occurred after 411.

It is equally clear that when Fortunius showed Augustine the letter of the pseudo-Sardican, or Philippopolitan, council in chapter 2, §6, Augustine did not yet know what it was. Yet in the books against Cresconius, written before 411, he already knew of it and rejects it as an Arian gathering in Book 3, chapter 34.

It is also evident from Augustine’s words in chapter 1, §1, that Fortunius was an older bishop than Augustine himself. Yet Fortunius was not alive in 411, since Januarius of Tibursicum, a bishop in Numidia, attended the Carthaginian Conference on behalf of the Donatists. Fortunius, therefore, cannot have survived beyond 411. We may consequently more easily believe that he was the very man listed tenth among the 310 bishops of the Council of Bagai, held by the Donatists in 394.

From these considerations, then, we conclude that this conference must be placed approximately fifteen years earlier than Baronius placed it.

Nor should the following point be passed over in silence. When Ambrose is mentioned in the same conference, Augustine’s words in Letter 44, chapter 4, §7, might lead one to believe that the holy bishop was still alive. Moreover, when the persecution of the Donatists against the Maximianists is discussed, nothing at all is said of Praetextatus and Felicianus, whom the Donatists had nevertheless received at the beginning of 397. From this someone might infer that the conference at Tibursicum was held no later than the beginning of 397.

For this to be established, however, one must first suppose that Megalius died around the middle of 395, since Profuturus survived Megalius and Augustine’s journey to ordain Profuturus’s successor was the occasion of his conference with Fortunius. Someone must then be inserted between Megalius and Crescentianus as primate; or it must at least be said that a full year passed before the man was announced who, by right of seniority, succeeded Megalius in the primatial office.

For Crescentianus did not become primate before 397, shortly before the Council of Carthage held on 28 August. At that council Aurelius testified that he had recently received a letter from Crescentianus, “of the first see of Numidia,” as he himself implied. From this final clause it is clear that Aurelius did not then know that Crescentianus was the primate, although he ought to have known it above all.

Although nothing prevents our inserting someone between Megalius and Crescentianus as primate, the arguments given above do not require us to believe that this happened. We have therefore preferred to place the conference at the end of 397, or rather at the beginning of 398. At that time the fall of the tyrant Gildo could have caused the Donatists to fear persecution because of their own Optatus, Gildo’s associate. The statements recorded in Letter 44, chapter 5, §11, seem to look toward this.

### XLV.—Written in 398.

Letter 45 to Paulinus, which is added to this edition from the Phimarcon manuscript, was written a full two years after Romanus and Agilis had returned to Paulinus. Augustine had sent them away from him around the beginning of 396. This letter, therefore, belongs to the beginning of 398.

### XLVI, XLVII.—Written around this time.

Letter 46 is Publicola’s letter consulting Saint Augustine as a bishop already endowed with authority and as one capable of removing the scruples by which this man of particularly sensitive conscience was troubled. This letter and the following one from Augustine to Publicola are assigned to this period because they seem to have been written while the worship of idols was still in force; that worship was prohibited in 399.

### XLVIII.—Perhaps written in 398.

Letter 48 to Eudoxius, whom the ancient manuscripts call abbot of the island of Capraria, is believed to have been written around 398. In §4 Augustine praises two monks of approved life who had crossed from there to Africa, Eustasius and Andreas; Eustasius had already died there.

They are thought to have been the very men who accompanied Mascezil, commander of the Roman army. At the beginning of this year Mascezil sailed to Africa against the tyrant Gildo and visited the island of Capraria, as Orosius writes in Book 7, chapter 36. From there he took with him, moved by his prayers, several holy servants of God. With these men he continued day and night in prayers, fasts, and psalms; thus he won victory without battle and vengeance without slaughter.

### XLIX.—Written around 398.

Concerning the date of Letter 49 to Honoratus, it can only be established that it is highly probable that it belongs to the earlier years of Augustine’s episcopate, when the Donatists had not yet opposed the truth with such hostility.

Honoratus, a bishop of their party who lived near Hippo, had indicated to Augustine through Erotes that he would gladly discuss the schism with him by letter, so that they might treat a matter of such importance with the gentleness and peace of mind it required. Augustine, who had long desired a conversation with him, replied in this letter that his proposal greatly pleased him; he then took up the case on behalf of the Catholic side and invited Honoratus to respond.

### L.—Perhaps written in 399.

Baronius refers to the imperial rescripts issued in 399 against idols the event about which Augustine complains in Letter 50 to the elders of the colony of Suffectum. In that colony, after a statue of Hercules had been pulled down and smashed, the pagans attacked the Christians with weapons and slaughtered sixty of them. They are listed in the Roman Martyrology among the holy martyrs on 30 August.

### LI.—Written in 399 or 400.

Letter 51 to Crispinus appeared after the death of Optatus of Thamugadi. Augustine recalls his memory with playful praise in §3, in these words: “Even the holy memory of that Optatus, your tribune, is proclaimed.” It was written before the death of Praetextatus of Assuri, of whom Augustine speaks here in the same way as of Felicianus of Musti, who was still alive. More directly relevant is what he says in §4 of both men: “Therefore, all who baptized at that time now have them with themselves and with you.”

Optatus died shortly after the killing of the tyrant Gildo in 398. Praetextatus, however, had already died when Augustine was placing the final touches on Book 3 against Parmenianus, around 400, as is clear from the last chapter of that book. We therefore note that this letter was written in 399 or 400.

When Augustine writes in §3 that the Donatists were accustomed to accuse the Catholics of persecuting them through earthly powers, this should be referred not to the edicts of 405 but to the earlier edicts, some of which were issued against them in 377 and afterward.

### LII.—Written around 400.

Letter 52 to Leverinus should apparently be counted among Augustine’s earliest writings against the Donatists. Yet it should not be placed much before 400, since in §3 he says: “So many wicked men arose among them, and they tolerated them for so many years, so as not to tear apart the party of Donatus.”

By these words he frequently signifies the ten-year tyranny of Optatus, now that Optatus had died.

### LII.—Written around 400.

Letter 53 to Generosus may likewise be assigned to approximately this period, since it was written while Anastasius was seated at Rome, as is clear from §3, and perhaps while Praetextatus was still alive, as is conjectured from §6.

### LIV, LV.—Written around 400.

[Col. 0025]

Letters 54 and 55, which are the two books concerning Januarius’s inquiries, occupy a middle place in the *Retractations* among the short works composed around 400. They are reviewed somewhat before the books against Petilianus’s letters, which were written no later than 402, since Anastasius, who died in that very year, was seated in the Roman chair on the day when Augustine was writing Book 2, chapter 51, against the aforementioned letters of Petilianus, as Augustine himself testifies there.

### LVI, LVII.—Written around 400.

Augustine undoubtedly gave Letters 56 and 57 to Celer before the Carthaginian Conference, since he says nothing about its proceedings, but after he had published several books against the Donatists, which he presents to Celer for reading. They therefore seem appropriately assigned to this same period.

### LVIII.—Written toward the end of 401.

Letter 58 to Pammachius was perhaps written toward the end of 401 and entrusted to the envoys who carried petitions to the emperors in the name of the Council of Carthage held on the Ides of September.

Just as the opening of that council notes the Donatists’ plots and abuses, by which they seriously harassed the Catholic Church of Africa, so at the end of this letter Augustine speaks of the plots of the heretics: “You will nevertheless hear these things,” he says, “from my brothers, whom I commend most highly to your Excellency.”

### LIX.—Written around the end of 401.

After receiving from Victorinus, on the fifth day before the Ides of November, the *Tractoria* by which Victorinus summoned the council as primate of Numidia, Augustine replied to him with Letter 59. He indicated that Xantippus of Tagaste was saying that the primacy belonged to him.

Xantippus had attained the primacy no later than 402, as is clear from Letter 65, addressed to him as “the Elder,” that is, to the primate, before Easter in that year. It is especially clear from the Council of Milevis held on 27 August of the same year, at which the same bishop is called first see of Numidia.

Therefore, if Victorinus persuaded his colleagues of his case, Letter 59 may belong to some earlier year after 397, when Crescentianus was proclaimed primate. But if, as is more probable, Victorinus lost his case, it is reasonably placed toward the end of 401.

### LX.—Written around the end of 401.

Letter 60 to Aurelius concerns two brothers who left the monastery without obtaining permission and went over to the same Aurelius. Augustine does not approve of Aurelius enrolling such deserters from their institution among the clergy.

Concerning one of them, named Donatus, who had been ordained before the enactment on this matter made by the Council of Carthage held on 13 September 401, Augustine leaves the matter to Aurelius’s prudence and discretion. Concerning the other, and especially because Donatus had left the monastery on his account, Augustine indicates that he has a different view.

From this we infer that the letter was written not long after that council.

### LXI.—Written toward the end of 401 or shortly afterward.

Letter 61 to Theodore appears to have been written at about the same time. In it Augustine promises under oath that he will preserve the honor of their own rank for Donatist clergy returning to the Church.

The decree of the aforementioned council had left this to the will and discretion of each Catholic bishop: if it seemed advantageous to him, he could thereafter receive those men with their honors and orders.

### LXII, LXIII.—Written around the same time.

Letters 62 and 63 to Severus were written in the case of Timothy. On this occasion, we believe, the canon was established by the Council of Milevis on 27 September 402: “Whoever has read even once in the Church shall not be accepted for the clerical office by another Church.”

Certainly, in Letter 63, §4, Augustine asks Severus to consider before God whether Timothy—who had performed the office of lector not merely once, and not in only one place within the diocese of Hippo—could or should be judged not to have been a lector. He makes no mention at all of this canon of the Council of Milevis, although the matter was clearly explained by it.

These letters therefore cannot be assigned to a period later than this.

### LXIV.—Written shortly after the Nativity of Christ in 401.

In the sixty-fourth letter to Quintianus, written shortly after Christ’s Nativity, as is shown by §2, Augustine indicates in §3 that a recent council had decreed that those who had withdrawn or been expelled from some monastery were not to become clerics or superiors of monasteries elsewhere. This is undoubtedly none other than the decree of the Council of Carthage of 13 September 401: “It was also decided that, if anyone is found from another monastery, etc.” In the African Code of Canons, ch. 80.

### LXV.—Written at the beginning of 402.

The sixty-fifth letter, written to the elderly Xantippus, was composed somewhat before the Sunday of Easter, which was to fall on 6 April, as §2 shows. But Easter did not fall on 6 April except in the year 402 while Xantippus the Elder—or, as that title seems to indicate, the holder of the primacy—was in office, as the Perronias most aptly observe in *Against the Answer of the King of Britain*, ch. 48, and Norisius in book 2 of the *History of the Pelagians*, ch. 8.

### LXVI.—Written around the same time.

It was no later than this period that Crispinus of Calama committed the offense over which Augustine reproaches him in the sixty-sixth letter. For in book 2 of *Against the Letters of Petilian*, ch. 83, which he was writing in 402, Augustine testifies that this had recently occurred and says that he was still mourning it. Nevertheless, since the meaning of the word “recently” sometimes extends over several years, Crispinus’s action could be assigned to one of the preceding years. But since we do not know in what year it occurred, it seemed best to place this letter here.

### LXVII, LXVIII.—Written around 402.

The sixty-seventh letter, to Jerome, and the sixty-eighth, from Jerome to Augustine, were written after Paulinianus’s return from the West to Palestine. Augustine greets him, and in turn is greeted by him through Jerome. Paulinianus had been sent by his brother Jerome to the West in 398 to sell their jointly inherited property, as Jerome relates in his twenty-sixth letter to Pammachius; he did not return to Bethlehem until near the end of 401.

Moreover, Jerome now sends Augustine his *Apology against Rufinus*, whether the first or the second; Augustine quotes some of its words in letter 166, ch. 5, §15. Rufinus had certainly already sent his insults to Jerome, as is said in this letter 68, §3. He did so after the first *Apology*, thereby providing the occasion for the second, as is clear from that later *Apology*, which belongs to the year 402.

Jerome uses Asterius as his courier, through whom six years earlier he had sent the first letter mentioned above in letter 39. Since he calls that earlier letter nothing more than an act of greeting, one may infer from this also that it differed from the reply now under discussion.

Finally, here in §1 it should be noted that copies of Augustine’s letters, brought by the deacon Sysinnius, reached Jerome at the time when Paula was ill. From this one understands that this deacon was not the same Sysinnius who sailed to Jerusalem in 406, that is, two years after Paula’s death—or, if he was the same man, that he crossed there a second time, contrary to what Baronius thought.

### LXIX.—Written toward the end of 402.

The sixty-ninth letter to Castorius should be considered in connection with the Council of Milevis held on 27 August 402. For that Maximianus whom Alypius and Augustine praise here, because he had laid down the episcopal burden, moved by peaceful devotion, and whose succession by his own brother Castorius in the administration of the Church of Vaga they desire—that Maximianus, in the judgment of certain learned men, was Maximianus of Bagai. He was permitted by the decree of that council to withdraw from the episcopal see, in the African Code of Canons, ch. 88.

Rivius held this view, and before him Baronius, under the year 402. Baronius nevertheless notes that he had once thought that this Maximianus was the bishop of Bagai who, according to Augustine in letter 185, §26, letter 88, §7, and book 3 of *Against Cresconius*, ch. 43, was beaten by the Donatists and thrown from a tower, and that he was the same man as the one discussed at the Council of Milevis. But he now thinks that he was different from that man, and that the Acts of that council should read *Maximianus of Vagia*, not *of Bagai*. There may be another occasion to discuss this matter.

### LXX.—Perhaps written around this time.

We believe that the seventieth letter to Naucellio was written after the year 400, or after Praetextatus had already died. No other reason occurs to explain why Augustine is now silent about him and mentions only Felicianus, unless it is that Felicianus alone remained alive.

For the two men had shared one cause, one sentence had been pronounced against both, and afterward the same lawsuits had been brought against both so that they might be expelled from their churches. On the same occasion—namely, under the compulsion of Optatus of Gildon—and finally under the same conditions, the two had been reconciled. Augustine had previously presented them together wherever the holy Doctor turned this argument against the Donatists, showing that the schismatics were vainly bringing against Catholics actions which they themselves had perpetrated in the case of the Maximianists, especially against Praetextatus and Felicianus.

### LXXI.—Written around 403.

Augustine had not yet received Jerome’s letter, brought by Asterius together with the *Apology against Rufinus*, when he gave his seventy-first letter to the deacon Cyprianus to carry to Jerome. For he says nothing about Jerome’s disagreement with Rufinus, and here too he freely reveals what he thought of Jerome’s labor in translating the books of the Old Testament from Hebrew. He would certainly not have done this if Jerome’s anger had not first been calmed, and if Augustine had understood that Jerome had been stirred up and offended by his earlier letters.

At the same time he sent three other letters written previously, as appears from ch. 1, §2. He knew that one of them, namely letter 28, had not been delivered; concerning the other two, letters 40 and 67, he was uncertain.

### LXXII.—Written in 403 or 404.

The following letter is understood to have been dictated by Jerome around this time, from ch. 2, §4, where he repeats certain words from letter 67, which Augustine had sent him the preceding year. In part it answers that letter 67; in part it also answers another letter, which has not survived. In that missing letter Augustine evidently stated that a certain letter, to which he requested a reply, had first been entrusted by him to Profuturus, then sent a second time through someone else; but that this person had feared the dangers of the sea and changed his plan of sailing.

Jerome did not send this reply, however, until after Cyprianus’s return. Cyprianus was the bearer both of this letter and of another, namely letter 75, written toward the end of 404 or somewhat later, according to letter 82, ch. 4, §30.

Finally, it should be observed that Jerome says in ch. 1, §1, that Augustine’s letter—namely letter 40, about which Jerome complains here—had been found by Sysinnius on the island of Adria approximately five years earlier.

### LXXIII.—Written around 404.

Meanwhile, after Cyprianus’s departure for Palestine, Augustine received letter 68 through Asterius and realized that Jerome was somewhat offended by his letters. Jerome complained that those letters had been circulated throughout Italy but had not reached him, the person to whom they had been written. Augustine therefore did not delay, but immediately replied with his seventy-third letter.

While attempting to satisfy Jerome’s complaints, he declares that he has received the *Apology against Rufinus*. He says that he was frightened by the example of the disagreement that had arisen between them, since in Jerome’s letter he had read certain indications of Jerome’s indignation toward himself.

This letter therefore belongs approximately to the year 404, by which time Augustine had already reached his fiftieth year. In ch. 2, §5, he professes himself an old man—not, as he sometimes does, using “old man” to designate the final period of life, which begins at the age of sixty-one. Otherwise the letter would have to be assigned to a date after the year 414.

### LXXIV.—Written together with the preceding letter.

The seventy-fourth letter, addressed to Praesidius, was occasioned by the preceding letter. Augustine asks that the preceding letter be sent through Praesidius to Jerome, and even asks that Jerome be reconciled to him through Praesidius’s letter.

Praesidius, who is here called a fellow priest—that is, a bishop—seems unquestionably to be the man whom Jerome, while passing from Palestine, commended to Augustine in letter 39, probably written in 397. Jerome calls him a deacon and says that he was especially dear to him.

### LXXV.—Written around the end of 404.

When Cyprianus was returning to Africa, Jerome gave him two letters for Augustine, letters 72 and 75, according to letter 82, ch. 5, §36. In this seventy-fifth letter Jerome replies to three of the letters brought to him by Cyprianus: letters 28, 40, and 71. He says nothing about letter 73, which he had doubtless not yet received.

He was therefore writing toward the end of 404, and certainly no earlier, since John Chrysostom had already been deposed, as he indicates fairly clearly here in ch. 3, §6.

### LXXVI.—Written at the beginning of 404 or around that time.

After the decree of the general council of all Africa, held on 25 August 403, the bishops of the Donatists were summoned by each Catholic bishop within his own diocese, in the form of public Acts, so that they would not hesitate to come to a peaceful conference. They replied with words full of deceit, curse, and bitterness, as Augustine relates in book 3 of *Against Cresconius*, ch. 45.

When Augustine himself questioned Proculeianus at Hippo, Proculeianus first replied that the bishops of his party would hold a council and deliberate there about what answer they should give. When pressed again, he openly refused the conference, according to letter 88, §7.

Augustine therefore judged that the Donatists’ own laypeople should be addressed in the seventy-sixth letter, which is inscribed “To the Donatists.”

“Let your bishops,” he says in §4, “answer these points to you laypeople, if they do not wish to speak with us, etc. If the wolves have held a council so as not to answer the shepherds, why have the sheep lost the sense to approach the wolves’ dens?”
