The letter was therefore written at the beginning of 404. It mentions Felicianus, but not Praetextatus, because, as we observed above, Praetextatus had already died.

### LXXVII, LXXVIII.—Perhaps written in 404, around 26 June.

Two letters concerning the case of Bonifacius and Spes follow. We understand that they were written while Proculeianus was still alive as bishop of the Donatists at Hippo, and also some time after the decree issued by the Council of Carthage on 13 September 401 concerning the reception of Donatist clerics. This is clear from letter 78, §8.

There the lapse of two deacons who had come from the party of Donatus to the Catholic Church is recalled. At the same time, certain Catholics are reproved because their minds had been stirred by a kind of empty glory: on account of the deacons’ lapse, they had insulted Proculeianus’s discipline.

These letters perhaps belong to the time of the council held at Carthage on 26 June 404. At that time, since the holy bishop could not immediately return to Hippo to remove the scandal that had arisen in his church, he did what he could by letter.

In the letter that he addressed to the clergy, elders, and people of Hippo, he finally conceded in §4 that the name of the presbyter Bonifacius should not be recited in the diptychs. Hence it is clear that this letter was sent shortly after the other letter addressed to Felix and Hilarinus. In §2 of that letter Augustine writes that he did not dare to anticipate God’s judgment by erasing or suppressing Bonifacius’s name.

Those two men were not bishops—although Erasmus and the Louvain scholars, by an authority whose basis we do not know, bestowed that dignity upon them—but certain leading men among the Catholics of Hippo. The letter itself makes this sufficiently clear.

Nor would it be unreasonable to believe that this Hilarinus was the same man whom Augustine commends to Aurelius at the end of letter 41: “Brother Hilarinus, physician and leading citizen of Hippo.”

### LXXIX.—Perhaps written in 404.

The seventy-ninth letter was addressed to a certain Manichaean presbyter, whom we suspect was none other than Felix, who was defeated by Augustine in a public disputation in December 404, according to the *Acts with Felix*, volume 6.

Bernard Vindingus holds this view because the presbyter’s predecessor is said to have been Fortunatus. Augustine seems to imply in book 1 of the *Retractations*, ch. 8, that this Fortunatus had been Felix’s predecessor.

### LXXX.—Written in 405, around March.

The eightieth letter to Paulinus discloses its own date in §1. It was written when the return of the bishops Theasius and Evodius was expected shortly. They had been sent to Honorius by the Council of Carthage of the preceding year and undoubtedly hastened their return to Africa after the Emperor promulgated laws against the Donatists on 12 February.

### LXXXI.—Perhaps written in 405.

Jerome sent the eighty-first letter through Firmus, excusing himself for having finally replied, even unwillingly, after Augustine had challenged and compelled him to answer—namely, in letter 75. For that reason letter 75 seems to have preceded this letter 81 by only a short time.

In the following letter, §1, Augustine also suspects that Jerome had received his letter 73 before dictating this letter 81 to him. Thus this letter 81 may reasonably be assigned approximately to the year 405.

### LXXXII.—Written around the same time.

After reading the preceding letter, Augustine immediately replied to Jerome with the eighty-second letter. He responds both to the latest letter brought by Firmus and to the other two letters brought by Cyprianus, namely letters 72 and 75.

### LXXXIII.—Written around 405.

The time when the matter discussed in the eighty-third letter to Alypius came under consideration is not otherwise known, except that Augustine writes in §4 that he had discussed the matter with Bishop Samsucius.

At the beginning of Augustine’s episcopate, Samsucius was already a bishop distinguished by faith and authority, as is understood from letter 32. After 407, however, nothing further is found concerning him.

The conjecture is supported by the fact that the people of Thiava are here said to have now joined Catholic peace, perhaps as a result of the laws against the Donatists issued in 405.

### LXXXIV.—Written around this time, or before 411.

The eighty-fourth letter to Novatus was written some time before the Carthaginian Conference. There is no doubt that Novatus—who took part in the conference as bishop of Sitifis—had approached Augustine about the restoration of his brother Lucillus, a deacon, which matter occasioned this letter, as soon as he had assumed the episcopal burden.

Augustine himself clearly suggests in his reply that Novatus had acquired that dignity only recently, since he had not yet personally appointed certain ministers of the Church.

### LXXXV.—Written around 405.

The eighty-fifth letter, in which Augustine rebukes Bishop Paulus for departing as far as possible from the holy purpose he had undertaken, could not be placed much earlier than this period. Paulus is said to have been begotten in Christ through Augustine’s preaching and subsequently to have rendered good service to the Church, having already brought many people into it.

Nor should it be placed later, since Bonifacius had already succeeded the deceased Paulus by 408, according to letter 96, §2, and is called bishop of Cataqua in letter 97, §3.

Verlinus, Vindingus, and Holstenius do not doubt that the same Paulus is indicated in letter 96 as in this eighty-fifth letter; this is clear from a comparison of the two letters.

### LXXXVI.—Perhaps written in 405.

The request made of Caecilianus in the eighty-sixth letter—that he who had assisted Catholic unity with remarkable effectiveness throughout the other regions of Africa should finally come to the aid of the region of Hippo and its neighboring districts by an edict issued in his capacity as governor—is plainly evidence that the letter was not written until after the laws against the Donatists had been issued by Honorius at the beginning of 405.

Since this Caecilianus is undoubtedly the same man who was Praetorian Prefect in 409, and since it does not seem likely that a man who had held that dignity would later have earned a provincial administration in Africa, we conjecture that this letter belongs approximately to 405.

### LXXXVII.—Perhaps written in 405, certainly before 411.

Two things concerning the date of the eighty-seventh letter to Emeritus are certain. First, Augustine had not yet seen Emeritus and knew him personally only by reputation, as appears from §§1, 4, and 10. Consequently, the Carthaginian Conference had not yet taken place. At that conference Emeritus, one of the seven whom the Donatists had chosen to defend their cause, worked especially hard on behalf of that cause, as Augustine says in book 2 of the *Retractations*, ch. 51.

Second, and no less certain, Honorius had already issued the laws of 405, somewhat more severe than the representatives of the Council of Carthage in 404 had wished to obtain.

When the representatives came to Rome, as is related in the following letter, §7, the horrible and very recent wounds of the Catholic bishop of Bagai had already moved the Emperor to send such laws as were in fact sent. This is precisely what Augustine tells Emeritus here in §8.

### LXXXVIII.—Written after the beginning of 406.

The letter of the clergy of Hippo to Januarius—“of the first see of the party of Donatus,” as our manuscripts read—was sent some time before the conference with the Donatists, which they repeatedly declare themselves eager to hold.

In §10 they make the following claim: “For your colleagues who had sailed away said before the prefects that they had come to be heard.” Since this unquestionably refers to those proceedings produced in the third Carthaginian Conference, §124, in the trial held before the prefecture—where the opposing party, that is, the schismatics, demanded so insistently to be heard—and since the same conference, §141, notes that these proceedings were drawn up at Ravenna on the third day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Our Lord Arcadius, perpetual Augustus, and Probus for the fourth time—that is, in the year 406—it demonstrably follows that the letter was written after the beginning of that year.

### LXXXIX.—Written around the same time.

The eighty-ninth letter to Festus was sent after the aforesaid laws of Honorius, as is understood from §§2, 6, and 7, but before the Carthaginian Conference. Augustine makes no mention whatsoever of the conference, although he pursues the Church’s case against the Donatists at length.

### XC, XCI.—Written in 408, after 1 June.

The date of the two following letters must be determined from Augustine’s words in his reply to Nectarius, §8: “Against the most recent laws, a sacrilegious festival of the pagans was celebrated on the Kalends of June.”

Baronius and certain other scholars refer these words to the laws issued by Honorius against the pagans in 399. We, however, have no doubt that they refer to the law addressed to Curtius on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December, in the Theodosian Code, book 16, title 10, law 19, or to the law issued at Rome on the eighth day before the Kalends of December and posted at Carthage on the Nones of June, in the consulship of Bassus and Philippus, according to the appendix to the Theodosian Code, p. 35.

For these are the very words of that law which Augustine took care to reproduce here, complaining that a festival had been celebrated in violation of the laws. Moreover, the laws promulgated in 399 prohibit sacrifices to idols, not the celebration of solemn festivals.

Indeed, in that same year, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September, Honorius issued a law in these words: “Just as we have now removed profane rites by a salutary law, so we do not permit the festive gatherings of citizens and the common joy of all to be removed.”

Furthermore, letters 94 and 95—which no one will doubt were written respectively in May and toward the end of the same year in which the crime of the people of Calama occurred—cannot be assigned to 399. For Melania the Elder was not in Africa in 398, whereas it is certainly clear from letter 94, §2, that Augustine had seen her shortly before the time of the Calaman affair.

It should now be observed that the law addressed to Curtius was promulgated first in Numidia and later at Carthage, where the law is recorded in the appendix to the Theodosian Code as posted on 5 June. Alternatively, the crime of the people of Calama in question occurred only in 409.

The latter view seems less probable to us when we recall that Possidius, who had approached the Emperor’s court because of that affair, did not leave the imperial retinue until April of the following year, and that he undertook another embassy to the Emperor at the Carthaginian Council of 410, on 14 June.

We have therefore thought it preferable to assign this letter of Nectarius, and Augustine’s reply, to the year 408. Augustine testifies in letter 104, §1, that he sent that reply approximately eight months before 27 March of the following year—that is, at the beginning of August.

### XCII.—Written around 408.

The ninety-second letter, in which Augustine consoles Italica for her husband’s death, was sent shortly before letter 99, which was addressed to the same Italica. For in letter 99, §3, Augustine greets her children and thereby indicates that she had been widowed only recently.

### XCIII.—Written around 408.

The ninety-third letter to Vincentius the Rogatist is everywhere completely silent about the Carthaginian Conference, although it argues expressly and at length against the Donatist schism.

Augustine also gives an extended discussion there of the laws enacted against them, in order to excuse the severity of those laws. Yet he says nothing either about the rescript issued by Honorius toward the end of 409, allowing everyone freely to profess whatever religion he wished, or about the events that occurred immediately after Stilicho’s death, around the end of 408.

At that time the pagans and Donatists in Africa were not only spreading false reports—that the laws had been issued against them not by Honorius’s will but through Stilicho’s hostility, and therefore no longer possessed any force—but were also violently attacking the Catholics, even killing certain bishops.

From this one may infer that the letter was written some time before 411, indeed before the end of 408, but at a time when Augustine was diligently working to make the heretics obey the laws.

Vincentius considered this contrary to Augustine’s character. “Although I know very well,” he says in his letter to Augustine here, §51, “that you were still far removed from the Christian faith, and that formerly, devoted to literary studies, you were a lover of tranquility and uprightness.”

Augustine displayed such exceptional uprightness among human beings even during that period which he pursues in the books of the *Confessions* with such bitter style and profound grief.

### XCIV, XCV.—Written in 408.

Paulinus indicates the month and day on which he received the ninety-fourth letter in §8, in these words: “On the day before the Ides of May, the deacon Quintus came to us to request replies, and on the Ides he obtained permission to depart before the sixth hour.”

Augustine himself indicates the year in letter 95, §1, where he replies: “Therefore, when you have heard from brother Possidius himself how sorrowful was the cause that compelled him, you will recognize that I am speaking the absolute truth concerning that joy in which brother Possidius is with you.”

That sorrowful cause which compelled Possidius to sail to Italy was none other than the disaster and destruction inflicted on his Church of Calama by the pagans in June 408.

Possidius, as he departed, undoubtedly received this reply to carry to Paulinus, or it was sent not long after his departure. Augustine wrote it while wintering at Carthage, according to letter 121, §14—that is, at the beginning or end of winter—for according to letter 97, §3, he was at Hippo in midwinter. Unless “midwinter” here indicates a time especially unfavorable for sailing.

We were somewhat troubled at this point by the opinion of a learned man who assigns these two letters to the year 399. He thinks that Publicola’s death, discussed as still recent in letter 94, cannot be assigned to a time close to 409.

His argument is as follows. The author of the life of Melania the Younger says that she was married to Pinianus at the age of fourteen. He then says that, after the death of her father Publicola, she renounced the world at the age of twenty.

Palladius, however, in the *Historia Lausiaca*, ch. 118, relates that Melania the Elder returned from Palestine to Rome after hearing that her granddaughter Melania had married and wished to renounce the world.

Finally, Melania the Elder is believed to have returned with Rufinus during the pontificate of Siricius. Therefore, the learned man concludes, in 397, the last year of Siricius’s pontificate, Melania the Younger was already married. Publicola’s death, which occurred when Melania was twenty and six or seven years after her marriage, could therefore not be assigned approximately to the year 409.

Nevertheless, after the matter had been carefully considered, the reasons by which the date of the Calaman affair was investigated above under letter 90 seemed far more certain. The learned man himself has no doubt that Augustine refers to that affair in the words of letter 95 cited here. It appeared to us less securely established that Melania was in Rufinus’s company when Rufinus landed in Italy while Siricius was Roman pontiff, since, in our reckoning, Melania’s return from Palestine can scarcely be placed before 402.

We have therefore thought it better not to determine the date of these letters on the basis of that opinion, but rather to proceed in the opposite direction.

### XCVI.—Written in 408, around the beginning of September.

After hearing that Olympius had been promoted to a higher dignity, Augustine soon wrote to him his ninety-sixth letter. The report of Olympius’s promotion that had reached Africa had not yet been confirmed, as Augustine says in §1.

The office of master of the offices mentioned here was acquired by Olympius after Stilicho was killed on 23 August 408. This letter therefore seems to have been sent not long after the beginning of September.

### XCVII.—Written toward the end of 408.

The ninety-seventh letter, the second sent to Olympius, was written after the preceding one and in midwinter, as §3 shows.

In this letter Augustine warns him about the disturbances stirred up in the African Church. After Stilicho’s death, the pagans and heretics were claiming that the laws against them had been sent without the Emperor’s will, or without his knowledge, and were thereby inflaming ignorant minds violently against the Church.

Augustine therefore asks Olympius to come to their aid as soon as possible and to use his authority so that the Church’s enemies might understand that those laws had been established by the Emperor’s will.

For this reason, at the Council of Carthage held on 13 October 408, the bishops Restitutus and Florentius undertook an embassy to the Emperor, at the time when Severus and Macarius were killed, as is recorded in the African Code of Canons, ch. 106.

### XCVIII.—Perhaps written in 408.

We have thought it appropriate to place here the ninety-eighth letter to Bishop Bonifacius, since it was not written before this period. He is clearly the same man who is praised in the preceding letters to Olympius: the successor of Paulus, who had died not long before, and bishop of Cataqua.

### XCIX.—Written toward the end of 408 or at the beginning of 409.

The ninety-ninth letter, addressed to Italica, belongs to the time of the disaster inflicted on the Roman people during Alaric’s first siege of the city, which is mentioned in §1.

The words of Zosimus, found in the note to this letter, compel us to assign that first siege to the end of 408.

### C.—Written around the same time.

In the hundredth letter, §2, Augustine asks the proconsul Donatus to issue an edict promptly, so that the Donatist heretics may learn that the laws enacted against their error remain in force. They already regarded those laws as ineffective and were publicly claiming that they had no force.

From this it is understood that Augustine was writing toward the end of 408, soon after new rescripts against the heretics had appeared. Among these is the law addressed to Donatus himself on 24 November.

Augustine also addresses Donatus at the beginning as though he had only recently assumed the proconsulship of Africa.

### CI.—Written around the same time.

Possidius, bishop of Calama, was the bearer of the hundred-and-first letter to Memorius, as §1 shows. Because of the case of his church against the pagans, he sailed to Italy, as we have already observed, either toward the end of 408 or, more probably, at the beginning of 409.

This is so first because on 27 March of that year Augustine still did not know whether Possidius had obtained anything against the criminals, according to letter 104, §1; and second because letter 95—which, as we have said, was sent to Paulinus when Possidius was departing or had only recently departed—was dictated in winter.

### CII.—Written around the same time.

The hundred-and-second letter to Deogratias, which Augustine entitled *Six Questions Explained against the Pagans*, bears no indication of its own date. We assign it this place because it is listed among the books published after 406 and before 411 in book 2 of the *Retractations*, ch. 31.

### CIII, CIV.—Written in 409, around March.

Augustine received the later letter from Nectarius, here numbered 103, on 27 March, and immediately sent him the hundred-and-fourth letter. In §1 he asks Nectarius why he had delayed sending his reply so long, since Augustine was answering letter 91 only after nearly eight months.

It is easy to suspect that after Stilicho’s death Nectarius had abandoned the task of replying because he saw the Church plunged into great disturbances and believed that the laws issued on its behalf while Stilicho was alive had already, as rumor reported, been completely repealed.

Now, however, he turned his attention to requesting pardon for the offense committed by his fellow citizens because he had learned that new laws had been issued by the Emperor on behalf of the Church, not only at the end of 408 but also at the beginning of 409.

There is, in fact, a law in these words: “Lest the Donatists … Jews and Gentiles … think that the provisions of the laws previously issued against them have grown weak, let all judges know that their commands must be obeyed with faithful devotion,” and so forth.

This law is correctly dated in the Theodosian Code, book 16, title 5, law 46, to 15 January of this year, 409. In Sirmond’s appendix, p. 45, however, it is dated the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Honorius for the ninth time and Theodosius for the fifth time, that is, in 412.

That is entirely wrong, since Caecilianus succeeded Theodorus, to whom the law is addressed as Praetorian Prefect, and Caecilianus obtained that office not long after the beginning of 409.

### CV.—Written at the beginning of 409.

We understand the hundred-and-fifth letter to the Donatists to have been written around this time, first from these words in §6: “What is better: to produce the true commands of the Emperors in support of unity, or false indulgences in support of perversity—as you have done, filling all Africa suddenly with your lie?” These words plainly refer to the deceitful rumors spread by the Donatists after Stilicho’s death concerning the repeal of the earlier laws.

The date is also indicated by what Augustine says in §8, speaking about the case of Caecilianus: “Demand this of us; let us prove it to you; and if we do not prove it, do with us whatever you can.” These words imply that no conference with the Donatists had yet been held concerning that matter, and indeed that the Emperor had not yet issued a rescript ordering that a conference be held.

### CVI–CVIII.—Perhaps written in 409.

Epistle 106 was written to Macrobius, recently ordained bishop, as appears from the subsequent letter of Maximus and Theodore to Augustine from the same period. Macrobius had been substituted for Proculeianus at Hippo, as is understood from Epistle 107, also addressed to Macrobius. For when he entered that city with a large retinue, he thereafter acted there as bishop, as is clear from no. 14, watching over the people together with Augustine and exercising pastoral care over the households divided into two factions, as appears from nos. 17 and 20. There can be no doubt that he is the same man who is called “Bishop of Hippo” in the Carthaginian Conference 1, no. 201.

Proculeianus, moreover, had not yet died at the end of 403. At that time Augustine, by decree of the Council of Carthage held on 25 August of the same year, arranged for him to be summoned once and again to the conference, according to Epistle 88, no. 7. Furthermore, when the clergy of Hippo mention him in a letter written as the year 406 was already advancing, they say nothing at all about his death. For this reason someone might perhaps think that Epistle 106 and the two immediately following letters were not written before 406.

For our part, at least this is certain: they are not earlier than the laws promulgated against the Donatists in 405. Those laws are shown in this Epistle 106, no. 14, in these words: “The Maximianists endured persecution from you not only afterward—that is, after they had returned to you—but also earlier and at your hands.” And more clearly in no. 18: “Unity is shunned, so that we may seek public laws against the wickedness of your people . . . and against those very laws the Circumcellions arm themselves; laws which, in the very fury with which they were raging, they despised when they stirred them up against you.”

Against such clear evidence it is useless to set Praetextatus of Assuras, who, as we observed above in connection with Epistle 51, is said here in no. 5 to have died recently, although he died around the year 400. It is much more reasonable here to take the word “recently” in a broader sense; everyone knows that writers sometimes extend it to fifteen years or more, especially in the course of debate, when they do not want their opponent to claim ignorance of or concealment regarding a matter.

We must also note the statement in no. 18: “Before that law by which you rejoice that liberty has been restored to you,” etc. If this does not perhaps refer to Julian’s rescript, it shows that the letter was written toward the end of 409, after the edict of Honorius himself by which he decreed that everyone should be permitted to follow whatever religion he preferred. See the annotation on this passage.

In any case, the state of affairs represented in the letter does not allow it to be assigned later than approximately the middle of 410. Accordingly, we think that the following words in no. 19 should be removed: “Writing about this Marcellinus, you call him a tenant of the Church.” For Marcellinus the tribune, who seems to be praised here, was not sent to Africa until the end of 410, to arrange the Carthaginian Conference; and there is no mention of that conference here.

The error is easily detected—not from the manuscript copies, of which none survive except the Vatican manuscript, but from the context itself. A scribe carelessly brought into the text something that an inexperienced reader had noted in the margin after seeing Epistle 139 to Marcellinus, where Augustine says that a certain deacon named Donatus, who had been rebaptized, was a tenant of the Church.

**CIX, CX.—Probably written around 409.**

The two following letters, whose date cannot be determined so precisely, are Epistle 109 from Severus to Augustine and Epistle 110 from Augustine to the same Severus. He was not an abbot, as Erasmus and the Louvain editors assigned him that title, but a bishop: Severus himself calls Augustine, who was certainly then a bishop, “brother,” while Augustine calls him “fellow priest.”

Nor is that Severus whom Augustine here professes to be so closely attached to any other than the bishop of Milevis. Augustine likewise writes of him in Epistle 84 to Novatus, no. 1: “However strong the kinship of your blood may be, it does not surpass the bond of friendship by which I and my brother Severus cling to one another . . . Yet he now speaks with me only with difficulty and occasionally through very short letters.”

Severus died in 426, as is clear from Epistle 213. The aforementioned Epistle 109 seems to have been written after Severus had read the books of the *Confessions* and other pious works of Augustine, from which he indicates that he derived great pleasure and benefit.

**CXI.—Written at the end of 409, perhaps in November.**

The circumstances expressed at the beginning of Epistle 111 to Victorianus fit the year 409 especially well: that most sorrowful picture of the whole world afflicted by such great disasters that scarcely any part of the earth remained where events such as those Victorianus had reported were not occurring and being lamented.

Augustine adds: “Even concerning the Spaniards, so many provinces which had seemed for a long time untouched by these evils, reports of such events have now begun to arrive.” In that same year, of course, the Vandals occupied Spain, according to Cassiodorus and Prosper in their *Chronicle*. The Alans and Suevi did so as well, according to the *Chronicle* of Hydatius, who reports that their incursion into Spain is dated by some to 28 September and by others to 13 October. Consequently, this letter may perhaps have been written in November.

Augustine also mentions here the killing of monks by barbarians in the solitude of Egypt. Cassian’s Sixth Conference concerns this same killing of the saints.

**CXII.—Written at the end of 409 or the beginning of 410.**

[Col. 0035]

Epistle 112 was written to Donatus, formerly proconsul, shortly after he had been released from public responsibilities, as is understood from no. 1. On what day or in what month Donatus laid down the proconsulship of Africa, however, we have not been able to discover, except that it happened before 25 June 410, as we learn from the law addressed on that day to Macrobius, proconsul of Africa.

**CXIII–CXVI.—Written around this period, that is, no earlier than 409 and no later than 423.**

The four immediately following letters—to Cresconius, Florentinus, Fortunatus, and Generosus—were written concerning the same matter and must be assigned neither before 409 nor after 423. In them Augustine cites a law enacted by Honorius on 21 January 409 concerning the production or transfer of defendants. In the *Theodosian Code*, book 9, title 2, law 6, it reads as follows:

“If anyone who has been made a defendant by the preliminary bond of accusation is ordered, by the direction of the judges, to be sent as an aid to his own curia, let him be questioned in the municipal records whether he wishes, in accordance with the command of our triumphant father, to remain in the city for the thirty days granted to him, under moderate and careful custody, in order to arrange his household affairs and provide himself with expenses. If he wishes this to be done, this kind of benefit must not be denied to those who desire it.”

As you can see, the very words of this law are reproduced in the letters mentioned above, so that there can be no doubt that Augustine had already seen this precise law. For the law issued by Theodosius on the same matter in 380 uses entirely different words in the same place of the *Theodosian Code*, law 2.

Augustine also implies that he is invoking the law of the emperor who was then administering the empire, since he consistently calls it “the emperor’s law”—that is, the law of Honorius, who died on 15 August 423.

**CXVII, CXVIII.—Probably written in 410 or at the beginning of 411.**

Epistle 117, from Dioscorus, and Epistle 118, Augustine’s reply to Dioscorus, were written when Augustine had already begun to grow gray, as he himself seems to attest in his reply, no. 9. They can scarcely be placed earlier than the year 410, when Augustine was 56 years old.

Nor can they be placed later than the beginning of 411. In no. 12, where Augustine urges Dioscorus to investigate thoroughly the errors of the heretics who at that time were attacking the faith of the Church, rather than reheating the long-settled disputes of the ancient philosophers, he lists the Donatists, Maximianists, and Manichaeans from Africa, and the Arians, Eunomians, and others from the East, but makes no mention of the Pelagians. Yet a synod against them was held at Carthage before the end of 411.

Thus Alypius is called an old man by Dioscorus in reference to age, not to rank, since he attained the dignity of primate in Numidia only toward the end of Augustine’s life.

**CXIX, CXX.—Probably written around the same period.**

Augustine had withdrawn to a country estate when Epistle 119 from Consentius was delivered to him, as is said in no. 1. If anyone wishes to connect this with what the same saint writes to Dioscorus, no. 34—namely, that after an illness he had withdrawn for a time from Hippo—we shall not object.

We observe only that Epistle 120, Augustine’s reply to Consentius, was written around this period. For Augustine indicates in no. 13 that by then he had already committed many matters concerning the question of the Trinity to writing. He had been working on the work on the Trinity, which he says in Epistle 174 he began as a young man and published as an old man, from approximately the year 400, although he did not complete it before 416.

**CXXI.—Written around 410.**

It is evident that this Epistle 121 from Paulinus was written somewhat later than Epistle 95, which was written toward the end of 408. In no. 14 Paulinus asks that another copy of the latter letter, which had already been sent to him, be forwarded to him. It was also written somewhat earlier than Epistle 149, composed around 414. Between that letter and this one, several letters passed back and forth, including Augustine’s reply to the questions Paulinus had posed here; all of these letters have nevertheless perished. Compare Epistle 149, no. 1.

**CXXII.—Written around the same period.**

[Col. 0036]

In Epistle 122 Augustine encourages his people of Hippo, who had grown cold in distributing alms because of fear of the impending disasters. Baronius assigns it to the end of 409, because it fits very well the period when the destruction of the Roman Empire was feared.

But it fits no less well the end of 410, when Alaric, after capturing Rome and ravaging Italy, was preparing to cross into Sicily, according to Orosius, book 7, chapter 43, and from there to sail toward the subjugation of Africa, according to Jordanes in his book on Gothic history.

**CXXIII.—Probably written toward the end of 410.**

The whole of Epistle 123, from Jerome, is enigmatic. Since interpreters have gone in different directions in explaining it, it is not easy to say whose understanding follows Jerome’s intention: whether those who understand the opening words as referring to the Pelagians condemned in Palestine, or rather those who interpret the whole letter either in relation to the capture of the City or to the Origenists. See the note on that letter and what we observe below concerning Epistle 195.

**THIRD CLASS OF LETTERS**, which Augustine wrote from the time of the conference held with the Donatists at Carthage and the introduction of the Pelagian heresy into Africa until his death—that is, from the year of Christ 411 to 430.

**CXXIV–CXXVI.—Written around the beginning of 411.**

Epistle 124 to Albina, Pinianus, and Melania was written in winter, not long after their arrival in Africa. They crossed over only toward the end of 410, namely from Sicily, as the author of the life of Melania the Younger reports. Rufinus likewise states in his letter to Ursacius that they remained on that island during the same year. See the note on Epistle 124.

After spending a few days at Thagaste, Pinianus and Melania, as it is easy to believe, went to Hippo to visit Augustine. There occurred the event discussed in the two immediately following letters. For that reason we assign them to the beginning of 411.

**CXXVII.—Probably written in 411.**

Epistle 127 to Armentarius and Paulina appeared around the year 411, as is clearly inferred from these words in no. 1: “Unless perhaps the world is still to be loved, though crushed by such universal ruin that it has even lost the appearance of seduction”; and from these words in no. 4: “Just now, when Rome itself, the dwelling place of the most illustrious empire, was being ravaged by barbarian invasion.”

**CXXVIII.—Written in 411, shortly before 1 June.**

In Marcellinus’ second edict, by which he announced, as Augustine says in the *Brief Account of the Conference*, day 1, chapter 3, while the bishops of both parties were already present at Carthage, what the place and procedure of the conference would be, he instructed each party to write back to him whether they approved what the edict contained. The Catholics’ response was Epistle 128.

That reply is found subscribed in the name of all the other bishops by only two primates, namely Aurelius of Carthage and Silvanus, already primate of Numidia. Nevertheless, Augustine reports in his book *On the Proceedings with Emeritus* that it was prepared in a very large gathering of almost three hundred bishops. From this it follows that it belongs to the days immediately preceding the Carthaginian Conference, which began on 1 June 411.

**CXXIX.—Written shortly after the preceding letter.**

Epistle 129 belongs to the same period. In it the Catholic bishops thought they should respond to the rescript—or “Notoria,” as they called it—of the Donatists, who had replied to Marcellinus on behalf of their own party that they did not approve his proposal in the edict: namely, that only those bishops whom the others had delegated to conduct the case should assemble at the place of the conference. They requested instead that all who had come to Carthage be permitted to attend, as appears from the *Brief Account of the Conference*, day 1, chapter 4.

**CXXX.—Written around 412.**

[Col. 0037]

Epistle 130 to Proba was written some time after her arrival in Africa and after she had already spoken several times with Augustine, as is clear from no. 1.

Proba, together with her daughter Juliana and her granddaughter Demetrias, withdrew to Africa as soon as they were able to escape the barbarian dangers into which they had fallen when the City was captured. Jerome’s Epistle 8 to Demetrias should be read on this subject.

Augustine’s first letter to Proba can therefore be assigned to 411 or 412, and certainly not much later. First, in no. 30, when he mentions her daughter-in-law, the widow Juliana, and urges the widows and virgins placed under Proba’s care to devote themselves to prayer, he says nothing about Demetrias. He would undoubtedly have praised her here if she had already professed virginity; but she did so in 413.

Moreover, Augustine mentions this letter at the end of his book *On the Good of Widowhood*, which he wrote after Demetrias had recently embraced the discipline of virginity, as is clear from the words there in chapter 19: “she who has only just begun.”

**CXXXI.—Written around the same period.**

Epistle 131 to the same Proba cannot be assigned to a much later time. By then, whether in 413 or thereabouts, Proba was already advanced in years and had reached old age, as is evident from the book *On the Good of Widowhood*, chapters 19 and 23.

**CXXXII.—Written around the beginning of 412.**

Epistle 132 to Volusianus was written some time before Epistles 135 and 136, which were composed around the beginning of 412.

**CXXXIII.—Written around the same period.**

When the Emperor Honorius wished the Donatists to be punished for their obstinacy after the Carthaginian Conference, and enacted a law against them on 30 January 412, preserved in the *Theodosian Code*, book 16, title 5, law 52, they began to rise up against the Catholics with greater violence and to rage more fiercely.

When Augustine heard that some of them had been brought before the judges and, at the same time, that they had been convicted of the murder of Restitutus the presbyter and of the killing of Innocentius, another Catholic presbyter, whose eye had been gouged out and whose finger had been cut off, he wrote Epistle 133 to Marcellinus the Tribune, earnestly asking that the death penalty not be inflicted upon them. We therefore think that this letter should be assigned shortly after the beginning of 412.

**CXXXIV.—Written at the same time as the preceding letter.**

Epistle 134 to the judge Apringius was delivered at the same time and concerning the same matter. He was Marcellinus’ brother, as appears from no. 2, and at that time held the proconsulship, as is clear from no. 3 of the preceding letter.

**CXXXV–CXXXVIII.—Written at the beginning of 412.**

The four following letters—Epistle 135 from Volusianus, Epistle 136 from Marcellinus to Augustine, Epistle 137 from Augustine to Volusianus, and Epistle 138 to Marcellinus—preceded Epistle 139 by not much time. In Epistle 139, no. 3, Augustine mentions these two letters as having recently been sent by him.

**CXXXIX.—Written in 412.**

Epistle 139 to Marcellinus is somewhat later than Epistles 133 and 134. Augustine says of them here in no. 2:

“If you, the Proconsul—or both of you together—are going to pronounce sentence against them, and if he perhaps persists in wishing to punish them with the sword, although he is a Christian and, as far as we have been able to observe, is not inclined toward such tortures, nevertheless, if it should be necessary, order my letters to be cited even in the official records. I thought that I should send each of them to you concerning this matter.”

**CXL.—Written after the preceding letter.**

We can establish the date of Epistle 140 to Honoratus, entitled *The Book on the Grace of the New Testament*, from book 2 of the *Retractations*, chapter 36. There Augustine testifies that the questions he undertakes to resolve in this letter were sent to him at the time when he was vigorously engaged against the Donatists and had already begun to be engaged against the Pelagians.

We can also establish it from the preceding Epistle 139, in which the holy Doctor says in no. 3:

“Now I have in hand a book for our Honoratus on five questions that he posed to me and communicated in writing. You see how little it is appropriate for me to reply to him immediately.”

**CXLI.—Written 14 June 412.**

Epistle 141, from the Council of Zerta to the Donatists, has the day and the consuls written on it.

**CXLII.—Written around the same period.**

We have placed immediately after it the letter addressed to Saturninus, Euphrates, and other clergy who had converted from the Donatist schism to the Church, because no. 3 speaks of Donatist bishops convicted at the Carthaginian Conference in the same words that are found in Epistle 141, nos. 4 and 6.

Moreover, toward the end Augustine urges prayer for those who still cling to the schism, so that their carnal weakness of mind, contracted through long habit, may be healed in them. From this you may understand that he wrote it some time after the Carthaginian Conference.

**CXLIII.—Written around the end of 412.**

Epistle 143 to Marcellinus appeared around the end of 412. This is clearly inferred from no. 12, where Augustine observes that something he had written about the virginity of Saint Mary, the Mother of God, in Epistle 137 was not for that reason unworthy of belief, merely because the matter was extraordinary and unique.

Add that in no. 1 he replies to a letter from Marcellinus received through the bishop Boniface. Boniface was with Marcellinus at the time when Epistle 139 was delivered, as is indicated there in no. 2, and he is thought to have brought the aforementioned letter with him on his return.

**CXLIV.—Written around this period.**

We think that Epistle 144 to the people of Cirta who had converted from the Donatist faction to Catholic unity was delivered around the same time. First, because their obstinacy is said to have been overcome by the force of truth—an obstinacy by which they had resisted the most evident and, in a sense, public truth, that is, a matter already fully settled through the Carthaginian Conference.

Second, because the holy Doctor carefully urges them here to attribute their conversion to a work of God, not of man, as though they needed to be fortified against another error recently revealed in Africa, the Pelagian error. Compare the beginning of this letter with the end of Epistle 141.

**CXLV.—Written around 412 or 413.**

In Epistle 145 to Anastasius Augustine shows that righteousness is fulfilled not through the law but through grace, and not at all through servile fear but only through free love. In no. 8 he says that he is treating this argument because of certain people who attribute too much to human will and think that, once the law has been given, it is sufficient for them to fulfill righteousness.

At this point he still spares the name of those heretics, whom he had decided to attack only after their obstinacy had become known. The letter should therefore be assigned to around 413.

**CXLVI.—Written around 413.**

Epistle 146 is likewise assigned to the year 413. Augustine wrote it to Pelagius after he had come to understand Pelagius’ heresy—not from writings published by Pelagius himself, but through rumor and conversation—as he testifies in the book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chapter 26:

“For I had already heard that, whenever some mention was made here of the grace by which we are justified, he openly and contentiously attempted to oppose it.”

**CXLVII, CXLVIII.—Apparently written in 413.**

Augustine lists the *Book on Seeing God* addressed to Paulina and the *Memorandum to Fortunatianus of Sicca* on the same subject—Epistles 147 and 148 here—in the *Retractations* immediately after the books he composed in 412 or 413.

Fortunatianus, who governed the church of Sicca in 411 after the Carthaginian Conference, had Urbanus as his successor around 413. For this Urbanus himself had undertaken a journey to Rome and had already returned from there in 415, as appears from fragment 1 of volume 10.

**CXLIX.—Written in 414.**

Epistle 149 to Paulinus can scarcely be assigned earlier than 414. Between this letter and Epistle 121, which Paulinus wrote in reply in 410 and whose questions Augustine answers again, several letters passed back and forth and have disappeared, as is clear from no. 2.

Furthermore, no. 32 mentions Urbanus, bishop of Sicca. If he is the same as the presbyter Urbanus mentioned in Epistle 143, no. 1, he had not yet attained episcopal rank toward the end of 412.

Nor can the letter easily be placed later. Peregrinus the deacon, who had departed together with Urbanus when Urbanus was going to undertake the burden of the episcopate, had not yet returned to Hippo when Augustine dictated this letter, as he testifies at the end.

**CL.—Written around the end of 413.**

Epistle 150 was written to Proba and Juliana on the occasion of the consecration of their daughter Demetrias. She had been inflamed by Augustine’s exhortation to despise the world and had professed virginity.

Although Demetrias had already heard Augustine at Carthage, when he went there to hold the conference with the Donatists, she does not seem to have taken the veil before 413. For Jerome’s Epistle 8 to Demetrias on the same consecration—which, as Augustine says here in no. 1, was proclaimed everywhere with extraordinary speed and widespread fame—was written only in that year, or, as is much more likely, in the following year.

Accordingly, we judge that Augustine’s letter belongs to the end of 413 or the beginning of the following year.

**CLI.—Written at the end of 413 or the beginning of 414.**

The discussion of the murder of Saint Marcellinus in Epistle 151 to Caecilianus is demonstrated in the notes on that letter. From this you may readily understand that it was delivered around the end of 413.

**CLII–CLV.—Written around 414.**

We establish the date of the four following letters in this way. In Epistle 152, no. 3, Macedonius says that he has not yet received the works Augustine had promised him and asks him to send them at last.

Then, in Epistle 154, he tells Augustine that he has received and read the books Augustine sent him. Anyone who examines Augustine’s reply—Epistle 155 here, no. 2—will understand that these books were the first three books of *The City of God*, which appeared in 413. Augustine added the fourth and fifth books in 415, according to Epistle 169, no. 1.

**CLVI, CLVII.—Written in 414.**

You will infer from our note on Epistle 157 that Epistle 156 from Hilary of Syracuse and Epistle 157, Augustine’s reply to the same Hilary, were written in 414.

At least, one should not agree with Baronius, who assigns them to 411. For in no. 22 Augustine testifies that he had already said much about the questions concerning the Pelagians that Hilary had proposed, both in other short works of his and in ecclesiastical sermons.

**CLVIII–CLXIV.—Written in 414.**

As for the letters of Evodius and Augustine’s replies to him, they were arranged very disorderly in the editions published up to the present.

It is clear that Epistle 158 from Evodius, formerly numbered 258, occasioned Epistle 159, which was numbered 100 and addressed to Evodius. Epistle 159 was written a short time before Epistle 162, in which Augustine, replying in no. 3 to Evodius’ Epistles 160 and 161, testifies that he had only recently answered that Epistle 159.

Soon afterward came Epistle 163 from Evodius, written before he had received Epistle 162. For Evodius repeats the questions from his earlier letters and adds two others.

After discussing these two questions in Epistle 164, Augustine says in no. 22 that he had already answered the questions sent previously, except the one concerning the vision of God through the body.

Since Epistles 161 and 162 concern a statement from Epistle 137, written to Volusianus in 412, it follows that all the letters under discussion were produced around this period. They seem to have been dictated shortly before Epistle 169 to the same Evodius, which belongs to the end of 415.

**CLXV.—Written not long after 410.**

Epistle 165 from Jerome was sent to Marcellinus the Tribune, who was serving in Africa, as is clear from no. 1. Marcellinus served in that region for approximately three years, from 410 to 413. In September of that year he was killed by the schemes of the heretics and entered the number of the martyrs. See the note on this letter.

**CLXVI.—Written in the spring of 415.**

Epistle 166 to Jerome was dictated on the occasion of the presbyter Orosius’ voyage to Palestine in 415, undertaken around springtime, as appears from no. 2.

**CLXVII.—Written at the same time as the preceding letter.**

Orosius also received this Epistle 167 to deliver to Jerome at the same time. It was written at the same time as the preceding letter, as is indicated not only by Augustine in this Epistle 167, no. 1; Epistle 169, chapter 4, no. 13; and book 2 of the *Retractations*, chapter 45, but also by Jerome in his reply, which is Epistle 172 here, no. 1.

**CLXVIII.—Probably written in 415.**

Epistle 168 is from Timasius and James. In it they offer Augustine thanks for his book *On Nature and Grace*, which we have no doubt was published in 415.

**CLXIX.—Written at the end of 415.**

Augustine sent Epistle 169 to Evodius after completing the book *On Nature and Grace*. It was written in the same year in which he dictated the fourth and fifth books of *The City of God* and Epistles 166 and 167 to Jerome, as he himself states here in nos. 1 and 13.

**CLXX, CLXXI.—Probably written in 415.**

Epistle 170 to Maximus and Epistle 171 to Peregrinus were delivered at the same time, and not before 415. Peregrinus, the bishop with whom Augustine and Alypius here interact so familiarly, seems to have been the same Peregrinus who was still serving as a deacon in 412, according to Epistles 139 and 149, and indeed after 413, according to Epistle 149, no. 34.

**CLXXII.—Written at the beginning of 416.**

Jerome’s Epistle 172 here is thought to have been delivered to Augustine by Orosius when he returned from Palestine to Africa in 416, around springtime.

**CLXXIII.—Written around this period.**

Epistle 173 to the presbyter Donatus is somewhat later than the Carthaginian Conference, whose proceedings Augustine discusses there in no. 7. It is also later than the laws subsequently issued by Honorius against the Donatists. Donatus would not have been forcibly seized and brought to the Church in the manner reported here in no. 1 if the authority of the imperial laws had not intervened.

In what year this happened is uncertain: whether immediately after the laws issued against the schismatics following the news of Marcellinus’ murder, or afterward, when Dulcitius the Tribune, the executor of the imperial laws, came to Africa.

**CLXXIV.—Written around this period.**

Epistle 174 to Aurelius cannot be assigned earlier than 416, since in book 13 of *On the Trinity*—a work completed in all its parts and sent here to Aurelius—there is mention of book 12 of *The City of God*, which was not completed before 416.

**CLXXV.—Written in 416.**

[Col. 0041]

The letter of the Council of Carthage to Innocent, numbered here as Epistle 175, is assigned to 416, first because the presbyter Orosius, who brought the African bishops the letters of Heros and Lazarus against Pelagius and thus gave the African fathers the occasion to write this letter while they were holding their customary synod, returned from Palestine in the spring of that very year.

Second, Innocent’s reply to the same synod is dated 27 January after the consulship of Theodosius VII and Junius Quartus, both *viri clarissimi*—that is, in 417.

**CLXXVI.—Written shortly after the preceding letter.**

On the same day Innocent replied to the fathers of Milevis, who, following the example of the Carthaginians, had sent him a synodal letter on the same matter—Epistle 176 here—as they say in no. 5. It therefore belongs to the same year, 416.

**CLXXVII.—Written around the same period.**

The date of Epistle 177 is established by the same arguments. It was dictated after the preceding synodal letters, as appears from no. 1.

**CLXXVIII.—Written at the same time.**

Epistle 178 to Bishop Hilary gives its own date in these words in no. 2:

“By the time I was writing this, we had already learned that in the Church of Carthage a decree of the episcopal council had been issued against them, to be sent by letter to the holy and venerable Pope Innocent; and we from the Council of Numidia had likewise already written to the same Apostolic See.”

**CLXXIX.—Written around the same period.**

Augustine had not yet received the proceedings of the Council of Diospolis, held toward the end of 415, when he gave Epistle 179 to John of Jerusalem to be delivered, as appears from no. 7.

He had, however, already seen an apology composed by Pelagius and sent to the Africans in place of those proceedings. In it Pelagius boasted that he had answered the charges of Heros and Lazarus. Augustine had also already written another letter to John on the same matter, after Orosius’ return, as we believe.

For in no. 1 Augustine thinks that John’s reply to him had not been delivered because no courier had been available to him.

**CLXXX.—Written around the end of 416.**

Epistle 180 to Oceanus was delivered some time after Orosius’ return to Africa, as appears from no. 5.

**CLXXXI–CLXXXIII.—Written at the beginning of 417.**

The three following letters, sent by Innocent to Africa, have the day and the consuls recorded. These dates fall in January 417.

**CLXXXIV.—Written around the same period.**

We believe that Epistle 184 from Innocent to Aurelius and Augustine was written around the same period, since Innocent died in 417, in March or July.

**CLXXXV.—Written around 417.**

In Epistle 185 to Boniface Augustine mentions the Carthaginian Conference in no. 6. But he indicates its date more precisely in the *Retractations*. There, after reviewing the book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, which was published around the beginning of 417, he testifies that he wrote this letter at the same time, assigning it immediately before the book to Dardanus, written in the summer of 417.

**CLXXXVI.—Written around the middle of 417.**

Several considerations establish the date of Epistle 186 to Paulinus. First, the proceedings of the Council of Diospolis had already reached Augustine’s hands, as appears from nos. 1, 31, and those that follow.

Next, he had read Innocent’s replies against the Pelagians, issued at the beginning of 417. For in no. 28 he begins to bring against the Pelagians the Lord’s statement, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man,” etc. Nevertheless, he carefully observes that the Apostolic See had employed this testimony for the purpose of preventing people from thinking that unbaptized children could have life.

[Col. 0042]

In addition, he had heard of Innocent’s death, as appears from no. 2. According to Baronius’ reckoning, supported by the *Acts of the Ancient Pontiffs* published by Bollandus, by Anastasius the librarian, and by the recent Roman Martyrology, this occurred on 28 July 417.

Or rather, it occurred on 12 March, as preferred by the Martyrologies of Bede, Usuard, Ado, and Notker—and before all of these, by the ancient Roman Martyrology used by Ado.

The Martyrologies are corroborated by a letter from Zosimus to the churches of Gaul, which is recorded by Sirmond as having been written on 22 March 417. They are also corroborated by a letter written in 443 by Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum, to Leo, the Roman pontiff. Paschasinus relates that in 417 the Westerners, when Zosimus was pope, made an error concerning the date of Easter: although Easter fell on 22 April, they celebrated it on 25 March.

Finally, Prosper reports in his *Chronicle* that Zosimus governed the Church for one year, nine months, and eight days—or, according to some editions, nine months and nine days. Zosimus died on 26 December 418. He therefore assumed the government of the Church on 17 or 18 March 417.

Another indication of the date of this letter to Paulinus is that Innocent’s successor, Zosimus, had not yet attempted anything either in favor of or against the Pelagians, since this letter contains no mention of him.

**CLXXXVII.—Written around the middle of 417.**
The book to Dardanus, listed among Augustine’s letters in the editions thus far published, belongs approximately to the middle of the year 417. For Augustine reveals in section 1 that it was written as summer was drawing to a close, and in the *Retractations* assigns it a position between the book on the Proceedings of Pelagius, composed toward the end of 416 or the beginning of 417, and the books *On Grace and Original Sin*, written around May 418.

**CLXXXVIII.—Written toward the end of 417 or the beginning of 418.**

The one-hundred-and-eighty-eighth letter, addressed to Juliana, is sent in the name of Alypius and Augustine, who wish to learn whether the anonymous book addressed to Demetrias—the work printed here in the Appendix as Letter XVII—originated with Pelagius. In his work *On the Grace of Christ*, however, Augustine attributes this same book to Pelagius, whose authorship was fully ascertained and established. This letter, therefore, was issued before the aforementioned work *On the Grace of Christ*, composed in 418; yet not a very long time before it, since in section 14 Augustine speaks of another letter of Pelagius, written to Innocent at the beginning of 417 and delivered to his successor Zosimus only around September.

**CLXXXIX.—Written around the year 418.**

At the beginning of the one-hundred-and-eighty-ninth letter to Boniface, Augustine says that a written reply had already been dictated by him and delivered into the hands of the bearer; and that, prompted by this same bearer, he was induced to add this further letter, writing something that might build him up toward eternal salvation. After Erasmus, the Louvain scholars understand this to refer to Letter CLXXXV, also addressed to Boniface. Although we do not agree with them, since Augustine in the *Retractations* regards that earlier work not as a letter but as a book, and since its subject was such that nothing further could have been desired for Boniface’s edification, nevertheless the letter under discussion, Letter CLXXXIX, can conveniently be assigned to this period: the time when Augustine had learned of Boniface’s virtues by report, as appears from section 8, but perhaps had not yet become sufficiently familiar with him through personal experience or association.

**CXC.—Written shortly after the middle of 418.**

The date of the one-hundred-and-ninetieth letter to Optatus may be inferred partly from sections 22 and 23, where mention is made of the Pelagians condemned by Zosimus and of the *Tractoria* which he himself issued against them throughout the world before the middle of 418; and partly from section 1, in which Augustine indicates that, while staying at Caesarea, he resolved to write this letter at the urging of Renatus and Muresis. He went to Caesarea after the Council of Carthage, held on 1 May 418, taking the route from Carthage directly into Mauretania, as appears from Letter 193, section 1; and he was still at Caesarea on 20 September of that same year, as is shown by the Proceedings concerning Emeritus.

**CXCI–CXCIII.—Written toward the end of 418.**

Augustine wrote the three following letters—the one-hundred-and-ninety-first to Sixtus, the one-hundred-and-ninety-second to Caelestine, and the one-hundred-and-ninety-third to Mercator—in response to one and the same occasion: the departure from Africa of Albinus, an acolyte of the Roman Church. He wrote them after returning to Hippo, as he himself states at the beginning of each letter—that is, after his return from Caesarean Mauretania, according to Letter CXCIII, section 1, and therefore after 20 September, the date on which the Proceedings concerning Emeritus are recorded as having been completed at Caesarea.

**CXCIV.—Written shortly after the preceding letters.**

The one-hundred-and-ninety-fourth letter to Sixtus was sent shortly after the departure of the acolyte Albinus, through the presbyter Firmus, as appears from section 1.

**CXCV.—Probably written in 418.**

In the one-hundred-and-ninety-fifth letter Jerome seems to congratulate Augustine on the Pelagians having now been condemned throughout the whole world. When he praises Augustine for having persevered with the ardor of faith against the blowing winds, he perhaps indicates the holy Doctor’s steadfastness in attacking the Pelagian heresy, at a time when the Romans, deceived by their machinations, seemed to be lending them their support.

Moreover, in two monastic manuscripts of the Vendôme collection, we observe that another very brief letter written by Jerome is appended to this letter. That letter is numbered CXXI above, and it is joined to the present one with these three words interposed: “Now after the subscription.” Many limp on both sides, and so forth.

**CXCVI.—Written toward the end of 418.**

The one-hundred-and-ninety-sixth letter to Asellicus was written at the time when Donatianus, by ancient right, held the position of primate of the province of Byzacena, as appears from section 1; this dignity is attributed to him at the Council of Carthage in 418. Furthermore, Augustine indicates in section 7 that the Pelagians had already been condemned by Innocent and Zosimus, in these words: “Who, by the recent judgment of God, through his diligent and faithful servants, have even been deprived of Catholic communion.”

**CXCVII and CXCVIII.—Written toward the end of 418 or the beginning of 419.**

**CXCIX.—Written in 419.**

From the three letters that immediately follow, the one-hundred-and-ninety-ninth, addressed to Hesychius, is understood from section 20 to have been sent in the year of Christ 419. Consequently, the one-hundred-and-ninety-seventh and one-hundred-and-ninety-eighth letters, which had been written somewhat earlier, appear to belong to the end of 418 or the beginning of 419. This conjecture is supported by the fact that in Letter CXCVIII, section 5, Hesychius says that signs had been seen in the heavens at that time. He was doubtless referring to events which historians report as having occurred in 418; moved by those signs, he took the opportunity to consult Augustine concerning the last day of the world.

**CC.—Written toward the end of 418 or the beginning of 419.**

The two-hundredth letter to the comes Valerius was sent together with Book One *On Marriage*, dedicated to him. We shall show in its proper place that this book was composed toward the end of 418 or the beginning of 419. Augustine himself says in Book One addressed to Boniface, chapter 5, that he published this work after the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius. He then adds immediately:

> I have thought it necessary to say this because he says that my words were received by his enemies out of hatred for the truth. Let no one therefore suppose that, on account of this book of mine, the enemies of Christ’s grace were condemned as new heretics.

This provides grounds for concluding that the same book appeared not long after the condemnation of those heretics.

**CCI.—Written in 419, in June.**

The two-hundred-and-first letter, issued by the Emperors Honorius and Theodosius to Aurelius and separately to Augustine in identical terms, bears an indication of the day and the consuls.

**CCII.—Apparently written toward the end of 419.**

Baronius considers the two-hundred-and-second letter, which is the last of all the letters written by Jerome, and assigns it to the year 420, in which Jerome’s death occurred according to Prosper’s *Chronicle*. Certainly the death, or “falling asleep,” of the virgin Eustochium, whose grief Jerome here testifies to have deeply overwhelmed him, cannot be placed much before the aforesaid year 420, since Palladius, writing his *Lausiac History* in 419 or 420, believes that she was still alive in chapter 125.

As for the bearer of the letter, the presbyter Innocentius, he had been sent in 419 by the African Fathers to Cyril to investigate the canons of Nicaea. From there he returned to Africa in the same year, before 26 November, as is clear from the title of chapter 137 of the *Code of the Canons of the African Church*. On that occasion, having undoubtedly seen Jerome, he received the letter under discussion for delivery—not in the following year. For at the beginning of the letter, when Jerome excuses Innocentius for not having carried his letter to Augustine the previous year, as though he would never return to Africa, he indicates Innocentius’s first and second journeys in the East. The first of these, if Innocentius was uncertain about his return to Africa, cannot be the same journey that he undertook in 419 on the authority of the African synod. Nor does Baronius rightly infer from Jerome’s words that the letter was sent in the year following Innocentius’s embassy.

**CCIII.—Probably written around 420.**

The two-hundred-and-third letter to Largus was written at a time when he, having formerly experienced prosperity, was now living amid adversity. It may be assigned approximately to the year 420, since this Largus, who is addressed as “illustrious and most distinguished lord” and honored with the title “Your Excellency,” is reasonably believed to be the same man who governed Africa as proconsul in the years 415, 418, and 419.

**CCIV.—Written around this time.**

It is clear from sections 4 and 9 that the two-hundred-and-fourth letter to Dulcitius, tribune and executor of the imperial commands against the Donatists, was sent shortly before the books against Gaudentius. Augustine issued this work, his final work against the Donatists, around the year 420.

**CCV.—Probably written toward 420.**

There is scarcely room for doubt that the two-hundred-and-fifth letter to Consentius was written to the same man as the book *Against Lying*, and at approximately the same time. The man to whom that book, composed around the year 420—as will be shown elsewhere—is dedicated lived among the Priscillianists, who were troubling Spain at that time, and had sent Augustine much material to read, as is stated at the beginning of the same book. Augustine was dealing with the use of lying to expose their heresy, which they habitually concealed even by means of perjury.

In this letter Augustine says that a letter had been sent to him by Consentius, together with an additional sheet containing the questions to which he is now replying. By the term “letter” he seems to mean more extensive writings, to which he later replied in the book *Against Lying*, where he also excuses the delay in his responses.

Furthermore, Augustine’s description here fits well with a man settled in Spain and considering fleeing from there to Africa. In chapter 1, section 1, Augustine says that he would indeed like to see Consentius, but amid circumstances in which human affairs were quieter and more peaceful, so that the meeting might be an act of honorable affection rather than an oppressive necessity.

In chapter 4, section 18, he mentions a book written by himself *On Faith and Works*, a book dating from 413.

**CCVI.—Written around this time.**

The two-hundred-and-sixth letter is addressed to that same Valerius, the comes to whom Book One *On Marriage* was sent around the beginning of 419. This letter too seems to belong to approximately the same period, since Augustine writes to him as though he had already been received into his friendship and intimacy.

**CCVII.—Written in 421 or shortly afterward.**

The two-hundred-and-seventh letter to Claudius was sent together with the four books against Julian. These books were published around the year 421, and not earlier, since in Book One, chapter 7, Augustine speaks of Jerome as though he were already dead; Jerome died on 30 September 420.

**CCVIII.—Probably written toward 423.**

If the two-hundred-and-eighth letter, addressed to Felicia, is compared with Letter CCIX to Caelestine, one is led to think that the disturbances which troubled that virgin, after she had been converted from the Donatist schism to the unity of the Church, may be attributed to the bishop Antonius. Antonius had charge of the people of Fussala, who had returned from the Donatists to Catholic communion, but he governed that Church so perversely through his depraved conduct that he was deprived of office by the judgment of the bishops. If our conjecture is not mistaken, this letter belongs approximately to the year 423.

**CCIX.—Probably written at the beginning of 423.**

The two-hundred-and-ninth letter to Caelestine is understood from section 1 to have been sent at the beginning of his pontificate, where Augustine congratulates the pope on his election having been carried out without any division among the Roman people.

Caelestine succeeded Boniface immediately. Baronius assigns Boniface’s death to 423, on the eighth day before the Kalends of November—that is, 25 October—following the authority of Anastasius. He assigns the year, however, on no other authority than the fact that Prosper and Marcellinus in their *Chronicles* record the accession of his successor in that same year. Yet it could have happened that, although Boniface died toward the end of 422, Caelestine was not installed until 423.

Indeed, in those same *Chronicles* the beginning of Caelestine’s pontificate is recorded before the death of the Emperor Honorius, which occurred in August 423. Moreover, both ancient and modern writers, Latin and Greek alike, agree in assigning Boniface a pontificate of three years and several months, with the exception of Nicephorus, whose authority is not so great, and some editions of Prosper, in which four years are attributed to Pope Boniface. These accounts can easily be reconciled with the others if the fourth year is understood as incomplete.

In a Corbie manuscript, written eleven hundred years ago and ending with Vigilius, there is a list of the Roman pontiffs. It assigns to Caelestine nine years, ten months, and six days, but to Boniface only three years, eight months, and six days. Boniface was elevated to the pontificate on 29 December 418. His death, and the election of his successor Caelestine, may therefore be assigned to the end of 422. The events may have been transferred in the *Chronicles* to the following year because they occurred only a few days before its beginning.

**CCX.—Probably written around this time.**

There is a substantial suspicion that the two-hundred-and-tenth letter to Felicitas and Rusticus was written on the occasion of a disturbance that had arisen within a community of holy women. To suppress it, Augustine sent the following letter to the women religious.

**CCXI.—Written around this time.**

The two-hundred-and-eleventh letter, addressed to the women religious, is later than the Conference at Carthage and the laws subsequently promulgated against the schismatics, since at that time the Church was especially rejoicing in the Donatists’ return to unity, as appears from section 4.

Nor was it written much before 424. Augustine’s sister, who had been superior of the same monastery, had not recently died, as appears from section 4. Possidius, however, says in chapter 26 that she “lived for a long time, serving God as a widow and as superior of the handmaids of God until the day of her death.”

**CCXII.—Written around 423.**

Toward the end of the two-hundred-and-twelfth letter, Augustine speaks to Quintilianus concerning the relics of the martyr Stephen, which, according to the *Chronicle* of Marcellinus, were first brought into the West in 416 by Orosius on his return from Jerusalem. He writes:

> Your Holiness, as we have done, is not unaware how appropriately you ought to honor them.

In our opinion, he indicates here that a memorial of the holy martyr had been established at Hippo.

Yet in Book 22, chapter 8, of *The City of God*, which Augustine was engaged in writing toward the end of 426, these words are found:

> It is not yet two years since this memorial began to exist at Hippo-Regius.

We therefore judge that this letter was written approximately in 425.

**CCXIII.—Written on 26 September 426.**

[Col. 0046]

The ecclesiastical proceedings concerning the designation of Heraclius as Augustine’s successor, which are presented here in place of the two-hundred-and-thirteenth letter, bear an indication of the day and the consuls.

**CCXIV, CCXV.—Written around Easter 426 or 427.**

The two-hundred-and-fourteenth and two-hundred-and-fifteenth letters, addressed to Valentinus, abbot of the monastery at Hadrumetum, are understood from their opening words to have been written at the same time: the former shortly before Easter, the latter shortly after that feast. They do not, however, belong to the year 418, as Baronius thought.

The longer letter to Sixtus, which is discussed in these two letters and whose faulty interpretation had given rise to certain disputes among the monks of Hadrumetum, was not dictated before the end of that same year 418, but in 426 or 427. The book *On Grace and Free Will*, with which these letters were sent together, as is clear from Letter CCXV, section 2, can scarcely be assigned to a later date, since it is listed in the *Retractations*, composed around 427; nor can it be assigned to an earlier date, since in the same *Retractations* it occupies, together with the book *On Rebuke and Grace*, the final position among the works addressed to these same monks.

**CCXVI.—Written shortly after the two preceding letters.**

In the preceding letters Augustine had asked that Florus, who was said to have been the author of the disturbance, should come to him. Since Florus went to Augustine very willingly and without any hesitation, Valentinus sent the two-hundred-and-sixteenth letter in reply, as appears from section 6.

**CCXVII.—Written around the same time.**

Regarding the two-hundred-and-seventeenth letter to Vitalis, one thing is certain: it appeared after the Pelagian heresy had already been condemned. A second point is highly probable: it was later than Letters CCXIV and CCXV, in which, among the writings issued against the Pelagians and especially useful for instructing the monks of Hadrumetum, it is not mentioned.

For after Augustine had stated at length in *On Grace and Free Will*, chapter 7 and the following chapters, that the beginning of good will and faith itself proceeds from God’s gift, Vitalis—unless we conjecture incorrectly—was moved to begin objecting and to respond with testimonies drawn from Philippians 2 and Psalm 36, which Augustine had employed in the same book, chapter 16. This is clear from the present letter, sections 1 and 4.

Here Augustine presses and explains against Vitalis the verse from Psalm 36, which in the book *On Free Will* he had merely indicated. He also refutes more thoroughly the argument drawn from the Church’s prayers, which he had touched upon only very briefly in chapter 14 of that work. As for the many other testimonies and arguments pertaining equally to the same issue, since they had been sufficiently and more than sufficiently explained there, it is not surprising that he did not undertake to treat them again here.

**CCXVIII.—Probably written at the same time.**

At this point we place the letter to Palatinus, in which Augustine urges him not to place his hope of living well in his own powers. For, he says in section 3, the very Lord’s Prayer admonishes him that he needs the help of his Lord. Then he says:

> Ask him that it may be brought to perfection by whom it was granted that it should begin.

He then adduces testimonies from Philippians 2 and Psalm 36, as in the preceding letter to Vitalis. These circumstances may suggest that both letters belong to the same period.

**CCXIX.—Written in 426 or 427.**

For the date of the two-hundred-and-nineteenth letter, addressed by Augustine and three other African bishops to the Gallic bishops Proculus and Cylinnius on the occasion of Leporius, consult the note to this letter.

**CCXX.—Written around the end of 427.**

The two-hundred-and-twentieth letter to Boniface was written during the war waged against him as a rebel against the Empire. Augustine therefore indicates at the beginning that he had never been able to find a more trustworthy bearer of his letters than Peter. In section 2 he says that letters could never have been sent to Boniface during his dangers because of the danger to the bearer:

> And lest my letter should reach those to whom I did not wish it to come.

This war took place during the consulship of Hierius and Ardaburius, that is, in 427. According to Prosper’s *Chronicle*, it was caused by the jealousy of Felix, the master of the soldiers; according to Paul the Deacon in *Miscellaneous History*, Book 44, by the treachery of the comes Aetius, who viewed with hostility the fact that Boniface possessed authority over western Libya and had increased his power in Africa.

Thus Augustine says to Boniface in section 5:

> You say, indeed, that you have a just cause, of which I am not the judge, and so forth.

And he adds:

> You ought to have accepted what was offered, so that you might use it for piety; but you ought not to seek what was denied or assigned elsewhere in such a way that, on account of it, you would be brought into this necessity.

This letter should not be assigned much later than the end of 427, since Augustine makes no complaint about the incursion of the Vandals, who, summoned by Boniface for assistance, entered Africa in May 428.

**CCXXI–CCXXIV.—Written in 427 and 428.**

The two letters of Quodvultdeus and Augustine’s replies to them belong to the same period and concern the same subject, except that the former probably belong to 427 and the latter to 428. Certainly, in Letter CCXXIV, Augustine testifies that the two books of the *Retractations*, which he published in 427 or, at the latest, in 428, had already been completed.

**CCXXV.—Written in 428 or 429.**

Prosper’s letter, numbered here as the two-hundred-and-twenty-fifth, was written at the time when Hilary presided over the Church of Arles, as appears from section 9. Hilary was appointed in place of Honoratus, who died eight or nine days before the holy feast of the Epiphany, in 428 or 429, as is clear from the note to the same letter.

**CCXXVI.—Written at the same time.**

The two-hundred-and-twenty-sixth letter, which belongs to Hilary the layman, was sent together with the preceding letter, as Hilary himself testifies in section 10.
