Augustine therefore replied to Prosper and Hilary together, dedicating to both of them the book *On the Predestination of the Saints*.

**CCXXVII.—Written after Easter, probably in 428 or 429.**

No one will doubt that the two-hundred-and-twenty-seventh letter to the elder Alypius should be assigned approximately to the year 429—unless someone thinks that another Alypius is intended here, distinct from Alypius, bishop of Thagaste, or that the title “elder” does not signify a primate. Augustine had not yet bestowed this title on Bishop Alypius in Letter CCXXIV, addressed to Quodvultdeus in 428; there he calls him simply “brother.”

**CCXXVIII.—Written in 428 or 429.**

The two-hundred-and-twenty-eighth letter to Honoratus, bishop of Thiava, was written when the Vandals were threatening as enemies, according to Possidius, chapter 30.

**CCXXIX–CCXXXI.—Written toward the end of Augustine’s life, probably in 429.**

Augustine wrote the two-hundred-and-twenty-ninth letter to the comes Darius in the final period of his old age, as appears from section 1. Darius had come to Africa to arrange peace, not to seek it through bloodshed, but to prevent anyone’s blood from being sought, having been sent on an embassy, as appears from section 2. He also came to bring a remedy and an end to evils that had increased to a certain summit of calamity, as Darius himself writes in Letter CCXXX, section 3.

Indicating what progress he had made in this undertaking, Augustine says:

> If we have not extinguished the wars, at least we have postponed them.

Apart from the war between Boniface and the Vandals, nothing else presents itself to which these words could refer at the end of Augustine’s life, or at least after the year 421; and this embassy of Darius certainly did not precede that year. For the *Enchiridion on Faith, Hope, and Charity*, a short work not published before the year just mentioned, was sent to Darius at this time to be read, together with Letter CCXXXI, section 5.

Procopius in Book One of *The Vandalic War* actually reports that some of Boniface’s friends, sailing to Carthage, met him at the command of Placidia. When Aetius’ treachery against Boniface was discovered, they swore that Placidia would be just toward Boniface if they could persuade him to avert the destruction of Roman affairs in Africa. Boniface then withdrew from the Vandals, who besieged Hippo-Regius, where he had taken refuge after being defeated in battle.

Possidius too writes of this siege of Hippo-Regius, with Boniface inside the city, adding in chapter 28 that Saint Augustine fell ill with fever in the third month of the siege and began to suffer his final illness.

**LETTERS OF THE FOURTH CLASS, whose dates are less certain**

There remain thirty-nine letters, included in the fourth class, for which it has not been possible to establish a definite and proper chronological position. It is easy enough to understand that they were all written when Augustine was already a bishop; but only a few of them bear any more precise indication of their date.

Thus there is a suspicion that the laws of Honorius against idols, enacted in 399 or alternatively in 408, are referred to in Letter CCXXXII to the people of Madaura, section 3, in these words:

> You certainly see the temples of the images partly demolished, partly closed, partly converted to other uses; and the images themselves either broken to pieces or burned, and so forth; and the very powers of this age . . . have turned their attacks and laws . . . against those same images.

The letters addressed to Pascentius, on the other hand, appear to have been written when Augustine was not yet elderly, since in Letter CCXXXVIII, section 1, he declares himself inferior to Pascentius in age and rank. Yet they belong to a time when the holy Doctor had already become highly renowned, as is apparent from the same letter, section 8.

Finally, Letter CCL to Auxilius seems to belong to the final years of Augustine’s life. There, concerning the sentence he had pronounced against Classicianus, he says in section 2:

> Here I am, an old man prepared to learn from a young man, and a bishop of so many years from a colleague who is not yet a year old.

The same applies to Letter CCLIX to Cornelius and Letter CCLXIX to Nobilius, in which Augustine indicates that he was living at a more advanced age.

We have therefore thought it appropriate to arrange these and many other letters whose dates are much less certain according to their subject matter. First come those concerning the enemies of the Christian faith—the pagans, Manichaeans, Priscillianists, and Arians—and finally those that contribute to the proper formation of morals, followed by several personal letters of the holy Doctor.

[Col. 0047]

**[NOTE.]**

Anyone who gives even a little consideration to the matter can see from this how much labor and deliberation we have devoted to arranging Augustine’s letters properly, and how much care we have taken to lighten, as far as possible, the work of students.

We established this order sometimes on firm grounds, or at least on grounds that were as highly probable as possible; but at other times on conjectures, or on the mutual connection and sequence of the letters among themselves, and at still other times on the authority of learned men who have written on the subject. We judged that arguments of this kind carry great weight in matters where certain and established evidence is lacking.

It is not our intention to advertise our own work here. Indeed, conscious of our own ignorance, we cannot deny that we have fallen into not a few errors deserving the criticism of learned men. When benevolent readers point these out, we shall gladly acknowledge them and strive to correct them as quickly as possible.

Nevertheless, we do not hesitate to promise, without any charge of boasting, that this new order established by us, whatever its ultimate merit, is far more useful than the arrangement previously accepted by custom. Nor do we fear that the inconvenience which some people opposed to this future alteration will bring with it will not be compensated by a substantial benefit and increase to scholarship.

May God grant that the matter turn out according to our wishes, and may fair-minded readers judge this labor of ours with fairness and goodwill.

**The Benedictine Fathers**

[Col. 0049]

After the completed edition of the Benedictine Fathers, the Reverend Godefridus Besselius, abbot of the monastery of Gottweig in Germany, discovered two letters of Augustine in manuscript codices. He published them at Vienna in 1732, furnishing them with a preface; Jacobus Martin, a Maurist, published them at Paris in 1734 with a new preface, warnings, and annotations.

The discovery is certainly of considerable importance. But so that the order of the earlier editions should not be disturbed, instead of assigning a special number to either letter, we prefixed the word “Bis” to the number under which it appears, as may be seen after Letters CXXXIV and CCII.

**M.**

[Col. 0049]

# PREFACE OF THE MOST REVEREND GODEFRIDUS BESSELIUS, ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF GOTTWEIG, PREFIXED TO THE VIENNA EDITION

## To the Learned Reader

### Concerning the Letters Mentioned Above

**I.** That human souls are created by God out of nothing and infused individually into individual human beings is today a most certain opinion and a Catholic truth, concerning which no orthodox person may safely entertain doubt.

At the beginning of the fifth century, however, not all teachers of the Catholic Church held the same view on this important question. This is especially clear from several works of the great Aurelius Augustine, which he composed for different people on this controversy.

The most celebrated of these are the four books *On the Soul and Its Origin*, written toward the end of the year 419. The first is addressed to the monk Renatus, the second to the presbyter Peter, and the remaining two to Vincentius Victor, who had given Augustine the occasion and opportunity to write so many little works.

We shall present the matter in Augustine’s own words. In Book Two of the *Retractations*, chapter 56, he writes:

> At that time a certain Vincentius Victor, in Caesarean Mauretania, found with a certain Spanish presbyter named Peter one of my little works, in which I had confessed at a certain point that I did not know whether the souls of individual human beings are propagated from that one soul of the first man and thereafter from their parents, or whether, as was the case with that one man, individual souls are given individually to individual human beings without any propagation. Nevertheless, I did know that the soul is not a body but a spirit.
>
> Against these statements of mine he wrote two books to the same Peter, which the monk Renatus sent to me from Caesarea. After reading them, I replied with four books: one to the monk Renatus and two to Victor himself. To Peter, although it has the length of a book, it is nevertheless a letter, which I did not wish to separate from the other three.
>
> In all of these works, in which many necessary matters are discussed, I defended my hesitation concerning the origin of the souls given to individual human beings, and I exposed the many errors and depraved presumptions of his argument.

This, then, is what Augustine says about his four books *On the Soul and Its Origin*.

**II.** Augustine’s investigation, however, did not remain confined to these books, which were published and circulated only later. He also sent to the most learned Jerome a substantial book *On the Origin of the Human Soul*. In it, after reviewing various opinions concerning the origin of the soul, Augustine wishes to be instructed which opinion ought chiefly to be followed and by what reasoning the view could be defended against the impious doctrine of the Pelagians—the view which Jerome had indicated in one of his letters to be his own, namely, that individual souls are newly made for those who are born.

Our most learned Benedictine Fathers of the Congregation of Saint Maur judge that this book was written in the spring of 415, in their new, exceptionally polished and accurate edition of the works of Saint Augustine, volume II, Letter 166.

Augustine himself discusses this book in Book Two of the *Retractations*, chapter 45:

> I also wrote two books to Jerome the presbyter, residing at Bethlehem: one *On the Origin of the Human Soul*, the other *On the Sentence of the Apostle James*, where he says, “Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all of it” (James 2:10). In both I consulted him.
>
> In the former, however, I did not solve the question that I had proposed; in the latter, I did not remain silent about what seemed to me to be its solution, but I consulted him as to whether he too approved of it.

Augustine then adds what Jerome replied to this consultation and what followed:

[Col. 0050]

> The most modest Doctor replied, praising my consultation, but saying that he did not have leisure to answer it.

Augustine continues:

> While he was still alive, I did not wish to publish these books, lest he should perhaps answer at some time and they should be published together with his answer. After his death, however, I published the former so that whoever reads it may be warned either not to ask at all how the soul is given to those who are born, or, at any rate, to accept concerning this most obscure matter a solution to the question that is not contrary to the clearest truths which the Catholic faith knows concerning original sin: namely, that infants are without doubt condemned unless they are regenerated in Christ. I published the latter so that the solution to the question treated there—which is the one that seemed satisfactory to us—might also become known.

**III.** When the bishop Optatus had written to the aforementioned Renatus at Caesarea in Mauretania concerning this same delicate and thorny subject, and had vigorously defended the creation of individual souls, Saint Augustine, at the request of Renatus and a certain Muresis, sent Optatus a substantial letter around the middle of 418.

In his customary acute and lucid manner, Augustine demonstrated to Optatus what concerning the origin of the soul was certain and established, what could rightly be called into question, and what effort was required in this controversy: above all, that the faith should remain intact, by which the Catholic Church believes that no human being is born from Adam without being bound by the chain of condemnation, and that no one is freed from it except by being reborn through Christ.

He further indicates to Optatus that he had written to Jerome a substantial book on this question:

> Consulting him, he says, and asking him first to teach me, and then to send me those whom I may teach.

Augustine continues:

> This book of mine may be read by me as belonging not to a teacher but to an investigator, and rather to one who desires to learn. It ought not, however, to be sent anywhere or given to anyone outside, except when, with the Lord’s help, I have received his written reply. I shall defend most readily and gladly what he thinks, if he is able to teach me how souls do not come from Adam and yet find in him a just share of condemnation, unless they attain remission of sins by being reborn.
>
> Far be it from us to believe either that the souls of infants receive a false cleansing from sins in the bath of regeneration, or that God—or any nature that God did not create—is the author of that defilement from which they are cleansed.
>
> Until he replies, or until I myself, if God wills, learn in some way whether, if the soul derives no sinful origin from that source, there is some other cause for its incurring original sin, which must exist in all infants—and into which neither God forces it while innocent, since he is not the author of sin, nor any evil nature, since no such nature exists—I dare to preach nothing of the kind.

Augustine concludes his letter with these words:

> As I have been able, I have replied to the letters of Your Holiness—not indeed to those addressed to me, but nevertheless to those of our dearest friends—not with the learning you desired, but with concerned affection, and so forth.

### IV

After Optatus had received this from Augustine, he allowed a two-year interval and did not wish to be more troublesome to Augustine, who was overwhelmed by other extremely weighty writings. But when, within that period, he had no doubt that Jerome’s reply to Augustine’s inquiry concerning the origin of the soul had arrived, and indeed believed that Augustine had by then reached the point at which he could give a definite judgment on the disputed question, he finally wrote a second letter to him. That letter of Optatus has indeed perished, but its subject can readily be learned from Augustine’s own reply. From this, therefore, it is clear, first, that Optatus was concerned not only with that book of inquiry and with Jerome’s reply to it; it is also evident that he most eagerly desired to discover the answer to the matter which Augustine had asked Jerome to resolve.

Second, Optatus had complained bitterly to Augustine about some number of old men and men trained by learned priests, whom he had been unable to recall to the understanding and affirmation of his own modest position, which was entirely filled with truth—that is, the opinion concerning the creation of individual souls. He had therefore feared, as a young and inexperienced teacher, that he might corrupt the traditions of so many and such great bishops, and had been afraid to turn people toward a better position because of the injury this might do to the departed.

Third, Optatus and his followers had placed their principal “Achilles” in the claim that, unless individual human souls were created, God could not be said to have made, to be making, or to be going to make human beings, nor could anything exist in heaven or on earth that had not been and was not established by him as its author. From this it followed, they said, that the defenders of transmission and propagation denied that our souls were God’s work.

Fourth, the opinion that souls are propagated through transmission had appeared to Optatus to be a new invention and an unheard-of doctrine.

Finally, Optatus had expressly demanded and insisted that Augustine define one of two alternatives: whether the remaining souls are made from that one human being, as bodies are through propagation, or whether, without propagation, they are made individually by the Creator, as that one soul—namely, Adam’s—was.

These were the principal points of Optatus’s letter to Augustine. To them Augustine here replied, as will be clear below, with the greatest modesty, judgment, and learning.

### V

The substance of Augustine’s letter—which we rightly call the second letter to Optatus—is this: he openly and humbly confesses his ignorance concerning the origin of the soul, and does not think that anything certain can be established in this controversy, whatever may have seemed so to Optatus and others, unless definite, clear, and fraud-proof testimonies from the divine Scriptures are brought forward. Those who deny transmission have thus far by no means accomplished this.

As for his own inquiry, he had still received no reply from Jerome, and he did not dare to publish his book of inquiry without it:

> “Otherwise,” he says, “the man who will perhaps answer me, as I desire, may justly be angry that my question, elaborated in a most laborious discussion, should be circulated among people and brought to their knowledge without his answer, which ought not yet to be despaired of; and he may judge that I have done this more boastfully than usefully, as though I had been able to ask what he had not been able to unravel, when perhaps he can do so and we ought to await him while he does it.”

At the end of the letter he warns Optatus, as earnestly as he can, to avoid the Pelagian heresy with the greatest caution whenever he is either considering or already discussing the origin of souls. He must take care lest the belief secretly steal upon him that absolutely no soul, except that of the one Mediator, draws original sin from Adam—original sin to which it is bound by generation and from which it is released by regeneration.

### VI

All the writings of St. Augustine on the origin of the soul reviewed thus far have already appeared publicly in print, except only two letters, which we learn from St. Fulgentius that Augustine wrote to Bishop Optatus in addition to the first letter already published. Fulgentius says in book 3, chapter 18, of *On the Truth of Predestination and Grace*:

> “In the three letters which he composed to Bishop Optatus on this question, Augustine’s discussion shines forth as no less abundant than profound, and is all the more praiseworthy because it is moderated with suitable restraint.”

Since, therefore, last summer, for the better and more solid instruction of our younger religious in literary matters and in the understanding of ancient manuscripts, we had summoned to our monastery as an assistant the Reverend Father Bernard Pez, a man already highly deserving of esteem on several grounds in literary affairs and renowned for so many learned works, we examined all the manuscripts of our library with the greatest care. Among many other things which, with God’s favor granting us life, we shall in due time communicate to the learned world, this second letter to the same Optatus was fortunately drawn out of the darkness like a treasure hidden in a field. It had until now escaped all learned and scholarly men, and perhaps exists only—unless we are greatly mistaken—in a single manuscript of our Gottweig library.

It is written on parchment of at least the twelfth century, in folio, as they say, and is now marked, after the restoration of our library, with the letter G. N. 10. From it we brought forth this illustrious relic and, as we hope, judged that it should be published for the benefit of the whole Church and the republic of letters.

### VII

In the same manuscript, after the second letter to Optatus, there remains another equally unpublished letter of the same Augustine, addressed to Peter and Abraham. The Bishop of Hippo calls them his most beloved lords and holy sons, and says that he had heard that they had ordered their lives in such a way that, while serving God, they had time to read his writings against the Pelagians and the pagans.

From this we understand that Peter and Abraham either practiced the monastic life or, at any rate, after abandoning the tumult of the world, lived in the countryside—as that age commonly did—in a private life devoted to more sacred pursuits.

After they had asked Augustine a number of questions, the most holy Doctor replied that he had already answered all, or nearly all, of them in several of his shorter works. The principal question of Peter and Abraham, as appears from Augustine’s reply, was whether infants who, by living wickedly, had added nothing to original sin would be condemned by God if they died before receiving Baptism. St. Augustine unequivocally and consistently affirms this both in this letter and elsewhere.

> “For when infants are baptized,” he says, “it is not said in vain but truly enacted that they are to be counted among believers; hence they are also called a new offspring by the mouth of all Christians. Therefore, if they do not believe, they will be condemned. And since by living wickedly they themselves have added nothing to original sin, it may be said, on account of their merit, that in that condemnation the punishment is the least, though not nothing.”

The great man then teaches that whatever is begotten among human beings through concupiscence must be born again.

> “For,” he says, “although one is born of parents who have been regenerated, carnal generation cannot provide this child with what spiritual regeneration provided for them. Thus, not only from the seed of a wild olive but also from the seed of an olive, nothing is born except a wild olive, although the olive is not a wild olive.”

Finally, he explains how one ought to deal with pagans who by no means acknowledge the authority of the divine Scriptures, so that they may be led rightly and successfully to the Christian faith. He also discusses at greater length his famous work *On the City of God*, whose fourteenth book, he says, will, if the Lord wills, contain the solutions to all the questions they had proposed in their letter.

From this it is established that Augustine wrote this letter before the year 420, since he published the fourteenth book of *On the City of God* in that same year. But on these matters see more in the Preface to volume VII of the Benedictine edition of the works of St. Augustine.

For us, enough has now been said about this pair of Augustine’s letters, unpublished until now; at last we must take our hand from the table, lest, as they say, the preface become longer than the subject. We note only that this later letter of St. Augustine is entitled in our Gottweig manuscript *On the Nature and Origin of the Soul*, whereas it ought more correctly to have been entitled *On the Punishments of Infants Who Die without Baptism*. We have therefore thought that this title should be retained at the head of our edition, although we are by no means unaware how closely these two topics are connected in Augustine’s present controversy. But this is not important enough to detain the learned reader, who is eager for Augustine’s letters, any longer.

[Col. 0053]

## PREFACE OF THE REVEREND JACOB MARTIN TO THE SAME LETTERS

How greatly the labors undertaken through wakeful days and nights, and the work spent in unfolding old archival documents and searching through the innermost recesses of chests, contribute to the benefit of the Church and of the republic of letters is demonstrated by these two letters of St. Augustine, newly discovered. Through their assistance alone, the treasure that we are today making public in France has been dug out for us.

It should be considered all the more precious because, from the time when that celebrated Benedictine edition of Augustine’s works appeared in Paris, we had no hope of finding other writings of the Doctor of Africa—or rather, of the Christian world—than those that had then been committed to print. Indeed, the most learned editors labored indefatigably both to restore Augustine to his former purity through the abundance of manuscript codices obtained from everywhere, or at least examined in their own places—Gallican, Vatican, Belgian, English, and others—and to bring to light any unpublished works of that distinguished bishop that might be found.

Since they had devoted to this undertaking an effort scarcely capable of being surpassed, nothing appeared to us to offer hope of repairing the loss of those writings which we know were composed by our Doctor but which, through the hostility of time or the negligence of library officials, have not come down to us.

But behold—may it be fortunate, propitious, and blessed—the Most Reverend Lord Godefridus Bessel, abbot of the monastery of Gottweig, while preparing immortal glory for himself not only by restoring buildings completely consumed by fire but also by properly educating his younger monks alike in learning and in regular discipline, opportunely summoned Bernard Pez, the most celebrated monk in Germany, to him, so that he might relieve and lessen for his pupils the weariness that very frequently arises when reading the characters of ancient parchments.

Bernard Pez, however, is a man to whom every kind of literature and script is accessible, and who knows very well how to judge writings not from opinion but from truth. As soon as he came upon a codex of approximately the thirteenth century containing these two letters, he immediately recognized the value of the hidden pearls and advised the most learned Abbot to communicate them shortly to the Church. This was certainly done promptly, for in the previous year [Note: [Col. 0053] 1732.] both letters were committed to print at Vienna, adorned with an elaborate preface and various magnificent engravings.

But this speed was of little benefit to our countrymen. Scarcely one or two copies of Augustine’s letters were transported and carried from Germany to us. We therefore took the occasion and resolved to submit them to the press again. And, so that France might not complain that she had for a time been deprived and dispossessed of them—or rather, so that she might think that matters had been arranged for her in the best possible way—we provided that our Paris edition should be more correct, more elegant, and more ample, and that its publication should uphold the reputation of the other Parisian editions that consecrate their homeland, editions which foreign nations eagerly seek to obtain or imitate and compete to acquire.

For this reason our attention and diligence were aroused for a long time and with great effort; the letters themselves were read and examined again and again; and even the writing, its traces, and its strokes were very frequently copied by us and, so to speak, boiled down and reboiled.

1. So that we might ascertain and establish that these works had proceeded not from a spurious and adulterine workshop but from Augustine’s genuine study. In this matter all our anxiety was soon cast aside, and we were filled with the greatest joy, since we found that both letters were recorded in the *Index* of Possidius and that the letter to Optatus was also mentioned and highly approved by St. Fulgentius.

2. So that we might not correct the readings corrupted and impaired by the antiquary’s haste, negligence, carelessness, or incompetence—for we considered it wrong even slightly to alter the text of the Gottweig manuscript—but might undertake, through meditation and the exercise of our judgment, to seek genuine readings from elsewhere and indicate them at the foot of the page, so that the letters could proceed whole and without stumbling.

3. So that each letter might be furnished with its own preliminary notice, and a summary of each letter might be affixed at the beginning; shorter notes, serving as summaries of complete sections, were also to be arranged opposite them.

4. So that we might compare very many passages of these letters with other similar passages collected here and there, in order that anyone might easily investigate the mind of the holy Bishop.

5. So that, for the sake of clarity, we might divide these letters into chapters and the chapters into various sections, as the meaning and subject matter required, and distribute the numerical designations of the chapters and sections in order through the margins.

6. So that we might illustrate and clarify whatever difficult matter arose during reading through critical, historical, and chronological observations; and even, wherever the Masters had erred in matters relevant to our subject, warn the reader and correct those errors to the best of our ability.

7. Finally, so that we might arrange and establish everything, both collectively and individually, in such a way that these two letters might appear to have come from that polished and famous Benedictine workshop. We always kept it before our eyes and directed and completed our work according to its standard.

Whether the undertaking we have assumed has succeeded according to our intention, let the learned decide; and if anything has been done wrongly, let them pardon us. But if they find anything good and if, henceforth, some ornament or improvement accrues to the collection of St. Augustine’s works from our labor, let them attribute it all either to the most holy Bishop, who supplied the subject of our exercises, or rather to God Almighty, from whom comes every good gift and every perfect gift (James 1:17).

How highly the Gottweig manuscript should be valued is apparent not only from the two letters that it alone supplies, but also from four excellent variant readings, through which the genuine text of a fragment of Jerome’s seventy-eighth letter is restored. For when all these readings are examined according to the rules of careful criticism, they must be accepted with both hands. They therefore testify both to the praise deserved by the copyist’s hand and skill and to the accuracy of the ancient codex that the copyist himself used.

The occasional slips that appear do not contradict our judgment. Such errors, as everyone highly skilled knows, more often occur by chance than through intention or negligence.

We shall not use a more extended discourse here to win goodwill and favor for Augustine’s letters. Both are sufficiently and abundantly commended by the dignity of their subject, their manner of treating the issues, the abundance of their recondite learning, and the name of the most distinguished Writer. Everywhere one will find either something to learn, or how to learn it, or how to become a better person.

Moreover, if fragments of ordinary authors are sought with such zeal by land and sea, gathered with such labor, and acquired and transported at such expense, with how much greater ardor, spirit, and willingness ought these two letters—and these complete letters—to be embraced, written by that exceptional Shepherd whose name itself is so many times a commendation!

We wish to warn the reader of only one thing: we have never departed by a hair’s breadth from the Gottweig manuscript, except with regard to the order in which Augustine’s letters are presented there. In that manuscript the first occupies the second place, and conversely the second occupies the first. We, however, paying particular attention to the time at which they were composed, have restored to each its proper place.

Perhaps someone will ask what sort of monastery it is from whose archive Augustine’s letters have emerged for the perpetual glory of the Christian republic. I shall transcribe word for word what I received three months ago on this subject from the distinguished man Bernard Pez, praised above.

The monastery of Gottweig is by far the largest and most celebrated in Germany. It is situated on the right bank of the Danube, about six miles above Vienna, on a very high but most pleasant mountain. See Mabillon’s *Annals*, century XI, where it is recorded that the monastery was founded and richly endowed by St. Altmann, bishop of Passau.

When it had been reduced to ashes around the seventeenth year of this century, it was restored so successfully by the Most Reverend Lord Godefridus Bessel, who now presides with the highest praise for the restored regular discipline and the revived reputation of learning and scholarship, that no monastery of our Order in Europe yields to it anything in splendor, size, or elegance.

In German it is called Gottweig, in the Middle Ages Gottwic, or the monastery of St. Mary at Gottwic, and sometimes Kottwic. Thus the manuscripts in the Gottweig library commonly read. The aforementioned Abbot has enriched this library with good literature to such an extent that I know of no monastic library in Germany worthy of comparison with it.

You will shortly learn more about this place from volume II of the *Chronicle of Gottweig*. Volume I, which has already emerged from the press, contains only matters concerning antiquarian affairs and, especially, diplomatic studies. I know of nothing more magnificent, august, or learned that has thus far been printed in Germany than this first volume; no somewhat better library in France will be able to lack it. Its author is the same Most Reverend Lord Abbot Godefridus, at whose expense this splendid work was also committed to print.

[Col. 0055]

## NOTICE BY THE SAME AUTHOR ON LETTER CLXXXIV BIS

Peter and Abraham, to whom this letter is addressed, were undoubtedly monks. St. Augustine indicates this sufficiently at the beginning of his discourse, saying that they had so ordered their lives in the service of God that they had time for reading.

Peter, unless I am greatly mistaken, is that very Peter of whom Cassiodorus says in *On Divine Instruction in Literature*, chapter 8:

> “Peter, abbot of the province of Tripoli, is said to have annotated the letters of St. Paul with excerpts from the works of the blessed Augustine, so that through another’s mouth he might disclose the secret of his own heart. He fitted these to the individual passages so appropriately that you may believe this work to have been completed more by the study of blessed Augustine. For it is remarkable that he so elucidated one through the other that, without any addition of his own words being mixed in, he appears to have fulfilled the desire of his own heart.”

This work, unpublished until now, exists at Venice in the library of St. Mark, with the title *Commentary on Paul’s Letters from the Books of Augustine, Attributed to Peter of Tripoli*. “I would not readily affirm this,” says the illustrious Mabillon. Whatever the truth of the matter, however, it cannot be called into question whether this letter truly belongs to Augustine, since Possidius mentions it in his *Index*.

We suppose that it was written at the beginning of approximately the year 417, because below, in chapter 2, number 5, St. Augustine testifies that, while writing it, he had the fourteenth book of *On the City of God* in his hands. Moreover, he praises this very book in chapter 14 of book 1 of *Against an Adversary of the Law and the Prophets*, and therefore at the beginning of the year 420. It is certain that the books *Against an Adversary of the Law* appeared at that time; the fourteenth book of *On the City of God* had therefore appeared shortly beforehand.

Since we know that Augustine was occupied with almost countless affairs throughout the whole year 418 and the beginning of the following year, it is scarcely credible that at that time he could have put the finishing touches to book 14 of *On the City of God*. It remains, therefore, that he completed it during the course of the year 417 and composed this letter as that year was advancing toward maturity.

[Col. 0055]

## NOTICE BY THE SAME AUTHOR ON LETTER CCII BIS

While Augustine was staying at Caesarea in the year 418, specifically in September, as is clear from the proceedings with Emeritus, in the town mentioned above—ecclesiastical necessity having drawn him there by the order imposed upon him by the venerable Pope Zosimus, bishop of the Apostolic See (Letter 190, no. 1)—Optatus’s letter was brought to him. In it Optatus indicated that he was distressed concerning the origin of the soul and wished to know whether it descended by propagation from the soul created by God and given to Adam, or whether God newly created individual souls for individual human beings.

Nevertheless, it appears that he had conceded the latter opinion (ibid., chapter 4, nos. 13 and 14). He had also published a short work on the same subject, as well as a letter addressed to certain very close friends of his. When these writings were brought to Caesarea, they were delivered to Augustine, who was still staying there, by a servant of God named Renatus. Renatus urged the holy Doctor so strongly to reply that, although occupied at that time with other matters, Augustine could not refuse to do so (ibid., chapter 1, no. 1).

Optatus himself also appears in his letter to have wished to become more certain of the holy Doctor’s opinion on the matter (ibid., chapter 6, no. 26). A certain Muressis, a friend of Optatus, further induced Augustine to do this. When Muressis came to Caesarea, he said that he too had received a letter from Optatus on the same subject, and he asked Augustine to disclose to him, either orally or in writing, what he thought about the matter, so that he might report it to Optatus (ibid., chapter 1, no. 1).

The holy Doctor therefore wrote a letter to Optatus himself from Caesarea, as those words clearly show: “while we were staying in the same town.” He replied concerning the proposed difficulty that he had no definite position to establish, because arguments existed on both sides. The only point that had to be guarded against was that no one, abusing this question, should wish to doubt original sin, which is a constant and catholic dogma, and thereby unwittingly admit the new heresy of Pelagius and Coelestius, recently condemned by councils and by the Roman bishops Innocent and Zosimus. Augustine enclosed their letters, or at least those of the latter, in case they had not yet reached Optatus.

Optatus was undoubtedly not satisfied with this response. Augustine consequently sent him two further letters on the same subject, which have perished through the injury of time. Fulgentius praises the learning and power of intellect with which the holy Doctor examined this question both in these three letters and in certain other works of his; but above all he praises Augustine’s modesty, since it deterred him from deciding anything concerning a matter equally grave and obscure.

> “Seeing the depth of this question to be inscrutable to him,” Fulgentius says, “he wished to pronounce no defined judgment concerning it, considering it wholly inappropriate to affirm without hesitation something that another person could overturn with a contrary answer” (*Life of St. Augustine*, book 7, chapter 13, no. 5).

This may perhaps have been reported at greater length, but certainly as briefly as we could manage, because it thereby becomes clear that the following letter is the second of those which Possidius and Fulgentius assert were sent by Augustine to Bishop Optatus concerning the origin of souls, and which they value highly. There is, however, this difference: Possidius assigns two letters to Optatus (*Index*), whereas Fulgentius assigns three (in the place cited above). Let the reader judge which of them should be trusted. Certainly the distinguished editors of Augustine’s works, as well as Tillemont and other most learned men, follow Fulgentius.

It is worth noting only this point: namely, that Possidius, when listing the letters addressed to Optatus, expressly teaches that they were written against the Priscillianists.

We judge that this letter was written either late in the year 419 or, rather, at the beginning of 420. For in number 1 Augustine indicates that he is replying to Optatus after almost five years have elapsed since he sent to the East the book containing not a presumption but an inquiry of his own.

The book sent to the East is clearly Augustine’s Letter 166 to Jerome, transmitted through Orosius. Orosius had arrived in Palestine from Africa shortly before July of the year 415, since in that same year and month he entered into a disputation against Pelagius at Jerusalem. He must therefore have set out from Africa at the beginning of that year.

At what precise time the first letter to Optatus, which is Letter 190 among the published letters, was written is not so clear. Dom. Dubois assigns it approximately to August of the year 418, but this is very far from the truth. Augustine could not have written it until after he had arrived at Caesarea from Carthage, and it is certain that this occurred only in September.

Indeed, Augustine himself indicates in these words that he composed this letter only after his withdrawal from Caesarea: “while we were staying in the aforementioned town.” The many and great affairs that the holy Doctor handled and completed at Caesarea within a few days point in the same direction. These matters prevented him from turning his attention to writing letters that were in no way urgent and did not concern him.

It is also highly probable that Augustine could not prepare this same letter while returning from Caesarea to Hippo, since, as he himself testifies, “through all those lands the various things presented to his senses were carrying his attention here and there.”

For these reasons we believe that the first letter to Optatus, numbered 190 among Augustine’s letters, could not have been written before November of the year 418. Indeed, with the leave of the learned, we think it should be placed after Letters 191, 192, and 193. Augustine had the greatest interest in replying to those three letters, and for that reason they are still full of haste. Letter 190, however, was extracted not by necessity but by the favor of friends; it is therefore reasonable to transfer it to a suitable and unoccupied time.

Again, from Augustine’s Letter 190, chapter 7, number 20, and also from the same holy Bishop’s Letter 166, chapter 4, number 8, we know for certain that Marcellinus had asked Jerome what ought to be thought concerning the origin of souls, after receiving Augustine’s reply on that question.

Now, Augustine’s Letter 143 establishes with complete certainty that this very reply from Augustine did not reach Marcellinus until the year 412 alone. Therefore Marcellinus could have written to Jerome only in that same year, and Jerome could not have replied to Marcellinus later than the year 413 at the latest.

Accordingly, in my judgment, contrary to the requirements of truth, Jerome’s reply to Marcellinus—which is Letter 78 in Jerome’s collection and Letter 165 in Augustine’s, and which both the Jerome and Augustine editors, as well as Dom. Dubois, assign to the year 410—should not be placed there. Tillemont, the most learned scholar, comes closer to the truth, though not quite close enough, when he assigns it to the year 411 or 412.

Who that Bishop Optatus was, to whom Augustine addressed these letters, is entirely unknown. It is certain that he was not the famous Optatus of Milevis, who pierced the Donatists with his writings, despite the fact that the Gottweig manuscript explicitly says so. That Optatus of Milevis had long since departed this life; already in the year 396 the most blessed Severus presided over the Church of Milevis as Augustine’s fellow disciple, and he continued to preside over it until the year 426, as is clear from Letters 31 and 213 of our most holy Bishop.

From this it is evident that the most learned men Dom. Louis Ellies Dupin, in his notes on chapter 215 of the first day of the Carthaginian Conference, and Dom. Thierry Ruinart, *History of the Vandal Persecution*, p. 297, wrongly assert that Severus, bishop of Milevis, had died shortly before the aforementioned Conference. The Acts of that Conference expressly state that he had watched and waited for it long beforehand, but then withdrew home because of weakness and illness, not because he had died.

Certainly the highly esteemed editors of the works of St. Augustine defend our opinion in the Preface to volume 2, in the chronological arrangement of Letters 109 and 110. Indeed, the learned Ruinart contradicts himself in the place cited: he praises the Council of Milevis held in the year 416, which Severus attended, as is clear from the letters numbered 175, 176, and 181 among Augustine’s letters; but that synod took place only four years after the Carthaginian Conference.

The late Baluze (ὁ μακαρίτης) conjectures in his notes on the Carthaginian Conference that the Optatus we seek was the man who attended that same Carthaginian Conference and who is called bishop of the people of Vesceris in the Acts of the first day.

But the people of Vesceris were in Numidia. On the other hand, the words of our Optatus inserted and incorporated into these letters of Augustine demonstrate that the people whom he governed inhabited one of the three Mauritanias.

If Dom. Dubois is to be trusted, Optatus was bishop of Tubuna, the man from whom Augustine orders Count Boniface in Letter 185 to obtain a brief record of the Conference. But the author supports his opinion with no arguments and does not indicate where he derived it. This is unsurprising, for Augustine’s own letter clearly proves it false. That Optatus mentioned there attended the Carthaginian Conference in 411 and the Council of Zerta in 412; he had therefore already held episcopal rank for many years when Augustine’s letters to Optatus were written.

The Optatus who concerns us here, however, boasts of himself in Letter 202 bis, number 7, as a young and inexperienced teacher. Moreover, in Letter 185 Augustine tells Boniface to obtain from the Church of Sitifis a brief record of the Conference if Optatus does not have one. He thus implies that the Optatus of whom he is speaking was accustomed to live in Numidia, whereas it has been shown that our Optatus must be sought in Mauritania.

A suspicion persists in the mind of a certain highly learned friend that our Optatus was indeed a bishop of Milevis, but the second of that name, successor to the great Optatus of Milevis; and that we should therefore abide by the judgment of the Gottweig copyist, who expressly calls him Optatus, Bishop of Milevis.

But this suspicion collapses in light of what has been said. Throughout all the years of Augustine’s episcopate, no one except Severus occupied the see of Milevis. Add that this Severus, always most closely connected with Augustine, consistently adhered to the holy Bishop’s teaching and friendship [Note: [Col. 0058] See Augustine, Letter 71, no. 1.]. Optatus, by contrast, opposed it as long as he could, sometimes rightly and sometimes wrongly.

It also follows that the people subject to the Optatus whom we wish to identify were enclosed within the boundaries of Mauritania, not Numidia. That Mauritania was not Caesariensis; [Col. 0059] otherwise Optatus would have attended the council held at Caesarea when his writings were brought to that city, and he would have asked the council’s Fathers in person, more conveniently than by letter, for what he was requesting from the Caesarean bishops.

Nor was that Mauritania Sitifensis. No bishop of that province could have been unaware of the condemnation of the Pelagians, for all the priests of Mauritania Sitifensis, being Numidians, were united under Augustine the Numidian in overthrowing the heretics.

Optatus, however, according to Augustine’s Letter 190, number 22, was ignorant—or could have been ignorant—of a matter of such importance.

It remains, therefore, that Optatus’s diocese must have been situated in Mauritania Tingitana, and thus in that farthest region of Africa separated from Spain by the Strait of Gades and inhabited only by barbarian peoples. This fits very well with the complaint recorded in Letter 202 bis, number 7, concerning the rustic and less instructed crowd of clergy who had caused Optatus trouble in matters in which they had been trained by learned priests.

# The Epistles of Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, Arranged Now for the First Time According to Their Chronological Order and Divided into Four Classes (C, S)*

Class I contains the letters he wrote before becoming bishop, namely from the year of Christ 386 to 395. Class II contains those he wrote as bishop before the conference held at Carthage with the Donatists and before the discovery of Pelagius’s heresy, from the year 396 to 410. Class III contains those he wrote during the remainder of his life, from 411 to 430. Class IV includes some letters also written while he was bishop, whose date is less certain.

# First Class

## Epistle I

[Note: [Col. 0061] This was reviewed against manuscripts bl., cb., gg., gv., n., r., sb., th., vc., two t. manuscripts, and two v. manuscripts, and against the Louvain edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0061] Formerly numbered 213; what was number 1 is now number 132. Written near the end of the year 386.]

Augustine discloses his plan concerning his books Against the Academics and asks Hermogenianus for his judgment concerning what he declared near the end of the third book about those philosophers.

### Augustine to Hermogenianus

1. I would never dare to attack the Academics, not even in jest; for how could the authority of such great men fail to move me, unless I thought that their position was far other than is commonly believed? Therefore I imitated them as much as I could, rather than defeated them—which I am wholly unable to do. For it seems to me quite appropriate to the circumstances of the time that, if anything genuine were flowing from the Platonic spring, it should be led into pasture among shady and thorny thickets for the benefit of very few people, rather than flowing openly, where cattle rushing about everywhere could in no way leave it clear and pure.

For what is more characteristic of cattle than to suppose that the soul is a body? Against people of this sort, I think, that art and method of the true God—[Note: [Col. 0061] Perhaps: “of concealing the truth.”]—was devised with good reason.

But in this age, when we see no philosophers except perhaps those wearing a little cloak—[Note: [Col. 0061] Twelve manuscripts have *clanculo corporis* (“secretly, of the body”).]—whom I would certainly not judge worthy of so venerable a name, people seem to me to have to be led back to hope of discovering the truth, if any have been deterred from grasping realities by the Academicians’ position through their verbal ingenuity—[Note: [Col. 0061] The Louvain edition has: “the perversity of their ingenuity had deterred them from grasping realities and had driven them into hope,” etc. But how could the Academicians be “perverse,” if—as was said shortly before—they had usefully devised an art and method of concealing the truth? We have therefore corrected the passage on the basis of ten manuscripts, which have *through verbal ingenuity ... deterred*, or *terrified*; of these, however, only two retain the word *position*.]—so that what was temporarily suited to uprooting the deepest errors may not now begin to obstruct the planting of knowledge.

2. At that time, indeed, the pursuits of the various schools were flourishing so vigorously that nothing needed to be feared except the approval of what was false. Once each person had been driven by their arguments from what he had believed himself to hold firmly and immovably, he sought something else all the more steadfastly and cautiously, in proportion as there was greater diligence in matters of conduct and as truth was sensed to lie deeply hidden and intricately concealed in the nature of things and souls.

But now there is such a flight from labor and such neglect of the liberal disciplines that, as soon as it has been heard that the most acute philosophers judged that nothing can be comprehended, people abandon their minds and cover them over forever. They do not dare to believe themselves more vigorous than those men, so that something might appear to them which Carneades, despite such intense study, intelligence, leisure, such abundant and varied learning, and finally such a very long life, was unable to discover. If, while making some effort against their laziness, they read the same books in which human apprehension is, as it were, shown to have been denied, they fall asleep in such torpor that not even a heavenly trumpet could awaken them.

3. Since, therefore, I value your faithful judgment of my little books very highly, and place such weight upon you that neither error can enter into your prudence nor dissimulation into your friendship, I ask you especially to consider more carefully and write back to me whether you approve what, at the end of the third book, I judged should be believed—perhaps with more suspicion than certainty, but, as I think, with more usefulness than incredibility.

For my part, whatever the case may be with that work, I am not so much pleased that I have conquered the Academicians—as you write, perhaps more affectionately than truthfully—as that I have broken off from myself the most hateful restraint by which despair of the truth—the nourishment of the soul—held me back from the breast of philosophy.

## Epistle II

[Note: [Col. 0063] This was checked against manuscripts cb., gg., gv., n., r., two sb. manuscripts, two t. manuscripts, and two v. manuscripts, and against the Louvain edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0063] Formerly numbered 214; what was number 2 is now number 135. Written about the same time.]

He explains to Zenobius his desire that they should complete between themselves the discussion they had begun.

### Augustine to Zenobius

[Note: [Col. 0063] This is undoubtedly the man to whom Augustine dedicated his books On Order in 386. See volume I, book 1 of On Order, chapters 1 and 2.]

1. We agreed well among ourselves, I think, that everything touched by bodily sensation cannot remain even for a moment in the same condition, but slips away, flows away, and possesses nothing present—in Latin terms, that it does not exist. True and divine philosophy therefore teaches us to restrain and lull to sleep our most destructive and punishment-filled love of these things, so that the soul, even while it acts through this body, may be carried and burn with its whole being toward those things that are always the same and are not pleasing because of some foreign beauty.

Although this is so, and although the mind sees you in yourself as true and simple, such that you can be loved without any anxiety, we nevertheless seek your company and presence when you withdraw bodily from us and are separated from us by distance; and, while it is permitted, we long for them. This fault, if I know you well, you love in us; and although you wish every good for those dearest and closest to you, you fear to cure them of this fault.

But if you possess a spirit so powerful that you can both recognize this snare and laugh at those caught by it, then indeed you are a great man and a different sort of man. For my part, as long as I long for someone absent, I want to be missed. Nevertheless, I keep watch as much as I can and strive to love nothing that can be absent from me against my will.

In carrying out this duty, I remind you meanwhile—whatever sort of person you are—that the discussion begun with you must be completed, if we are concerned for ourselves. I would never allow Alypius to complete it with me, even if he wished to. But he does not wish to. For it is not characteristic of his humanity now to work with me so that we might keep you with us in as many letters as possible, while you are fleeing, I do not know under what necessity.

## Epistle III

[Note: [Col. 0063] In preparing this recension we used a., bn., bg., c., cc., ff., gv., n., r., s., t., two a. manuscripts, two sb. manuscripts, four v. manuscripts, and the editions Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0063] Formerly numbered 151; what was number 3 is now number 137. Written in 387.]

Augustine replies to Nebridius that he is undeservedly called blessed by him, since he is ignorant of so many things. He explains where true blessedness lies.

### Augustine to Nebridius

[Note: [Col. 0063] Nebridius, Augustine’s dear friend, is praised in the books of the Confessions, especially in book 9, chapter 3, where it is said that he died not long after Augustine’s baptism—that is, before Augustine became a presbyter, and therefore before the year of Christ 391. Augustine began writing to him from the estate at Cassiciacum, according to Confessions 9.4; he lived on that estate for several months at the end of 386 and the beginning of 387.]

1. I am uncertain whether I should think this has happened through some sort of flattery of yours, so to speak, or whether the matter really stands as you say. It happened suddenly, and it has not been sufficiently considered how far it ought to be entrusted to faith.

You are waiting to hear what this is. What do you think? You have almost persuaded me that I am not indeed blessed—for that is the possession of the wise alone—but at least as though blessed; just as we call someone “almost a man” in comparison with the man whom Plato knew, or call things “almost round” and “almost square” when we see them, although they are far from the things perceived by the minds of the few.

I read your letter by lamplight after dinner; bedtime was near, though not yet sleep. For a long time I lay in bed thinking with myself and held this conversation, Augustine himself with Augustine:

“Is it not true that Nebridius approves of our being blessed?”

“Certainly not; for he himself does not dare deny that we are still foolish.”

“What if even fools attain the blessed life?”

“Hardly! As though folly itself were a small misery, or any other misery!”

“Where, then, did he get that impression? Or, having read those little books, did he dare to believe me wise?”

His joy is not so rashly extravagant—especially since we know very well how weighty a man his judgment is. The explanation is this: he wrote what he thought would be most pleasing to us, because whatever we put in those letters also became sweet to him; and he wrote rejoicing, without caring what should be entrusted to a rejoicing pen.

What if he had read the Soliloquies? He would have rejoiced much more abundantly, and yet he would not have found anything more by which to call me blessed. Thus he quickly poured the highest title upon me and reserved nothing for himself with which he could make a more joyful assertion about me. See what joy can do!

2. But where is this blessed life? Where? Where, I ask? [Note: [Col. 0064] One Vatican codex has: “the blessed life—where, unless in the soul? If only it were itself.” Two other Vatican manuscripts have: “the blessed life—where is the true one? If only it were itself,” etc.] If it were itself, it would reject Epicurus’s atoms. If it were itself, it would know that there is nothing below except the world. If it were itself, it would know that the outermost sphere revolves more slowly than the middle one, and other similar things that we likewise know.

But how, in fact, am I blessed in any sense, when I do not know why the world is so vast, since the principles of the figures by which it exists do not prevent it from being as large as anyone wishes? Or how could it not be said to me—or rather, how could we not be compelled to admit—that bodies are divisible without limit, so that from a definite sort of base a definite number of little bodies might rise to a definite quantity?

Therefore, since no smallest body is allowed to exist, how can we allow the existence of something so vast that nothing greater could exist—unless perhaps that very obscure point which I once made to Alypius has great force: since that intelligible number increases infinitely, yet does not diminish infinitely—for it cannot be resolved beyond the monad—whereas sensible number (for what else is sensible number than the quantity of bodies or bodily things?) can indeed diminish infinitely, but cannot increase infinitely.

For this reason, perhaps, philosophers rightly place riches in intelligible things and poverty in sensible things. What is more miserable than always being able to become smaller and smaller? What is richer than to grow as much as you wish, go wherever you wish, return whenever you wish, continue as long as you wish, and love greatly what cannot be diminished?

For whoever understands these numbers loves nothing so much as the monad; [Col. 0065] and this is not surprising, since through it the others are made lovable. Yet why is the world so vast? It could have been larger or smaller. I do not know; it is simply this way. And why is it here rather than there? There should be no question about a matter in which, whatever the answer were, there would still be a question.

Only one thing troubled me greatly: that bodies could be divided infinitely. Perhaps the answer to this is found in the contrary force of intelligible number.

3. But wait; let us see what this something or other is that is suggested to the mind. Certainly, the sensible world is said to be an image of some intelligible world.

It is remarkable, however, what we see in images reflected by mirrors. For no matter how large the mirrors are, they do not return images larger than the bodies—even the very smallest bodies—that are placed before them. In small mirrors, on the other hand, as in the pupils of the eyes, even if a large face is presented, a very small image is formed according to the size of the mirror.

Thus images of bodies may be made smaller if mirrors are made smaller; but they cannot be made larger if the mirrors are enlarged. Something is certainly hidden here, but now it is time to sleep. For I do not seem blessed to Nebridius by searching, but perhaps by discovering something.

But what is that something? Is it perhaps that reasoning which I habitually flatter as my sole possession, and in which I take too much delight?

4. Of what do we consist? Of soul and body. Which of these is better? Obviously, the soul. What do they praise in the body? I see nothing other than beauty. What is bodily beauty? The harmony of its parts together with a certain sweetness of color.

Where is this form better: where it is true, or where it is false? Who could doubt that it is better where it is true? Where, then, is it true? In the soul, of course. The soul, therefore, is more deserving of love than the body.

But in what part of the soul is this truth found? In the mind and understanding. What opposes this? The senses. Must we therefore resist the senses with all the soul’s strength? Clearly. What if sensible things give too much pleasure? Let it happen that they no longer give pleasure. How does that happen? Through the habit of doing without them and desiring better things.

What if the soul dies? Then either truth dies, or understanding is not truth, or understanding is not in the soul, or something in which there is something immortal can die. But our Soliloquies already establish that none of these things can happen, and this has been sufficiently made convincing; nevertheless, through some habit of evil things, we are terrified and stagger.

Finally, even if the soul dies—which I see no way could happen—the fact that the blessed life does not consist in delight in sensible things has been sufficiently examined during this leisure.

By such matters, and perhaps others like them, I seem to my Nebridius to be not blessed but at least almost blessed. Let me seem so to myself as well; what do I lose by it, or why should I spare a good opinion? This is what I said to myself; then I prayed as usual and went to sleep.

5. I decided to write this to you. For I am pleased that you thank me if I conceal nothing from you that comes into my mouth, and I rejoice because you are pleased with me. With whom, then, should I more willingly make a fool of myself than with someone whom I cannot displease?

But if it lies in Fortune’s power for one human being to love another, consider how blessed I am, since I rejoice so greatly in things dependent on chance and, I confess, desire such goods to increase for me abundantly.

As for Fortune’s goods, let the truest wise men—who alone may rightly be called blessed—neither fear nor desire them—or whether they should be desired, you may decide. And this has turned out beautifully. For I want you to make me familiar with the inflection of this word.

When I join similar verbs together, I become more uncertain. The form is *cupio*, like *fugio*, *sapio*, *jacio*, and *capio*; but whether the infinitive is *fugiri* or *fugi*, *sapiri* or *sapi*, I do not know.

I could look to *jaci* and *capi*, if I were not afraid that the man who proved that one thing is *jactum* and *captum*, and another *fugitum*, *cupitum*, and *sapitum*, might seize me and throw me wherever he wished as an object of ridicule.

Likewise, I do not know whether these three forms should be pronounced with the penultimate syllable long and rising, or with a grave and short accent. I have challenged you to write a longer letter; I ask you to let me read you a little longer. For I cannot say enough how delightful it is to read you.

## Epistle IV

[Note: [Col. 0066] We reviewed this against a., bl., bg., cb., gg., gv., n., r., sb., two t. manuscripts, two v. manuscripts, and the editions Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0066] Formerly numbered 117; what was number 4 is now number 136. Written about the same time.]

Augustine to Nebridius, indicating how much progress he has made in retreat through contemplation of eternal things.

### Augustine to Nebridius

1. It is extraordinarily surprising how something has happened to me beyond my expectation. When I considered which of your letters still remained for me to answer, I found only one that still held me in your debt: the one in which you ask us to tell you, amid the great leisure which you suppose we have and wish were yours with us, what progress we have made in distinguishing sensible from intelligible nature.

But I do not think it is hidden from you that, just as each person is more deeply and familiarly entangled in false opinions the more he dwells among them, so the same thing happens much more easily to the mind in matters that are true. This happens gradually, however, as we advance with age.

Although there is a great difference between a child and a young man, no one, if questioned every day from childhood, will say that he will at some time become a young man.

2. I do not want you to take this in such a way that you imagine we have reached, in these matters, a kind of intellectual maturity through the strength of firmer understanding. We are children, but, as the saying goes, perhaps fine children, and not bad ones. [Note: [Col. 0066] Am., Er., and two manuscripts have “not badly.”]

For that little argument, so well known to you, often gives breathing-space to the eyes of the mind, disturbed and filled with anxieties by the blows of sensible things—[Note: [Col. 0066] That is, by phantasies.]—[Note: [Col. 0066] Most manuscripts have “in respiration.”]: that the mind and understanding are better than the eyes and this ordinary act of seeing. That would not be so unless the things we understand were more real than the things we see.

I ask you to consider with me whether anything powerful is wholly opposed to this reasoning. In the meantime, when I have been refreshed by it, and after I have prayed to God for assistance and begun to be lifted toward him and toward those things that are most truly true, I am sometimes filled with such a strong presumption of the permanence of things that I am astonished that I need reasoning in order to believe that these things exist—things that are present with such force as each person is present to himself.

You too should recall this; for I admit that you are more diligent in this matter, lest I perhaps unknowingly remain in your debt for further replies. For the sudden laying down of so many burdens, which I had once counted, does not convince me, although I have no doubt that you received my letters, to which I have no written responses.

## Epistle V

[Note: [Col. 0067] Reviewed against a., bl., bg., cb., g., gg., gv., n., r., sb., two t. manuscripts, two v. manuscripts, and the editions Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0067] Formerly numbered 114; what was number 5 is now number 138. Written near the end of 388.]

Nebridius laments that Augustine is excessively interrupted by the affairs of his fellow citizens and kept from the leisure of contemplation.

### Nebridius to Augustine

Is it really so, my Augustine? You devote strength and endurance to the affairs of your fellow citizens, and that long-desired rest has still not been restored to you? I ask you: what sort of people interrupt you? I suppose people who do not know what you love and what you desire.

Have you no friend who can report your loves to them? Neither Romanianus nor Lucinianus? [Note: [Col. 0067] In several manuscripts this is written *Lucianus* here, and *Lucilianus* in Epistle 10. Shortly afterward the Victorinus codex reads: “let them hear me, at least.”]

Let them hear me, at least. I will cry out; I will testify that you love God, desire to serve him and cling to him. I would like to invite you to my countryside estate and rest there. For I shall not fear being called your seducer by your fellow citizens, whom you love too much and by whom you are loved too much.

## Epistle VI

[Note: [Col. 0067] For correcting Epistles VI and VII to Nebridius, we used a., bl., bg., cb., ff., gg., gv., n., r., sb., vc., two t. manuscripts, two v. manuscripts, and the editions Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0067] Formerly numbered 71; what was number 6 is now number 92. Written near the beginning of 389.]

Nebridius writes that it seems impossible to him for memory to exist without phantasy; he also argues that phantasy obtains its power to form images of things not from sensation but rather from itself.

### Nebridius to Augustine

1. I take great pleasure in preserving your letters as I would my eyes. They are great, not in size but in content, and they contain great proofs of great matters. They will speak to me of Christ, of Plato, and of Plotinus.

They will therefore be sweet to me when heard, because of their eloquence; easy to read, because of their brevity; and beneficial to understand, because of their wisdom. You will therefore take care to teach me whatever has appeared holy or good to your mind.

You will answer these letters when you have discussed something more subtly concerning phantasy and memory. It seems to me that, although not every phantasy is accompanied by memory, no memory can exist without phantasy.

But you say: “What happens when we remember that we understood or thought something?” To this I reply and say that it happened for this reason: when we understood or thought something corporeal and temporal, we generated something belonging to phantasy. For either we joined words to our understanding and thoughts—and words do not exist without time and belong to sense or phantasy—or our understanding underwent in thought something that could have produced memory in the phantastic soul. [Note: [Col. 0067] Thus three manuscripts. The editions have: “which could have produced a phantastic memory in the soul,” etc.]

I have said this carelessly and confusedly, as is my habit. You will investigate it, reject what is false, and bring the truth back to me in writing.

2. Hear another point. Why, I ask you, do we say that all images belong to phantasy from itself rather than from sensation? For just as the intellectual soul is prompted by sensation to see its intelligible objects rather than receiving anything from sensation, so perhaps the phantastic soul is prompted by sensation to contemplate its images rather than taking anything from it.

For perhaps this is why it happens that it can look upon things that sensation does not see: which is a sign that it possesses all images in itself and from itself. You will also reply what you think about this matter.

## Epistle VII

[Note: [Col. 0068] Formerly numbered 72; what was number 7 is now number 143. Written about the same time.]

Augustine discusses both questions raised by Nebridius: whether memory can exist without phantasy, and whether the soul, without using the senses, is without phantasies. The objection is resolved.

### Augustine to Nebridius

### Chapter I — That Memory Can Exist without Phantasy

1. I shall dispense with a preface and quickly begin what you are already urging me to say—especially since I shall not be stopping quickly. You think that no memory can exist without images or imagined perceptions, which you have wished to call by the name *phantasies*. I think otherwise.

First, then, we must see that we do not always remember things that pass away, but very often things that remain. Therefore, although memory claims for itself the retention of past time, it nevertheless belongs partly to things that leave us and partly to things from which we depart.

When I remember my father, I certainly remember someone who has left me and is no longer here; when I remember Carthage, I remember something that exists and that I myself have left. In both kinds of case, however, memory holds past time. For I remember both that man and that city from what I saw, not from what I see.

2. Here you may perhaps ask: “What is the point of this?”—especially since you notice that neither of these things can come into memory unless that imagined perception has been seen. [Note: [Col. 0068] Manuscript a. has: “unless by that imagined perception.” Other codices have “unless seen.”]

For the present, however, it is enough for me to have shown that memory can also be said to belong to things that have not yet perished. But listen attentively to how this helps me.

Some people criticize that most celebrated Socratic discovery, by which it is asserted that the things we learn are not inserted into us as something new but recalled into memory through recollection. They say that memory belongs to past things, whereas the things we learn by understanding, according to Plato himself, always remain and cannot perish, and therefore are not past.

They fail to notice that the vision by which we once saw these things with the mind is past. Because we have flowed away from that vision and begun to see some things differently, we revisit them through recollection—that is, through memory.

Therefore, leaving other matters aside, if eternity itself always remains and does not acquire any imaginary fictions by which it might come into the mind as though by vehicles, yet could not come unless we remembered it, there can be memory of certain things without any imagination at all.

### Chapter II — That a Soul Not Using the Senses Is without Phantasies

3. But the opinion that seems to you to hold that the soul, even without using the bodily senses, can imagine corporeal things is shown to be false in the following way.

If the soul can imagine the same bodies before it uses the body to sense bodies, and if it was in a better condition before it became entangled in these deceptive senses—as no sane person doubts—then the souls of sleepers are in a better condition than those of the waking, and the souls of the delirious in a better condition than those free from such a disease. For they are affected by images by which they were affected before these most deceitful messengers, the senses.

Either the sun they see will be truer than the sun seen by the sane and wakeful, or false things will be better than true ones. Since both alternatives are absurd, as they are, that imagination is nothing else, my Nebridius, than a blow inflicted through the senses.

Through the senses, as you write, there is not some recollection by which such things are formed in the soul; rather, it is the very introduction of this falsity—or, to put it more explicitly, its imprinting.

Your question—how it happens that we think of faces and forms we have never seen—certainly troubles you, and rightly so. I shall therefore do what makes this letter longer than usual; but not for you, since no page is more welcome to you than one that brings me to you as more talkative.

4. I see that all these images, which you and many others call phantasies, can most conveniently and truly be divided into three classes. One is impressed by things sensed; the second consists of things supposed; the third of things reasoned or inferred.

Examples of the first class occur when the soul forms within itself an image of your face, of Carthage, or of Verecundus, once our companion—[Note: [Col. 0069] A grammarian and citizen of Milan, to whose country estate Augustine, while not yet baptized, withdrew with his companions. See Confessions 9.3.]—or of anything else, whether enduring or dead, that I have nevertheless seen and sensed.

The second class includes things that we suppose to have been or to be a certain way. For example, for the sake of discussion we invent certain things that in no way obstruct the truth; or we form images of things of the sort we encounter when reading histories, and when we hear, compose, or suspect fictional tales.

For I form, as I please and as it occurs to my mind, the face of Aeneas; Medea with her winged serpents yoked together; Chremes and some Parmeno. The images of this class also include things that either wise men, wrapping some truth in such figures, or fools, the authors of various superstitions, have presented as true: the Tartarean Phlegethon; the five caves of the race of darkness; the northern axle holding up the heavens; and a thousand other monstrosities of poets and heretics.

Yet even in argument we say, “Suppose there are three worlds one above another, each like this one”; and, “Suppose the earth is contained within a square figure”; and similar things. We invent and suppose all these things according to the storm of thought.

As for the third class of images, it chiefly concerns numbers and dimensions. Part of it exists in the nature of things, as when the figure of the entire world is discovered and an image of that discovery follows in the mind of the person thinking; part of it exists in the disciplines, such as geometrical figures, musical rhythms, and the infinite variety of numbers.

Although these things are grasped as true, in my judgment, they nevertheless give rise to false imaginations against which reason itself scarcely struggles. It is not even easy for the discipline of argumentation itself to be free from this defect, since in divisions and conclusions we imagine certain calculations, as it were.

5. In this entire forest of images, I believe you do not think that the first class belongs to the soul before it becomes attached to the senses; nor need we argue about this any longer.
