Concerning the remaining two classes, one could rightly continue to ask questions, unless it were clear that the soul is less exposed to falsities before it has suffered the vanity of sensible things and of the senses. For who would doubt that these images are much more false than sensible things?

Those things that we suppose, believe, or invent are either wholly false in every respect or, as you see, are certainly much less true than the things we see and sense.

Now, in that third class, I may figure any bodily space in my mind, although thought seems to have produced it through the disciplines’ unfailing principles; yet, when those same principles again argue the point, I prove it to be false.

It follows that I cannot in any way believe that a soul not yet sensing through the body, not yet beaten by the most deceitful senses with the blows of mortal and fleeting substance, lay in such disgraceful falsity.

### Chapter III — The Objection Resolved

6. How, then, does it happen that we think of things we have not seen? What do you think, unless there is some power implanted in the soul to diminish and enlarge, which it must necessarily carry with it wherever it goes?

This power can be observed especially in numbers. Through it, for example, when the image of a crow has been set, so to speak, before the eyes—an image familiar to sight—by subtracting and adding certain features it can be brought to an image that has never been seen at all.

Through this power it happens that, when souls are accustomed to turning such things over within themselves, figures of this kind burst into their thoughts as though spontaneously.

Thus, by subtracting from and adding to what the senses have introduced into it, the imagining soul can produce things that it has never encountered through any sense at all; but it can also produce parts of things it had encountered in various other objects.

Thus we, born and raised in inland regions, could already imagine seas from seeing water in a small cup; but before tasting strawberries and acorns in Italy, their flavor could in no way come to mind.

This is why people blind from birth, when asked about light and colors, cannot find what to answer. They do not undergo any colored images, because they have sensed none.

7. Nor should you wonder how things that are represented and can be represented in the nature of things can be formed and circulate within the soul that is present in everyone, even though it has never sensed them externally.

For when, through indignation, joy, or other movements of this kind, we form many facial expressions and colors in our own body, our thought first conceives such images as things we can produce.

Those forms follow in those marvelous ways. Consider them and entrust them to your thought, when hidden numbers are set in motion in the soul without any bodily figure of falsities. [Note: [Col. 0070] Thus the more elegant manuscripts. The printed editions have: “without any bodily figure.”]

From this, I would like you to understand the following. Since you perceive that there are so many movements of the soul devoid of all the images about which you are now asking, you should understand that the soul receives a body through some movement other than the thought of sensible forms, which, before it uses the body and the senses, I believe it cannot undergo in any way.

Therefore, for the sake of our friendship and out of reverence for the divine law itself, I earnestly warn you, dearest and most delightful to me: do not join any friendship with those infernal shadows, and do not delay tearing apart the friendship that has already been joined.

For one cannot in any way resist the senses of the body—which is for us a most sacred discipline—if we caress the blows and wounds inflicted upon us through them. [Note: [Col. 0071] The editions have “through them” with a feminine pronoun; but the manuscripts, with broad agreement, prefer the masculine, which refers to the senses. A little earlier it is said: “Imagination of sensible things in this body is nothing other than a blow inflicted through the senses.” From this you will understand the passage in On True Religion, chapter 34, section 64, where Augustine says against the Manichaeans: “Provide someone who can resist the senses of the flesh and the blows by which, through them, he has been beaten in the soul.” Nor does he seem to understand by the infernal shadows from which he is here calling Nebridius any others than those phantasies or phantasms which the Manichaeans embraced, as appears from Confessions 3.6 and 9.4.]

## Epistle VIII

[Note: [Col. 0071] In correcting this letter we used cb., gg., gv., n., r., sb., vc., two t. manuscripts, two v. manuscripts, and Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0071] Formerly numbered 245; what was number 8 is now number 27. Written shortly after the preceding letter.]

By what action of the heavenly powers images and dreams slip into the soul of a sleeping person.

### Nebridius to Augustine
1. Since I am eager to get to the matter itself, I approve of no preface or introduction. How does it happen, my Augustine—or what is that method employed by the higher powers, whom I wish to understand as celestial beings—when they are pleased to show us, while we sleep, certain dreams? What, I ask, is their method—that is, how do they do it, by what art, by what contrivances (*manganis*), and by what instruments or drugs?

[Note: [Col. 0071] Lov. reads *machinis* (“machines”), whereas the manuscripts read *manganis*. The meaning is the same; hence *magganella*, certain implements of war. Suidas, moreover, interprets *magganon paradoxon ti* as “some wondrous thing”; some interpret it as “conjuring tricks.”] [Note: [Col. 0071] Lov. reads “or drugs [do they drive] our mind.” We have altered the text somewhat in accordance with the manuscripts.]

Do they drive our mind through their thoughts, so that we too imagine these things by thinking of them? Or do they themselves, in their own body or in their own imagination, make and present these things to us?

But if they make them in their own body, it follows that, when we sleep, we too have other bodily eyes internally, with which we see what they have formed in their own body. If, however, they are not aided in these matters by their body, but arrange them in their imagination and thus come into contact with our imagination, and what is a dream becomes visible—why, I ask you, do I not compel your imagination through my own to produce such dreams as I first formed in it myself? Certainly I too have an imagination, and it is capable of fabricating whatever I wish, while I produce no dream for you at all; yet I see that our own body itself generates dreams within us.

For when it has once acquired, through the affection by which it is joined to the soul, a certain disposition, it compels us in wondrous ways to imitate that same thing through the imagination. Often, when we are thirsty in sleep, we dream that we are drinking; when hungry, we seem to be eating; and there are many similar experiences, which, as though by a kind of commerce, are transferred imaginatively from the body to the soul. Do not be surprised if these matters, obscure as they are in themselves and given our own ignorance, have been explained less elegantly and less subtly than they might be. You will work to do so as far as you can.

**EPISTLE IX**  
[Note: Epistles IX and X were corrected against a, bl, bg, cb, g, gg, gv, n, r, sb, two copies of t, two of v, and Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]  
[Note: Formerly 115, first; what was 9 is now 40. Written at approximately the same time.]  
*He responds to the question concerning dreams sent by the higher powers.*

[Col. 0072]

**AUGUSTINE TO NEBRIDIUS**

1. Although you are acquainted with my mind, perhaps you nevertheless do not know how greatly I wish to enjoy your presence. Yet God will one day grant us this great benefit. I have read your very proper letter, in which you complained of solitude and of a kind of abandonment by your friends, with whom life is most sweet.

But what else can I say to you here except what I have no doubt you already do? Withdraw into your own mind, and raise it to God as much as you can. There you possess us more surely—not through bodily images, which we must now use in our recollection, but through that thought by which you understand that we are together not in place.

2. As I considered your letters, in which, as you sought great answers, I undoubtedly gave you great ones, I was greatly alarmed by that letter in which you ask how it happens that certain thoughts and dreams are inserted into us by higher powers or by demons. This is a great matter, and you yourself, with your prudence, perceive that it calls for an answer not in a letter but either in a personal conversation or in some little book.

Nevertheless, I shall attempt, knowing your intelligence, to sow beforehand certain lights concerning this question

[Note: Lov. reads *limina* (“thresholds”); the manuscripts and older editions read *lumina* (“lights”).]

so that either you may weave the rest together by yourself or may not despair that a probable investigation of so great a matter can be reached.

3. For I believe that every movement of the soul does something in the body. When the movements of the soul are greater, they reach even our senses, dull and slow as they are—for example, when we are angry, sad, or joyful. From this one may infer that, when we are also thinking something, although it does not appear to us in our own body, it may nevertheless appear to beings of air or ether, whose sense is exceedingly sharp and in comparison with which our own sense should scarcely be called sense at all.

Thus the things that the soul, so to speak, imprints upon the body as traces of its movement can both remain and form a kind of habit. When these traces have been secretly stirred and handled, they implant thoughts and dreams in us according to the will of the one who stirs and handles them; and this happens with astonishing ease.

For if it is evident that the exercises of our earthly and extremely sluggish bodies, in playing musical instruments, walking the tightrope, and countless spectacles of this kind, have reached certain incredible achievements, it is by no means absurd that those who act upon bodies with an airy or ethereal body—bodies which they penetrate according to the natural order—should use far greater ease to move whatever they wish, while we do not perceive it, yet nevertheless suffer some effect from it.

For we do not even perceive how an excess of bile drives us to more frequent anger; yet it does drive us, once that very excess I mentioned has arisen in us when we are angry.

4. But if you do not wish to accept this as something similar to our own case, turn it over in your mind as far as you can. If some difficulty in doing and accomplishing what it desires continually arises in the soul, it is continually angry. Anger, in my opinion, is a turbulent desire to remove whatever obstructs ease of action.

Accordingly, we are often angry not only with human beings but with a pen while writing, and we dash it against something and break it; gamblers become angry with their dice, painters with their brush, and everyone with whatever instrument he thinks is causing him difficulty. Physicians also affirm that, through this continual habit of anger, the bile grows. As the bile increases, we again become angry easily and for almost no reason. Thus what the soul has produced in the body by its own movement becomes capable in turn of moving the soul itself.

5. These matters could be treated at great length and brought, through many testimonies drawn from experience, to a more certain and fuller understanding. But attach to this letter the one I recently sent you concerning images and memory, and examine it more carefully; for your reply showed me that you had not understood it fully.

When you add to the letter you are now reading what was said there concerning a certain natural power of the soul that diminishes and increases any thought, perhaps even bodily forms that we have never seen may be shaped either by thinking them within ourselves or by dreaming them.

[Note: Here the epistle ends in Lov. and in the older manuscripts. But in Bad., Am., and Er., it is joined continuously to the most recent editions at the words “although acts,” with the beginning removed; the following words belong to Epistle XIV.]

**EPISTLE X**  
[Note: Formerly 116; what was 10 is now 71. Written at approximately the same time.]  
*Concerning living together with Nebridius and withdrawing from the turmoil of worldly affairs.*

**AUGUSTINE TO NEBRIDIUS**

1. Nothing in your inquiries has ever held me so feverishly occupied in thought as what I read in your most recent letter, where you reproach us for neglecting to arrange that we might live together. A serious accusation—and, unless it were false, an extremely dangerous one.

But since a plausible argument seems to show that we can, according to our wishes, live here rather than at Carthage, or even in the countryside, I am entirely uncertain what I should do with you, my Nebridius. Should the most suitable vehicle for you be sent? Our Lucinianus assures us that you could travel safely in a *basterna*.

[Note: In the editions, *bastarna*. But in the old books it is written *basterna*. Isidore explains the word in his *Glossary* as “a covered hand-carried vehicle”; hence some think it was a portable chair or litter carried in the hands of attendants, while others think it was a litter customarily placed on the back of pack animals, according to the same Isidore, *Etymologies* 20.12. Such was the vehicle mentioned by Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks* 3.26.]

Yet I think of my mother: she did not tolerate my absence when I was well, and she would tolerate it much less in my weakness. Should I come to you myself? But here are people who cannot come with me and whom I would consider it wrong to abandon. You can live pleasantly within your own mind; these people, however, are struggling so that they too may be able to do so.

Should I go and return frequently, being now with you and now with them? But that is neither to live with both at once nor to live according to one’s wishes.

[Note: The conjunction *neque* (“nor”) is omitted in the manuscripts.] The journey is not short, but so long that frequently undertaking the business of completing it is not the same as reaching the leisure we desire.

Added to this is the weakness of my body, by which, as you know, I too cannot do what I wish unless I altogether cease wishing for anything beyond what I am able to do.

2. To spend one’s whole life thinking about journeys that one cannot make quietly and easily is not the conduct of a person thinking about that one final journey called death—which alone, or at least chiefly, you understand must truly be contemplated.

God has indeed granted to certain few, whom he wished to be governors of the churches, that they should not merely await death courageously but even desire it eagerly, and undertake without anguish the labors of discharging those offices. Yet I do not think that this great blessing is granted either to those who are swept into such offices by love of temporal honor, or, again, to those who, although private persons, seek a life full of business: namely, that amid restless noise, gatherings, and comings and goings, they should acquire the familiarity with death that we seek. For both groups could have become divine in leisure.

Or, if this is false, then I am the most—perhaps I should not say foolish, but certainly the most sluggish—of all people, since unless a secure cessation from activity comes to me, I cannot taste or love that genuine good. Believe me, a great withdrawal from the tumult of passing things is necessary, so that a person may come to fear nothing—not through hardness, boldness, desire for empty glory, or superstitious credulity. From this arises that solid joy as well, which no other delight can match in any part.

3. But if such a life does not fall within human nature, why does this security ever occur?

[Note: Earlier editions read *cui aliquando*; we have substituted *cur* (“why”) from the manuscripts.] Why does it occur more frequently in proportion as a person worships God in the inner sanctuary of the mind? Why does this tranquility usually remain even in human action if one proceeds to act from that inner shrine? Why, sometimes even while speaking, do we not fear death, whereas when we are silent we even desire it?

I speak to you—for I would not say this to just anyone. I speak, I say, to you, whose journeys toward the heavenly realms I know well. When you have often experienced how sweetly the soul lives when it dies to bodily love, will you finally deny that the whole of human life can become fearless, so that a person may rightly be called wise? Or will you dare to assert that this disposition toward which reason strives, has ever come upon you except when you are distressed in your inmost self?

[Note: Thus Lov. Er. has “when you were distressed in your inmost self.” Bad., Am., and the Gemmeticensis manuscript have “when you are acted upon in your inmost self.” Most manuscripts have “when you are acted upon in your inmost self”; perhaps the reading should be *ageres*, “when you acted.”]

Since this is so, you see that one thing remains: that you too should contribute to a common plan by which we may live together. What should be done about my mother—whom, certainly, our brother Victor does not abandon—you know far better than I do. I did not wish to write anything else, lest I turn you away from this thought.

**EPISTLE XI**  
[Note: XI and XII are found only in the Vatican manuscript.]  
[Note: Formerly 268; what was 11 is now 75. Written at approximately the same time.]  
*Why the assumption of humanity is attributed to the Son alone, although the divine persons are inseparable.*

[Col. 0075]

**AUGUSTINE TO NEBRIDIUS**

1. The question you proposed some time ago, with a certain familiar reproach, concerning how we might live together was greatly troubling me. I had decided to write back to you about this alone, and to demand a reply, without turning my pen to anything else relevant to our studies, so that this very matter might be settled between us.

But the very brief and truthful reasoning of your recent letter quickly made me secure: namely, that we need not think about this now, because either we shall necessarily come to you when we can, or you will necessarily come to us when you can.

Thus, as I have said, having been made secure, I examined all your letters to see which replies I owe you. In them I found so many questions that, even if they could easily be resolved, their sheer accumulation would surpass anyone’s intelligence and leisure. They are, however, so difficult that, even if only one of them had been imposed upon me, I would not hesitate to confess that I was heavily burdened.

This preface serves to ask you to stop seeking new answers for a while, until we are freed from our entire debt, and to write back to me about my judgment alone. Yet I know how contrary this is to me, since I delay even briefly sharing in your divine thoughts.

2. Hear, then, what I think concerning the mystical assumption of humanity, which the religion in which we have been instructed commends to us as something to be believed and understood, and which was made for our salvation. I have chosen this question as the one most suitable for answering—not because it is the easiest of all.

For the questions asked about this world do not seem to me sufficiently relevant to attaining the blessed life; and if investigating them brings some pleasure, we must nevertheless fear that they may occupy time which ought to be devoted to better things.

Accordingly, concerning this assumption now under discussion, I am first surprised that you were disturbed by the question why the Son, rather than the Father, is said to have assumed humanity, and likewise why the Holy Spirit is not said to have done so.

For Catholic faith commends and believes this Trinity to be so inseparable, and it is understood by so few holy and blessed people in such a way, that whatever is done by it must be considered to be done simultaneously by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: the Father does nothing that the Son and the Holy Spirit do not also do; the Holy Spirit does nothing that the Father and the Son do not also do; nor does the Son do anything that the Father and the Holy Spirit do not also do.

It therefore seems to follow that the whole Trinity assumed humanity. For if the Son assumed it but the Father and the Holy Spirit did not, they would do something separately from one another.

Why, then, is the assumption of humanity celebrated in our mysteries and sacred rites as attributed to the Son? This is a very full question, so difficult and concerning so great a matter that neither the judgment here can be sufficiently straightforward nor its proof sufficiently secure.

Since I am writing to you, however, I dare to indicate what my mind contains rather than explain it, so that you may infer the rest for yourself, according to your intelligence and our intimacy, through which you know me very well.

3. There is no nature, Nebridius, and absolutely no substance, that does not possess and display these three things within itself: first, that it is; then, that it is this or that; and third, that it remains, as far as it can, in what it is.

The first displays the very cause of nature, from which all things exist; the second, the form through which all things are made and, in a certain sense, shaped; the third, a kind of permanence, so to speak, in which all things exist.

If it is possible for something to exist without being this or that and without remaining in its own kind; or for it to be this or that without existing and without remaining in its own kind as far as it can; or for it to remain in its own kind according to the powers of that kind while nevertheless neither existing nor being this or that—then it is also possible for one person of that Trinity to do something apart from the others.

But if you see that whatever exists must immediately be this or that and remain in its own kind as far as it can, then those three do nothing apart from one another.

I see that I have so far dealt only with one part of this question, which is what makes its solution difficult. But I wanted briefly to disclose to you—if indeed I have accomplished what I intended—how subtly and with how much truth the inseparability of this Trinity is understood in the Catholic faith.

4. Now understand how the thing that causes difficulty may fail to disturb the mind. The form properly attributed to the Son also pertains to instruction and to a certain art, if we use that word correctly in these matters, and to the understanding by which the mind itself is formed through thought of things.

Therefore, since through that assumption of humanity the purpose was to insinuate into us a certain discipline of living and an example of instruction under the majesty and clarity of certain sayings, this whole matter is attributed to the Son for good reason.

In many matters which I entrust to your thought and prudence, although many elements are present, one nevertheless stands out and therefore not unreasonably claims a certain distinctiveness for itself. For example, in the three kinds of questions: even when one asks whether something exists, the question of what it is is also present, since it certainly cannot exist unless it is something; and the question of whether it should be approved or rejected is also present, since whatever exists is worthy of some evaluation.

Thus, when one asks what something is, it is necessary both that it exist and that it be weighed by some evaluation. In the same way, when one asks what quality it has, it certainly exists in some way, although, since everything is inseparably joined, the question takes its name not from all the elements but from the intention of the questioner.

Accordingly, discipline is necessary for human beings, so that they may be instructed by it and formed according to its pattern. Yet we cannot say that what is produced in human beings through this discipline either does not exist or is not desirable. We first direct our attention to knowing, and to that through which we may infer something and in which we may remain.

A certain norm and rule of discipline therefore had to be demonstrated first. This was accomplished through the dispensation of the assumed humanity, which is properly attributed to the Son. It follows that knowledge of the Father himself—that is, of the one principle from which all things exist—comes through the Son, as does a certain inward and ineffable life and sweetness of remaining in that knowledge and scorning all mortal things; this gift and endowment is properly attributed to the Holy Spirit.

Thus, although everything is accomplished in the highest communion and inseparability, the elements had nevertheless to be demonstrated distinctly because of our weakness, since we have fallen from unity into multiplicity. No one raises another to the level at which he himself is unless he descends somewhat toward the level at which the other is.

You have here a letter that has not ended your concern about this matter, but perhaps has begun your thoughts upon some firm foundation, so that you may pursue the rest with the intelligence that is very familiar to me and attain it through the piety on which one must chiefly rely.

**EPISTLE XII**  
[Note: Formerly 269; what was 12 is now 67. Written at approximately the same time.]  
*He takes up again the question briefly treated in the preceding epistle.*

**AUGUSTINE TO NEBRIDIUS**

1. You say that you sent more letters than we received. Yet I can neither fail to believe you nor fail to believe myself. Although I am unable to equal you in writing replies, your letters are preserved by me with no less care than they are sent by you.

We agree that you received no more than two of our longer letters; for we did not send a third. On reviewing the copies, I noticed that approximately five of your questions had been answered, except that one question, touched upon only in passing, although it was not rashly entrusted to your intelligence, perhaps did not satisfy your greed for answers. You must restrain this appetite somewhat and willingly tolerate certain abbreviations.

Indeed, if I defraud your understanding by being sparing with words, spare me nothing; but demand from me, by the right that would perhaps make me more vigorous—if anything could be more pleasant—the whole of what is owed.

You will therefore count this among my shorter letters; it does nothing to reduce the heap of what I owe you. For you too do not send short letters without increasing that same heap.

Accordingly, concerning what you ask about the Son of God—why he himself is said to have assumed humanity rather than the Father, although both acted together—you will recognize the answer very easily if you recall our conversations in which, as best we could—for it is something ineffable—we discussed what the Son of God is, with whom we are united.

To touch upon it briefly here: the Son is called the discipline itself and the form of God, through which all things that have been made were made. Whatever was accomplished through that assumed human being was accomplished for our instruction and formation.

[Sixty-seven lines are missing in the Vatican manuscript from which this epistle was extracted.]

**EPISTLE XIII**  
[Note: We collated this epistle in bl., cb., gg., gv., n., r., sb., vc., two copies of t, two of v, and Lov.]  
[Note: Formerly 218; what was 13 is now 68. Written perhaps in 389, certainly before 391.]  
*He asks that they abandon the question concerning a certain body of the soul, as irrelevant to him.*

**AUGUSTINE TO NEBRIDIUS**

1. I do not wish to write you the usual things; I am not permitted to write new things. I see that the former does not suit you, while I have no leisure for the latter.

For ever since I left you, I have had no opportunity and no leisure to examine and turn over the matters we usually investigate together. The winter nights are indeed exceedingly long, and I do not spend all of them asleep; but when I have leisure, they present matters that demand more thought, matters which require leisure in order to be resolved.

[Note: Lov. reads *definiendo* (“defining”); all the manuscripts we examined, along with one Vatican manuscript, read *diffirmando* (“refuting” or “resolving”).]

What, then, shall I do? Should I be mute or silent before you? You want neither, and I want neither. Come, then, and accept what the final part of the night, while it lasted, was able to draw out of me—the time during which this letter was written.

2. You must remember what has often been thrown about in conversation between us, and what has made us gasp and burn with eagerness: namely, the question of the soul’s perpetual body, or quasi-body,

[Note: Lov. reads *velut perpetuo* (“as though perpetual”) instead of *vel perpetuo* (“or perpetual”).] which, as you recall, some people also call its vehicle.

It is clear that this thing, if it moves from place to place, is not intelligible. Whatever is not intelligible cannot be understood.

But if something escapes the understanding while at least not escaping the senses, it is not altogether impossible to form some estimate of it with probability.

[Note: Lov. reads *verisimile* (“probable”); the manuscripts read *verisimiliter* (“with probability”).] What can neither be understood nor perceived by the senses, however, generates an excessively rash and foolish opinion; and the thing we are discussing is of this kind, if it exists at all.

Why, then, I ask you, do we not declare a holiday from this little question and, having prayed to God, raise our whole selves into the highest serenity of the highest living nature?

3. Perhaps you will say that, although bodies cannot be perceived, we can nevertheless perceive intelligibly many things pertaining to a body—for example, that we know that a body exists. Who could deny this, or who would admit that it is merely probable rather than true?

Thus, although the body itself is something probable, it is nevertheless most truly the case that something of this kind exists in nature. Therefore the sensible body is judged to exist, while “body” itself is intelligible; otherwise it could not be perceived.

In the same way, that body about which we are asking, upon which the soul is thought to rest so that it may pass from place to place, may be sensible to certain beings far more vigorous than our senses, even if it is not sensible to our own. Yet whether it exists may still be known intelligibly.

4. If you say this, let us recall that what we call understanding occurs in us in two ways: either inwardly, through the mind and reason themselves, as when we understand that understanding itself exists; or by an admonition from the senses, as in the case already mentioned, when we understand that a body exists.

In these two kinds, we understand the first through ourselves—that is, by consulting God concerning what is present within us—and the second, concerning what is announced by the body and by sense, nevertheless by consulting God.

If these points are sound, no one can understand whether that body exists unless some sense has reported something about it. If there is any living creature among those whose senses report this, we plainly see that we are not among them. I therefore think that the conclusion I began to state above is complete: this question does not concern us.

I wish you to think over these matters again and again, and to take care that I learn what your thinking has brought forth.

**EPISTLE XIV**  
[Note: We corrected this epistle against a., bl., bg., cb., g., gg., gv., n., r., sb., two copies of t, two of v, and Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]  
[Note: Formerly 115, second; what was 14 is now 72. Written at approximately the same time.]  
*Why the sun does not produce the same effect as the other heavenly bodies. Whether the highest truth contains the rational principle of every human being.*

**AUGUSTINE TO NEBRIDIUS**

1. I preferred to answer your most recent letters—not because I despised your earlier questions or found them less enjoyable, but because in replying I am undertaking greater things than you suppose.

Although you instructed me to send you a letter longer than the longest possible, we do not have as much leisure as you think, and as you know we have always desired and still desire. Do not ask why this is so; I could more easily explain the things that impede me than the reason why I am impeded.

2. You write asking why you and I, although each of us is an individual, do many of the same things, whereas the sun does not do what the other stars do. I would try to explain the reason for this.

For if we do the same things, it too does many things with the other stars; if it does not, neither do we. I walk and you walk; it moves and they move. I am awake and you are awake; it shines and they shine. I argue and you argue; it revolves and they revolve.

[Note: In Bad., Am., and Er., the remaining part of this epistle is confused with Epistle IX, with the words prefixed here removed. Nevertheless, two ancient Vatican manuscripts, the codex of the Gervasian College in Paris, the Corbeiensis manuscript of approximately nine hundred years, and other manuscripts of the highest quality, as well as Lov., present this entire epistle separately, as it is printed here.]

Yet the activity of the soul cannot in any way be compared with the things we see. If you compare soul with soul, as is proper, then the stars, if any soul is in them, should be considered more alike in thinking, contemplating, or whatever more suitable term may be used, than human beings are.

In bodily movements, however, if you pay close attention, as you customarily do, absolutely nothing can be done in exactly the same way by two people. When we walk together, do you really think that we immediately perform the same action? Far be that from your prudence.

The one of us who walks nearer the north must either move ahead of the other with an equal motion or proceed more slowly; yet neither difference can be perceived. But, unless I am mistaken, you are asking what we understand, not what we perceive.

If, moving from the north toward the south, we joined and adhered to one another as closely as we could, leaning upon smooth and level marble, or even upon ivory, our movement could no more be identical than the pulse of our veins, our form, or our face.

Remove us and put Glaucia’s offspring in our place.

[Note: Almost all manuscripts have *Clauciam prolem*, “Claucia’s offspring.”]

You will have accomplished nothing. Even in twins who resemble each other as closely as possible, there is as much necessity for each to move in his own way as there was for each to be born separately.

3. “But,” you will say, “this applies only to reason. The fact that the sun differs from the stars is also clear and manifest to the senses.”

If you force me to consider size, you know how much is said about distances and how uncertain this apparent clarity becomes. But even if I grant that things are as they appear—for I do believe that they are—whose sense, after all, was ever deceived by the stature of Naevius, a foot taller than the tallest six-foot man?

[Note: Bad., Am., and Er. have: “lest he be seven feet taller, although six is the greatest.” Lov. has: “lest he be taller by seven feet than those who are six feet tall.” The reading must undoubtedly be as we have corrected it from the manuscripts, although in them it is written in such a way that *ne vij nomen* might appear to mean “lest seven”; but our reading is confirmed by what the manuscripts prefer at the end of the epistle, *excessisse Naevium*, “that Naevius exceeded,” whereas the editions again corruptly read *excesserim veniam*.]

I believe that you searched too long for a man equal to him and, when you could not find one, wished to extend our letter all the way to his dimensions. Since something of this sort exists even on earth, I think nothing about heaven should be surprising.

But if it troubles you that, apart from the sun, the light of no heavenly body fills the day, who, I ask you, ever appeared as great among human beings as that human being whom God assumed—so unlike the other holy and wise people?

If you compare him with other wise men

[Note: Thus the two Vatican manuscripts: *hominibus* (“human beings”).]

the distance separating him is greater than the distance by which the sun surpasses the other stars.

Consider this likeness carefully. It may be that, through the intellectual power in which you excel, we have passed over and resolved a question you proposed concerning the human Christ.

4. You also ask whether that highest truth, highest wisdom, and form of things through which all things were made, whom our sacred faith proclaims to be the only Son of God, contains in general the rational principle of humanity or also that of each one of us individually.

A great question. But it seems to me that, insofar as it concerns the making of a human being, the rational principle there is that of humanity, not of me or of you individually; whereas, insofar as it concerns the temporal world, the various rational principles of human beings live within that purity.

Since this is extremely obscure, I do not know what likeness could illuminate it, unless perhaps we must turn to the arts that exist in our mind.

In the discipline of measurement, there is one principle of the angle and one of the square. Thus whenever I wish to demonstrate an angle, only one principle of the angle occurs to me. But I would not draw a square unless I contemplated simultaneously the principle of all four angles.

So each human being was made according to one principle, by which he is understood as human. But when a people is made, although there too there is one principle, it is not the principle of one human being but of human beings.

If, then, Nebridius is a part of this universe, as he is, and every universe consists of parts, the God who created the universe could not lack the rational principle of its parts.

Therefore, although the rational principle of many human beings exists there, it does not pertain to the individual human being, although in wondrous ways everything is again reduced to unity.

You will think this through more suitably yourself. For now, I ask you to be content with this, although I have already exceeded Naevius.

**EPISTLE XV**  
[Note: Collated against a., bl., cb., g., gg., gv., n., r., sb., two copies of t, two of v, and Lov.]  
[Note: Formerly 113; what was 15 is now 73. Written in 390.]  
*He announces that he has written a little work on religion, which is to be sent to Romanianus, and urges him to make good use of the leisure granted to him.*

**AUGUSTINE TO ROMANIANUS**

1. This letter does not reveal such a shortage of paper that it can at least testify to an abundance of parchment. I sent the ivory writing tablets I have to your uncle along with the letter.

You will more readily forgive this little sheet, because what I wrote to him could not be delayed, and I thought it exceedingly foolish not to write to you as well. But if any of our tablets are there, I ask you to send them, for needs of this kind.

I have written something on the Catholic religion, as much as the Lord has deigned to grant me. I want to send it to you before my arrival, if paper is not lacking in the meantime. You will tolerate whatever sort of writing comes from the workshop of the elders.

[Note: Seven manuscripts have “from the workshop of Majorinus”; the older editions give in the margin “from the workshop of my people.” Perhaps the text should be punctuated as follows: “from the workshop of the elders—from the books,” and so forth.]

As for the books, apart from the books *On the Orator*, the whole matter has escaped me. But I could write nothing more than that you should take whichever books you wished, and I remain of the same opinion now. In my absence I do not see what more I can do.

2. It gives me the greatest pleasure that, in your last letter, you wished to make me a participant in your domestic happiness. But:

> Do you bid me be ignorant of the face and quiet waves  
> of the tranquil sea?  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* V)

Although you do not bid me, nor are you yourself ignorant. Therefore, if some rest has been granted you for better thinking, make use of the divine gift.

For when such things come to us, we ought not to congratulate ourselves but those through whom they come, since a just, dutiful, and, according to its kind, more peaceful and tranquil administration of temporal affairs generates merit for receiving eternal things—provided it does not hold one captive when held, entangle one when multiplied, or wrap one up when it is pacified.

[Note: Nearly all the manuscripts read *putatur* (“is thought”); perhaps this stands for *portatur* (“is carried”).]

For the mouth of Truth itself said: “If you were not faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is yours?” (Luke 16:12).

Let us therefore loosen our cares for changing things, seek goods that are stable and sure, and soar above our earthly riches. Even when honey is plentiful, the little bee does not have wings for nothing; for it kills what clings to it.

**EPISTLE XVI**  
[Note: This epistle and XVII, addressed to Maximus, were reviewed against a., a., bl., bn., bg., c., cc., ff., g., gv., j., n., r., s., sb., t., two copies of vc., five of v, and Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]  
[Note: Formerly 43; what was 16 is now 74. Written perhaps around 390.]  
*Maximus, a grammarian of Madaura, excuses the pagans for worshiping one God under various names; expresses indignation that dead human beings are preferred to the gods of the nations; mocks certain Punic names; apparently reproaches the Christians for venerating the tombs of martyrs; and observes that they do not admit profane people to their sacred rites.*

**MAXIMUS OF MADAURA**  
[Note: In three manuscripts Maximus of Madaura is given the title “the Grammarian.”]  
**TO AUGUSTINE**
1. Eager to be gladdened frequently by your utterances, and, prompted by your speech—with which shortly before, while preserving our friendship, you most pleasantly challenged me—I have not ceased to return the favor, lest you should call my silence repentance. But I ask you, if you should regard these as, so to speak, the limbs of an old man, to treat them with the indulgence of kindly ears.

Greece, on uncertain faith, tells of Mount Olympus as the dwelling place of the gods. But we see and acknowledge that the forum of our city is occupied by a throng of saving divinities. Indeed, who is so mad, so deranged in mind, as to deny that there is one supreme God, without beginning, without offspring by nature, like a great and magnificent father? We invoke his powers, spread throughout the work of the universe, by many names, since evidently we all alike do not know his proper name. For “God” is a name common to all religions. Thus, while we pursue what are, as it were, certain parts of him piecemeal with various supplications, we seem, in fact, to worship him in his entirety.

2. But I cannot conceal my impatience with so great an error. Who could endure that Mygdon [Note: [Col. 0082] Twelve manuscripts have *Migginem*, and shortly afterward most have *Sanamen* instead of *Sanaem*; some also have *Namphamonem* instead of *Namphanionem*. Moreover, the martyr Namphanius is commemorated in the Roman Martyrology on July 4.] should be preferred to Jupiter wielding the thunderbolts, and Sanaes to Juno, Minerva, Venus, and Vesta, and—shameful to say!—the archmartyr Namphanio to all the immortal gods? Among these, Lucitas too is held in no lesser honor [Note: [Col. 0082] Five manuscripts have *suscipitur*, “is received.”], along with others whose number is without limit—names hateful to gods and men—which, conscious of unspeakable crimes, having heaped crime upon crime under the appearance of a glorious death, found for themselves, stained as they were, an end worthy of their character and deeds.

If it is worth mentioning, fools frequent their tombs, abandoning the temples and neglecting the spirits of their ancestors, so that the prophecy of that poet who indignantly complained stands out:

> And Rome swore by the shades in the temples of God.  
> (*Lucan*)

But to me, in this present age, the Actian War [Note: [Col. 0082] Eight manuscripts have: “The Actian War has broken out again.” Four Vatican manuscripts have *Asiaticum*, “Asian.” Other codices have *Actiacum*, “Actian.”] seems almost to have broken out again, in which Egyptian monsters dare to hurl weapons against the gods of Rome—though they will not endure for long.

3. But I ask you, most learned man, setting aside and rejecting the power of your eloquence, by which you are renowned among all, laying aside also the Chrysippean arguments with which you used to fight, and postponing for a little while the dialectic which, by the struggle of its sinews, tries to leave no certainty to anyone: prove by the matter itself who this God is whom you Christians claim as your own and whom you represent yourselves as seeing present in hidden places.

For we worship our gods openly, in the light of day, before the eyes and ears of all mortals, with pious prayers; by means of pleasing sacrifices we make them favorable to us; and we insist that all can see and approve this.

4. But I, an old and feeble man, now withdraw from this contest, and gladly adopt the judgment of the Mantuan rhetorician:

> Each person is drawn by his own pleasure.  
> (*Virgil, Eclogue 2*)

After this, illustrious man, I do not doubt that you, who have deserted my sect, will have this letter stolen away by someone and destroyed by fire or by some other means. If that happens, the loss will be to the little sheet of paper, not to our conversation, whose copy I shall preserve forever among all religious people.

May the gods preserve you, through whom all mortals whom the earth sustains worship and honor, in a thousand ways amid harmonious discord, the common father of those gods and of all mortals.

## LETTER XVII [Note: [Col. 0083] Formerly 44; the letter that was formerly 17 is now 39. Written at about the same time.]

Augustine replies to the foregoing letter of Maximus the grammarian, but in such a way as to show that its contents are unworthy of a reply and worthy of ridicule.

### TO MAXIMUS OF MADURA [Note: [Col. 0083] In three manuscripts Maximus is given the title “Maximus of Madura, Grammarian.”]

1. Are we engaged in something serious with one another, or do you wish to jest? For, judging from the way your letter speaks, I am uncertain whether it happened through the weakness of your case or through the courtesy of your character that you preferred to be more amusing than prepared.

First, you made a comparison between Mount Olympus and your forum. I do not know what purpose this served, unless it was to remind me that Jupiter established a camp on that mountain when he was waging war against his father, as the history teaches—the history which your people also call sacred—and to remind me that in that forum there are two statues, in one of which Mars is naked and in the other armed, and that their demon, most hostile to the citizens, is restrained by a human statue set opposite it, with three fingers extended.

Could I ever have believed, when you mentioned that forum, that you wished to renew for me the memory of such divinities, unless you preferred to jest rather than speak seriously? But regarding your statement that such gods are certain parts of one great God, I admonish you—since you deign to listen—to abstain most carefully from such sacrilegious jokes.

If you call that one God whom, as the ancients are said to have taught, learned and unlearned alike acknowledge, do you call these beings his parts, whose monstrousness—or, if you prefer, power—is restrained by the image of a dead man? I could say more on this subject. You see, in your wisdom, how broad a field for criticism lies open here. But I restrain myself, lest I be thought to be acting rhetorically rather than truthfully.

2. As for your collecting certain Punic names of the dead, with which you thought you could cast what seemed to you festive insults at our religion, I do not know whether I ought to refute you or pass over the matter in silence.

If these matters seem as trivial to your gravity as they actually are, I have little leisure for jesting. But if they seem serious to you, I am surprised that, being disturbed by the absurdity of the names, it did not occur to you that your own people have Eucaddires among their priests [Note: [Col. 0083] Several manuscripts have *Eucaddares*.] and Abaddires among their divinities. I do not think that, when you wrote these things, you failed to bear this in mind; rather, in keeping with your humanity and wit, you wished to remind us how much there is in your superstition that deserves laughter.

For you could not have forgotten yourself so completely that, as an African writing to Africans—for both of us live in Africa—you would think Punic names deserving of ridicule. If we interpret those names, what else does *Namphanio* mean than “a man of a good foot,” that is, one whose arrival brings some good fortune, just as we commonly say that someone “entered with the right foot” when prosperity followed his entrance?

[Col. 0084] If you disapprove of this language, deny that Punic books, as men of the greatest learning report, have committed many wise things to memory. Certainly you should regret having been born where the cradle of this language is still warm.

But if both the sound of the word does not reasonably displease us and you acknowledge that I have correctly interpreted it, you have reason to be angry with your Virgil, who invites your Hercules to the rites celebrated for him by Evander in these words:

> Come also, and with your right foot attend your rites.  
> (*Virgil, Aeneid VIII*)

He wishes Hercules to come with the right foot. Therefore he wishes Namphanio to come—the Namphanio whom you deign to insult us so greatly.

Yet if you enjoy laughter, you have among your own people abundant material for jokes: the god Stercutius, the goddess Cloacina, Venus Calva, the god Fear, the god Pallor, the goddess Fever, and countless other beings of this kind, for whom the ancient Romans, worshipers of statues, built temples and decreed that worship should be offered. If you disregard these, you disregard the Roman gods. From this it is clear that you have not been initiated into the Roman rites, and yet you despise and scorn Punic names [Note: [Col. 0084] Lov. has *numina*, “divinities,” but the manuscripts more correctly have *nomina*, “names.”] as though you were devoted to the altars of the Roman divinities [Note: [Col. 0084] So in eight manuscripts; *nimium*, “too much,” in another reading.].

3. But you seem to me altogether to attach perhaps even less value than we do to those rites, and to seek from them I know not what pleasure for the passage through this life. Indeed, you did not hesitate to take refuge in Maro, as you write, and to defend yourself with his verse:

> Each person is drawn by his own pleasure.  
> (*The same, Eclogue 3*)

For if you approve of Maro’s authority, as you indicate that you do, then surely you also approve of this:

> Saturn first came from heavenly Olympus,  
> Fleeing Jupiter’s weapons, an exile from his kingdom, now taken from him.  
> (*The same, Aeneid VIII*)

And the rest of the passage, by which he wishes it to be understood that Saturn and gods of this kind were human beings. For he had read a great deal of history strengthened by ancient authority [Note: [Col. 0084] Thus in fifteen manuscripts and in the older editions. Lov. has: “He had read Euhemerus’s history.”], which Cicero too had read; in his dialogues Cicero mentions this very matter more boldly than we might have dared to ask, and endeavors to bring it to human knowledge as far as those times permitted.

4. As for your statement that your rites are preferred to ours because you worship your gods publicly, whereas we use more secret assemblies: first I ask how you forgot that Liber is entrusted to the eyes of only a few initiates.

Then you yourself make clear that, when you mentioned the public celebration of your rites, you intended nothing other than to place before our eyes, as spectacles, the decurions and leading men of your city raging and running mad through the streets of your town. In that festival, if you are possessed by a divinity, surely you see what sort of thing it is that takes away the mind. But if you are pretending, what are these secrets of yours even in public, and what purpose does such shameful falsehood serve? And why, if you are prophets, do you sing no things to come? Or why, if you are sane, do you strip those standing around you?

[Col. 0085] 5. Since, through your letter, you have reminded us of these and other matters that I now think should be passed over, what is there that we should not ridicule in your gods? Anyone who knows your talent and has read your letters understands that you yourself subtly ridicule them.

Therefore, if you wish us to discuss these matters with one another in a way suitable to your age and wisdom—and, finally, in a way that our dearest friends may rightly demand from us regarding our purpose—seek something worthy of our discussion. Take care to speak on behalf of your divinities in such a way that we do not think you a betrayer of your case, reminding us more of what can be said against them than saying anything on their behalf.

In short, however, lest this escape you and draw you unwittingly into sacrilegious abuse, know that among Catholic Christians—whose church has also been established in your town—no dead person is worshiped, and nothing is adored as a divinity that has been made and created by God. They worship the one God himself, who made and created all things.

These matters will be discussed at greater length, with the help of the true and only God, when I learn that you wish to proceed seriously.

## LETTER XVIII [Note: [Col. 0085] This letter was collated against a. bl. cb. ff. g. gg. sb. th. gv. n. vc., two t. and two v. manuscripts, and against Am. Bad. Er. Lov.] [Note: [Col. 0085] Formerly 63; the letter that was formerly 18 is now 81. Written perhaps at about the same time.]

Three kinds of nature are briefly touched upon.

### AUGUSTINE TO CAELESTINUS

1. If only I could always say something to you! That “something” would be this: that we might strip ourselves of empty cares and clothe ourselves with useful cares. For I do not know whether anything secure should be hoped for in this world.

I wrote, but received no reply. I sent books against the Manichaeans, as prepared and corrected as I was able to send them, but I have received no indication of your judgment or response concerning them. Now it is appropriate that I should ask for them again and that you return them. I therefore ask you not to delay sending them back with a reply, by which I wish to know what you think of them, or what weapons you still believe you need in order to defeat that error.

2. Since I know you well, accept this grand yet brief thought. There is a nature that is changeable both with respect to place and with respect to time, like a body. There is a nature that is in no way changeable with respect to place, but is changeable only with respect to time, like a soul. And there is a nature that cannot be changed either with respect to place or with respect to time: this is God.

Whatever I have here suggested to be changeable in any way is called a creature; what is immutable is called the Creator. Since, however, whenever we say that something exists, we say it insofar as it remains, and since the form of every beauty is unity insofar as it is one, you surely see in this arrangement of natures what is highest, what is lowest, and nevertheless exists; and what is intermediate, greater than the lowest and less than the highest.

The highest is blessedness itself. The lowest is that which can be neither blessed nor miserable. The intermediate lives miserably when it inclines toward the lowest, but lives blessedly when it turns toward the highest. Whoever believes in Christ does not love the lowest, does not become proud in the intermediate, and thus becomes fit to cling to the highest. This is the whole of what we are commanded, admonished, and kindled to do.

## LETTER XIX [Note: [Col. 0086] Reviewed against a. bl. cb. ff. g. gg. gv. n. r. sb. th. vc., two t., two v. manuscripts, and against Am. Bad. Er. Lov.] [Note: [Col. 0086] Formerly 84; the letter that was formerly 19 is now 82. Written perhaps at about the same time.]

Augustine sends Gaius, whom he had perhaps drawn to the Church through discussion, his books to read, urging him to persevere in his good purpose.

### AUGUSTINE TO GAIUS [Note: [Col. 0086] Lov. writes *Caius*. The manuscripts and older editions have *Gaius*.]

1. After we left you, it cannot be said with what sweetness the recollection of you filled us, and often still fills us. We remember that, although the ardor of your inquiry was extraordinary, the modesty of your discussion was not disturbed. I could hardly find anyone who questioned more eagerly or listened more calmly.

I would therefore like to speak with you at length; for however long I spoke with you, it would not be long. But since this is difficult, what need is there to seek reasons? It is indeed difficult. Perhaps someday it will become very easy—God grant that it may—but for now it is otherwise.

Therefore I instructed the brother through whom I sent this letter to make all our writings available for your most prudent Charity to read. He will not force anything of mine upon you against your will. For I know the good will that you hold toward us. Yet if, after reading them, you approve them and perceive them to be true, do not think them ours merely because they were given to you; rather, turn to the source from which you were also given the ability to approve them.

No one sees that what he reads is true in the book itself or in the person who wrote it, but rather in himself—if a light, not ordinary but far removed from the dregs of the body, has impressed the truth upon his mind. If you discover anything false or unacceptable, know that it has been sprinkled with human cloudiness, and consider that genuinely ours.

I would urge you to seek, if I did not seem to see certain openings in your heart. I would also urge you to hold courageously what you have recognized as true, if you did not display the most evident strength of mind and judgment. For in a short time, with the coverings of the body almost laid open, everything living within you revealed itself to me.

Nor could the most merciful providence of our Lord in any way have permitted you, so good and so eminently intelligent a man, to remain separated from the Catholic flock of Christ.

## LETTER XX [Note: [Col. 0086] This was collated against the same codices, except r.] [Note: [Col. 0086] Formerly 126; the letter that was formerly 20 is now 233. Written at about the same time.]

Augustine thanks Antoninus for the good opinion and affection he has shown him, and wishes that his entire household may profess the Catholic religion.

### AUGUSTINE TO ANTONINUS [Note: [Col. 0086] Bad. Am. Er. write *Antonio*. Lov. and the better manuscripts have *Antonino*.]

1. Since letters were owed to you from two of us, you have received the greater part of the response in fullest measure, because you see one of us present; through his mouth, you also receive me. I might have refrained from replying, unless I had done so at his command, though, when he was departing, what I did seemed unnecessary.

For this reason I perhaps converse with you more fruitfully than if I were present in person, since you both read my letter and hear him in whose heart you know very well that I dwell.

I considered and pondered the letter of Your Holiness with great joy, because it displays your Christian spirit without any disguise prompted by these unjust times, and as most friendly toward us.

2. I congratulate you and give thanks to God and our Lord for your hope, faith, and charity, and for you before him, because you think so well of us as to believe that we are faithful servants of God, and because you love in us, with a most pure heart, that very quality.

Yet in this matter congratulations are due to your benevolence rather than thanks to you. For it benefits you to love goodness itself; and surely the person who loves someone whom he believes to be good loves goodness, whether that person is as he is believed to be or otherwise.

There is only one error to be avoided here: that someone should think differently about the good of a person—not about the person himself—than the truth requires. But you, dearest brother, who are in no way mistaken in believing or knowing that it is a great good to serve God willingly and chastely, when you love any human being for the reason that you believe him to share in this good, possess your reward even if he is not in fact such. Therefore you are to be congratulated on this account; but the other person is to be congratulated not merely if he is loved for that reason, but if he is actually what the one who loves him for that reason believes him to be.

What sort of people we are, and how far we have advanced toward God, let him see whose judgment cannot err, not only concerning the good of a person but concerning the person himself. For the reward of blessedness, so far as this matter is concerned, it is enough for you that, believing us to be such as God’s servants ought to be, you embrace us with the full breadth of your heart.

We give you abundant thanks because, when you praise us as though we were such, you wonderfully urge us to desire to be such. We give you still greater thanks if you not only commend yourself to our prayers but also do not fail to pray for us. Prayer offered to God for a brother is more pleasing when the sacrifice of charity is offered with it.

3. I greet your little one most warmly, and, in accordance with the Lord’s saving commandments, I wish him to grow. I also desire and pray that your entire household may come to possess the one true faith and devotion—which alone is Catholic.

If you think that any other service of ours may be necessary for this purpose, do not hesitate to claim it for yourself, relying both on our common Lord and on the right of charity.

I would also admonish your most religious prudence to instill or nourish in your weaker vessel a fear of God that is not irrational, through divine reading and serious conversation. For scarcely anyone is concerned about the state of his soul and, for that reason, intent without obstinacy on seeking the will of the Lord, who, with a good guide, fails to recognize the difference between any schism and the one Catholic Church.

## LETTER XXI [Note: [Col. 0088] For its correction we used manuscripts a. bl. c. cc. cb. ff. g. gg. gv. n. r. s. t. vc., three sb., four v., and Am. Bad. Er. Lov.] [Note: [Col. 0088] Formerly 148; the letter that was formerly 21 is now 234. Written at the beginning of 391.]

Augustine, ordained presbyter at Hippo, especially for administering the word of God, reflects on how difficult it is to act as a godly priest and beseeches Valerius to allow him to undertake this through prayer and study in retirement, so that he may be fit for the office imposed upon him.

[Col. 0088]

To the most blessed and venerable lord, sincerely and in the sight of the Lord most dearly loved father, Valerius the bishop: Augustine the presbyter sends greetings in the Lord.

1. Above all, I ask Your Religious Prudence to consider that nothing in this life, and especially at the present time, is easier, more pleasant, or more acceptable to people than the office of bishop, presbyter, or deacon, if the matter is handled superficially and flatteringly; but nothing is more miserable, sadder, or more liable to condemnation before God.

Likewise, nothing in this life, and especially at the present time, is more difficult, laborious, or dangerous than the office of bishop, presbyter, or deacon; but before God nothing is more blessed, if one serves in the manner commanded by our emperor.

But I learned what that manner is neither in childhood nor in adolescence. At the time when I was beginning to learn it, force was used against me—deservedly, because of my sins, for I do not know what else to think—and the second position at the helm was entrusted to me, although I did not know how to hold an oar.

2. But I think that my Lord wished to correct me in this way because, before I had experienced what is done there, I had dared, as though I were more learned and better, to criticize the sins of many sailors. Thus, after I had been sent into the midst of things, I began to feel the rashness of my criticisms, although even before that I had judged this ministry exceedingly dangerous.

This was the source of those tears which some brothers noticed me shedding in the city at the time of my ordination. Not knowing the causes of my grief, they nevertheless consoled me with whatever words they could, though those words had no relevance at all to my wound.

But I have experienced far, far more than I thought I would—not because I saw new waves or storms that I had not previously known, heard of, read about, or considered, but because I had no knowledge at all of my own skill and strength for avoiding or enduring them, although I had thought them of some importance. The Lord, however, mocked me and wished to show me to myself.

3. If he did this not by condemning me but by having mercy on me—and this is certainly what I hope—now that I have come to know my sickness, I ought to examine all the medicines of his Scriptures and, by praying and reading, strive to obtain sound health of soul sufficient for such dangerous affairs. I did not do this before, because I had no time.

I was ordained at the very time when we were considering using a period of leisure to learn the divine Scriptures and were planning to arrange matters so that we might have free time for this task. And, to speak truthfully, I did not yet know what I lacked for such work as now torments and crushes me.

If, therefore, I learned through the work itself what is necessary for a man who ministers the sacrament and word of God to the people, only to discover that I am no longer permitted to obtain what I have learned I lack, then you command me to perish, Father Valerius! Where is your charity? Surely you love me? Surely you love the Church itself, which you wished me to serve in this way? Yet I am certain that you love both me and the Church. But you think me fit, whereas I know myself better—although even I would not have known myself if experience had not taught me.

4. But perhaps Your Holiness will say: “I should like to know what is lacking in your instruction.” There is so much that I could more easily enumerate what I possess than what I desire to possess.

I would dare to say that I know and hold with full faith what pertains to our salvation. But how am I to minister this for the salvation of others, seeking not what is useful to me but what is useful to many, so that they may be saved?

Perhaps there are—or rather, there certainly are—counsels written in the holy Books by which, once they have been known and grasped, a man of God may minister more orderly in ecclesiastical affairs [Note: [Col. 0089] Thus Lov. Er. and the Gemmet manuscript have *et ordinationibus*, “and in ordinances.” Bad. and most manuscripts, without the conjunction, have *ecclesiasticis ordinationibus*, “in ecclesiastical ordinances.”], or at least, among the hands of wicked men, live with a sounder conscience or die in such a way that he does not lose that life for which alone humble and meek Christian hearts sigh.

But how can this be done except as the Lord himself says—by asking, seeking, and knocking; that is, by praying, reading, and grieving? For this task I wished through the brothers to obtain from your most sincere and venerable charity a short period of time, up to Easter, and now I wish to obtain it through this petition.

5. What will I answer the Lord my judge?

“I could not seek these things because I was hindered by ecclesiastical business.”

Suppose he then says to me:

“Wicked servant, if some slanderous person were laying claim to a farm belonging to the Church, whose produce requires great labor to gather, and if, neglecting the field that I watered with my blood, you could do something for it before an earthly judge, would you not go, with everyone agreeing and some even ordering and compelling you? And if judgment were given against you, would you not even travel across the sea? In this way no complaint would recall you from an absence of a year or more, lest another possess land necessary not to the soul but to the bodies of the poor—whose hunger, nevertheless, my living trees would satisfy much more easily and more pleasingly for me if they were carefully cultivated.

Why, then, do you claim that you lacked time to learn how to cultivate my field? Tell me, I beg you, what am I to answer?”

Or perhaps you want me to say:

“Old Valerius, believing that I was instructed in every matter, allowed me the less to learn these things, the more he loved me”?

6. Consider all this, old Valerius, I beseech you by the goodness and severity of Christ, by his mercy and judgment, and by him who inspired you with such charity toward us [Col. 0090] that we dare not offend you, even for the profit of our souls.

You make God and Christ witnesses to your innocence, charity, and sincere affection toward us as though I could not swear to all these things myself.

I therefore implore that very charity and affection: have mercy on me, grant me the amount of time I have requested for the purpose I have requested, assist me with your prayers, and do not let my desire be empty or my absence unfruitful for the Church of Christ, for the benefit of my brothers and fellow servants.

I know that the Lord will not despise that charity praying for me, especially in such a matter. Receiving it as an offering of sweetness, he may perhaps, in a shorter time than I have requested, return me instructed by the most salutary counsels of his Scriptures.

## LETTER XXII [Note: [Col. 0090] For its correction assistance was provided by cb. ff. gg. gv. n. r. t. vc., two sb., two v. manuscripts, and Am. Bad. Er. Lov.] [Note: [Col. 0090] Formerly 64; the letter that was formerly 22 is now 235. Written around 392.]

Augustine the presbyter, to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, lamenting that feasting and drunkenness are frequently practiced throughout Africa in cemeteries and at the memorials of martyrs under the pretext of religion; he earnestly begs him to remedy this evil. He also grieves that contention and the desire for human praise have not been banished from the clerical order itself.

### TO AURELIUS THE BISHOP, FROM AUGUSTINE THE PRESBYTER

## CHAPTER ONE.—After greeting Aurelius, he discusses the removal of feasting from the Church.

1. Since, after hesitating for a long time, I could not find how to reply to the letter of Your Holiness—for the affection of my heart overcame everything, and the reading of your letter stirred that affection, already spontaneously arising, much more ardently—I nevertheless entrusted myself to God, that he might work in me according to my strength, enabling me to write what would accord with our mutual zeal in the Lord and ecclesiastical concern, with your excellence and my obedience.

First, as for your belief that you are assisted by my prayers, I not only do not avoid this but gladly embrace it. Thus our Lord will hear me, if not because of my prayers, certainly because of yours.

You received with the greatest kindness the fact that our brother Alypius remained in our fellowship, so that he might be an example to brothers who desire to avoid the cares of this world. I give thanks in words that could never adequately express them. May the Lord repay this to your soul.

The whole assembly of brothers that has begun to grow together among us is therefore bound to you by such a great privilege that, although separated from us by the vast distances of the earth, you have cared for us as though you were present in spirit. Therefore we devote ourselves to prayer as much as we can, asking that the Lord deign to sustain with you the flock entrusted to you, never abandon you anywhere, but be present as your helper in times of need, showing mercy with his Church through your priesthood—such mercy as spiritual men entreat him with tears and groans to grant.

[Col. 0091] 2. Know, therefore, most blessed lord and venerable man of fullest charity, that we do not despair; indeed, we strongly hope that our Lord and God, through the authority of the office you hold—which we trust has been imposed not upon your flesh but upon your spirit—may heal, by the gravity of your counsel [Note: [Col. 0091] Several manuscripts have *consiliorum gravi esse*, “to be serious in counsel.” Others have *consiliorum gravitate*, “by the gravity of counsel.” Perhaps *conciliorum*, “of councils,” should be read.], many carnal foulnesses and diseases from which the African Church suffers in many of its members and laments in a few.

When the Apostle, in one place, briefly set down three kinds of vices to be detested and avoided, from which a harvest of innumerable vices arises, one of these—the one he placed second—is punished with the utmost severity in the Church. The other two, however, that is, the first and the last, seem tolerable to people, and so it may gradually happen that they are no longer even considered vices.

For the chosen vessel says:

> Not in revelries and drunkenness, not in beds and sexual immorality, not in contention and deceit; but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh in its desires.  
> *(Romans 13:13–14)*

3. Of these three, beds and sexual immorality are considered so great a crime that no one who has stained himself with this sin seems worthy not only of ecclesiastical ministry but even of communion in the sacraments [Note: [Col. 0091] Four manuscripts have *maculaverit*, “has stained himself.” This is preferable.], and entirely rightly.

But why only this? Feasting and drunkenness are thought so permitted and lawful that they are celebrated even in honor of the most blessed martyrs—not only on solemn days, which surely anyone who does not view these things with merely fleshly eyes must consider lamentable, but also every day.

If this foulness were merely scandalous and not also sacrilegious, we would think that it should be endured by every possible means of forbearance. Yet what of the statement that, after listing many vices, among them drunkenness, the same Apostle concluded by saying that we should not even eat bread with such people? (1 Corinthians 5:11).

Let us tolerate these things amid domestic luxury and corruption, and let us accept the body of Christ with those with whom we are forbidden to eat bread. But at least let such disgrace be kept away from the tombs of holy bodies, from places of the sacraments, and from houses of prayer. For who dares forbid privately what, when practiced in holy places, is called an honor paid to the martyrs?

4. If Africa were the first, in contrast to the other lands, to attempt to remove this practice, it ought to be worthy of imitation. But when throughout most of Italy, and in all or nearly all the churches overseas, such practices have either never existed or, having arisen or become deeply established, have been extinguished and erased through the diligence and discipline of holy bishops who truly think about the life to come, how can we hope to correct so great a corruption of morals by so widely established an example [Note: [Col. 0091] So in the manuscripts; *lato*, “broad,” in another reading.]?

We do have a bishop from those regions, for which we give great thanks [Col. 0092] to God. His modesty and gentleness, and finally his prudence and concern in the Lord, are such that even if he were an African, he would quickly be persuaded from the Scriptures that the wound inflicted by a permissive and badly unrestrained custom must be treated.

But the plague of this evil is so great that, as it seems to me, it cannot be healed except by the authority of a council. Or, if the remedy must begin with one church, just as it seems audacious to attempt to change what the Church of Carthage maintains, so it is a great impudence to wish to preserve what the Church of Carthage has corrected.

For this task, what other bishop could be desired except one who, when he was a deacon, used to execrate these practices? [Note: [Col. 0092] Aurelius was made bishop of the Church of Carthage perhaps in 391, certainly not before 390; for in that year his predecessor Genethlius presided over the Second Council of Carthage. The Council of Hippo was held under Aurelius in 393.]

5. But what was then to be lamented must now be removed—not harshly, but as it is written, in a spirit of gentleness and meekness (Galatians 6:1). For the letters that bear witness to your genuine charity give me confidence to dare speak with you as with myself.

These things should therefore be removed, as I think, neither harshly, nor sternly, nor in a merely authoritative manner, but more by teaching than by commanding, more by admonishing than by threatening. For this is how one must deal with the multitude; severity, however, must be exercised against the sins of the few.

And if we threaten anything, let it be done with grief: let us threaten punishment from the Scriptures, so that it is not we ourselves who are feared in our own authority, but God who is feared in our speech [Note: [Col. 0092] Augustine conducted himself in this way, as may be seen in Letter 29.].

In this way the spiritual, or those close to the spiritual, will first be moved, and through their authority the rest of the multitude will be broken by admonitions that are indeed gentle but most persistent.

6. But since these drunken revels and luxurious banquets in the cemeteries are accustomed to be regarded by the carnal and uninstructed populace not only as honors paid to the martyrs, but also as consolations for the dead, it seems to me that this disgrace and depravity could more easily be discouraged there [Note: [Col. 0092] Seven manuscripts read *illis* (“those”); others, *illic* (“there”).] if it were prohibited both by the Scriptures and if offerings for the spirits of the sleeping—which must truly be believed to help in some way—were not sumptuous at the memorials themselves, but were supplied to all who ask, without arrogance [Note: [Col. 0092] One manuscript has *typo* (“with a mistake”).], and with cheerful willingness.
