Nor should they be sold; rather, if anyone wishes to offer some money out of religious devotion, let him distribute it at once to the poor [Note: [Col. 0092] Two manuscripts have *erogetur* (“let it be distributed”); others have *eroget* (“let him distribute it”).]. Thus they will not seem to be abandoning the memorials of their relatives—a practice that can generate no slight grief of heart—and what is celebrated in the Church will be celebrated piously and honorably. Let this suffice for the present concerning feasting and drunkenness.

## CHAPTER II  
### On Contention and the Desire for Praise: How Honor and Praise Should Be Accepted by Prelates

7. But why should I speak of contention and deceit, when these vices are more serious not among the common people but among our own number? The mother of these maladies is pride and eagerness for human praise, which also often produces hypocrisy. It cannot be resisted unless fear and love of God are instilled through frequent testimonies from the divine Books—provided that the one who does this offers himself as an example of patience and humility, taking less for himself than is offered; yet neither accepting everything nor nothing from those who honor him, and accepting whatever praise or honor is received not on his own account—for he ought to be wholly before God and to despise human things—but on account of those for whose benefit he cannot act if he becomes worthless through excessive abasement. To this belongs what was said: “Let no one despise your youth” (1 Tim. 4:12), although the one who said this also says elsewhere: “If I still pleased human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. 1:10).

8. It is a great thing not to rejoice in human honors and praises, but also to cut off every empty display, and, if anything necessary is retained from it, to devote the whole of it to the benefit and salvation of those who bestow the honor. For it was not said without reason: “God will break the bones of those who wish to please human beings” (Ps. 52:6). What is more feeble, what so lacking in stability and strength—qualities signified by bones—than a person whom the tongue of malicious speakers weakens, even though he knows that what is said is false? The pain of this matter would in no way tear apart the innermost parts of the soul if love of praise did not break its bones.

I presume upon the strength of your spirit; and so, what I discuss with you I say to myself. Nevertheless, I believe that you are willing to consider with me how serious and difficult these things are. No one feels the power of this enemy except one who has declared war against him. For although it is easy for anyone to lack praise when it is withheld, it is difficult not to take pleasure in it when it is offered. Yet the mind must be so suspended upon God that, if we are praised without deserving it, we correct those whom we can, lest they suppose either that what is not in us is in us, or that what belongs to God belongs to us, or lest they praise things which, even if they are not lacking in us—or even abound in us—are nevertheless not praiseworthy, such as all the goods that we share either with animals or with ungodly people.

But if we are rightly praised because of God, let us rejoice for those who take pleasure in the true good—not for ourselves because we please human beings, but if before God we are such as they believe us to be. And let the credit be given not to us but to God, whose gifts are all the things that are truly and deservedly praised.

I sing these things to myself every day—or rather, he sings them whose saving precepts they are, whether they are found in the divine Readings or are suggested inwardly to the soul. Yet while fighting vigorously with the adversary, I often receive wounds from him, since I cannot keep myself from taking pleasure in offered praise.

9. I have written these things so that, even if they are no longer necessary for Your Holiness—either because you yourself consider many things of this kind, and more useful ones, or because this medicine is not needed by Your Holiness—my evils may nevertheless be known to you, and you may know how to pray to God for me in my weakness. I beg you to do this with the greatest earnestness, by the humanity of him who gave the command that we should bear one another’s burdens.

There are many things concerning our life and conduct that I would lament, which I would not wish to come to you by letter [Col. 0094] if there were any means [Note: [Col. 0094] Am., Bad., and three manuscripts read *nulla* (“no”); others, *ulla* (“any”).] between my heart and yours other than my mouth and your ears. But if the venerable Saturninus [Note: [Col. 0094] We do not know whether this is the same man who is praised in *The City of God*, book 22, chapter 8, as “Saturninus of blessed memory, once bishop of Uzalum,” whom Augustine evidently saw at Carthage together with Aurelius in 388.]—dear to us and to all of us with complete sincerity, whose truly brotherly kindness and devotion toward you I observed when I was present—should deign to come to us when it seems opportune, whatever we may be able to discuss with His Holiness in spiritual affection will differ little, if at all, from what we would discuss with Your Dignity.

I beg you with prayers for which no words suffice to ask and obtain this from him together with us. For the Hipponians fear my absence so intensely and excessively that they are in no way willing to trust me in such a manner that I might see the field which, as we learned through our holy brother and fellow servant Parthenius, had been given to the brothers through your foresight and generosity even before your letter—Parthenius from whom we heard many other things that we desired to hear. The Lord will grant that the other things we still desire may also be fulfilled.

---

## LETTER XXIII [Note: [Col. 0094] Compared with manuscripts and editions designated a, bg, c, cc, cb, ff, g, gg, gv, j, n, r, s, two bn manuscripts, two sb manuscripts, two t manuscripts, two vc manuscripts, four v manuscripts, and with Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.] [Note: [Col. 0094] In other enumerations, Letter 203; the letter that was formerly numbered 23 is now 98. Written at approximately the same time.]

Augustine to Maximinus, a Donatist bishop who was said to have rebaptized a Catholic deacon, inviting him either to acknowledge the deed or to declare himself orthodox, and inviting him either to a conference or to write back, so that the unity of the Church might be repaired.

To the most beloved and honorable brother MAXIMINUS [Note: [Col. 0094] In the Gervasian manuscript and five others, *Maximianus* is written; in the Corbie manuscript, *Macrovius*. Maximinus was then a Donatist bishop of Siniti, near Hippo; later he embraced Catholic peace and, according to Letter 105, remained in the same see. Augustine speaks of him honorably in *The City of God*, book 22, chapter 8.], AUGUSTINE, presbyter of the Catholic Church, sends greetings in the Lord.

### 1

Before I come to the matter about which I wished to write to Your Benevolence, I shall briefly explain the reason for the title of this letter, lest it disturb either you or anyone else.

I wrote “Lord” because it is written: “You were called to freedom, brothers; only do not use freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another” (Gal. 5:13). Since, then, even by this service of writing I serve you through love, I do not improperly call you “lord,” on account of our one and true Lord, who commanded these things of us.

As for my writing “most beloved,” God knows that I not only love you, but love you as I love myself, since I am well aware that I wish for you the good things that I wish for myself.

As for the word “honorable,” I added it not in order to honor your episcopate. You are not a bishop to me—and do not take this as an insult—but I speak from the disposition that ought to be in our mouth: “Yes, yes; no, no.” Neither are you ignorant, nor is anyone who knows us ignorant, that you are not my bishop and I am not your presbyter.

I therefore gladly call you honorable according to the standard by which I know you to be a human being. I know that the human being was made in the image and likeness of God and was placed in honor by the very order and law of nature—provided that, by understanding what ought to be understood, he preserves his honor. For it is written: “The human being, when placed in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless animals and became like them” (Ps. 48:21).

Why, then, should I not call you honorable insofar as you are a human being, especially since, as long as you are in this life, I dare not despair of your salvation and correction?

As for calling you “brother,” you are not unaware that we have received a divine command to say even to those who deny that they are our brothers, “You are our brothers.” This bears strongly upon the matter for which I wished to write to Your Fraternity. Now that I have explained why I gave the letter such an opening, listen with complete calm to what follows.

### 2

When, in this region, I was lamenting and deploring the custom of people who boast of the Christian name yet do not hesitate to rebaptize Christians, there were some who praised you and told me that you did not do this. I confess that at first I did not believe them.

Then, considering that it might happen that fear of God would seize a human soul reflecting upon the life to come, so that it would refrain from an utterly manifest crime, I rejoiced and believed it, thinking that by such a resolve you had chosen not to be excessively alienated from the Catholic Church.

I was indeed seeking an opportunity to speak with you, so that, if possible, the small disagreement that remained between us might be removed. But behold, a few days ago it was reported that you had rebaptized our deacon from Mutugenna. I was deeply grieved both by his pitiable fall and by your unexpected crime, brother.

For I know what the Catholic Church is. “The nations are Christ’s inheritance, and the ends of the earth are Christ’s possession.” You know this too—or, if you do not know it, take notice; it can very easily be learned by those who wish to know.

To rebaptize a heretical person who has received those holy signs that Christian discipline has handed down is certainly a sin; but to rebaptize a Catholic is a monstrous crime.

Nevertheless, since I did not believe it so readily—for I had formed a favorable opinion of you—I myself went to Mutugenna. I could not see that wretched man, but I heard from his parents that he had now also become your deacon. And yet I still think so well of your heart that I do not believe he was rebaptized.

### 3

Therefore, most beloved brother, I beseech you by the divinity and humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ to deign to write back to me concerning what happened, and to write in such a way that you know I intend to read your letter aloud to our brothers in the Church.

I have written this so that, if afterward I should do what you did not expect me to do, I would not offend Your Charity, and you would not lodge a justified complaint against me with our mutual friends.

I do not see what prevents you from writing back. If you do rebaptize, there is no reason for you to fear the people of your fellowship, since you will have written back that you do what they would order you to do even if you were unwilling. And when you defend, with as much evidence as you can, that this ought to be done, they will not merely refrain from being angry; they will even praise you.

But if you do not rebaptize, seize Christian freedom, brother Maximinus—seize it, I beg you. In contemplation of Christ, do not fear anyone’s reproach or shrink from anyone’s power. The honor of this age passes away; ambition passes away.

At Christ’s future judgment, neither stepped platforms nor veiled chairs nor crowds of nuns coming forward and singing will be brought forward in defense, when consciences begin to accuse and the judge of consciences begins to judge. What honors us here burdens us there; what lifts us up here weighs us down there. Those things that, for the time being and for the benefit of the Church, are offered to our honor may perhaps be defended by a good conscience; but they will not be able to defend a bad one.

If, then, you act with such a pious and religious disposition—if indeed you do so—that you do not repeat the baptism of the Catholic Church but rather approve it as belonging to the one true mother, who offers her bosom to all nations for regeneration and pours out her milk upon the regenerated; as belonging to the one possession of Christ, extending itself to the ends of the earth—if you truly do this, why do you not burst forth in a joyful and free declaration?

Why do you press the useful brightness of your lamp beneath a bushel? Why do you not tear apart and cast away the old skins of timid servitude, put on Christian confidence instead, come forth, and say:

“I know one baptism, consecrated and sealed in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Wherever I find this form, I must approve it. I do not destroy what I recognize as the Lord’s; I do not spit upon the standard of my King.”

Even those who divided Christ’s garment did not tear it (John 19:24); and at that time they still believed that Christ would not rise again, but saw him dying. If the garment of the one hanging on the cross was not torn by persecutors, why is the sacrament of the one seated in heaven destroyed by Christians?

If I had been a Jew in the days of the ancient people, when I could not have had anything better, I would certainly have accepted circumcision. That seal of the righteousness of faith had such force at that time, before it was annulled by the Lord’s coming, that the Angel would have strangled Moses’ infant son unless his mother had seized a knife, circumcised the child, and by this sacrament driven away the impending destruction (Exod. 4:24–25).

This sacrament also restrained the Jordan River and turned it back toward its source. The Lord himself, although he annulled it when crucified, nevertheless received it when he was born. For those seals were not condemned; they passed away when more suitable ones succeeded them.

Just as the Lord’s first coming removed circumcision, so his second coming will remove baptism. For just as now, after freedom of faith has come and the yoke of servitude has been removed, no Christian is circumcised in the flesh, so then, when the righteous reign with the Lord and the ungodly have been condemned, no one will be baptized. Rather, what these things prefigure—that is, circumcision of the heart and purity of conscience—will remain forever.

If, then, I had been a Jew at that time, and a Samaritan had come to me wishing, after abandoning the error that the Lord himself rejected by saying, “You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, because salvation is from the Jews” (John 4:22), to become a Jew—the Samaritan whom the Samaritans had circumcised—there would certainly have been no occasion for the audacity of repetition. We would have been compelled not to repeat but to approve what had been done among heretics and what God had commanded.

And if, in a circumcised person’s flesh, I could not find a place where I might repeat circumcision, because there is only one such member, much less can a place be found in one heart where Christ’s baptism may be repeated. Therefore, you who wish to duplicate baptism must necessarily seek double hearts.

### 5

So declare openly that you are right to do so if you do not rebaptize, and write back to me about it not only without hesitation but also with joy. Let none of your councils terrify you, brother.

For if they are displeased by this, they are not worthy to have you; but if they are pleased, we trust in the mercy of the Lord—who never abandons those who fear displeasing him and strive to please him—that peace between you and us will soon exist. Otherwise, because of our honors, for which we shall have to render an account as for a dangerous burden, wretched common people who believe in Christ may have common food in their homes but be unable to have Christ’s common table.

Do we not groan that a husband and wife, in order faithfully to join their bodies, often swear to each other by Christ, yet tear apart Christ’s own body by differing communion?

If, through your modesty, prudence, and love for him who shed his blood for us, this scandal—this great triumph of the devil, this great destruction of souls—were removed from these regions, who could put into words the crown the Lord would prepare for you, so that from you might proceed an example of healing worthy of imitation for the healing of the other members that lie miserably diseased throughout Africa?

How I fear—for you cannot see my heart—that I may seem to be speaking to you more in mockery than in love! But certainly I find nothing more I can do except offer you my words for inspection, and my spirit to God.

### 6

Let us remove from our midst the empty accusations that the uninstructed parties are accustomed to hurl against one another. Do not bring up the times of Macarius, and I will not bring up the violence of the Circumcellions. If the former does not concern you, neither does the latter concern me.

The Lord’s threshing floor has not yet been winnowed; it cannot be without straw. Let us pray and act as much as we can so that we may be grain.

I cannot remain silent about our rebaptized deacon, for I know how harmful silence would be for me. I do not intend to pass my time amid ecclesiastical honors, blown about by the wind; I intend to render an account to the chief Shepherd of all for the sheep entrusted to me.

If perhaps you did not want me to write these things to you, brother, you ought to forgive my fear. I am very much afraid that, if I remain silent and pretend not to notice, others among you will also be rebaptized.

Therefore I have resolved, insofar as the Lord grants strength and opportunity, to conduct this matter in such a way that, through peaceful conferences between us, all who communicate with us may know how far the Catholic Church differs from heresies and schisms, and how greatly they must beware of the destruction represented either by weeds or by branches cut off from the Lord’s vine.

If you willingly undertake such a conference with me, so that the letters of both of us may be read to the people in agreement, I shall rejoice with unspeakable joy. But if you do not accept this with equanimity, what am I to do, brother, except read our letters to the Catholic people even against your will, so that they may be better instructed?

And if you do not deign to write back, I have decided to read my own letters, so that at least, once your distrust is known, they may be ashamed to rebaptize.

### 7

I will not do this while the soldier is present, lest any of you think that I wished to act more tumultuously than the cause of peace requires. I will do it after the soldier’s departure, so that all who hear us may understand that my purpose is not to compel unwilling people to join anyone’s communion, but to make the truth known as quietly as possible to those who seek it.

Let the terror of temporal powers cease on our side; let the terror of assembled Circumcellions also cease on your side. Let us conduct the matter by fact, by reason, and by the authority of the divine Scriptures. Let us ask, seek, and knock as quietly and peacefully as we can, so that we may receive and find, and that it may be opened to us, lest perhaps it prove possible that, with the Lord’s help and through our united efforts and prayers, so great a deformity and impiety in the regions of Africa may begin to be abolished from our lands [Note: [Col. 0098] This is the reading of all editions, but it is obscure. Perhaps *ne* should be read as *an* or *num* (“whether”).].

If you do not believe that I intend to act after the soldiers’ departure, then write back after the soldiers’ departure. For if I wish to read my letters to the people while the soldier is present, my published letter will show that I am a violator of faith. May the Lord’s mercy avert this from my character and purpose—the purpose he has deigned to inspire in me through his yoke.

### 8

My bishop might perhaps have written to Your Benevolence himself if he had been present, or I might have written either at his command or with his permission. But since he is absent, and the rebaptism of the deacon is said to be recent, I did not allow the action itself to grow cold through delay. I was roused by the sharpest goads of grief over a brother’s true and spiritual death.

With the help of the Lord’s mercy and providence, some compensation of peace may perhaps soften this grief of mine. May our God and Lord deign to inspire in you a peaceful mind, most beloved and honorable brother.

---

## LETTER XXIV [Note: [Col. 0098] Compared with manuscripts and editions designated a, bn, bg, cc, ff, g, gv, j, l, n, r, s, sb, t, vc, vd, two a manuscripts, four v manuscripts, and with Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.] [Note: [Col. 0098] In other enumerations, Letter 35; the letter formerly numbered 24 is now 201. Written near the end of 394, before winter.]

Paulinus to Alypius, concerning the books of Augustine that he received, apologizing for having sent Eusebius’ *Chronicle* to him late. He wishes to be informed about Alypius’ family and life, while in turn revealing some things about himself. He sends him one loaf as a gift.

To the deservedly honorable and most blessed father ALYPIUS, PAULINUS and THERASIA, sinners.

### 1

This is true charity; this is perfect love, which you have shown to exist toward our humility, truly holy lord, deservedly most blessed and greatly desired.

For, through our man Julianus, returning from Carthage, we received a letter bringing us so great a light from Your Holiness that we seemed not to recognize but to recognize anew your charity. For this charity flowed from the one who predestined us for himself from the foundation of the world, in whom we were made before we were born, because “he made us, and not we ourselves” (Ps. 99:3)—he who made the things that are to come.

Formed, therefore, by his foreknowledge and work into likeness of wills and unity of faith—or into the faith of unity—and joined together by charity preceding acquaintance, we came to know one another through the revealing Spirit before we came into bodily sight.

Therefore we rejoice and glory in the Lord, who, one and the same throughout the whole world, works his love in his own through the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon all flesh, making his city glad with the rushing of a river. Among the citizens of this city, he has deservedly placed you in a leading position, among the princes of his people, in the apostolic seat. He also wished us—those whom he raised when broken down and lifted from the earth in our poverty—to be numbered in your portion.

But we rejoice even more in that gift of the Lord by which he established us in the dwelling place of your heart, and by which he has deigned to introduce us so deeply into your innermost being that we may claim a special confidence in your charity. We have been summoned by such services and gifts that we cannot love you timidly or lightly.

### 2

For we have received a distinguished and exceptional token of your love and concern: a work of the holy and perfect man in Christ, our brother Augustine, composed in five books. We admire and revere it so greatly that we believe its words were dictated by God.

Thus, trusting that we might receive your fellowship, we have dared to write to him as well, presuming that through you we might both be excused to him for our lack of learning and be commended to his charity. We presume that you will care with equal affection for all the saints as well, whose services, even in absence, you have deigned to secure for us, so that through Your Holiness they may exchange mutual greetings and courtesies—your companions in the clergy and imitators of your faith and virtue in the monasteries.

For although you act among the people and over the people, guiding the sheep of the Lord’s pasture with the vigilant watchfulness of a careful shepherd, yet through renunciation of the world and rejection of flesh and blood you have yourself made a desert, withdrawn from the many and called among the few.

### 3

As a kind of substitute, though unequal to you in every respect, I have, as you ordered, procured the history of all times by the venerable bishop Eusebius of Constantinople. The delay in obeying you arose because, following your direction, I found in Rome, since I did not possess this codex myself, a copy with our truly holy father Domnio. Without doubt he complied with me more readily in this service because I told him that it was to be conveyed to you [Note: [Col. 0099] The editions read: “which he judged should be conveyed to you.” Two v manuscripts have *judicavi* (“I judged”); two other v manuscripts, together with thirteen of ours, have *indicavi* (“I indicated”).].

Nevertheless, since you also deigned to indicate your whereabouts to me, as you yourself had requested, we wrote to the venerable partner of your crown, our father Aurelius, asking that, if you were then staying at Hippo Regius, he would deign to send you our letter and the parchment copied at Carthage.

We also asked the holy men, the Count and Evodius—whom through your letter we had recognized as tokens of their charity—to arrange this themselves, so that the codex might not remain away from our father Domnio for too long or, once sent to you, remain with you without need of being returned.

### 4

In particular, I ask this of you because you have filled me, undeserving and unprepared, with such great love for you: tell me, concerning this history of the ages, the whole history of Your Holiness. Explain to me your family, your origin, where your home was, how, so greatly called by the Lord, you were separated from your mother’s womb and, after renouncing the stock of flesh and blood, passed over to the mother rejoicing in the offspring of God’s children, and how you were transferred into a royal and priestly lineage.

You indicated that you had already learned at Milan, when you were initiated there, something about the name of our humility. I confess that I wish to learn more fully, so that I may know you in every respect and rejoice the more if, through being received by our father Ambrose, you were either invited to the faith or consecrated to the priesthood, so that we may both appear to have him as our guide.

For although I was baptized by Delphinus at Bordeaux and consecrated by Lampius at Barcelona in Spain amid the sudden violence of an inflamed crowd, I have nevertheless always been nourished in the faith by love for Ambrose, and now I am cherished in the order of the priesthood. Finally, he wished to claim me for his clergy, so that, although I live in different places, I might be reckoned his presbyter.

### 5

But so that you may know nothing about me only incompletely, know that I am an ancient sinner, not long ago brought out of darkness and the shadow of death, and that I have only recently drawn the breath of life-giving air. I have only recently placed my hand upon the plow and taken up the Lord’s cross. Help me with your prayers, so that we may be able to carry it through to the end.

This reward will be added to your merits if, through your intercession, you lighten our burdens. For the holy person who helps one who is laboring—for we do not dare to call you “brother”—will be exalted like a great city.

And you are indeed a city built upon a mountain, or a lamp lit upon a lampstand, shining with sevenfold brightness. We lie hidden beneath the bushel of sins. Visit us by your letters and bring us into the light in which you yourself dwell, conspicuous upon golden lampstands.

Your words will be a light for our paths, and our head will be enriched with the oil of your lamp. Faith will be kindled when, through the spirit of your mouth, we receive food for the mind and light for the soul.

### 6

May the peace and grace of God be with you, and may the crown of righteousness remain for you on that day, lord and father, deservedly most beloved, venerable, and greatly desired.

We earnestly and respectfully ask you to greet, with great affection and devotion, the blessed companions and fellow imitators of Your Holiness—our brothers in the Lord—if they deign to regard us as their brothers, both in the churches and monasteries of Carthage, Thagaste, and Hippo Regius, throughout all your parishes, and in all the places in Africa known to you where they serve the Lord in the Catholic faith.

If you receive the parchment of the holy Domnio, please deign to send us a copy. And I ask you to write to me which hymn of mine you have come to know.

We have sent one loaf to Your Holiness as a sign of unity; in it is also contained the solidity of the Trinity. You will make this bread an *eulogia*—a blessing—by deigning to partake of it.

---

## LETTER XXV [Note: [Col. 0101] Compared with manuscripts and editions designated a, bg, bl, bn, c, cc, ff, g, gv, j, r, s, sb, vc, vd, two a manuscripts, five v manuscripts, and with Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.] [Note: [Col. 0101] In other enumerations, Letter 31; the letter formerly numbered 25 is now 195. Written at the same time as the preceding letter.]

Paulinus to Augustine, adorning him with elaborate praises for his five books against the Manichaeans, which he had received from Alypius. He sends him a loaf as a gift.

[Col. 0101]

To his united and venerable brother AUGUSTINE, PAULINUS and THERASIA, sinners.

### 1

The charity of Christ, which presses upon us and binds us together even when absent through the unity of faith, itself gave me confidence to write to you after dispelling my shame. Through your letters it has brought you into the innermost parts of my heart. Those letters, rich in scholastic learning and sweet as heavenly honeycombs, I now hold in five books as physicians and nourishers of my soul. We received them as a gift from our blessed and venerable bishop Alypius, not only for our instruction but also for the benefit of the Church in many cities.

I now have these books in hand for reading; in them I delight; from them I receive food—not the food that perishes, but that which, through our faith by which we are incorporated into Christ Jesus our Lord, produces the substance of eternal life. Our faith, which disregards visible things and longs for invisible ones, is strengthened by letters and by the examples of the faithful, believing all things according to the truth of almighty God through love.

O true salt of the earth, by which our innermost hearts are seasoned so that they cannot waste away in the vanity of the world’s error! O lamp worthy to be placed upon the lampstand of the Church, which, nourished by the oil of joy and shining from a seven-branched lamp, pours light broadly over Catholic cities, scatters the dense darknesses of heretics, and by the radiance of splendid speech clears the light of truth from the clouds of confusion and darkness!

### 2

Do you see, united brother, admirable in Christ the Lord and worthy of reception, how familiarly I have come to know you, with what astonishment I admire you, and with how great a love I embrace you? Every day I enjoy conversation with your letters and feed upon the spirit of your mouth.

I would rightly call your mouth a channel of living water and a vein of the eternal fountain, because Christ has become in you “a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4:14) [Note: [Col. 0101] This is the reading of twelve manuscripts. The editions have: “because Christ is the fountain of the water of life.”].

My soul has thirsted for him in you, and my land has longed to be intoxicated by the abundance of your stream.

Therefore, since with this Pentateuch of yours you have sufficiently armed me against the Manichaeans, if you have also prepared defenses against other enemies of the Catholic faith—for our enemy, who has a thousand arts of causing harm, must be attacked with as many weapons as he employs stratagems—I ask you to draw weapons of righteousness for me from your armory and not refuse to supply them.

For I am a laborer, even now a sinner under a great burden [Note: [Col. 0101] Seven manuscripts have “under great honor, a sinner.” One Vatican manuscript has “under a burden of sins.”], long-serving among the ranks of sinners but a new recruit in the body of the eternal King.

Until now, miserable man that I was, I admired the wisdom of the world, and through useless writings and condemned prudence I was foolish and mute before God. After growing old among my enemies and wasting away in my thoughts, I lifted my eyes to the mountains, looking toward the precepts of the law and the gifts of grace. From there came my help from the Lord, who, not repaying according to my iniquities, enlightened the blind, released the chained, humbled the person wrongly raised up, so that he might raise up the one humbly brought low.

### 3

Therefore I follow, though not yet with equal steps, the great footprints of the righteous, so that by your prayers I may attain him in whom I have been apprehended by the mercies of God.

So guide the little one crawling upon the earth, and teach me to walk in your footsteps. For I do not want you to consider my age according to bodily birth more than according to spiritual birth. Indeed, in bodily age I am now the age of the man who was healed by the apostles at the Beautiful Gate through the power of the word (Acts 3:7; 4:22).

But in the birth of the soul I am still at the infancy of her who, sacrificed amid wounds inflicted for Christ, preceded the victim of the Lamb by worthy blood and inaugurated the Lord’s Passion.

Therefore, as one still an infant in the word of God and in spiritual age, nurture me with your words, while I long for the breasts of faith, wisdom, and charity.

If you consider our common office, you are my brother; if you consider the maturity of your intellect and understanding, you are my father to me, even if you are perhaps younger in years, because gray-haired prudence has advanced you, while still young, to maturity of merit and the honor of elders [Note: [Col. 0102] The editions read: “Gray-haired prudence advanced you, young, to maturity of merit and the honor of an elder.” Nine manuscripts have “to the maturity of merit and the honor of elders.” Two Vatican manuscripts read more suitably: “and advanced you, young, to the honor of elders.”].

Therefore cherish and strengthen me in the Sacred Scriptures and spiritual pursuits: as I said, recent in time and therefore unpractised after long dangers and many shipwrecks, scarcely emerging from the waves of the world. You, who already stand upon solid shore, receive me safely into your embrace [Note: [Col. 0102] This is the reading in the printed editions. Most manuscripts have: “You have already stood upon solid shore; receive me safely,” etc.], so that, if you consider me worthy, we may sail together into the harbor of salvation.

Meanwhile, as I strive to escape the dangers of this life and the depths of sin, sustain me by your prayers like a plank, so that I may escape naked from this world as from a shipwreck.

4. For this reason I have taken care to lighten my burdens and strip off the clothing that weighs me down, so that, at Christ’s command and with his help, I may swim out across the stormy sea of this present life—which, with sins barking between, separates us from God—unencumbered by every garment of the flesh and by concern for the following day. I do not boast that I have accomplished this; even if I could boast, I would boast in the Lord, whose work it is to accomplish what lies before us to will. Yet my soul still longs to desire the judgments of the Lord. See when he who still desires to desire it may attain, in the accomplishment of God’s will [Note: [Col. 0102] The editors read: “May he attain the effect of God’s wills.” Two manuscripts: “The effect by God’s will.” Two others: “God’s will.” One Vatican manuscript: “God’s will in deed.” We follow the latter reading.].

Nevertheless, insofar as it lay within me, I loved the beauty of the holy house, and, as far as I was able, I had chosen to be despised in the house of the Lord. But he who was pleased to set me apart from my mother’s womb and to draw me from the friendship of flesh and blood into his grace was also pleased—though I lacked every good merit—to raise me from the earth and from the pit of miseries, and to draw me out of the mire of filth, so that he might place me among the princes of his people and put my portion in your lot, so that, through your merits, I might be made equal to you by association in office [Note: [Col. 0102] Cistercian manuscript: “that I might be made equal by the office of the senate,” that is, by the dignity of the presbyterate.].

5. Therefore, not by my own presumption but by the Lord’s approval and ordinance, claiming the bond of your Brotherhood, I deem myself worthy of so great an honor, though unworthy of it; for I know with certainty that, because of your holiness, you are wise in truth—not in thinking highly of yourself, but in keeping company with the humble. And so I hope that you will readily and deeply receive the love of our humility, which, I am confident, you have already received through the most blessed priest Alypius—because he deigns to be our father. For without doubt he offered you an example in himself of loving us, before knowing us and beyond our deserts. Though we were unknown to him and separated from him by a great interval of land or sea, he was able, through the spirit of true love, which is everywhere and pours itself everywhere, both to see us by loving us and to reach us by addressing us. He gave us the first proofs of his affection and pledges of your charity in the worthy gift of books mentioned above. And because he took such pains, we believe that he cared so greatly that we should know your Holiness—not merely through his words but more fully through your eloquence and faith—that we could not help loving you so greatly, and that, in turn, by imitating him, you might love us very much.

May the grace of God remain with you forever, as it does, brother unanimous with us in the Lord Christ, venerable and most earnestly desired. We greet your entire household, every companion, and every fellow-striver in the holiness of the Lord with the greatest affection of unanimous brotherhood. We ask you to bless, by accepting it, the one loaf that we have sent to your charity as a sign of our unanimity.

## LETTER XXVI

[Note: [Col. 0103] We have revised this letter with the aid of manuscripts a, bg, bl, bn, c, cc, ff, g, gv, j, l, n, r, s, sb, t, vc, vd, five Vatican manuscripts, and the editions of Ambrose, Badius, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis.]

[Note: [Col. 0103] Also numbered 39; the letter that was 26 is now 123. It was probably written at the beginning of 395 and sent with the following letter.]

Augustine exhorts the young, noble, and learned Licentius, formerly his pupil, to despise the world, making use for this purpose of a poem by Licentius himself, which he had written to his teacher.

### AUGUSTINE TO LICENTIUS

1. I scarcely found an opportunity to write to you—who would believe it? Yet I must believe you, Licentius. I do not want you to investigate the causes and reasons, which, even if they could be given, I do not owe to the trust with which you believe me. For I did not receive your letter through persons by whom I could send back a written reply. As for what you asked me to request, I took care to set it forth by letter as far as seemed called for [Note: [Col. 0103] Three manuscripts read *petendum*, “to be requested”; most others, *promendum*, “to be set forth”]; but you will see what I have accomplished. If it has not yet been accomplished, I shall act more urgently when I know this, or when you yourself remind me again.

Thus far I may have spoken with you about the chains of this life that resound around us. Now, in a few words, receive the stirrings of my heart concerning your hope—not a transitory hope—and the way by which the road to God may lie open for you.

2. My Licentius, because you repeatedly refuse and fear the fetters of wisdom, I fear that you are being bound most firmly and most disastrously by mortal things. Wisdom, after first binding those whom it has taken hold of and taming them through certain exercises and labors, later releases them and gives itself to them for their enjoyment. Those whom it first trains through temporal bonds, it later binds with eternal embraces [Note: [Col. 0103] Fourteen manuscripts read “will later release … will bind with eternal embraces]”—a bond than which nothing more delightful or more secure can be imagined.

I admit that the first bonds are somewhat harsh; but I would not call the last harsh, because they are sweetest, nor soft, because they are strongest. What, then, are they, except something that cannot be spoken but can nevertheless be believed, hoped for, and loved?

The bonds of this world, however, have real harshness and false delight; certain pain and uncertain pleasure; hard labor and fearful repose; a condition full of misery and an empty hope of blessedness. Do you insert your neck, hands, and feet into these bonds, when you seek to be subjected to honors of this kind, when you consider your actions fruitful in no other way, and when you strive to cling to that place to which you ought to have gone neither invited nor compelled?

Here you might perhaps give me the answer of Terence’s slave:

> “Ho! You are pouring out wise words here!”  
> (Terence, *The Adelphoe*)

Take it, then, so that I may pour rather than spill. Or, if I sing while you dance to another tune, I still do not regret it. The singing itself has its own cheerfulness, even when the limbs of the person to whom it is sung do not move in response to it with a rhythm full of love. Certain words in your letters moved me, but I thought it foolish to discuss them while concern for your actions and your entire manner of life burns me up.

### Poem of Licentius to Augustine, his teacher

[Note: [Col. 0104] Also called Letter XL.]

3.

> In probing Varro’s mysterious, profound path,  
> My mind grows dull and, terrified, flees the hostile light.  
> Nor is this strange: all my care in reading lies helpless,  
> For, when you do not give your hand, it fears to rise alone.  
>   
> For as soon as love urged me to unravel  
> The tangled summaries of so great a man  
> And to touch his sacred meanings,  
> He who gave tones their number, who, by sounding forth,  
> Explained the world and taught it to sing,  
> And made equal dances move in harmony,  
> Entangled my breast in varied darkness  
> And brought upon my mind a cloud of violent confusion.  
>   
> From there, madly, I ask for the forms of figures  
> Set down without dust, and encounter other heavy darknesses.  
> Finally [Note: [Col. 0104] Three manuscripts read *adsumam*, “I shall take up”; not badly], I seek the causes and bright courses of the stars,  
> Whose obscure positions he shows through the clouds.  
>   
> Thus I lay there, wavering, so that neither he who prevents us from recognizing the hidden places of heaven nor a *persona* could furnish so utter a ruin, the *treta* of the dyed caves [text materially uncertain].  
>   
> For the old tales say that Proteus, the Pelasgian,  
> While unwilling to disclose the future to anxious men,  
> Foams as a boar, flows as water, roars as a lion,  
> Hisses as a serpent,  
> Yet is eventually captured in the small forms of birds.  
>   
> But I, who am oppressed by cares too heavy,  
> Seek every sweetness, food somewhat sweet for my soul;  
> Varro’s answers lie hidden.  
> With supplicating song, shall I ask a nymph for protection,  
> Or beg the rivers?  
>   
> Or shall I call upon you with my voice,  
> You whom the ruler of bright Olympus  
> Set over the fountains of the young  
> And commanded to pour forth from the abundance of your spirit  
> Streams hidden far away?  
>   
> Bring help, teacher; and do not, do not abandon  
> My feeble powers. Begin with me to overturn  
> The sacred clods. For time, unless mortal things deceive me,  
> Slips away and draws us into old age.  
>   
> Our Apollo fills your heart,  
> And reconciles his father and the father of the gods.  
> He displays a good law and a bloody peace,  
> And, when the veil has been drawn away, reveals everything.  
>   
> You had perhaps measured twenty long circuits of the sun  
> When the most beautiful reason of the universe,  
> Richer than empires and sweeter than every nectar,  
> Seized you, established you, and set you in the middle,  
> From which place you could direct your sight upon all things.  
>   
> O good man, pursue the road of the years,  
> As wisdom grows through love of itself,  
> Always discovering new summits.  
> Continue along the road by which the glorious offspring  
> Of the thunderer leads you,  
> Making high places into level plains.  
>   
> And when evening has postponed the dawns of light  
> And has blessed the holy fire above,  
> Remember me yourself. You who set your thirsty ear  
> To invincible laws, strike your breasts with your palms,  
> Lay your limbs upon the ground, summon deserved sorrows,  
> And forbid wickedness. God commands one thing for all;  
> The bishop gives warning, and future thunderbolts terrify  
> [Note: [Col. 0105] The editions read “rivers”; five manuscripts, “thunderbolts.”].  
>   
> Would that the former dawn, with its joyful wheels,  
> Should recall for me the days already passed—  
> Those days when, trying the freedom of leisure with you  
> And the bright laws of the good,  
> We traveled through central Italy and across the high mountains!  
>   
> Neither harsh frosts, hard with hoary cold,  
> Nor savage storm, nor the blasts of Zephyrus and the North Wind,  
> Would keep me from pressing upon your footsteps  
> With anxious tread.  
>   
> Command only this task, and blood will water my limbs;  
> In summer we shall follow the Neuri,  
> In winter the Danube.  
>   
> The unknown Garamantes will loosen the bonds of my people  
> [Note: [Col. 0105] Badius and Erasmus read “Gerris”],  
> And the river Hypanis, fleeing the Xampaean lakes  
> [Note: [Col. 0105] Most manuscripts read: “and the Hypanis, fleeing the Xampoean lakes, where it is bitter”],  
> Will resound foaming among the Scythian waters of the Callipidae.  
>   
> We shall go also to Leucos, where Leucia stretches  
> Toward the rising of the sun; and to the deserted summits  
> Of vast Cassius, whose Cassian cliff  
> Makes itself equal to Epidamnian heights.  
>   
> From there, at your urging, I shall seek to see  
> The resting dawn, the loosened chariots,  
> And the day put to sleep in the middle of night.  
> For no labor or fear terrifies me  
> Where God hears the innocent with open prayers.  
>   
> Even now I would abandon the seats of Romulus,  
> The empty roof-tops of their houses,  
> The frenzied homes and vain tumults,  
> And come wholly at once into your heart,  
> If my mind, intent upon marriage, did not hold me back as I went.  
>   
> Believe my miseries, learned man, and my true sorrow:  
> Without you, my sails promise no harbors,  
> And we wander far away through the troubled seas of life,  
> Like sailors driven headlong through dense fog,  
> Whom the southern fury, shrieking,  
> And a blast from the east has struck,  
> While a whirlwind has deprived them of their snatched-away pilots.  
>   
> At once, wretched men, they are rolled through the broken waves.  
> Neither the deck nor the prow, nor the sails thereafter,  
> Can withstand the storms, and the reason that should guide them lies stunned.  
> Thus the wind drives me, and the waves of desire roll me  
> Into a death-bearing sea, though land is not far away.  
>   
> But as I reflect with myself, teacher, upon your bright words,  
> I think you believe these things still more:  
> Desire is a crafty thing; it deceives  
> And weaves its nets around our minds.  
>   
> For, forgetting the past, I am now present to you in the present;  
> Dear one, I now slip from your heart.  
> Alas, where shall I be carried? From where may I wish  
> To reveal my mind to you?  
>   
> Before pious doves will fit out their homes beneath the Aegean  
> [Note: [Col. 0105] All manuscripts read *optabunt*, “will desire,” except Corbie, which has *aptabunt*; *optabunt* is better],  
> And the halcyon, turning, will arrange its nests in a tree;  
> Before a hungry lioness will feed following calves,  
> And an unfed she-wolf will nurse tender lambs;  
>   
> Before, with the world changing and divided into its parts,  
> Either Barca will feed a bull, or Hyrcania lizards  
> [Note: [Col. 0105] The editions read “bulls”; ten manuscripts, “lizards”];  
> Before a mind once more terrified by Thyestean feasts  
> Will see the interrupted day vanish back toward the west;  
>   
> Before deer will give rains to the Nile,  
> Wandering above the sky; mountains will sing  
> And rivers will clap their hands—  
> Before your gifts, teacher, will come to me from behind.  
>   
> Love prevents this and preserves the bond of our shared honor.  
> Here, here, friendship’s glory reigns once the enemy has been put to flight.  
>   
> For we do not join our agreement of minds  
> Because of glassy wealth or rebellious gold;  
> Nor has the falling fortune of the crowd,  
> Which separates the lofty, joined us.  
>   
> Rather, it is the labor of reading inward things,  
> Things published in books, and discoveries made in your minds,  
> And a noble doctrine proclaimed,  
> With good answers brought back in reply.  
>   
> And my Calliope, although she shudders  
> To approach your height and hides her face,  
> Handling something useless—  
> Yet this bond of the spirit, these faithful connections,  
> Not even the one who broke the Alps,  
> Strengthened by mountainous rocks,  
> And pressed Italian cities with their walls,  
> Could break, nor could he frighten anything  
> By his strength from ours.  
>   
> Let the waters of the Oxus go far away  
> In swollen winding channels; let the Rhiphaean mountains  
> Or the cities of the Caspians be separated from the Aremphaeans  
> By a broad river;  
> Let the Maeotian regions, which the Hellespont overwhelms,  
> Stretch far apart the boundaries of Europe and Asia.  
>   
> Did Dodona not cut off, from either side,  
> The cattle-wearying Molossians  
> And their kinsmen the Arabs from Thalarius  
> [Note: [Col. 0105] The editions read *lateri*, “side”; most manuscripts read *thalari*]  
> By its boundaries? Nor did the friendly treaty of peace  
> Remain between the Sidonian kingdom and that of Pelops,  
> Or between the sacrilegious Phrygians,  
> Although for a time hospitality was shared by all.  
>   
> Why, finally, should I sing of the division of brothers  
> And their battles? Why of the honorable blows of parents,  
> The madness of mothers, and arrogant sons?  
>   
> There is even harmonious discord among the affairs of the heavenly powers,  
> And as many rites flow forth as opinion gives laws.  
>   
> Not even if Boreas gave me a hundred murmurs,  
> As many spirits, and a hundred tongues,  
> And my tongue, stiff as adamant, thundered through a hundred mouths,  
> Would I be able to recount the things  
> That the nature of ancient places, once joined together,  
> Separated and smoothed with rounded gravel into a world.  
>   
> But I pass over us: that we arose from one city,  
> That one house brought us forth,  
> That we are touched by one blood,  
> That Christian faith has bound us together,  
> And that an immense journey separates us,  
> While the expanse of sea between us confines us—  
> Love despises both obstacles.  
>   
> He who scorns the joys of the eyes  
> Always enjoys the absent friend,  
> Since the friend hangs upon the depth of the heart  
> And searches out the nourishment of the inner being.  
>   
> Meanwhile, whatever future things are written  
> In the life-giving message of the good,  
> And whatever from the writings of the ancients  
> Should be compared with honeycombs,  
> Considering what you have poured forth from your deep heart  
> As nectar and honey brought into the light,  
> Will themselves make you present to me,  
> If you will grant my request  
> And hand over the books in which the slow music  
> Reposes within you—for I burn wholly for them.  
>   
> Grant this, so that the truth may open before us through reason;  
> So that the Eridanus may flow more abundantly;  
> And so that the contagions of the world  
> May fly in vain around the fields of our husbandman.

4. [Note: [Col. 0106] Also called Letter 41.]

If your verse were distorted by irregular intervals, if it did not stand according to its own laws, if it offended the listener’s ears with unequal measures, you would certainly be ashamed, and you would neither delay nor desist until you had ordered, corrected, established, and balanced your verse by learning and practicing the art of meter with the utmost zeal and every kind of labor. What then, when you yourself are perverted in disorder, when you do not stand by the laws of your God, and when, in the conduct of your life, you are not in harmony with the honorable objects of your own desires and with this very education of yours, do you think these things should be cast behind your back and neglected? It is as though you were cheaper in your own eyes than the sound of your tongue, and as though offending God’s ears by disordered conduct were less serious than if grammatical authority were angered by your disordered syllables.

You write:

> Would that the former dawn, with its joyful wheels,  
> Should recall for me the days already passed—  
> Those days when, trying the freedom of leisure with you  
> And the bright laws of the good,  
> We traveled through central Italy and across the high mountains!  
>   
> Neither harsh frosts, hard with hoary cold,  
> Nor savage storm, nor the blasts of Zephyrus and the North Wind,  
> Would keep me from pressing upon your footsteps  
> With anxious tread.  
>   
> Command only this task.

Wretched me, if I do not command, if I do not compel and order, if I do not ask and beg! But if your ears are closed against my voice, let them be opened to your own mouth—let them be opened to your poem. Hear yourself, most hard, most savage, most deaf of men. What use to me is a golden tongue and an iron heart? With what shall I be able to lament your poems—not with songs, but with lamentations—in which I see the soul and talent that I am not permitted to grasp and offer in sacrifice to our God?

Do you expect me to command you: “Be good, be tranquil, be blessed,” as though anything more welcome could dawn upon my days than that I should enjoy your talent in the Lord? Or do you truly not know how I hunger and thirst for you? Or do you not confess this very thing in that poem?

Recall the state of mind in which you wrote these words, and now say to me: “Command only this task.” Here is my command: give yourself to me, if this is only a task; give yourself to my Lord, who is Lord of us all, who gave you that talent. For what am I except your servant through him, and your fellow servant under him?

5. Does he himself not command? Hear the Gospel:

> “Jesus stood,” it says, “and cried out” (John 7:37): “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:28–30).

If these words are not heard, or are heard only as far as the ears, do you expect Augustine to command his fellow servant, rather than mourn that his Lord commands in vain—or rather, does not command, but in some way invites and entreats, so that those who labor may be refreshed by him?

But evidently, with a very strong and confident neck, you find the yoke of the world more pleasant than the yoke of Christ. If he compelled us to labor, consider who would compel us and for what reward he would compel us.

Go to Campania and learn from Paulinus, that outstanding and holy servant of God, how unhesitatingly he shook off the great pride of this age with a neck all the nobler because it was humbler, so that he might place that neck beneath Christ’s yoke, as he did. Now, with Christ guiding his journey, he rejoices in quietness and moderation.

Go and learn with what resources of talent he offers sacrifices of praise to Christ, returning to him whatever good he has received from him, lest he lose everything if he does not place it in the one from whom he has received it.

6. Why are you agitated? Why do you waver? Why do you lend your ear to the imaginings of deadly pleasures and turn away from us? They lie; they die; they drag us into death. They lie, Licentius:

> “So may the truth open before us through reason;  
> So may the Eridanus flow more abundantly.”

No one speaks truth except Truth. Christ is the Truth. Let us come to him, so that we may not labor. Let us take his yoke upon us, so that he himself may refresh us, and let us learn from him, because he is gentle and humble of heart; then we shall find rest for our souls. For his yoke is easy and his burden is light.

The devil seeks to adorn himself through you. If you had found a golden cup lying on the ground, you would give it to the Church of God. You have received from God a spiritually golden talent, and you use it to serve lusts; with it you offer yourself as a drink to Satan! Do not do this, I beg you. May you someday feel how miserably and with what a pitiable heart I have written these words; and now take pity on me, if you have made yourself cheap.

## LETTER XXVII

[Note: [Col. 0107] Revised with the aid of manuscripts a, bg, bl, c, cc, ff, gv, j, n, r, s, t, vc, vd, two a manuscripts, two sb manuscripts, five Vatican manuscripts, and the editions of Ambrose, Badius, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis.]

[Note: [Col. 0107] Also numbered 32; the letter that was 27 is now 165. Written around the beginning of 395.]

Augustine to Paulinus, embracing his goodwill and declaring their mutual love; mentioning Romanianus and Alypius, as well as Licentius, whose youth he feared might incline toward worldly things.

To the truly holy and venerable Lord, and to the brother PAULINUS, celebrated and worthy of exceptional praise in Christ, whom one must honor and embrace with the service of sincere love, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

### 1.

O good man and good brother, you were hiding from my soul. I tell it to endure that you still hide from my eyes, and it scarcely obeys me—indeed, it does not obey me. But does it really endure it? Why, then, does the desire for you torture me within that very soul?

If I were suffering bodily discomforts, and if they did not disturb the balance of my mind, I would rightly be said to endure them. But when I do not bear with equanimity the fact that I do not see you, it is intolerable to call this endurance. Yet since you are such a person, perhaps being without you would be even more intolerable to endure.

It is therefore good that I cannot bear with equanimity what, if I bore with equanimity, I ought not to bear with equanimity. What has happened to me is strange but true: I grieve because I do not see you, and the grief itself consoles me. I dislike the strength by which the absence of good things—such as you—might be borne patiently.

For we certainly desire the future Jerusalem; and the more impatiently we desire it, the more patiently we endure everything for its sake. Who, then, can fail to rejoice when he sees you, so that he can fail to grieve while he does not see you?

I can do neither. And since, if I could, I would do either one with monstrous intensity, I take pleasure in being unable to do so; and in that pleasure there is some consolation. Thus it is not a calmed but a considered grief that consoles me in my grief.

Please do not rebuke me with the holier gravity in which you excel, saying that I do not rightly grieve because I do not yet know you, since you have opened your soul to me to behold—that is, your inner self. For what if I had learned somewhere in your earthly city that you were my brother and beloved, and such a man in the Lord, and you did not permit me to know your house? Would you suppose that I would feel no grief?

How, then, should I not grieve that I have not yet seen your face—that is, the house of your soul, which I know as I know my own?

### 2.

For I have read your letters, flowing with milk and honey, displaying the simplicity of your heart, in which you seek the Lord, sensing him in goodness, and bringing him glory and honor. The brothers have read them and rejoice tirelessly and ineffably in such abundant and excellent gifts of God—in your good qualities.

All who read them snatch them up, because they are themselves carried away while reading. It cannot be said how sweet the fragrance of Christ is, or how strongly it pours forth from them. When those letters offer you to our sight, how they stir us to seek you! They make you both visible and desirable.

The more they somehow present your presence to us, the less they allow us to endure your absence. Everyone loves you in them and longs to be loved by you. God is praised and blessed, by whose grace you are such a person.

There Christ is invoked, that he may deign to calm winds and seas for you as you make your way toward his steadfastness. There, to those who read, a wife is seen—not a guide leading her husband toward softness, but one returning him to strength within his bones [Note: [Col. 0108] Thus twenty-one manuscripts. The printed editions have: “May he deign to lead you toward his stability. There a wife is stirred up, not a guide,” etc.].

We return greetings, with the services owed to your Holiness, in you alone—she having been brought back and restored to your unity, and joined to you by spiritual bonds all the stronger because they are chaster. There the cedars of Lebanon, brought down to the earth and raised upright for the construction of the ark by the joining of love, cut through the waves of this world without decaying.

There glory is despised in order to acquire it, and the world is abandoned in order to possess it. There the little ones—or even the rather large sons—of Babylon are dashed against the rock: namely, the vices of worldly confusion and pride.

### 3.

Your letters offer these and similar spectacles, most sweet and most sacred, to those who read them: letters of unfeigned faith, letters of good hope, letters of pure love. How they breathe forth your thirst and the longing and weariness of your soul for the courts of the Lord! What holy love they exhale! What abundance of a sincere heart they pour forth! What thanks they give to God! What things they obtain from God!

Are they more flattering or more ardent? More luminous or more fruitful? What is it that makes them soothe us so, kindle us so, drench us so, and yet remain so serene? What is it, I ask you, and what can I repay you for them, except that I am wholly yours in him of whom you are wholly the possession?

If that is too little, I certainly have nothing more. Yet you have made it seem not too little to me, since in that letter you deigned to honor me with such great praise that, when I pour myself back into you, if I should think this too little, I would be convicted of not believing you.

I am ashamed to believe so much good about myself, but I am more reluctant not to believe you. Here is what I shall do: I shall not believe myself to be the sort of person you think me, since I do not recognize myself as such; but I shall believe that I am loved by you, since I feel and clearly perceive it. Thus I shall be neither reckless toward myself nor ungrateful toward you.

And when I offer myself wholly to you, it is not little: I offer you the one whom you love most intensely. And if I am not as you suppose me to be, I nevertheless offer you the one for whom you pray that I may deserve to become such. For this is what I now ask you especially to do: do not desire less to have added to what I am, because you think that I already am what I am not.

### 4.

Here is my dearest friend, and one most familiarly close to me from the beginning of adolescence [Note: [Col. 0109] Romanianus, praised in *On True Religion*, chapter 7, section 12], who is bringing this letter to your Excellency and outstanding Charity.

His name is found in the book *On Religion*, which your Holiness, as you indicate in your letters, reads with the greatest pleasure [Note: [Col. 0109] The editions have *de vera Religione* (“On True Religion”); twenty manuscripts lack the word *vera* (“true”).]. That book has become more pleasing to you also through the recommendation of so great a man, who sent it to you.

Nevertheless, I would not have you believe this intimate friend of mine in whatever he may perhaps say in praise of me. I have often sensed that he too, not from a desire to lie but from an inclination to love, is mistaken in his judgment, thinking that I have already received certain things for which I still gape with open-hearted mouth as I await their reception from the Lord.

And if he says this to my face, who could fail to infer how much better than truer things he joyfully pours forth about me in my absence?

He will make the books we have available to your venerable devotion. For I do not know that I have written anything either for the ears of those outside the Church of God or for the ears of the brothers that he himself does not possess.

But when you read, my holy Paulinus, do not let those things which Truth speaks through our weakness carry you away so completely that you pay less careful attention to what I myself say. Otherwise, while greedily drinking in the good and correct things granted to the minister, you will fail to pray for the sins and errors that I myself commit.

In those things that will rightly displease you, if you pay attention, I myself am visible. But in those things that rightly please you in my books through the gift of the Spirit that you have received, he is to be loved and proclaimed—he with whom is the fountain of life, and in whose light we shall see light (Psalm 35:10), without a riddle but face to face, whereas now we see in a riddle (1 Corinthians 13:12).

In those matters, therefore, that I have belched forth from the old leaven, I recognize him as I read them and judge myself with grief. But in those things that I have spoken from the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, by God’s gift, I rejoice with trembling.

For what do we have that we have not received? Yet the person who is rich in greater and more numerous gifts of God is indeed better than the person rich in fewer and smaller gifts. Who denies it? But again, it is better to give thanks to God even for a small gift of God than to want thanks to be given to oneself for a great one.

Brother, pray for me, so that I may always confess this from my heart and my heart may not disagree with my tongue. Pray, I beg you, that I may invoke the Lord not as one wishing to be praised but as one praising him, and that I may be saved from my enemies.

### 5.

There is another reason for you to love this brother more: he is a relative of the venerable and truly blessed bishop Alypius, whom you embrace with your whole heart—and rightly so. For whoever thinks kindly of that man is thinking of God’s great mercy and of God’s wondrous gifts.

When he read your request, in which you indicated that you desired him to write his story for you, he wanted to do so because of your goodwill, but did not want to because of his own modesty. When I saw him wavering between affection and embarrassment, I transferred the burden from him to my own shoulders; he even ordered me to do this by letter.

Therefore, if the Lord helps, I shall soon insert the whole of Alypius into your inmost heart. For I was especially afraid that he would hesitate to disclose everything that the Lord had bestowed upon him, lest he seem, to someone less discerning—for you will not be the only one to read these things—to be proclaiming not divine gifts granted to human beings but himself; and lest you, who know how to read such matters, be deprived of the knowledge owed to brotherly love because of the need to guard against the weakness of others.

I would already have done this, and you would already be reading him, if the brother’s sudden departure had not unexpectedly seemed best.

I commend him to your heart and tongue in such a way that you should show yourself friendly toward him as though you had learned to know him not now but previously with me. For if he does not hesitate to open himself to your heart, he will be healed, either entirely or to a great extent, through your speech.

I want him to be beaten down more thoroughly by the voices of those who love a friend not in a worldly manner.

### 6.

As for his son, our son [Note: [Col. 0110] Licentius, whose name you will find in some of our books, including *Against the Academics*], even if he did not himself travel to the presence of your charity, I had decided to place in your hands a letter by which you might console, exhort, and instruct him—not so much by the sound of your voice as by the example of your strength.

For I burn with desire that, while his age is still in the green grass, he may turn weeds into grain and believe those who have experience in the things he dangerously desires to experience.

Now, from his poem and from the letter that I sent to him [Note: [Col. 0111] The preceding letter], your most benevolent and gentle wisdom understands what I grieve over in him, what I fear, and what I desire. Nor do I despair that the Lord will be present, so that through you, his minister, I may be freed from such great surges of anxiety.

Since you are going to read many of our writings, your love will be much more pleasing to me if, among the things that displease you, you correct me as a just man in mercy and rebuke me. For you are not the sort of person whose oil I fear will make my head fat.

The brothers—not only those who live with us and those who live anywhere while serving God together, but nearly all who willingly know us in Christ—greet, honor, and long for your Brotherliness, Blessedness, and Kindness.

I do not dare to ask; but if you have time away from ecclesiastical duties, you see what Africa thirsts for with me [Note: [Col. 0111] The editions have: “Come and see what Africa feels with me.” The manuscripts lack the words “come and see” and have “you see what,” and three of them finally read “what Africa thirsts for with me”—a word with which Augustine beautifully alludes to Africa’s dryness, as he does again in Letter 31, section 42.].

## LETTER XXVIII

[Note: [Col. 0111] In revising this letter, manuscripts a, bl, bn, cc, j, fs, mr, gg, r, sb, t, vc, ten Vatican manuscripts, and the editions of Ambrose, Badius, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis were compared.]

[Note: [Col. 0111] Also numbered 8; the letter that was 28 is now 166. Written in 394 or 395.]

Augustine to Jerome, concerning a new version of the Old Testament after the Septuagint; and concerning Peter, rebuked by Paul in Galatians 2, complaining about Jerome’s acceptance here of a defense of a “useful lie.”

To the most beloved Lord, a brother and fellow presbyter, whom one must serve, honor, and embrace with the purest devotion of love, JEROME, AUGUSTINE sends greetings.

## CHAPTER ONE

1. No one has ever become so familiar to anyone by his face as your tranquil, joyful [Note: [Col. 0111] The editions have *quieta laetitia* (“tranquil joy”); several manuscripts have *laeta* (“joyful”).], and truly liberal exercise in the Lord has become familiar to me.

Although I greatly desire to know you altogether, I lack only a small part of you—namely, the presence of your body. Even this, after the most blessed Alypius, now a bishop but then already worthy of the episcopate, saw you and appeared to me on his return, I cannot deny has been impressed upon me to a considerable extent by his report. Before his return, when he saw you there, I saw you too—but through his eyes.

No one who knows us would say that he and I are two in spirit, but only in body: we are united by harmony and the most faithful intimacy, though not by those merits in which he surpasses me.

Since, then, you first love me through the communion of the spirit by which we are joined together, and then through his mouth, I am certainly not immodestly commending to your Brotherliness, as though he were unknown, our brother Profuturus [Note: [Col. 0111] While preparing to depart, he was made bishop and soon died, according to Letter 71. Therefore this letter, which Augustine there says was the first he sent to Jerome and was written while he was still a presbyter, was not delivered at that time. This Profuturus seems to be the man praised as bishop of Cirta in *On the Single Baptism against Petilian*, chapter 16, and to whom Letter 38 was addressed. Paulinus mentions the same Profuturus in Letter 32. Finally, in Letter 158, section 9, Evodius reports that Profuturus, whom he had formerly known in the monastery, appeared to him in a dream and foretold something future.], whom we hope will truly be profitable to our efforts and, subsequently, through your assistance—unless perhaps, because he is such a man, I myself may become more commendable to you through him than he through me.

Perhaps I should have written only this much if I wished to remain content with the customary manner of formal letters. But my spirit overflows with the desire to share with you conversation about our studies in Christ Jesus our Lord, who deigns, through your charity also, to provide us with many benefits and certain provisions for the journey he has shown us.

## CHAPTER TWO
## 2.

We therefore ask—and with us the entire devoted fellowship of the African Churches asks—that you not shrink from applying care and effort to interpreting the works of those who have treated our Scriptures most excellently in Greek. For you can enable us also to possess such men, and especially that one whom you more willingly bring forth in your writings. As for translating the canonical Holy Scriptures into Latin, I would not wish you to labor at this unless in the manner in which you interpreted Job: namely, so that, by means of signs, it may be evident how your version differs from that of the Seventy, whose authority is of the greatest weight.

I cannot sufficiently marvel, however, if something is still found in the Hebrew copies that escaped all those interpreters most skilled in that language. I set aside the Seventy, concerning whose greater agreement—whether of purpose or of spirit—than if they had been one man, I do not dare to form a definite judgment in any direction, except that I consider their pre-eminent authority in this task unquestionably deserving of recognition. I am more impressed by those who, when they interpreted later and, as is reported, clung tenaciously to the force [Note: [Col. 0112] Perhaps, “force.”] and rules of Hebrew words and expressions [Note: [Col. 0112] Amerbach, Bad., and all the manuscripts read mordacius, “more sharply.” Lovaniensis follows Erasmus in the reading printed here, mordicus, “tenaciously.”], not only failed to agree among themselves, but also left many things that had to be dug out and brought to light so long afterward. And these are either obscure or clear. If they are obscure, it is believed that you too could have been mistaken in them; if clear, it is not believed that they could have been mistaken in them. For this reason, then, in view of your charity, I beg you to make me certain of the matter after setting out the reasons.

## CHAPTER III.—A Pernicious Pretense

### 3.

I have also read certain writings said to be yours on the Epistles of the apostle Paul. When, in wishing to unravel the Epistle to the Galatians, you came to that passage where the apostle Peter is recalled from a pernicious pretense, I confess that I am exceedingly grieved that there a defense of falsehood was undertaken either by you, such a man, or by someone else, if another wrote those things—until the arguments that trouble me are refuted, if indeed they can be refuted.

For it seems to me most destructive to believe that any falsehood is found in the Holy Books—that is, that the men through whom that Scripture was supplied and written for us lied in any part of their books. One question, of course, is whether good men ever lie; another question is whether the writer of the Holy Scriptures ought to have lied. Indeed, it is not another question but no question at all. For once an officious falsehood has been admitted into so great a pinnacle of authority [Note: [Col. 0112] Three manuscripts read: “in the pinnacle of such great authority.”] [Note: [Col. 0112] The phrase “correctione, mordicus” appears corrupt in the transmitted text; its precise sense is uncertain.] [Col. 0113] no part of those books will remain that cannot, whenever it seems difficult for anyone’s morals or incredible for anyone’s faith, be referred by that same most destructive rule to the intention and service of a lying author.

### 4.

For if the apostle Paul was lying when, rebuking the apostle Peter, he said, “If you, though you are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?”—and if Peter seemed to him to have acted rightly, although he both said and wrote that Peter had not acted rightly, supposedly to calm the spirits of those who were in turmoil (Gal. 2:11–14)—what will we answer when perverse men arise forbidding marriage, whom he himself foretold would come (1 Tim. 4:3), and say that everything the same apostle said to establish the rights of marriage (1 Cor. 7:10–16) was a lie told for the sake of people who might be thrown into turmoil by love of their spouses—that he did not really think this, but said it in order to calm their hostility?

There is no need to recall many examples. Even officious falsehoods concerning the praises of God may seem possible, so that love for him may burn more ardently among people who are sluggish; and thus the authority of chaste truth in the Holy Books will nowhere be certain. Do we not observe the same apostle, with immense care for commending truth, saying: “But if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is empty, and your faith is empty also; moreover, we are found to be false witnesses of God, because we testified against God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise” (ibid. 15:14–15)?

If someone said to him, “Why do you recoil from this falsehood, since you have said something which, even if false, pertains above all to the praise of God?”—would he not, abhorring that madness, open the inner recesses of his heart to the light with whatever words and expressions he could, crying out that to praise falsehood in God is no less, or perhaps even greater, a crime than to condemn truth?
