It must therefore be ensured that such a person approaches the knowledge of the divine Scriptures with such a holy and truthful estimation of the Holy Books that he does not wish to take delight in any part of them through officious falsehoods, and would rather pass over what he does not understand than set his own heart above that truth. Certainly, when he says this, he seeks to have us believe him, and he acts so that we do not believe the authority of the divine Scriptures.

### 5.

For my part, with whatever strength the Lord supplies, I would show that all those testimonies which have been brought forward to establish the usefulness of falsehood ought to be understood otherwise, so that their firm truth might everywhere be taught. For just as the testimonies ought not to be false, so they ought not to favor falsehood. But I leave this to your intelligence. If you apply more careful consideration to the reading, you will perhaps see it much more easily than I do.

Piety will compel you to this consideration, for you recognize that the authority of the divine Scriptures is made to waver if it is once persuaded that those men through whom these Scriptures were supplied to us could have lied officiously in their writings. Otherwise, perhaps you are going to give us certain rules by which we may know where it is appropriate to lie and where it is not. [Col. 0114] But if this can be done, I beg you not to explain it by any means through deceitful and doubtful arguments; nor judge me burdensome or impudent, by the very truthfulness of the humanity of our Lord. For, to say nothing of there being no fault, certainly my error is not a great one if it favors truth, provided that truth can rightly favor falsehood in you.

## CHAPTER IV

### 6.

I would like to speak many other things with your most sincere heart and to confer about Christian devotion, but no letter is sufficient for this desire of mine. I can communicate the same matter more fully through the brother whom I rejoice to have sent so that he might be mingled with and nourished by your sweet and useful conversations.

And yet, perhaps even he does not contain as much as I would wish—if I may say this without offending him—although I would not place myself above him in the slightest. I confess that I am more capable of receiving you; but I see that he is becoming fuller, and in this he surpasses me without doubt. After he returns, as I hope will happen successfully with the Lord’s help, when I have shared in what your presence has heaped into his breast, he will not fill what in me will still be empty and eager for your thoughts. Thus I too will then be more needy, while he will be more abundant.

That same brother is carrying some of our writings with him. If you deem them worthy of reading, I beg you to apply to them sincere and fraternal severity as well. For I understand what is written—“Let the righteous correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head” (Ps. 140:5)—in no other way than that the rebuker who heals is loved more than the flatterer who anoints the head.

I am, however, a very poor judge when I read what I have written, being either more timid than is right or more eager than is right. Sometimes I also see my faults, but I prefer to hear of them from better men [Note: [Col. 0114] Four manuscripts read “older men”; one reads “greater men.”], lest, when I have perhaps rightly criticized myself, I flatter myself again and seem to myself to have passed a sentence upon myself that was timid rather than just.

# LETTER XXIX

[Note: [Col. 0114] Now published for the first time, and revised after publication against the oldest copy of the library of the Fathers of the Cistercian monastery of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem at Rome.]

[Note: [Col. 0114] What was formerly Letter 29 is now Letter 167. Written in the year 395.]

Augustine the presbyter to Alypius, bishop of Thagaste, relating by what exhortations he finally prevailed upon the Catholics of Hippo to recoil from the luxurious banquets that it had been customary to celebrate in the African Churches on the anniversaries of the saints.

## Letter of the Presbyter of the Hippo-Regians to Alypius, Bishop of the Thagastensians, concerning the Feast of the Birth of Leontius, formerly Bishop of Hippo

[Note: [Col. 0114] Saint Leontius is praised in Sermon 13 on Various Subjects, chapter 2, and is said to have founded a basilica called Leontiana after his name. Several sermons of Augustine are identified as having been delivered in that basilica.]

### 1.

Meanwhile, concerning the matter which I cannot fail to care about, I have been able to write nothing certain in the absence of brother Macharius, who is said to be returning soon; and whatever can be accomplished with God’s help will be accomplished.

As for our anxiety on their behalf, although our brothers and fellow citizens who were present could reassure their own people [Note: [Col. 0114] Perhaps read, “could reassure you.”], nevertheless the Lord granted us a matter worthy of an exchange of letters, by which we console one another. In this we believe that your very anxiety has greatly helped us to win the Lord’s favor, since it certainly could not have existed without prayer for us.

### 2.

Therefore, so that we may not fail to tell Your Charity what happened, and so that you may give thanks to God with us for the benefit we received—you who poured out prayers with us to receive it—after your departure we were informed that people were in an uproar and saying that they could not bear that the festival called Laetitia should be prohibited, though by calling it “Joy” they vainly attempted to conceal the name of drunkenness, just as had already been announced in your presence.

It happened opportunely, by the hidden ordering of almighty God, that on Wednesday the passage in the Gospel was treated in due course: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine” (Matt. 7:6). The discussion therefore concerned dogs and swine, so that both those who quarreled against God’s commands with obstinate barking and those devoted to the filth of carnal pleasures were compelled to blush. The conclusion was such that they saw how wicked it was to do within the walls of the church, in the name of religion, what, if they persisted in doing it in their own homes, would require that they be kept away from the holy things and ecclesiastical pearls.

### 3.

Although these things were gratefully received, the great matter had not yet been settled, because only a few had gathered. As this sermon was discussed outside by those who had been present, each according to his ability and zeal, it acquired many opponents.

Afterward, when the days of Lent had dawned and a large crowd had gathered for the hour of instruction, this passage in the Gospel was read: after the Lord had expelled from the temple the sellers of animals and overturned the tables of the money-changers, he said that they had made his Father’s house, which was a house of prayer, a den of robbers (ibid. 21:12). When I had made them attentive to the question of drunkenness, I myself recited this passage and added an argument showing how much more impetuously and vehemently our Lord would expel drunken banquets—which are shameful everywhere—from the temple, since he had expelled permitted commercial transactions, when what was sold was necessary for the sacrifices lawful at that time.

I asked them whom they thought more like a den of robbers: those who sold necessary things, or those who drank immoderately.

### 4.

Since the readings prepared for me to suggest were being held ready, I then added that the Jewish people themselves, while still carnal, had never celebrated banquets in that temple—neither drunken banquets nor even sober ones—where the body and blood of the Lord were not yet being offered. Nor are they found in the history to have become drunk publicly in the name of religion, except when they celebrated a feast for an idol they had fashioned [Note: [Col. 0115] The manuscripts read “for a fabricated deception” [that is, “the fabrication of an idol”].] [Col. 0116] (Exod. 32:6).

As I said these things, I also took up the codex and read the whole passage. I added, with as much sorrow as I could, that since the Apostle says—distinguishing the Christian people from the hardness of the Jews—that his letter was written not on tablets of stone but on tablets of fleshly hearts (2 Cor. 3:3), while Moses, the servant of God, had broken the two stone tablets because of those leaders (Exod. 32:19), how could we not break the hearts of these people who, as human beings of the New Testament, wanted solemnly to display on the days of the saints’ celebrations what the people of the Old Testament had celebrated only once, and then for an idol?

### 5.

After returning the copy of Exodus, I enlarged upon the crime of drunkenness as much as time allowed. I took up the apostle Paul and showed among what sins drunkenness had been placed, reading the passage: “If anyone who bears the name of brother is a fornicator, or an idolater, or greedy, or abusive, or drunkard, or robber, with such a one not even to eat” (1 Cor. 5:11). With groaning I warned them of the great danger in which we would be dining with those who became drunk even in their homes [Note: [Col. 0116] So the manuscripts; perhaps, “who are drunk.”].

I also read the passage that follows not far afterward: “Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor idolaters, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor the abusive, nor robbers will possess the kingdom of God. And such were some of you; but you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (ibid. 6:9–11).

After these words had been read, I told them to consider how the faithful could hear “but you were washed” when they still allowed such filth of desire—against which the kingdom of heaven is closed—to remain in their hearts, that is, in the inner temple of God.

From there we came to the passage: “When you come together, it is not to eat the Lord’s supper; for each one takes his own supper beforehand in eating, and one is hungry while another is drunk. Do you not have houses in which to eat and drink? Or do you despise the church of God?” (ibid. 11:20–22).

After reciting it, I emphasized more carefully that not even respectable and sober banquets ought to be celebrated in the church. For the Apostle did not say, “Do you not have houses in which to make yourselves drunk?”—as though it were permitted to become drunk in the church only in some particular way—but “to eat and drink,” something that can be done respectably, yet outside the church, by those who have houses where they can be refreshed with necessary food. And yet we have been brought to such straits by corrupt times and dissolute morals that we wish for them not yet modest banquets, but at least the domestic reign of drunkenness.

### 6.

I also recalled the Gospel passage that I had treated on the previous day, where it is said of false prophets: “You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. 7:16). Then I brought back to memory that the fruits mentioned in that passage meant nothing other than works. I asked among what fruits drunkenness had been named, and I read the passage to the Galatians:

“The works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, impurity, debauchery, idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousy, animosity, dissensions, heresies, envy, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5:19–21).

After these words I asked how we Christians could be recognized by the fruit of drunkenness, when the Lord commanded that we be recognized by our fruits.

I also added that what follows should be read: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control” (ibid. 5:22–23). I urged them to consider how shameful and lamentable it was that they wished not only to live privately by those fruits of the flesh, but also to offer them as an honor to the Church; and, if they were given the power, to fill the whole space of so great a basilica with crowds of banqueters and drunkards.

As for the spiritual fruits, to which both the authority of the divine Scriptures and our groans invited them, they did not wish to offer gifts to God or to celebrate the feasts of the saints chiefly with those fruits.

### 7.

When these things had been done, I returned the codex and ordered prayer. Then, to the extent that I was able, to the extent that the danger itself pressed upon me, and to the extent that the Lord deigned to supply strength, I set before their eyes the common danger—both that of those entrusted to us and that of us shepherds, who would have to give an account of them to the chief Shepherd.

By the humility of the one who, for our sake, endured notable insults, blows, spitting in the face, slaps, a crown of thorns, the cross, and blood, I begged them: if they had offended against anything themselves, to have mercy on us also; and to consider the unspeakable charity toward me of the venerable old man Valerius, who, for their sake, had not hesitated to impose upon me the dangerously burdensome task of speaking the words of truth. He had often told them that his prayers concerning our arrival had been heard. He rejoiced that we had come to him, not for a common death or the spectacle of their death, but for a common effort toward eternal life.

Finally, I also said that I was certain and trusted in him who cannot lie, who through the mouth of his prophet promised concerning our Lord Jesus Christ, saying: “If his sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments; if they profane my statutes, I will visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with scourges; but I will not remove my mercy from them” (Ps. 88:31–34).

I therefore trusted in him that, if they despised all these great things that had been read and said to them, he would visit them with the rod and with the scourge, and would not permit them to be condemned with this world.

In this appeal, everything was done as our protector and governor supplied courage and ability in proportion to the magnitude of the matter and the danger. I did not move their tears by my tears; but when such things were being said, I confess that, overcome by their weeping, I could not hold back my own. And when we had all wept together, my sermon came to an end with the fullest hope for their correction.

### 8.

The next day [Note: [Col. 0117] Besides this feast of Saint Leontius, which occurred in February—either during Lent or immediately after the day of Lent mentioned above in section 3—in this year 395, when Easter fell on March 25, another celebration was held around the feast of the Ascension, as is clear from Sermon 13 on Various Subjects, delivered on that day, which was solemn because of the Lord’s Ascension and Leontius’s burial. Although in section 3 above one might suspect that the reading should be “when the day of the fortieth day had dawned,” that is, the day of the Ascension, especially because Augustine nowhere here opposed the observance of the Lenten fast to the banquets and drinking parties to which the Catholics wished to devote themselves and to which the Donatists devoted themselves throughout that day.] when the day dawned on which they were accustomed to prepare their throats and bellies, I was informed that some people, including some who had attended the sermon, had not yet ceased their murmuring. The force of the worst habit had such power over them that they used only this expression and said: “Why now? Those who did not prohibit these things before were not therefore not Christians.”

When I heard this, I had absolutely no idea what greater devices for moving them I should prepare. Nevertheless, I was planning, if they thought the matter should be continued, to read the passage from the prophet Ezekiel: “The watchman is acquitted if he has announced the danger, even if those to whom it is announced are unwilling to take precautions” (Ezek. 33:9), then to shake out my garments and depart.

But then the Lord showed that he does not abandon us, and by what means he encourages us to place our confidence in him. Before the hour at which we were to ascend the platform, those very men whom I had heard complaining about the attack upon the old custom entered to see me. I received them kindly and, with a few words, brought them over to a sound opinion. When the time for discussion arrived, I omitted the reading I had prepared because it was no longer necessary, and said a little about this very question: that we could bring nothing shorter or truer against those who say, “Why now?” than to say ourselves, “At least now.”

### 9.

Nevertheless, lest those who had gone before us—who had either permitted such obvious crimes of an ignorant multitude or had not dared to prohibit them—should seem to be subjected by us to any insult, I explained by what necessity these practices appeared to have arisen in the Church [Note: [Col. 0118] For this same reason, Gregory Thaumaturgus, as his biographer Gregory of Nyssa testifies, allowed that on festivals established in honor of the holy martyrs the faithful should refresh themselves. Pope Gregory I was led by the same consideration to recommend the following to Abbot Mellitus, who was going to Britain, in Book 9, Letter 71: “And since oxen are accustomed to be slaughtered in great numbers in sacrifices to demons, some solemnity ought also to be changed for them in this matter, so that on the day of the dedication or on the birthdays of the holy martyrs they may celebrate the solemnity with religious banquets … so that, while some outward joys are reserved for them, they may more easily consent to the inward joys.”]:

After so many and such severe persecutions, when peace had been made, crowds of Gentiles wishing to enter the Christian name were hindered because they were accustomed to spend their feast days with their idols amid an abundance of food and drunkenness, and could not easily abstain from these most destructive and deeply rooted pleasures. It therefore seemed to our elders that this aspect of their weakness should for the time being be spared, and that, after abandoning their former feast days, they should celebrate others in honor of the holy martyrs—not with a similar sacrilege, although with similar luxury.

Then, once they had been gathered under the name of Christ and subjected to the yoke of such great authority, they could be given saving commands of sobriety, which they would no longer be able to resist because of the honor and fear owed to the one commanding them. For this reason, the time had now come [Col. 0119] for those who did not dare deny that they were Christians to begin living according to Christ’s will, so that, once they were Christians, they would reject what had been permitted so that they might become Christians.

### 10.

Then I urged that we should wish to imitate the transmarine Churches, in some of which these practices were never accepted and in others of which they had already been corrected by good leaders with the people’s obedience [Note: [Col. 0119] He praises Ambrose in Book 6 of the Confessions, chapter 2, because at Milan he prohibited food from being brought to the memorials of the saints, “so that no opportunity might be given to drunkards to gorge themselves, and because that practice was almost exactly like the parental rites of pagan superstition.”]

And because examples of daily drunkenness were being cited from the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter [Note: [Col. 0119] Pammachius is praised by Paulinus in a letter written to him for having provided an especially lavish banquet for the poor in the basilica of Saint Peter at the funeral of his wife Paulina, around the year 397; see Paulinus Illustratus, pp. 29–30.], I said that we had often heard that it had been prohibited, but that, because the place was far from the bishop’s daily oversight and because in so great a city there was a large multitude of carnal people—especially foreigners who continually arrived, retaining that custom with all the greater violence because they were more ignorant—it had not yet been possible to restrain and calm so monstrous a plague.

Nevertheless, if we honored the apostle Peter, we ought to hear his commands and look far more devoutly upon the Epistle in which his will appears than upon the basilica in which it does not appear. I immediately took up the codex and read where he says:

“Since Christ suffered for us in the flesh, arm yourselves also with the same thought, because one who has suffered in the flesh has ceased from the flesh, so that for the remaining time he may live in the flesh no longer according to human desires but according to the will of God. For the past time is sufficient for you to have fulfilled the will of men, walking in licentiousness, desires, drunkenness, revelries, and abominable idolatries” (1 Pet. 4:1–3).

When these things had been done, and I saw that everyone was proceeding with one mind toward a good intention, having rejected the evil custom, I urged them to attend the divine readings and psalms at midday. In this way, they would celebrate that day much more purely and sincerely; and from the multitude that gathered it could readily be seen who followed the mind and who followed the belly.

After all the readings, the sermon came to an end.

### 11.

In the afternoon a larger crowd was present than in the morning, and until the hour when we departed with the bishop, readings and psalm-singing continued alternately. After we had gone out, two psalms were read.

Then, against my will—for I already wanted such a dangerous day to be over—the old man compelled me, by ordering me, to say something to them [Note: [Col. 0119] In Sermon 252, “On the Two Fish,” chapter 4: “In this city, my brothers, have we not experienced what Your Holiness remembers with us—at what danger to us God expelled drunkenness from this basilica? Was not the ship almost sunk with us by the uprising of the carnal people?” These words, however, are somewhat too severe to be referred to what is here narrated as having happened at Hippo; they seem rather to have been spoken near Carthage, or in a city where there were “many spectators of the theaters.”]

I gave a short sermon in which I thanked God. Since we heard that the customary banquets were being celebrated in the basilica of the heretics, and since even at that very time when these things were being done by us they were persisting in their drinking, I said that the beauty of the day was enhanced by comparison with the night, and that a white color is more pleasing through its proximity to black.

In the same way, our gathering for a spiritual celebration would perhaps have been less joyful if carnal gluttony had not been displayed on the other side. I urged them to desire such banquets eagerly, if they had tasted how sweet the Lord is. But I said that those people should fear who pursue as primary what will someday be destroyed, since each becomes the companion of the thing he worships; the Apostle mocked such people when he said, “Their god is the belly” (Phil. 3:19), while in another place he said, “Food is for the belly and the belly for food; but God will destroy both it and them” (1 Cor. 6:13).

We, therefore, ought to follow what is not destroyed, what is retained through the sanctification of the spirit, as far removed as possible from the inclination of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0120] This should be read as transmitted: “he will destroy both it and them; therefore …”]. In accordance with this thought, after, as the occasion allowed, the things that the Lord deigned to suggest had been said, the evening rites that are customarily performed each day took place. As we departed with the bishop, the brothers sang a hymn in the same place, while a considerable crowd of both [Note: [Col. 0120] Perhaps “both sexes” is intended.] [Note: [Col. 0120] Perhaps the text should read “remaining and singing until the day grew dark.”] remained and sang until daylight had faded.

### 12.

I have related to you, as briefly as I could, what no one could doubt that you desired to hear. Pray that God may deign to turn away from our efforts every scandal and every weariness.

In a considerable measure we rest with you in the joyful ardor of our zeal, because we are told of such frequent gifts from the spiritual Church of the Thagastensians.

The ship with the brothers has not yet arrived. At Hasna [Note: [Col. 0120] The manuscript reads “Asna.”], where brother Argentius is presbyter, the Circumcellions attacked our basilica and smashed the altar. The case is now being heard. We ask you earnestly to pray that it may be conducted peacefully and as befits the Catholic Church, for the suppression of the tongues of the unruly heresy.

We have sent a letter to the Asiarch.

Most blessed brothers, persevere in the Lord, remembering us. Amen.

# LETTER XXX

[Note: [Col. 0120] This letter has been reviewed against manuscripts and editions designated a, bg, bl, bn, c, cc, ff, g, gv, j, n, r, s, sb, t, vc, vd, two copies designated a, four copies designated v, and the editions of Amerbach, Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0120] Formerly Letter 33; what was Letter 30 is now Letter 172. Written at approximately the same time.]

Paulinus writes again to Augustine through others, having received no reply from him.

## To the holy and like-minded lord and brother AUGUSTINE, PAULINUS and THERASIA, sinners.

### 1.

For some time now, my like-minded brother in Christ the Lord, since I learned that you were unaware of me amid your holy and devout labors, and saw that you were absent, I have embraced you with my whole mind and hastened to address you through a familiar and brotherly exchange of letters [Note: [Col. 0120] Perhaps the reading should be “hastened to approach you.”].

I trust that, in the hand and by the grace of the Lord, my message has been brought to you. But since the boy whom we had sent before winter to you and to the other beloved people whom God likewise wished to greet has still been delayed [Note: [Col. 0120] Toward the end of the year 394.], we could neither suspend our duty any longer [Col. 0121] nor restrain our keen desire for your message.

Therefore we have written again now, if our earlier letter has been deemed worthy of reaching you—or for the first time, if it did not have the good fortune of reaching your hands.

### 2.

But you, spiritual brother [Note: [Col. 0121] The editions read “spiritually”; the manuscripts read “spiritual brother.”], who judge all things, should not measure our love for you solely by our duty or by the timing of our letters. For the Lord is witness, he who alone and alike works his charity everywhere in his own people.

From the time when, through the benefit of the venerable bishops Aurelius and Alypius, we came to know you through your work against the Manichaeans, your love was so impressed upon us that we seemed not to take up some new friendship but, as it were, to resume an old affection.

Thus, although we now write to you in words, we do not write as though we were inexperienced in affection; and in turn we recognize you in spirit through the inner person, as though we had known you before. Nor is it surprising that, though absent, we are present to one another, and that, though unknown, we know one another, since we are members of one body, have one head, are drenched with one grace, live by one bread, walk along one way, and dwell in the same house.

Finally, in all that we are, with the entire hope and faith by which we stand in the present and strive toward the future, we are one both in the spirit and in the body of the Lord, lest we be nothing if we fall away from the One.

### 3.

How little, then, is the bodily absence that grudges us to one another [Col. 0122], unless perhaps it grudges us that fruit by which the eyes of those who await temporal things are nourished? Yet even bodily grace ought not to be called temporal in the case of spiritual things, since the resurrection will also grant eternity to bodies, so that we dare, through the power of Christ and the goodness [Note: [Col. 0122] Fourteen manuscripts read “and the goodness” rather than “and the goodness of.”] of God the Father, to presume even this, though unworthy.

Would that the grace of God, through our Lord Jesus Christ, might grant us this gift also, so that we might see your face in the flesh! It would not only bring great joy to our desires; it would also increase light in our minds, and our poverty would be enriched from your abundance.

You can grant this even to us while absent, especially on this occasion, when our sons, like-minded and most dear to us in the Lord, Romanus and Agilis—whom we commend to you as though they were our other selves—will return in the Lord’s name after completing this work of charity. We ask that they especially enjoy the affection of your charity.

For you know how exalted a promise the Most High makes to the brother who helps his brother. Through them, if you wish to repay me with some gift from the grace that has been given to you, you may safely do so. Believe me: they are one heart and one soul with us in the Lord.

May the grace of God remain with you eternally, as it does now, my like-minded brother in Christ the Lord, venerable, most beloved, and longed for.

Greet from us all the holy people in Christ who, as is beyond doubt, are joined to you. Commend us to all the saints, so that they may deign to pray for us with you.

# SECOND CLASS

Letters that Augustine, already a bishop, wrote before the conference held at Carthage with the Donatists and before the Pelagian heresy was discovered in Africa, from the year of Christ 396 to 410.

[Col. 0121]

# LETTER XXXI

[Note: [Col. 0121] Corrected against manuscripts designated a, bg, bl, bn, c, cc, ff, g, gv, j, n, r, s, t, vc, vd, two copies designated a, two designated sb, five designated v, and the editions of Amerbach, Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0121] Formerly Letter 34; what was Letter 31 is now Letter 25. Written at the beginning of the year 396.]

Augustine presents a dutiful expression of gratitude to Paulinus for the second letter received from him, and reports that he has been ordained co-bishop of Valerius at Hippo. He expresses the wish that Paulinus himself might cross over to Africa, which would be a great consolation to him and an example to the other Christians.

[Col. 0121]

## To the most beloved and most sincere lords, truly most blessed brothers and outstanding through the most abundant grace of God, PAULINUS and THERASIA, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

1. When I most eagerly wished that my letter, in which I replied to your earlier one—if your letter could in any way be answered by me—might reach the hands of Your Charity as quickly as possible, so that, though absent, I might somehow soon be with you, my own delay brought me the benefit of your letter. Good is the Lord, who often does not grant what we want, in order to give us what we would prefer. For what you will write after receiving my letter is one thing; what you wrote without receiving it is another. When we read this with the greatest joy, we would certainly have been deprived of that joy if, as we most earnestly wished and desired, our letter had quickly reached Your Holiness. But now [Col. 0122] it delights us with a joy all the fuller to have both this letter in hand and the hope of a reply to it. Thus neither can our fault be blamed, and the Lord’s more generous goodness has brought about what he judged more conducive to our desire.

2. We received the holy brothers Romanus and Agile, who brought and returned another letter from you, a letter that heard your voice and gave it back, and that was a most sweet part of your presence—though it made us yearn all the more eagerly to see you—with great joy in the Lord. How, when, or in what manner could either you have given, or we have demanded, such a report about you as we learned from their lips? Moreover, there was something that no sheet of paper can contain: such joy in the narrators that, through the very faces and eyes of the speakers, we read you written in their hearts with ineffable delight. There was also this further point: however excellent the writing contained in any page may be, it contributes nothing by itself, though it may be read for the benefit of others; but we read your letter—your brotherly soul, that is—in their conversation, so that it appeared to us happier in proportion as it had been more richly composed from you. Thus, by eagerly questioning them about everything concerning you, we transcribed it into our hearts for imitation of that same blessedness.

3. Yet we did not endure their departure from us so quickly, although they were returning to you, without distress. See [Col. 0123], I ask you, in what feelings we were caught. They had to be dismissed more quickly precisely because they desired so earnestly to obey you; but the more they desired this, the more fully they displayed you to us. For they showed thereby how dear your inner being was to them; therefore we wanted to let them go all the less, the more justly they insisted that they should be released. What an intolerable thing this would be, unless by this departure we were not departing from one another—unless we were members of one body, had one head, were poured over by one grace, lived by one bread, walked along one way, and dwelt in the same house! Why, then, should we not use the same words? I believe you recognize [Note: All editions read *agnoscis*, certainly corruptly. M.] that these are words from your letter [Note: From Letter XXX, no. 2.]. But why should these be your words rather than mine, since, insofar as they are true, they proceed for us from communion with the same head? And if they have been given to you as something especially your own, I have loved them all the more, so that they occupied the passage of my breast and would not allow words to pass from my heart to my tongue until words as much earlier as they are yours had gone forth [Note: Earlier editions read *puriōra*, “purer,” but the manuscripts more suitably read *priora*, “earlier.”]. Holy brothers, beloved of God and mutually our members: who would doubt that we are enlivened by one Spirit, unless he does not perceive the love by which we are bound together?

4. Yet I should like to know whether you endure this bodily absence more patiently and easily than we do. If so, I confess that I do not like this strength of yours—unless perhaps we are such that we ought to be less missed by you than you are missed by us. If I possessed your patience for enduring your absence, I should dislike it; for I would be sluggish in trying to see you. What, however, is more absurd than becoming more sluggish through strength? Your Charity ought to understand how I am bound by care for the Church from this fact: the most blessed father Valerius—through our brothers you will hear how much he greets you with us and how greatly he thirsts for you—would not allow me to remain merely his presbyter unless he imposed upon me the greater burden of the co-episcopate [Note: Possidius, chapter 8: “He refused, contrary to the custom of the Church, to accept the episcopate while his bishop was alive; and while everyone urged him that this was customarily done, and the practice was shown to him by examples from overseas and African Churches unknown to him, he was compelled and forced to yield . . . . . Later he both said and wrote that this ought not to have been done to him—that he should have been ordained while his bishop was alive—because of the prohibition of the universal council (Nicaea). This dignity he obtained in the year 395, according to Prosper’s Chronicle, around Christmas, as appears from Homily 25 among the Fifty.].

Because I believed that the Lord willed this on account of Valerius’s great affection and the people’s great desire, and because several preceding examples had closed off every excuse for me, I was exceedingly afraid to offer resistance. Yet although Christ’s yoke is in itself easy and his burden light (Matthew 11:30), nevertheless, because of our harshness and weakness, if this bond bites me at all and this burden presses upon me, your presence would make it incomparably more tolerable and bearable for me. I hear that you live more free and unencumbered from such cares [Note: At that time Paulinus lived free from ecclesiastical cares. For he scarcely consented to be ordained presbyter in the Church at Barcelona, finally agreeing on the condition—as he writes to Severus in Letter 6—that he would not be tied to that Church: “I was dedicated only to the priesthood of the Lord, not also to a place in the Church.” Accordingly, after being ordained at Barcelona on the Lord’s Nativity, he withdrew from there to Nola after Easter of the following year, namely 393 or 394. It is not clear that he himself assumed the episcopate of this place before the year 409. See the note on Letter 95.]. Therefore [Col. 0124], without shame, I ask, request, and implore you to deign to come to Africa, which suffers from a greater thirst for such men than from the renown of its dryness.

5. God knows that we desire you to be bodily present in these lands not only because of my longing, nor only because of those who have learned through us of your purpose, or from whatever source has proclaimed it by reputation, but also because of the others who partly do not hear and partly do not believe what they hear, yet can love what they come to know. For although you carry out this work diligently and mercifully, let your works also shine before the people of our regions, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven (ibid., 5:16). When the Lord called the fishermen, they rejoiced even in recalling that, because they had left their boats and nets, they had left everything and followed the Lord (ibid., 19:27). Indeed, he despises everything who despises not only as much as he could have, but also as much as he wished to have. In the first case, God’s eyes are witnesses; in the second, human eyes as well. Somehow, however, when superfluous and earthly things are loved, what has been acquired binds more tightly than what has merely been desired. For why did that man who was seeking from the Lord the counsel for attaining eternal life depart sorrowful, when he heard that he must sell all he possessed, distribute it to the poor, and have treasure in heaven if he wished to be perfect, unless it was because, as the Gospel says, he had great riches? (Luke 18:22–23.) It is one thing not to want to incorporate what is lacking; it is another to tear away what has already been incorporated. The former are rejected like food; the latter are cut away like limbs. How great, therefore, and with what wondrous joy does Christian love in our times behold, through the Lord’s Gospel, being done gladly what the rich man heard from the Lord’s mouth with sorrow?

6. Although I cannot express in words the conception and birth of my heart, you wisely and devoutly understand that this is not your glory—that is, human glory—but the Lord’s glory in you. For you look upon the enemy with the greatest caution and act with the deepest devotion, so that, as disciples of Christ, you may be humble and meek in heart. Earthly wealth is more usefully possessed humbly than abandoned arrogantly. Since, therefore, you rightly understand that this is not your glory but the Lord’s, you see how small and slight my words have been. I have spoken of the praises of Christ, to which even the tongues of angels are unequal. We therefore desire that this glory of Christ be brought before the eyes of our people: examples, set forth in one marriage, by which pride may be trampled down for both sexes without despairing of perfection. I do not know whether you act more mercifully in anything than by refusing to let it remain hidden that you are as much what you wished to be as you are.

7. I commend to your kindness and affection Vetustinum, a boy pitiable even to the impious. You will hear from him the causes of his misfortune and exile. His purpose—by which he promises that he will serve God—the greater length of time, his more mature age, and the fear he has overcome will reveal more certainly [Col. 0125]. I have sent to Your Holiness and Charity three books—and would that they were as adequate to explain so great a question as they are large—being the less afraid of imposing the labor of reading upon you the more I perceive your ardor for loving. Their subject is free will.

I know that our brother Romanus does not possess these books, or does not possess all of them. Through him, out of your zeal for us, I entrusted almost everything I could write suited to any audience not to be carried to you but to be pointed out for reading. He already had everything and carried it with him; through him I sent my first replies [Note: Letter 27.]. I believe that Your Holiness has already discerned, through the spiritual insight the Lord has granted you, what good this man carries in his mind and in what respect his weakness limps. Therefore, I hope you have read with what concern I commended both him and his son to your humanity and affection, and how closely they are joined to me. May the Lord build them up through you. This is more properly to be asked of him, for I know how much you desire it.

8. I have learned from the brothers that you are writing against the pagans. If we deserve anything from your heart, send whatever comes from it without distinction, so that we may read it. For your heart is such an oracle of the Lord that we presume that from it responses will be given to us both pleasing and fully explanatory against the most talkative questions. I believe Your Holiness possesses the books of the most blessed Pope Ambrose, but I greatly desire those which he wrote with the greatest diligence and fullness against certain extremely ignorant and arrogant men who maintain that the Lord learned from Plato’s books [Note: These books of Ambrose no longer survive.].

9. The most blessed brother Severus, bishop of the Church at Milevis, well known among the brothers of that city from our shared schooling [Note: The editions read *condisciplinatu*; eighteen manuscripts read *condiscipulatu*, “shared schooling.”], greets Your Holiness with us in the duty owed to you. All the brothers who serve the Lord with us do the same, and they desire you as much as you desire them; they desire you as much as they love you, and they love you as much as you are good. The bread we have sent will become a more abundant blessing through the affection of your kindness in receiving it. May the Lord guard you forever from this generation (Psalm 11:8), most beloved and sincere lords, truly kind and most excellent brothers through the Lord’s abundant grace.

## LETTER XXXII

[Note: Corrected against manuscripts a, bg, bl, bn, c, cc, ff, g, gv, j, n, r, s, sb, t, vc, vd, five v, and the editions Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: Formerly numbered 36; the letter formerly numbered 32 is now 27. Written shortly after the preceding letter.]

Paulinus to Romanianus, rejoicing that the Church at Hippo has deserved Augustine as a colleague in the episcopate. He urges Licentius, in prose and verse, to despise the vanity of the court and dedicate himself to Christ.

To the deservedly esteemed, renowned, and honorable brother ROMANIANUS, PAULINUS and THERASIA.

1. On the day before we gave this letter, our brothers had returned from Africa—those whose arrival you saw us awaiting, most desired of holy and beloved men—and we had received letters from them, namely [Col. 0126] from Aurelius, Alypius, Augustine, Profuturus, and Severus, now all alike bishops. Rejoicing, therefore, in the most recent messages of so many such holy men, we hastened to report our joy to you, so that in your anxious exile we might bring you the longed-for news through the most festive signs. If you have learned the same things about those venerable and beloved men through the arrival of other ships, receive them repeated from us as well, and rejoice again with joy as though renewed. But if this is the first message to reach you from us, rejoice that, by Christ’s gift, such affection has been formed in your homeland that whatever divine Providence does there we always know—first or among the first—wonderful, as it is written, in his saints (Psalm 67:36).

2. We do not write merely to congratulate you that Augustine has received the episcopate, but that the African Churches have deserved this care from God, so that they might receive heavenly words from the mouth of Augustine, who, advanced in a new manner to a greater grace of the Lord’s gift, was consecrated not to succeed a bishop in his seat but to join him. While Valerius, bishop of the Church at Hippo, remains alive [Note: The Benedictine editors do not include the word *episcopo*, “bishop,” which is found in other editions and manuscripts.], Augustine is his co-bishop.

And that blessed old man, whose pure mind no stain of dark envy ever touched, now receives from the Most High fruits worthy of the peace of his heart: the man whom he had simply desired as successor to his priesthood he has deserved to hold as his colleague. Could this have been believed before it happened? Yet here too, in this work of the Almighty, that evangelical saying may be uttered: “These things are difficult for human beings; but with God all things are possible” (Luke 18:27). Let us therefore exult and rejoice in him who alone does wonders, who makes people dwell together in unity in a house, because he has regarded our humility and visited his people with goodness; he who raised up a horn in the house of David his servant, and now has exalted the horn of his Church in his chosen ones, so that, as he promises through the prophet, he may break the horns of sinners—that is, of the Donatists and Manichaeans.

3. Would that the Lord’s trumpet, which now resounds through Augustine, might strike the ears of our son Licentius—but that he might hear with the ear through which Christ enters, from which the enemy does not snatch God’s seed! Then Augustine will truly appear to himself a supreme pontiff of Christ, because he will feel that he has been heard on high if, in Christ, he worthily brings forth as his own son the man whom he has begotten worthy of you in letters.

For even now, believe me, he has written to us with the most ardent concern for him. We trust in almighty Christ that Augustine’s spiritual desires will prevail over the fleshly desires of our young man. He will be conquered even against his will—believe me; he will be conquered by the faith of his most devout father, lest he win a disastrous victory if he should prefer to conquer for his own ruin rather than be overcome for his salvation.

So that the duty of brotherly kindness might not seem empty, we have sent you and our son Licentius five loaves of *buccellatum*, the bread of the Christian campaign, in whose military service we daily fight for the ration of frugality [Note: *Buccellatum* was a military bread made approximately in the form of a small mouthful, so that it could be baked more readily for long-term use, as Ammianus relates in book 17. In the manuscripts here it is written *buccillato*.]. We could not separate from our blessing one [Col. 0127] whom we desire to bind completely to us by the same grace. Yet let us address him briefly as well, lest he deny that what was written to you was written about him. It is said of Aeschinus that he hears what Micio hears. But why speak of others, when we can speak everything concerning our own—and it is not usually the mark of a sound head to speak of others? By God’s grace we are sound and safe, since Christ is our head. May we have you safe for many years and always blessed, together with your whole household, as we desire, in Christ, lord brother, most deservedly honorable and most desired.

4. Hear, then, son, the law of your father—that is, Augustine’s faith—and do not reject the counsels of your mother, a name which Augustine’s devotion likewise rightly claims for itself toward you. He carried you, so small, in his bosom; and after you were first imbued from childhood with the milk of secular learning, he now desires to suckle and nourish you with the spiritual breasts of the Lord.

He sees you grown in bodily age but still wandering in spiritual cradles, still an infant in the word of God, scarcely crawling in Christ with your first steps and stumbling track—provided Augustine’s teaching, like a mother’s hand and a nurse’s arm, guides the unstable child. If you listen to him and follow him, let me once more entice you with Solomon’s words: “Son, you will receive a crown of graces upon your head” (Proverbs 4:9).

Then you will truly be that consul and pontiff—not dreamed in the fantasy of sleep, but formed by truth itself—with Christ filling empty images of false achievement with the solid effects of his work. For you will truly be a pontiff and truly a consul, Licentius, if you cling to Augustine’s prophetic and apostolic disciplines, as blessed Elisha clung to Elijah and the young Timothy to the illustrious Apostle, accompanying him without separation along the divine roads. Thus you will learn both to deserve the priesthood with a perfect heart and, with a teacher’s mouth, to counsel peoples toward salvation.

5. Enough of admonition and exhortation. I think that with a brief speech and little effort you can be urged, my Licentius, toward Christ, since from childhood you have been devoted to the studies of truth and wisdom, both of which truly are Christ, the highest good of every good, kindled by the spirit and mouth of the venerable Augustine.

If he has had little influence with you on your own behalf, what shall I accomplish, so much later than he and poor in all his resources? Yet trusting both in the power of his ability and in the humanity of your talent, and hoping that more and greater things have been worked in you than remain to be worked, I have dared to speak with a twofold motive: both to make myself his partner, through the affection owed to him, in concern for you [Note: The editions read *devincta charitate compararet*; eight manuscripts read *de vita et charitate*; six others read *debita charitate*.], and to have myself counted, by openly declaring my feeling, among those who love your salvation.

For I know that the outcome in your perfection assigns the palm chiefly to Augustine [Note: Twelve manuscripts read *affectus*, “affection,” rather than *effectus*, “outcome.”]. I fear, son, that I have offended your ears by the harshness of a reckless speech, and through your ears have inflicted the wound of my weariness upon your mind as well. But I remembered your letter, in which I understood that you were familiar with musical modes [Note: The poem of Licentius is contained in Letter 26.]. I too was once not alien to that study in an earlier period of my own life.

Thus, if I had wounded your mind in any respect, I found a remedy for soothing it by recalling your letter: I might summon you to the Lord, the craftsman of every kind of harmony, through the measured music of verse. I ask you [Col. 0128] to listen with your ear and not despise the cause of your salvation because of my words; but gladly receive the devout care and fatherly mind even in words you may disregard. The name of Christ is implanted in them, and because that name is above every name, it makes this reverence due, so that it cannot be despised by one who believes.

## PAULINUS’S ELEGIAC POEM TO LICENTIUS

Come, then, break your delays and the tenacious chains of the age;

Do not fear the gentle yoke of the peaceful Lord.

The present things are indeed beautiful, but wondrous to wandering minds;

A wise spirit is not astonished by them.

Now ambition troubles you with varied and misleading appearances—

Alas, powerful Rome can even turn the strong aside.

But may your father Augustine, my son, always meet you

Against all the allurements of the City.

If you behold him amid such great dangers of fragile life

And hold him in your heart, you will be safe.

Yet I shall repeat this warning again and again:

Flee the slippery path of harsh military service.

The name of honor is pleasing, slavery is evil, the end is painful—

What now delights one to desire, soon pains one to have desired.

It is pleasing to climb high places; trembling comes from descending them.

If you stumble, you fall worse from the highest citadel.

Now false goods please you; now ambition seizes every ear,

And hollow fame carries them in a glassy bosom.

But when the belt, bought at great cost, has girded you

And barren labor has broken you thereafter,

Late and in vain you will accuse your empty hopes,

And wish to break the chains you are now weaving.

Then you will remember, grieving, that you foolishly despised

The truthful warnings of your father Augustine.

Therefore, if you are wise and a devout boy, listen,

And take the words of fathers and the counsel of elders.

Why draw back your savage neck from the yoke? My burden is gentle;

The yoke of Christ is sweet. Believe God’s devout voice.

Add your head to the yoke, give your mouth to the soft bridle,

And place your lowered shoulders beneath the light burden.

Now you can do this, while you act as a free man,

While no chains hold you, no concern for a marriage-bed, no lofty honor.

This is true freedom: to serve Christ, and in him

To be above all—not a servant of human masters,

Not a servant of vices, not of proud kings—

Only the one who has given himself to Christ the Lord.

Nor should the nobility seem free to you which you now see

Riding sublimely through the astonished City.

You see how free it considers itself,

That it disdains to bend its neck to God.

That wretched man serves many mortals, and even slaves;

He buys slave-women so that they may rule him.

The eunuchs know, and those who have endured the great palaces,

And everyone who, wretched by choice, endures Rome.

At what cost of sweat and loss of dignity

the cloak there and the honor of office here are obtained.

Yet even the powerful man who buys himself a position

Higher than everyone else, so that he may serve no one, does not attain it.

When he has proudly proclaimed himself master of the whole City,

He serves demons if he worships images.

Alas, Licentius, because of these men you delay in the City,

And scorn Christ’s kingdom in order to please them.

You call them masters and greet them with bent neck,

Though you see that they are slaves of wood and stone!

In the divine name they venerate silver and gold;

Their religion is what the disease of avarice loves.

May he who does not love Augustine love these men,

and may he who delights in worshiping them not worship Christ.

Therefore God himself says that it is impossible

To serve two masters, since one mind pleases God:

One faith, one God, and one Christ from the Father;

There is no double service to one master.

For as great as the distance between heaven and earth,

So great is the difference between Caesar’s and Christ’s affairs and commands.

Lift yourself from the earth—but now, while the spirit rules these limbs,

Penetrate heaven with your mind; no delay of the flesh hinders you.

Die even now to bodily actions,

And clearly contemplate the good of heavenly life in your mind.

You are spirit, although you are held by a body,

If now, victorious through a devout mind, you destroy the work of the flesh.

These things, dear boy, compelled by faithful love,

I have written to you; if you receive them, you will be received by God.

Believe that Augustine has now been doubled for you in me;

Receive two fathers with a single devotion.

Are we despised? You will be torn from two with greater grief;

[Col. 0129] Are we heard? You will be a sweet pledge to two.

The glad care of two fathers has labored for you,

And it is a great honor for you to have made two rejoice.

When I join myself to Augustine, I do not boast that I am his equal in merit;

I compare myself with him only in love for you.

For what can I pour out, sprinkling you from my poor stream?

Apart from me, you will be washed by a twofold river:

Brother Alypius is one, and Augustine the teacher;

The one is your partner in blood, the other the sower of your talent.

You are strong with so great a brother and teacher, Licentius,

And do you hesitate to follow the stars on such wings?

Whatever you do—for the world may not hope to have you as its friend—

You will not be given to the earth, a soul owed to Christ.

Even if you contemplate marriage and lofty honors,

you will one day restore yourself to your Lord.

I believe that two just men will conquer one sinner,

and that your brother's vows and prayers will drive you away.

Therefore return: by voice as father, by blood as brother,

Both priests command you to come back.

They draw you back to what is yours, for now you seek what is foreign [Note: The editions read *petisses*, “you had sought”; the manuscripts read *petescis*, “you seek.”].

These realms that hold you fast are more truly your own.

Return to them; yearn for them; do not wear away your time on outsiders.

If you do not want what is yours, who will give you what belongs to others?

You will not belong to yourself; sent far through foreign lands,

Alas, you will live an exile from the feelings of your own heart.

I have sung these things sufficiently to a concerned father,

While telling you what I myself both desire and fear.

If you receive it, this page will one day bring life to you;

If you reject it, this same page will bear witness.

May Christ grant that you remain safe for me, most beloved son,

And make you his servant forever.

Live, I pray—but live for God; for living for the world

Is the work of death. To live for God is living life [Note: The Regius manuscript reads, “true is living life for God”; others read, “living.”].

## LETTER XXXIII

[Note: Collated for correction against manuscripts a, bg, bl, c, cc, ff, g, gv, r, s, t, vc, two sb, and four v, and against the editions Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: Formerly numbered 147; the letter formerly numbered 33 is now 30. Written at the beginning of Augustine’s episcopate.]

Augustine to Proculeianus, bishop of the Donatist party at Hippo, inviting him to settle the schism through a mutual conference.

To the honorable and most beloved lord PROCULEIANUS [Note: In Bad., Am., Er., and two Vatican manuscripts, *Proculianus*. The same spelling appears below in Lov. and most manuscripts.], AUGUSTINE.

1. Because of the vanities of ignorant people, I ought not to dispute with you for so long about the title of my letter. For although, before the fullest discussion of the matter, it may seem to some uncertain which of us is in error, when we try to recall one another from error, we nevertheless serve one another if we act toward each other with good will, so that we may be freed from the perversity of discord.

That I am acting from a sincere heart, with the trembling of Christian humility, even if it is not evident to most people, is seen by him from whom no hearts are closed. You can easily understand what I do not hesitate to honor in you. I do not consider the error of schism—an error from which, insofar as it concerns me, I desire all people to be healed—worthy of any honor. But I consider you worthy of honor above all because you are bound to us by the bond of human fellowship itself, and because certain signs of a gentler mind stand out in you. Through them there is no reason to despair that, once truth has been demonstrated, you can embrace it without any agitation of doubt. I owe you as much love as the one who loved us even to the shame of the cross commands us to owe.

2. But do not wonder that I remained silent before Your Benevolence for so long. I did not think that you held the position [Col. 0130] which brother Evodius—whose word I cannot distrust—joyfully reported to me. It happened by chance that you came together in one house, and conversation arose between you about our hope, that is, about Christ’s inheritance. He said that Your Kindness declared that you wished to confer with us before good men seated.

I rejoice greatly that you have deigned to offer yourself to our humility, and I cannot in any way abandon so great an opportunity for your kindly disposition. I shall therefore seek and discuss with you, insofar as the Lord grants strength, what cause, origin, and rationale brought about in the Church of Christ—of which he said, “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27)—such a grievous and lamentable division.

3. I did hear from the brother mentioned that you complained because he answered you with some kind of insult. I ask you not to count it as an insult, since I am certain that it did not proceed from a proud spirit. I know my brother; but if, while arguing for his faith and for the love of the Church, he perhaps spoke too fervently, in a manner your dignity did not wish to hear, that should be called not insolence but confidence. He wished to be a partner in discussion and an interlocutor, not an assentor and flatterer.

For this is the oil of the sinner with which the prophet does not wish his head to be fattened. Thus he says: “The righteous will correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but the oil of the sinner will not fatten my head” (Psalm 140:5). He prefers to be corrected by the severe mercy of the righteous rather than praised by the gentle anointing of flattery. Hence there is also that prophetic saying: “Those who call you happy lead you into error” (Isaiah 3:12).

For this reason, of a man whom false blandishments make arrogant, it is rightly said in common speech, “His head has grown”: he has been fattened with the sinner’s oil—that is, not corrected by harsh truth, but praised by gentle falsehood.

I do not ask you to understand this as though I wished you to be regarded as corrected by brother Evodius as by a righteous man. I fear that you might think I too had spoken something insulting against you, which I avoid as much as I can. But righteous is the one who said, “I am the truth” (John 14:6). Therefore, whenever truth sounds to us with some harshness from the mouth of any person, we are corrected not by that person, who may perhaps be a sinner, but by Truth itself—that is, by Christ, who is righteous—lest the anointing of flattering but harmful praise, the sinner’s oil, fatten our head.

Even if brother Evodius, somewhat disturbed in defending his communion, had said something with an elevated manner and a more agitated spirit, you ought to forgive him because of the man’s age and the necessity of the cause.

4. I ask you to remember what you deigned to promise: that, with those whom you yourself choose seated as witnesses—provided that our words are not scattered uselessly but recorded with a pen, so that we may discuss more calmly and orderly, and so that, if anything said by us should slip from memory, it may be recalled by reading—we may examine together, in harmony, so great a matter, one that concerns everyone’s salvation.

Or, if you prefer, let us first confer without any intermediary, whether by letters or by conversation [Col. 0131] and reading, wherever you please. Some intemperate hearers might perhaps prefer to await what they regard as our contest rather than think about our salvation in our conversation. Then, whatever has been settled between us, the people may afterward learn through us.

Alternatively, if you prefer to proceed by letters, let the letters themselves be read to the congregations, so that at some point they may be called not congregations but one congregation. In every respect—as you wish, command, or prefer—I gladly accept it. And concerning the mind of the most blessed and venerable father Valerius, who is now absent, I promise with complete confidence that he will learn of this with great joy. I know how much he loves peace and how little he is puffed up by any empty vanity of conceit.

5. I ask you: what have we to do with ancient dissensions? Let those wounds last no longer, wounds which the arrogance of proud men inflicted upon our members. Through the putrefaction of those wounds we have even lost the pain by which a physician is usually summoned.

You see with what great and pitiable ugliness Christian households and families have been disturbed [Note: Six manuscripts read “defiled.”]. Husbands and wives agree with one another in their bed but disagree over Christ’s altar. By him they swear to one another so that they may have peace among themselves, but in him they cannot have it. Children share one home with their parents, but they do not share one house of God. They desire to succeed to the inheritance of those with whom they quarrel over Christ’s inheritance.

Slaves and masters divide the one Lord who took the form of a slave in order to free all by serving. Your people honor us; our people honor you. Your people adjure us by our crown; our people adjure you by yours. We receive everyone’s words and do not wish to offend anyone. Why does Christ alone offend us, whose members we tear apart?

People who wish to settle their secular affairs before us call us holy men and servants of God when they need us, so that they may conduct their earthly business. Let us sometimes conduct the business of our salvation and theirs—not about gold, silver, estates, or livestock, for the sake of which we are daily greeted with bowed heads so that we may settle human disputes, but about our very head, concerning which there is among us such a shameful and destructive disagreement.

However much those who greet us bow their heads, so that we may make them concordant on earth, our head was bowed from heaven even to the cross, in which we are not concordant.

6. I ask and implore you: if there is in you any humanity, let the goodness that many proclaim appear here. If it is not being feigned for the sake of passing honors, let the inward parts of mercy be stirred within you. Be willing at last to examine the matter, persevering with us in prayers and discussing everything peacefully, lest the miserable congregations who obey our honors oppress us by their obedience in God’s judgment.

Rather, may they be recalled from errors and dissensions through our genuine love, together with us, and directed onto the paths of truth and peace. I desire you to be blessed before the eyes of God, honorable and most beloved lord.

## LETTER XXXIV

[Note: Corrected against manuscripts a, bg, c, cc, ff, g, gv, n, r, s, sb, t, two vc, four v, and the editions Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: Formerly numbered 168; the letter formerly numbered 34 is now 31. Written after the preceding letter.]

Concerning a young man who was accustomed to beat his mother and finally, after threatening her with death, passed over to the Donatists and was baptized again by them. Augustine requests an inquiry into whether this was done at the command of the Donatist bishop Proculeianus, as his presbyter Victor had reported in an official communication, meanwhile declaring himself ready, if Proculeianus wishes, to discuss the entire case of the schism calmly.

[Col. 0132]

To the eminent and deservedly respected [Note: Six manuscripts read “deservedly esteemed.”] and honorable brother EUSEBIUS, AUGUSTINE.

1. God knows—for the secrets of the human heart are manifest to him—how much I love Christian peace, and how deeply I am moved by the sacrilegious deeds of those who persist unworthily and impiously in their dissension. Yet the movement of my spirit is peaceable. I am not striving to compel anyone unwillingly to enter Catholic communion, but rather that the truth, openly declared to all who are in error, may, once manifested through our ministry with God’s help, itself sufficiently persuade them that it must be embraced and followed.

2. For what, I ask you, is more execrable—leaving other matters aside—than what is now happening? A young man, crazed by repeatedly beating his mother, is rebuked by his bishop; yet he does not restrain his impious hands from the womb from which he was born, not even on those days when the severity of the laws spares the most criminal offenders. He threatens the same mother that he will go over to the party of Donatus and kill her, whom he habitually beats with unbelievable fury. He threatens her, goes over to the party of Donatus, is rebaptized in his frenzy, and, raging for his mother’s blood, is clothed in white garments. He is placed within the railings, prominent and conspicuous, and is presented, as though renewed, to the eyes of all who mourn, as one plotting matricide.

3. Can this finally please you, most serious of men? I could never believe this of you: I know your thoughtful character. His bodily mother is beaten in the limbs with which she gave birth to and nourished an ungrateful son; his spiritual mother, the Church, forbids this, and she too is beaten in the Sacraments by which she gave birth to and nourished an ungrateful son. Does it not seem to you that he has said, gnashing his teeth like a parricide: “What shall I do to the Church that forbids me to beat my mother? I have found what I shall do: let her herself also be struck by whatever injuries I can inflict; let something happen to me by which her members may suffer. I shall go to those who know how to blow away the grace in which I was born to her and destroy the form that I received in her womb. I shall torture both my mothers with savage torments: let the latter, who gave birth to me, carry off the former. For the grief of this one, I shall die spiritually; for the slaughter of that one, I shall live carnally.”

What else are we waiting for, honorable Eusebius, except that he should now, as a Donatist, confidently arm himself against the wretched woman, worn out by old age and deprived of her husband, from whose beatings he was being restrained in the Catholic Church? For what else did he conceive in his frenzied heart when he said to his mother, “I shall go over to the party of Donatus, and I shall drink your blood”? Behold, already bloodstained in conscience but clothed in white, he has fulfilled one part of his promise; the other remains, that he drink his mother’s blood. If, then, these things please them, they are being pressed by their clerics and sanctifiers to fulfill within their octave everything that they vowed.

4. The right hand of the Lord is indeed powerful enough to restrain his fury from the miserable and desolate widow, and to deter him, by means known to it, from so wicked a resolution. Nevertheless, struck by such profound anguish of spirit, what could I do except at least speak? Or are they permitted to do these things while I am told, “Be silent”? May the Lord avert from me such madness, that when he himself commands me through his Apostle, saying that those who teach what they ought not must be refuted (Tit. 1:9), I should, terrified by their indignation, keep silent. I wanted this sacrilegious crime to be attached to the public records for precisely this reason: so that no one—especially in other cities where it might be useful—might suppose that I was inventing something when I lamented these events, since it is now even being said at Hippo itself that Proculeianus did not order what the public official reported.

5. What more moderate course can we take than for me to pursue so grave a matter through you, a man endowed with the highest dignity and tranquil in your very considerate disposition? I therefore ask—as I have already asked through our brothers, good and honorable men whom I sent to Your Excellency—that you deign to inquire whether Proculeianus’s presbyter Victor did not receive from his bishop the order that he reported as having been given to him in the public office; or whether, perhaps, although Victor himself said something else, those men of the same communion prosecuted a false statement against him in the official records.

Or, if he agrees, I gladly accept the proposal that we calmly examine the whole question of our dissension, so that the error, already manifest, may become more plainly known. For I have heard that he said that, without popular tumult, ten serious and honorable men from each side should meet with us, and that we should investigate from the Scriptures what is true.

But what some have reported to me that he said again—why I did not go to Constantina when more of his people were there, or that I ought to go to Milevis [Note: Six manuscripts have Mileum; Bad. and Am., Milenum; Er., Milevum.] because, as they say, they will soon hold a council there—is ridiculous to say, as though responsibility for this properly concerned me except in the Church of Hippo. The whole basis of this question concerns me chiefly with Proculeianus. But if he perhaps considers himself unequal to the task, let him seek the assistance of whatever colleague he wishes. In other cities we undertake only as much concerning the Church as the bishops of those same cities—our brothers and fellow priests—either permit us or impose upon us.

6. Yet I do not sufficiently understand what this man, who says he has been a bishop for so many years, fears from me, a novice, so that he is unwilling to confer with me. If it is the training of the liberal arts—which perhaps he himself has either not learned or learned less thoroughly—what does that have to do with a question that must be examined from the holy Scriptures or from ecclesiastical or public documents, with which he has been occupied for so many years and in which he ought therefore to be more expert? [Col. 0134]

Finally, here is my brother and colleague, Samsucius, bishop of the Church of Turris, who has learned none of the things that this man is said to fear. Let him attend and deal with him. I shall ask him, and, as I trust in the name of Christ, he will readily grant my request that he undertake my role in this matter. The Lord will help him, as we trust, contending for the truth: although unpolished in speech, he is nevertheless instructed in true faith.

There is therefore no reason for him to refer the matter to I know not whom else [Note: Eleven manuscripts have differat; the editions have deferat.], lest we settle among ourselves what concerns us. Yet, as I said, I do not avoid those others either, if he himself requests their assistance.

## EPISTOLA XXXV

[Note: The following witnesses were used in this recension: a. bg. bl. c. cc. ff. g. gv. n. r. s. sb. vc.; two copies of t.; four of v.; and Am. Bad. Er. Lov.]

[Note: Elsewhere 169; what was formerly 35 is now 24. Written shortly after the preceding letter.]

Augustine again appeals to Eusebius to see that the license of the Donatist clerics is restrained through the bishop Proculeianus; otherwise, no one should complain of him if he brings this matter to Proculeianus’s attention through the public records.

To his distinguished, deservedly honored, and beloved brother EUSEBIUS, AUGUSTINE.

1. I did not, as you say, impose upon your unwillingness to undergo judgment among the bishops by becoming an importunate exhorter or petitioner. Indeed, even if I had wished to persuade you of this, I might perhaps easily have shown how capable you are of judging between us in a matter so manifest and obvious, and what sort of conduct yours is when, without hearing both sides, you do not hesitate to pronounce judgment for one side, although you shrink from judgment. But, as I said, I set this aside for the moment.

What I had requested from your honorable kindness—and I ask you finally to notice this, at least in this letter—was simply that you inquire of Proculeianus whether he himself had said to his presbyter Victor what Victor reported as having been said to him in the public office; or whether perhaps those who were sent did not pursue in the official records what they had heard from Victor, but a falsehood. Then I asked what he thought about the whole question that must be examined between us.

I think that a man is not made a judge when he is asked to question someone and to write back what answer he receives. This, therefore, I now again ask you not to find burdensome, because he does not wish to receive my letters, as I have also discovered by experience. If he had wished to receive them, I would certainly not be conducting this matter through Your Excellency.

Since he does not wish to receive them, what milder course can I take than to have such a man as you, who also love him, ask him something about which my responsibility prevents me from remaining silent? As for the fact that a mother was beaten by her son and that this displeased your gravity, you said, “But if he knew, he would have excluded so wicked a young man from his communion.” My brief reply is: now he knows; now let him exclude him.

2. I add something else. A former subdeacon of the Church of Spania, named Primus, was forbidden to approach the consecrated women because of his undisciplined conduct, and he despised orderly and sound commands. He was removed from the clergy; and, angered against God’s discipline, he transferred himself to those people and was rebaptized.

He also transferred two of his fellow tenants [Note: So Lov. and most manuscripts. At., Bad., Am., and Er. have “together with his tenants.”] from the estate of Catholic Christians—or whether he himself transferred them or they followed him, they too were nevertheless rebaptized. Now, among the bands of Circumcellions, amid roving groups of women who refused to have husbands for the very reason that they might thereby avoid discipline, he proudly revels in detestable drunken debauchery, rejoicing that the broadest license for wicked conduct—conduct from which he was restrained in the Catholic Church—has been opened to him.

Perhaps Proculeianus is unaware of this. Therefore, let it be brought to his attention through your dignity and moderation. Let him order that the man who chose that communion for no other reason than that he had lost his clerical rank in the Catholic Church because of disobedience and depraved conduct be removed from his communion.

3. For my part, if it pleases the Lord, I maintain this practice: whoever has been degraded among them on disciplinary grounds and wishes to pass over to the Catholic Church is received into the humility of repentance, into which they themselves might perhaps have compelled him had he wished to remain among them.

But consider, I ask you, how execrably they act: those whom we correct for living badly through ecclesiastical discipline are persuaded to come to another washing, and, in order to be deemed worthy to receive it, they must declare that they are pagans. To prevent such a statement from proceeding from a Christian mouth, so much blood of martyrs was shed. Then, as though renewed and sanctified, made worse than before by the discipline they could not bear, they insult the discipline under the appearance of a new grace, through the sacrilege of a new frenzy.
