Or, if I am acting wrongly, arrange through your kindness for these matters to be corrected; but let no one complain about me if I have these things brought to his attention through public records, which, as I think, cannot be denied me in the Roman city [Note: Understand Hippo, which enjoyed the rights of a Roman city or colony. It is also called a Roman city in *Against the Letter of Petilianus*, book 2, chapter 83, section 184, and a colony in *The City of God*, book 22, chapter 8.].

For since God commands us to speak and preach the word, to refute those who teach what they ought not, and to insist upon it in season and out of season, as I demonstrate from the Lord’s and the Apostles’ Letters (II Tim. 4:2; Tit. 1:9–11), let no human being suppose that silence about these matters can be imposed upon me. If they think they can venture anything by force or brigandage [Note: Lov. has “but if they venture anything violently or as brigands.” Am., Bad., and Er. have “if they think they can venture anything by force or brigandage.”], the Lord will not be absent to protect his Church—he who, with his yoke spread throughout the whole world in her bosom, has subjected all earthly kingdoms to it.

4. For when a certain tenant of the Church wished, with paternal severity, to recall to Catholic communion his daughter—who had been a catechumen among us but had been led astray by them against her parents’ wishes, so that, once baptized there, she might also assume the status of a consecrated woman—and I refused to receive a woman of corrupted mind unless she came willingly and chose the better course by her free will, that rustic began to press her even with blows, so that his daughter would agree with him. I immediately forbade this by every means.

Nevertheless, as we were passing through Spania, his presbyter, standing in the midst of the estate of a Catholic and praiseworthy woman, shouted after us in the most shameless voice that we were traditors and persecutors. He hurled this insult also at the woman, who belonged to our communion and in whose estate he was standing. When I heard these words, I restrained not only myself from an altercation but also the crowd accompanying me.

And yet, if I say, “Let it be investigated who are or were the traditors or persecutors,” the answer given to me is: “We do not wish to dispute; we wish to rebaptize. Let us prey upon your sheep like wolves with ambushes and biting attacks; you, if you are good shepherds, be silent.” For what else did Proculeianus command, if he truly gave that command? “If you are a Christian, preserve this by the judgment of God: unless we do it, you be silent.”

The same presbyter even dared to threaten a rustic tenant of the Church’s estate.

5. Let Proculeianus also learn all these matters through you, I ask, and let him restrain the madness of his clerics. For this reason, honorable Eusebius, I have not kept silent before you.

You will therefore deign to write back not what you think about all these matters—as though you should imagine that I am imposing upon you the burden of a judge—but what they answer me. May God’s mercy preserve you unharmed, distinguished, deservedly honored, and beloved brother.

## EPISTOLA XXXVI

[Note: Corrected against bl. cb. ff. gg. m. rm. vc.; four copies of v.; and Am. Bad. Er. Lov.]

[Note: Elsewhere 86; what was formerly 36 is now 32. Perhaps written in 396 or at the beginning of 397.]

Augustine to the presbyter Casulanus, refuting the dissertation of Urbicus— that is, of a certain man from Rome—in favor of fasting on the Sabbath, written with extreme incompetence.

To his most beloved and most earnestly desired brother and fellow presbyter CASULANUS, AUGUSTINE, greetings in the Lord.

## CHAPTER ONE

1. I do not know how it happened that I did not reply to your first letters; yet I know that I did not do so out of contempt. I take pleasure both in your studies and in your very manner of speaking, and I both wish and exhort you, in this youthful age, to advance in the word of God and abound for the building up of the Church.

Now that I have received your second writings, in which at last you rightly demand, by the brotherly and most equitable charity in which we are one, that a response be made to you, I did not think that I should delay your loving desire any longer. Amid my most pressing occupations, I have undertaken to discharge toward you this obligation [Note: Three Vatican manuscripts have *exsolvere* (“to fulfill”); others have *absolvere* (“to discharge”).].

2. As to your consultation—whether it is permissible to fast on the Sabbath—I answer: if it were in no way permissible, surely neither Moses, nor Elijah, nor the Lord himself would have fasted for forty consecutive days. But this reasoning also establishes that fasting on the Lord’s Day is not unlawful.

Nevertheless, whoever thinks that this day should be devoted to fasting, just as some observe the Sabbath by fasting, will cause no small scandal to the Church, and not without reason. In matters about which divine Scripture has established nothing certain, the custom of the people of God or the institutions of our ancestors must be held as law. If we wish to dispute about these matters and condemn some people because of the practice of others, an interminable struggle will arise. Since the labor of argument, without any certain proofs, conveys no truth, we must certainly take care lest the calm of charity be obscured by the storm of contention.

The man whose lengthy dissertation you thought should be sent to me, together with your earlier letters, so that I might answer him, neglected to avoid this danger.

## CHAPTER TWO

3. I do not, however, have such ample stretches of time that I can spend them refuting each of his individual assertions, for I need them to explain other works that are more urgently pressing. But, judging from the intelligence you display in your letters—an endowment of God in you that I greatly value—consider somewhat more carefully the same discourse of a certain Urbicus, as you call him [Note: This surname was assigned from the city of Rome. Hence Pope Zephyrinus is called *Urbicus* by Optatus in book 1, and Siricius by Paulinus in Letter 1 to Severus; and in the First Council of Arles there is discussion of *urbic* deacons, that is, Roman deacons.], and you will see that he did not hesitate to tear apart almost the entire Church of Christ, from the rising of the sun to its setting, with words of the greatest insult.

I should not say “almost the entire,” but plainly “the entire.” For he is found not to have spared even the Romans, whose custom he seems to be defending. He does not realize how the force of his abuse also rebounds upon them, because he has not noticed it.

For when his arguments fail by which he might prove that one ought to fast on the Sabbath, he attacks the pleasures of banquets, drunken feasts, and the most shameful drunkenness, as though not fasting were the same as being drunk. But if that is so, what benefit does it give the Romans to fast on the Sabbath? For on the other days, when they do not fast, they must, according to this man’s argument, be judged drunkards and belly-worshipers.

Moreover, if it is one thing to burden the heart with gluttony and drunkenness—which is always evil—and another to relax the fast while preserving moderation and temperance, which certainly, when it happens on the Lord’s Day, has no Christian accuser, let him first distinguish the meals of holy people from the greed and drunkenness of belly-worshipers. Otherwise, when the Romans do not fast, he will make them belly-worshipers; and then let him investigate not whether it is permissible to be drunk on the Sabbath—which is not permissible on the Lord’s Day either—but whether one ought not to fast on the Sabbath, as one ordinarily does not fast on the Lord’s Day.

4. Would that he asked or affirmed this in such a way that he did not openly blaspheme the Church spread throughout the whole world, except for the Romans and a few others in the West. But now, who could tolerate his saying of all the Eastern peoples and also many Western Christian peoples—of so many servants and handmaids of Christ who dine soberly and moderately on the Sabbath—that they are carnal, cannot please God, and are the people of whom it is written, “Let the wicked depart from me; I do not wish to know their way”? He says that they are belly-worshipers, preferring the synagogue to the Church, and sons of the slave woman; that they follow a law not just but pleasure-seeking, consulting their belly rather than submitting to discipline; that they are flesh, that they savor death, and other things of this kind.

If he said these things about even one servant of God, who ought to listen to him, and who ought not to avoid him? But when he persecutes with these insults and curses the Church that bears fruit and grows throughout the whole world and that dines almost everywhere on the Sabbath, I admonish whoever he is to restrain himself. For since you wished me not to know the name of the man, you surely did not wish me to pass judgment on him.

## CHAPTER THREE

5. “The Son of Man,” he says, “is Lord of the Sabbath: on it one may chiefly do good rather than evil” (Matt. 12:8–12). If, then, we do evil when we dine, we never live well on the Lord’s Day.

As for the fact that he admits that the Apostle ate on the Sabbath and says that the time for fasting had not yet come—because the Lord said, “The days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast, the children of the bridegroom” (ibid. 9:15)—since there is “a time for joy and a time for mourning” (Eccl. 3:4), he ought first to have observed that the Lord there spoke of fasting, not of fasting on the Sabbath.

Further, since he wishes mourning to be understood as assigned to fasting and joy to food, why does he not consider that whatever God wished to signify by the statement that he rested on the seventh day from all his works (Gen. 2:2) did not signify mourning there but joy? Unless perhaps he is going to say that, in God’s rest and sanctification of the Sabbath, joy was signified for the Jews but mourning for Christians.

Yet when God sanctified the seventh day because he rested on it from all his works, he expressed nothing about fasting or dining on the Sabbath. Nor, when he later commanded the Hebrew people concerning the observance of that day, did he say anything about foods either to be eaten or not to be eaten. Only abstention from one’s own or servile works is commanded to human beings.

The earlier people, receiving this as a shadow of future things, abstained from works just as we now see the Jews abstaining—not because, as is supposed, carnal Jews wrongly understand what Christians rightly understand. For we do not understand this better than the Prophets, who nevertheless, at the time when it was proper for it to be done, observed this Sabbath abstention, which the Jews think must still be observed.

That is why God ordered a man to be stoned who had gathered wood on the Sabbath (Num. 15:35). Yet nowhere do we read that anyone was stoned or judged worthy of any punishment, whether for fasting on the Sabbath or for dining on it.

Let this man himself see, however, which of these two is appropriate to rest and which to labor—he who assigned joy to those who eat and mourning to those who fast, or understood the Lord to assign them so, when he answered concerning fasting: “The children of the bridegroom cannot mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them” (Matt. 9:15).

6. As for his saying that the Apostles ate on the Sabbath because the time had not yet come for them to fast on the Sabbath, since the tradition of the ancients prohibited it: was it therefore already time for them not to abstain on the Sabbath? Did not the tradition of the ancients prohibit this too and compel abstention?

And yet, on that very Sabbath day on which we read that Christ’s disciples ate, they certainly plucked ears of grain (ibid. 12:1)—something that was not permitted on the Sabbath because the tradition of the ancients prohibited it.

Let him therefore consider whether a more fitting answer might perhaps be given him: that the Lord wished these two things to be done by his disciples on that day—one, the plucking of ears; the other, the eating of food. The first was directed against those who wished to keep Sabbath rest; the second against those who compelled fasting on the Sabbath. By the first he indicated that such Sabbath rest had become superstitious after the time had changed; by the second he wished eating to remain free at both times.

I do not say this as an assertion of doctrine; I have merely shown what answer could be given him, much more suitably than the things he says.

## CHAPTER FOUR

7. “How,” he says, “will we not be condemned along with the Pharisee, if we fast twice on the Sabbath?”—as though the Pharisee were condemned because he fasted twice on the Sabbath, and not because he proudly exalted himself above the tax collector (Luke 18:11–12).

This man could also say that those who give a tenth of all their produce to the poor are condemned with the Pharisee, because the Pharisee also proclaimed this among his works—something we desire many Christians to do and scarcely find even a very few doing. Or he could say that anyone who has not been unjust, adulterous, or a robber will be condemned with the Pharisee, because the Pharisee boasted that he was not such a person. Anyone who thinks this is certainly insane.

But if these things, undoubtedly good, which the Pharisee declared to be present in himself, are not to be rejected together with the proud boastfulness that appeared in him, but are nevertheless to be retained together with the humble piety that was absent from him, then so also twice fasting on the Sabbath is fruitless in a person such as that Pharisee was, but religious in a humbly faithful—or faithfully humble—person.

The Gospel, however, did not say that the Pharisee was condemned; rather, it said that the tax collector was justified.

8. But if this man thinks that the Lord’s statement, “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:21), must be understood in this way, and that unless we fast more than twice on the Sabbath we cannot fulfill this command, it is fortunate that there are seven days, which return in their appointed sequence through the cycle of time.

When, therefore, someone removes two of these days so as not to fast on the Sabbath and the Lord’s Day, five days remain in which he can surpass the Pharisee who fasted twice on the Sabbath. For I think that if someone fasts three times on the Sabbath, he already surpasses the Pharisee who fasted twice on the Sabbath.

And if he fasts four times—or even, so that no day except the Sabbath and the Lord’s Day is omitted, fasts five times in the week, as many people do throughout their lives, especially those established in monasteries—not only will the Pharisee who fasted twice on the Sabbath be surpassed in the labor of fasting, but also the Christian who is accustomed to fast on Wednesday, Friday, and the Sabbath, as the Roman populace frequently does [Note: The editions have *sexta feria* (“Friday”). The manuscripts lack the word *feria* here and in other places where the editions have added it.].

And yet this Urbicus, whoever he is, the disputant you mention, calls a person carnal even if he fasts in such a way on five consecutive days apart from the Sabbath and the Lord’s Day that he does not refresh his body at all on any day—as though food and drink on the other days did not pertain to the flesh. He judges him a belly-worshiper, as though only the Sabbath meal descended into the belly.

## CHAPTER FIVE

9. It is not enough for this man that, to surpass the Pharisee, it already suffices to fast three times on the Sabbath. Except for the Lord’s Day, he compels fasting on the other six days in such a way that he says:

“Once the ancient stain has been removed, the two who remain under Christ’s discipline in one flesh ought not to celebrate pleasure-seeking Sabbath banquets with the lawless and with the princes of Sodom and the people of Gomorrah; rather, with the inhabitants of holiness and those devoted to God, they ought more and more legitimately to fast according to solemn and ecclesiastical law, so that the slight error of six days may be washed away by the fountains of fasting, prayer, and almsgiving, whereby, refreshed by the Sunday *alogia*, we may all sing with equal heart in a worthy manner: ‘You have satisfied, O Lord, the empty soul, and given drink to the thirsty soul.’”

By saying this, and excepting only the Lord’s Day from frequent fasting, he rashly and incautiously accuses not only the Christian peoples of East and West, among whom no one fasts on the Sabbath, but even the Roman Church itself.

For when he says that those who remain under Christ’s discipline ought not to celebrate pleasure-seeking Sabbath banquets with the lawless, the princes of Sodom, and the people of Gomorrah, but ought, with the inhabitants of holiness and those devoted to God, to fast more and more legitimately according to solemn and ecclesiastical law, and then, defining what it means to fast legitimately, adds, “so that the slight error of six days may be washed away by the fountains of fasting, prayer, and almsgiving,” he plainly does not think that those who fast fewer than six days in the week practice fasting legitimately, are devoted to God, or wash away the stains of error contracted from this mortality.

Let the Romans therefore see what they are doing, since they too are treated with excessive insult in this dissertation. Among them, apart from a very few clerics or monks, how many are found to practice frequent daily fasting on all those six days? Especially since fasting on Thursday does not seem to be customary there.

10. Next I ask: if the slight error of each day is removed or washed away by that day’s fasting—for this is what he says, that “the slight error of six days may also be washed away by the fountains of fasting”—what shall we do about the error that creeps in on the Lord’s Day, when fasting is a scandal?

Or, if no error creeps in upon Christians on that day, let this man, who accuses belly-worshipers as though he were a great faster, see how much honor and usefulness he attributes to bellies if error does not occur when people dine.

Perhaps he has placed such great good in fasting on the Sabbath that the fasting of the Sabbath alone can abolish the slight error, as he calls it, of the other six days—that is, even of the Lord’s Day—and that only on the day on which one fasts throughout the whole day does one not err.

Why, then, does he place the Lord’s Day before the Sabbath, as though by Christian law? Behold: according to him, the Sabbath is found to be much holier, since on it no error is committed when the whole day is spent fasting, and by that same fasting the errors of the other six days—and therefore even the error of the Lord’s Day—are washed away. I think you do not approve of this presumption.

11. Now, since he wishes to appear a spiritual man and accuses those who dine on the Sabbath as carnal, observe how he is refreshed on the Lord’s Day—not by a moderate meal, but by *alogia*.

What is *alogia*, a word borrowed from the Greek language, except indulgence in banquets whereby one deviates from the path of reason? Hence animals lacking reason are called *aloga* (ἄλογα), and those devoted to the belly are like them. For this reason, an immoderate banquet, by which the mind—where reason holds dominion—is in a manner overwhelmed by the stuffing of eating and drinking, is called *alogia*.

Moreover, because of food and drink, not of the mind but of the belly, he says that on the Lord’s Day this *alogia* is to be sung:

“You have satisfied, O Lord, the empty soul, and given drink to the thirsty soul.”

O spiritual man! O reprover of the carnal! O great faster—and not belly-worshiper! Behold the man who warns us not to corrupt the law of the Lord by the law of the belly, not to sell the bread of heaven for earthly food, and who adds:

“For by food Adam perished from paradise; by food Esau lost his birthright.”

Behold the man who says:

“For it is Satan’s customary slander—the temptation of the belly—which persuades one to take a little in order to remove everything.”

“And,” he says, “the interpretation of these commands bends belly-worshipers less.”

12. Does he not seem, by these words of his, to be working toward fasting even on the Lord’s Day? Otherwise the Sabbath, on which the Lord rested in the tomb, will be holier than the Lord’s Day, on which he rose from the dead.

The Sabbath is certainly holier if, according to this man’s words, every sin is avoided by fasting on the Sabbath and whatever has been contracted on the other days is abolished; whereas on the Lord’s Day temptation through food in the belly is not avoided, an opportunity for the devil’s slander is given, paradise is lost, and the birthright is forfeited.

What, then, is the meaning of his once again contradicting himself by urging us not to be refreshed by a moderate, sober, Christian meal on the Lord’s Day, but to rejoice and applaud in *alogia* while singing:

“You have satisfied, O Lord, the empty soul, and given drink to the thirsty soul”?

Surely, if we do not err when we fast, and if we wash away the errors of the other six days when we fast on the Sabbath, there will be no day worse than the Lord’s Day and none better than the Sabbath.

Believe me, most beloved brother: no one understands the law as this man does except one who does not understand it.

For if Adam was ruined not by food but by forbidden food (Gen. 3:6), and if Esau, the grandson of holy Abraham, was condemned not by food but by food desired even to the point of despising the sacrament that he possessed in his birthright (Gen. 25:33–34), then holy and faithful people dine piously just as sacrilegious and unbelieving people fast impiously.

The Lord’s Day is placed before the Sabbath by faith in the resurrection, not by the custom of refreshment or by the license of drunken singing.

## CHAPTER SIX

13. “Moses,” he says, “did not eat bread or drink water for forty days.” Then he adds why he has said this:

“Behold Moses, the friend of God, the inhabitant of the cloud, the bearer of the Law, and leader of the people, celebrating three pairs of Sabbaths in fasting, established not an offense but a merit.”

Does he not consider what can consequently be opposed to this? For if he sets forth the example of Moses fasting because during those forty days he fasted three pairs of Sabbaths, as he puts it, and from this wishes to persuade us to fast on the Sabbath, then from this he should also persuade us to fast on the Lord’s Day, because during those same forty days Moses likewise fasted three pairs of Lord’s Days.

But he adds and says, “And even then, with Christ, the Lord’s Day was being reserved for the approaching Church.” I do not know why he said this.

For if it is because one ought to fast much more after the Lord’s Day came with Christ, then—God forbid—one should fast even on the Lord’s Day itself.

But if he feared that, because of the forty-day fast, someone might object that one should also fast on the Lord’s Day, and therefore added that, with Christ still approaching, the Lord’s Day was being reserved for the Church—so that Moses is understood to have fasted even on the day following the Sabbath because Christ had not yet come, through whom the Lord’s Day itself was made, on which it would not be appropriate to fast—why, then, did Christ himself fast for forty days in the same way?

Why, during those forty days, did he not break his fast on the three pairs of days following the Sabbaths, so that even before his resurrection he might commend the meal of the Lord’s Day, just as before his passion he gave his blood to be drunk?

You see clearly that the forty-day fast he mentions is no more relevant to fasting on the Sabbath than it is to fasting on the Lord’s Day.

14. He plainly does not consider what can be opposed to him concerning the Lord’s Day. Just as drunken banquets and every greedy and drunken indulgence must be condemned, so he condemns Sabbath meals, although these too may be those of moderate and sober people.

Therefore, it is unnecessary to answer him point by point, since, by reproving the vices of luxury in place of the Sabbath meal, he repeats the same things again and again. He finds nothing else to say except what he says vainly and irrelevantly.

The question is whether one ought to fast on the Sabbath, not whether one ought to indulge in luxury on the Sabbath—a practice that those who fear God do not engage in even on the Lord’s Day, although they certainly do not fast on that day.

Who would say what this man has dared to say?

“How,” he says, “will things be ratified for God on our behalf or through us, or be worthy, if they compel us to sin on a sanctified day?”

He confesses that the Sabbath is a sanctified day, and says that people are compelled to sin because they dine. Consequently, according to this man, either the Lord’s Day has not been sanctified and the Sabbath is beginning to be better, or, if the Lord’s Day too has been sanctified, we are compelled to sin because we dine.

## CHAPTER SEVEN
15. And he tries to prove by divine testimonies that one ought to fast on the Sabbath; but he finds absolutely no basis for proving this. “Jacob ate,” he says, “and drank wine, and was filled, and departed from his saving God, and twenty-three thousand fell on one day” (Exod. 32:6, 8, 28)—as though it had been said: “Jacob dined on the Sabbath and departed from his saving God.” And when the Apostle recalled that so many had fallen, he did not say, “Let us not dine on the Sabbath, as they dined”; rather, he said, “Let us not commit fornication, as some of them committed fornication, and twenty-three thousand fell on one day.” What, moreover, does he mean by saying, “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (1 Cor. 10:7–8)? The Apostle did indeed include this testimony, but in order to prohibit bondage to idols, not a Sabbath meal. This event’s having occurred on the Sabbath, however, he does not prove; he merely conjectures it as he pleases.

Just as it can happen that someone fasts and, when the fast is broken, if he is a drunkard, becomes drunk then, so it can happen that one does not fast and, if people are temperate, dines with the greatest moderation. What, then, is the point of his bringing forward the Apostle as a witness when he wishes to persuade us to fast on the Sabbath, saying, “Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is all debauchery” (Eph. 5:18)—as though he were saying, “Do not dine on the Sabbath, because there is all debauchery there”? Yet just as this apostolic command—not to become drunk with wine, in which there is all debauchery—is observed by Christians who fear God when they dine on the Lord’s Day, so it is observed when they dine on the Sabbath.

16. “To contradict those in error more explicitly,” he says, “no one offends God by fasting, even if he does not win His favor; moreover, not offending Him is itself a way of winning His favor.” Who would say this except one unwilling to consider what he was saying? Thus, when pagans fast, they do not thereby offend God more; or, if he intended what he said to be understood of Christians, who would not offend God if he wished to fast on the Lord’s Day with the scandal of the whole Church spread throughout the world?

Next he brings forward testimonies from Scripture that have no force whatsoever for the case he has undertaken. “By fasting,” he says, “Elijah was granted paradise and reigns in the body”—as though those who do not fast on the Sabbath did not commend fasting, just as those who commend fasting nevertheless do not fast on the Lord’s Day; or as though Elijah fasted at a time when God’s people were also fasting on the Sabbath. What we replied concerning Moses’ forty-day fast—consider that same reply made concerning Elijah’s forty days as well.

“By fasting,” he says, “Daniel escaped unharmed the lions’ dry rage”—as though he had read that Daniel fasted on the Sabbath, or even that he was with the lions on the Sabbath; although we read that he also dined. “By fasting,” he says, “the faithful brotherhood of the three men, having mastered the blazing prison, worshiped the Lord who had been received as a guest in the lodging of the pyre.”

These examples of holy persons have no force for persuading anyone to fast on any particular day—how much less on the Sabbath? For not only is it not read that the three men were cast into the burning furnace on the Sabbath; it is not even read that they remained there long enough for anyone to say that they fasted. Indeed, scarcely an hour’s interval is occupied while their confession and hymn are sung; they did not walk unharmed amid those flames any longer than it took them to complete that song. Unless perhaps he counts even an hour’s interval as a fast. If that is so, he has no reason to be angry with those who dine on the Sabbath: until the hour of the meal, the fast lasts much longer than it did in that furnace.

17. He also brings forward that testimony of the Apostle where he says: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Rom. 14:17); and he wants the kingdom of God to be understood as the Church, in which God reigns. I ask you: was the Apostle concerned, when he spoke these words, that Christians should fast on the Sabbath? But he was not speaking even about fasting on any particular day when he said this. For it was spoken against those who, in the manner of the Jews, thought under the old Law that purity consisted in the observance of certain foods, and for the admonition of those brethren through whose food and drink, accepted without distinction, the weak were being scandalized.

Therefore, after saying, “Do not destroy by your food the one for whom Christ died” (ibid., 15), and, “Let not our good be blasphemed” (ibid., 16), he added: “For the kingdom of God is not food and drink.” For if this man understands the Apostle’s words in such a way that the kingdom of God, which is the Church, consists not in food and drink but in fasting, then—not to say that we ought to fast on the Sabbath—we ought never to take food or drink at all, lest we ever depart from this kingdom of God. Yet I think that, by his own admission, we belong to the Church somewhat more religiously on the Lord’s Day, even though, by his own concession, we dine then.

## CHAPTER VIII

18. “Why,” he says, “do we murmur that we should offer to the superior Lord a sacrifice dear to Him, which the spirit desires and the angel praises?” Then he adds the testimony of the angel who says: “Prayer is good with fasting and almsgiving” (Tob. 12:8). What he means by “the superior Lord,” I do not know—unless perhaps the copyist made a mistake and it escaped you, so that you did not correct what you sent me to read.

Thus he wants fasting to be understood as a sacrifice dear to the Lord, as though this question concerned fasting in general and not fasting on the Sabbath. For the Lord’s Day does not pass without a sacrifice dear to God simply because there is no fasting.

He continues and presses into service testimonies wholly unrelated to the case he has undertaken to defend. “Sacrifice,” he says, “a sacrifice of praise to God” (Ps. 49:14); and, wishing somehow to connect this verse of the divine psalm with the matter at hand, he says: “Certainly not a feast of blood or drunkenness, in which not praises due to God but blasphemies flourish with the devil’s support.”

O reckless presumption! Thus, because there is no fasting on the Lord’s Day, the sacrifice of praise is not offered; instead, a feast of drunkenness is conducted, and blasphemies flourish with the devil’s support. If it is sacrilegious to say this, let him understand that fasting is not signified by what is written: “Sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise.” Fasting is not practiced on certain days, especially feast days, but the sacrifice of praise is offered by the Church spread throughout the whole world every day.

Otherwise—something no one, I do not say a Christian, but not even a madman, would dare to say—the fifty days after Easter until Pentecost, during which there is no fasting, would, according to this man, be excluded from the sacrifice of praise. Yet on those very days Alleluia is sung in many churches—and especially in all churches; and no Christian, however unlearned, is unaware that this is a word of praise.

19. Nevertheless, he admits that even on the Lord’s Day people dine not in drunkenness but in joy, when he says that we—many Christians in name from Jews and Gentiles, but few elect in faith—ought, at the evening incense of the Sabbaths, to offer to God in praise a fast pleasing to Him in place of animal victims, so that by its heat the works of sins may be burned up and fail.

“And in the morning,” he says, “may He whom we hear hear us, and we shall have houses for eating and drinking, not in drunkenness but in joy, with the celebration of the Lord’s Day completed.” Thus it is *eulogia*—a blessing—that is celebrated, not, as he said above, *alogia*—a senseless or irrational thing.

But what offense the Sabbath day, which the Lord sanctified, has given him, I do not know, so that he does not think that on it one can eat and drink with a joy free from drunkenness, even though we can fast before the Sabbath in the same way he says we ought to fast on the Sabbath before the Lord’s Day. Or does he think that it is sacrilegious to dine on two successive days?

Let him see, then, what an insult he also inflicts on the Roman Church, where, even in those weeks during which fasting occurs on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday, people nevertheless dine for three successive days—namely, on the Lord’s Day and then on Monday and Tuesday.

20. “It is certain,” he says, “that the life of sheep depends on the shepherds’ judgment. But ‘Woe to those who call evil good, and darkness light, and light darkness, and bitter sweet, and sweet bitter’” (Isa. 5:20). I do not sufficiently understand what he intends by these words.

For if Urbicus says this, as you write, then in Rome the people, dependent on their shepherd’s judgment, fast on the Sabbath with their bishop. But if he wrote this to you because you yourself wrote something of the kind in your letter, let him not persuade you to praise the Christian city for fasting on the Sabbath in such a way that you are forced to condemn the Christian world for dining.

For when he says, “Woe to those who call evil good, and darkness light, and light darkness, and bitter sweet, and sweet bitter,” wishing “good,” “light,” and “sweet” to mean Sabbath fasting, and “evil,” “darkness,” and “bitter” to mean dining, who could doubt that he is condemning the whole world in all Christians who dine on the Sabbath? He does not consider himself, nor attend to what he says, so as to restrain this rash audacity by his own writings.

For immediately he added: “Therefore let no one judge you in food or drink” (Col. 2:16)—something he certainly does himself, since he condemns in this way those who take food and drink on the Sabbath. [Note: Lov. reads: “He errs so greatly that it is to be feared that even this may happen to him,” etc. But the other manuscripts, like ours, read: “How fitting it would have been,” etc.] How fitting it would have been for even this to come to his mind, what the same Apostle says elsewhere: “He who eats, let him not despise him who does not eat; and he who does not eat, let him not judge him who eats” (Rom. 14:3)?

He should maintain this rule and moderation, by which he would avoid scandals, between those who fast on the Sabbath and those who eat: so that the one who eats would not despise the one who does not eat, and the one who does not eat would not judge the one who eats.

## CHAPTER IX

21. “Peter also,” he says, “the head of the Apostles, the gatekeeper of heaven, and the foundation of the Church, taught the Romans this very thing. Simon, who had been the devil’s figure and could be conquered only by fasting, having been destroyed, Peter taught the Romans, whose faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world.”

Did the other Apostles, then, teach Christians throughout the whole world to dine contrary to Peter? Therefore, just as Peter and his fellow disciples lived together in harmony, so let those whom Peter planted, who fast on the Sabbath, and those whom his fellow disciples planted, who dine on the Sabbath, live together in harmony.

There is indeed an opinion held by many—although most Romans declare it false—that the Apostle Peter, when he was about to contend with Simon Magus on the Lord’s Day, fasted on the preceding day with the Church of that city because of the danger of that great temptation, and that after achieving such a prosperous and glorious success he maintained the same custom, which certain Churches of the West imitated.

But if, as this man says, Simon Magus was a figure of the devil, that tempter is not specifically a Sabbath or Lord’s Day tempter, but a daily one. Yet people do not fast against him every day, since they dine on every Lord’s Day, on all fifty days after Easter, and in various places on the solemn days of the martyrs and on every feast. Nevertheless, the devil is conquered if our eyes are always turned toward the Lord, so that He Himself may draw our feet from the snare (Ps. 24:15); and whether we eat or drink, or do anything else, we may do everything to the glory of God; and, so far as it depends on us, may be without offense to Jews, Greeks, and the Church of God (1 Cor. 10:31–32).

Those who eat with offense or fast with offense think little about this. By either kind of intemperance they stir up scandals, by which the devil is not overcome but rejoices.

22. If it is answered that James in Jerusalem, John in Ephesus, and the other Apostles in other places taught what Peter taught in Rome—that is, that people should fast on the Sabbath—but that the other lands departed from this teaching while Rome remained in it; and if, conversely, it is reported that certain places in the West, including Rome, did not preserve what the Apostles handed down, while the lands of the East, from which the preaching of the Gospel itself began, remained without variation in what was handed down by all the Apostles together with Peter—namely, that people should not fast on the Sabbath—then this is an endless dispute, producing quarrels rather than settling questions.

Let there therefore be one faith throughout the whole Church spread everywhere, as within its members, even if this unity of faith is celebrated through certain diverse observances by which what is true in the faith is in no way impeded. For “all the beauty of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. 44:14); those observances that are celebrated in varied ways are understood in her clothing, and therefore it is said there: “Clothed in a garment fringed with gold, adorned with variety” (ibid., 15). But let that garment also be varied through diverse celebrations in such a way that it is not torn apart by hostile disputes.

## CHAPTER X

23. “Finally,” he says, “if a Jew, by honoring the Sabbath, denies the Lord’s Day, how does a Christian observe the Sabbath? Let us either be Christians and honor the Lord’s Day, or let us be Jews and observe the Sabbath; ‘for no one can serve two masters’” (Matt. 6:24).

Does he not speak as though the Sabbath had one master and the Lord’s Day another? Does he not hear what he himself also mentioned: “The Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath” (Luke 6:5)?

And when he wants us to be as far removed from the Sabbath as Jews are from the Lord’s Day, does he not err so greatly that he could also say that we ought not to accept the Law and the Prophets, just as Jews do not accept the Gospel and the Apostles? You understand what evil he would be thinking if he held this view.

“But the old things,” he says, “have passed away, and in Christ all things have become new” (2 Cor. 5:17). This is true. For that reason, just as we do not spend the Sabbath at leisure as the Jews do, so, even though we relax the constraint of fasting in order to signify the rest signified by that day, we preserve Christian sobriety and moderation.

And if some of our brethren do not think that the Sabbath rest ought to be signified by relaxing the fast, we do not quarrel at all about the variety of the royal garment, lest we trouble the inner members of the queen herself, in whom we retain one faith even concerning that rest.

For although, because the old things have passed away, the carnal observance of Sabbath leisure has also passed away with them, nevertheless, because we dine on the Sabbath and the Lord’s Day without superstitious observance, we do not thereby serve two masters, since the Sabbath and the Lord’s Day have one Lord.

24. Yet this man, who says that the old things have passed away in such a way that altar gave way to altar in Christ, sword to fasting, fire to prayers, animal sacrifice to bread, and blood to the cup, does not know that the name “altar” occurs much more frequently in the letters of the Law and the Prophets, and that an altar was first placed for God in the tabernacle made through Moses (Exod. 40:24). He does not know that an altar is also found in the apostolic writings, where the martyrs cry out beneath the altar of God (Rev. 6:9–10).

He says that the sword gave way to fasting, without remembering that sword with which the Gospel soldiers are armed from both Testaments—the two-edged sword (Eph. 6:17; Heb. 4:12).

He says that fire gave way to prayers, as though prayers were not even then brought into the temple, and as though Christ had not now sent fire into the world (Luke 12:49).

He says that the animal gave way to bread, as though he did not know that even then the bread of the Presence was customarily placed on the Lord’s table (Exod. 25:30), and that now he himself receives a portion of the body of the immaculate Lamb.

He says that blood gave way to the cup, without considering that even now he receives blood in the cup (Luke 22:7–20).

How much better and more appropriately he would say that the old things have passed away and the new things have been made in Christ, so that altar gave way to altar, sword to sword, fire to fire, bread to bread, animal to animal, and blood to blood. For in all these things we see the carnal antiquity yielding to spiritual newness.

Thus it must be understood that, whether one dines on this revolving seventh day or some people also fast, nevertheless the spiritual Sabbath has replaced the carnal Sabbath: in the former, eternal and true rest is desired; in the latter, temporary leisure, now superstitious, is despised.

## CHAPTER XI

25. The remaining matters with which this man concludes his discussion, like certain other things that I did not think should be mentioned from it, are even more irrelevant to the question at issue, in which the dispute concerns fasting or dining on the Sabbath. I leave it to you yourself to notice and judge them, especially if you have been helped in any way by what I have said.

But since I think that I have answered him sufficiently, as far as I could, if you ask my opinion on this matter, I have turned it over in my mind in the light of the evangelical and apostolic writings and the whole instrument called the New Testament, and I see that fasting is commanded. On which days, however, one ought not to fast and on which days one ought to fast, I do not find defined by any command of the Lord or the Apostles.

Accordingly, I judge that—not indeed for attaining eternal rest, which faith and righteousness attain and in which is the inner beauty of the king’s daughter, but nevertheless for signifying the eternal rest where the true Sabbath is—relaxing the fast is more suitable than tightening it.

26. Nevertheless, whether in fasting or dining on this Sabbath, nothing seems to me safer or more peaceful to preserve than that “he who eats should not despise him who does not eat, and he who does not eat should not judge him who eats,” because “whether we eat, we shall not abound, nor, if we do not eat, shall we lack” (Rom. 14:3)—provided that the fellowship of those among whom we live and with whom we live for God is preserved without offense in these matters.

For just as what the Apostle says is true—that a person does wrong when he eats through giving offense (ibid., 20; 1 Cor. 8:8)—so a person does wrong when he fasts through giving offense.

Let us therefore not be like those who, seeing John neither eating nor drinking, said, “He has a demon.” But let us also not be like those who, seeing Christ eating and drinking, said, “Behold, a glutton and a wine-drinker, a friend of tax collectors and sinners” (Matt. 11:19). For the Lord Himself added a very necessary point to these words, saying: “And wisdom is justified by her children” (ibid.).

If you ask who these are, read what is written: “The children of wisdom are the assembly of the righteous” (Sir. 3:1). These are the people who, when they eat, do not despise those who do not eat; when they do not eat, do not judge those who eat. But they certainly despise or judge those who, whether they do not eat or do eat, do so through giving offense.

## CHAPTER XII

27. The matter of the Sabbath is easier, since the Roman Church fasts, as do some other Churches, although they are few, whether near or far from Rome. But fasting on the Lord’s Day is a great scandal, especially after the extremely detestable heresy of the Manichaeans became known—so plainly contrary to the Catholic faith and the divine Scriptures. They seem to have established this day for their hearers as a lawful day for fasting; and thus fasting on the Lord’s Day came to be regarded as more horrible.

Unless, perhaps, someone is capable of continuing a fast beyond a week without inserting any refreshment, so as to approach as closely as he can the forty-day fast, as we know some have done. We have even been assured by brethren entirely worthy of belief that one person reached the full number of forty days.

For just as Moses and Elijah did nothing against Sabbath meals when they fasted for forty days in the times of the ancient fathers, so one who is able to pass seven days fasting has not chosen the Lord’s Day for fasting; rather, he found it among the days during which he vowed to fast for many days.

Yet if a continuous fast is to be broken during the week, it is broken on no day more appropriately than the Lord’s Day. But if the body is refreshed only after a full week, then the Lord’s Day is not chosen for fasting; it merely falls within the number of days one has decided to vow.

28. Nor should the fact that the Priscillianists, very similar to the Manichaeans, customarily bring forward a testimony from the Acts of the Apostles for fasting on the Lord’s Day disturb us. The Apostle Paul was in Troas, and the text reads:

“On the first day of the week, when we had assembled to break bread, Paul was speaking to them, intending to depart on the next day, and he prolonged his discourse until midnight” (Acts 20:7).

Then, after he had gone down from the upper room where they had assembled, in order to restore to life the young man who, overcome by sleep, had fallen from the window and was reported dead, Scripture speaks of the Apostle himself in this way:

“And when he had gone up and broken bread and tasted it, and had spoken sufficiently until dawn, he departed” (ibid., 11).

Far be it from us to understand this as though the Apostles customarily fasted solemnly on the Lord’s Day. At that time “the first day of the week” was the name of the day now called the Lord’s Day, as is found more clearly in the Gospels. For the day of the Lord’s resurrection is called “the first of the Sabbath” by Matthew, but by the other three evangelists “the first day of the week” (Matt. 28:1; Mark 16:2; Luke 24:1; John 20:1). It is clear that this is the day afterward called the Lord’s Day.

Either, then, after the Sabbath day had ended, they had assembled at the beginning of the night—which night certainly already belonged to the Lord’s Day, that is, to the first day of the week—and thus, because he was going to break bread that same night as it is broken in the sacrament of Christ’s body, he prolonged his discourse until midnight. After the sacraments had been celebrated, he again spoke to those assembled until dawn, since he was in great haste to depart at daybreak on the Lord’s Day.

Or, if they had assembled on the first day of the week not during the night but during the day, the words “Paul was speaking to them, intending to depart on the next day” themselves state the reason for prolonging the discourse: he was going to depart and wished to instruct them adequately.

They were not therefore solemnly fasting on the Lord’s Day. Rather, the necessary discourse, listened to with the ardor of the most fervent devotion, did not seem to be interrupted for the sake of bodily refreshment by the Apostle who was about to depart and who, because of his constant journeys elsewhere, either never or very rarely visited them. This was especially so because, as the subsequent events indicate, he was then about to depart from those regions in such a way that he would not see them again in the flesh.

This makes it clearer that their customary practice was not to fast on the Lord’s Days. For, lest anyone should believe this, the writer of the book took care to explain the reason for prolonging the discourse, so that we might know that, if some necessity arises, food should not be preferred to a more urgent task.

Although these listeners, hearing him with such eagerness and considering that the very fountain was about to depart, and therefore drawing in with great thirst—not for water but for the word—whatever flowed forth without satiety, disregarded not only a bodily meal but even supper.

29. At that time, although fasting on the Lord’s Day was not their customary practice, it would nevertheless not have been such a notable offense to the Church if, because of a necessity like the one the Apostle Paul faced, they had neglected to refresh their bodies throughout the Lord’s Day until midnight or even until dawn.

But now, after heretics—especially the most impious Manichaeans—began to fast on the Lord’s Day not because of some necessity that arose, but to dogmatize this as though it were an established sacred solemnity, and this became known among Christian peoples, I certainly think that what the Apostle did should not be done even in such a necessity as his, lest one incur a greater evil through scandal than good is received from the word. [Note: Am., Bad., Er., and six manuscripts omit “Manichaeans,” reading “especially the most impious fasts.”]

Nevertheless, whatever reason or necessity may arise that compels a Christian to fast on the Lord’s Day—as we also find in the Acts of the Apostles, where, in the danger of shipwreck, the Apostle himself was sailing, and people fasted for fourteen days, and therefore through two Lord’s Days (Acts 27:33)—we ought in no way to doubt that, when no vow has been made to continue for many days without any refreshment, the Lord’s Day should not be counted among the days of fasting.

## CHAPTER XIII

30. As for why the Church fasts especially on Wednesday and Friday, the following explanation seems to be given. When the Gospel is considered, it is found that on Wednesday—the day commonly called the fourth day of the week—the Jews made their plan to kill the Lord.

One day was then interposed, on the evening of which the Lord ate the Passover with His disciples. That was the conclusion of the day we call Thursday. He was then betrayed during the night that already belonged to Friday, the day of His manifest passion.

This was the first day of Unleavened Bread, beginning at evening. But the evangelist Matthew says that Thursday was the first day of Unleavened Bread, because on its following evening the Passover meal was to take place, at which meal the eating of unleavened bread and the sacrifice of the lamb began.

From this it is inferred that it was Wednesday when the Lord said: “You know that after two days the Passover will take place, and the Son of Man will be delivered up to be crucified” (Matt. 26:2). Accordingly, that day itself was assigned to fasting, because, as the Evangelist continues and says:

“Then the chief priests and the elders of the people gathered in the courtyard of the high priest, who was called Caiaphas, and they took counsel to seize Jesus by deceit and kill Him” (ibid., 3–4).

One day was then interposed, of which the Gospel says: “On the first day of Unleavened Bread the disciples came to Jesus, saying, ‘Where do You want us to prepare for You to eat the Passover?’” (ibid., 17).

After that day had intervened, the Lord suffered, which no one doubts occurred on Friday; therefore Friday itself is rightly assigned to fasting. For fasts signify humility. Hence it is said: “I humbled my soul with fasting” (Ps. 34:13).

31. The Sabbath follows. On that day Christ’s flesh rested in the tomb, just as, in the first works of the world, God rested on that day from all His works.

From this arose the variety in the garment of that queen, so that some—especially the peoples of the East—preferred to relax the fast in order to signify rest, while others, on account of the humility of the Lord’s death, preferred to fast, as do the Roman Church and certain Churches of the West.

On the one day when Easter is celebrated, however, because the event is commemorated anew—the disciples having experienced human grief over the Lord’s death—all fast in such a way that even those who dine on the Sabbath throughout the rest of the year observe the Sabbath fast with the utmost devotion. Thus they signify both the disciples’ mourning on that one anniversary day and the goodness of rest on the other Sabbaths.

For there are two things that cause the blessedness of the righteous and the end of all misery to be hoped for: death and the resurrection of the dead. In death there is rest, concerning which the Prophet says: “My people, enter into your chambers; hide yourselves for a little while, until the Lord’s anger has passed” (Isa. 26:20). In the resurrection there is perfect happiness in the whole human being—that is, in flesh and spirit.

Thus it came about that people thought neither of these two things should be signified by the labor of fasting, but rather by the joy of refreshment, except on the one Sabbath of Easter, when, as we have said, the disciples’ mourning, because of the commemoration of the event, had to be marked by a more prolonged fast.

## CHAPTER XIV

32. But since, as I have already mentioned above, we do not find in the evangelical and apostolic writings—which properly concern the revelation of the New Testament—any clear command that fasts must be observed on particular days, this matter too, like many others that would be difficult to enumerate, has found a place for variety in the garment of that king’s daughter, namely, the Church.

I shall tell you what the venerable Ambrose, from whom I was baptized and who was bishop of Milan, answered me when I asked him about this.

When my mother was with me in that same city, and we were still catechumens, giving little attention to such matters while she was anxious about whether, according to the custom of our city, she ought to fast on the Sabbath or dine according to the custom of the Church of Milan, I questioned the aforesaid man of God so that I might free her from this uncertainty.

He replied: “What more can I teach about this than what I myself do?”

I had thought that by this answer he had prescribed nothing except that we should dine on the Sabbath; for I knew that this was what he himself did. But he continued:

“When I am here, I do not fast on the Sabbath; when I am in Rome, I fast on the Sabbath. And wherever you come,” he said, “follow the custom of that Church, if you do not wish either to suffer scandal or to cause it.”

I reported this answer to my mother, and it was sufficient for her; she did not doubt that she ought to obey. We followed this practice as well.

But since it happens, especially in Africa, that one Church, or the Churches of one region, has some people who dine on the Sabbath and others who fast, it seems to me that the custom of those to whom the governance of these peoples’ congregations has been entrusted should be followed.

Therefore, if you willingly accept my advice—especially since, at your request and insistence, I have perhaps said more in this matter than was sufficient—do not resist your bishop in this matter, but follow without any scruple or dispute what he himself does.

# LETTER XXXVII

[Note: This letter was missing from this volume. It is published here after comparison with the books that contain it prefixed to the books of Questions to Simplicianus.]

[Note: From Volume 4: what was Letter 37 is now Letter 109. Written around the year 397.]

Augustine congratulates himself that his literary labors are being read and approved by Simplicianus; he submits to Simplicianus’ judgment both his other books and those that he composed concerning the questions proposed by Simplicianus.

To his most blessed lord and father, to be embraced with most venerably sincere charity, SIMPLICIANUS,

AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

[Note: Simplicianus, bishop of the Church of Milan, succeeded the most blessed Ambrose. This occurred in the year 397, according to Book 2 of the *Retractions*, chapter 1. For Ambrose died on the day before Easter, according to Paulinus, the writer of his life—namely, on April 4, according to the evidence of the martyrologies; Easter, moreover, fell on April 5 in the year 397.]

1. I received, as a gift from Your Holiness, a letter full of good joys: you remembered me, loved me as you customarily do, and took great pleasure in whatever gifts the Lord in His mercy has deigned to confer upon me—not because of my merits. In it I drank in the paternal affection toward me that came from your most kindly heart, an affection not sudden or new, but one that I had certainly experienced and known before and now encountered again, my most blessed lord, to be embraced with most venerably sincere charity.

2. But how has such great good fortune arisen for our literary labor, over which we have sweated in composing certain books, that they should be read by Your Dignity? It can only be because the Lord, to whom my soul is subject, wished to console my anxieties and revive me from the fear that necessarily makes me solicitous in such works, lest somewhere I should stumble, whether through insufficient learning or through carelessness, even in the clearest field of truth.

When what I write pleases you, I know whom it pleases, since I know who dwells in you. The same distributor and giver of all spiritual gifts will, through your judgment, confirm my obedience. Whatever those writings possess that is worthy of your delight, God said in my ministry, “Let there be,” and it came to be; but in your approval God saw that it was good (Gen. 1:3–4).

3. As for the little questions that you deigned to command me to unravel, even if I did not understand them because of my own slowness and entanglement, I would open them with the help of your merits. I ask only this: that you pray to God for my weakness, and that, whether in the matters with which you kindly and fatherly wished to exercise me or in any others of ours that may perhaps come into your holy hands, since I recognize them as gifts of God and likewise recognize my errors, you devote not merely the care of a reader but also assume the judgment of one who corrects.

Farewell.

# LETTER XXXVIII

[Note: Revised according to the editions and manuscripts designated a, a, bg, bl, c, cc, ff, g, gv, n, r, s, t, vc, vd, two copies of sb, four copies of v, and according to Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: Elsewhere Letter 149; what was Letter 38 is now Letter 243. Written around the middle of the year 397.]

Augustine to Profuturus, concerning enduring adverse health, the death of Megalius, and the restraint of anger.

AUGUSTINE to his brother PROFUTURUS.

1. In spirit, insofar as it pleases the Lord and He Himself deigns to provide strength, we are well; but physically I am in bed. For I cannot walk, stand, or sit because of the pain and swelling of fissures or external hemorrhoids.

[Note: Physicians classify fissures and external hemorrhoids among disorders of the seat: *rhagades*, from the verb *resso*, “I break,” are fissures around the anus in the veins, which are called hemorrhoids because of the flow of blood; *exochas*, from *execho*, “I project,” are swellings in the seat, with the same veins protruding.]

But even in this condition, since it pleases the Lord, what else should be said except that we are well? If we do not want what He wills, we are the ones who must be blamed; He should not be thought to do or permit anything improperly.

You know all this. But because you are my other self, what would I speak with you more willingly about than what I speak with myself?

We therefore commend our days and nights to your holy prayers, so that you may pray for us: that we may not use our days intemperately, that we may endure our nights with an even spirit, and that, even if we walk in the midst of the shadow of death, the Lord may be with us, so that we do not fear evils.

## 2

Who could doubt that you have already heard that the old man Megalius [Note: [Col. 0153] This Megalius was bishop of Calama and primate of Numidia. Possidius apparently succeeded him in the episcopate, and Crescentianus in the primacy, as is understood from the Council of Carthage of 397. He ordained Saint Augustine bishop. Nevertheless, while Augustine was still a presbyter, he wrote an angry letter to Megalius; afterward he sought pardon for the insult and, in a council of bishops, condemned the slander and falsehood in writing. See *Against the Letter of Petilianus*, Book 3, chapter 16, no. 19; *Against Cresconius*, Book 3, chapter 80, no. 92; and Book 4 against the same, chapter 64, no. 79, etc. Perhaps Augustine refers to this in what he adds after announcing Megalius’s death: “There are no lack of scandals,” etc.] has died? For when I wrote this, it was approximately twenty-four days since his body had been laid to rest. Whether you have already seen [Note: [Col. 0153] Lov. has *found*. But Bad., Am., Er., and fourteen manuscripts have “whether you have already seen.”]—for you were planning to do so—we wish, if possible, to know his successor in the primacy.

There are no lack of scandals, but neither is there any lack of refuge; there are no lack of sorrows, but neither are there any lack of consolations. In the midst of all this, you know, excellent brother, how greatly we must keep watch lest hatred of anyone occupy the inmost recesses of the heart, and prevent us from praying to God in our room with the door closed (Matt. 6:6), but instead close the door against God himself. Yet anger creeps in while no angry person thinks his anger unjust. For as anger grows old, it becomes hatred: as though a sweetness belonging to supposedly righteous pain were mixed into it, it is kept longer in the vessel, until the whole contents grow sour and corrupt the vessel itself. Therefore it is much better that we be angry with someone, even without justification, than that, while becoming angry as though justly, we should slip by the hidden facility of anger into hatred of someone.

When receiving unknown guests, we customarily say that it is much better to suffer a bad person than perhaps, through ignorance, to shut out a good one while taking precautions lest a bad person be admitted. But with the emotions of the soul the reverse is true. For it is incomparably healthier not to open the inner chamber of the heart even to anger that knocks with justification than to admit an anger that will not readily withdraw and that will grow from a twig into a beam. In its shamelessness it dares to increase more quickly than one would think. It is not ashamed in the darkness, when the sun has set upon it (Eph. 4:26). You surely remember with what care and great concern I wrote these things, if you remember what you recently said to me on a certain journey.

## 3

We salute our brother Severus and those who are with him. We might perhaps also have written to them, if the haste of the messenger had permitted it. I ask you to assist me with our same brother Victor—whom I also thank in the presence of Your Holiness for informing me, as he was proceeding, about Constantina—by asking him, on account of the matter which he himself knows—and because I bear the very heavy burden of the elder Nectarius’s urgent entreaties in this affair—not to consider it burdensome to return through Calama. For that is what he promised me. Farewell.

# LETTER XXXIX [Note: [Col. 0154] This letter was collated with a. b. cc. fs. j. mr. r. sb. t. tt. vc.; ten copies marked v.; and Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.] [Note: [Col. 0154] Formerly 17; the letter that was 39 is now 26. Written around the year 397.]

Jerome to Augustine, commending Praesidius to him and greeting Alypius.

[Col. 0154]

To the truly holy and most blessed lord, Pope AUGUSTINE, JEROME sends greetings in Christ.

## CHAPTER I

### 1

Last year, through our brother Asterius the subdeacon, I sent a letter to Your Dignity, thereby promptly fulfilling my duty of greeting; I believe it was delivered to you. Now also, through my holy brother Praesidius the deacon, I ask first that you remember me; then that you receive the bearer of this letter as one commended to you, know him to be most closely attached to me, and, whenever necessity requires, cherish and support him—not because, by Christ’s gift, he lacks anything, but because he eagerly seeks the friendship of good men and considers himself to have received the greatest benefit when he forms such friendships. You will be able to learn from him why he has sailed to the West.

## CHAPTER II

### 2

We who are established in the monastery are shaken by various waves from every side and endure the hardships of exile. But we trust in him who said, “Take courage; I have conquered the world” (John 16:33), believing that, with him as giver and protector, we shall gain victory over the enemy, the devil. I ask you to greet the holy and venerable brother of ours, Pope Alypius, as a service from me. The holy brothers who are hastening to serve the Lord with us in the monastery greet you warmly. May Christ our almighty God preserve you unharmed and mindful of me, truly holy and venerable lord and pope.

# LETTER XL [Note: [Col. 0154] We revised this letter against a. bl. bn. cc. fs. j. mr. r. sb. t. tt. vc.; nine copies marked v.; and Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.] [Note: [Col. 0154] Formerly 9; the letter that was 40 is now included as 26. Written around the year 397.]

Augustine to Jerome concerning the title of the book on ecclesiastical writers published by Jerome; then concerning Peter’s being reproved truthfully by Paul, about which he had already written to Jerome in Letter 28. Finally, he urges him to publish the errors of Origen and of each of the heretics.

To his most beloved brother Jerome, worthy of observance and embrace with the purest devotion of charity, and his fellow presbyter, AUGUSTINE.

## CHAPTER I

### 1

I am grateful that, in response to the greeting written below, you sent me a full letter, though much shorter than I would wish to receive from you. From such a man, no matter how occupied he may be, no conversation is too long. Although, therefore, we are surrounded by immense cares arising from the affairs of others, and from worldly affairs at that, I would not readily forgive the brevity of your letter unless I considered how few words my own letter would receive in return. Therefore, I beg you, enter with us into this literary conversation, lest bodily absence have too much power to separate us—although we are joined in the Lord by unity of spirit, even when we rest from writing and remain silent.

The books which you have produced from the Lord’s granary display almost your whole self to us. If we do not know you because we have not seen your bodily face, then you do not know yourself in this way either, since you too do not see it. But if you are known to yourself for no other reason than that you know your own mind, then we also know it to no small degree through your writings. In them we bless the Lord, because he has given you such a character—to you, to us, and to all the brothers who read you.

## CHAPTER II

### 2

One of your books, among others, has not long since come into our hands. We still do not know its title, for the book itself did not display it, as is customary, on the title page. Yet the brother in whose possession it was found said that it was called an *Epitaph*. We would believe that you wished this name to be given to it if we had found there only the lives or writings of those who had already died. But since the works of many who were living both at the time it was written and still now are mentioned there, we wonder why you either gave it this title or are believed to have given it so. We certainly approve the book as having been usefully composed by you.

## CHAPTER III

### 3

In your exposition of Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, we also found something that greatly troubles us. For if what might be called well-intentioned lies are admitted into the sacred Scriptures, what authority will remain in them? What judgment will finally be pronounced concerning those Scriptures whose weight could crush the insolence of contentious falsehood? As soon as you put forward a statement, if the person opposing it thinks otherwise, he will say that the writer lied in that passage out of some honorable sense of duty. For where could this not be asserted, if it could be asserted in the narrative that the Apostle began by saying, “As for what I am writing to you, behold, before God, I am not lying” (Gal. 1:20), and yet could be believed and declared to have lied in the passage where he said of Peter and Barnabas, “When I saw that they were not walking uprightly according to the truth of the Gospel” (ibid. 2:14)?

For if they were walking uprightly, he lied; but if he lied there, where did he tell the truth? Will he be thought to have told the truth wherever he said what the reader thinks, while, whenever something contrary to the reader’s understanding occurs, it will be attributed to a well-intentioned lie? There will be no shortage of reasons for thinking that he not only could but even ought to have lied, if this principle is granted a place. There is no need to pursue this matter at length, especially with you, for one need only state it to someone whose wisdom is sufficiently provident. I would certainly not presume to enrich your divinely bestowed golden intellect with my pennies; nor is anyone more qualified than you to correct that work.

## CHAPTER IV

### 4

Nor do you need me to teach you how to understand what the same Apostle says: “I became to the Jews as a Jew, in order to win Jews” (1 Cor. 9:20), and the other statements made there out of compassionate mercy, not deceitful pretense. One becomes as though ill when ministering to the ill—not by pretending to have fevers, but by considering, with a compassionate mind, how one would wish to be served if one were ill oneself.

For Paul was certainly a Jew; but after becoming a Christian, he had not abandoned the sacraments of the Jews, which that people had appropriately received at the lawful time appointed for them. Accordingly, he undertook to celebrate them even when he was already an Apostle of Christ, in order to teach that it was not harmful for those who wished to preserve them as they had received them from their parents through the Law, even after they had believed in Christ—provided that they did not place their hope of salvation in them. For through the Lord Jesus the salvation itself, which those sacraments signified, had arrived. Therefore he judged that they should in no way be imposed upon the Gentiles, since they would recall people unaccustomed to them from the faith by a heavy and unnecessary burden (Acts 15:28).

### 5

Therefore Paul did not correct Peter because Peter observed the traditions of his fathers. If he had wished to do so, he would have acted neither deceitfully nor improperly; for although those practices were already superfluous, customary observances were not harmful. Rather, Paul corrected him because Peter was compelling the Gentiles to Judaize (Gal. 2:14), which he could not possibly have done unless he acted as though those observances were still necessary for salvation even after the Lord’s coming. The truth, through Paul’s apostleship, strongly rejected this.

The Apostle Peter was not ignorant of this; but he acted as he did because he feared those who were of the circumcision. Thus Peter was truly corrected, and Paul truthfully narrated the event, so that the holy Scripture, published for the faith of posterity, would not totter and fluctuate in complete uncertainty once the authority of lying had been admitted. It cannot, nor ought it to, be expressed in writing how many and how unspeakable evils would follow if we granted this. But it could be demonstrated suitably and with less danger if we were conversing face to face.

### 6

Paul had therefore abandoned in the Jews what was evil; above all, the fact that, “being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own righteousness, they were not subject to the righteousness of God” (Rom. 10:3). Next, after Christ’s passion and resurrection, once the sacrament of grace according to the order of Melchizedek had been given and revealed, they still thought that the old sacraments had to be celebrated not merely as customary solemnities but as necessary for salvation. Yet if those sacraments had never been necessary, the Maccabean martyrs would have suffered martyrdom for them fruitlessly and in vain (2 Macc. 7:1).

Finally, there was the fact that the Jews persecuted Christians, the preachers of grace [Note: [Col. 0156] Perhaps *Christian grace*.], as enemies of the Law. He says that he regarded these and similar errors and vices as “loss” and “dung” [Note: [Col. 0156] Nearly all the manuscripts read, “he says that he regarded [them as] losses,” whereas the editions have, “he says that he condemns,” etc.], in order to gain Christ (Phil. 3:8)—not observances of the Law if they were celebrated according to ancestral custom, as Paul himself celebrated them without any necessity for salvation [Note: [Col. 0156] The word “not” is absent in Bad., Am., Er., and most manuscripts.]; not as the Jews thought they ought to be celebrated, nor with the deceptive pretense that he had reproved in Peter. For if he celebrated those sacraments because he pretended to be a Jew in order to win them, why did he not also sacrifice with the Gentiles, since he became as one without the Law to those who were without the Law, in order to win them also? He did so because, as a Jew by nature, he did the former, and he spoke of all this not in order deceitfully to pretend to be what he was not, but in order mercifully to recognize that he ought to come to their aid as though he himself were struggling with the same error—not with the cunning of one who lies, but with the feeling of one who sympathizes.

Thus, in that very passage, he added generally, “I became weak to the weak, in order to win the weak” (1 Cor. 9:22), so that the following conclusion, “I have become all things to all people, in order to win all” (ibid.), may be understood as referring to his appearing to pity each person’s weakness as though it were his own. For when he said, “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (2 Cor. 11:29), he did not wish it to be understood that he had pretended to another’s weakness rather than sympathized with it.

### 7

Therefore, I beg you, take up the frank and truly Christian severity of charity in order to correct and amend that work, and sing a *palinode* (*παλινῳδίαν*), as the expression goes. The truth of Christians is incomparably more beautiful than the Helen of the Greeks. For this truth our martyrs fought more bravely against this Sodom than those heroes fought for Helen against Troy.

I do not say this so that you may recover the eyes of your heart—for heaven forbid that you should have lost them—but so that you may notice that, although you possess them sound and watchful, you have turned them away through some dissimulation, so as not to consider the consequences that would follow if it were once believed that the writer of the divine Books could honorably and devoutly lie in some part of his work [Note: [Col. 0157] The editions have: “that the writer could be honorably understood.” But thirteen manuscripts have: “that the writer of the divine Books could honorably and devoutly lie.” We embrace this reading.].

# CHAPTER V

### 8

I had previously written you a letter that was not delivered, because the person to whom I had entrusted it did not proceed to deliver it. While dictating this present letter, that circumstance suggested something to me which I ought not to omit here also: if your view is different, and that view of yours is the better one—for unless it is true, it cannot be better—then readily forgive my fear. For if you think otherwise, and what you think is true—for unless it is true, it cannot be better—then, not to say that my error is no fault at all, it is certainly not a great fault that it favors truth, if truth can rightly favor falsehood in anyone.

# CHAPTER VI

### 9

As for Origen, regarding whom you were kind enough to write back, I already knew that you approve and praise whatever is right and true that we find, not only in ecclesiastical writings but in all writings, and that you disapprove and criticize what is false and corrupt. But I desired—and still desire—this from your prudence and learning: that you make known to us the very errors by which that great man is shown to have departed from the faith of the truth.

In the book in which you mentioned all the ecclesiastical writers and their writings whom you were able to recall, I think it would have been more useful if, after naming those whom you know to have been heretics—since you did not wish even to omit them—you had also added in what respects they should be avoided. Although you omitted some others as well, I would like to know for what reason this was done.

Or, if you did not wish to burden that volume, so that, after mentioning the heretics, you would not add in what respects Catholic authority condemned them, I ask that you not consider it burdensome to your literary labor—through which, by the grace of the Lord our God, you have to no small degree kindled and assisted the studies of the saints in the Latin language—to do what fraternal charity, through my humility, urges you to do.
