If your occupations permit, publish in a single short book an organized account of the perverse doctrines of all the heretics who, up to the present time, have tried through shamelessness, ignorance, or stubbornness to corrupt the rightness of the Christian faith. This would make them known to those who either do not have time to read and learn so much because of other business, or cannot do so because of their unfamiliarity with the language. I would ask you at length, unless prolonged asking were usually a sign of less confidence in charity.

In the meantime, I warmly commend to your kindness our brother Paulus in Christ, whose good reputation in our regions we affirm before God with good testimony.

# LETTER XLI [Note: [Col. 0158] We collated this letter with a. bl. bn. bg. cb. ff. g. gg. gv. j. n. s. t. vc.; two copies marked a.; two marked sb.; four marked v.; and Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.] [Note: [Col. 0158] Formerly 77; the letter that was 41 is now included as 26. Written at the beginning of Augustine’s episcopate.]

Alypius and Augustine congratulate Aurelius on the sermons which the presbyters had begun to deliver to the people in his presence, and ask him to send them some of those sermons.

To the most blessed, reverently honored, and most sincerely beloved brother and fellow priest, Pope AURELIUS, ALYPIUS and AUGUSTINE send greetings in the Lord.

### 1

“Our mouth was filled with joy, and our tongue with exultation” (Ps. 125:2), when your letter announced that your holy intention, with the Lord’s assistance—he who inspired it—had been brought to completion concerning all our ordained brothers, and especially concerning the sermon of the presbyters, which is poured into the people in your presence. Through their tongues your charity cries out in human hearts with a louder voice than they do in human ears. Thanks be to God!

For what better thing can we carry in our hearts, utter with our mouths, and express with our pen than “Thanks be to God”? Nothing can be said more briefly, heard more joyfully, understood more magnificently, or put into practice more fruitfully. Thanks be to God, who has enriched you with such a faithful heart toward your sons and has brought into the light what you held in the inmost part of your soul, where no human eye penetrates, granting you not only the will to do good but also the means by which what you will could become visible.

So let it plainly happen—let it happen! Let these works shine before human beings, so that they may see, rejoice, and glorify the Father who is in heaven (Matt. 5:16). May you delight in such people in the Lord. May he himself deign to hear you praying for them, whom you do not disdain to hear speaking through them.

Let us go, walk, and run upon the Lord’s way. Let the small be blessed together with the great, rejoicing in those who say to them, “We will go into the house of the Lord” (Ps. 121:1). Let the former go before and the latter follow, becoming imitators of them as they are imitators of Christ. Let the path of the holy ants be fervent; let the works of the holy bees give off fragrance; let fruit be borne in endurance, together with the salvation of persevering to the end. May the Lord not allow us to be tempted beyond what we can bear, but with the temptation may he also provide a way out, so that we may be able to endure (1 Cor. 10:13).

[Col. 0159]

### 2

Pray for us, you who are worthy to be heard. With so great a sacrifice of sincere love and praise do you approach God in your works; pray that these things may also shine in us. For he whom you pray to knows with what great joy they shine in you.

These are our wishes; these are the multitudes of consolations which, in proportion to the multitude of our sorrows, gladden our soul (Ps. 93:19). So it is, because so it has been promised; what remains will be so, just as it has been promised.

We beseech you by him who has granted you these things and, through you, has poured this blessing upon the people whom you serve, to order that whichever individual sermons of theirs you wish be written out, corrected, and sent to us. I too do not neglect what you commanded, and, as I have already often written, I await word of what you think about Tyconius’s seven rules, or keys [Note: [Col. 0159] The remaining lines are missing from all editions published thus far and are not found in more than two of our manuscripts, the excellent Germanensis and Corbeiensis.].

We warmly commend our brother Hilarinus, the chief physician of Hippo and a man of high standing. As for our brother Romanus, we know what you are doing, and nothing remains to be requested except that the Lord assist you on his behalf. Amen.

# LETTER XLII [Note: [Col. 0159] Previously unpublished; it comes from a cork-bound codex of Phimarcon.] [Note: [Col. 0159] The letter formerly numbered 42 is now 232. Written in late summer of 397.]

Augustine to Paulinus, demanding that he discharge the debt of correspondence, unpaid for more than a full year, and send him his work against the pagans when he has completed it.

Now published for the first time [Note: [Col. 0159] The letter formerly numbered 42 is now 232. Written in late summer of 397.] from a cork-bound codex that once belonged to the church of Narbonne and now belongs to the distinguished Phimarcon family:

To the praiseworthy and most holy brothers in Christ, PAULINUS and THERASIA, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

Could we even have hoped or expected that we would have to demand a reply through our brother Severus, after such a long time during which your Charity has not answered us, despite our burning desire? Why must we be made to thirst through two summers—and both of them in Africa? What more can I say? You who daily give away your possessions, pay what you owe.

Or perhaps, because I had heard that you were writing against the worshipers of demons and had shown that I greatly desired that work [Note: [Col. 0159] In Letter 31.], you have delayed sending me letters for so long because you wished to complete and send it? Would that at least you might now receive my year-long fast from your pen with such a rich banquet! If it is not yet ready, we shall not cease complaining if, while you complete it, you do not meanwhile refresh us.

Greet the brothers, especially Romanus and Agilis. Those who are here with us greet you, and they are somewhat angry with us if they love you only a little.

# LETTER XLIII [Note: [Col. 0159] Letters XLIII and XLIV were collated with a. bg. bl. c. cc. ff. g. gv. n. r. s. sb. t. vc.; four copies marked v.; and Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.] [Note: [Col. 0159] Formerly 162; the letter that was 43 is now 16. Written around the end of 397 or the beginning of 398.]

The great shamelessness with which the Donatists persist in their schism, though convicted by so many judgments.

To our most beloved and deservedly praised brothers GLORIOSUS, ELEUSIUS, FELIX, GRAMMATICUS [Note: [Col. 0160] Bad., Am., Er., and one Vatican manuscript have *Felix*. Another Vatican manuscript has *Felices grammatici*.], and all the others to whom this is agreeable, AUGUSTINE.

## CHAPTER I

### 1

The Apostle Paul indeed said: “After one admonition, avoid a heretical person, knowing that such a one is perverted and sins, being self-condemned” (Titus 3:10–11). But those who do not defend their opinion, however false and perverse, with stubborn hostility—especially when they did not produce it through the audacity of their own presumption but received it from parents who had been misled and had fallen into error—while they seek the truth with cautious concern and are ready to be corrected when they find it, are by no means to be counted among heretics.

I would perhaps send you no letter if I did not believe that you are such men. Yet even a heretic swollen with however hateful a pride and maddened by the stubbornness of wicked contention, just as we warn that he must be avoided lest he deceive the weak and the immature, so we do not refuse to correct by whatever means we can.

For this reason we have even written to certain prominent Donatists—not letters of communion, which, because of their perversity, they have long refused to accept from the Catholic unity spread throughout the whole world, but private letters of the sort which we are permitted to use even with pagans. Although they have sometimes read such letters, they have either refused to answer them or, as is more likely, have been unable to do so.

In this we thought that we had fulfilled the duty of charity, which the Holy Spirit teaches us we owe not only to our own people but to everyone. Through the Apostle he says to us: “May the Lord multiply you and make you abound in love for one another and for all” (1 Thess. 3:12). Elsewhere he also instructs that those who think differently should be corrected with gentleness: “Perhaps,” he says, “God may grant them repentance leading to knowledge of the truth, and they may recover from the snares of the devil, having been captured by him for his will” (2 Tim. 2:25–26).

### 2

I have prefaced this so that no one may think that I sent you a letter more rashly than prudently, and that in this way I wished to conduct some business concerning your souls with you because you are not in our communion. Yet if I were writing you something about a matter concerning a property or the settlement of some financial dispute, perhaps no one would criticize me.

So precious is this world to human beings, and so cheap have they become in their own eyes! This letter, therefore, will be a witness on my behalf in the judgment of God, who knows with what intention I acted and who said: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. 5:9).

## CHAPTER II

### 3

Therefore, as you may remember, when we were in your city and were discussing with you certain matters concerning the communion of Christian unity, your party produced certain official records in which it was recited that approximately seventy bishops had condemned Caecilian, formerly bishop of the Church of Carthage and a member of our communion, together with his colleagues and ordainers. There also the case of Felix of Aptunga [Note: [Col. 0160] In Am., Er., and ten manuscripts it is written: “Felix of Autumnitana.”] was treated with much greater hostility and accusation than the others.

After everything had been read aloud, we replied that it was not surprising if the men who at that time created that schism, not without fabricating official records, had rashly thought that those against whom they had been stirred up by rivals and corrupt men ought to be condemned in their absence and without the case having been investigated.

But we have other ecclesiastical official records [Note: [Col. 0161] “Official records” refers to those produced at Cirta in 305 at a council of eleven or twelve bishops presided over by Secundus, then primate of Numidia—not by right of a particular see, but by right of seniority. For in the provinces of Africa the primacy was not attached to a fixed see, except in the Proconsular Province, where the bishop of Carthage permanently enjoyed that preeminence. Optatus discusses the Council of Cirta in Book 1 against Parmenianus and reports its Acts; Augustine also reports them in *Against Cresconius*, Book 3, chapter 27, no. 30. In the latter passage, however, there is an error in the designation of the consuls, which should be corrected from the *Brief Account of the Conference*, day 3, chapter 17, no. 31.], in which Secundus of Tigisis, who at that time held the primacy in Numidia, left present and confessed traditors to the judgment of God and permitted them to remain in their episcopal seats as they were. Their names are counted among the condemners of Caecilian, even though Secundus himself presided over that council, where he condemned as traditors, in their absence, those whom he had pardoned when they were present and confessed.

### 4

Then we said that, somewhat later, after the ordination of Majorinus—whom they had wickedly raised up against Caecilian, setting altar against altar and scattering the unity of Christ through frenzied dissensions—they had asked the emperor Constantine for episcopal judges who, as impartial arbiters, might judge their disputes, which had arisen in Africa and were breaking the bond of peace [Note: [Col. 0161] They asked for bishops from Gaul, since that region was, as they said, “free from” the crime of traditio under discussion. Maternus of Cologne, Rheticius of Autun, and Marinus of Arles were appointed and sent to Rome together with fifteen other Italian bishops. In their assembly, Pope Miltiades declared Caecilian innocent, according to Optatus, Book 1 against Parmenianus; this occurred in 313, according to Augustine, *After the Conference*, chapter 33, no. 56.].

After this had happened, with Caecilian present and those who had sailed against him also present, and with Miltiades [Note: [Col. 0161] Ancient manuscripts generally read *Militiades*.] then bishop of the city of Rome judging together with his colleagues whom the emperor had sent at the Donatists’ request, it was impossible to prove anything against Caecilian. Accordingly, Caecilian was confirmed in the episcopate, while Donatus, who was then present against him, was rejected.

When these proceedings had been completed, and those men nevertheless persisted in the obstinacy of their criminal schism, the emperor later ordered the same case to be examined and settled more carefully at Arles [Note: [Col. 0161] At the First Council of Arles, in 314.]. But they appealed from the ecclesiastical judgment, so that Constantine himself might hear the case. When the matter was eventually brought before him, with both parties present, Caecilian was judged innocent [Note: [Col. 0161] By the emperor at Milan, in 316, according to Augustine, *After the Conference*, chapter 33, no. 56.], while they withdrew defeated and nevertheless remained in the same perversity.

Nor was the case of Felix of Aptunga neglected. At the command of the same ruler [Col. 0162], he too was cleared by the proconsular official records [Note: [Col. 0162] The judgment of the proconsul Helianus, or Aelianus, given in the official records mentioned here, was in favor of Felix of Aptunga; Augustine reports it in *Against Cresconius*, Book 3, chapter 70, no. 81. Optatus of Milevis also mentions these proconsular Acts. They belong to the year 314, according to Augustine, *After the Conference*, chapter 33, no. 56.].

### 5

But because we were merely saying all these things and were not also reading them, you plainly thought that we were doing less than you expected from our insistence. When we perceived this, we did not delay sending the documents which we had promised to read.

While we were making an excursion to the Church of Gelizitana, intending to return from there to your town, all these documents arrived after an interval of less than two days, and, as you know, they were read aloud to you in a single day, as much as the time allowed.

First came the ecclesiastical Acts in which Secundus of Tigisis was shown not to have dared to remove confessed traditors from his fellowship, although afterward he dared to condemn Caecilian, who was not confessed and was absent, together with his other colleagues. Then came the proconsular Acts, in which Felix was proved innocent by the most careful investigation. You remember that these were read to you before noon.

After noon we read their petitions to Constantine, together with the ecclesiastical Acts held in the city of Rome by the judges whom he had appointed. In those Acts they were rejected, while Caecilian was confirmed in episcopal honor. Finally, we read the letters of the emperor Constantine, in which everything was made especially well attested and clear.

## CHAPTER III

### 6

What more do you want, men? What more do you want? This is not a question of your gold and silver; your land and estates are not at stake; finally, the safety of your bodies is not being endangered. We are addressing your souls concerning the attainment of eternal life and the avoidance of eternal death.

Awaken at last! We are not dealing with some obscure question, nor searching out hidden secrets whose penetration might be beyond the capacity of all but a few human hearts. The matter is in the open. What is more conspicuous? What is seen more quickly?

We say that innocent and absent men were condemned by a rash council, however numerous it was. We prove this from the proconsular Acts, in which the man whom the council Acts produced by your party declared to be especially criminal was judged free from every charge of traditio.

We say that sentences were pronounced against those called traditors by traditors who had confessed. We prove this from the ecclesiastical Acts, where those men are named and where it is made clear that Secundus of Tigisis, as though looking upon the interests of peace, forgave those whose case he had examined, while afterward he condemned those whose case he had not examined, once peace had been torn apart [Note: [Col. 0162] Thus the manuscripts and the older editions. Lov. has: “after he had examined.”].

From this it became apparent that at first he had not been concerned for peace but for himself. For Purpurius of Limata [Note: [Col. 0162] Thus most manuscripts, and also Optatus. The editions Lov., Er., etc., read “of Liniata.” The Gervasian manuscript has “of Laniata.”] had charged him with the fact that he too, when he had been detained by the curator and the council in order to hand over the Scriptures, had been released—surely not without cause, unless he had handed them over or ordered something to be handed over.

Fearing this highly plausible suspicion, he took counsel with his younger relative Secundus and consulted the other bishops who were with him. He left these manifest crimes to the judgment of God and thus appeared to have protected the peace. But this was false, since he had protected himself.

### 7

For if the thought of peace had dwelt in his heart, he would not afterward at Carthage have condemned as traditors those whom, present and confessing, he had left to God, although no one had convicted them before him when they were absent. Indeed, he ought to have feared all the more that the peace of unity might be violated, since Carthage was a large and distinguished city, from which whatever evil had arisen there might pour forth, as from a summit, through the whole body of Africa.

It was also near the transmarine regions and renowned for its exceedingly famous reputation. Consequently its bishop possessed no small authority: he could disregard a conspiring multitude of enemies, since he saw that he was joined by letters of communion both to the Roman Church—in which the primacy of the apostolic see had always flourished—and to the other lands from which the Gospel had come to Africa itself. He would have been ready to state his case there, if his adversaries attempted to alienate those Churches from him.

Since, then, he refused to come to the lodging of colleagues whom he believed—or suspected—to have been perverted by his enemies against the truth of his case, or, as they themselves claim, merely pretended this, Secundus ought all the more, if he wished to be a guardian of true peace, to have taken care that those absent should not be condemned who had altogether refused to be present at their judgment.

For the matter concerned not presbyters, deacons, or clerics of a lower order, but colleagues—men who could reserve their case intact for the judgment of other colleagues, especially of the apostolic Churches. Before those Churches, sentences pronounced against them in their absence would have had no force whatever, since they had not first approached that tribunal and afterward abandoned it; rather, they had always regarded it with suspicion and had never wished to approach it.

### 8

This consideration ought especially to have troubled Secundus, who was then primate, if he was presiding over the council in order to promote peace. He could perhaps easily have silenced or restrained the rabid tongues attacking the absent by saying:

“You see, brothers, that after so great a slaughter during the persecution, God’s mercy has granted peace through the rulers of this world. We Christians and bishops must not tear apart the Christian unity which the pagan enemy no longer pursues. Therefore, either let us leave to God the Judge all these cases which the calamity of that most turbulent time inflicted upon the Church; or, if there are among you some who know the certain crimes of these men so thoroughly that they can readily make them known and convict those who deny them, and who fear to communicate with such persons, let them go to our brothers and colleagues, the bishops of the transmarine Churches, and first there complain about the deeds and contumacy of these men, because, conscious of their guilt, they refused to come to the judgment of their African colleagues. Let it then be announced to them from there that they must come and answer the charges there brought against them.

“If they do not do so, their depravity and perversity will also become known there, and, once a *tractatoria* [Col. 0163] has been sent concerning their name throughout [Col. 0164] the whole world, wherever the Church of Christ has now spread, their communion will be cut off by all the Churches, lest any error arise in the Chair of the Church of Carthage. Only then, when these men have been separated from the whole Church, shall we safely ordain another bishop for the people of Carthage. Otherwise, if another were ordained now, the transmarine Church might not communicate with him, because the man already ordained would not appear to have been deposed from his office, and fame has celebrated him and caused letters of communion to be sent to him. Thus a great scandal of schism might arise within Christ’s unity in these now-pacified times, while we hastily seek to rush through our sentences and dare to erect another altar—not against Caecilianus alone, but against the whole world, which through ignorance communicates with him.”

[Note: [Col. 0163] In some manuscripts, *tractoria*; here it means nothing other than a synodical letter. Sometimes, however, it denotes a diploma authorizing the use of public conveyance, as in Constantine’s Edict to Ablavius [Col. 0164], where he orders *tractoriae* to be given to bishops traveling to the Council of Arles.]

### 9

Whoever, being unrestrained, refused to obey such a sound and upright counsel—what would he have done? Or how could he have condemned any absent colleague when he did not possess the Acts of the council, with the primate opposing him?

And if so great a sedition arose even against the chief see that some now wished to condemn those whom the primate wished to defer, would it not have been far better to dissent from such men, who were attempting disturbances and unrest, than to dissent from the communion of the whole world?

But because there was nothing that could be proved against Caecilianus and those who ordained him before a transmarine judgment, they neither wished to refer the matter before pronouncing sentences against him, nor, after pronouncing them, persevered in making the matter known to the transmarine Church, so that it might be determined whose communion among the condemned traditors in Africa ought to be avoided.

For if they had attempted this, Caecilianus and the others would have been present, and they would have carefully cleared their case before the transmarine ecclesiastical judges against their deceitful accusers.

### 10

That council, therefore, was perverse and wicked, and, as is generally believed, belonged chiefly to traditors whom Secundus Tigisitanus had forgiven when they confessed. Since rumor about betrayal had grown widespread, they sought to turn suspicion away from themselves by disgracing others. While people throughout Africa, trusting the bishops, repeated falsehoods about innocent men—that traditors had been condemned at Carthage—the men who had truly handed things over were able to remain concealed, as it were, within a cloud of most deceitful rumor.

Thus you see, dearest brothers, how something could have happened which some of you said was improbable: that men who had confessed their own betrayal and obtained the concession that their case ought to be left to God should afterward sit as judges and condemners of absent persons as traditors.

They embraced the opportunity to cover others with false accusation and, in this way, to divert men’s tongues from investigating their own crimes. Otherwise, if it were impossible for anyone to judge in another the evils he himself had committed, the Apostle Paul would not have said to certain people:

[Col. 0165] “Therefore you are without excuse, O man, every one who judges. For in judging another you condemn yourself, since you do the same things that you judge.” [Romans 2:1.]

They did this altogether, so that these apostolic words apply to them completely and appropriately.

### 11

Secundus, then, did not promote peace and unity at the time when he left their crimes to God. Otherwise, he would have taken greater care of this at Carthage, lest a schism arise, where there was no one whose confessed crime he would be compelled to forgive. The easiest way to preserve peace would have been simply to refuse to condemn the absent.

They would therefore have done an injury to innocent men even if they had refused to pardon them when they had not been convicted, had not confessed, and were not present at all. For forgiveness is granted to the man whose guilt is completely certain. How much more monstrous and blind, then, were those who thought they could condemn matters which, being unknown, they could not even have forgiven?

There, known crimes were left to God so that other matters would not be sought; here, unknown crimes were condemned so that those matters might be concealed.

Someone will say: “They knew them.” Even if I grant this, the absent nevertheless ought to have been spared. They had not abandoned a judgment at which they had never been present; nor was the Church confined to those African bishops, so that those who refused to present themselves before their judgment would appear to have avoided every ecclesiastical judgment.

Thousands of transmarine colleagues remained, before whom it was evident that men who seemed to regard their African or Numidian colleagues with suspicion could be judged.

Where, then, is what Scripture proclaims: “Before you question anyone, do not blame him; and when you have questioned him, rebuke him justly” (Ecclesiasticus 11:7)?

If, therefore, the Holy Spirit wished no one to be blamed or rebuked without being questioned, how much more criminally were those not merely blamed or rebuked, but altogether condemned, though, being absent, they could not be questioned at all about their crimes?

### 12

Yet these men—although they say that they condemned known crimes belonging to absent persons who had in no way abandoned a judgment, since they had never been present and had always made clear that they suspected that very faction—tell me, my brothers, I beg you: how did they know them?

You answer: “We do not know, since the knowledge itself is not explained in those Acts.”

But I shall show you how they knew. Consider the case of Felix of Aptunga, and first read how much more vehemently they proceeded against him. Thus they knew the cases of the others in the same way as they knew the case of this man, who was afterward proved completely innocent by a careful and terrifying investigation.

How much more justly, safely, and quickly, therefore, ought we to regard as innocent those whose crimes were accused by these men more lightly and condemned with milder reproach, when the man against whom they raged far more savagely was found innocent?

## Chapter IV

### 13

Or perhaps, as someone said—a remark which displeased you when it was made to you, but which nevertheless must not be passed over—someone said: “A bishop ought not to have been cleared by a proconsular judgment,” as though he had arranged this for himself, rather than the emperor having ordered an investigation, since the matter chiefly belonged to the emperor’s care, for which he would have to render an account to God.

They had made him the arbiter and judge of the case concerning the betrayal and the schism: they had even sent petitions to him, and afterward appealed to him; yet they refused to abide by his judgment.

Therefore, if the man whom an earthly judge acquitted is to be blamed, although he himself had not sought this judgment, [Col. 0166] how much more must those be blamed who wished an earthly king to be the judge of their case?

But if it is not a crime to appeal to the emperor, neither is it a crime to be heard by the emperor; therefore it is not a crime to be heard by one to whom the emperor delegated the case.

That friend also wished to bring an accusation against someone who had been suspended on the rack in the case of the bishop Felix, so that it might be said that he had been tortured even by claws. Could Felix have objected to such a thorough or severe investigation when an examiner was pursuing the discovery of his case? For what else would refusing to be investigated in this way have meant than confessing the crime?

Yet that very proconsul, amid the terrifying voices of heralds and the bloody hands of executioners, would never condemn an absent colleague who refused to present himself at his judgment, provided that he had another means by which he could be heard. Or if he did condemn him, he would certainly suffer the just and deserved penalties even under the secular laws.

[Note: Four Vatican manuscripts read *saecularibus*; others read *securalibus*.]

## Chapter V

### 14

But if the proconsular Acts displease you, yield to the ecclesiastical ones. Everything has been recited to you in order.

Or perhaps Melchiades, bishop of the Roman Church, ought not, together with his transmarine colleagues, to have assumed the judgment which had been concluded by seventy Africans under the presidency of Secundus Tigisitanus?

And what if he did not even assume it? When the emperor was petitioned, he sent bishops to sit with him and to decide whatever seemed just concerning the whole case.

We prove this both from the petitions of the Donatists and from the emperor’s own words. You remember that both have been read to you, and you now have permission to inspect and copy them. Read and consider everything.

See with what care all matters were examined for the preservation or restoration of peace and unity; how the persons of the accusers were handled; with what blemishes some of them were branded; and how it was clearly established from the testimony of those present that they had nothing to say against Caecilianus. They wished instead to transfer the whole case to the people of Majorinus’ party—that is, to a seditious multitude alienated from the peace of the Church—so that Caecilianus might be accused by that crowd, which they thought they could bend the minds of the judges to their will by tumultuous shouting alone, without any documentary testimony and without any examination of the truth.

Unless, perhaps, that frenzied multitude, drunk with the cup of error and corruption, was speaking true accusations against Caecilianus, when seventy bishops, as was established in the case of Felix of Aptunga, condemned absent and innocent colleagues with such insane recklessness.

They had agreed with such a crowd that they should pronounce sentences against innocent men who had not been questioned; and they now wished Caecilianus to be accused again by the same crowd. But they had plainly not found judges to whom they could persuade that madness.

### 15

For, in accordance with your prudence, you can observe there both their perversity and the gravity of the judges: how in the end they could not be persuaded to allow Caecilianus to be accused by the people of Majorinus’ party, which had no definite representative.

When questioned, the judges also demanded either accusers, witnesses, or persons in any way [Col. 0167] necessary to the case—men who had come from Africa together with them and were said to have been present and to have been taken away by Donatus.

Donatus himself promised that he would produce them. Although he made this promise not once but repeatedly, he no longer wished to appear at that judgment, where he had already confessed so much that by failing to appear thereafter he seemed to have wished nothing other than not to be condemned while present—even though the matters deserving condemnation had been brought to light while he was present and being questioned.

[Note: Bad., Am., Er., and the Gervasian manuscript read *interrogante*, “while he was questioning.”]

Another matter was added: certain persons submitted a written indictment against Caecilianus. After this had been done, the investigation was again conducted. What can I say about how it proceeded, what persons submitted that indictment, and how nothing could be proved against Caecilianus, when you have heard everything and can read it as often as you wish?

### 16

As for the number of the seventy bishops, when their authority was advanced as though it were most weighty, you remember what was said. Yet those very serious men preferred to restrain their judgment amid countless questions linked together in an inextricable chain. They paid no attention to how many those bishops were or from where they had been assembled, since they saw that they had been blinded by such recklessness that they dared to pronounce hasty sentences against absent and unquestioned colleagues.

And yet what was the final sentence pronounced by the blessed Melchiades himself? How innocent, complete, prudent, and peaceable it was! He did not dare remove from his college colleagues concerning whom nothing had been established; he placed the chief blame upon Donatus alone, whom he had discovered to be the originator of the whole evil; and he gave the others a free choice to recover their soundness.

He was even prepared to send letters of communion to those who were known to have been ordained by Majorinus, so that wherever there were two bishops, whom dissension had multiplied, he wished the one who had been ordained first to be confirmed, while provision would be made for the other to govern another people.

O excellent man! O son of Christian peace and father of the Christian people!

Now compare this small number with that multitude of bishops—not number with number, but weight with weight: on this side modesty, on that recklessness; on this side vigilance, on that blindness.

Here gentleness did not corrupt integrity, nor did integrity conflict with gentleness. There, however, fear was concealed by fury, and fury was provoked by fear.

These men had assembled to reject falsehood by investigating true crimes; those others sought to conceal the truth by condemning falsehoods.

## Chapter VI

### 17

Would Caecilianus finally entrust himself to those men to be heard and judged, when he had such persons before whom, if his case were brought, he could very easily demonstrate his innocence?

He would not entrust himself to them at all—not even if he had suddenly been ordained bishop of the Church of Carthage as a stranger and were unaware of what a certain exceedingly wealthy woman named Lucilla might then be able to do to corrupt the minds of wicked or ignorant people. Caecilianus had offended her when, while he was a deacon, he rebuked her in the interest of ecclesiastical discipline. This too [Col. 0168] had been added to the evil by which that iniquity was completed.

For in that council, where absent and innocent men were condemned by confessed traditors, there were a few who wished to conceal their own crimes by disgracing others, so that people might be diverted from investigating the truth and distracted by false rumors.

There were therefore only a few who chiefly managed this affair, although they possessed greater authority because of their association with Secundus, who had spared them through fear.

The rest, however, are said to have been chiefly bought and incited against Caecilianus by Lucilla’s money.

The Acts before Zenophilus, the consular governor, remain. There a certain deacon named Nundinarius, apparently degraded by Silvanus, bishop of Cirta, after unsuccessfully attempting to satisfy them through letters from other bishops, revealed many matters in anger and brought them into public court. Among them, it is recorded that, after bishops had been corrupted by Lucilla’s money, altar was raised against altar in the Church of Carthage, the capital of Africa.

[Note: [Col. 0168] These Acts were compiled in the year 320 and are found in Book 3 of *Against Cresconius*, chapter 29, section 33. Optatus also mentions them in Book 1 of *Against Parmenianus*.]

I know that we did not read these Acts to you, but you remember that there was not enough time. There was also a certain resentment of spirit arising from the arrogance of pride: they themselves had not ordained the bishop of Carthage.

### 18

When Caecilianus recognized, in all these circumstances, that he had encountered not true judges but enemies and corrupt men, how could it happen that he himself would wish—or that the people over whom he presided would permit him—to leave the Church and go into a private house, there to be slaughtered not by the examination of colleagues but by a factional clique and feminine hatreds?

Especially since he saw that, before the transmarine Church, which was free from private enmities and from the dissension of either side, an incorrupt and complete examination of his case remained.

If his adversaries did nothing there, they would cut themselves off from the most innocent communion of the whole world. If they attempted to accuse him there, he would then appear to answer them and would defend his innocence against their schemes, as you later learned had happened.

Yet they had sought a transmarine judgment far too late, already guilty of schism and already stained by the dreadful crime of erecting another altar.

They should have done this first if they relied upon the truth. But after false rumors had been strengthened by the passage of time, they wished to come to judgment as though ancient reputation had already prejudged the case.

[Note: [Col. 0168] Lov. reads *noluerunt*, “they did not wish”; other manuscripts read *voluerunt*, “they wished.”]

Or, what is more credible, after condemning Caecilianus as they pleased, they seemed to themselves secure, relying on their numbers, and did not dare to bring so bad a case elsewhere, where truth could be found because no corruption was at work.

## Chapter VII

### 19

But after they had learned by experience that the communion of the whole world remained with Caecilianus, and that letters of communion were being sent to him by the transmarine Churches rather than to the man whom they had wickedly ordained, they were ashamed to remain silent.

People could have charged them with allowing the Church, ignorant throughout so many nations, to communicate with condemned men; and with cutting themselves off from the communion of the innocent whole world, while by their silence they allowed the bishop whom they had ordained for the Carthaginians to be denied communion by the entire world.

They chose, as it is said, to pursue their case against Caecilianus before the transmarine Churches in two [ways], prepared for either outcome. [Note: [Col. 0169] So Lov. and the manuscripts. The older editions and the Fulda manuscript read “with two frauds.”]

If by any deceit of false accusation they could overcome him, they would fully satisfy their desire. If they could not, they would remain in the same perversity but would at least seem to have something to say: that they had suffered unjust judges. This is the cry of all wicked litigants when they have been defeated even by the clearest truth.

Could it not justly have been said to them: “Let us suppose that those bishops who judged at Rome were not good judges. There still remained a plenary council of the universal Church, where the case could be argued even with those judges themselves, so that, if they were convicted of having judged badly, their sentences could be overturned”?

Let them prove whether they did this. We easily prove that they did not, from the fact that the whole world does not communicate with them. Or, if it was done, they were defeated there as well; their very separation makes this clear.

### 20

Yet the emperor’s letters show most adequately what they did afterward. They dared to accuse before the emperor—not before other colleagues—the ecclesiastical judges, bishops of such authority, by whose judgment both Caecilianus’ innocence and their own wickedness had been made clear, alleging that they had judged badly.

He provided another judgment at Arles, that is, of other bishops—not because it was already necessary, but yielding to their perversity and desiring by every means to restrain such shamelessness.

For the Christian emperor did not dare accept their tumultuous and deceitful complaints in such a way as to judge himself the decision of the bishops who had sat at Rome. Instead, as I have said, he appointed other bishops. Yet from these they preferred to appeal again to the emperor himself; and you have heard how he detested them for this.

Would that at least by his judgment they had put an end to their utterly mad animosities, and that, just as he yielded to them by judging that case after the bishops—though he would afterward seek pardon from the holy prelates—they too might at last have yielded to the truth, since they had nothing further to say if they refused to obey the judgment of the one to whom they themselves had appealed.

For he ordered the parties to come to Rome to conduct the case. When Caecilianus failed to appear there, for some reason unknown to me, and they brought the matter to his attention, he ordered them to proceed to Milan.

Then some of them began to withdraw, perhaps indignant that Constantine had not imitated them by immediately and swiftly condemning Caecilianus in his absence.

When the prudent emperor learned this, he had the rest escorted by his officials to Milan. When Caecilianus also arrived there, the emperor produced him as well, as he wrote; and after examining the case, with what diligence, caution, and foresight his letters reveal, [Col. 0170] he judged Caecilianus completely innocent and them utterly wicked.

## Chapter VIII

### 21

They still baptize outside the Church and, if they can, rebaptize the Church. They offer sacrifice in dissension and schism, and greet as “peace” peoples whom they expel from the peace of salvation.

The unity of Christ is torn apart, Christ’s inheritance is blasphemed, and Christ’s Baptism is contemptuously blown upon (*exsufflatur*). Yet they do not wish to be corrected for these things by the scourges of temporal punishments through the ordinary human authorities, lest they be consigned to eternal punishments for such great sacrileges.

We accuse them of the madness of schism, the insanity of rebaptization, and the wicked separation from Christ’s inheritance, which has been spread among all nations.

From the books—not only ours but also theirs—we read the names of Churches which they themselves read today but with which they do not communicate today. When these names are read in their conventicles, they say to their readers, “Peace be with you,” while they have no peace with the very peoples to whom those letters were written.

They, in turn, bring against us either false crimes of the dead or, even if true, crimes belonging to others. They do not understand that, in the matters we bring against them, all of them are implicated; whereas in the matters they bring against us, the chaff or weeds of the Lord’s harvest are being reproved, and the crime does not belong to the wheat.

Nor do they consider that those who approve of wicked people within unity themselves communicate with the wicked; but those who disapprove of them and cannot correct them, and who do not dare uproot the weeds before harvest lest they uproot the [Col. 0171] wheat along with them (Matthew 13:29), communicate not with their deeds but with Christ’s altar.

Thus they are not only untouched by those people’s defilement, but also deserve to be praised and proclaimed by the divine words, because, lest the name of Christ be blasphemed through terrible schisms, they tolerate for the sake of the good of unity what they hate for the sake of the good of justice.

### 22

If they have ears, let them hear what the Spirit says to the Churches.

For it is written in the Apocalypse of John:

“Write to the angel of the Church in Ephesus: Thus says he who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who walks among the seven golden lampstands: I know your works, your labor, and your patience, and that you cannot tolerate the wicked; you tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and you found them liars; you have patience and endured for my name, and you have not failed” (Revelation 2:1–3).

If this were meant to be understood of an angel of the higher heavens, rather than of the leaders of the Churches, it would not then consistently say:

“But I have this against you: that you have abandoned your first love. Remember, therefore, from where you have fallen, repent, and do your former works; otherwise I am coming to you and will move your lampstand from its place, unless you repent” (ibid. 2:4–5).

This cannot be said to the higher angels, who retain perpetual love. Those who fell and lapsed are the devil and his angels.

Therefore he speaks of “first love” because the angel endured false apostles for Christ’s name; he commands him to recover that love and perform his former works.

The crimes of wicked people are brought against us—not our own but those of others—and some of those crimes are even unknown. If we saw them as true and present, and tolerated them for the sake of unity while sparing the weeds for the sake of the wheat, anyone who heard the Holy Scriptures without deafness of heart would say that we deserve not reproach but considerable praise.

### 23

Aaron tolerates the multitude demanding, making, and worshiping an idol.

Moses tolerates the many thousands murmuring against God and repeatedly offending his holy name.

David tolerates Saul, his persecutor, who abandons heavenly things through his wicked conduct and seeks the underworld through magical arts. He avenges his death and even calls him “the Lord’s anointed” because of the sacrament of venerable anointing.

Samuel tolerates the wicked sons of Eli and his own perverse sons. Because the people refused to tolerate them, they were accused by divine truth and corrected by divine severity.

Finally, he tolerates that proud people who despised God.

Isaiah tolerates those against whom he hurls so many true accusations.

Jeremiah tolerates those from whom he suffers so much.

Zechariah tolerates the Pharisees and scribes, such as Scripture testifies that they were at that time.

I know that I have passed over many examples. Let those who wish read; let those who can read the heavenly utterances. They will find that all God’s holy servants and friends always had people whom they tolerated within his people. Although they shared with them in the sacraments of that time, they were not only not defiled, but also commendably endured them, striving, as the Apostle says, “to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4:3).

Consider also the period after the Lord’s coming. We would find many more examples of this tolerance throughout the whole world if everything could have been written down and established as authoritative. Nevertheless, consider these examples that we do possess.

The Lord himself tolerates Judas, his devil, thief, and betrayer. He allows him to receive among the innocent disciples what the faithful know to be the price of our redemption.

The Apostles tolerate false apostles. And while seeking not their own interests but those of Jesus Christ, Paul, who sought not his own things but those of Jesus Christ, lives among them with most glorious tolerance.

Finally, as I mentioned shortly before, Scripture praises in the voice of God the leader of the Church under the name of an angel because, although he hated the wicked, he nevertheless tolerated them after testing and discovering them, for the Lord’s name.

### 24

In short, let them question themselves: are not the massacres and arsons of the Circumcellions tolerated by them? [Col. 0171] These are the men who venerate those who have voluntarily thrown themselves to their deaths, while the whole of Africa has groaned for so many years under the incredible evils of one Optatus.

[Note: Optatus, bishop of Thamugadi. See the note on Letter 53.]

I shall refrain from mentioning the tyrannical powers and public brigandage of the individual regions, cities, and estates throughout Africa. It is better that you yourselves say these things to yourselves, either privately or openly, as you wish.

Wherever you turn your eyes, what I am saying—or rather what I am leaving unsaid—will confront you.

Nor do we accuse those whom you love there. They do not displease us because they tolerate the wicked, but because they are intolerably wicked on account of the schism, the altar raised against altar, and the separation from Christ’s inheritance, spread throughout the whole world as was promised [Col. 0172] so long before.

We lament and mourn the violated peace, the torn unity, the repeated baptisms, and the sacraments contemptuously blown upon—sacraments which remain holy even among wicked people.

If they regard these things as trivial, let them look at the examples by which God has shown how highly he valued them. Those who made the idol were killed by the ordinary death of the sword (Exodus 32:27–28); but those who wished to create a schism were swallowed up when the earth opened, and the consenting crowd was consumed by fire (Numbers 16:31–35).

The difference in punishments reveals the difference in merits.

## Chapter IX

### 25

In persecution, the holy Books are handed over; the traditors confess, and they are left to God. Innocent men are not questioned, yet are condemned by reckless men.

The man accused far more vehemently than the rest among those condemned in their absence is proved unimpaired—innocent—by decisive judgments.

An appeal is made from the judgment of bishops to the emperor; the emperor is chosen as judge; the emperor is despised when he judges.

You have read what was done then; you see what is being done now. If you have any doubts about those former events, observe these present ones.

Let us not deal merely with old documents, public archives, or forensic or ecclesiastical Acts. Our greater book is the whole world. In it I read fulfilled what I read promised in the Book of God:

“The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 2:7–8).

Whoever does not share in this inheritance, whatever books he may possess, should recognize that he has been disinherited.

Whoever attacks this inheritance clearly shows that he is a stranger to the household of God.

Certainly the dispute concerns the handing over of the divine Books, in which this inheritance was promised. Let the man be believed to have handed the testament over to the flames who litigates against the will of the testator.

What has the Church of Corinth done to you, O party of Donatus? What has it done to you? And what I say of that Church, I wish to be understood of all similar Churches, however far away.

What have those Churches done to you, which could not possibly have known either what you had done or whom you had disgraced? Was it because Caecilianus injured Lucilla in Africa that the world lost the light of Christ?

### 26

At last, let them perceive what they have done. After a definite interval of years, their own deed has rightly been thrown back into their faces.

Ask by what woman Maximianus—said to be a relative of Donatus—separated himself from the communion of Primianus; how he gathered a faction of bishops, condemned Primianus in his absence, and had a bishop ordained against him.

Ask how Majorinus, through Lucilla, gathered a faction of bishops, condemned Caecilianus in his absence, and had a bishop ordained against him.

[Note: Maximianus, a Donatist deacon of Carthage hostile to his bishop Primianus, became the author of a new schism around the year 393, “cutting off a piece from a piece,” as Augustine says in his *Exposition of Psalm 36*, sermon 2, section 20. There he also reports the synodical letter of the Donatist bishops who condemned Primianus at the Council of Cabarsussis and substituted Maximianus in his place. In the following year, however, the other Donatists held the Council of Bagai against the schism that had arisen, and Maximianus was condemned by them.]

Or do you perhaps wish it to count for something that Primianus was cleared by the other African bishops of his communion against Maximianus’ faction, while you do not wish it to count for something that Caecilianus was cleared by the transmarine bishops of unity [Col. 0173] against Majorinus’ faction?

I ask you, my brothers: what great thing am I asking? What difficult matter do I wish you to understand?

There is indeed a great and incomparable difference in authority and number between the African Church and the other regions of the world. Even if unity existed here, it would still be far smaller in comparison with all the other Christian nations than the party of Maximianus was in comparison with the party of Primianus.

Nevertheless, I ask—and I think it just—that the council of Secundus of Tigisi, which Lucilla brought together against the absent Caecilianus, the apostolic see,

[Note: Nearly all manuscripts read “the apostolic sees,” which may be the genuine reading.]

and the whole world communicating with Caecilianus, should have as much force as the council of the Maximianists, which a certain woman likewise brought together against the absent Primianus and the rest of Africa communicating with Primianus.

What could be seen more clearly? What could be requested more fairly?

27. You see all these things, and you know them, and you grieve; yet God also sees that nothing compels you to remain in so pestilential and sacrilegious a separation, if, in order to attain the spiritual kingdom, you overcome carnal attachment, and if, to avoid everlasting punishments, you do not fear to offend human friendships that will profit nothing in God’s judgment. Go, then, and consult them; find out what they can answer to these arguments of ours. If they produce documents, we produce documents; if they say that ours are false, let them not object if we say the same about theirs. No one erases God’s decree from heaven; no one erases God’s Church from the earth. He promised the whole world, and she has filled the whole world. She has both wicked and good, but on earth she loses none except the wicked, and into heaven she admits none except the good. This discourse of ours—which God himself knows how much love both for peace and for you drew from us—will be correction for you, if you wish it, but a witness even if you do not.

## LETTER XLIV

[Note: Elsewhere 163; the one that was 44 is now 17. Written at the end of 397 or the beginning of 398.]

Augustine reports what has begun to be done toward reconciliation with Fortunius, a bishop of the Donatists, wishing that what has begun peacefully may be completed without tumult through a more numerous gathering.

To his most beloved and praiseworthy lords and brothers ELEUSIUS, GLORIUS, and FELICIBUS,

[Note: Bad., Am., Er., one manuscript, and the Vatican codex read “Felici”; others, “Felicibus.”]

AUGUSTINE.

### CHAPTER I

1. We found Fortunius, whom you have as bishop of Tubursicum, passing through that same city, although we were hurrying as fast as possible on our way to the Church of Cirta, exactly as you are accustomed to describe him to us with the greatest kindness.

[Note: Two Vatican codices read: “Tybursicum.”]

[Note: They were going there to ordain bishops, as is said below, no. 13, namely to fill the place of Profuturus, who died shortly after assuming the episcopate. He was succeeded by Fortunatus, praised in Book 2 against Petilian’s Letters, ch. 99, no. 228, and one of the seven bishops chosen to defend the cause of the Catholic Church at the Conference of Carthage in 411.]

When we told him what you had said about him, wishing to see him, he did not refuse. We therefore went to him, since we thought that, out of regard for his age, we ought to come to him rather than require him first to come to us. We proceeded, accompanied by quite a few people whom that occasion happened to have gathered around us. When we had sat down with him, a considerable crowd also flocked together after the rumor had spread; but among all that multitude very few seemed to us to desire that the matter, and so great a question in so important a case, should be handled profitably and salubriously and examined prudently and devoutly.

The rest had come more for the spectacle of our altercation, almost in theatrical fashion, than for instruction in Christian devotion and salvation. Consequently, apart from the few I have mentioned, whose intention appeared religious and sincere, they could provide us neither silence nor even an attentive, modest, and orderly conversation. Everything was thrown into confusion by the noise of those speaking immoderately, according to the impulse of each person’s mind; and neither he nor we could prevail, whether by requests or sometimes even by rebukes, in securing respectful silence.

2. Nevertheless, the matter somehow began to be discussed, and we continued the alternating conversation for several hours, as far as we were allowed by the interruptions of those who were making various disturbances. But at the very beginning of the debate, when we saw that the things being said were repeatedly slipping from the memory either of us or of those whose salvation we were especially concerned for, and so that the discussion might be conducted with greater care and moderation, and also so that you and the other brothers who were absent might learn by reading what had taken place between us, we requested that our words be recorded by the notaries.

He and those who agreed with him resisted this for a long time; later, however, he himself gave permission. But the notaries who were present, and who could have carried this out diligently, refused for some reason to take it down. At least we arranged for the brothers who were with us to record it, although they might be slower at this task, promising that we would leave the same tablets there. This was agreed. They began to record our words, and some things said by each side were entered on the tablets.

Afterward, however, because the notaries were unable to endure the disorderly interruptions of those who kept shouting and, consequently, our own more turbulent disputation as well, they withdrew, although we did not stop and continued saying many things as each of us was given the opportunity. From all our words, insofar as I could remember them, I did not wish to deprive Your Charity of the proceedings of the whole case. You can read my letter to him, so that he may either approve that I have written what is true, or himself freely explain to you anything he remembers better.

### CHAPTER II

3. First he deigned to praise our way of life, which he said he had learned from what you had reported to him—perhaps more favorably than accurately—adding that he had told you that we could have done everything you had represented about us well, if we had done it in the Church.

Then we began to ask what Church that was in which one ought to live in this way: whether it was the Church that, as holy Scripture had foretold so long before, would spread throughout the world, or the one contained by a small part either of the Africans or of Africa. At first he tried to assert that his communion existed throughout the whole world. I asked whether he could give me, wherever I wished, letters of communion, which we call *formatae*, and I affirmed—what was evident to everyone—that in this way the question could most easily be brought to an end.

[Note: On this point Optatus also pressed the Donatists in Book 2: “The whole world,” he says, “agrees with us through the exchange of *formatae* in one fellowship of communion.” In the code of the African Church canons there is Canon 23, according to which a bishop traveling overseas is to receive a *formata* from the primate.]

I was preparing, if he agreed, to send such letters from us to those churches which we could at that time read as having been founded under apostolic authority.

4. But because the matter was plainly false, the discussion soon moved away from it amid a mixture of words. During this exchange he recalled that evangelical admonition of the Lord in which he said: “Beware of false prophets. Many will come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves. You will know them by their fruits” (Matthew 7:15–16).

When we said that the same words of the Lord could be recited by us concerning them, the discussion turned to an exaggeration of the persecution which he said his party had often endured. By this he wished to show that his people were Christians because they suffered persecution.

While I was preparing to answer from the Gospel, he first recalled the passage in which the Lord says: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (the same, 5:10). At this point I expressed my satisfaction and immediately added that what had to be investigated, therefore, was whether they had suffered persecution for righteousness.

In this inquiry I wanted to examine what was clear to everyone: whether the times of Macarius had found them established in the unity of the Church, or already divided by schism.

[Note: Macarius, whose actions against the Catholics the Donatists maliciously brought forward as accusations—so much so that they called them “Macarians” after his name—was sent to Africa by the emperor Constans around the year 348, together with Paulus, both to distribute alms to the poor and to exhort individuals to Catholic unity. The Donatist bishops, especially Donatus of Carthage and Donatus of Bagai, vigorously opposed him; indeed, they incited against him the fury of the Circumcellions. Very many of these were killed by soldiers and adorned among the Donatists with the title of martyrs; the more famous among them were Marculus and Donatus, namely Donatus of Bagai. The other Donatus, together with those who refused to be recalled to concord, later fled, or was banished into exile, according to Optatus in Book 3 and partly also according to Augustine, and so forth.]

Thus, if they wished to see whether they had suffered persecution for righteousness, they should consider instead whether they had rightly cut themselves off from the unity of the whole world. If they were found to have acted unjustly, it would be clear that they had suffered persecution on account of injustice rather than righteousness, and therefore could not be added to the number of the blessed, concerning whom it is said: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake.”

There the more famous than reliable tradition of the Books was brought forward. Our side replied that their leaders, rather, had been traditors; and that if they did not wish to believe our writings on this matter, we ought not to be compelled to believe theirs.

### CHAPTER III

5. But, setting aside that disputed question, I asked how these men had justly separated themselves from the innocence of the other Christians who, established in the most ancient churches and preserving throughout the world the order of succession, were completely unaware who the traditors in Africa had been. Certainly, they could communicate only with those whom they heard occupying episcopal sees.

He replied that the Churches of the overseas regions had remained innocent only until they consented to the bloodshed of those whom he said had endured the persecution of Macarius.

Here I could indeed have said that the innocence of the overseas Churches could not be contaminated by hatred of the time of Macarius, since it could in no way be proved that they had carried out even what had been done under their authority. But, for the sake of brevity, I preferred to ask whether, if the overseas Churches were said to have consented to the savagery of Macarius and had thereby lost their innocence, it could at least be proved that the Donatists had remained in unity with the Eastern Churches and the other regions of the world down to that time.

6. Then he produced a certain volume in which he wished to show that the Council of Sardica had sent a letter to the African bishops who belonged to the communion of Donatus. When it was read, we heard the name of Donatus among the other bishops to whom they had written.

Accordingly, we began to insist that it be stated whether this was the Donatus from whose party these people take their name. For it could have happened that they had written to some Donatus who was a bishop of another heresy, especially since no mention of Africa had been made in those names.

How, then, could he prove that “Donatus” was to be understood as the bishop of Donatus’ party, when he could not even prove whether those letters had been sent specifically to the bishops of the African Churches? Although the name Donatus is usually African, it would not conflict with the truth that someone from those regions might have borne an African name, or that an African might have been established as bishop in those regions.

Nor did we find in the document either a date or a consul, so that at least something certain might emerge from consideration of the times. Since, moreover, we had once heard that the Arians, after separating from Catholic communion, had tried to ally the Donatists with themselves in Africa, Brother Alypius whispered this very point in my ear.

Then, having taken the volume and examining the decrees of that council, I read that Athanasius, the Catholic bishop of Alexandria, whose conflicts in the fiercest debates against the Arians had been especially prominent, and Julius, likewise a Catholic bishop of the Roman Church, had been condemned by that Council of Sardica.

[Note: Bad., Am., Er., and several manuscripts read *legit* (“he read”).]

From this it became clear to us that it was a council of the Arians, whom these Catholic bishops were vehemently resisting. We therefore wished to take the volume and carry it away with us for a more careful examination of the dates. He refused to give it, saying that we could have it there whenever we wished to examine something in it. I also asked him to permit me to mark it with my own hand; I confess that I feared that, if circumstances required me later to request it, another volume might perhaps be produced in its place. He refused this as well.

### CHAPTER IV

7. Next he began to press me to answer briefly his question: whether I considered the just person to be the one who persecuted, or the one who suffered persecution.

I replied that the question was not correctly framed. It could happen that both were unjust; it could also happen that a more just person persecuted a more unjust one. It does not therefore follow that someone is more just merely because he suffers persecution, although that is often the case.

Then, seeing that he was dwelling at length on this point because he wanted the justice of his party to be recognized as certain on the ground that it had suffered persecution, I asked him whether he considered Ambrose, bishop of the Church of Milan, just and Christian.

He was compelled to deny that this man was Christian and just, because if he admitted it, we would immediately object that he judged him to require rebaptism. When, therefore, he was forced to say things by which Ambrose was not to be regarded as Christian and just, I recalled how great a persecution Ambrose had endured, even with the church surrounded by armed soldiers.

I also asked whether he considered Maximian, who had created a schism against them at Carthage, just and Christian. He could only deny it. I therefore recalled that Maximian too had suffered such persecution that his church was demolished down to its foundations.

By these examples I was trying, if I could, to persuade him to stop saying that enduring persecution was the most certain proof of Christian righteousness.

8. He also related that, at the very beginning of the schism, his elders, while considering the fault of Caecilian and wishing somehow to suppress it so that a schism would not arise, had appointed a certain *interventor* among the people of their communion at Carthage, before Majorinus was ordained against Caecilian.

[Note: An *interventor* was someone who governed a Church while its see was vacant.]

He said that this *interventor* had been killed by our people in their meeting-place. I confess that I had never heard this at all before, although so many crimes alleged by them had been refuted and rebutted by our people, and more and greater charges had been hurled against them.

Nevertheless, after he had related this, he again began to ask me insistently whom I considered just: the one who had killed, or the one who had been killed—as though he had already proved to me that the matter had occurred as he had narrated it.

I therefore replied that it first had to be investigated whether it was true; for one ought not rashly to believe whatever is said. Nevertheless, it could have happened that both were equally wicked, or even that a wicked person had killed someone worse than himself.

For it can truly happen that the rebaptizer of the whole person is more criminal than the one who kills only the body.

9. Consequently, the question he later put to me was no longer necessary. For he said that even an evil person ought not to have been killed by Christians and just men, as though we called those who do such things in the Catholic Church just.

Yet these are things they more readily say about us than prove, since many of their own bishops, presbyters, and clergy of every kind, having gathered crowds of utterly frenzied people, do not cease to inflict, wherever they can, many extremely violent killings and massacres not only upon Catholics but sometimes even upon their own people.

Although this was the case, he concealed the most criminal deeds of his own people—of which he himself knew more—and pressed me to say which of the just had killed any evil person.

Even if this no longer pertained to the case—for we admitted that wherever such things were done under the Christian name, they were not done by good people—we nevertheless replied, so that he might be reminded what needed to be investigated, by asking whether Elijah seemed to him to have been just. He could not deny it.

Then we added how many false prophets he had slain with his own hand (1 Kings 18:40). Here he truly saw what needed to be seen: that such things were permitted to the just at that time. For they did these things by the prophetic spirit and by God’s authority, who undoubtedly knows whom it may benefit to be killed.

He therefore demanded that I show, in the times of the New Testament, which of the just had killed anyone, even a criminal and an impious person.

### CHAPTER V

10. Then we returned to the earlier discussion, in which we wished to show that neither ought we to reproach them with the crimes of their people, nor they us if any such deeds were found among ours.

From the New Testament I did indeed show that it could not be proved that any just person had killed anyone. Nevertheless, it could be proved by the Lord’s own example that criminals had been tolerated by the innocent.

He endured the presence among the innocent of his own traditor, who had already received the price of his betrayal, until the final kiss of peace. He did not conceal from them that a man guilty of so great a crime was among them; and yet, before that man had been excluded, he gave the first Sacrament of his body and blood to them all together (Matthew 26:20–28).

When almost everyone was moved by this example, he attempted to say that, before the Lord’s Passion, the Apostles’ communion with that criminal had not harmed them because they did not yet have Christ’s baptism, but John’s baptism.

After he had said this, I began to ask him how it was therefore written that Jesus baptized more people than John, although Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples did—that is, he baptized through his disciples (John 4:1–2).

How, then, were they giving what they had not received? That is precisely what they themselves are accustomed to say. Or was Christ perhaps baptizing with John’s baptism?

Then I was going to ask many questions about this position: how John himself was then questioned about the Lord’s baptism and replied that the Lord had the bride and that he was the bridegroom (the same, 3:29). Was it therefore proper for the bridegroom to baptize with John’s baptism—that is, with the baptism of a friend or servant?

Moreover, how could they receive the Eucharist while not yet baptized? Or how could he have replied to Peter, who wanted him to wash his whole body: “The one who has been washed once does not need to be washed again, but is wholly clean”? (the same, 13:10.)

For complete cleansing is found not in John’s baptism but in the Lord’s baptism—

[Note: Eight manuscripts read: “But the baptism is in the name of the Lord.”]

—provided that the one who receives it makes himself worthy of it; but if he is unworthy, the Sacraments will remain in him not for salvation but for destruction.

Since I was therefore going to ask these questions, he too saw that he ought not to have raised the issue of the baptism of the Lord’s disciples.

11. From there the discussion moved to another matter, with many people speaking on both sides as best they could. During this exchange it was said that our people would still persecute them. He told us that he wanted to see what sort of people we would show ourselves to be in that persecution—whether we would consent to such savagery or refuse to lend it any support.

We replied that God sees our hearts, which they could not see; and that they were still fearing such things for no reason. If such things occurred, they would occur through evil people, whom they themselves have in greater number and of worse character. Nevertheless, we ought not for that reason to separate ourselves from Catholic communion if something were done against our will, or even, if we were able, despite our opposition, since we had learned peaceful endurance, as the Apostle says: “Bearing with one another in love, striving to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4:2–3).

We said that those who created the schism had not maintained this peace and endurance: now, among their own people who are more moderate, they tolerate worse things so that what has been divided may not be split apart, although they were unwilling to tolerate lesser things for the sake of unity itself.

We also said that, in the times of the ancients, the peace of unity and the practice of endurance had not yet been proclaimed with such emphasis as in the example of the Lord and the love of the New Testament. Yet those Prophets and holy men were accustomed to denounce the crimes of their people while never attempting to tear themselves away from the unity of that people or from communion in receiving together the Sacraments that existed at that time.

12. From there, I do not know how, the discussion came to recall the blessed Genethlius, bishop of Carthage before Aurelius, who, they said, had suppressed some decree issued against them and had not allowed it to take effect.

Everyone praised him and spoke of him with the greatest warmth. In the midst of these praises we added that even Genethlius himself, if he had fallen into their hands, would be judged to require rebaptism.

We were already standing as we spoke, because the time for departure was pressing. At that point the old man plainly said that a rule had already been established: whoever of our faithful came to them was to be baptized. It was evident, as far as possible, that he was saying this unwillingly and with distress of heart.

Since he too openly lamented many of the evil deeds of his own people, and showed—something confirmed by the testimony of his entire city—how far he was removed from such actions, and since he brought forward in a modest complaint what he was accustomed to say to his own people, we recalled the passage of the prophet Ezekiel where it is plainly written that neither the son’s guilt is imputed to the father nor the father’s guilt to the son, where it says: “For just as the soul of the father is mine, so also the soul of the son is mine; the soul that sins, it alone shall die” (Ezekiel 18:20, 4).

It pleased everyone that in such discussions the violent deeds of wicked people ought not to be brought against one another.

The question of the schism therefore remained. Accordingly, we urged him again and again, with a calm and peaceful spirit, to strive together with us so that such a great inquiry might reach its conclusion through careful examination.

When he kindly said that we alone were asking these questions, while our people did not want them asked, we departed after making this promise: that we would bring him several of our colleagues—certainly at least ten—who would wish the matter to be investigated with as much benevolence, gentleness, and devout zeal as we sensed he had already observed and approved in us. He himself made the same promise concerning people from his own side.

### CHAPTER VI

13. Therefore I exhort and beseech you, by the blood of the Lord, to remind him of his promise and press him earnestly, so that the matter begun may proceed; you already see that it has nearly reached its end.

For, in my judgment, you can scarcely find among your bishops a disposition and willingness so useful as those we observed in this old man.

On the following day he himself came to us, and we began again to discuss these questions. But because the necessity of ordaining a bishop was already carrying us away from there at any moment, we could not remain with him longer.

For we had already sent for Major of the Coelicolists,

[Note: The name Coelicolists occurs in several laws issued by Honorius, under which they are required to suffer the penalties established against heretics “unless they have been converted to the worship and Christian veneration of God.”]

whom we had heard to be the founder of the new baptism among them,

[Note: The editions read *instituisse* (“to have instituted”). Fourteen manuscripts read *institisse*. The Gemmet manuscript reads *extitisse* (“to have been”). The latter is much better.]
