and to have led many astray by that sacrilege, so that we might speak with him about something, insofar as the constraints of time permitted.

When he learned that Major was about to come, and saw that we had undertaken another task, while some necessity of departure also pressed Major himself, he kindly and peacefully took his leave of us.

14. It seems to me that we ought entirely to avoid turbulent crowds that bring hindrance rather than help, and, with the Lord’s assistance, complete so great a matter—undertaken in a genuinely friendly and tranquil spirit—by meeting at some small estate where none of us had a church. Nevertheless, people belonging both to our communion and to his jointly possess such an estate, as is the case with the estate of Titiana.

Whether such a place is found in Tubursicum or in Thagaste—either the one I have mentioned or some other—let us arrange for the canonical books to be present. If documents can be produced from either side, then, setting everything else aside, and, if it pleases the Lord, without any troublesome interruption, let us devote as many days as we can to this matter. Let each of us entreat the Lord at his own host’s house, with the help of him to whom Christian peace is most pleasing, so that we may bring this great matter, begun with good will, to the conclusion of its investigation.

Write back and tell us what you and he think about this matter.

## LETTER XLV

[Note: Now published for the first time from the Phimarcon manuscript. The one that was 45 is now 127. Written around the beginning of 398.]

Augustine to Paulinus, asking him at last to write back after two years of silence and to send him the work against the Pagans which he had long ago heard Paulinus was preparing.

To their most intimate, beloved, and praiseworthy lords in Christ, PAULINUS and THERASIA,

ALYPIUS and AUGUSTINE send greetings in the Lord.

1. Your failure to write—whatever the reason for it—which has resulted in our receiving no letter from you for the entire two years since our sweetest brothers Romanus and Agilis returned to you, has certainly not made us slow to write.

For although in other matters the more someone is loved, the more worthy of imitation he seems to be, the opposite is true here. The more ardently we love you, the less we endure your not writing to us; nor do we wish to imitate you in this.

So here we are greeting you—not by replying to your letters, since none reach us, but by making a complaint, and not a slight one, although perhaps Your Charity is likewise complaining, if you know that letters sent by you did not reach us, and that those sent by us were in turn not delivered to you.

If this is so, let us turn our complaints into prayers to the Lord, lest he deny us such great consolations.

2. We had heard that you were writing against the Pagans. If the work is finished, please do not delay sending it by the bearer of this letter.

He is dear to us, and in our regions we can safely give a good testimony concerning his reputation. Through us he asks Your Holiness to deign to commend him to those with whom he has business and before whom he fears that his good cause may be suppressed.

He himself will explain more conveniently what is taking place; and whatever concerns the individual matters that may perhaps trouble your mind, we are most grateful for it among …

We give thanks to our Lord God for your most sincere kindness if, through your efforts, we may rejoice in the safety of a Christian brother.

## LETTER XLVI

[Note: Letters XLVI and XLVII have been revised in manuscripts and editions designated a, b, g, bl, c, cc, ff, g, gv, n, r, s, t, vc, two manuscripts marked sb, and four marked v, as well as in Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: Elsewhere 153; the one that was 46 is now 214. Possibly written in 398.]

Publicola submits many questions to Augustine.

To the beloved and venerable father, AUGUSTINE, bishop,

PUBLICOLA.

It is written: “Ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will declare it to you” (Deut. 32:7). Accordingly, in such a matter I have judged that I must inquire into the law from the mouth of a priest. I explain the matter in writing, both so that you may instruct me and so that I may be instructed in various cases. I have arranged the individual and distinct questions by chapters; deign to answer them one by one.

—Among the Arzuges, as I have heard, the barbarians customarily swear to the decurion who commands the frontier [Note: In Ambrosianus, Badianus, and seven manuscripts, *militi* (“soldier”) is read. The other witnesses, however, have the better reading, *limiti* (“the frontier”). See the *Notitia Dignitatum Imperii*.], or to the tribune, swearing by their demons. Some have contracted to transport baggage loads [Note: *Bastaga*, from *bastazo*, “to carry,” means a burden; according to the *Legal Lexicon*, it is “something suited to carrying fiscal goods.” *Bastagia* was the term for the actual load of goods carried by pack animals.], while others undertake individually, as landowners or tenants, to guard the crops themselves—almost as though they were already trustworthy—when the decurion sends a letter, or when individual travelers pass through and necessarily have to travel by way of them.

A question has arisen in my mind: whether the landowner who accepts a barbarian, whose loyalty appears to have been secured by an oath sworn by demons, is himself defiled, or whether the crops that he guards are defiled, or whether the person who is escorted by the barbarian escort is defiled. But you must know that the barbarian who swears receives gold from the landowner for guarding the crops, or from the traveler for providing an escort. Yet together with this payment, as is customarily given by the landowner or traveler, there is also that deadly oath, sworn to the decurion or tribune. This troubles me: whether it defiles the person who accepts the barbarian’s oath, or the crops that the barbarian guards. For whatever the arrangement—although, as I have heard, gold and hostages are also given—an impious oath has nevertheless intervened. Deign to write me a definitive answer, and not one expressed with hesitation. For if you yourself write hesitantly, I may fall into greater doubts than I had before asking.

—I have also heard that the tenant-managers themselves who oversee my property accept an oath from barbarians who swear by their demons, in exchange for guarding the crops. Deign to make clear whether, when they swear by their demons that they will guard the crops, they defile the crops themselves, so that a Christian who knowingly eats from them, or receives money derived from those goods, is defiled.

—I have likewise heard from one person that a barbarian does not swear to a tenant-manager, while another said that he does swear to one. If the man who said that the barbarian swears to the tenant-manager told me falsely, must I nevertheless, merely because I heard this, refrain from using the crops themselves or their proceeds, on account of the mere report, since it is said: “But if someone says, ‘This has been offered in sacrifice to idols,’ do not eat it, because of the one who disclosed it”? (1 Cor. 10:28.) Yet this case may perhaps be analogous to the case of food offered in sacrifice. If so, what ought I to do with the crops themselves or with their proceeds?

—Must I investigate both men who told me these things—the one who said that the barbarian does not swear to the tenant-manager and the one who said that he does—and establish by witnesses which of the two spoke the truth, and meanwhile refrain from touching the crops themselves or their proceeds until it has been proved whether the man who said that the barbarian does not swear to the tenant-manager spoke the truth?

—If a barbarian who swears an evil oath makes the Christian tenant-manager, or the tribune who commands the frontier, swear to him, for the sake of preserving faith with him and guarding the crops, by the same deadly oath by which he himself swears, is only that Christian defiled? Or are the things on whose behalf he swears also defiled? Or if a pagan who commands the frontier swears to the barbarian, by a deadly oath, in order to preserve faith with him, does that defile the things on whose behalf he swears? If I send someone to the Arzuges, is he permitted to accept that deadly oath from a barbarian? And if accepting such an oath does not defile him, may a Christian accept it?

—If, from a threshing floor containing wheat or any kind of legume, or from a winepress, something has been offered to a demon, is a Christian knowingly permitted to eat what comes from there?

—Is a Christian knowingly permitted to take wood from a sacred grove for some personal use?

—If someone going to the market buys meat that has not been offered in sacrifice, but has two thoughts in his heart—that it has been sacrificed and that it has not been sacrificed—and he retains the thought that it was not sacrificed, does he sin if he eats it?

—If someone does a good deed about which he is uncertain whether it is good or evil, believing it to be good, although he had also thought it might be evil, is sin attributed to him?

—If someone says that something has been offered in sacrifice, while lying, and later says again that he was lying—and truly was lying—is a Christian permitted to eat from it, or sell it, and make use of the proceeds, on the basis of what he heard?

—If a Christian, while traveling, suffers necessity and is overcome by hunger for one day, two days, or many days, so that he can endure no longer, and in that very necessity of hunger, when he sees death already approaching, finds food placed in an idol’s shrine, where there is no one, and cannot find any other food, ought he to die or take nourishment from it?

—If a Christian sees that a barbarian or Roman intends to kill him, ought that Christian kill them so as not to be killed by them? Or is it permitted to repel or resist them without killing them, since it is said: “Do not resist evil”? (Matt. 5:39.)

—Should a Christian build a wall around his property because of the enemy, and does the Christian who built the wall incur guilt for homicide when some people begin fighting from it and killing enemies?

—Is it permitted to drink from a spring or well into which something from a sacrifice has been thrown? If there is a well in a temple that has been abandoned, ought a Christian drink from it? If, in a temple where an idol is worshiped, there is a well or spring, and nothing has been done in that well or spring, ought a Christian draw water from it and drink?

—Ought a Christian bathe in bathhouses or hot baths in which sacrifices are offered to images?

—Ought a Christian bathe in bathhouses where pagans have bathed on their festival day, whether with them or without them?

—If, in a bathing basin [Note: That is, a vessel in which people sat while bathing.] into which pagans descended after coming from idols on their festival day, they have performed some sacrilegious act, and a Christian knows this, ought he descend into the same basin?

—If a Christian, invited by someone, has had meat placed before him as food, and has been told that it was sacrificial, but has not eaten it; and afterward, by some circumstance, finds that same meat transferred elsewhere and offered for sale, and buys it; or if, having been invited by someone else, he has had the meat placed before him without recognizing it and eats it, does he sin?

—If a Christian knowingly ought to buy and eat a vegetable or some fruit from a garden or estate belonging to idols or to their priests?

Concerning oaths and idols, so that you may not have to labor in searching, I have wished to set before you what we have found, by the Lord’s favor. If you find anything else stated more clearly or more appropriately in Scripture, deign to make it known to me. What we have found is this: when Laban said to Jacob, “The God of Abraham and the God of Nahor” (Gen. 31:53), Scripture did not indicate which God he meant. Again, “When Abimelech came to Isaac, where he swore, or those who were with him” (ibid. 26:31), Scripture did not indicate what kind of oath it was. Again, concerning idols, in the Book of Judges, when the Lord commanded Gideon to make a burnt offering from the bull that he had killed (Judg. 6:26). And in Joshua, concerning Jericho, that all the gold, silver, and bronze should be brought into the treasuries of the Lord, and that the city which was under the ban was called holy (Josh. 6:19). And what is the meaning of the passage in Deuteronomy: “You shall not bring an abomination into your house, and you shall be under the ban, just as it is itself”? (Deut. 7:26.)

May the Lord preserve you. I greet you; pray for me.

## LETTER XLVII

[Note: Formerly numbered 154; the letter that was 47 is now 215. Written at approximately the same time.] Augustine resolves several of Publicola’s proposed questions.

To the honorable and most beloved son PUBLICOLA, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

### 1

After I learned from your letter of the agitation of your mind, it immediately became my own as well—not because everything of the kind that you indicated had disturbed you would likewise disturb me, but because, I confess, I became agitated over how those agitations might be removed from you; especially since you ask me to write you a definitive answer, lest you fall into greater doubts than you had before asking.

This is not within my power. For however I write what seems most certain to me, if I do not persuade you, you will undoubtedly be more uncertain. Just as it lies within my power to offer reasons for persuasion, it does not likewise lie within my power to persuade everyone. Nevertheless, so as not to deny your affection the service you request, after some deliberation I thought I should write back.

### 2

You are certainly troubled as to whether one may rely on the loyalty of someone who has sworn by demons in order to preserve it. I want you first to consider whether, if someone swore by false gods that he would keep faith and then did not keep it, you would not think that he had sinned twice. If he preserved the faith promised by such an oath, he would be judged to have sinned only because he had sworn by such gods; no one, however, would rightly criticize the fact that he kept faith. But now, because he both swore by those by whom he ought not to have sworn and did what he ought not to have done against his pledged faith, he certainly sinned twice.

Accordingly, the person who makes use of the loyalty of one whom he knows to have sworn by false gods, and who uses it not for something evil but for something lawful and good, does not associate himself with the man’s sin in swearing by demons, but with the good act by which he kept his agreement. I am not speaking here of that faith by which those who are baptized in Christ are called faithful. That faith is altogether different and distinct from the faith involved in human agreements and contracts.

Nevertheless, without any doubt, it is a lesser evil to swear truthfully by a false god than falsely by the true God. For the holier the one by whom the oath is sworn, the more grievous is the perjury.

The question is therefore a different one: whether the person who has another swear by false gods does not sin because the one who swears to him worships false gods. The testimonies that you yourself cited concerning Laban and Abimelech may support this question—provided that Abimelech swore by his gods, just as Laban swore by the God of Nahor [Note: The printed editions and manuscripts read “by the God of Jacob.” The citation is more accurately given by the canonists as “by the God of Nahor.”].

As I said, this is a different question, and it might reasonably trouble me if the examples concerning Isaac and Jacob, and any others that may be found, had not occurred to me. Unless perhaps what is said in the New Testament—that we should not swear at all (Matt. 5:34, 36)—no longer troubles you. I understand this to have been said not because swearing truthfully is a sin, but because perjury is an enormous sin; and the one who warned us not to swear in any manner wished us to be far from it.

But I know that you understand the matter differently. It is therefore not now necessary to discuss that point; rather, let us deal with the matter on which you thought you should consult me. Accordingly, just as you do not swear, so do not compel another to swear, if that is your conviction. Although it is said that we should not swear, I do not remember reading anywhere in the holy Scriptures that we should not accept an oath from another.

There is, however, another question: whether we ought to make use of the peace that has been established among people who have sworn to one another. If we refuse to do so, I do not know whether we could find anywhere on earth to live. For peace is established not only along the frontier but throughout all the provinces by barbarian oaths. It would therefore follow that not only the crops guarded by those who have sworn by false gods, but everything everywhere secured by that peace confirmed by their oath, would be defiled. Since it would be utterly absurd to say this, let the points that troubled you no longer trouble you.

### 3

Again, if something is taken from a threshing floor or winepress for sacrifices to demons, a Christian sins if he permits it when he has the power to prevent it. But if he discovers that it has happened, or did not have the power to prevent it, he makes use of the other clean produce from which those things were taken, just as we make use of springs from which we certainly know that water has been drawn for sacrificial purposes.

The same principle applies to baths. For we have no hesitation about drawing breath from the air into which we know smoke from all the altars and fires of demons rises. From this it is evident that what is prohibited is using, or appearing to use, something in honor of foreign gods—receiving it in such a way that, although we despise them in our hearts, we nevertheless encourage those who do not know our hearts to honor them.

When temples, idols, sacred groves, and anything of this kind are overthrown with lawful authority, it is obvious that in doing so we do not honor them but rather detest them. Nevertheless, we ought not to appropriate anything from them for our own private and personal uses, so that it may be clear that we destroy them out of piety, not greed. When, however, they are converted to common rather than private and personal uses, or to the honor of the true God, what happens to them is like what happens to the people themselves when they are transformed from sacrilegious and impious persons into the true religion.

God is understood to have taught this through the testimonies that you cited: when he commanded that wood from the sacred grove of foreign gods be used for a burnt offering, and concerning Jericho, that all the gold, silver, and bronze should be brought into the treasuries of the Lord.

Therefore, the passage written in Deuteronomy also appears sufficiently clear:

“You shall not covet their silver or gold, nor take any of it for yourself, lest you transgress because of it, for it is an abomination to the Lord your God. You shall not bring an accursed thing into your house, and you shall be under the ban like it; you shall utterly detest it and be defiled by it, for it is under the ban” (Deut. 7:25–26).

Either private uses of such things are prohibited, or they must not be brought into one’s house in such a way that they are honored. They are an abomination and a curse when the honor of such sacrilege is not overturned by its complete destruction [Note: The printed editions read *talibus sacrilegiis* (“such sacrileges”). The manuscripts, however, have *talium sacrilegus* (“the sacrilegious honor of such things”), which is the better reading.].

### 4

You may be certain that, concerning food offered to idols, we ought to observe nothing beyond what the Apostle commanded. Recall his words on this subject; if they were obscure, we would explain them according to our limited ability.

A person does not sin if, without knowing it, he later eats food that he had previously rejected as food offered to an idol. A vegetable, or any fruit born in any field, belongs to the one who created it, because “the earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness,” and “every creature of God is good” (Ps. 23:1; 1 Cor. 10:25–26; 1 Tim. 4:4). But if what grows in the fields is consecrated to an idol or sacrificed, then it must be classified among food offered to idols.

One must beware lest, if we think that a vegetable growing in the garden of an idol’s temple may not be eaten, it follows that we should think the Apostle ought not to have eaten food at Athens, because the city was consecrated to Minerva and her divinity [Note: This is correctly read in the Gemmetic manuscript as *Apostolos* (“the Apostles”).].

I would give the same answer concerning a well or spring located in a temple. It is indeed more troubling if something from a sacrifice is thrown into a spring or well. But the same reasoning applies to the air, which receives all the smoke mentioned above. Or, if someone thinks there is a difference because the sacrifice whose smoke is mixed with the air is not offered to the air itself but to some idol or demon, while at other times sacrifices are thrown into waters so that the waters themselves are sacrificed to, the answer is still that we do not for that reason cease to use the light of the sun, although sacrilegious people do not cease to sacrifice to it wherever they can.

Sacrifices are also offered to the winds, yet we use them for many of our needs, even though they seem in a certain sense to inhale and swallow the smoke of those same sacrifices.

If someone is uncertain whether some meat has been offered in sacrifice, and it has not been, and he retains the conviction that it has not been sacrificed and eats it, he certainly does not sin. For it neither is nor is now believed to be sacrificial, even though it was previously thought to be. It is certainly permissible to correct one’s thoughts from falsehood to truth.

But if someone thinks that something evil is good and does it, he sins precisely because of that belief. These are all sins of ignorance: when a person thinks that something is being done well although it is being done badly.

### 5

As for killing people so that one may not be killed by them, I do not approve of that course of action [Note: Augustine had already explained his view elsewhere in *On Free Choice of the Will* 1.5, where he ultimately approved Evodius’s position, section 13: namely, that those who have stained themselves with human blood for the sake of things that ought to be despised are by no means free from sin before divine providence. He absorbed this teaching from Ambrose, who in *On the Duties* 3.4 writes: “It does not seem that a Christian, just, and wise man ought to seek his own life through another’s death; accordingly, even if he encounters an armed robber, he cannot strike back at the one striking him, lest, while defending his life, he stain his piety.” He also drew it from Cyprian, who states absolutely in Letter 56: “It is not permitted to kill, but it is necessary to be killed”; and in Letter 57: “Nor may even the innocent kill one who does harm.”].

There may be an exception if the person is a soldier or holds a public office, so that he does this not for himself but for others or for the state in which he too lives, having received lawful authority, if such action is appropriate to his position.

Those who are restrained by some fear from doing evil may perhaps themselves also receive some benefit. This is why it is said, “Let us not resist evil” (Matt. 5:39): not so that we may neglect the correction of people, but so that we may not delight in vengeance, which feeds the mind on another’s misfortune.

Accordingly, a person is not guilty of another’s death if he builds a wall around his property and someone is struck and killed by the collapse of part of it [Note: Seven manuscripts, Badianus, and Erasmus read: “who, while he was enclosing his property, is not guilty if someone is struck and killed by the use of those materials.”].

A Christian is not guilty if his ox kills someone by goring him, or his horse kills someone by kicking him. Nor, for that reason, should Christians refrain from having oxen with horns, horses with hooves, or dogs with teeth. Or, because the Apostle Paul took sufficient care to have it reported to the tribune that certain wicked men were plotting against him, and for that reason received armed escorts (Acts 23:17–24), if those criminals had fallen upon those weapons, would Paul have acknowledged his own guilt in their shedding of blood?

Far be it from us to think that, if something harmful happens to someone against our will through things that we do or possess for a good and lawful purpose, it should be attributed to us. Otherwise, we should not possess household or agricultural tools, lest someone kill himself or another with them; nor a tree or rope, lest someone hang himself from it; nor should we make a window, lest someone throw himself through it.

Why should I say more, when I could not finish listing such examples? What is there in good and lawful human use from which harm could not also be inflicted?

### 6

It remains, if I am not mistaken, to say something about the Christian traveler whom you mentioned: overcome by hunger, if he finds nowhere anything except food placed in an idol’s shrine, where no other human being is present, is it better for him to die of hunger than to take that food for nourishment?

Since it does not follow that the food is food offered to an idol—for it could have been left there forgetfully or intentionally by people who had turned aside from their journey to refresh themselves, or it could have been placed there for any other reason—I shall answer briefly.

It is either certain that it is food offered to an idol, certain that it is not, or unknown. If it is certainly such food, it is better to reject it with Christian fortitude. But if it is known not to be such food, or if this is unknown, it may be taken for the necessities of life without any scruple of conscience.

## LETTER XLVIII

[Note: We have collated this letter with manuscripts A, BG, C, CC, FF, G, GV, N, R, SB, VC, two T manuscripts, two V manuscripts, and with Ambrosianus, Badianus, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis.]  
[Note: Formerly numbered 81; the letter that was 48 is now 93. Written perhaps in A.D. 398.] Augustine to Eudoxius, abbot of the monks of the island of Capraria, exhorting them to use their leisure for piety, not idleness, and, whenever the Church requires their service, not to decline it.

To the lord, beloved and most longed-for brother and fellow presbyter EUDOXIUS, and to the brothers who are with you, AUGUSTINE and the brothers who are with me send greetings in the Lord.

### 1

When we think of the quiet that you possess in Christ, we too, although we are engaged in various harsh and difficult labors, find rest in your love. For we are one body under one head, so that you are active in us and we are at rest in you, because “if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; and if one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it” (1 Cor. 12:26).

We therefore admonish, ask, and beseech you, through the sublime humility and most merciful majesty of Christ, to remember us in your holy prayers, which we believe you offer with greater wakefulness and sobriety. For the darkness and turmoil of secular affairs often wound and weaken us. Even if these affairs are not our own, the affairs of those who compel us to go one mile and command us to go with them another two (Matt. 5:41) are imposed upon us in such abundance that we can scarcely breathe.

Nevertheless, we believe that he in whose presence “the groaning of the prisoners enters” (Ps. 79:11), if we persevere in the ministry in which he has deigned to place us with the promised reward, will free us from every distress through the assistance of your prayers.

### 2

But we exhort you, brothers, in the Lord to preserve your vocation and persevere to the end. If Mother Church should ever desire your service, do not undertake it with the proud eagerness of ambition, nor reject it through the flattering appeal of laziness. Obey God with a gentle heart, bearing with meekness the one who governs you, who guides the meek in judgment and teaches the humble his ways (Ps. 24:9).

Do not place your leisure above the needs of the Church. If, when she was in labor, no good people had been willing to minister to her, you would not have found her giving birth to you.

Just as a path must be kept between fire and water, so that a person is neither burned nor drowned, we must regulate our course between the summit of pride and the abyss of laziness, as it is written: “Not turning aside either to the right or to the left” (Deut. 17:11).

There are people who, while fearing too much that they might be carried away and exalted as though to the right, fall to the left and are submerged. Others, while withdrawing too far from the left lest they be swallowed up by the torpid softness of inactivity, are corrupted and consumed on the other side by the arrogance of self-display, and vanish into ash and smoke.

Therefore, beloved, love leisure in such a way that you restrain yourselves from every earthly delight, and remember that there is no place where the one who fears that we may fly back to God cannot lay his snares. Let us regard as an enemy the enemy of every good thing, whose captives we were [Note: This is the reading of all our manuscripts and two Vatican manuscripts. The printed editions have *vindicemus* (“let us avenge”).], and let us think that we have no perfect rest until iniquity passes away (Ps. 56:2) and justice is transformed into judgment (Ps. 93:15) [Note: All the manuscripts read *cogitetis* (“you should think”), rather than *cogitemus* (“let us think”).].

### 3

Whenever you act vigorously and eagerly and work diligently—whether in prayers, fasts, or almsgiving; whether by giving something to those in need or forgiving offenses, just as God in Christ forgave us (Eph. 4:32); whether by mastering destructive habits, disciplining the body, and bringing it into servitude (1 Cor. 9:27); whether by enduring tribulation, and above all by bearing with one another in love—for what does someone endure who does not endure his brother?; whether by watching for the craft and snares of the tempter and repelling and extinguishing his flaming arrows with the shield of faith (Eph. 6:16); whether by singing and chanting in your hearts to the Lord (Eph. 5:19), or with voices that do not disagree with the heart—do everything for the glory of God (1 Cor. 10:31), who works all things in all people (ibid. 12:6).

Be fervent in spirit (Rom. 12:11), so that your soul may glory in the Lord (Ps. 33:3). This is the activity of the right path: it always keeps its eyes upon the Lord, because he will draw the feet out of the snare (Ps. 24:15). Such activity is neither broken by business nor chilled by leisure; it is neither turbulent nor languid, neither rash nor evasive, neither headlong nor prostrate. Do these things, and the God of peace will be with you (2 Cor. 13:11).

### 4

Let your Charity not think me intrusive because I wished to speak to you, even by letter. I did not admonish you about something that I suppose you are not doing. Rather, I believed that I would be commended to God by you to no small degree if, while doing the things you do by his gift, you also did them with the remembrance of our conversation.

Even before this, report had brought us word, and now the brothers who came from you—Eustasius [Note: The printed editions have *Eusthatius*. In the parchment manuscripts, however, the name is consistently written *Eustasius*.] and Andreas—have brought us the good fragrance of your holy way of life.

Of these, Eustasius has gone ahead into that rest which, unlike an island, is battered by no waves and does not long for Capraria, since he no longer seeks to be clothed in sackcloth.

## LETTER XLIX

[Note: We have revised this letter against manuscripts A, BG, C, CC, FF, G, GV, N, R, S, SB, T, VC, four V manuscripts, and against Ambrosianus, Badianus, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis.]  
[Note: Formerly numbered 161; the letter that was 49 is now 102. Written at approximately the same time.] Augustine to Honoratus of the Donatist party, asking him to explain calmly by letter how the name of the Church—which Scripture clearly foretold would exist throughout the whole world—came to be restricted to them alone.

To HONORATUS, bishop of the Donatist party, AUGUSTINE, bishop [Note: The printed editions read “bishop of the party of the Catholic Church.” The manuscripts lack the word *partis* (“party”), and Verlinus and Vindingus observed that the expression “party of the Catholic Church” is inappropriate and that Augustine does not customarily attribute it to him.] of the Catholic Church.

### 1

We were greatly pleased by your plan, which you deigned to communicate through our most beloved and praiseworthy brother in Christ, Herotes [Note: This is the reading of the manuscripts. The printed editions have *Erotes*. The bracketed form is *Erotem*.], namely, that we should deal with one another by letter, where no tumult of disturbances could disrupt our discussion—a discussion that ought to be undertaken and conducted with complete gentleness and peace of mind, as the Apostle says: “The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward all, teachable, patient, correcting those who think differently with restraint” (2 Tim. 2:24–25).

We therefore briefly indicate what we would like you to answer.

### 2

Since we see the Church of God, which is called Catholic, spread throughout the world, just as it was prophesied concerning her, we think that we ought not to doubt the fulfillment of such an evident holy prophecy—one that the Lord also confirmed in the Gospel, as did the Apostles through whom that same Church was extended, just as it had been foretold.

At the beginning of the sacred Psalter it is written concerning the Son of God:

“The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 2:7–8).

The Lord Jesus Christ himself says that his Gospel will be preached among all nations (Matt. 24:14). The Apostle Paul, before the word of God had reached Africa, wrote at the very beginning of his Letter to the Romans: “Through him we have received grace and apostleship for the obedience of faith among all the nations for his name” (Rom. 1:5).

Afterward he himself preached the Gospel from Jerusalem and in the surrounding regions throughout all Asia as far as Illyricum, establishing and founding churches—not he alone, but the grace of God with him (1 Cor. 15:10), as he himself testifies.

What could appear more evident than the fact that in his letters we even find the names of regions and cities? He writes to the Romans, Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Thessalonians, and Colossians [Note: The manuscripts read *scripta* (“written”), which is not inappropriate if our punctuation is changed.].

John also writes to seven churches, which he mentions as established in those regions; through their number seven we understand the whole Church to be symbolically commended: Ephesus, Smyrna, Sardis [Note: Lovaniensis has *Sardes*. Other manuscripts have *Sardos*.], Philadelphia, Laodicea, Pergamum, and Thyatira (Rev. 1:11).

It is evident that we are in communion with all these churches today, just as it is evident that you are not in communion with them.

### 3

We therefore ask you not to hesitate to answer us: what reason, perhaps, do you know for Christ’s having lost his inheritance, spread throughout the whole world, so that it suddenly remained only among Africans—and not even among all of them?

The Catholic Church is also in Africa, because God willed and foretold that she would exist throughout all lands. But your party, which is called Donatist, is not present in all those places through which the writings, preaching, and deeds of the Apostles have spread.

But lest you say that our Church is not called Catholic but Macarian, as you call it, you should know something that can easily be established: throughout all those regions from which the Gospel of Christ has poured over these lands, neither the name of Donatus nor the name of Macarius is known.

You cannot deny that yours is called the party of Donatus, and it is known to everyone wherever your communion exists.

Deign therefore to write back to us, so that we may know how it could be that Christ lost his Church from the whole world and began to possess her among you alone. It is your responsibility to demonstrate this. For our case is sufficiently established by the fact that we see prophecy and the holy Scriptures fulfilled throughout the world.

I, Augustine, dictated this letter because I have long wished to speak with you about this matter. It seems to me that, especially because of our proximity, we may be able to discuss it by letter without any disturbance, with God’s help, to the extent that the situation requires.

## LETTER L

[Note: This letter has been found only in the Vatican manuscript.]  
[Note: Formerly numbered 267; the letter that was 50 is now 105. Written perhaps in A.D. 399.] Augustine reproaches the inhabitants of Suffecte for the killing of sixty Christians and promises that their Hercules will be returned to them.

To the authors and leaders, or elders, of the colony of Suffecte, AUGUSTINE, bishop.

The notorious crime of your brutality and your unexpected cruelty shakes the earth and strikes heaven, so that blood shines in your streets and shrines, and murder resounds. Among you Roman laws lie buried, and the authority of lawful judgments has been trampled underfoot. Certainly, there is neither reverence nor fear of the emperors among you.

Among you the innocent blood of sixty brothers has been shed [Note: The memory of these martyrs is celebrated in the Roman Martyrology on August 30.], and if someone has killed more, he has been rewarded with praise and has held the chief position in your council.

Come now, let us turn to the principal issue. If you say that Hercules is yours, we shall return him to you. There is metal available; stones are not lacking; varieties of marble are at hand; there is an abundant supply of craftsmen. In any event, your god is carefully sculpted, turned, and decorated. We shall add the red pigment that paints a blush, so that your sacred vows may resound.

For if you say that Hercules is yours, we shall collect the individual coins and buy the god from your craftsman for you. Therefore, return the lives that your hands have violently wrenched away; and just as your Hercules is returned to you by us, so let the lives of so many people be returned by you.

## LETTER LI

[Note: This letter has been corrected against manuscripts A, BG, BL, C, CC, FF, G, GV, N, R, S, SB, VC, two T manuscripts, four V manuscripts, and against Ambrosianus, Badianus, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis.]  
[Note: Formerly numbered 172; the letter that was 51 is now 154. Written in A.D. 399 or 400.] Augustine presses Crispinus, bishop of the Donatist party at Calama [Note: Crispinus is mentioned in Letter 105, section 4, and in *Against Cresconius* 3.46, sections 50 and following, as well as in Possidius, chapter 12.], with several arguments briefly presented, asking him to answer them by letter if he can.

### 1.

Because your people criticize our humility, I have therefore prefixed the letter in this way; for it might seem that I have done so as an insult to you, unless I expect you to reply to me in the same manner. As for your promise—or ours—regarding Carthage, or our persistence, why should I say much? However we handled those matters, let them be past, so that they may not obstruct what remains. Now, if I am not mistaken, there is no excuse left, with the Lord’s help: we are both in Numidia, and in our respective locations we are near one another. Rumor has brought me word that you still wish to test me by disputing the question that divides our communion. See how briefly all evasions may be removed: reply to this letter, if you please, and perhaps that will be sufficient—not only for us, but also for those who desire to hear us. Or, if it is not sufficient, let letters and replies be exchanged until they are sufficient. What advantage could the great proximity of the cities in which we live offer us more conveniently? For I have decided to deal with you concerning this matter only by letter, either so that nothing said may slip from the memory of either of us, or so that those interested in such matters, who perhaps cannot be present, may not be deprived of them.

You are accustomed to boast falsely about past events, whenever it suits you—perhaps not out of a desire to lie, but through error. Therefore, if you please, let us measure that matter against the present. Without doubt you remember that in the time of the former people both the sacrilege of idolatry was committed and the prophetic book was burned by a contemptuous king (Jer. 36:23); yet the evil of schism would not have been punished more severely for either of these crimes, unless it had been weighed more gravely. Surely you remember how the earth, splitting open, swallowed alive the authors of the schism, and how fire rushing down from heaven consumed those who had consented to them (Num. 16:31–35). Thus neither a fabricated and worshiped idol nor the sacred Book deserved to be avenged so severely.

### 2.

Why, then, when you are accustomed to charge us with crimes—not merely crimes unapproved among our people, but rather crimes approved among your own, committed by those who, driven by fear of persecution, handed the Lord’s books over to be burned—did you receive, within that very episcopate in which you had condemned them, those whom you condemned for the crime of schism with the supposedly truthful voice of your plenary council, as it is written there? I mean Felicianus of Musti and Praetextatus of Assuri.

[Note: This indicates the Council of Bagaï, held by 310 bishops against the Maximianists; see above, the note on Letter 43. Although Felicianus and Praetextatus, both among the twelve bishops who had ordained Maximianus, were condemned by the council’s sentence, they could never be expelled from their sees. Their opponents attempted this even by bringing suit against them before two or three proconsuls—the proceedings here called the “proconsular Acts”—but ultimately received them back in their offices, although Rogatus had already been ordained in Praetextatus’s place; see Book 1 *Against Gaudentius*, chapter 39, section 54, and other passages. This was evidently compelled by Optatus Gildonianus, as is said in Letter 53, section 6.]

For, contrary to what you tell the ignorant, these men were not among those to whom your council extended and fixed a period, within which, unless they returned to your communion, they would be held by the same sentence. Rather, they were among those whom you condemned without delay on the very day on which you granted them a delay. I shall prove it, if you deny it: your council speaks; we have the proconsular Acts in our hands, and you yourselves have cited them more than once. Prepare another defense, if you can, lest, while you deny what I shall establish, we waste time.

If Felicianus and Praetextatus were innocent, why were they condemned in this way? If they were criminals, why were they received in this way? If you prove that they were innocent, why should we not believe that your forefathers, far fewer in number, could have condemned innocent men on a false charge of handing over the Scriptures, if their three hundred and ten successors could condemn innocent men on a false charge of schism with the truthful voice of a plenary council—where this is even recorded as a great achievement? But if you prove that they were rightly condemned, what defense remains for their being received into the same episcopate, except that, while magnifying the usefulness and health-giving power of peace, you should show that even such things must be tolerated for the bond of unity? Would that you did this with strength of heart, not merely of mouth! You would surely perceive that the peace of Christ throughout the world ought not to be violated by any calumnies, if, in Africa also, men condemned for sacrilegious schism may, for the sake of Donatus’s peace, be received into that very episcopate.

### 3.

You are likewise accustomed to charge us with persecuting you through earthly authorities. On this point I do not argue either what you deserve for the enormity of so great a sacrilege or how much Christian gentleness restrains us. I say only this: if it is a crime, why did you fiercely harass those same Maximianists through judges sent by the emperors whom our communion brought forth through the Gospel? You drove them from the basilicas they occupied, in which the very investigation found them, disturbing them both through the tumult of lawsuits, the power of official commands, and the force of assistance.

The traces of recent events testify to what they suffered in each place; the documents indicate what orders were given; the earth cries out what was done. Among these events the sacred memory of that Optatus, your tribune, is also proclaimed.

[Note: Optatus, bishop of Thamugadi, from the Donatist schism, a notorious devastator of Africa.]

### 4.

You likewise customarily say that we do not possess Christ’s baptism, and that it exists nowhere outside your communion. I could discuss this at somewhat greater length. But there is no need to do so against you, since, together with Felicianus and Praetextatus, you also accepted the baptism of the Maximianists.

For all those whom they baptized while they were in communion with Maximianus—you were even attempting, as the Acts testify, to expel Felicianus and Praetextatus by a prolonged course of litigation from their basilicas—all those baptized at that time now retain baptism with them and with you, not only amid the dangers of illness but also during the Easter solemnities, in the many churches belonging to their cities. Even in those great cities, those who had been baptized outside in the crime of schism are with you, and none of them received baptism again.

Would that you could prove that those whom Felicianus and Praetextatus had baptized outside, in the crime of schism, as though their baptism were useless, were baptized again inside, after their reception, as though it were useful. For if these men were to be baptized again, those others were to be ordained again. They had lost the episcopate when they withdrew from you, if they could not baptize outside your communion. For if, on departing, they had not lost the episcopate, then surely they could baptize. But if they had lost it, then, so that what they had lost might be restored to them, they ought to have been ordained again when they returned.

But do not be afraid: just as it is certain that they returned with the same episcopate with which they had departed, so it is certain that all whom they baptized in Maximian’s schism they reconciled to your communion with them without any repetition of baptism.

### 5.

With what tears, then, are we to lament that the baptism of the Maximianists is received, while the baptism of the whole world is blown away? Whether you heard Felicianus and Praetextatus or not, whether you condemned them justly or unjustly—you condemned Felicianus; you condemned Praetextatus. Tell me: which bishop of the Corinthians did any one of you hear or condemn? Which of the Galatians, which of the Ephesians, which of the Colossians, Philippians, Thessalonians, or any of all the other cities concerning which it is said: “All the nations of the earth shall worship in his presence” (Ps. 21:28)?

Therefore the baptism of these men is accepted, while that of those men is blown away—yet baptism belongs neither to these nor to those, but to him of whom it was said: “This is he who baptizes” (John 1:33). But I am not dealing with that point here. Turn your attention to what is before us; look at what strikes even blind eyes: those who were condemned have baptism, while those who were not heard do not have it! Those explicitly named, condemned and expelled for the crime of schism, have it; while unknown men, foreigners from far away, never accused and never judged, do not have it! Those who were cut off from a severed part of Africa and then severed again have it; while those from whom the Gospel itself came into Africa do not have it!

Why burden you with more? Respond to these things.

Pay attention to the sacrilege of schism that your council charged against the Maximianists; pay attention to the persecutions you inflicted upon them through judicial authorities; pay attention to their baptism, which you received together with those whom you condemned. And answer, if you can, whether you possess anything by which you may cast mists before the unlearned, explaining why you are separated from the greater part of the world by a far greater crime of schism than the one you boast of having condemned in the Maximianists.

May Christ’s peace prevail in your heart.

ΕΥΤΥΧΩΣ — “Farewell.”

[Note: At the end of the letter we have added *eutuchōs* from the manuscripts; the word is absent from the printed editions.]

## LETTER LII

[Note: Collated with manuscripts and editions designated a, bg, bl, ff, g, gv, n, r, s, t, vc, two t manuscripts, four v manuscripts, and with Am, Bad, Er, and Lov.]

[Note: Formerly numbered 170; the letter formerly numbered 52 is now 155. It was perhaps written at about the same time.]

Augustine to Severinus, his kinsman, a Donatist, urging him to abandon the criminal and shameless schism.

To his greatly desired and very dear brother SEVERINUS, AUGUSTINE:

### 1.

Although very late, and although it was not what I had hoped for, I nevertheless received your letter with joy. I was especially filled with greater happiness when I learned that one of your people had come to Hippo for this very reason alone: to bring me a letter from your Fraternity.

I reflected that this had not arisen in your mind without cause—that you had recalled our kinship—unless perhaps you perceive, as I know you do, given the considerable weight of your good sense, how grievous it is that although we are brothers according to the flesh, we do not live in one fellowship within Christ’s body. This is especially so because it is easy for you to attend to and see the city set upon a mountain, of which the Lord says in the Gospel that it cannot be hidden (Matt. 5:14). This is the Catholic Church; hence it is called *καθολική* (*katholikē*) in Greek, because it is spread throughout the whole world. No one is permitted to be ignorant of it; therefore, in accordance with the word of our Lord Jesus Christ, it cannot be hidden.

### 2.

The party of Donatus, however, confined to the Africans alone, slanders the whole world and does not consider that, through the barrenness by which it refused to bear the fruit of peace and charity, it has been cut off from the root of the Eastern Churches, from which the Gospel came into Africa. Therefore, if soil from there is brought to them, they worship it; but if a faithful person comes from there, they blow him away and rebaptize him.

For the Son of God, who is the truth, also foretold this: that he is the vine, that his disciples are the branches, and that his Father is the cultivator: “The branch,” he says, “that does not bear fruit in me, my Father will remove; but the branch that bears fruit in me, he cleanses, so that it may bear more fruit” (John 15:1–2). It is therefore not surprising that those who refused to bear the fruit of charity have been cut off from that vine which grew and filled all the lands.

### 3.

If they had brought true charges against their colleagues, their ancestors, when they made the schism, would themselves have prevailed in their case before the overseas Church, from which the authority of the Christian faith flowed into these regions; thus those against whom they brought the same charges would have been the ones outside.

But now, when those men are found to be in communion within the apostolic Churches—whose names they possess and recite from the sacred Books—while these men are placed outside and separated from that communion, who would not understand that those who were able to prevail in their case before impartial judges had the better cause?

Or, if they had a good case but could not prove it to the overseas Churches, what harm did the whole world do to them, where the bishops could not rashly condemn colleagues who had not been convicted among them of the charges brought against them?

Thus innocent people are rebaptized, and Christ is blown away in the innocent. But if these same Donatists knew the true crimes of their African colleagues and neglected to demonstrate and prove them to the overseas Churches, they themselves cut themselves off from Christ’s unity through a most criminal schism. They have no excuse—and you know it—especially since so many criminals arose among them, whom they tolerated for so many years lest they tear apart Donatus’s party. Yet at that time they did not hesitate, by bringing forward their false suspicions, to shatter the peace and unity of Christ—and you see this.

### 4.

But I do not know what carnal custom, brother Severinus, keeps you there. For a long time I have grieved and groaned, especially when I think of your good sense, and for a long time I have desired to see you, so that I might speak with you about this matter.

What benefit is there in either temporal safety or kinship, if in our family relationship we despise Christ’s eternal inheritance and everlasting salvation?

For the present, let it suffice that I have written these things—very few and almost nothing to hardened hearts, but very many and very great to your mind, which I know well. For they are not my words, since I am nothing except one who awaits God’s mercy; they belong to God Almighty himself, whom anyone who despises as Father in this world will find as Judge in the next.

## LETTER LIII

[Note: Collated with manuscripts and editions designated a, bg, bl, c, cc, ff, g, gv, n, r, s, sb, t, vc, four v manuscripts, and with Am, Bad, Er, and Lov.]

[Note: Formerly numbered 165; the letter formerly numbered 53 is now 152. It was written around the year 400.]

A letter of a certain Donatist presbyter is refuted. He was attempting to seduce Generosus, a Catholic of Constantina, pretending that an angel had warned him to bring Generosus over to the Donatist party.

To their most beloved and honored brother GENEROSUS, FORTUNATUS, ALYPIUS, and AUGUSTINE send greetings in the Lord.

## CHAPTER ONE

### 1.

Since you wished us to know the letter which a Donatist presbyter gave you—although you too, with a Catholic mind, laughed at it—we nevertheless ask you to deliver this reply to him, so that you may advise him, if he is not hopelessly insane.

He wrote that an angel had ordered him to explain to you the Christian order of your city, although you possess Christianity not merely of your city, nor merely of Africa or the Africans, but of the whole world, which has been and is being announced to all nations.

It is therefore not enough for them that they are not ashamed to be cut off, nor that they do not help themselves by returning to the root whenever they can. They also attempt to cut off others with themselves and, like dry wood, consign them to the fire.

Accordingly, if an angel himself had appeared to you—whom that man, as we suppose, cunningly and vainly pretends appeared to him on your account—and had said to you the very things that he claims to be conveying to you at the angel’s command, you ought to remember the apostolic judgment, which says: “Even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel contrary to what we preached to you, let him be accursed” (Gal. 1:8).

For it has been announced to you by the voice of the Lord Jesus himself that his Gospel will be proclaimed to all nations, and then the end will come (Matt. 24:14). It has been announced to you through the prophetic and apostolic Letters that the promises were made to Abraham and to his seed, which is Christ (Gal. 3:16), when God said to him: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 12:3).

If, then, while you held these promises, an angel from heaven were to say to you, “Abandon the Christianity of the whole world and hold to the Christianity of Donatus’s party”—the order of which is explained to you in the letter of the bishop of your city—he ought to be accursed, because he would be trying to cut you off from the whole and confine you within a part, alienating you from God’s promises.

[Note: Lov. reads *partes*, “the parts.” Other editions read *partem*, “the part.” The manuscripts have *partis*, which must be supplied as “the Christianity of the part.”]

### 2.

For if the order of succeeding bishops is to be considered, how much more certainly and truly for our salvation do we count from Peter himself, who represented the figure of the whole Church and to whom the Lord said: “Upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. 16:18).

Peter was succeeded by Linus; Linus by Clement; Clement by Anacletus; Anacletus by Evaristus; Evaristus by Alexander; Alexander by Sixtus; Sixtus by Telesphorus; Telesphorus by Hyginus; Hyginus by Anicetus; Anicetus by Pius; Pius by Soter; Soter by Eleutherius; Eleutherius by Victor; Victor by Zephyrinus; Zephyrinus by Callistus; Callistus by Urban; Urban by Pontian; Pontian by Anterus; Anterus by Fabian; Fabian by Cornelius; Cornelius by Lucius; Lucius by Stephen; Stephen by Xystus; Xystus by Dionysius; Dionysius by Felix; Felix by Eutychianus; Eutychianus by Gaius; Gaius by Marcellinus; Marcellinus by Marcellus; Marcellus by Eusebius; Eusebius by Miltiades; Miltiades by Sylvester; Sylvester by Marcus; Marcus by Julius; Julius by Liberius; Liberius by Damasus; Damasus by Siricius; Siricius by Anastasius.

[Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “Linus, Cletus; Cletus, Clement,” against the other manuscripts. Shortly afterward, most manuscripts have *Anencletus* for *Anacletus*. Further, twelve manuscripts, including four Vatican codices, list Alexander after Soter, omitting Eleutherius altogether: “Soter, Alexander; Alexander, Victor”; they do not place Alexander after Evaristus, as do the printed editions and Optatus, Book 2. The same codices also omit Marcellinus later in the list.]

No Donatist bishop is found in this succession. Instead, they sent someone ordained from Africa across to Rome, who, presiding over a few Africans, spread in the city the name of the Montensians or Cutzupitans.

[Note: They acquired this designation because they began to have their first church in Rome on a hill, according to Jerome in his *Chronicle* under the year 360; or, as Optatus reports in Book 2, from a cave which they enclosed there outside the city with steps, where they held their assemblies. This cave undoubtedly lay in a higher place. From this perhaps also arose the name Cutzupitans, which is how it is read in most manuscripts. In the printed editions, with the *t* removed, it is *Cuzupitans*; in two Vatican manuscripts, *Cutrunpitans*. Whether the reading here should instead be *Rupitans* or *Rupitanans*, as in *On the Unity of the Church*, chapter 3; or *Scototopitans*, deriving the word from *scotos*, “darkness,” and *topos*, “place,” as the distinguished Joannes Baptista Cotelerius wishes it to be read in Isidore’s *Etymologies*, Book 8—where the printed editions and the old Corbie manuscript have *Cotopites*, and another Corbie manuscript has *Contopites*; or whether this passage should finally be corrected from Jerome’s *Against the Luciferians*, where some printed editions have *Campites* and others *Campates*—we cannot easily say.]

### 3.

As for the succession of bishops extending from Peter himself to Anastasius, who now occupies that same chair, even if some betrayer had slipped into it during that period, this would prejudice neither the Church nor innocent Christians. The Lord, in his providence, said concerning evil overseers: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do; for they say things and do not do them” (Matt. 23:3).

Thus the faithful may possess a sure hope, placed not in a human being but in the Lord, and it will never be scattered by the storm of sacrilegious schism—unlike these people, who have themselves been scattered. They read in the sacred books about the Churches to which the Apostles wrote, yet they have no bishop in any of them.

What could be more perverse and insane than to say “Peace be with you” to readers reading those same Letters, while being separated from the peace of the Churches to which the Letters themselves were written?

## CHAPTER TWO

### 4.

Nevertheless, lest they flatter themselves even concerning the episcopal succession of Constantina—that is, of your city—read to him the Acts held before Munatius Felix, perpetual curator and *flamen*, at that time of your same city.

[Note: We have restored this wording from the copy of the Acts reproduced in Book 3 *Against Cresconius*, chapter 29. The printed editions read “Numacius Felix Flavius, procurator,” and most manuscripts “Munatius,” or “Mannatius Felix Flavius, through a procurator”; the error arose from abbreviations. These Acts were drawn up in 303.]

They were drawn up in the consulship of Diocletian for the eighth time and Maximian for the seventh time, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June. These Acts clearly established that the bishop Paul had handed over the Scriptures, and that Sylvanus was then his subdeacon and had handed them over with him, producing the Lord’s instruments, including those that had been carefully concealed: a silver vessel and a silver lamp. A certain Victor said to him: “You would have died if you had not found them.”

This Sylvanus—a most manifest betrayer—is mentioned by that man in the letter he writes to you as having then been ordained bishop by Secundus of Tigisis, the bishop of the first see.

[Note: The printed editions read, “This Sylvanus … in the letter in which he writes,” and so forth. We have corrected the text with the help of the manuscripts, from which it is clear that the pronoun “this man” refers to the presbyter whose letter is being refuted.]

Let their proud tongue therefore be silent and let them acknowledge their own crimes, lest, in their madness, they speak of those of others.

Read to him also, if he wishes, the ecclesiastical Acts of that same Secundus of Tigisis, held in the house of Urban Donatus, where he handed over confessed betrayers to God the Judge: Donatus of Masculula, Marinus from Aquae Tibilitanae, and Donatus of Calama. Along with these confessed betrayers, he ordained the aforementioned betrayer, Silvanus, as bishop.

[Note: Optatus, Book 1, has “in the house of Urban Carisius,” because, as he says, the basilicas had not yet been restored.]

Read to him the Acts held before Zenophilus, the *consularis*, where a certain deacon, Nundinarius, enraged at Silvanus because he had been excommunicated by him, revealed all these matters before the courts. They were established more clearly than daylight by reliable documents, the answers of witnesses, the reading of the Acts, and numerous letters.

### 5.

There are many other things you may read to him, if he wishes to listen prudently rather than act contentiously: the petitions of the Donatists to Constantine, asking him to send judges from Gaul—bishops—to settle the dispute among the African bishops.

Read to him also the letters of that same emperor, in which he sent bishops to the city of Rome; the Acts in the city of Rome, where the case was heard and examined by the bishops whom he had sent; and other letters in which the emperor declares that they had complained to him about the judgment of their colleagues—that is, the bishops whom he had sent to Rome.

Read also the documents in which he wished other bishops to judge at Arles; where these men appealed from the judgment of those bishops to the same emperor; and where, finally, he himself heard the case between the parties. There he vehemently declares that they had been defeated by Caecilianus’s innocence.

If he wishes, he will hear these things, fall silent, and cease plotting against the truth.

## CHAPTER THREE

### 6.

Although we rely not so much upon these documents as upon the sacred Scriptures, where Christ’s inheritance is promised among all nations to the ends of the earth, these people, separated by their wicked schism, heap accusations upon the chaff of the Lord’s harvest. This chaff must necessarily be tolerated as mixed with the grain until the end, when the whole threshing floor will be winnowed at the final judgment.

It is therefore clear that these accusations, whether true or false, do not concern the Lord’s grain, which ought to grow throughout the entire field—that is, throughout this world—until the end of the age, just as it is not a false angel speaking in this matter of error, but the Lord in the Gospel (Matt. 13:30).

Therefore God justly repaid these wretched Donatists, who cast many false and empty accusations against innocent Christians mixed throughout the world with wicked Christians as with their chaff or weeds. He caused them to condemn the Maximianists of Carthage—their own schismatics, who condemned Primianus; their own baptizers outside Primianus; and their own rebaptizers after Primianus—with their universal council.

Then, after a considerable interval, compelled by Optatus Gildonianus, they received into the dignities of their episcopates certain men from that number, Felicianus of Musti and Praetextatus of Assuri, together with all those whom the condemned men had baptized outside.

[Note: Optatus, whose surname was Gildonianus because he exercised tyranny in Africa together with Count Gildo, was a Donatist bishop and predecessor of Gaudentius of Thamugadi, according to Book 1 of *Against Gaudentius*, chapter 38, section 52. Hence Augustine reproaches the Donatists in Book 2 of *Against the Letter of Parmenianus*, chapter 2, section 4: “They honored and retained in communion Optatus Gildonianus, the ten-year groan of all Africa”—that is, from the year 388 to 398, when, accused of belonging to Gildo’s following, he died in prison, according to Book 2 of *Against the Letters of Petilianus*, chapter 92, section 209—“as a priest and colleague.”]

If they are not polluted by receiving again into their own honor and communicating with those whom, with their own mouths, they condemned as criminals and sacrilegious persons, and whom they compared with those first schismatics whom the earth swallowed alive (Num. 16:31–33), let them finally awaken. Let them consider with what blindness and madness they say that the whole world has been polluted by the unknown crimes of Africans, and that Christ’s inheritance—promised and manifested among all nations—was erased by the sins of Africans through the contagion of communion, while they themselves refuse to appear erased and polluted when they communicate with men whose crimes they judged after learning them.

### 7.

Since the Apostle Paul also says that Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light, it is therefore not surprising if his ministers disguise themselves as ministers of righteousness (2 Cor. 11:13–15).

If this man truly saw an angel announcing error and wishing to separate Christians from Catholic unity, then he himself suffered an angel of Satan disguising himself as an angel of light. But if he is lying and saw nothing of the kind, then he himself is a minister of Satan, disguising himself as a minister of righteousness.

Nevertheless, if he considers all these things and does not wish to be excessively perverse and obstinate, he may be freed from every deception, whether another’s or his own.

For your sake we have approached him without hatred, observing toward him what the Apostle says: “The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward everyone, teachable, patient, correcting those who think differently with humility, so that God may perhaps grant them repentance for the recognition of the truth, and they may recover from the devil’s snares, having been captured by him for his will” (2 Tim. 2:24–26).

If, therefore, we have said anything harshly, let him understand that it was intended not for the bitterness of disagreement, but for the correction that love brings.

May you remain unharmed in Christ, most beloved and honored brother.

## CONCERNING THE TWO LETTERS THAT FOLLOW

(*Book II of the Retractions, chapter 20*)

The two books entitled “To the Inquiries of Januarius” contain many discussions concerning the sacraments—both those which the Church observes universally and those which it observes in particular places, that is, not equally everywhere. It was not possible to mention everything, but the matters inquired about received an adequate answer.

The first of these books is a letter, for it has at its beginning an indication of who writes to whom. Nevertheless, this work is counted among the books because the following work, which does not bear our names, is much longer and treats many more matters.

In the first book, then, concerning the manna I said “because it tasted in each person’s mouth according to his own desire.” I did not recall where this could be proved, except from the Book of Wisdom (Wis. 16:21), which the Jews do not accept as canonical authority. Yet this could have happened to believers, not to those who murmured against God; they would surely not have desired other foods if the manna had tasted to them as they wished.

This work begins as follows: “Concerning the things you asked me.”

# TO THE INQUIRIES OF JANUARIUS, BOOK ONE, OR LETTER LIV

[Note: The following manuscripts and editions were used for correction: bl, bn, cc, cl, f, j, r, vv, two sb manuscripts, two t manuscripts, three vc manuscripts, three v manuscripts, and Am, Bad, Er, and Lov.]

[Note: Formerly numbered 118; the letter formerly numbered 54 is now 153. It was written around the year 400.]

Augustine replies to Januarius, explaining what should be done concerning matters in which the customs of regions or Churches differ, and concerning those in which they agree—for example, the sacraments, feast days, fasting, and the Eucharist.

[Col. 0200] To his beloved son JANUARIUS,

[Note: In the Florentine manuscript it is inscribed “To Januarius the Notary.” One of the Sorbonne manuscripts also supports this.]

AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

## CHAPTER ONE

### 1.

Concerning the things you asked me, I would have preferred first to know what you yourself would answer if questioned. In that way, by approving or correcting your answers, I could respond much more briefly, and could very easily either confirm or correct you.

[Note: Several manuscripts read “what you would have answered”; shortly afterward, “I would confirm or correct.”]

That is what I would have preferred, as I said. Nevertheless, since I am replying now, I preferred to make the discussion longer rather than delay it.

First, then, I want you to hold firmly to the central point of this discussion: our Lord Jesus Christ, as he himself speaks in the Gospel, has subjected us to his gentle yoke and light burden (Matt. 11:30). Therefore he has bound together the fellowship of the new people by very few sacraments, easy to observe, and most excellent in their significance. Such are baptism consecrated in the name of the Trinity, communion in his body and blood, and whatever else is commended in the canonical Scriptures—apart from those observances which, in keeping with the disposition of the hearts of that people and with the prophetic period, burdened the former people’s servitude, and which are also read in the five books of Moses.

As for those practices that we preserve not as written but as handed down, and that are observed throughout the whole world, it is to be understood that they were commended and established for retention either by the Apostles themselves or by plenary councils, whose authority in the Church is most salutary. Such practices include the annual celebration of the Lord’s passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, the coming of the Holy Spirit from heaven, and whatever other such observance is found to be maintained by the universal Church, wherever it extends.

## CHAPTER TWO

### 2.

Other practices, however, vary according to places and regions of the world. For example, some fast on Saturday and others do not; some communicate daily in the Lord’s body and blood, while others receive it on appointed days. In some places no day is omitted on which it is not offered; elsewhere it is offered only on Saturday and Sunday; elsewhere only on Sunday.

Whatever other practices of this kind may be observed, this entire class of matters has free observance. No discipline is better for a serious and prudent Christian in these things than to act in the manner in which he sees the Church act wherever he happens to arrive.

For whatever is not shown to be contrary either to the faith or to good morals is to be regarded as indifferent, and, for the sake of the fellowship of those among whom one lives, is to be observed.

[Note: So most manuscripts. The printed editions read, “whatever is not enjoined contrary to good morals.”]

### 3.

I believe you once heard me say this, but I shall mention it again now. My mother, having followed me to Milan, found that the Church there did not fast on Saturday. She began to be disturbed and uncertain about what she should do. Since I paid no attention to such matters, I nevertheless consulted the blessed Ambrose, of revered memory, on her behalf.

He replied that he could teach me nothing except what he himself did, because if he knew anything better, he would observe that instead. When I supposed that, without giving any reason, he wished to instruct us by his authority alone not to fast on Saturday, he continued and said to me: “When I am in Rome, I fast on Saturday; when I am here, I do not fast.”

“So you too,” he said, “should observe the custom of whatever Church you happen to enter, if you do not wish to be a cause of scandal to anyone, nor anyone to you.”

When I reported this to my mother, she readily accepted it. But as I reflected again and again upon this opinion, I always held it as though I had received it from a heavenly oracle.

For I have often felt sorrow and groaned when I saw many disturbances among the weak arise through the contentious obstinacy or superstitious timidity of certain brothers. In matters of this kind—which cannot be brought to a definite conclusion either by the authority of sacred Scripture, the tradition of the universal Church, or the usefulness of correcting one’s life—they raise such quarrelsome questions, merely because some sort of reasoning occurs to the person thinking, or because he has been accustomed to do things that way in his own country, or because he saw it practiced elsewhere and, the farther he has traveled from his own people, supposes himself to have become wiser—

[Note: Correctly as found in several manuscripts: “or because he saw it there, where, the farther his journey had taken him from his own people, he supposed himself to have become wiser.”]

They raise such contentious questions that, unless others do what they themselves do, they consider nothing right.

## CHAPTER THREE
4. Someone may say that the Eucharist should not be received every day. You ask why. “Because,” he says, “one ought to choose the days on which a person lives more purely and more continently [Note: Lov. has *vivat* (‘may live’), and shortly afterward *dignius accedat* (‘may approach more worthily’). The older editions and manuscripts, however, prefer our reading.], so that he may approach so great a Sacrament worthily: ‘For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself’ (1 Cor. 11:29).

“Another, on the contrary, says: ‘No; if the wound of sin and the force of the illness are so great that such medicines must be deferred, each person should, by the authority of the bishop, be removed from the altar to do penance, and by that same authority be reconciled. For this is to receive unworthily: to receive at a time when one ought to be doing penance—not to withdraw from communion or return to it at one’s own discretion, whenever one pleases. But if the sins are not so great that anyone ought to be judged excommunicated [Note: Correctly so in several manuscripts: ‘that any person should be judged excommunicated.’], he ought not to separate himself from the daily medicine of the Lord’s body.’

Perhaps someone who urges that they remain especially in the peace of Christ settles the dispute between them more rightly; but let each person do what he devoutly believes ought to be done according to his faith. Neither of them dishonors the body and blood of the Lord; rather, in their rivalry they strive to honor the most salutary Sacrament.

For Zacchaeus and that centurion did not quarrel with one another, nor did either of them set himself above the other, when one joyfully received the Lord into his house (Luke 19:6), while the other said, ‘I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof’ (Matt. 8:8): both honoring the Savior in different and seemingly contrary ways; both miserable because of their sins, both obtaining mercy.

This comparison is also supported by the fact that, among the first people, the manna tasted in each person’s mouth according to his own desire [Note: See *Retractationes* II.20.]. So too, in the heart of each Christian, that Sacrament by which the world has been subjected [Col. 0202] has its own savor [Note: Thus in four manuscripts. The printed editions have: ‘so in the mouth of every Christian, that sacrament—how it is to be received must be considered.’ Bad. and Am. have: ‘by which he is to be considered subjected.’ But in all the manuscripts, as well as in the Vatican and Gallican witnesses, the reading is: ‘by which the world has been subjected.’ This reading is confirmed by the commonly transmitted text of Bede on 1 Corinthians 11.].

For one, by honoring it, dares not receive it every day; the other, by honoring it, dares not omit it on any day. This food desires only not to be despised, just as the manna did not desire to become loathsome. For this reason the Apostle says that it was received unworthily by those who did not distinguish it from other foods by the singular veneration that is due to it. Immediately after saying, ‘He eats and drinks judgment upon himself,’ he added, ‘not discerning the body of the Lord’ (1 Cor. 11:29). This becomes sufficiently clear throughout that entire passage in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, if it is carefully considered.

## CHAPTER IV

5.
