Suppose a traveler is in a place where people persist in observing Lent and neither bathe nor relax their fast on Thursday [Note: Lov. has *levant* (‘raise’), but Bad., Am., Er., and the manuscripts more correctly have *lavant* (‘bathe’)]. “I shall not fast today,” he says. The reason is sought. “Because,” he says, “this is not done in my country.” What else is he attempting but to prefer his own custom to another person’s custom?

He will not recite this to me from the Book of God, nor will he contend in a full voice throughout the universal Church, wherever it is spread, nor will he demonstrate that the other acts against the faith while he acts according to the faith, proving either that the other violates the best customs or that he himself preserves them. By quarreling over a superfluous question, they are certainly violating their own tranquility and peace.

Nevertheless, in matters of this kind I would prefer that the one, in the other’s country, and the other, in the first one’s country, should not recoil from what the rest do. But if someone, while traveling in a foreign country where the people of God are more numerous, more frequent, and more fervent, saw, for example, that the Eucharist was offered twice on Thursday of the final week of Lent, both in the morning and in the evening, and then, on returning to his own country where the custom is to offer it at the end of the day, were to insist that this was done wrongly and unlawfully because he had seen it done differently elsewhere, that is a childish attitude: it must be avoided in ourselves, tolerated in others, and corrected among our own people [Note: Am., Er., and four manuscripts have: ‘tolerated and corrected among our own people.’ Bad. and one of the royal manuscripts have: ‘removed and corrected among our own people.’].

## CHAPTER V

6. Consider, then, which of these three categories contains your first question, which you set out in your memorandum. You ask in these words:

“What ought to be done on Thursday of the final week of Lent? Should the Eucharist be offered in the morning and again after supper, because of what was said, ‘Likewise after supper’ (Luke 22:20)? Or should one fast and offer it only after supper? Or should one fast and, after the offering, eat supper, as we usually do?”

To this I reply as follows. If the authority of divine Scripture prescribes which of these things is to be done, there can be no doubt that we ought to do what we read, so that the question is no longer how it should be done, but how the Sacrament should be understood. Likewise, if the whole Church throughout the world frequently does one of these things, it is the height of insolent madness to dispute whether it ought to be done in that way.

But neither of these applies to what you ask. It remains, therefore, that this belongs to the third category, which varies according to places and regions. Let each person do what he finds practiced in the Church to which he comes. Nothing is done on either side contrary to the faith, or contrary to customs that are better here or there. For these are the reasons—either faith or customs—for which something wrongly done ought to be corrected, or something not previously done ought to be instituted.

A change of custom, even when it is beneficial, disturbs people by its novelty. Consequently, what is not useful is harmful as well as unprofitably disturbing.

7. One should not therefore suppose that it was instituted in many places that the Eucharist should be offered after the meal on that day because it is written: “Likewise the cup after supper,” and so forth. He could have called the meal itself the supper at which they had already received the body, so that afterward they received the cup. For elsewhere the Apostle says: “When you come together, it is not to eat the Lord’s supper” (1 Cor. 11:20), calling this very reception of the Eucharist the Lord’s supper.

## CHAPTER VI

What may have moved people more was the question whether on that day they should offer or receive the Eucharist after already eating, since the Gospel says: “While they were eating, Jesus took bread and blessed it,” after having also said above: “When evening had come, he was reclining with the twelve; and while they were eating he said, ‘One of you will betray me’” (Matt. 26:20–21, 26). He afterward gave them the Sacrament. It is plainly evident when the disciples first received the body and blood of the Lord: they did not receive them fasting.

8. Should the universal Church therefore be accused because the Eucharist is always received by those who are fasting? It pleased the Holy Spirit that, in honor of so great a Sacrament, the Lord’s body should first enter the Christian’s mouth before any other food [Note: Thus Lov. and the manuscripts. Bad., Am., and Er. have: ‘before external foods.’]; this is why the custom is observed throughout the world.

Nor, because the Lord gave it after food, ought brothers who have eaten or supped to assemble in order to receive that Sacrament, or, as those whom the Apostle rebukes and corrects were doing, to mix this sacred meal with their own tables. The Savior, in order to impress more forcefully the greatness of that mystery, wished to fix this final act more deeply in the hearts and memory of the disciples, from whom he was about to depart for his passion.

For this reason he did not prescribe in what order it should afterward be received, reserving this matter for the Apostles, through whom he was going to organize the Churches. If he had instructed them always to receive it after other food, I believe that no one would have changed that custom. But when the Apostle speaks of this Sacrament, he says:

“Therefore, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another. If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, so that you may not come together for judgment.” Immediately he adds: “I shall arrange the other matters when I come” (1 Cor. 11:20, 34).

From this it is understood—for it would have been too much to indicate in the Epistle the entire order of observance that the universal Church throughout the world follows—that what is not varied by any diversity of customs was ordered by the Apostle himself.

## CHAPTER VII

[Col. 0204]

9. Nevertheless, a certain plausible reason has pleased some people: that on one fixed day each year, the day on which the Lord gave that supper, the body and blood of the Lord may, as a more solemn commemoration, be offered and received after food.

I think it more proper for this to take place at an hour when even someone who has fasted may, after the meal that takes place at the ninth hour [Note: Seven manuscripts have *ante* (‘before’), while others have *post* (‘after’).], still be able to arrive for the offering. Accordingly, we compel no one to eat before that Lord’s supper [Note: Several manuscripts have: ‘that Lord’s supper compels no one to eat.’ Bad., Am., and Er. have: ‘we compel no one to eat at that Lord’s supper.’], but neither do we dare contradict anyone.

I do not think, however, that this custom was instituted except because most people, and nearly everyone in many places, have been accustomed to bathe on that day. Since some also observe a fast, the Eucharist is offered in the morning for those who eat, because they cannot endure both fasting and bathing; but in the evening it is offered for those who fast.

10. If you ask why the custom of bathing arose, nothing more plausible occurs to me, as I consider the matter, than that the bodies of those who were to be baptized had become dirty through the observance of Lent and would have been brought to the font with an offensive appearance unless they bathed on some day.

This day was chosen for that purpose because the Lord’s supper is celebrated annually on it. Since this bathing was permitted to those who were about to receive Baptism, many wished to bathe with them and relax their fast.

Having discussed these matters as best I could, I urge you to observe as far as you can what I said earlier, as befits a prudent and peaceable son of the Church. The other matters about which you asked I shall, if the Lord wills, resolve at another time.

# SECOND BOOK TO JANUARY’S QUESTIONS, OR LETTER 55

[Note: Elsewhere numbered 119; the letter that was 55 is now 117. It was written somewhat later than the preceding letter.]

On the rites of the Church: those which it is wrong to neglect, and those which ought to be abolished if this can be done without greater inconvenience. The mystery of the Sabbath, and so forth. The fast of Lent. The washing of the feet. Various customs. The singing of the Church, and so forth.

## CHAPTER I

1. After reading your letter, in which you reminded me that I ought to discharge my obligation by disentangling the remaining questions that you had asked long ago, I could not bear to delay any longer your most welcome and dear desire for study. Although I was surrounded by the heaps of my occupations, I made this my chief concern, so that I might answer what you had asked.

I do not wish to discuss your letter at greater length, lest this very discussion prevent me from at last rendering what I owe.

2. You ask why the anniversary of the celebration of the Lord’s passion does not return on the same day of the year as the day on which his birth is commemorated. You then add that, if this is because of the Sabbath and the moon, what the observance of the Sabbath and the moon signifies in this matter.

First, you ought to know [Col. 0205] that the Lord’s Nativity is not celebrated as a sacrament, but only recalled as the fact that he was born. Consequently, nothing was necessary except to mark with festive devotion the returning day of the year on which the event itself occurred.

A sacrament, however, is present in a celebration when the commemoration of an event is conducted in such a way that something is also understood to be signified, something that must be received in holiness. Accordingly, we celebrate Easter not merely by recalling what happened—that Christ died and rose again—but also by not omitting the other matters connected with these events that belong to the sacramental meaning [Note: The Floriacensis manuscript has: ‘so that we do not fail to turn it toward the sacred meaning.’].

For, as the Apostle says, “He died for our sins and rose for our justification” (Rom. 4:25): a kind of passage from death to life was consecrated in the Lord’s passion and resurrection.

Even the very name *Pascha*, those who know both languages say, is not Greek, as it is commonly thought [Note: This was the view of Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* IV.33; Tertullian, *Against the Jews* 10; Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* IV.26; and Ambrose, *On the Mystical Passover*, chapter 1.]. It is Hebrew. For it was not named from the passion—since in Greek πάσχειν (*paschein*) means “to suffer”—but, as I have said, from the fact that one passes from death to life; in the Hebrew language the word is said to mean “passage,” according to those who understand the matter.

The Lord himself wished to allude to this when he said: “Whoever believes in me will pass from death to life” (John 5:24) [Note: The Floriacensis manuscript has *transit* (‘passes’), perhaps in place of *transiit* (‘has passed’), as in the Vulgate and the Greek text, *metabébēken*.].

The same evangelist is understood to have wished especially to express this when, speaking of the Lord’s celebration of Passover with his disciples, at which he gave them the mystical supper, he says: “When Jesus saw that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father” (John 13:1).

Thus the passage from this mortal life to another, immortal life—that is, from death to life—is commended in the passion and resurrection of the Lord.

## CHAPTER II

3. This passage is now enacted by us through faith, which brings us forgiveness of sins and the hope of eternal life when we love God and our neighbor, because “faith works through love” (Gal. 5:6), and “the righteous person lives by faith” (Hab. 2:4).

“Hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. 8:24).

According to this faith, hope, and love, through which we have begun to exist under grace, we have already died with Christ and been buried with him through baptism into death (Col. 3), as the Apostle says: “Our old self was crucified together with him,” and “we rose with him” (Rom. 6:6). For he raised us together and made us sit together in the heavenly places.

Hence also comes the exhortation:

“If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on things above, not on things on earth.”

But what follows—“For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:1–4) [Col. 0206]—sufficiently indicates what is meant: our passage now from death to life, which takes place through faith, is completed in hope of the resurrection and glory that will come at the end, when this corruptible thing—that is, this flesh in which we now groan—puts on incorruption, and this mortal thing puts on immortality (1 Cor. 15:53).

For now we do indeed possess the first fruits of the Spirit through faith, but we still groan within ourselves, awaiting adoption, the redemption of our body; “for by hope we were saved.” While we are in this hope, “the body is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness.”

But see what follows:

“If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. 8:23–24, 10–11).

This, then, is what the whole Church, found on pilgrimage amid mortality, awaits at the end of the age: what was prefigured in the body of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is “the firstborn from the dead,” because his body, of which he is the head, is nothing other than the Church (Col. 1:18).

## CHAPTER III

4. Some people, attending to the words that the Apostle repeatedly says—that we have died with Christ and risen with him—without understanding the sense in which these things are said, have thought that the resurrection has already taken place and that no further resurrection should be expected at the end of time:

“Among them,” he says, “are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have deviated from the truth by saying that the resurrection has already taken place, and they have overturned the faith of some” (2 Tim. 2:17).

The same Apostle condemns and detests those people, although he himself says that we have risen with Christ. Why, then, except because he says that this has happened in us through faith, hope, and love, according to the first fruits of the Spirit?

But since “hope that is seen is not hope,” and therefore “if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience,” it necessarily remains that the redemption of our body is still future. Awaiting it, we groan within ourselves. Hence also the saying: “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Rom. 12:12).

5. This renewal of our life, then, is a kind of passage from death to life. It begins through faith, so that we may rejoice in hope and be patient in tribulation, while our outward self is still being corrupted but our inward self is renewed day by day (2 Cor. 4:16).

Because of this very beginning of the new life, because of the new person whom we are commanded to put on [Note: Three manuscripts have: ‘Because of this very beginning …’; others continue: ‘Because of the beginning of the new life itself, we are commanded to put on the new person.’] and to put off the old (Col. 3:9–10), “purging out the old leaven so that we may be a new dough, because Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5:7), the first month among the months of the year has been assigned to this celebration.

It is itself called the month of new things (Exod. 23:15). Since the third period has now appeared in the whole span of the world’s history, the Lord’s resurrection lasts three days.

The first period was before the Law, the second under the Law, and the third under Grace, where the manifestation has now appeared of the mystery previously hidden in prophetic riddles.

This is also signified in the lunar number. Since the number seven commonly appears in Scripture as a mystical sign of a certain perfection, Easter is celebrated in the third week of the moon, on a day falling between the fourteenth and the twenty-first.

## CHAPTER IV

6. There is another Sacrament there as well. If it is obscure to you because you are less learned in such investigations, do not be distressed; nor should you think me better because I learned these things in my childhood studies. “Let the one who boasts,” he says, “boast in this: that he knows and understands that I am the Lord” (Jer. 9:24).

Some students of such matters therefore investigated many things concerning numbers [Note: Thus the more authoritative manuscripts. Lov. has: ‘students of such matters investigated many things concerning gifts,’ and so forth.] and the movements of the stars. Those who examined these matters more subtly inferred the moon’s waxing and waning from the turning of its sphere—not because any part of its substance is added to it when it grows or removed when it diminishes, as the delirious ignorance of the Manichaeans maintains [Note: The printed editions have: ‘as the delusion of the ignorant Manichaeans maintains.’ Four manuscripts have: ‘as the ignorance of the Manichaeans, in its delirium, maintains.’ Two others have: ‘delirious ignorance.’].

They say that the moon is filled as a ship is filled, with that part of God which has escaped and which, mixed with the powers of darkness and polluted by their filth, they do not hesitate to believe and utter with sacrilegious heart and mouth.

They therefore say that the moon is filled when that same part of God, cleansed with great labor from its pollution, flees from the whole world and all its sewers and is returned to the grieving God while awaiting its return. It is filled for half the month and poured back into the sun during the other half, as into another ship.

Yet amid these blasphemies, which must be anathematized, they have never been able to devise any explanation for why the moon, whether beginning to shine or ceasing, glows with horn-shaped light, or why it begins to diminish from the middle of the month and does not reach fullness before being poured back [Note: Seven manuscripts have: ‘reach fullness before being brought to completion.’].

7. Those, however, who investigated these matters by fixed calculations, so that they could predict not only why eclipses of the sun and moon occur but also when they would occur long beforehand, fixing them by canonical calculations at determined intervals of time and committing them to writing—so that those who now read and understand these writings still predict them—such people predicted them, and the eclipses occur neither otherwise nor at other times than they predicted.

The sacred Scripture says that such people are not to be excused: “For if they had the power to know so much that they could investigate the age of the world, why did they not more easily find its Lord, whom they could have discovered with humble devotion?” (Wis. 13:9).

From the horns of the moon that face away from the sun, whether during its waxing or waning, they inferred either that the moon is illuminated by the sun and that, the farther it recedes from the sun, the more it receives the sun’s rays on that side which is turned toward the earth; but that, after the middle of the month, the closer it approaches the sun from the other semicircle, the more it is illuminated on its upper side and the less able to receive rays on the side it turns toward the earth, and therefore appears to diminish.

Or, if it possesses its own light, they inferred that it has that light on one side of its hemisphere [Col. 0208]. As it gradually recedes from the sun, it reveals that side little by little to the earth [Note: Seven manuscripts have: ‘as it receded from the sun … until it displayed the whole of it.’], until it displays the whole, seeming to show an increase—not because anything lacking is added, but because what was already present is revealed. Then it gradually conceals what had been visible, and for that reason appears to diminish.

Whichever of these two explanations is correct, this at least is clear and easily recognized by anyone who pays attention: the moon does not increase before our eyes except by receding from the sun, nor does it diminish except by approaching the sun from the other side.

## CHAPTER V

8. Now consider what is read in Proverbs: “The wise person remains like the sun, but the fool changes like the moon” (Sir. 27:12).

Who is the wise person who remains except that sun of righteousness of whom it is said, “The sun of righteousness has risen for me,” and concerning whom the wicked, lamenting that he did not rise for them on the last day, will say: “The light of righteousness did not shine for us, and the sun [Note: Lov. has: ‘and the sun of righteousness did not rise,’ and so forth. The word ‘righteousness’ is absent from the manuscripts and older editions, as well as from the Greek version of the Septuagint, followed by Ambrose, Sermons 3 and 16, and Gregory, *Moralia* XXXIV.6, and others. The Vulgate has: ‘the sun of understanding.’] did not rise for us” (Wis. 5:6)?

God causes this visible sun to rise on the eyes of the flesh over the good and the evil; he also causes rain to fall on the just and the unjust (Matt. 5:45). Appropriate likenesses are often drawn from visible things to invisible things.

Who, then, is the fool who changes like the moon except Adam, in whom all have sinned? The human soul, when it withdraws from the sun of righteousness—that is, from the inward contemplation of unchanging truth—turns all its powers outward and becomes increasingly darkened in its inner and higher parts.

But when it begins to return to that unchanging wisdom, the more closely it approaches it in devout affection, the more the outward self is corrupted, while the inward self is renewed day by day. All that light of understanding which had been directed toward lower things is turned toward higher things and is, as it were, taken away from earthly matters, so that it may die more and more to this age and its life may be hidden with Christ in God.

9. It therefore changes for the worse as it advances outward and casts its innermost things aside in its life. This appears better to the earth—that is, to those who set their minds on earthly things—when “the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the one who practices iniquity is blessed” (Ps. 9:3).

But it changes for the better when it gradually turns its attention and glory away from earthly things that appear in this age and directs them toward higher and inward things [Note: Thus the manuscripts, joined by Bad. and Am. Lov. and Er. have: ‘and turns it from lower things toward higher things.’]. This appears worse to the earth—that is, to those who set their minds on earthly things.

Hence those wicked people, finally practicing fruitless repentance, will say among many other things:

“These are the ones whom we once held up to ridicule and made an object of reproach; we foolishly regarded their way of life as madness” (Wis. 5:3–4).

Accordingly, the Holy Spirit, drawing a likeness from visible to invisible things and from bodily to spiritual matters, wished that the passage from one life to another—the event called Passover—should be observed from the fourteenth day of the moon. This was so that, not only because of the third period mentioned above, since the third week begins from that point, but also because of the very turning from outward things to inward things, a likeness might be drawn from the moon.

It extends to the twenty-first day because of the number seven itself, by which the signification of the whole is often represented and which is also assigned to the Church because it resembles the whole.

## CHAPTER VI

10. For this reason the apostle John writes in the Apocalypse to seven Churches. The Church, while it remains in this mortality of the flesh, is signified in Scripture by the name of the moon because of its very mutability.

Hence the saying: “They have prepared their arrows in the quiver, to shoot at the upright in heart in the dark moon” (Ps. 10:3, according to the Septuagint).

Before what the Apostle says comes to pass—“When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:4)—the Church appears dark during the time of her pilgrimage, groaning amid many iniquities. At that time the plots of deceptive seducers must be feared; these he wished to be understood by the name of arrows.

Elsewhere, because of the most faithful messengers of truth whom the Church continually brings forth everywhere, it is said: “The moon is a faithful witness in heaven” (Ps. 88:38).

And when the Psalmist was singing of the Lord’s kingdom, he said: “In his days righteousness shall rise, and abundance of peace, until the moon is destroyed” (Ps. 71:7)—that is, abundance of peace will increase until it consumes all the mutability of mortality.

Then the last enemy, death, will be destroyed, and whatever resists us because of the weakness of the flesh, on account of which we do not yet possess perfect peace, will be entirely consumed when this corruptible thing has put on incorruption and this mortal thing has put on immortality (1 Cor. 15:26, 53–54).

For this reason also the walls of that city called Jericho—which is said to be interpreted as “Moon” in the Hebrew language—fell when the Ark of the Testament had been carried around them for the seventh circuit (Josh. 6:20).

What else does the proclamation of the kingdom of heaven now accomplish, which the circling of the Ark signified, except that all the fortifications of mortal life—that is, every hope of this age that resists hope of the age to come—should be destroyed through free will by the sevenfold gift of the Holy Spirit?

For this reason, when the Ark went around them, those walls did not fall through a violent assault but by themselves.

There are also other testimonies of Scripture that, by mentioning the moon, impress upon us the signification of the Church. In this mortality it makes its pilgrimage away from that Jerusalem whose citizens are the holy angels, amid hardships and labors.

11. Foolish people who refuse to be changed for the better should not therefore think that those heavenly lights are to be worshiped merely because a likeness is sometimes drawn from them to represent divine mysteries. A likeness is drawn from every creature.

Nor should we therefore fall under the sentence of condemnation pronounced by the Apostle’s mouth against certain people who “worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever” (Rom. 1:25).

For just as we do not worship cattle, although Christ is called both a lamb (John 1:29) and a calf (Ezek. 43:19); nor a wild beast, because he is called the lion of the tribe of Judah (Rev. 5:5); nor a stone, because Christ was the rock (1 Cor. 10:4); nor Mount Zion, because the Church is represented in it (1 Pet. 2:4); so neither do we worship the sun or the moon, although figures of the sacraments are taken from this heavenly creature, as from many earthly creatures, for mystical instruction.

## CHAPTER VII

12. The ravings of the astrologers must therefore be mocked with abhorrence. When we have opposed their empty theories—by which they rush human beings into the error into which they themselves first rushed—they think themselves clever when they say to us: “Why do you also celebrate Easter according to the calculation of the sun and the moon?”

They speak as though we were criticizing the orders of the stars or the alternations of the seasons that were established by the supreme and good God, rather than their perversity, which abuses things created with the greatest wisdom for the most foolish opinions [Note: Ten manuscripts have: ‘for the most vain opinions of their folly.’].

If an astrologer is going to object that we draw likenesses from the stars and the lights of heaven for the mystical representation of the sacraments, let the diviners object as well, so that it may not be said to us, “Be innocent as doves.” Let the Marsians object as well, so that it may not be said to us, “Be shrewd as serpents” (Matt. 10:16). Let the actors object, so that we may not mention the lyre in the Psalms.

Or, because signs of likeness are taken from these things for the mysteries of the word of God [Note: The editions have: ‘for the mysteries of the words of God.’ Twelve manuscripts have: ‘of the word of God.’], let them say, if they please, that we are practicing divination, preparing poisons, or pursuing theatrical lusts. To say this would be the height of madness.

13. We do not therefore infer the outcomes of our actions from the sun and moon, or from the yearly and monthly seasons, lest, striking against the rocks of miserable servitude amid the most dangerous storms of human life, we suffer shipwreck with respect to free will.

Rather, with deeply religious devotion we receive suitable likenesses for the sacred signification of a matter, just as we do from the rest of creation: from winds, sea, earth, birds, fish, cattle, trees, and human beings—using them abundantly in speech, but, in the celebration of the Sacraments, now very sparingly in Christian freedom; for example, from water, grain, wine, and oil.

Under the servitude of the former people, many things were also commanded to be celebrated which are handed down to us only for understanding.

We do not therefore observe days, years, months, and seasons, lest we hear the Apostle say: “I fear that perhaps I have labored over you in vain” (Gal. 4:11) [Note: The editions have: ‘over you’ or ‘in you’ (*in vobis*). The manuscripts have *in vos* (‘toward you’), corresponding to the Greek text, *eis humas*.].

He condemns those who say: “I will not travel today because it is an unlucky day,” or “because the moon is in such a position”; or, “I will travel so that things may turn out favorably because the stars are arranged in this way.”

They say: “I will not conduct business this month because that star is governing my month”; or, “I will conduct business because it has taken charge of the month”; or, “I will not plant a vineyard this year because it is a leap year.”

No wise person, however, should think that those who observe the seasons are to be reproved when they say: “I will not travel today because a storm has arisen”; or, “I will not sail because the remnants of winter are still present”; or, “It is time to sow because the earth has been filled with autumn rains.”

The same applies if certain other natural effects concerning the movement of the air and the fluids, by which the qualities of the seasons vary, have been observed in the most orderly movement of the stars. Of these it was said when they were created: “Let them be for signs and seasons and days and years” (Gen. 1:14).

If figures of likeness are drawn not only from heaven and the stars but also from lower creation for the ordering of the sacraments, this is a certain eloquence of salutary teaching, adapted to move the affections of learners: from visible things to invisible, from bodily things to spiritual, and from temporal things to eternal.

## CHAPTER VIII

14. Nor does any one of us attend to the fact that, at the time when we celebrate Easter, the sun is in Aries, as they call a certain region of the stars where the sun is in fact found during the month of new things.

But whether they wish to call that region Aries or something else, we have learned from the holy Scriptures that God created all the stars and arranged them in whatever heavenly positions he wished. Let them divide the heavens, distinguished and ordered by stars, into whatever regions they please and mark them with whatever names they please. Wherever the sun happens to be during the month of new things, this celebration will find it there, because of the sacramental likeness of renewed life, which we have discussed sufficiently above.

And if that region of the stars could also be called Aries because of some correspondence of figure, divine discourse would not hesitate to draw from such a thing a sacramental likeness, just as it does from other creatures, both heavenly and earthly.

It has done so with Orion and the Pleiades, with Mount Sinai and Mount Zion, with the rivers called Gihon, Pishon, Tigris, and Euphrates, and with the river Jordan itself, so often mentioned and honored [Note: The editions and several manuscripts have *nobilitato* (‘honored’); seven others have *nominato* (‘mentioned’).] in the holy mysteries. From these it has drawn mystical likenesses of things to be represented figuratively.

15. But who does not understand how great the difference is between observing the stars for purposes suited to atmospheric conditions, as farmers and sailors do; or for marking the regions of the world and directing one’s course from one place to another, as ship pilots do, and as those do who travel through sandy deserts into the interior regions of the south without any definite or straight path; or when some mention of the stars is made to signify figuratively something useful in teaching—how great, then, is the difference between these uses and the vanities of people who observe the stars for the sake of investigating not atmospheric conditions, not routes through regions, not merely the number of seasons, and not spiritual likenesses, but as though the events of things were already fixed by fate? Who could fail to understand this?

## CHAPTER IX
16. But from this point let us see why, even when Easter is celebrated, it is also observed that the Sabbath should occur [within it]; for this is proper to the Christian religion. The Jews observe only the month of new produce and the moon from the fourteenth through the twenty-first day. But because that Passover of theirs on which the Lord suffered occurred in such a way that the day of the Sabbath fell between his death and resurrection, our fathers judged that this should be added, so that our festival might also be distinguished from the festival of the Jews. And it ought to be believed that this was not done without reason by him who exists before the times, through whom the times were made, and who came in the fullness of time, who had the power to lay down his life and to take it up again, and therefore awaited not a fated but an opportune hour for the sacrament he had undertaken to commend, when he said, “My hour has not yet come” (John 2:4); thus, at the annual celebration of his Passion, this arrangement was to be preserved by posterity.

[Note: [Col. 0212] The editions read: “And because sometimes Easter … that it might be distinguished. That this was not done without reason … so that at the annual celebration …” Here we have preferred the reading of the manuscripts, which more clearly expresses the twofold reason why we preserve this arrangement in the celebration of Easter, namely, that the Sabbath should fall between the solemnity of the Lord’s Passion and resurrection: first, so that our festival might thereby be distinguished from the festival of the Jews; second, because it was not without reason that the Lord arranged for the Sabbath day to fall between his death and resurrection.]

17. For what we now do in faith and hope, as I said above, and toward which we strive through love, is a kind of rest from every labor and from all troubles, holy and everlasting. From this life we pass into it, and our Lord Jesus Christ deigned to foreshadow and consecrate it by his Passion. In that rest there is not sluggish idleness, but a certain ineffable tranquility of unburdened activity. For at the end we rest from the works of this life in such a way that we rejoice in the activity of the other life. But because that activity is exercised in the praise of God, without labor of the limbs and without the anguish of cares, we do not pass into it through rest in such a way that labor succeeds rest—that is, activity does not begin in such a way that rest ceases. We do not return to labors and cares; rather, in the activity there remains what belongs to rest: neither laboring in our work nor wavering in our thought.

Because, therefore, through rest we return to the first life from which the soul fell into sin, rest is signified by the Sabbath. That first life, which is restored to those returning from pilgrimage and receiving the first robe, is signified by the first day of the week, which we call the Lord’s Day. Read the seven days in Genesis: you will find the seventh without evening, because it signifies rest without end. The first life, therefore, was not everlasting for the sinner; but the final rest is everlasting. Accordingly, the eighth day too will possess everlasting blessedness, because that rest, which is eternal, is received by the eighth day, not extinguished by it—for otherwise it would not be eternal. Thus the eighth will be the first in such a way that the first life is not taken away but restored as eternal.

CHAPTER X

18. Nevertheless, the Sabbath was commended to the former people to be celebrated bodily in idleness [Note: [Col. 0212] Am. Bad. Er.: “to be celebrated temporarily in bodily idleness”], so that it might be a figure of sanctification in the rest of the Holy Spirit. For nowhere do we read in Genesis of sanctification on all the preceding days; only of the Sabbath is it said: “And God sanctified the seventh day” (Gen. 2:3). Both pious and wicked souls love rest, but most do not know by what route they may reach what they love. Even bodies themselves seek nothing through their own weights except what souls seek through their loves [Note: [Col. 0212] Am. Bad. Er.: “except to rest from their own movements”]. For just as a body strives by its weight, whether downward or upward, until, arriving at the place toward which it strives, it comes to rest—for the weight of oil, if released in air, strives downward, but beneath water upward—so souls strive toward what they love in order that, by reaching it, they may rest.

Many things delight us through the body, but there is in them neither eternal nor even lasting rest; and therefore they rather defile the soul and weigh it down, hindering its pure weight by which it is borne toward higher things. When the soul delights in itself, it is not yet delighting in an unchangeable reality; and therefore it is still proud, because it regards itself as the highest thing, although God is higher. Nor is it left unpunished in such sin, because “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6). But when it delights in God, there it finds true, certain, eternal rest—the rest it was seeking and could not find in other things. Therefore it is admonished in the Psalm: “Delight in the Lord, and he will give you the desires of your heart” (Ps. 36:4).

19. Since, therefore, “the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5), sanctification is commemorated on the seventh day, where rest is commended. But since we cannot work well unless aided by his gift, as the Apostle says, “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:13), nor can we rest after all the good works we perform in this life unless, by his gift, we have been sanctified and perfected for eternity [Note: [Col. 0213] The Floriac manuscript reads: “and have reached the perfected Sabbath”; hence, “therefore …”], therefore it is said of God himself that, when he had made all his works very good, “on the seventh day he rested from all his works that he had made” (Gen. 1:31; 2:2). For he signified the future rest that he would give us human beings after our good works. Just as, when we work well, he is said to work in us, by whose gift we work well, so, when we rest, he is said to rest, by whose gift we rest.

CHAPTER XI

20. Hence it is that, among the first three commandments of the Decalogue that pertain to God—for the remaining seven pertain to one’s neighbor, that is, to the human being, since “the whole law depends on” two commandments (Matt. 22:40)—the third is placed there concerning the observance of the Sabbath.

Thus, in the first commandment we are to understand the Father, where it is forbidden to worship any likeness of God made by human art—not because God does not have an image, but because no image of him ought to be worshiped except that which is what he himself is; and even that image not in his place, but together with him. And because creation is changeable, and therefore it is said that “every creature has been subjected to vanity” (Rom. 8:20), since the nature of the whole universe is displayed even in a part of it, lest anyone should think that the Son of God, the Word through whom all things were made, is a creature, the next commandment follows: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain” (Exod. 20:7; Deut. 5:11).

The Holy Spirit, in whom that rest is granted to us which we love everywhere but do not find unless we love God, is insinuated in the third commandment of the Law, written concerning the observance of the Sabbath. For God sanctified the seventh day on which he rested, and his love is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5). This commandment is not given so that we should suppose ourselves to rest already in this life, but so that everything we do well may have no other aim than the future, everlasting rest. Remember especially what I have already mentioned above: “We have been saved in hope; but hope that is seen is not hope” (Rom. 8:24).

[Note: [Col. 0214] The editions read: “who has been given to us. For since he sanctified …” But the more harmonious reading results from changing the punctuation and removing the particle “therefore,” which is absent from all the manuscripts.]

21. All these things that are figuratively conveyed to us belong, in a manner of speaking, to nourishing and fanning that very fire of love, by which, as though by a weight, we may be carried upward or inward toward rest. For they move and kindle love more strongly than if they were set forth plainly, without any likenesses of the sacraments. It is difficult to state the reason for this. Nevertheless, the matter is such that what is conveyed through allegorical signification moves more, delights more, and is honored more than if it were stated most openly in proper words.

I believe that the soul’s movement, so long as it is still entangled in earthly things, is kindled more sluggishly; but if it is carried toward bodily likenesses and from them brought back to spiritual realities, which are figured by those likenesses, it is invigorated by that very transition, as though a fire were stirred in a torch, and it is carried toward rest by a more ardent love.

[Note: [Col. 0214] Thus the Colbert manuscripts: “and, in a manner of speaking, fanning it.” Earlier editions corruptly read “kindling it” (*flammandum*) instead. Augustine uses this word in *Confessions*, Book 7, chapter 6, section 8: “they were fanning the fire of their heart toward those trifles” (*flatabant in eas nugas ignem cordis sui*). [*flandum*]]

CHAPTER XII

22. Therefore, among all those ten commandments, only the commandment concerning the Sabbath is prescribed to be observed figuratively; and we have undertaken to understand that figure, not to celebrate it through bodily idleness. Since the Sabbath signifies spiritual rest, of which it is said in the Psalm, “Be still and know that I am God” (Ps. 45:11), and to which people are called by the Lord himself when he says, “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:28–29), we nevertheless observe the other commandments there as commandments properly understood, without any figurative signification.

For we have plainly learned not to worship idols; not to take the name of the Lord our God in vain; to honor father and mother; not to commit adultery, kill, steal, or bear false witness; not to covet our neighbor’s wife; and not to covet any possession of our neighbor (Exod. 20:1–17; Deut. 5:6–21). These do not figuratively present one thing while mystically signifying another; they are observed just as they sound. But we are not commanded to observe the Sabbath literally, as bodily rest from work, in the manner observed by the Jews. Indeed, their observance, which was prescribed in that way, is judged laughable unless it signifies some other kind of spiritual rest.

Accordingly, we understand not inappropriately that everything said figuratively in the Scriptures is effective in stirring up love, by which we strive toward rest, since the only figurative commandment in the Decalogue is the one in which rest is commended—rest that is loved everywhere but found securely and holily only in God.

CHAPTER XIII

23. The Lord’s Day, however, was declared not to the Jews but to Christians by the Lord’s resurrection, and from that event it began to have its festival. The souls of all the saints are indeed in rest before the resurrection of the body, but they are not yet engaged in that activity by which they will be invigorated after receiving their bodies. The eighth day, which is also the first, signifies such activity, because it does not take away that rest but glorifies it.

Difficulty does not return with the body from the body, because corruption does not return either: “For this corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:53). Therefore, although before the Lord’s resurrection the holy fathers, filled with the prophetic Spirit, were by no means ignorant of the sacrament of the eighth day, by which the resurrection is signified—for a Psalm is also entitled “For the eighth” (Pss. 6 and 11), infants were circumcised on the eighth day, and in Ecclesiastes, with reference to the two Testaments, it is said, “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight” (Eccles. 11:2)—nevertheless, it was reserved and concealed, and only the Sabbath was handed down for celebration.

For at that time there was the rest of the dead; but there was no resurrection of anyone who, rising from the dead, would no longer die, and over whom death would no longer have dominion. Thus, after such a resurrection had taken place in the Lord’s body—so that he might go before, as the head of the Church, that which the body of the Church hoped for at the end—the Lord’s Day too, that is, the eighth, which is also the first, began to be celebrated.

The reason is also understood why, in the observance of Passover, when they are commanded to kill and eat a sheep [Note: [Col. 0215] The editions read “to kill a lamb.” The manuscripts, however, have “a sheep,” a word Augustine frequently uses in this matter, in accordance with the Greek text, which has probaton, as he observes in Question 42 on Exodus], this was not prescribed to them in such a way that they should take care that the Sabbath occur and coincide with the third week of the month of new produce, so that the Lord might also mark by his Passion that same day—the Lord who had come to declare the Lord’s Day, that is, the eighth, which is also the first.

CHAPTER XIV

24. Consider, then, the most sacred triduum of the crucified, buried, and risen one. What the cross signifies we enact in the present life; what burial and resurrection signify we enact in faith and hope. For now it is said to the human being, “Take up your cross and follow me” (Matt. 16:24).

The flesh is crucified when our members that are upon the earth are put to death: fornication, uncleanness, lust, greed, and other things of this kind. Concerning these he likewise says: “If you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live” (Rom. 8:13). Hence he also says of himself: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14). And elsewhere: “Knowing,” he says, “that our old man was crucified with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed, that we might no longer serve sin” (Rom. 6:6).

Therefore, as long as our works are directed toward destroying the body of sin, as long as the outward person is being corrupted so that the inward person may be renewed day by day, it is the time of the cross.

25. These are indeed good works, but they are still laborious; their reward is rest. Yet it is said, “Rejoicing in hope,” so that, while considering the future rest, we may work cheerfully amid our labors. This cheerfulness is signified by the breadth of the cross, in the transverse beam where the hands are fixed. By the hands we understand works; by the breadth, the cheerfulness of the worker, because sadness creates narrowness. By the height, to which the head is attached, we understand the expectation of reward from the sublimity of God’s justice, who “will repay each one according to his works: to those who, by perseverance in good work, seek glory, honor, and incorruption, eternal life” (Rom. 2:6–7).

Accordingly, the length, by which the whole body is extended, signifies perseverance, which is why those who endure are called long-suffering. The depth, however, which is fixed in the earth, prefigures the hiddenness of the sacrament. For you remember, unless I am mistaken, what words of the Apostle I shall explain in this designation of the cross, where he says: “Rooted and founded in love, so that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the length, breadth, height, and depth” (Eph. 3:17–18).

Those things that we do not yet see and do not yet possess, but enact in faith and hope, are figured in the other two days. For what we are now doing, fixed as though by the nails of the commandments in the fear of God, as it is written, “Pierce my flesh with the nails of your fear” (Ps. 118:120), is counted among necessary things, not among those that are desirable and to be coveted for their own sake.

Hence he says that he has the excellent desire “to depart and to be with Christ,” but that “to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Phil. 1:23–24). What he calls departing and being with Christ is the point at which rest begins. That rest is not interrupted by the resurrection but glorified. It is nevertheless now held by faith, because “the righteous lives by faith” (Hab. 2:4).

“Do you not know,” he says, “that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? Therefore we were buried with him through baptism into death” (Rom. 6:3–4). How else than by faith? For it is not yet perfected in us, while we still groan within ourselves and await adoption, the redemption of our body: “For in hope we were saved; but hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. 8:24–25).

26. Remember how often I mention this, lest we suppose that we ought already in this life to become blessed and free from every difficulty, and thus murmur against God in sacrilegious speech amid the narrow straits of temporal circumstances, as though he were not providing what he promised. He did indeed promise necessities even for this life; but the consolations of the miserable are one thing, and the joys of the blessed another.

“Lord,” he says, “according to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul” (Ps. 93:19). Therefore let us not murmur in difficulties, lest we lose the breadth of cheerfulness of which it is said, “Rejoicing in hope,” for what follows is, “patient in tribulation” (Rom. 12:12).

The new life is therefore now begun in faith and enacted in hope. It will then be perfect when the mortal is swallowed up by life, when death is swallowed up in victory, when that last enemy, death, is destroyed, and when we have been changed and made equal to the angels. “We shall all rise,” he says, “but we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. 15:54, 26, 51). And the Lord says, “They will be equal to the angels of God” (Luke 20:36).

Now we have been apprehended in fear through faith; then we shall apprehend [Note: [Col. 0217] Lov. reads, “then we shall be apprehended.” But the other manuscripts more correctly read, “then we shall apprehend”] in love through sight. For as long as we are in the body, we are away from the Lord; “for we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Cor. 5:6). The Apostle himself, therefore, who says “that I may apprehend as I have been apprehended,” openly confesses that he has not yet apprehended: “Brothers,” he says, “I do not consider that I have apprehended” (Phil. 3:12–13).

Nevertheless, because this hope is made certain for us by the promise of truth, when he had said, “Therefore we were buried with him through baptism into death,” he added: “so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life” (Rom. 6:4).

We therefore walk in the reality of labor, but in the hope of rest; in the flesh of oldness, but in the faith of newness. For he says, “The body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness.” And “if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus Christ from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. 8:10–11).

[Note: [Col. 0217] The editions read “lives.” The manuscripts read “is life,” in accordance with the Greek, zōē dia dikaiosynēn—“life because of righteousness.”]

27. These things are celebrated at the annual Easter through the authority of the divine Scriptures and the agreement of the whole Church, which is spread throughout the world,

CHAPTER XV

in a very great sacrament, as you now understand. In the older Scriptures, no time is prescribed for celebrating Passover except that it be in the month of new produce, from the fourteenth through the twenty-first day of the moon. From the Gospel, however, since it is clear on which day the Lord was crucified, buried, and rose again, the observance of those very days was added through the councils of the fathers, and the entire Christian world was persuaded that Easter ought to be celebrated in that manner.

28. The forty-day period certainly has the authority of fasting, both in the older Books, from the fasting of Moses (Exod. 34:28) and Elijah (1 Kings 19:8), and from the Gospel, because the Lord fasted for the same number of days (Matt. 4:2), demonstrating that the Gospel does not disagree with the Law and the Prophets. In the person of Moses, the Law is understood; in the person of Elijah, the Prophets, between whom he also appeared gloriously on the mountain, so that what the Apostle says of him might stand out more clearly: “Having testimony from the Law and the Prophets” (Rom. 3:21).

In what part of the year, then, could the observance of the forty-day period be established more suitably than immediately beside and contiguous with the Lord’s Passion? For it signifies this laborious life, which requires self-restraint, so that we may fast from friendship with the world itself—a world that does not cease falsely to flatter, to scatter about, and to flaunt the cosmetics of its enticements.

I think that this life is figured by the number forty for the following reason. The number ten, in which the perfection of our blessedness is found, seems to be expressed here as it is in the number eight, because eight returns to the beginning. The creature, which is figured by the number seven, cleaves to the Creator, in whom the unity of the Trinity is to be proclaimed throughout the temporal world. That world is bounded by the four winds, raised up by the four elements, and varied by the four changes of the seasons.

Four times ten are completed in forty; and forty, reckoned through its parts, adds the ten itself, making fifty, as it were the reward of labor and self-restraint. For it was not without reason that the Lord himself remained with the disciples for forty days after his resurrection, in this earth and in this life; and after he ascended into heaven, when ten days had intervened, he sent the promised Holy Spirit when the day of Pentecost was complete.

This number fifty has another sacrament: seven times seven makes forty-nine, and when one returns to the beginning, which is the eighth day, which is also the first, fifty is completed. These fifty days are celebrated after the Lord’s resurrection, now as a figure not of labor but of rest and joy. For this reason fasts are relaxed, and we pray standing, which is a sign of the resurrection.

Hence this is observed at the altar on all the Lord’s Days, and the Alleluia is sung, signifying that our future activity will consist in nothing but praising God, as it is written: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, Lord; for ever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. 83:5).

CHAPTER XVI

29. The fiftieth day is also commended in the Scriptures—not only in the Gospel, because the Holy Spirit came then, but also in the older Books. For there, after they had celebrated Passover by killing the lamb, fifty days are counted until the day on which the Law was given on Mount Sinai to God’s servant Moses, written by the finger of God (Exod. 12, 19, 20, 31).

In the books of the Gospel it is made perfectly clear that “the finger of God” signifies the Holy Spirit. For when one Evangelist had said, “By the finger of God I cast out demons” (Luke 11:20), another expressed the same thing in this way: “By the Spirit of God I cast out demons” (Matt. 12:28).

Who would not prefer the joy of the divine sacraments, when they shine with the light of sound doctrine [Note: [Col. 0218] The Floriac manuscript reads, “when profits increase”], to all the kingdoms of this world, even those pacified by extraordinary prosperity? Do not two Seraphim, singing the praises of the Most High in harmony, cry out to one another: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts” (Isa. 6:3)? In the same way, do not the two Testaments, faithfully agreeing, sing together the sacred truth?

A sheep is killed, Passover is celebrated, and after fifty days the Law, written by the finger of God, is given for fear. Christ is killed, who was led like a sheep to slaughter, as Isaiah testifies (Isa. 53:7); the true Passover is celebrated; and after fifty days the Holy Spirit, who is the finger of God, is given for love. He is contrary to people who seek what belongs to themselves and therefore bear a harsh yoke and a heavy burden, finding no rest for their souls, because “love does not seek its own” (1 Cor. 13:5).

Therefore the contentious spirit of heretics is always restless. The Apostle shows that they possess the endeavor of Pharaoh’s magicians when he says: “Just as Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth, people corrupted in mind, disqualified regarding the faith. But they will make no further progress; for their folly will be manifest to all, as theirs also was” (2 Tim. 3:8).

Because they were exceedingly restless through that very corruption of mind, they failed at the third sign, confessing that the Holy Spirit who was in Moses was against them. For, when they failed, they said: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. 8:19). Just as the Holy Spirit, when reconciled and appeased, grants rest to the gentle and humble in heart, so, when opposed and hostile, he agitates the harsh and proud with restlessness. That restlessness was signified by those very small flies [Note: [Col. 0219] The editions read “very troublesome.” But the manuscripts more correctly read “very small,” as is clear from Book 3 of On the Trinity, chapter 7], under which Pharaoh’s magicians failed, saying: “This is the finger of God.”

30. Read Exodus and see where they celebrated Passover and how many days later the Law was given. God speaks to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai on the first day of the third month [Note: [Col. 0219] Lov. reads, “on the third day of the third month.” We have corrected it according to two Vatican manuscripts and one Sorbonne manuscript: “on the first day”].

Count one day from the beginning of that third month, and see what he says among other things: “Go down,” he says, “testify to the people, and purify them today and tomorrow; let them wash their garments and be ready for the third day. For on the third day the Lord will descend upon Mount Sinai before all the people” (Exod. 19:10–11). Then the Law was given, namely on the third day of the third month.

Count, therefore, from the fourteenth day of the first month, on which Passover took place, to the third day of the third month, and you will find seventeen days of the first month, thirty of the second, and three of the third—making fifty.

The Law in the ark is sanctification in the body of the Lord, through whose resurrection future rest is promised to us, and to obtain it love is inspired by the Holy Spirit. “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:39). Hence that prophecy was sung: “Arise, Lord, into your rest, you and the ark of your sanctification” (Ps. 131:8). Where there is rest, there is sanctification. Therefore we have now received a pledge, so that we may love and desire it. All are called to the rest of the other life, into which one passes from this life, by the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

CHAPTER XVII

31. Therefore the number fifty, multiplied three times and with the triad itself added to heighten the sacrament, is also found in those large fish which, after his resurrection, the Lord commanded to be brought up from the right side, thereby demonstrating the new life; and the nets were not torn (John 21:6, 11), because then there will be no restlessness of heretics.

Then the perfect and peaceful human being, cleansed in soul and body by the pure utterances of the Lord—“silver tested in the furnace of the earth, purified sevenfold” (Ps. 11:7)—will receive the reward of the ten, so that the total will be seventeen.

This number too, like others that display multiple figures, contains a wonderful sacrament. Nor is it without reason that the seventeenth Psalm alone is read in full in the Books of Kings (2 Kings 22:2–51), because it signifies that kingdom in which we will have no adversary. Its title is: “On the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul.”

For who is figured in David except the one who came according to the flesh from the seed of David (Rom. 1:3)? He still suffers enemies in his body, which is the Church. Hence from heaven there sounded to that persecutor whom he struck down by his voice, and whom, by transferring him in a manner into his own body, he somehow consumed: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4).

When will this body of his be delivered from the hand of all its enemies except when that last enemy, death, is destroyed? To this time the number of those 153 fish pertained. For the number seventeen itself, rising to a triangular figure, completes the sum of 153. Add together all the intermediate numbers as they rise from one through seventeen, and you will find the result: add two to one, and the total is three; add three, and it is six; add four, and it is ten; add five, and it is fifteen; add six, and it is twenty-one; continue in this way through the remaining numbers, and when the seventeenth itself is included, the total is 153.

32. These things are held most firmly from the Scriptures, namely Easter and Pentecost. The Church’s custom has given authority to the observance of those forty days before Easter [Note: [Col. 0220] Am. Bad. Er. and three manuscripts: “the agreement of the Church has strengthened it”]. Likewise, it has given authority to distinguishing eight days for the newly baptized from the rest—that is, so that the eighth may correspond to the first.

But the practice of singing the Alleluia in the Church only during those fifty days is not observed everywhere. In some places it is sung on other days as well, in various ways; but during those days it is sung everywhere. As to whether praying while standing during those days and on all the Lord’s Days is observed everywhere, I do not know. Nevertheless, I have stated as best I could what practice the Church follows in this matter, and I think it is clear.

CHAPTER XVIII

33. Concerning the washing of feet: since the Lord commended this on account of the form of humility that he had come to teach, as he himself subsequently explained, it was asked at what time such a great thing might most suitably be taught also by an act. The time presented itself when that commendation would take hold most religiously.

But lest it appear to pertain to the sacrament of Baptism itself, many refused to receive this into their customary practice. Some did not hesitate to remove it from their custom. Others, in order both to commend it at a more sacred time and to distinguish it from the sacrament of Baptism, chose either the third day of the octave—for the number three also excels greatly in many sacraments—or the eighth day itself, in order to perform this rite.

34. I am certainly surprised that you wished me to write something to you about those practices that are observed variously in different places, since this is neither necessary, and one most salutary rule must be retained in such matters: wherever we see, or learn of, practices rightly instituted that are not contrary to the faith or to good morals and that contribute something to exhorting people toward a better life, we should not merely refrain from disapproving them; we should also follow them with praise and imitation, unless someone’s weakness prevents this in such a way that the harm becomes greater.

For if it hinders them in such a way that greater gains may be hoped for among the zealous than losses feared from the slanderers, it must unquestionably be done—especially what can also be defended from the Scriptures, as with the singing of hymns and psalms, since we possess the Lord’s and the Apostles’ teachings, examples, and commandments on the matter [Note: [Col. 0221] Several manuscripts read: “we have an example and commandments concerning this matter, and so forth”].

There is a variety of custom concerning this matter, so useful for moving the soul toward piety and kindling the affection of divine love; and most of the churches in Africa are rather sluggish in this respect. Thus the Donatists criticize us because we soberly sing the divine songs of the Prophets in church, while they inflame their drunkenness to the singing of psalms composed by human ingenuity, as though to trumpets of exhortation [Note: [Col. 0221] We have restored from the manuscripts the particle “to,” which is absent from the editions].

When is there not time for holy singing, when the brothers gather in church, except when something is being read or discussed, when the bishop prays aloud, or when common prayer is announced by the deacon?

CHAPTER XIX

35. As for the other portions of time, I see absolutely nothing better, more useful, or holier for assembled Christians to do. But when something is instituted beyond customary practice, as though it were an observance of a sacrament, I cannot approve it. Nevertheless, even if many such practices are introduced to avoid the scandals of certain persons, whether holy or turbulent, I do not dare to disapprove of them too freely.

But I grieve deeply over this: many things most beneficially commanded in the divine books are neglected, while everything is so filled with numerous presumptions that a person is more severely censured for touching the ground barefoot during his octaves than for burying his mind in drunkenness.

I therefore judge that all such practices—those contained neither in the authority of the Holy Scriptures, nor established in the councils of bishops, nor strengthened by the custom of the universal Church, but varying innumerably according to the diverse customs of diverse places, so that the reasons people followed in instituting them can scarcely, or perhaps never, be discovered—should, wherever the opportunity is given, be cut away without hesitation.

For although it may not be possible to establish that these practices are contrary to the faith, they nevertheless burden the religion that God’s mercy intended to make free through very few and very clear celebrations of the sacraments with servile loads, so that the condition of the Jews becomes more tolerable. Even if they did not recognize the time of freedom, they are at least subjected to legal burdens, not to human presumptions.

But the Church of God, established amid much chaff and many weeds, tolerates many things; nevertheless, things that are contrary to the faith [Note: [Col. 0222] Thus in the earlier printed editions. But most manuscripts read: “things that are contrary to the faith, neither does the good person approve nor keep silent about them, and so forth”] or to a good life it neither approves, nor keeps silent about, nor practices.

CHAPTER XX
36. Therefore, what you wrote—that certain brothers so abstain from eating meat as to regard it as unclean—is most plainly contrary to sound faith and doctrine. If, then, I wished to continue discussing this at length, some might think that the Apostle had obscurely commanded it here. Yet among the many things he said about this matter, he so denounced the impious opinion of the heretics that he declared:

> “But the Spirit expressly says that in the latter times some will depart from the faith, devoting themselves to deceitful spirits and teachings of demons, through the hypocrisy of liars whose consciences are seared, forbidding marriage and abstaining from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who have come to know the truth. For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving; for it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer” (1 Tim. 4:1–5).

And elsewhere he speaks of these matters:

> “To the pure all things are pure; but to the impure and unbelieving nothing is pure; rather, both their mind and their conscience are defiled” (Tit. 1:15).

You yourself should read the rest and recite it to as many as you can, so that they do not make God’s grace void in themselves, since they have been called to freedom; only let them not use freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, and therefore refuse any longer to abstain from whatever foods in order to restrain the desires of the flesh, on the grounds that they are not permitted to do so superstitiously and unbelievingly.

37. As for those who read lots from the pages of the Gospels [Note: [Col. 0222] Among the Capitularies of the Frankish Kings, in the Third Capitular of the year 789, chapter 4 states: “That no one should presume to cast lots in the Psalter, or in the Gospel, or in other matters, nor observe any divinations”; something that the councils of Agde in 506, canon 42; Orléans in 511, canon 30; and Auxerre in 578, canon 4, had already forbidden. You will learn how this kind of divination was carried out through the divine Books from the notes of V. C. Stephen Baluze on that same chapter.], although it is to be hoped that they do this rather than rush to consult demons, nevertheless this practice too displeases me: they wish to turn the divine oracles, which speak for the sake of the life to come, toward secular affairs and the vanity of this present life.

CHAPTER XXI

38. If you do not think that these answers are sufficient for what you asked, you are greatly mistaken about both my abilities and my occupations. I am so far from what you supposed—that nothing is hidden from me—that I have read nothing in your letter with greater sadness, since it is most plainly false. And I am astonished that this should be hidden from you: not only are many things unknown to me in countless other matters, but even in the Holy Scriptures I know far more that I do not know than that I do know. Yet for this reason I hold a hope in the name of Christ that is not fruitless: not only have I believed in my God that the whole Law and the Prophets depend upon those two commandments (Matt. 22:40), but I have also tested this and test it every day. Whenever some sacrament or some particularly obscure passage from the sacred Scriptures is opened to me, I find those same commandments there:

> “The aim of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unhypocritical faith” (1 Tim. 1:5);

and:

> “Love is the fullness of the law” (Rom. 13:10).

39. Therefore, dearest brother, whether you read these things or others, and whether you learn them, do so in such a way that you remember the saying to be utterly true:

> “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Cor. 8:1).

“Love,” moreover, “does not envy and is not puffed up.” Knowledge should therefore be employed as a kind of scaffolding by which the structure of love may rise—a structure that will endure forever, even when knowledge is destroyed (1 Cor. 13:4, 8). When applied to the end of love, knowledge is extremely useful; by itself, without such an end, it has proved not merely superfluous but harmful. I know how a holy thought guards you beneath the shelter of the wings of the Lord our God. Yet I have offered these brief admonitions because I know that this very love of yours, which does not envy, will cause many to receive and read this letter.

EPISTLE LVI [Note: [Col. 0223] Found only in the Corbie manuscript and two Vatican manuscripts, besides the Louvain edition.] [Note: [Col. 0223] Otherwise numbered 237; the one that was 56 is now 118. It was perhaps written around the year 400.] Augustine to Celer, urging him to devote himself to the study of the sacred Scriptures, so that by comparison with eternal life he may learn that this life is smoke; and that he may renounce the sect of the Donatists.

To the distinguished, deservedly honorable, and most beloved son CELER, AUGUSTINE [Note: [Col. 0223] The Vatican manuscripts add, “greeting in the Lord.” Celer, to whom this letter is addressed, held the proconsulship of Africa in the year 429, as may be understood from the laws issued to him.].

1. I am not forgetful of my promise or of your wish. But since I had to set out to visit the churches entrusted to my care, and could not personally discharge my obligation at once, I nevertheless did not wish to remain longer in your debt—something that could have been repaid even while I was present. Accordingly, I assigned the task to my very dear son, the presbyter Optatus, so that at whatever hours you find most convenient he might read with you what I promised. When he has realized that the whole can be accomplished, he will urge Your Excellency to carry this out as vigorously and keenly as you receive the proposal gratefully. I believe you understand very well how much I love you, and how much I wish you to take pleasure and exercise yourself in salutary studies concerning knowledge of divine and human matters.

2. If you do not disdain the affection expressed in my duty, I hope that, in the Christian faith itself and in conduct suited to your already established position, you will make such progress that you may await the final day of this smoke or vapor—this life that is called human life, a day that no mortal is permitted to escape—whether eagerly, securely, or at least with a concern that is not despairing, not in the vanity of error but in the solidity of truth. For just as it is certain to you that you are alive, so let it be certain that this life, lived amid temporal pleasures, must be reckoned not life but death in comparison with the eternal life promised to us through Christ and in Christ. I would in no way doubt your character: if you do not esteem Christian purity lightly, you will very easily withdraw yourself from this Donatist custom. It is not difficult even for those of slow understanding to perceive, if only they listen patiently and attentively, by how unshakable a foundation of evidence that error is refuted. But to pursue an unfamiliar uprightness and break the bond of a customary and almost familiar perversity requires greater strength. Yet there is no reason to despair that, with our Lord God Himself assisting and exhorting you, you will act from your noble freedom and entirely manly courage. May the mercy of the Lord our God preserve you safe, distinguished, deservedly honorable, and most beloved son.

EPISTLE LVII [Note: [Col. 0224] Reviewed against the Corbie manuscript, two Vatican manuscripts, and the Louvain edition.] [Note: [Col. 0224] Otherwise numbered 210; the one that was 57 is now 187. Written somewhat later than the preceding letter.] Augustine had instructed Celer, in a book of his composed on this matter, that the Donatists had separated themselves from the Catholic Church through sheer frivolity. If that book has not satisfied him, he promises further writings. At the end, he wishes to confer with a certain Donatist, a subordinate of Celer.

To his most beloved, deservedly honorable, and worthy-to-be-received son CELER, AUGUSTINE, greeting in the Lord.

1. I believe that, the more your prudence considers it, the more easily you understand that there was no just reason for the party of Donatus to sever itself from the whole world, throughout which the Catholic Church is spread according to the prophetic and evangelical promises. If a more careful discussion of this matter is necessary, I remember that I gave your good will a book to read, when your son Caecilius, who is very dear to me, informed me that you had requested it [Note: [Col. 0224] The Louvain edition omits “your.” It is found in the Vatican and Gallican manuscripts.]. That book remained with you for several days. If, out of a desire to learn about this matter, you either wished or were able to read it amid your occupations, I do not doubt that your prudence discovered that they have nothing with which they can plausibly disagree. And if something still perhaps troubles you, insofar as God grants and permits, perhaps we shall be able to answer you when you ask, or likewise give you something to read, most beloved, distinguished, deservedly honorable, and worthy-to-be-received son.

2. Therefore I ask you to commend the Catholic unity of the Hipponian region [Note: [Col. 0224] One of the Vatican manuscripts reads, “of the Hipponian region.”] more diligently to your people, especially Paternus and Maurusius. I know the vigilance of your heart, and I think it is unnecessary to write more, since, if you wish, you can very easily learn both what others are doing and guarding against on your estates and what is happening in your affairs. I have been emphatically assured that there is, on your estate, a friend with whom I desire to be reconciled. I ask you to favor this matter, so that you may have both great praise among men and a great reward with God.
