For he had already sent me word through a certain Carus [Note: [Col. 0224] The Louvain edition omits “Carus,” a name restored from the manuscripts.]—who served as an intermediary between us—that he feared that some violent men of his might do something which, in your affairs and with your support, he will not be able to fear. Nor should you yourself prize in him not constancy but sheer obstinacy. It is shameful to change one’s judgment when it is true and right; but when it is foolish and harmful, to change it is both praiseworthy and salutary. Just as constancy does not allow a person to be corrupted, so obstinacy does not allow him to be corrected. Therefore, just as the former deserves praise, so the latter must be amended. The presbyter whom I sent will explain the rest more clearly to your prudence. May the mercy of God preserve you safe and prosperous, most beloved, distinguished, deservedly honorable, and worthy-to-be-received son.

EPISTLE LVIII [Note: [Col. 0225] Corrected with the assistance of manuscripts a, bg, bl, c, cc, ff, g, gv, j, n, r, s, t, vc, two sb manuscripts, four Vatican manuscripts, and the editions of Ambrose, Badius, Erasmus, and Louvain.] [Note: [Col. 0225] Otherwise numbered 134; the one that was 58 is now 121. Written at the end of the year 401.] Augustine congratulates Pammachius, a senator, because through his exhortations he had brought his Donatist tenants in Numidia to the Catholic Church.

To the distinguished, deservedly worthy-to-be-received, and in the heart of Christ most beloved son PAMMACHIUS [Note: [Col. 0225] Four manuscripts spell the name “Palmachius.” We have no doubt that this is the Roman citizen and senator Pammachius, who was Paula’s son-in-law, Paulina’s husband, and very intimate with Jerome.], AUGUSTINE, greeting in the Lord.

1. Your good works, springing from the grace of Christ, have made you honorable to us as one of His members, and plainly known and most beloved. For if I saw your face every day, you would not be more familiar to me than when I saw, recognized, and loved your inner self—beautiful with the dignity of peace [Note: [Col. 0225] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have “the beauty of peace.”] and radiant with the light of truth—in the brightness of your single deed. Now I speak to that inner self; to that inner self I write, to my beloved friend who, though absent in body, became known to me. Yet we were already together, joined beneath one head and living under it. If you were not rooted in that head’s love, Catholic unity would not be so dear to you, nor would you have addressed your African tenants—situated in that part of the world from which the fury of the Donatists arose, namely, in the heart of consular Numidia—with such an exhortation and animated them with such fervor of spirit that, with the greatest readiness of devotion, they chose to follow, thinking that they ought to follow so great and distinguished a man as you only after recognizing the truth. Though separated from you by such great distances, they went beneath the same head and were counted forever with you among its members, by whose command they serve you temporarily.

2. Embracing you as one whom I had come to know through this deed, I rejoiced and congratulated you in Christ Jesus our Lord, and sent you this congratulatory letter as some token of my heart and affection toward you; I could do no more. But please do not measure how much I love you by this alone. Having read this letter, pass beyond it by that invisible passage which takes place within, and proceed by thought into my heart; see what is happening there concerning you. The eye of love will reveal the chamber of love, which we close against the noisy trifles of the world when we worship God there. You will see there the delights of my joy over your good deed—delights that I can express neither with my tongue nor with my pen—burning and blazing in the sacrifice of His praise, under whose inspiration you wished this and with whose help you were able to do it. Thanks be to God for His indescribable gift (2 Cor. 9:15).

3. How greatly, together with you, we long for such a deed in Africa from the many senators who are likewise sons of the holy Church, as we rejoice over your deed! Yet it is dangerous to exhort them, whereas it is safe to congratulate you. They may perhaps do nothing, and, as though the enemies of the Church had prevailed in their hearts, they may lie in wait to deceive the weak. But you have already acted, so that the enemies of the Church may be put to shame and the weak set free. Therefore it seemed sufficient that you yourself should read this letter with friendly confidence to those to whom you can, by Christian right. For from your deed they may come to believe that what perhaps makes them sluggish because they think it impossible can be done in Africa. As for the plots that the heretics themselves contrive with twisted hearts, I did not wish to write them to you, because I laughed at the thought that they believed them to have any power in Christ’s possession [Note: [Col. 0226] The Louvain edition reads: “because they themselves think that these plots have power,” and so forth. Here we have preferred the reading of Badius, Ambrose, Erasmus, and eleven manuscripts.]. Yet you will hear of these things from my brothers, whom I commend very highly to your Excellency, so that amid such a great and unexpected salvation of those people over whom the Catholic mother rejoices through you, you may not reject even those who fear what is superfluous.

EPISTLE LIX [Note: [Col. 0226] Corrected with the assistance of the Corbie manuscript, two Vatican manuscripts, and the Louvain edition.] [Note: [Col. 0226] Otherwise numbered 217; the one that was 59 is now 149. Written around the end of the year 401.] Augustine to Victorinus, who was convening a council, explaining why he would not attend; asking him first to settle peacefully with Xantippus the question of primacy and of convening the council.

To the most blessed and venerable father and fellow priest VICTORINUS, AUGUSTINE, greeting in the Lord.

1. The circular summons [Note: [Col. 0226] One of the Vatican manuscripts consistently reads “circular letter.”] reached me on the fifth day before the Ides of November, after the day had already ended, and found me in such poor health that I could not come at all. Nevertheless, whether this was due to my incompetence or whether I have been justly moved, it is for Your Holiness and Dignity to judge. I also read in the same circular summons that a letter had been sent to the Mauritanias, provinces which we know have their own primates. If a council was to be summoned to Numidia from those provinces as well, it was surely proper that the names of some Moorish bishops who hold senior rank there should have been placed in the summons. Since I did not find them in this circular letter, I was greatly astonished. Then the letter was sent to the Numidians themselves in such a confused and negligent order that I found my name in third place, though I know how long after many bishops I was appointed. This is sufficiently insulting to others and prejudicial to me. Moreover, our venerable brother and colleague Xantippus of Tagosa [Note: [Col. 0226] The Louvain edition has “Xantippus of Thagaste.” But learned judgment requires a different reading: at the time when Augustine was writing, Alypius occupied the Numidian see of Thagaste. Barely two manuscript copies of this letter came into our hands. One of them, the Victorinus manuscript, has “Sanctippus of Tagosa”; the other, the very ancient and excellent Corbie manuscript, has “Sanctippus of Tagosa.” Of the two Vatican manuscripts formerly examined at the command of Clement VIII for a more accurate edition of this letter, one agrees with the Corbie manuscript. Indeed, R. P. M. Henry de Noris, an Augustinian and professor of theology, states in book 2, chapter 8 of his *History of Pelagianism* that “Xantippus of Tagosa” is read in three Vatican manuscripts, and he advises that the editions be corrected in accordance with them. “Nor is it surprising,” he says, “that the city of Tagosa is not found on geographical maps. For the African primates, as Gregory says in book 1, letter 72, to Gennadius, resided throughout the countryside, not in the principal cities; and at the time of the Carthaginian conference there were 567 bishops throughout Africa, although neither the maps of Ptolemy nor those of Ortelius represent so many towns.” In the *List of the African Bishoprics*, among the Numidians there is a Timothy of Tagura; two bishops of Tagora also appear in the first Carthaginian conference. Could it be that the name, written differently because letters are often transposed, designates the same see rather than different sees?], says that the primacy itself belongs to him; he is regarded in this way by many, and he sends letters of that sort. Even if this error can easily be recognized and corrected between Your Holiness and him, nevertheless his name ought not to have been omitted from the circular summons sent by Your Venerability. If it had been written among the names in the middle rather than placed first, I would have been very surprised; how much more surprising is it that no mention at all was made there of someone who above all ought to have come to the council, so that the question of the order of primacy itself could first be dealt with before all the Numidian bishops?

2. For these reasons I would even hesitate to come, lest the circular summons prove to be false, since it displays such great perversity; although the shortness of time and other serious necessities would also hinder me in many ways. Therefore I ask Your Beatitude to forgive me, and first to take care that it be agreed between Your Holiness and the aged Xantippus which of you ought to convene the council. Or, better still, as I think, convene our fellow bishops together without prejudice to either party—especially those who are close to you in the age of their episcopates, who can easily recognize which of you is speaking truth—so that the same question may be settled between the two of you, who are few [Note: [Col. 0227] The Corbie manuscript reads: “so that the same question may be settled between the two of you, who in this matter speak as much as we do, and so forth.”], and, once the error has been removed, the younger bishops may be summoned by the others. They neither can nor ought to do anything except trust you as their seniors in this matter, and at present they do not know which of you they ought chiefly to believe. I sent this letter sealed with a ring bearing the face of a man looking to the side.

EPISTLE LX [Note: [Col. 0227] Reviewed against manuscripts bl, cb, ff, gg, r, sb, two t manuscripts, two Vatican manuscripts, and the editions of Ambrose, Badius, Erasmus, and Louvain.] [Note: [Col. 0227] Otherwise numbered 76; the one that was 60 is now 86. Perhaps written around the same time.] Augustine informs Aurelius that Donatus and his brother withdrew from the monastery when he was away; moreover, that an easy fall is being offered to monks and an injury done to the clerical order when such men are admitted to the clergy.

To the most blessed, deserving of due respect, venerable, sincere, and dearly beloved brother and fellow priest, Pope AURELIUS, AUGUSTINE, greeting in the Lord.

1. I have received no letter from Your Venerability since we physically departed from one another. Now, however, I have read your Kindly One’s letter concerning Donatus and his brother, and for a long time I wavered over what I should answer. Yet, considering again and again what is useful for the salvation of those whom we serve by nurturing them in Christ, I could think of nothing else than that this path must not be opened to the servants of God: they must not think that they will more easily be chosen for something better if they have become worse. For it is an easy fall for them, and a most unworthy injury is done to the clerical order, if deserters from monasteries are chosen for clerical service, when from those who remain in the monastery we customarily admit to the clergy only the more tested and better men. Unless perhaps, just as the common people say, “A bad chorus-master is a good instrumentalist,” those same common people will joke about us by saying, “A bad monk is a good cleric.” It would be exceedingly lamentable if we raised monks to such a ruinous pride and considered clerics worthy of so grave an insult—among whose number we are—when sometimes even a good monk scarcely makes a good cleric, if he possesses sufficient continence but lacks the necessary instruction or the integrity proper to his person.

2. But concerning these men, I believe Your Beatitude supposed that they had left the monastery with our consent, so that they might be useful to their fellow countrymen. That is false: they went away of their own accord, deserted of their own accord, while we resisted them as much as we could for the sake of their salvation. As for Donatus, since what has happened has already happened—he was ordained before we could establish anything about this matter in council [Note: [Col. 0228] Council of Carthage, 13 September 401.]—if he has perhaps been corrected from his perverse pride, let your prudence do what it wishes. But concerning his brother, especially on whose account Donatus himself left the monastery, now that you understand what I think, I do not know what to answer. Nevertheless, I do not dare oppose your prudence, honor, and charity; and I truly hope that you will do what you perceive to be beneficial for the members of the Church.

EPISTLE LXI [Note: [Col. 0228] Corrected against the Corbie manuscript, one Vatican manuscript, and the Louvain edition.] [Note: [Col. 0228] Otherwise numbered 223; the one that was 61 is now 204. Written at the end of the year 401 or shortly afterward.] Augustine to Theodore, so that, when this letter is produced, he may assure people that clerics coming from the party of Donatus are to be received into the Catholic Church in their own clerical order.

To the most beloved and honored brother THEODORE [Note: [Col. 0228] So the manuscripts. The Louvain edition has only “To the most beloved brother Theodore, Augustine,” and in the prefixed summary Theodore is called a bishop. We do not know on what basis that dignity is attributed to him; certainly not from the title “brother,” which Augustine gives above in Epistle 53 to Generosus, a layman, and sometimes even to heretics and pagans, as may be seen in Epistles 90 and 232. Finally, we think that this Theodore is designated together with Maximus by Augustine in Epistle 85 in these words: “My most beloved sons, honorable men”—to whom, presumably, he had written Epistle 84.], AUGUSTINE, Bishop, greeting in the Lord.

1. When Your Benevolence was speaking with me about how we should receive clerics from the party of Donatus if they wished to become Catholics, I was pleased with what I answered you. I have therefore also set it down in this letter sent to you, so that if anyone asks you about this matter, you may show him, brought forth in my own hand, what we think and do about it. Know, then, that we detest in them nothing except their dissension, by which they have become schismatics or heretics, because they do not hold the unity and truth of the Catholic Church: they do not have peace with the people of God, which is spread throughout the whole world, and they do not recognize Christ’s Baptism in other people. We therefore reject the evil error that they possess; but the good name of God that they possess, and His sacrament, we recognize in them, revere, and embrace. For this reason we grieve over those who err and desire, through the love of Christ, to win them for God, so that the holy sacrament which outside the Church they possess to their destruction they may possess in the peace of the Church for their salvation. If, then, the evil belonging to men is removed and the good belonging to God is honored in men, there will be fraternal concord and an amiable peace, so that in human hearts the love of Christ may prevail over the devil’s persuasion.

2. Therefore, when they come to us from the party of Donatus, we do not receive their evils—that is, their dissension and error—but these are removed as obstacles to concord, and we embrace our brothers who stand with them, as the Apostle says, “in the unity of the Spirit” [Note: [Col. 0229] The manuscripts of better quality read, “in the unity of Christ.”], “in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4:3). We recognize in them the good things of God, whether the holy Baptism, or the blessing of ordination, or the profession of continence, or the consecration of virginity, or faith in the Trinity, and whatever else there may be. Even though all these things existed in them, they were of no benefit when love was absent. For who can truly say that he possesses the love of Christ when he does not embrace Christ’s unity? Therefore, when they come to the Catholic Church, they do not receive here what they already had; rather, so that what they had may begin to benefit them, they receive here what they did not have. Here they receive the root of love in the bond of peace and in the fellowship of unity, so that all the sacraments of truth that they possess may serve not for their condemnation but for their liberation. The branches ought not to boast because they are not the wood of thorns but of the vine. For if they do not live in the root, they will be thrown into the fire with their entire appearance. Concerning certain broken branches the Apostle said that God is able to graft them in again (Rom. 11:23). Therefore, dearest brother, if you happen to see any of them uncertain about the order in which they are to be received by us, show them this hand of mine, which you know well; and if they wish to keep it among themselves, let them have it. For I call God to witness over my soul that I shall receive them in such a way that they will possess not only the Baptism of Christ which they received, but also the honor of holiness and continence [Note: [Col. 0229] So the old Corbie manuscript. The Louvain edition has “the fellowship and continence.”].

EPISTLE LXII [Note: [Col. 0229] Epistles LXII and LXIII have been reviewed against the Corbie manuscript, two Vatican manuscripts, and the Louvain edition.] [Note: [Col. 0229] Otherwise numbered 241; the one that was 62 is now 192. Perhaps written toward the end of the year 401.] Alypius, Augustine, and Samsucius to Severus, explaining and excusing what was done in the affair of Timothy.

To the most blessed, venerable, dearly beloved, and very sincere brother and fellow priest SEVERUS [Note: [Col. 0229] Unless we are mistaken, this is the very man whom Augustine greets by name in Epistle 31, section 3: “The most blessed brother Severus, our fellow student and bishop of the Church of Milevis, and so forth.”], and to the brothers who are with you, ALYPIUS, AUGUSTINE, and SAMSUCIUS, and to the brothers who are with us, greeting in the Lord.

1. When we came to Subsanum and inquired into what had been done there in our absence and against our will, some things were as we had heard, while others had happened differently; nevertheless, everything was to be grieved over and endured [Note: [Col. 0230] The Louvain edition has “and removed.” The manuscripts have “and endured.”]. With the Lord’s help we corrected matters partly by rebuking, partly by warning, and partly by praying. There is one thing that greatly saddened us after Your Holiness’s departure: the brothers were sent away from there without a guide for the journey. We ask you to forgive this, and to understand that it was done more through timidity than through malice. For when they thought that our son Timothy was sending them for the purpose of provoking Your Charity especially against us, while they themselves wished to preserve everything intact for our arrival, which they hoped would take place with you, they thought that the brothers would not depart if they did not receive a guide for the journey. Yet who could doubt that this was a sin? From this also arose the report given to Fossor that Timothy had already departed with the brothers. That was certainly false, though it was not said by the presbyter; and it has been made perfectly clear to us that our brother Carcedonius was entirely unaware of all these matters, insofar as such things can be made clear.

2. But why delay over this at greater length? Our aforementioned son Timothy, deeply disturbed that he had unwillingly experienced such an unexpected uncertainty, told us that when you were dealing with him so that he might serve God at Subsanum, he burst out and swore that he would not withdraw from you at all. When we asked what he wished, he replied that this oath prevented him from being where we had wanted him to be even before, especially since he was now secure concerning the declaration of his freedom. We explained to him that he would not be guilty of perjury if, not through his own agency but through yours, he could not be with you in order to avoid scandal—since he could have sworn concerning not your will but his own, and he acknowledged that you had not in turn sworn anything to him. Finally he said what a servant of God and son of the Church ought to say: whatever we decided should be done concerning him in consultation with Your Holiness, he would undoubtedly follow. Therefore we ask, and through the love of Christ implore, your prudence to remember everything we have said and to gladden us by your reply. We must, as the Apostle says, “bear the burdens of the weak” (Rom. 15:1)—if, amid such great dangers of temptation, we may dare to say that we are the stronger. Brother Timothy did not write to Your Holiness because your holy brother has reported everything that happened. Remember us, and may you glory in the Lord, most blessed, venerable, dearly beloved, and very sincere brother.

EPISTLE LXIII [Note: [Col. 0230] Otherwise numbered 240; the one that was 63 is now 18. Written shortly after the preceding letter.] Again concerning Timothy, who, after swearing that he would not withdraw from Severus, had been ordained subdeacon at Subsanum in the diocese of Hippo. Augustine testifies that this was done against his will. Nevertheless, he declares that Timothy, whom he wished to return to Severus, had already fulfilled the office of lector in the churches of the diocese of Hippo and had thereby fulfilled the oath previously sworn to Severus; consequently, he was to be sent back to him.

[Col. 0231] To the most blessed, venerable, and most sincerely beloved brother and fellow priest SEVERUS, and to the brothers who are with you, AUGUSTINE and the brothers who are with me, greeting in the Lord.

1. If I say what the matter itself compels me to say, where will be the concern of love? But if I do not say it, where will be the freedom of friendship? Nevertheless, wavering for the moment, I have chosen to clear myself rather than accuse you. You wrote that you were surprised that we had been willing, with our own grief, to tolerate what could have been corrected by amendment—as though things badly done ought not to be grieved over even when they are later corrected as far as possible, or as though that should not be tolerated above all which, although plainly done wrongly, cannot be made undone. Therefore, dearest and most sincere brother, cease to wonder. Timothy was ordained subdeacon at Subsanum against my advice and will, while deliberation about what ought to be done with him still wavered between our opposing judgments. I still grieve over this, although he has now returned to you; yet in this we do not regret having obeyed your will.

2. Hear also what we corrected by rebuking, warning, and praying, even before he had departed from here, lest you should still think that nothing had then been corrected by us because he himself had not yet returned to you. By rebuking, we first corrected Timothy himself, because he had not obeyed you and had set out for Your Holiness without consulting Brother Carcedonius, from which the beginning of our present distress arose. Then we rebuked the presbyter and Verinus, through whom we discovered that the ordination had taken place. When all of them, under our rebuke, confessed that these things had not been done rightly and asked to be forgiven, we would have acted with excessive arrogance if we had not believed them corrected. They could not act so as to make what had happened not have happened; but in rebuking them we were doing nothing other than making them recognize and grieve that they had acted badly.

By warning, we corrected everyone, first so that thereafter they would not dare such things and thereby experience God’s anger. Then we especially corrected Timothy, who said that he was compelled by his oath alone to go to Your Charity. We told him that if Your Holiness, as we hoped, should consider what we had said together and, for the sake of the scandal of the weak, for whom Christ died, and for the discipline of the Church, which they were dangerously neglecting, should not wish him to be with you—since he had already begun to be a lector here—he would then be free from the bond of his oath and could serve God with an entirely tranquil mind, to whom we shall render an account of our actions. By warning, we had also brought Brother Carcedonius himself, as far as we could, to the point that he too would accept most patiently whatever the provision and necessity of preserving ecclesiastical discipline compelled to be done concerning him.

By praying, we corrected ourselves, commending both the direction and the outcome of our counsels to God’s mercy, and, if some indignation had wounded us, taking refuge beneath His healing hand so that we might be cured. See how many things we corrected, partly by rebuking, partly by warning, and partly by praying.

3. And now, considering the bond of love, so that we might not be possessed by Satan—for we are not ignorant of his designs [Col. 0232]—what else ought we to have done except obey your will? You did not think that what had been done could be corrected unless the very man in whom you complain that an injury had been done to you was restored to your jurisdiction. Brother Carcedonius himself did this, although not without considerable disturbance of mind, for which I ask you to pray for him, nevertheless thinking of Christ in you and acting with equanimity. While I was still considering whether, with Timothy remaining here, I should send another letter to Your Integrity, he feared your paternal agitation [Note: [Col. 0232] The Louvain edition has “admonition.” All the manuscripts have “agitation.”] and cut short my deliberation, not merely allowing but even urging Timothy to be restored to you.

4. But as for me, brother Severus, I leave my case to your judgment. For I am certain that Christ dwells in your heart; and through him I beg you to consult him, who presides over your mind when it is subject to him, whether a man who had already begun to read in the church entrusted to my administration—and had done so not once, but a second and a third time, at Subsanum, accompanied by the presbyter of the Church of Subsanum, and at Turres, Cizan [Note: In the old Corbie manuscript, Cizau.], and Verbalis—could or should be judged not to have been a reader [Note: This matter seems to have supplied the occasion for the promulgation of that canon at the Council of Milevis, celebrated on 27 August 402: “That whoever has read even once in a church shall not be retained by another church.”]. And just as we corrected what was afterward done against our will, at God’s command, so you too should similarly correct what was previously done without your knowledge, at that same command. For I do not fear that you fail to understand how great an opening is made for dissolving the order of ecclesiastical discipline if a cleric of another church has sworn to someone that he will not withdraw from him, and that person allows the cleric to remain with him, asserting that he does this lest he become the cause of the cleric’s perjury; when in fact the man who does not allow this and does not permit the cleric to remain with himself—because the cleric could swear concerning himself, not concerning another—is himself preserving the peaceful rule without any reproach.

## LETTER LXIV

[Note: Letters LXIV and LXV have been revised against the Corbie manuscript, two Vatican manuscripts, and Lovaniensis.]  
[Note: Formerly 235; the letter that was 64 is now 22. Written shortly after Christmas in 401.]

Augustine to Quintianus, exhorting him to patience and desiring his reconciliation with Bishop Aurelius, and dealing with Privatio, whom Quintianus complained had been received into Augustine’s monastery as a cleric of his church.

To his most beloved brother and fellow presbyter QUINTIANUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

### 1

We do not disdain to look upon bodies that are less beautiful, especially since our own souls are not yet beautiful, as we hope they will be when he who is ineffably beautiful appears to us—he in whom we now believe without seeing. For then we shall be like him, when we see him as he is (1 John 3:2). We admonish you to feel the same about your soul, if you receive me gladly and as a brother: do not presume that it is already beautiful, but, as the Apostle commands, “rejoice in hope,” and do what follows; for he says, “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Romans 12:12). “For we have been saved in hope”; and again the same Apostle says, “Hope that is seen is not hope: for what a man sees, why does he hope for it? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Romans 8:24–25). May this patience not fail in you; “wait for the Lord with a good conscience, act manfully, let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord” (Psalm 26:14).

### 2

It is certainly clear that, if you came to us without communicating with the venerable Bishop Aurelius, you could not communicate with us either; but we would do this out of the same charity by which we do not doubt that he also acts. Nevertheless, your arrival would not be burdensome to us, since you too ought to act with equanimity for the sake of ecclesiastical discipline, especially with your conscience intact—a conscience known to you and to God. For if he has deferred examining your case, he did not do so out of hatred for you, but because of his own necessities. If you knew them as well as you know your own, you would neither be surprised nor saddened.

We ask you also to believe this concerning our own circumstances, since you cannot know them in the same way. There are bishops senior to us in age, more distinguished in authority, and nearer in place, through whom you can more easily deal with matters pertaining to the care of your church. Nevertheless, I did not keep silent before my venerable brother and colleague, the aged Aurelius, whom I must receive with the honor due to his merits, about your distress and the complaint contained in your letters; rather, by means of a copy of your letter, I took care to convey your innocence to him.

I received your letters either the day before or two days before Christmas, when you indicated that he was going to the Church of Badesilis, from which you fear that God’s people may be disturbed and corrupted. Therefore, although I do not dare address your people by letter, I could write back to those who wrote to me; but how could I take it upon myself to write of my own accord to a people who have not been entrusted to my administration?

### 3

Nevertheless, let what I say to you alone, since you wrote to me, reach through you those to whom it needs to be said. First, do not yourselves put the Church into scandal by reading publicly Scriptures that the ecclesiastical canon has not received. Heretics, and especially the Manichaeans, commonly overturn uninstructed minds with such writings; and I hear that they are willingly lying in wait in your territory.

I therefore wonder at your prudence: you admonished me to order that those who come from you to us for the monastery should not be received, so that what had been established by us in council might remain in force; yet you do not remember what was established in the council [Note: At Hippo, in 393, canon 38; and at Carthage III, in 397, canon 47.] concerning which Scriptures are canonical and ought to be read among God’s people.

Review the council, therefore, and commit to memory everything you read there. There too you will find that the rule was made only concerning clerics [Note: Ibid., canon 21.], not also concerning laymen, so that people coming from anywhere should not be received into the monastery. This is not because the monastery was mentioned, but because the rule was established that no one should receive a cleric belonging to another church.

At a recent council [Note: Held at Carthage on 13 September 401.] it was established that those who have withdrawn from, or have been expelled from, a monastery should not elsewhere become clerics or superiors of monasteries. If, therefore, something concerning Privatio [Note: Perhaps Privatianus.] has disturbed you, know that he has not yet been received by us into the monastery. I have sent his case to the aged Aurelius, so that I may do whatever he decides concerning him.

For I wonder whether a man who has read noncanonical Scriptures only once can already be appointed a reader. If, because of this, he is already an ecclesiastical reader, then that writing too is ecclesiastical. But if that writing is not ecclesiastical, whoever has read it, even in a church, is not an ecclesiastical reader. Nevertheless, concerning this young man, I must observe whatever seems right to the bishop mentioned above.

### 4

The people of Vigesilis, most dear to us with you in the depths of Christ, will act with sound judgment if they refuse to receive a bishop degraded in the plenary council of Africa [Note: Carthage, 13 September 401.]; they neither can nor ought to be compelled. And whoever violently compels them will show what sort of person he is; he will also make clear what sort of person he was previously, when he was unwilling to have anything evil believed about himself.

No one reveals the nature of his case so plainly as the man who, through secular powers or any kind of violence, and amid disturbance and complaint, tries to recover the honor he has lost. He does not wish to serve Christ willingly, but to rule over Christians against their will. Brothers, be cautious: the devil is exceedingly crafty; but Christ is the Wisdom of God.

## LETTER LXV

[Note: Formerly 236; the letter that was 65 is now 80. Written at the beginning of 402.]

Augustine to Xantippus, primate of Numidia, explaining why he refused to entrust a church to the disreputable presbyter Abundantius.

To the most blessed and venerably received father and fellow priest, the aged XANTIPPUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

### 1

In the performance of the duty owed to your merits, I greet Your Dignity and commend myself most earnestly to your prayers. I inform your prudence that a certain Abundantius was ordained presbyter in the estate of Strabonianus, which belongs to our pastoral care [Note: Lovaniensis has “your pastoral care.” But the manuscripts have “our.”].

When he did not walk in the ways of God’s servants, he began to lack a good reputation. Alarmed by this—not rashly believing anything, but becoming distinctly more concerned—I took pains to discover, if possible, some certain indications of his bad conduct.

First I learned that he had misappropriated money belonging to a certain countryman, money entrusted to him in the name of God, so that he could give no plausible account of it. Then he was convicted and confessed that, on the fast day of Christmas, when the Church of Gippita, like the others, was also fasting, he had taken leave of his fellow presbyter of Gippita at about the fifth hour, as though he were going to his own church; that, although he had no cleric with him, he had remained on the same estate; [Col. 0235] and that at the house of a woman of bad reputation he had both dined and supped, and had stayed overnight in the same house [Note: All the manuscripts have: “And in the neighboring house and in that house.”].

A cleric of ours from Hippo had already been removed from that lodging; and because this man knew it very well, he could not deny it. As for what he denied, I left it to God, judging what he had not been permitted to conceal.

I feared entrusting a church to him, especially one situated amid the barking fury of heretics. When he asked me to write to the presbyter of the estate of Armemanus [Note: In the Vatican manuscripts, “to the presbytery.” In one of them, as also in the Corbie manuscript, “of the estate of Armenianus.”] in the Bullensian territory, from which he had come to us, explaining his case so that the man there would not form an excessively harsh opinion of him, and asking that he live there, if possible, more corrected and without the office of presbyter, I acted out of compassion. I have especially needed to disclose these things to your prudence, lest some deception creep upon you.

### 2

I heard his case when there were one hundred days until the Lord’s Pasch, which will fall on the eighth day before the Ides of April. I have taken care to make this known to Your Venerability on account of the council; I did not conceal it from him either, but faithfully explained to him what had been established [Note: At the council held at Carthage on 13 September 401.]: that if within a year he neglected to pursue his case, should he think that he had something to pursue, thereafter no one should hear his complaint.

But if we, most blessed lord and venerably received father, do not think that these indications of clerics’ bad conduct—especially when an evil reputation has begun to accompany them—should be punished in the manner established by the council, we begin to be forced to investigate things that cannot be known, either condemning what is uncertain or passing over what is genuinely unknown.

For my part, I judged that a presbyter who, on a fast day when the Church of that same place was also fasting, after taking leave of his fellow presbyter of that place, dared to remain, dine, and sup at the house of a notorious woman, with no cleric accompanying him, and to sleep in the same house, should be removed from the office of presbyter. I feared thereafter to entrust God’s Church to him.

But if ecclesiastical judges should think otherwise, since the council established that a presbyter’s case must be settled by six bishops [Note: At the Council of Carthage under Gratus, in 348 or 349, canon 11.], let whoever wishes entrust him with the church committed to his care. I confess that I fear entrusting any people to men of this kind, especially when no good reputation protects them in such a way that their conduct could be forgiven; lest, if something more harmful should break out, I should blame myself while already weakened.

## LETTER LXVI

[Note: Collated against manuscripts cb, cc, ff, g, gv, n, r, s, sb, vc, two t, four v, and against Am. Bad. Er. Lov.]  
[Note: Formerly 173; the letter that was 66 is now 170. Written around the same period.]

He reproaches Crispinus of Calama, who, having overcome the Mappalians by fear, rebaptized them.

[Note: In eight manuscripts this title is prefixed: “The booklet of Saint Augustine the Catholic against Crispinianus the schismatic.”]

### 1

You ought indeed to have feared God. But since, in rebaptizing the Mappalians [Note: In Book 2 of *Against the Letter of Petilianus*, chapter 83, section 184, Augustine says that he still grieves over this crime of Crispinus, bishop of Calama among the Donatists, who, after purchasing an estate, did not hesitate, “in one onslaught of terror, as he says, to plunge nearly eighty souls, murmuring with pitiable groans, into rebaptism.”], you wished to be feared as a man, why should a royal command in the province not prevail, if a provincial command prevailed so greatly in a village?

If you compare the persons, you are a landowner, he is an emperor. If you compare the places, you are on an estate, he is in a kingdom. If you compare the causes, he acts so that division may be repaired, whereas you act so that unity may be divided.

But we are not frightening you with a man. For we could act so that, in accordance with the emperor’s commands, you would pay ten pounds of gold. Or perhaps you have nothing with which to repay what the rebaptizers were ordered to pay, because you spend so much purchasing those whom you rebaptize?

But, as I said, we are not frightening you with a man; rather, let Christ frighten you. I want to know what you would answer if he said to you:

“Crispinus, your price was costly for purchasing the fear of the Mappalians, while my death was of little value for purchasing the love of all nations? Was what was paid from your worldly wealth worth more for rebaptizing your colonists than what flowed from my side for baptizing my peoples?”

I know that you could hear more if you lent your ear to Christ, and that from your own estate you could be reminded how impiously you speak against Christ. For if, under human law, you confidently claim firm possession of what you purchased with your silver, how much more firmly does Christ possess under divine law what he purchased with his blood!

And he will certainly possess without disturbance all that he purchased, concerning whom it is said: “He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 71:8). But how can you be confident that you will not lose what you appear to have purchased in Africa, when you say that Christ, after the whole world was lost, remained only in Africa?

### 2

Why say more? If the Mappalians crossed into your communion of their own will, let them hear both of us, so that what we say may be written down and, signed by us, interpreted for them in Punic; then, with fear of domination removed, let them choose what they wish. For from what we say it will become clear whether they remain in falsehood under compulsion or hold the truth willingly.

If they do not understand these matters, with what rashness did you lead over people who did not understand? But if they do understand, let them hear both of us, as I have said, and do what they wish.

If any peoples have also passed from you to us, whom you think were compelled by their masters, let the same procedure be followed there: let them hear both of us and choose what pleases them. But if you do not wish this to happen, who could fail to see that you do not rely on the truth?

Yet God’s anger must be feared, both in this age and in the age to come. I adjure you by Christ to answer these points.

## LETTER LXVII

[Note: Revised against manuscripts a, bl, bn, cc, fs, j, mr, r, sb, t, tt, vc, ten v, and against Am. Bad. Er. Lov.]  
[Note: Formerly 12; the letter that was 67 is now 227. Written around 402.]

Augustine to Jerome: denying that he wrote a book against him; mistaken in this respect because someone had called a lengthy letter a book.

To his most beloved and most desired lord, and his honored brother and fellow presbyter in Christ, HIERONYMUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

## CHAPTER ONE

### 1

I have heard that my letters have reached your hands. But since I have not yet deserved a reply, I would by no means attribute this to your affection: without doubt some obstacle intervened. From this I recognize that I ought rather to beseech the Lord to grant your will the opportunity to send what you will write back; for he has already granted the opportunity to reply, since whenever you wish, you can do so very easily.

## CHAPTER TWO

### 2

I hesitated whether to believe this report, which was indeed conveyed to me; but I ought not on that account to have hesitated about writing something to you. I was told that certain brothers had briefly suggested to Your Charity that I had written a book against you and sent it to Rome.

Know that this is false. I call our God to witness that I did not do this. But if perhaps in some of my writings there are passages in which I am found to have thought differently from you, you should understand that they were not written against you, but that I wrote what seemed right to me; or, if this cannot be understood, you should believe it.

I say this in such a way that I am not merely fully prepared, if anything in my writings has disturbed you, to receive fraternally what you think to the contrary—ready to rejoice either in my correction or in your very kindness—but also that I ask and earnestly implore this of you.

### 3

Oh, if only it were permitted me to enjoy you in the Lord in frequent and sweet conversation—not living with you, at least having you nearby! But since this has not been granted, I ask you to strive to preserve, increase, and perfect the very fellowship by which, in the Lord, we are together as far as we can be; and do not disdain replies, even if they are rare.

Give my dutiful greetings to the holy brother Paulinianus and to all the brothers who rejoice with you and concerning you in the Lord [Note: Eight manuscripts have “glory.”]. May you be heard by the Lord in every holy desire of yours, remembering us, most beloved and most desired lord and honored brother in Christ.

## LETTER LXVIII

[Note: Revised against manuscripts bl, bn, cc, fs, j, mr, r, sb, t, tt, vc, eleven v, and against Am. Bad. Er. Lov.]  
[Note: Formerly 13; the letter that was 68 is now 88. Written shortly after the preceding letter.]

Jerome to Augustine, having now received the letter containing the question about a useful lie, but still doubting whether it is Augustine’s; he refuses to reply unless certain of its author. He also mentions Rufinus under an assumed name.

To the truly holy and most blessed Pope AUGUSTINE, HIERONYMUS sends greetings in Christ.

### 1

At the very moment of the departure of our holy son Asterius the subdeacon, my close associate [Note: Omitted in eleven manuscripts: “my close associate.”], Your Beatitude’s letter arrived. In it you assure me that you did not send a book against my insignificance to Rome.

I had not heard that this had happened. But copies of a certain letter, supposedly written to me, reached here through our brother the deacon Sysinnius. In it you urge me to sing a *palinode* (*παλινῳδίαν*) concerning a certain passage of the Apostle, and to imitate Stesichorus, who vacillated between censuring and praising Helen, so that the man who had lost his sight by reviling her might recover it by praising her.

I frankly confess to Your Dignity that, although your style and arguments (*ἐπιχειρήματα*) seemed to me to be present, I did not think that copies of letters should be trusted rashly. I feared that, if you were offended by my reply, you might justly reproach me for failing first to establish that the discourse was yours before writing back.

The prolonged illness of the holy and venerable Paula added to the delay. For while we sat with her during her long illness, we almost forgot your letter—or the letter of whoever had written under your name—remembering that verse: “Music in mourning is an untimely narration” (Ecclesiasticus 22:6).

Therefore, if the letter is yours, write openly, or send more reliable copies, so that, without any bitterness of spirit, we may engage in discussion of the Scriptures, either correct our own error or learn that we have reproved another without cause.

### 2

Far be it from me to dare touch anything from the books of Your Beatitude. It is enough for me to establish my own positions and not disparage those of another. Your prudence knows very well that each person should abound in his own judgment, and that it is childish boastfulness—something young men once commonly did—to seek fame for one’s own name by accusing distinguished men.

Nor am I so foolish as to think myself injured by the diversity of your explanations, since you are not injured if we think differently. But there is a true reproach among friends when, not seeing our own bag [Note: Lovaniensis has “our works.” Erasmus, more accurately, has “our bag.” Jerome alludes to Aesop’s fable, in which every mortal is imagined to carry a bag, or wallet, filled with his own faults and hanging behind him, while he looks at the bag of others in front of him. The allusion is also to Persius in the satires:

“No one attempts to descend into himself, no one;

Yet the wallet hanging on the back before him is observed!”], we examine, in Persius’ phrase, the wallet of others.

It remains for you to love one who loves you diligently, and not, as a young man, challenge an old man on the field of Scripture. We have had our own time and have run as far as we could. Now that you are running and crossing long distances, leisure is owed to us; and, speaking with your pardon and honor, do not seem to me to be the only one who has proposed something from the poets. Remember Dares and Entellus [Note: Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book 5.], and the common proverb that a tired ox plants its foot more firmly.

We dictated these things sadly. Would that we might deserve your embraces, and that by mutual exchange we might either teach something or learn!

### 3

Calphurnius, surnamed Lanarius [Note: Thirteen manuscripts have Calpurnius.], sent me his usual reckless insults, which, through his efforts, I learned had reached Africa as well. I replied to them briefly and in part; I sent you copies of his pamphlet, intending to send the longer work at the first suitable opportunity.

In it I took care not to damage anyone’s Christian reputation, but only to refute the falsehood and folly of a deranged and ignorant man. Remember me, holy and venerable pope. See how much I love you: even when provoked, I did not wish to reply, nor do I believe that what I might otherwise have reproved belongs to you.

Our common brother sends you his humble greetings.

## LETTER LXIX

[Note: Revised against manuscript cb, sb, two v, and Lovaniensis.]  
[Note: Formerly 238; the letter that was 69 is now 249. Written toward the end of 402.]

Alypius and Augustine to Castorius, exhorting him to succeed his brother Maximianus, who was yielding his episcopate of the Church of Vaga with glory.

[Col. 0239] To their deservedly beloved, worthy of honor, and to be received as a son, CASTORIUS, ALYPIUS and AUGUSTINE send greetings in the Lord.

### 1

The adversary of Christians did indeed attempt, through our most beloved and sweetest son, your brother, to stir up a most dangerous scandal against the Catholic mother who, when you were fleeing from the disinherited severance, received you with pious affection into Christ’s inheritance. He wished, of course, to cloud with shameful sadness the serenity of our joy, which had arisen for us from the goodness of your conversion.

But our merciful and compassionate Lord God, comforting the afflicted, nourishing the little ones, and healing the sick, permitted him to accomplish something only so that we might rejoice much more over the matter’s correction than we had grieved over its disturbance.

For it is far more glorious to lay down the burden of the episcopate to avoid dangers to the Church than to assume it in order to direct its governance. The man who does not unworthily defend the honor he has received shows that he could worthily have received it, had the requirements of peace allowed it.

God therefore wished, even through your brother, our son Maximianus, to show the enemies of his Church that there are within her heart those who seek not their own interests but those of Jesus Christ. He did not abandon that ministry of administering the mysteries of God because he had been overcome by some worldly desire; rather, moved by peaceful piety, he laid it down lest shameful, dangerous, or perhaps even destructive disagreement arise among the members of Christ on account of his honor.

For what would be more blind and more deserving of every curse than to abandon schism for the peace of the Catholic Church and then disturb that very Catholic peace by disputing one’s own honor? What could be more praiseworthy or more beneficial to Christian charity than, after abandoning the mad pride of the Donatists, to cling to Christ’s inheritance in such a way that testimony to humility would be proved by love of unity?

Therefore, so far as he is concerned, just as we rejoice that he was found to be such a man that the divine word built in his heart was not at all overturned by the storm of this temptation, so we desire and beseech the Lord that by his subsequent life and conduct he may increasingly show how well he would have discharged what he would certainly have discharged had it been necessary.

May the eternal peace promised to the Church be repaid to him, since he understood that what was not beneficial to the Church’s peace was not beneficial to him.

### 2

But you, dearest son, who are not prevented by any such necessity from accepting the episcopate, ought to dedicate to Christ the gift he has given you; you are no small source of joy to us. Your intelligence, prudence, eloquence, seriousness, sobriety, and the other qualities with which your character is adorned are gifts of God.

Whom do they serve better than the one from whom they were given, so that they may be guarded, increased, perfected, and rewarded? Let them not serve this age, lest they vanish and perish with it.

We know how readily you consider the hopes of empty men, their insatiable desires, and their uncertain life. Therefore cast from your mind whatever it had conceived in expectation of earthly and false happiness. Work in God’s field, where the harvest is certain, where so many promises were fulfilled so long beforehand that it would be utter madness to despair of those that remain.

We beseech you by the divinity and humanity of Christ, by the peace of that heavenly city from which, as pilgrims through temporal labor, we obtain eternal rest, that in the episcopate of the Church of Vaga [Note: Thus in the Vatican and Gallican manuscripts. Some nevertheless think that Dagaiensis should be read: first, because this is how it is read in the Council of Milevis of 402, in the canon issued concerning this very case of Maximianus; and second, because they wish this man to be the same as Maximianus of Bagai, whom Augustine reports in Book 3 against Cresconius, chapter 43, to have been gravely wounded by the Donatists and thrown down from a lofty tower. Furthermore, when the manuscripts at this passage and at that place, as well as in Letters 88 and 185, where the same killing of Maximianus is discussed, are compared, we find considerable disagreement, which we have noted in the appropriate places.] you may succeed your brother—not one who fell dishonorably, but one who yielded gloriously.

Let that people, for whom we hope for abundant growth through your mind and tongue, made fertile and adorned by God’s gifts, understand in you that your brother did what he did not because of his own negligence, but for the sake of its peace.

We arranged that this letter should not be read to you until those who need you had already taken possession of you. For we hold you by the bond of spiritual love, since you are also greatly needed by our fellowship. Why we have not also presented our bodily presence, you will learn later.

## LETTER LXX

[Note: Revised against manuscripts cb, vc, v, and Lovaniensis.]  
[Note: Formerly 207; the letter that was 70 is now 220. Written perhaps around this period.]

The rashness of the Donatists, who accuse Catholics of handing over the Scriptures, exposes itself in the case of Felicianus, whom they themselves first solemnly condemned and afterward restored to his office.

To their most beloved and honorable brother NAUCELIONI [Note: The Corbie manuscript has Naucellioni.] [Note: Verlinus and Vindingus suspect that “our brother Clarentius” should be read here, rather than “our father,” as in Lovaniensis, since Clarentius was a Donatist. But manuscripts cb and V read “our bishop.” Perhaps “your [bishop]” should be read instead.] ALYPIUS and AUGUSTINE.

### 1

You reported to us what our father Clarentius had answered—namely, that concerning Felicianus of Mustitanum he did not deny that the man had been condemned by them and afterward restored to his office, but said that an innocent man had been condemned because he had been absent and had proved his absence.

We say this so that he may answer the point: it was not lawful to condemn unheard the man whom they now themselves say was innocent. Therefore either an innocent man ought not to have been condemned, or a condemned guilty man ought not to have been restored. If he was restored as innocent, he was condemned as innocent; if he was condemned as guilty, he was restored as guilty.

If those who condemned him did not know whether he was innocent, they must be charged with rashness, because they dared to condemn unheard an innocent man concerning whom they had no knowledge. From what they have now done, we understand that by the same rashness they also condemned those whom they branded with the crime of handing over the Scriptures. For if an innocent man could be condemned by them, then people who were not traditors could also be called traditors by them.

### 2

Moreover, after being condemned by them, this same Felicianus communicated with Maximianus for a long time. If he was innocent when he was condemned, why afterward, while communicating with the criminal Maximianus, did he baptize many outside their communion?

They themselves are witnesses: they acted before the proconsul so that Felicianus, as one associated with Maximianus, might be expelled from the basilica. Was it not enough to condemn an absent man, to condemn an unheard man, to condemn, as they say, an innocent man? In addition, action was brought before the proconsul against him so that he might be expelled from the church.

At the time when they were expelling him from the church, they admit that they counted him among the condemned, the criminals, and the Maximianists. Therefore, when he was baptizing people while communicating with Maximianus, was he giving true baptism or false?

If he was giving true baptism while communicating with Maximianus, why is the baptism of the whole world accused? But if he was giving false baptism while communicating with Maximianus, why were those whom he baptized in Maximianus’ schism received with him in such a way that no one rebaptized them in your party [Note: Lovaniensis has “in our party.” But manuscript cb has “in your party,” which is the correct reading.]?

## LETTER LXXI

[Note: Revised against manuscripts a, bl, bn, c, cc, fs, gg, j, mr, sb, t, vc, ten v, and against Am. Bad. Er. Lov.]  
[Note: Formerly 10; the letter that was 71 is now 6. Written in 403.]

Augustine to Jerome, dissuading him from translating the books of the Old Testament from Hebrew and urging him to restore the greatly corrupted and divergent Septuagint version to its integrity. He approves Jerome’s correction of the New Testament.

To the venerable, desired, holy brother and fellow presbyter HIERONYMUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

## CHAPTER ONE

### 1

Since I began writing to you and desiring your writings, no better opportunity has occurred for my letter to be brought to you by a servant and most faithful minister of God, and one most dear to me, than our son Cyprian the deacon.

Through him I hope for your letters with as much confidence as I can hope for anything in this realm. For our son will lack neither eagerness in seeking your replies, nor favor in obtaining them, nor diligence in preserving them, nor alacrity in conveying them, nor fidelity in delivering them. If in some way I may deserve this, may the Lord help me and attend to your heart and my desire, so that no greater will may obstruct fraternal affection.

### 2

Since, therefore, I have already sent two letters but have received none of yours afterward, I wished to send those same letters again, believing that they had not arrived. Even if they did arrive, and perhaps your letters simply could not reach me, send again the writings you have already sent, if they have been kept; and if not, write again what I may read, provided only that you do not find it burdensome to answer them, since I have been waiting for this for a long time.

I have also wished to send now the first letters that, while still a presbyter, I had prepared to send to you through a certain brother of ours, Profuturus, who afterward became our colleague and has now departed this life. At that time he himself could not carry them, because, as he was preparing to depart, he was immediately detained by the burden of the episcopate and then died shortly afterward.

I send them now so that you may know how long I have burned for conversation with you, and how I suffer because the bodily senses of you, through which my mind might approach your mind, are so far removed from me, my sweetest brother and honored among the members of the Lord.

## CHAPTER TWO

### 3

In this letter I add something we learned afterward: that you interpreted Job from Hebrew, although we already possessed a translation of the same prophet rendered into Latin from the Greek. In that earlier version, however, you marked with asterisks what is in Hebrew but absent from Greek, and with obelisks what is found in Greek but absent from Hebrew, with such admirable diligence that in some places we see individual stars attached to individual words, signifying that those same words are present in Hebrew but absent from Greek.

But in this later translation, made from Hebrew, the same fidelity to the words is not found. This greatly troubles anyone considering either why, in the first version, asterisks are affixed with such care that they indicate even the smallest particles of speech missing from the Greek manuscripts but present in the Hebrew ones, or why, in this second version, which is from Hebrew, the matter was handled more carelessly, so that these same particles might be found in their proper places.

I wished to set down an example of this, but at the moment I lacked the manuscript that is from Hebrew. Nevertheless, since you surpass others in intelligence, you understand well enough, I think, not only what I have said but also what I wished to say, so that, having given the reason, you may explain what troubles me [Note: Thus fifteen manuscripts; one has “what.”].

## 4.

I would certainly prefer that you translate for us the Greek canonical Scriptures that are said to possess the authority of the Seventy Translators. *[Col. 0242: The editions read “by the authority of the translators”; the manuscripts do not contain “by authority.”]* For it will be exceedingly difficult if your translation begins to be read more frequently throughout the churches, and the Latin churches consequently differ from the Greek churches—especially since an opponent is easily convicted by producing a Greek book, that is, in the language most widely known. But whoever is disturbed by something unusual in what has been translated from Hebrew and brings an accusation of falsity will scarcely, or never, be able to reach the Hebrew testimonies by which the allegation could be refuted. And even if he does reach them, who would tolerate the condemnation of so many Latin and Greek authorities? In addition, informed Jews may give another answer, so that you alone may appear indispensable, since you might even be able to convict them themselves; yet it would be remarkable if you could find a judge by whom this could be established.

## CHAPTER III

### 5.

For one of our brother bishops, when he had arranged for your translation to be read in the church over which he presides, encountered in the prophet Jonah (Jonah 4:6) something expressed quite differently by you from what had been fixed in everyone’s understanding and memory and sung through the succession of so many generations. Such a great uproar arose among the people—especially when the Greeks accused and loudly cried out against the alleged falsification—that *[Col. 0242: Lov. reads “inflaming”; some manuscripts, “crying out.”]* the bishop (for the city was Oea) was compelled to demand the testimony of the Jews. *[Col. 0242: Several manuscripts and two Vatican codices read: “the bishop of the city [was compelled], [to demand the testimony] of the Jews,” etc.]* [Col. 0243] Whether through ignorance or malice, they replied that the Hebrew manuscripts contained what the Greek and Latin texts both had and reported. What more need be said? The man was forced, as though correcting an error, to amend the text, since after so great a danger he did not wish to remain without his congregation. Hence it seems to us that you too may at times have been mistaken in certain matters. And consider how serious this is in writings that cannot be corrected by comparing the testimony of the customary languages.

## CHAPTER IV

### 6.

Accordingly, we give no small thanks to God for your work, by which you translated the Gospel from the Greek, because there is almost no offense anywhere when we compare it with the Greek Scripture. Therefore, if anyone stubbornly favors an old error, he is either very easily instructed or refuted when manuscripts are produced and compared. And if a few exceedingly rare matters reasonably cause concern, who is so harsh that he would not readily pardon work so useful, to which he cannot adequately repay an equivalent measure of praise?

But I would like you to be willing to explain why, in many places, the authority of the Hebrew manuscripts differs from that of the Greek manuscripts called those of the Seventy. For that version possesses no small weight, since it has earned such wide renown; and not only does the matter itself indicate that the Apostles used it, but I remember that you yourself have borne witness to this. Accordingly, you would render a very great service if you restored to Latin truth that Greek Scripture which the Seventy produced. It varies so greatly in different manuscripts that it can scarcely be tolerated, and it is so suspect—lest something else be found in the Greek—that one hesitates to bring forward or establish anything from it.

I thought this letter would be short; but somehow it has become so pleasant for me to proceed in it, as though I were speaking with you. But I beseech you by the Lord not to be reluctant to answer everything, and to grant me, insofar as you can, your presence.

# LETTER 72

*[Col. 0243: The text was collated with manuscripts designated a, bl, bn, cc, fs, j, mr, r, sb, vc, and eleven manuscripts designated v, and with the editions of Amerbach, Bad., Erasmus, and Lov.]*

*[Elsewhere numbered 14; the letter that was 72 is now 7. Written in A.D. 403 or 404.]*

Jerome reproaches Augustine concerning a letter of his circulated throughout Italy, in which a passage not correctly expounded in the Epistle to the Galatians was criticized.

To the truly holy and most blessed pope AUGUSTINE, JEROME sends greetings in the Lord.

## CHAPTER I

### 1.

You send me frequent letters, and often compel me to reply to one of your letters, copies of which, as I have already written, had reached me through the deacon Sysinnius, without your subscription; and you indicate that you first sent it through our brother Profuturus, and a second time through someone else. Meanwhile Profuturus was called back from his journey and, having been made a bishop, was taken away by a swift death; while the man whose name you conceal feared the dangers of the sea and changed his plan of sailing.

Since this is so, I cannot sufficiently wonder how that letter is said to be in the possession of many people both at Rome and throughout Italy, while it alone has not reached me, to whom alone it was sent—especially since the same brother Sysinnius said that, among your other works, he found it not in Africa, nor with you, but on an Adriatic island, nearly five years ago.

### 2.

All suspicion must be removed from friendship, and one ought to speak with a friend as with another self. Some of my close companions, vessels of Christ—of whom there is a very great abundance at Jerusalem and in the holy places—suggested that you had not acted with a straightforward intention, but were seeking praise, popular gossip, and a little glory, so that you might rise at our expense; so that many would learn that you challenged me while I was afraid, that you wrote as the learned man while I kept silent as the ignorant one, and that you had finally found someone to impose a limit on my loquacity.

But, to confess the truth plainly, I initially did not wish to answer Your Dignity for this reason: I did not clearly believe that the letter was yours, and I did not wish to “smear a sword with honey,” as the popular proverb says about certain matters. Then I was taking care lest I should seem to answer insolently a bishop of my communion and to criticize something in a letter that criticized me—especially since I judged certain things in it to be heretical.

## CHAPTER II

### 3.

Finally, I did not want you justly to reproach me and say: “What then? Had you seen my letter and recognized in its subscription the marks of a hand known to you, that you should so easily injure a friend and turn another’s malice into an insult against me?”

Therefore, as I have already written, either send me that same letter with your own subscription, or stop troubling an old man hiding in his little cell. But if you wish either to exercise or to display your learning, seek out young, eloquent, and noble men—there are said to be very many of them at Rome—who can and dare to engage with you and, in disputing the holy Scriptures, to share the yoke with a bishop.

I was once a soldier; now I am a veteran. I ought to praise both your victories and those of others, not once again fight with an exhausted body—lest, if you frequently compel me to write back, I remember the story of how Quintus Fabius Maximus, by his patience, broke Hannibal when he was exulting in youthful fashion (Livy, Decade 3, book 2).

> “Age bears away all things, the mind as well. Often I remember  
> > that as a boy I used to bury long suns in song;  
> > now so many songs are forgotten by me; even my voice  
> > itself has fled from Moeris.”  
> > *(Virgil, Eclogue 9.)*

And, to speak more in terms of the holy Scriptures, that Gileadite Barzillai, leaving to the young man his son all the benefits and delights offered by King David (2 Samuel 19:32–37), showed that old age ought neither to desire such things nor to accept them when offered.

### 4.

As for your swearing that you did not write a book against me, nor send to Rome something you had not written, but that if anything in your writings should be found to differ from my understanding, I should consider myself not injured by you, but that you had written what seemed right to you: I ask you to listen to me patiently.

You did not write a book; then how were writings criticizing me by you brought to me through others? Why does Italy possess what you did not write? On what grounds do you demand that I reply to things you deny having written?

I am not so dull that, if you held different opinions, I would think myself injured by you. But if you criticize things I said face to face, demand an account of my writings, compel me to correct what I have written, and call upon me for a *palinode* (*palinōidia*, a recantation), giving me back my eyesight, then friendship is injured and the rights of our relationship are violated.

Let us not seem to quarrel childishly and provide material for our supporters or detractors to contend with one another. I write these things because I wish to love you purely and as a Christian, and to retain in my mind nothing that differs from my lips.

For it is not fitting that, from my youth to this age, laboring in a little monastery with holy brothers, I should dare to write anything against a bishop of my communion—especially against a bishop whom I began to love before I knew him, who first invited me to friendship, and whose rise after me in the learning of the Scriptures I rejoiced to see.

Therefore, either deny that the book is yours, if it is not in fact yours, and stop demanding a reply to things you did not write; or, if it is yours, openly acknowledge it, so that if I write anything in my defense, the fault may lie with you, who provoked me, not with me, who was compelled to respond.

## CHAPTER III

### 5.

Moreover, you add that you are prepared, if anything in your writings has disturbed me, or if I should wish to correct anything, to receive it fraternally; and you even entreat me not merely to rejoice in your goodwill toward me, but to do this very thing.

Again I say what I feel: you provoke an old man, stimulate one who is silent, and seem to flaunt your learning. Yet it is not appropriate to my age to be thought ill-disposed toward one to whom I owe greater favor.

And if perverse men find in the Gospels and the Prophets something on which they can base criticism, do you wonder if in your books—and especially in your exposition of the Scriptures, which are often exceedingly obscure—some things seem to depart from the straight line?

I say this not because I already judge that certain things in your works deserve criticism. I have never devoted myself to reading them, nor are copies of them plentiful among us, apart from your books of the *Soliloquies* and some commentaries on the Psalms. If I wished to examine these, I would show them to differ—not, I will not say, from me, who am nothing, but from the interpretations of the ancient Greeks.

Farewell, my friend, most dear to me, my son in age, my father in dignity. And observe this request of mine: whatever you write to me, make sure that it reaches me first.

# LETTER 73

*[In correcting this letter we used manuscripts a, bl, bn, j, mr, r, s, sb, t, vc, two copies of cc, eleven copies of v, and the editions of Amerbach, Bad., Erasmus, and Lov.]*

*[Elsewhere numbered 15; the letter that was 73 is now 245. Written in A.D. 404.]*

Augustine endeavors to soothe Jerome, who had been somewhat offended by his letters. He testifies that he has received Jerome’s defense against Rufinus, and laments that so bitter a disagreement has arisen between men once bound by the closest friendship.

To the revered and most dearly beloved brother, fellow presbyter HIERONYMUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

## CHAPTER I

### 1.

Although I think that, before you took up these letters, there had come into your hands my letter, which I sent through God’s servant, our son the deacon Cyprian—by which you would have recognized with complete certainty that I was the author of the letter whose copies you say reached you, and from which I now imagine that I have begun to be struck and tossed about by your replies like Entellus by leaden balls and sharp boxing gloves, as though I were the audacious Dares—nevertheless I now answer those very letters of yours which you were pleased to send me through our holy son Asterius.

In them I found many signs of your most benevolent affection toward me, and again certain indications of some displeasure on your part toward me. Thus, where I was soothed as I read, there I was immediately wounded as well.

I was especially astonished by this: you say that you did not think copies of my letters should rashly be trusted, lest, if you replied, I should justly complain that you ought first to have proved that the words were mine and only then written back; yet afterward you order me, if the letter is mine, either to write openly or to send more accurate copies, so that we may engage in discussion of the Scriptures without any rancor.

How can we engage in this discussion without rancor if you are preparing to injure me? Or, if you are not preparing to do so, how could I, without being injured by you, justly reproach you for having first had to prove that the words were mine and then write back—that is, write back in a manner that would injure me? Unless you had injured me by writing back, I could not justly have reproached you.

Therefore, when you write back in a way that causes injury, what room is left for us to engage in the discussion of the Scriptures without any rancor?

For my part, far be it from me to be injured if you should wish and be able to demonstrate by sound reasoning that you have understood something in the Apostle’s Epistle, or in any other part of the holy Scriptures, more truly than I have. Indeed, far be it from me not to count it among my gains, with thanksgiving, if I am instructed by your teaching or corrected by your correction.

### 2.

Nevertheless, my dearest brother, unless you thought that you had been injured by my writings, you would not have thought that I could be injured by your replies. For I would never have entertained the opinion of you that you did not consider yourself injured, if you nevertheless wrote back in such a way as to cause injury.

Or, if I—because of my excessive foolishness—thought that I could be injured even though you did not write in a way that injured me, then you plainly injured me by judging me in this fashion.

But you would never rashly have believed me, whom you had never found to be such a person, to be the sort of person who could be injured even by such a reply from you—just as you were unwilling rashly to trust copies of my letters even when you knew my style. For if you rightly saw that I would justly have reproached you had you rashly believed a letter to be mine when it was not mine, how much more justly would I reproach you for rashly thinking me to be such a person as you had not found me to be?

You would therefore never have fallen so far as to think that, even though you did not write anything by which I could be injured, I was nevertheless so senseless that I could have been injured by such a reply from you.

## CHAPTER II

### 3.

It remains, then, that you intended to injure me by writing back if you knew by certain evidence that those letters were mine. And since I do not believe that you would unjustly have thought me deserving of injury, it remains for me to acknowledge my fault: I injured you first by those letters, which I cannot deny are mine.

Why then do I struggle against the current instead of asking forgiveness? I beseech you, therefore, by the gentleness of Christ, that if I have injured you, you forgive me and not return evil for evil by injuring me in turn.

You will injure me, however, if you remain silent about an error of mine which you may have discovered in my deeds or words. For if you criticize in me things that ought not to be criticized, you injure yourself more than me. Far be it from your character and holy purpose to do this out of a desire to injure, blaming me with a malicious tongue for something that you know, with a truthful mind, ought not to be blamed.
