Accordingly, either criticize with a benevolent heart—even if the person whom you think should be criticized is free from fault—or soothe with fatherly affection one whom you cannot cast aside. *[Col. 0247: Bad., Amerbach, and Erasmus read “cast aside” (*abjicere*) instead of “add” (*adjicere*).]* It may happen that something seems to you different from what the truth holds, provided that you do nothing different from what charity requires.

For I will most gratefully accept friendly criticism, even if what has been criticized did not deserve criticism but can rightly be defended. Or I will recognize at once your goodwill and my fault and, insofar as the Lord grants it, find myself grateful in one respect and corrected in another.

### 4.

What, then? Shall I fear your perhaps harsh but certainly salutary words like the boxing gloves of Entellus? He was beaten, not treated; and therefore he was defeated, not healed.

But if I calmly receive your medicinal correction, I shall not suffer. If, however, human weakness—or my own weakness—cannot help but be somewhat saddened even when I am truthfully reproved, then it is better for the swelling of the head to hurt while it is being treated than, because it is spared, to remain unhealed.

For this is what the man keenly perceived who said that quarreling enemies are often more useful than friends who are afraid to rebuke. While quarreling, the former sometimes speak truths that we may correct; the latter show less freedom in the cause of justice than they ought, fearing to embitter the sweetness of friendship.

Therefore, although you may perhaps seem to yourself to be an ox wearied by old age in body but not in strength of spirit, laboring fruitfully in the Lord’s threshing floor, here I am: if I have spoken wrongly, plant your foot more firmly. The burden of your age ought not to trouble me, provided that the straw of my fault is crushed.

### 5.

Accordingly, I either read or recall, with a sigh of great longing, what you wrote at the end of your letter:

> “Would that we might deserve your embraces, and that through mutual conversation we might either teach or learn something!”

I reply: Would that at least we lived in neighboring regions, so that, if our conversations could not mingle, our letters might be more frequent!

But now we are separated from one another’s presence by so great a distance that I remember having written to Your Holiness, when I was still a young man, about those words of the Apostle to the Galatians; and now, behold, I am already old and have not yet deserved a reply. The copies of my letter reached you more easily—because of I know not what prior circumstance—than the letter itself reached me through my own efforts. For the man who had then received it neither delivered it to you nor brought it back to me.

Yet such great things appear to me in your letters that have been able to reach our hands that, if I could, I would prefer none of my studies to remaining at your side. Since I cannot do this, I am considering sending one of our sons in the Lord to you to be instructed, if I should also deserve a reply from you concerning this matter.

For I do not possess, nor can I now possess, as much knowledge of the divine Scriptures as I see to be present in you. And whatever ability I have in this matter I spend, as best I can, on the people of God. But, because of ecclesiastical duties, I cannot devote myself to study more diligently than to instruct the people in what they hear.

## CHAPTER III

### 6.

[Col. 0248] I do not know what malicious writings concerning your name have reached Africa. *[The editions read “we have heard that [they] reached”; the better reading of nine manuscripts is “reached.” Jerome complains in Letter 68 that Rufinus’s insults reached Africa through Rufinus’s efforts; Augustine replies that he does not know which insults against Jerome reached Africa.]* Nevertheless, we have received what you were pleased to send in reply to those insults.

After reading it, I confess that I grieved deeply that so great an evil of discord had arisen between persons so dear and familiar, joined by a bond of friendship known to almost all the churches.

Your letters clearly show how much restraint you exercise and how firmly you hold back the goads of your indignation, lest you return insult for insult. Nevertheless, when I read those very words, I wasted away with grief and stiffened with fear. What would the things he wrote against you have done to me if they had perhaps reached my hands?

“Woe to the world because of scandals” (Matthew 18:7). Behold, it happens; indeed, precisely what the Truth says is fulfilled: “Because iniquity will abound, the love of many will grow cold” (Matthew 24:12).

To what trustworthy hearts, then, may people safely pour themselves out? Into whose bosom may secure affection throw itself entirely? Finally, what friend would not be feared as a future enemy, if what we lament could arise between Jerome and Rufinus?

O miserable and pitiable condition! O unreliable knowledge of present circumstances in the wills of friends, where there is no foreknowledge of the future!

But why should I lament this about one person in relation to another, when a human being is not even known to himself with regard to the future? He knows, however imperfectly and scarcely perhaps, what he is now; but what he will later be, he does not know.

### 7.

Furthermore, if not only knowledge of what each person is but also foreknowledge of what each will be exists in the holy and blessed angels, I entirely fail to see how the devil could once have been blessed while he was still a good angel, knowing his future wickedness and everlasting punishment.

If it is nevertheless necessary for us to know about this matter, I would like to hear from you what you think. See what the lands and seas that physically separate us are doing. If this letter of mine, which you are reading, were myself, you would already tell me what I have asked. But now, when will you write back? When will you send it? When will it arrive? When will I receive it?

And yet, would that what we sustain with as much patience as we can, since it cannot happen as quickly as we wish, might someday happen!

Therefore I return to those sweetest words of your letter, so full of your holy longing, and make them mine in turn:

> “Would that we might deserve your embraces, and that through mutual conversation we might either teach or learn something!”

—if there could in any way be something that I might teach you.

### 8.

In these words, now not only yours but also mine, in which I delight and am refreshed, and by which—even while the longing of both of us hangs suspended and does not reach fulfillment—I am consoled to no small extent, I am again pierced by the sharpest goads of grief.

I think that, among you two, to whom God had lavishly and abundantly granted precisely what each of us desired—that, joined in the closest familiarity, you might together taste the honey of the holy Scriptures—such a ruin of bitterness has crept in: bitterness to be feared by every person, at every time and in every place.

This happened even though, having already cast aside your worldly burdens and being unencumbered, you were following the Lord and living together in that land in which the Lord, walking with human feet, said: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27). It happened to men mature in age and dwelling in the word of the Lord.

“Truly, human life upon earth is a trial” (Job 7:1).

Alas for me, who cannot find you together anywhere! Perhaps, moved as I am, grieving and fearful, I would fall at your feet, weep as much as I could, and entreat you as much as I loved you: now each of you on his own behalf, now both of you on behalf of each other, and on behalf of others—especially the weak, for whom Christ died (1 Corinthians 8:11).

They watch you as though in the theater of this life, at great risk to themselves, lest you scatter abroad by writing about one another things which, if you refuse to be reconciled now, you will not be able to erase when you are at last reconciled; or things which, once reconciled, you would fear to read lest you quarrel again. *[Col. 0249: Ten manuscripts read: “which, since you will not be able to erase them when reconciled, you are unwilling to be reconciled.” One Cistercian manuscript reads: “which, since you will not be able to erase them when at some time [reconciled], you are unwilling to be reconciled.”]*

### 9.

I speak the truth to your charity: nothing made me tremble more than this example when I read in your letter certain indications of your indignation—not so much the passage about Entellus and the weary ox, where you seemed to me to be joking cheerfully rather than threatening angrily, as that other passage which plainly shows that you wrote seriously, and from which I have spoken above, perhaps at greater length than I ought, but not at greater length than I feared, where you said:

> “Lest, if injured, you should justly reproach me.”

I ask you, if it can be done, let us seek and discuss among ourselves something by which our hearts may be nourished without the bitterness of discord. Let it be so.

But if I cannot say what seems to me in need of correction in your writings, nor you in mine, except with the suspicion of envy or the injury of friendship, let us cease from these matters and spare our life and salvation.

Let that which puffs up gain less, provided that that which builds up is not offended (1 Corinthians 8:2). *[Col. 0249: Lov. reads “that knowledge”; the word “knowledge,” absent from the manuscripts, is redundant.]*

I feel myself to be far from that perfection of which it is written: “If anyone does not stumble in word, he is a perfect man” (James 3:2). But I plainly think that, through God’s mercy, I can easily ask forgiveness from you if I have given offense. You ought to disclose this to me, so that, when I have heard you, you may “gain your brother” (Matthew 18:15).

For although, because of the distance between our lands, you cannot do this between me and yourself, you ought not for that reason to allow me to remain in error.

As for the matters themselves that we wish to know, if I know, believe, or think that I possess some truth about which you think differently, I will try to maintain it, insofar as the Lord grants, without injuring you. But as for your offense, whenever I perceive that you are angry, I will do nothing other than beg forgiveness.

### 10.

Nor do I think that you could have become angry unless either I said something I ought not to have said, or said it in a way I ought not to have used. For I am no less surprised that we know one another less than we are known by our closest and most familiar friends.

As for the affection of those friends, I confess that I readily throw myself entirely into it, especially when wearied by the scandals of the world, and rest in it without any anxiety. For I sense God to be there, into whom I cast myself securely and in whom I rest securely.

Nor, in this security of mine, do I at all fear that uncertainty of human frailty concerning tomorrow about which I lamented above. For when I sense that a person is burning with Christian charity and has become a faithful friend to me through that faith, whatever counsels and thoughts of mine I entrust to him, I entrust not to a human being but to the one in whom he remains such a person.

“For God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God, and God in him” (1 John 4:16). If he abandons that love, he must cause as much grief as his remaining in it had brought joy.

Nevertheless, if an intimate friend becomes an enemy, let him, when shrewd, seek something to invent for himself; when angry, let him find nothing that he can betray. Everyone easily achieves this not by concealing what he has done, but by not doing what he would wish to be concealed.

God’s mercy grants the good and pious this privilege: that, among any friends who may later become enemies, they may move about freely and securely, not betray sins entrusted to them by others, and themselves commit nothing they would fear to have exposed. *[Col. 0250: The editions read “enemies”; six manuscripts have “friends.”]*

When something false is invented by a malicious person, it is either not believed at all, or else the person’s reputation alone is troubled while his safety remains intact. But when an evil is actually committed, the intimate enemy exists, even if it is not made public by the talk or quarrel of any intimate person. *[Col. 0250: Fourteen manuscripts read: “But when an evil is committed, he is an enemy,” etc.; this reading is by no means to be despised.]*

Therefore, what prudent person would not see how tolerably you endure the incredible hostility of one who was once your closest friend and most familiar companion, comforted by your conscience—and how you count either what he boasts or what some perhaps believe as among the weapons of the left hand, with which one fights against the devil no less than with those of the right?

Nevertheless, I would prefer him to be somehow gentler rather than you more heavily armed in this manner.

It is a great and grievous miracle that friendships of such a kind have arrived at such hostility. It will be joyful, and a much greater miracle, if from such hostility you return to your former concord.

# LETTER 74

*[Revised with manuscripts bl, bn, fs, j, mr, r, t, vc, two copies of sb, ten copies of v, and the editions of Amerbach, Bad., Erasmus, and Lov.]*

*[Elsewhere numbered 16; the letter that was 74 is now 236. Written together with the preceding letter.]*

Augustine asks Praesidius to see that the preceding letter is delivered to Jerome and to please him with a letter of his own as well.

To the most blessed and deservedly revered brother and fellow priest PRAESIDIUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

### 1.

Just as I asked Your Sincerity in person, so now I remind you not to hesitate to send my letter to our holy brother and fellow presbyter Jerome.

And so that Your Charity may know how you ought also to write to him on my behalf, I have sent copies both of my letter to him and of his letter to me. When you have read them, your holy prudence will easily see both the manner I thought should be observed and the agitation that I did not fear without cause.

Or, if I wrote something I ought not to have written, or wrote it in a way I ought not to have used, send not a message about me to him but, in brotherly affection, a message to me myself, so that, once corrected, I may ask him to forgive me if I recognize my own fault.

# LETTER 75

*[Purged of many errors on the authority of manuscripts bl, bn, c, cc, gg, fs, j, mr, r, sb, t, tt, vc, ten copies of v, and the editions of Amerbach, Bad., Erasmus, and Lov.]*

*[Elsewhere numbered 11; the letter that was 75 is now 250. Written toward the end of A.D. 404.]*

Jerome finally replies to the questions Augustine had proposed in Letters 28, 40, and 71—namely, concerning the title of the book representing ecclesiastical writers, concerning Peter’s being rebuked by Paul in the Epistle to the Galatians, concerning the translation of the Old Testament, and concerning the word for “ivy” in Jonah—vigorously defending his writings and translations against Augustine.

To the truly holy and most blessed pope AUGUSTINE, JEROME sends greetings in Christ.

## CHAPTER I

### 1.

I have received through the deacon Cyprian, sent by Your Dignity, three letters together—or rather, brief treatises—containing, as you call them, different questions, but, as I understand them, criticisms of my little works. If I wished to answer them, a book of considerable size would be required.

Nevertheless, I shall try, insofar as I can, not to exceed the limits of a rather long letter and not to delay the brother who is in haste. He demanded these letters from me three days before he was to depart, so that I was compelled to pour out whatever these writings may be almost while already marching for battle, and to answer in an improvised style—not with the maturity of a writer but with the rashness of one dictating. Such a method often results not in instruction but in accident; just as sudden wars throw even the strongest soldiers into confusion and compel them to flee before they can seize their weapons.

### 2.

Our armor, however, is Christ and the instruction of the Apostle Paul, who writes to the Ephesians:

> “Take up the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day.”

And again:

> “Stand, having girded your loins with truth, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, and having shod your feet in preparation for the gospel of peace; above all, taking up the shield of faith, with which you may be able to extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one; and receive the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6:13–17).

Once armed with such weapons, King David went forth to battle. Taking five smooth stones from the stream, he showed that amid the whirlwinds of this age there was no roughness or filth in his thoughts, drinking from the stream on the way. And therefore, being exalted, he cut off the exceedingly proud head of Goliath with Goliath’s own sword, striking the blasphemer in the forehead (1 Samuel 17:40–51), and wounding him in that part of the body in which Uzziah, who presumptuously seized the priesthood, was also struck with leprosy (2 Chronicles 26:19).

The holy man exults in the Lord, saying:

> “The light of your countenance, Lord, has been marked upon us” (Psalm 4:7).

Let us therefore also say:

> “My heart is ready, God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make melody in my glory. Awake, psaltery and lyre; I will awake at dawn” (Psalm 56:8–9),

so that this may be fulfilled in us:

> “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Psalm 81:11);

and:

> “The Lord will give the word to those who proclaim the gospel with great power” (Psalm 68:12).

I do not doubt that you yourself pray that, while we contend with one another, truth may prevail. For you are not seeking your own glory but Christ’s. When you are victorious, I too am victorious if I understand my error; and, conversely, when I am victorious, you prevail, because “parents ought to store up for their children, not children for their parents” (2 Corinthians 12:14).

And in the Book of Chronicles we read that the children of Israel went forth to battle “with a peaceful mind” (1 Chronicles 12:17–18), thinking, even amid swords, the shedding of blood, and the corpses of the fallen, not of victory for themselves but of victory for peace.

Let us therefore answer everything and, if Christ commands it, resolve the many questions in a brief discourse. I pass over the duties of greeting with which you soothe my head; I say nothing of the flatteries with which you try to console me for your criticism. I shall come to the matters themselves.

## CHAPTER II

### 3.

You say that you received from a certain brother my book, which had no title, in which I listed ecclesiastical writers, both Greek and Latin. When you asked him—using your own words—why the opening page had not been inscribed, or under what name it was to be classified, he replied that it was called an *Epitaphium*. You argue that it would rightly be called this if you had read there only the lives or writings of those who had already died. But since the little works of many are mentioned who were living both at the time when it was written and even now, you wonder why I gave it this title.

I think Your Prudence can understand that you were able to grasp the title from the work itself. For you have read both Greek and Latin authors who described the lives of illustrious men, and you know that they never wrote “Epitaph” as the title of such a work, but rather “On Illustrious Men”—for example, commanders, philosophers, orators, historians, epic poets, tragic poets, and comic poets.

An *epitaphium*, properly speaking, is written for the dead. I know that I once composed such a work on the death of the presbyter Nepotianus, whose memory is holy.

Therefore this book ought to be called either *On Illustrious Men* or, more properly, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, although by many unskilled correctors it is said to be inscribed *On Authors*.

## CHAPTER III
### 4.

In the second place you ask why I said in my commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians that Paul could not have reproved Peter for something he himself had done (Gal. II, 11), nor accuse another of hypocrisy of which he himself was guilty. You assert that the apostolic rebuke was not a matter of expediency but a genuine one, and that I ought not to teach falsehood, but that everything written should sound exactly as it is written.

To this I answer first that your prudence ought to have remembered the preface to my commentary, where I said in my own person:

> “What then? Am I foolish and reckless, promising something which he could not accomplish? Certainly not. Rather, as it seems to me, I am more cautious and timid in this matter, since, conscious of my weakness, I have followed Origen’s commentaries. That man wrote five volumes specifically on Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians, and completed the tenth book of his *Stromata* in a concise discourse on its exposition. He also composed various treatises and excerpts which, by themselves, could have sufficed. I pass over my seeing Didymus, and the Laodicean [Note: [Col. 0252] The editions read, “and Apollinaris the Laodicean.” Here in the manuscripts Apollinaris’s name also intruded in several places [Col. 0253], although it had been omitted in the exemplar, as is clear from Epistle 82, chapter 3. It is likewise absent from the Vatican manuscript and other codices of better quality.], who recently emerged from the Church [Col. 0253], and Alexander the ancient heretic, as well as Eusebius of Emesa and Theodore of Heraclea, who likewise left behind brief commentaries on this subject. If I were to select even a little from them, it would produce something that could not be wholly despised. Therefore, to confess the matter plainly, I read all these works, heaping much into my mind, and then, summoning a secretary, dictated either my own words or those of others, without sometimes remembering the order, the wording, or even the meanings. It is now a matter for the mercy of the Lord that through our inexperience the things well said by others should not perish, and that what pleases among our own people should not fail to please among outsiders.”

If, therefore, you thought that anything in my exposition deserved criticism, it was the task of your learning to ask whether what we wrote was found in the Greek authors, so that, if they had not said it, you might then condemn it as my own opinion—especially since I freely confessed in the preface that I had followed Origen’s commentaries and had dictated either my own words or those of others. At the end of the very chapter you criticize I also wrote:

> “If anyone does not approve this interpretation, by which neither Peter is shown to have sinned nor Paul to have insolently rebuked his superior, he must explain by what logic Paul reproved in another what he himself had committed.”

By this I showed that I was not deliberately defending as my own what I had read in the Greek authors, but had expressed what I had read, leaving it to the reader’s judgment whether it should be approved or rejected.

### 5.

You, therefore, in order not to do what I had asked, discovered a new argument: you asserted that Gentiles who had believed in Christ were free from the burden of the Law, while those who believed from among the Jews remained subject to the Law. Thus, through the persons of both, Paul could rightly rebuke those who observed the Law, as the teacher of the Gentiles; and Peter could justly be rebuked because, as the leader of the circumcision (Gal. II, 8), he had commanded the Gentiles to observe what only those who came from the Jews ought to have observed.

If this pleases you—or rather, since it does please you—then, as a bishop renowned throughout the world, you ought to promulgate this opinion and draw all your fellow bishops into agreement with you. I, in my little hut, together with monks—that is, my fellow sinners—do not dare to decide great matters, except frankly to confess that I read the writings of earlier authorities and, in my commentaries, following everyone’s practice, set forth various interpretations, so that each person may choose from among them whatever he wishes. I think you have read and approved this practice both in secular literature and in the divine Scriptures.

### 6.

This interpretation, which Origen first introduced in the tenth book of his *Stromata*, where he interprets Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians, and which the later interpreters followed, they introduce above all for the purpose of answering Porphyry, the blasphemer who attacks Paul’s insolence for daring to rebuke and confront Peter, the chief of the Apostles, and to convict him by argument of having acted wrongly—that is, of having fallen into the very error in which he himself stood who rebuked another offender.

What shall I say about John, who long ago governed the Church of Constantinople in the pontifical rank [Col. 0254], and specifically wrote a very extensive book on this chapter, in which he followed the opinion of Origen and the earlier authorities? [Note: [Col. 0254] John Chrysostom was first deposed in July of 403, and then again in 404, on the very day of the Great Sabbath.] If, then, you criticize me for being in error, please allow me to err along with such men; and when you see that I have many companions in my error, you ought at least to produce one supporter of your truth.

This concludes what I have to say about the interpretation of one chapter of the Epistle to the Galatians.

### 7.

But lest I seem to resist your reasoning by relying on the number of witnesses and to evade the truth under cover of illustrious men, without daring to engage directly, I shall briefly present examples from Scripture.

In the Acts of the Apostles, a voice came to Peter saying: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat”—that is, all four-footed animals, reptiles of the earth, and birds of the air. By this utterance it is shown that no human being is unclean by nature, but that all alike are summoned to the Gospel of Christ.

Peter replied: “By no means, Lord, for I have never eaten anything common or unclean.” And a voice came to him a second time from heaven, saying: “What God has cleansed, you must not call common.” Thus he went to Caesarea and, entering Cornelius’s house, “opened his mouth and said: In truth I have discovered that God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever fears him and practices righteousness is acceptable to him.”

Finally, “the Holy Spirit fell upon them, and the faithful of the circumcision who had come with Peter were astonished that the grace of the Holy Spirit had also been poured out upon the Gentiles. Then Peter answered: Can anyone forbid water, so that these should not be baptized who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have? And he ordered them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ” (Acts X, 13–48).

The Apostles and the brethren who were in Judea heard that the Gentiles too had received the word of God. When Peter had gone up to Jerusalem, those who were of the circumcision argued against him, saying: “Why did you enter men who were uncircumcised and eat with them?”

After explaining everything in due order, he concluded his speech with these words:

> “If, therefore, God gave them the same grace as he gave us who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could hinder God?”

When they heard this, they fell silent and glorified God, saying: “Then God has granted repentance unto life also to the Gentiles” (ibid. XI, 1–18).

Again, much later, when Paul and Barnabas had come to Antioch and, after the Church had assembled, had reported “how great things God had done with them, and that God had opened the door of faith to the Gentiles” (ibid. XIV, 26), certain men came down from Judea and taught the brethren, saying: “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.”

When a considerable dispute had arisen against Paul and Barnabas, they determined that both those who were accused and those who accused them should go up to the Apostles and presbyters in Jerusalem concerning this question. When they had arrived in Jerusalem, certain men of the Pharisaic sect who had believed in Christ rose up, saying: “They must be circumcised, and they must be commanded to observe the Law of Moses.”

When a great dispute had arisen over this statement, Peter, with his customary freedom, said:

> “Men and brethren, you know that from ancient days God chose among us that through my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the Gospel and believe. And God, who knows the hearts, bore witness to them, giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us, and making no distinction between us and them, purifying their hearts by faith. Now, therefore, why do you test God by placing upon the necks of the disciples a yoke which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear? But we believe that we are saved through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, just as they are.”

Then the whole multitude fell silent (Acts XV, 1–12), and the apostle James and all the presbyters together agreed with his judgment.

### 8.

These matters ought not to be burdensome to the reader, but useful both to him and to me, so that we may establish that, even before the apostle Paul, Peter was not ignorant of this matter; indeed, he was the chief author of the decree that the Law was not to be observed after the Gospel.

Peter possessed such great authority that Paul wrote in his Epistle:

> “Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to see Peter, and remained with him fifteen days” (Gal. I, 18).

Again, later on:

> “Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus with me. I went up according to a revelation, and I laid before them the Gospel which I preach among the Gentiles,”

showing that he did not regard himself as secure in preaching the Gospel until the judgment of Peter and those who were with him had confirmed it.

He immediately adds:

> “But privately before those who seemed to be something, lest perhaps I should run, or had run, in vain.”

Why privately, and not publicly? So that no stumbling-block might arise for the believers from among the Jews, who thought that the Law was to be observed and that one must believe in the Lord and Savior in this manner.

Therefore, even at the time when Peter came to Antioch—although the Acts of the Apostles do not record this, we must believe Paul, who affirms it—Paul writes that he withstood him to his face because he was blameworthy.

Before certain men came from James, Peter ate with the Gentiles; but when they came, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision. The other Jews joined him in this, so that even Barnabas was led away by them into that hypocrisy.

“But when I saw,” he says, “that they were not walking rightly according to the truth of the Gospel, I said to Peter before them all: If you, though you are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how do you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?” (Gal. II, 1, 2, 14), and so forth.

No one, therefore, can doubt that the apostle Peter was the first author of the very judgment for which he is now accused of being a transgressor. The cause of his transgression was fear of the Jews. Scripture says that at first he ate with the Gentiles, but when certain men came from James, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision.

He feared the Jews of whom he was the apostle, lest through the occasion provided by the Gentiles they should withdraw from the faith of Christ; and, as an imitator of the good shepherd, he did not wish to lose the flock entrusted to him.

### 9.

As we have shown, Peter held a correct opinion concerning the abolition of the Mosaic Law, but was compelled by fear to pretend to observe it [Note: [Col. 0255] In one Vatican manuscript, *observantiae* (“of observance”). In the Cistercian manuscript, *observationis* (“of observation”).]. Let us see whether Paul himself, who rebuked another, did something of the same kind.

We read in the same book:

> “Paul went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches. He came to Derbe and Lystra; and behold, there was a certain disciple there named Timothy, the son of a believing Jewish woman, but of a Gentile father. The brethren who were in Lystra and Iconium bore witness to him. Paul wanted him to set out with him; and taking him, he circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Gentile” (Acts XV, 41, and XVI, 1–3).

O blessed apostle Paul, who had rebuked in Peter the hypocrisy by which he withdrew from the Gentiles out of fear of the Jews who had come from James: why are you compelled to circumcise Timothy, the son of a Gentile—and certainly himself a Gentile, since he was not a Jew, having not been circumcised—against your own judgment?

You will answer me: “Because of the Jews who were in those places.” If, then, you pardon yourself for circumcising a disciple who came from the Gentiles, pardon Peter, your predecessor, for doing something out of fear of Jewish believers.

Again it is written:

> “But Paul, after remaining many days, took leave of the brethren and sailed for Syria, with Priscilla and Aquila; and he had his head shorn at Cenchreae, for he had a vow” (ibid. XVIII, 18).

Suppose that there he was compelled by fear of the Jews to do what he did not wish to do. Why did he grow his hair under a vow and afterward cut it at Cenchreae according to the Law, as those who had consecrated themselves to God as Nazirites customarily did in accordance with the command of Moses? (Num. VI, 18.)

### 10.

Yet these matters are small compared with what follows.

Luke, the writer of sacred history, reports:

> “When we had come to Jerusalem, the brethren received us gladly.” On the following day James and all the elders who were with him, “after approving his Gospel, said to him: You see, brother, how many thousands there are in Judea who have believed in Christ, and they are all zealous for the Law. They have heard about you, that you teach the Jews who are among the Gentiles to depart from Moses, saying that they ought not to circumcise their children or walk according to the customs. What then is to be done? The multitude will certainly assemble, for they will hear that you have arrived. Therefore do what we tell you. We have four men who have a vow upon themselves. Take them with you, sanctify yourself with them, and pay their expenses so that they may shave their heads; and everyone will know that the things they have heard about you are false, but that you yourself walk in observance of the Law.”

Then Paul took the men, and on the following day, after being purified, entered the temple with them, announcing the completion of the days of purification, until the offering should be made for each one of them (Acts XXI, 17–26).

O Paul, here again I ask you: Why did you shave your head? Why did you practice going barefoot according to Jewish ceremonies? Why did you offer sacrifices, and why were victims sacrificed according to the Law on your behalf?

You will surely answer: “So that those who had believed from among the Jews might not be scandalized.”

You therefore pretended to be a Jew in order to win the Jews; and James and the other presbyters taught you this very hypocrisy. Yet you could not escape. For when a riot arose and you were about to be killed, you were seized by the tribune and sent by him to Caesarea under careful military guard, lest the Jews should kill you as a pretender and destroyer of the Law. From there, arriving at Rome, you preached Christ to both Jews and Gentiles in the lodging you had rented; and your judgment was confirmed by Nero’s sword (Acts XXIII, 23, and XXVIII, 14, 30).

### 11.

We have learned that, because of fear of the Jews, Peter and Paul alike pretended to observe the precepts of the Law. With what face, then, with what audacity, can Paul rebuke in another what he himself committed?

I—or rather, others before me—explained the matter as they thought it should be explained, not defending a useful falsehood, as you write, but teaching an honorable accommodation. In this way they both demonstrated the prudence of the Apostles and restrained the insolence of the blasphemer Porphyry, who says that Peter and Paul fought with one another in a childish quarrel—or rather that Paul burned with envy of Peter’s virtues and wrote boastfully things which he either had not done or, if he had done them, had done insolently, rebuking in another what he himself had committed.

They interpreted the passage as best they could. How will you explain it? You will surely give a better interpretation, since you rejected the opinion of the earlier authorities.

## CHAPTER IV

### 12.

In your letter you write to me [Note: [Col. 0257] Epistle 40, no. 4.]:

> “For you do not need me to teach you how to understand what the same Apostle says: ‘I became to the Jews as a Jew, that I might win the Jews’ (1 Cor. IX, 20), and the other things said there—not through the simulation of deceit, but through compassionate mercy [Note: [Col. 0257] Eight manuscripts read: “through compassionate mercy, not through deceitful simulation.”]. For he becomes like a sick man who ministers to the sick—not by pretending that he has a fever, but by compassionately considering how he would wish to be served if he himself were ill.
>
> “For he was certainly a Jew; but having become a Christian, he had not abandoned the Jewish sacraments, which that people had received appropriately and at the proper lawful time. Therefore, even when he was already an apostle of Christ, he undertook to celebrate them, in order to teach that they were not harmful to those who wished to preserve them as they had received them from their parents through the Law, even after believing in Christ—though they were not to place their hope of salvation in them, since through the Lord Jesus salvation itself, which those sacraments signified, had arrived.”

The entire meaning of your speech, which you extended through a very lengthy discussion, is this: Peter did not err in thinking that the Law ought to be observed by those who had believed from among the Jews; rather, he deviated from the straight path by compelling the Gentiles to Judaize. He compelled them, however, not by the command of a teacher but by the example of his conduct. And Paul did not speak contrary to what he himself had done; rather, the question is why Peter compelled those who were from the Gentiles to Judaize.

### 13.

This, then, is the substance of the question—or rather, of your opinion: after the Gospel of Christ, believing Jews do well if they observe the commandments of the Law; that is, if they offer the sacrifices Paul offered, circumcise their sons, observe the Sabbath, as Paul did in the case of Timothy and as all the Jews observed.

If this is true, we fall into the heresy of Cerinthus and Ebion, who, although they believed in Christ, were anathematized by the Fathers for this one reason: they mixed the ceremonies of the Law with the Gospel of Christ and thus professed the new faith without abandoning the old.

What shall I say about the Ebionites, who pretend to be Christians? [Col. 0258] To this day throughout the synagogues of the East there is a sect among the Jews called the Mineans, still condemned by the Pharisees. They are commonly called Nazarenes. They believe in Christ the Son of God, born of the Virgin Mary; they say that he is the one who suffered under Pontius Pilate and rose again, in whom we too believe. But while they wish to be both Jews and Christians, they are neither Jews nor Christians.

I therefore beg you: you think that our little wound needs to be treated because it has been pierced—or rather pricked, as the saying goes. Treat the wound of this opinion, which has been struck by a lance and, so to speak, by the bulk of a *phalarica* [Note: [Col. 0258] A *phalarica* is a type of weapon, like a spear reinforced with a very large iron head, which was hurled with great force by twisted sinews or by some military engine.].

For it is not the same offense to set forth different opinions of earlier authorities in an exposition of Scripture and to introduce once again into the Church a most wicked heresy.

But if this necessity is imposed upon us—that we receive Jews together with their lawful practices, and that they may observe in the churches of Christ what they practiced in the synagogues of Satan—I shall say what I think. They will not become Christians; rather, they will make us Jews.

### 14.

What Christian could patiently hear what is contained in your letter?

> “Paul was a Jew; but having become a Christian, he had not abandoned the Jewish sacraments, which that people had received appropriately and at the proper lawful time. Therefore he undertook to celebrate them when he was already an apostle of Christ, in order to teach that they were not harmful to those who wished to preserve them as they had received them from their parents through the Law.”

Again I beg you to hear my grief without offense. Paul observed the ceremonies of the Jews when he was already an apostle of Christ, and you say that “they are not harmful to those who wish to preserve them as they received them from their parents.”

I shall speak in opposition, and, with the whole world protesting, I shall declare in a free voice that the ceremonies of the Jews are both harmful and deadly to Christians; and that whoever observes them, whether from the Jews or from the Gentiles, has been cast down into the devil’s abyss.

“For Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes, to the Jew namely and to the Gentile” (Rom. X, 4). For he would not be the end for righteousness to everyone who believes if the Jew were excluded.

And in the Gospel we read:

> “The Law and the Prophets were until John the Baptist” (Matt. XI, 13, and Luke XVI, 16).

And elsewhere:

> “For this reason the Jews sought all the more to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God” (John V, 18).

And again:

> “From his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace, because the Law was given through Moses; but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (ibid. I, 16–17).

In place of the grace of the Law that has passed away, we have received the enduring grace of the Gospel; and in place of the shadows and images of the Old Testament, truth has come through Jesus Christ.

Jeremiah also prophesies in the person of God:

> “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will consummate a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not according to the covenant which I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt” (Jer. XXXI, 31–32). [Col. 0259]

Observe what he says. He promises the new covenant of the Gospel not to the Gentile people, who had previously received no covenant [Note: [Col. 0259] Eleven manuscripts read: “with whom he had not previously made a covenant.”], but to the Jewish people, to whom he had given the Law through Moses, so that they should no longer live in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the Spirit.

Paul, however, whose name is now the subject of controversy, repeatedly expresses opinions of this kind. For the sake of brevity I shall append a few of them:

> “Behold, I Paul say to you that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing.”

And again:

> “You are severed from Christ, you who are justified in the Law; you have fallen away from grace.”

And below:

> “If you are led by the Spirit, you are no longer under the Law” (Gal. V, 2, 4, 18).

From this it is evident that the person who is under the Law does not possess the Holy Spirit in an expedient or accommodating sense, as our predecessors wished, but in truth, as you understand it.

Let us learn from God himself what the legal commandments are:

> “I gave them,” he says, “statutes that were not good, and ordinances by which they should not live” (Ezek. XX, 25).

We say these things not because, like Manichaeus and Marcion, we destroy the Law—for, in accordance with the Apostle, we know it to be holy and spiritual—but because, after faith came and the fullness of time arrived, God sent his Son, made [Note: [Col. 0259] The editions read, “born of a woman.” Ten manuscripts instead read, “made of a woman,” as Jerome elsewhere commonly does in accordance with the Greek text.] of a woman, made under the Law, in order to redeem those who were under the Law, so that we might receive adoption as sons (Gal. IV, 4), and might no longer live under a pedagogue but as adults and heirs under the Lord.

### 15.

Your letter continues:

> “Peter was not corrected because he observed the traditions of his fathers; if he had wished to do so, he would have acted neither deceitfully nor improperly.”

I say again: since you are a bishop and teacher of the Churches of Christ, if you wish to prove that what you assert is true, receive some Jew who has become a Christian and let him circumcise a son born to him, observe the Sabbath, abstain from the foods which God created to be used with thanksgiving, and slaughter a lamb at evening on the fourteenth day of the first month.

When you have done this—or rather, when you have not done it, for I know that you are a Christian and would not commit such a sacrilegious act—you will, whether you wish it or not, reject your own opinion. Then you will know that it is more difficult to establish one’s own position by deeds than to criticize another’s.

And lest perhaps we should not believe you—or rather, lest we should not understand what you are saying—for speech drawn out at length frequently lacks intelligibility, and when it is not understood it is less criticized by the unlearned—you repeat and emphasize:

> “Paul had abandoned that part of Judaism which was evil. What is the evil of Judaism which Paul had abandoned? Certainly what follows: ‘Being ignorant,’ he says, ‘of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they were not subject to the righteousness of God’ (Rom. X, 3).
>
> “Then, after the passion and resurrection of Christ, once the sacrament of grace had been given and revealed according to the order of Melchizedek, they still thought that the ancient sacraments were to be celebrated not from customary observance but from necessity for salvation. Yet if they had never been necessary, the Maccabean martyrs would have suffered martyrdom for them without fruit or purpose. Finally, they persecuted the preachers of grace, the Christians, as enemies of the Law. These and similar errors and vices, he says he condemned and regarded as refuse, in order to gain Christ” (Phil. III, 8). [Col. 0260]

### 16.

Through you we have learned what evils the apostle Paul abandoned among the Jews [Note: [Col. 0260] This is the reading in fifteen manuscripts: “what evils he had abandoned.”]. Let us now learn from you what good things he retained among them.

“The observances,” you will say, “of the Law, which they celebrate according to ancestral custom, just as Paul himself celebrated them, without any necessity for salvation.”

I do not sufficiently understand what you mean by “without any necessity for salvation.” If they do not bring salvation, why are they observed? But if they ought to be observed, then certainly they bring salvation—especially those whose observance makes martyrs. They would not be observed unless they brought salvation.

Nor are they indifferent between good and evil, as the philosophers argue. Continence is good; luxury is evil. Between the two are indifferent acts such as walking, digesting the excrement of the bowels, expelling nasal impurities through the nostrils, and casting out phlegm by spitting. These are neither good nor evil: whether you do them or do not do them, you possess neither justice nor injustice.

Observing the ceremonies of the Law, however, cannot be indifferent. It is either evil or good. You say it is good; I assert that it is evil—and evil not only for those who come from the Gentiles, but also for those who have believed from the Jewish people.

In this passage, unless I am mistaken, while avoiding one danger you have fallen into another. While fearing Porphyry the blasphemer, you have fallen into the snares of Ebion, deciding that those who believe from among the Jews must observe the Law.

And because you understand that what you say is dangerous, you again attempt to soften it with superfluous words:

> “Without any necessity for salvation, as the Jews thought they ought to celebrate them, or through the deceitful simulation which Paul had reproved in Peter.”

### 17.

Peter, then, pretended to observe the Law; but Paul, Peter’s bold rebuker, observed the legal rites openly.

Your letter continues:

> “For if he celebrated those sacraments because he pretended to be a Jew in order to win them, why did he not also sacrifice with the Gentiles, since he became as one without the Law to those who were without the Law, in order to win them also (1 Cor. IX, 21)? The reason is that he did the former as a Jew by nature, and said all this not so that Paul might pretend to be what he was not, but because in compassion he judged that he ought to assist them as though he himself were struggling in that error—not through the cunning of one who lies, but through the affection of one who sympathizes.”

You defend Paul well, asserting that he did not pretend to share the error of the Jews but truly was in error; that he did not wish to imitate Peter in lying by concealing, out of fear of the Jews, what he was [Note: [Col. 0260] Two Vatican manuscripts read, “by pretending out of fear of the Jews to be what he was not.”], but declared with complete freedom that he was a Jew.

What a novel mercy of the Apostle! While wishing to make Jews Christians, he himself became a Jew. For he could not restore the luxurious to frugality unless he had proved himself luxurious, nor could he mercifully, as you say, assist the wretched unless he himself felt wretched.

Truly pitiable and deserving of compassionate lament are those who, by their dispute and love for the abolished Law, made the apostle of Christ a Jew.

There is not much difference between my opinion and yours, because I say that both Peter and Paul, out of fear of believing Jews, practiced—or rather pretended to practice—the commandments of the Law [Col. 0261]; while you assert that they did this compassionately, “not through the cunning of one who lies, but through the affection of one who sympathizes.” Let it at least be agreed that, whether from fear or from mercy, they pretended to be what they were not.

The argument you use against us—that he ought to have become a Gentile to the Gentiles if he became a Jew to the Jews—supports us even more. Just as he was not truly a Jew, so he was not truly a Gentile; and just as he was not truly a Gentile, so he was not truly a Jew.

He imitates the Gentiles in this respect: that he accepts uncircumcision in the faith of Christ and permits the eating, without distinction, of the foods condemned by the Jews—not the worship of idols, as you suppose. For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision is anything, but the observance of the commandments of God (Gal. V, 6, and VI, 15).

### 18.

I therefore beg you, and again and again implore you, to forgive my little disputation; and attribute to yourself the fact that I have gone beyond my proper measure, since you compelled me to write back and, with Stesichorus, took out my eyes.

Do not think me a teacher of falsehood, since I follow Christ, who says:

> “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6).

It cannot happen that I, a worshiper of truth, should submit my neck to falsehood.

Nor should you stir up against me the ignorant crowd who revere you as a bishop and, when you declaim in church, look up to you with the honor due to the priesthood; while they despise me, now at the end of life and almost decrepit, pursuing the seclusion of a monastery and the countryside. You should seek others whom you may teach or rebuke.

For, separated from you by such vast distances of sea and land, we scarcely hear the sound of your voice. And if you should perhaps write a letter, Italy and Rome will receive it before it can be delivered to me, to whom it is sent.

## CHAPTER V

### 19.

In other letters you ask why my earlier translation of the canonical books has asterisks and prefixed obeli, and why I later published another translation without these signs. With your permission, I shall say that you seem not to understand what you have asked.

That earlier translation is the translation of the Seventy interpreters. Wherever there are little strokes—that is, obeli—it signifies that the Seventy have said more than is found in the Hebrew. Wherever there are asterisks, that is, shining stars, material has been added from the edition of Theodotion by Origen. There we translated the Greek; here we expressed what we understood from the Hebrew itself, preserving sometimes the truth of the meaning rather than the order of the words.

I am amazed that you read the books of the Seventy interpreters not in their pure form, as they were published by them, but as corrected—or corrupted [Note: [Col. 0261] Lovaniensis reads, “corrected.” Most codices, editions, and manuscripts more correctly read, “corrupted.”]—by Origen through obeli and asterisks, and that you do not follow the little translation of a Christian, especially since he translated what had been added from the edition of a Jewish and blasphemous man after the passion of Christ.

Do you wish to be a true lover of the Seventy interpreters? Do not read what is under the asterisks. Rather, scrape it out of the volumes, so that you may prove yourself a supporter of the ancients. If you do this, you will be forced to condemn all the libraries of the Churches. For scarcely one or another book will be found that does not contain these additions.

## CHAPTER VI
## 20

Furthermore, when you say that I ought not to have interpreted after the ancient translators, you employ a new syllogism: “Either the things interpreted by the Seventy were obscure or they were clear. If obscure, it must be acknowledged that you too could have been mistaken in them; if clear, it is evident that they could not have been mistaken in them.” I answer you in your own language.

All the ancient commentators who preceded us in the Lord and who interpreted the Holy Scriptures interpreted either obscure or clear matters. If obscure, how did you dare to discuss them after them, when they were unable to explain them? If clear, it is superfluous for you to have wished to discuss what could not have escaped them—especially in your explanation of the Psalms, which among the Greeks were interpreted in many volumes: first by Origen, second by Eusebius of Caesarea, third by Theodore of Heraclea, fourth by Asterius of Scythopolis, fifth by Apollinaris of Laodicea, and sixth by Didymus of Alexandria. Works by various authors on a few Psalms are also in circulation; but now we are speaking of the Psalter as a whole.

Among the Latins, however, the bishops Hilary of Poitiers and Eusebius of Vercelli translated Origen and Eusebius; and our Ambrose followed the former in certain passages. Let your prudence answer me: why, after so many and such interpreters, have you held a different view in your explanation of the Psalms? For if the Psalms are obscure, it must be believed that you too could have been mistaken in them. If they are clear, it is not believed that those men could have been mistaken in them. Thus, either way, your interpretation will be superfluous; and according to this rule, no one will dare to speak after his predecessors, and whatever subject one person has taken up, another will have no permission to write about.

Rather, it is a mark of your humanity that, in the matter where you grant pardon to yourself, you should extend indulgence to others as well. For I have not so much attempted to abolish the old translations as to bring forward those testimonies—which I translated, corrected, from Greek into Latin for people who speak my language—that the Jews omitted or corrupted, so that our people might know what the Hebrew truth contained. If anyone does not wish to read them, no one compels him against his will. Let him drink the old wine with pleasure and disdain our new wine, which has been published in an explanation of the earlier translations, so that wherever those are not understood, our versions may make them clearer.

As for what kind of method of interpretation should be followed in the Holy Scriptures, the book I wrote, *On the Best Kind of Interpretation*, and all the prefaces to the divine books that I placed before my edition explain this. I think that the prudent reader should be referred to those works. And if, as you say, you accept me in the correction of the New Testament and explain why you accept me—because many who possess knowledge of Greek can judge my work—you ought to have trusted the same integrity also in the Old Testament, which we did not fabricate, but translated the divine Scriptures as we found them among the Hebrews. If you doubt anything, ask the Hebrews.

## 21

But perhaps you will say: “What if the Hebrews either refuse to answer or wish to lie? Will the entire multitude of Jews be silent about my interpretation, and will no one be found who has any knowledge of the Hebrew language? Or will they all imitate those Jews whom you say were found in a little town in Africa and conspired against me in slander?”

For in your letter you weave the following story [Note: [Col. 0262] *Letter* 71, §5]:

> “A certain bishop, our brother, when he had begun to have your interpretation read aloud in the church over which he presides, encountered something placed by you quite differently in the prophet Jonah from what had become fixed in everyone’s understanding and memory and had been sung through the succession of so many generations. A tremendous disturbance arose among the people, especially when the Greeks accused it and loudly denounced the charge of falsification, so that the bishop was compelled—for the city was Oea—to seek the testimony of the Jews. Whether from ignorance or malice, they replied that the Hebrew manuscripts contained what the Greek and Latin manuscripts had and proclaimed. What more need be said? The man was compelled, as though correcting an error, to make an amendment, wishing after the great danger not to remain without his people. Hence it also seems to us that you too may sometimes have been mistaken in certain matters.”

# CHAPTER VII

## 22

You say that I interpreted something badly in the prophet Jonah and that, when the people were shouting in tumult over the difference of a single word, a bishop nearly lost his priesthood. Yet you suppress what that thing was which I supposedly interpreted badly, depriving me of the opportunity to defend myself, lest whatever you said be dissolved when I replied—unless perhaps, as many years ago, the *gourd* was brought forward, with Cornelius and Asinius Pollio of that period asserting that I had translated *ivy* instead of *gourd*.

[Note: [Col. 0263] Jerome identifies that censor by name and wittily mocks him in his commentary on Jonah, chapter 4, verse 6, in these words: “At this place a certain Canthelius, of the very ancient family of the Ceraelii—or, as he himself boasts, of the stock of Asinius Pollio—is said to have accused me at Rome some time ago of sacrilege, because I translated *ivy* instead of *gourd*. Clearly he feared that, if ivy grew instead of gourds, he would have no place from which to drink secretly and in darkness.”]

On this matter we have given a fuller answer in the commentary on the prophet Jonah. For the present, it is enough to say that in the passage where the Seventy translators rendered the word as *gourd*, while Aquila and the others rendered it as *ivy*, that is, κισσόν (*kissón*, “ivy”), the Hebrew manuscript has written *ciceion*, which the Syrians commonly call *ciceia*. It is a kind of shrub with broad leaves, shaped like those of a vine. Once planted, it quickly rises into a little tree without any support from reeds or poles, which both gourds and ivy require, sustaining itself by its own trunk.

Therefore, if, explaining this word literally, I had wished to translate *ciceion*, no one would have understood it; if I had translated *gourd*, I would have said what is not found in the Hebrew. I used *ivy* in order to agree with the other translators.

But if your Jews, as you yourself assert, said through malice or ignorance that the Hebrew manuscripts contain what is found in the Greek and Latin books, it is clear either that they do not know Hebrew letters or that they wished to lie in order to mock the advocates of the gourd.

At the end of the letter I ask you not to compel an old man at rest, long since a veteran, to take up arms and once more endanger his life. You are young and established at the summit of the episcopate: teach the peoples and enrich the Roman roofs with the new fruits of Africa. For me, it is enough to whisper with a poor listener and reader in a corner of the monastery.

# LETTER LXXVI

[Note: [Col. 0263] Collated and corrected with the assistance of manuscripts a, bg, bl, c, cc, ff, g, gv, n, s, sb, vc; two r manuscripts; two t manuscripts; four v manuscripts; and editions Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0263] Elsewhere 171; the letter that was 76 is now 60. Written toward the end of the year 403 or shortly afterward.]

Under the persona of the Catholic Church, he exhorts all the Donatists to come to their senses and return to Catholic communion.

## 1

To you, Donatists, the Catholic Church says:

“Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Psalm 4:3.)

Why have you separated yourselves from the unity of the whole world by the sacrilegious crime of an accursed schism? You heed the false things said to you by men—whether lying or mistaken—about the handing over of the divine books, so that you may die in heretical separation; yet you do not heed what those very books say to you, so that you may live in Catholic peace.

Why do you open your ears to the speech of men who say what they have never been able to prove, while you are deaf to the speech of God, who says:

> “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and your possession to the ends of the earth.” (Psalm 2:7.)

The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. Scripture does not say, “And to seeds,” as though to many, but as though to one: “And to your seed,” which is Christ (Galatians 3:16). “In your seed,” it says, “all nations shall be blessed” (Genesis 22:18).

Lift up the eyes of your hearts and consider the whole world: how all nations are blessed in the seed of Abraham. Then, what was not yet seen was believed by one man; now you see it, and still you are envious.

The Lord’s Passion is the price of the whole world. He redeemed the whole world; yet you do not agree with the whole world for your own gain, but rather quarrel in a faction to your own loss, so that you may lose everything.

Hear in the Psalm the price by which we were redeemed:

> “They pierced my hands and feet; they counted all my bones. They themselves looked and saw me; they divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast lots.” (Psalm 21:18–19.)

Why do you wish to be dividers of the Lord’s garments, and why do you refuse to hold together with the whole world that tunic of charity woven from above, which not even his persecutors divided?

The same Psalm says that the whole world holds it:

> “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship in his presence, because the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he shall rule the nations.” (Psalm 21:28–29.)

Open the ears of your hearts and hear that the God of gods, the Lord, has spoken and summoned the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting:

> “From Zion comes the beauty of his splendor.” (Psalm 49:1–2.)

If you do not wish to understand this, hear the Gospel, where the Lord himself is now speaking through his own mouth and saying:

> “It was necessary that everything written about Christ in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms should be fulfilled, and that repentance and the forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.” (Luke 24:44, 47.)

What he said in the Psalm—“He summoned the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting”—he said in the Gospel as “among all nations.” And what he said in the Psalm—“From Zion comes the beauty of his splendor”—he said in the Gospel as “beginning from Jerusalem.”

## 2

You pretend that you flee before the time of harvest from the weeds mixed in with the wheat, because you yourselves are the only weeds. For if you were wheat, you would tolerate the weeds mixed with you and would not separate yourselves from Christ’s field.

It was said of the weeds:

> “Because iniquity will abound, the love of many will grow cold.”

But it was also said of the wheat:

> “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved.” (Matthew 24:12–13.)

Why do you believe that the weeds have grown and filled the world, while the wheat has diminished and remained only in Africa? You call yourselves Christians, yet you contradict Christ.

He said, “Let both grow together until the harvest”; he did not say, “Let the weeds grow and the wheat diminish.” He said, “The field is this world”; he did not say, “The field is Africa.” He said, “The harvest is the end of the age”; he did not say, “The harvest is the time of Donatus” [Note: [Col. 0265] The editions read “part”; eighteen manuscripts read “time.”]. He said, “The harvesters are angels” (Matthew 13:30, 38–39); he did not say, “The harvesters are the leaders of the Circumcellions.”

But because you accused the wheat on account of the weeds, you demonstrated that you are the weeds; and, what is more serious, you separated yourselves from the wheat before the proper time.

For your ancestors, in whose sacrilegious division you persist, some handed over the sacred books and the church’s property to the persecutors, according to municipal records [Note: [Col. 0265] Drawn up before Munatius Felix]; others, confessing this, let those men go and communicated with them. Both groups then came together at Carthage in a frenzied faction and, concerning the crime of handing over the books—a crime about which they had already agreed among themselves—condemned men without a hearing, ordained bishop against bishop, and raised altar against altar.

Afterward they sent letters to the emperor Constantine, asking that bishops from overseas judge among the Africans. When the judges whom they had requested had been appointed and had judged at Rome, they did not obey them; they accused the bishops before the Emperor as though they had judged wrongly. Again, when other bishops had been sent to Arles, they appealed to the Emperor himself. After being heard by him and found to be false accusers, they persisted in the same crime.

Awaken to salvation, love peace, return to unity. Whenever you wish, we shall recite to you in full how all these things took place.

## 3

The one who consents to the deeds of the wicked communicates with the wicked; it is not the one who tolerates weeds in the Lord’s field until the harvest, or chaff until the final winnowing.

If you hate the wicked, change yourselves from the crime of schism. If you feared association with the wicked, you would not have retained among you for so many years Optatus, living in the most open iniquity.

[Note: [Col. 0265] Optatus of Thamugadi died in prison on account of Gildo, according to *Against the Letter of Petilianus*, book 2, chapter 92, §209.]

Now that you call him a martyr, it remains only for you to call Christ, for whose sake he died, a Christ.

Finally, what offense has the Christian world committed against you, from which you have cut yourselves off in accursed fury? And what have the Maximianists done to deserve your favor, whom, after you condemned them and expelled them from the basilicas through public judgments, you have again received into their former honor?

What offense has the peace of Christ committed against you, against which you divide yourselves from those whom you defame? And what has the peace of Donatus done to deserve your favor, for whose sake you receive those whom you condemn?

Felicianus of Musti is now with you. We read that he was first condemned in your council, afterward accused by you in the proconsul’s court, and attacked by you in the municipal records of the city of Musti.

## 4

If the handing over of the books is a crime—which God avenged with military death [Note: [Col. 0265] Eleven manuscripts read “military”; the editions read “public.”] upon the king who burned Jeremiah’s book (Jeremiah 36:23, 30)—how much more criminal is the sacrilege of schism, whose authors, whom you have compared with the Maximianists, the earth swallowed alive after opening its mouth (Numbers 16:31–33)!

How, then, do you charge us with the crime of handing over the books, which you do not prove, while you both condemn and accept your schismatics?

If you are righteous because you suffered persecution from emperors, the Maximianists are more righteous than you, since you yourselves persecuted them through judges sent by Catholic emperors.

If you alone possess Baptism, what is the baptism of the Maximianists doing among you in those whom Felicianus baptized after being condemned, and with whom he was later recalled to you?

Let your bishops answer these questions to you laypeople, if they do not wish to speak with us. And consider, for your salvation, what kind of thing it is that they do not wish to speak with us.

If wolves have held a council so that they may not answer the shepherds, why have the sheep lost their council, so as to approach the wolves’ dens?

# LETTER LXXVII

[Note: [Col. 0266] Collated with manuscripts a, bg, c, cc, ff, gv, j, n, r, s, sb, t, vc; four v manuscripts; and editions Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0266] Elsewhere 136; the letter that was 77 is now 41. Written shortly before the following letter.]

Augustine to Felix and Hilarinus, urging them not to be disturbed by scandals that have arisen in the Church. Concerning Boniface, who had been found guilty of no offense before him, he says that he could not decree that his name be removed from the list of presbyters, especially since he had committed the case to God’s judgment.

To his beloved and deservedly honored brothers Felix and Hilarinus [Note: [Col. 0266] Five manuscripts read *Hilarius*; five others, *Hilarianus*], Augustine sends greetings in the Lord.

## 1

I am not surprised that Satan disturbs the minds of the faithful. Resist him, remaining firm in hope of the promises of God, who cannot deceive; who has not only deigned to promise eternal rewards to us who believe in him, hope in him, and persevere to the end in his love, but has also foretold that temporal scandals would not be lacking, by which our faith would have to be exercised and tested.

For he says:

> “Because iniquity will abound, the love of many will grow cold.”

But immediately he adds:

> “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved.” (Matthew 24:12–13.)

What wonder, then, if men slander the servants of God and, because they cannot corrupt their lives, try to disfigure their reputation, when they do not cease daily to blaspheme the God and Lord of those servants themselves, whenever they are displeased by whatever he does against their will through a just and hidden judgment?

Therefore I exhort your prudence, my beloved and deservedly honored brothers, to reflect with a thoroughly Christian heart upon the Scripture of God, which foretold all these things to us and warned us that we ought to stand firm against them, rather than upon the slanderous empty talk and rash suspicions of men.

## 2

So I say briefly to your Charity: the presbyter Boniface was found guilty of no offense before me; I have in no way believed or do believe anything of that kind about him.

How, then, could I order his name removed from the number of presbyters, when the Gospel strongly warns me, where the Lord says:

> “In the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged.” (Matthew 7:2.)

Since the case that arose between him and Spes remains subject to divine examination, according to their agreement—which, if you wish, can be read to you—who am I to dare anticipate God’s sentence by deleting or suppressing the name of a man concerning whom, as a bishop, I ought neither rashly to suspect anything evil nor, as a human being, judge clearly about hidden matters?

Even in secular cases, when the authority to judge is referred to a higher power, with everything remaining as it was, that judgment is awaited from which there can no longer be an appeal; otherwise injury would be done to the superior judge if, while his judgment was pending, something were changed.

And there is certainly a great difference between divine power and any human authority, however exalted.

May the mercy of the Lord our God never abandon you, my beloved and honored brothers.

# LETTER LXXVIII

[Note: [Col. 0267] Collated with manuscripts a, a, bg, bl, c, cc, cb, ff, g, gg, gv, j, n, r, s, t; two sb manuscripts; two vc manuscripts; four v manuscripts; and editions Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0267] Elsewhere 137; the letter that was 78 is now 197. Probably written in the year 404, around June 26.]

A certain man from Augustine’s monastery, named Spes, was accused by the presbyter Boniface and transferred the charge to Boniface himself. Since Augustine could not investigate the matter by evident proofs, both men were ordered to visit the tomb of Saint Felix of Nola, so that the judgment might be settled by a miracle. Augustine had arranged this secretly. But because the matter had become known, he meanwhile allows Boniface’s name not to be recited among the presbyters; he exhorts everyone not to judge rashly, nor, on account of the offenses of a few, to fall away from piety themselves or suspect everyone of wrongdoing. He observes that there has never been a community so fortunate that some criminal person did not arise in it.

To his beloved brothers, the clergy, elders, and all the people of the Church of Hippo, whom he serves in the love of Christ, Augustine sends greetings in the Lord.

## 1

Would that, applying your minds attentively to the Scriptures of God, you did not need the help of our speech amid the various scandals, but that the one who consoles us—and who consoles you as well—might console you instead.

He not only foretold the good things that he will grant to his saints and faithful, but also the evils with which this world would abound. He caused them to be written beforehand so that we might await the good things that would follow the end of the age with greater certainty than we would experience the similarly foretold evils that would precede that end.

Hence the Apostle also says:

> “Whatever was written beforehand was written for our instruction, so that through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope in God.” (Romans 15:4.)

What need was there for the Lord Jesus himself not only to say, “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matthew 13:43)—something that will occur after the end of the age—but also to cry out, “Woe to the world because of scandals” (Matthew 18:7), unless it was so that we would not flatter ourselves that we could reach the seats of eternal happiness unless we had been tested by temporal evils and had not fallen away?

Why did he need to say, “Because iniquity will abound, the love of many will grow cold,” unless it was so that those of whom he immediately went on to say, “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 24:12–13), would not be disturbed, terrified, or fail as though distressed by unexpected and unforeseen events when they saw love growing cold amid this abundance of iniquity? Rather, seeing the events occur that had been foretold as future before the end, they would persevere patiently to the end, so that, secure, they might deserve to reign after the end in the life that has no end.

## 2

Therefore, beloved, concerning this scandal by which some are disturbed over the presbyter Boniface, I do not tell you not to grieve. Those who do not grieve over such things do not have the love of Christ; but those who even rejoice over them are filled with the devil’s malignity.

This is not because anything appeared in the presbyter mentioned that was judged worthy of condemnation, but because two men from our household have such a case that one of them is undoubtedly considered lost, while the reputation of the other is bad in the eyes of some and doubtful in the eyes of others, even though his conscience may not be stained.

Grieve over these things, because they ought to be grieved over; yet do not grieve in such a way that your love grows cold toward righteous living. Rather, let it burn more ardently toward entreating the Lord.

If your presbyter is innocent [Note: [Col. 0268] Lov. reads “our presbyter”; the other manuscripts, “your presbyter”], as I more strongly believe—for when he perceived the other man’s impudent and unclean advance, he was unwilling either to consent or to remain silent—may divine judgment quickly restore him, once vindicated, to his own ministry.

But if, as I dare not suspect, he was conscious of wrongdoing in himself and wished to injure the other man’s reputation, since he could not contaminate his chastity, as the man with whom he has the case himself says, may God not allow him to conceal his wickedness, so that what human beings cannot discover may be revealed by divine judgment concerning either of them.

## 3

When this matter had long tormented me and I could not find a way to convict one of the two, although I had been more inclined to believe the presbyter, I had first considered leaving them both to God until something arose in the one whom I suspected by which he might be expelled from our dwelling, not without just and manifest cause.

But when he began with great insistence to seek promotion to the clergy, either there through me or elsewhere by means of my letters, while I could in no way be persuaded to lay the hands of ordination upon a man of whom I had such a poor opinion, or to introduce him to one of my brothers through my recommendation, he began to act more turbulently, so that if he himself was not promoted to the clergy, neither would the presbyter Boniface be allowed to remain in his rank.
