When I saw, in this provocation of his, that Boniface did not wish to become a scandal to any weak people inclined to suspicion concerning doubts about his life, and that he was prepared to endure the loss of his honor among men rather than proceed uselessly, even to the disturbance of the Church, in a dispute in which he could not demonstrate his conscience to the ignorant, the doubtful, or those inclined to suspect evil, I chose a middle course.

I arranged that both men should bind themselves by a definite agreement to go to a holy place, where the more fearsome works of God might much more readily disclose the unsound conscience of either one and compel him to confession either through punishment or fear.

[Col. 0269] God is everywhere, certainly, and the one who created all things is contained or enclosed by no place. He must be worshiped by true worshipers in spirit and truth (John 4:24), so that, hearing in secret, he may also justify and crown in secret.

Nevertheless, concerning those things that become visibly known to human beings, who can search out his counsel as to why these miracles occur in some places and not in others? Many people know very well the holiness of the place where the body of blessed Felix of Nola was buried, and I wished them to go there because from that place it could more easily and reliably be written to us whatever might be divinely revealed concerning either of them.

For we too know that at Milan, at the memorial of the saints—where demons confess in a wondrous and terrifying manner—a certain thief who had come there to deceive by swearing falsely was compelled to confess the theft and return what he had taken.

Yet is not Africa also full of the bodies of holy martyrs? And still we do not know of such things happening anywhere here.

For just as, in the Apostle’s words, not all the saints possess gifts of healing, nor do all possess the discernment of spirits (1 Corinthians 12:30), so he who distributes to each person individually as he wills did not wish such things to occur at every shrine of the saints.

## 4

Therefore, since I had not wished this most grievous sorrow of my heart to be brought to your knowledge, lest I disturb you by causing you atrocious and needless grief, perhaps God did not wish it to remain hidden from you so that you might join us in prayer, and so that he might also deign to reveal to us what he himself knows in this matter but we cannot know.

I did not dare to suppress or delete the presbyter’s name from the number of his colleagues, lest I appear to injure the divine power, under whose examination the case still remains pending, if I wished to anticipate its judgment by my own prejudice. Even secular judges do not do this when the uncertainty of a case is referred to a higher authority: while the report is pending, they do not dare to alter anything.

It was also decreed in a council of bishops [Note: [Col. 0269] Carthage 3, in the year 397, canons 7 and 8] that no cleric who has not yet been convicted should be suspended from communion, unless he fails to present himself for examination of his case.

Boniface, however, accepted this humility: he would not even accept letters by which he might seek to preserve his honor while traveling, so that, in the place where both men were unknown, equality might be maintained concerning them both.

And now, if it pleases you that his name not be recited, lest, as the Apostle says, we give those who do not wish to come to the Church an occasion for seeking an occasion (2 Corinthians 11:12), this will not be our act but that of those on whose account it is done.

For what harm does it do a man that human ignorance does not wish him to be recited from that register, if an unjust conscience does not delete him from the book of the living?

[Col. 0270]

## 5

Therefore, my brothers who fear God, remember what the Apostle Peter said:

> “Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.” (1 Peter 5:8.)

When he cannot devour someone seduced into wickedness, he tries to stain that person’s reputation, so that, if possible, the person may fail through human reproaches and the slander of evil tongues and thus fall into his jaws.

But if he cannot even stain the reputation of an innocent person, he tries to persuade that person to judge his brother through malicious suspicions, so that, entangled by this, he may himself be swallowed up.

Who would be sufficient either to comprehend or enumerate all his traps and circumventions?

Nevertheless, concerning the three matters more directly related to the present case, so that you may not be led into wickedness by imitating evil examples, God addresses you through the Apostle:

> “Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership has righteousness with iniquity, or what fellowship has light with darkness?” (2 Corinthians 6:14.)

Again, in another place:

> “Do not be deceived: evil conversations corrupt good morals. Be sober, righteous, and do not sin.” (1 Corinthians 15:33–34.)

And so that you may not fail because of the tongues of slanderers, he says through the Prophet:

> “Hear me, you who know judgment, my people, in whose heart is my law: do not fear the reproach of men, and do not be overcome by their slander; do not consider it a great thing that they despise you. For like a garment they will be consumed in time, and like wool they will be eaten by the moth; but my righteousness remains forever.” (Isaiah 51:7–8.)

And finally, so that you may not perish by suspecting falsely and with a malicious mind concerning the servants of God, remember the Apostle’s words:

> “Do not judge anything before the time, until the Lord comes, who will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and disclose the purposes of hearts; then each person will receive praise from God.” (1 Corinthians 4:5.)

And also what is written:

> “The things that are manifest belong to you; but the things that are hidden belong to the Lord your God.” (Deuteronomy 29:29.)

## 6

It is clear that such things do not occur in the Church without great sorrow to the saints and faithful. Nevertheless, let him console us who foretold everything and warned us not to grow cold amid the abundance of iniquity, but to persevere to the end, so that we might be saved.

For as far as I am concerned, if there is in me even a little love of Christ, “who among you is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not on fire?” (2 Corinthians 11:29.)

Therefore do not increase my sufferings by failing either through false suspicions or through the sins of others.

Do not, I beg you, make me say of you:

> “And they added to the pain of my wounds.”

Those who rejoice in these our sufferings—of whom it was long ago foretold in the person of Christ’s body:

> “Those who sat at the gate insulted me, and those who drank wine sang against me” (Psalm 68:27, 13)—

are much easier to endure. Yet we have learned to pray even for them and to wish them well.

For what else are these people sitting and seeking except that, whenever a bishop, cleric, monk, or consecrated woman falls, they may believe, proclaim, and insist that all such people are alike, though not all can be exposed?

And yet, when an adulteress is found among married women, they neither cast away their wives nor accuse their mothers. But when some crime concerning those who profess the holy name has either been falsely reported or actually revealed, they persist, labor, and strive to make everyone believe it of all.

It is easy, therefore, to compare those who seek to draw the sweetness of their evil tongues from our sufferings with those dogs—if they are to be understood as wicked—who licked the wounds of that poor man who lay before the rich man’s door and endured every hardship, laborious and undeserved, until he came to the rest of Abraham’s bosom (Luke 16:21–23).

## 7

Do not torment me further, you who have some hope in God. Do not multiply the very wounds that those people lick. You, for whom we are in danger every hour, “with conflicts outside and fears within” (2 Corinthians 7:5), danger in the city, danger in the desert, danger from the nations, danger from false brothers (2 Corinthians 11:26)—do not add to my suffering.

I know that you grieve; but can you grieve more bitterly than I? I know that you are troubled, and I fear that, amid the tongues of slanderers, the weak person for whom Christ died may fail and perish.

Do not let our sorrow increase because of you, since your sorrow was not caused by our fault.

For this is what I tried to prevent: if possible, that this evil should neither be neglected, though it had to be avoided, nor brought to your knowledge, where the strong would be tormented fruitlessly and the weak dangerously disturbed.

But the one who, after making this known, allowed you to be tested should give you strength to endure and instruct you from his law. May he teach you and bring you relief from the evil days, until the pit is dug for the sinner (Psalm 94:12–13).

8. I hear that some of you are distressed more deeply by this than by the fall of those two deacons who had come over from the party of Donatus, as though they had insulted Proculeianus’s discipline, or as though they were boasting over us that nothing of this kind had arisen among the clergy of our discipline. Whoever among you did this, I confess, did not do well. Behold, God has taught you that “whoever boasts, let him boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:31). Nor should you reproach heretics with anything except that they are not Catholics, lest you become like them. Since they have nothing to defend in the cause of their division, they seek only to collect the crimes of men, and they falsely broadcast those crimes in even greater number. Since they cannot accuse or obscure the very truth of divine Scripture, by which the Church of Christ, spread everywhere, is commended, they bring into hatred the people through whom it is preached; and concerning these people they can invent whatever occurs to them.

But you did not learn Christ in this way—if, indeed, you heard him and were taught in him (Eph. 4:20–21). For he himself made his faithful secure even concerning wicked stewards who do their own evil deeds while speaking his good words, when he said: “Do whatever they say; but do not do what they do, for they say and do not do” (Matt. 23:3). Pray, indeed, for me, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should be found disqualified (1 Cor. 9:27). Nevertheless, when you boast, boast not in me but in the Lord.

However vigilant the discipline of my household may be, I am a human being and live among human beings. I do not dare claim that my household is better than Noah’s ark, where, among eight people, one was nevertheless found reprobate (Gen. 9:27); or better than Abraham’s household, where it was said, “Cast out the slave woman and her son” (Gen. 21:10); or better than Isaac’s household, concerning whose two twin sons it was said, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. 1:2).

[Note: [Col. 0272] The editors have *cui*. But the better manuscripts have *cujus*.]

Nor is it better than Jacob’s household, where a son violated his father’s bed (Gen. 49:4); or better than David’s household, whose son had intercourse with his sister (2 Sam. 13:14), and whose other son rebelled against his father’s most holy gentleness (ibid. 15:12); or better than the householding of the apostle Paul. Yet, even if he had lived among all good people, he would not have said, “Outside there are conflicts, inside fears” (2 Cor. 7:5). Nor, when speaking of Timothy’s holiness and faith, would he have said, “I have no one who is genuinely concerned for you. For all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Phil. 2:20–21).

Nor is it better than the companionship of the Lord Christ himself, in which eleven good men endured the treacherous thief Judas. Finally, nor is it better than heaven, from which angels fell.

9. But I frankly confess to Your Charity, before the Lord our God, who is witness over my soul, that ever since I began to serve God I have found none better than those who have made progress in monasteries; likewise, I have found none worse than those who have fallen in monasteries. Hence I think that it was written in the Apocalypse: “Let the righteous become more righteous, and let the filthy become filthier still” (Rev. 22:11).

[Note: [Col. 0272] Manuscript *gg* has *ex monasterio* (“from the monastery”). The same codex, together with *cb* and one *v.*, adds *defecerunt* (“have fallen away”).]

Therefore, although we are distressed by certain refuse, we are also comforted by the greater number of ornaments. Do not, then, detest the winepresses because of the dregs that offend your eyes, for from them the Lord’s storehouses are filled with the fruit of more luminous oil.

May the mercy of the Lord our God preserve you, most beloved brothers, in his peace against every ambush of the enemy.

# LETTER LXXIX

[Note: [Col. 0272] It is found only in the Vatican manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 0272] Elsewhere numbered 244; what was 79 is now 198. It was perhaps written in the year 404.]

Augustine, bishop, to a certain Manichaean presbyter, warning him either to resolve the question at which his predecessor Fortunatus had failed, or to depart far from his Church.

You are evading the matter without cause, since it is plainly evident what sort of person you are. The brothers have told me what they discussed with you. It is well that you do not fear death; but you ought to fear that death which you yourself bring upon yourself by blaspheming God. And that you understand this visible death, known to all human beings, to be the separation of the mind from the body is not a great achievement of understanding. But as for what you add concerning your doctrine—that it is the separation of good from evil—if the mind is good and the body evil, then the one who mingled them was not good. Yet you say that God, who is good, mingled them. Therefore either he is evil, or he feared evil.

And you boast that you do not fear a human being, while imagining for yourself a God of such a kind that he feared darkness and therefore mingled good and evil? Do not become puffed up in spirit, as you wrote, because we make you great by wishing to prevent your poisons from spreading pestilence among human beings. The Apostle does not make those whom he calls dogs great when he says, “Beware of dogs” (Phil. 3:2); nor did he make great those whose speech he said spread like gangrene (2 Tim. 2:17).

Therefore I warn you in the name of Christ: if you are prepared, resolve the question at which your predecessor Fortunatus failed.

[Note: [Col. 0273] Augustine defeated Fortunatus in a disputation while he was still a presbyter, according to *Retractions* 1.16. Later, when he was already a bishop, he held another disputation with Felix, who, as he says in *Retractions* 2.8, “had come to Hippo to sow the same error.” This occurred in the year 404, according to the Acts of the disputation with Felix. It may therefore be conjectured that this letter was written to him.]

He had gone away from here in such a manner that he would not return unless, after comparing the disputation with his associates, he found what he could answer in reply, while arguing with the brothers. But if you are not prepared for this, depart from here. Do not pervert the ways of the Lord or entangle and infect the souls of the weak with poisons, lest, with the help of the right hand of our Lord, you blush in shame in a way you had not expected.

# LETTER LXXX

[Note: [Col. 0273] Reviewed against manuscripts *a, bg, bl, c, cc, ff, ggv, j, l, n, r, sb, th, vc*, two *t.*, four *v.*, and the editions of Amerbach, Bad., Erasmus, and Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 0273] Elsewhere numbered 65; what was 80 is now 199. Written in the year 405, around the month of March.]

Augustine asks Paulinus to explain more clearly how we can know the will of God, which must be preferred to our own.

To the holy and beloved of God, deservedly venerable and greatly desired brothers, PAULINUS and THERASIA, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

1. When our dearest brother Celsus was returning your letters, I hastened to discharge my obligation; indeed, I hastened very much. For I had thought that he would remain with us for several more days, but suddenly, having learned of an opportunity to sail, he informed me during the night that he would depart the following day. What could I do, since I could not keep him, and since he was hastening to you, with whom it would be better for him to be? Even if I could have kept him, I ought not to have done so.

Accordingly, I immediately seized upon these few words to dictate and send, while confessing myself indebted to you for a longer letter, once I have been somewhat satisfied concerning you through the return of our venerable brothers and fellow bishops, Theasius

[Note: [Col. 0273] Erasmus and Louvain have *Therasii*. In the Gervasian manuscript, *Thesii*. Several others have *Theasii*. This is also how the name is written in the council held at Carthage on June 26, 404, whose decree sent envoys to the emperor Honorius against the Donatists: Theasius and Evodius, or Evhodius, as the manuscripts have it. These are doubtless the same men who were going to visit Paulinus.]

and Evodius. For we already hope, in the name and with the help of Christ, that you will soon come to us more fully in their hearts and mouths.

As I was writing this, I had already, a few days before, sent another letter through our like-minded son Fortunatianus, a presbyter of the Church of Thagaste,

[Note: [Col. 0273] Bad., Amerbach, and Erasmus have “of the Carthaginian Church.” One Vatican manuscript has “of the Thaganian Church.”]

who was sailing to Rome. Now, therefore, I ask what I usually ask, so that you may do what you usually do: pray for us, that God may see our humility and our labor and forgive all our sins.

2. I desire, if you deem me worthy, to converse with you in writing about such matters as we could discuss if we were present before your senses. Behold, you have solved, with thoroughly Christian understanding and devotion, that little question which I recently proposed, as though, being present before one another amid sweet conversation, I had placed it before you.

But you did so too hurriedly and briefly. The grace of your speech could have dwelt there somewhat longer and more fully if, after saying that you had resolved to persevere in that place which you happily occupy, you had explained somewhat more openly that, if anything else concerning you should please the Lord, you would prefer his will to your own.

[Note: [Col. 0274] Seven manuscripts read *propterea volentes* (“therefore willingly”); Bad., Amerbach, and Erasmus have *propterea praeferre debemus* (“we ought therefore to prefer”), and Louvain has *propterea voluntati praeferre debemus* (“we ought therefore to prefer to [our] will”). The same four editions subsequently read: “There indeed is what we want, but therefore we are compelled,” etc. The reading found in the better manuscripts has been adopted.]

In what way, then, do we know the will of God, which must be preferred to our own will? Is it only in that matter which we must therefore willingly endure because we would be compelled to endure it even unwillingly? For there what we do not want does indeed happen; but for that very reason we correct ourselves so that we may want it, because he wills it—he whose will it is not lawful to refuse on account of its excellence, nor possible to escape on account of its omnipotence. Thus, another girded Peter and carried him where he did not want to go (John 21:18); nevertheless, he went where he did not want to go, and willingly overcame the bitter death.

Or is it also the case where we have the power not to change a decision, although something else presents itself in which the will of God calling us to change our decision appears more clearly—not because our former decision was bad, but because it was right to remain in it unless he called us to another? For it was not evil for Abraham to nourish and raise his son, as far as it depended on him, for the whole course of his life. But when he was suddenly commanded to kill him, he certainly changed not a previously bad decision, but one that would have become bad had it not been changed after the command.

[Note: [Col. 0274] Louvain has “which would rather have been bad if changed.” Bad. and several manuscripts have “if it had rather been altered.” Erasmus has “if changed for better things.” But the reading in manuscript *j* is better: “if it had been changed after the command.”]

In this matter also, I have no doubt that you see it in the same way.

3. But very often it is not by a voice from heaven, not through a prophet, not by a revelation, whether of a dream or of that departure of mind called ecstasy, but through events themselves, which occur and call us to something other than we had decided, that we are compelled to recognize that God’s will is different from what ours had been.

It is as though we had decided to depart, and something arose which, after the truth had been consulted concerning our duty, forbade us to leave; or as though, while we were deciding to remain there, something were announced which, after that same truth had been consulted, compelled us to depart.

Concerning this third kind of circumstance that leads us to change a decision, I ask you to discuss with me more fully and clearly what you think. It often troubles us, and it is difficult not to omit something that ought rather to be done, while we do not want to change what we had previously decided to continue doing.

[Note: [Col. 0274] The editions have *mutare volumus* (“we want to change”); but nine manuscripts read *mutare nolumus* (“we do not want to change”), so that the preferable course which presents itself is abandoned.]

That former undertaking was not in itself evil; it becomes evil because, when something preferable to it presents itself, the latter is abandoned. If the new circumstance had not arisen, we could have continued in the former course not only without blame but even with praise.

Here it is difficult not to go astray. Here the prophetic voice prevails entirely: “Who understands his transgressions?” (Ps. 18:13). I beg you to make me a participant in your thoughts: in such circumstances, what do you usually do, or what do you discover ought to be done?

# LETTER LXXXI

[Note: [Col. 0275] Reviewed against manuscripts *a, bg, bl, bn, c, cc, fs, g, gv, j, l, n, r, sb, t, vc*, nine *v.*, and the editions of Amerbach, Bad., Erasmus, and Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 0275] Elsewhere numbered 18; what was 81 is now 48. Perhaps written in the year 405.]

Jerome to Augustine, excusing himself for having replied too freely to Augustine’s letter in Letter 75, and asking that, setting aside contentious questions, they should henceforth confer with one another as friends and converse peacefully in the field of the sacred Scriptures.

To the truly holy and most blessed pope AUGUSTINE, JEROME sends greetings in Christ.

When I anxiously asked our holy brother Firmus

[Note: [Col. 0275] The name Firmus is omitted here in eight Vatican manuscripts and in six others among our manuscripts, but it appears in almost all of them at the beginning of the following letter.]

what you were doing, I was glad to hear that you were safe. Again, when I not only hoped for but demanded a letter from you, he told me—without your knowing—that you had departed from Africa. Therefore, through him who embraces you with unique love, I return your greetings and at the same time beg you to forgive my modesty, since I could not refuse one who had long been urging me to write back.

I did not answer you, but the case itself. And if it is a fault to have answered, I ask you to hear patiently that it is a much greater fault to have provoked the answer. But let such complaints be dismissed. Let there be pure brotherhood between us, and henceforth let us send one another letters not of contentious questions but of charity.

The holy brothers

[Note: [Col. 0275] Manuscript *t.* has “holy fathers.” All the others more correctly have “brothers.” Jerome rejects the former designation in chapter 4 of his letter to the Galatians.]

who serve the Lord with us greet you abundantly. I beg you to discharge my duty of respect by greeting the holy men who bear Christ’s easy yoke with you, especially the holy and worthy pope Alypius. May Christ our omnipotent God preserve you safe and mindful of me, truly holy and most blessed pope.

If you have read my book of Expositions on Jonah, I think you will not accept the ridiculous question concerning the gourd. But if the friend who first attacked me with a sword has been driven back by the pen, it belongs to your humanity and justice to rebuke the accuser, not the respondent. If you please, let us play with one another in the field of the Scriptures without causing each other pain.

# LETTER LXXXII

[Note: [Col. 0275] For this revision, manuscripts *a, a, bg, bl, bn, c, cc, fs, g, gv, j, l, n, r, s, sb, t, vc*, nine *v.*, and the editions of Amerbach, Bad., Erasmus, and Louvain were collated.]

[Note: [Col. 0275] Elsewhere numbered 19; what was 81 is now 202. Written shortly after the preceding letter.]

Having received Jerome’s preceding Letters 72, 75, and 81, Augustine replies more fully concerning the interpretation of the passage in the Epistle to the Galatians, affirming that Peter was rightly and truthfully rebuked by Paul. For the rest, he asks pardon if certain incautious expressions offended Jerome, explaining that, through no fault of his own, the letter had wandered through many hands before reaching the person to whom it had been written.

[Col. 0276] To his most beloved lord, honored in the compassion of Christ, his holy brother and fellow presbyter HIERONYMUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

## CHAPTER ONE

1. Some time ago I sent Your Charity a lengthy letter in reply to the one you recall sending through your holy son Asterius, now not only my brother but also my fellow bishop. I still do not know whether that letter deserved to reach your hands, except that through our most sincere brother Firmus you write: “If the one who first attacked you with a sword has been driven back by the pen, it belongs to my humanity and justice to rebuke the accuser, not the respondent.” From this very slight indication I somehow infer that you have read my letter.

In it I lamented that such discord had arisen between you, whose great friendship—spread everywhere by report—had delighted fraternal charity. I did not do this by censuring Your Brotherhood, whose fault in that matter I would not dare claim to have recognized; I did it by grieving over human misery, since, in retaining friendships through mutual charity, permanence remains uncertain however great that charity may be.

Yet I had preferred to learn from your reply whether you had granted me the pardon I had requested. I wish this to be made clearer to me, although a certain cheerful expression in your letter seems to indicate that I have obtained this also—if, that is, your letter was sent after you had read mine, which is by no means apparent from it.

2. You ask—or rather, with the confidence of charity, you command—that we “play with one another in the field of the Scriptures without causing each other pain.” As far as I am concerned, I would prefer that we engage in this matter seriously rather than playfully.

But if you were pleased to use this word because of the ease it conveys, I confess that I expect something greater from the kindness of your powers and from your wisdom, with its learned, leisurely, long-standing, studious, ingenious diligence,

[Note: [Col. 0276] Louvain has *diligenti* (“diligent”). Most of the manuscripts have *diligentia* (“diligence”).]

which the Holy Spirit has not merely granted you but also dictated to you, so that in great and laborious questions you may help me—not as one playing in the field of the Scriptures, but as one gasping for breath in the mountains.

But if, because of the cheerfulness that ought to exist among the dearest of friends when they discuss matters together, you thought it appropriate to say, “Let us play”—whether what we are discussing is open and level ground, or steep and difficult—then please teach me how we can accomplish this. Suppose something moves us which, whether because we attend insufficiently carefully or because we understand too slowly, has not persuaded us, and we try to assert what seems right to us against it. If we speak with somewhat freer confidence, how can we avoid falling under suspicion of childish boasting, as though we were seeking renown for our own name by accusing distinguished men?

And if something harsh must be brought forth because refutation requires it, how can we surround it with gentler language so that it becomes tolerable, lest we be judged to be drawing a sword smeared with honey?

[Note: [Col. 0276] So the editions read. Nineteen manuscripts lack the particle *ne* (“lest”).]

Unless perhaps the way to avoid both this fault and the suspicion of this fault is to argue with a more learned friend in such a way that whatever he says must be approved, and that we are not permitted even for the sake of inquiry to resist slightly.

[Col. 0277] 3. Then indeed one plays in the field without any fear of causing offense; but it would be astonishing if we were not being mocked. I confess to Your Charity that I have learned to show this fear and honor only to those books of Scripture that are called canonical: I firmly believe that none of their authors erred in writing.

If I encounter in them anything that seems contrary to the truth, I will not hesitate to conclude that either the manuscript is corrupt, or the translator has failed to grasp what was said, or I myself have not understood it.

I read other authors in such a way that, however great their holiness and learning, I do not consider something true because they themselves thought it so, but because, either through those canonical authors or through a probable line of reasoning, they have been able to persuade me that it does not depart from the truth.

Nor do I think that you, my brother, think otherwise. I certainly do not suppose that you wish your books to be read as though they were the books of the Prophets or Apostles, concerning whose freedom from every error it is sacrilegious to doubt.

Far be this from pious humility and a truthful judgment about yourself. If you were not endowed with such humility, you would certainly not have said: “Would that we might deserve your embraces and, through mutual discussion, either teach or learn something.”

## CHAPTER TWO

4. If I believe that you said this about yourself, considering your life and character, not deceptively or falsely, how much more reasonable is it for me to believe that the apostle Paul meant precisely what he wrote when he said of Peter and Barnabas: “When I saw that they were not walking rightly toward the truth of the Gospel, I said to Peter before everyone: If you, though you are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how do you compel the Gentiles to judaize?” (Gal. 2:14).

If I cannot be certain that someone will not deceive me in writing or speaking, how can I be certain that the Apostle did not deceive his children, whom he was again in labor with until Christ—that is, the truth—was formed in them (Gal. 4:19)? After prefacing his words by saying, “As for what I am writing to you, behold, before God, I do not lie” (Gal. 1:20), was he nevertheless not writing truthfully, but deceiving them through some dispensational pretense, claiming that he had seen Peter and Barnabas not walking rightly toward the truth of the Gospel and had opposed Peter to his face for no other reason than that he was compelling the Gentiles to judaize?

5. But, someone may say, it is better to believe that the apostle Paul wrote something untrue than that the apostle Peter did something wrong. If this is so, let us say—God forbid—that it is better to believe that the Gospel lies than that Peter denied Christ (Matt. 26:75), and that the Book of Kings lies than that so great a prophet, so remarkably chosen by the Lord God, committed adultery by desiring and taking another man’s wife, and committed so dreadful a murder by having her husband killed (2 Sam. 11:4, 17).

No. I shall read Holy Scripture, placed at the highest and heavenly summit of authority, with certainty and confidence in its truth, and in it I shall learn truthfully which human beings were approved, corrected, or condemned, rather than, because I sometimes fear believing that reprehensible actions occurred in persons of otherwise admirable excellence, allow the divine utterances themselves to become suspect to me everywhere.

6. The Manichaeans assert that many passages of the divine Scriptures, by whose crystal clarity of meaning their wicked error is convicted, are false because they cannot twist them into another meaning. Yet they do not attribute this falsity to the apostles who wrote them, but to certain corrupters of the manuscripts.

Because they have never been able to prove this either from a larger number of manuscripts or from more ancient copies, or from the authority of the earlier language from which the Latin books were translated, they depart defeated and confounded by the truth known to all.

Does your holy prudence not understand how great an opportunity for their wickedness would be opened if we said that the apostolic writings had not been falsified by others but that the Apostles themselves had written falsehoods?

7. “It is not credible,” you say, “that Paul reproved Peter for doing what Paul himself had done.” I am not now asking what he did; I am asking what he wrote. This bears above all on the question I have undertaken, so that the truth of the divine Scriptures, entrusted to memory for the building up of our faith—not by just anyone but by the Apostles themselves, and therefore received into the supreme authority of the canon—may remain truthful and beyond doubt in every respect.

For if Peter did what he ought to have done, then Paul lied when he said that he saw him not walking rightly toward the truth of the Gospel. Whoever does what he ought to do certainly acts rightly. Therefore the person who says that someone did not act rightly in doing what he knows that person ought to have done speaks falsely about him.

But if Paul wrote the truth, then it is true that Peter was not at that time walking rightly toward the truth of the Gospel. He was therefore doing what he ought not to do. And if Paul himself had already done something of that kind, I would much rather believe that he himself was corrected and could not disregard the correction of his fellow apostle than that he inserted a falsehood somewhere in his Epistle—and in any Epistle, how much more in the one in which he had first declared: “As for what I am writing to you, behold, before God, I do not lie” (Gal. 1:20)?

8. I believe that Peter acted in such a way as to compel the Gentiles to judaize. For this is what I read Paul to have written, and I do not believe that he lied. Therefore Peter was not acting rightly in this matter.

It was contrary to the truth of the Gospel for those who believed in Christ to think that they could not be saved without those ancient sacraments. This was the position argued at Antioch by those who had believed from circumcision, against whom Paul fought steadfastly and vigorously.

Paul himself, however, did not act as he did in order to suggest that Christian salvation was given through those sacraments—whether when he circumcised Timothy (Acts 16:3), fulfilled a vow at Cenchreae (Acts 18:18), or, after being admonished by James at Jerusalem, undertook with those who understood the matter to celebrate those lawful rites (Acts 21:26). Rather, he acted so that it would not be thought that he condemned as idolatry those practices which God had commanded to be performed in earlier times, appropriately, as shadows of things to come.

For this is what James said had been heard about him: that he taught apostasy from Moses (Acts 21:21). It would certainly be wicked for those who believe in Christ to be severed from Christ’s prophet as though they detested and condemned his teaching. Christ himself says of Moses: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also, for he wrote about me” (John 5:46).

9. Consider, I beg you, James’s actual words: “You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews who have believed in Christ, and they are all zealous for the Law. They have heard about you that you teach apostasy from Moses among the Jews who live among the Gentiles, saying that they ought not to circumcise their children or walk according to the custom.

“What, then, is to be done? The multitude will certainly assemble, for they will hear that you have arrived. Therefore do what we tell you. We have four men who have a vow upon them. Take them, sanctify yourself with them, and pay their expenses so that they may shave their heads. Then everyone will know that what they have heard about you is false, but that you yourself also keep the Law.

“As for the Gentiles who have believed, we have sent our judgment that they should observe nothing of this kind, except that they should keep themselves from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, and from fornication” (Acts 21:20–25).

I do not think it obscure that James gave this advice so that those who had heard these things about Paul might know them to be false—those who, although they had believed in Christ from among the Jews, were nevertheless zealous for the Law. He did this lest they should think that, through Christ’s teaching, the practices delivered through Moses to the fathers—as though they were sacrilegious and not written at God’s command—were being condemned.

This accusation against Paul had not been spread by those who understood the spirit in which these practices should then be observed by Jewish believers: namely, to commend the divine authority and the prophetic holiness of those sacraments, not to obtain the salvation that had already been revealed in Christ and administered through the sacrament of Baptism. Rather, it had been spread by those who wanted these practices observed as though salvation in the Gospel were impossible for believers without them.

They had recognized Paul as an especially forceful preacher of grace and as most opposed to their intention, teaching that a person is not justified through those practices but through the grace of Jesus Christ, on whose announcement those shadows in the Law had been commanded. Therefore, seeking to arouse envy and stir up persecution against him, they accused him as an enemy of the Law and of the divine commandments.

He could not more appropriately avoid the hostility generated by this false accusation than by himself celebrating the practices that he was thought to condemn as sacrilegious. In this way he showed that Jews at that time were not to be prohibited from them as wicked rites, while Gentiles were not to be compelled to them as necessary rites.

10. For if he really rejected these practices in the way that had been reported about him, and accepted their celebration in order to conceal his position through a simulated action, James would not have said, “Everyone will know,” but, “Everyone will think that what they have heard about you is false”—especially since, in Jerusalem itself, the Apostles had already decreed that no one should compel the Gentiles to judaize (Acts 15:28).

They had not, however, decreed that no one should at that time prevent Jews from judaizing, although Christian teaching no longer compelled even the Jews themselves to do so.

Therefore, if after the Apostles’ decree Peter maintained at Antioch that pretense by which he compelled the Gentiles to judaize—something that he himself was no longer compelled to do, although, for the sake of commending the divine utterances entrusted to the Jews, he was not prohibited from it—what wonder that Paul constrained him openly to affirm what he remembered having decreed with the other Apostles at Jerusalem?

11. But if Peter did this—as I am more inclined to believe—before that council at Jerusalem, it is still not surprising that Paul wanted him not timidly to conceal but confidently to affirm what he already knew Peter shared with him.

Perhaps this was because he had discussed the Gospel with him; or because, at the calling of Cornelius the centurion, he had learned that Peter had been divinely instructed about this matter; or because, before those whom Peter feared had come to Antioch, he had seen Peter eat with Gentiles.

For we do not deny that Peter already held the position held by Paul. Paul was therefore not then teaching him what was true in this matter. Rather, he was reproving his pretense, by which the Gentiles were being compelled to judaize. The sole reason was that all those practices were being performed in a pretended manner, as though what those people were saying were true: that believers could not be saved without circumcision of the foreskin and the other observances that were shadows of things to come.

12. He circumcised Timothy, therefore, so that the Jews—and especially Timothy’s maternal relatives—would not think that those who from among the Gentiles had believed in Christ detested circumcision as they detest idolatry. God had commanded the former, whereas Satan had persuaded people to practice the latter.

He did not circumcise Titus so that he would not give an opportunity to those who said that believers could not be saved without circumcision, and who might falsely claim, to the deception of the Gentiles, that Paul himself held this view.

Paul himself makes this sufficiently clear when he says: “But even Titus, who was with me, although he was a Greek, was not compelled to be circumcised—because of the false brothers who had slipped in, who had entered secretly to spy out our freedom, which we have in Christ Jesus, in order to bring us into slavery. We did not yield in submission to them even for an hour, so that the truth of the Gospel might remain with you” (Gal. 2:3–5).

Here it is clear what he understood them to be seeking. For this reason he did not do what he had done in Timothy, although he was able to do so in the freedom by which he had shown that those sacraments ought neither to be sought as necessary nor condemned as sacrilegious.

[Note: [Col. 0280] Six manuscripts have *ostenderet* (“he might show”) instead of *ostenderat* (“he had shown”).]

[Note: [Col. 0280] Two Vatican manuscripts have: “could not be saved, and that the Teacher of the Gentiles himself held this view.”]

13. But in this discussion we must evidently take care lest, like the philosophers, we call certain human actions intermediate between right action and sin—actions that are counted neither among right actions nor among sins—and thus be pressed by the argument that observance of the ceremonies of the Law cannot be indifferent but must be either good or evil.

If we call it good, we too will be compelled to observe them; but if we call it evil, we will have to believe that the Apostles observed them not truthfully but deceptively.

For my part, I fear for the Apostles not so much the example of the philosophers—even though the philosophers do say something true in their disputations—as that of courtroom advocates, who lie when pleading the cases of others.

If this comparison was thought suitable for confirming the pretense of Peter and Paul in the exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians,

[Note: [Col. 0281] Jerome introduces it in this way.]

why should I fear before you the name of philosophers? They are not vain because they say everything falsely, but because they rely on many falsehoods and, even when they happen to say what is true, they are alienated from the grace of Christ, who is truth itself.

14. Why should I not say that those commands concerning the ancient sacraments were neither good, because people are not justified by them—for they are shadows announcing the grace by which we are justified—nor evil, because they were divinely commanded and appropriate to their time and persons?

A prophetic statement even assists me here, in which God says that he gave that people commands that were not good (Ezek. 20:25). Perhaps for this reason he did not call them evil but merely “not good”: that is, not of such a kind that people are made good by them, or cannot be good without them.

I would like Your Kindly Sincerity to teach me whether, when some holy Easterner comes to Rome, he fasts on Saturday as a matter of pretense, except on the day of the Easter vigil. If we say that this is evil, we will condemn not only the Roman Church but also many churches near it and somewhat farther away, where the same custom is observed and remains.

But if we think that not fasting on Saturday is evil, with what rashness shall we accuse all the churches of the East and the much greater part of the Christian world? Does it please you that we call this something intermediate, yet acceptable to the person who does it not deceptively but in accordance with an appropriate fellowship and observance?

And yet we do not read that anything of this kind was commanded to Christians in the canonical books. How much less do I dare call evil what I cannot deny, while holding the Christian faith itself, that God commanded, since I have learned that I am not justified by it but by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord?

### 15

I therefore say that circumcision of the foreskin and other practices of this kind were divinely given to the former people through the Testament called the Old, as signs of future things that had to be fulfilled through Christ. When those things arrived, these practices remained for Christians to read about, merely for understanding the prophecy previously given, but not necessarily to perform—as though the revelation of faith, which these things signified as something yet to come, were still awaited.

Although, therefore, these practices were not to be imposed upon the Gentiles, they ought not for that reason to have been removed from Jewish custom as though they were detestable and condemnable. Accordingly, as the sound preaching of the grace of Christ gradually grew stronger—the grace by which alone believers would know that they were justified and saved—the whole practice of those shadows of things formerly future, but then already arriving and present, was to be brought to an end in the case of those Jews whom the presence of the Lord’s flesh and the apostolic age had encountered in that condition.

For their commendation, it was enough that these practices should not be avoided as detestable and akin to idolatry. Beyond that they should not proceed, lest they be thought necessary—as though salvation came from them or could not exist without them. This was the belief of the heretics who, while wishing to be both Jews and Christians, were able to be neither Jews nor Christians. You graciously and most kindly warned me that I must avoid their view, although I was never part of it.

Peter had fallen into not agreement with that view but a pretense of it, through fear; hence Paul wrote of him with complete truth that he had seen him “not walking straightforwardly according to the truth of the gospel,” and said to him with complete truth that he was compelling the Gentiles to Judaize. Paul certainly did not compel them to do so. For this reason he truthfully observed those ancient practices, wherever there was need, in order to show that they were not to be condemned. Yet he persistently preached that the faithful were saved not by those practices but by the revealed grace of faith, so that he might not compel anyone to accept them as necessary.

Thus, I believe, the Apostle Paul truthfully carried out all those practices. Yet I neither compel nor permit anyone now made a Christian from the Jews to celebrate them truthfully—just as you, who think that Paul pretended to perform them, neither compel nor permit this man to pretend to perform them.

### 16

Or would you have me also say that this is the substance of the question—or rather, of your position: that after the gospel of Christ, believing Jews do well if they offer the sacrifices that Paul offered; if they circumcise their sons; if they observe the Sabbath, as Paul did in the case of Timothy and as all the Jews observed, provided that they do these things falsely and deceptively?

If this is so, we are no longer falling into the heresy of Ebion or of those commonly called Nazarenes, or into any other ancient heresy, but I do not know what new one—one all the more pernicious because it arises not from error but from deliberate and willful deception.

But if, in order to clear yourself of this position, you reply that the Apostles commendably pretended to do these things so that the weak, many of whom had believed from among the Jews and did not yet understand that these practices should be rejected, would not be scandalized; and that now, since the teaching of Christian grace has been confirmed among so many nations, and also confirmed throughout all the Churches of Christ by the reading of the Law and the Prophets, so that these things may be recited for understanding but not observed, anyone who wished to perform them by pretending would be insane—why may I not say that the Apostle Paul and other Christians sound in faith ought then, by observing those ancient sacraments truthfully for a short time, to commend them, lest it be thought that the observances of those prophetic signs, preserved by the most devout fathers, were to be detested by later generations as diabolical sacrileges?

For when the faith that had previously been foretold by those observances had come and had been revealed after the Lord’s death and resurrection, they had lost, as it were, the life of their function. Nevertheless, just as dead bodies had to be conveyed in some manner to burial with the offices required by the occasion—not by pretense but religiously—and not immediately abandoned or cast away to be mangled by the bites of enemies like dogs, so now any Christian, even if he is from the Jews, who wishes similarly to celebrate those practices is not a pious escort or bearer of a body, but an impious violator of a burial, digging up ashes that should have been left at rest.

[Note: At Col. 0282, *officiis* (“offices”) is absent in twenty-two manuscripts.]

### 17

I freely admit that in what my letter contains—namely, that Paul had undertaken to celebrate the Jewish sacraments, although he was already Christ’s apostle, in order to teach that it was not harmful for those who wished to preserve them as they had received them from their parents through the Law—I failed to add the qualification “only at that time when the grace of faith was first revealed.” At that time this was not harmful.

[Note: Editions read: “As time progressed, however, it was harmful unless those observances were abandoned by all Christians; lest, if they then occurred, they should not be distinguished,” etc. Twenty manuscripts lack the words *erat perniciosum, nisi* (“it was harmful, unless”); they then read: “lest, if they then occurred,” that is, “lest they should be abandoned at that first time.”]

As time progressed, however, those observances had to be abandoned by all Christians. Otherwise, if this happened at once, it would not be understood that what God commanded his people through Moses was different from what the unclean spirit instituted in the temples of demons. Therefore my negligence is to be blamed, because I did not add this, rather than your rebuke.

Nevertheless, long before I received your letter, when writing against Faustus the Manichaean, I explained—though briefly—how I understood this same passage, and I did not omit this point there. Your Kindness may read it, if you do not disdain to do so; and through our dear friends, by whom I have now sent this writing, you may obtain whatever assurance you wish that I had dictated this earlier.

Believe me concerning my mind: speaking before God, and making this claim by the right of charity, I have never thought that Christians now made from the Jews ought to celebrate those ancient sacraments in any spirit or frame of mind, or that they are in any way permitted to do so. I have always understood Paul in this way, from the time when his writings became known to me—just as you too think that no one in the present age should pretend to perform these things, since you believe that this is what the Apostles did.

### 18

Therefore, just as you speak in the opposite way and, as you write, proclaim in a free voice—even though the world protests—that the ceremonies of the Jews are both harmful and deadly to Christians, and that whoever observes them, whether Jew or Gentile, is cast down into the abyss of the devil, so I entirely affirm this statement of yours and add: whoever observes them, whether Jew or Gentile, is cast down into the abyss of the devil—not only if he does so truthfully, but also if he does so by pretense. What more do you seek?

But just as you distinguish the Apostles’ pretense from the circumstances of the present time, so I distinguish the truthful conduct at that time of the Apostle Paul in all these matters from observance at the present time of Jewish ceremonies, even if that observance is entirely without pretense. For then it was to be approved; now it is to be detested.

Thus, although we read, “The Law and the Prophets were until John the Baptist” (Luke 16:16); and although the Jews sought to kill Christ because he not only broke the Sabbath but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God (John 5:18); and although “we have received grace for grace,” and “the Law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:16–17); and although God promised through Jeremiah that he would give a new covenant to the house of Judah, “not according to the covenant which I made with their fathers” (Jer. 31:31)—nevertheless, I do not think that the Lord himself was deceitfully circumcised by his parents.

Or, if his age did not at all prevent this, I do not think that he deceitfully said to the leper—whom certainly not that observance commanded through Moses but he himself had ordered—“Go and offer for yourself the sacrifice that Moses commanded, as a testimony to them” (Mark 1:44). Nor did he go up deceitfully to the feast. So far was this from being done for display before human beings that he did not go up openly but secretly (John 7:10).

### 19

But, someone says, the same Apostle declared: “Behold, I Paul say to you that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. 5:2). Did he therefore deceive Timothy and make Christ profit him nothing? Or, because this was done deceitfully, did it therefore do no harm?

Yet Paul did not qualify his statement in this way. He did not say, “If you are circumcised truthfully,” any more than he said, “If you are circumcised deceitfully”; rather, without any exception, he said: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing.”

Therefore, just as you wish to make room here for your position, so that “unless it is deceitfully” is to be understood, I reasonably insist that you also allow us to understand there that the words “If you are circumcised” were spoken of those who wished to be circumcised because they thought that otherwise they could not be saved in Christ.

Whoever, then, was circumcised at that time with this disposition, this will, and this intention received absolutely no benefit from Christ. As he says openly elsewhere: “For if righteousness is through the Law, then Christ died for nothing” (Gal. 2:21).

This is also made clear by the passage you yourself cited: “You are severed from Christ, you who are justified in the Law; you have fallen away from grace.” He therefore rebukes those who believed that they were justified in the Law, not those who observed those lawful practices in honor of him by whom they had been commanded, understanding both the reason for which they had been commanded—as foretellers of the truth—and how long they were to remain in force.

Hence his statement: “If you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the Law” (Gal. 5:18). From this, as you seem to infer, it becomes apparent that the person who is under the Law—not dispensatively, as you think our ancestors intended, but truly, as I understand it—does not possess the Holy Spirit.

[Note: Editions read *apparere* (“to become apparent”); two Vatican manuscripts read *apparet* (“it becomes apparent”).]

### 20

It seems to me a substantial question what it means to be under the Law in the manner condemned by the Apostle. I do not think that he says this because of circumcision, or those sacrifices that were then offered by the fathers but are not now offered by Christians, or other practices of this kind. Rather, he also means the very command of the Law, “You shall not covet” (Exod. 20:17; Deut. 5:21), which we certainly acknowledge Christians ought to observe and which is especially proclaimed in the light of the gospel.

He calls the Law holy, and the commandment holy, righteous, and good. Then it adds: “Therefore, did what is good become death to me? By no means! Rather, sin, so that it might be shown to be sin, worked death in me through what is good, so that through the commandment sin might become exceedingly sinful” (Rom. 7:12–13).

What he says here—that sin becomes exceedingly sinful through the commandment—he says elsewhere in these words: “The Law entered so that the trespass might increase. But where the trespass increased, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. 5:20). And elsewhere, when he had spoken above about the dispensation of grace, by which grace itself justifies, he asks as if inquiring: “What then is the Law?” He immediately answers: “It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made” (Gal. 3:19).

He therefore says that those are damnably under the Law whom the Law makes guilty because they do not fulfill it. They do not understand the benefit of grace for carrying out God’s commands, and in proud arrogance presume as though they relied on their own strength.

“For the fullness of the Law is love” (Rom. 13:10). “The love of God has been poured into our hearts,” not through ourselves, “but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). A longer treatment, perhaps in a work of its own, is owed to explaining this matter as fully as necessary.

If, then, the command of the Law, “You shall not covet” (Rom. 13:9), holds a person guilty under itself, when human weakness has not been helped by God’s grace, and condemns the transgressor rather than freeing the sinner, how much less could those practices that were commanded for the sake of signification—circumcision and the rest—justify anyone, since, as the revelation of grace became more widely known, they necessarily had to be abolished?

Nevertheless, they were not for that reason to be avoided as the diabolical sacrileges of the Gentiles, even when the grace that had been foretold by such shadows had already begun to be revealed. Rather, they were to be permitted for a short time, especially to those who had come from the people to whom they had been given. Afterward, once they had been buried with honor, they were to be abandoned irreparably by all Christians.

### 21

But what do you mean, I ask you, by saying, “Not dispensatively, as our ancestors intended”? Either this is what I call an officious lie—that this dispensation is a duty consisting, as it were, in honorable lying—or I simply cannot see what else it could be. Unless perhaps, by adding the name “dispensation,” a lie ceases to be a lie. But if that is absurd, why do you not openly say that an officious lie must be defended?

Unless perhaps the word itself troubles you, because the term *officium* is not so customary in ecclesiastical books. Our Ambrose was not afraid of it: he chose to call some of his books, full of useful instructions, *On Duties*.

Is a person to be blamed if he lies dutifully, but approved if he lies dispensatively? I ask you: let the person who thinks this lie wherever he chooses. For this too is a major question—whether a good man, indeed a Christian man, may ever lie, when such men have been told, “Let your ‘Yes’ be yes and your ‘No’ be no, so that you may not fall under judgment” (James 5:12; Matt. 5:37), and when they hear in faith, “You will destroy all who speak lies” (Ps. 5:7).

### 22

But this, as I said, is another and a substantial question. Let the person who holds this view choose where he will lie, provided that he firmly believe and wholly defend that lying is absent from the writers of the sacred Scriptures, especially the canonical Scriptures.

Otherwise the stewards of Christ, of whom it is said, “What is required of stewards is that they be found faithful” (1 Cor. 4:2), might seem to have learned something great and to lie faithfully in place of dispensing the truth, although in Latin the word *faith* is said to have received its name from the fact that what is said is done. Where what is said is done, there is certainly no place for lying.

The Apostle Paul, therefore, as a faithful steward, unquestionably displays faithfulness to us in writing, because he was a steward of truth, not of falsehood. Accordingly, he truly wrote that he had seen Peter not walking straightforwardly according to the truth of the gospel, and that he had opposed him to his face because he was compelling the Gentiles to Judaize.

Peter, for his part, accepted what Paul had done usefully through the freedom of charity with the piety of holy and gracious humility. In this way he offered posterity a rarer and holier example: they should not disdain, if they had perhaps abandoned the path of righteousness somewhere, to be corrected even by those who came later.

Paul offered another example, so that even lesser persons might confidently dare to resist their superiors in defense of evangelical truth, while preserving brotherly charity. For although it is better to deviate from the path not at all than in any respect, it is nevertheless far more remarkable and praiseworthy willingly to accept correction than boldly to correct one who has gone astray.

There is therefore praise for righteous freedom in Paul and for holy humility in Peter. As far as I can judge according to my limited ability, this ought rather to have been defended against the calumniating Porphyry than to have given him a greater opportunity for abuse—an opportunity to accuse Christians much more bitterly either of writing their own writings deceitfully or of bearing the sacraments of their God deceitfully.

## CHAPTER III

### 23

You demand that I show at least one person whose opinion I have followed in this matter, since you have mentioned by name so many who preceded you in what you assert. You ask that, if I rebuke you for erring, I allow you to err along with such men, none of whom, I confess, I have read.

Although there are nearly six or seven of them, you yourself weaken the authority of four. You say that the Laodicean, whose name you do not mention, has recently departed from the Church; Alexander was an ancient heretic; and I read in your more recent works that Origen and Didymus have been criticized by you—not moderately, nor concerning insignificant questions, although you previously praised Origen admirably.

I therefore think that I should not err with these men, because you yourself would not tolerate it—although this is said as though they had not erred in this opinion. For who would wish to err with just anyone?

Three, then, remain: Eusebius of Emesa, Theodore of Heraclea, and John, whom you mention a little later and who long ago governed the Church of Constantinople in the episcopal office.

### 24

Furthermore, if you ask or recall what our Ambrose and likewise our Cyprian thought about this, you may perhaps find that we too have not lacked men whom we could follow in what we assert. [Ambrose, *Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians*; Cyprian, Letter 71 to Quintus.]

Yet, as I said shortly before, I owe this frank servitude only to the canonical Scriptures. I follow them alone in such a way that I have no doubt that their authors made no mistake in them at all and inserted nothing deceitfully.

Therefore, when I look for a third person, so that I may set three against your three, I could perhaps easily find one, as I think, if I had read much. Nevertheless, the Apostle Paul himself comes to mind in place of all these—or rather, above them all.

I take refuge in him. Against all interpreters of his writings who think otherwise, I appeal to him himself. I question and interrogate him concerning what he wrote to the Galatians: when he said that he had seen Peter not walking straightforwardly according to the truth of the gospel and had therefore opposed him to his face because by that pretense he was compelling the Gentiles to Judaize, did he write the truth, or did he perhaps lie through some dispensative falsehood of which I know nothing?

And I hear him crying out to me shortly before, at the beginning of the same narrative, in a devout voice: “Now concerning the things that I write to you, behold, before God, I do not lie” (Gal. 1:20).

### 25

Let those who think otherwise forgive me; I place greater trust in so great an Apostle swearing in his own writings and on behalf of his own writings than in any highly educated person arguing about the writings of another.

Nor am I afraid to say that I defend Paul in such a way as to maintain that he did not pretend to the error of the Jews but was truly in error. For he was not pretending to error when, with apostolic freedom—as suited that time—he commended those ancient sacraments by performing them wherever there was need. They had been established prophetically not by Satan’s cunning for deceiving human beings, but by God’s providence for foretelling future events.

Nor was he truly in the error of the Jews, since he not only knew but also persistently and vigorously preached that those who thought these practices should be imposed upon the Gentiles or were necessary for the justification of any believers were in error.

### 26

When I said that he became as a Jew to the Jews and as a Gentile to the Gentiles—not through the craft of a liar but through the feeling of one who shares another’s weakness—you seem not to have paid sufficient attention to what I meant; or perhaps I myself was unable to explain it adequately.

I did not say this because he mercifully feigned those practices. Rather, he did not pretend to the things in which his conduct resembled that of Jews, any more than he pretended to those things in which his conduct resembled that of Gentiles, which you too have mentioned. In this you have helped me, and I acknowledge it without resentment.

For when I asked in my letter how he could be thought to have become as a Jew to Jews because he deceitfully undertook the Jewish sacraments, since he also became as a Gentile to Gentiles but nevertheless did not deceitfully undertake the sacrifices of the Gentiles, you replied that he became as a Gentile to Gentiles in that he retained the foreskin and freely allowed himself to eat foods condemned by the Jews.

Here I ask whether he did this too by pretense. If that is utterly absurd and false, then in the same way, in those matters in which he conformed to Jewish custom, he acted through prudent freedom, not slavish necessity—or, what is more disgraceful, through deceitful rather than faithful dispensation.

### 27

For, as he himself testifies, to the faithful and to those who have recognized the truth—unless perhaps he is deceiving us here too—“every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving” (1 Tim. 4:4).

Therefore, for Paul himself—not merely as a man but especially as a most faithful steward; not merely as one who recognized the truth but also as its teacher—every creature of God in the realm of food was good, not by pretense but truly.

Why, then, although he did not pretend to accept the sacred rites and ceremonies of the Gentiles, but truly thought and taught this about food and the foreskin, did he become as a Gentile to Gentiles, while he could become as a Jew to Jews only by deceitfully accepting the Jewish sacraments?

Why, when grafted into the wild olive, did he preserve the faithful truth of his dispensation, but when dealing with the natural branches established not outside the tree but within it, did he put forward some veil of dispensative pretense?

Why, when he became as a Gentile to Gentiles, did he teach what he thought and say what he thought; but when he became as a Jew to Jews, did he conceal one thing in his heart and bring forth another in words, deeds, and writings?

Far be it from us to think this. For he owed charity to both groups “from a pure heart and a good conscience and a sincere faith” (1 Tim. 1:5). Accordingly, he became all things to all people, so that he might win all (1 Cor. 9:19–22), not through the craft of a liar but through the feeling of one who shares another’s weakness—that is, not by deceitfully committing all the evils of human beings, but by taking compassionate and healing care for all the evils of all others as though they were his own.

[Note: The Lovaniensian edition reads *vero* (“indeed”) where other editions and sixteen manuscripts read *viro* (“man”). Fourteen manuscripts read *agit* (“does”) rather than *ait* (“says”) in the phrase rendered above “he teach[es] what he thought and say[s] what he thought.”]

### 28

When, therefore, he did not refuse to perform even for himself those sacraments of the Old Testament, he was not mercifully deceiving anyone. He was not deceiving at all; rather, by this very conduct he commended that those practices had been commanded by the Lord God to last until a definite period of dispensation, and he distinguished them from the sacrilegious rites of the Gentiles.

At that time he became as a Jew to Jews—not through the craft of a liar but through the feeling of one who shares another’s weakness—when he wished to free them from the error by which they either refused to believe in Christ or thought that through their ancient priesthoods and observance of ceremonies they could be cleansed from sins and made safe, as though he himself were held by that error.

He was loving his neighbor as himself and doing for others what he would wish others to do for him if he needed it. When the Lord had given this instruction, he added: “For this is the Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 22:40).

### 29

In the same Epistle to the Galatians he commands this feeling of sharing another’s weakness, saying: “If a person is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself lest you also be tempted” (Gal. 6:1).

[Note: Editions read *fieri* (“to become”); one Vatican manuscript reads *fias* (“become!”), while several others read *fiere*, an imperative form Augustine uses elsewhere.]

See whether he did not say, “Become as that person, so that you may win that person.” Certainly he did not mean that one should deceitfully act as the beloved person or pretend to possess that person’s condition. Rather, he meant that one should consider what could also happen to oneself through another’s offense, and so mercifully help another as one would wish to be helped by another.

This is not the craft of a liar but the feeling of one who shares another’s weakness. Thus Paul became as a Jew to a Jew, as a Gentile to a Gentile, and as any other human being to anyone established in error or some sin—not by pretending to be what he was not, but by sharing the weakness of what he might have become. He became all things to all people, so that he might win all.

## CHAPTER IV

### 30

If you please, I beg you to look at yourself for a little while—to look, I say, at yourself in your dealings with me—and recall, or, if you have them written down, reread your words in that letter which you sent me through our brother Cyprian, now my fellow bishop.

You had complained gravely that I had committed certain offenses against you, and then added these words, with what truthfulness, what sincerity, and what full affection of charity:

“In this friendship is injured; in this the rights of our relationship are violated: that we should not seem to quarrel childishly and provide our supporters or detractors with material for contention.”

I understand that these words of yours were spoken not only from your heart but also with a kindly intention, for my benefit. Finally, you add what would have been evident even had you not added it: “I write this because I wish to love you purely and as a Christian, and to retain in my mind nothing that differs from my lips.”

O holy man, and, as God sees my soul, beloved by me with a truthful heart: what you set down in your letter, and what I do not doubt you displayed toward me, I believe that the Apostle Paul displayed in his writings—not toward just one person, but toward Jews, Greeks, and all the Gentiles who were his children, whom he had begotten in the gospel and for whom he was in labor until they were born; and afterward toward the many thousands of faithful Christians for whose sake that letter was committed to memory, so that he would retain in his mind nothing that differed from his lips.

### 31

You too became as I am—not through the craft of a liar but through the feeling of one who shares another’s weakness—when you considered that I should no more be abandoned in the fault into which you thought I had fallen than you would wish to be abandoned if you had fallen in the same way.

Therefore, while I give thanks for your benevolent attitude toward me, I ask at the same time that you not be angry with me because, when certain things in your works disturbed me, I disclosed my disturbance to you.

I wish everyone to show me the same consideration that I have shown you: whatever they think should be censured in my writings, let them neither praise it with a deceitful heart nor criticize it before others while remaining silent before me. Rather, let them understand that friendship is injured and the rights of our relationship violated by such conduct.

For I do not know whether those friendships should be called Christian in which the common proverb has greater force—“Compliance wins friends; truth produces hatred” (Terence, *Andria*, act 1, scene 1)—than the ecclesiastical saying, “The wounds of a friend are more faithful than the voluntary kisses of an enemy” (Prov. 27:6).

### 32

Therefore, with all the insistence we can muster, let us teach our dearest friends, who sincerely support our labors, this point above all: they should know that it is possible for something to be said against one another even among the closest friends, without charity itself being diminished and without truth producing the hatred that is owed to friendship.

Whether what is said in opposition is true, or whether it is simply stated with a truthful heart, let nothing that differs from the lips be retained in the mind.

Let our brothers, your associates, to whom you bear witness that they are vessels of Christ, believe that what happened occurred against my will. I am not without considerable grief over the fact that my letter came into the hands of many before it could reach you, the person to whom it was written.

How this happened would take a long time to explain, and, unless I am mistaken, it would be unnecessary. It is enough if you believe this about me: it was not done with the intention you suppose; indeed, it was not at all my will, arrangement, agreement, or even thought that it should happen.

If they do not believe this—although I speak with God as my witness—I have no more that I can do. Nevertheless, far be it from me to believe that they maliciously suggested these things to Your Holiness in order to stir up enmity between us. May the mercy of our Lord God turn such enmity away from us.

Rather, with no intention of causing harm, they readily suspect human failings in a human being. This is what it is fair for me to believe about them, if they are vessels of Christ, made and arranged not for dishonor but for honor in the great house of God, for a good work (2 Tim. 2:20–21).

If, after this testimony of mine has come to their knowledge, they wish to act otherwise, you too see how wrong their conduct would be.

### 33

What I had written—that I had sent no book against you to Rome—I wrote for this reason: I distinguished the title “book” from that letter, and therefore thought that you had heard of something entirely different; moreover, I had not sent the letter itself to Rome but had sent it to you; and I did not think that it was against you, since I knew that I had written it in the sincerity of friendship, either to admonish you or to correct you—or to be corrected by you.

Apart from your associates, I beg you by the grace by which we have been redeemed: whatever good qualities of yours, granted to you by the goodness of the Lord, I have set down in my letters, do not think that I included them through treacherous flattery. But if I have sinned against you in anything, forgive me.

Nor should you take more personally than I intended what I perhaps mentioned too awkwardly rather than elegantly concerning the action of some poet whom I do not know. I immediately added that I had not said this so that you might recover the eyes of your heart—far be it from me ever to think that you had lost them—but so that you might recognize the healthy and vigilant eyes you possessed.

I therefore thought that the matter should be touched upon solely because of a *palinodia*—a recantation, that is, if we have written something that we ought to undo in a later writing—not because of the blindness of Stesichorus, which I neither attributed nor feared in your heart.

[Note: Jerome appears later to have approached Augustine’s view in *Against the Pelagians*, book 1, chapter 8, where he says that among bishops an irreproachable one is either nonexistent or rare, since even Peter himself, according to the apostle Paul, was blameworthy: “Who will be indignant that he is denied what the chief of the Apostles did not possess?”]

I repeatedly ask you to correct me confidently wherever you see that this is necessary for me. Although, according to the titles of honor now established by ecclesiastical usage, the episcopate is higher than the presbyterate, Augustine is nevertheless inferior to Jerome in many matters; and correction ought not to be rejected or disdained even when it comes from anyone who is inferior.

## CHAPTER V

### 34

You have now persuaded me concerning the usefulness of your translation, namely, that you wish to translate the Scriptures from the Hebrew so that you may bring into public view those things that have been omitted or corrupted by the Jews.

But I ask you to explain whether you mean by “the Jews” those very people who translated the Scriptures before the Lord’s coming; and, if so, which of them or who among them.
