Or do you mean those who came later, who might therefore be thought either to have removed certain things from the Greek manuscripts or to have corrupted them in order not to be convicted by those testimonies concerning the Christian faith?

I cannot discover why the earlier translators would have wished to do this.

Next, I beg you to send us your translation from the Septuagint, which I did not know you had published. I also wish to read your book, which you mentioned, *On the Best Kind of Translation*, and to learn how, in your view, the translator’s linguistic expertise should be balanced against the conjectures of those who interpret and expound the Scriptures.

Even if such interpreters are sound and united in one faith, they must produce differing opinions concerning the obscurity of many passages. Yet this variety does not at all conflict with the unity of the same faith. A single interpreter too can expound the same passage in different ways according to that same faith, because its obscurity permits this.

### 35

I desire your translation from the Septuagint for two reasons: first, so that we may, as far as possible, avoid the incompetence of the many Latin translators who, whatever their quality, have dared to undertake this work; and second, so that those who think I envy your useful labors may finally understand, if possible, that I do not want your translation from the Hebrew to be read in the churches lest we disturb the congregations of Christ with a great scandal by introducing something new against the authority of the Septuagint.

Their ears and hearts are accustomed to hearing that translation, which has also been approved by the Apostles.

Thus, if in the Hebrew text the plant in Jonah (Jonah 4:6) is neither ivy nor gourd but some other thing that, resting on its trunk, rises without needing any supporting props, I would nevertheless prefer that “gourd” now be read in all the Latin churches. I do not think that the Septuagint translators rendered it this way without reason, unless they knew that this plant too was similar to a gourd.

### 36

I think that I have answered your three letters—indeed, perhaps more than sufficiently. [Letters 72, 75, and 81.] I received two of them through Cyprian and one through Firmus.

Write back whatever you think will instruct us or others. I shall take greater care, as far as the Lord helps me, to ensure that the letters I write to you reach you before they reach anyone through whom they might be more widely circulated.

For I admit that I do not wish done to me, in the case of your letters to me, what you most rightly complain was done with mine to you.

Nevertheless, let us mutually value not only charity but also the freedom of friendship, so that you do not remain silent before me, nor I before you, about what in our letters respectively disturbs us—provided that we do so with an intention that does not displease the eyes of God in brotherly love.

But if you think this cannot happen between us without the destructive offense of love itself, then let it not happen. The charity I would wish to have with you is certainly greater; but this lesser charity is better than none.

[Note: Editions read *melior* (“better”); the manuscripts read *melius* (“better”).]

## LETTER LXXXIII

*[Found only in manuscripts cb and two v., apart from the Lovaniensian edition.]*

*[Formerly Letter 239; formerly numbered 83, now 224. Written around A.D. 405.]*

Augustine informs Alypius that he has adopted another view concerning the possessions that had belonged to Honoratus, a monk from Thagaste and presbyter of the Church of Thiava, and that he now finally thinks it preferable that all these possessions should pass, as it were by hereditary right, not to the monastery of Thagaste but to the Church of Thiava.

To the most blessed, venerably beloved, and most greatly desired brother and fellow bishop Alypius, and to the brothers who are with you, Augustine, and the brothers who are with me, sends greetings in the Lord.

## EPISTLE LXXXIII

1. The distress of the Church at Thiava [Note: Lov. reads *Thianensis*. The old Corbie codex prefers *Thiavensis*, a spelling which we approve more, because in Possidius’s *Index*, in manuscript copies, certain letters are reckoned as written to the Thiavenses—or, with *v* changed to *b*, to the Thiabenses.] does not permit my heart to rest [Col. 0292] until I hear, together with you, that they have been restored to their former disposition; and this must be done quickly. For if the Apostle takes such pains even over one man, saying, “lest one such as this be swallowed up by excessive sorrow,” where he also says, “that we may not be overreached by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs” (2 Cor. 2:7, 11), how much more ought we to act watchfully, lest we have cause to mourn this in the whole flock, especially among those who have now [Note: Thus the manuscripts. Lov. has, “who have already come to Catholic,” etc.] come to Catholic peace and whom I cannot possibly abandon. But because the shortness of time did not allow us jointly to extract, after careful deliberation, a settled opinion on this matter, let Your Holiness receive what has seemed good to me after much thought since our departure; and, if it also seems good to you, let the letter which I wrote to them in our common name [Note: This letter is not extant.] be sent without delay.

2. You said that they should have one half, and that I should provide for them from some source or other the other half. But I think that, if the whole were taken from them, there would be ground for saying that we had labored so earnestly not over money but over justice. Yet when we grant them half and at some point settle with them on those terms, it will be sufficiently evident that our concern was nothing other than financial; and you see what ruin follows. For we shall seem to them to have taken half of another’s property; and they will seem to us to have suffered dishonestly and unjustly, so as to be helped from half of what had wholly belonged to the poor. As for what you said—“Care must be taken, when we wish to remedy a doubtful matter, not to make greater wounds”—this will have equal force if half is granted to them. Precisely on account of that half, those for whose conversion we wish to provide [Note: *Consulere* is omitted in Lov.; we restore it from the manuscripts.] will postpone the sale of their property under those delaying excuses, so that this precedent may be followed in their case. Moreover, it is strange if so great a scandal of the entire people should arise from a doubtful matter, when they think that their bishops, whom they hold in high esteem, are stained with filthy avarice because an evil appearance is not avoided.

3. For when anyone is converted to a monastery, if he is converted with a true heart, he does not contemplate this—especially after being warned how great an evil it is. But if he is false and seeks his own interests, not those of Jesus Christ (Phil. 2:21), he certainly does not possess charity. And what does it profit him if he distributes all that he has to the poor and delivers his body to be burned (1 Cor. 13:3)? In addition, as we have already discussed, this can henceforth be avoided: in dealing with one who is converted, he should not be admitted to the fellowship of the brothers before he has stripped himself of all those encumbrances, and, when his property has ceased to be his, he may be brought forward from retirement [reading uncertain]. But this death of the weak, and such a hindrance to the salvation of those for whom we labor so earnestly in order to win them to Catholic peace, cannot otherwise be avoided, except by making them understand most clearly that in such causes we are in no way concerned about money. They will in no way understand this unless we leave for their use that property which the presbyters have always believed to be theirs; for even if it was not his, they ought to have known this from the beginning.

[Col. 0293] 4. Therefore it seems to me that the following rule must be retained in matters of this kind: whatever, by the legal right by which such things are possessed, belonged to a man who is ordained cleric anywhere, belongs to the Church in which he is ordained. Indeed, the property at issue belonged to the presbyter Honoratus by that same legal right to such an extent that, if he had died while ordained elsewhere, or even while still resident in the monastery at Thagaste, without having sold his property or transferred it to anyone by a formal donation, none but his heirs would have succeeded to it, just as Brother Aemilianus succeeded Brother Privatus in those thirty solidi. These things, therefore, must be guarded against beforehand; but if they have not been guarded against, it is proper to preserve for them those rights which, according to civil society, have been established concerning the possession or non-possession of such things, so that we may refrain, as far as possible, from every evil thing and even every evil appearance, and preserve a good reputation, which is very necessary to our stewardship. Let Your Holy Prudence consider how evil that appearance is. Apart from the distress which we experienced among them, lest I myself perhaps be deceived—as often happens when I incline too readily toward my own opinion—I related the case to our brother and fellow bishop Samsucius [Note: Bishop of Turris.], not yet saying what now seems to me, but rather adding what had seemed right to both of us when we opposed them. He shuddered greatly and was astonished that this had seemed right to us, moved by nothing else than the very foul appearance, wholly unworthy not of our life alone but of anyone’s life and character.

5. Therefore I beg you not to delay sending the letter which I wrote to them in our common name, with your subscription. And if perhaps you see most clearly there that course to be just, let not the weak be compelled now to learn what I do not yet understand, so that in this case there may be observed toward them what the Lord said: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16:12). For, sparing such weakness, he also said concerning the payment of tribute: “Then the sons are free; but lest we offend them,” and so forth, when he sent Peter to pay the didrachmas then being demanded (Matt. 17:26). For he knew another legal right by which he owed no such thing; but that man paid him tribute by the legal right by which, as we have said, the heir of the presbyter Honoratus would have succeeded, had he died before giving away or selling his property. Even in the Church’s own right the Apostle Paul spares the weak and does not claim the wage due to him, although his conscience assured him that he could claim it with perfect justice; but, avoiding nothing other than a suspicion which disturbed the good fragrance of Christ, and abstaining from that evil appearance, he did this in those regions where he knew it was necessary (1 Cor. 9:1–23), perhaps before he had experienced people’s distress. But we, slower to perceive, should correct through experience what we ought to have foreseen.

6. Finally, because I fear everything and remember what you proposed when we parted—that the brothers at Thagaste hold me indebted for half of that price—if you see clearly that this is just, I do not refuse, but only on the condition that I repay it when I have it; that is, when so much comes to the monastery at Hippo [Col. 0294] that this can be done without hardship, so that, after so large a sum has been deducted there, a portion no less equal in proportion to the number of residents may come to our people.

## EPISTLE LXXXIV

[Note: Epistles LXXXIV and LXXXV were compared with manuscripts cb, vc, two v manuscripts, and Lov.]  
[Note: Formerly numbered 242; what was Epistle 84 is now 19. Written perhaps about this time, or before A.D. 411.]

Augustine to Bishop Novatus, explaining why he cannot send him his brother Lucillus the deacon, whom the Churches of the diocese of Hippo cannot do without because of his knowledge of Latin.

To his most blessed, venerable, and beloved lord, brother and fellow priest NOVATUS [Note: Novatus, bishop of Sitifis, took part in the Conference of Carthage; perhaps he is the same man to whom this letter was written.], and to the brothers who are with you, AUGUSTINE and the brothers who are with him send greetings in the Lord.

1. I too feel how harsh [Note: Thus from three manuscripts; one has “although.”] I seem, and can scarcely bear myself, because I neither send nor permit my son, the deacon Lucillus, your brother, to go to Your Holiness. But when you too begin to yield up some persons, most dear and sweet, nurtured by you, to the needs of Churches far away from you, then you will feel with what goads of longing I am pierced because certain men most closely and sweetly joined to me are not even physically with me. For, not to carry your thought far away, however much the brotherhood of your blood may avail, it does not surpass the bond of friendship by which Brother Severus and I cling to one another; yet you know how seldom I have the opportunity of seeing him. This was certainly brought about neither by his will nor mine, but because we set the needs of Mother Church in our present time before the needs of the age to come, in which we shall live together inseparably. How much fairer, then, is it that you should bear, for the benefit of that same Mother Church, the absence of the brother with whom you have not for so long ruminated upon the Lord’s food as I have with my sweetest fellow-citizen Severus—who even now scarcely speaks with me, and then only sometimes through small letters, more full of other cares and business than bearing anything from our meadows in Christ’s sweetness?

2. Here perhaps you will say: “What then? Will my brother not be useful to the Church among us, or do I desire to have him with me for some other reason?” Certainly, if his presence seemed to you as useful there as it does to me here for winning or governing the Lord’s sheep, no one would fail justly to blame not merely my harshness but my unfairness. But since the Latin language [Note: Perhaps read, “But since he knows Latin.” In those times Latin speech was extremely familiar in Africa; Augustine began learning it, “even amid the endearments of nurses,” according to *Confessions* 1.14.23. Hence, when about to cite a Punic proverb in Sermon 167 on the words of the Apostle, chapter 3, section 4, he says: “I shall speak to you in Latin, because not all of you know Punic.”], for want of which the evangelical ministry greatly suffers in our regions, is in universal use there, do you think that we ought to provide for the salvation of the Lord’s peoples by sending this ability [Col. 0295] there and taking it away from here, where we seek it with great anxiety of heart? Grant me pardon, therefore, because I do what is not only against your desire but also against my own feeling, being compelled to do it by concern for our burden. May the Lord, in whom you have placed your heart, grant that your labors may be such that you are rewarded for this service; for it is you who have rather granted the deacon Lucillus to the burning thirst of our regions. Nor will you render a small service if you burden me no further with any request on this matter, lest I appear nothing other than harsher to your venerable and holy Benevolence.

## EPISTLE LXXXV

[Note: Formerly numbered 216; what was Epistle 85 is contained in Epistle 120. Written perhaps about A.D. 405.]

Augustine rebukes a certain Bishop Paul, who by his frivolity gravely offended the Church, urging him to return to an upright life worthy of a bishop.

To his most sincerely beloved lord, brother and fellow priest PAUL [Note: Paul administered the Church of Cataqua; he is, we think, the predecessor of Boniface, bishop of Cataqua, mentioned in Epistle 96.2 and Epistle 97.3.], worthy to be made blessed by every prayer, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

1. You would not call me so inexorable unless you also thought me a liar. For what else do you believe about my mind when you write such things to me, except that I harbor against you a blemish of discord and detestable hatred? It is as though, in a manifest matter, I did not take care lest, while preaching to others, I myself should be found reprobate (1 Cor. 9:27), or as though I wished to cast the speck from your eye while nourishing a beam in my own (Matt. 7:4). It is not as you think. Behold, I say again and call God to witness that, if you wished for yourself the things that I wish for you, you would long ago be living securely in Christ and making his whole Church rejoice in the glory of his name. Behold, I have already written that you are not merely my brother but also my colleague. For no bishop of the Catholic Church, whatever his character, can fail to be my colleague so long as he has not been condemned by any ecclesiastical judgment. Yet I have no reason not to communicate with you except that I cannot flatter you. For I owe you especially this: by truly rebuking you with the salutary sharpness of charity, I have begotten you in Christ Jesus through the Gospel. Nor do I rejoice so greatly that, with the Lord’s help, many have been gathered into the Catholic Church through you that I ought not to mourn that more have been scattered from it. For you have wounded the Church at Hippo in such a way that, unless the Lord recalls you—freed from every worldly care and burden—to a true episcopal life and manner of living, such a wound cannot be healed.

2. But since you do not cease to entangle yourself more and more, so that you have involved yourself even after your renunciation in the affairs which you renounced—something that cannot in any way be defended even under human laws—and since you are said to live in a profession for which the frugality of your Church cannot suffice, why do you seek communion with me when you have never been willing to hear my admonition? Is it so that people may impute to me whatever you do, though I cannot bear their complaints? You wrongly suspect [Col. 0296] that those who are your detractors are the people who always opposed you, even in your former life. It is not so; nor is it surprising that much is hidden from you. But even if this were true, they ought not to have found anything in your conduct which they could rightly rebuke and from which they could blaspheme the Church. Perhaps you still think that I say these things because I have not received satisfaction from you. On the contrary, I say them lest I myself be unable to make sufficient satisfaction to God for my sins if I keep silent about these things to you. I know that you have a heart; but a slow heart is safe when it is in heaven, and a sharp heart is nothing when it is on earth. The episcopate is not an art of carrying on a deceitful life. The Lord God, who has blocked all the ways in which you wished to use it, will teach you what I say, so that, if you understand, he may direct you into that way for whose walking so holy a burden was laid upon you.

## EPISTLE LXXXVI

[Note: Compared with manuscripts bl, cb, ff, gg, r, t, vc, three v manuscripts, and with Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]  
[Note: Formerly numbered 60; what was Epistle 86 is now 36. Written perhaps in A.D. 405.]

Augustine asks Caecilianus the governor to restrain the Donatists in the region of Hippo and neighboring places by his edict.

To his distinguished lord, son CAECILIANUS [Note: Some manuscripts read “to be received”; and in the body of the letter, “most worthy son to be received.” This is thought to be the same Caecilianus who later became praetorian prefect in A.D. 409 and to whom Augustine wrote another letter in A.D. 413.], truly and deservedly honorable and worthy of respect in the charity of Christ, AUGUSTINE, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord.

The splendor of your administration, your reputation for virtues, and your praiseworthy devotion and faithful sincerity in Christian piety—divine gifts which you rejoice to have been bestowed upon you by him who gives them, and from whom you hope, on his promise, for greater things—have prompted me to share with Your Excellency, by this epistolary address, the anxieties of my causes [Note: Thus almost all manuscripts. The editions read, “to disclose them to your Excellency.”]. For as greatly as we rejoice that throughout other regions of Africa you have furthered Catholic unity with marvelous effectiveness, so greatly do we grieve that the territory of Hippo Regius and the neighboring bordering parts of Numidia have not yet deserved to be aided by the force of your gubernatorial [Note: The Tellerian manuscript reads “gubernatorial.”] edict, most distinguished lord, son truly and deservedly honorable and worthy of respect in the charity of Christ. Lest this be imputed rather to my negligence, as one who bears the episcopal burden at Hippo, I thought it should not be concealed from Your Magnificence. If you deign to hear, either from my brothers and fellow bishops who can report these things to Your Sublimity, or from the presbyter whom I have sent with this letter, how great an audacity heresy displays even in the territory of Hippo, then, with the help of our Lord God, you will undoubtedly take care that the swelling of sacrilegious vanity be healed by intimidation rather than cut away by punishment.

## EPISTLE LXXXVII

[Note: We have reviewed this letter against manuscripts a, bg, bl, c, cc, ff, g, gv, n, r, s, sb, t, vc, four v manuscripts, and Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]  
[Note: Formerly numbered 164; what was Epistle 87 is now 210. Written in A.D. 405 or later, but before A.D. 411.]

Augustine to the Donatist Emeritus, urging him to consider and answer on what just ground they initiated the schism.

To his desired and beloved brother EMERITUS [Note: Emeritus was a citizen of Caesarea in Mauretania and bishop of the Donatists there [Col. 0297], one of the seven whom they delegated to defend their cause at the Conference of Carthage; see *Retractations* 2.51.], AUGUSTINE.

1. When I hear of anyone endowed with a good intellect and educated in the liberal disciplines, although the salvation of the soul is not located in these, yet holding in a very easy question an opinion other than that required by truth, the more I wonder, the more I burn to know the man and converse with him; or, if I cannot do that, at least to reach his mind with letters that fly very far, and in return to be reached by him. I hear that you are such a man, and I grieve that you are torn away and cut off from the Catholic Church, which, as was foretold by the Holy Spirit, is spread throughout the whole world; I do not know for what reason. For it is certain that the party of Donatus is unknown to a great part of the Roman world—not to speak also of the barbarian peoples, to whom the Apostle said that he too was a debtor (Rom. 1:14), and with whose Christian faith our communion is woven together—and that they do not at all know when or on what grounds this dissension arose. Unless you confess that all these Christians are innocent of the charges which you bring against the Africans, you are compelled to say that they are liable for the evil deeds of all, because, if men who are corrupt among you lie hidden, all of you are polluted, to put it mildly. For you do not expel no one from your communion; nor do you expel someone as soon as he first commits the act for which he must be expelled. Do you not condemn a person who lies hidden for some time and is afterwards exposed and convicted? I ask, then, whether he contaminated you while he was hidden. You will answer: “In no way.” Therefore he would not contaminate you at any time even if he always remained hidden; for some deeds of the dead are often disclosed, and Christians who communicated with them while they lived are not harmed. Why then have you, by so rash and sacrilegious a rupture, cut yourselves off from the communion of the innumerable Eastern Churches, which have always been unaware and still are unaware of what you either teach or invent to have been done in Africa?

2. For another question is whether what you say is true; indeed, we prove it false by much more probable evidence, and demonstrate that the very charges which you bring are proved rather among you. But this, as I have said, is another question, to be undertaken and discussed when necessary. Let the vigilance of your mind now attend to this: no one can be contaminated by crimes unknown to one who is unaware of them. Hence it is manifest that you have separated yourselves by sacrilegious schism from communion with the world, to which the charges against the Africans that you make—whether false or true—are wholly unknown and have always been unknown. Yet this also must not be left unsaid: even known evil persons do not harm good persons in the Church if there is either no power to prevent them from communion or some consideration for preserving peace stands in the way. For who are those who, in the prophet Ezekiel, deserved to be marked before the devastation of the wicked and to escape unharmed while they were devastated (Ezek. 9:4–6), unless they were those who, as is shown there most clearly, mourn and grieve the sins and iniquities of God’s people which are done in their midst? But who grieves and mourns over what he does not know? By the same reasoning the Apostle Paul also tolerates false brothers. For he does not say of unknown persons: “For all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” [Col. 0298] (Phil. 2:21); yet he makes clear that they were with him. And from what class are those who preferred either to burn incense to idols or to hand over the divine books rather than die, if not from those who seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ?

3. I pass over many testimonies of Scripture, lest I make the letter longer than necessary, and leave more matters for your learning to consider by yourself. Yet, I beg you, observe what is sufficient: if so many wicked persons in the one people of God did not make those who lived among them [Note: Eight manuscripts read “testified with them.”] like themselves; if that multitude of false brothers did not make the Apostle Paul, who belonged to the same Church with them, a man who sought his own interests and not those of Jesus Christ; then it is clear that a person does not become what some wicked person is with whom he approaches Christ’s altar—even if that person is not unknown—provided that he does not approve him and separates himself from him by the disapproval of a good conscience.

It is therefore clear that to associate with a thief means nothing other than either to steal with him or to approve his theft in one’s heart. We say this so that we may remove the endless and superfluous questions about people’s deeds, which do not impede our reasoning at all.

4. But if you do not hold this view, you will all be such as Optatus was among you, while you knew it—something far be it from the character of Emeritus and of others like him, whom I do not doubt are among you and are far removed from his deeds.

For we charge you with nothing except the crime of schism, which by your persistence you have also made heresy. But read what I do not doubt you have read, and see how highly this crime is valued in the judgment of God. You will find that Dathan and Abiram were swallowed by an opening in the earth, while all the others who had consented to them were consumed by fire issuing from their midst (Num. 16:31–35).

The Lord God marked that crime by a present punishment as an example for avoiding it, so that, when he spares such people with the greatest patience, he might show what punishment he reserves for the final judgment.

We do not criticize your reasons if, at the time when Optatus was raging in his deranged power, while the groaning of all Africa joined with your own because you were his accusers—if indeed you are such as report portrays you, and as God knows I both believe and wish you to be—you refused to excommunicate him lest, though excommunicated, he drag many along with him and cut your communion apart through the frenzy of schism.

But this very thing condemns you in the judgment of God, Brother Emeritus: when you saw that it was such a great evil for the party of Donatus to be divided that Optatus was judged preferable to tolerate within the communion rather than admit that division, you nevertheless remain in the evil that your ancestors perpetrated when they divided Christ’s Church.

5. Perhaps, driven into the narrowness of having to answer, you will try to defend Optatus. Do not, brother, I beg you, do not. It does not suit you; and even if it might suit someone else—if anything suits wicked people—it certainly does not suit Emeritus to defend Optatus.

But perhaps you should not accuse him either. Very well. [Col. 0299] Use a middle position and say: “Each will bear his own burden” (Gal. 6:5). “Who are you to judge another’s servant?” (Rom. 14:4).

If, then, on the testimony of all Africa—or rather of all the lands wherever the fame of Gildo was spreading—for he too was known—you never dared to judge Optatus, lest you rashly judge unknown matters, can we now, on the basis of your testimony alone, pass a rash judgment on people who lived before us concerning matters unknown to us? Must what you accuse as unknown be insufficient, unless we also judge what is unknown?

You do not defend Optatus, even if perhaps he is suffering under a false accusation; you defend yourself when you say, “I do not know what kind of man he was.” How much more, then, does the Eastern world not know what kind of men the Africans were, whom you accuse even though they are still more unknown? Yet you separate yourself from Churches whose names you have in the books and recite: the Churches of Corinth, Ephesus, Colossae, Philippi, Thessalonica, Antioch, Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, and the other regions of the world built up by the Apostles in Christ.

If your own colleague, the bishop of Thamugadi, a man of great notoriety and very bad reputation, was unknown—not to the bishop of Caesarea but even to his colleague at Sitifis, who was of the same time—how could the Church of the Corinthians, Ephesians, Colossians, Philippians, Thessalonians, Antiochenes, Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, and the other parts of the world founded by the Apostles have known the African traditors, whoever they were? How could they have deserved to be condemned by you, since they could not know them?

Yet you refuse communion with those Churches, say that they are not Christians, and attempt to rebaptize them. What can I say? What can I lament? What can I cry out? If I am speaking with a reasonable man, I share with you the goads of this indignation. For you surely see what I would say if I wished to say it.

6. Or did your ancestors perhaps hold a council among themselves and condemn the entire Christian world apart from themselves? Has the evaluation of matters been brought to such a point that the council of the Maximianists—who were cut off from your own separation, but are very few compared with you—has no force against you, while your council has force against the nations that are Christ’s inheritance and the ends of his possession (Ps. 2:8)?

I wonder whether a person who is not ashamed of this matter has any blood in his body. Please write back to these points. I have heard from certain people whom I could not fail to believe that you would reply if I wrote to you.

Some time ago I also sent a letter, but I do not know whether you received it or answered it, and perhaps I did not receive your reply. For now, I ask you not to consider it burdensome to answer what I have written, according to your judgment. But do not divert yourself into other questions; this is the starting point of the most orderly inquiry: why was the schism made?

7. For when earthly powers persecute schismatics, they defend themselves by the rule expressed by the Apostle: “Whoever resists authority resists what God has appointed; and those who resist will bring judgment upon themselves. For rulers are not a terror to good conduct but to bad. Do you wish not to fear the authority? Do what is good, and you will have its praise; for it is God’s servant for your good. But if you do what is wrong, be afraid; for it does not carry the sword without reason. It is God’s servant, an avenger for wrath against the one who does evil” (Rom. 13:2–4).

The entire question, therefore, is whether schism is no evil, or whether you did not create schism in order to resist the authorities for good conduct rather than for evil, thereby bringing judgment upon yourselves.

For this reason the Lord most prudently did not say, “Blessed are those who merely suffer persecution,” but added, “for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. 5:10). If, then, the separation in which you also persist is righteousness, I want you to explain this to me in light of what I have said above.

But if it is wickedness to condemn a Christian world that has not been heard—either because it did not hear what you heard, or because it did not accept as proven what you rashly believed or accused without reliable evidence—and therefore to wish to rebaptize so many Churches of the Lord himself, founded while he was still in the flesh by the preaching and labor of his Apostles; if you are permitted either not to know that your African colleagues, living with you and administering the sacraments with you, are evil, or even to know it but tolerate them lest the party of Donatus be divided; while those established in the remotest parts of the world are not permitted to be ignorant of what you either know, believe, have heard, or imagine concerning the Africans—what perversity is this, to embrace your own wickedness and accuse the severity of the authorities?

8. “But,” you say, “Christians are not permitted to persecute the wicked.” Granted; let it not be permitted. But is it lawful to make this objection to the authorities appointed precisely for this purpose? Shall we erase the Apostle? Or do your books not contain what I quoted shortly before?

“But,” you say, “you ought not to communicate with such people.” What then? Did you refuse communion with Flavianus, once a deputy prefect and a man of your party, because, in obedience to the laws, he killed the criminals he found?

“But,” you say, “the Roman authorities are provoked against us by our people.” Rather, they are provoked by you against yourselves, because you dared to tear apart and persist in rebaptizing the Church whose members they already are there, as was foretold so long ago—for it was said of Christ, “All the kings of the earth shall adore him” (Ps. 71:11).

Our people, however, seek protection from the appointed authorities against the unlawful and private violence of your members—violence that even you, who do not commit such acts, lament and mourn there—not so that the authorities may persecute you, but so that they may defend your victims. The Apostle Paul acted similarly against the Jews who had conspired to kill him (Acts 23:21), before the Roman empire was Christian, arranging for protection to be provided to him even by armed men.

Those rulers, however, learning by whatever means about the crime of your schism, establish against you, according to their own concern and authority, whatever they decide. For they do not carry the sword without reason; they are God’s ministers, avengers for wrath against those who do evil.

Finally, even if some of our people act in these matters without Christian moderation, it displeases us. Nevertheless, we do not abandon the Catholic Church because of them, if we cannot purge it of chaff before the final time of winnowing—just as you did not abandon the party of Donatus because of Optatus, when you did not dare to expel him.

9. “But,” you say, “why do you want us joined to you if we are criminals?” Because you are still alive and can be corrected if you wish. When you are joined to us—that is, to the Church of God, Christ’s inheritance, whose possession is the ends of the earth—you are corrected so that you may live in the root.

Concerning broken branches the Apostle says: “For God is able to graft them in again” (Rom. 11:23). You must therefore be changed in that part in which you have dissented, although the sacraments you possess are holy, since they are the same everywhere.

For this reason we wish you to be changed from your perversity: namely, so that your separation may be rooted again. The sacraments that you have not changed are approved by us as you possess them, lest, when we wish to correct your wickedness, we commit a sacrilegious injury against Christ’s mysteries, which have not themselves been corrupted by your wickedness.

Saul, after all, had not corrupted the anointing that he had received; and the devout servant of God, King David, showed the anointing great honor. We therefore do not rebaptize you because we wish to restore the root to you. We approve the form of the severed branch, if it has not been altered; yet, however intact it may be, it is in no way fruitful without a root.

The question of the persecutions that you say you suffer amid the great gentleness and mildness of our people, while your own members truly act unlawfully and privately in more serious ways, is one question. The question of baptism is another: we do not ask where it is, but where it is beneficial. Wherever it is, it is itself; but the person who receives it is not himself wherever it is.

Thus we detest the private impiety of people within the schism, but everywhere we venerate Christ’s baptism. For if deserters carry away their emperor’s standards, the standards are received back intact, whether the deserters are punished by condemnation or corrected by pardon, provided that the standards have remained intact.

If anything more carefully needs to be asked about this matter, that is another question, as I have said. What must be observed in these matters is what the Church of God observes.

10. The question is whether your Church or ours is the Church of God. Therefore the inquiry must begin at the source: why did you create the schism?

If you do not reply, I believe that I have an easy case before God, because I have sent a peace-making letter to a man whom I have heard to be good and liberally educated apart from the schism. You will see what you answer to him whose patience must now be praised but whose judgment at the end must be feared.

But if you reply with the concern appropriate to the letter you have received, God’s mercy will be present, so that at last the error that divides us may perish through love of peace and the reason of truth.

Let me not speak of the Rogatists [Note: Lov. has “Rucatists.” But Bad., Am., Er., and all the manuscripts have “Rogatists,” that is, the followers of Rogatus of Cartenna in Caesarean Mauretania, as is understood from Epistle 93. He was a bishop who, after defecting from the Donatists, suffered many bitter things from them, while Firmus, the tyrant and brother of Gildo, assisted their party. Hence Augustine says in *Against the Letter of Petilian* II.83: “Who could suffice to recount what Rogatus the Moor suffered from you in the war of Firmus?”], whom you are said to call Firmians, just as we are called Macarians by you. Nor will I speak of your bishop of Rusicade [Note: So Lov. The older editions and four manuscripts have “Rusicazensis”; four other reputable manuscripts have “Ruficatensis”; another has “Rusicarsensis.”], who is said to have made a pact with Firmus to secure the safety of his own people, provided that the gates were opened to him, the Catholics were delivered over to destruction, and countless other things were done.

Stop, then, exaggerating by commonplaces the deeds of people, whether heard about or known. You see what I leave unsaid concerning your own people, so that the matter may be conducted concerning the origin of the schism, where the whole issue lies.

May the Lord God inspire you with a peaceful thought, desirable and beloved brother.

## EPISTLE LXXXVIII

[Note: Assistance in correcting this letter was supplied by manuscripts a, bg, bl, c, cc, ff, g, gv, n, r, vc, two sb manuscripts, two others, four further manuscripts, and the editions of Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]  
[Note: Formerly numbered 68; what was Epistle 88 is now 156. Written after the beginning of A.D. 406.]

The Catholic clergy of Hippo Regius to Januarius [Note: He was bishop of Casæ Nigrae in Numidia, then advanced in age, and was called the chief bishop of the Donatist party in Possidius’s *Index*, chapter 3. At the council of Bagai in 394 he is named fifth; at the Conference of Carthage he subscribes immediately before Primianus himself.], the Donatist bishop, protesting the violence of the Circumcellions against Catholics. The style is Augustine’s, although the letter was written in the common name of the clergy.

To JANUARIUS, from the Catholic clergy of the region of Hippo Regius.

1. Your clergy and your Circumcelliones rage against us with a persecution of a new kind and unheard-of cruelty. Even if they were returning evil for evil, they would still be acting contrary to the law of Christ. But now, when all our deeds and yours are taken into consideration, we are found to be suffering what is written: “They repaid me evil for good” (Ps. 34:12); and in another psalm: “With those who hated peace I was peaceful; when I spoke to them, they warred against me without cause” (Ps. 119:7).

For since you are advanced to so great an age, we think you know very well that the party of Donatus, which was first called the party of Majorinus at Carthage, voluntarily accused Caecilian, then bishop of the Church of Carthage, before that ancient emperor Constantine. But lest perhaps your dignity has forgotten this, or you pretend not to know it, or even—something we do not suppose—perhaps do not know it, we insert in this letter the text of the report then made by Anulinus the proconsul, whom the party of Majorinus at that time appealed to, so that the charges it brought against Caecilian might be sent by that proconsul to the aforesaid emperor.

**A. GGG. NNN** [Note: These letters stand before the manuscripts, and the Gervasian codex explains them in the margin as *Augusto Constantino* (“to Augustus Constantine”). Henricus Valesius, who published this same report with the heading “To Constantine Maximus Augustus: Anulinus, etc.,” supports this interpretation. But in the Carthaginian Conference 3.216 it is headed “To our Augusti,” perhaps through a copyist’s error. For when Constantine was consul for the third time—that is, in the year 313, when this report was written—two Augusti, Constantine and Licinius, were ruling, not three, as those letters would seem to imply.]

**ANULINUS, vir consularis** (“a man of consular rank”), proconsul of Africa. [Note: The printed editions read “now proconsul.” But the manuscripts and Valesius more correctly have *vc*, that is, according to the interpretation of the Gemeticensis codex, *vir consularis* (“a man of consular rank”); according to the example in the Carthaginian Conference, *vir clarissimus* (“a most illustrious man”). The latter interpretation must be attributed to a copyist’s error. For a proconsul writing to an emperor would certainly not have called himself a most illustrious man.]

2. “The heavenly letters of Your Majesty, received and revered, caused my devotion, in the records of my humble office, to bring to the attention of Caecilian and those who serve under him, who are called clergy, and urged them, once unity had been established by the agreement of all, to appear freed from every public obligation by the indulgence of Your Majesty, while preserving the Catholic faith and serving divine things with the reverence owed to the sanctity of the law.” [Note: Eusebius reports this letter in *Ecclesiastical History* 10.7. In it the Emperor wishes the clergy “to be kept wholly exempt from all public functions, lest through some error or sacrilegious accident they be drawn away from the worship owed to the supreme divinity, but rather that without any disturbance they may devote themselves to their proper law.” These are Constantine’s words, necessarily cited here to elucidate this report.]

“But after a few days certain men appeared with a gathered crowd, thinking that Caecilian ought to be opposed. They presented to my jurisdiction a sealed packet in a leather case and an unsealed petition, and urgently requested that I send them to the sacred and venerable court of Your Divinity. Since Caecilian remained in his position, I sent them, together with the attached records, so that Your Majesty might discern everything. I transmitted two petitions: one enclosed in the leather case and bearing this superscription: ‘Petition of the Catholic Church concerning the crimes of Caecilian, submitted by the party of Majorinus’; and another, unsealed, attached to the same leather case.” [Note: The editions read, “Two petitions were transmitted, one enclosed in the leather case and subscribed,” etc. We have corrected the passage according to the manuscripts and, partly, the example in the Carthaginian Conference. As for the other petition, which is said to have lacked a seal, Valesius and others think it was the petition presented by the bishops of the party of Majorinus to Constantine, asking him to provide judges from Gaul who would judge between them and Caecilian and his colleagues. Optatus gives a copy of this petition in Book 1, and Augustine mentions it in Letters 43.13 and 76.2.]

“Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, at Carthage, in the third consulship of Our Lord Constantine Augustus.”

3. After this report had been sent to him, the Emperor ordered the parties to come to an episcopal judgment at Rome. The ecclesiastical records indicate how the case was heard and concluded there, and how Caecilian was judged innocent. Surely, after the peaceful moderation of the episcopal judgment, all stubbornness of contention and hostility ought to have been extinguished.

But again your elders returned to the Emperor and complained that judgment had not been rightly given and that the whole case had not been heard. Consequently, he granted a second episcopal judgment to be held at Arles, a city of Gaul. There many of your party, after their empty and diabolical dissension had been condemned, returned to concord with Caecilian; but others, most stubborn and quarrelsome, appealed to the same Emperor.

Afterward the Emperor himself, compelled to do so, examined and concluded the episcopal case between the parties, and was the first to establish a law against your party, ordering that the places of your assemblies be claimed for the imperial treasury. If we wished to insert documentary evidence of all these matters, our letter would become excessively long.

Nevertheless, it must in no way be passed over how the case of Felix of Aptunga was investigated and concluded in a public trial, under pressure from your party before the Emperor. Your fathers had said at the Council of Carthage, through Secundus of Tigisis, the primate, that Felix was the source of all their evils. For the aforesaid Emperor testifies in this very case that your accusers and persistent appellants appeared before him; we have copied his letter below.

**The Emperors Caesars, FLAVIUS CONSTANTINE MAXIMUS and VALERIUS LICINIANUS, to PROBIANUS, proconsul of Africa.**

4. “Your predecessor Aelianus, rightly, while the most perfect man Verus, deputy of the prefects, was then confined by ill health throughout our Africa, exercising his functions in his place, considered that, among other matters, the business—or controversy—which appeared to have arisen concerning Caecilian, bishop of the Catholic Church, ought to be referred to his own investigation and decision.

“For when he had caused Superius the centurion, Caecilian the magistrate of the people of Aptunga, Saturninus the curator, and the younger Calibius, curator of the same city, as well as Solon, the public slave of the aforesaid city, to be present, he granted a proper hearing. Thus, when it had been alleged against Caecilian that the episcopate seemed to have been conferred upon him by Felix, against whom the delivery up and burning of the divine Scriptures appeared to have been alleged, it became clear that Felix was innocent of this charge.” [Note: This was Calidius, or Claudius Saturianus, as he is read in Optatus, Book 1. He had been curator of the city of Aptunga during the persecution involving the delivery up of the books, that is, under the eighth consulship of Diocletian and the seventh of Maximian, in the year 303. He was therefore brought to trial so that, on the basis of his testimony and the municipal records previously drawn up under his authority, it might be investigated whether Felix, the ordainer of Caecilian, had delivered up the sacred books. For the same reason Superius the centurion was summoned, since officials used soldiers and centurions when forcibly taking the Scriptures from Christians; and Alfius Caecilianus was summoned because during that persecution he had held the magistracy, or duumvirate, of the municipality of Aptunga, and his letter to Felix had to be examined. The younger Calibius, whom Optatus calls Calidius Gratianus, was curator for that year—namely, 314, when the question concerning Felix was being pursued—and was perhaps summoned to produce the municipal records of the magistrates of the preceding period.]

“Finally, when Maximus claimed that Ingentius, a decurion of the city of Ziqua, had forged the letter of Caecilian, the former duumvir, we examined Ingentius himself in light of the records that lay before us; and for that reason we did not subject him to torture, since he asserted that he was a decurion of the city of Ziqua.” [Note: The editions read *ex divino jure* (“from divine law”); most manuscripts read *ex duumviris*. It should certainly be read as one word, *exduumviri*. The letter at issue is Alfius Caecilianus’s letter, written by him after his duumvirate, as is clear from the records of Felix’s acquittal.]

“Therefore we wish you to send this same Ingentius, under suitable escort, to the court of Constantine Augustus, so that it may be made clear and declared, before those who are currently acting and who do not cease to appeal day after day, with them hearing and standing present in person, that they have vainly sought to stir up hatred against Bishop Caecilian and to rise violently against him.” [Note: Baronius thinks that this letter to Probianus was written before the Council of Arles in 314, and says that Ingentius was presented to that council. Henricus Valesius, on the other hand, maintains that the letter was issued in the fourth consulship of Constantine and Licinius, that is, in 315. Petronius Probianus is known to have been proconsul of Africa in that year, both from the Theodosian Code, under the title *De appellationibus*, and from the fact that Aelianus, here called his predecessor, held the proconsulship of Africa in the consulship of Volusianus and Annianus, that is, in 314. Valesius does not, however, show in what month Probianus assumed the proconsulship, or whether he did so before the beginning of 315. There is also a constitution of Constantine addressed to Probus, dated 1 April 314, where Godofredus conjectures that *Probianum* should be read.]

“For thus it will come about that, once such disputes have been set aside, as is proper, the people may serve their own religion with due reverence and without any dissension.”

5. Since you see that these things happened in this way, why do you stir up hatred against us on account of the emperors’ orders issued against you, when you yourselves did all this earlier? If emperors ought to order nothing in such cases, if this concern ought not to belong to Christian emperors, who compelled your elders to send Caecilian’s case to the Emperor through the proconsul, and to accuse before the Emperor a bishop against whom, though absent, you had already pronounced judgments of one kind or another, and, after he was declared innocent, to devise before that same Emperor further accusations against Felix, his ordainer?

And now what else survives than the judgment of the great Constantine himself against your party—the judgment your elders chose, extorted through persistent appeals, and preferred to episcopal judgment? If imperial judgments displease you, who first compelled the emperors to undertake them on your behalf?

For now you cry out against the Catholic Church concerning what the emperors decree against you, just as if those who, after Daniel had been delivered, were sent to be consumed by the same lions by whom they themselves had first wished him to be consumed, wished to cry out against Daniel. For it is written: “There is no difference between the king’s threats and the lion’s rage” (Prov. 19:12).

Daniel’s calumniating enemies compelled him to be thrown into the lions’ den. His innocence conquered their wickedness; he was lifted out unharmed; they themselves were thrown into it and perished. Similarly, your elders exposed Caecilian and his fellowship to be consumed by royal wrath. His innocence freed them, and you now suffer from those same rulers what your people wished them to suffer, since it is written: “Whoever digs a pit for his neighbor will fall into it himself” (Ecclus. 27:29).

6. Therefore you have no grounds for complaining about us. Yet the gentleness of the Catholic Church had entirely remained quiet even in the face of these imperial orders, unless your clergy and Circumcelliones, disturbing and ravaging our peace through their most savage outrages and frenzied violence, had compelled these measures against you to be recalled and renewed.

For before the more recent laws of which you now complain came to Africa, they laid ambushes for our bishops on the roads, battered our fellow clergy with atrocious beatings, inflicted grievous blows even on laypeople, and set fire to their buildings. They also seized a certain presbyter—because by his own free and deliberate choice he had chosen the unity of our communion—from his house, savagely beat him as they pleased, rolled him in a muddy pool, clothed him in a *buda* [Note: The printed editions have *burda*; three manuscripts have *bsuda*; but most others read *buda*, as does Letter 105, where the presbyter in question is named Restitutus of Victorianum. Augustine explains what *buda* means in *Against Cresconius* 3.48, where, recounting the same story, he says that Restitutus was dishonored by being wrapped in a reed garment. It is therefore either a reed, or certainly a mat made of reeds, according to Isidore’s Glossary, though there one finds corruptly written *buda, historia* instead of “it is a reed mat.” Donatus, in his commentary on *Aeneid* 2, says that “many call *ulva* the plant commonly called *buda*.”], and displayed him in a procession of their crime—an object of pity to some and laughter to others. Then they carried him away wherever they wished and released him only after twelve days.

Consequently, when Proculeianus was summoned by our bishop before the municipal records but evaded investigating the matter, and was summoned again immediately afterward, he stated explicitly in the records that he would say nothing further. And today those who did this are your presbyters; they still threaten us and persecute us as far as they are able.

7. Yet our bishop did not complain to the emperors about these injuries and persecutions that the Catholic Church at that time suffered in our region. Instead, after a council had been held [Note: At Carthage, on 25 August 403], it was resolved that you should be approached peacefully, so that, if possible, you might hold a conference among yourselves [Note: The editions read “that you might hold a conference among us.” Nearly all the manuscripts read “among yourselves.” The clerics of Hippo are clearly speaking not of themselves but of the Catholic and Donatist bishops, as is evident from section 10.], and, once the error had been removed, fraternal charity might rejoice in the bond of peace [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “might be bound together.”].

The records themselves will inform Your Gravitas what Proculeianus first replied—namely, that you would hold a council and there see what you ought to answer—and then what he later recorded when, because of his promise, he was summoned again, refusing a peaceful conference. Moreover, when the notorious savagery of your clergy and Circumcelliones, known to everyone, did not cease, the case was brought forward: Crispinus was judged a heretic, but through Catholic gentleness he was not allowed to be struck with the penalty of ten pounds of gold that the emperors had established against heretics; nevertheless, he thought he should appeal to the emperors. [Note: See *Against Cresconius* 3.46.50 and 3.47.51, and Possidius, chapter 12.]

When that appeal received the response it did, was it not your party’s preceding outrage, together with his own appeal, that forced the matter to be handled in this way? Yet even after the rescript, when our bishops intervened with the Emperor, he was not subjected to that same condemnation of ten pounds of gold. Instead, our bishops sent representatives from the council [Note: The Council of Carthage, 26 June 404] to the imperial court to obtain that not all the bishops and clergy of your party should be subject to the same condemnation of ten pounds of gold established against all heretics, but only those in whose districts the Catholic Church suffered violence at your hands. [Note: See Letter 185.7.25–26.]

But when the representatives arrived at Rome, the Emperor had already been moved by the dreadful and very recent scars of the Catholic bishop of Bagai [Note: Maximianus.] [Note: The editions of Lovaniensis and Erasmus read *Vagitani*; seven good manuscripts read *Bagaitani*, and the others are not very different: three Vatican manuscripts have *Bagaetani*, another Vatican manuscript *Bagartani*, the Cistercian manuscript *Ligaitani*, and the editions of Badianus and Amerbachius *Bacaitani*. Compare *Against Cresconius* 3.43.] so that laws of the kind were sent—and sent they were.

When these laws arrived in Africa, and you had begun to be pressed, clearly not toward evil but toward good, what ought you to have done except send to our bishops, so that, just as you yourselves had approached them, they might in turn be approached by you, and the truth might rather become apparent through a conference?

[Col. 0307] 8. But you not only failed to do this; your people now inflict worse evils upon us. They do not merely batter us with clubs and cut us down with iron; with astonishing ingenuity in wickedness, they also put lime mixed with vinegar into our eyes to destroy them.

Moreover, after plundering our houses, they have forged huge and terrifying weapons for themselves. Armed with these, they roam through various places, threatening and panting for massacres, plunder, fires, and blindness.

Driven by these things, we were compelled first of all to complain to you, so that Your Gravitas might consider how many of your people—or rather all of you—who claim to suffer persecution sit safely in your own and others’ possessions under the supposedly terrible laws of the Catholic emperors, while we suffer such unheard-of evils at your hands.

You say that you suffer persecution; we are cut down by your armed men’s clubs and iron. You say that you suffer persecution; our houses are plundered and devastated by your armed men. You say that you suffer persecution; our eyes are destroyed by your armed men with lime and vinegar.

Moreover, if they inflict death upon themselves by their own choice, they want this to bring hatred upon us and glory upon you. They do not attribute to themselves what they do to us, and they attribute to us what they do to themselves. They live like robbers, die like Circumcelliones, and are honored like martyrs. Yet we have never even heard that robbers blind those whom they have plundered. They take the slain away from the light; they do not take the light away from the living. [Note: The editions omit *non* (“not”); this negation is found in fifteen manuscripts.]

9. Meanwhile, whenever we capture any of your people, we keep them unharmed with great affection, speak with them, and read to them all the passages by which the error itself is refuted—the error that separates brothers from brothers. We do what the Lord commanded through the prophet Isaiah, saying:

“Listen, you who fear the word of the Lord. Say to those who hate you and curse you, ‘You are our brothers,’ so that the name of the Lord may be honored and he may appear to them in gladness; but they themselves shall be put to shame” (Isa. 66:5).

Thus, when we consider that some of them recognize the clarity of the truth and the beauty of peace, we join them not to Baptism—which they had already received like a royal mark, as deserters—but to the faith they lacked, to the charity of the Holy Spirit, and to the body of Christ. For it is written: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15:9); and again it is written: “Charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8).

But if, whether because of excessive hardness, or because they cannot bear the shame of the insults of those with whom they had spread so many falsehoods against us and devised so many evils, or rather because they fear that they may now suffer at our hands the same things they formerly inflicted upon us, they refuse to consent to the unity of Christ, then, just as they were kept unharmed, so they are released by us unharmed.

As far as we can, we also admonish our laypeople to keep them unharmed and bring them to us for correction and instruction. Some listen to us and do this if they can; others treat them as they treat robbers, because they really do experience them as such. Some repel by striking blows directed at their own bodies, lest they be struck first by them; some hand over those whom they have seized to the judges and, despite our intercession, do not spare them, because they fear suffering monstrous evils at their hands. In all these matters, those men do not lay aside the deeds of robbers, yet they demand for themselves the honor of martyrs.

10. This, then, is our desire, which through this letter and through the brothers whom we have sent we lay before Your Gravitas. First, if it can be done, we ask that you confer peacefully with our bishops, so that wherever anything is found, it may be the error itself, not human beings, that is removed; so that people may not be punished but corrected; and so that you may now approach them, since previously you despised their approach to you.

How much better it would be for you to do this among yourselves, so that what you have done may be written down, signed, and sent to the Emperor, rather than for this to be done before earthly powers, which can do nothing except serve the laws already enacted against you [Note: This is the reading of thirteen manuscripts. Earlier editions have “which can do nothing except rage against you.”]!

For your colleagues who had sailed there said before the prefects that they had come to be heard. [Note: The records relevant here appear in the third Carthaginian Conference, section 121: “in the court held by the prefecture, where the opposing party, that is, the Donatists, demanded so insistently to be heard”; and in the same conference, section 141, they are noted as having been drawn up at Ravenna on the third day before the Kalends of February, in the fourth consulship of Arcadius and Probus, that is, in the year 406.] They named our holy father Valentinus, a Catholic bishop who was then at the imperial court, saying that they wished to be heard with him. The judge could not grant this, since he was already judging according to the laws enacted against you; nor had that bishop come in this capacity, or received any such commission from his bishops.

How much better, then, that the Emperor himself—who is not subject to those same laws and has the power to enact other laws—should be able, once your conference has been read to him, to judge the entire matter, although it was long ago heard and concluded?

But we wish you to confer for this reason: not that the case may be concluded again, but that it may be shown to those who do not know that it has already been concluded. If your bishops are willing to do this, what do you lose by it, and what do you not rather gain, since your willingness becomes known and you cannot rightly be accused of distrust?

Or perhaps you think that this is not permitted, when you cannot be unaware that the Lord Christ himself spoke with the devil about the Law (Matt. 4:4); and that not only Jews but also Gentile philosophers from the schools of the Stoics and Epicureans conferred with the apostle Paul (Acts 17:18)?

Or perhaps the Emperor’s laws do not permit you to approach our bishops? In the meantime, approach your bishops who are in the region of Hippo, where we suffer such evils at the hands of your people. How much more freely and easily your written words can reach us through your people than their weapons can reach us!

11. Finally, through these same brothers whom we have sent to you, write such a reply. But if you do not wish even this, at least listen to us together with your people, from whom we suffer such things.

Show us the truth for which you say you suffer persecution, while we suffer such great cruelty from your people. For if you convict us of being in error, perhaps you will grant us that we not be rebaptized by you, judging it just to grant this to us, who have been baptized by those whom you condemned without any judicial process.

You granted this to those whom Felicianus of Musti and Praetextatus of Assuri had baptized for such a long time, when you were trying, by the orders of judges, to drive them from the basilicas because they were in communion with Maximianus, with whom they were explicitly and by name condemned by you at the Council of Bagai.

We demonstrate all these matters through judicial and municipal records, where you also cited your own council when you wished to show the judges that you had driven your own schismatics from the basilicas.

And yet, although you have made a schism from the very seed of Abraham, in whom all nations are blessed (Gen. 22:18), you do not wish to be driven from the basilicas—not by judges, as you drove out your own schismatics, but by the very kings of the earth who, in fulfillment of prophecy, worship Christ, before whom you withdrew defeated after accusing Caecilian.

12. But if you are unwilling either to hear us or to instruct us, come with us—or send people with us—to the region of Hippo, so that they may see your armed army, although no soldier, judging by the number of his weapons, has ever added lime and vinegar to the eyes of barbarians.

If you do not wish even this, at least write to those men, telling them not to do these things any longer and to restrain themselves from killing, plundering, and blinding us.

We do not wish to say, “Condemn them.” You will see for yourselves how those whom we have just shown to be robbers within your communion do not defile you, while those whom you have never been able to show to be traditors defile us.

Choose from all these options whichever you wish. But if you despise our complaints, we shall have no regret that we wished to proceed in a peaceful manner. The Lord will be present to his Church, so that you may rather regret having despised our humility.

## LETTER LXXXIX

[Note: Compared against manuscripts a, bg, bl, c, cc, ff, g, gv, n, r, s, sb, t, two vc manuscripts, and four v manuscripts, and against the editions of Amerbachius, Badianus, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis.] [Note: Formerly Letter 167; the letter formerly numbered 89 is now 157. Written at approximately the same time.]

Augustine to Festus, explaining that the Donatists are rightly restrained by the laws and indicating that in the region of Hippo they have not yet been corrected by Festus’s letters but are still carrying on intolerably.

**To the most beloved and honorable Lord and esteemed son FESTUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.**

1. If people, on behalf of error, damnable dissension, and falsehood convicted in every respect, presume so greatly that they do not cease to plot against and threaten the Catholic Church, which seeks their salvation, how much more fitting and necessary it is for those who assert the truth of Christian peace and unity—truth made manifest even though everyone may dissemble or restrain it—to labor earnestly and diligently, not only for the protection of those who are already Catholic but also for the correction of those who are not yet so.

For if stubbornness attempts to possess unconquerable strength, how much steadfastness ought to be possessed by the cause which, in the good it pursues perseveringly and tirelessly, knows that it pleases God and certainly cannot displease prudent human beings?

2. What is more unhappy and perverse than what the Donatists do? They boast that they suffer persecution, yet concerning the restraint of their wickedness they not only do not know how to be ashamed [Col. 0310] but even wish to be praised. Through astonishing blindness—or pretending, with damnable hostility, not to know—they fail to understand that it is not punishment but the cause that makes true martyrs.

I would say this against those whose only covering was the darkness of heretical error, for which they would undergo punishments fully deserved, yet who did not dare to harm anyone through violent madness. But what shall I say against these men, whose most destructive perversity is restrained either by fear of penalties or taught by exile how widely the Church is spread, as it was foretold would happen—though they prefer to attack it rather than acknowledge it? [Note: Earlier editions read “how widely it is spread everywhere.” The manuscripts more elegantly omit *quod*, reading “how widely spread it is.”]

And if what they suffer through the most merciful discipline is compared with the deeds they commit in their frenzied recklessness, who does not see which of them ought rather to be called persecutors?

Even wicked children, simply by living depraved lives, persecute the piety of their parents more grievously—even when they inflict no violence—than when their father or mother, the more they love them, the more strongly compel them, without any concealment, to live a good life.

3. There are the firmest proofs in the public records, which you can read if you wish—indeed, I ask and urge you to read them. They establish that the elders of those who first separated themselves from the peace of the Church voluntarily dared to accuse Caecilian before the Emperor Constantine through Anulinus, then proconsul.

If they had won in that judgment, what would Caecilian have suffered from the Emperor except what the Emperor later pronounced against them after their defeat? But evidently, if Caecilian and his colleagues had been driven from the seats they held, or even punished more severely while persisting in their conspiracy—for royal authority could not disregard the defeated if they continued to resist—then these men would have publicized their own foresight and zealous concern for the Church with lavish praise.

Now, however, because they were defeated, because they were entirely unable to prove what they alleged, whatever they suffer for their wickedness they call persecution. They do not restrain their utterly ruined frenzy; indeed, they seek the honor of martyrs.

As though Christian Catholic emperors were pursuing anything against their most stubborn wickedness other than the judgment of Constantine, before whom they themselves voluntarily appeared as Caecilian’s accusers, preferring his authority to that of all the bishops overseas, so that they would refer the Church’s case not to those bishops but to him; so that they would accuse before him again the episcopal judgment given at Rome, in which they were first defeated; and so that they would appeal to him from the second episcopal judgment given at Arles.

Yet, finally defeated before him, they remained in their perversity. I think that even the devil himself, if he were defeated so many times by the authority of a judge whom he had voluntarily chosen, would not be so shameless as to persist in that case.

4. But let these human judgments be set aside, and let it be said that they could have been circumvented, deceived, or even corrupted. Why, then, is the Christian world still accused and branded with the crimes of certain traditors, since it could and ought to trust none but the judges who were chosen, rather than the litigants who were defeated?

Those judges have their own case before God, whether good or bad. But what has the Church, spread throughout the whole world, done? It is judged by these men to require rebaptism for no other reason than that, in a case where it could not judge what was true, it decided to trust those who were able to judge rather than those who, though defeated, refused to yield.

O great crime of all the nations whom God promised would be blessed in the seed of Abraham (Gen. 22:18), and whom he displayed as blessed, just as he had promised! When they all say with one voice, “Why do you wish to rebaptize us?” the answer given to them is: “Because you do not know who in Africa were the traditors of the sacred books, and, in what you did not know, you preferred to trust judges rather than accusers.”

If another person’s crime burdens no one, what does it matter to the whole world what someone committed in Africa? If an unknown crime burdens no one, how could the whole world have known either the crime of the judges or that of the accused?

Judge, you who have hearts. This is heretical justice: because the whole world does not condemn an unknown crime, the party of Donatus condemns the world without hearing its case.

But it is enough for the whole world to hold fast to God’s promises and to see fulfilled in itself what the Prophets sang so long ago; to recognize the Church in those same Scriptures where its king, Christ, is also recognized. For wherever such things were foretold about Christ as we read fulfilled in the Gospel, there things were foretold about the Church such as we now see fulfilled throughout the whole world.

5. Unless perhaps it will trouble any prudent person that they customarily say that Christ’s baptism is true only when it is given by a just human being. Yet here too the whole world holds the clearest evangelical truth, where John says:

“He who sent me to baptize in water himself said to me: ‘Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit’” (John 1:33).

Therefore the Church confidently places its hope not in a human being, lest it fall under the sentence written in Scripture: “Cursed is everyone who places his hope in a human being” (Jer. 17:5). Rather, it places its hope in Christ, who so took the form of a servant that he did not lose the form of God; of him it was said, “He is the one who baptizes.”

Accordingly, whatever burden the human minister of his baptism may carry, it is not this man but the one upon whom the dove descended who baptizes.

Those who think otherwise are followed by such absurdity that they cannot find anywhere to flee from it. For when they admit that baptism is valid and true when a criminal baptizes among them, although his crimes are hidden, we ask them: “Who, then, baptizes?” They have no answer except “God.” For they cannot say that an adulterous human being sanctifies anyone.

We reply to them: “If, then, when a manifestly just person baptizes, that person sanctifies, but when a secretly wicked person baptizes, it is not that person but God who sanctifies, those being baptized ought to prefer to be baptized by secretly wicked people rather than by openly good people. For God sanctifies them much better than any just human being.”

But if it is absurd for someone being baptized to wish to be baptized by a secret adulterer rather than by a manifestly chaste person, it remains that, whoever among human ministers approaches, baptism is valid for this reason: the one upon whom the dove descended is himself the one who baptizes.

6. And yet, although such clear truth strikes the ears and hearts of human beings, the abyss of evil custom has so engulfed some that they prefer resisting every authority and argument to giving their assent. They resist in two ways: either by raging or by becoming sluggish. What, then, should the Church’s medicine do, seeking the salvation of all with maternal charity, as though feverishly laboring among the delirious and the lethargic? Should it despise them? Should it desist? Ought it, or can it? It must be troublesome to both groups, because it is the enemy of neither. For the delirious do not want to be restrained, and the lethargic do not want to be awakened. Yet the diligence of charity perseveres: it rebukes the delirious, stirs the lethargic, and loves both. Both are offended, but both are loved; both, while they are ill, resent being troubled, but once healed both rejoice.

7. Finally, we do not receive them, as they think and boast, in the condition in which they were, but wholly changed; for they do not begin to be Catholics until they have ceased to be heretics. Their sacraments are not hostile to us, since we share them with them; for they are not human but divine. What must be taken away is their distinctive error, which they wrongly absorbed—not the sacraments that they received in the same way, which they carry and possess to their own condemnation. They possess them all the more culpably, but they nevertheless possess them. Thus, after abandoning error and correcting the perversity of separation, they pass from heresy to the peace of the Church, which they did not have, and without which what they possessed had been harmful to them.

But if, when they cross over, they are hypocrites, that is no longer our judgment but God’s. And yet some who were thought to be hypocrites, because they had crossed over to us under the pressure of the command’s terror, were later found, in certain trials, to be such that they were preferred to some long-standing Catholics. Therefore, nothing is accomplished when action is taken persistently? No: something is indeed accomplished. The wall of hardened custom is not stormed by human terrors alone; faith and understanding of mind are also instructed by divine authorities and arguments.

8. Since this is so, let Your Benevolence know that your people who are in the region of Hippo are still Donatists, and that your letter has had no effect among them. It is unnecessary to write why it had no effect; instead, send one of your own people—whether a member of your household or a friend—to whom you can entrust this matter, someone who will come first to us, not to those places, without their knowing anything about it. After first discussing the matter with us and deciding, with the Lord’s help, what seems ought to be done, let him carry it out.
