For when we do this, we are acting not only for their sake but also for the sake of our own people who have already become Catholics, for whom the proximity of those others is so hostile that we cannot possibly disregard it. I could have written this briefly, but I wanted you to have something from my correspondence by which you might not only understand the reason for my concern yourself, but also have an answer to anyone who dissuaded you from applying yourself persistently to correcting your people, or who criticized us because we wanted such action.

If I have done more than necessary—if you had already learned or considered these matters yourself, or if I have burdened you, so occupied with public responsibilities, by thrusting upon you a lengthy letter—please forgive me, provided that you do not disregard what I have suggested and requested. May God’s mercy thus protect you.

## LETTER XC

[Note: [Col. 0313] For correcting Letters 90 and 91, the following witnesses assisted: a. bg. bl. bn. c. cc. g. gv. ff. j. n. r. s. sb. vc. vd.; two t.; four v.; and Am. Bad. Er. Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0313] Previously 201; the letter formerly numbered 90 is now 175. Probably written in 408, after June 1.]

Nectarius the pagan to Augustine, acting so that the penalties which ought to be exacted from his fellow citizens of the colony of Calama might be remitted—not only the penalties for violating the emperor’s most recent edict forbidding the performance of sacred rites to idols, but also those for the injuries which they themselves had inflicted upon Christians on the occasion of their sacred rites.

To the distinguished and deservedly honored brother AUGUSTINE, bishop, NECTARIUS.

Since you know how great is the love of one’s homeland, I pass over it. It alone surpasses the affection owed to parents. If there were any way or limit by which good people might give counsel to it, we should already have deserved to be excused from its obligations. But since the affection and gratitude of the community increase day by day, and since, the nearer one’s age is to its end, the more one desires to leave one’s homeland safe and flourishing [Note: [Col. 0313] Thus all manuscripts. Correctly, with the reference being to affection: “we desire”], I rejoice first of all that my discussion here is with a man equipped with every discipline.

There are many things in the colony of Calama that we rightly love, whether because we were born there or because we seem to have rendered it important services. This community, then, most excellent and deservedly honored lord, has fallen through no slight error on the part of its people. If we measure the matter by the strictness of public law, it ought to be punished with more severe judgment. But it is not lawful for a bishop to do anything except confer salvation upon people, assist their causes for the sake of a better condition, and obtain forgiveness from almighty God for the offenses of others.

Therefore, with all the supplication I can make, I beg that, if the matter must be defended, the innocent be defended and injury be kept away from the innocent. Grant what, in accordance with your nature, you clearly see is being requested. The damages can readily be assessed; we ask only that punishments be remitted. May you live in greater favor with God, distinguished and deservedly honored brother.

## LETTER XCI

[Note: [Col. 0313] For correcting Letters 90 and 91, the following witnesses assisted: a. bg. bl. bn. c. cc. g. gv. ff. j. n. r. s. sb. vc. vd.; two t.; four v.; and Am. Bad. Er. Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0313] Previously 202; the letter formerly numbered 91 is now 182. Written in the same year, around the beginning of August.]

Augustine attacks the pagan rites and enumerates the recent injuries inflicted upon Christians by the people of Calama, showing that their salvation would be far more kindly served if they were not, by leaving such a crime unpunished, encouraged to attempt similar acts.

To the distinguished and deservedly honored brother NECTARIUS, AUGUSTINE.

### 1

Although your limbs are already growing cold with old age, I neither wonder at nor fail to praise the fervor of your spirit for your homeland. I willingly accept—not reluctantly, but gladly—that you not only keep in mind but also demonstrate by your life and conduct that there is no limit or end to what good people may do for their homeland.

This is why we would wish you also to be such a citizen of that heavenly homeland whose holy love we, according to our ability, risk and labor among those whom we counsel to seek it: that you should consider there to be no limit or end to your duty of caring for even the smallest portion of it, while it journeys here on earth. You would become better in proportion as you rendered the duties owed to a better community, and in its eternal peace you would find no end to rejoicing, since in its temporary hardships you had set no limit to your concern for it.

### 2

But until that happens—for we must not despair that you may acquire that homeland, or that you may already be wisely considering acquiring it, the homeland to which your father, who begot you in this one, has gone before you—until that happens, forgive us if, because of our own homeland, which we desire never to abandon, we grieve your homeland, which you desire to leave flourishing.

If we discuss its flourishing with your wisdom, there is no danger that it will be difficult to persuade you, or that you will not readily see how a community ought to flourish. That famous poet of your illustrious literature mentioned certain “flowers of Italy”; but in your homeland we have experienced less the men by whom that land flourished than the weapons by which it burned—or rather, not weapons but flames; and not burned, but burned it.

If so great a crime is left unpunished, without any fitting correction of the wicked, do you think you will leave your homeland flourishing? O flowers plainly not of fruits but of thorns! Compare now whether you would rather have your homeland flourish through piety or through impunity [Note: [Col. 0314] Lov. reads “impiety”; the manuscripts, however, read “impunity”], through corrected morals or through reckless license. Compare these things and see whether you surpass us in love of your homeland, whether you desire its flourishing more truly and more deeply than we do.

### 3

Look for a little while at the books on the Republic, from which you drank that feeling of the most devoted citizen—that there is no limit or end to what good people may do for their homeland. Look at them, I beg you, and observe how highly frugality and self-restraint are praised there, as well as fidelity to the marriage bond and chaste, honorable, and upright conduct. When these qualities prevail in a community, it truly deserves to be called flourishing.

These virtues are taught and learned in the churches growing throughout the world, as in holy lecture halls for the peoples; above all, piety toward the true and truthful God is taught—the God who not only commands people to undertake all those things by which the human spirit is instructed and fitted for fellowship with God and for inhabiting the eternal heavenly city, but also grants that they be fulfilled [Note: [Col. 0314] Thus the editions; but the Vatican manuscripts and fourteen of ours read: “by divine fellowship” (*divina societate*)].

This is why the images of many false gods were both foretold to be overthrown and commanded to be overthrown. Nothing makes people so incapable of living together through the depravity of their lives as imitation of such gods as are described and commended in their writings.

### 4

Finally, those highly learned men who sought or even described the earthly republic and community as they thought it ought to be, more by discussions within their own circles than by establishing and shaping it through public action, set before the uneducated youth for imitation outstanding and praiseworthy human beings rather than their gods.

And indeed, that young man in Terence who, gazing at a painted picture on a wall depicting the adultery of the king of the gods, inflamed the lust by which he was being carried away with the stimulus of such great authority [Note: [Col. 0315] In *The Eunuch*, act 3, scene 5], would in no way have slipped into or plunged himself into that disgraceful act, whether by desiring or committing it, if he had preferred to imitate Cato rather than Jupiter. But how could he do that, when in the temples he was compelled to worship Jupiter rather than Cato?

Perhaps we ought not to bring forward such examples from comedy, by which the luxury and sacrilegious superstition of the impious are exposed. Read, or recall, in those same books how prudently it is argued that the writings and performances of comedies could in no way have been admitted unless the morals of those who admitted them were in harmony with them. Thus, on the authority of the most illustrious men who excelled in public life and discussed the public good, it is firmly established that the worst human beings are made worse by imitating the gods—not true gods, certainly, but false and fabricated ones.

### 5

But, they say, everything that was written in ancient times about the life and morals of the gods must be understood and interpreted quite differently by the wise. Yet only yesterday and the day before yesterday we heard such salutary interpretations recited before crowds gathered in the temples.

I ask you: is the human race so blind in opposition to truth that it does not perceive things so open and manifest? In so many places Jupiter is painted, cast, beaten, sculpted, written about, read about, acted, sung, and danced, committing so many adulteries. How difficult would it have been to read, at least in his own Capitol, a prohibition of such things?

When these evils, so full of disgrace and impiety, flourish among the people without anyone prohibiting them; when they are worshiped in temples and laughed at in theaters; when, while sacrifices are offered to them, even the livestock of the poor is slaughtered; when, while actors perform and dance these things, the estates of the rich are squandered—are such communities said to flourish?

The mother worthy of such flowers is plainly not fertile soil or some wealthy virtue, but that goddess Flora, whose theatrical games are celebrated with such lavish and unrestrained obscenity that anyone can understand what sort of demon is being appeased—one that cannot be placated otherwise than by causing not birds, not four-footed animals, and finally not even human blood, but, far more criminally, human modesty itself to perish as though sacrificed there.

### 6

I have said this because you wrote that, as your age approaches its end, you desire to leave your homeland safe and flourishing. Let all those empty and insane practices be removed; let people turn to the true worship of God and to chaste and devout morals. Then you will see your homeland flourishing—not according to the opinion of fools, but according to the truth recognized by the wise—when this homeland of your bodily birth has become a portion of that homeland into which we are born not by the body but by faith, where all God’s saints and faithful people, after the wintry hardships of this life, will flourish in unending eternity.

Therefore, we are determined neither to lose Christian gentleness nor to leave that community a harmful example for others to imitate. God will grant that we may accomplish this, if he does not become too greatly angered against them. Otherwise, both the gentleness we wish to preserve and the discipline we strive to exercise with moderation may be obstructed, if God secretly wills something else—whether, in his judgment, he decides that so great an evil must be punished with a sharper scourge, or whether, in his more intense anger, he chooses to leave it unpunished for a time because they have neither been corrected nor turned to him.

### 7

Your wisdom, in a certain sense, prescribes for us what befits the person of a bishop, and you say that your homeland has fallen through no slight error on the part of its people. If we measure this by the strictness of public law, you say, it ought to be punished with more severe judgment. But you add that it is not lawful for a bishop to do anything except confer salvation upon people, assist their causes for the sake of a better condition, and obtain forgiveness from almighty God for the offenses of others.

We are trying wholly to preserve this principle: that no one be punished with more severe judgment, either by us or by anyone else with our intervention. We wish to confer upon people the salvation that consists in the happiness of living rightly, not in the security of doing evil. We also strive to obtain forgiveness not only for our own offenses but for those of others, though we cannot obtain it at all except for those who have been corrected.

You also add: “With all the supplication I can make, I beg that, if the matter must be defended, the innocent be defended and injury be kept away from the innocent.”

### 8

Briefly learn what was done, and distinguish the guilty from the innocent yourself.

Against the most recent laws [Note: [Col. 0316] He means the law of Honorius forbidding pagans “to perform any solemn rite,” issued to Curtius on November 24, 407, according to the appendix to the *Theodosian Code*, p. 35], on the Kalends of June, a pagan festival [Note: [Col. 0316] Six manuscripts read *festa*, “festivals.” Am. Bad. and Er. read *sexto*, “on the sixth”] was celebrated in a sacrilegious manner, without anyone prohibiting it, with such insolent boldness that a most wanton crowd of dancers passed along the very same street in front of the church—something that had not even happened in the time of Julian.

When the clergy attempted to prohibit this utterly unlawful and disgraceful activity, the church was stoned. Then, about eight days later, after the bishop had repeated the well-known laws to the municipal council, and while they were preparing as though to carry out what had been ordered, the church was stoned again.

On the following day, so as to instill fear in our people, public justice was denied to those who appeared before the official records wishing to make a statement. On that same day, as though they were to be terrified by divine intervention, hail answered the stonings. When it had passed, they immediately carried out a third stoning and finally set fire to ecclesiastical buildings and to people. They killed one servant of God who happened to encounter them while wandering about. The others hid wherever they could, or fled by whatever route they could find.

Meanwhile the bishop, driven and compressed into a certain place, was hiding there; he heard the voices of those searching for him in order to kill him and reproaching him because, since they had not found him, they had committed such a great crime for nothing.

These events continued from approximately the tenth hour until a considerable part of the night had passed. No one among those whose authority might have been influential attempted to restrain them or come to the aid of the victims, except one outsider. Through him, many servants of God were rescued from the hands of those attempting to kill them, and much was taken away from the plunderers. Through him it became clear how easily these events either would not have occurred at all or would have been abandoned once begun, if the citizens, and especially the leading men, had forbidden them to occur and continue.

### 9

Accordingly, throughout that entire community you may perhaps distinguish not the innocent from the guilty, but the less guilty from the guiltier.

Those are guilty of a lesser offense who, overcome by fear—and especially by fear of offending those whom they knew to possess great power in that town and to be enemies of the Church—did not dare to offer assistance. All those are wicked through whose will these deeds were committed, even if they did not carry them out or instigate them. Guiltier are those who committed them; most guilty are those who instigated them.

But let us suppose that the suspicion of instigation is not certainty, and let us not investigate matters that cannot be discovered except through the torture of those by whom they are being investigated. Let us also forgive the fear of those who thought it better to pray to God for the bishop and his servants than to offend powerful enemies of the Church.

What of those who remain? Do you think none should be restrained by discipline, and do you think so monstrous an example of fury should be presented as unpunished? We are not seeking to nourish our anger by avenging the past; we are working mercifully to provide for the future.

Evil people have a place where they may be punished by Christians not only gently but also usefully and beneficially. They retain their bodies unharmed; they retain the means by which they live; they retain the means by which they live wickedly. Let the first two be preserved, so that those who may repent remain alive. This is what we desire, and to the extent that it lies within us, this is what we earnestly pursue through diligent effort.

But if God wills the third to be cut away as rotten and harmful, he will punish them very mercifully. If he wills something more, or does not even permit this, the reason belongs to a higher and certainly more just judgment that rests with him. Our duty is to expend care and service as long as we are permitted to see what is happening, entreating him to approve our intention: that we wish to provide for everyone and that he should allow nothing to be done through us that he knows far better than we do to be harmful to us and to his Church.

### 10

Just now, when we were at Calama, we dealt with the Christians as much as we could and considered appropriate at the time, so that those who were ours might either be comforted in their profound grief or calmed in their fury.

Then we also admitted the pagans themselves—the source and cause of so great an evil—when they asked to be received by us. We did this so that on this occasion we might admonish them about what they ought to do if they had wisdom, not only to remove their present anxiety but also to seek eternal salvation.

They heard much from us, and they themselves made many requests. But far be it from us to be servants of the sort who are pleased to be petitioned by those who do not petition our Lord. You therefore see, with your lively understanding, that we must persevere in this while preserving gentleness and Christian moderation, so that either we may deter others from imitating their perversity or may wish others to imitate their correction.

The damages inflicted are either endured by Christians or repaired through Christians. We desire the gains of souls—souls whose acquisition we long for even at the risk of our blood—to arise more abundantly in that place and not to be obstructed elsewhere by its example. May God’s mercy grant us the joy of rejoicing in your salvation.

## LETTER XCII

[Note: [Col. 0318] We reviewed this letter with the aid of a. bg. bl. bn. c. cc. cb. ff. g. gg. gv. j. l. n. s. t. vd.; two a.; two vc.; five v.; and Am. Bad. Er. Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0318] Previously 6; the letter formerly numbered 92 is now 176. Written around 408.]

Augustine to the widow Italica, consoling her over the death of her husband and refuting the opinion of those who said that God is seen with bodily eyes.

To the distinguished and deservedly excellent lady, and daughter honored in the love of Christ, ITALICA [Note: [Col. 0318] It seems that John Chrysostom’s Letter 170 was written to this same Italica. In it he urges a powerful Roman woman, according to her ability, personally or through others, to apply diligence toward calming the storm that had arisen in the Eastern Church], AUGUSTINE, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord.

### 1

I have learned, not only from your letter but also from the report of the person who brought it, that you have been earnestly requesting a letter from me, believing that you might receive great consolation from it. You will see what benefit you derive from it; nevertheless, I ought not to have refused or delayed writing.

May your faith and hope console you, as well as that love which is poured into the hearts of the devout through the Holy Spirit (Rom. 5:5). We have now received a portion of that love as a pledge, so that we may learn to desire its fullness.

You should not think yourself abandoned, since in the inner person you have Christ present through faith in your heart. Nor ought you to grieve as the Gentiles do, who have no hope, since by the most truthful promise we hope that, after departing from this life, we shall come to that life where those of our own whom we have seen departing have not been lost to us but sent ahead. There they will be all the more known to us and therefore all the dearer, and lovable without fear of any separation.

### 2

Here, although your husband, whose departure has made you a widow, was very well known to you, he was nevertheless better known to himself than to you. How can this be, when you saw his bodily face, which he himself certainly did not see? It is because knowledge of ourselves is more certain within, where no one knows the things belonging to a human being except the human spirit that is within him (1 Cor. 2:11).

But when the Lord comes and “brings to light the things now hidden in darkness and discloses the purposes of the heart” (ibid., 4:5), then nothing near one person will be hidden from another, and there will be nothing that each person must reveal to friends while concealing it from strangers, since no one will be a stranger.

What, or how great, is that light by which all the things now hidden in hearts will be illuminated? What tongue could express it, or even a weak mind apprehend it? Surely that light is God himself, since “God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all” (1 John 1:5)—but it is the light of purified minds, not of these bodily eyes. The mind will then be capable of seeing that light, though it is not yet so capable.

### 3

The bodily eye can neither see this now nor will it be able to see it then. Everything that can be perceived by bodily eyes must exist in some place; it cannot be wholly everywhere, but occupies a smaller place with its smaller part and a larger place with its larger part.

The invisible and incorruptible God is not like this—he alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light, “whom no human being has ever seen or can see” (1 Tim. 6:16). For he cannot be seen by a human being by that faculty by which a human being sees bodies with the body.

If God were inaccessible to the minds of the devout, it would not be said, “Draw near to him, and be enlightened” (Ps. 33:6). And if he were invisible to the minds of the devout, it would not be said, “We shall see him as he is.” Consider the whole sentence in John’s Epistle:

“Beloved,” he says, “we are God’s children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared. We know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

Therefore, we shall see him insofar as we shall be like him, just as now we do not see him insofar as we are unlike him. We shall see him from that by which we shall be like him.

Who would be so deranged as to say that we are, or shall be, bodily like God? This likeness therefore exists in the inner person, which “is being renewed in knowledge according to the image of its creator” (Col. 3:10). We become more like him in proportion as we advance in knowledge and love of him.

Although our outer person is wasting away, our inner person is renewed day by day (2 Cor. 4:16). Even so, however great our progress may be in this life, it remains far from that perfection of likeness which will make us capable of seeing God, as the Apostle says, “face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12).

If in these words we take “face” in a bodily sense, it will follow that God also has such a face, and that there is some interval between ours and his when we see him face to face. And if there is an interval, then there is a boundary, a defined shape of limbs, and other absurd and impious consequences in speech and thought—consequences by which the merely natural person, who does not perceive the things of God’s Spirit (ibid., 2:14), is mocked by the most deceptive vanities.

### 4

Some of those who chatter such things—as far as their words have reached me—say that we see God now with the mind, but then with the body, and they even assert that the impious will see him in the same manner.

See how they have progressed toward worse things, while unrestrained talk, wandering here and there, is carried along without fear or shame and goes unpunished. Formerly they said that Christ granted this only to his flesh: that it would see God with bodily eyes. Then they added that all the saints, once they had received their bodies in the resurrection, would see God in the same way. Now they have granted this possibility even to the impious.

Let them grant as much as they wish, and to whomever they wish. Who would dare contradict people who give away what belongs to them? “Whoever speaks falsehood speaks from his own resources” (John 8:44).

But you, together with those who hold sound doctrine, must not presume to claim any of these things from your own resources. When you read, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8), understand that the impious will not see him; for the impious are not blessed and pure in heart.

Likewise, when you read, “Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12), understand that we shall then see face to face from that by which we now see through a mirror and in an enigma.

Both of these are functions of the inner person, whether while we still walk by faith in this pilgrimage, in which we use a mirror and an enigma, or in that homeland, when we shall contemplate through direct vision. It is in reference to that vision that “face to face” is written.

### 5

Let the flesh, drunk with carnal thoughts, hear this: “God is spirit, and those who worship God must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:24). If this is so in worship, how much more in seeing?

Who would dare assert that the substance of God is seen bodily, when he would not have it worshiped bodily?

But they think they speak cleverly and seem to press the matter by asking: “Could Christ grant his flesh that it should see the Father with bodily eyes, or could he not?” If we answer that he could not, they will proclaim that we have detracted from God’s omnipotence; but if we concede that he could, they will use our answer to complete their argument.

How much more tolerably do those people rave who assert that flesh will be changed into the substance of God and will become what God is, so that, at least by seeing God, they may make it capable of seeing him, although it is now so unlike him! I believe that these people reject such vanity from their faith, perhaps even from their hearing.

Yet if they are similarly pressed by the question whether God could accomplish this or could not, will they detract from his power if they answer that he cannot, or will they admit that this will happen if they concede that he can? Just as they escape from that foreign snare, so let them escape from their own.

Moreover, why do they insist that this gift was granted only to Christ’s bodily eyes and not also to his other senses? Will God therefore be sound, so that he can also be perceived by the ears? Will he be breath, so that he can be sensed by smell? Will he be some kind of liquid, so that he can be drunk? Will he be a mass, so that he can also be touched?

“No,” they say.

“What then? Can God do that, but not this? If they say he cannot, why do they detract from God’s omnipotence? If they answer that he can but does not wish to, why do they favor the eyes alone and begrudge the other bodily senses of Christ?”

Or do they rave as far as they wish? How much better are we, who do not set limits to their folly but refuse to let them rave at all!

### 6

Much could be said to refute this madness. But if such people ever assail your ears, read them these points for now, and do not hesitate to write back to me, as you are able, with what they answer.

For this reason our hearts are purified by faith: because the reward of faith promised to us is the vision of God. If that vision will come through bodily eyes, then the spirit of the saints is exercised in vain to attain it. Indeed, when the spirit thinks in this perverse manner, it is not exercising itself in itself but is wholly in the flesh.

For where would it dwell more tenaciously and firmly than in that from which it presumes it will see God? How great an evil this certainly is, I entrust rather to your understanding than undertake to explain at length [Note: [Col. 0320] The remaining words are entirely absent from sixteen manuscripts].

May your heart always dwell under the Lord’s protection, distinguished and deservedly excellent lady, daughter honored in the love of Christ. Greet in return your honorable sons, most dear to you and to us in the Lord, with the service owed to your merits.

## LETTER XCIII

[Note: [Col. 0321] Corrected with the aid of a. bg. bl. bn. c. cc. ff. g. gv. j. n. r. s. vc. vd.; three sb.; two t.; five v.; and Am. Bad. Er. Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0321] Previously 48; the letter formerly numbered 93 is now 181. Written around 408.]

Augustine refutes a letter of Vincentius, bishop of Cartenna from the Rogatist schism. He says that he once thought one should proceed against heretics not by force but by the word of God and reason; but, overcome by the arguments and examples of others, he changed his view and now believes that the laws of rulers may rightly be invoked against enemies of the faith, provided this is done with the intention of correcting, not from a desire for revenge. He adds many other arguments against the obstinacy and rebaptism of the Donatists.

To his dearly beloved brother VINCENTIUS, AUGUSTINE.

## FIRST CHAPTER

### 1

I received the letter that I found it not implausible was yours. It was brought by a man whose identity as a Catholic Christian was certain and who, as I think, would not dare to lie to me. But even if the letter is perhaps not yours, I thought I ought to reply to the person who wrote it.

You knew me at Carthage when I was a young man and Rogatus, whom you succeeded, was still alive; now I am more eager for and desirous of quiet than I was then. But the Donatists are excessively restless, and it does not seem useless to me that they should be restrained and corrected by the powers ordained by God.

For we already rejoice over the correction of many who now hold and defend Catholic unity so sincerely, and rejoice that they have been freed from their former error, that we regard them with great rejoicing and admiration. Yet, through some force of habit, they would not have thought of changing for the better at all unless, struck by this terror, they had turned their anxious minds toward consideration of the truth.

Otherwise, if they endured temporary troubles not for justice but for human perversity and presumption, through an unproductive and vain endurance, they would later find before God nothing but the deserved punishments of the impious, who had despised his gentle admonition and fatherly scourges. Thus, made teachable by this reflection, they found in the divine books, not in human accusations and fables, the Church promised throughout all nations, and saw it made manifest before their own eyes; in those books they had no doubt that Christ, though unseen above the heavens, had been foretold as exalted above the heavens.

Should I have envied these people their salvation, so that I would recall my colleagues from such fatherly diligence, through which we have come to see many of them denouncing their former blindness? They believed Christ exalted above the heavens, even though they did not see him; yet, although they saw his glory throughout the whole earth, they denied it, even though the Prophet embraced both things in one sentence with such clarity, saying: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory over all the earth” (Ps. 107:6).

### 2

These former fierce enemies of ours, who severely harassed our peace and quiet by various kinds of violence and ambushes—if we were to disregard and tolerate them in such a way that we neither devised nor undertook anything at all that might be effective in frightening and correcting them, we would truly be returning evil for evil.

If someone saw an enemy who had become delirious with dangerous fevers running headlong toward destruction, would he not then be returning evil for evil if he allowed him to run on, rather than taking care to seize and restrain him? Yet at that moment he would seem most burdensome and hostile to him, precisely when he proved most useful and merciful. Once his health was restored, he would thank him all the more abundantly, recognizing that he had spared him least of all.

If only I could show you how many manifest Catholics we now have from among the Circumcellions themselves, condemning their former life and the pitiable error by which they thought that whatever they did with restless rashness they were doing on behalf of God’s Church! Yet they would not have been brought to this health unless they had been bound like delirious people by the chains of those laws that displease you.

What of that other kind of very serious illness among them—the people who did not possess turbulent boldness but were weighed down by a kind of long-standing dullness, saying to us: “What you say is true; there is nothing to answer. But it is hard for us to abandon the tradition of our ancestors”? Was it not salutary that they be shaken free by the discipline of temporary troubles, so that they might emerge from lethargic sleep and awaken to the salvation of unity?

How many of them now rejoice with us, reproach the former burden of their destructive conduct, and admit that it was necessary for us to trouble them, lest, like people in a deadly sleep, they perish from the illness of their antiquated custom!

3. But these measures are of no benefit to some. Is medicine therefore to be neglected because the pestilence afflicting certain people is incurable? You pay attention only to those who are so hard-hearted that they will not accept even this discipline. Of such people it is written: “In vain I chastised your children; they did not accept discipline” (Jer. II, 30). Yet I think they were chastised out of love, not hatred.

But you must also consider the very many whose salvation makes us rejoice. For if they were frightened but not instructed, it would seem like an oppressive form of domination. Conversely, if they were instructed but not frightened, hardened by the age-old force of habit, they would be moved more sluggishly to take up the path of salvation. Indeed, many whom we know well, after reasons had been given them and the truth had been made clear through divine testimonies, replied to us that they desired to enter into communion with the Catholic Church, but feared the violent hostility of wicked men. They certainly ought to have despised such hostility for the sake of justice and eternal life; but the weakness of such people, until they become strong, must be borne with, not abandoned in despair.

Nor must we forget that the Lord Himself said to Peter, while he was still weak: “You cannot follow me now; but you will follow afterward” (John XIII, 36). When useful fear is joined to saving instruction—so that not only does the light of truth drive away the darkness of error, but the force of fear also breaks the bonds of evil habit—we rejoice, as I have said, in the salvation of many. They join us in blessing God and give thanks to Him because, having fulfilled His promise that the kings of the earth would serve Christ, He has thus cared for the sick and healed the weak.

## CHAPTER II

4. Not everyone who spares is a friend, nor is everyone who strikes an enemy. “The wounds of a friend are better than the voluntary kisses of an enemy” (Prov. XXVII, 6). It is better to love with severity than to deceive with gentleness. It is more beneficial to take bread away from a hungry person if, secure in his food, he neglects justice, than to break bread for a hungry person so that, deceived by it, he acquiesces in injustice. Both the person who binds a madman and the person who awakens one sunk in lethargy cause them distress, yet both love them.

Who can love us more than God? And yet He does not cease not only to teach us gently, but also to frighten us beneficially. Along with the mild remedies by which He consoles us, He often adds the most biting medicine of tribulation. He exercises even pious and devout patriarchs through hunger (Gen. XII, XXVI, XLII, and XLIII); He drives a rebellious people through harsher punishments; and, though asked three times, He does not remove from the Apostle the thorn of the flesh, so that power may be perfected in weakness (II Cor. XII, 7–9).

Let us love our enemies also, because this is just and this is what God commands: that we be sons of our Father who is in heaven, “who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. V, 45). But just as we praise these gifts of His, so let us also consider His chastisements upon those whom He loves.

5. Do you think no one ought to be compelled toward justice, when you read that the master of the household said to his servants, “Compel whoever you find to enter” (Luke XIV, 23)? When you also read that Saul, later Paul, was compelled to learn and hold the truth by the great force of Christ compelling him (Acts IX, 3–7)?—unless perhaps you think money, or any kind of property, dearer to human beings than this light, which is apprehended by the eyes. After he had suddenly lost this light when struck down by a heavenly voice, he did not recover it until he was incorporated into the holy Church.

And do you think no force should be applied to a person so that he may be freed from the peril of error, when you see God Himself—whom no one loves us more usefully than—doing this by the clearest examples, and hear Christ saying, “No one comes to me unless the Father has drawn him” (John VI, 44), which takes place in the hearts of all who turn to Him through fear of divine wrath? And do you not know that sometimes a thief scatters fodder to divert sheep, while at other times a shepherd recalls wandering animals to the flock with a whip?

6. Did not Sarah, having received authority, afflict the defiant slave-woman? Certainly she did not hate cruelly the woman whom she had previously made a mother through her own favor; rather, she beneficially subdued her pride (Gen. XVI, 5). You are not unaware that these two women, Sarah and Hagar, and their two sons, Isaac and Ishmael, are figures of spiritual and carnal realities.

Although we read that the slave-woman and her son suffered severe mistreatment from Sarah, the Apostle Paul nevertheless says that Isaac suffered persecution from Ishmael: “But just as then he who was according to the flesh persecuted him who was according to the spirit, so also now” (Gal. IV, 29). Thus those who can understand may recognize rather that the Catholic Church suffers persecution from the pride and impiety of carnal people, whom she tries to correct through temporal afflictions and fears.

Whatever the true and legitimate mother does, even if it is felt as harsh and bitter, she does not repay evil with evil; rather, by driving out the evil of iniquity, she applies the good of discipline—not from hatred of harming, but from love of healing. When good and evil people do the same things and suffer the same things, they are to be distinguished not by their actions and punishments, but by their purposes. Pharaoh crushed God’s people with harsh labors (Exod. V, 9); Moses afflicted that same people, when it acted impiously, with harsh restraints (ibid., XXXII, 27). They did similar things, but did not intend to benefit in the same way: the former was puffed up by domination, the latter inflamed by love.

Jezebel killed the prophets; Elijah killed the false prophets (III Kings XVIII, 4, 40). I think the merits of those who acted and of those who suffered were different.

[Note: [Col. 0324] The editions read “zeal” (*zelo*). But sixteen manuscripts have “love” (*dilectione*).]

7. Consider also the times of the New Testament, when the gentleness of charity itself had to be preserved not only in the heart but also displayed openly; when Christ sends Peter’s sword back into its sheath and shows that it ought not to have been drawn, not even for Christ (Matt. XXVI, 52).

Yet we read not only that the Jews struck the Apostle Paul, but also that the Greeks struck Sosthenes the Jew on Paul’s behalf (Acts XVI, 22–23, and XVIII, 17). Does not the similarity of the deed seem to unite them both, while the difference of their purposes nevertheless distinguishes them? Certainly God “did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. VIII, 32). Certainly it is said of the Son Himself, “He loved me and delivered himself up for me” (Gal. II, 20). Certainly it is also said of Judas that Satan entered into him so that he might betray Christ (John XIII, 2).

Since, then, the Father delivered up His Son, Christ His own body, and Judas his Lord, why is God pious in this betrayal while the human being is guilty, unless it is because, although they performed one deed, the reason for performing it was not one and the same?

Three crosses stood in one place: on one, a thief to be freed; on another, a thief to be condemned; in the middle, Christ, about to free one and condemn the other. What was more alike than these crosses? What was more unlike than those hanging upon them?

Paul was handed over to be confined and bound (Acts XXI, 23–24), but Satan is certainly worse than any prison guard. Yet Paul himself handed a man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit might be saved on the day of the Lord Jesus (I Cor. V, 5). What shall we say here? Behold: the cruel betrayer handed someone over to a gentler one; the merciful betrayer handed someone over to a more cruel one.

Let us learn, brother, to distinguish the dispositions of those who act amid the similarity of their deeds. Let us not slander with closed eyes, nor accuse the well-intentioned as though they were guilty. Likewise, when the same Apostle says that he handed certain people over to Satan so that they might learn not to blaspheme (I Tim. I, 20), did he repay evil with evil, or rather judge that correcting evil people even through evil was a good work?

[Note: [Col. 0325] Am., Bad., Er., and manuscript *gv* read “indicated” (*indicavit*).]

8. If it were always praiseworthy to suffer persecution, it would have been enough for the Lord to say, “Blessed are those who suffer persecution,” and He would not have added, “for the sake of justice” (Matt. V, 10). Likewise, if it were always blameworthy to inflict persecution, it would not have been written in the holy Books: “The one who secretly slanders his neighbor, him I persecuted” (Ps. C, 5).

Therefore, sometimes the one who suffers persecution is unjust, and the one who inflicts it is just. But certainly the wicked have always persecuted the good, and the good have persecuted the wicked: the former by harming through injustice, the latter by helping through discipline; the former savagely, the latter with restraint; the former in the service of desire, the latter in the service of love.

For the one who slaughters does not consider how he may tear; but the one who heals considers how he may make an incision. The former persecutes health; the latter, putrefaction. The impious killed the prophets, and the prophets also killed the impious. The Jews scourged Christ, and Christ also scourged the Jews. The Apostles were handed over by human beings to human authority, and the Apostles also handed human beings over to Satan’s authority.

In all these cases, what is considered except who acted for the truth and who for iniquity, who in order to harm and who in order to correct?

## CHAPTER III

9. No example is found in the evangelical and apostolic writings of anything being requested from the kings of the earth on behalf of the Church against the Church’s enemies. Who denies that it is not found? But that prophecy had not yet been fulfilled: “And now, kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth; serve the Lord in fear.”

For what is said somewhat earlier in the same psalm was still being fulfilled: “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise vain things? The kings of the earth stood by, and the princes gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Ps. II, 10–11, 1–2).

Nevertheless, if past events in the prophetic books were figures of future events, both periods were figured in that king who was called Nebuchadnezzar: the period that occurred under the Apostles, and the period that the Church now possesses.

In the time of the Apostles and martyrs, what was figured was being fulfilled when that king compelled pious and just people to worship an image and cast those who refused into the flames. But now what was figured somewhat later in the same king is being fulfilled: after he had been converted to honoring the true God, he decreed throughout his kingdom that whoever blasphemed the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego should suffer the penalties he deserved (Dan. III, 96).

Thus the earlier period of that king signified the earlier periods of the unbelieving kings, for the sake of whose impiety Christians suffered; the later period of that king signified the periods of the later kings who had already become faithful, for the sake of whom the impious suffer.

10. But among those who, deceived by perversity, err under the name of Christ—lest they perhaps be Christ’s wandering sheep and need to be recalled to the flock in this manner—measured severity and, even more, gentleness are maintained. Thus, through the coercion of exile and financial penalties, they are urged to consider what they are suffering and why, and to learn to place above human rumors and slanders the Scriptures they read.

Who among us—who among you—does not praise the laws issued by the emperors against pagan sacrifices? Certainly a much harsher penalty has been established there, for the punishment for that impiety is capital. But in your case, provision has been made for correction and restraint so that you might be admonished to abandon error rather than punished for crime.

Perhaps what the Apostle said about the Jews may also be said about you: “I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. For, being ignorant of God’s justice and wishing to establish their own, they are not subject to God’s justice” (Rom. X, 2–3).

For what else do you wish to establish except your own justice, when you say that only those can be justified who are able to be baptized by you? In this apostolic judgment that he pronounced concerning the Jews, you differ from the Jews in this respect: you possess the Christian sacraments, whereas they still lack them. But in regard to what he says—“being ignorant of God’s justice and wishing to establish their own,” and that “they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge”—you are entirely their equals, except only for those among you who know what is true and, because of the animosity of their perversity, fight even against a truth they know perfectly well.

The impiety of such people perhaps even surpasses idolatry.

[Note: [Col. 0326] Five Gallican manuscripts read: “They defend impiety even against the truth, which perhaps surpasses idolatry.” Three Vatican manuscripts read: “Fighting even against the truth known perfectly well, they defend impiety. The impiety of such people,” and so forth.]

But because this evil lies hidden in the mind and cannot easily be proved, you are all restrained with milder severity, as though you were less alien from us.

[Note: [Col. 0326] Eight manuscripts read: “As though not excessively alien from us.”]

This I would say either of all heretics who are instructed in the Christian sacraments but dissent from Christ’s truth or unity, or of all Donatists.

11. As for you, who are called not only Donatists in common with them, after Donatus, but also specifically Rogatists, after Rogatus, you certainly seem gentler because you do not rage with the most savage bands of the Circumcellions. But no beast is called tame merely because it has no teeth and claws, if it harms no one.

You say that you do not wish to rage; I think you are unable to do so. For you are so few in number that you dare not set yourselves against the multitudes opposed to you, even if you wished to. But let us suppose that you also do not wish what you are unable to do. Let us suppose that you understand and hold the evangelical saying—“If anyone wishes to take your tunic and contend with you in judgment, let him have your cloak as well” (Matt. V, 40)—in such a way that you think no injury and no legal resistance at all should be offered to those who persecute you.

Certainly Rogatus, your founder, either did not possess this understanding or did not put it into practice. For, concerning I know not what matters, as you yourselves say, he fought with the fiercest persistence, even in a legal proceeding. If someone had said to him, “Which of the Apostles ever defended his own property in a public court in a matter of faith?”—just as you wrote in your letter, “Which of the Apostles ever seized another’s property in a matter of faith?”—he would indeed have found no example of this deed in the divine writings. Yet perhaps he would have found some genuine defense if he had held to the true Church and had not shamelessly possessed something under the name of the true Church.

## CHAPTER IV

12. As for commands of earthly powers, whether they are to be sought or exercised against schismatics or heretics, those from whom you separated were certainly very vigorous in this matter, as far as we have been able to learn—both against you and against the Maximianists, as we prove by the certain documents of the official proceedings. Yet you had not yet separated from them when, in their petition to the emperor Julian, they said that justice alone had a place with him.

[Note: [Col. 0327] From this it is further understood that the Rogatist schism did not arise before the year 361, at the end of which, after Constantius died, Julian gained control. On that flattering petition of the Donatists, by which they requested that basilicas taken from them by Constantine’s command be restored to them, Augustine should be consulted in *Against the Letter of Petilian*, book 2, ch. 92, no. 203; ch. 97, no. 224; and Epistle 105, no. 9; likewise Optatus, book 2.]

They certainly knew him to be an apostate and saw that he was devoted to idolatries. Thus they must either have admitted that idolatry was justice or been unable to deny that they had wickedly lied when they said that justice alone had a place with him, although they saw that idolatry had a great place with him.

But let there have been an error in the wording. What do you say about the deed itself? If nothing just is to be requested from an emperor, why was something considered just requested from Julian?

[Note: [Col. 0327] Lov. reads: “If nothing unjust is to be requested from the emperor,” and shortly afterward, “what was considered unjust.” But the manuscripts and the earlier editions have *justum*—“just”—in both places, and this is better.]

13. Is it permissible to request that each person recover his own property, but not to accuse someone so that he may be restrained by the emperor? For the moment, even in the demand for the return of their own property they depart from apostolic examples, since none of the Apostles is found to have done this.

Yet when your ancestors accused Caecilian, then bishop of the Church of Carthage, before the emperor Constantine through the proconsul Anulinus, although they refused to communicate with him as though he were a criminal, they did not seek the return of property they had lost. Rather, as we judge, and as the outcome of the trials itself showed, they maliciously attacked an innocent man. What more wicked thing could they have done?

But if, as you falsely suppose, they handed over a man whom they judged truly criminal to the earthly authorities, what do you object to us that the presumption of your own people first did? We would not blame them for having done it if they had done it not with an envious and harmful intention, but with the desire to amend and correct.

But we certainly blame you, since you regard it as a crime to complain to a Christian emperor about the enemies of our communion, although the petition given by your ancestors to the proconsul Anulinus, and intended to be sent to the emperor Constantine, bore this heading:

“Petition of the Catholic Church concerning the crimes of Caecilian, delivered by the party of Majorinus.”

[Note: [Col. 0327] The petition referred to in Epistle 88, §2.]

We blame them even more for this: after they had voluntarily accused Caecilian before the emperor—although they ought first of all to have convicted him before their overseas colleagues—when the emperor acted much more orderly and sent the episcopal case brought before him to the bishops, they refused, even after being defeated, to maintain peace with their brothers. Instead, they came again before the same emperor; again they accused before an earthly king not only Caecilian but also the bishops given to them as judges; again they appealed from another episcopal judgment to the same emperor. Even when that emperor himself was hearing and judging the case between the parties, they did not think they ought to yield either to truth or to peace.

14. What else would Constantine have decreed against Caecilian and his associates, if they had been defeated by the accusations of your ancestors, than what he decreed against those very people who had voluntarily brought the accusations but could not prove what they alleged, and who, even after being defeated, refused to consent to the truth?

[Note: [Col. 0328] The editions add: “For they refused to consent to the truth.” *For* is absent from the manuscripts and ought to be absent.]

That emperor was the first to establish in this case that the property of those who had been convicted and who stubbornly resisted unity should be confiscated for the treasury.

But naturally, if the emperor had issued some such decree against Caecilian’s communion after your ancestors had accused and overcome him, you would have wanted to be called the Church’s guardians and defenders of peace and unity. But when such decrees are issued by emperors against those who voluntarily accused others yet could prove nothing, and who refused to consent even when the embrace of peace was offered to them so that they might be received after correction, you loudly proclaim that this is an unworthy deed. You insist that no one should be compelled to unity and that no one should repay evil with evil.

What is this other than what one of your own people wrote: “What we want is holy”?

[Note: [Col. 0328] A half-line of Tyconius.]

Even now it was neither difficult nor beyond your ability to consider and reflect that Constantine’s judgment and sentence against you remain in force. It was promulgated against you when your ancestors repeatedly accused Caecilian before the emperor but failed to convict him; and the other emperors, especially Catholic Christians, necessarily follow it whenever the necessity created by your obstinacy compels them to do something concerning you.

15. It would have been easy for you to think about these matters and at some point say to yourselves: If Caecilian was either innocent or could not be convicted as guilty, what did the Christian society spread so far and wide do wrong in this affair? Why was the Christian world not permitted to remain ignorant of what those who had brought the accusation could not demonstrate?

Why are those whom Christ sowed in His field—that is, in this world—and whom He commanded to grow among the weeds until the harvest (Matt. XIII, 24–30)—why are the many thousands of faithful in all nations, whose multitude the Lord compared with the stars of heaven and the sand of the sea, whom He promised and brought to blessing in the seed of Abraham (Gen. XXII, 17–18), denied the name of Christians merely because in this case, in which they were not present for the investigation, they preferred to trust the judges who judged at their own peril rather than the defeated litigants?

Certainly no one’s crime stains a person who is ignorant of it. How could the faithful spread throughout the whole world have known the crime of the traditors—a crime which, even if the accusers knew it, they were nevertheless unable to demonstrate to them?

Their innocence in this matter, then, is most easily shown by their very ignorance. Why, therefore, are innocent people accused of false crimes because they did not know the crimes of others, whether false or true? What room is left for innocence if it is itself a crime not to know another person’s crime?

Moreover, if the ignorance of so many peoples, as has been said, shows them to be innocent, how great a crime it is to separate from the communion of these innocent people! For even the deeds of the guilty—deeds that cannot be demonstrated to the innocent or believed by them—do not defile anyone if, for the sake of association with the innocent, they endure even what they have come to know.

The good are not to be abandoned on account of the wicked; rather, the wicked are to be tolerated for the sake of the good. The prophets tolerated those against whom such things were said, and they did not abandon communion in the sacraments of that people. The Lord Himself tolerated the guilty Judas until the end appropriate to him and allowed him to share the sacred supper with the innocent. The Apostles tolerated those who proclaimed Christ out of envy, which is the devil’s vice (Phil. I, 15–18). Cyprian tolerated the avarice of his colleagues, which, according to the Apostle, he calls idolatry (Col. III, 5).

Finally, whatever was done at that time among those bishops—even if some of them perhaps knew about it—is now unknown to everyone, unless there is partiality.

[Note: [Col. 0329] The manuscripts and editions other than Lov. read “is now unknown to everyone.” Lov. has “now.”]

Why, then, is peace not loved by everyone? You could very easily have considered these things, or perhaps you do consider them. But it would have been better for you to love the earthly possessions that, from fear of losing them, would lead you to consent to known truth than to love the utterly empty glory of human beings, which you think you will lose if you consent to known truth.

## CHAPTER V

16. You see now, I think, that what must be considered is not what someone is compelled to do, but the character of that by which he is compelled—whether it is good or evil. The point is not that anyone can become good unwillingly, but that, fearing what he does not wish to suffer, he either abandons the obstinacy that obstructs his mind or is compelled to learn a truth previously unknown to him. Thus, through fear, he may reject the falsehood he was defending or seek the truth he did not know, and willingly hold what he had previously been unwilling to hold.

This might perhaps be said needlessly in any number of words if it were not demonstrated by so many examples. We see that not merely this or that individual, but many cities, were once Donatist and are now Catholic; they vehemently detest the devilish separation and ardently love unity. Yet they became Catholic through the opportunities provided by this fear that displeases you, through the laws of the emperors—from Constantine, before whom your people first voluntarily accused Caecilian, down to the present emperors, who most justly decree that the judgment of the man whom your people chose and preferred to episcopal judges must be upheld against you.

17. Therefore, when these examples were presented to me by my colleagues, I yielded. At first my own position had been that no one should be compelled to the unity of Christ: we should act by words, fight by debate, and conquer by reason, lest we have as Catholics those whom we knew to be open heretics.

But my opinion was overcome not by the words of those who contradicted me, but by the examples they demonstrated. First they confronted me with my own city. Although it had been entirely on the Donatist side, it was converted to Catholic unity through fear of the imperial laws. Now we see it detest the destructive force of your hostility so completely that one would think it had never been there.

Many other cities were also mentioned to me by name, so that I could recognize from the facts themselves that in this matter too the saying could rightly be understood: “Give an opportunity to the wise person, and he will become wiser” (Prov. IX, 9).

How many, as we know for certain, already wished to be Catholics, moved by the clearest truth, but, out of respect for the offense of their own people, postponed it day after day! How many were bound not by the truth—in which you have never placed your trust—but by the heavy bond of hardened custom, so that the divine saying might be fulfilled in them: “A stubborn servant will not be corrected by words; even if he understands, he will not obey” (ibid. XXIX, 19)!

How many therefore thought the true Church was the party of Donatus because security made them torpid, disdainful, and lazy about coming to know Catholic truth! How many were barred from entering by the rumors of slanderers, who kept claiming that we placed I know not what else upon God’s altar! How many, thinking it made no difference in which party someone was a Christian, remained in the Donatist party because they had been born there, since no one compelled them to leave it and cross over to the Catholic Church!

18. The fear of these laws, through which kings serve the Lord in fear, benefited all these people so greatly that some now say: “We already wanted this; but thanks be to God, who gave us the opportunity to do now what we had long intended to do and cut short our little delays.”

Others say: “We already knew this was true, but we were held by some kind of habit. Thanks be to the Lord, who broke our bonds and transferred us to the bond of peace.”

Others say: “We did not know that the truth was here, nor did we wish to learn it. But fear made us attentive to learning it, because we feared that we might be struck by the loss of temporal things without gaining anything eternal. Thanks be to the Lord, who shook our negligence with the goad of fear, so that at least in our anxiety we might seek what, in our security, we had never taken care to know.”

Others say: “We were frightened from entering by false rumors, which we would not have known to be false if we had not entered; and we would not have entered unless we had been compelled. Thanks be to the Lord, who removed our trembling with the whip and, by experience, taught us how vain and empty were the things that lying rumor had spread about His Church. From this we now believe that those other accusations too were false—those accusations made by the founders of this heresy—since their descendants have invented things even more false and worse.”

Others say: “We thought it made no difference where we held the faith of Christ. But thanks be to the Lord, who gathered us from division and showed that it is fitting for the one God to be worshiped in unity.”

19. To prevent these gains for the Lord, then, should I have opposed my colleagues, so that Christ’s wandering sheep would not be gathered from your mountains and hills—that is, from the swellings of your pride—into the fold of peace, where there is “one flock and one shepherd” (John X, 16)?

Should I really have opposed this provision so that you would not lose the possessions you call yours, and could safely proscribe Christ? So that you could draw up wills under Roman law, yet by slanderous accusations tear apart the Testament established for the patriarchs under divine law, where it is written, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXVI, 4)? So that you could have free contracts in purchases and sales, yet dare to divide among yourselves what Christ purchased by being sold? So that whatever one of you gave to another might have force, while what the God of gods gave to His sons, called “from the rising of the sun to its setting” (Ps. LXIX, 1), would have no force?

So that you would not be sent into exile from the land of your bodies, while you tried to make Christ an exile from the kingdom of His blood, “from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Ps. LXXI, 8)?

On the contrary, let the kings of the earth serve Christ, even by making laws on Christ’s behalf. Your ancestors falsely accused Caecilian and his associates before the kings of the earth so that they might be punished. Let the lions now turn to crush the bones of the slanderers; let not even Daniel intercede for them, since he was proved innocent and delivered from the pit in which they perish (Dan. XIV, 39–42). For “the one who digs a pit for his neighbor will himself more justly fall into it” (Prov. XXVI, 27).

## CHAPTER VI

20. Brother, rescue yourself, while you live in this flesh, from the wrath that is to come upon the stubborn and proud. The terror of temporal powers, when it attacks the truth, is a glorious trial for the strong in justice, but a dangerous temptation for the weak. When, however, it proclaims the truth, it is a useful admonition for those who err and a useless affliction for the insensitive.

[Note: [Col. 0331] Bad., Am., and Er. read: “for those who err and are at odds.”]

Nevertheless, authority exists only from God; and whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance. For rulers are not a cause of fear to good conduct, but to evil. Do you wish not to fear authority? Do what is good, and you will receive praise from it (Rom. XIII, 1–3).

Whether authority, favoring the truth, corrects someone, or, hostile to the truth, rages against someone, the person who is corrected has praise from it in the first case, and the person who is crowned as victor has praise from it in the second.

But you do not do what is good, so that you ought not to fear authority—unless perhaps it is good to sit idle and not slander your brother (Ps. XLIX, 20), yet to slander all the brothers established among all the nations, to whom the prophets, Christ, and the Apostles bear witness.

For it is written, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXVI, 4). It is written, “From the rising of the sun to its setting a pure sacrifice is offered to my name; for my name is glorified among the nations, says the Lord” (Mal. I, 11). Listen: “says the Lord”—not “says Donatus,” or “Rogatus,” or “Vincentius,” or “Hilary,” or “Ambrose,” or “Augustine.” It is the Lord who speaks.

It is written: “And all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed in him; all nations shall magnify him. Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, who alone does wonders; and blessed is the name of his glory forever and ever. And all the earth shall be filled with his glory. Let it be, let it be” (Ps. LXXI, 17–19).

And you sit in Cartennas and say, with the ten Rogatists who remain: “Let it not be; let it not be.”

21. You hear the Gospel speaking: “It was necessary that all things written about me in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms be fulfilled.” Then He opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures, and He said to them: “Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and for repentance and forgiveness of sins to be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke XXIV, 44, 47).

You also read in the Acts of the Apostles how this Gospel began from Jerusalem, where the Holy Spirit first filled those one hundred and twenty people, and from there went out into Judea and Samaria and among all nations, just as He had told them when He was about to ascend into heaven: “You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (Acts I, 15, 8, and II). For “their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII, 5).

Yet you contradict divine testimonies, strengthened by such great firmness and made manifest by such great light. You try to confine Christ’s inheritance within this proscription, so that although repentance is preached in His name among all nations, as He said, no one moved by this preaching anywhere in the world can have his sins forgiven unless he seeks out and finds Vincent of Cartennas, hidden in Caesarean Mauretania, or one of his nine or ten companions.

What would the conceit of a decaying skin not dare? Where would the presumption of flesh and blood not plunge itself? Is this your good work, on account of which you should not fear authority?

You place such a great stumbling block before the son of your mother (Ps. XLIX, 20)—that is, the little and weak person for whom Christ died (I Cor. VIII, 11), not yet fit for paternal food but still needing to be nourished with maternal milk (ibid. III, 2). And you set Hilary’s books against me in order to deny the Church’s growth among all nations until the end of the age, which God promised against your unbelief with an oath.

You would have been most wretched if you had resisted when this was being promised; but now, even when it is being fulfilled, you contradict it.

## CHAPTER VII

22. But as a learned historian, you have discovered something great which you thought ought to be brought forward against God’s testimonies. For you say: “In relation to the regions of the whole world, the part in which the Christian faith is named is small in comparison with the whole world.”

You do not wish to consider—or you pretend not to know—among how many barbarian nations the Gospel has already come in so short a time. Thus even Christ’s enemies can no longer doubt that what He replied to the disciples who asked about the end of the age will soon come to pass: “This Gospel will be preached throughout the whole world, as a testimony to all nations; and then the end will come” (Matt. XXIV, 14).

On this point, cry out and contend as much as you can, even if the Gospel is preached among the Persians and Indians—where indeed it has long been preached—unless you mean that anyone who hears this but does not come to Cartennas, or to the neighborhood of the people of Cartennas, cannot be cleansed at all from his sins.

So, if you lack this voice, do you fear being mocked, while, when you do not lack it, you refuse to weep?

### Chapter VII

**23.** But you seem to say something clever when you interpret the name *Catholic* not from communion with the whole world, but from observance of all the divine precepts and all the Sacraments—as though, even if it was perhaps called Catholic because it truly possesses the whole truth, some fragments of that truth are also found in various heresies, we were relying on the testimony of this name to demonstrate the Church among all nations, rather than on God’s promises and on so many clear and manifest oracles of truth itself.

But surely this is the whole point you are trying to persuade us of: that only the Rogatists remain who ought rightly to be called Catholics, on the basis of observance of all the divine precepts and all the Sacraments; and that you alone are those in whom the Son of Man will find faith when he comes (Luke 18:8). Forgive us: we do not believe it.

For even if you dare perhaps to say that the faith which the Lord said he would not find on earth could be found among you, and that you should therefore be reckoned not as being on earth but in heaven, the Apostle has nevertheless made us so cautious that he commanded even an angel from heaven who should announce to us another gospel than the one we received to be accursed (Gal. 1:8).

How, then, can we be confident that from the divine Scriptures we have received Christ made manifest, if from them we have not also received the Church made manifest? Let anyone weave whatever handles and hooks he pleases against the simplicity of truth, let him spread whatever clouds of cunning falsehood he pleases: just as the one who announces that Christ neither suffered nor rose on the third day will be accursed—for in the gospel truth we received that “Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead on the third day” (Luke 24:46)—so shall anyone be accursed who announces a Church apart from the communion of all nations. For by that same truth we have consequently received that “repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem”; and we must hold without wavering that “whoever announces to you anything other than what you received, let him be accursed” (ibid., 47).

### Chapter VIII

**24.** If, then, we do not listen to all the Donatists when they put themselves forward as the Church of Christ [Note: [Col. 0333] Seventeen manuscripts read *opponentes* (“opposing”) instead of *supponentes* (“putting themselves forward”).], because they produce no testimony from the divine Books in their own support by which they can teach this, how much less, I ask you, ought we to listen to the Rogatists, who will not even attempt to interpret for themselves what is written: “Where do you pasture, where do you lie down at midday?” (Song 1:6)?

For if in this passage of Scripture “midday” is to be understood as Africa in the party of Donatus, because it lies beneath a hotter region of the sky, all the Maximianists will surpass you, since their schism broke out in Byzantium and Tripolis. But let the Arzuges fight with them and contend that this applies more to themselves. Mauritania Caesariensis, however, being nearer the western than the southern region, when it does not even wish to be called Africa, how will it boast of midday—not, I say, against the whole world, but against the very party of Donatus, from which the party of Rogatus is a tiny fragment cut off from a larger fragment? Who, moreover, would not most shamelessly attempt to interpret something placed in an allegory in his own favor unless he also possessed clear testimonies by whose light obscure passages might be illuminated?

**25.** But what we are accustomed to say to all the Donatists, we say to you with even greater force: If some people could have—and this is impossible—a just cause by which they separated their communion from the communion of the whole world and called it the Church of Christ, because they had justly separated themselves from the communion of all nations, how do you know that, in the Christian society spread so far and wide, some people may not already have separated themselves for a just cause in the most distant lands before you separated yourselves, so that the reputation of their justice could not have reached you?

How can the Church be among you rather than among those who perhaps separated themselves earlier? Thus, because you do not know this, you are uncertain even about yourselves. This must necessarily happen to all who use as testimony for their society not something divine, but their own testimony.

For you cannot say, “If this had happened, it could not have escaped our notice,” since, if you were asked how many parties have already been formed in Africa itself out of the party of Donatus, you would not be able to say—especially because those who do this seem to themselves more righteous the fewer they are, and therefore they are all the less conspicuous.

Accordingly, you are uncertain lest perhaps a few righteous people, and therefore people hardly known, somewhere far away, opposite Africa’s southern region, may have separated themselves first on the northern side, moved by an entirely just cause, before the party of Donatus separated its own justice from the wickedness of the rest of humanity; and lest that group should rather be the Church of God, like a spiritual Zion, which by a just separation anticipated all of you. It would interpret for itself, with much greater presumption, what is written, “Mount Zion, the sides of the north, the city of the great King” (Ps. 47:3), than the party of Donatus interprets for itself, “Where do you pasture, where do you lie down at midday?” (Song 1:6).

**26.** And yet you fear that, when you are compelled to unity by imperial laws, the name of God may be blasphemed longer by Jews and pagans—as though the Jews did not know how their first people, Israel, even wished to destroy in war those two and a half tribes which had received lands beyond the Jordan, when they thought that those tribes had separated themselves from the unity of their people (Josh. 22:9–12).

Pagans, on the other hand, can blaspheme us more on account of the laws which Christian emperors have enacted against the worshipers of idols; and yet many of them have been corrected and converted to the living and true God, and are converted every day.

But plainly, if Jews and pagans thought there were as few Christians as there are of you who claim that you alone are Christians, they would not even consider us worthy of blasphemy; they would never stop laughing.

Do you not fear that the Jews may say to you: “Where is what your Paul understands as your Church, where he says, ‘Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, for the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband’” (Gal. 4:27)—placing the multitude of Christians above the multitude of Jews—if the Church of Christ is your small number?

Will you say to them, “We are more righteous precisely because we are few”? And do you not consider that they will reply: “However many you claim yourselves to be, you are nevertheless not those of whom it was said, ‘The children of the deserted woman are many,’ if so very few of you have remained”?

**27.** Here you will bring forward the example of that righteous man in the Flood who, together with his household, was found worthy to be saved alone. You see, then, how far you still are from righteousness. We certainly do not call you righteous until you remain with seven others, making yourself the eighth—unless, as I was saying, someone had already seized this righteousness before the party of Donatus and, moved by some just cause, separated himself elsewhere with his seven companions and was saved from the flood of this world.

Since you do not know whether this happened, and since the name of Donatus is just as unheard of to many Christian peoples living in distant lands as this is unheard of to you, you are uncertain where the Church is. For it will be there where what you later did was perhaps first done, if there could have been any just cause by which you could separate yourselves from the communion of all nations.

### Chapter IX
