**28.** We, however, are certain that no one could justly separate himself from the communion of all nations, because each of us seeks the Church not in his own righteousness but in the divine Scriptures, and sees it restored as it was promised.

For it is the Church of which it is said, “As a lily among thorns, so is my near one among the daughters” (Song 2:2): and the thorns can be called such only because of wickedness of conduct, while the daughters can be called such only because of communion in the Sacraments.

It is the Church that says, “From the ends of the earth I cried to you when my heart was in distress” (Ps. 60:3). In another psalm it says, “Weariness seized me because of sinners who abandon your law,” and, “I saw the senseless, and I wasted away” (Ps. 118:53, 158).

It is the Church that says to her bridegroom, “Where do you pasture, where do you lie down at midday, lest I become like one who is veiled among the flocks of your companions?” (Song 1:6). This is what is said elsewhere: “Make your right hand known to me, and those instructed in heart in wisdom” (Ps. 89:12)—among whom, shining with light and burning with love, you rest as at midday. Otherwise, like one who is veiled—that is, hidden and unknown—I might rush not upon your flock but upon the flocks of your companions, that is, of heretics.

He calls them companions in the same way as he calls those daughters thorns, because of their communion in the Sacraments. Of them it is said elsewhere: “But you, my equal, my leader, and my acquaintance, who together with me took sweet food; we walked in agreement in the house of God. Let death come upon them, and let them descend alive into hell” (Ps. 54:14–16), like Dathan and Abiram, authors of impious separation.

**29.** It is to this Church that the following reply is immediately made: “Unless you know yourself, O beautiful among women, go out in the footsteps of the flocks and pasture your kids in the tents of the shepherds” (Song 1:7).

O reply of the sweetest bridegroom! “Unless you know yourself,” he says—for surely “a city cannot be hidden when set upon a mountain” (Matt. 5:14). Therefore you are not hidden, so that you may rush upon the flocks of my companions [Note: [Col. 0335] The editions read “your companions”; seventeen manuscripts read “my companions.”].

For I am the mountain prepared on the summit of the mountains, to which all nations shall come (Isa. 2:2). Unless, then, you know yourself—not in the words of slanderers, but in the testimonies of my Books.

Unless you know yourself, because it was said concerning you: “Lengthen your cords and strengthen your firm stakes; extend yourself further and further to the right and to the left. For your seed shall inherit the nations, and you shall inhabit cities that were deserted. There is no reason for you to fear, for you shall prevail; and do not be ashamed because you were detested. For you shall forget your confusion forever, and you shall not remember the disgrace of your widowhood. For I am the Lord who made you; the Lord is his name. And the one who redeemed you, he himself shall be called the God of Israel of the whole earth” (Isa. 54:2–5).

Unless you know yourself, O beautiful among women, because it was said concerning you, “The king desired your beauty”; because it was said concerning you, “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them princes over all the earth” (Ps. 44:12, 17).

Unless, then, you know yourself, “go out” (Song 1:7). It is not I who cast you out, but you go out, so that it may be said of you, “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19).

Go out in the footsteps of the flocks—not in my footsteps, but in the footsteps of flocks; not of one flock, but of divided and wandering flocks.

And pasture your kids—not as Peter, to whom it is said, “Pasture my sheep” (John 21:17), but pasture your kids in the tents of the shepherds; not in the tent of the shepherd, where there is one flock and one shepherd (ibid. 10:16).

For she knows herself, lest this happen to her, because it happened to those who did not know themselves in her.

**30.** It is the Church of whose small number it is said in comparison with the multitude of the wicked that “the way is narrow and constricted that leads to life, and few are those who walk in it” (Matt. 7:14).

And again it is the Church of whose multitude it is said, “So shall your seed be, like the stars of heaven and like the sand of the sea” (Gen. 22:17).

For the same faithful, holy, and good people are few in comparison with the greater number of the wicked, yet they are many in themselves: for “the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband”; and “many shall come from the east and the west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 8:11); and because God provides for himself “a people abundant in number, zealous for good works” (Titus 2:14); and in the Apocalypse a multitude that no one can number is seen, from every tribe and tongue, in white robes and with victorious palms (Rev. 7:9).

It is the Church that is sometimes darkened and, as it were, covered with cloud by the multitude of scandals, when sinners bend the bow “to shoot at the upright in heart in the dark moon” (Ps. 10:3). Yet even then she stands out in her strongest members.

And if some distribution is to be made in these divine words, perhaps it was not without reason that Abraham’s seed was compared both to “the stars of heaven” and to “the sand that is on the shore of the sea”: so that in the stars of heaven the fewer, stronger, and brighter may be understood, while in the sand of the seashore the great multitude of the weak and carnal may be understood—sometimes appearing peaceful and free in the calm of the times, but at other times covered and disturbed by the waves of tribulations and temptations.

**31.** Such was the time about which Hilary wrote [Col. 0337] [Note: [Col. 0337] Vincent was misusing this testimony of Hilary from his book *On the Synods*, against the Arians, where he says: “For apart from Eleusius and the few with him, most of the ten provinces of Asia in which I reside truly do not know God.” This is easily understood from Augustine’s reply: Hilary was reproving the tares of the ten provinces of Asia.], and you thought that you could lay an ambush against so many divine testimonies, as though the Church had perished from the whole world.

By this method you could also say that there were not so many Churches of Galatia at the time when the Apostle said, “O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you, that after beginning with the Spirit you are now being completed in the flesh?” (Gal. 3:1).

For this is how you slander the learned man, who severely rebuked the slow-hearted and timid, whom he was laboring over again until Christ should be formed in them (ibid. 4:19).

Who does not know that at that time many people of small understanding were deceived by obscure words, so that they thought the Arians believed what they themselves also believed? Others yielded through fear and gave a pretended assent, not walking rightly according to the truth of the Gospel. Yet when these people were later corrected, you would not wish them to be forgiven in the manner—whatever it may have been—that is unknown to you.

You plainly do not know the Scriptures of God. Read what Paul wrote about Peter, and what Cyprian also understood from it; and do not be displeased with the gentleness of the Church, which gathers together the scattered members of Christ rather than scattering those already gathered.

Even those who were firmest at that time, and who were able to understand the deceptive words of the heretics, were few in comparison with the others; yet some of them were bravely enduring exile for the faith, while others were hiding throughout the whole world.

Thus the Church, which grows among all nations, was preserved in the Lord’s wheat, and will be preserved until the end, until it possesses all nations, even the barbarian ones.

For it is the Church represented by the good seed which the Son of Man sowed, and which he foretold would grow among the tares until the harvest. The field, however, is the world, and the harvest is the end of the age (Matt. 13:24–39).

**32.** Hilary, then, was either reproving the tares, not the wheat, of the ten provinces of Asia, or else he considered that the wheat itself, which was endangered by some failing, ought to be reproved all the more strongly—and therefore all the more usefully.

The canonical Scriptures also have this manner of reproving, in which something is said as though to everyone, while the word reaches only certain people. For when the Apostle says to the Corinthians, “How do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?” (1 Cor. 15:12), he clearly shows that not all were like this; nevertheless, he testifies that such people were among them, not outside them.

So that those who did not hold this view might not be led astray by them, he shortly afterward warned them, saying: “Do not be deceived: bad conversations corrupt good morals. Be sober, righteous [Note: [Col. 0337] Erasmus and Louvain read *juste*, “justly,” following the Greek text, *dikaiōs*. Badius, Amerbach, and sixteen manuscripts, together with the Vulgate, read *justi*, “righteous.”], and do not sin; for some possess ignorance of God. I speak this to your shame” (ibid., 33–34).

And when he says, “Since there are jealousy and contention among you, are you not carnal and walking according to human ways?” (ibid. 3:3), he speaks as though to everyone; and you see how serious his statement is.

Therefore, unless we read in that same Epistle, “I give thanks to my God always for you, for the grace of God which was given to you in Christ Jesus, because in everything you have been enriched in him, in every word and in all knowledge, just as the testimony of Christ was confirmed in you, so that you lack nothing in any grace” (1 Cor. 1:4–7), we would think that all the Corinthians were carnal and merely natural, unable to receive the things of the Spirit of God (ibid. 2:14), contentious, jealous, and walking according to human ways.

Thus the whole world is “placed in the evil one” (1 John 5:19), because of the tares that are throughout the whole world; and Christ is “the propitiation for our sins, not for ours only but also for those of the whole world” (ibid. 2:2), because of the wheat that is throughout the whole world.

**33.** Love grows cold in many because of the abundance of scandals, as the name of Christ is glorified more and more and even the wicked, utterly and persistently perverse, are gathered into communion in his Sacraments; nevertheless, they are like chaff from the Lord’s threshing floor, to be separated only by the final winnowing (Matt. 3:12).

These people do not extinguish the Lord’s wheat—which, compared with them, is few, but in itself is many. They do not extinguish God’s elect, who are to be gathered at the end of the age, as the Gospel says, “from the four winds, from the highest heavens to their boundaries” (ibid. 24:31).

For their voice is: “Save me, Lord, for the holy one has failed, for truths have been diminished among the children of men” (Ps. 11:2). Concerning them the Lord also says, amid the abundance of iniquity, “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 24:12–13).

Finally, the context shows that more than one person speaks in the same psalm, where it says: “You, Lord, will preserve us and guard us from this generation forever” (Ps. 11:2, 8).

Because of this abundance of iniquity, which the Lord foretold would come, the following was also stated: “When the Son of Man comes, do you suppose he will find faith on earth?” (Luke 18:8).

The doubt of the one who knows all things foreshadowed our doubt in him, when the Church, often deceived by many from whom she had hoped much because they turned out otherwise than they were believed to be, is so disturbed in her own members that she is reluctant to believe anything good easily of anyone.

Nevertheless, there can be no doubt that those whose faith he will find on earth are growing throughout the entire field together with the tares.

**34.** It is therefore the Church that swims within the Lord’s net together with the bad fish, from whom she is always separated and withdrawn in heart and conduct, so that she may be presented to her husband glorious, “not having spot or wrinkle” (Eph. 5:27).

She awaits bodily separation on the shore of the sea—that is, at the end of the age (Matt. 13:47–49)—correcting those whom she can and tolerating those whom she cannot correct. Yet because of the wickedness of those whom she does not correct, she does not abandon the gentleness of the good.

### Chapter X

**35.** Therefore, brother, do not wish to gather accusations from the writings of bishops against so many, so clear, and so certain divine testimonies—whether from our bishops, such as Hilary, or from bishops of the very unity itself, before the party of Donatus separated, such as Cyprian and Agrippinus.

First, because this kind of writing must be distinguished from the authority of the canon [Col. 0339] [Note: [Col. 0339] The better manuscripts read “from canonical writings.”]. For these writings are not read as though testimony were to be produced from them in such a way that it would be impermissible to hold a contrary view if they happened in some place to have understood matters differently from what truth requires.

For we are among those to whom we should not disdain to apply what the Apostle said: “If you think anything differently, God will reveal this also to you. Nevertheless, in what we have attained, let us walk” (Phil. 3:15–16)—namely, in that way which is Christ.

Concerning this way the Psalm speaks: “May God have mercy on us and bless us; may he make his face shine upon us, so that we may know your way on earth, your salvation among all nations” (Ps. 65:2–3).

**36.** Next, if you take pleasure in the authority of the holy bishop and glorious martyr Cyprian—an authority which, as I said, we distinguish from canonical authority—why do you not take pleasure in the fact that he both cherished and defended the unity of the whole world and of all nations?

Why do you not take pleasure in the fact that he judged those who wished, as though they were righteous, to separate themselves from it to be extremely arrogant and proud? He ridiculed their presumption in claiming for themselves what the Lord did not grant even to the Apostles: to gather the tares before the proper time, or, as though they had been permitted to carry the chaff and cleanse the threshing floor, to attempt to separate the chaff from the wheat.

Why do you not take pleasure in the fact that he showed that no one could be defiled by the sins of others—a claim which all the authors of impious sedition adopt as the sole reason for their separation?

Why do you not take pleasure in the fact that, in the very matter on which he held a different opinion, he decided that colleagues who thought differently were neither to be judged nor removed from the right of communion?

Why do you not take pleasure in the fact that in the very letter to Jubaianus, which was first read aloud at the council [Note: [Col. 0339] Held at Carthage in the year 256.] whose authority you claim to follow in rebaptizing, he admits that in the past people who had been baptized elsewhere were admitted into the Church without being baptized again, and therefore he thinks that they were without Baptism; yet he places such usefulness and saving benefit in the peace of the Church that, for its sake, he does not believe they should be separated from the Church’s gifts?

**37.** In this matter, as I know your intelligence, you can very easily see that your entire case has been utterly overturned and extinguished.

For if, as you think, the Church that had existed throughout the world perished by communicating the Sacraments with sinners—for this reason you separated yourselves—then it had already wholly perished earlier, when, as Cyprian says, people were admitted into it without Baptism.

Thus Cyprian himself had no Church in which to be born; how much less did your much later founder and father, Donatus?

But if at that time, when people were admitted into it without Baptism, there was nevertheless a Church which gave birth to Cyprian and would also give birth to Donatus, it is clear that the righteous are not contaminated by the sins of others when they share the Sacraments with them.

Accordingly, you have no excuse by which you can cleanse yourselves of the separation by which you have withdrawn from unity, and the oracle of Holy Scripture is fulfilled in you: “The wicked son declares himself righteous, but he does not cleanse his departure” [Note: [Col. 0339] Proverbs 24 according to the Septuagint. These words are absent from the Vulgate but are found in the Septuagint, inserted between verses 22 and 23. The Greek text reads: “A wicked son declares himself righteous; but he has not washed his departure.” Jerome cites the passage in *Against the Pelagians*, book 1, chapter 12, in these words: “The wicked son makes himself righteous, and does not wash his departure.”] [Col. 0340].

**38.** No one equals Cyprian’s merits who, because of the identical Sacraments, does not dare to rebaptize even heretics—just as no one equals Peter’s merits who does not compel the nations to Judaize.

But Peter’s stumbling, and also his correction, are contained in the canonical Scriptures. Cyprian’s having thought differently about Baptism from the form and custom which the Church had is found not in the canonical writings but in his own letters and those of the council.

It is not found that he corrected this opinion. Nevertheless, it is not inappropriate to suppose of such a man that he did correct it, and that this may have been suppressed by those who took excessive pleasure in this error and did not wish to be deprived of such apparent patronage.

Although there are also people who insist that Cyprian did not hold this view at all, but that it was fabricated under his name by presumptuous liars.

For the integrity and recognition of the writings of any illustrious bishop could not be preserved in the same way as canonical Scripture, which is preserved through written transmission in so many languages and through the order and succession of ecclesiastical celebration. Yet even against canonical Scripture there have been people who fabricated many things under the names of the Apostles.

They did so in vain, because Scripture has been so authoritatively commended, so widely read, and so well known. Nevertheless, the audacity of impious efforts has demonstrated what may be attempted against writings that are not founded upon canonical authority: it has not refrained even from rising against writings fortified by so great a mass of public knowledge.

**39.** Nevertheless, for two reasons we do not deny that Cyprian held that view.

First, his style has a certain distinctive character by which it can be recognized. Second, our case is shown to be all the more invincible against you there: the presumption of your separation, namely that you should not be defiled by the sins of others, is entirely overturned with the greatest ease.

For Cyprian’s writings show that the Sacraments were shared with sinners when people were admitted into the Church who, according to your view—and according to the opinion which you attribute to him—did not possess Baptism.

Yet the Church did not perish. Rather, the Lord’s wheat remained scattered throughout the whole world in the dignity proper to its kind.

Accordingly, if, in your distress, you flee to Cyprian’s authority as though to some harbor, you see what reef your error strikes there. But if you no longer dare to flee there, you are shipwrecked without any struggle.

**40.** Moreover, Cyprian either did not hold at all what you quote him as having held; or he later corrected it according to the rule of truth; or he covered this blemish, as it were, on his most spotless breast with the abundance of love, while he both most fully defended the unity of the Church growing throughout the whole world and most steadfastly maintained the bond of peace.

For it is written, “Love covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8).

To this was added the fact that, like a most fruitful branch, whatever in him needed correction was cleansed by the Father with the pruning knife of suffering: “The branch,” says the Lord, “that bears fruit in me, my Father purifies it so that it may bear more fruit” (John 15:2).

Why was this so, unless because, remaining attached to the spreading vine, he did not abandon the root of unity? For even if he were to hand over his body to be burned, but did not have love, it would profit him nothing (1 Cor. 13:3).

**41.** Pay attention a little longer to Cyprian’s writings, so that you may perceive how he showed to be beyond excuse anyone who wished to separate himself from the unity of the Church—which God promised and brought about among all nations—as though for the sake of his own righteousness.

You will understand more clearly how true is the statement I mentioned shortly before: “The wicked son declares himself righteous, but he does not cleanse his departure.”

In one of his letters, which he wrote to Antonianus, he sets forth a matter quite relevant to the subject now before us; but it is better that we insert his own words.

“Our predecessors,” he says, “some of the bishops here in our province, did not think peace ought to be granted to adulterers, and entirely closed the way of repentance against adultery. Yet they did not withdraw from the college of their fellow bishops, nor did they break the unity of the Catholic Church either through harshness or through the obstinacy of their judgment, so that because peace was granted to adulterers by others, the one who did not grant it would be separated from the Church.

“With the bond of concord remaining, and with the indivisible sacrament of the Catholic Church persevering, each bishop arranges and directs his own action, destined to render an account of his purpose to the Lord” (Letter 52).

What do you say to this, brother Vincentius? Surely you see this great man, a peaceful bishop and most courageous martyr, striving for nothing more earnestly than that the bond of unity should not be broken.

You see him laboring not only so that the little ones conceived in Christ might be born, but also so that those already born might not be shaken from their mother’s bosom and die.

**42.** Moreover, consider the very matter which he cited against the impious separatists.

If those who granted peace to repentant adulterers were sharing communion with adulterers, were not those who did not do this defiled by their fellowship?

But if, as truth teaches and as the Church rightly maintains, peace was rightly granted to repentant adulterers, then those who entirely closed the way of repentance against adulterers were acting impiously. They denied healing to Christ’s members, withheld the keys of the Church from those who knocked, and with harsh cruelty opposed the most merciful patience of God, which allowed those people to live for the very purpose that they might be healed through repentance by offering a sacrifice of a contrite spirit and a broken heart.

Yet their enormous error and impiety did not defile these merciful and peaceful people, who shared the Christian Sacraments with them and tolerated them within the nets of unity until they were brought to shore and separated.

Or, if it did defile them, then the Church had already been destroyed by communion with the wicked, and there was no Church to give birth to Cyprian himself.

But if, as is certain, the Church remained, then it is also certain that no one can be defiled by the sins of others within the unity of Christ, provided that he does not consent to the deeds of the wicked and is not polluted by sharing in their sins, but tolerates the wicked as chaff in the Lord’s threshing floor until the final winnowing, for the sake of fellowship with the good.

Since this is so, where is the presumption of your separation? Are you not wicked sons, declaring yourselves righteous but failing to cleanse your departure?

**43.** Now if I wished also to recall what Tychonius, a man of your communion, inserts in his writings—he who wrote more in favor of the Catholic Church against you, although he vainly separated himself from communion with the Africans, whom he regarded as traditors, and by this one point Parmenianus strangles him—what could you reply except what Tychonius himself said about you, and what I recalled shortly before: “What we wish is holy”?

For that Tychonius, a man, as I said, of your communion, writes that a council was held at Carthage by 270 of your bishops [Note: [Col. 0342] No other trace of this council can be found. It seems, however, to have been held no earlier than the year 330, since in Tychonius’s time—who, according to Gennadius, is understood to have flourished after the year 380—many people were still living who, as Augustine says here, “could demonstrate that the matters he alleged were most certain and entirely clear.” Certainly the Donatist schism, begun in 305 and not fully consolidated until 311, had already become strong and firmly established when so great a number of bishops gathered in Africa’s principal city. Henry Valesius rightly observes this, and subsequently argues that the synod belonged to the time of Donatus of Carthage, not to the year 308. The view of Baldwin and Baronius, however, seems largely to have arisen from this very passage of Augustine, imperfectly understood, where Valesius suggests that it may instead be read: “But also to all the bishops of the Moors, whom he says, for forty years, up to the persecution carried out by Macarius,” and so forth. The common reading, although less clear, is nevertheless found in all the manuscripts.], at which council, after all previous matters had been set aside for seventy-five days, a carefully considered opinion was formed and decreed: that traditors, guilty of an immense crime, should be admitted to communion as though they were blameless if they did not wish to be baptized.

He also says that the bishop Deuterius of Macriana [Note: [Col. 0342] Louvain reads *Macrinensis*. Badius, Amerbach, Erasmus, and the manuscripts read *Macrianensis*.], a member of your communion, mingled an assembled people of traditors with the Church; that, according to the decree made by that council of 270 of your bishops, he established unity with the traditors; and that Donatus thereafter continued in communion with Deuterius. He says also that all the bishops of the Moors communicated with traditors without Baptism for forty years, until the persecution carried out by Macarius.

**44.** But you say, “Who is this Tychonius to me?”

He is that Tychonius whom Parmenianus rebukes in his reply and frightens away from writing such things. Yet Parmenianus does not refute the very things Tychonius writes. Rather, as I said above, he presses him on one point: although Tychonius said such things about the Church spread throughout the whole world, and although he said that the sins of others did not defile anyone within its unity, he nevertheless removed himself from the supposed contagion of the Africans as though they were traditors and remained in the party of Donatus.

Parmenianus could have said that Tychonius had fabricated all these things. But, as Tychonius himself recalls, many people were still alive who could show that these matters were most certain and entirely clear.

**45.** But I say nothing about these matters. Contend that Tychonius was lying. I bring you back to Cyprian, whom you yourself mentioned.

Plainly, according to Cyprian’s writings, if anyone is defiled by the sins of others within unity, then the Church had already perished before Cyprian, and there was no source from which Cyprian himself could arise.

But if it is sacrilegious to hold this view [Col. 0343], and if it is certain that the Church remains, then no one is defiled by the sins of others within her unity. In vain, then, do you wicked sons call yourselves righteous: you do not cleanse, you do not purify, your departure.

### Chapter XI
46. “Why, then,” you ask, “do you seek us? Why do you receive in this way those whom you call heretics?” See how easily and briefly I can answer. We seek you because you have perished, so that we may rejoice over those whom we have found, whereas we grieved over you when you were lost. We call you heretics—but only before you turn to Catholic peace, before you strip away the error in which you are entangled. When you pass over to us, you first leave behind what you were, so that you do not pass over to us as heretics.

“Then baptize me,” you say. I would do so if you had not been baptized, or if you had been baptized with the baptism of Donatus or Rogatus rather than with Christ’s baptism. It is not the Christian Sacraments that make you a heretic, but perverse dissent. The good that has remained in you must not be denied because of the evil that has proceeded from you—something you possess to your own detriment, if you do not possess there the source from which the good you have comes.

For all the Lord’s Sacraments belong to the Catholic Church; you possess and administer them in the same manner in which they were possessed and administered before you departed from it. Yet you do not therefore fail to possess them because you are not in the place from which the things you possess come. We do not alter in you the things in which you are with us; for in many respects you are with us. Indeed, it was said of such people, “For they were with me in many things” (Ps. LIV, 19). But we correct in you the things in which you are not with us, and here we wish you to receive those things which you do not possess there, where you are.

You are with us in Baptism, in the creed, and in the other Lord’s Sacraments. But in the spirit of unity and the bond of peace—and, finally, in the Catholic Church itself—you are not with us. If you accept these things, then what you possess will not merely be present; it will become beneficial to you. We therefore do not receive what is yours in the way you suppose. Rather, by receiving those who withdraw from you, we make them ours, so that they may be received by us; and in order to begin to be ours, they first cease to be yours. Nor do we compel the workers of error whom we detest to be joined to us. We wish those people to be joined to us precisely so that they may no longer be what we detest.

47. “But,” you say, “the apostle Paul baptized after John.” Was it, then, after a heretic? Or, if you dare to call that friend of the Bridegroom a heretic and say that he was not in the Church’s unity, I want you to write that as well. But if it is utterly mad either to think or to say this, it is for your own intelligence to consider why the apostle Paul baptized after John.

If he baptized after an equal, then all ought to be baptized after you. If after a superior, then you ought also to baptize after Rogatus. If after an inferior, Rogatus ought to have baptized after you, when you, a presbyter, baptized. But if the baptism now administered has equal efficacy in those who receive it, although the people through whom it is administered have unequal merit, because it belongs to Christ and not to those by whom it is administered, I think you now understand why Paul gave Christ’s baptism to certain people: they had been baptized with John’s baptism, not Christ’s.

That baptism is called John’s baptism, as divine Scripture testifies in many places. The Lord himself says: “John’s baptism—where was it from, from heaven or from human beings?” (Matt. XXI, 25). But the baptism Peter gave was not Peter’s, but Christ’s; and the baptism Paul gave was not Paul’s, but Christ’s. The baptism given by those who, in the time of the apostles, proclaimed Christ not with purity but out of envy (Phil. I, 15, 17), was not theirs, but Christ’s. And the baptism given by those who, in Cyprian’s time, seized estates through treacherous frauds and increased their capital through multiplying interest was not theirs, but Christ’s.

Because it belonged to Christ, it benefited those to whom it was given equally, even though it was not given through equals. For if a person is baptized more effectively the better the one is who baptizes him, the Apostle gives no proper thanks that he baptized none of the Corinthians except Crispus, Gaius, and the household of Stephanas (I Cor. I, 14). They would have been baptized so much better the better Paul was, if they had been baptized by him. Finally, when he says, “I planted, Apollos watered” (ibid., III, 6), he seems to indicate that he evangelized and Apollos baptized. Was Apollos better than John? Why, then, did the one who had baptized after John not baptize after Apollos, unless it was because the baptism administered by anyone was Christ’s, whereas the other baptism, although administered by anyone and preparing the way for Christ, was John’s?

48. It may sound malicious to say, “Baptism was administered after John, but it is not administered after heretics.” But one may also say maliciously, “Baptism was administered after John, but it is not administered after drunkards.” I mention this vice because it is one that those in whom it rules cannot conceal; and who is ignorant of how widespread it is everywhere—even someone blind?

Nevertheless, among the works of the flesh, whose practitioners will not possess the kingdom of God, the Apostle also lists this vice, where he likewise enumerates heresies: “Now the works of the flesh are manifest: fornications, impurities, licentiousness, idolatry, sorceries, enmities, strife, jealousies, hostilities, dissensions, heresies, envy, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you, that those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God” (Gal. V, 19–21).

For this reason, although baptism was administered after John, it is not administered after a heretic; and for the same reason, although baptism was administered after John, it is not administered after a drunkard. Heresies and drunkenness alike belong to those works which their practitioners will not possess the kingdom of God.

Does it not seem intolerably incongruous to you that, although baptism was administered after the one who, not drinking wine soberly but abstaining from wine altogether, prepared the way for the kingdom of God, it is not administered after a drunkard, who will not possess the kingdom of God? What answer can be given here except that the baptism was John’s, after which the Apostle baptized with Christ’s baptism, whereas the baptism with which the drunkard baptized is Christ’s?

There is therefore a great contrary difference between John and the drunkard; between Christ’s baptism and John’s baptism there is likewise a great difference, though not a contrary one. There is a great difference between the Apostle and the drunkard; between the baptism of Christ given by the Apostle and the baptism of Christ given by the drunkard there is no difference at all.

So too there is a great contrary difference between John and a heretic; and between John’s baptism and Christ’s baptism given by a heretic there is a great difference, though not a contrary one. But between Christ’s baptism given by the Apostle and Christ’s baptism given by a heretic there is no difference at all. The form of the Sacraments is recognized as equal even when there is a great difference in the merits of the people who administer them.

49. But pardon me: I was mistaken when I tried to convict you by reference to a drunken baptizer. I had forgotten that I am dealing with a Rogatist, not with just any Donatist. Perhaps among your few colleagues and all your clergy you can find no drunkard at all.

For you are the people who hold the Catholic faith not from the communion of the whole world, but from observance of all divine commandments and all the Sacraments. In whom, then, will he find it when the Son of Man comes, since he will not find faith on earth? For you are neither earth nor on earth, but heavenly beings dwelling in heaven!

Do you neither fear nor consider that “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James IV, 6)? Does the very passage of the Gospel not pierce you, where the Lord says, “When the Son of Man comes, do you suppose he will find faith on earth?” (Luke XVIII, 8). Immediately afterward, as though foreseeing that some would arrogantly claim this faith for themselves, he spoke this parable to certain people who considered themselves righteous and despised others: “Two people went up to the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector” (ibid., 10), and so forth.

You yourself supply the answer to what follows. Nevertheless, examine your own few people more carefully, to see whether no drunkard baptizes among them. For this plague ravages souls so extensively and rules with such freedom that I should be greatly surprised if it had not penetrated even your little flock—although you boast that, before the coming of the Son of Man, the one good shepherd, you have already separated the sheep from the goats.

## CHAPTER XII

50. Listen, then, through me, to the voice of the Lord’s wheat, laboring among the chaff in the Lord’s threshing floor until the final winnowing (Matt. III, 12)—that is, throughout the whole world, since God called the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting (Ps. XLIX, 1), where even children praise the Lord (Ps. CXII, 1–3):

“Whoever persecutes you by exploiting this imperial law—not out of love for correction, but from hatred and a desire to make you enemies—is displeasing to us. And although no earthly property can rightly be possessed by anyone except either by divine right, according to which all things belong to the righteous, or by human right, which places the earth under the authority of kings—and although you therefore falsely call these things yours, since you do not possess them as righteous people and have been ordered to surrender them according to the laws of earthly kings—and although you say in vain, ‘We labored to gather them,’ while you read, ‘The righteous will eat the labors of the impious’ (Prov. XIII, 22)—nevertheless, whoever, taking advantage of this law, which the kings of the earth who serve Christ promulgated to correct your impiety, greedily desires your private property is displeasing to us.

“Finally, whoever holds the very property of the poor, or the basilicas of the congregations which you held under the name of the Church—things that are owed exclusively to that Church which is truly Christ’s Church—not through justice but through greed, is displeasing to us. Whoever, because of some disgrace or crime, receives someone whom you have cast out in the same manner as those who, apart from the error by which you are separated from us, lived among you without crime, is displeasing to us.

“But you do not readily show us such people; and if you do, we tolerate some whom we cannot correct or punish. We do not abandon the Lord’s threshing floor because of the chaff; we do not tear the Lord’s nets because of the bad fish; we do not abandon the Lord’s flock because of the goats who are to be separated at the end; and we do not leave the Lord’s house because of the vessels made for dishonor.”

## CHAPTER XIII

51. But you, brother, as it seems to me, if you pay no attention to human vanity and disregard the insults of fools—who will say, “Why are you now destroying what you were previously building?” [Note: Most manuscripts and the older editions lack the words “destroying what you were previously building.”]—will undoubtedly pass over to the Church which I understand you to recognize as true. I do not need to seek far for testimony to this conviction of yours.

At the beginning of that same letter of yours to which I am now replying, you wrote these words: “Although,” you say, “I knew very well that you were still far removed from the Christian faith and had formerly devoted yourself to literary studies and been a lover of tranquility and integrity; and although afterward, having turned to the Christian faith—as I learned from the reports of many—you applied yourself to legal disputations.”

Certainly, if you sent that letter to me, these are your words. Since, then, you confess that I turned to the Christian faith, and since I did not turn either to the Donatists or to the Rogatists, you affirm without any doubt that the Christian faith exists both beyond the Rogatists and beyond the Donatists.

This faith, as we say, is spreading among all nations, which according to God’s testimony are blessed in the seed of Abraham (Gen. XXII, 18). Why, then, do you still hesitate to hold what you believe, unless you are ashamed either that you once did not believe what you now believe or that you once defended something else? And while you are ashamed to correct your error, you are not ashamed to remain in error—something of which you ought rather to have been ashamed.

52. This is what Scripture has not concealed: “There is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that brings grace and glory” (Ecclus. IV, 25).

Shame brings sin when someone is ashamed to change a wrong opinion, lest he be thought fickle or, in his own judgment, be held to have been in error for a long time. Thus “they descend alive into hell” (Ps. LIV, 16), that is, conscious of their own destruction [Note: Most manuscripts and the Badian, Amerbach, and Erasmus editions read thus; Lov. has: “or be considered, by his own judgment, different from himself.”]. Dathan, Abiram, and Korah, swallowed up by the earth’s chasm (Num. XVI, 31–33), prefigured such people long beforehand.

Shame brings grace and glory, however, when someone is ashamed of his own wrongdoing and, through repentance, is changed for the better. You are reluctant to do this because you have been overcome by that destructive shame, lest people who do not know what they are saying throw at you that apostolic statement: “For if I rebuild the things I destroyed, I establish myself as a transgressor” (Gal. II, 18).

If this could be said even of those who, after being corrected, proclaim the truth that they previously attacked in their perversity, it would first have been said of Paul himself. In him the churches glorified God when they heard that he was preaching the faith which he had once been ravaging (Gal. I, 23).

53. Do not suppose that anyone can pass from error to truth, or from any sin, whether great or small, to correction, without repentance. But it is an exceedingly shameless error to wish to slander the Church on this account, although it is established by so many divine testimonies as Christ’s Church: it treats differently those who abandon it if they correct that very act through repentance, and those who have not yet been in it and then, for the first time, receive its peace. It humbles the former more deeply, receives the latter more gently, loves both, and serves the healing of both with motherly affection.

You have a letter perhaps longer than you wished. It would have been much shorter if I had been thinking only of you in writing my reply. But now, even if it benefits you nothing, I do not think it will benefit nothing those who take care to read it with fear of God and without partiality. Amen.

## LETTER XCIV

[Note: Formerly published from a Vatican manuscript; now restored to its proper purity with the aid of the Rhimarcon manuscript.]

[Note: Formerly numbered 249; the letter that was 94 is now 178. It appears to have been written in the year 408, on May 15.]

Paulinus, giving thanks to Augustine for a book or letter received from him, continues with praise of the elder Melania and of her only son Publicola, recently deceased; he also says something about the future activity of the blessed in heaven after the resurrection.

To the holy, most blessed Lord, uniquely united with us, and venerable father, brother, and teacher, AUGUSTINE the bishop: PAULINUS and THERASIA, sinners.

### 1

“Your word is always a lamp for my feet and a light for my paths.” Thus, whenever I receive a letter from Your most blessed Holiness, I feel that the darkness of my ignorance is dispelled; and, as though the eyes of my mind had been anointed with the collyrium of illumination [Note: Lov. reads “delight”], I see more clearly, the night of ignorance driven away and the mist of doubt wiped clean.

Although I have often felt this gift bestowed on me through the offerings of your letters, I experienced it especially through this recent little volume of correspondence. Its bearer was our blessed brother Quintus the deacon, a man as welcome to me as he was worthy. After he had come to Rome, and after a considerable interval had passed, I came with him, according to my customary practice, after the Lord’s Pascha, in veneration of the apostles and martyrs. He brought us back the blessing of your lips.

Yet, although he had spent time in Rome without my knowing it, that time seemed erased from my memory; he appeared to me to have come most recently from your presence, so that when I first saw him and he offered me the full fragrance of your sweetness, exhaling in your words the purity of heavenly ointment, I could scarcely believe that he had just then come to me from you.

Nevertheless, I confess to Your venerable Unity that I could not read the volume itself in Rome as soon as I had received it. Such crowds were there that I could not examine your gift carefully or enjoy it as I wished—namely, by reading it through without interruption once I had begun.

And so, as one does when confidently awaiting a prepared feast, I restrained the hunger of my eager mind. With certain hope of being satisfied, I held in my hands the bread of my desire in the volume that I was to devour; and because it afterward proved most sweet to me, both in mouth and in stomach, I easily suspended my throat, already gaping at the honeycombs of your letters, until I could depart from the City and devote the entire day that we spent at Formiae, an intermediate station on the journey, to this work. Thus, freed from every dreg and suffocation of the disturbances, I could feast on the spiritual delights of your letter.

### 2

What, then, can I, humble and earthly, reply to this wisdom that has been given to you from above, which this world cannot contain, and which no one understands unless he is wise with God’s wisdom and speaks with God’s word?

Since I have experienced Christ speaking in you, I shall praise your words in God and shall not fear the terror of the night. For you taught me, in the spirit of truth, the salutary moderation with which the soul should be balanced amid dying mortals. You saw that blessed mother and grandmother Melania mourned the bodily death of her only son with silent grief, but not with a grief devoid of a mother’s tears.

You understood her restrained and solemn tears more deeply, as one whose spirit was closer or more akin to her soul. With the likeness of your own heart, you contemplated more justly the maternal heart of this woman perfected in Christ, without compromising the strength of a manly spirit. You thus recognized that she first wept because she had been moved by natural affection, and then was pierced by a more compelling cause: not so much because, by mortal condition, she had lost in the present age her only son who had died, but because he had been almost overtaken in worldly vanity—for the ambition of senatorial rank had not yet abandoned him—and she did not consider him to have been taken up according to the holy “avarice” of her vows, so that he might pass from the glory of conversion to the glory of resurrection, obtaining rest and a crown together with his mother, if, following his mother’s example, he had preferred sackcloth to the toga and the monastery to the Senate.

### 3

Nevertheless, that same man, as I think I previously reported to Your Holiness [Note: Lov. reads, “I reported in accordance with Your Holiness’s wish”], departed enriched by such works that, even if he did not wear the nobility of his mother’s humility in his clothing, he preferred it in his mind.

For he was so gentle in character and humble in heart, according to the Lord’s word (Matt. XI, 29), that he may rightly be believed to have entered the Lord’s rest. “There are remains for the peaceful person” (Ps. XXXVI, 37), and “the meek will possess the earth” (Matt. V, 4), pleasing God “in the land of the living” (Ps. CXIV, 9).

Indeed, he fulfilled the Apostle’s teaching not only through the silent affection of his mind but also through visible religious duties. Although, in rank and honor, he was a companion of the great ones of this age, he did not, as one glorified by the earth, set his mind on high things; rather, as a perfect imitator of Christ, he associated with the lowly (Rom. XII, 16), and continued throughout the whole day to show mercy and lend assistance.

Therefore his offspring became powerful on earth, among those who are excessively exalted as the strong gods of the earth. The sacred merit of the man is also revealed by the visitation of his most blessed family and household. “The generation of the upright,” he says, “will be blessed. Glory”—not glory that perishes—“and riches”—not riches that slip away—“are in his house” (Ps. CXI, 2–3), a house built in heaven, not by the labor of hands but by the holiness of works.

But I shall stop recounting more about a man so dear to me and so devoted to Christ. I believe that in my earlier letters I narrated quite a few things about him; and I could say nothing about the blessed mother of this son, and the equal [Note: Lov. reads “father”] root of the branches of the saints, better or more reverently than Your Holiness deigned to speak and write about Melania.

For I, a sinner with unclean lips, could say nothing worthy, being far removed from the merits of her faith and the virtues of her soul. You, that man of Christ, the teacher of Israel in the Church of truth, prepared by God’s grace for better things, were made the more worthy preacher of such a manly soul in Christ: you saw her mind, strengthened by divine power, with a spirit closer to hers, and praised her piety joined with virtue in more worthy speech.

### 4

You were pleased to ask me what the activity of the blessed will be in that age after the resurrection of the flesh [Note: Lov. reads “what our activity will be”]. But I consult you instead about the present state of my life, as I consult a spiritual teacher and physician, so that you may teach me to do God’s will and to walk after Christ in your footsteps, and first to die this evangelical death by which we voluntarily anticipate the dissolution of the flesh [Note: Lov. reads “so that we may anticipate this evangelical death …”]—departing from the life of this age not by death but by judgment, for this life is wholly temptation, or, as you once said to me, is itself wholly temptation.

Would that my ways might thus be directed after your footsteps, so that, following your example, I might remove the old sandal from my feet, break my chains, and, set free, leap for joy as I run the course. Then I might attain that death by which you died to this age, so that you might live to God in Christ living in you. His death and life are recognized in your body, heart, and mouth.

Your heart does not savor earthly things, nor does your mouth speak human works. Rather, Christ’s word abounds in your breast, and the spirit of truth pours from your tongue like the force of a heavenly river, gladdening the city of God.

### 5

What virtue produces this death in us except love, which is strong as death? It so blots out and destroys this age for us that, through affection for Christ, it fulfills the effect of death. Turned toward him, we turn away from the world, and while living we die to the elements of this world.

We do not make decisions, as though we were living under their observation and gaze [Note: The Phimarc manuscript reads “use”], because Christ’s death is our portion. We cannot attain the glory of his resurrection from the dead unless we imitate his death by putting to death the members and sensations of the flesh on the cross.

Thus we should no longer live according to our own will, but according to the will of him whose will is our sanctification. He died and rose again for us so that we might no longer live for ourselves but for him who died and rose again for us. He also gave us the pledge of his promise through his Spirit, just as he placed the pledge of our life in heaven in his body, which is the head [Note: The Phimarc manuscript omits “head”] of our body.

Therefore our expectation now is the Lord, and our substance is that which was made by him, with him, in him, and through him. He was conformed to the body of our humility so that he might conform us to the body of his glory and place us with himself in the heavenly realms.

For this reason those who are found worthy of eternal life will be in the glory of his kingdom, so that they may be with him, as the Apostle says (I Thess. IV, 16), and remain with him, as the Lord himself said to the Father: “I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John XVII, 24).

### 6

Without doubt, this is what you find in the Psalms: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; forever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. LXXXIII, 5).

I think that this praise will be expressed by the voices of those singing together. Although the bodies of the saints who rise again will be changed, so that they are like the Lord’s body appeared after the resurrection, in that resurrection a living image of human resurrection shone forth. The Lord himself, in the very body in which he had suffered and risen again, became like a mirror of contemplation for all.

When he had risen in the same flesh in which he had died and been buried, he repeatedly displayed before human eyes and ears the full functions of all his members [Note: Lov. reads “displayed,” feminine]. If even angels, whose nature is simply spiritual, are said to have tongues with which they sing praises to the Lord their creator and never cease to give thanks, how much more will human beings, even though their bodies will be spiritual after the resurrection, still retain all the members of glorified flesh, with their forms and proportions in every member; they will have tongues in their mouths and will give voice through speaking tongues, by which they may express in words divine praises and the affections of their perceptions and joys.

Perhaps the Lord will add this to the grace and glory of his saints in the ages of his kingdom: they will sing with tongues and voices all the more excellent as, through blessed transformation, they have advanced toward the more blessed nature of their bodies. Established in spiritual bodies, they may perhaps speak no longer in human but in angelic and heavenly words, of the kind the Apostle heard in paradise (II Cor. XII, 4).

Perhaps for this reason he testified that those words were ineffable to human beings, because among the various kinds of rewards, new tongues are prepared for the saints—tongues which people of this age are not yet permitted to use. Then the immortals will speak with them, as is fitting for their glory. Of them it is said: “They will indeed cry out and sing a hymn” (Ps. LXIV, 14), undoubtedly in the heavenly realms where they will be with the Lord and delight in the abundance of peace.

They will rejoice before the throne, casting bowls and crowns before the feet of the Lamb and singing to him a new song. Joined to the choirs of Angels, Virtues, Dominations, and Thrones, they too, with the Cherubim, Seraphim, and those four living creatures, will sing together in perpetual voice: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts” (Isa. VI, 3; Rev. IV, 8–10), and the rest that you know.

### 7

This, then, is what I, that needy and poor, foolish and little one of yours, whom you have accustomed yourself to bear as a true wise man, ask you to explain to me: your knowledge or opinion concerning this matter. I know that you have been illumined by the spirit of revelation from the very guide and source of the wise, so that, just as you have known the past and see the present, you may also assess the future [Note: Lov. reads “what you assess concerning the future”].

What do you think about the voices of these heavenly creatures—or even of those acting above the heavens in the presence of the Most High—in their everlasting praise, and by what instruments they are finally expressed?

Although the Apostle, by saying, “If I speak in the tongues of angels” (I Cor. XIII, 1), seems to show that they have a language proper to their nature or, so to speak, to their race, one so much higher than human senses and speech as the angelic creature and station surpasses mortal inhabitants and earthly dwellings [Note: Lov. reads “in heaven,” rather than “earthly dwellings”], perhaps he called the languages of angels “tongues” in the sense of kinds of voices and speech.

In discussing the variety of spiritual gifts, he likewise counts among the gifts “kinds of tongues” (ibid., XII), clearly signifying by this sign that the ability to speak in the language of many nations would be granted to individuals.

Yet the voice of God, often sent forth from a cloud to the saints, shows that speech can exist without a tongue. The tongue is a small bodily member, and yet it is great. But perhaps precisely because God placed the function of voice in this member, he called the speech and voices of the incorporeal angelic creature a tongue, just as Scripture customarily assigns bodily names to God according to the forms of his activity [Note: Lov. reads: “Because God can create even in the body of angels [a voice], without this member in which the function of voice resides.”].

Pray for us and teach us.

### 8

Our dearest and sweetest brother Quintus, as slowly as he returns to us from you, so quickly does he hurry to return from us to you. His urgency in demanding letters—and this letter, more crowded with erasures than with verses, speaks of it—was caused by the excessive haste of the collector who had been mentioned.

He came to us on the day before the Ides of May to ask for written replies, and he obtained permission to be dismissed before the sixth hour on the Ides. Consider, then, whether I have commended or accused him by this testimony.

Perhaps—or rather, without doubt—he will be judged more worthy of praise than of blame, since he hastened back with complete justice from darkness, which we are in comparison with your light, to his own light.”

## LETTER XCV

[Note: Revised according to the Vatican manuscript and according to Lov.]

[Note: Formerly numbered 250; the letter that was 95 is now 177. Written in the winter, toward the end of 408 or the beginning of 409.]

Augustine, replying to the preceding letter, discusses the condition of the present life, as well as the nature of the bodies of the blessed and the functions of their members after the resurrection.

To the dearest, most sincere, holy, desirable, and venerable brothers, fellow disciples under the teacher, the Lord Jesus [Note: Since Augustine was greeted as Teacher and Bishop in the preceding letter, he returns the greeting in these words. From this we may incidentally infer that the episcopal dignity had not been conferred on Paulinus before the year 409; otherwise a more elevated title, appropriate to him and one Augustine ought to have assigned him, would have been due. This inference is supported by Rufinus, who in the dedicatory letter of Book 2 of On the Blessings of the Patriarchs, apparently written around that time, calls him not bishop but brother. Later Augustine calls him bishop in Letter 149, written around 413, and in Book 1 of The City of God, chapter 10, where he discusses an event that occurred in 410.]: PAULINUS and THERASIA, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

### 1

When our brothers, most closely joined to us, continually see you—brothers whom, when they are desired along with us, you are accustomed to desire, and, when greeted, to greet again—our blessings are not so much increased as our troubles are consoled.

We try, insofar as we are able, to avoid the causes and necessities themselves, yet somehow, I believe because of our merits, they cannot be absent. But when they come to us and see us, what is written takes place: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul” (Ps. XCIII, 19).

Therefore, when you hear from our brother Possidius, who is with you for this joy, how grievous a cause compelled him, you will recognize that I am speaking with complete truth. Yet if one of us were to cross the sea for this sole purpose—to enjoy your presence—what cause could be more just, or what more worthy cause could be found?

But our bonds would not bear this. We are bound to serve the illnesses of the weak and not to abandon them bodily, except when their illness compels us to do so with greater urgency because of the greater danger. Whether we are being exercised by these burdens or rather punished, I do not know, except that he “does not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our iniquities” (Ps. CII, 10). He mingles such consolations with our sorrows and works through a wondrous medicine, so that we may neither love the world nor fail within the world.

[Note: Possidius, bishop of Calama, sailed to the Emperor to plead the cause of his Church, which had suffered plundering, fires, and killings at the hands of the pagan inhabitants of Calama, as Letters 91 and 104 show. According to Letter 104, he traveled toward the end of 408, the year in which that uprising appears to have occurred, or at the beginning of 409. He was doubtless the bearer of this Letter 95, written to Paulinus at Carthage while Augustine was wintering there, according to Letter 121.]

### 2

In my earlier letters I asked you what you thought the future eternal life of the saints would be. You answered me well that the condition of the present life must still be considered. Yet you wished to consult me about something that you either do not know with me, know with me, or perhaps know better than I do: namely, that we must first die an evangelical death before we voluntarily anticipate the dissolution of the flesh—not by dying, but by judgment, departing from the life of this age.

This matter is simple and does not fluctuate amid the storm of doubt: we judge that we ought to live in this mortal life in such a way that we may somehow be fitted to immortal life.

But the question that disturbs people who act and inquire, such as I am, is how one ought to live among, or for the sake of, those who do not yet know how to live by dying—not through dissolution of the body, but through a certain affection of the mind by which they turn away from bodily allurements.

For the most part, it seems to us that unless we accommodate ourselves somewhat to them in those very things from which we want to draw them out, we can do nothing beneficial with them. But when we do this, the pleasure of such things steals into us as well. We often take pleasure in speaking empty words and in lending an ear to those who speak; we are not merely amused but overcome and released by laughter.

Thus, weighing down our souls with certain dusty or even muddy affections, we raise them to God with greater labor and sluggishness, so that we may live an evangelical life by dying an evangelical death.

If this should ever succeed, immediately there follows an “Excellent! Excellent!”—not from human beings, for no human being perceives such an acknowledgment of the mind in another; rather, in some inner silence, I do not know from where, there is a cry of “Excellent! Excellent!”

Because of this kind of temptation, so great an Apostle confesses that he was buffeted by an angel (II Cor. XII, 7).

This is why human life upon earth is wholly temptation: a person is tempted even there where, as far as possible, he is being conformed to the likeness of heavenly life.

### 3

What shall I say about administering punishment, or not administering it, since in all this we desire to promote the salvation of those whom we judge ought to be punished or not punished? What the proper measure of punishment is—not only according to the nature or extent of the offenses, but also according to the differing capacities of people’s minds, what each person can endure and what each refuses—how profound and obscure a matter this is! And when we fear the punishment that hangs over us, which is feared by human beings, I do not know whether more people have been corrected by it than have deteriorated.

What, moreover, when it often happens that, if you punish one person, that person perishes, whereas, if you leave the matter unpunished, another perishes? I confess that I sin daily in such matters and do not know when or how I shall observe what is written: “Reprove sinners in the presence of all, so that the others may have fear” (1 Tim. 5:20); and what is written: “Reprove him between yourself and him alone” (Matt. 18:15); and what is written: “Do not judge before the proper time, so that you may not be judged” (1 Cor. 4:5)—for here he did not add “before the proper time”; and what is written: “Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master; and he will stand, for God is able to make him stand” (Rom. 14:4). From this he makes clear that he is speaking of those who are within; yet elsewhere he commands them to judge, when he says: “For what have I to do with judging those who are outside? Is it not those who are within whom you judge? Remove the evil person from among yourselves” (1 Cor. 5:12–13).

Even when this appears to have to be done, how great a matter of care and fear it is to determine how it should be done! We must be careful lest what is understood to be said of that very man in the second Letter to the same people come to pass: that the person of this kind might be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow. And lest anyone think that this need not be taken very seriously, he says there: “So that we may not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs” (2 Cor. 2:7, 11).

What trembling there is in all these matters, holy man of God, my Pauline! What trembling, what darkness! Do we not think that this was said of such things?

“Fear and trembling came upon me,  
and darkness covered me;  
and I said, ‘Who will give me wings like a dove,  
so that I may fly away and rest?’  
Behold, I have fled far away  
and remained in the wilderness.”

Yet perhaps even in that wilderness he experienced what follows:

“I was waiting for the one who would save me  
from faintheartedness and storm” (Ps. 54:6–9).

Indeed, then, “human life upon earth is a trial” (Job 7:1).

### 4

What? Are not the divine utterances themselves rather felt about than handled by us, since in many more matters we seek what ought to be understood than possess any definite and fixed understanding? And although such caution is full of anxiety, it is nevertheless far better than the rashness of making assertions.

In many matters, if a person does not think according to the flesh—which the Apostle calls death—will he not be a great scandal to one who still thinks according to the flesh (Rom. 8:5–6)? Here it is most dangerous to say what one thinks, most burdensome not to say it, and most destructive to say something other than what one thinks.

What happens when, in speech or writing among those who are within, we disapprove of certain things, and, supposing that this belongs to the freedom of fraternal charity, do not conceal our judgment—yet are believed to do this not out of goodwill but out of envy? How greatly we are sinned against! And when, similarly, we suspect that those who criticize our opinions wish rather to injure than to correct us, how greatly do we sin against others!

Certainly, this is often the source of enmities even among the dearest and most intimate persons, when, beyond what is written, one person is puffed up on behalf of another against another (1 Cor. 4:6); and when they bite and devour one another, we must fear that they may be consumed by one another (Gal. 5:15).

Who, then, will give me wings like a dove, so that I may fly away and rest (Ps. 54:7)? Whether because the dangers in which each person is involved are more serious than dangers not yet experienced, or because the matter really is so, any faintheartedness and storm of the wilderness seem less troublesome to me than what we either suffer or fear amid the crowds.

### 5

Accordingly, I greatly approve your view that we should deal with the condition—or rather, the course—of this life. I add something else: this must first be sought and held before we ask what the destination will be toward which this course is carrying us.

For that reason I asked what you think, as though, once the proper rule of this life had been grasped and preserved, we should already be secure, although in so many matters—and especially in those I have mentioned as briefly as I could—I feel that I struggle amid the greatest dangers.

But since all this ignorance and difficulty seems to me to arise from the fact that, amid great variety of conduct and of souls possessing most hidden desires and weaknesses, we administer the affairs of a people—not an earthly and Roman people, but the heavenly Jerusalem—I have preferred to speak with you about what we shall be rather than about what we are.

For there, although we do not know what good things will be in store, we are nevertheless certain about one matter of no small importance: those evils will not be there.

### 6

Concerning the conduct of this temporal life, by which we must come to eternal life, I know that carnal desires must be restrained; that indulgence in the pleasures of the bodily senses must be limited to what is sufficient to sustain and carry on this kind of life; and that all temporal troubles must be endured patiently and courageously for the truth of God and for our eternal salvation and that of our neighbor.

I also know that every effort of charity must be devoted to the welfare of our neighbor, so that he may conduct this life rightly for the sake of eternal life. Spiritual things must also be preferred to carnal things, unchangeable things to changeable things; and I know that a person can do all these things to a greater or lesser extent according as he is helped more or less by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

But why one person is helped in this way and another in that way, or is not helped, I do not know. I do know, however, that God acts with the highest equity, known to himself alone.

For the reasons I mentioned above, if you have any clear and certain knowledge of how one ought to live with other people, I beg you to teach me. But if these matters trouble you as they trouble me, discuss them with some gentle physician of the heart—whether you find one there where you are staying, or when you travel annually to Rome—and write to me what the Lord may have disclosed to you through him speaking to you, or as you discuss the matter together.

### 7

Since you in turn asked me what I think about the resurrection of bodies and about the future functions of the members in that incorruption and immortality, hear briefly what I think. If it is not sufficient, then, with the Lord’s help, it can be discussed at greater length.

We must hold most firmly what is established by the truthful and clear teaching of Scripture: that these visible and earthly bodies, which are now called animal bodies, will be spiritual in the resurrection of the faithful and righteous.

Moreover, what the quality of a spiritual body is—since we have no experience of it—how it can either be understood or conveyed, I do not know. Certainly there will be no corruption there, and consequently they will not then need the corruptible food on which they now depend. Yet they will not be unable to receive it and truly consume it, by power and not by necessity.

Otherwise the Lord would not have received food after his resurrection. He gave us an example of bodily resurrection such that the Apostle says: “If the dead are not raised, then Christ has not been raised” (1 Cor. 15:16).

When he appeared with all his limbs and made use of their functions, he also displayed the places of his wounds. As for me, I have always understood these as scars rather than as the wounds themselves, and as present by power, not by necessity. He displayed the ease of this power most clearly when he showed himself in another form, or when, while the disciples were gathered in the house and the doors were closed, he appeared as a real human being (Luke 24:15–43; John 20:14–29; Mark 16:12, 14).

### 8

From this arises the question concerning angels: do they have bodies suited to their functions and movements, or are they merely spirits? If we say that they have bodies, the following passage confronts us: “He makes his angels spirits” (Ps. 103:4). But if we say that they do not have bodies, there is an even greater difficulty: how are we to understand that they were presented to the bodily senses of human beings without bodies, received as guests, had their feet washed, and were served food and drink (Gen. 18:2–9; 19:1–3)?

It may more easily be supposed that angels are called spirits in the same way that human beings are called souls, as when it is written that so many souls descended with Jacob into Egypt (Gen. 46:2)—for they certainly did not lack bodies—than that all those events should be believed to have taken place without bodies.

Furthermore, in the Apocalypse a certain stature of an angel is specified (Rev. 10), in a measure that can belong only to bodies. Thus his appearance to human beings should be attributed not to deception but to the power and facility of spiritual bodies.

But whether angels have bodies, or whether someone can show how, without having bodies, they were able to perform all those things, in that city of the saints, where those redeemed through Christ from this generation will be joined forever to thousands of angels, bodily voices will reveal minds that are not hidden. For in that divine fellowship no thought will be capable of being concealed from one’s neighbor. There will be harmony in the praise of God, expressed not only in spirit but also through a spiritual body. This is how it seems to me.

### 9

In the meantime, if you already hold, or are able to hear from teachers, anything more consistent with the truth, I eagerly await the opportunity to learn it through you.

Read over my letter [Note: [Col. 0356] This letter is not extant]. Since you excused your very hasty reply then by the urgency of the deacon, I do not complain; rather, I mention it so that what was omitted then may now be supplied.

And inquire also what you think about Christian leisure for acquiring or discussing Christian wisdom, and about the leisure which I supposed was yours, although incredible reports have reached me of your occupations. See what I asked to learn from you.

*(In another hand.)* Remember us; live happily, holy servants of God, our great joys and consolations.

## LETTER XCVI

[Note: [Col. 0356] Collated with a, bl, c, cc, ff, g, gv, j, n, r, s, sb, t, vc, four copies of v, and with Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0356] Formerly 124; the letter formerly numbered 96 is now 183. Written in 408, around the beginning of September.]

Augustine warmly commends to Olympius, whom he had heard had recently been advanced to a new dignity—namely, Master of Offices, an office conferred upon him after the death of Stilicho in 408—the case of Boniface, bishop of Cataquum, concerning a certain possession of the Church acquired by Boniface’s predecessor not without fraud.

**To his most beloved lord and son Olympius, honorably to be embraced as a member of Christ, AUGUSTINE.**

### 1

Whatever your position may be according to the course of this world, we nevertheless write with complete confidence to our dearest and most sincere fellow-servant Olympius, a Christian. For we know that this is more glorious than every glory and more exalted than every elevation.

Rumor has brought us word that you have obtained a higher office. Whether this was true had not yet been confirmed among us when the opportunity to write arose. But since we know that you have learned from the Lord not to set your mind on high things but to associate with the lowly, we presume, whatever height you may have attained, that you will receive our letter in no other way than you ordinarily do, most beloved lord and son, honorably to be embraced as a member of Christ.

We have no doubt that you will wisely use temporal prosperity for eternal gain: the more power you possess in this earthly commonwealth, the more you will devote to that heavenly city which gave birth to you in Christ, so that it may repay you more abundantly in the land of the living, and in the true peace of those who are secure and whose joys remain without end.

### 2

I again commend to your charity the petition of my holy brother and fellow bishop Boniface, lest what could not be done before may perhaps now be accomplished.

Since he could perhaps have retained without any difficulty what his predecessor had acquired—even under another person’s name—and had already begun to possess in the name of the Church, we nevertheless do not wish him, because he was a debtor to the treasury, to have this scruple upon his conscience. For a fraud does not cease to be a fraud merely because it is committed against the treasury.

That Paul, after he had become a bishop and was about to renounce all his possessions because of the immense accumulation of his debts to the treasury, obtained a certain security in which a fixed quantity of silver was owed to him. He purchased these small fields, from which he might support his livelihood, as though they belonged to the Church, under the name of a then most powerful household. By following his customary practice, he would thus not pay the treasury even from these properties and would suffer no harassment from the collectors.

But the man who was ordained to that same Church after Paul’s death was afraid to accept these fields. Although he could have requested an imperial favor for the sole amount of the treasury debts that Paul had contracted on account of the possessions mentioned, he preferred to confess everything: namely, that Paul had purchased them with his own silver, although he was liable to the treasury, from the *hastarium* [Note: [Col. 0357] Bad., Am., and Er. have *de Ascario*. Lov. and the manuscripts, however, have *de hastario*. A *hastarium* was a place where the spoils or property of proscribed persons were sold]. Thus, if possible, the Church might possess them not through the hidden iniquity of a bishop but through the manifest generosity of a Christian emperor.

If this cannot be done, it is better for the servants of God to endure the hardship of poverty than to possess the means necessary for life with a guilty conscience of fraud.

### 3
