We ask that you deign to grant your support in this matter. He did not wish to cite what had first been obtained, lest he close off his ability to petition again; for the response had not addressed what he had requested.

Now, however, since you possess the same kindness as always but greater power, we do not despair that, with the Lord’s help, this may easily be granted through your merits. Even if you were to request these same places in your own name and then give them to the Church mentioned, who would criticize you? Who would not praise your petition to the highest degree, since it would serve not earthly greed but Christian piety?

May the mercy of the Lord our God protect you in Christ, happier in him, my lord and son.

## LETTER XCVII

[Note: [Col. 0357] Collated with a, bg, bl, c, cc, ff, g, gv, j, n, s, sb, t, vc, four copies of v, and with Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0357] Formerly 129; the letter formerly numbered 97 is now 184. Written toward the end of 408.]

Augustine writes to Olympius, asking him to uphold the laws concerning the destruction of idols and the correction of heretics that were sent to Africa while Stilicho was alive, and to use his authority and diligence to ensure that they understand that these laws were enacted by the emperor’s will and therefore remain in force even after Stilicho’s death.

**To his distinguished and most deserving son Olympius, greatly to be honored in the charity of Christ, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.**

### 1

Although, as soon as we heard that you had deservedly been elevated—and although the report itself was not yet entirely certain to us—we believed nothing else about your attitude toward the Church of God, whose true son we rejoice that you are, than what you soon revealed in your letter, nevertheless, after reading the letter which you deigned to send voluntarily, we write to you with even greater confidence.

In that letter you deigned of your own accord, even if we were sluggish and hesitant, to send us a most benevolent exhortation: that, with our humility instructing you, through your religious obedience the Lord—by whose gift you are such a man—might very soon come to the aid of his Church. Therefore we write with greater confidence to you, distinguished lord, most deserving son, and one greatly to be honored in the charity of Christ.

### 2

Many holy brothers, my colleagues, departed in grave disturbance of the Church, almost as fugitives, to the most glorious imperial court. Whether you have already seen them, or whether you have received letters from them from the city of Rome on some suitable occasion, I nevertheless, although I have not been able to consult with them, could not fail, through this brother and fellow presbyter of mine, to greet and admonish your charity, which you possess in Christ Jesus our Lord.

Urgent necessity compelled him, for the salvation of one of his fellow citizens, to come to those regions by whatever means he could, even in the middle of winter. I ask that your good work be hastened by the most diligent urgency, so that the enemies of the Church may understand that the laws concerning the destruction of idols and the correction of heretics, which were sent to Africa while Stilicho was alive, were established by the will of the most pious and faithful emperor.

Those enemies either falsely claim that these measures were taken without Stilicho’s knowledge or against his wishes, or gladly suppose that this was the case. As a result, they make the minds of the uninstructed exceedingly turbulent and turn them dangerously and violently against us.

### 3

In making this request and suggestion to your Excellency, I do not doubt that I am expressing the will of all my colleagues throughout Africa. I think that, at the first opportunity, the matter can and ought to be brought to completion with the greatest ease, so that those foolish men—whose salvation, even though they oppose us, we desire—may understand, as I have said, that the laws sent on behalf of Christ’s Church were arranged to be sent by the son of Theodosius rather than by Stilicho.

For this reason the presbyter who carries this letter, since he is from the region of Milevis, was ordered by his bishop, my venerable brother Severus, who sends many greetings to your most sincere Affection together with mine, to pass through Hippo Regius, where I am.

When we happened to be together amid the Church’s great troubles and disturbances, we were seeking an opportunity to write to your Excellency and could not find one. I had already sent one letter concerning the matter of my holy brother and colleague Boniface, bishop of Cataquum; but the more serious events that would have agitated us more intensely had not yet reached us.

The bishops who have sailed for this purpose will act with such kindness of heart that, having deliberated more carefully in common counsel, they can bring a more suitable remedy for suppressing or correcting these matters according to the way of Christ, insofar as the limited time allows.

Yet I suggest, request, beg, and implore that the province learn what the most merciful and religious ruler’s attitude toward the Church is. This matter must in no way be delayed; indeed, before you see the bishops who have departed, it should be hastened as soon as your most distinguished vigilance can manage, for the sake of Christ’s members who are placed in the greatest distress.

The Lord has offered no small consolation amid these evils by willing that you should now be able to do much more than you could before, at a time when we were already rejoicing in your many great good works.

### 4

We rejoice greatly over the firm and steadfast faith of certain people—not a few—who, because of these very laws, have been converted to the Christian religion or to Catholic peace. For their eternal salvation, we are glad even to face danger in this temporal life.

For this reason above all, we now endure more severe attacks of hostility from people who are excessively harsh and perverse. Some of those converts endure these attacks with us most patiently. Yet we fear greatly for their weakness until, with the help of the Lord’s most merciful grace, they learn and are able to despise the present age and the day of human judgment with stronger courage of heart.

If the memorandum that I sent to the brother bishops is not yet there, as I think it is not, let your Excellency hand it over to them when they arrive. We have such confidence in your most sincere heart that, with the help of the Lord our God, we desire you to be not merely a provider of assistance but also a participant in our counsel.

## LETTER XCVIII

[Note: [Col. 0359] In preparing this recension, the following were examined: a, bg, bl, bn, c, cc, ff, g, gv, j, n, r, s, t, vd, two copies of a, two of vc, three of sb, six of v, and Am., Bad., Er., and Lov., as well as the manuscript collection of Anselm of Lucca.]

[Note: [Col. 0359] Formerly 23; the letter formerly numbered 98 is now 163. Perhaps written around the same time.]

Augustine replies to Bishop Boniface, explaining how the faith of parents benefits infants in Baptism, although the parents’ impiety does not harm them after Baptism; and then explaining how sponsors in Baptism answer that the infants believe, although infants in fact do not believe and it is uncertain whether they will come to believe.

**To Boniface [Note: [Col. 0359] In most manuscripts the name is consistently written *Bonefacius], his fellow bishop, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.**

[Note: [Col. 0359] Since this Boniface was endowed with such religious scrupulousness that, as is said below in section 7, he “was accustomed to take great care to avoid lying,” it is not unreasonable to suppose that he was the very same Cataquum bishop who, out of the sincerity of his conscience, was reluctant to accept for the Church the fields acquired by his predecessor with some fraud against the treasury. Augustine mentions “his holy brother and fellow bishop” Boniface in Letters 143 and 149. Boniface of Cataquum took part in the Carthaginian conference.]

### 1

You ask me whether parents harm their baptized infants when they attempt to heal them through sacrifices to demons. And if they do not harm them, how does the parents’ faith benefit them when they are baptized, since the parents’ unbelief cannot harm them?

My answer is that the power of that sacrament—namely, saving Baptism—is so great within the holy structure of Christ’s body that one who has once been generated through the carnal pleasure of others, once regenerated through the spiritual will of others, cannot thereafter be bound by another person’s iniquity when he has given it no consent by his own will.

“For the soul of the father is mine,” he says, “and the soul of the son is mine. The soul that sins shall die” (Ezek. 18:4). But the child does not itself sin when the parents, while the child is wholly unaware, or anyone else, applies the sacrileges of demons to it.

The child therefore drew from Adam what the grace of that sacrament would remove because it was not yet a separately living soul—that is, another soul of which it could be said, “The soul of the father is mine, and the soul of the son is mine.”

Once a person exists in himself, having become another than the one who generated him, he is not held liable for another’s sin without his own consent. He therefore drew guilt because he was one with and in the person from whom he drew it when the act that he drew had been committed. But one person does not draw guilt from another once each is already living his own individual life, so that it may be said: “The soul that sins shall die.”

### 2

In order that he may be regenerated through the action of another person’s will, when he is brought forward to be consecrated, the one Spirit accomplishes this, and the person brought forward is regenerated through that Spirit.

For it is not written, “Unless someone is reborn through the will of his parents,” or “through the faith of those who bring or minister the sacrament,” but: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit” (John 3:5).

Thus water, externally presenting the sacrament of grace, and the Spirit, internally effecting the gift of grace, releasing the bond of guilt and restoring the good of nature, regenerate in the one Christ the person generated from the one Adam.

The regenerating Spirit is common to the adults who bring the child forward and to the child who is brought forward and regenerated. Therefore, through this fellowship of one and the same Spirit, the will of those who bring the child forward benefits the child.

But when adults sin against an infant by bringing it forward and attempting to bind it with the sacrilegious bonds of demons, the souls of the adults and the child are not common, so that they could also share a common guilt. Guilt is not communicated through another person’s will in the way that grace is communicated through the unity of the Holy Spirit.

The one Holy Spirit can be in both this person and that person, even if they do not know one another through whom their shared grace exists. But the spirit of a human being cannot belong both to this person and that person, so that, when one sins and the other does not sin, they nevertheless share a common guilt.

Accordingly, an infant once generated from its parents’ flesh can be regenerated by the Spirit of God, so that the obligation contracted from them may be dissolved. But once regenerated by the Spirit of God, it cannot be regenerated from its parents’ flesh so that the obligation already dissolved may be contracted again.

Therefore, once an infant has received the grace of Christ, it does not lose it except through its own impiety, if, with advancing age, it becomes wicked. For then it will also begin to have sins of its own, which are not removed by regeneration but healed by another remedy.

### 3

Nevertheless, parents—or any adults—who attempt to bind baptized children or infants through the sacrileges of demons are rightly called spiritual murderers. They do not actually kill the children, but insofar as it lies within them, they become their killers.

They are rightly told, when they are restrained from this crime: “Do not kill your children.” For the Apostle also says: “Do not extinguish the Spirit” (1 Thess. 5:19)—not because the Spirit can be extinguished, but because those who act in such a way that they wish it extinguished are rightly called, insofar as it lies within them, its extinguishers.

In this sense what the most blessed Cyprian wrote in his letter *On the Lapsed* can rightly be understood. In reproving those who had sacrificed to idols during the persecution, he says:

“And, as though something were still lacking to complete the accumulation of their crime, infants also, placed in or touched by the hands of their parents, lost what they had obtained at once at the very beginning of their birth.”

He said “they lost it” insofar as this pertained to the crime of those by whom they were compelled to lose it. They lost it in the mind and will of those who committed so great a crime against them.

For if they had lost it in themselves, they would certainly have remained, by the divine judgment, condemned without any defense. But if the holy Cyprian had thought that they had no defense, he would not immediately have added the following, saying:

“When the day of judgment comes, will they not say: ‘We did nothing; we did not voluntarily hasten to profane contagions after abandoning the food and cup of the Lord. Another’s faithlessness destroyed us; we experienced our parents as murderers. They denied us the Church as mother and the Lord as father, so that, while we were small, unsuspecting, and ignorant of so great a crime, we were joined through others to participation in the crime and were ensnared by another’s fraud’?”

He would not have added this defense unless he believed it to be most just and beneficial to the infants in the judgment of God.

For if it is truly said, “We did nothing,” and “The soul that sins shall die,” then those whom their parents, by their crime, destroyed insofar as it depended on the parents themselves will not perish under God’s just judgment.

### 4

Nor does the incident mentioned in the same letter disturb me: a little girl, whose parents had been thrown into confusion and fled, was left with her nurse; the nurse then afflicted her with the sacrileges of demons. Later, when the child was brought into the church, she rejected the Eucharist that was given to her by miraculous movements.

It seems to me that this happened by divine action so that the adults would not think that they were doing no wrong against the infants in that iniquity. Rather, they were to understand that, through the bodily gesture meaningfully performed by one who could not speak, they were being wonderfully admonished about what they themselves ought to do: after committing so great a crime, they ought to refrain through repentance from approaching the saving sacraments.

When divine providence does something of this kind through infants, we must not believe that the infants themselves do it knowingly or rationally. For when God wished to restrain the madness of a certain prophet even through a speaking she-donkey (Num. 22:28), this does not mean that we should admire the wisdom of donkeys.

If an irrational animal uttered something resembling human speech, that utterance must be attributed to a divine miracle and not to the donkey’s mind. In the same way, the Almighty could show, through the soul of an infant—not where reason was entirely absent, but where it was still dormant—by means of the infant’s bodily gesture, what those who had sinned both against themselves and against their children ought to remedy.

In any case, since the infant does not return into its parent so as to be one person with and in the parent, but is altogether another person, possessing its own flesh and its own soul, “The soul that sins shall die.”

### 5

Nor should the fact that some people bring infants to Baptism with an intention other than that they be regenerated by spiritual grace for eternal life disturb you. They bring them because they think that through this remedy the infants will retain or recover temporal health.

The infants are not therefore left unregenerated simply because those people do not present them with this intention. The necessary ministries and sacramental words are performed through them, without which the infant cannot be consecrated [Note: [Col. 0362] Bad., Am., Er., and Lov. inserted here certain words taken from section 3, which disturb the sense and are entirely absent from the manuscripts—both the six Vatican manuscripts and seventeen others that we examined. Those editions read as follows: “For the necessary ministries are performed through them. But those who attempt to bind their sons or any infants through the sacrileges of demons are spiritual murderers. They do not actually kill them, but insofar as it lies within them they become killers. And they are rightly told, when they are restrained from this crime: ‘Do not kill your children.’ But it is not rightly said to these people: ‘Do not recite the sacramental words, without which an infant cannot be consecrated.’ But the Spirit …” Anselm has slightly earlier: “necessary mysteries and words.”].

The Holy Spirit who dwells in the saints—from whom that one silver-colored dove is formed by the fire of charity—accomplishes what he accomplishes even through servitude, sometimes not only through those who are simply ignorant but also through those who are damnably unworthy.

Infants are brought forward to receive spiritual grace not so much by those whose hands carry them—although also by those people, if they themselves are good believers—as by the entire fellowship of the saints and faithful.

They are rightly understood to be brought forward by all who are pleased that they are brought forward, and whose holy and indivisible charity assists them toward participation in the Holy Spirit.

The whole mother Church, therefore, which exists in the saints, performs this act, because the whole Church gives birth to all and the whole Church gives birth to each individual.

For if the sacrament of Christian Baptism, when it is one and the same sacrament, is valid and sufficient for consecration even among heretics, although it is not sufficient for participation in eternal life—so that this consecration makes the heretic guilty, since he possesses the Lord’s character outside the Lord’s flock, while sound doctrine teaches that he must be corrected and not consecrated again—how much more, in the Catholic Church, is grain to be carried for purification even through the ministry of straw, so that it may be brought through the threshing floor into fellowship with the mass?

### 6

Do not let this escape you: you must not think that the bond of guilt drawn from Adam cannot be broken in any other way than by parents presenting their infants to receive the grace of Christ.

For you write as follows: “Just as parents were the cause of their punishment, so through the faith of their parents they may likewise be justified.” Yet you see that many infants are not presented by their parents, but by any outsiders—for example, slaves are sometimes presented by their masters.

Sometimes infants are baptized after their parents have died, being presented by those who are able to show them this kind of mercy. Sometimes children whom their parents have cruelly exposed to be cared for by anyone who would take them in [Note: [Col. 0362] Er. and Lov. have *nutriendos*. Most manuscripts, as well as the edition of Bad., have *nutriendi*] are gathered up by holy virgins and presented by them for Baptism. These virgins certainly have had no children of their own and do not intend to have any.

Thus you see that nothing else is happening here than what is written in the Gospel, when the Lord asked who had been neighbor to the man wounded by robbers and left half-dead on the road. The answer was: “The one who showed him mercy” (Luke 10:37).

### 7

At the end of your inquiry, you seem to have proposed to me a very difficult question, with the intention you customarily display of taking great care to avoid lying.

“If I place an infant before you,” you say, “and ask whether, when he grows up, he will be chaste or will not become a thief, you will undoubtedly answer: ‘I do not know.’ And if I ask whether, while still at that same infant age, he thinks anything good or evil, you will say: ‘I do not know.’

“If, then, you do not dare promise anything certain about his future conduct, what of his present thought? When infants are brought to Baptism, their parents answer on their behalf as guarantors of faith, saying that they do what that age cannot think—or, if it can, that the matter is hidden.

“For we ask those by whom they are brought and say: ‘Does he believe in God?’ Concerning an age that does not know whether God exists, they answer: ‘He believes.’ And similarly they answer each of the other questions that are asked.

“I am therefore amazed that parents answer so confidently on behalf of an infant in these matters, saying that he performs such great good deeds at the very hour when the baptizer asks him the questions. Yet if, at that same hour, I were to ask: ‘Will the one being baptized be chaste, or will he not be a thief?’ I do not know whether anyone would dare to say: ‘He will be one or the other,’ just as he answers me without hesitation that the infant believes in God and turns toward God.

“Then, concluding your letter, you add and say: ‘I therefore ask that you deign to answer these questions briefly, without appealing to custom against me, but by giving a reason.’”

## 8.

After reading and rereading your letter, and considering it as far as the narrowness of my time allowed, I remembered my friend Nebridius. He was a most diligent and acute investigator of obscure matters bearing especially upon the teaching of piety, and he strongly disliked a brief answer to a great question. Whoever asked this of him, he endured with the greatest difficulty; and, if the person’s status permitted it, he would restrain him with an indignant look and voice, judging him unworthy to ask such questions when he did not know how many things could and ought to be said about so important a matter.

But I am not angry with you in the same way he used to be. You are a bishop occupied with many cares, as I am; consequently, you have little leisure to read anything lengthy, and I have little leisure to write it. For Nebridius, then a young man who did not want to hear such things briefly and asked about many matters in our conversations, was an idle man asking an idle man. But you, considering now who you are and from whom you demand these things, order me to answer briefly concerning so great a matter. Behold, I am doing as much as I can; may the Lord help me to do what you ask.

## 9.

We often speak in such a way that, as Easter approaches, we say that the Lord’s Passion will take place tomorrow or the day after tomorrow, although He suffered so many years ago and that Passion occurred only once. On the very Lord’s Day we say, “Today the Lord has risen,” although so many years have passed since He rose. Who is so foolish as to accuse us of lying when we speak in this way? No one—because we name these days according to their likeness to those on which these events occurred. Thus the day itself is said to be the day, although it is not that day itself but a day resembling it through the passage of time; and the event is said to occur on that day because of the celebration of the sacrament, although it did not occur on that day but long ago.

Was Christ not sacrificed once for all in Himself? And yet, in the sacrament, He is sacrificed for the people not only throughout all the solemnities of Easter but every day; and the person who, when asked, answers that He is being sacrificed is certainly not lying. For if sacraments did not possess a certain likeness to the things of which they are sacraments, they would not be sacraments at all. From this likeness they often also receive the names of the things themselves. **[Note: Twenty manuscripts read *jam*, “already.”]** Thus, in a certain sense, the sacrament of Christ’s body is Christ’s body, and the sacrament of Christ’s blood is Christ’s blood; in the same way, the sacrament of faith is faith. Now believing is nothing other than having faith. Accordingly, when it is answered that an infant believes, although the infant does not yet possess the inclination of faith, the answer means that the infant has faith because of the sacrament of faith, and turns to God because of the sacrament of conversion; for the answer itself also belongs to the celebration of the sacrament.

Thus the Apostle says of Baptism itself: “We were buried with Christ through Baptism into death” (Romans 6:4). He does not say, “We signified burial,” but says outright, “We were buried.” He therefore named the sacrament of so great a reality by the name of that very reality.

## 10.

Therefore, although the infant does not yet possess that faith which consists in the will of believers, the sacrament of that faith already makes the infant faithful. For just as the infant is said to believe, so the infant is also called faithful—not by assenting to the reality in the mind, but by receiving the sacrament of that reality.

When the person begins to understand, he will not repeat that sacrament, but will understand it and will also conform his will to its truth. Until he is able to do this, the sacrament will serve for his protection against hostile powers; and it will serve so effectively that, if he departs from this life before attaining the use of reason **[Note: Nearly all manuscripts read *ante majoris usum aetatis*, “before attaining the use of greater age.”]**, through that sacrament and through the Church’s charity commending him, he will be delivered by Christian assistance from the condemnation that entered the world through one man (the same, 5:12).

Whoever does not believe this, and judges that it cannot happen, is certainly an unbeliever, even if he possesses the sacrament of faith. Far better than such a person **[Note: Thus one Vatican manuscript, and rightly. [Illegible text in the source note.]]** is the infant who, although he does not yet possess faith in his thoughts, nevertheless does not set up against it the obstacle of an opposing thought, and therefore receives its sacrament for salvation.

I have answered your questions as I think appropriate: as regards those who are less capable and those who are contentious, not adequately; but as regards the peaceful and understanding, perhaps more than is enough. Nor, in my defense, did I invoke the authority of an established custom; rather, I supplied as best I could the rationale of a most salutary custom.

**[Note: At [Col. 0364], nearly all manuscripts read *ante majoris usum aetatis*, “before attaining the use of greater age”; one Vatican manuscript, rightly, has the reading indicated above.]**

---

# LETTER XCIX

**[Note: Revised against manuscripts a, b, bg, bl, bn, c, cc, ff, g, gv, j, n, r, s, t, vc; against two manuscripts designated sb; against four designated v; and against Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]**

**[Note: Formerly Letter 133; formerly numbered 99, now 164. Written at the end of 408 or the beginning of 409.]**

He expresses sorrow and sympathy arising from the calamity of the Romans.

To the most religious and deservedly and rightly praiseworthy handmaid of God, **ITALICA**, a member of Christ, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

## 1.

I had received three letters from Your Goodness when I wrote this reply. One still requested a letter from me; another indicated that one of my letters had already reached you; and the third contained your most benevolent concern for us, including your concern for the household of the illustrious and excellent young Julian, which adjoins our walls.

As soon as I received it, I did not delay replying, because your Excellency’s steward wrote that he could soon send someone to Rome. We were deeply saddened by his letter, since he had taken care to inform us of what was happening there in the City or around the City, so that we might become certain of what we had been unwilling to believe on the basis of uncertain rumor.

**[Note: Here he refers to the calamity brought upon the Roman people in Alaric’s first siege of the City, apparently at the end of 408. After Alaric had withdrawn upon receiving gold from the Romans, “this seemed already to be a moderate relief from these evils, at the time when the emperor Honorius was entering upon the consulship at Ravenna, having held this honor eight times, while in the East Augustus Theodosius was already consul for the third time,” as Zosimus writes in Book 5—that is, at the beginning of 409.]**

For although letters previously sent by the brethren had reported matters that were distressing and severe, they had nevertheless reported them as much lighter than they truly were. I was more astonished than can be expressed that, despite so great an opportunity, neither the holy bishops among your people had written to us nor your letter had communicated anything about your great tribulations—tribulations that, through the bonds of charity, are certainly ours as well. Perhaps you thought it should not be done because you judged it of no benefit, or you did not wish our spirits to be saddened by your letters. Yet, in my opinion, it is beneficial even to know these things.

First, because it is unjust to wish to rejoice with those who rejoice but not to wish to weep with those who weep (Romans 12:15). Second, because “tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces proven character, and proven character produces hope; and hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:3–5).

## 2.

Let us therefore not refuse to hear even what is bitter and sorrowful concerning those dearest to us. For somehow what one member suffers becomes less burdensome when the other members suffer with it (1 Corinthians 12:26). The evil itself is not relieved by sharing in the calamity, but by the consolation of charity. Thus, although some suffer by enduring and others suffer with them by learning of their suffering, the tribulation is nevertheless common to those who share in the same testing, hope, love, and spirit.

The Lord consoles us all. He both foretold these temporal evils and promised eternal goods after them. Nor should the person who wishes to be crowned after the battle be broken when he is fighting, since the One who prepares ineffable gifts for the victors supplies strength to those who fight.

## 3.

Let that earlier reply of ours not take away your confidence in writing to us, especially since you have softened our fear with a defense that is not implausible.

We greet your little ones and wish that they may grow in Christ. Already at their present age they perceive how dangerous and harmful is the love of this world. Would that, when they are shaken by great and difficult things, their small and pliable dispositions might be corrected.

What can I say about that household except that I should give thanks for your most benevolent concern? They do not want the house we are able to give, while the one they want we are unable to give. For, contrary to what they have falsely heard, it was not left to the Church by my predecessor; rather, it is possessed among its ancient estates and is attached to another ancient church in the same way as the property in question is attached to another church.

**[Note: Editors read *patiuntur*, “suffer”; the manuscripts read *quatiuntur*, “are shaken.”]**

---

# LETTER C

**[Note: Compared with a, bg, bl, c, cc, ff, g, gv, j, n, r, s, t, vc; two manuscripts designated sb; four designated v; and with Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]**

**[Note: Formerly Letter 127; formerly numbered 100, now 159. Written at approximately the same time.]**

Augustine to Donatus, proconsul of Africa, asking him to restrain the Donatists, not kill them.

To the illustrious, deservedly honorable, and exceptionally praiseworthy son, **DONATUS**, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

**[Note: Donatus was serving as proconsul of Africa at the end of 408, as may be gathered from a law addressed to him on November 24. He did not hold that office beyond the middle of 410, since another law addressed to Macrobius, the proconsul of Africa, is found dated June 25 of that year.]**

## 1.

I would not wish the African Church to be placed amid these afflictions in such a way that it needed the aid of any earthly power. But since, as the Apostle says, “There is no authority except from God” (Romans 13:1), when assistance is given to her through you, the most sincere sons of the Catholic mother, our assistance is certainly given in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth (Psalm 120:2).

Who would not perceive that, amid such great evils, a considerable consolation has been sent to us by God, since you—a man of such character and most devoted to the name of Christ—have been raised to the insignia of the proconsulate, so that power joined to your good will might restrain the enemies of the good Church from criminal and sacrilegious attempts?

Yet there is one thing we fear in your justice: perhaps, because whatever wickedness impious and ungrateful people commit against the Christian community is more serious and atrocious than if such things were committed against others, you too may judge that they should be restrained on account of the enormity of their crimes rather than with consideration for Christian gentleness. We beseech you through Jesus Christ not to do this.

We do not seek vengeance upon our enemies in this world. Nor should the hardships we endure so constrict our hearts that we forget what He commanded us, for whose truth and name we suffer: “We love our enemies and pray for them.”

Therefore, taking advantage of the terror inspired by judgments and laws, we wish them to be corrected so that they do not fall into the punishments of eternal judgment, not killed. We do not wish discipline to be neglected in their case, but neither do we wish them to be subjected to punishments that they deserve. **[Note: Three Vatican and three Gallican manuscripts read *nec supplicia*, “nor punishments.”]** Thus restrain their sins in such a way that they remain people who repent of having sinned.

**[Note: All manuscripts except one read, “through Christ Himself” (*per ipsum Christum*).]**

## 2.

We therefore ask that, when you hear the Church’s cases, however wickedly you discover that she has been attacked or afflicted, you forget that you possess the power to kill, but do not forget our petition.

Do not regard as insignificant or contemptible, most honorably beloved son, what we ask of you: that those for whom we ask the Lord that they may be corrected should not be killed. Apart from the fact that we must not withdraw from our constant purpose of overcoming evil with good, let your prudence also consider that no one except ecclesiastics takes care to bring ecclesiastical cases before you.

Accordingly, if you think that the people involved in these crimes should be killed, you will deter us from bringing any such matter before your judgment through our efforts. Once they learn this, they will attack us with more unrestrained boldness, forcing and compelling us to choose even to be killed by them rather than to bring them before your judgments for execution.

I ask you not to receive this admonition, petition, and supplication of mine with disdain. I do not think you have forgotten that, even if I were not a bishop, I could nevertheless have had great confidence in you when you were raised to a much higher position than the one you now hold.

Meanwhile, let the heretics, the Donatists, quickly learn through an edict of Your Excellency that the laws enacted against their error remain in force—laws that they now think and proclaim to be powerless, so that even in this way they may be able to spare us to some extent.

You will greatly assist in making our labors and dangers fruitful if you do not simply arrange for their sect, full of empty vanity and impious pride, to be suppressed by imperial laws, so that they and their people may imagine that they are enduring some sort of hardship for the sake of truth and justice. Rather, when this is requested of you, allow them to be convicted and instructed by the clearest evidence of established facts in the records either of Your Eminence or of the lesser judges.

Then those who are detained at your command may, if possible, bend their hardened will toward what is better, and others may read these proceedings to their benefit. Diligence that merely compels people without teaching them is more burdensome than useful, even when its purpose is to abandon a great evil and hold fast to a great good.

---

# LETTER CI

**[Note: Revised against a, bg, bl, bn, c, cc, g, gv, j, n, r, s, sb, t, vc, four manuscripts designated v, and Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]**

**[Note: Formerly Letter 131; formerly numbered 101, now 162. Written at the end of 408 or the beginning of 409.]**

Augustine sends Bishop Memorius the sixth book of his work on Music, which Memorius had requested, and promises to send the others if he finds them. On this occasion he discusses the disciplines that are falsely called liberal unless the study of Christian piety is present.

To the most blessed, reverently beloved, and sincerely longed-for brother and fellow bishop, **MEMORIUS**, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

**[Note: This name is written *Memorium* in all manuscripts and printed editions at this point. Perhaps it should read *Memori*, as in Book 1 of *Against Julian*, chapter 4, and also according to Mercator, in Book *Subnotatus*, chapter 4, where he addresses Julian in these words: “Are you the son of Memorius, of holy and blessed memory, the bishop? Were you born from the womb of Juliana, a foremost woman, than whom no one more honorable can be found among the most revered matrons? … No one who knows the holy character, holy life, and discipline of those men will doubt that they have degenerated in you.” Ughellus counts Memorius among the bishops of Capua in volume 6 of *Sacred Italy*, relying on no authority other than that of Baronius and Bellarmine.]**

## 1.

I should no longer have sent any letter to Your Holy Charity without these books, which you demanded from me with the most forceful right of holy love, so that at least by this obedience I might answer your letters—letters by which you have deigned to burden me more than to honor me.

Yet where I yield because I am burdened, there too, because I am loved, I am relieved. For I am not loved, relieved, and chosen by just anyone **[Note: Perhaps read *erigor*, “I am raised.”]**, but by a man and priest of the Lord whom I perceive to be so acceptable to God that, when you raise your good soul to the Lord—because you have me within it—you also raise me.

I ought therefore now to have sent the books that I had promised to revise. I did not send them because I did not revise them—not because I was unwilling, but because I was unable, being occupied by many cares that were exceedingly pressing.

It would have been extremely ungrateful and hardhearted if you, who love us so greatly, had not learned this from our holy brother and colleague Possidius, in whom you will find a considerable presence of us, or if you had learned it without a letter from us. Through our ministry he has been nourished not by those writings that slaves of various lusts call liberal, but by the Lord’s bread, as much of it as could be distributed amid our limitations.

## 2.

What else should be said to those who, although wicked and impious, think themselves liberally educated, except what we read in writings that are truly liberal: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free”?

Through Him it is granted that we may recognize what those disciplines which are called liberal by people who have not been called to freedom actually contain that is liberal. For they possess nothing compatible with freedom except what they possess compatible with truth. Hence that very Son says, “The truth will set you free” (John 8:36, 32).

Therefore, the countless and impious fables with which the poems of empty-headed poets are filled do not in any way accord with our freedom; nor do the inflated and polished lies of orators; nor, finally, the chattering subtleties of philosophers themselves. Either they did not know God at all, or, when they knew God, they did not glorify Him as God or give thanks to Him. Instead, they became futile in their thoughts; their foolish heart was darkened; and, claiming to be wise, they became fools. They exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible man, birds, four-footed animals, and serpents; or, although they were not devoted—or were not excessively devoted—to these images, they nevertheless worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator (Romans 1:21–25).

Far be it from us to call such vanities and deceitful insanities, such windy trifles and proud error, rightly liberal literature—literature belonging to unhappy people who did not know the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, by which alone we are freed from this body of death (the same, 7:24–25), nor did they recognize it even in those things that they perceived to be true.

History, certainly, whose writers profess that they owe their chief duty of faithfulness to their narratives, may perhaps contain something worthy of knowledge for free people, since it recounts true events, whether good or evil, concerning human beings. Yet when we consider how those who were not assisted by the Holy Spirit, and who were compelled by the condition of human weakness to gather rumors, could avoid being deceived in very many matters, I altogether fail to see. Still, there is in them some proximity to freedom if they have no desire to lie and do not deceive people except when they themselves are deceived by human weakness.

## 3.

But because, in all the movements of things, the power of numbers is more easily considered in sounds, and because that consideration rises by certain graduated paths toward the innermost heights of truth—on those paths Wisdom reveals herself joyfully and meets those who love her in every act of providence (Wisdom 6:17)—at the beginning of our leisure, when my mind was free from greater and more necessary cares, I wished to make a preliminary exercise through the writings you requested.

At that time I wrote six books on rhythm alone, and, I confess, I intended to write perhaps another six on melody, expecting that I would have leisure. But after the burden of ecclesiastical cares was laid upon me, all those delights slipped from my hands, so that I can scarcely find the book itself now, since I cannot disregard your will—your request, which is not merely a request but a command.

If I am able to send you that little work, you will perhaps regret that you pressed me so greatly—not because I obeyed you, but because you demanded it so insistently. For the five books are extremely difficult to understand unless there is someone who can distinguish not only the speakers in the discussion but also, by pronouncing them, sound the syllabic intervals in such a way that the kinds of numbers are expressed through them and strike the sense of hearing. This is especially so because in some places measured intervals of silences are also interwoven, and these cannot be perceived at all unless the reader’s pronunciation instructs the listener.

## 4.

The sixth book, which I found revised and in which the entire fruit of the others is contained, I did not delay sending to Your Charity. Perhaps it will not shrink from your dignity. The preceding five books will scarcely seem worthy of reading and study except to our son and fellow deacon Julian, since he too is now serving alongside us.

I would not dare to say that I love him more than you, because I would not be speaking truthfully; yet I do dare to say that I long for him more than for you. It may seem strange how I can long more greatly for someone whom I love equally. But this is caused by my greater hope of seeing him. For I think that, if he comes to us at your command or is sent by you, he will do what is fitting for a young man—especially since he is not yet detained by greater cares—and he will bring you to me more readily.

I have not written in what numerical patterns the verses of David are composed, because I do not know. The translator could not express their numbers from the Hebrew language, which I do not know, since the necessity of meter might have forced him to depart from the truth of the translation more than the meaning of the sentences allowed. I nevertheless believe those who know that language thoroughly when they say that the verses are composed according to definite numerical patterns.

That holy man loved sacred music, and through those studies he himself kindled us more than any other author. May you all dwell forever under the protection of the Most High (Psalm 90:1)—you who dwell together in unity in one household (Psalm 67:7): father and mother, brothers and children, and all the children of one Father—remembering us.

---

# CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING LETTER

*(Book 2 of the Retractations, chapter 31)*

During this period, six questions were sent to me from Carthage. They had been proposed by a certain friend whom I wished to become a Christian, so that they might be answered against the pagans, especially because he said that some of them had been proposed by the philosopher Porphyry. I do not think, however, that this was that famous Porphyry of Sicily.

I brought discussions of these questions together in one book, not a lengthy one, entitled **“Six Questions Explained against the Pagans.”** The first question concerns the Resurrection; the second, the time of the Christian religion; the third, the distinction of sacrifices; the fourth, the statement, “With the measure you use, it will be measured back to you” (Matthew 7:2); the fifth, the Son of God according to Solomon; and the sixth, the prophet Jonah.

In the second question I said: “The salvation of this religion, through which alone true salvation is truly promised, has never been lacking for anyone who was worthy; and the person to whom it was lacking was not worthy.” I did not say this as though anyone had been made worthy by his own merits, but in the manner in which the Apostle says: “Not because of works, but because of Him who calls, it was said, ‘The elder shall serve the younger’” (Romans 9:12–13). He asserts that this calling belongs to God’s purpose. Hence he says: “Not according to our works but according to His own purpose and grace” (2 Timothy 1:9). He also says: “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called as saints according to His purpose” (Romans 8:28). Concerning this calling he says: “That He may count you worthy of His holy calling” (2 Thessalonians 1:11).

After the letter that was later added at the beginning, this book begins as follows: “Some are troubled and ask…”

---

# SIX QUESTIONS EXPLAINED AGAINST THE PAGANS, ONE BOOK, OR LETTER CII

**[Note: Corrected with the assistance of a, bg, bl, c, cc, gg, gv, j, n, r, s, vc; two manuscripts designated bn; two designated s; two designated t; two designated vc; five designated v; and Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]**

**[Note: Formerly Letter 49; formerly numbered 102, now 169. Written at approximately the same time.]**

Augustine sends to the presbyter Deogratias the solution of six questions proposed by a certain pagan, which Deogratias had sent to Augustine to solve.

To his most sincere brother and fellow presbyter, **DEOGRATIAS**, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

## 1.

You preferred to delegate to me the questions proposed to you—not, as I suppose, out of laziness, but because, in your great affection for me, you more willingly hear even what you know through me. I, however, preferred that you explain them yourself because the very friend who proposed them appears, from the fact that he did not reply to some letters of mine, to be somewhat ashamed to follow us. Let him determine the reason.

I nevertheless suspect this, and my suspicion is neither malicious nor absurd, since you know very well how much I love him and how painful it is to me that he is not yet a Christian. I consider it quite plausible that the man whom I see unwilling to reply to me did not want anything written to him by me.

Therefore I beg you: just as I obeyed you and, amid my extremely pressing occupations, feared offending your holy and most beloved will if I did not do what you asked, so you too should do what I ask. I ask that you not refuse to answer all his questions briefly, just as he requested from you, as you have told me; you could have done this earlier.

When you read my work, you will know that I have said almost nothing that you did not already know or could not have known without my saying it. But I ask you to regard this work of mine as belonging with the others whose usefulness to students you know. Let the work I am requesting from you belong to the man to whom it is especially appropriate, and to the others who take no small pleasure in such matters, in whatever form they can be explained by you—and I too am among them.

May you live always in Christ, remembering us.

---

# FIRST QUESTION: On the Resurrection

## 2.

Some are troubled and ask which of two resurrections corresponds to the promised resurrection: Christ’s or Lazarus’s.

“If Christ’s,” they say, “how can this correspond to the resurrection of those born from seed, when He was born without the condition of seed? But if Lazarus’s resurrection is said to correspond to it, even that seems not to fit. Lazarus’s resurrection occurred from a body that had not yet decayed, from the body by which Lazarus was known; but our bodies will be restored many centuries later from a confused mass after their elements have been scattered.

“Furthermore, if the condition after the resurrection is to be blessed, with no injury to the body and no necessity of hunger, what is the meaning of Christ’s having eaten and shown His wounds? But if He did this for the sake of the unbeliever, then He pretended; and if He showed something real, then wounds will also be present in the resurrection that is to come.”

## 3.

The answer is that it is not Lazarus’s resurrection but rather Christ’s that corresponds to the promised resurrection, because Lazarus rose in such a way that he would die again, whereas Christ, as it is written of Him, “having risen from the dead, dies no more, and death shall no longer rule over Him” (Romans 6:9). This too has been promised to those who will rise at the end of the age and reign with Him forever.

The difference between Christ’s birth and ours—He was born without male seed, whereas we were created from man and woman—has no bearing on this resurrection, just as it has no bearing on the difference in death itself. His death was not unreal because He was born without male seed. Likewise, the fact that the flesh of the first man arose differently from ours—he was created from the earth without parents, whereas we are born from parents—contributed nothing to a difference in death, so that he would die in one way and we in another. Just as different birth makes no difference to death, so it makes no difference to resurrection.

## 4.

But lest unbelieving people also refuse to believe what is written about the first man, let them ask or observe, if they can, how many kinds of animals are produced from the earth without parents, although they themselves reproduce by mating and bear offspring like themselves. Yet because of the difference in their birth, there is no difference in the nature of those produced from the earth and those that arise from animals mating with one another.

They live in the same way and die in the same way, although they are born in different ways. Thus it is not absurd that bodies which arose in different ways should rise in the same way.

People of this sort cannot see in what respect a difference matters and in what respect it does not. Whenever they notice a difference in origins, they insist that everything that follows must also differ. Such people might think that oil made from animal fat ought not to float on water as oil made from olives does, because the origin of the two is greatly different: one flows from wood, the other from flesh.

## 5.

As for the difference that Christ’s body, not dissolved by decay and putrefaction, rose on the third day, whereas ours will be restored after a long time from the dispersed condition into which they had dissolved: both are impossible for human ability, but both are extremely easy for divine power.

Just as the ray of our eye does not reach what is nearer more quickly and what is farther away more slowly, but touches both distances with equal speed, so, when the resurrection of the dead occurs “in the twinkling of an eye” (1 Corinthians 15:52), as the Apostle says, it is equally easy for God’s omnipotence and ineffable command to raise recent bodies and corpses scattered over a long period of time.

These things seem incredible to some because they are unfamiliar. Yet all nature is so full of miracles that things seem not marvelous because of an easy investigation by reason but because of habitual observation; and for that reason they appear unworthy of consideration or inquiry.

For I—and everyone who, with me, strives to understand the invisible things of God through the things that have been made (Romans 1:20)—admire no less, or perhaps even more, that in one tiny grain of seed all the things we praise in a tree lay hidden as though compressed, than that the vast expanse of this world, which receives human bodies as they dissolve, will restore them whole and entire for the future resurrection.

## 6.

How is it contradictory that Christ ate after the resurrection while the resurrection that is promised will involve no need for food, when we also read that angels consumed food of the same kind and in the same manner—not through a false and empty apparition but in manifest reality, and yet not from necessity but from power?

The earth absorbs water when it is thirsty in one way; the burning ray of the sun acts in another way. The former does so from need, the latter from power.

The body of the future resurrection will therefore possess imperfect blessedness if it cannot take food; and it will possess imperfect blessedness if it needs food.

I could discuss at greater length the changes in bodily qualities and the surpassing power exercised by higher bodies over lower bodies. But I have set out to answer briefly, and this has been written for minds that need only a reminder.

## 7.

Let the person who proposed these questions know that, after His resurrection, Christ showed scars—not wounds—to those who doubted. For their sake He also wished to take food and drink, not once but repeatedly, lest they think that what appeared to them was not a body but a spirit, and that it appeared not solidly but as an image.

Those scars would have been false if no wounds had preceded them. Yet even the scars would not exist if He had not wished them to exist. He wished, for the sake of a definite dispensation, to show those whom He was building up in an unfabricated faith that what had risen was not something else in place of what they had seen crucified, but that very thing.

What, then, does the statement mean, “If He did it for the unbeliever, He pretended”? It is as though a brave man, fighting for his country and receiving many grievous wounds, should say to a highly skilled physician—one capable of treating those wounds so that no scars appeared—that he wanted to be healed in such a way that the traces of the wounds would remain on his body as titles of glory. Would the physician therefore be said to have fabricated the scars merely because, although by his skill he could have made them disappear, he had deliberately caused them to remain for a definite reason?

The scars would be proved false in only one way, as I said above: if no wounds had been healed.

---

# SECOND QUESTION: On the Time of the Christian Religion

## 8.

They also proposed another matter, saying that they had extracted it from Porphyry against the Christians as though it were a stronger argument.

“If Christ,” they say, “calls Himself the way of salvation, grace, and truth, and places in Himself alone the return of souls that believe in Him (John 14:6), what became of all the people who lived through so many ages before Christ?

“To leave aside the periods before Latium was ruled, let us take Latium itself as the beginning of the human name. In Latium, gods were worshiped before Alba. In Alba likewise the religious observances and rites of temples flourished. Rome itself existed for no fewer centuries, over a long span of ages, without the Christian law.

“What,” they say, “became of the countless souls who were entirely without guilt, if the One whom they could believe in had not yet granted His arrival to humanity? The world, together with Rome itself, also burned with zeal for the rites of temples.

“Why,” they ask, “did the Savior who was so named withdraw Himself for so many ages?

“But,” they continue, “let them not say that the human race was healed by the ancient Jewish law. The law of the Jews appeared and flourished much later in a narrow region of Syria; afterward it spread even to the boundaries of Italy—but only after Gaius Caesar, or at least during his reign.

“What, then, became of the Roman or Latin souls who were deprived of the grace of Christ, who had not yet come, all the way up to the time of the Caesars?”

## 9.

The answer to this argument should begin by asking them whether the sacred rites of their gods, which were established at particular times, benefited human beings. If they deny that those rites contributed anything to the salvation of souls, they destroy them together with us and confess that they are empty. We indeed show that they were harmful as well; but it is already something significant if, for the moment, they first admit that they were empty.

If, on the other hand, they defend those rites and assert that they were established wisely and usefully, I ask what became of those who died before these rites were established. They were certainly deprived of that salvation and benefit. But if they could be purified in some other way, why did that way not continue for later generations? What need was there to establish new consecrations that had not existed in ancient times?

10. If they say that the gods themselves have always existed and have likewise always been able to liberate their worshipers, but that, because of the varying circumstances of temporal and earthly affairs—[Col. 0374] which they knew were appropriate at particular times and places—they wished to be served in one way at one time and place, in another way at another, why do they raise this question against the Christian religion? In this matter they either cannot answer us on behalf of their gods, or, if they can, let them answer on that very point also on behalf of our religion: namely, that it makes no difference, according to the suitability of different times and places, by what different sacraments something holy is worshiped, just as it makes no difference, according to the differing languages and audiences of speakers, by what different sounds something true is expressed. There is, however, this difference: human beings can establish among themselves, by a kind of social agreement, the sounds of languages by which they communicate their thoughts to one another; but those who judged rightly followed God’s will concerning which sacred rites were fitting for divinity. This will has never been lacking for the salvation of mortals who live justly and devoutly. And if different practices are celebrated among different peoples joined in one and the same religion, it matters greatly in what manner this is done, so that human weakness may be encouraged or supported and divine authority not opposed.

11. Therefore, when we say that Christ is the Word of God through whom all things were made, and therefore the Son because he is the Word—not a word spoken and completed, but the immutable Word himself, abiding immutably and unchangeably with the immutable Father, under whose governance the whole spiritual and bodily creation is administered according to the suitability of times and places; since wisdom and knowledge belong to him concerning what, when, and where things ought to occur for the ordering and governance of creation—then certainly, both before he propagated the Hebrew nation through which he would prefigure, by appropriate sacraments, the manifestation of his coming, and during the times of the Israelite kingdom, and afterward, when he manifested himself to mortals in mortal flesh received from a virgin, and from then until now, as he fulfills everything he previously foretold through the Prophets, and from now until the end of the age, when he will separate the holy from the impious and repay each person according to his deeds, he is the very same Son of God, coeternal with the Father and the immutable Wisdom through whom all nature was created, and by participation in whom every rational soul becomes blessed.

12. Thus, from the beginning of the human race, whoever believed in him, understood him in whatever way they could, and lived piously and justly according to his commandments was undoubtedly saved through him, whenever and wherever that person lived. For just as we believe in him as one who remains with the Father and has already come in the flesh, so the ancients believed in him as one who remained with the Father and was to come in the flesh. Nor, because what was then foretold as future is now announced as having happened in accordance with the variation of times, has the faith itself therefore changed, or salvation itself become different. Nor, because one and the same reality is proclaimed or prophesied through different sacred rites and sacraments to different peoples, should we therefore understand different realities or different salvations. As for when whatever belongs to the single and same deliverance of the faithful and devout takes place, let us attribute the plan to God and maintain obedience on our part. Accordingly, the one true religion is signified and observed under different names and signs at different times—formerly more obscurely, afterward more openly; formerly by fewer people, afterward by more.

13. We do not object to them that Numa Pompilius instituted a different manner of worshiping the gods for the Romans from that in which they had previously been worshiped by the Romans or Italians. Nor do we object that, in the time of Pythagoras, a philosophy was celebrated that previously either did not exist at all or perhaps lay concealed among a very few who held the same opinions, though they did not live according to the same rite. Rather, we debate with them whether those gods are true and ought to be worshiped, and whether that philosophy contributes anything to the salvation of souls. This is what we call into question and overthrow by argument. Let them therefore cease objecting to us what can be objected to every sect and every religious name. Since they acknowledge that the times are ordered not by chance but by divine providence, what is suitable and opportune for each time surpasses human judgment and is distributed from the source from which providence itself cares for the world.

14. For if they say that Pythagorean discipline did not exist always and everywhere because Pythagoras was a human being and could not have had this power, can they also say that, during the very time in which he lived and in those regions where that philosophy flourished, everyone who was able to hear him also wished to believe and follow him? Indeed, if Pythagoras had possessed such great power that he could proclaim his doctrines wherever and whenever he wished, and if, in addition to that power, he had possessed complete foreknowledge of events, he would have appeared nowhere and never except where and when he foresaw that people would believe him.

Since they do not object to Christ that not everyone follows his teaching—for they themselves understand that such an objection cannot rightly be made either against the wisdom of philosophers or against the divinity of their gods—what will they answer if, setting aside the lofty depth of God’s wisdom and knowledge, where perhaps another divine plan lies hidden far more secretly, and without prejudicing whatever other causes prudent people may investigate, we say this briefly in the course of the present debate: that Christ then wished to appear to human beings and have his teaching proclaimed among them when and where he knew that there would be people who would believe in him? [Col. 0375]

[Note: [Col. 0375] The Semipelagians of Marseilles brought forward this passage in support of their error. When Hilary had drawn Augustine’s attention to this matter in Letter 219, Augustine finally defended and explained his position in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 9: “Do you see that, without prejudice to God’s hidden plan and to other causes, I wished to say this about Christ’s foreknowledge because it seemed sufficient to refute the unbelief of the pagans who had raised this question? For what is truer than that Christ foreknew who would believe in him, and when and in what places they would believe? But whether, when Christ was preached to them, they would have faith of themselves or receive it as God’s gift—that is, whether God merely foreknew them or also predestined them—I did not then consider it necessary to ask or discuss. Accordingly, what I said—that Christ then wished to appear to human beings and have his teaching preached among them when and where he knew that there would be those who would believe in him—could also be expressed in this way: Christ then wished to appear to human beings and have his teaching preached among them when and where he knew that there would be those who had been chosen in him before the foundation of the world.”]

For he knew that, in those times and places where his Gospel was not preached, all such people would have been in his preaching as were those—[Col. 0376] though not all, nevertheless many—who were present with him bodily and still refused to believe in him, even after he had raised the dead. We also now see many such people: although the Prophets’ proclamations concerning him are being fulfilled with such manifest clarity, they still refuse to believe, preferring to resist by human cleverness rather than yield to divine authority so clear, evident, lofty, and sublimely proclaimed.

[Note: [Col. 0376] The Benedictine edition lacks the words *sublimi et*, which are found in other editions. M.]

[Note: [Col. 0376] The better manuscripts have this reading. The editions here and below have *credere* (“to believe”).]

As long as human understanding is small and weak, it ought to yield to divine truth. What wonder, then, if Christ knew that the world was so full of unbelievers in earlier ages that he rightly did not wish to appear or be preached to those whom he foreknew would not believe either his words or his miracles? It is not unbelievable that all people then were such as we are astonished to find so many have been and still are from his coming until the present time.

15. Nevertheless, from the beginning of the human race, sometimes more secretly and sometimes more clearly, as God judged appropriate to the times, prophecy did not cease, nor were those who believed in him lacking: from Adam to Moses, among the people of Israel itself—which, by a particular mystery, was a prophetic nation—and among other peoples before he came in the flesh. Since certain people are mentioned in the sacred Hebrew Books, from the time of Abraham onward, who were neither descended from his flesh nor from the people of Israel nor joined to Israel as outsiders, and yet were participants in this sacrament, why should we not believe that among the other peoples here and there there were also others, even though we do not read of them in those same authoritative writings?

Thus, the salvation of this religion—through which alone true salvation is truly promised—has never been lacking to anyone who was worthy of it, and whoever lacked it was not worthy.

[Note: [Col. 0376] Augustine says concerning these words in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 10: “If it is debated and asked from what source each person is worthy, there are those who say, ‘From human will’; but we say, ‘From divine grace or predestination.’” See also *Retractions*, book 2, chapter 31.]

From the beginning of the propagation of the human race until the end, it is proclaimed to some for reward and to others for judgment. Accordingly, those to whom it was not proclaimed at all were foreknown as people who would not believe; those to whom it was proclaimed even though they would not believe are displayed as an example to others; and those to whom it is proclaimed because they would believe are prepared for the kingdom of heaven and fellowship with the holy Angels.

## THIRD QUESTION  
### On the Distinction of Sacrifices

16. Let us now examine the question that follows. “They criticize,” he says, “the rites of sacrifices, victims, incense, and the other practices by which temple worship was conducted, although,” he says, “this same worship originated with them—or with the God whom they worship—in ancient times, when God is represented as having needed first fruits.”

17. The answer to this is that, since the question is recognized as having been proposed from that passage in our Scriptures where it is written that Cain offered God fruit from the earth, while Abel offered a gift from the firstborn of his sheep (Genesis 4:3–4), we should understand from this rather how ancient sacrifice is—a practice that truthful and sacred Scriptures teach ought to be offered to the one true God alone. This is not because God needs it, since those same Scriptures state most plainly: “I said to the Lord, ‘You are my God, for you have no need of my goods’” (Psalm 15:2); rather, in accepting, rejecting, or receiving these things, God acts solely for the benefit of human beings. It benefits us to worship God, not God himself. Therefore, when he inspires and teaches us how he is to be worshiped, he does so not from any need of his own, but for our greatest benefit.

All such sacrifices are symbolic, as are the likenesses of certain things by which we ought to be admonished to investigate, learn, or remember the realities of which they are likenesses. To discuss this matter as much as is sufficient would require not a brief speech, which is what we have proposed to offer in this response—especially since we have already said much about it in other small works of ours.

[Note: [Col. 0377] In book 22 of *Against Faustus*.]

Those who before us expounded the utterances of God have also spoken at length of the likenesses in the sacrifices of the Old Testament, as shadows and figures of things to come.

18. Certainly, this must not be passed over even in this brief treatment: if the false gods—that is, demons, who are transgressing angels—did not know that temple, priesthood, sacrifice, and everything else belonging to these things were owed to the one true God, they would never have demanded such things from their worshipers, whom they deceive. When these things are offered to God according to his inspiration and teaching, it is true religion; when they are offered to demons according to their impious pride, it is harmful superstition.

Therefore, those who know the Christian Scriptures of both Testaments do not condemn pagan sacrilegious rites because they build temples, establish priesthoods, and offer sacrifices, but because they offer these things to idols and demons. Who could doubt that idols lack every sense? Yet when they are placed in seats of honor and elevated prominence, so that they may be attended by those who pray and sacrifice, they affect weak minds through the very likeness of living limbs and senses. Though they are senseless and lifeless, they seem to live and breathe, especially when the veneration of the multitude is added—the great worship that is lavished upon them.

19. The divine Scripture heals these diseased and pestilential affections. It impresses upon us a matter that is well known, yet does so as a wholesome remedy of admonition, saying: “They have eyes and do not see; they have ears and do not hear” (Psalm 113:5), and other statements of the same kind.

The more plainly and popularly true these words are, the more wholesome shame they instill in those who, while offering fearful divine worship to such images and revering and adoring them as resembling living beings, gaze upon them and address prayers to them as though they were present, sacrifice victims to them, and fulfill vows to them. They are affected in such a way that they scarcely dare to regard these objects as devoid of sensation.

[Col. 0378] But lest such people think that our Books intend to say only that this kind of emotion arises in the human heart from idols, it is written most plainly: “For all the gods of the nations are demons” (Psalm 95:5). Hence the apostolic teaching not only says what is read in John: “Brothers, beware of idols” (1 John 5:21), but also what is found in Paul: “What then? Do I say that something sacrificed to idols is anything, or that an idol is anything? But the things that the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God; and I do not want you to become partners with demons” (1 Corinthians 10:19–20).

From this it can be sufficiently understood that true religion condemns in the superstitions of the Gentiles not sacrifice itself—for the ancient saints did sacrifice to God—but sacrifice offered to false gods and impious demons. For just as truth urges human beings to become companions of the holy Angels, so impiety leads them into fellowship with demons, for which eternal fire is prepared, just as the eternal kingdom is prepared for fellowship with the holy.

20. Nor do the impious excuse their sacrilegious rites and images by elegantly interpreting what each thing signifies. For all that interpretation refers to the creature, not to the Creator, to whom alone is owed that religious service which in Greek is called by the single name *λατρεία* (*latreia*, worship or service).

We do not say that the earth, seas, sky, sun, moon, stars, and certain heavenly powers not immediately evident are demons. But since every creature is partly bodily and partly incorporeal—the latter of which we also call spiritual—it is clear that what is done by us piously and religiously proceeds from the will of the mind, which is a spiritual creature and must be preferred to every bodily creature. From this it follows that sacrifice must not be offered to a bodily creature.

What remains is the spiritual creature, which is either pious or impious: pious in human beings and just Angels who rightly serve God; impious in wicked human beings and angels, whom we also call demons. Accordingly, sacrifice must not be offered even to a spiritual creature, however just. For the more pious and subject to God it is, the less it considers itself worthy of such an honor, knowing that it is owed to God alone.

How much more pernicious, then, is it to sacrifice to demons—that is, to an iniquitous spiritual creature which, dwelling in this lower and shadowy heaven as though in its aerial prison, has been destined for everlasting punishment! Therefore, even when human beings claim that they sacrifice to higher heavenly powers that are not demons, and think that the only difference is one of name—that they call them gods, while we call them Angels—they cannot be deceived by those powers through manifold fraud unless those powers are demons, who delight in error and, in a manner, feed upon human beings.

The holy Angels do not approve any sacrifice except that which, according to the teaching of true wisdom and true religion, is offered to the one true God, whom they serve in holy fellowship. Accordingly, just as the impious pride of human beings or demons either commands or desires that these divine honors be offered to them, so the pious humility of human beings or holy Angels has refused honors offered to them and has shown to whom those honors are owed. Our sacred Scriptures provide unmistakable examples of this.

[Col. 0379] 21. The sacrifices distributed in the divine utterances according to the suitability of the times—some being offered before the manifestation of the New Testament, which is administered through the true and unique priestly victim, namely, through the outpoured blood of Christ, and another being offered now, appropriate to this manifestation, since we are now called Christians by a declared name—are demonstrated not only by the Gospel writings but also by the prophetic Scriptures.

A change not of God, nor of religion itself, but of sacrifices and sacraments, would now seem to have been proclaimed shamelessly unless it had first been foretold. Just as one and the same person, if he offers one thing to God in the morning and another in the evening according to the suitability of the times of day, does not thereby change God or religion—just as he does not change salvation when he greets someone in one way in the morning and another way in the evening—so throughout the whole course of the ages, when one thing was offered by the ancient saints and another is offered by those who live now, sacred mysteries appropriate to the times are celebrated not by human presumption but by divine authority. God and religion are not changed.

## FOURTH QUESTION  
### On the Saying: “With the Measure You Use, It Will Be Measured Back to You” (Matthew 7:2)

22. Let us next examine what he proposed concerning the measure of sin and punishment, thus slandering the Gospel: “Christ,” he says, “threatens eternal punishments to those who do not believe in him” (John 3:18); and elsewhere he says: “With the measure you use, it will be measured back to you.” “This,” he says, “is sufficiently ridiculous and contradictory. For if he is going to return punishment according to measure, and every measure is bounded by time, what do threats of infinite punishment mean?”

23. It is difficult to believe that this question was raised and proposed by any philosopher, since he says, “Every measure is bounded by time,” as though measure ordinarily belonged only to time, as in the measure of hours, days, and years, or as when we say that a short syllable has one unit of time in comparison with a long syllable.

I think, however, that bushels and gallons, urns and amphorae are not measures of time. How, then, is every measure bounded by time? Do they not themselves say that this sun is eternal, while nevertheless daring to investigate and report its size in geometrical measurements?
