Whether they can do so or not, it is nevertheless clear that the sun has a measure proper to its own sphere. If they comprehend how large it is, they comprehend its measure; if they do not achieve this, they nevertheless fail to comprehend its measure. It does not therefore have no measure simply because human beings cannot know it.

Something can therefore be both eternal and have a definite measure of its own kind. I have spoken of the sun’s eternity according to their own views, so that they may be refuted by their own position and concede that something eternal can exist with a measure. Thus they should not think that the eternal punishment threatened by Christ is unbelievable merely because he also said: “With the measure you use, it will be measured back to you.”

24. If he had said, “What you measure, that will be measured [Col. 0380] for you,” even then it would not necessarily be right to refer the statement in every respect to the same thing. We can rightly say, “What you plant, that you will harvest,” although no one plants an apple but rather a tree, while harvesting usually means harvesting an apple rather than a tree. We say this according to the kind of tree, because no one plants a fig tree from which to harvest a nut.

In the same way, one could say, “What you do, you will suffer,” not meaning that if someone commits adultery, that person will suffer adultery, but that the law will do to that person what the person has done through the sin: because the person has removed from his own life the law that forbids such acts, the law itself will remove him from the life of the human community over which it rules.

Again, if he had said, “As much as you measure, so much will be measured back to you,” it still would not follow that we ought to understand the punishments as equal in every respect to the sins. Wheat and barley, for example, are not equal; yet one could say, “As much as you measure, so much will be measured back to you,” meaning, “As much wheat, so much barley.”

If the subject were pains, and it were said, “As much pain as you inflict, so much will be inflicted upon you,” the pain could be just as great even if it lasted longer—that is, even if its duration were greater, its force could be equal. Nor, if we say of two lamps, “This fire was as hot as that one,” will the statement be false merely because one of them happened to go out sooner. Thus, if something is equal in one respect but not in another, it does not follow that the measure in which it is equal is false merely because it is not equal in every respect.

25. But when he says, “With the measure you use, it will be measured back to you,” and when it is clear that the measure by which something is measured is one thing, while the thing being measured is another, it can happen that the measure with which people measured—for example, a bushel of wheat—is the measure in which thousands of bushels are measured back to them. Thus the quantity of grain would differ greatly, while the measure would remain the same.

I say nothing of the difference between the things themselves: for it can happen not only that the measure with which someone measured barley is the measure in which wheat is measured back to him, but also that the measure with which someone measured grain is the measure in which gold is measured back to him—one bushel of grain, but many bushels’ worth of gold.

Thus, although the kind and quantity differ in the things themselves without comparison, it can nevertheless be said with complete correctness: “In the measure with which he measured, it was measured back to him.”

The reason Christ said this becomes sufficiently clear from what precedes: “Do not judge,” he says, “so that you may not be judged. For with the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged.” Will they be judged with an unjust judgment if they judge with an unjust judgment? Certainly not. There is no injustice with God. Rather, it is as though he had said: “With the disposition in which you do good, you will be liberated; or, with the disposition in which you do evil, you will be punished.”

If someone used his eyes for shameful desire and were ordered to be blinded, he would rightly hear: “In the eyes with which you sinned, you have deserved punishment.” For each person uses the judgment of his mind—whether good or evil—to do good or to sin. It is therefore not unjust that a person should be judged in the very faculty by which he judges: that is, that he should suffer punishment in the judgment of his own mind when he undergoes the evils that follow upon a mind that judges wrongly.

[Col. 0381] 26. There are, moreover, other manifest torments prepared for the future, themselves drawn from the same root of evil will.

[Note: [Col. 0381] Thus fourteen manuscripts. The editions have *extracta* (“drawn out”).]

But in the mind itself, where the inclination of the will is the measure of all human actions, punishment immediately follows guilt, usually becoming greater through the more grievous blindness of the person who does not perceive it.

Therefore, after saying, “With the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged,” he added: “And with the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you.” In his own will, the good person will measure good deeds, and in that same will blessedness will be measured out to him. Likewise, in his own will, the wicked person will measure evil works, and in that same will misery will be measured out to him. For wherever a person is good—when he wills what is good—there also he is wicked when he wills what is evil. Accordingly, it is there also that he becomes either blessed or miserable: namely, in the very affection of his will, which is the measure of all actions and merits.

We measure deeds, whether rightly performed or sinful, by the qualities of wills, not by the spans of time. Otherwise, cutting down a tree would be considered a greater sin than killing a human being. The former is done over a long period and with many blows; the latter with a single blow and in a very short time. Yet if, for this grave sin committed in a short time, a person were punished by perpetual exile, it would be said that he had been treated more mildly than he deserved, even though the length of the punishment in time could in no way be compared with the brevity of the crime.

What contradiction is there, then, if the punishments are equally long, or even equally eternal, but some are milder and others harsher, so that, although their duration is equal, their severity is not equal because of the measure of the sins—not in the extension of time, but in the will of those who sin?

27. The will itself is punished, whether by punishment of the mind or of the body, so that the very will that delights in sins is chastised in punishments, and the person who judges without mercy is judged without mercy. In this sentence, the measure is the same only in this respect: that what the person did not grant is not granted to him. Thus what he himself is judged to receive will be eternal, although what he judged could not be eternal.

Accordingly, within the same measure—although the evil deeds themselves are not eternal—eternal punishments are measured out, so that, because the person wished to have eternal enjoyment of sin, he finds the severity of vengeance to be eternal.

[Note: [Col. 0381] Lov. has *perfruitionem* (“enjoyment”). Most of the other manuscripts have *perfructionem*.]

The brevity proposed for my response does not permit me to gather everything, or at least very much, that the sacred Books contain concerning sins and the punishments of sinners, and from these to extract a single unambiguous judgment—if indeed I would be capable of doing so by the strength of my mind, even if I found suitable leisure. For now, however, I think it has been shown sufficiently that the eternity of punishments is not contradicted by their being repaid according to the same measure in which the sins were committed.

## FIFTH QUESTION  
### On the Son of God According to Solomon

28. [Col. 0382] After this question, the person who introduced these matters from Porphyry added: “You will surely also deign to instruct me about this, if Solomon truly said, ‘God has no Son.’”

29. The answer is quickly given: he not only did not say this, but also said that God has a Son. For Wisdom, speaking in his book, says: “Before all the hills he begot me” (Proverbs 8:25). And what is Christ except the Wisdom of God?

Likewise, in a certain passage of Proverbs: “God,” he says, “taught me wisdom, and I have learned the knowledge of the holy ones. Who has ascended into heaven and descended? Who has gathered the winds into his bosom? Who has wrapped up the water in a garment? Who has held the ends of the earth? What is his name, or what is the name of his Son?” (Proverbs 30:4).

Of the two things I have mentioned at the end, he referred one to the Father—that is, “What is his name?”—because he had said, “God taught me wisdom”; and he clearly referred the other to the Son when he said, “Or what is the name of his Son?” This is because the other statements are more properly understood of the Son, namely: “Who has ascended into heaven and descended?” Paul recalls this in the following words: “He who descended is also the one who ascended above all the heavens” (Ephesians 4:10).

“Who has gathered the winds into his bosom?” That is, the souls of believers into what is hidden and secret, to whom it is said: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:3).

“Who has wrapped up the water in a garment?” So that it could be said: “As many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians 3:27).

“Who has held the ends of the earth?” He who said to his disciples: “You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and throughout all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (Acts 1:8).

## SIXTH QUESTION  
### On the Prophet Jonah

30. The final question proposed concerns Jonah, and it is not presented as though it came from Porphyry, but rather as a mockery by the pagans. It was stated as follows:

“What, then,” he says, “should we think about Jonah, who is said to have been in the belly of a sea monster for three days? This is ἀπίθανον (*apithanon*, implausible) and unbelievable: that a man, swallowed with his clothing, should have been in the heart of a fish. Or, if it is a figure, will you deign to explain it? And what is also meant by the gourd that grew above Jonah after he had been vomited out (Jonah 2:1 and 4:6)? What was the reason for its growing?”

I have observed that this kind of question was ridiculed by the pagans with much laughter.

31. The answer is that either none of the divine miracles should be believed, or there is no reason why this one should not be believed. We would not believe that Christ rose on the third day if Christian faith feared the laughter of the pagans.

Since our friend did not raise the question of whether we ought to believe that Lazarus was raised on the fourth day or that Christ himself rose on the third day, I am greatly surprised that he presented what happened to Jonah as unbelievable—unless perhaps he thinks it easier for a dead man to be raised from a tomb than for a living man to have been preserved in the vast belly of a beast.

To say nothing of the great size of sea monsters reported by those who have experienced them, who could fail to infer how widely that mouth gaped which, like the entrance to a cavern, led into the belly protected by those ribs that are publicly displayed and known to the people at Carthage? [Col. 0383] Unless perhaps, as he proposed, clothing was an impediment preventing Jonah from being swallowed unharmed—as though the man who had been hurled down through a sheer descent had squeezed himself through a narrow passage, and had been received by the beast’s belly before its teeth could tear him apart.

Although Scripture does not say that he was thrown into that cavern either naked or clothed, it could be understood that he entered it naked as well, if that was necessary—as though, just as an egg’s shell is removed, his clothing were stripped from him so that he might be swallowed more easily.

These people are so concerned about the prophet’s clothing as though he were said either to have crawled through a small window or to have entered a bathhouse. Even if it had been necessary for him to enter clothed, this would scarcely have been inconvenient, though it would not have been remarkable.

32. They do indeed have one reason for refusing to believe in the divine miracle: they think that the vapor of the belly, by which food decays, could not have been regulated in such a way as to preserve a human life. How much more unbelievable, then, would they have considered it if those three men thrown by an impious king into a furnace had walked unharmed in the midst of the fire?

Therefore, if these people are unwilling to believe any divine miracles, they must be refuted in another discussion. They ought not to single out one thing as unbelievable and call it into question, but should address everything that is reported as similar or even more miraculous.

And yet if what is written about Jonah were said to have been done by Apuleius of Madaura or Apollonius of Tyana—men whose many marvels are proclaimed without any trustworthy authority—then, although demons also perform certain deeds resembling those of the holy Angels, not in truth but in appearance, not in wisdom but in sheer deception, still, if such a thing were related about those men whom they honorably call magicians or philosophers, laughter would no longer burst from their lips, but arrogance.

Let them laugh at our Scriptures; let them laugh as much as they can, while day by day they see themselves becoming rarer and fewer, either by dying or by believing. Meanwhile, everything is being fulfilled that those who long ago laughed at these people foretold: that they would fight vainly against the truth, bark in empty defiance, and gradually fail. They left these predictions not only for us, their descendants, to read, but promised that we would experience them.

33. It is certainly neither absurd nor inappropriate to ask what these events signify, so that, once this has been explained, they may be believed to have been written not merely because they happened, but also because they signify something.

Let the person who wishes to investigate why this happened first have no doubt that the prophet Jonah was in the belly of a huge sea monster for three days. It did not happen without reason, but it did happen.

If events that were merely spoken figuratively and were not enacted move people to faith, how much more ought those things to move them that were not merely spoken figuratively but also enacted? For just as human custom speaks through words, divine power also speaks through deeds. And just as new or less familiar words, sprinkled moderately and appropriately into human speech, add brilliance to it, so in marvelous deeds that signify something fittingly, divine eloquence becomes in a certain way more luminous.

34. Why, then, are we [Col. 0384] asked what was prefigured when the monster devoured the prophet and restored him alive on the third day, when Christ himself explains this? He says:

“An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. For just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea monster for three days and three nights, so the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights” (Matthew 12:39–40).

How the three-day period of the Lord Christ’s death is to be explained—when, by taking the part for the whole, the first and last days are counted so that the three days, together with their nights, are complete—would take too long to discuss, and has already been said very often in other sermons.

Thus, just as Jonah went from the ship into the belly of the sea monster, so Christ went from the wood of the cross into the tomb or into the depths of death. And just as Jonah did so for those who were in danger from the storm, so Christ did so for those who are tossed about in this world. And just as Jonah was first commanded to preach to the people of Nineveh, but Jonah’s preaching did not reach them until after the sea monster vomited him out, so prophecy was first directed toward the Gentiles, but did not reach the Gentiles until after Christ’s resurrection.

35. Now, in setting up a shelter for himself and sitting opposite the city of Nineveh, awaiting what would happen to it, the Prophet was taking on the role of another signification. For he prefigured the carnal people of Israel. This people was saddened over the salvation of the Ninevites—that is, over the redemption and liberation of the Gentiles. Hence Christ came to call not the righteous, but sinners to repentance (Luke 5:32). The shelter of the gourd over his head therefore represented the promises of the Old Testament, or the gifts themselves already bestowed, in which there was indeed, as the Apostle says, “a shadow of things to come” (Colossians 2:17), providing, as it were, a protection from the heat of temporal evils in the land of promise. But the morning worm, by whose gnawing the gourd withered, is again Christ himself. From his mouth, when the Gospel was proclaimed abroad, all those things that had previously flourished among the Israelites temporally, or under a shadowy signification, withered away and were abolished. And now that people, having lost the Jerusalem kingdom, priesthood, and sacrifice—which was all a shadow of what was to come—is scorched in captivity and dispersion by the great heat of tribulation, like Jonah, who, as it is written, suffered from the sun’s heat (Jonah 4:8), and grieves bitterly. Yet the salvation of the Gentiles and of those who repent is preferred to its grief and to the shadow it loved.

[Note: [Col. 0384] Three Vatican manuscripts and two others of ours read *poenitentiaque* (“and of those who repent”).]

36. Let the pagans still laugh, and let them mock Christ as a worm, and this interpretation of the prophetic mystery with even more arrogant chatter—yet meanwhile he gradually and little by little consumes them as well. For Isaiah prophesies concerning all such people, through whom God says to us: “Hear me, you who know judgment, my people, in whose heart is my law: do not fear the reproaches of men, and do not be overcome by their slander, nor consider it important that they despise you. For as a garment, so they shall be consumed in time, and as wool, so they shall be devoured by the moth; but my righteousness remains forever” (Isaiah 51:7–8).

[Col. 0385]

Let us therefore recognize the morning worm, since in that psalm whose title is written “For the morning reception,” he himself deigned to call himself by this name: “I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people.” This reproach belongs to those reproaches that through Isaiah we are commanded not to fear, when he says: “Do not fear the reproaches of men.” By this worm, as by a moth, those are devoured who, under his evangelical tooth, marvel as their small number diminishes day by day. Let us recognize him, and for the sake of divine salvation endure human reproaches.

He is a worm because of the lowliness of the flesh; perhaps also because of his birth from a virgin. For this creature is generally born from flesh, or from some earthly substance, without any sexual union. He is “morning” because he rose at dawn. That gourd could certainly have withered without any little worm. Finally, if God needed a worm for this purpose, why was “morning” added, unless that worm was to be recognized who sings “for the morning reception”: “But I am a worm and not a man”?

37. What could be clearer in this prophecy now that the event itself has been accomplished? [Note: [Col. 0385] All manuscripts read *lucidius?* (“clearer?”). “For surely, if he was mocked” does not fit the sense. Perhaps the reading should be *Numquid enim* (“For is he perhaps…?”).] If this worm was mocked when he hung upon the cross, as it is written in the same psalm: “They spoke with their lips and shook their head. He hoped in God; let him deliver him. Let him save him, since he desires him,” when the things foretold there were fulfilled: “They pierced my hands and feet; they counted all my bones. They themselves looked upon me and saw me; they divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast lots.” What was prophesied in such manifest terms in the ancient book is recounted as having occurred in the new Gospel with equal clarity. But if, in this humiliation, as I had begun to say, this worm was mocked, is he still to be mocked when we see fulfilled what follows in the psalm itself: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship before him; for the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he shall rule the nations” (Psalm 21:7–29)?

Thus the Ninevites remembered, and they turned to the Lord. Israel grieved over this salvation of the repentant Gentiles, prefigured so long beforehand in Jonah, just as it now grieves, stripped of its shadow and wounded by the heat. Certainly, anyone may explain the other things hidden under mysteries in the Prophet Jonah in whatever manner he wishes, provided that everything is according to the rule of faith. But that he was in the belly of the sea-monster for three days cannot rightly be understood in any other way than as we have shown it to have been revealed by the heavenly Teacher himself in the Gospel.

38. We have explained the matters proposed as best we could. But let the one who proposed them already be a Christian, lest, while he waits to finish his questions about the holy Books, he should finish this life first, before passing from death to life. It is understandable that, before being instructed in the Christian mysteries, he should inquire about the resurrection of the dead. Perhaps it is also permissible that he should have asked why Christ came so late, or about a few other great questions to which the rest are subordinate.

But if someone intends to finish all questions of this sort before becoming a Christian—such as “With what measure you measure, it shall be measured to you,” or this question about Jonah—he thinks very little either about the human condition or about his own age. For there are innumerable questions that must not be finished before faith, lest life end without faith. Once faith has been embraced, however, they should be sought with the greatest zeal for the pious delight of faithful minds; whatever comes to light in them should be shared without the arrogance of boasting, while whatever remains hidden should be endured without peril to salvation.

[Note: [Col. 0386] Lov.: *perperam* (“wrongly”); but the manuscripts more correctly read *perparum* (“too little”).]

[Note: [Col. 0386] The manuscripts read *typo* for *typho*, with the letter *h* omitted, as is commonly written; it is enough to note this once.]

## EPISTLE 103

[Note: [Col. 0386] We searched for Epistles 103 and 104 in vain in the Gallic manuscripts. They have been corrected from the Vatican exemplar, from which they had previously been published.]

[Note: Formerly 253, second series; the letter that was 103 is now 212. Written before the end of March 409.]

Augustine had replied in Epistle 97 to Nectarius, who was requesting pardon for his fellow citizens, that Christian benevolence did not permit the notorious crime of the people of Calama to be dismissed altogether with impunity. Nectarius now writes to him again, flattering him and humbly urging that they be spared without exception.

To the lord brother AUGUSTINE, rightly and deservedly to be received and honored in every way, NECTARIUS sends greetings in the Lord.

### 1.

When I received the letter of Your Eminence, in which you destroyed the worship of idols and the ceremonies of the temples, I seemed to hear the voice of a philosopher—not that one whom they recall as sitting in the dark corners of the earth in the Lyceum of the Academy, sunk in some profound meditation, with his knees drawn up to his forehead and his head enclosed between them, so that, being some impoverished slanderer of doctrine, he might attack the distinguished discoveries of others and, while defending nothing of his own, accuse what had been nobly asserted—but plainly, awakened by your speech, Marcus Tullius, the consular, stood before my eyes. Having preserved the lives of countless citizens, he would bring back, crowned with the laurels of victory, the standards of the law courts to the astonished schools of Greece; and panting, he would turn around that trumpet of melodious voice and tongue which he had inflated with the breath of righteous indignation against criminals and traitors to the state, and would throw back that very toga, its pages of folds unfolded, imitating the appearance of a cloak.

### 2.

Therefore, when you compelled us to the worship and religion of the most exalted God, I listened willingly; when you urged us to contemplate the heavenly homeland, I received it gratefully. For you did not seem to be speaking to me of that city bounded by some circuit of walls, nor of that city which the treatises of philosophers call worldly and profess to be common to all; rather, you spoke of the city inhabited and occupied by the great God and by souls that have deserved well of him, which all laws pursue by different roads and paths, which we cannot express in speech, though perhaps we might discover it by thought.

Although this city is to be sought and loved above all, I do not think that the earthly city in which we were born and begotten should be abandoned: the city that first gave us the use of this light, that nourished us, that raised us, and—to speak specifically to the matter at hand—of which, learned men assert, dwellings are prepared in heaven after the death of the body for men who have deserved well of their native cities, so that a kind of promotion to the heavenly realm may be granted to those who have deserved well of their birthplace; and that those dwell with God more closely who are shown to have given their homeland salvation either by their counsels or by their deeds.

As for what you jokingly deigned to say, that our city blazes not with arms but with flames and conflagrations, and produces thorns rather than flowers: this is not the greatest reproach, since we know that flowers are often produced from thorns. For who doubts that roses grow from thorns, or that crops themselves are enclosed by a barrier of ears of grain, so that harsh things are often mingled with pleasant ones?

### 3.

[Col. 0387]

The final point in Your Eminence’s letter was that the Church was not seeking the punishment of their heads or blood, but that they be stripped of the things they fear most. Unless my judgment deceives me, I think that to be stripped of one’s resources is worse than to be killed. For, as you know is frequently said in letters, death removes the perception of all evils, whereas a life of poverty produces eternal misery; it is worse to live badly than to end in a bad death.

Your own work also indicates this, since you support the poor, relieve the sick by treatment, and apply medicine to afflicted bodies. Finally, you do everything possible so that those afflicted may not feel the prolonged duration of their calamity. As for the degree of their sins, it makes no difference what kind of sin appears to be involved when pardon is requested. For if repentance both obtains pardon and cleanses the offense, then surely the one who asks and embraces your feet is repentant; and if, as certain philosophers hold, all sins are equal, pardon should be common to all.

Someone spoke too insolently: he sinned. He hurled insults or accusations: he likewise sinned. Someone seized another’s property: this is counted among offenses. He violated profane or sacred places: he is not to be excluded from pardon. Finally, there would be no place for forgiveness if sins did not come first.

### 4.

Now, since I have replied not as much as I ought, but as much as I could—whether more or less, as the saying goes—I beg and implore you: would that I could be present, so that you might see my tears as well, and so that you might think again and again about who you are, what you profess, and what you are doing. Consider what kind of city it is from which men led away to punishment are dragged; what is the lamentation of mothers, wives, children, and parents; with what shame those who have been released but tortured can return to their homeland; and what pains or groans are renewed by the sight of wounds and scars.

After considering all these things, consider God first, and think of the reputation of men, of goodness, of friendly and familial affection; seek praise by forgiving rather than by exacting vengeance. Let this be said concerning those whom the genuine guilt of their confession binds. To them, as I never cease praising, you have granted pardon in accordance with the contemplation of the law.

But it is scarcely possible to explain how great a cruelty it is to attack the innocent and summon to a capital trial those who are known to be distinct from the crime. If they should happen to be acquitted, consider, I beg you, how much envy will be removed from their accusers when, defeated, they voluntarily release the accused and leave them innocent.

May the supreme God protect you and preserve you, the support and ornament of his law.

## EPISTLE 104

[Note: [Col. 0388] Formerly 254; the letter that was 104 is now 191. Written perhaps in 409, after the sixth day before the Kalends of March.]

Augustine responds point by point to the preceding letter, refuting among other things the claim Nectarius had introduced from the Stoics, that all sins are equal.

[Col. 0388]

To the eminent, deservedly honorable, and worthy-to-be-received brother NECTARIUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

### CHAPTER ONE

#### 1.

I read the letter of Your Goodness, in which you replied to me long after I had sent my letter to be delivered to you. I had written my reply while he was still with us and before my holy brother and fellow bishop Possidius had sailed away. I received the letter you deigned to give him on my account on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, almost eight months after I had written.

Why my letter reached you so late, or yours reached me so late, I entirely do not know—unless perhaps it has now pleased Your Prudence to reply, whereas earlier you had scorned to do so. If that is so, I wonder why. Or have you heard something that remains unknown to us—that my brother Possidius obtained harsher punishment against your fellow citizens (whom, with your permission, I will say that he loves much more beneficially than you do)? For your letter shows that you fear this, when you urge me to place before my eyes what kind of city it is from which men led away to punishment are dragged; what is the lamentation of mothers, wives, children, and parents; with what shame those who have been released but tortured can return to their homeland; and what pains or groans are renewed by the sight of wounds and scars.

Far be it from us to press that such things be inflicted on any of our enemies, whether through us or through anyone else. But, as I said, if rumor has brought any such report to you, explain it more openly, so that we may know either what to do to prevent these things or what we ought to say in reply to those who believe them.

#### 2.

Look instead at my letter, which you were reluctant to answer. For there I sufficiently expressed our purpose. But, as I think, having forgotten what I wrote in reply to you, you reported something altogether different and unlike it. As though recalling what I had put in my letter, you inserted into yours something I had not put there at all.

You say that the final point in my letter was that the Church was not seeking the punishment of their heads or blood, but that they be stripped of the things they fear most. Then, showing how serious this evil is, you add and connect the claim that, unless your judgment deceives you, you think it worse to be stripped of one’s resources than to be killed. To explain more clearly what resources you mean, you continue and add that you know it is frequently said in letters that death removes the perception of all evils, whereas a life of poverty produces eternal misery. You concluded that it is worse to live amid evils than to end in an evil death.

#### 3.

I do not recall ever reading, either in our own writings—which I confess I began studying later than I would have wished—or in yours, which I learned from early childhood, that a life of poverty produces eternal misery. For poverty itself is never a sin, and some degree of restriction and restraint is a curb upon sins. Therefore, there is no need to fear that, after this brief life, the fact that someone lived here in poverty could contribute to the eternal misery of his soul. And in this very life that we live on earth, no calamity can in any way be eternal, since that same life cannot be eternal, nor even long-lasting, however far it may have extended into age and old age.

What I have rather read in those writings is that the life itself that we enjoy is brief, while in it, you think—and now remind us is frequently stated in letters—that misery can be eternal. Your writings do indeed say that death is the end of all evils, but not all of them say this. It is the opinion of the Epicureans and of others who think the soul mortal.

But those whom Tullius calls, as it were, consular philosophers—because he greatly values their authority—believe that when we perform our final day, the soul is not extinguished but departs, and that according to its merits, whether good or evil, it remains either for blessedness or for misery. This agrees with the sacred Scriptures, whose learned interpreter I desire to be.

Death, then, is the end of evils—but of evils suffered by those whose life is chaste, pious, faithful, and innocent, not by those who burn with desire for temporal trifles and vanities and who, while they seem happy to themselves here, are proved miserable by the very perversity of their will and are compelled after death not only to have but also to feel greater miseries.

#### 4.

Since these things are repeatedly affirmed both in some of your writings, which you hold in higher honor, and in all of ours, good lover even of your earthly homeland, fear an extravagant life for your fellow citizens, not a life of poverty. Or, if you fear poverty, warn them instead to avoid that poverty which, although surrounded by great prosperity in earthly possessions, nevertheless, by its insatiable craving for them—to use the words of your own authors—is diminished neither by abundance nor by want.

Yet in the letter to which you replied, I did not say that your fellow citizens, the enemies of the Church, should be corrected by that poverty in which the necessities of nature are lacking and to which mercy comes to the aid—a mercy concerning which you thought it necessary to lecture us, since, as you claim, the pattern of our works shows that we support the poor, relieve the sick by treatment, and apply medicine to afflicted bodies. Although even in this respect it is more useful to be in need than to abound in everything for the satisfaction of wickedness, far be it from me to have judged that those about whom we are speaking should be reduced to this distress by such restraint.

### CHAPTER TWO

#### 5.

Review my letter—if you considered it worthy of review, or, if not of rereading when you had to answer it, at least of preserving it so that, when you commanded it to be produced, it could be brought forth whenever you wished—and attend to what I said. You will certainly find there something to which, as I think, you will admit that you did not reply.

For I now insert words from that letter of mine:

“We do not strive to feed our anger by taking vengeance for the past; rather, out of mercy, we labor to provide for the future. Wicked men have a place where, through Christians, they may be punished not only gently but also usefully and beneficially. They have the fact that they live with their bodies unharmed; they have the means by which they live; they have the means by which they live wickedly. Let the first two remain safe, so that those who repent may continue to exist; this is what we desire, and, insofar as it lies within us, we press for it with strenuous effort. But if the Lord wills to cut away the third as something rotten and harmful, he will punish with great mercy.”

If you had reviewed these words when you deigned to reply to me, you would have regarded a request to us, on behalf of those for whom you plead, to spare them not only death but also bodily tortures as more invidious than dutiful. For I said that we want what they possess to remain safe: that they live with their bodies unharmed.

You would not have feared for them a life of poverty in which they would need food distributed by others, since I also said that we want the second thing they possess to remain safe: the means by which they live.

But as for the third thing they possess—the means by which they live wickedly—this means, to say nothing else, the means by which the silver images of false gods are truly manufactured, images for the preservation, worship, or continued veneration of which by sacrilegious rites people rush even to the burning of God’s Church, while the means of supporting the most devout poor are offered for plunder to the miserable mob and blood is shed: you who are concerned for your city, why do you fear that this should be cut away, lest a thoroughly unpunished and destructive audacity be nourished and strengthened?

Explain this to us; teach us by a careful argument what the harm is. Pay close attention to what we say, lest you appear to be making an indirect accusation against us under the guise of asking for what you say to us.

#### 6.

Let your fellow citizens be honorable, of upright character, not of excessive wealth. We do not want to bring them, through this restraint, to the plow of Quintius or the hearth of Fabricius. By that poverty those leaders of the Roman republic did not become despicable to their fellow citizens; rather, on account of it they became especially dear to them and better suited to govern their homeland’s resources.

Nor do we desire or seek this: that only ten pounds of silver should remain to the wealthy people of your homeland, as in the case of Rufinus, twice consul.

[Note: [Col. 0390] Lov.: “let a little silver remain to be torn away.”]

At that time, strict censorship rightly judged even that amount worthy of being cut away as a vice. The custom of a morally discolored age persuades us to handle the excessively enervated souls of today with such excessive gentleness that what seemed just to those censors appears too severe for Christian mildness.

And you see how great the difference is between these two things: whether merely possessing so much is already a punishable fault, or whether, on account of other very serious faults, one permits someone to possess so much. What was then already a sin, we now want to be at least the punishment of sin.

Yet something can and should be done so that severity neither proceeds as far as this nor impunity, growing too secure, rejoices and runs riot; and lest an example for imitation leading to the gravest and most hidden punishments be set before the unfortunate. At least grant that those who plot to burn and devastate what is necessary for us should fear their own excessive superfluities.

Let us grant this benefit even to our enemies: while they fear losing possessions that it is not harmful to lose, they may not attempt to commit what is harmful to them. For this should not be called vengeance for sin, but protection of prudent counsel; it is not the imposition of punishment, but fortification against receiving punishment.

#### 7.

Whoever deprives an imprudent person of something while allowing him some awareness of pain, so that, accustomed to needless crimes, he may not pay the most atrocious penalties, is like someone who pulls a child’s hair lest he applaud snakes. Thus, where love is troublesome, no limb is injured; but the thing from which it deters one places safety and life in peril.

We are not beneficial when we do what is asked of us, but when we do what does not harm those who ask. In many matters we benefit by not giving, and we would do harm if we gave. Hence the proverb: “Not even a sword to a child.” But, says Tullius, “not even to an only son.” For the more we love someone, the less we ought to entrust to him those things in which one sins at great risk. And, unless I am mistaken, he was speaking about riches when he said this.

Accordingly, what is entrusted to people who use it wrongly and dangerously is often beneficially taken away. When physicians see that rottenness must be cut and burned, they often mercifully become deaf to many tears.

If, whenever we children—or even grown children—asked pardon for our offenses, we had received it from parents or teachers, who among us would have grown up fit to be tolerated? Who would have learned anything useful? These things are done providently, not cruelly.

I beg you, do not focus in this matter on anything else except how to achieve among us what your fellow citizens ask of you. Consider everything carefully. If you neglect the past, which can no longer be undone, look somewhat toward the future. Prudently attend not to what those who petition you desire, but to what is advantageous for them.

We are certainly not proved to love them faithfully if we look only to this: that, by not doing what they ask, we may be loved less by them. And where is the principle praised even in your writings—that ruler of a homeland who cares more for the people’s welfare than for their will?

### CHAPTER THREE

#### 8.

“It makes no difference,” you say, “what sort of sin it appears to be when pardon is requested.” You would say this rightly if we were dealing with punishing, not correcting, human beings.

Far be it from a Christian heart to be carried to anyone’s punishment by the lust for vengeance. Far be it that, in forgiving anyone’s sin, either the petitioner’s prayers should not come first, or forgiveness should not immediately follow. But this is so that he may not hate the person, repay evil with evil, be inflamed with the desire to harm, or wish to feed upon vengeance even when it is required by law—not so that he may fail to provide for him, fail to look ahead, or fail to restrain him from evil.

For it can happen that, by opposing someone too vehemently, a person neglects the correction of one whom he hates more intensely, and by imposing some unpleasantness makes better the one whom he loves most.

#### 9.

For repentance, as you write, does obtain pardon and cleanse the offense—but the repentance practiced in true religion, which considers God’s future judgment; not that which is either displayed or feigned for the moment before human beings, not so that the soul may be cleansed forever from sin, but so that, for the time being, a life soon to perish may be freed from present fear and trouble.

This is why, when Christians confessed and pleaded—men who had been implicated in that crime either by failing to come to the aid of the burning Church or by taking something from the most criminal plunder—we believed that the pain of their repentance was fruitful for them and judged that it was sufficient for their correction that they possessed in their hearts the faith by which they could consider what they ought to fear from divine judgment.

But what repentance can heal those who not only neglect to recognize the very source of pardon, but do not cease to mock and blaspheme it? Nevertheless, we do not retain hostility in our hearts toward such people; this is plain and open to him whose judgment, both in the present life and in the life to come, we fear, and whose aid we hope for.

But we also think that we provide something for them if people who do not fear God fear something else—not so that their advantage may be harmed, but so that their vanity may be chastened. This is so that God himself, whom they despise, may not be offended more grievously by their bolder deeds in their harmful security, and so that this same security may not be presented to others for imitation with far greater danger.

Finally, for those on whose behalf you ask us, we ask God to turn them to himself, so that, cleansing their hearts by faith, he may teach them to practice true and salutary repentance.

#### 10.

See how much more orderly and beneficially we love those whom you think we are angry with—let me say this with your permission—for whom we pray both to avoid far greater evils and to obtain far greater goods.

If you too loved them not according to the earthly custom of men but according to God’s heavenly gift, and if you had sincerely written back to me that you had gladly listened when I compelled you to the worship and religion of the most exalted God, you would not merely wish these things for them; you yourself would lead them toward them. Thus the whole business of your petition among us would have been concluded with great and sound joy.

Thus, by the true and pious love with which you love this homeland that physically gave birth to you, you would earn the heavenly homeland, which, when I urged you to contemplate it, you said you had gladly received. You would truly be concerned for your people—not toward the vanity of temporal joy or the most destructive impunity of crime, but toward the grace of everlasting happiness.

#### 11.

You have before you the thoughts and desires of my heart in this matter. But what may lie hidden in God’s plan—I confess that I am a human being and do not know. Whatever it is, it is more just, wiser, and more firmly established, with incomparable excellence, than all human minds.

For what is read in our books is true: “There are many thoughts in a man’s heart, but the counsel of the Lord remains forever” (Proverbs 19:21).

Accordingly, what time may bring, what ability or difficulty may arise for us, and finally what intention may suddenly emerge from present circumstances, whether through correction or hope; whether God is so indignant at these deeds that they will be punished more severely by the impunity they seek, or whether he may mercifully judge that they should be restrained in the manner pleasing to us; or whether, after some harsher but more salutary correction of them has preceded, he may avert and transform into joy whatever terror was being prepared, through their genuine conversion not to human mercy but to his own—he himself already knows; we do not.

Why, then, should Your Eminence and I labor here fruitlessly before the time? Let us set aside for a little while the concern whose hour has not come, and, if you please, let us do what is always urgent. No time is empty in which it is not fitting and necessary to do something by which we may please God.

To fulfill this in the present life all the way to such perfection that no sin at all exists in a human being is either impossible or perhaps exceedingly difficult. Therefore, cutting off every delay, we must flee to his grace, to whom the following words can most truly be spoken—words that a flattering poet addressed, I do not know to what nobleman, though he confessed that he had received them from the Cumaean poem as from a prophetic song:

> With you as guide, if any traces of our crime remain,  
> They shall release the earth from perpetual fear, annulled.

(Virgil, *Eclogue* 4.)

Under this guide, with all sins released and dismissed, we reach the heavenly homeland by this road. When I commended its dwelling to you as much as I could, so that you might love it, you were greatly delighted.

### CHAPTER FOUR

#### 12.

But since you said that all laws pursue it by different roads and paths, I fear that, thinking the path on which you now stand also leads there, you may be slower to hold to the path that alone leads there.

Yet, attending carefully to the word you used, I think I can disclose your meaning without presumption. You did not say that all laws attain, show, discover, enter, or possess it by different roads and paths, or anything of that kind. By saying “pursue,” a measured and carefully chosen word, you signified not attainment but the desire to attain.

Thus you neither excluded the true path nor admitted the false ones. For the path that leads there does indeed seek it, but not every path that seeks it leads there. Whoever is led there is without any doubt blessed.

We all wish to be blessed—that is, we pursue blessedness—yet not all who wish can do so; that is, not all attain what they pursue. The one who attains it, therefore, holds the road not merely by which he pursues it, but by which he also arrives, leaving others on the roads of pursuing without the end of attaining.

For there would be no error if nothing were pursued, nor if the truth that was pursued were held.

But if by “different roads” you meant roads that are not opposed to one another, as we speak of different commands that nevertheless all build a good life—some concerning chastity, others patience, others faith, others mercy, and so on—not only is that homeland pursued by such different roads and paths; it is also found.

For in the sacred Scriptures both “roads” and “the road” are read of: “roads,” as in, “I will teach the wicked your ways, and the impious shall turn to you” (Psalm 50:15); “the road,” as in, “Lead me in your way, and I shall walk in your truth” (Psalm 85:11).

These are not some roads and that one another; rather, they are all one road, concerning which the same sacred Scripture says elsewhere: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Psalm 24:10). If these words are carefully considered, they produce abundant discussion and an exceedingly pleasant understanding. If necessary, I will defer that matter to another time.

#### 13.

For now, since I think this is sufficient for the duty I have undertaken in replying to Your Eminence, because Christ said, “I am the way” (John 14:6), mercy and truth must be sought in him. Otherwise, if we seek them elsewhere, we shall go astray, holding a road that pursues but does not also lead to the destination.

For example, if we wished to follow that very path on which you mentioned that all sins are equal, would it not send us far into exile from that homeland of truth and blessedness?

For what could be said more absurdly or insanely than that someone who laughed somewhat too immoderately and someone who burned down his homeland with excessive savagery should be judged to have sinned equally?

You thought that this principle, according to the opinion of certain philosophers, should be employed—not as a different road that nevertheless leads to the heavenly dwelling, but as a thoroughly perverse road leading to the most destructive error—not according to your own judgment, but on behalf of your fellow citizens. Thus we should forgive those whose raging fires burned the Church in the same way as we would forgive them if they had attacked us with some insolent insult.

#### 14.

But see how you have established this claim. “And if,” you say, “as certain philosophers hold, all sins are equal, pardon ought to be common to all.”

Then, as though you were preparing to show that all sins are equal, you add and say: “Someone spoke too insolently; he sinned. He hurled insults or accusations; he likewise sinned.”

This is not to teach, but to present what is perversely believed without any supporting evidence. To your statement “he likewise sinned,” the answer is quickly given: “He did not sin likewise.”

Perhaps you demand that I prove this. But what have you proved by saying that he sinned likewise? Or should we listen to what you add? “Someone seized another’s property; this is counted among offenses.”

Here you yourself were also embarrassed. You were ashamed to say that he sinned equally; instead you said, “it is counted among offenses.” But the question is not whether this too is counted among offenses; the question is whether it is joined to that offense as its equal.

Or, if things are equal for the reason that both are offenses, then mice and elephants will be equal because both are animals; flies and eagles because both are flying creatures.

#### 15.

You proceed still further and conjecture: “He violated profane or sacred places; he is not to be excluded from pardon.”

Here, certainly, from the violation of sacred places you came to the crime committed by your fellow citizens. Yet you did not yourself make it equal to insolent speech; you merely requested pardon for them—a pardon rightly requested from Christians because of abundant mercy, not because of an equality among sins.

I had already cited from our Scriptures: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Psalm 24:10). They will obtain mercy if they do not hate truth. This mercy is not owed to those who have sinned equally, as though they had merely spoken too insolently; rather, according to Christian law, it is rightly owed to those who repent of an immense and impious crime.

But you, a man deservedly worthy of praise, please do not teach your *Paradoxus* to embrace these Stoic paradoxes. We wish that he may grow up in true piety and happiness, for what could a noble young man think more wrongly, or more dangerously for you yourself, than that, if someone hurled an insult at any stranger, he should consider it equal not merely to parricide but even to an insult against his father?

16. Accordingly, you act among us on behalf of your fellow citizens by pressing upon us the mercy of Christians, not the harshness of the Stoics—a cause which, undertaken by you, not only gives no support but greatly works against you. For the Stoics place mercy itself, without which—if we do not possess it—we could be moved by none of your petitions or by any entreaties of theirs, among vices; they banish it completely from the mind of the wise person, whom they want to be wholly iron and unyielding. It would therefore have occurred to you more aptly to say something from your Cicero, who, praising Caesar, says: “No one of your virtues is more admirable or more welcome than mercy” (*Oration for Quintus Ligarius*). How much more ought it to prevail in the churches, since they follow him who said, “I am the way” (John 14:6), and read, “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.”

Do not, then, fear that we are plotting destruction against the innocent, since we do not even wish the guilty to reach a punishment proportionate to their offense—prevented as we are by that mercy which we love in Christ together with truth. But whoever spares and fosters vices lest he distress the will of sinners is no more merciful than one who refuses to take a knife away from a child lest he hear the child crying, and does not fear that he may grieve over the child’s being wounded or killed. Therefore reserve for a suitable time what you are doing among us on behalf of these men, in whose affection—pardon me—you not only fall far short of surpassing us, but do not yet even follow us. Rather, write back what moves you about this way which we hold, and in which we urge you to walk with us toward the heavenly homeland, which we know and rejoice delights you.

17. As for the citizens of your earthly homeland, although you said that not all but some of them were innocent, you nevertheless did not defend what you ought to have noticed after rereading my letter. When I said that we had felt not flowers but thorns, in reply to what you had written—that you wished to leave your homeland flourishing—you thought I was joking. Surely such a thing is enjoyable amid such great evils! It is exactly so: the ruins of the burned church are still smoking, and we are joking in that matter!

For my part, although no innocent persons there came to mind except those who had either been absent, or suffered those evils, or had possessed no power or authority to prevent them, nevertheless in my reply I distinguished the more guilty from the less guilty. I assigned one cause to those who feared offending powerful enemies of the Church, another to those who wished this to be done; another to those who did it; and another to those who instigated it. I deliberately said nothing about the instigators, since perhaps this cannot be discovered without bodily tortures, which are contrary to our purpose.

But all your Stoics grant that all are equally guilty, since they hold that all sins are equal. Joining their harshness—which condemns mercy—to this opinion, they in no way judge that all should be forgiven equally; rather, they hold that all should be punished equally. Remove those men, therefore, as far as you possibly can from the defense of this case, and prefer to hope that we may act as Christians, so that, as we desire, we may win in Christ those whom we spare, lest by a ruinous laxity we spare them to their own destruction. May the merciful and truthful God deign to bestow true happiness.

## EPISTLE 105

[Note: [Col. 0396] Compared with a, bg, bl, c, cc, ff, g, gv, n, r, s, sb, t, vc, four copies designated v, and with Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0396] Formerly 166; formerly numbered 105, now 194. It appears to have been written at the beginning of the year 409.]

He exhorts the Donatists to unity and shows that the laws enacted against them by the Catholic emperors were just and necessary. He proves that the holiness of baptism depends on the grace of the divine gift, not on the merits of the human minister. He then shows that the Catholic Church is recognized in the sacred Scriptures, and finally that the wicked found within it ought to be tolerated.

[Col. 0396]

**AUGUSTINE, Catholic bishop, to the Donatists.**

### CHAPTER I

1. The charity of Christ, by which we wish to win every person, insofar as our will is concerned, does not permit us to remain silent. If you hate us because we preach Catholic peace to you, we serve the Lord who says, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:9); and it is written in the Psalm: “With those who hated peace I was peaceable; when I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause” (Psalm 119:7).

For this reason certain presbyters of your party sent us a message, saying: “Withdraw from our congregations, if you do not want us to kill you.” How much more justly should we say to them: “Rather, do not withdraw, but come peacefully to congregations that are not ours but his, to whom we all belong. Or, if you do not want this and remain hostile, withdraw yourselves instead from the congregations for which Christ shed his blood. You wish to make them yours so that they may not be Christ’s, although you attempt to possess them under his name—just as if a slave stole sheep from his master’s flock and stamped his master’s mark upon all that were born from them, so that his theft could not be recognized.”

For this is what your ancestors did: they separated from Christ’s Church peoples who possessed Christ’s baptism, and they baptized with Christ’s baptism everyone who joined them.

[Note: [Col. 0396] Lov. has “a people possessing baptism.” Other manuscripts have “peoples possessing baptism.”]

[Note: [Col. 0396] The editions have “they rebaptized them.” The manuscripts more correctly read, “they baptized them.”]

But the Lord punishes both the fathers and the children if they do not correct themselves, and he recalls the sheep from their error to the flock; nor does he destroy his own mark in them. [The preceding corrupted reading *fieres* is contextually corrected as “thieves”: “the Lord punishes thieves if they do not correct themselves.”]

2. You call us traditors—a charge which neither your ancestors were able to prove against ours, nor will you ever be able to prove against us. What do you want us to do for you, when, whenever we tell you to listen patiently to both our case and yours, you know only how to rage and grow arrogant?

We would certainly show you that it was rather those who condemned Caecilian and his associates on the supposed charge of betrayal who were the traditors. And you say, “Withdraw from our congregations”—congregations whom you teach to believe you and not Christ. For you tell them that, because of traditors whom you do not prove to exist, the Church of Christ remained only in Africa, in the party of Donatus. You repeat this not from the Law, not from the Prophets, not from the Psalms, not from the Apostle, not from the Gospel, but from your own heart and from the accusations of your ancestors.

But Christ says that repentance and the forgiveness of sins are to be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem (Luke 24:47). You do not share in that Church made manifest from Christ’s mouth, and, dragging others into your destruction, you do not wish them to be liberated.

### CHAPTER II

3. But if we displease you because you are compelled to unity by the commands of the emperors, you yourselves caused this. Wherever we wished to preach the truth, so that everyone might hear it freely and choose it willingly, you never permitted us to do so because of your violence and threats.

Do not hiss and disturb your souls. If possible, consider patiently what we say, and recall the deeds of your Circumcellions and of the clerics who were always their leaders; then you will see what cause has provoked this situation for you. Thus you complain unjustly, since you yourselves compelled all these things to be ordered against you.

To avoid recounting matters long past and many in number, at least consider your recent deeds. Marcus, a presbyter of Casphalianum, became a Catholic voluntarily, compelled by no one. Why did your people persecute him and nearly kill him, unless the hand of God, acting through men who arrived, had restrained their violence?

Victorianus of Victorianum transferred himself to the Catholic Church without compulsion. Why was he dragged from his house, beaten, rolled about in water, clothed in a *buda*?

[Note: [Col. 0397] Bad., Am., Er., and four manuscripts have *bruda*.]

Why was he kept captive for I do not know how many days, and perhaps would not have been restored to his proper freedom unless Proculeianus had already seen that a summons was nearly impending against him on that very account?

Marcianus of Urga chose Catholic unity of his own will. Why did your clerics, when he himself had fled, beat his subdeacon almost to death and bury him beneath stones? Their houses were overturned in punishment for their crime.

4. What more can we say? Just now you sent a herald to shout at Siniti: “Whoever communicates with Maximinus, let his house be burned!”

[Note: [Col. 0397] Three Vatican manuscripts, together with two others, have *Maximianus*. Bad., Am., and Er. have *Maximinianus*. But Lov. and the majority of manuscripts more correctly have *Maximinus*, as it is written in Epistle 23 addressed to the same man and in Book 22, chapter 8, of *The City of God*.]

Before he himself had been converted to the Catholic Church, and while he had not yet returned from overseas, why else had we sent a presbyter to Siniti except that he might visit our people without troubling anyone and, while staying in a house under his own jurisdiction, preach Catholic peace to those who desired it? You drove him from there with grave insult.

What else were we doing when Possidius, one of our number and bishop of Calama, was going to the estate of Figulinum?

[Note: [Col. 0397] Lov. reads *Fugilinensem*. Bad., Am., Er., and nine manuscripts have *Figulinensem*.]

It was simply that our people, although few who were there, might be visited and that those who wished might be converted to Christ’s unity after hearing the word of God.

They lay in wait for him as robbers while he was traveling along his road. Because he did not fall into their ambush, they attacked him with open violence at the estate of Livetum and nearly burned him alive together with the house into which he had fled.

[Note: [Col. 0397] Seven manuscripts have “at the estate of Olivetum.”]

The tenants of that estate, fearing for their own safety, extinguished for the third time the flames which had been set beneath it. Yet when Crispinus was convicted of heresy before the proconsular court for this deed, he was not required to pay ten pounds of gold, through the intercession of that same bishop Possidius.

Ungrateful for such kindness and gentleness, he dared to appeal to the Catholic emperors. Thus he provoked against you, much more offensively and violently, this wrath of God about which you complain.

5. You see that you rise up violently against the peace of Christ, and that you suffer not for Christ himself but for your own iniquities. What madness is this—that when you live wickedly, you imitate the deeds of robbers, and when you are justly punished, you seek the glory of martyrs?

If, then, by your private daring you so violently compel people either to enter into error or to remain in error, how much more ought we, through the most orderly authorities whom God, according to his prophecy, has subjected to Christ, to resist your fury, so that miserable souls, freed from your domination, may be rescued from an ancient falsehood and become accustomed to the most open truth?

For as to what you unwillingly say—that we compel people—many even wish to be compelled, as they confess to us both before and afterward, so that in this way at least they may escape your oppression.

6. Yet what is better: to produce the true commands of the emperors in support of unity, or false indulgences in support of perversity? You did the latter, and by your lie you suddenly filled all Africa.

By this act you showed nothing other than that the party of Donatus, always presuming upon falsehood, is tossed and carried about by every wind, as it is written: “He who trusts in lies feeds the winds” (Proverbs 10:4).

Just as this indulgence was genuine, so too are the crimes of Caecilian and the betrayal of Felix of Aptunga, by whom he was ordained, along with everything else which you customarily say against Catholics in order to separate unhappy people from the peace of Christ’s Church and to separate yourselves from it unhappily.

We do not presume upon the power of any human being—although it is certainly much more honorable to presume upon emperors than upon Circumcellions, upon laws than upon seditions. But we remember that it is written: “Cursed is everyone who places his hope in a human being” (Jeremiah 17:5).

If you wish to know, then, upon whom we presume, consider the one of whom the prophet foretold, saying: “All the kings of the earth shall adore him, and all nations shall serve him” (Psalm 72:11). Therefore we use the authority of the Church, which the Lord both promised and gave to it.

7. If the emperors were in error—which God forbid—and issued laws for their error against the truth, by which the righteous would be tested and crowned, they should not do what the emperors commanded, because God would forbid it. Thus Nebuchadnezzar ordered a golden statue to be worshiped; those who refused to do so pleased God, who prohibited such acts.

But when emperors hold the truth, they command on behalf of the truth and against error. Whoever despises this acquires judgment against himself. He both pays penalties among human beings and, before God, “will not have a brow”—

[Note: [Col. 0398] Lov. reads “will not have a lot.” The older editions have “will not have a brow,” a reading supported by thirteen manuscripts. Augustine appears to allude to the Apostle’s words at Romans 13:5: “Therefore it is necessary to be subject, not only because of wrath but also because of conscience.”]

—because he refused to do what the truth itself commanded him through the heart of the king.

Nebuchadnezzar himself, later moved and changed by the miracle of the three youths’ deliverance, issued an edict in favor of the truth and against error: whoever blasphemed the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego was to be put to death, and his house destroyed (Daniel 3:96).

And you do not want Christian emperors to issue something of this kind against you, when they know that, in those whom you rebaptize, Christ is exsufflated (*exsufflari*, ritually breathed upon in renunciation)?

If royal commands have nothing to do with proclaiming religion and prohibiting sacrilege, why do you yourselves mark the king’s edict when it commands such things? Or do you not know that these are the words of the king:

“Signs and wonders which the Most High God has done for me—it has pleased me to announce in my presence how great and powerful his kingdom is, an everlasting kingdom, and his power throughout the ages of ages” (Daniel 3:99–100)?

[Note: [Col. 0399] Lov. reads, “that the words of the king are those of Nebuchadnezzar.” Am., Bad., and Er. have, “that the words of the king are: ‘I displayed to King Nebuchadnezzar the signs.’” The manuscripts have, “that the words of the king are: ‘Signs,’ etc.”]

When you hear this, do you not respond, “Amen,” and, at this statement, mark yourselves with a loud voice during the king’s edict at the holy solemnity?

[Note: [Col. 0399] In the Gothic rite these words were said on Holy Saturday, and the response was “Amen.”]

But now, because you have no influence with the emperors, you wish to make us odious on that account. If you had any influence, how much would you do, since you do not cease even when you have none!

8. Know that your first ancestors brought Caecilian’s case before the emperor Constantine. Demand that we prove this to you; and if we do not prove it, do to us whatever you can.

But because Constantine did not dare to judge the case of a bishop, he delegated it to bishops for investigation and settlement. This was done in the city of Rome, with Melchiades, the bishop of that Church, presiding together with many of his colleagues.

When they had pronounced Caecilian innocent and condemned Donatus, the bishop of Casis Nigris who had created the schism at Carthage—

[Note: [Col. 0399] “The bishop from Casis Nigris.”]

—your people again came to the emperor and complained about the judgment of the bishops, in which they had been defeated. For how can a bad litigant praise judges by whose judgment he has been defeated?

Nevertheless, the most merciful emperor again appointed other bishops as judges at Arles, a city of Gaul. From them your people appealed to the emperor himself, until he too investigated the case and pronounced Caecilian innocent and them slanderers.

Even after being defeated so many times, they did not remain quiet. Through daily appeals they wearied the emperor concerning Felix of Aptunga, by whom Caecilian had been ordained, saying that he was a traditor and that Caecilian therefore could not be a bishop because he had been ordained by a traditor. At last Felix himself, after the case had been investigated at the emperor’s command by Aelianus, the proconsul, was proved innocent.

9. Then Constantine first issued a very severe law against the party of Donatus. His sons, following his example, issued similar orders.

After them came Julian, the apostate from Christ and his enemy. At the entreaty of your men Rogatianus and Pontius, he granted the party of Donatus freedom for its destruction.

Finally, he restored the basilicas to the heretics at the time when he restored temples to demons, thinking that the Christian name could thus perish from the earth: he envied the unity of the Church from which he had fallen and allowed sacrilegious dissensions to be free.

This was the justice they had to praise, and Rogatianus and Pontius praised it when they entreated him, an apostate, saying that justice alone found a place with him.

Jovian succeeded him.

[Note: [Col. 0400] Am., Bad., Er., and three manuscripts designated v, together with sb, read *Jovinianus*. Manuscripts cc and s read *Juvinianus*.]

Because Jovian died quickly, he issued no orders concerning such matters. Then came Valentinian: read what he ordered against you. After him came Gratian and Theodosius: read, whenever you wish, what they established concerning you.

Why, then, do you wonder at the sons of Theodosius, as though they ought to have followed any other course in this matter than the judgment of Constantine, so firmly preserved through so many Christian emperors?

10. As we have said—and as we have shown you whenever you wish, if indeed you are ignorant of it—your ancestors voluntarily brought Caecilian’s case before Constantine.

Constantine has died, but Constantine’s judgment against you lives on: the judgment before whom your people brought the case; before whom they criticized the episcopal judges; to whom they appealed from the episcopal judges; whom they wearied with their complaints about Felix of Aptunga; from whom they returned so many times convicted and confounded, without withdrawing from the destructive course of their own fury and obstinacy.

They left this inheritance to their descendants, so that you so shamelessly make Christian emperors’ commands odious. If it were permitted you, you would not now appeal to Constantine the Christian against us, since he favored the truth; instead, you would summon the apostate Julian from the underworld—as if, even if such a thing occurred, it would be a great evil for anyone except you.

For what death of the soul is worse than freedom for error?

### CHAPTER III

11. But let us now remove all these matters from the way. Let us love peace, which every educated and uneducated person understands ought to be preferred to discord; let us also love and hold unity.

The emperors command this, and Christ also commands it, because when they command what is good, it is Christ alone who commands through them.

Through the Apostle he also entreats us all to say the same thing, and that there be no schisms among us, and that we not say, “I belong to Paul,” or “I to Apollos,” or “I to Cephas,” or “I to Christ”; but that altogether we belong only to Christ, because Christ was not divided, and Paul was not crucified for us—how much less Donatus? Nor were we baptized in the name of Paul (1 Corinthians 1:10–13)—how much less in the name of Donatus?

The emperors say this too, because they are Catholic Christians, not servants of idols like your Julian; not heretics, as some were who persecuted the Catholic Church, when true Christians endured most glorious sufferings not for heretical error, as you do, but for Catholic truth.

12. Consider the clearest truth spoken by God through the heart of the king, which is in God’s hand, in that very law which you say was issued against you. If you understand it, it was issued for you.

Consider what the words of the ruler contain:

“For if, among those who were first initiated, the religion of baptism is judged weak on the ground that those by whom it is received are thought to be sinners, the sacrament once given will have to be renewed as often as the administrator of the baptism conferred is found unworthy; and our faith will depend not on the judgment of our own will, nor on the grace of the divine gift, but on the merits of priests and the quality of clerics.”

[Note: [Col. 0401] These words perhaps belong to that law of Constantine, Constantius, and Valentinian mentioned in the *Theodosian Code*, Book 16, title 6, “That Holy Baptism Be Not Repeated,” law 2.]

Let your bishops hold a thousand councils; let them answer this one judgment, and we will agree with you in whatever you wish.

See how perversely and impiously it is said—what you are accustomed to say—that if a man is good, he himself sanctifies the person whom he baptizes; but if he is evil, and the person being baptized does not know it, then God sanctifies him.

If this is true, people ought to wish to be baptized by wicked men whom they do not know rather than by known good men, so that they might be sanctified more by God than by a human being. But far be such madness from us.

Why, then, do we not speak the truth and think rightly: that this grace and sacrament always belong to God, while the human being supplies only the ministry? If the minister is good, he clings to God and works with God; but if he is evil, God works through him the visible form of the sacrament, while God himself grants the invisible grace.

Let this be the understanding of us all, and let there be no schisms among us.

### CHAPTER IV

13. Agree with us, brothers. We love you, and we want for you what we want for ourselves. If you hate us more deeply because we do not permit you to wander and perish, say this to God, whom we fear when he threatens wicked shepherds and says: “You did not bring back what had gone astray, and you did not seek what had perished” (Ezekiel 34:4).

God himself does this for you through us, whether by entreating, threatening, correcting, losses, labors, his hidden admonitions or visitations, or the laws of temporal authorities.

Understand what is happening to you. God does not want you to perish, alienated in sacrilegious discord from your Catholic mother.

You have never been able to prove anything against us. Your bishops, when summoned by us, have never been willing to confer peacefully with us, as though they were fleeing from speaking with sinners.

Who could tolerate such arrogance? As though the Apostle Paul had not conferred with sinners and with people guilty of great sacrilege! Read the Acts of the Apostles and see.

As though the Lord himself had not held discussions about the Law with the Jews, by whom he was crucified, and answered them appropriately.

Finally, the devil is the first of all sinners, one who can never be converted to righteousness; yet the Lord himself did not disdain to answer even him concerning the Law, so that you may understand that these men refuse to confer with us because they know that their case is lost.

14. We do not know what people who delight in slanderous dissensions boast against themselves.

[Note: [Col. 0401] One Vatican manuscript has “We are not ignorant.” This may be better.]

In the Scriptures we learn about Christ; in the Scriptures we learn about the Church. We possess these Scriptures in common. Why, then, do we not hold Christ and the Church in common through them?

Where we recognize him of whom the Apostle says, “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed”—he does not say, “and to seeds,” as though to many, but as to one, “and to your seed,” which is Christ (Galatians 3:16)—there we recognize the Church, of which God says to Abraham, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:3).

Where we recognize Christ prophesying about himself in the Psalm, “The Lord said to me, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you,’” there we recognize the Church in what follows: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession the ends of the earth” (Psalm 2:7–8).

Where we recognize Christ in what is written, “The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken,” there we recognize the Church in what follows: “And I called the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting” (Psalm 50:1).
