Where we recognize Christ in what is written, “And he, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber, rejoiced like a giant to run his course,” there we recognize the Church in what is said shortly before: “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world. In the sun he has placed his tabernacle” (Psalm 19:5–6). This is the Church placed in the sun—that is, in a manifestation known to all—extending to the ends of the earth.

Where we recognize Christ in what is written, “They pierced my hands and feet; they counted all my bones. They themselves considered and looked upon me; they divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast lots,” there we recognize the Church in what is said shortly afterward in the same Psalm: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship in his sight; for the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he shall rule the nations” (Psalm 22:16–18, 27–28).

Where we recognize Christ in what is written, “Be exalted above the heavens, O God,” there we recognize the Church in what follows: “And your glory over all the earth” (Psalm 57:5).

Where we recognize Christ in what is written, “O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king’s son,” there we recognize the Church in what is said about him in the same Psalm: “And he shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth. Before him the Ethiopians shall fall, and his enemies shall lick the earth. The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of Arabia and Sheba shall bring presents; and all the kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations shall serve him” (Psalm 72:2, 8–11).

15. Where we recognize Christ in what is written—that a stone cut from the mountain without hands shattered all the kingdoms of the earth, namely those that presumed upon the worship of demons—there we recognize the Church in what is said: that the stone itself grew, became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth (Daniel 2:34–35).

Where we recognize Christ in what is written, “The Lord will prevail against them and destroy all the gods of the nations of the earth,” there we recognize the Church in what follows there: “And all the islands of the nations shall worship him, each from his place” (Zephaniah 2:11).

Where we recognize Christ in what is written, “God will come from the south, and the Holy One from the shadowed mountain; his power will cover the heavens,” there we recognize the Church in what follows: “And the earth is full of his praise” (Habakkuk 3:3).

Jerusalem lies toward the south, as is read in the Book of Joshua (Joshua 15:8), and from there the name of Christ spread. There too is the shadowed mountain, the Mount of Olives, from which he ascended into heaven, so that his power might cover the heavens and the Church might be filled throughout the whole earth with his praise.

Where we recognize Christ in what is written, “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he was without a voice; so he did not open his mouth,” together with the other things said there about his passion, there we recognize the Church in what is said there:

“Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not give birth, because the children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband.”

For the Lord said:

“Enlarge the place of your tent, and stretch out your curtains; do not spare. Extend your cords farther, and strengthen your stakes. Extend again and again to the right and to the left. For your seed shall inherit the nations, and you shall inhabit cities that had been deserted. Do not fear, for you shall prevail; do not be ashamed because you were detested. You shall forget your shame forever, and you shall remember no more the disgrace of your widowhood; for I am the Lord who made you, the Lord is his name. The one who redeemed you shall be called the God of Israel, the God of the whole earth” (Isaiah 53:7 and 54:1–5).

### CHAPTER V

16. We do not know what you say about the traditors, whom you have never been able to convict or point out. I do not say that your own people are rather revealed as having been detected and confessed in such a crime—for what do the burdens of others have to do with us?—except that we correct those whom we can, either by correction or by whatever discipline, in a spirit of gentleness and with careful charity.

As for those whom we cannot correct, even if necessity compels us, for the salvation of the rest, to share with them God’s sacraments, let us not share in their sins. This happens only by consenting and favoring them.

Thus, in this world—where the Catholic Church is spread among all nations, which the Lord calls his field—we tolerate them like weeds among the wheat, or in this threshing floor of unity like chaff mixed with grain, or within the nets of word and sacrament like bad fish enclosed with good fish, until the time of the harvest (Matthew 13:24–43), or of winnowing (Matthew 3:12), or of the shore (Matthew 13:47–50).

[Note: [Col. 0403] Some manuscripts have “sacraments.”]

We do this so that on their account we do not uproot the wheat; or, before the proper time, separate the bare grains from the threshing floor and, instead of cleansing them for placement in the granary, throw them out to be gathered by birds; or, by tearing apart the nets through schisms, flee into the sea of destructive freedom while supposedly avoiding the bad fish.

For this reason the Lord strengthened the tolerance of his servants through these and other parables: lest, while the good think themselves defiled by association with the wicked, they destroy the little ones or the little ones perish through human and rash dissensions.

The heavenly teacher warned that this must be avoided to such an extent that he even made the people secure concerning wicked leaders, lest the seat of saving doctrine be abandoned on their account—the seat in which even the wicked are compelled to speak good things. For what they say is not their own but God’s, who placed the doctrine of truth in the seat of unity.

Therefore that truthful one, who is himself the truth, said concerning leaders who do evil but speak God’s good things: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do; for they say and do not do” (Matthew 23:3). He certainly would not have said, “Do not do what they do,” unless the evil things they do were manifest.

17. Let us not therefore perish because of the wicked in an evil dissension. Although, if you wish, we can show that your ancestors were not accusers of the wicked but accusers of the innocent. But whoever they were, and whatever their character, let them carry their own burdens.

Here are the Scriptures we share. Here is where we know Christ. Here is where we know the Church.

If you hold Christ himself, why do you not hold the Church herself? If you believe in Christ himself, whom you read about but do not see, because of the truth of the Scriptures, why do you deny the Church, whom you both read about and see?

By saying these things to you and compelling you toward the good of peace, unity, and charity, we have become your enemies. You issue orders that you will kill us because we tell you the truth and, insofar as we can, do not permit you to perish in error.

May God avenge us upon you by killing your error within you, so that you may rejoice with us in the truth. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0404] Bad., Am., Er., and some manuscripts lack “Amen.” Other manuscripts have “Farewell” in its place.]

## EPISTLE 106

[Note: [Col. 0404] Epistles 106, 107, and 108 are not contained in the Gallican manuscripts. They have been purged of many errors on the authority of a Vatican exemplar. Nevertheless, certain rather substantial errors also had to be corrected by conjecture. We attempted this in such a way that the ancient reading might nevertheless be displayed here.]

[Note: [Col. 0404] Formerly 265; formerly numbered 106, now 186. Possibly written in 409.]

Augustine to Macrobius, a bishop of the Donatian party at Hippo, as is understood from Epistle 108, urging him not to rebaptize a certain subdeacon.

**To his beloved brother Macrobius, Augustine.**

I have heard that you intend to rebaptize one of our subdeacons. Do not do it. May you live for God in this way, please God in this way, not hold Christ’s sacraments in vain in this way, and not be separated forever from Christ’s body in this way.

Do not, I beg you, brother—for I beg you especially for your own sake—pay a little attention to what I say.

Felicianus of Musti condemned Primianus of Carthage, and in turn was himself condemned by him. Felicianus remained for a long time in the sacrilegious schism of Maximianus, and there baptized many people throughout his churches. Now he is your bishop together with Primianus, who nevertheless baptizes no one after him.

By what right, then, do you still think that people should be rebaptized after joining us? Answer this question for me, and baptize me. But if you cannot answer it, spare another person’s soul; spare your own.

Or if you accuse me of having said something false about Felicianus, demand that I prove it. Certainly, if I do not prove it, then do what you think right. I add this as well: if I do not prove it, let me not be bishop of my communion. But if I do prove it, do not be an enemy to your own salvation.

I wish you, my lord and brother, to be at peace with us.

## EPISTLE 107

[Note: [Col. 0404] Formerly 266; formerly numbered 107, now 216. Written after the preceding letter.]

Maximus and Theodorus report to Augustine what Macrobius answered them in person concerning Augustine’s letter to him.

**To the most blessed, venerable, and greatly desired father Augustine, Maximus and Theodorus send greetings in the Lord.**

1. At the command of Your Holiness we went to Bishop Macrobius. When we brought him the letter of Your Blessedness, he first refused even to allow it to be read to him. Later, moved at length by our urging, he wished it to be read aloud to him. After it had been read, he said:

> “I can receive only those who come to me, and give them the faith which they request.”

When we then asked him what he had to say about Primianus’s action, he said that, having been recently ordained, he could not be the judge of his father, but that he would remain in what he had received from his predecessors.

We have therefore found it necessary to report this to Your Holiness in this letter. May the Lord preserve Your Blessedness for us, lord and father.

## LETTER 108

[Note: [Col. 0405] Formerly 256; what was 108 is now 265. Written shortly after the preceding letter.]

He deals with the non-repetition of Baptism, refuting the Donatists’ obstinacy in this matter, since they accepted as valid the baptism of the Maximianists. He subsequently proves that they had no just cause for producing a schism.

To the beloved brother MACROBIUS, AUGUSTINE.

### CHAPTER ONE

1. When my dear sons, honorable men, had brought Your Benevolence my letter, in which I admonished and begged you not to rebaptize our subdeacon, they wrote back to me that you had replied: “I can receive only those who come to me, and give them the faith which they request.” And yet, if someone baptized in your communion comes to you—someone who has long been separated from you and, through ignorance, thinks that he ought to be baptized again and asks for this—when you inquire and learn where he was baptized, you do indeed receive him when he comes to you; nevertheless, you do not give him what he asks, but teach the man that he already has what he seeks. You do not attend to the words of the one who is in error, but apply yourself to correcting him. Thus his error accuses the man who wrongly gives what ought not now to be given and violates a Sacrament that has already been given; it does not excuse the one who asks. Tell me, then, I beg you, how can the one who asked this of you not have what he had already received through me?

If it is on account of “alien water” and an “alien fountain”—as those who do not understand usually say, because it is written, “Abstain from alien water, and do not drink from an alien fountain” [Note: [Col. 0405] You will search for these words in vain in the Vulgate; but you will find them in the Septuagint, Proverbs 9:18. These words were once brought forward in this matter of repeating Baptism after heretics not only by the Donatists but also by Cyprian.]—then, when Felicianus separated from you into the party of Maximianus, he was being dragged along by the chain of sacrilege as “an adulterer of truth,” as the words of your council [Note: [Col. 0405] Bagaitanum.] indicate. If he had taken your fountain with him, what fountain was there in which you baptized your people after he had separated? For now your bishop sits together with Primianus, whom he had condemned and who had condemned him.

2. But, as our people who saw you in this matter informed me in their letter (Epistle 107), when they asked what you said about it, you replied that, having only recently been ordained, you could not be the judge of the deeds of your father [Note: [Col. 0405] That Macrobius was the Donatist bishop at Hippo is established both by this letter and by the Carthaginian conference. He was doubtless ordained in the place of Proculeianus, who was still alive after the Carthaginian council held on August 25, 403, as is understood from Epistle 88, section 8.], but that you would remain in what you had received from your predecessors. Here I certainly grieved over your predicament, since I consider you, as I hear, a young man of good character. What but the necessity of a bad cause compels you to make this reply? But if you pay attention, my brother; if you think correctly; if you fear God, no necessity compels you to persist in a bad cause.

For your reply does not solve the question I put to you; rather, it frees our cause from every slander arising from your pretext. You say that, having only recently been ordained, you cannot judge the deeds of your father, but that you remain in what you received from your predecessors. Why, then, do we not rather remain in the Church which, as Scripture testifies, began from Jerusalem and, through all the nations, bears fruit and grows (Acts 1:8), and which we received from the Lord Christ through the Apostles? Why are we now judged on account of the deeds of I know not which fathers, said to have been committed nearly a hundred years ago?

If you do not dare to judge your father, who is still alive and whom you can question, why am I told to judge a dead man long before I was born? And why are Christian nations told to judge the deeds of African traditors who died so many years ago—men whom not even all the Christians who were then living in distant lands could have heard or known while they were alive? You do not dare to judge Primianus, whose continuing presence is known to you; why do you wish to impose on me the judgment of Caecilianus, ancient and unknown? If you do not judge your fathers for their own deeds, why do you judge your brothers for the deeds of others?

3. Or do you perhaps deny that we are brothers? But we hear the Holy Spirit more correctly speaking through the prophet and commanding: “Hear, you who fear the word of the Lord: Say, ‘You are our brothers,’ to those who hate you and who detest you, so that the name of the Lord may be honored and may appear to them in joy; but they themselves shall be put to shame” (Isaiah 66:5, according to the Septuagint).

Indeed, if the name of the Lord were more pleasing to human beings than the names of human beings, would Christ—who cries, “I give you my peace” (John 14:27)—be divided in his members by those who say, “I belong to Paul,” “I to Apollos,” “I to Cephas” (1 Corinthians 3:4), and who are torn apart by human names?

Would Christ be blown away in his own Baptism, of which it was said, “This is the one who baptizes” (John 1:33), and of which it was said, “Christ loved the Church and gave himself for her, to sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water with the word” (Ephesians 5:25–26)? Would he, then, be blown away in that very washing of his, if the name of the Lord—to whom the Baptism itself belongs—were more pleasing than the names of human beings, concerning whom you say: “It is holy because he gives it, not because that man gives it”?

### CHAPTER TWO

4. And yet your colleagues, whenever they wished, paid attention rather to the truth. They judged holy not only the Baptism which Primianus administered in your communion, but also that which Felicianus gave in the sacrilegious schism of Maximianus, for the sake of the honor belonging to the Lord. Nor did they dare to violate the character—not only the one he himself had received among you, but also the one which, after deserting us, he had impressed upon others outside us—when he was corrected, because they recognized it as royal.

You do not wish to judge this very good deed of theirs, where you ought laudably to imitate them; instead, you follow the judgment by which they deserve to be detested by all. You fear judging Primianus, lest you be compelled to hear something that you might condemn. Rather, judge him, and there you will be better able to find something to praise. For we do not want you to remember what Primianus did badly, but what he did most excellently: when he received those whom his condemner had baptized during that most wicked separation, he corrected human error; he did not destroy God’s Sacraments. He recognized Christ’s good in wicked people; he corrected human evil without violating Christ’s good.

Or, if this deed displeases you, at least consider this; prudently observe it for the sake of your good character: you do not judge one Primianus for the deeds of that same Primianus, yet you judge the Christian world for the deeds of Caecilianus. You fear that it may defile you if you acknowledge what you do not dare to punish. Therefore acquit the nations, which could not even have known what you accuse.

5. Yet this was not the deed of Primianus alone. You too, I think, know that nearly a hundred of your bishops, conspiring with Maximianus in a damnable faction, dared to condemn Primianus. And the council of 310 at Bagai, as the words of its decree resound, hurled the thunderbolt of its sentence from the bosom of peace against Maximianus, “a rival of the faith, an adulterer of truth, an enemy of the mother Church, a minister of Dathan, Korah, and Abiron.”

After this, twelve others who had taken part in his ordination when he was raised up against Primianus were joined to him in condemnation without delay. For the others, however, lest excessive severity be shown, a fixed day was appointed and a postponement for returning was granted, with their honors preserved if they returned within the allotted time.

Nor did the 310 fear to recall to their fellowship those accused of such great sacrilege with Maximianus, perhaps observing what is written: “Love covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8).

Those who were granted the time of postponement baptized outside your communion everyone whom they were able to baptize. For unless they had been outside, they could not have been invited to return by the concession of a postponement.

Then, both before the postponement had ended and after it had ended, those twelve who had been condemned with Maximianus were accused before three or more proconsuls, so that they might be expelled from their sees by judicial force. Among them were Felicianus of Musti, about whom I am not now speaking, and Praetextatus of Assuri, who recently died, in whose place, after his condemnation, another had already been ordained.

These two were received with their honors intact—not by Primianus alone, but by many of your fellow bishops—while, with a very great throng, they were celebrating the anniversary festival of Optatus of Thamugadi [Note: [Col. 0407] In Lovaniensis, “optata natalitia”; nor is it read otherwise in the Vatican manuscript, the only copy of this letter that has so far been found. This and several other passages had to be emended so that the sense might be clear, while the ancient reading was nevertheless preserved in the Variants. The reference is to the passage in Book 2 Against the Letters of Petilianus, chapter 23: “I mention the man who lived with you, whose anniversary you celebrated with such great solemnity, to whom you joined the kiss of peace among the Sacraments,” etc. There “anniversary” is understood as the anniversary of the see—that is, the day on which Optatus was ordained bishop.]—after their condemnation without postponement, after the postponement granted to the others had ended, and after their accusation had been publicized even amid the bustle of the courts before so many consuls. They received them with their honors unimpaired, and afterward baptized no one again.

If this assertion is resisted, or if any part of it is denied, I shall be required, at the peril of my episcopate, to prove what I say.

6. The case is finished, brother Macrobius. God brought this about; God willed this. It was the work of his hidden providence that, in the case of Maximianus, a mirror of correction should be set before you, so that every calumny against us—or rather against the Church of Christ, which is growing throughout the whole world [Note: [Col. 0408] Lovaniensis: “of the world.”]—might come to an end. I do not say your calumny, lest I seem insulting toward you, but certainly the criminal calumny of your people.

Nothing at all remains of the arguments which those who do not understand Scripture are accustomed to bring against us as though they came from Scripture. They commonly have these words in their mouths: “Abstain from alien water” (Proverbs 9:18). But the answer is: It is not alien water, even though it is among aliens—just as that water of Maximianus was not alien, from which you did not abstain.

Again, this is brought forward against us: “They have become to me like deceitful water, which has no faith” (Jeremiah 15:18). But the answer is: This was said about deceitful people, who do not belong to the Sacraments of God; and those Sacraments cannot become deceitful even in deceitful people.

For certainly those who condemned Primianus on false charges, as you yourselves claim, were liars. Yet the water in which, after separating from you, they baptized those whom they could was not deceitful. For when you received that water in those whom Felicianus and Praetextatus had baptized outside, you recognized that it had been true in liars.

This is brought forward against us: “What benefit is there in the washing of one who is baptized by the dead?” (Sirach 34:30). The answer is: If this was written about the Baptism by which those who have been expelled from the Church as dead baptize, it did not say that the washing does not exist, but that it profits nothing. This is also what we say.

Nevertheless, when the baptized person comes with him to the Church, what harmed him outside will benefit him inside—not when Baptism itself is repeated, but when the baptized person is corrected.

The council of Bagai speaks of Maximianus and his associates, whom your assembly had called dead, as though they had been buried and then revived: “The members of some shipwrecked men were cast upon harsh cliffs by the truthful wave. The shores are filled, as it were after the example of the Egyptians, with the funerals of the perishing; and their punishment is greater even in death, because, after their souls have been torn away by avenging waters [Note: [Col. 0408] Lovaniensis: “cast out by avenging waters.”], they do not even find burial” [Note: [Col. 0408] See Book 4 Against Cresconius, chapters 31 and 16.]

From this crowd of the dead, as though coming back to life, you received Felicianus and Praetextatus with their honors intact, and you did not rebaptize those baptized by them in that death. You acknowledged that the Baptism of Christ, given outside by the dead, does not profit the dead, yet that it does profit those who come back to life inside.

This is brought forward against us: “Let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head” (Psalm 140:5). The answer is that this is understood as referring to the gentle and deceitful flattery of a smooth-tongued flatterer, by which their head is anointed and grows fat when sinners are praised in the desires of their souls and those who have done evil are blessed. This is clear enough from the preceding verse, for the whole sentence is arranged as follows: “The righteous shall correct me in mercy and reprove me; but the oil of the sinner shall not fatten my head.” He said that he preferred to be crushed by the truthful severity of the merciful rather than raised up by the deceptive praise of one who deceives [Note: [Col. 0409] Lovaniensis: “joined together.”].

But however you understand it, certainly, in those whom Felicianus and Praetextatus baptized in the sacrilege of Maximianus, either you accepted the oil of sinners, or you recognized that the oil given by sinners who ministered it was Christ’s oil. For they were certainly sinners when the council of Bagai said of them: “Know that those convicted of a notorious crime, who by the deadly work of destruction glued together a filthy vessel with accumulated foulness” [Note: [Col. 0409] Lovaniensis: “of glues.”], had been condemned.

### CHAPTER THREE

7. Let what I have said about Baptism suffice. The cause of your separation, however, is commonly given an appearance of legitimacy through testimonies that are not understood.

It is written: “Do not share in the sins of others” (1 Timothy 5:22). But the answer is that the person shares in the sins of others who consents to evil deeds—not the person who, while himself being wheat, nevertheless shares in the divine Sacraments together with the chaff for as long as the threshing floor is being threshed.

For it is written: “Go out from there, and do not touch what is unclean”; and, “Whoever touches what is polluted is polluted” (Isaiah 52:11). This refers to the consent of the will by which the first human being was deceived, not to bodily association, by which Judas also kissed Christ.

Those fish of which the Lord speaks in the Gospel—the good and the bad—swim together, bodily mixed, within the same nets by which he joins the unity of the gathered Church, until the end of the age, which is prefigured by the shore (Matthew 13:48–49); they are separated in conduct, though mixed in body.

For it is written: “A little leaven corrupts the whole mass” (1 Corinthians 5:6). But this concerns those who consent to people doing evil, not those who, according to the prophet Ezekiel, sigh and mourn over the iniquities of the people of God that are committed in their midst (Ezekiel 9:4).

8. Daniel too mourns this mingling with the wicked (Daniel 9:5–16); and the three young men also mourned it (Daniel 3:28–31). The one bears witness to it in prayer, the others in the furnace. Yet they did not separate themselves bodily from the unity of the people whose sins they confessed.

What did all the prophets say—how much they said—against the very people among whom they lived! Yet they did not seek another people in which to live by bodily departure or separation.

The Apostles themselves endured Judas, the devil mixed among them, until the end, when he destroyed himself even by the noose, without any contamination of their own. Thus the Lord said to them, because of his presence among them: “And you are clean, but not all” (John 13:10). Nor was the mass of those whose conduct differed from theirs corrupted in them by his uncleanness, as by leaven.

Nor can it rightly be claimed that his wickedness was hidden from them—unless perhaps they were unaware that he was even going to betray the Lord. For they themselves wrote of him that he was a thief and that he carried away everything placed in the Lord’s money-box (John 12:6). No one could slander them with the testimony: “You saw a thief, and you ran with him” (Psalm 50:18). For one runs together with the deeds of the wicked not by sharing their Sacraments, but by consenting to those deeds.

How much does the Apostle Paul complain about false brothers (2 Corinthians 11:26)! Yet their bodily association did not stain him, because he was separated from them by the difference of a pure heart. For he rejoices that Christ is preached even by some whom he knew to be envious (Philippians 1:15–18); and envy is certainly a devilish vice.

9. Finally, Bishop Cyprian—whose authority you sometimes invoke in support of the repetition of Baptism—was nearer to our own times, when the Church had spread more abundantly. His council [Note: [Col. 0410] The Carthaginian council of the year 256, concerning the rebaptizing of heretics.] and those writings—if they truly belong to him and were not, as some think, composed and fabricated under his name—show how much he loved unity and how, in the clearest exhortation, he advised that those who thought differently from him should nevertheless be tolerated within it, lest the bond of peace be broken [Note: [Col. 0410] Lovaniensis: “even against whom … he advised.”].

He paid particular attention to this: if human error should creep in among people on either side who think something other than what the truth holds, then, provided brotherly harmony is preserved, love also covers a multitude of sins.

He held and loved this so firmly that, if he had understood anything concerning the Sacrament of Baptism differently from the truth, God might also reveal that to him, just as the Apostle says to brothers walking in love: “Therefore, let those of us who are perfect think this; and if you think anything differently, God will reveal that also to you. Nevertheless, let us walk according to what we have attained” (Philippians 3:15–16).

Moreover, if that fruitful branch still had anything requiring purification, it was purified by the glorious sickle of martyrdom—not because he was killed for the name of Christ, but because he was killed for the name of Christ within the bosom of unity.

For he himself wrote, and asserts with the greatest confidence, that those who are outside unity, even if they die for that name, can be killed but cannot be crowned (Book On the Unity of the Church). Such power does love of unity possess, whether for removing sins or for confirming them, depending on whether that love is preserved or violated.

10. That same Cyprian, then, when the Church had been devastated by the persecution of the impious Gentiles and he mourned many who had lapsed, attributing this to the evil conduct of those who lived in the Church itself in a damnable manner, mourns the conduct of his fellow bishops and does not conceal his grief in silence. Rather, he says that they had advanced to such great greed that, while their brothers in the Church were hungry, they wanted to possess silver in abundance; that they seized estates through treacherous frauds; and that, as interest multiplied, they increased their usury (Sermon on the Lapsed, beginning).

I suppose Cyprian was not stained by the avarice, estates, and usury of these men; yet he was not separated from them bodily, but by the dissimilarity of his life. He touched the altar with them; but he did not touch their unclean life when he condemned and rebuked it in this way.

What is pleasing is approached; what is displeasing is rejected. Therefore that excellent bishop lacked neither the discipline by which he restrained sins nor the prudence by which he guarded the bond of unity.

In one of his letters to the presbyter Maximus, a clear and explicit statement on this matter is read. Holding to the prophetic rule, he commanded absolutely that the unity of the Church must not be abandoned because of the mingling of the wicked. “For,” he says, “although tares appear to be in the Church, our faith or love must not be hindered so that, because we see that there are tares in the Church, we withdraw from the Church. We must work only to be able to be wheat” (Epistle 51).

11. This law of love was proclaimed from the mouth of the Lord Christ. For these likenesses are his: the likeness of the tares, tolerated in unity throughout the field of the world until the time of harvest (Matthew 13:24–43), and that of the bad fish, tolerated within the same nets until the shore (Matthew 13:47–50).

If your ancestors had kept this law of love in mind, if they had considered it with the fear of God, they would not have torn themselves away by wicked separation from so many Christian nations that entirely did not know who, what, or against whom they were bringing charges—not on account of Caecilianus and I know not which Africans, whether they were truly criminals, as you think, or—which is more credible—attacked by slanders.

They would not, I say, have torn themselves away from the Church which Cyprian himself described as extending its rays throughout all nations and spreading its branches throughout the whole earth in abundant fertility. They would not have separated themselves from the Christian peoples who knew nothing of these matters, unless this was done either from private hostility rather than concern for the common good, or through that vice which Cyprian himself subsequently lists and recalls as something to be avoided.

For after commanding that the Church must not be abandoned because of the tares seen within it, he continues and adds: “We must work only to be wheat, so that, when the wheat begins to be stored in the Lord’s granaries, we may receive fruit according to our work and labor. The Apostle says in his Epistle: ‘In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay; some indeed for honor, others for dishonor’ (2 Timothy 2:20). Let us apply ourselves and labor as much as we can to be a vessel of gold or silver. But the breaking of clay vessels has been granted to the Lord alone” [Note: [Col. 0411] Lovaniensis: “has been entrusted.” It may perhaps be necessary to read, “permitted to him alone.”]—to him also was given the iron rod.

“A servant cannot be greater than his lord. No one should claim for himself what the Father granted to the Son alone, so as to think that he can already openly carry the chaff and the winnowing fan, or separate all the tares from the wheat by human judgment” [Note: [Col. 0411] Lovaniensis omits “the chaff and the winnowing fan,” etc. But in Cyprian it reads: “to carry it openly already.” The same is found in Augustine, Book 2 Against Cresconius, chapter 34, and Book 2 Against Gaudentius, chapter 13, except that “himself” is omitted.].

This is proud presumption and sacrilegious obstinacy, which perverse rage takes upon itself. While they always assume more for themselves than gentle justice demands [Note: [Col. 0411] In Cyprian it reads: “and while some claim for themselves continually more than lordship,” etc.], they perish from the Church; and while they insolently exalt themselves, blinded by their own swelling, they lose the light of truth.

12. What could be clearer than this testimony of Cyprian? What more truthful? You see how brightly it shines with evangelical and apostolic light. You see that those who, as though offended on behalf of their own righteousness by the iniquities of others, abandon the unity of the Church are themselves rather the most iniquitous.

You see that the tares are outside: those who were unwilling to tolerate tares in the unity of the Lord’s field. You see that the chaff is outside: those who were unwilling to tolerate such things in the unity of the great house.

You see how truly it is written: “A wicked son declares himself righteous, but he does not cleanse his way” (Proverbs 24, according to the Septuagint). That is, he does not cleanse, excuse, defend, or show as pure and without guilt the departure by which he leaves the Church. This is what “he does not cleanse” means.

For if he did not declare himself righteous but were truly and legitimately righteous, he would not impiously abandon the good on account of the wicked; rather, he would patiently endure the wicked for the sake of the good, until the Lord himself—either through himself or through his angels—separated at the end of the age the tares from the wheat, the chaff from the grain, the vessels of wrath from the vessels of mercy, the goats from the sheep, and the bad fish from the good.

### CHAPTER FOUR

13. But if you attempt to receive those testimonies of Scripture which your ancestors believed should be understood or brought forward to divide the people of God in a way other than the sense required by the divine words, stop now. Consider the mirror which God, in his most merciful providence, has set before you for your admonition—if you have understanding.

I speak of the case of Felicianus, “a rival of the faith, an adulterer of truth, an enemy of the mother Church,” as was proclaimed in the council of Bagai, and “a minister of Dathan, Korah, and Abiron.” They added further that the open earth had not swallowed him, but had reserved him above for a greater punishment [Note: [Col. 0412] Lovaniensis: “but for a greater punishment upon them.”].

“For,” they say, “by the shortcut of a funeral he had gained release from his punishment; now he gathers heavier interest on his funeral, since he, alive, is among the dead” [Note: [Col. 0412] In the books Against Cresconius, “of usury.”].

I ask whether those who, conspiring with him, condemned the innocence of Primianus touched him when he was then unclean and dead. If they touched him, then by touching what was polluted they were polluted.

Why, then, was a postponement for returning granted to them, as though they were innocent, in the same communion as he and separated from yours, so that, returning with their honor and faith intact, they might have foundations for their restoration? Why were they allowed to hear that the sacrilegious branch had not polluted their plantings, when they were situated in the same party, joined in the same schism, separated from you, associated with those men, established together in Africa, well known to them, their closest friends and associates?

Even if they were not physically present when he was ordained, they nevertheless condemned Primianus, who was absent, on his account. And yet it is said that Caecilianus’s branch polluted the immense, distant, and unknown Christian peoples throughout the world—peoples of whom many could not know, I do not say his case, but even his name.

Those who not only knew of Maximianus’s sin but also raised him up against Primianus by ordaining him do not share in the sins of others; yet those who either did not know that Caecilianus had been made bishop in distant nations, or had merely heard of him in nearer places, or had simply and peacefully learned that he had been ordained in Africa, or had not raised him against anyone in Carthage, do share in the sins of others!

Those who shared with the thief did not run with a thief, although Nummasius the advocate, speaking for your bishop Restitutus who was present, says that he had seized the primacy of the episcopal name by a hidden, almost sacrilegious theft. Those who shared with the adulterer of truth did not take their portion with an adulterer. Their whole mass was not corrupted by a little leaven when they favored him and remained in his party—not as people ignorant of the matter, cut off from you, but as people who worked to be raised up against you, to be cut off, and to be established.

Then you yourselves, who invited them to return in such a way that you declared those so closely joined to Maximianus unpolluted by the sacrilegious branch—since you also received Praetextatus and Felicianus with their honors intact, and live in peaceful concord with them, as you see Felicianus sitting together with you even today—are not stained by any sharing in the sins of others, nor polluted by any contact with uncleanness, nor corrupted by the leaven of any wickedness.

Yet through these testimonies a foreign crime is charged against the Christian world; the division of unity is defended as though by a disastrous separation; and the branch that remained in the root of the true mother is accused by the severed branch as though it were an unclean branch!

### CHAPTER FIVE

14. What of that boasting in which you are accustomed to glory over the persecutions you have endured? If it is not the cause but the punishment that makes martyrs, then when it was said, “Blessed are those who suffer persecution,” the words “for righteousness’ sake” (Matthew 5:10) were added in vain.

Do not the Maximianists easily defeat you even in the glory of this title? They endured persecution not only afterward together with you, but first from you.

The words of the advocates who accused Maximianus, in the presence of your colleague Restitutus—who had already been ordained in place of Salvius of Membressa [Note: [Col. 0413] Lovaniensis: “Salvi.” See Book 3 Against Cresconius, chapter 53.] before the day of the postponement had passed, after he and those other eleven had been condemned without postponement—are the words I mentioned shortly before.

Titianus too, on the very day the postponement expired, accused Felicianus and Praetextatus, in the gravest terms, of the whole conspiracy against Primianus.

The council of Bagai was also cited more than once in the proconsular records and afterward in the municipal records. Judgments were set in motion, the most threatening orders were obtained, and it was requested and commanded that those resisting should be brought to punishment. Official assistance was supplied, and aid from the cities was granted so that what had been judged might be carried out.

Why, then, do you quarrel with us over the persecution imposed by authority, when we shared these things with you on equal terms? For since it is not always the case that one who endures persecution reaches martyrdom, your clerics and Circumcellions arranged matters among us so that you should endure persecution and we should endure martyrdom.

But, as I said, compete with the Maximianists in this praise. They produce against you the court records in which you persecuted them through judges. Yet afterward you made peace with some of them after they had been corrected by such coercion. Therefore our reconciliation should not be despaired of, if God deigns to help and inspire you with a peaceful mind.

For that saying which your party commonly directs against us more with a slanderous than a truthful mouth—“Their feet are swift to shed blood” (Psalm 13:3)—we have experienced rather in the case of the great banditry of your Circumcellions and clerics. They tore human bodies apart with the most savage slaughter and stained so many places with the blood of our people.

When you entered this region, their leaders escorted you with their bands, loudly crying praises to God amid songs. They had such cries as though they were the sounds of trumpets in battle throughout all their acts of banditry.

On another day, however, shaken and pricked by the goads of your words—which you hurled against them through a Punic interpreter with honorable and free indignation—and provoked by their deeds rather than pleased by their services, they tore themselves from the middle of the congregation in furious agitation, as we were able to hear from those who were present.

Nor, after their feet had been swift to shed blood, did you salt the pavements with any water [Note: [Col. 0414] The Donatists thought that sacred places and vessels had to be washed if Catholics had touched them. Thus they scraped their altars, broke their chalices, washed their cloths, and sprinkled the hair of consecrated virgins with salted water, as Optatus testifies in Book 6, where he says, among other things: “In many places you wanted to wash the walls, and you ordered enclosed spaces to be sprinkled with salted water.”]—which your clerics later thought ought to be done after our people.

15. But, as I had begun to say, this testimony from Scripture, which you habitually throw at us more by abuse than by proof—“Their feet are swift to shed blood”—was also vomited forth against Felicianus and Praetextatus in that vehement attack, in the council of Bagai’s grandiloquent sentence.

For when they had said what they thought should be said about Maximianus, they continued: “Nor does the just death of his crime condemn this man alone. The chain of sacrilege also drags many into partnership in the crime, concerning whom it is written: ‘The poison of asps is under their lips; their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness. Their feet are swift to shed blood’ (Psalm 13:3),” and so forth.

After saying this, in order to show who those were whom the chain of sacrilege dragged into partnership in the crime, and to condemn them with Maximianus with similar severity, they continued: “Therefore know that the following are guilty of a notorious crime: Victorianus of Carcaviana, together with the eleven whom they add to him, among whom are Felicianus of Musti and Praetextatus of Assuri.”

After these words had been spoken against them, such concord was established with them that nothing was taken away from their honors. No one washed by them was judged to require washing again, after the feet of those who washed them had been swift to shed blood [Note: [Col. 0414] Lovaniensis: “judges.”].

Why, then, should our concord be despaired of? May God turn away the envy of the devil, and may the peace of Christ prevail in our hearts. And, as the same Apostle says, “Let us forgive one another, if anyone has a complaint against another, just as God in Christ forgave us” (Colossians 3:15, 13), so that—as I have already said and must often say—“love may cover a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8).

### CHAPTER SIX

[Col. 0415]

### 16

But you, brother, with whom I am now dealing, and concerning whom I desire to rejoice in Christ—as He Himself knows—if you should wish, by the resources of your intelligence and eloquence, to undertake the defense of Donatus’s party in this case of Maximianus, and not to act falsely—for the memory of these events is still fresh among the people against whom they occurred, who are still alive, and there are also so many proconsular and municipal records in which the Catholic Church has always admonished you—then you must not, as is your custom, admit that those passages about “another’s water,” “the water of deceit,” “the washing of the dead,” and any other such expressions are to be understood in that way. Rather, you must maintain that the baptism of Christ, given to the Church for participation in eternal salvation, is judged neither extraneous outside the Church nor alien among those who are alien, but is effective for destruction among strangers and aliens, while for those who are its own and belong to it, it is effective for salvation. Among the former, when they turn to the peace of the Church, their error should be corrected; the Sacrament itself should not be destroyed in order to punish the error. What was harmful outside, when perversely administered, should begin to be beneficial within, once the recipient has been corrected.

Nor will you accept, as you usually do, those passages about not sharing in the sins of others, separation from the wicked, not touching what is unclean and polluted, avoiding the corruption of a little leaven, and other such expressions, lest they entangle you inexplicably in the case of Maximianus. Instead, you will wisely assert and hold to what sound doctrine commends and what the true rule establishes by prophetic and apostolic examples: that the wicked should rather be tolerated so that the good are not abandoned than that the good should be abandoned so that the wicked may be separated [Note: [Col. 0415] Lov., “the good.”]. The reprobate must be separated only from imitation, agreement, and similarity of life and conduct—though they grow together, are mingled together in tribulation, and are gathered together within the nets until the time of harvest, winnowing, and the shore.

But concerning the persecution: how will you defend whatever your people have done through the judges to expel the Maximianists and disturb them in their homes, unless you say that your more prudent men did it with the intention of correcting them and with restrained intimidation, not of harming them? If some exceeded human measure—as in the case of what the city itself testifies that Salvius of Membressa endured—will you say that such acts do not prejudice the others, who are established with the wheat in one communion of the Sacraments, though separated from them by difference of life, just as chaff is separated from wheat?

### 17

Since these things are so, I embrace this defense of yours. For this will be your defense, if it is truthful; and it will be overcome by truth if it is not. I embrace, I say, your defense—but you see that it is also mine. Why, then, do we not work together to be wheat in the Lord’s threshing floor and together tolerate the chaff? Why not, I beg you? What is the reason, for what benefit, for what advantage? Tell me.

Unity is avoided so that peoples bought by the blood of the one Lamb may be inflamed against one another by hostile zeal and the sheep may be divided—as though they were ours among ourselves, rather than belonging to that master of the household who said to his servant, “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17), not “Feed your sheep”; those of whom it was said, “There shall be one flock and one shepherd” (John 10:16). He cries out in the Gospel, “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have true love among yourselves” [Col. 0416] (John 13:35), and, “Let both grow until the harvest, lest while you wish to gather the weeds, you uproot the wheat along with them” (Matthew 13:30).

Unity is avoided so that the husband may come together in one place and the wife in another. Let him say, “Hold unity with me, because I am your husband”; let her reply, “There I shall die, where my father is.” Thus, in one bed they divide Christ—people whom we would detest if they divided the bed.

Unity is avoided so that relatives, fellow citizens, friends, guests, and all who are bound together by human ties—both Christians—may be united when they hold banquets, give and receive spouses in marriage, buy and sell, make agreements and arrangements, exchange greetings, share decisions, converse, and conduct all their affairs and business, yet be at odds at the altar of God. For wherever they have conceived discord, they ought to end it there, and, according to the Lord’s command, first be reconciled to their brothers and then offer their gift at the altar (Matthew 5:24); but although they are united elsewhere, they are divided there.

### 18

Unity is avoided so that we may seek public laws against the wickednesses of your people—for I do not wish to call those wickednesses yours—and so that the Circumcellions may be armed against those very laws. They despise them with the very frenzy with which, when raging against you, they provoked their enactment.

Unity is avoided so that peasant insolence may rise against its owners, and fugitive slaves, contrary to apostolic discipline, may not only be alienated from their masters but even threaten their masters; and not merely threaten them, but plunder them in the most violent attacks [Note: [Col. 0416] Lov., “most conspicuous attacks.”], under the direction and leadership—and, in the crime itself, the foremost champions—of your agonistic confessors. These men adorn your honor in praise of God, yet shed the blood of others in praise of God, so that, because of the resentment of men, in your gatherings and excursions you promise to restore the spoils to those from whom they were taken.

Yet you do not wish even this to be carried out, lest you be forced to offend their audacity, which your presbyters have judged excessively necessary to themselves. For they boast of their previous merits in your cause, pointing out and enumerating what they did before the law by which you rejoice that your liberty was restored [Note: [Col. 0416] Liberty had already been restored to the Donatists by the law of the emperor Julian. Augustine writes of this in Letter 105, chapter 2, section 9: “Julian, the deserter of Christ and His enemy, at the request of your men Rogatianus and Pontius, granted the party of Donatus the liberty of perdition; finally, he restored the basilicas to the heretics at the very time when he ordered the temples to be opened to the demons.” Before Augustine, Optatus likewise wrote in Book 2: “With the same voice,” he says, “with which the temples of idols were ordered to be opened, liberty was restored to you.” More about this rescript of Julian may be found in Book 2 Against the Letters of Petilianus, chapter 97. In addition, toward the end of the year 409, Honorius issued another edict on behalf of the Donatists, by which he granted “that anyone might freely accept Christian worship,” as is recorded in the council held at Carthage on June 14, 410. By decree of that council, the bishops Florentius, Possidius, Praesidius, and Benenatus were sent to the same emperor to ask him to rescind that edict; he did so shortly afterward, as appears from the law addressed to Heraclianus, Count of Africa, issued on August 25 of that same year, 410.].

They say that your presbyters devastated our places and basilicas and took possession of them after driving us out; thus, if you wish to be severe toward them, you will appear ungrateful for their services.

### 19

Unity is avoided so that whoever among us refuses to endure discipline may flee to them for protection and be offered to you for rebaptism.

Such was the case of Rusticianus, a subdeacon from the countryside [Col. 0417] [Note: [Col. 0417] In the Vatican manuscript, Rusticanus.], whose case has compelled me to write these things to you with great sorrow and fear. Excommunicated by his presbyter because of his reprobate and perverse conduct, and having also become a debtor to many people in that region, he sought no other refuge, contrary both to ecclesiastical discipline and to his creditors, than to be rebaptized by you and loved by them as though he were perfectly pure [Note: [Col. 0417] The following phrase once stood here: “Writing about this Marcellinus, you call him a tenant of the Church.” But these words should be deleted, as we observe concerning this letter in the preface to this volume.].

Your predecessor rebaptized such a deacon of ours—himself also excommunicated by his own presbyter—and made him your deacon. Not many days later, having joined himself, as he desired, to the audacity of those same lost men, he was killed during a nocturnal attack, in the midst of his robbery and arson, when a crowd came running to assist [Note: [Col. 0417] Proculeianus.].

These are the fruits of this division, which you refuse to heal by fleeing unity in the same way that division itself ought to have been avoided. Division is filthy in itself and condemned by God, even if it did not produce these and other such horrible and wicked acts.

## CHAPTER VII

### 20

Let us therefore recognize the peace of Christ, brother, and hold it together. As far as God grants, let us strive to be good together; and, preserving unity, let us correct the wicked together with as much discipline as we can, and for the sake of that same unity let us tolerate them with as much patience as we can. Otherwise, as Christ warned, when we wish to gather the weeds before the proper time—those weeds which the blessed Cyprian testified are seen and discerned not outside but within the Church—we may uproot the wheat along with them.

For you do not truly possess certain privileges of holiness of your own, so that our wicked people pollute us but your wicked people do not pollute you; so that an ancient timidity concerning traitors, of which we know nothing, contaminates us, but the present audacity of the reprobate, which you see, does not contaminate you.

Let us recognize that ark which prefigured the Church. Let us be clean animals together there, and let us not refuse to carry with us in it unclean animals as well, until the end of the flood. Clean and unclean animals were together in the ark, but Noah did not offer the unclean animals together with the clean ones to the Lord as a sacrifice of pleasing fragrance (Genesis 7–8). Nevertheless, no clean animal abandoned the ark before the appointed time because of the unclean ones.

Only the raven abandoned it and separated itself before the time from communion with that ark; but it was one of the two unclean animals, not one of the seven clean ones. Let us detest the uncleanness of this separation. For whoever is otherwise commendable in conduct, that separation alone makes him blameworthy, because the wicked son himself calls himself righteous but does not wash away his departure. Although arrogantly puffed up and blinded by his own swelling pride, he dares to say what the Prophet foresaw and condemned: “Do not touch me, for I am clean” (Isaiah 65:5).

Whoever, then, abandons the congregation of this unity before the proper time, supposedly because of the uncleanness of certain people, like an ark in the flood carrying both clean and unclean creatures, shows himself rather to be what he flees.

The Lord willed that even in this city your people, through the mouth of a certain . . . .

[Col. 0418]

[In the Vatican manuscript from which Letter 108 was extracted, a space of twenty-seven lines is left blank.]

## LETTER 109

[Note: [Col. 0418] Revised according to manuscripts a, bg, ll, bn, c, cc, ff, g, gv, j, l, n, r, s, sb, t, vc, vd, five copies marked v, and the editions of Am, Ead, Er, and Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0418] Formerly numbered 37; what was 109 is now 211. Probably written in 409.]

Severus, bishop of Milevis, declares that he derives the greatest pleasure and benefit from reading Augustine, praising him highly and finally urging him to write a reply.

**To the venerable and beloved bishop AUGUSTINE, whom I embrace with the whole bosom of my love, SEVERUS.**

### 1

Thanks be to God, brother Augustine, whose gift is whatever good joy there is in us. I confess that I am well with you; I read you often. I shall say something remarkable, but entirely true: just as presence is usually absent to me, so your absence has become present to me.

No turbulent activities of temporal affairs come between us. I do as much as I can, though I cannot do as much as I wish. Why should I say how much I wish? You know very well how greedy I am for you. Yet I do not complain that I do not do as much as I wish, because, in turn, I do no less than I can.

Thanks, then, to God, dearest brother. I am well with you; I rejoice that I am more closely joined to you, and, so to speak, clinging to you as closely as one can, gathering strength from the abundance of your breasts. If I could become capable of shaking and expressing them, may your very entrails, if possible, deign to pour out for me whatever they guard more secretly and inwardly, enclosed beneath the skins which they still offer to a nursing infant to suck.

I desire, I say, that your entrails be poured back into me: your entrails, rich entrails, fattened by heavenly nourishment and seasoned with every spiritual sweetness; your entrails, pure entrails, simple entrails—except that they are bound about with the twofold bond of a double love; your entrails, suffused with the light of truth and shining back the truth.

I submit myself to their outpouring or radiance, so that my night may fade in your light and we may walk together in the brightness of day [Note: [Col. 0418] Four Vatican manuscripts read “of God.”].

O truly skillful bee of God, building honeycombs full of divine nectar, dripping mercy and truth! Through them my soul delights as it moves about, and by their life-giving nourishment it strives to repair and support whatever it finds lacking or feels weak within itself.

### 2

The Lord is blessed through the proclamation of your mouth and your faithful ministry. You make yourself harmonize and respond so well to the Lord who sings to you that whatever flows down to us from His fullness becomes more pleasing and welcome through your elegant service, your concise purity, and your faithful, chaste, and simple ministry.

You make it shine so brilliantly through your wit and vigilance that it dazzles the eyes and draws them to itself—unless you yourself suggest that the Lord is responsible, so that, by referring whatever delightfully shines in you back to Him, we may recognize it as belonging to Him, whose goodness makes you good, and whose purity, simplicity, and beauty make you pure, simple, and beautiful.

As we give thanks to Him for your goodness, may He deign, by His gift [Note: [Col. 0418] So read sixteen manuscripts. The editions have: “and, giving thanks to the Lord for your goodness, who has deigned by His gift,” etc.], to join us to you, or somehow subordinate us to you [Col. 0419], so that we may be more fully subjected to Him. Under whose guidance and direction we rejoice that you are such a man that you may also rejoice in us.

I do not doubt that this will happen if you assist me with your prayers. By imitating you I have already made some progress, so that I desire to become such a man.

You see what you do by being so good: how you draw us into love of our neighbor, who is for us both the first step toward the love of God and the final one, and, as it were, the boundary by which love of God and love of neighbor are joined to each other. Standing, as I said, upon this boundary, we are touched by the warmth of both and burn with love for both.

But the more this fire has burned and purified us in relation to our neighbor, the more it compels us to go, purified, toward God. In this matter no limit is imposed upon how much we should love, since there the measure is to love without measure. We must not fear, then, that we may love the Lord our God too much; what we must fear is loving Him too little.

### 3

This preceding letter, which presents me to you as happier—as though my sadness had been wiped away—because of the joyful activity of the generous leisure I was permitted to enjoy with you in this rural place (for such leisure could indeed be permitted), was written before the venerable bishop graciously visited us, as though it marked the culmination of those joys. What I truly find remarkable is that he came on the very day on which it was written.

What is this, I ask, my soul, unless it is perhaps something that delights us? Yet although it is honorable, it is not sufficiently useful, because it is only partial. In the meantime, let us strive to fit this very part—namely, ourselves—to the whole, insofar as the material yields to us because of our sins; that is, insofar as we ourselves yield, becoming more worthy and better fitted together, if you permit me to use that word.

You have here a letter longer than befits your greatness but suited to my smallness. By it I have challenged you to send me a letter not suited to my smallness but to your greatness. However long it may be, it will not be long for me, since all time is too short for reading you.

Write to me when or where I should come to meet you, concerning the matter for which you ordered me to come. If that plan remains in force and something else has not perhaps seemed preferable, then I shall come. If not, I beg you not to call me back from my journey, for that was the only thing I thought should take precedence over everything else.

I greatly long for and salute all the brothers who are our fellow servants in the Lord.

## LETTER 110

[Note: [Col. 0419] Corrected according to manuscripts a, a, bg, bl, c, cb, cc, ff, g, gg, gv, j, n, r, s, t, two copies marked sb, two marked vc, four marked v, and the editions of Am, Bad, Er, and Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0419] Formerly numbered 135; what was 110 is now 213. Written after the preceding letter.]

Augustine to Bishop Severus, gently protesting and asking why Severus praised him so greatly in the preceding letter.

**To the most blessed and sweetest lord, the highly venerable and greatly desired brother and fellow priest SEVERUS, and to the brothers who are with you, AUGUSTINE and the brothers who are with me send greetings in the Lord.**

### 1

My letter, which our beloved son and fellow deacon Timothy carried, was already prepared for departure when our sons Quodvultdeus and Gaudentius came to us with your letters. Consequently, when he departed immediately, he did not carry my reply, because after their arrival he remained with us only a very short time and seemed about to leave from hour to hour.

But even if I had replied through him, I would still have been in your debt. Even now, when I seem to have replied, I remain in debt—not, I say, in the debt of love, which we owe all the more the more we expend it, and of which the Apostle shows us to be perpetual debtors when he says, “Owe no one anything except to love one another” (Romans 13:8), but in the debt of your letter itself.

For when shall I be equal to your sweetness and to such eagerness of spirit as your letter revealed to me when I read it? It introduced to me something already very well known to me about you; yet although it did not introduce a new subject, it was a new demand for a reply.

### 2

Perhaps you wonder why I say that I am unequal to repaying this debt, since you think so highly of me and know me as though you knew my own soul. But this very thing has made it very difficult for me to reply to your letter: I spare saying how great you seem to me out of consideration for your modesty; yet if I say less, after you have bestowed such praise upon me, what shall I remain except a debtor?

I would not care about this if I knew that what you said about me to me had not been spoken from the most sincere love, but from flattery hostile to friendship. In that case I would not become a debtor, because I would not be obliged to return such things. But the more I know how faithfully you speak, the more I see how heavily I am burdened by my debt.

### 3

Consider what has happened to me: I have somehow praised myself by saying that you faithfully praised me. But what else could I say except what I reminded you about yourself—which you know [Note: Ten manuscripts read, “which you know.”]?

Behold, I have created for myself a new question that you did not propose, and perhaps you are waiting for me to solve it. It was not enough that I was a debtor; I have even burdened myself with a still greater debt. Yet this is easy to demonstrate, and, if I do not demonstrate it, easy for you to see: things that are untrue can be said faithfully, and things that are true can be said unfaithfully.

Whoever believes what he says speaks faithfully, even if he says what is untrue. Whoever does not believe what he says speaks unfaithfully, even if he says what is true. Do I therefore doubt that you believe about me what you wrote? Since I do not recognize these qualities in myself, you may have faithfully said things about me that are not true.

### 4

But I do not wish you to be deceived in this way even by goodwill. I owe a debt to that goodwill, since I can speak about you both faithfully and benevolently of the things that are true—unless, as I said above, I were sparing your modesty.

When I am praised by the closest and most intimate companion of my soul, as though by myself, that is how I regard it. You can see how troublesome this is, even when what is said is true. How much more troublesome it is because, although you are another soul of mine—or rather, although your soul and mine are one—you are mistaken about me by thinking that I possess what I lack, just as one person can be mistaken about himself.

I do not wish this merely so that you, whom I love, may not be deceived, but also so that you may not pray less for me to become what you already believe me to be. Nor am I your debtor in the sense that, as benevolence advances, I should believe and say the same good things about you that you yourself still recognize to be lacking in you. Rather, with a spirit indeed so benevolent, I should speak only of those good qualities of yours which are God’s gifts and of which I am certain in you.

I do not refrain from doing this because I fear being mistaken about those qualities, but lest, when praised by me, you should seem to have praised yourself, and because of that rule of justice which I do not wish done to me. If it ought to be done, I choose to remain a debtor as long as I think it ought not to be done; but if it ought not to be done, then I am not a debtor.

### 5

But I know what you may reply to me: “You speak as though I had desired your lengthy letter praising me.” Far be it from me to believe this of you. Yet your letter, I do not say how full of true or untrue praise, but nevertheless full of praise of me, demanded—even against your will—that I criticize this judgment concerning me.

For if you wanted me to write about something else, you desired me to be a giver, not a repayer. The order of justice, however, is that we first repay what is owed; then, if it pleases us, we may also give something to the person to whom we have repaid it.

Indeed, even such things as you wanted me to write, if we consider the Lord’s commands more carefully, we repay rather than give, since we owe no one anything except to love one another. Love itself demands the debt: as servants of fraternal love, we should assist, insofar as we can, the person who rightly wishes to be helped.

But, my brother, I believe you know how much is in my hands. Because of the various concerns required by our service, only the smallest drops of time scarcely trickle down to me; and if I spend them on other matters, I seem to be acting contrary to my duty.

### 6

You want me to write you a lengthy letter, and I admit that I owe you this. I certainly owe it to your sweet, sincere, and unalloyed desire. But because you are a good lover of justice, I remind you of this so that you may hear it from me all the more willingly, since you love justice.

You see that what I owe both to you and to others comes before what I owe to you alone, and that I do not have enough time for everything, since I do not even have enough for those matters that take precedence.

Therefore all my dearest and closest friends—among whom, in Christ’s name, you are one of the first—will perform their duty if they not only refrain from imposing other letters upon me to write, but also, with as much authority and holy kindness as they can, restrain others from doing so. Otherwise I may seem harsh when I do not give what each person asks, while I wish rather to repay what I owe to everyone.

Finally, when, as we hope and hold by promise, Your Venerability has come to us, you will learn with what literary tasks and how greatly I am occupied. Then you will more urgently do what I have asked: remove from me the obligation to write something else imposed by anyone whom you can persuade.

May the Lord our God fill your heart’s great and holy bosom, which He Himself created, most blessed lord.

## LETTER 111

[Note: [Col. 0421] We have corrected this according to manuscripts a, bl, c, cc, cb, ff, g, gg, gv, j, n, r, s, sb, t, two copies marked bn, two marked vc, four marked v, and the editions of Am, Bad, Er, and Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0421] Formerly numbered 122; what was 111 is now 148. Written toward the end of 409, perhaps in November.]

Augustine to the presbyter Victorianus, consoling him and urging him patiently to accept the evils inflicted upon holy men and sacred virgins by the barbarians invading Italy and Spain.

[Col. 0422]

**To his most beloved and greatly desired brother and fellow presbyter VICTORIANUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.**

### 1

Your letter filled our heart with great sorrow. You asked me to respond at length, although such evils call for lengthy groans and tears more than for lengthy books.

The whole world is afflicted by such great disasters that scarcely any part of the earth exists where events such as those you described are not being committed and mourned. A short time ago, even in the deserts of Egypt, where monasteries had chosen to lodge apart from all noise, as though in safety [Note: [Col. 0422] Lov., “were living.” Other editions and manuscripts read, “had chosen.”], brothers were killed by barbarians.

As for the wicked deeds recently committed in the regions of Italy and Gaul, I do not suppose they are unknown to you. In Spain, too, such things have begun to be reported from so many provinces that previously seemed to have remained untouched by these evils.

But why go farther away? Here in our own region of Hippo, since the barbarians have not reached it, the robberies of the Donatist clergy and the Circumcellions devastate the churches so thoroughly that the deeds of the barbarians may perhaps seem milder.

What barbarian could have devised what these men have done—throwing lime and vinegar into the eyes of our clergy, whose other limbs they also mangled with horrifying blows and wounds? They plunder and burn some houses, seize dry crops, pour out liquids, and, by threatening others with similar acts, compel many to be rebaptized. The day before I dictated these things to you, I was informed that forty-eight souls from one place had been rebaptized through terrors of this kind.

### 2

These things should be mourned, not wondered at, and we should cry out to God that He may free us from such great evils, not according to our merits but according to His mercy.

For what could the human race have hoped for, since such things were foretold long ago both in the Prophets and in the Gospel? We must not be so self-contradictory as to believe when these passages are read and complain when they are fulfilled. Rather, even those who were unbelieving when they read or heard these things written in the holy books should now at least believe, when they see them already being fulfilled.

Thus, from these great pressures—as from the winepress of the Lord our God—just as the dregs of unbelievers who murmur and blaspheme flow out, so may the oil of the faithful who confess and pray continue to be pressed out and rendered.

To those who do not cease to hurl impious complaints against the Christian faith, saying that before this teaching was preached throughout the world the human race did not suffer such great evils, it is easy to reply from the Gospel. For the Lord says:

“The servant who did not know his master’s will and did things deserving of blows shall receive few blows; but the servant who knew his master’s will and did things deserving of blows shall receive many blows” (Luke 12:47–48).

What wonder, then, if in Christian times this world, like a servant who now knows his master’s will and does things deserving of blows, receives many blows? They observe how rapidly the Gospel is preached, but they do not observe how perversely it is despised.

The humble and holy servants of God, who suffer temporal evils in two ways—both from the impious and together with the impious—have their consolations and the hope of the age to come. Hence the Apostle says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18).

### 3

Therefore, dearest brother, respond humbly, truthfully, and piously even to those whose words you say you cannot endure, because they ask: “If we sinners deserved these things, why were the servants of God killed by the barbarians’ sword, and why were the handmaids of God led away captive?”

However much justice we preserve, however much obedience we offer to the Lord, can we possibly be better than those three men who were thrown into a furnace of blazing fire in order to preserve God’s law?

Yet read what Azariah says there, one of the three who opened his mouth in the midst of the fire:

“Blessed are You, Lord, God of our fathers, and worthy of praise; and glorious is Your name forever. For You are just in all that You have done for us, and all Your works are true, Your ways are right, and all Your judgments are truth. You have executed true judgments in all that You have brought upon us and upon the holy city of our fathers, Jerusalem; for in truth and judgment You have brought all these things upon us because of our sins. For we have sinned and have not obeyed Your law, nor have we heeded Your commandments, so that it might be well with us; and all that You have brought upon us, You have brought in true judgment.

You have delivered us into the hands of lawless enemies, hateful apostates, and an unjust and worst of kings, beyond the whole earth. And now we cannot open our mouths; we have truly become a shame and a reproach to Your servants and to those who worship You.

Do not deliver us forever because of Your name, Lord, and do not reject Your covenant. Do not withdraw Your mercy from us, for the sake of Abraham whom You loved, and Isaac Your servant, and Israel Your holy one, to whom You spoke, promising that You would multiply their offspring like the stars of heaven and the sand of the sea.

For, Lord, we have become less than all the nations, and today we are humbled throughout the earth because of our sins” (Daniel 3:26–37).

You certainly see, brother, what kind of men these were—how holy and how courageous in the midst of tribulation, although they were being spared there and the very flame feared to burn them. They confessed their sins, for which they knew they were being humbled deservedly and justly, and they did not remain silent.

## 4

Can we perhaps be better than Daniel himself, concerning whom God says through the prophet Ezekiel to the prince of Tyre: “Are you wiser than Daniel?” (Ezek. 28:3)? He is also counted among the three righteous whom God says he alone would deliver, thereby showing in them three kinds of righteous persons whom he says he would deliver in such a way that they themselves alone would be delivered, not even their sons along with them: Noah, Daniel, and Job (Ezek. 14:14, 16).

[Note: “In Noah,” as he says in *On the Destruction of the City*, chapter 1, “the good superiors are signified, who rule and govern the Church, just as Noah governed the ark in the flood. In Daniel all the holy continent are signified. In Job all married people who live justly and well are signified.” Consult Bernard, Sermon 6, *On the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord*, and Sermon 3, *On the Assumption of the Blessed Mary*.]

Read Daniel’s prayer as well, and see how, while placed in captivity, he confesses not only the sins of his people but also his own, and declares that, on account of them, he had reached that punishment and disgrace of captivity through God’s justice. For it is written:

“And I turned my face to the Lord God, seeking prayers and supplications with fasting and sackcloth; and I prayed to the Lord my God, and confessed, and said:

‘O great and wondrous Lord God, who keeps your covenant and mercy with those who love you and keep your commandments, we have sinned, we have acted against the Law, we have acted wickedly, and we have withdrawn and turned aside from your commandments and from your judgments; and we have not listened to your servants the Prophets, who spoke in your name to our kings and to all the people of the land.
