To you, Lord, belongs righteousness; but to us, confusion of face, as on this day—to the men of Judah, to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and to all Israel, those who are near and those who are far away, in every land where you scattered them, because of their defiance by which they rejected you, Lord.

But to us belongs confusion of face—to our kings, our princes, and our fathers, because we have sinned. To the Lord our God belong mercies and acts of forgiveness,

[Note: Thus it stands in nearly all manuscripts and also among the Septuagint. But in Badius, Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain it reads: “Because we have sinned against you, Lord our God of mercy and forgiveness.” The editions likewise give a little later: “Which he brought before us through the hands of his servants the Prophets of all Israel. For they sinned,” and so forth. We have restored this passage according to the authority of the manuscripts.]

because we have withdrawn and have not listened to the voice of the Lord our God, so as to walk in the precepts of this law which he set before us through the hand of his servants the Prophets.

And all Israel have transgressed your law and turned aside, refusing to listen to your voice. Therefore the curse and the oath have come upon us, which are written in the law of Moses, the servant of God, because we have sinned; and he has confirmed his words, which he spoke against us and against our judges who judged us, bringing upon us great evils such as had never been done under all heaven, according to what was done in Jerusalem.

As it is written in the Law of Moses, all these evils have come upon us; yet we did not entreat the Lord our God to turn our offenses away from us and to make us understand all your truth.

And the Lord our God kept watch over all his holy things and brought upon us what he had done, because the Lord our God is just in all the works that he has made, and we did not listen to his voice.

And now, Lord our God, who brought your people out of the land of Egypt with a strong hand and made yourself a name, as at this day, we have sinned against your law.

Lord, in all your mercy, let your anger and your wrath be turned away from your city Jerusalem and from your holy mountain. For because of our sins and the iniquities of our fathers, Jerusalem and your people have become a reproach to all who surround us.

And now hear, our God, the prayers of your servant and his supplication, and show us your face for the sake of your sanctuary, which is desolate.

For your own sake, incline your ear, my God, and hear; open your eyes and see our desolation and that of your city Jerusalem, over which your name has been invoked,

[Note: The earlier editions omit “over which”; it is found, however, in the manuscripts and in the Septuagint.]

because we have not cast our prayer before you on the basis of our righteousness, but on the basis of your great mercy.

Hear, Lord; be gracious, Lord; attend, Lord, and do not delay,

[Note: The editions read, “and do not hand us over.” But most manuscripts more correctly have “and do not delay,” in accordance with the Septuagint, *mē chronisēs* (“do not delay”), and the Vulgate, “do not tarry.”]

for your own sake, my God, because your name has been invoked upon your city, upon your city and your people.’

And while I was still speaking and praying and confessing my sins and the sins of my people—

[Note: Louvain adds here: “I heard a voice saying to me, ‘Daniel, understand the words that I speak to you, for I have been sent to you,’” and then continues: “See how …” But in nine manuscripts, after “I have been sent to you,” these further words are added: “For Michael, one of the chief princes of the angels, has also come to my aid, and strengthened me, and restored health to me from the sorrow by which I was greatly oppressed.” This addition does not sufficiently agree with the sacred text and is in fact entirely absent from the better-quality manuscripts and from Erasmus’s edition.]

(Dan. 9:3–20).

See how he first mentioned his own sins and afterward those of his people. He commends this justice of God and declares this to be God’s praise: that he scourges even his holy ones, not unjustly but on account of their sins. If, then, such things are said by those who, with the highest holiness, had fire and lions harmlessly around them, what ought we to say in our lowliness, who are so far inferior to them, however much justice we may appear to maintain?

## 5

But lest anyone suppose that those servants of God whom you say were killed by barbarians ought to have escaped that death in the same way as those three men were delivered from the fires and Daniel from the lions, let him know that those miracles were performed so that the kings by whom they were handed over to those punishments might believe that they worshiped the true God.

For this was part of God’s hidden judgment and mercy: that by this means he might provide for the salvation of those kings. But he did not wish to provide for King Antiochus in this way. He had cruelly put the Maccabees to death, and by their most glorious sufferings he punished the heart of that harsh king with still greater severity.

Read also what one of them—the one who suffered in the sixth place—says. For it is written:

“And after him they brought forward the sixth. When he had been tortured by torments and was dying, he said: ‘Do not deceive yourself because of us. We are suffering these things because we have sinned against our God, and these things have happened to us deservedly. But do not suppose that you will remain unpunished, since you have chosen to fight against God and his Law by means of your laws’” (2 Macc. 7:18–19).

You see how humbly and truthfully these men also understand matters: they confess that they are scourged by the Lord on account of their sins. Of him it is written: “For whom the Lord loves, he corrects” (Prov. 3:12); and, “He scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6). Hence the Apostle also says: “For if we judged ourselves, we would not be judged by the Lord. But when we are judged, we are corrected by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world” (1 Cor. 11:31–32).

## 6

Read these things faithfully, preach them faithfully, and take every possible care—and teach others to take care—not to murmur against God in these temptations and tribulations.

You say that good, faithful, and holy servants of God were killed by the sword of the barbarians. But what difference does it make whether fever or iron released them from the body? The Lord considers not by what circumstance they depart, but what kind of people they are when they depart to him in his servants. Except that prolonged illness entails a greater punishment than a very swift departure. Yet even that prolonged and dreadful illness is something we read of: it was the kind suffered by that Job whose righteousness God himself, who cannot be deceived, bears such testimony.

## 7

That captivity of chaste and holy women is certainly most grievous and deeply to be lamented. But their God is not captive, nor does he abandon those who are his, if he knows them to be his. For those holy persons whose sufferings and confessions I have recalled from the holy Scriptures were led away by enemies and placed in captivity; yet they spoke the words that were written down for us to read, so that we might learn that the captive servants of God are not abandoned by their Lord.

How do we know what the almighty and merciful God may also wish to accomplish through these women in that barbarian land, by his wondrous works? Only do not cease to groan to God on their behalf, and, as far as you can and as far as he permits, when he provides the time and opportunity, seek to discover what has happened to them or what consolations you may be able to offer them.

For a few years ago a consecrated virgin, the niece of Severus, bishop of Sitifis—

[Note: Louvain has “the Sitifian woman.” Badius, Amerbach, and Erasmus have “the Sitisian woman.” But all the manuscripts have “the niece of Severus, bishop of Sitifis.” Supply “from the region,” or something similar, as in the immediately following letter, where we read: “those whom you have in the region of Sinitis or Hippo.”]

—was carried away by barbarians and, through God’s wondrous mercy, was restored with great honor to her parents.

For the house of those barbarians into which she entered as a captive suddenly began to be shaken by the illness of its masters, so that all those barbarians—three brothers, if I am not mistaken, or more—were suffering from a most dangerous illness. Their mother noticed that the girl was devoted to God and believed that, through her prayers, her sons could be delivered from the danger of death that was already threatening them. She asked her to pray for them, promising that, if they recovered, they would return her to her parents.

She fasted and prayed, and was immediately heard. For this was why it had happened, as the outcome showed. Thus, having received health through so sudden a benefit from God, they marveled at and honored her and fulfilled what their mother had promised.

## 8

Pray, then, to God for them, and ask him to teach them also to say such things as the holy Azariah mentioned above poured forth to God, among other things, in his prayer and confession.

For they are in the land of their captivity just as those men were in that land where they could not sacrifice to the Lord according to their custom, just as these women cannot: either carry an offering to God’s altar or find there a priest through whom they may offer to God.

May the Lord therefore grant them to say to him what Azariah said in the continuation of his prayers:

“‘At this time there is no prince, prophet, or leader; no burnt offering, offering, or supplications; no place to sacrifice before you and to find mercy. But may we be received with a contrite soul and a spirit of humility.

As with the burnt offerings of rams and bulls and with the multitude of fat lambs, so may our sacrifice be today in your sight, to bring to completion those who follow you, for there will be no shame for those who trust in you.

And now we follow you with all our heart and fear you, and we seek your face, Lord. Do not put us to shame, but deal with us according to your gentleness and according to the multitude of your mercy. Deliver us according to your wonders, and give glory to your name, Lord.

Let all who inflict evils upon your servants be put to shame and fear; let them be confounded by your almighty power, and let their strength be crushed; and let them know that you alone are the Lord God, glorious throughout the whole world’” (Dan. 3:38–45).

## 9

When they say these things and groan to God, he who is accustomed to be present with his own will assuredly be present with his own. Either he will permit nothing to be perpetrated by hostile lust against their most chaste bodies, or, if he permits it, he will not count it against them.

For when the soul is stained by no shameful consent, it also defends its own flesh from guilt; and whatever lust inflicted upon the body of the sufferer, which she neither committed nor permitted, will belong solely to the guilt of the perpetrator. All that violence will be reckoned not as the shame of corruption but as the wound of suffering.

The integrity of chastity has such power in the mind that, while it remains inviolate, modesty cannot be violated even in the body, although its members may have been overpowered.

[Note: See *On the City of God*, book 1, chapters 16 and 18.]

Let this letter, brief in accordance with your desire but nevertheless very long in view of my occupations, and written with excessive haste because of the courier’s urgency, suffice for your affection. The Lord will console you much more abundantly if you read his Scriptures with the greatest attention.

# LETTER 112

[Note: It was collated with manuscripts a, bg, bl, c, cc, fi, g, gv, n, r, s, t, vc; three sb manuscripts; two v manuscripts; and with the editions of Amerbach, Badius, Erasmus, and Louvain.]

[Note: Formerly numbered 128; the letter that was formerly 112 is now 147. Written at the end of 409 or the beginning of 410.]

Augustine urges Donatus, a former proconsul, to abandon all pride and follow Christ, and to attract his associates to communion with the Catholic Church.

To the distinguished lord and brother Donatus, honorable for his most sincere affection, Augustine sends greetings in the Lord.

### 1

Because, while greatly longing to see you in office, I was unable to do so even when you came to Tibilis—

[Note: Badius, Amerbach, and Erasmus have “Cibilis.”]

—I believe this happened so that I might enjoy your mind, freed from public cares, rather than have that greeting, with me at leisure and you occupied, fail to temper the longing of either of us as fully as would have been fitting.

Recalling the integrity of your character from your earliest years, I consider your heart abundantly suitable for Christ to pour himself into it most generously, so that you may bear fruit for him worthy of eternal and heavenly glory rather than of temporal and earthly praise.

### 2

For many people—indeed, practically everyone whom I have been able either to question or even spontaneously to hear praising you—consistently and emphatically praise and commend the chastity and excellence of your administration. I received this testimony without any hesitation concerning its varied agreement, and all the more confidently because those who praised you were unaware of our relationship and did not know at all whether I even knew you slightly; otherwise I might have thought that they had merely adapted themselves to my ears rather than spread what was true about you.

Praise is far removed from vanity when even blame is free from offense.

Nevertheless, distinguished brother, honorable for your most sincere affection, you do not now need instruction, but perhaps admonition: all this glory and popular reputation should not be pleasing because it is on the lips of the crowd, but because it exists in the realities themselves. Even if these things displease the crowd, they are precious through their own brilliance and weight, not through the commendation of the ignorant. The person who condemns such things is more deserving of pity than the person who is judged miserable because of them.

When they do please people and are also publicly proclaimed with the praise due to them, they do not thereby become greater or better through another’s judgment; for they are perfected by their inner truth and made firm by the strength of conscience alone. Thus something of happiness comes rather to people who judge rightly than to the one whom the crowd judges favorably.

### 3

Since you know these things very well, good man, look—as you have begun to do—with the strongest gaze of your heart upon our Lord Jesus Christ. Completely swelling down from all empty pride, rise toward him who does not inflate those who turn to him with empty wind, but places those who lean upon and ascend by sure steps of faith upon the eternal summit of heavenly and angelic dignity.

Through him I beg you to write back to me and to urge, courteously and kindly, all your people whom you have in the region of Sinitis or Hippo to communion with the Catholic Church.

I have learned that your praiseworthy and distinguished father was also begotten by you in her bosom. I ask you to greet him for me with the honor due to his merits, and not to consider it burdensome to visit us. I also make this request—not presumptuously—for the sake of making your affairs, which you have here, better before God.

May God’s mercy surround you and preserve you from every iniquity.

# LETTER 113

[Note: Letters 113, 114, 115, and 116 are not found in the manuscripts except in two Vatican manuscripts and one very ancient manuscript of Corbie.]

[Note: Formerly numbered 229; the letter that was formerly 113 is now 15. Written around this time, no earlier than 409 and no later than 413.]

Augustine asks Cresconius to assist his petition on behalf of Faventius.

To the most beloved, deservedly honorable, and worthy brother Cresconius—

[Note: Cresconius, to whom Augustine testifies here that he wrote once and again concerning Faventius’s case, is suspected to be that same tribune placed in charge of guarding the coast, to whom he immediately sent word after hearing of Faventius’s abduction, as he later says in Letter 115.]

—Augustine sends greetings in the Lord.

If I were to disregard this case, concerning which I am writing to your religious office for the second time, not only would Your Excellency, but also the man himself—whoever he may be, in whose case Faventius was abducted in this manner—rightly blame me and justly reproach me, judging that if he himself had fled to the Church for help and something similar had happened to him, I would likewise have disregarded his need and tribulation.

Moreover, if human opinion is to be despised, what shall I say to the Lord our God, and what account shall I give if I do not do everything I can for the safety of one who has entrusted himself to the Church that I serve, to be protected and assisted by it, most beloved and venerable son?

I therefore ask Your Kindness—for it is difficult and incredible that you do not already know, or cannot come to know, in what case he is being detained—to deign for the present to assist my petition with the official who holds him, so that he may do what the Emperor’s law commands:

[Note: A law on this matter was issued by Theodosius on 30 December 380. Here, however, Augustine reports almost the exact words of another law promulgated by Honorius in 409, on 21 January, in the Theodosian Code, book 9, title 2.]

that he should have him questioned before the municipal records, whether he wishes to be granted thirty days during which he may remain under moderate custody in the city where he is detained, so that he may put his affairs in order and provide for his expenses.

If, during that period of days, with your benevolent consent, we can settle his case through a friendly discussion, we shall rejoice. But if we cannot, the outcome of the legal proceedings will find him according to what pleases God, in keeping with the merits of his case or the will of the almighty Lord.

# LETTER 114

[Note: Formerly numbered 228; the letter that was formerly 114 is now 5. Written at the same time, after the preceding letter.]

To Florentinus concerning the same case of Faventius.

To the most beloved son Florentinus, Augustine sends greetings in the Lord.

You may determine by whose order and authority you abducted Faventius. But this I know: every power established under authority is subject to the laws of its emperor.

Although I have already sent, through my brother and fellow presbyter Caelestinus, the law—which, indeed, you ought not to have been unaware of even before I sent it—which grants to those ordered by any authority to be brought before a court that they be taken to the municipal records and questioned there whether they wish to spend thirty days in the city where they are held, under moderate custody, in order to prepare their resources or arrange their affairs as necessity requires, nevertheless I have now sent it again with this letter.

I do not send it to frighten you, but to ask you, and to intercede on behalf of a human being with the humanity and episcopal mercy that humanity and piety permit, my son and lord: deign to grant this both to your reputation and to my petition, and do not consider it burdensome to carry out, with my intervention and entreaty added, what the Emperor’s law commands, since you serve the state of that Emperor.

# LETTER 115

[Note: Formerly numbered 230; the letter that was formerly 115 is now 9 and 14. Written shortly after the preceding letter.]

To Fortunatus, bishop of Cirta, concerning the same matter.

To the most blessed and venerably beloved brother and fellow priest Fortunatus, and to the brothers who are with you, Augustine sends greetings in the Lord.

Your Holiness knows Faventius well; he was tenant of the Paratian estate. Since he feared some danger from the owner of that same property, he fled to the church at Hippo. There he was, as fugitives customarily are, awaiting the way in which his affairs might be settled through our intercession.

As often happens, he became less and less concerned with each passing day and, as though his adversary had ceased to act, grew confident. When he was leaving dinner at a friend’s house, he was suddenly seized by a certain Florentinus, they say an official of the Count, by a band of armed men as large as seemed sufficient for this deed.

When this was reported to me, and it was still unknown by whom or by what persons he had been abducted, there was nevertheless suspicion of the man from whom he had been protecting himself through the Church. I immediately sent to the tribune appointed to guard the coast. He sent soldiers; no one could be found.

But in the morning we learned both in what house he had been and that, after cockcrow, he had departed with the man who had held him. I also sent there where he was said to have been taken. When the aforesaid official was found there, he refused to allow the presbyter whom I had sent even to see him.

On another day I sent a letter asking that what the Emperor had commanded in such cases be granted to him: namely, that those ordered to be brought before the authorities should be questioned in the municipal records whether they wished to spend thirty days in that city under moderate custody, in order to arrange their affairs or prepare their expenses. I certainly thought that during those days we might perhaps settle his case through a friendly discussion.

But he has now been taken away in the company of that official. There is fear that, if he has been brought to the office of the Consular, he may suffer some harm. For he has a case against a very wealthy man, although the judge’s integrity is proclaimed by the clearest reputation.

Nevertheless, lest money prevail in the office, I ask Your Holiness, most beloved and venerable brother and lord, to deign to deliver my letter to the honorable and very dear Consular, and to read this letter to him. I did not think it necessary to present the same case twice. Ask him to postpone the hearing of the case, since I do not know whether Faventius is guilty or innocent.

Let him also not disregard the fact that the laws concerning him were not observed: that he was abducted in this manner, nor that, as the Emperor commanded, he was not taken to the municipal records to be questioned whether he wished to accept the benefit of a postponement. In this way we may be able to settle the matter with his adversary.

# LETTER 116

[Note: Formerly numbered 231; the letter that was formerly 116 is now 10. Written together with the preceding letter.]

Augustine commends the case of Faventius to Generosus, the Consular of Numidia.

To the distinguished, deservedly eminent, and honorably beloved son Generosus, Augustine sends greetings in the Lord.

The praise and commendation of your administration and your outstanding reputation have greatly delighted me, in view of the affection that we owe to your merits and kindness. Until now, my intercession has never burdened Your Excellency in requesting any favor, most beloved and venerable son and lord.

But now, when Your Eminence learns from the letter that I sent to my venerable brother and fellow bishop Fortunatus what happened in the city in which I serve God’s Church, your kindness will perceive what necessity compelled me to press my petition upon your occupations.

You will certainly do what befits not only an upright but also a Christian judge, displaying toward us the disposition that in Christ’s name we had every reason to expect.

# LETTER 117

[Note: Letters 117 and 118 were collated with manuscripts a, bg, bl, bn, c, cc, ff, g, gv, n, r, s, sb, vc, vd; two t manuscripts; four v manuscripts; and with the editions of Amerbach, Badius, Erasmus, and Louvain.]

[Note: Formerly numbered 55; the letter that was formerly 117 is now 4. Perhaps written at the beginning of 410.]

Dioscorus sends Augustine many questions from Cicero’s books, asking him to answer them promptly.

Offering a preface to you is not only superfluous but also troublesome, since you desire the matter rather than the words. Therefore listen simply.

The old man Alypius, when I asked him, had repeatedly promised to answer with you a few little questions from the dialogues. Since he is said still to be in Mauritania, I ask with all my strength and beg you to deign to answer alone—something you would undoubtedly have done even in the presence of that brother of yours.

There is no sum of money, no gold, that you would undoubtedly have given for anything, if you had it; but now you can say without effort what I ask. I could entreat you more insistently and through many of your dear friends, but I know your mind: it does not desire to be asked, but to provide for everyone, provided only that what is dishonorable is absent—and in this matter there is absolutely nothing dishonorable.

Nevertheless, whatever it is, I ask you to provide it for one who is about to sail. You know how exceedingly burdensome it is to me to be a burden—not to Your Sincerity, but to anyone at all. God alone knows how necessity, too great to resist, drove me to do this.

For I am going to sail with you safe and with God’s favor. You know human customs, which are prone to blame, and you see how, if someone does not answer when questioned, he will be considered ignorant and dull.

Therefore, I beg you, answer everything without hesitation, lest you send me away sad. So may I see my parents; for it is solely for this reason that I sent Cerdon, and I am waiting only for him.

Brother Zenobius has been made Master of the Records—

[Note: The “Master of the Records,” as the *Notitia Dignitatum* of the Empire states, “dictates and issues all annotations and responds to petitions”; that is, what the emperor answered orally, the Master dictated briefly and recorded. He issued diplomas for use in the public transport system—hence the reference here to his having “sent a travel warrant with provisions”—and finally dictated the replies given by the emperor to petitioners’ written appeals.]

—and he sent us a travel warrant with provisions. If I am not worthy for you to answer my little questions, at least let the provisions be feared.

May the Most High Divinity preserve you unharmed for us through a long life. Papas sends Your Dignity his warmest greetings.

# LETTER 118

[Note: Formerly numbered 56; the letter that was formerly 118 is now 54. Written shortly after the preceding letter.]

Augustine replies to Dioscorus that questions of this kind are neither becoming for a bishop to handle nor useful for a Christian to learn. He discusses the goal of study and the highest good, exhorting Dioscorus to pursue Christian philosophy, which alone was able to persuade people of the truth by setting before them the example of divine humility. Finally, he elucidates certain passages in which Cicero criticizes the philosophers’ opinions about God.

## CHAPTER ONE

### 1

You thought that you could suddenly surround me—or rather overwhelm me—with an innumerable host of questions, even if you believed me free and at leisure. For when could I, in any leisure, untie so many knots of so many matters for someone in such haste and, as you write, already almost departing?

The very number of the matters would hinder me, even if the knots were easy to untie. But they are entangled in such complexity and bound with such tenacity that, even if they were few, they would occupy me in the deepest leisure, exhaust my attention through a considerable delay of time, and wear down my fingernails.

I wish I could snatch you away from the midst of your delightful inquiries and pack you in among my cares, so that you might either learn not to be pointlessly curious or not dare to impose the feeding and nourishing of your curiosity upon those whose greatest concern among their cares is to restrain and curb the curious.

How much better and more fruitful it would be—if time and effort are spent in sending you any letter at all—to spend them instead cutting away your vain and deceptive desires. They must be avoided all the more because they deceive so easily, concealed and disguised, I do not know by what shadow of respectability and under the name of liberal studies, rather than to have them, through our service and, so to speak, our attendance, stirred up more vigorously into a domination—

[Note: Badius has “into a hardened attendance”; Erasmus has “of hardened attendance.”]

—in which they would oppress your good mind.

### 2

For look: if all the dialogues you have read have not helped you to see the goal and attain the end of all your actions, what use are they? Tell me.

Your letter sufficiently indicates where you have placed the end of this entire passionate study of yours, fruitless for you and troublesome for us. When you were writing to me about resolving the questions you sent, you wrote as follows:

“I could,” you say, “entreat you more insistently and through many of your dear friends; but I know your mind, which does not desire to be asked but to provide for everyone, provided only that what is dishonorable is absent—and in this matter there is absolutely nothing dishonorable. Nevertheless, whatever it is, I ask you to provide it for one who is about to sail.”

In these words of your letter you correctly judge of me that I desire to provide for everyone if what is dishonorable is absent. But that there is nothing dishonorable in this matter does not seem correct to me.

The fair appearance of such things does not affect my judgment when I think of a bishop constrained and overwhelmed by the uproar of ecclesiastical cares, suddenly stopping all those activities as though he had become deaf, in order to explain to a single schoolman the little questions of Cicero’s dialogues.

However much, carried away by the ardor of your studies, you may refuse to attend to how dishonorable this is, you nevertheless perceive it yourself. For what else does it indicate that, after saying that there was absolutely nothing dishonorable in this matter, you immediately added: “Nevertheless, whatever it is, I ask you to provide it for one who is about to sail”?

This means that it seems to you that there is indeed nothing dishonorable in this matter, but that, whatever dishonor there may be, you nevertheless ask me to provide it for one who is about to sail.

But why, I ask you, did you add “for one who is about to sail”? Would I not owe you something dishonorable if you were not about to sail? Surely you think that the shame is washed away by seawater. If that were so, at least my shame, since I am not about to sail, would remain unpurged.

### 3

You also write that you know how exceedingly burdensome it is to me to be a burden to anyone, and you affirm that God alone knows that excessive necessity drove you to do this.

When I read your letter at this point, I certainly noticed that you understood your need, when suddenly you bring forward and say to me:

“You know human customs, which are prone to blame, and how, if someone does not answer when questioned, he will be considered ignorant and dull.”

At this point I burned to write back to you. Through this sickness of your mind you entered my heart and burst into my cares, so that I could not conceal how much God was helping me to heal you—not so that I might think about unraveling and explaining your questions, but so that I might tear your happiness away from its dependence on human tongues, trembling from such an unhappy tether, and bind it to a seat entirely unshaken and firm.

Do you, Dioscorus, not even look at your Persius insulting you in a twisted verse, striking and restraining your childish head—if you have any understanding—with a thoroughly appropriate blow?

> “Your knowledge is nothing, unless another knows that you know it.”  
> (Persius, *Satire* 1.)

As I said above, you have read so many dialogues and absorbed into your heart so many disputes among philosophers. Tell me: which of them placed the end of their actions in the reputation of the crowd, or in the speech of good and wise people?

And yet you—not to mention what is more shameful, now that you are about to sail—testify quite plainly that you have made progress in Africa, since you assert that you do not wish to be a burden to the busiest bishops, occupied with matters altogether different, so that they might explain Cicero to you, for no other reason than that you fear people who are prone to blame and do not want, if questioned by them and unable to answer, to be considered ignorant and dull.

What a subject worthy of bishops’ vigils and nocturnal labors!

4. You do not seem to spend your days and nights thinking about anything other than being praised by people for your studies and learning. Although I have always judged this dangerous for those who are striving toward what is certain and right, I now experience it especially in your case. For it was only because of this same destructive influence that you failed to see by what consideration we might be moved to give you what you were asking. Just as you yourself are perversely driven to learn the things you ask about for no other reason than to be praised by people, or not criticized by them, so perversely you suppose that we too are moved in granting your request by such considerations.

And would that we could bring it about that you, too, would be entirely unmoved by such an empty and deceptive good as human praise, when we made clear to you [Col. 0434] that we were moved—not to provide you with what you ask because you write these things about yourself, but to correct you! “People’s character,” you say, “is inclined to criticize.” What follows? “If someone is questioned and does not answer,” you say, “he will be thought unlearned and dull.” Very well: I question you—not about something in Cicero’s books whose meaning readers perhaps cannot discover, but about your own letter and the meaning of your words. For I ask why you did not say, “Anyone who does not answer will be shown to be unlearned and dull,” but instead said, “He will be thought unlearned and dull”—unless it is because you yourself understand well enough that one who does not answer such questions is not unlearned and dull, but merely thought to be so. But I warn you that anyone who fears being cut to pieces by the pruning-hook tongues of such “thinkers” is dry wood; and therefore he is not merely thought unlearned and dull, but truly is so and is proved to be so.

5. Perhaps you will say: “But since I am not dull in mind, and especially since I strive not to be so, I do not want to be thought dull in mind either.” Quite properly; but I am asking for what purpose you do not want this. For when you did not hesitate to say that the reason and purpose for which you wanted those questions opened up and explained to you—and for which you did not hesitate to burden us—was so necessary that you called it an “urgent necessity,” it was, plainly, lest, if questioned about these matters and unable to answer, you should be thought dull and unlearned by people inclined to criticize.

I, however, ask whether this is the whole reason why you desire these things from us, or whether there is some other reason why you do not want to be thought unlearned and dull. If this is the whole reason, you see, I think, that this is the end of your vehement exertion, by which, as you admit, you burden us as well. But what can Dioscorus be a burden to us for, except something that burdens Dioscorus himself, even though he does not know it? He will not feel it until he wants to rise; and would that these burdens were not so tightly fastened that he should try in vain to shake them from his shoulders! I do not say this because these questions are being learned, but because they are being learned for such an end.

You certainly now perceive that this end is trifling, empty, and wind-filled. It also contains swelling, beneath which corruption is generated, and a film spreads over the eye of the mind so that it cannot see the abundance of truth. Believe me, my Dioscorus, it is so—so may I enjoy you in the very will, and in the very dignity of truth, from whose shadow you turn away. For I find no way to convince you of this matter except perhaps in this manner. You do not see it; nor can you see it in any way so long as you build ruinous joys out of human tongues.

6. But if that is not the end of these actions and of your purpose, and you do not want to be thought unlearned and dull for some other reason, what is that reason, I ask? If it is so that your access may not be narrowed to acquiring temporal riches, obtaining a wife, seeking honors, and other such things—which rush past in headlong flow and drag those who fall into them down to the bottom—then it is not right for us to serve you even toward this end; indeed, it is right for us to draw you away from it as well.

For we do not forbid you to make uncertain reputation the ultimate end of your actions in such a way that you would migrate, as it were, from the Mincius into the Eridanus; indeed, the Mincius itself might perhaps drive you into it even without your migrating. When the vanity of human praise has not satisfied the greedy spirit—for it offers nothing with which to feed it except something empty and inflated—greed itself forces it to transfer its desire to something else, as though that were richer and more fruitful. Yet if this too flows past in temporal decline, it is as though one river should lead into another, so that misery has no end so long as the end of our actions is placed in something unstable [Note: [Col. 0435] Most manuscripts: “is not placed in a stable thing.”].

We therefore want to fix you in some firm and unchanging good, the home of your most steadfast purpose and the most secure rest of all your good and honorable action. Or do you perhaps intend to transfer even that earthly happiness I mentioned—if you are able to reach it by spreading your sails before a breeze, or even before gusts, of favorable rumor—to some other certain, true, and complete good? But this does not seem so to me; indeed, truth itself wholly denies that one can reach what is so near by such lengthy detours, or what is so freely given by such great expenditures.

7. Or do you think that human praise should be used as an instrument, so that through it you may prepare access to people’s minds in order to persuade them of what is true and salutary? And do you fear that, once they have thought you unlearned and dull, they will consider you unworthy of receiving their attentive or patient ear, whether you exhort someone to right conduct or rebuke the wickedness and depravity of a sinner?

If you had this end in mind when asking us those questions, then we have treated you badly by placing in your letter something other than what would move us—something that would either make us gladly give you what you asked, or make us refuse it for some other reason that might perhaps prevent us, but not because we were ashamed not only to serve your empty desire but even to resist it.

How much better and more salutary it would be, I ask you, if you received the very principles of truth themselves, much more certainly and briefly, so that you could refute all falsehoods yourself. Otherwise, if you learn the old and decrepit falsehoods of many people with more ostentatious than prudent zeal, you may come to think yourself learned and intelligent—although I no longer suppose that this seems so to you. For it was not without reason that we spoke such true things to Dioscorus for so long; and from that point we proceed in this letter.

**CHAPTER II**

8. Let us therefore now consider this matter: since you judge yourself neither unlearned nor dull through ignorance of these things, but rather through ignorance of truth itself, so that whatever anyone has written or may write about them either consists of matters you already hold with certainty or, if false, may safely be ignored; and since you are not to be tormented by empty anxiety about learning the differing opinions of others lest you remain apparently unlearned and dull—since this is so, let us also consider, if you please, whether the false opinion of others, who, as you write, are inclined to criticize, so that if they discover that you are ignorant of these matters they may falsely, yet nevertheless, think you unlearned and dull, ought to move you so far that you should not incongruously ask bishops to explain these things to you.

For we already believe that you desire these things for the purpose of assisting them in persuading to the truth and correcting the lives of those who, if they think you unlearned and dull in Cicero’s books, will regard you as unworthy to be someone from whom they should receive useful and salutary knowledge. But believe me, that is not how things stand.

First, I see no possibility that there are people in those regions where you fear appearing inexperienced and insufficiently sharp who will ask you anything about these questions. For here, where you came to learn such matters, you have discovered in Rome how negligently they are regarded and, for that reason, neither taught nor learned. And in Africa you tolerate no questioner about them to such an extent that you cannot even find anyone—including yourself—who will tolerate you; consequently, because of this lack, you are forced to send these matters to be explained to bishops.

It is as though these bishops, even if they were adolescents, had pursued the study of these matters with the same fervor—or rather error—that carries you away, and had allowed them to remain in their memories until their episcopal gray hairs and ecclesiastical chairs; or as though, even if they wanted to do so, they could prevent other greater and heavier concerns from excluding them from the hearts of unwilling people; or as though, if some of these matters remained in their minds through excessive familiarity, they would not prefer to bury them in forgetfulness rather than recall them in order to answer foolish questions.

And yet, even in the very lightness of their student days and rhetorical chairs, they seem to have fallen so silent and become so stupefied that they are thought to have to be sent from Carthage to Hippo, where such things can be explained. These matters are so unusual and altogether foreign there that, if I wished to examine something in order to prepare an answer—wishing to see how one arrives at the point that would have to be explained to me, or what discourse could subsequently be woven from it—I could not find a book at all.

But if the Carthaginian rhetoricians have failed your zeal, I not only do not criticize them, I even approve them, if perhaps they now remember that such contests belong not to the courts of Rome but to the gymnasia of Greece. Yet when you turned your thoughts toward the gymnasia and found even them bare and cold with respect to such matters, the basilica of the Christians at Hippo came to mind, because a bishop now sits there who once sold these things to boys.

But I do not want you still to be a boy; and it is not fitting that I, just as I am no longer a seller of childish things, should be a distributor of them either. Since this is so—that is, since the two great cities, Rome and Carthage, the craftsmen of Latin literature, neither trouble themselves enough about these matters to inquire after them from you nor care enough about your troubles to listen to you while you inquire after them—I am astonished beyond words that you, a young man of such good talent, fear that in the Greek and Eastern cities you may encounter some troublesome questioner about these matters. You will hear jackdaws more easily in Africa than this kind of voice in those regions.

10. Next, if I am mistaken, and someone there has perhaps appeared as a questioner of such matters—one all the more detestable because such questioning is more foolish in those places—should you not rather fear that there will be people who, when you are established in Greece and have first been imbued with the Greek language, will ask you questions from the very books of the philosophers about matters that Cicero did not include in his writings?

If this happens, what will you answer? That you preferred to know these things from the books of Latin authors rather than from the Greek ones? In that answer you will first insult Greece—and you know how unwilling those people are to endure this. Then, already wounded and angry, how quickly they will judge you—something you very much do not want—as dull, because you preferred to learn in Latin dialogues the doctrines of the Greek philosophers, or rather certain torn and scattered fragments of their doctrines, rather than learning them whole and coherently in the Greek books of their own authors; and unlearned, because, while you do not know so many things in your own language, you have striven vainly to gather such matters in a foreign one.

Or perhaps you will answer that you have not despised Greek books on these subjects, but first took care to learn the Latin ones, and now, having become learned in Latin, wish to seek the Greek? If a Greek is not ashamed to have learned Latin like a child, and now wishes to learn Greek like a barbarian, will you finally not be ashamed to be ignorant in Latin of matters that, as you yourself perceive from the fact that you say you are a burden to us out of great necessity, so many learned Latins in the great multitude of learned people at Carthage do not know along with you?

11. Finally, suppose that you were able to answer questions about everything you ask from us. There you are, now called extremely learned and sharp; there you are, now lifted to heaven by a Greekling’s puff of praise. You need only remember your dignity and decide for what purpose you wish to deserve that praise: namely, that you should teach those who have lightly admired these light matters and who, with the greatest goodwill and eagerness, now hang upon your lips something most serious and salutary.

I would like to know whether you possess and know how to convey that very thing—whatever it is—that is most serious and salutary. For it is ridiculous to have learned many unnecessary things for the purpose of preparing people’s ears to receive what is necessary, and then not to possess the necessary things for receiving which you prepared their ears through the unnecessary ones; and while you are occupied in learning how to make people attentive, to refuse to learn what should be poured into those who are attentive.

But if you now say that you know this, and answer that it is precisely Christian doctrine—which we know you place above everything and in which alone you presume there is hope of eternal salvation—then there is no need to procure hearers for it through knowledge of Cicero’s dialogues and the collection of other people’s conflicting opinions gathered by begging. Let those who are going to receive such a thing from you become attentive to your conduct. I do not want you first to teach something that must later be unlearned, so that you may teach the truth.

12. For if knowledge of the differing and conflicting opinions of others helps the proclaimer of Christian truth, so that he may know how to destroy opposing falsehoods, this is useful only lest someone who argues against him fix his eyes exclusively on refuting your position while carefully concealing his own. For knowledge of the truth is capable of judging and overthrowing all falsehoods, provided they are brought forward—even those that were previously unheard.

But if, in order that not only what is openly displayed may be struck down but also what is hidden may be drawn out, it is necessary to know the errors of others, raise your eyes and ears, I beg you, and see and listen whether anyone is bringing anything against us concerning Anaximenes or Anaxagoras. By now, even the ashes of the much later and very talkative Stoics or Epicureans are no longer warm enough to kindle some spark against the Christian faith. Instead, circles and gatherings—some evasive, others boldly forward—of Donatists, Maximianists, Manichaeans, and even Arians, Eunomians, Macedonians, Cataphrygians, and countless other plagues, among whose flocks and crowds you are going to arrive, are resounding everywhere.

If you are reluctant to learn the errors of all these people, why should we, for the defense of the Christian religion, seek to know what Anaximenes thought and rekindle long-dormant disputes through empty curiosity, when the disputes and questions of certain heretics who wished to glory in the Christian name—such as the Marcionites and Sabellians, and many others besides—are already being left unmentioned?

Nevertheless, if, as I said, it is necessary to know beforehand some opinions opposed to the truth and to have examined them, we ought to have thought about heretics who call themselves Christians rather than about Anaxagoras and Democritus.

**CHAPTER III**

13. Whoever asks you the questions you ask us should hear from you that you do not know them more learnedly and wisely. For if Themistocles did not care that he was considered less learned when he refused to play the lyre at banquets—when he admitted that he did not know how to do so and, after someone said to him, “What, then, do you know?” replied, “How to make a small state great”—should you hesitate to say that you do not know these things, when, if someone asks what you do know, you can answer that you know how a person can be happy even without them?

If you still do not possess this knowledge, you pursue these matters as perversely as someone who, weighed down by a dangerous bodily illness, should seek delicacies and the softest clothing rather than medicines and physicians. This knowledge must not in any way be postponed, nor—especially at your age—should any order of learning be preferred to it.

Consider, however, how easily you could know this if you wished. For whoever asks how [Note: [Col. 0438] Most manuscripts: “For whoever asks by what [route] to, etc.” One Vatican manuscript: “by what way.”] to reach the happy life is certainly asking nothing other than where the end of the good lies—that is, where the highest good of human beings has been established, not by a perverse and reckless opinion, but by certain and unshakable truth. Wherever anyone establishes this, it is found to be either in the body, or in the mind, or in God, or in two of these, or certainly in all of them.

If you learn that neither the highest good nor any part of the highest good is in the body, two things remain: mind and God, and it must be in one of them or in both. If you then add and learn the same concerning the mind as concerning the body, what else will present itself but God, in whom the highest good of human beings is established? This does not mean that other goods do not exist; rather, that is called the highest good to which everything is referred.

For each person is happy by enjoying that for whose sake he wishes to possess the other things, while he loves this one not for the sake of anything else but for its own sake. And therefore it is called the end, because nothing remains toward which it may advance or to which it may be referred. There is the rest of desire, the security of enjoyment, and the most tranquil joy of the best will.

14. Grant that someone may quickly see that the good of the mind is not the body, but rather that the good of the body is the mind; then the inquiry will already cease as to whether that highest good, or any part of it, is in the body [Col. 0439]. For what is most foolishly denied is that the mind is better than the body. It is equally foolish to deny that the one who gives blessed life, or some part of blessed life, is better than the one who receives it.

The mind therefore does not receive from the body either the highest good or any part of the highest good. Those who do not see this have been blinded by the sweetness of bodily pleasures; they do not perceive that this sweetness arises from a lack of health. Perfect bodily health, however, will be the final immortality of the whole human being.

For God made the soul with such powerful a nature that, from the soul’s fullest blessedness—which is promised to the saints at the end of time—there will also overflow into the lower nature, the body, not the blessedness proper to one who enjoys and understands, but the fullness of health, that is, the vigor of incorruption.

Those who do not see this, as I said, engage in restless disputes and, each according to his own capacity, establish the highest human good in the body and stir up seditious crowds of the flesh. Among these, the Epicureans flourished with greater authority among the unlearned multitude.

15. Grant also that someone may quickly see that the mind itself is not blessed by its own good when it is blessed; otherwise it would never be miserable. Then the inquiry will cease as to whether that highest and, so to speak, beatifying good—or any part of it—is in the mind.

For when the mind rejoices in itself as though it were its own good, it is proud. But when it perceives that it is changeable—even in the one respect that it becomes wise from being foolish—and sees that wisdom is unchangeable, it must at the same time perceive that wisdom is above its own nature, and that through wisdom’s participation and illumination it rejoices more fully and more certainly than in itself.

Thus, ceasing and subsiding from its own boasting and inflation, it strives to cling to God and to be restored and refashioned by that unchangeable one. From him it begins to derive not only the beauty of all things—whether those reached by bodily sensation or those reached by the understanding of the mind—but also the very capacity for formation before formation, when something is called formless because it can be formed.

Accordingly, the less it clings to God, who supremely is, the less stable it feels itself to be. And therefore God supremely is because he neither advances nor declines through any change; whereas the change by which the mind advances is beneficial to it, so that it may cling perfectly to God, while the change that involves decline is vicious.

Every decline tends toward destruction. Whether or not a thing reaches this point, it is nevertheless evident that everything tends toward destruction so that it is no longer what it was. Hence he concludes that things decline, or can decline, for no other reason than that they were made from nothing.

Thus whatever they possess by which they are what they are and remain what they are, and by which, even through their declines, they are ordered into the whole universe, belongs to the goodness and omnipotence of the one who supremely is and who is the creator—who is powerful enough to make from nothing not merely something but even something great.

The first sin, that is, the first voluntary decline, is rejoicing in one’s own power; for one rejoices in something lesser than if one rejoices in the power of God, which is certainly greater. Those who do not see this, and who attend to the powers of the human mind and to the great beauty of its deeds and words, even if they were ashamed to place the highest good in the body, nevertheless placed it in the mind itself, and thus placed it below where it ought to be placed according to the purest reason.

Among the Greek philosophers who held this view, the Stoics prevailed both in number and in subtlety of argument. Yet, because they thought everything in nature corporeal, they were able to turn the mind away from flesh more readily than from the body.

16. Among those who say that our one and highest good is enjoyment of God, from whom both we and all things were made, the Platonists were preeminent. They rightly considered it their duty to resist the Stoics and especially the Epicureans—indeed, almost the Epicureans alone.

The Academics were the same as the Platonists, as the succession of their students itself demonstrates. For when you ask whom Arcesilas succeeded—Arcesilas being the first to conceal his own position and decide to do nothing other than refute them—you will find Polemo. Ask whom Polemo succeeded, and you will find Xenocrates. Plato left his own school, the Academy, to Xenocrates, his pupil.

So, as far as the question of the highest human good is concerned, remove the persons from the discussion and set out the dispute itself. You will certainly find two errors clashing face to face: one placing the highest good in the body, the other placing it in the mind.

The principle of truth, by which God is understood to be our highest good, resists both. Yet it does not teach what is true without first unteaching what is wrong. Now set out the same matter with the persons included, and you will find Epicureans and Stoics fighting one another with the greatest vehemence; while the Platonists attempt to judge their dispute, concealing the truth of their own position and convicting and refuting the others’ empty confidence in falsehood.

17. But the Platonists were unable to fulfill the role of true reason as those others fulfilled the role of their errors. For all of them lacked the example of divine [Note: [Col. 0440] Five manuscripts: “true.”] humility, which was revealed at the most fitting time through our Lord Jesus Christ. Before this one example, all pride in any mind that arrogantly claims superiority yields, breaks, and dies.

Therefore, since they lacked the authority to lead crowds blinded by love [Note: [Col. 0440] Bad., Am., Er.: delectatione, “delight.”] of earthly things to faith in invisible realities, and since they saw those crowds stirred especially by Epicurean arguments—not only to imbibe bodily pleasure, toward which they were already spontaneously inclined, but also to defend it, so that the highest human good might be established in it—they observed that those who were moved against this pleasure by the praise of virtue could less difficultly contemplate virtue in human minds, from which good deeds, which they could judge at least somewhat, proceeded.

At the same time they saw that, if they attempted to introduce to such people some divine reality, unchangeable above all things, which could be reached by no bodily sense but understood by the mind alone, and which nevertheless surpassed the very nature of the mind; if they proposed that this reality was God, set before the human mind for enjoyment once it had been cleansed of every stain of human desires, in whom alone every desire for blessedness would find rest, and in whom alone the end of all our goods would lie—such people would not understand.

And if Epicureans or Stoics opposed them, they would much more easily win the palm than the Platonists themselves. Thus the true and salutary position would be degraded by the mockery of unlearned peoples—an outcome most destructive to the human race. This was the situation in moral matters.

18. In natural questions, if the Platonists said that incorporeal Wisdom was the maker of all natures, while the others never withdrew from the body—some assigning atoms as the principles of things, others the four elements, among which fire was dominant in producing everything—who would not see that the multitude of fools, devoted to the body, would be unable to contemplate the incorporeal power that created things, and would instead be swept into the support of those others?

19. The rational questions remained. For you know that whatever is sought for the attainment of wisdom involves a question either of morals, of nature, or of reason.

Since the Epicureans said that the bodily senses never deceive, while the Stoics admitted that they sometimes deceive, yet both placed in the senses the rule for grasping truth, who would listen to the Platonists when these people opposed them?

Who would think them worthy to be counted not merely among the wise but among human beings at all, if they openly said that there is something that cannot be perceived by bodily touch, smell, or taste, nor by these ears or eyes, nor even imagined through any representation of things perceived in such ways; but that only this truly exists, and only this can be perceived, because it is unchangeable and everlasting—and that it is perceived by understanding alone, through which alone truth is reached, however it can be reached?

20. Since the Platonists held such views—views that they could neither teach to people devoted to the flesh nor persuade the crowds to believe on the authority they possessed, until the mind had been brought to the condition in which such things can be grasped—they chose to conceal their position and argue against those who boasted that they had found the truth, when they placed the discovery of truth itself in the senses of the flesh.

What need is there to ask what their plan was? Certainly it was not divine, nor endowed with any divine authority. Attend only to this: Cicero very clearly shows in many ways that Plato placed the end of the good, the causes of things, and confidence in reasoning in wisdom—not human but plainly divine—from which human wisdom was in some way kindled; that is, in the wholly unchangeable wisdom and truth that always remains the same [Note: [Col. 0441] Lov. reads *veritatem constituisse* (“to have established truth”). But the other editions and almost all manuscripts have *veritate* (“in truth”).].

The Platonists, under the names of Epicureans and Stoics, opposed those who placed in the nature either of the body or of the mind the end of the good, the causes of things, and confidence in reasoning. In the course of time the matter came to this: at the beginning of the Christian age, when faith in invisible and eternal realities was salutarily proclaimed to people through visible miracles—people who were unable either to see or to conceive anything except bodies—the very Epicureans and Stoics are found, in the Acts of the Apostles, to have opposed the blessed apostle Paul, who was sowing that same message among the Gentiles.

21. In this matter it seems to me sufficiently demonstrated that the errors of the Gentiles—whether concerning morals, the nature of things, or the method of investigating truth—which, although numerous and manifold, were especially prominent in these two schools, endured into Christian times, despite the learned attacking them and overturning them through arguments of such subtlety and abundance.

In our own age we see them now so silenced that their opinions are scarcely even mentioned in the schools of rhetoricians. Their disputes have nevertheless been uprooted and suppressed even from the most talkative Greek gymnasia, so that if any sect of error now arises against the truth—that is, against the Church of Christ—it does not dare to advance into combat unless it is covered by the Christian name.

From this it is understood that even the philosophers of the Platonic school ought, with a few changes in matters rejected by Christian discipline, to submit their devout necks to Christ, the one unconquerable king, and to understand that the Word of God was clothed with humanity—he who commanded, and what they feared even to utter was believed.

22. I would like you, my Dioscorus, to submit yourself wholly and devoutly to him, and not to construct for yourself any other road for taking hold of and attaining the truth than the road constructed by him who, as God, saw the weakness of our steps.

The first thing is humility; the second thing is humility; the third thing is humility. And however often you might ask me, I would say this. I do not mean that there are no other precepts to be given, but unless humility both precedes and accompanies and follows everything we do well—being set before us as the object we contemplate, placed beside us as the support to which we cling, and imposed upon us as the restraint by which we are checked—pride snatches everything from our hand even when we are rejoicing in some good deed.

For the other vices are to be feared in sins, but pride is to be feared even in right actions, lest things done laudably be lost through desire for the very praise they receive.

Thus, just as that most celebrated rhetorician [Note: [Col. 0442] Demosthenes.] is said to have answered “Delivery” when asked what he thought should first be observed among the precepts of eloquence; and, when asked what should come second, answered the same, “Delivery”; and, when asked what should come third, said nothing other than “Delivery”—so, if you asked me, and however often you asked me, about the precepts of the Christian religion, it would please me to answer nothing other than humility, even if some necessity should compel me to mention other things.

**CHAPTER IV**

23. The most salutary humility that our Lord Jesus Christ assumed humility in order to teach—this humility, I say, is especially opposed by a certain, so to speak, utterly unlearned knowledge, when we rejoice in knowing what Anaximenes, Anaxagoras, Pythagoras, Democritus, and others of this sort thought, so that we may appear learned and educated, although this is very far from true learning and education.

Anyone who has learned that God is not extended or spread through places—whether finite or infinite—as though he were larger in one part and smaller in another, but is wholly present everywhere, just as truth is, since no sober person says that one part of truth is in this place and another part in that place—for truth is certainly God—will not at all be disturbed by what anyone who thought that God himself was air believed about infinity.

What does it matter to him if he does not know what these people say the form of a body is? They say that it is something bounded on every side. And whether Cicero, in order to refute Anaximenes as an Academic, objected that God must have form and beauty [Note: [Col. 0443] Cicero’s words here are: “Next, Anaximenes declared air to be God, and said that it is begotten, immense, infinite, and always in motion—as though air could be God without any form, especially since God ought to possess not merely some appearance but the most beautiful appearance; or as though mortality did not follow everything that has come into being.” *On the Nature of the Gods* 1.]—thinking of a bodily appearance because Anaximenes had said that God was corporeal, since air is a body—or whether Cicero himself understood form and beauty to be incorporeal qualities of the truth by which the mind itself is formed and through which we judge all the deeds of the wise to be beautiful, so that he spoke not merely for the sake of refutation but with complete truth when he said that God ought to possess the most beautiful appearance, because nothing is more beautiful than intelligible and unchangeable truth—this should not trouble him.

Nor does the statement that Anaximenes said air was begotten, although he nevertheless considered it God, trouble the man who understands that the Word of God—God with God—was not begotten as air is begotten, that is, brought into being by some cause, since air is not God at all; rather, the Word was begotten in a wholly different manner, which no one understands unless God himself has inspired him [Note: [Col. 0443] Two Vatican manuscripts: “unless God and the one whom he himself has inspired.”].

Who would not see that Anaximenes was foolish even in bodily matters, when he says that air is begotten and wants it to be God, but does not call the one from whom air is begotten God? For it cannot be begotten from nothing.

Nor will the statement that air is always in motion disturb someone into thinking that it is therefore God, if he knows that the motion of every body is inferior to the motion of the mind, and that the motion of the mind is far slower than the motion of supreme and unchangeable Wisdom.

24. Likewise, if Anaxagoras—or anyone else—calls the mind itself truth and wisdom, what need have I to quarrel with the man over a word? It is clear that the ordering and arrangement of all things are made by that wisdom, and that it can appropriately be called infinite—not through extension in space, but through a power that human thought cannot comprehend.

Nor does it follow that wisdom itself is something formless. For formlessness belongs to bodies, so that whatever is infinite is also formless. Cicero, however, apparently with the intention of refuting his opponents, who think corporeally, denies that anything can be joined to the infinite, because on the side where anything is joined to it there must necessarily be some limit in bodies.

For this reason he says that Anaxagoras did not see that there could be no motion joined to and contained by the infinite—that is, adhering to an infinite thing through continuous connection—as though he were speaking of bodies, to which nothing can be joined except through spatial boundaries [Col. 0444].

He adds: “Nor any sense at all, by which the whole of nature would perceive when struck,” as though Anaxagoras had said that the mind which orders and governs all things possesses a sense like that which the soul possesses through the body.

It is clear that the whole soul perceives when it perceives something through the body; for nothing that is perceived is hidden from the whole soul. Cicero therefore said “the whole of nature perceives” in order, as it were, to take away from Anaxagoras what he had said about the mind being infinite. For how could it perceive as a whole if it were infinite?

Bodily sensation begins from some place and does not traverse the whole unless it reaches its limit; but this cannot be said of what is infinite. Yet Anaxagoras had not said anything about bodily sensation.

There is another sense in which something incorporeal is called “whole”: it is understood without spatial boundaries, so that it can be called both whole and infinite—“whole” because of its integrity, and “infinite” because it is not enclosed by the boundaries of places.

25. “Next,” he says, “if he wished the mind itself to be some sort of living creature, there would have to be something within from which that living creature would receive its name; so that this mind would be, as it were, a body, and would have within it a soul from which it would be called a living creature.” See how he speaks according to bodily usage, as animals ordinarily appear to be, because of the coarse understanding, I suppose, of those against whom he is arguing. And yet he said something that, if they were able to awaken, would sufficiently admonish them that everything which presents itself to the mind like a living body ought rather to be thought to have a soul and to be a living creature than to be a soul. For this is what he says: “There will be something within, from which that living creature will receive its name.” But he adds: “What, then, is within the mind?” Therefore the mind cannot have an inner soul so as to be a living creature, because it is itself the inner thing. Let it therefore have a body outside itself, to which it is inner, so that it may be a living creature. For this is what he says: “It is therefore enclosed by an external body,” as though Anaxagoras had said that the mind could not exist unless it belonged to some living creature. If he understood the mind itself as the highest wisdom, which is not the possession of any particular living being, because truth is commonly available to all souls capable of enjoying it. And so see how elegantly he concludes: “Since this is not acceptable,” he says—that is, it is not acceptable to Anaxagoras that the mind which he calls God should be enclosed by an external body so that it could be a living creature—“an open and simple mind, joined to nothing by which it could perceive”—that is, joined to no body through which it could perceive—“seems to elude the power and conception of our understanding” (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book 1).

26. Nothing is more true than that this eludes the power and conception of the understanding of the Stoics and Epicureans, who are unable to think of anything except bodily things. By saying “our,” he meant “human”; and rightly he did not say, “It eludes,” but, “It seems to elude.” For this is what seems to them: that no one can understand such a thing, and therefore they suppose that nothing of this kind exists. But for some people, insofar as this has been granted to human beings, it is clear to the understanding that there is an open and simple wisdom and truth, which is not the possession of any living creature, but by which every soul that is capable of it is commonly made wise and truthful. If Anaxagoras perceived this, saw that it was God, and called it “mind,” then not only does the name of Anaxagoras—which, because of its literary antiquity, all the “lettered soldiery” (*litteriones*), as I may speak in military fashion, eagerly puff up—fail to make us learned and wise, but neither does his knowledge itself, by which he knew this to be true. [Note: [Col. 0445] The editions read *litteriores* (“more learned”); four manuscripts, *litterationes*. Several other and better manuscripts have *litteriones*, the contemptuous term by which Augustine calls grammarians in book 1 of *Against the Adversary of the Law*, ch. 24.] For truth ought not to be dear to me because it was not hidden from Anaxagoras, but because it is truth, even if none of them had recognized it.

27. If, then, neither the knowledge of the man who perhaps perceived the truth ought to puff us up, so that we may appear to be learned in it, nor even the solid reality of truth itself, through which we can truly become learned [Note: [Col. 0445] The particle *nec* (“nor”) is absent from twelve manuscripts and from the editions Bad., Am., and Er.], how much less can the names and doctrines of those who held false opinions assist our learning or make hidden things known? Since, if we are human beings, we ought rather to be saddened by the errors of so many and such illustrious men when it happens that we hear them than to seek these things eagerly so that, among those who do not know them, we may be bandied about in the most empty boasting.

How much better it would have been never to have heard the name of Democritus than to think with sorrow of someone—regarded as a great man in his own time, for all I know—who supposed that the gods were images flowing from solid bodies, although the images themselves were not solid, and that, by circling here and there through their own motion and entering human minds, they caused a divine power to be imagined. Yet surely the body from which the image flowed would be judged to be as much more excellent as it was more solid.

For this reason, his opinion, as these people say, fluctuated and wavered, so that at one time he declared that a certain nature from which the images flowed was God. Yet he held that this nature could not be thought of except through the images it poured forth and emitted—that is, images which, from that supposedly corporeal and eternal, and therefore also divine, nature, were carried along by a continuous emanation resembling vapor [Note: [Col. 0445] Twelve manuscripts read *vaporis similitudinem* (“a likeness of vapor”).], and came into and entered our minds, so that we might be able to think of God or the gods.

For they suppose that there is no other cause of any thought of ours than that images come from and enter our minds from the bodies which we are thinking about—as though those who know how to think of such things did not think of many, indeed almost innumerable, incorporeal and intelligible things, such as wisdom and truth themselves. If these people do not think of wisdom and truth, I wonder how they can discuss them at all; but if they do think of them, I should like them to tell me either from what body, or what sort of image of truth, enters their minds.

28. Yet Democritus is also said to differ from Epicurus in natural questions in this respect: Democritus holds that there is in the collision of atoms a certain animal and breathing power [Note: The editions read *spiritualem* (“spiritual”); most manuscripts read *spirabilem* (“breathing” or “respirable”).]. By this power, I believe, he says that the images themselves are endowed with divinity—not images of all things, but of the gods—and that the principles of mind exist throughout the universe, to which he attributes divinity, as well as living images that are accustomed either to benefit or to harm us.

[Col. 0446]

Epicurus, however, holds that there is nothing at all in the principles of things besides atoms—that is, certain particles so minute that they can no longer be divided and cannot be perceived either by sight or by touch. He says that through the fortuitous collision of these particles innumerable worlds, living creatures, souls themselves, and the gods are produced. He places the gods in human form, not in some world but outside the worlds and between the worlds. And he does not wish anything to be thought of apart from bodies. Yet, in order that he may think of these bodies, he says that images flow from the very things which he supposes to be formed from atoms, and enter the mind, subtler than the images that come to the eyes.

For he also says that this is the cause of seeing: certain enormous images, so large that they encompass the entire world externally. But by now, I suppose, you understand what sort of images these people imagine.

29. I am surprised that Democritus was not led by this very point to recognize that the things he says are false. For when such enormous images enter our very small mind—if, as they maintain, the mind is enclosed within such a small body—they cannot touch it in its entirety. When a large body touches a small body, it cannot possibly be touched by the whole of it at once. How, then, are the images thought of as whole at once, if they are thought of insofar as, coming and entering, they touch the mind, when they can neither enter wholly through such a small body nor wholly touch such a small mind?

Remember that I am speaking according to their views; for I do not hold such an understanding of the mind. Or, if Democritus considers the mind incorporeal, then Epicurus alone can be pressed by this argument. But why did Epicurus not see that it is neither necessary nor possible for an incorporeal mind to think through the arrival and contact of corporeal images [Note: Lov. reads *cogitetur* (“be thought of”). But the better reading, found in some other editions and manuscripts, is *cogitet* (“think”).]?

As for the sight of the eyes, both of them are equally refuted. For eyes so small can in no way be touched in their entirety by bodies of images so immense.

30. But when they are asked why a single image of some body is seen, although images flow from it innumerably, they reply that, precisely because the images flow and pass by frequently, it comes about through a sort of compacting and thickening of them that one image is seen from many.

Cicero refutes this absurdity by denying that their eternal god can be thought of precisely because he is thought of through images flowing and slipping away in innumerable numbers.
