And since they say that the eternal forms of the gods are produced through the supply of innumerable atoms—when certain particles depart from the divine body and others take their place, so that the same succession prevents that nature from dissolving—he says:

“Then everything would be eternal, since nothing lacks that limitless supply of atoms which continually replenishes perpetual ruin. Next, how can this god not fear perishing, when he is struck and shaken without interruption by the everlasting impact of atoms? For he says that a body is struck when atoms rush against it, and shaken when they penetrate it. Moreover, since images, about which enough has already been said, continually flow from it, how can it have confidence in immortality?” (*On the Nature of the Gods*, book 1).

31. [Col. 0447] Amid all these ravings of those who hold such opinions, the chief cause for sorrow is that it is not enough merely to recount them, so that they may be rejected without anyone’s opposing argument; instead, the intellects of very sharp men have also undertaken the task of copiously refuting things that, as soon as they were stated, ought to have been ridiculed and cast aside even by the dullest people.

For if you grant that atoms exist, and if you also grant that through fortuitous collision they strike and agitate one another, must you also grant them the right to say that atoms, colliding fortuitously with one another, can produce something in such a way as to fashion it by form [Note: So read in Bad., Am., Er., and the manuscripts. Lov. reads *aedificent* (“build”).], define it by shape, polish it by proportion, illuminate it by color, and animate it by a soul? Whoever loves to see with the mind more than with the eyes, and seeks this from the one by whom he was made, sees that none of these things can occur except through the art of divine providence.

Nor should the atoms themselves be granted to exist in any way. Leaving aside the subtle argument taught by learned men concerning the division of bodies, see how easily this can be demonstrated according to their own opinion. They themselves certainly say that everything belonging to nature is nothing other than bodies and void, together with the attributes of these—which, I believe, means motion and impact, and the forms that follow from them.

Let them say, then, in what category they place the images which they suppose to flow from more solid bodies, although the images themselves are not solid, so that they cannot be perceived by touch except by the eyes when we see, and by the mind when we think, if these images too are bodies. For this is what they maintain: that the images can leave a body and come to the eyes or to the mind, while nevertheless they say that the mind itself is corporeal.

I ask whether images also flow from the atoms themselves. If they do flow from them, how are they still atoms, since some bodies are separated from them? If they do not flow from them, then either something can be thought of without images—which they vehemently reject—or how do they know the atoms, which they were unable to think of?

But I am already ashamed to refute these things, since they were not ashamed to hold them. And when they have even dared to defend them, I am ashamed—not now of them, but of the human race itself, whose ears have been able to endure such things.

## CHAPTER V

32. Since the blindness of minds, through the filth of sins and the love of the flesh, is so great that even these monstrous opinions have been able to consume the leisure of learned men in argument, will you, Dioscorus—or anyone endowed with an alert intelligence—doubt that no better counsel could in any way have been given to the human race for pursuing the truth than that a human being, taken up by Truth itself ineffably and wonderfully, and representing Truth’s own person on earth, should persuade people, by giving sound commands and performing divine deeds, to believe beneficially what they were not yet able prudently to understand?

We serve the glory of this one; we urge you to believe in him immovably and steadfastly. Through him it has come about that not merely a few, but even peoples who cannot judge such matters by reason, believe by faith [Note: Four Vatican manuscripts and twelve others of ours read *fide irrideant* (“mock by faith”), not without plausibility if this is referred to the philosophical doctrines explained above. But the reading in Lov. and other editions, *fide credant* (“believe by faith”), is also appropriate, namely if it is referred to what Christ commanded and did.], until, supported by saving precepts, they escape from these perplexities into the air of the purest and most sincere truth.

The more we see that no error now dares to raise itself up without gathering crowds of the ignorant under the cloak of the Christian name, the more devotedly we ought to obey this authority [Col. 0448]. Yet among the ancients, only those who possess the Scriptures through which they understand and see that the Lord Jesus Christ himself was announced continue somewhat longer or more frequently in their little gatherings [Note: Lov. reads *aliquanto diutius vel frequentius* (“somewhat longer or more frequently”). Other manuscripts lack *diutius vel*.], while concealing this fact.

Those who, although they are not in Catholic unity and communion, nevertheless boast of the Christian name are compelled to oppose believers, and dare to misrepresent the ignorant as though by reason, precisely when the Lord came with this medicine so that he might command the peoples to have faith. But, as I have said, they are compelled to do this because they feel themselves lying utterly prostrate if their authority is compared with Catholic authority.

Therefore they attempt to overcome the most firmly established authority of the deeply founded Church by the name and promise of reason. For this rashness is, as it were, the common rule of all heretics. But that most merciful commander of the faith fortified the Church through the most celebrated assemblies of peoples and nations, and through the very seats of the Apostles, the citadel of authority; and through a few piously learned and truly spiritual men he armed it also with the most abundant resources of unconquerable reason.

Yet that most correct discipline is to admit the weak as fully as possible into the citadel of faith, so that, once they have been placed there in complete safety, the strongest arguments may be fought on their behalf.

33. The Platonists, however, when the errors of false philosophers were barking about at that time, had no divine person by whom they could command faith. They preferred to conceal their doctrine as something to be sought out rather than profane it by openly proclaiming it. But when the name of Christ began to spread, as earthly kingdoms marveled and were thrown into confusion, they began to emerge and to set forth and disclose what Plato had thought.

At that time Plotinus’ school flourished at Rome, and he had as fellow students many very acute and highly capable men. But some of them were corrupted by curiosity about magical arts; others, recognizing that the Lord Jesus Christ bore the person of that very truth and unchanging wisdom which they were striving to attain, entered his service.

Thus the entire summit of authority and the light of reason were established for the renewal and restoration of the human race in that one saving name and in his one Church.

34. I do not at all regret having spoken to you at such length in this letter, even if you might perhaps have preferred something else. You will approve these things more as you make greater progress in the truth; and then you will approve my counsel, which you now think has attended insufficiently to the usefulness of your studies.

Moreover, I have replied, as briefly as I could, not only to some of those questions of yours in this letter, but also to nearly all the others in the very sheets on which you sent them, by making annotations. If you think that in these I have done too little, or something other than you wished, you are not thinking rightly, my Dioscorus, about the one from whom you now seek these things.

But I passed over all the questions concerning the *Orator* and the books *On the Orator* [Col. 0449]. For I seemed to myself to be some sort of trifler if I pursued them by way of exposition. In the case of the others, I could perhaps appropriately be questioned if someone brought forward matters to be treated and resolved in themselves, not matters taken from Cicero’s books. But in those books the matters themselves are at present less suited to our profession.

I would not have done all this if, after my illness—the illness I was suffering from when your servant arrived—I had not withdrawn for a while from Hippo. During those same days I was again overtaken by disturbed health and fevers. This is why these things were sent to you more slowly than they might have been. I urgently request that you write back to tell me how you received them.

## LETTER CXIX

[Note: We have corrected this letter according to r, s, b, two t manuscripts, and two v manuscripts, to which was finally added the old Bertinian codex, by far the most excellent.]

[Note: Elsewhere 221; the letter that was formerly 119 is now 55. It was perhaps written around the year 410.]

**Consentius proposes questions about the Trinity to Augustine.**

To the holy and most blessed lord, Pope Augustine, Consentius.

1. I had already briefly presented the nature of my request to your brother Alypius, a holy man and one whom I admire for all the virtues of his soul, hoping that he might be willing to act as an assistant for my prayers before you. But because the circumstance that compelled you to go to the country deprived me of your presence, I preferred to insert my petition in a letter rather than leave my mind wavering in expectation—especially since, if you should see that what I ask ought to be granted, the solitude of the place in which you now reside, as I believe, may assist your understanding as it searches into the deepest mysteries.

I have determined within myself that the truth of divine matters ought to be apprehended more by faith than by reason. For if the faith of the holy Church were grasped through the reasoning of disputation, rather than through the piety of belief, no one except philosophers and orators would possess blessedness.

But because it pleased God, who chose the weak things of this world in order to confound the strong, to save believers through the foolishness of preaching, it is not so much an explanation of God that must be sought as the authority of the saints that must be followed. For surely neither the Arians, who consider the Son whom we confess to have been begotten inferior, would persist in this impiety, nor would the Macedonians, insofar as they can, thrust the Holy Spirit—whom we believe to be neither begotten nor unbegotten—from the citadel of divinity, if they preferred to place their faith in the Holy Scriptures rather than in their own reasonings.

2. Yet you, remarkable man, if that Father of ours, alone conscious of the secrets, who holds the key of David (Rev. 3:7), has granted you, through the gaze of your serene heart, to penetrate the structure of the heavens and, with unveiled face, as it is written, to contemplate the glory of the Lord (2 Cor. 3:18), then, insofar as the one who gave you such a thought grants you the ability to express it, declare to us some portion of the ineffable substance, and strive, insofar as you can, to give verbal expression to an image of its likeness with his assistance.

For unless you are present as guide and teacher in so great a matter, our thought fears to gaze upon it, like eyes suffering from inflammation, when the radiance of so great a light is reflected upon them. Enter, therefore, into that most obscure cloud of God’s mysteries which bars our sight. Correct, first in me and then in my books, the little questions in whose solution I recognize that I am in error, since I wish to follow the authority of Your Holiness by faith rather than be corrupted by the false image of a reasoning conceived by the heart.

3. Indeed, with very cautious simplicity, hearing and believing that the Lord Jesus Christ is light from light, as it is written, “Announce his salvation from day to day” (Ps. 95:2), and in the Wisdom of Solomon, “For she is the brightness of eternal light” (Wis. 7:26), I believed that God—although I was not able to believe worthily what it is right to believe—was an infinite magnitude of some immeasurable light, whose quality I could neither estimate, nor measure its quantity, nor form an image of its appearance, although the human mind, however sublime its thoughts, might be sufficient for this. Yet I believed that there was something—whatever it may be—to which belonged an incomparable form and immeasurable beauty, which even Christ might behold, at least with bodily eyes.

When, therefore, toward the end of the first book, as you undoubtedly deign to remember, I was wishing to prove that the Lord Jesus Christ—that is, the human being assumed by him—possessed divine power in such a way that the material of human flesh which he had assumed remained, and when I had taught that in those members it had perished as nothing other than weakness [Note: So reads the manuscript bt., and better. The supplied bracketed word is *dicimus* (“we say”).], this question was presented to me as a knot:

“If that human being whom Christ assumed was changed into God, then he ought not to have been local. Why, then, after the resurrection, did he say, ‘Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father’?” (John 20:17).

4. As I was therefore laboring to prove that Christ is everywhere by power, not by activity; by divinity, not by flesh, I wrote the following concerning the unity of God and the Trinity of persons:

“God is one, and there are three persons. God is undivided; the persons are distinct. God is within all things and beyond all things; he contains the lowest, fills the middle, transcends the highest; he is beyond all things and diffused through all things. The persons, however, are constant in themselves [Note: [Col. 0450] So it should be read with manuscript bt.: *sunt* (“are”).] and are distinguished by their properties; they are not mingled by confusion.

“God, therefore, is one and is everywhere, because there is no other besides him, and there is no place empty where another could exist. All things are full of God, and apart from God there is nothing. He himself is in the Father, he himself in the Son, he himself in the Holy Spirit. Accordingly, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not several gods, but the one same God. Yet the Father is not himself the Son, nor is the Son the Holy Spirit.

“The Father is in the Son, the Son in the Father, and the Holy Spirit in both, because in the three persons—distinguished by number, not by order, that is, distinguished in persons, not in power—the one and indivisible God dwells. All that belongs to the Father belongs to the Son; what belongs to the Son belongs to the Father; and what belongs to both belongs to the Holy Spirit. For they possess not, as it were, an equal substance, but the same—that is, the one [Note: [Col. 0450] So manuscript bt., correctly reads; the other reading is *quia aequalem* (“because [they possess] an equal [substance]”).] and undivided [Note: All manuscripts read *unitam* (“united”).]—substance of the Godhead. Therefore neither in majesty nor in age does one precede another, because what is full cannot be divided, nor is there anything in fullness that could separate fullness and make a greater portion for one and a lesser for another [Note: So it should be read with manuscript bt.; the reading in other witnesses is *reparare* (“restore”).].

“But in the persons it is not so, because the person of the Father is not the person of the Son, nor is the person of the Son identical with that of the Holy Spirit. There is one power possessed by the threefold power; there is one substance in which the three subsisting persons exist.

“Therefore the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are everywhere in majesty, because they are one; but they are with one another only in their persons, because they are three.”

After weaving together other statements of this kind, I carried the matter to the point of affirming that the persons are indeed present and everywhere, but that the one and same majesty exists above the heavens, beyond the seas, and beyond the underworld.

From this I showed that it ought to be understood that the human being whom Christ assumed, although changed into God, did not lose the nature he had assumed, yet could not be believed to be a fourth person [Note: So reads manuscript bt.: *credi personam* (“to be believed a person”).].

5. But you, man to whom, as I believe, heaven itself has been granted to enter through the subtlety of your thoughts—for he who says, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8), is truthful—you raise the height of a pure heart above all the stars toward contemplation itself. You say that God ought not to be thought of as some sort of body.

For even if someone were to imagine in his mind a light a thousand times brighter and more intense than that of this sun, no likeness of God could be comprehended there, because everything that can be seen is a body. But just as we cannot think of justice or piety as corporeal, unless perhaps, in pagan vanity, we fashion some bodily images of women, so also God must be thought of, insofar as we can, without any contrived image of the imagination.

But to me, who can scarcely grasp the subtlety of disputation with a mind that is extremely dull, it seemed that nothing living according to substance exists in justice. Therefore I still cannot think of God—that is, a living nature—as resembling justice, because justice does not live in itself but in us; indeed, rather, we live according to justice, while justice itself does not live independently, unless perhaps it is maintained that not this human equity but that justice which is God alone is justice.

6. Therefore I wish to be strengthened by all your words—not only those now present [Note: So manuscript bt. reads: *non solum praesens tibi* (“not only the present one to you”).], but also by a fuller letter. For it is not right that only our feet should be called back, at your admonition, from this road of error on which many of us walk.

When many people in the islands where we live, while heading straight along the raised road, have run into the track of this winding error, will there be some Augustine there whose authority they will obey, whose teaching they will believe, whose ingenuity will overcome them? Or perhaps, out of that paternal affection, you prefer to direct me by a hidden admonition rather than rebuke me as a companion on a wrong journey.

But for me, who wish to run for the benefit of my soul more than for worldly praise, your correction is not useless, and therefore not bitter either—especially since it will bring life and praise both to me and to others at the same time. Surely no one can be so unjust, as I believe, as to prefer to mark me as foolish because I once followed a wrong path rather than hesitate to judge me prudent because I have chosen the right one [Note: So reads manuscript bt., and more neatly: “because I have chosen it.”].

For those whom the Apostle Paul admonished not to run uncertainly, saying, “Run in such a way that you may obtain” (1 Cor. 9:24), are not to be considered fools. Therefore this road on which we are running must not only be abandoned by us, but also blocked and cut off, lest it perhaps deceive even those whom it frustrates by a deceptive show of affection [Note: So reads manuscript bt.; shortly afterward it has: “As though the crime of a certain idolatry.”].

For you have been chosen, if I am not mistaken, not as a reader of the books I have already published, but as the corrector of those that must be approved. In the letter which I placed before those little books of mine as a kind of preface, I wrote words of this kind:

“‘It has pleased me,’ I said, ‘to stabilize the wavering boat of our faith by the judgment of Bishop Augustine.’”

Why, then, man who are the summit of this doctrine which is in Christ, do you hesitate openly to rebuke a son who must henceforth be corrected, when the anchor of your judgment cannot stabilize us more securely unless it presses its hold deeper?

For this is no slight or blameworthy question, in which our blindness of thought not only made no progress but afterward, as you very forcefully said, incurred the crime of idolatry. I should like you to examine this carefully and wisely, so that the clarity of your teaching and intellect may wipe away the cloud from our mind, and so that what we cannot now think may, once revealed by you through the light of understanding, become visible to the eyes of our hearts.

May you, safe and blessed forever, possess the heavenly kingdoms, remembering me, holy and most blessed lord and pope.

## LETTER CXX

[Note: This letter is found mutilated in many manuscripts and in the editions of Am., Bad., and Er. It is complete only in bt., r., sb., two t manuscripts, two v manuscripts, and Lov.]

[Note: Elsewhere 222; the letter that was formerly 120 is now 140. It was written shortly after the preceding one.]

**Augustine’s reply to Consentius concerning the questions about the Trinity proposed to him.**

To his beloved brother and honored in the heart of Christ, Consentius, Augustine sends greeting in the Lord.

## CHAPTER ONE

1. I asked you to come to us because I was greatly pleased by your ability in your books. Therefore I wanted you to read certain of our little works—which I judged necessary for you—not while living far from us, but rather here with us, so that if there were things you perhaps understood less well, you might ask about them in person without difficulty and, through our conversation and mutual exchange, might yourself recognize and correct what needed correction in your books, insofar as the Lord granted us the ability to express and you the ability to grasp it.

You possess the ability to explain what you have understood; and you possess the integrity and humility to deserve to understand the truth. And I now hold the same opinion, which ought not to displease you. For this reason I recently urged you, when you read at your own place the works on which we have labored, to mark the passages that trouble you and come to me with them and ask about each one.

I am not urging you now to do what you have already done. You would rightly feel embarrassed and be reluctant to do so if you had once wished to do it and had found me difficult to approach. I had also said, when I heard from you that you were being worn out by very faulty manuscripts, that you should read ours, which you might find more accurately corrected than the others.

2. But as for your request that I examine cautiously and wisely the question of the Trinity—that is, concerning the unity of the Godhead and the distinction of the persons—so that, as you say, the clarity of my teaching and intellect might remove the cloud from your mind, and so that what you cannot now think might, once revealed by me through the light of understanding, become somehow visible to your eyes: first consider whether this request agrees with your earlier definition.

For earlier, in that very letter in which you make this request, you say that you have determined within yourself that truth should be apprehended more by faith than by reason. “For if,” you say, “the faith of the holy Church were grasped through the reasoning of disputation and not through the piety of belief, no one except philosophers and orators would possess blessedness. But because it pleased God, who chose the weak things of this world in order to confound the strong, to save believers through the foolishness of preaching” (1 Cor. 1:27), “it is not so much an explanation that must be sought as the authority of the saints that must be followed.”

Consider, then, according to these words of yours, whether you ought instead—especially concerning this matter, in which our faith principally consists—to follow the authority of the saints alone and not seek from me an explanation of its intelligibility.

For when I begin, in whatever way I can, to introduce you into the understanding of so great a secret—which I shall absolutely be unable to do unless God assists inwardly—I shall be doing nothing other than offering an explanation as best I can. If you reasonably demand this explanation from me or from any teacher, so that you may understand what you believe, correct your definition—not so as to reject faith, but so that what you already hold firmly by faith may also be seen in the light of reason.

3. Far be it from us to suppose that God hates in us that by which he created us superior to the other living creatures. Far be it, I say, that we should believe so as not to receive or seek reason, since we could not even believe unless we possessed rational souls [Note: [Col. 0453] We have corrected this from one Vatican manuscript. Other codices read: “Far be it, I say, that we should believe so as [to avoid] reason,” and so forth.].

Therefore, that in certain matters pertaining to saving doctrine—which we are not yet able to grasp by reason, but will one day be able to grasp—faith may precede reason so that the heart may be cleansed and made capable of receiving and enduring the light of great reason: this itself is a matter of reason.

And therefore it was reasonably said through the prophet: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. 7:9 according to the Septuagint). There he clearly distinguished these two and gave the instruction that we should first believe, so that we might be able to understand what we believe.

Accordingly, it has rightly been judged reasonable that faith should precede reason. For if this command is not reasonable, then it is unreasonable—which is impossible. If, then, it is reasonable that, in approaching certain great things which cannot yet be grasped, faith should precede reason, then undoubtedly however little reason persuades us of this, that reason itself also precedes faith.

4. For this reason the Apostle Peter urges us to be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks us for a reason concerning our faith and hope (1 Pet. 3:15). If an unbeliever asks me for the reason of my faith and hope, and I see that he cannot grasp it before he believes, I give him precisely this explanation: if possible, he may see how perversely he asks, before faith, for an explanation of things he cannot grasp.

But if a believer asks for an explanation so that he may understand what he believes, his capacity must be considered, so that, once an explanation has been given according to it, he may receive as much understanding of his faith as he is able to grasp: more, if he is capable of more; less, if he is capable of less. Nevertheless, until he reaches the fullness and perfection of knowledge, he must not depart from the path of faith.

This is why the Apostle says: “And if in anything you think differently, God will reveal that also to you; nevertheless, let us walk by the same rule to which we have attained” (Phil. 3:15–16) [Note: [Col. 0454] So manuscript bt.; a little later it reads, *si quid aliter sapitis* (“if you think differently”). The other reading is *ut secundum rationem redditam ... aliter scitis* (“that according to the explanation given ... you know differently”).].

If, then, we are believers, we have reached the road of faith. If we do not abandon it, we shall undoubtedly arrive not only at as great an understanding of incorporeal and unchangeable realities as can be grasped in this life—not by everyone—but also at the summit of contemplation which the Apostle calls “face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12).

For some who are very lowly indeed, yet advance with the greatest perseverance along the road of faith, reach that most blessed contemplation. Others, however, who already have some understanding of what an invisible, unchangeable, incorporeal nature is, and who refuse to hold to the road leading to the dwelling of such blessedness because what they see as foolish is Christ crucified, cannot reach the innermost sanctuary of that rest, whose light already strikes their minds as though it were radiating from far away.

5. There are certain things which, when we hear them, we do not grant our belief to them, yet when an explanation is supplied to us, we recognize them as true—things we are unable to believe. Indeed, all God’s miracles are not believed by unbelievers for this reason: their rationale is not apparent. And in truth there are things for which no explanation can be given, although an explanation does exist—for what is there in the nature of things that God has done irrationally? Yet for some of his wondrous works it is even advantageous that their rationale remain hidden for a while, lest, among minds weakened by boredom, they lose their value when that rationale is understood.

For there are, and there are many, who are held more by their admiration of things than by knowledge of their causes; once miracles cease to be astonishing, such people must be aroused to faith in invisible things by visible miracles, so that, purified by love, they may arrive where, through familiarity with truth, they cease to wonder. For in theaters people marvel at a tightrope walker and take pleasure in musicians: in the former, difficulty produces astonishment; in the latter, pleasure holds and nourishes them.

[Note: [Col. 0454] In manuscript bt. it reads “and these too,” referring to those who shortly afterward are said to “cease wondering.”]

6. I have said this in order to encourage your faith toward love of understanding, to which true reason leads and for which faith prepares the mind. Those opinions which persuaded people that, in the Trinity which is God, the Son is not coeternal with the Father, or is of another substance and in some respect unlike him, and that the Holy Spirit is inferior in this way; likewise those opinions which persuaded people that the Father and the Son are of one and the same substance, but the Holy Spirit of another—not because they are reasoned conclusions, but because they are false reasoning—must be avoided and condemned. For if the reasoning were true, it would certainly not have gone astray.

Therefore, just as you should not avoid every kind of discourse merely because false discourse also exists, so you should not avoid every kind of reasoning merely because false reasoning also exists. I would say the same about wisdom. Wisdom is not to be avoided merely because there is also a false wisdom, to which Christ crucified is foolishness, although he is the Power of God and the Wisdom of God. For this reason it pleased God, through the foolishness of preaching, to save those who believe, since what is foolish in God is wiser than human beings.

Some philosophers and rhetoricians who pursued not the true way but what resembled the truth, and who deceived themselves and others in it, could not be persuaded of this; some, however, could. For those to whom it could be persuaded, Christ crucified is neither a stumbling block nor foolishness. They belong to those who are called Jews and Greeks, for to them he is the Power of God and the Wisdom of God.

Those who were able, by God’s grace, to grasp the straightness of this way—that is, of faith in Christ crucified—even if they were called philosophers or rhetoricians, humbly and devoutly confessed that fishermen had gone before them in it by a far greater measure, not only by the firmest strength of believing but also by the most certain truth of understanding.

[Note: [Col. 0455] Manuscript bt. reads: “by the firmest strength of believing, and also by the most certain truth of understanding.”]

When they had learned that the foolish things and weak things of the world had been chosen so that the strong and wise might be confounded (I Cor. I, 21–29), and had recognized that they were deceptively wise and weakly powerful, they were salutarily confounded. They became foolish and weak, so that through the foolish and weak thing of God—which is wiser and stronger than human beings—they might, among the chosen foolish and weak things, become truly wise and effectively strong.

## CHAPTER II

7. To what, except the truest reason, does faithful piety yield, so that we do not hesitate to overthrow a kind of idolatry which the weakness of human thought attempts to establish in our hearts from the habit of visible things? We must not dare to believe that the Trinity whom we worship as invisible, incorporeal, and immutable is like three living masses, however great and beautiful, each nevertheless bounded by the limits of its own space and joined to the others by contiguous proximity in their respective places—whether one of them is set in the middle, separating the other two joined to it on either side, or whether the other two are each touched by the first in the form of a triangle, so that none is separated from any other.

Nor should we believe that among three persons so great and such as these—although their masses are very large, they are nevertheless bounded above, below, and on every side—there is some fourth divinity, one and common to all, not such as any one of them is, but like a divine power common to all, wholly present both in all three and in each individually; that through this one divinity the same Trinity is called one God; that its three persons exist nowhere except in heaven, while that divinity exists nowhere in such a way as not to be present everywhere; and that, consequently, it is correct to say that God is both in heaven and on earth, because of that divinity which is everywhere and common to the three, but incorrect to say that the Father, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit is on earth, since this Trinity has its dwelling only in heaven.

When true reason, with the one who inwardly assists and enlightens us—he who does not wish to dwell in our hearts together with such idols—begins to undermine this composition of carnal thought and empty fiction, we hasten to reshape it and to shake it, so to speak, out of our faith, allowing not even a speck of such fantasies to remain there.

[Note: [Col. 0455] Thus it is read with manuscript bt.: “and its three persons [such as is one . . . its three persons].”]

[Note: [Col. 0455] Lov., “one.” But the manuscripts here have “divine power.”]

[Note: [Col. 0456] Thus manuscript bt., and better: “is.”]

[Note: [Col. 0456] In another version, Epistle 85; from this word it began: “of thought,” etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0456] Thus nine manuscripts: “in our hearts.”]

8. Therefore, unless faith had preceded in our hearts—the faith that clothes us with devotion—would we not hear in vain the reasoning of the discussion by which, admonished from without and with the inward truth shining within, we perceive these things to be false? Since faith accomplished what belonged to it, the reasoning that followed consequently discovered something of what it was seeking.

Thus true reason, by which we understand what we believe, and faith itself in matters not yet understood must unquestionably be preferred to false reasoning. It is better to believe what is true though not yet seen than to think that you see as true what is false. Faith has its own eyes, by which it somehow sees that what it does not yet see is true, and by which it sees with complete certainty that it does not yet see what it believes.

Moreover, one who already understands by true reasoning what he had previously only believed is certainly to be preferred to one who still desires to understand what he believes. But if he does not even desire this, and thinks that things requiring understanding are to be believed only, he does not know what good faith serves. For devout faith does not wish to exist without hope and without love. Thus a faithful person ought to believe what he does not yet see in such a way that he both hopes for and loves the vision.

9. Of visible things in the past, which have passed away in time, there is faith alone, since they are not still hoped for as things to be seen but are believed as things done and completed. Such is the fact that Christ died once for our sins and rose again, and now dies no more, and death will no longer rule over him (Rom. VI, 9–10).

Things which do not yet exist but are still future—such as the resurrection of our spiritual bodies—are believed in such a way that they are also hoped for as things to be seen; but they cannot in any way be displayed at present.

Things which exist in such a way that they neither pass away nor are future, but remain eternal, are partly invisible, such as justice and wisdom, and partly visible, such as Christ’s immortal body, which already exists. Invisible things are seen when understood, and therefore they too are seen in a manner appropriate to themselves. When they are seen, they are much more certain than the things touched by bodily sensation. Yet they are called invisible because they cannot possibly be seen by these mortal eyes.

Those permanent things which are visible can, if they are displayed, also be seen by these mortal eyes. Thus the Lord displayed himself to his disciples after the resurrection (Matt. XXVIII; Mark XVI; Luke XXIV; and John XX, XXI), and likewise, after the ascension, to the apostle Paul (Acts IX, 3–4) and to the deacon Stephen (Acts VII, 55).

10. We therefore believe these permanent visible things in such a way that, even if they are not displayed, we hope that one day we shall see them. We should not attempt to comprehend them by reason or understanding except insofar as, because they are visible, we conceive them more distinctly as distinct from invisible things. When we imagine what they are like in thought, we know well enough that they are not known to us.

I can think of Antioch, which I do not know, but not in the same way as I think of Carthage, which I do know. My thought invents a vision of the former, while it recalls the latter. Nevertheless, I have no doubt about either: in the one case because I have believed witnesses concerning it, and in the other because I have believed my own sight.

Justice, wisdom, and whatever is of this kind are not imagined in one way and contemplated in another; rather, we behold these invisible things when they are understood through the simple attention of mind and reason, without any bodily forms or masses, without any outlines or shapes of limbs, and without any spatial limits—whether finite or infinite.

The very light by which we distinguish all these things, in which it becomes sufficiently evident to us what we believe without knowing, what we hold as known, what bodily form we remember, what we invent in thought, what bodily sensation touches, what the mind imagines as resembling a body, and what understanding contemplates as certain and utterly unlike all bodies—this light, then, in which all these things are judged, is not spread through surrounding spatial regions like the radiance of the sun or of any bodily light, nor does it illuminate our mind with something like visible brightness. Rather, it shines invisibly, ineffably, and yet intelligibly. It is as certain to us as are the things which, in accordance with it, we perceive with certainty.

11. Since there are three kinds of things that are seen, one kind consists of bodies, such as this heaven and this earth and whatever bodily sensation perceives and touches in them. A second kind resembles bodies: these are the things that we imagine in spirit when we think, or remember, or forget them, contemplating them as though they were bodies. To this category also belong visions which, in dreams or in some mental rapture, are impressed upon us with quasi-spatial dimensions.

The third kind is distinct from both: it is neither a body nor does it have any likeness to a body. Such is wisdom, which is seen when understood by the mind, and in whose light sound judgment is passed on all these things.

To which of these kinds should we believe the Trinity we wish to know belongs? It must belong either to one of them or to none. If to one, then surely to that which is superior to the other two, such as wisdom. If its gift is in us, and it is less than that supreme and immutable wisdom called the Wisdom of God, I think we must not conceive the giver as inferior to his gift.

[Note: [Col. 0457] Some manuscripts: “If its gift in us is less than”; [Col. 0458] another Vatican manuscript: “if it is no less in us than,” etc.]

If some splendor of that wisdom exists in us—what is called our wisdom—however much of it we can grasp through a mirror and in an enigma, we must nevertheless distinguish it both from all bodies and from all likenesses of bodies.

12. But if the Trinity is to be thought to belong to none of these kinds, and is so invisible that it is not even seen by the mind, then we ought much less to hold such an opinion about it that we believe it resembles bodily things or images of bodily things.

It surpasses bodies not by the beauty or size of its mass, but by the dissimilarity and disparity of its nature. And if it is distinct from comparison with the goods of our mind—such as wisdom, justice, love, chastity, and other things of this kind, which we do not measure by bodily mass or represent in thought as though they had bodily forms, but which, when we understand them correctly, we behold in the light of the mind without any corporeality or likeness of corporeality—how much more distinct must it be from comparison with all bodily qualities and quantities?

The Apostle nevertheless testifies that it is not wholly alien to our understanding, when he says: “For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are understood and seen through the things that have been made; his eternal power also and divinity” (Rom. I, 20).

Since this same Trinity made both body and soul, it is unquestionably superior to both. If, therefore, the soul is considered—especially the human, rational, and intellectual soul, which was made in his image—and if it does not overcome our thoughts and understandings, but we are able to grasp with mind and understanding what is most excellent in it, namely the mind itself and understanding, it will perhaps not be absurd for us, with his help, to raise it toward understanding its Creator as well.

But if it fails within itself and succumbs to itself, let it be content with devout faith so long as it is away from the Lord, until what was promised in the human being comes to pass through him who is powerful, as the Apostle says, “to do above and beyond what we ask or understand” (Eph. III, 20).

[Note: [Col. 0458] What follows, up to the words “It remains, therefore,” etc., no. 17, was absent from the epistle formerly numbered 85.]

## CHAPTER III

13. Since these things are so, for the present I want you to read what we have already written at length concerning this question, including what we now have in hand but cannot yet explain because of the magnitude and difficulty of the question.

For now, however, hold with unshaken faith that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are a Trinity and yet one God—not because they possess some common fourth divinity, but because the Trinity itself is ineffably inseparable; that the Father alone begot the Son, and the Son alone was begotten by the Father; and that the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of both the Father and the Son.

Whatever bodily likeness occurs to you while you think about these things, drive it away, reject it, deny it, repudiate it, cast it aside, and flee from it.

[Note: [Col. 0458] “Drive it away” is absent from the manuscripts.]

For it is no small beginning of knowledge of God if, before we are able to know what he is, we begin already to know what he is not.

Love understanding very greatly. For even the holy Scriptures, which urge faith before understanding great matters, cannot benefit you unless you understand them correctly. All heretics who accept the Scriptures as authoritative think that they are following the Scriptures, when in fact they are following their own errors. Thus they are heretics not because they despise the Scriptures, but because they do not understand them.

14. But you, dearest brother, pray strongly and faithfully that the Lord grant you understanding, so that the things supplied outwardly through the diligence of a teacher or instructor may bear fruit. “Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase” (I Cor. III, 7).

To him we say, “Our Father who are in heaven” (Matt. VI, 9), not because he is there and is not here—for, being incorporeal, he is wholly present everywhere—but because he is said to dwell in those whose devotion he attends, and these are especially in heaven, where our citizenship also is, if our answer that we truly have our heart raised upward corresponds to reality.

Even if we were to understand bodily what is written, “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. LXVI, 1), we would have to believe that he is both there and here; though not wholly there, since his feet would be here, nor wholly here, since the upper parts of his body would be there.

That carnal notion can again be shaken from us by what is written of him: “He measured heaven with the span and the earth with a handful” (ibid., XL, 12). For who could sit within the space of his own span, or place his feet in as much space as his fist could grasp?

Unless, perhaps, empty fleshly thinking goes so far that it is not enough for it to attribute human limbs to the substance of God, unless it also imagines them monstrously—where the span is broader than the loins and the handful broader than both palms joined together.

But these things are said so that, when what we hear in a bodily sense does not fit together, we may be admonished by those very things to think ineffably of spiritual realities.

15. Therefore, even if we think of the Lord’s body—which was raised from the tomb and carried up into heaven—as having only human form and limbs, we must not nevertheless think that he sits at the right hand of the Father in such a way that the Father appears to sit at his left hand.

In that blessedness which surpasses all human understanding, there is only a right hand, and that same right hand is the name of blessedness itself.

Nor should what he said to Mary after his resurrection—“Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John XX, 17)—be understood so absurdly that we suppose he wanted to be touched by women after he had ascended, although before ascending he allowed himself to be touched by men.

Rather, when he said this to Mary, in whom the Church was represented, he plainly wished it to be understood that he had ascended to the Father when she recognized him as equal to the Father. With such faith she touched him unto salvation; for if she had believed that he was only what had appeared in the flesh, she would not have touched him correctly.

This is how the heretic Photinus touched him: he believed him to be merely human.

16. And even if these words of the Lord can perhaps be understood in another, more suitable and better way, the opinion must nevertheless be rejected that the Father’s substance is in heaven, insofar as the Father is one person in the Trinity, while divinity is not only in heaven but everywhere—as though the Father were one thing and his divinity, which he shares with the Son and the Holy Spirit, another; as though the Trinity were corporeal and existed in bodily places, while the one divinity of the three persons were present everywhere, and this alone, as incorporeal, were wholly everywhere.

If their divinity were a quality—which God forbid, since in the Father, Son, or Holy Spirit quality is not one thing and substance another—even if it could be their quality, it could not be more fully somewhere than in its own substance.

[Note: [Col. 0460] Lov. reads, “than it could be its own”; but the manuscripts have, “than it could be in its own substance,” apart from some in which the word “substance” is omitted.]

But if it is a substance, and is other than they themselves are, it is another substance. This too is believed most falsely.

17. But if perhaps you understand less clearly what distinction there is between substance and quality, at least you can more easily notice this: the divinity of the Trinity—which is thought to be something other than the Trinity itself, and on account of which it is said that there are not three gods but one God, since this divinity is one and common to the three—is either a substance or it is not a substance.

If it is a substance, and is other than the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit, or other than the Trinity itself considered together, then unquestionably it is another substance. But truth refutes and rejects this.

If this divinity is not a substance, and it is God because it alone is wholly everywhere, while the Trinity is not, then God is not a substance. What Catholic would say this?

Again, if this divinity is not a substance, and according to it the Trinity is one God because this divinity is one in the three, then the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit should not have been said to be of one substance, but of one divinity that is not a substance.

You recognize, however, that in the Catholic faith this is true and established: the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, although they are a Trinity, are one God because they are inseparably of one and the same substance—or, if this is better said, essence.

Some of our writers, especially the Greeks, have said that the Trinity, which is God, is more properly an essence [Greek: οὐσία, ousia] than one substance, believing or understanding that there is some difference between these two names. There is no need to discuss that now. For even if we call this divinity, which is thought to be something other than the Trinity itself, not a substance but an essence, the same falsehood will follow. If it is other than the Trinity itself, it will be another essence. God forbid that a Catholic should think this.

It remains, therefore, that we should believe the Trinity to be of one substance in such a way that the essence itself is nothing other than the Trinity itself.

However far we progress in this life toward seeing it, what we shall see will be “through a mirror and in an enigma.” But when we begin to possess the spiritual body promised in the resurrection, then—whether we see it with the mind or, in a wondrous manner, with the body as well, since the grace of the spiritual body is ineffable—we shall see it not through intervals of place, nor smaller in one part and greater in another, since it is not a body and is wholly everywhere, but according to our capacity.

[Note: [Col. 0460] In several manuscripts: “in an irrational manner.”]

## CHAPTER IV

18. In your letter you stated—or rather, this was what seemed to you to be the case—that nothing living according to substance exists in justice, and therefore that you were not yet able to think of God, that is, a living nature, as resembling justice. For, as you say, justice does not live in itself but in us; rather, we live according to it, while justice itself, in itself, does not live at all.

To answer yourself on this point, consider whether it can rightly be said that the very life by which everything lives that we rightly call living does not itself live. For I think it would seem absurd to you that something should live through life while life itself did not live.

But if that life itself lives preeminently, by which everything that lives lives, recall, I ask you, whom divine Scripture calls dead souls. You will certainly find them to be the unjust, the impious, and the unbelieving.

Although their bodies are alive through them—bodies of impious people, of whom it was said that “the dead bury their own dead” (Matt. VIII, 22)—and although wicked souls are thereby understood not to be without some kind of life (for otherwise bodies could not live through them, unless through some kind of life of which souls cannot be entirely deprived, and for which reason they are rightly called immortal), nevertheless they are called dead after losing justice for no other reason than that, although souls live with some kind of immortal life, justice is a truer and greater life for souls: it is, as it were, the life of lives. When souls are in bodies, the bodies themselves are alive through them, although they cannot live by themselves.

Therefore, if souls cannot exist without living to some extent in themselves, since bodies live through them and die when abandoned by them, how much more must true justice be understood to live in itself, since souls live through it in such a way that, when it is lost, they are called dead, although they do not cease to live with however little life remains to them?

19. That justice which lives in itself is unquestionably God, and he lives immutably.

Just as, although this life exists in itself, it also becomes life for us when we become in some way participants in it, so, although it is justice in itself, it also becomes justice for us when, by clinging to it, we live justly.

We are just in greater or lesser degree according as we cling to it more or less.

Thus it is written concerning the only-begotten Son of God, who is certainly the Wisdom and Justice of the Father and always exists in himself: he was made for us by God “wisdom and justice, sanctification and redemption,” so that, as it is written, “Whoever glories, let him glory in the Lord” (I Cor. I, 30–31).

You yourself saw this when you added and said: “Unless perhaps it is maintained that not the justice of human equity, but that justice which is God, is justice alone.”

Indeed, the supreme God is true justice, or the true God is supreme justice. To hunger and thirst for this justice is our justice during this pilgrimage; to be filled with it afterward is our full justice in eternity.

Let us not, then, think of God as resembling our justice. Rather, let us think that we are so much more like God as we can become more just through participation in him.

20. If, then, we must take care not to think of God as resembling our justice, since the light that illuminates is incomparably superior to that which is illuminated, how much more must we beware of believing him to be something inferior and, so to speak, more discolored than our justice?

What else is justice, when it is in us—or any virtue by which one lives rightly and wisely—than the beauty of the inner person?

Certainly, we were made in the image of God according to this beauty more than according to the body. Hence it is said to us: “Do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed in the renewal of your mind, so that you may prove what is the will of God, what is good and pleasing and perfect” (Rom. XII, 2).

If, then, we say—or know, or wish—that the mind is beautiful not in mass or in parts separated by their respective locations, as bodies are either perceived or conceived, but in an intelligible virtue such as justice; and if according to this beauty we are reformed into the image of God, then the beauty of God himself, who formed us and reforms us according to his image, must certainly not be imagined as existing in any bodily mass.

He must therefore be believed to be incomparably more beautiful to the minds of the just inasmuch as he is incomparably more just.

[Note: [Col. 0462] The epistle formerly numbered 85 ended here.]

These matters, in relation to the customary length of letters, have perhaps been addressed to Your Love at greater length than you expected; but in relation to the question of so great a matter, it will have been sufficient to offer a brief reminder—not as though this were enough for your education, but so that, carefully instructed by reading or hearing these things from others as well, you yourself may refute more fully what you have said otherwise. This is certainly better in proportion as it is more humble and more faithful.

## EPISTLE CXXI

[Note: [Col. 0462] Corrected according to manuscripts a, bg, bl, bn, c, cc, ff, g, gv, n, r, s, sb, vc; two manuscripts marked t; four marked v; and according to Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0462] Formerly numbered 58; what was 121 is now 130. Written around the year 410.]

Paulinus, bishop of Nola, proposes several questions to Augustine, first about the Psalms, then about the Apostle, and finally about the Gospel.

### FIRST CHAPTER

1. Since the bearer of this letter is already hurrying to the ship, and I too am hastening because of his haste, I shall propose some questions that have just now occurred to me, so that you may not write back to me without some small supplement.

If they happen to be clear but seem obscure to me, let none of the prudent sons who may perhaps be standing around you from among our number at the hour of this little reading laugh at my foolishness. Rather, let them favor me with the goodwill of brotherly love by instructing me, so that I may become a participant in the company of those who see and, enlightened by your teaching, may contemplate the wonders of the Lord’s law with illuminated minds.

2. Tell me, then, blessed teacher of Israel, what is meant by what is said in Psalm 15: “He has made all his desires wondrous among his holy ones who are in the earth. For their infirmities have been multiplied; afterward they hastened.”

Whom does he call holy—the holy ones who are in the earth? Does he mean those Jews who are children of Abraham according to the flesh, but not children of the promise, and who are excluded from the seed called in Isaac (Rom. IX, 8, 7)? Are they called holy in the earth because they are holy by carnal descent but earthly in life and understanding—those who set their minds on earthly things and grow old in the observance of the letter, according to the oldness of the letter, not being reborn into a new creation because they did not receive him through whom old things passed away and all things became new?

Perhaps this is how he calls them holy in this Psalm, just as in the Gospel he calls them just when he says, “I have not come to call the just, but sinners” (Matt. IX, 13)—that is, those just people who glory in the holiness of their descent and in the letter of the Law.

To them it is said, “Do not glory in Abraham as your father, for God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (ibid., III, 9).

Their type is presented in that Pharisee who, recalling his own righteousness as though the Lord were unaware of it, proclaimed it in the temple—not praying to be heard, but demanding, as though it were a debt owed for his merit, a reward for good works that nevertheless displeased God, because pride destroyed what righteousness had built.

Nor did he keep this silent; he proclaimed it aloud, so that it might be evident that he was not speaking to divine ears, since he also wished to be heard by human beings. For this reason he did not please God: he pleased himself.

“God has scattered the bones of those who please themselves. They were confounded,” he says, “because he despised them” (Ps. LII, 6)—he who does not despise a humble and contrite heart.

3. Finally, in the very parable in the Gospel in which the persons of the Pharisee and the tax collector are contrasted, the Lord himself clearly shows what he accepts in a person and what he rejects (Luke XVIII, 10–14), just as it is written: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James IV, 6).

Thus he declares that the tax collector went away from the temple more justified by his confession of sins than the Pharisee by his accounting of his own righteousness.

With good reason, that self-praiser was rejected and departed from the presence of God. Though by his very title he displayed his knowledge of the Law, he had forgotten the saying of the prophet concerning the Lord: “Upon whom shall I rest, except upon the humble and peaceful one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI, 2).

But the tax collector, an accuser of himself in a contrite heart, is accepted and obtains forgiveness for his confessed sins through the grace of humility, while that holy Pharisee—such as the Jews are who are holy in this sense—carries away a burden of sins from his boastful holiness.

The Jews in question are plainly represented by those of whom the Apostle says that, desiring to establish their own righteousness, they were not subject to the righteousness of God (Rom. X, 3), which is from faith—the faith reckoned to our father Abraham as righteousness, not from works (ibid., IV, 2–3), because he believed God according to God’s omnipotence.

Before God, the truly just person is the one who lives from faith. Such a person is not holy in the earth but in heaven, because he walks not according to the flesh but according to the spirit; his citizenship is in heaven. He does not glory in circumcision of the flesh but in circumcision of the heart, which is performed invisibly not by the letter but by the spirit.

Therefore his praise is not from human beings but from God.

[Note: [Col. 0463] Lov. reads “the Spirit of God.” The word “God” is absent from the other manuscripts.]

4. Next, concerning what he adds in the same verse—“He made his desires wondrous among them”—I believe he says this because he first lit for them the lamp of the Law and gave them commandments for living. For, he says, “He made his ways known to Moses and his desires to the children of Israel” (Ps. CII, 7).

Then he worked among them the mystery of piety: God was born in the flesh from a virgin among their people, and from their flesh, from the seed of David, he became human.

Then came the mighty works of healing which he performed among them and in their presence. Yet through these things he was not only not believed by them but also blasphemed, when they said, “If this man were from God, he would not perform cures on the Sabbaths” (John IX, 16), and, “He casts out demons only by Beelzebul, the prince of demons” (Matt. XII, 24).

Because of this mind, blinded by hardened impiety, their infirmities and darkness were multiplied.

5. But what does he mean when he says, “Afterward they hastened”? Does he mean that they hastened to repentance, like those in the Acts of the Apostles who, pierced by the preaching of blessed Peter, believed in him whom they had crucified and, hastening to be cleansed from so great a sin, ran toward the gift of grace (Acts II, 37–41)?

Or does he mean that, because the virtues of the soul are strengthened by faith and love of God, the infirmities of the soul were multiplied in those impious people, empty of both, whose souls were seized by the deadly sicknesses of their crimes?

Christ is the light and life of believers, and healing is under his wings. It is therefore no wonder that the darkness and infirmities of those who did not receive life and light, and did not wish to remain under his wings, were multiplied unto destruction. As he himself testifies with tears in his Gospel, he often wished to gather them under his wings, as a hen gathers her chicks, but they refused (Matt. XXIII, 37).

When their infirmities had multiplied, where did they hasten? Perhaps to shout for the Lord’s crucifixion and to extort it from Pilate, against his will, with wicked cries, so that they might fill up the measure of their fathers; so that these people might kill the Lord of the prophets, whose fathers had killed the prophets themselves, from whom it had been announced that this Savior of the world would come.

“Afterward they hastened”—for “their feet are swift to shed blood. Destruction and misery are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace” (Ps. XIII, 3)—that is, Christ, who says, “I am the way” (John XIV, 6).

6. In the following Psalm I desire an explanation of what he says: “Their belly has been filled from your hidden things. They have been satisfied with swine,” or, as I hear it written in some Psalters, “They have been satisfied with sons,” “and they have left what remained for their little ones.”

[Note: [Col. 0464] Greek: υἱῶν (huiōn), “of sons”; ὑῶν (huōn), “of swine.” Jerome, however, translated from the Hebrew, “with sons.”]

7. Again, in another psalm I am accustomed to wonder, understanding the Son to be speaking to the Father. In Psalm 58, concerning the Jewish enemies of whom he had said above, “Behold, they will speak with their mouth, and a sword is in their lips,” he says a little farther on: “Do not kill them, lest they at any time forget your Law. Scatter them by your power, and destroy them, O Lord.” We see this fulfilled in them even to the present day: they have been destroyed from their former glory, living dispersed among all nations, without a temple, sacrifices, or prophets.

But why are we surprised that through the Prophet he was already asking that they not be killed, when even at the time of his Passion, while they were leading him to the cross, he prayed for them, saying, “Father, forgive them; for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34)?

Yet what he added—“lest they ever forget your Law”—as though their life required this even without faith in the Gospel, I confess is obscure to me. For what benefit does it bring them, with regard to the salvation that is sought only through faith, to occupy themselves with remembering and meditating upon the Law? Unless perhaps it is for the sake of the honor of the Law itself, or of Abraham’s race, so that even among the earthly portion of his carnal offspring, which appears to be counted “like the sand of the sea,” the letter of the ancient Law might remain—lest perhaps some, by reading the Law, be enlightened unto faith in Christ, who is the end of both the Law and the Prophets, and who shines forth prefigured and foretold throughout all their books [Col. 0465].

Or perhaps it is because from those very impious people the generation of the elect is to come—those who are chosen from each tribe and designated in groups of twelve thousand (Revelation 7:5–8). The revelation itself of blessed John bears witness to them through the voice of the angel who foretells this: they will cling more familiarly to the retinue of the eternal King, completely undefiled and untouched by human union. Of them he says specifically: “They follow the Lamb wherever he goes, because they have not defiled themselves with women; for they are virgins” (ibid. 14:4).

8. In Psalm 67, among other things, this is especially obscure to me: “Nevertheless, God has shattered the heads of his enemies, the crown of the hair of those who walk about in their sins.” What does it mean “to walk about the crown of the hair in sins”? For he did not say, “the crown of the head,” but “the crown of the hair,” which is without sensation. Or does he wish to indicate a person filled with sins? It is written: “Every heart is in anguish, from the feet even to the head” (Isaiah 1:6).

And a little farther on he says: “The tongue of your dogs from the enemies, from him.” From whom? And can the Gentiles be called God’s dogs, whom he himself calls dogs in the Gospel (Matthew 15:26)? Or perhaps he calls those people God’s dogs who may be regarded as such if they live as Gentiles under the Christian name—people whose portion is placed with unbelievers because, although they honor God in words, they deny him by their deeds?

## CHAPTER II

9. So much for the Psalms for now. I shall now propose whatever questions I may have concerning the Apostle. In his Letter to the Ephesians he says what he had said in another Letter (1 Corinthians 12:28) concerning the ranks or orders of God’s arrangements, the Holy Spirit effecting distributions of graces:

“And he gave some as apostles, some as prophets, others as evangelists, others as pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints” (Ephesians 4:11–12), and so forth.

I wish you to distinguish for me, amid this diversity of names, what particular function or grace belongs to each name: what is proper to the Apostles, what to the Prophets, what to the Evangelists, what to the Pastors, and what to the Teachers. For in all these different names I see an office of teaching that was carried out in a similar and almost identical way.

As for the Prophets whom he placed after the Apostles, I do not think he means those who existed before the Apostles in the order of time, but those who, already under the Apostles, were endowed by grace either with the interpretation of Scripture, the discernment of minds, or the prediction of future events—such as Agabus, who foresaw and foretold both the impending famine (Acts 11:28) and what blessed Paul would suffer in Jerusalem, announcing it in words and showing it by means of Paul’s belt (ibid. 21:10–11).

I wish to understand what distinction there is specifically between Pastors and Teachers, since both names are ordinarily attributed to the leaders of the Church.

10. Likewise, concerning what he says to Timothy—“Therefore, first of all I ask that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people” (1 Timothy 2:1)—I ask you to explain to me what distinction there is in this diversity of words, since everything he says is to be done appears to me to belong to the office of prayer [Col. 0466].

11. Likewise, concerning what he says to the Romans, I ask and beg you to explain the following to me, for I confess that I am very blind in this statement of the Apostle about the Jews:

“According to the Gospel, they are enemies for your sake; but according to election, they are beloved for the sake of the fathers” (Romans 11:28).

How are the same people both enemies for our sake—we who have believed from the Gentiles—as though the Gentiles could not have believed unless the Jews had not believed? Or was the one Creator of all, God, who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2:4), unable to acquire both peoples unless he possessed one in place of the other?

Then he says, “Beloved for the sake of the fathers.” If they are “beloved,” how, or from what cause, do they not believe and persist in being enemies of God? “Do I not hate those who hate you, O God,” he says, “and do I not waste away over your enemies? With perfect hatred I hate them”?

Surely, I think, this is the voice of the Father speaking to the Son through the Prophet in that same psalm, where above he had spoken of the portion of believers:

“But to me your friends, O God, have been exceedingly honored; their rule has been exceedingly strengthened” (Psalm 138:21–22, 17).

But what benefit does it bring them toward salvation—which is obtained only through faith and the grace of Christ—if they are beloved by God because of the faith of their fathers? To what advantage are those loved whom it is necessary to condemn for this reason: that because of their unbelief they differ from the faith of their prophetic and patriarchal ancestors and are enemies of the Gospel of Christ?

If, then, they are beloved by God, how will they perish? And if they do not believe, how will they not perish? If they are loved for the sake of their fathers without any merit of their own, how will they also not be saved for the sake of their fathers? Yet even if Noah, Daniel, and Job were in their midst, they would not save their impious children; they alone would be saved (Ezekiel 14:14, 16).

12. Draw another, still more obscure matter up for me from the depths, and bring it into shallow water. In the Letter to the Colossians I cannot understand at all what he says:

“Let no one deceive you, taking delight in humility and the worship of angels, entering upon things he has not seen, vainly puffed up by the thought of his flesh, and not holding fast to the Head” (Colossians 2:18–19).

Of which angels is he speaking? If he means enemies and evil spirits, what worship or what humility belongs to them? And who is the teacher of this deception, who, under the pretext of some angelic worship, teaches as though seen and discovered things that he has not seen?

Without doubt, these are the heretics who both follow and proclaim doctrines of demons, inventions conceived by their spirit. They fabricate phantasms they have not seen as though they had seen them, and sow them through deadly disputations in hearts inclined to believe wrongly (1 Timothy 4:1–2). These are the people who do not hold fast to the Head—that is, to Christ, the source of truth; whatever opposes his teaching is insanity.

And these are the blind leaders of the blind (Matthew 15:14), of whom I think it may be said: “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns that cannot hold water” (Jeremiah 2:13).

13. Then, in the following chapter, he added:

“Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle—things that all perish in their use according to the commandments and doctrines of human beings. These matters indeed have an appearance of wisdom in superstition and humility, and in not sparing the body, but they have no honor of any kind, only for the satisfying of the flesh” (Colossians 2:21–23).

What are these things in which the teacher of truth testifies that there is a semblance of wisdom, and yet denies that the truth of religion itself is present? Is he perhaps speaking of things such as those about which he says to Timothy: “Having an appearance of godliness, but denying its power” (2 Timothy 3:5)?

Therefore I ask you especially to explain these two chapters of the Letter to the Colossians to me, word by word, because he has mixed reprehensible things with praiseworthy ones. For what is as praiseworthy as a principle of wisdom, and what is as detestable as the superstition of error?

Humility too is pleasing to God and especially praiseworthy in true religion; yet, along with a semblance of wisdom, it is attributed to those whose doctrines and actions are the ones about which he says to us, “Do not touch, do not taste—things that lead to destruction” (Colossians 2:21–22), because they are not from God; and everything that is not from faith is sin (Romans 14:23).

But God has destroyed the counsels of the wise (Psalm 27:10), who through the wisdom of the flesh are foolish toward God; for the fleshly mind cannot be subject to the law of God (Romans 8:7). He knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are futile (Psalm 94:11).

I ask what sort of humility and what sort of semblance of wisdom he says is present in superstition arising from human doctrines.

And what he says—“in not sparing the body, but having no honor of any kind, only for the satisfying of the flesh” (ibid. 23)—I understand very poorly indeed, because in the same statement there appears to me to be a great distinction. I think he is speaking of some fabricated or useless abstinence, such as heretics commonly affect, when he says, “in not sparing the body.”

But what he added—“having no honor of any kind”—means, I think, that although they do not practice the appearance of a holy work in the faith of truth, they perform it without any honor of glory or benefit, thereby bringing about a grave condemnation of perverse error, since they transform themselves into ministers of righteousness.

But what he added—“for the satisfying of the flesh”—seems contrary to what he says, “in not sparing the body.” For it seems to me that the person who subdues the flesh with fasts does not spare the body, as the Apostle says: “I bruise my body and bring it into subjection” (1 Corinthians 9:27). The satisfying of the flesh is alien to this practice.

Unless perhaps he also calls the very care taken to satisfy the flesh—which is especially disgraceful in those who claim to practice religion—“not sparing the body,” in accordance with that honorable command which he gives elsewhere: that each person should know how to possess his own vessel honorably (1 Thessalonians 4:4), and should present his body as a living sacrifice, pleasing to God (Romans 12:1), not for the satisfying of the flesh—for bodily overindulgence destroys the soul’s sobriety and is hostile to chastity [Col. 0467].

## CHAPTER III

14. It remains for me to suggest something also concerning passages in the Gospels to Your Blessedness—not as many as usually occur to someone reading at leisure (for I shall not now have time to search through scattered books or to stir my memory in recalling them), but I shall ask about the few that come to mind at the moment of dictating this letter.

Concerning the form of the resurrection, I ask you to send me, if you have it copied in your papers, the letter that you wrote in response to my second inquiry while you were wintering at Carthage—a letter not extensive, but full of instruction in the faith—or at least to rewrite it for me; this will be easy for you.

[Note: Fifteen manuscripts read *exhiemarem* (“while I was spending the winter”); others, with the editions, read *hiemarem* (“while I was wintering”). But we believe *hiemares* (“while you were wintering”) should be read. For Augustine, replying to this request of Paulinus in Letter 149, §2, writes: “At the same time, as you ordered, I sent a copy of that letter which I had written in reply to your Charity at Carthage concerning the resurrection of bodies, where the question of the use of the members had arisen.” By these words he appears to indicate Letter 95, §7, in which he discusses the functions of the members after the resurrection; that letter was written to Paulinus while he was staying in Italy, about the end of the year 408.]

For even if it no longer exists in writing—perhaps because it was a brief letter and, being composed hastily among your books, was neglected—renew it for me, ready in the same sense, from the treasury of your heart. Send it to me along with the other replies that, I hope, you will return to me, if Christ grants both you and me a period of travel.

In this way I may receive from you, so that your labor may bear fruit in me, answers to these passages of Scripture about which I have questioned you, since you see, as it were, through God.

[Note: Manuscript *a* and one Vatican manuscript read, “as though I had questioned God.”]

I ask you so that I may hear what God speaks to me in you or through you [Col. 0468].

15. I ask you to make clear to me in what way or for what reason the Lord, after the resurrection, was both unrecognized and recognized—first by the women who came to the tomb, then by those two on the road, and afterward by his disciples (Luke 24:16). For he rose in the same body in which he suffered.

How, then, was the form of that body not the same as it had been? Or, if it was the same, how was he not recognized by those who knew it? I believe that the following contains a sacramental meaning: he who was not recognized by those walking along the road was revealed in the breaking of the bread. Nevertheless, I wish to grasp this according to your understanding, not my own.

16. And concerning what he said to Mary—“Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father” (John 20:17)—if he did not permit her to touch him while he stood nearby, how would she touch him after he had ascended to the Father, unless perhaps by progress in faith and the ascent of the mind, by which God becomes distant from or near to a human being?
