And perhaps she had doubted concerning Christ, whom she had thought to be the gardener.

[Note: Five manuscripts read “she may have doubted”; the others read “she had doubted.”]

For this reason she may have deserved to hear, “Do not touch me.” She was judged unworthy to touch with her hand the Christ whom she had not yet grasped by faith and had not understood to be God, since she had thought him to be the gardener, concerning whom shortly before she had heard from the angels: “Why do you seek the living among the dead?” (Luke 24:6).

Therefore, “Do not touch me, because I have not yet ascended to the Father” for you, since I still appear to you merely as a human being. Later you will touch me, when by believing you have ascended to the recognition of me.

17. Explain to me also what you think concerning the words of the most blessed Simeon, so that I may follow your understanding. When he had come into the temple, moved by the Spirit and by God’s oracle, to see Christ, and had received the infant Lord into his arms and blessed him, he said to Mary:

“Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel, and as a sign that will be opposed; and your own soul a sword will pierce, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed” (ibid. 2:34–35).

Are we to believe that he prophesied this concerning Mary’s Passion, which is nowhere recorded? Or rather concerning her maternal affection, by which later, at the time of the Passion, as she stood beside the cross to which the one she had borne was fastened, she was pierced by the pain of her maternal entrails? And the sword of the cross that had pierced the one who, in her sight, was her son according to the flesh was penetrating her soul.

For I see that it is also said in the Psalms concerning Joseph: “They humbled his feet in fetters; iron passed through his soul” (Psalm 105:18), just as Simeon said in the Gospel, “And your own soul a sword will pierce” (Luke 2:35).

He did not say “the flesh,” but “the soul,” in which the affection of devotion is contained and in which the sting of grief works like a sword—whether someone is afflicted by an injury to his flesh, as Joseph was, who suffered not death but injuries, having been sold as a slave, bound as an accused man, and handed over to prison; or whether someone is tormented by the sadness and pain of an inward affection, as Mary was.

Maternal feeling had certainly led her to the cross of the Lord, in whom at that time she thought only of the son of her own body, so that when she saw him dead, she might mourn with human weakness and gather him for burial, presuming nothing about his resurrection, because the punishment of the Passion before her eyes blinded her to faith in the wonder that was to follow.

[Note: Six manuscripts read “which”; eight others read “by which.”]

Nevertheless, when she stood beside his cross, the Lord did not console her in the trembling weakness of one who was dying. Rather, possessing in full power the death he was undergoing willingly, and with the steadfastness of one who would rise again, he admonished her from the cross, speaking of the blessed apostle John:

“Woman, behold, your son”; and likewise to him, as he stood there: “Behold, your mother” (John 19:26–27).

Already, as he was passing through the death of the cross from the human frailty in which he had been born of a woman into the eternity of God, so that he might be in the glory of God the Father, he entrusted to a human being the obligations of human affection. From among his disciples he chose the younger one, so that he might appropriately assign a virgin mother to a virgin apostle.

[Note: Five manuscripts read: “From among his disciples he chose his younger one, choosing the younger.”]

In the same statement he taught two things at once: he left us an example of devotion, since he showed concern for his mother, so that although he was leaving her bodily, he would not abandon her in his care; indeed, he was not going to leave her bodily either, because the one whom she saw dying she would soon see restored to life.

He also, by the hidden plan of divine counsel, set forth under these words the saving mystery of his filial devotion, which concerned the faith of all: he assigned another man to be regarded as his mother in place of his own mother, and to console her in his place; and in turn he gave her a new son in place of his own bodily presence—or, rather, so to speak, begot one for her.

[Note: Several manuscripts read “designating.”]

By this he showed that apart from himself, who had been born from that virgin, she neither had had nor had a son; for the Savior would not have shown such great concern for her consolation if he had not been her only son.

[Note: The Badian, American, and Erasmian editions, together with several manuscripts, read “concern for her desolation.”]

18. But let us return to Simeon’s words, in whose conclusion I confess that my understanding grows dim:

“And your soul,” he says, “a spear”—or “sword”—“will pierce, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.”

According to the literal sense, this is entirely obscure to me, because we have nowhere read that the most blessed Mary was killed, so that the holy man might appear to have prophesied a future bodily suffering for her by a physical sword.

But the statement he added is also obscure: “so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.” For it is written: “God searches hearts and reins” (Psalm 7:10). And concerning the future judgment the Apostle says that then “God will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and will reveal the counsels of hearts” (1 Corinthians 4:5).

Likewise, when the Apostle expresses spiritually the heavenly weapons with which we ought to arm ourselves within, he calls the word of God “the sword of the Spirit” (Ephesians 6:17). Concerning this he says to the Hebrews:

“The word of God is living and effective, and sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching,” he says, “even to the division of soul and spirit” (Hebrews 4:12), and the rest that you know [Col. 0470].

What wonder is it, then, if the fiery power of this word, and the sharper edge of the two-edged sword, pierced the soul of holy Joseph long ago, and afterward that of blessed Mary? For we know that iron passed through the body of neither of them.

And so that it may become still clearer that the Prophet used “iron” in place of the sword of the word, he immediately adds in the following verse: “The word of the Lord set him on fire.” For the word of God is both fire and sword, the Word himself saying both things concerning himself:

“I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it already be kindled?” (Luke 12:49).

Likewise, elsewhere he says: “I have not come to bring peace, but a sword” (Matthew 10:34). You see that he designated the one power of his teaching by the different names of fire and sword.

But how would suffering or tribulation inflicted upon Mary by a sword persist? Therefore I wish to know what concerned Mary about the thoughts of many hearts being revealed, or where it became apparent that, because her soul had been pierced either by a bodily sword of iron or by a spiritual sword in the word of God, the thoughts of many hearts were thereafter revealed.

Explain this conclusion of Simeon’s words to me above all, for I do not doubt that it shines clearly to your holy soul, which has deserved the illumination of the Holy Spirit through the purity of its inward eye, so that through him it may search out and contemplate even the deep things of God.

May God have mercy on me through your prayers, and may he illuminate his face upon me through the lamp of your word, holy lord, most blessed brother, united with me in the Lord Christ, my teacher in the faith of truth and my protector in the depths of charity.

[Note: Several manuscripts read “the charity of Christ.”]

## LETTER 122

[Note: Collated with manuscripts a, id, c, cc, g, gv, j, n, r, s, t, vc, four sb, four v, and with the editions of Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: Formerly numbered 138; the letter that was 122 is now 111. Written around the year 410.]

Augustine excuses his absence to the clergy and people of Hippo, exhorting them to be more eager than usual in relieving the poor, on account of temporary afflictions.

To the most beloved brothers, fellow clergy, and to the whole people, Augustine sends greetings in the Lord.

1. First of all I ask your charity, and I implore you through Christ not to let my bodily absence grieve you. In spirit and in the affection of my heart, I think you cannot possibly doubt that I am unable to depart from you, although it grieves me more than perhaps it does you yourselves that my weakness is not sufficient for all the concerns that the members of Christ demand of me, whom both fear of him and charity compel me to serve.

Let Your Affection know this: I have never been absent through an unrestrained freedom, but through a necessary servitude, which has often compelled my holy brothers and fellow clergy to endure even journeys by sea and overseas. I have always been excused from these journeys not by lack of devotion in mind, but by the inadequate strength of my body.

Therefore, my most beloved brothers, act in such a way that, as the Apostle says, whether he comes and sees you or is absent, he may hear concerning you that you are standing firm in one spirit, striving together with one mind for the faith of the Gospel (Philippians 1:27).

If some temporary affliction is troubling you, this ought rather to remind you how you should think about that life where you will live without any labor, escaping not the distressing hardships of a brief period but the dreadful punishments of eternal fire.

For if you now act with such great care, attention, and labor to avoid falling into some temporary suffering, how solicitous ought you to be in fleeing everlasting misery! And if death is feared in this way, although it brings temporal labor to an end, how greatly must that death be feared which sends a person into eternal grief!

And if the pleasures of this age, brief and sordid, are loved in this way, with how much greater intensity must the pure and boundless joys of the age to come be sought!

Thinking upon these things, do not be sluggish in good works, so that in due time you may come to the harvest of your seed.

2. For it has been reported to me that you have forgotten your customary practice of clothing the poor. When I was present, I urged you to this mercy, and now I urge you again, lest the devastation of this world, in which you see such things occurring as our Lord and Redeemer, who cannot lie, foretold would come, overcome you and make you sluggish.

Therefore you ought not merely to perform fewer works of mercy; you ought to do more than usual. For just as those who see the collapse of a house approaching because its walls are crumbling migrate more quickly to safer places, so, the more Christian hearts perceive the ruin of this world drawing near through ever-increasing tribulations, the more eagerly ought they to transfer to the heavenly treasury, with tireless speed, the good things they had been planning to store up on earth.

Then, if some human disaster occurs, the person who has migrated from a collapsing place will rejoice. If nothing of the sort follows, the person will not grieve who, destined eventually to die, has entrusted his possessions to the immortal Lord to whom he is going.

Therefore, my most beloved brothers, from what each person possesses, according to the strength that he himself knows, do what you usually do, but with more eager spirits than usual. Amid all the troubles of this age, retain in your hearts the Apostle’s exhortation, where he says: “The Lord is near; do not be anxious about anything” (Philippians 4:5–6).

Let such reports about you reach me that I may know you are accustomed to do—not because I am present, but because of God’s command, who is never absent—what you have done for many years when I was present, and sometimes even when I was absent.

May the Lord preserve you in peace; and, my most beloved brothers, pray for us [Col. 0471].

## LETTER 123

[Note: Reviewed against manuscripts bl, c, fs, mr, tt, two vd, six v, and the editions of Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: Formerly numbered 26; the letter that was 123 is now 257. Written perhaps toward the end of the year 410.]

Jerome reports certain matters to Augustine through an enigma.

Many people limp with both feet, and, even with their necks broken, do not bend down; they retain their former inclination to error, although they no longer have the freedom to preach it.

[Note: In manuscript mr this letter is joined to Letter 195 and follows it continuously. In the vd codices, however, it is attached to that letter after the subscription, with these three intervening words: “Now after the subscription.”]

The holy brothers who are here with our insignificance, especially your holy and venerable daughters, respectfully greet you.

I beg you, my crown, to greet in my name your brothers, my lords Alypius and Evodius.

Jerusalem has been captured and is held by Nebuchadnezzar.

[Note: By the name “Nebuchadnezzar,” the editors of Jerome’s works, Erasmus and Marianus, understand him to be hinting secretly and indirectly at a Jerusalem bishop who defended condemned heresies. But in Augustine’s edition, that same Erasmus, followed by the Louvain theologians, teaches in the commentary on this letter that the reference is to Rome, captured by the Goths, refusing to recognize God’s hand and attempting rebellion by summoning auxiliary forces. Baronius likewise thinks the statement refers to the city captured in the year 410.]

Nor does it wish to heed Jeremiah’s counsels; indeed, it longs for Egypt, so that it may die at Taphnes and perish there in everlasting servitude.

## THIRD CLASS

Letters that Augustine wrote from the year of the conference held with the Donatists and the discovery of the Pelagian heresy in Africa onward, during the remaining years of his life—that is, from the year 411 to 430.

[Col. 0471]

## LETTER 124

[Note: Formerly numbered 227; the letter that was 124 is now 96. Written around the beginning of the year 411.]

Augustine excuses himself to Albina, Pinianus, and Melania, who had come to Africa out of their desire to see him and were staying at Thagaste, explaining that he had not been able to go to them—not so much because of the severity of winter as because of the precarious condition of the Church at Hippo.

[Col. 0471]

To the distinguished lords in the Lord, and brothers most dear and most desired for their holiness, Albina, Pinianus, and Melania, Augustine sends greetings in the Lord.

[Note: In Lov., “Albino, Piniano, and Meliano.” We restore “Albina” and “Melania” on the authority of the very ancient Corbie manuscript, the only manuscript of this letter that has come into our hands. They are likewise named in the catalogue of Possidius, chapter 7. Albina was the elder Melania’s daughter-in-law, the mother of the younger Melania, who was married to Pinianus. Some time before the invasion of the Goths, the elder Melania led them out of Rome together with her son Publicola, according to Palladius in the Lausiac History. Palladius calls this Publicola, or Poplicola, “the younger,” perhaps indicating that he was the son of Publicola, Albina’s husband, whose death is discussed above in Letters 94 and 95. Ruffinus accompanied this religious group of refugees, and he was with them in Sicily in the year 410, when the Goths devastated Rhegium Julianum with flames, as he himself testifies in the preface, or letter to Ursacius, prefixed to his translation of Origen’s work on the Book of Numbers and published by Henri Valois with notes on Eusebius, book 6, chapter 38. Not long afterward, after Ruffinus had died, they sailed to Carthage and finally withdrew to Thagaste. This is attested not only by this letter of Augustine but also by the Metaphrast in the Life of the younger Melania, under January 31.]

[Col. 0472]

1. Although by habit of health or by nature I cannot bear the cold, I have never endured greater heat than during this dreadful winter, since I was unable not merely to go but even to fly to you, though you were so near, to whom I would have had to cross the seas by flight, and who, coming from so far away to see us, are now established so close at hand.

Perhaps Your Holiness has thought that the severity of this winter was the only cause of my suffering.

[Note: We have not found this reading in the manuscripts except cb and two V.]

Far be it from you, my beloved ones. For what hardship, trouble, or even danger do these rains present that I would not have had to undertake and endure in order to come to you—such great consolations amid our great evils; lights kindled so ardently from the highest light in this crooked and perverse generation; lofty people who have embraced humility; people made more glorious by having despised worldly glory?

At the same time I would have enjoyed the spiritual happiness of my earthly homeland, which has deserved to have you present as well. When it heard what you were by birth and what you had become through the grace of Christ, although it believed this through charity, it perhaps hesitated to speak of it, lest it not be believed [Col. 0473].

2. I shall therefore explain why I did not come and by what troubles I was prevented from receiving so great a blessing, so that I may deserve from you not only pardon but also, through your prayers, mercy from the one who works in you that for which you live to him.

The people of Hippo, to whom the Lord has given me as a servant, are so weak in great measure, indeed almost in every respect, that even the pressure of a lighter tribulation could make them seriously ill. Now they are being struck by such a great tribulation that, even if they were not so weak, they could scarcely endure it with any spiritual well-being.

When I returned, I found them in the most dangerous state of scandal on account of my absence. Yet, concerning you, whose spiritual strength we rejoice in the Lord, healthy throats surely know how to savor the meaning of the words: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?” (2 Corinthians 11:29).

Especially since there are many here who, by speaking against us, try to disturb the minds of others who appear to love us, so that they may make room for the devil in them. When those whose salvation we are concerned for become angry with us, their great plan for taking revenge is a desire to die—not in body but in heart, where a hidden corpse is sensed by its stench before it can be seen by our thought.

You certainly willingly forgive this anxiety of mine, especially since, if you were angry and wished to take revenge, you might find nothing more grievous than what I suffer when I do not see you at Thagaste.

Yet, aided by your prayers, I hope that, wherever in Africa you may be, I shall soon be permitted to come to you once what now holds me here has passed—if this city in which we labor is not unworthy, since I myself do not dare to consider it worthy of rejoicing with us over your presence.

## LETTER 125

[Note: Letters 125 and 126 have been reviewed against manuscripts cb, sb, vc, two v, and Lov.]

[Note: Formerly numbered 224; the letter that was 125 is now 259. Written shortly after the preceding letter.]

When Pinianus had come to Hippo to visit Augustine and was attending a sacred service there, he was suddenly summoned to the presbytery amid a riot of the people. He was not permitted to escape until he had sworn that he would not leave Hippo and that, if at any time he chose to consent to receiving clerical office, he would accept that office only in the Church of Hippo itself.

Albina and her children—namely, Pinianus and Melania—complained that the people of Hippo had attempted to claim this very wealthy man out of greed for money, and they maintained that an oath extorted by force and fear had no validity.

For this reason Augustine writes to Alypius, explaining how these suspicions and complaints should be addressed and with what religious principle the oath given by Pinianus should be dissolved.

[Col. 0473]

[Col. 0474]

To the most blessed and venerably beloved lord, brother, and fellow priest Alypius, and to the brothers who are with you, Augustine and the brothers who are with me send greetings in the Lord.

1. We certainly grieve deeply, and we cannot regard as insignificant the fact that the people of Hippo shouted so much in insult to Your Holiness. But it is far more grievous that such things are thought about us than that they were shouted.

For when we are believed to wish to retain the servants of God out of greed for money rather than love of justice, is it not desirable that those who believe this should testify to it with the voice of their hearts, so that, if possible, remedies might be sought that are much greater than allowing them to perish silently, poisoned by deadly suspicions?

Therefore, we must take greater care to persuade the people—those to whom we are commanded to offer ourselves as an example of good works—that what they suspect is false. We spoke about this even before it happened. The question is not how to rebuke those who express their suspicions in voices and words, but how to persuade people that their suspicions are false.

2. Accordingly, I do not resent the holy Albina, nor do I judge that she should be reproved, but rather that she should be healed of such a suspicion. Although she directed the same words [Note: [Col. 0474] Lov. reads, “had said”; but the manuscripts read, “directed.”] not against my person, but as though she were complaining about the people of Hippo—that they had disclosed their desire to keep among them a rich man, not for the sake of the clerical office but for the sake of his money, despite his contempt for and generosity with such wealth—nevertheless, what she thought about us she nearly shouted aloud; and not she alone, but also her holy sons, who said this very thing in the apse that same day. I therefore think that they, as I said, should be healed of such suspicions rather than reproved on account of them. For where can security and rest from such thorns be prepared or provided for us, if they could spring up against us in hearts so holy and so dear to us? The uneducated crowd, after all, formed this opinion about you; about us, the lights of the Church. You see, therefore, which of the two is more grievous. I judge that neither party should be accused, but both should be healed: they are human beings, and they suspect such things about human beings—false, certainly, but not incredible.

For surely such people are not so foolish as to believe that the people desired their own money, especially since they had already experienced that the people of Thagaste had received nothing from it; and so too, then, with the people of Hippo. But all this hostility burns only against the clergy, and especially against bishops, whose authority appears to stand above the rest, and who are thought to use and enjoy the Church’s possessions as owners and masters. My Alypius, if possible, let us not by our conduct build up the weak toward this desire, so harmful and deadly. Recall what we said before this temptation occurred—a temptation that presses us all the more strongly toward this course. Let us rather, by taking counsel together, [Col. 0475] seek, with the Lord’s help, to provide for the matter; and let our own conscience not suffice us, because this is not a case in which it ought to suffice by itself. For if we are not rejected servants of God, if there still burns in us some spark of that fire by which charity does not seek its own, we must certainly take care to do what is good not only before God but also before human beings, lest, while we drink tranquil water in our conscience, we be convicted of walking heedlessly, so that the Lord’s sheep drink turbid water.

3. As for what you wrote about the type of oath violently extorted, let us inquire into the matter among ourselves: I beg you, do not let our discussion make clear matters obscure. If certain death were threatened, so that a servant of God were compelled to swear that he would do something unlawful and wicked, he ought to prefer death to swearing, lest he fulfill an oath by committing a crime. But now, when the most persistent uproar of the people was compelling no one to any wickedness, but to something which, if it were done, would be lawful; and when there was indeed fear that certain dissolute persons, who are often mixed in with a crowd even of good people, might, finding an opportunity in the sedition and in what seemed a just indignation, burst out into some criminal act of violence from desire for plunder, yet the thing feared was uncertain. Who would judge that, to avoid uncertain things—not to mention losses or any bodily injuries, but even death itself—a certain perjury ought to be committed?

That Regulus, whoever he was, had heard nothing in the holy Scriptures about the impiety of a false oath, nothing about Zechariah’s sickle [Note: [Col. 0475] Lov., “Zechariah’s book”; concerning this, in the Vulgate, Zechariah, chapter 5. But the manuscripts we were able to inspect—the Sorbonicus and the very ancient and excellent Corbeiensis—have “Zechariah’s sickle,” which we do not doubt is the genuine reading; for the Septuagint, whose version Augustine consistently follows, renders Zechariah as follows: “I see a flying sickle … everyone who is in it will be punished from this point onward until death, and every perjurer will be tortured from this point onward.” Chrysostom likewise read “sickle” there, as is clear from Homily 9, To the People of Antioch.]—and evidently had sworn to the Carthaginians not by the sacraments of Christ but by the defilements of demons. Yet he did not fear certain torments and a death of terrifying example because necessity compelled him to swear; rather, because he had sworn, he freely endured them so as not to commit perjury.

The Roman judgment of that time was unwilling to retain—not among the saints, but among the senators; not in heavenly glory, but in the earthly senate—not only those who, from fear of death and cruel punishments, had most openly preferred to commit perjury rather than return to savage enemies, but also the man who had thought himself absolved from the guilt of perjury because, after swearing, he had returned under some fictitious necessity. Those who expelled him from the Senate did not consider what he himself had intended when he swore, but what those to whom he had sworn expected from him. Nor had they read what we sing everywhere:

> “The one who swears to his neighbor and does not deceive” (Psalm 14:4).

We customarily praise such conduct with immense admiration, even when found in people alien to the grace and name of Christ; yet we still think that we must search the divine Books to discover whether we may sometimes lawfully commit perjury, when we have even been commanded not to swear, lest through the ease of swearing we slide into perjury! [Col. 0476]

4. I do not doubt that this is rightly said: the oath is fulfilled not according to the words of the person swearing, but according to the expectation of the person to whom the oath is sworn—an expectation known to the one who swears. For words, especially brief ones, very rarely encompass the meaning whose fulfillment is demanded of the one swearing. Hence those are perjurers who, while preserving the words, deceive the expectation of those to whom they swore; and those are not perjurers who, even without preserving the words, fulfill what was expected of them when they swore.

Accordingly, since the people of Hippo wished to have the holy Pinianus among them not as a condemned man but as a most beloved inhabitant of their city, even if his words could not sufficiently encompass this, nevertheless what they expected of him is so evident that the fact that he is now absent after his oath troubles none of those who were able to hear that he would depart for a definite reason while intending to return. Therefore he will neither be a perjurer nor be thought one by them, unless he has deceived their expectation. He will not deceive it unless he has either changed his intention of living among them or at some point departed without arranging to return—something far removed from his character and from the faith which he maintains as due to Christ and the Church.

To omit what you know along with me—how dreadful the divine judgment concerning perjury is—I certainly know this: henceforth we ought not to resent anyone who does not believe us when we swear, if we should think that the perjury of such a man ought not merely to be endured with equanimity but even defended. May the mercy of the One who rescues those who hope in Him turn this away both from us and from him.

Therefore, just as you wrote in your memorandum, let him fulfill the promise by which he promised that he would not depart from Hippo, in the same manner as I, or the people of Hippo themselves, do not depart, although we have the freedom both to leave and to return. The only difference is that those who are not held by an oath also have complete freedom to migrate and not return without incurring the guilt of perjury.

5. Whether our clergy, or the brothers living in the monastery, took part in or encouraged the insults directed at you, I do not know whether it can be proved. When I asked about this, I was told that only one Carthaginian [Note: [Col. 0476] All the manuscripts read “a Carthaginian.”] from the monastery had shouted along with the people when they were demanding that he be made a presbyter—not when they were hurling unworthy insults at you. I have appended to this letter a copy of the example of the promise, transcribed from the same little document that he himself signed and that was corrected while I was examining it.

## LETTER 126

[Note: [Col. 0476] Elsewhere 225; what was 126 is now 20. Written shortly after the preceding letter.]

The subject is the same as that of the preceding letter: Augustine explains to Albina how matters concerning Pinianus took place at Hippo, satisfying her complaints and ill-founded suspicions.

To the holy, venerable lady and servant of God ALBINA, AUGUSTINE, greetings in the Lord.

1. It is right to console the distress of your soul, which you write that you cannot express, not to increase it; so that, if possible, we may heal your suspicions rather than, by resenting them as directed against us, disturb still further your venerable heart dedicated to God.

No fear of death was inflicted by the people of Hippo upon our holy brother, your son Pinianus, even if he himself perhaps feared something of the kind. We too were afraid that certain dissolute persons, who often mingle with a crowd through secret conspiracy, might break out into violent recklessness, having found an opportunity for sedition which they would stir up as though from just indignation. But, as we were later able to learn, no such thing was said or attempted by anyone. Rather, they were shouting many insulting and unworthy things against my brother Alypius; would that through his prayers they might deserve to be absolved from so great a guilt.

After their first shouts, I told them that I was bound by a promise already made that he could not be ordained while I was unwilling, and I added that if they had him as presbyter while my pledge was violated, they would not have me as bishop. I then returned to our benches, leaving the crowd behind. At that my unexpected answer made them hesitate and unsettled them for a while; but then, like a flame briefly pressed down by the wind, they began to flare up much more fiercely, thinking that either I might be forced not to keep my promise, or that, while I maintained the fidelity of my promise, he might be ordained by another bishop.

I told those whom I could—the more honorable and influential men who had come up to us in the apse—that I could neither be moved from keeping my promise nor allow him to be ordained by another bishop in the church entrusted to me without being consulted and giving permission; and that, if I gave permission, I would nonetheless deviate from my pledge. I also added that they would gain nothing by his being ordained against his will except that, once ordained, he would depart. They did not believe that this could happen. Meanwhile the multitude, arranged according to its groups, persisted in the same intention with a terrible and unremitting roar of shouting, leaving us uncertain in mind and counsel. It was then that those unworthy shouts were directed against my brother, and then that we feared worse things.

2. Although I was moved by so great an agitation of the people and so great a disturbance of the Church, I had said nothing else to that packed assembly except that I could not ordain him against my will. Yet even so I was not induced to do what I had promised not to do: namely, to persuade him to accept the presbyterate. If I had been able to persuade him, he would no longer have been ordained against his will.

I kept faith with both promises—not only with the one I had already disclosed to the people, but also with the one by which, as far as human beings were concerned, I was bound by a single witness. I kept, I say, the faith of a promise, not of an oath, in a situation of such danger—a danger that, although later we discovered that it was falsely feared, nevertheless threatened everyone in common, if it existed at all. The fear itself was shared by all; and, because I was especially afraid for the church in which we were, I was considering leaving. But it had to be feared that, in my absence, something of the kind might be done more readily, both because reverence would be diminished and because resentment would burn more fiercely.

Moreover, if I were to leave with brother Alypius while the crowd surrounded us, we had to fear that someone might dare to lay hands on him. But if I were to leave without him, what would happen to our reputation if something should perhaps befall him and I appeared to have abandoned him for the very purpose of handing him over to the raging crowd?

3. Amid these anxieties, this profound grief, and the absence of any breathing space for counsel, suddenly and unexpectedly our holy son Pinianus sent to me a servant of God to tell me that he wished to swear to the people that, if he were ordained against his will, he would leave Africa altogether. I suppose he thought that, since he could not commit perjury, they would no longer continue their fruitless persistence in shouting to drive from here a man whom at least we ought to have as a neighbor.

I kept silent about this, because I seemed to fear that their grief would become more violent after the oath; but since he had at the same time asked me to come to him, I did not delay. When he told me this, he immediately added to the oath the further point which, as I was going to him, he had sent me through another servant of God—namely, that he would remain present if no one imposed the burden of the clerical office upon him against his will.

Here, in such great distress, I was refreshed as though by a breath of air. I made him no reply, but went at a quicker pace to brother Alypius and told him what Pinianus had said. Alypius, as I think, wishing to avoid anything being done on his authority that might offend you, said: “Let no one consult me about this.” On hearing this, I went to the agitated people. When silence had been made, I disclosed what had been promised, together with the oath.

Those who were thinking of and desiring only his presbyterate did not receive the offer as I had expected. After muttering among themselves for a while, they asked that the same promise and oath should include the provision that, if he should ever decide to consent to accept the clerical office, he should consent only in the church of Hippo. I reported this to him, and he agreed without hesitation. I announced it to them; they rejoiced, and immediately demanded the promised oath.

4. I returned to our son and found him hesitating over what words could encompass that promise together with the oath, because of unforeseen necessities that might compel him to depart. At the same time he explained what he feared: that some hostile incursion might occur, one that would have to be avoided by departure. Saint Melania wanted herself and the excuse of unhealthy air to be added; but she was rebuked by his reply.

I said that he had presented a serious and not negligible necessity, one that would compel even citizens to emigrate. But if these things were told to the people, we had to fear that we might appear to be uttering an ill omen; whereas, if an excuse were made under the general heading of “necessity” [Note: [Col. 0478] Thus the manuscripts: “if, however, an excuse were made under the name of necessity.”], it would be thought nothing but a fraudulent necessity.

Nevertheless, it seemed good to test the people’s attitude on this matter, and we found nothing other than what we had expected. When his words were recited by the deacon and everything had pleased them, as soon as the name of the proposed necessity was heard, they immediately protested. The promise displeased them, the tumult revived, and the people thought that nothing but deceit was being attempted against them. When our holy son saw this, he ordered the word “necessity” to be removed from the document, and the people returned once more to rejoicing.

[Col. 0479]

5. When I excused myself on the grounds of weariness, he refused to approach the people without me; we went together. He told them that he had given the deacon the instructions they had heard, that he had sworn, and that he would carry them out. He then went through everything in the precise form in which he had dictated it.

The response was, “Thanks be to God,” and they requested that the entire document be signed. We dismissed the catechumens, and he immediately signed the document. Then we bishops began to be asked—not by the voices of the people, but nevertheless by the people through respectable and faithful men—to sign as well. But when I began to sign, holy Melania objected. I wondered why she had objected so late, as though by refusing to sign we could make that promise and oath void; nevertheless, I obeyed. Thus my signature remained incomplete, and no one thereafter thought that we should be pressed to sign.

6. Whatever disturbances or words arose among the people on the following day, after they had learned that he himself had departed, I have taken care to report to Your Holiness in a memorandum, insofar as I thought sufficient. Therefore, whoever may have told you anything contrary to what I have related either lies or is mistaken. I realize that I omitted certain matters which seemed not to belong to my responsibility; nevertheless, I have said nothing false.

Accordingly, it is true that our holy son Pinianus swore in my presence and with my permission; but it is false that he swore at my command. He knows this, as do the servants of God whom he sent to me—first Saint Barnabas, and then Timasius, through whom he also sent me word about his promise to remain present.

The people themselves were compelling him by their shouts to accept the presbyterate, not to take an oath [Note: [Col. 0479] Lov., “The people were not shouting for the presbyterate.” The word “not” is absent from all the manuscripts.]. Yet he did not reject what was offered to them, since they hoped that, while he remained among us, his will might be brought to the point of consenting to ordination, and that he would not depart, as he had sworn he would if ordained against his will.

Thus they shouted for the work of God—for the sanctification of the presbyterate is indeed the work of God—and the reason why, after rejoicing over his promised presence, they were not satisfied unless it was added that, if he should ever wish to consent to accept the clerical office, he would consent only in the church of Hippo, is readily apparent. They also hoped for his dwelling among them, and for that reason did not withdraw from their desire for the work of God.

7. How, then, do you say that they did this from a most shameful desire for money? First, because that accusation has no bearing at all upon the people who were shouting. Just as the people of Thagaste have no share in what you contributed to the Church of Thagaste except the joy of your good work, so too the people of Hippo—and the people of any other place where you have carried out, or may anywhere carry out, the Lord’s commands concerning the mammon of unrighteousness—have no such share.

Therefore, when the people urgently demanded that such a great man be assigned to their Church, they were not seeking a financial advantage for themselves from you; rather, they loved in you your contempt for money. For if they loved in me what they had heard—that, after despising a few small paternal plots, I had turned to the free service of God—they did not begrudge this even to the Church of Thagaste, my earthly homeland. But when [Col. 0480] that Church had not imposed the clerical office upon me, they seized me for their own whenever they could.

How much more ardently, then, could they love in our Pinianus such a desire for this world, such wealth, and such hope, overcome and trampled underfoot by so great a conversion! For, according to the judgment of many who compare themselves with one another, I seem not to have left riches but to have come to riches. My paternal property can scarcely be reckoned a twentieth part of the estates of the Church, which I am now thought to possess as a master.

But in whatever Church—especially in the Churches of Africa—our man may be, I do not say as presbyter but as bishop, when compared with his former wealth he will be extremely poor, even if he acts with the mind of a master. Christian poverty is therefore loved here much more clearly and securely, since no desire for greater possessions can be suspected.

This inflamed the people’s spirits; this raised them to that persistent and violent shouting. Let us not additionally accuse them of shameful greed; rather, let us permit them, without guilt, at least to love in others the good which they themselves do not possess. Even if poor or beggars were mixed into that crowd, shouting along with the rest and hoping to supplement their need from your venerable abundance, I do not think that even this desire is shameful.

8. It remains, then, that this most shameful desire for money is directed obliquely against the clergy, and especially against the bishop. We are thought to dominate the Church’s possessions; we are thought to enjoy its wealth. Finally, whatever we have received from these resources, we have either continued to possess or distributed as seemed appropriate; from it we have given nothing to the people outside the clergy or monastery except to a very few persons in need.

I do not say that such things should have been said about us above all; nevertheless, they could credibly have been said about us alone. What, then, shall we do? By what reasoning shall we clear ourselves before you, if we cannot do so before our enemies? This matter concerns the soul; it is inward, hidden far from mortal eyes, and known only to God. What remains, then, except to call God as witness, since he knows it?

When you form such an opinion about us, you do not command us—as would be much better, and as you thought fit to charge me with as a fault in your letter—but altogether compel us to swear. You do not threaten us with fear of the death of our flesh, as the people of Hippo were thought to have done; you threaten us with fear for our reputation. For the sake of the weak, to whom we strive to present ourselves as examples of good works by whatever manner of life we lead, that reputation must certainly be preferred even to the life of this flesh.

9. Nevertheless, when you compel us to swear, we do not resent it, as you resent it in the case of the people of Hippo. For, as human beings, you believe such things of human beings: things which are not in us, but which nevertheless could be in us. These suspicions must be healed in you, not accused; and our reputation must be cleared before you, if our conscience has been cleared before the Lord.

Perhaps he will grant—just as my brother Alypius and I discussed before this temptation occurred—that it may become known not only to you, our most beloved fellow members, but also to [Col. 0481] our bitterest enemies, that we are not defiled by any desire for money in matters belonging to the Church.

Until that happens, if the Lord grants that it happen, here is what we are compelled to do for the present, lest we postpone for any length of time the medicine for your heart. God is my witness that I endure all this administration of the Church’s affairs, which we are believed to love ruling over, because of the service I owe to the love of the brethren and the fear of God; I do not love it. Indeed, if I could be free of it without failing in my duty, I would wish to be.

God himself is witness that I feel no differently about my brother Alypius. Yet the people, and more grievously the people of Hippo, formed a different opinion about him and plunged him into such great insults. And you, holy people of God, full of compassion, by believing such things about us and invoking the name of that same people—which has absolutely no connection with a desire of this kind—wished to touch and admonish us; surely for the purpose of correcting us, not out of hatred, which God forbid should be found in you.

Therefore I ought not to become angry but to give thanks, since you could not have acted either more modestly or more freely: you did not reproach the bishop insultingly for what you thought, but left it to be understood indirectly.

10. Do not be troubled, then, as though you should consider yourselves burdened because I thought it necessary to swear. For the Apostle did not burden, nor did he love too little, those to whom he said:

> “We never came with words of flattery, as you know, nor with a pretext for greed—God is witness” (1 Thessalonians 2:5).

In an evident matter he called human beings as witnesses; but for an inward matter, whom could he call except God? If he rightly feared that human ignorance might form such an opinion about him, although everyone could see his labor—since he took nothing for his own use from the peoples among whom he dispensed the grace of Christ except in the greatest necessity, and otherwise supplied the necessities of his own sustenance by the work of his hands—how much more must we labor to be believed, who are far inferior both in the merit of holiness and in strength of character, and who cannot work with our hands to support this life? Even if we could, our many occupations—which I do not believe those men had to endure at that time—would certainly not allow it.

Let the Christian people, therefore, which is the Church of God, no longer be accused in this matter of the most shameful desire for money. It is more tolerable that this accusation should be made against us, upon whom, although falsely, a plausible suspicion of this evil could fall, than against those who are known to be alien to such desire and suspicion.

11. With regard to refusing an oath, it is not lawful for minds endowed with any faith, and still more with Christian faith, I do not say to maintain the contrary, but even to entertain doubt. On this subject I have explained my view fully enough, I think, in the letter I wrote to my brother.

Your Holiness wrote to me: “If either I or the people of Hippo hold that satisfaction should be made by an oath violently extorted.” What then do you yourself think? Does it seem right to you that, even when certain death is imminent—which was then feared without cause—a Christian should invoke the name of the Lord his God for deception, and call upon his God as witness to a falsehood? If a Christian were compelled by imminent death [Col. 0482] to give false testimony apart from an oath, he ought surely to fear defiling his life more than ending it.”

Hostile and armed ranks certainly clash with one another under the clearest threat of death; yet when they swear to one another, we praise those who keep faith and rightly detest those who deceive. What did each side fear from the other when they swore, except being killed or captured? Accordingly, if an oath extorted by fear either of death or of captivity is not obeyed, if the faith pledged in it is not kept, they remain bound by the crime of sacrilege and perjury—even such people as fear committing perjury more than killing a human being.

And are we to raise the question for debate as to whether an oath extorted from servants of God—men outstanding in the gift of holiness, monks hastening toward perfection in Christ’s commandments even through the distribution of their own possessions—ought to be fulfilled?

12. Why, I beg you, should that promise of remaining present be burdened with the names of exile, deportation, or banishment? I suppose that the presbyterate is not exile. Would our son choose this rather than exile? Far be it from us to defend this holy man of God, so dear to us, in such a way. Far be it, I say, that it should be said that he preferred exile to the presbyterate, or perjury to exile.

I would say this if an oath promising his presence had truly been extorted from him by us or by the people. But it was not extorted while he was refusing it; he accepted it while it was being offered. And he accepted it with the hope, as we said above, that through that presence he might perhaps consent to the clerical office when those who desired this believed he could be persuaded.

Finally, whatever opinion may be held about us or about the people of Hippo, the case of those who compelled him to swear is very different from that of those who—not to say compelled him, but—persuaded him to commit perjury. Let the man himself, too, not refuse to consider which is worse: taking an oath under any sort of fear, or committing perjury once that fear has been removed.

13. Thanks be to God, because the people of Hippo understand the promise made to them to be fulfilled in no other way than that he be present with the intention of living among them, and go wherever necessity requires with arrangements to return. If they attended to and demanded the literal words of the oath, the servant of God ought no more to have departed in any way than to have committed perjury in any way.

But since it would be their crime to hold in such a manner not merely such a man but any human being, they have themselves shown that they had no other expectation: when they heard that he had departed in order to return, they rejoiced. Nor does a truthful oath owe them anything other than what they expected from it.

What, then, does it mean to say that, in the oath expressed by his own mouth, he made an exception for necessity? As though he had not likewise ordered this to be removed with his own mouth. Certainly, when he himself spoke to the people, he would then also have inserted the qualification. If he had done so, they would surely not have replied, “Thanks be to God”; rather, they would have returned to the protest that had occurred when the words were recited by the deacon.

And does it matter whether an excuse of necessity for departing was inserted or not? Nothing else was expected of him than what we stated above. Whoever deceives the expectation of those to whom he swears cannot fail to be a perjurer.

[Col. 0483]

14. Let what was promised therefore be fulfilled, and let the hearts of the weak be healed, lest those who approve this be built up by so great an example to imitate perjury; while those who disapprove may most justly say that none of us should be believed—not merely when promising something, but even when swearing.

This is where we must rather guard against the tongues of our enemies, whom that enemy uses as arrows to destroy the weak. But far be it from us to expect from such a soul anything other than what the fear of God inspires and the great excellence of holiness within it encourages.

As for me, whom you say ought also to have forbidden it, I confess that I could not think in such a way that I would prefer the Church to which I serve to be overturned by so great a tumult or offense rather than accept what such a man was offering us.

## LETTER 127

[Note: [Col. 0483] Corrected according to a. bl. bg. bn. c. cc. ff. gv. j. n. r. s. t., two sb. manuscripts, two vc. manuscripts, six v. manuscripts, and according to Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0483] Elsewhere 45; what was 127 is now 100. Perhaps written in 411.]

Augustine exhorts Armentarius [Note: [Col. 0483] The heading prefixed to this letter in all editions hitherto added to Armentarius the surname Riparius, on the authority of no manuscript copy known to us. Nor does the title of the same letter in Possidius’s index, chapter 7, have anything other than “To Armentarius and Paulina.”] and his wife Paulina to despise the world and fulfill the vow of continence by which they bound themselves together.

To the distinguished, deservedly honorable and beloved children, ARMENTARIUS and PAULINA, AUGUSTINE, greetings in the Lord.

1. The distinguished man, my son Ruferius, your relative, told me what you have vowed to the Lord. His account delighted me, but at the same time I feared that the tempter who has long begrudged such good things might suggest something else. I therefore thought I should briefly exhort Your Charity, my distinguished, deservedly honorable and beloved son, to consider what is read in the divine utterances:

> “Do not delay to turn to the Lord, and do not postpone it from day to day” (Ecclesiasticus 5:8);

and to seize and take care to return what you know you vowed to him who both exacts what is owed and fulfills what is promised.

For it is also written:

> “Vow and pay your vows to the Lord your God” (Psalm 75:12).

Yet even if you had not made a vow, what else ought to have been urged upon you, or what better thing can a human being do, than to restore himself to the one by whom he was formed? This is especially true because God’s love toward us has appeared and shone forth in such a great sign that he sent his only-begotten Son to die for us.

It remains, therefore, that what the Apostle says should be fulfilled: Christ died so that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who died and rose again for them (2 Corinthians 5:15).

Unless, perhaps, the world is still to be loved, although it has been crushed by so great a corruption that it has even lost the appearance of seduction. For as greatly as those deserve praise and proclamation who did not deign to flourish even when the world was flourishing, so greatly must those be rebuked and accused who delight in perishing along with what is perishing.

2. The labors, dangers, and disasters of this passing life are endured for the sake of that same life, which must at some point end, so that its death may not be removed altogether but merely postponed for a little while. How much more, then, must such things be endured for eternal life, where death is neither anxiously avoided by nature, nor shamefully feared by cowardice, nor bravely endured by wisdom—for no one will have death, since death will not exist.

Let eternal life therefore possess you among its lovers. Do you not see how forceful and how demanding this miserable and needy life is toward its lovers? Yet they, often disturbed by its dangers, bring it to an end more quickly, by the very means by which they fear to end it; and, while avoiding death, they hasten it, as though someone were to rush into a river that would carry him away, or flee from a robber or a wild beast.

When a storm rages, people sometimes throw even their provisions into the sea; and, in order to live, they cast away the things by which they live, lest what is lived through toil should quickly end. With what labors is life prolonged so that one may labor for a longer time! And when death begins to threaten, it is avoided so that it may be feared for a longer time.

Amid so many accidents of human frailty, how many deaths are feared, although when one of them comes, there remains no need to fear the others! Yet one is fled so that all may be feared. What sufferings torment those who are treated and cut by physicians? Is it so that they will not die? No, but so that they may die somewhat later.

Many certain torments are undertaken so that a few uncertain days may be added. Sometimes, overcome by those very pains, people die immediately—people who endure them out of fear of death. And although they do not at all choose to end life in order to avoid pain, but choose to suffer in order not to end life, it happens to them that they both suffer and die.

This is so not only because those who are cured eventually end their lives after their sufferings—a life which, when compared with such punishments, can be neither everlasting, because it is mortal, nor long-lasting, because it is wholly brief, nor secure even within its brief span, because it is always uncertain—but also because they sometimes end that life through pain which they were willing to suffer in order not to end.

3. This excessive love of the present life also has the great, exceedingly detestable and dreadful evil that many people, while wishing to live a little longer, gravely offend God, with whom is the fountain of life. Thus, while they vainly fear the end of life—which must necessarily come—they are prevented from reaching the place where life is lived without end.

Moreover, even if this miserable life could be everlasting, it could in no way be compared with even the briefest blessed life. Yet by loving what is most miserable and brief, such people lose what is most blessed and eternal, since in this very life, which they love wrongly, they desire what they lose in the other.

For in this life they do not love misery, since they wish to be blessed; nor do they love brevity, since they do not want it to end. It is simply because it is life that they love it in such a way that, often for its sake—although it is miserable and brief—they lose what is blessed and everlasting.

### 4

Having considered these things, what great command does eternal life give its lovers, when it commands them to be loved in the same way as this life is loved by its devotees? Is it really worthy or tolerable that everything loved in the world should be despised so that a life destined shortly to end may at least be held for that short while; yet that the world should not be despised so that the life which exists without end with him by whom the world was made may be obtained?

[Col. 0485] Recently, when Rome itself, the dwelling-place of the most glorious empire, was being ravaged by a barbarian attack, how many lovers of this temporal life gave up everything they possessed—not only what they had kept for its enjoyment and adornment, but even what they had kept for its support and protection—in order to redeem it, however unhappily and in its nakedness, so that it might be prolonged? Lovers commonly give many things to those whom they love, in order to have them. These people would not have had their beloved life unless, by loving it, they had made it destitute; nor did they give it many things, but rather took everything away, lest the enemy take it away from them. I do not condemn their decision: for who does not know that life itself would have perished if those things stored up for it had not perished? Yet some lost those possessions first and then life itself; while others, although ready to lose everything for its sake, lost life itself first. From this, however, we must learn what kind of lovers of eternal life we ought to be: for its sake we should despise all superfluous things, since, for the sake of this transitory life, things necessary to it were despised.

### 5

For we do not strip our beloved life, as those people stripped theirs, in order to keep it; rather, in order to attain eternal life, we make this temporal life serve it as a more manageable handmaid. We do so if we neither bind it with the fetters of empty ornaments nor burden it with the weight of harmful cares. Let us listen to the Lord, who most faithfully promises us that life, which we ought to desire with the greatest ardor, as though crying out publicly before the whole world:

> Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light.  
> *(Matthew 11:28–30.)*

This discipline of devout humility drives from the soul and, so to speak, exhales the boastful and turbulent desire that craves things placed beyond our control. For there is labor where many things are sought and loved, things for whose attainment and retention the will is not sufficient, because it does not possess the capacity to secure them. But a righteous life is present whenever we will it, because to will it fully is itself righteousness; and the completion of righteousness requires nothing more than a perfect will. See whether there is labor where willing is enough.

Hence it was divinely said:

> Peace on earth to people of good will.  
> *(Luke 2:14.)*

Where there is peace, there is rest; where there is rest, there is an end to striving, and no reason for labor. But for this will to be complete, it must be healthy. It will be healthy if it does not avoid the physician, by whose grace alone it can be healed from the disease of harmful desires.

He is therefore the physician who cries out, “Come to me, all you who labor,” saying that his yoke is easy and his burden light. For when charity has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, what is commanded will certainly be loved [Note: This is how it appears in Lovaniensis and in several manuscripts. But in the editions of Bade and Erasmus it reads *quod videbitur* (“what will seem right”); eight manuscripts support that reading. Other manuscripts finally have *quod jubebitur* (“what will be commanded”).], and it will not be harsh or burdensome if, under this one yoke, we serve with a neck all the freer the less swollen with pride. This is the one burden by which its bearer is not weighed down but lifted up.

If riches are loved, let them be stored where they cannot perish. [Col. 0486] If honor is loved, let it be possessed where no unworthy person is honored. If health is loved, let it be desired and attained where, once attained, nothing is feared. If life is loved, let it be acquired where it is ended by no death.

### 6

Therefore return what you have vowed, because you yourselves are what you return, and you return yourselves to him from whom you are. Return it, I beg you. For what you return will not be diminished by being returned; rather, it will be preserved and increased. He is a generous exactor, not one in need; and he does not grow through what is returned to him, but causes those who return it to grow in themselves.

What is not returned to him is therefore lost; what is returned is added to the one who returns it—or rather, in the one to whom it is returned, the one who returns it is himself preserved. For the thing returned and the one who returns it will be identical, because the debt and the debtor were identical. A human being owes himself to God, and must be returned to him in order to be blessed, since from him he received existence.

This is signified by what the Lord says in the Gospel:

> Render to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God.  
> *(Matthew 22:21.)*

He said this when a coin had been shown to him and they had been asked whose image it bore; they answered, “Caesar’s.” From this they were to understand that God demands his image from the human being in the human being himself, just as Caesar demanded his image on the coin. How much more, then, must it be returned when it has been promised to him to whom it is owed even without a promise!

### 7

Therefore, dearest one, I could indeed, according to my very limited ability, praise more fully the fruit of the holy purpose which I have learned that you have vowed to God, and show what difference there is between Christians who love this world and those who despise it, although both are called faithful. Both have been washed in the same bath of the sacred font, imbued and consecrated with the same mysteries; both are not merely hearers but also preachers of the same Gospel. Yet both are not participants in the kingdom of God, in the light, and in eternal life, which alone is blessed, as co-heirs.

For the Lord Jesus distinguished not those who do not hear, but hearers of his words among themselves, by a very broad boundary and not by a narrow distinction:

> Whoever hears these words of mine and does them, I will compare him to a prudent man who built his house upon rock: the rain descended, the rivers came, the winds blew and struck that house, and it did not fall, because it had been founded upon rock. But whoever hears these words of mine and does not do them, I will compare him to a foolish man who built his house upon sand: the rain descended, the rivers came, the winds blew and struck that house, and it fell, and its ruin was great.  
> *(Matthew 7:24–27; and Luke 6:47–49.)*

To hear those words, then, is to build; in this respect both are equal. But in doing or not doing what they hear, they are as different as a building founded upon the solidity of rock differs from one that, without any foundation, is easily overturned by the shifting nature of sand.

Nor does anyone who does not hear at all thereby secure something safer for himself. For, building nothing and having no roof, he is much more easily overwhelmed, carried away, and scattered by the rains, rivers, and winds that are given free rein.

### 8

I could also, according to my ability, distinguish among those same people who belong on the right hand and to the kingdom of heaven, according to their degrees and merits; and I could show how the married life of fathers and mothers of families who beget children, though religious and devout, differs from the life [Note: The editions of Bade, Ambrose, and Erasmus, and four manuscripts, read “from the blessed life” (*a beata vita*).] which you have vowed to God [Col. 0487]—if you were now to be exhorted to vow it. But since you have already vowed it, since you have already bound yourself, you may not do otherwise.

Before you became bound by your vow, it was free for you to occupy an inferior position, although that freedom is not to be celebrated by which a person is enabled not to return what he owes when it is returned with profit. But now, because your pledge is held before God, I am not inviting you to great righteousness; I am deterring you from great iniquity. For if you do not fulfill what you have vowed, you will not be what you would have remained if you had vowed nothing of the kind. Then you would have been lesser, not worse; but now, God forbid, you will be all the more wretched if you break faith with God, just as you will be all the more blessed if you fulfill your vow.

Do not therefore regret having vowed; rather, rejoice that you are no longer permitted to do what would have been permitted to your detriment. Begin without fear, and fulfill your words by your deeds. He who desires your vows will himself assist you. Blessed is the necessity that compels us toward better things.

### 9

There could be one reason alone why we should not merely fail to urge you to fulfill what you have vowed, but should even forbid you to fulfill it: if your wife should refuse to undertake this with you because of some weakness of mind or body. Such vows ought not to be made by married people except with mutual agreement and consent. If something of this kind has been done rashly, the rashness should be corrected rather than the promise fulfilled. For God does not demand that anyone vow something belonging to another; rather, he forbids the usurpation of what belongs to another.

The Apostle has given a divine ruling on this matter:

> The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband; likewise, the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife.

He used the word “body” to designate the sex. But since I hear that she is so ready to dedicate her continence to God that the only thing preventing her is that she is compelled by conjugal right to render to you what is owed, return to God what both of you have vowed, so that what you do not demand from one another may be fulfilled to him.

If continence is a virtue, as indeed it is, why is the weaker sex more ready for it, when virtue appears to have been named from the man, as the similarity of the word suggests? Therefore, man, do not recoil from the virtue which a woman is ready to undertake. Let your mutual agreement be an offering upon the exalted altar of the Creator, and let conquered desire become the bond of charity—stronger in proportion as it is holier.

Let us rejoice over you in the abundant grace of Christ, outstanding lords and deservedly honored and beloved sons.

## LETTER 128

[Note: Letters 128 and 129 have been transferred here from the Acts of the Carthaginian conference, except that the former also appears in the book *On the Proceedings with Emeritus*.]

[Note: Marcellinus was sent into Africa by Honorius to arrange a conference between Catholics and Donatists concerning their controversies. After the imperial rescript issued to him at Ravenna on 14 or 12 October, in the consulship of Varane (that is, in 410)—as a fragment of that rescript is noted in the *Theodosian Code*, book 16, title 11—had first been published, he himself issued two edicts in the following year. By one he appointed that the bishops of both parties should assemble at Carthage by the day of the Kalends of June for the purpose of conference; by the other, once the bishops had arrived at Carthage, he prescribed the place and manner of the conference, warning each party to declare in written replies whether the provisions of the edict pleased them, according to Augustine, *Brief Account of the Conference*, chapters 2 and 3. The Catholics therefore answered this latter edict with the letter which we have taken care to publish here among Augustine’s letters, because in style and sense it wholly bears Augustine’s stamp. Possidius says, chapter 13, that in all that was done for the peace of the Church the palm was given to Augustine by the Lord: “For,” he says, “that entire good was both begun and completed through that holy man, while our bishops took counsel with him and labored together.” Hence Augustine himself writes in *On the Proceedings of Pelagius* that he was then “most occupied with the care” of this conference, when he first saw Pelagius once or twice at Carthage.]

[Note: Added from Volume 7, part 1. What was formerly numbered 128 is now 112. Written in the year 411.]

The Catholic bishops declare their agreement with the conditions prescribed in Marcellinus’s edict for the conference to be held at Carthage. They also voluntarily promise that, if defeated, they will not demand that their episcopal office be preserved for them, although they wish the dignity of the Donatist bishops, even if defeated, to remain intact for each of them.

To the honorable and beloved son, the most illustrious and distinguished man, tribune and notary, [Col. 0488] MARCELLINUS: AURELIUS, SILVANUS, and all the Catholic bishops.

### 1

By this letter we inform you that, as you were pleased to urge us, we agree in every respect with the edict of Your Excellency, by which provision has been made for preserving the tranquility and peace of our conference and for establishing and defending the truth. That is, we agree concerning the place and time of the conference itself and concerning the number of those who ought to be present.

We also agree that those to whom we delegate the task of holding the conference should subscribe to their written statements; and in the document by which we impose this duty upon them and promise that we will approve what they do, you should not only have the signatures of all of us, but should yourself watch them being made.

With the Lord’s help, we will also admonish the Christian people to keep completely away from the place of the conference, for the sake of peace and tranquility, and to hasten to hear what is being done—not while it is being done, but afterward, when it has been written down—so that they may learn it, just as you have promised to publish it for all.

### 2

Relying also upon the truth, we bind ourselves by this condition: if those with whom we are dealing can demonstrate that, although the Christian people, in accordance with God’s promises, were increasing everywhere, already filling a large part of the world and spreading so as to fill the rest, the Church of Christ suddenly perished through the contagion of the sins of certain people whom they accuse, and remained only in the party of Donatus—if they can demonstrate this, as stated—then we will demand no episcopal honors from them, but will follow the counsel of those to whom, for the sake of eternal salvation alone, we shall owe gratitude for so great a benefit, once the truth has been recognized.

But if we are able instead to show that the Church of Christ already possesses the most fertile expanses of all the provinces—not only African but also overseas—and of many nations, abounding in peoples, and that, as it is written, it is bearing fruit and growing throughout the whole world; if finally we demonstrate that the case of those whom they then preferred to accuse rather than convict has been brought to an end, although the cause of the Church does not rest upon them; and if we show that Caecilian was judged [Col. 0489] innocent, while they were judged violent and slanderous by the emperor to whose tribunal they themselves voluntarily brought their accusations; finally, if we prove, by human records or divine testimony, whatever they say about the sins of any persons either that their innocence was attacked by false accusations or that the Church of Christ, whose communion we share, was not destroyed by any of their offenses—then let them preserve unity with us in such a way that they may not only find the way of salvation but also not lose the honor of the episcopate.

For it is not the divine sacraments of truth in them that we detest, but the inventions of human error. When these have been removed, we embrace the brotherly heart joined to us by Christian charity, which we now grieve to see separated by diabolical dissension.

### 3

Each of us will be able, with the colleague associated with him in office, to sit alternately in the more prominent place, just as a visiting bishop sits beside his colleague. When this is granted alternately in the two basilicas on either side, each will be anticipated by the other in mutual honor. For where the commandment of charity has enlarged hearts, the possession of peace does not become narrow.

Then, when one of them has died, each may subsequently be succeeded individually, according to the former custom. Nor will anything new be done. From the very beginning of the separation, Catholic charity has preserved this practice among those who, after condemning the wicked error of schismatic division, however late, came to taste the sweetness of unity.

Or, if perhaps the Christian people prefer individual bishops and cannot tolerate the association of two because of the unusual appearance of things, let both of us withdraw from office. Once the condemned cause of schism has been established in peaceful unity in the individual churches, let individual bishops be appointed in the necessary places by those who will be found individually in the individual churches, after unity has been restored.

For why should we hesitate to offer our Redeemer the sacrifice of this humility? Did he descend from heaven into human members so that we might be his members, while we fear to descend from our seats lest his very members be torn apart by cruel division?

For our sake there is nothing more sufficient than that we are faithful and obedient Christians; let us therefore always remain so. We are ordained as bishops for the sake of Christian peoples. Therefore let us do with our episcopate whatever benefits Christian peoples for Christian peace.

If we are useful servants, why should we begrudge the Lord’s eternal gains for the sake of our temporal exaltation? The dignity of the episcopate will be more fruitful for us if, once laid down, it gathers Christ’s flock rather than, when retained, scatters it. For with what face shall we hope for the honor promised by Christ in the future age if our honor in this age prevents Christian unity? [Note: In *On the Proceedings with Emeritus*, Augustine ordered this letter to be read in full. When these words were being read, he recalls saying in the book concerning those same proceedings: “Brothers, if we are thinking of the Lord, this higher place is the watchtower of a vinedresser, not the summit of one who is proud. If, when I wish to retain my episcopate, I scatter Christ’s flock, how can the honor of the shepherd be anything but the loss of the flock?”]

### 4

We have taken care to write these things to Your Excellency so that they may also become known to everyone through you. We ask that, with the help of the Lord our God—by whose prompting [Col. 0490] we make these promises and by whose assistance we trust that we can fulfill them—even before the conference, if possible, pious charity may either heal or subdue the hearts of people, whether weak or hardened. Thus, with minds already at peace, let us not resist the most evident truth, but let our agreement either precede or follow our discussion.

For we ought not to despair if they remember that the peacemakers are blessed, because they will be called sons of God (Matthew 5:9). It is much more fitting and easier for them to wish that the party of Donatus be reconciled to the entire Christian world than for the entire Christian world to be rebaptized by the party of Donatus.

This is especially so since, when people came from the sacrilegious and condemned schism of Maximianus—people whom they had tried to correct by persecuting them even through the commands of earthly authorities—they sought them with such great charity that they did not dare to invalidate the baptism given by them. They received some of those who had been condemned without diminishing their honor at all, while they judged others to have remained undefiled in the fellowship of that division.

We do not envy their agreement among themselves. But they should certainly consider how piously and zealously the Catholic root seeks the branch broken from it, if that branch itself labored in the same way to gather a small fragment cut off from it.

*(In another hand):* We wish you, son, good health in the Lord.

I, Aurelius, bishop of the Catholic Church of Carthage, have subscribed to this letter.

*(Again in another hand):* I, Silvanus, elder of the Church of Summis, have subscribed.

## LETTER 129
