[Note: It was missing from the printed editions. What was formerly numbered 129 is now 97. Written shortly after the preceding letter.]

The Catholic bishops reply to the Notoria [Note: The Donatist *Notoria* survives in the first Carthaginian conference, section 14. In it, replying to Marcellinus’s second edict, they make known that, coming together from various parts of Africa, they entered Carthage on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June, and ask Marcellinus to order all who had come to be present at the conference.], declaring to Marcellinus that they grant what the Donatists had requested: that all their bishops who had come should be present at the place where the conference was to be held. They also defend the cause of the Catholic Church against their schism with powerful arguments.

To the honorable and beloved son, V. C. and distinguished tribune and notary, MARCELLINUS: AURELIUS, SILVANUS, and all the Catholic bishops.

### 1

The *Notoria*, or the letter of our brothers—whom we desire to be converted from pernicious dissension to Catholic peace—made us very anxious, because they did not wish to agree with the edict of Your Nobility, by which you provided for the tranquility and peace of our discussion. We feared that, even if not all of them, at least some might obstruct the conference, which ought to be peaceful and orderly, through the tumult or uproar of the crowd.

Would that this thought does not trouble them and that this suspicion deceives us! Therefore, if they wish all to be present, so that, whenever they deem it appropriate, we too may assemble there with them and depart from there together, united and at peace, with their schismatic division corrected and bound by the fraternal bond of Christ’s unity—while all good people marvel and rejoice, and only the devil and [Col. 0491] those like him grieve—then let us proceed together into the Church with the most fervent and radiant charity, to give thanks and offer praise to God.

### 2

For what great difficulty is there if a peaceful eye observes, and Christian thought does not cease to consider and see, that, once human accusations—whether true or false—have been set aside, the Church must be sought in those writings in which Christ, its Redeemer, has been made known?

Just as we do not listen to those who speak against Christ by saying that his body was stolen from the tomb by his disciples, so we ought not to listen to those who speak against his Church by saying that it exists only among the Africans and their few associates.

For the Apostle says that truthful Christians are members of Christ (Ephesians 4:25). Therefore, just as we do not believe that the dead flesh of Christ perished from the tomb through someone’s theft, so we ought not to believe that his living members perished from the world through someone’s sin.

Since Christ is the head and the Church is the body, it is therefore not difficult to see that both the head and the body are commended together in the Gospel: the head against the accusations of the Jews, and the body against the accusations of heretics.

For what is written—“It was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day”—is directed against those who say that the dead man was taken away from the tomb. But what follows—“and that repentance and the forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:46–47)—is directed against those who say that the Church does not exist throughout the world.

Thus, in one brief passage and with only a few words, both the enemy of the head and the enemy of the body are rejected—and, if he pays faithful attention, corrected.

### 3

We grieve all the more that our brothers retain these hostilities because it is evident that they hold, together with us, the same Scriptures in which these clearest testimonies are contained.

The Jews who deny that Christ rose do not at least accept the Gospel. But these brothers of ours are bound by the authority of both Testaments; nevertheless, they wish to accuse us concerning the Gospel that has been handed down, and they refuse to believe what has been read aloud.

But perhaps now, having undertaken the care of this conference, they have examined the sacred Scriptures more diligently. They have found in them countless testimonies promising that the Church would exist among all nations and throughout the whole world. They see that its fulfillment and manifestation have begun in the Gospel, in the Apostolic Letters, and in the Acts of the Apostles, where the very places, cities, and provinces through which it grew are recorded.

Beginning from Jerusalem, it spread from there even into Africa—not by migrating, but by growing. Yet they have found no testimony in the divine utterances stating that it would perish from the other regions of the world and remain only in the African party of Donatus.

They have seen how absurd it would be for so many divine testimonies to be recited on behalf of the Church that was destined to perish, while no testimony of God could be found for the Church that, as they think, was destined to please the Lord.

Perhaps, reflecting on these things, they wished to come together to our place of conference in order to end their empty, pernicious hostilities opposed to eternal salvation—not so that a new tumult might arise, but so that an ancient discord might end.

[Col. 0492] ### 4

They may also have reflected upon the matter that commonly provokes them greatly against us: namely, that earthly kings, who were foretold long beforehand as destined to serve Christ the Lord, establish laws against heretics and schismatics for the sake of Catholic peace.

We believe that they may at some point have considered this not blameworthy. For the ancient kings, not only of the Hebrew nation but also foreigners, terrified all the peoples of their kingdoms with extremely threatening commands, so that no one would do anything—or even say anything—against the God of Israel, that is, the true God.

Moreover, the elders of these people sent the very case of Caecilianus, from which this dissension arose, to the emperor Constantine through the proconsul Anulinus, by bringing an accusation. They seem certainly to have done this for no other reason than that the emperor Constantine should, by royal authority, decree something against those who were defeated in favor of those who prevailed.

They could have discovered, and perhaps did discover—because of the necessity of this very conference—by searching the public archives, that the whole case had long ago been concluded after the ecclesiastical judgments by which Caecilianus was acquitted. The emperor himself had judged it, to whose tribunal they had first sent the entire matter and afterward brought it.

There too they could have found that the case of Felix of Aptunga, the ordainer of Caecilianus, whom they had called the source of all evils in their council, had been cleared when the proconsul Aelianus investigated it by order of that same emperor.

### 5

Even if they paid attention to this—and it would have been easy to do so—they could have noticed that the sacred Scriptures promised that the Church of Christ would exist, mixed with weeds, chaff, and bad fish, until the time of the harvest (Matthew 13:24–30), of winnowing (Matthew 3:12), and of the shore and the sorting of fish (Matthew 13:47–48).

They could certainly have understood that, even if Caecilianus and his fellow bishops had had a bad case, this could have prejudiced nothing against the Christian world, which God had promised long beforehand to a few believers and has now granted to many who can see it.

Unless, perhaps, a sinful human being had more power against the Church than God, who swore on behalf of the Church; or unless iniquity had more power through what it lost than truth through what God promised.

They may by now have seen how foolish and impious it is to think such things. They may also have reflected that, through earthly authorities, they themselves had taken care to drive the Maximianists whom they had condemned—and who had condemned Primianus—from their basilicas.

There they learned more certainly, through their own recent example, that it is not a sin if the Church requests such action against its rebels from authorities of this kind.

They also later received some of those whom they had condemned. When condemning them, they had granted a delay to many others who were established in the same fellowship of schism, saying that they had remained undefiled in communion with the sacrilegious offshoot of Maximianus. They did not dare to invalidate and repeat the baptism administered either by those who had been condemned or by their associates, although it had been administered outside, in schism.

They must certainly have judged that the things they said against us were condemned by their own example. We must believe that they now understand how unworthy and intolerable it is that, while they sit in episcopal chairs together with these people, and while the condemned and the condemners of Primianus sit together with him in his cause, so that there may be peace within the party of Donatus, the Christian world should be slandered on account of Caecilianus, lest the unity of Christ live in peace.

[Col. 0493] ### 6

Perhaps reflecting upon all these things and moved by fear of God, they wished to be present at the place of the conference—not with the intention of creating tumult, but of creating peace.

As for their statement that they wished all to be present because their number might thereby become evident, since their opponents had often falsely claimed that they were few: if our people have ever said this, it could most truthfully have been said of those places where the number of our fellow bishops, clergy, and laity is far greater, especially in the proconsular province.

Indeed, except in consular Numidia, they are easily outnumbered by us even in the other African provinces. Or, certainly, in comparison with all the nations throughout which the Catholic communion is spreading, we are entirely correct to call them very few.

But if they wished to make their number known now, would it not become known more orderly and peacefully through their subscriptions, which you instructed them by your edict to append in your presence and under your supervision?

What, then, do they mean by desiring that all be present at the place of the conference? If they are not thinking of peace, what will they not disturb by speaking, or what will they do there by remaining silent? For even if there is no shouting, the mere whispering of so many people will itself create enough uproar to obstruct the conference.

### 7

What did they mean by thinking it should be included in their *Notoria* that they had justly demanded that all should be present because all had been summoned to come? As though a few could be selected who ought to be present, unless from among all who had come, so that they might subscribe to their selection in your presence; thus all would be present in the few, once the few had been selected by all.

Therefore either they are contemplating tumult or peace. We desire the latter and guard against the former. For this reason, lest—God forbid—what we guard against be prepared rather than what we desire, we agree that all of them may be present, provided that on our side there is a number as large as seemed sufficient to Your Excellency.

Thus, if anything tumultuous emerges through the crowds, it may rightly be attributed only to the party in whose presence there was a wholly unnecessary multitude for a matter that ought to be conducted by a few.

But if the multitude necessary for creating unity is what we all desire, what we ardently seek, and what we humbly implore from the Lord, then, whenever they wish it, we will all be present and, with the help of him who grants this gift, will hasten eagerly toward so great a good, saying:

> You are our brothers.  
> *(Isaiah 66:5, according to the Septuagint.)*

We will say this no longer to those who detest us, but to those who, their hatred ended, embrace us, so that the name of the Lord may be honored and so that, rejoicing together with us, they may see how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity (Psalm 132:1).

*(In another hand):* We wish you, son, good health in God.

*(Again):* I, Aurelius, bishop of the Catholic Church of Carthage, have subscribed.

*(Again):* I, Silvanus, of the first see of the province of Numidia, have subscribed.

## LETTER 130

[Note: In correcting this letter we were assisted by manuscripts a, bg, bl, c, cc, ff, g, gv, j, n, r, s, th, vc; two manuscripts of bn, two of sb, two of t, five of v; and by the editions of Ambrose, Bade, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis.]

[Note: Elsewhere numbered 121; what was formerly 130 is now 144. Written in the year 411 or 412.]

Augustine prescribes for the wealthy widow Proba how God should be prayed to.

[Col. 0494] AUGUSTINE, bishop, servant of Christ and of the servants of Christ, to the devout handmaid of God PROBA [Note: Proba, whose cognomen was Faltonia, had fled to Africa after the destruction of the City. She was the wife of Probus, prefect of the praetorium and ordinary consul in the year 371; the grandmother of the virgin Demetrias; and the mother-in-law, not the true mother, of Demetrias’s mother Juliana, according to Augustine in *On the Good of Widowhood*, chapter 19. Jerome likewise indicates in Letter 8 to Demetrias that Demetrias was born to Olibrius, Proba’s son. He then praises Proba’s family at length, saying: “That Proba was more illustrious in the Roman world than any other name of every dignity and all nobility; her holiness and goodness, poured out upon everyone, were venerable even among barbarians; and the ordinary consulships of her three sons, Probinus, Olibrius, and Probus, did not weary her,” and so forth.], greetings in the Lord of lords.

## CHAPTER ONE

### 1

Remembering that you asked me and that I promised to write something to you about praying to God, now that, by the gift of the one whom we pray to, time and opportunity have been granted, I ought at last to discharge my debt and serve your devout purpose in the charity of Christ.

I cannot express in words how much your request itself has rejoiced me, since through it I learned how great a concern you have for so important a matter. For what business ought to be more important for your widowhood than to persist in prayer night and day, in accordance with the Apostle’s admonition? He says:

> But she who is truly a widow and desolate has hoped in the Lord and persists in prayer night and day.  
> *(1 Timothy 5:5.)*

It may therefore seem surprising that, although according to this world you are noble, wealthy, and the mother of so great a family—and, though a widow, not desolate—you have allowed the concern for prayer to occupy your heart and claim it especially for itself. Yet this is because you wisely understand that in this world and in this life no soul can be secure.

### 2

Accordingly, the one who gave you that thought is surely doing what he did for his disciples, who were grieving not for themselves but for the human race and despairing that anyone could be saved after hearing from him that it was easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven. He answered with a wonderful and most merciful promise: what is impossible for human beings is possible for God (Matthew 19:24–26).

The one for whom it is easy even for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven inspired you with the devout concern about which you thought you should consult me: how you ought to pray. For while he was still here in the flesh, he sent the rich Zacchaeus into the kingdom of heaven (Luke 19:9); and after he had been glorified by his resurrection and ascension, he afterward made many rich people, by granting them the Holy Spirit, despise this world and become richer through the end of their desire for riches.

How would you be so eager to pray to God unless you hoped in him? And how would you hope in him if you hoped in the uncertainty of riches and despised the most salutary command in which the Apostle says:

> Command the rich of this world not to be proud in mind, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who gives us all things abundantly for enjoyment; let them be rich in good works, freely give, share, and store up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of the true life.  
> *(1 Timothy 6:17–19.)*

## CHAPTER TWO
### 3

You ought, therefore, because of your love for this true life, to consider yourself desolate in this world, however great the happiness may be in which you live. For just as that is the true life, in comparison with which this life—which is nevertheless greatly loved—however pleasant and prolonged it may be, ought not even to be called life, so there is also a true consolation which the Lord promises through the prophet, saying: “I will give him true consolation, peace upon peace” (Isa. 57:18–19, according to the Septuagint). Without this consolation, whatever earthly consolations there may be contain more desolation than consolation.

For what consolation do riches, lofty dignities, and other things of this kind bring to mortals who think themselves happy but are deprived of that true happiness, when it is better for them not to need such things than to excel in them? Once acquired, these things torment them more through fear of losing them than the ardor of acquiring them tormented them when they were desired [Note: [Col. 0495] In Louvain, this negative particle is omitted; it is found in the other editions and in nearly all the manuscripts.] [Note: [Col. 0495] The Benignian manuscript reads: “Which torment the person who has acquired them more through fear of loss than the person who desires them through the ardor of acquisition.”]. Such goods do not make people good; rather, people who have been made good by another source make these things good by using them well. True consolations are therefore not found in these things, but rather where true life is found. For a person must become blessed from the same source from which he becomes good.

### 4

Good people, however, seem even in this life to provide no small consolations. If poverty causes distress, if mourning brings sadness, if bodily pain troubles us, if exile grieves us, or if any other calamity afflicts us, let good people be present who know not only how to rejoice with those who rejoice but also to weep with those who weep (Rom. 12:15), and who know how to address and converse with us for our benefit: harsh things are greatly softened, heavy burdens relieved, adversities overcome. But it is he who acts in them and through them who has made them good by his Spirit [Note: [Col. 0495] Two Vatican manuscripts read: “who makes good people good by his good Spirit.”].

Conversely, if riches overflow, if no bereavement occurs, if bodily health is present, if one lives safely in one’s homeland, but wicked people live alongside one, among whom there is no one whom one can trust, from whom deceit, fraud, anger, discord, and ambushes need not be feared and endured, do not all those things become bitter and harsh, with nothing joyful or sweet in them? Thus, in all human circumstances, nothing is friendly to a person without a friendly person.

But how many people of this kind are found, concerning whose mind and character one can have secure confidence in this life? For just as no one is fully known by another, so no one is so fully known even to himself that he can be confident about his conduct tomorrow. Therefore, although many people are known by their fruits, and some by living well bring joy to their neighbors while others by living badly cause them grief, nevertheless, because human hearts are unknown and uncertain, the Apostle very rightly warns us not to judge anything before the proper time, until the Lord comes, brings to light what is hidden in darkness, and discloses the purposes of the heart; then each person will receive praise from God (1 Cor. 4:5).

### 5

In the darkness of this life, therefore, in which we are absent from the Lord as long as we walk by faith and not by sight (2 Cor. 5:6–7), the Christian soul ought to consider itself desolate, so that it does not cease to pray. It should learn to direct the eye of faith toward the words of the divine and holy Scriptures, as toward a lamp placed in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in our hearts (2 Pet. 1:19).

For the light of this lamp has an ineffable source: that light shines in the darkness and is not grasped by the darkness. To see it, hearts must be cleansed by faith: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8); and, “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

Then there will be true life after death and true consolation after desolation: that life will deliver our soul from death, and that consolation our eyes from tears. And because there will then be no temptation, the same psalm continues: “My feet from falling.” Moreover, if there is no temptation, there is no longer any prayer; for there will no longer be an expectation of the promised good, but the contemplation of the good that has been received. Hence he says: “I shall please the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 114:8–9), where we shall then be, not in the desert of the dead, where we now are.

“For you have died,” the Apostle says, “and your life is hidden with Christ in God. But when Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:3–4). This is the true life which the rich are commanded to attain through good works. And there is true consolation there. In view of that consolation, the desolate widow—although she has children and grandchildren and piously manages her household, dealing with all her family so that they place their hope in God—nevertheless says in prayer:

“My soul has thirsted for you; how greatly my flesh has thirsted for you, in a desert land, pathless and waterless” (Ps. 62:2–3).

What is this dying life, whatever mortal consolations may fill it, whatever companions may accompany travelers through it, and however great an abundance of things may heap it up? You know how uncertain all these things are; and, in comparison with that promised happiness, what would they be even if they were not uncertain?

### 6

I have said this because you, a wealthy and noble widow and the mother of so great a household, asked me about prayer, so that even while your attendants remain with you in this life and obey you, you may feel yourself desolate—not yet having attained that life where there is true and certain consolation, where what was said in prophecy will be fulfilled:

“We have been satisfied in the morning with your mercy; we have rejoiced and been glad in all our days. We have rejoiced in proportion to the days in which you humbled us, the years in which we saw evil” (Ps. 89:14–15).

## CHAPTER III

### 7

Before that consolation comes, therefore, remember that you are desolate, however abundantly you may be surrounded by the happiness of temporal goods, so that you may persist in prayer day and night. For the Apostle did not assign this duty to just any widow:

“But she who is truly a widow and desolate,” he says, “has set her hope on the Lord and persists in prayer day and night.”

But what follows, guard against with the utmost vigilance: “She who lives in pleasures is dead while she lives” (1 Tim. 5:5–6). A person lives amid the things he loves, the things he desires as something great, the things in which he believes himself to be happy.

Therefore, what Scripture says about riches—“If riches increase, do not set your heart on them” (Ps. 61:11)—I say to you also about pleasures: “If pleasures increase, do not set your heart on them.” Do not think highly of yourself because they are not lacking, because they are available in abundance, because they flow as though from a most lavish fountain of earthly happiness. Despise and reject all these things in yourself, and seek nothing in them except the sound health of your body.

For sound health must not be despised because of the necessary uses of life, before this mortal nature puts on immortality (1 Cor. 15:54)—that is, true, perfect, and perpetual health, which is not restored by corruptible pleasure after being weakened by earthly infirmity, but, remaining firm through heavenly strength, is invigorated by eternal incorruption.

The Apostle himself says: “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13:14), because we care for the flesh, but only as necessity for salvation requires. “No one ever hated his own flesh” (Eph. 5:29), as he likewise says. For this reason he also admonishes Timothy, who, as it appears, was excessively severe with his body, to use a little wine because of his stomach and his frequent illnesses (1 Tim. 5:23).

### 8

Many holy men and women, therefore, exercising every possible caution, rejected these pleasures—if a widow lives in them, that is, if she clings to and dwells in them with the delight of her heart while she is dead in life [Note: [Col. 0497] So the Gallican manuscripts. Four Vatican manuscripts read: “if she clings and dwells in the love of the heart” (*si in dilectione cordis*); other Vatican manuscripts: “if [she clings and dwells] in love of heart” (*si dilectione cordis*); the editions: “with the delight of the flesh” (*si in delectatione carnis*).]—by distributing to the poor the riches that are, as it were, the mothers of pleasures, and in this way stored them more securely in heavenly treasures.

If you do not do this because you are bound by some duty of piety, you know how you will give an account of these things to God. “No one knows what is in a person except the spirit of the person that is in him” (1 Cor. 2:11). We ought not to judge anything before the proper time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light what is hidden in darkness and disclose the purposes of the heart; then each person will receive praise from God (ibid. 4:5).

Nevertheless, it is part of your widow’s duty that, if pleasures increase, you do not set your heart on them, lest what ought to be above, so that it may live, die by rotting in them. Count yourself among those of whom it is written: “Their hearts shall live for ever and ever” (Ps. 21:27).

## CHAPTER IV

### 9

You have heard what kind of prayer you should offer [Note: [Col. 0497] Erasmus and Louvain read “how”; the other editions and manuscripts read “what kind of prayer.”]; now hear also what you should pray for—the matter about which you thought it especially necessary to consult me—since you are troubled by what the Apostle says: “For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought” (Rom. 8:26). You feared that praying otherwise than as one ought might harm you more than not praying.

What can be said briefly is this: pray for the blessed life. Everyone wants to possess it; for even those who live most wickedly and ruinously would not live that way at all unless they thought that they were, or could become, blessed in that condition. What else, then, ought you to pray for except what both the wicked and the good desire, but which only the good attain?

## CHAPTER V

### 10

Perhaps you will now ask what the blessed life itself is. In considering this question, the intellectual powers and leisure of many philosophers have been worn out. Yet they were able to find it all the less because they honored its source all the less and did not give thanks to it.

First, then, consider whether we should agree with those who say that the person is blessed who lives according to his own will. But far be it from us to believe that this is true. What if he wishes to live wickedly? Is he not proved to be all the more miserable the more easily his evil will is fulfilled?

Even those who philosophized without worshiping God rightly rejected this opinion. For one of them, a most eloquent man, says:

“Behold, others, not philosophers indeed, but nevertheless ready for argument, all say that those are blessed who live as they themselves wish. That is certainly false. To wish what is unbecoming is itself the greatest misery; and it is not so miserable to fail to obtain what you wish as to wish to obtain what you ought not” (Cicero, *Hortensius*).

What do you think? Were these words not spoken by Truth itself through whatever human being uttered them? We may therefore say here what the Apostle said of a certain Cretan prophet when he approved that man’s statement: “This testimony is true” (Titus 1:13).

### 11

That person, then, is blessed who has everything he wants and wants nothing that is unbecoming. If this is so, consider now what people may rightly desire.

One person wants to marry; another, bereaved of a spouse, chooses thereafter to live continently; another wishes to experience no sexual intercourse, even within marriage. And although one of these may be found better than another, we cannot say that any of them desires something unbecoming. So too, it is not unbecoming to desire children—the fruit, of course, of marriage—and life and health for those who have been born. This desire often occupies even a widow’s continence; for although, having renounced marriage, she no longer desires to bear more children, she still desires that those she has borne may live in safety.

Virgin integrity is free from all this concern. Yet all these people have dear men and women for whom they rightly desire even temporal health. But once people have obtained this health for themselves and for those whom they love, can we call them blessed already? They possess something that it is not unbecoming to desire; but if they do not possess other things that are greater and better, and more fully endowed with usefulness and dignity, they are still far from the blessed life.

## CHAPTER VI

### 12

Is it therefore fitting that, beyond this temporal health, they should desire honors and powers for themselves and their own? Certainly, if they desire these things so that through them they may benefit those who live under their authority—not for the sake of the honors and powers themselves, but for the sake of the good that results from them—it is fitting to desire them. But if they desire them for empty ostentation, proud display, or the excessive and even harmful pomp of vanity, it is not fitting.

Accordingly, if they also desire for themselves and their own a sufficiency of necessary things, concerning which the Apostle speaks as follows:

“Godliness with sufficiency is great gain. For we brought nothing into this world, and we can take nothing out of it. But having food and clothing, let us be content with these. For those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and a snare and many foolish and harmful desires, which plunge people into destruction and perdition. For the root of all evils is greed; by craving it, some have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows” (1 Tim. 6:6–10),

then whoever desires this sufficiency, and desires nothing more, does not desire anything unbecoming. Otherwise he does not desire sufficiency itself, and therefore does not desire it rightly.

This is what the person desired and prayed for who said:

“Do not give me riches or poverty; but appoint for me what is necessary in sufficient measure, lest, when satisfied, I become a liar and say, ‘Who sees me?’ or, having become poor, I steal and swear falsely by the name of my God” (Prov. 30:8–9).

You see clearly that this sufficiency is not desired for its own sake, but for the sake of bodily health and a manner of life appropriate to the person, so that one may not be out of place among those with whom one must live honorably and dutifully.

### 13

In all these matters, therefore, human health and friendship are desired for their own sake. Sufficiency of necessary things, however, is ordinarily sought—not for its own sake, but for the sake of those two higher goods—when it is sought rightly.

Health consists in life itself, in well-being, and in the soundness of mind and body. Nor should friendship be confined within narrow limits: it embraces all to whom love and affection are owed, although the heart may incline more readily toward some and more cautiously toward others. It extends even to enemies, for whom we are commanded to pray. Thus there is no one in the human race to whom affection is not owed—not necessarily because of mutual love, but because of our fellowship in the common nature of humanity.

## CHAPTER VII

Yet those who in turn love us in holiness and purity greatly and rightly delight us. When these relationships are present, we should pray that they may be preserved; when they are absent, we should pray that they may be obtained.

### 14

Is this the whole of it? Are these all the things from which the sum of the blessed life is gathered? Or does Truth teach something else that should be preferred to all these things?

For that sufficiency, and health itself—whether our own or that of our friends—as long as it is temporal, must be rejected for the sake of attaining eternal life. Perhaps, indeed, a body may be considered healthy, but certainly not a healthy mind, if it does not prefer eternal things to temporal ones. For life is not lived usefully in time unless it is lived in order to acquire the merit by which one may live in eternity.

To that one life, therefore, in which we live with God and from God, all other things that are usefully and rightly desired must unquestionably be referred. We love ourselves in the true sense if we love God; and, according to another commandment, we truly love our neighbors as ourselves if, as far as lies within us, we lead them toward a love like ours for God.

We therefore love God for his own sake, and ourselves and our neighbors for his sake. But when we live in this way, we must not yet consider ourselves established in the blessed life, as though there were nothing more for which we should pray. For how are we already living blessedly when that for the sake of which alone we live well is still lacking?

## CHAPTER VIII

### 15

Why, then, do we scatter ourselves among many things and ask what we should pray for, fearing that perhaps we may not pray as we ought, instead of saying with the psalm:

“One thing I have asked from the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, to behold the delight of God and to visit his temple” (Ps. 26:4)?

There all the days become “all” not by coming and passing away, nor is the beginning of one the end of another; all are together without end, where life itself, whose days they are, has no end.

To obtain this life, the blessed true Life itself taught us to pray—not with many words, as though we were heard because we were more talkative when we prayed to the one who, as the Lord himself says, knows what we need before we ask him (Matt. 6:7–8).

It may therefore seem surprising that, although he forbade many words, he urged us to pray in this way. Since he knows what we need before we ask him, why did he say, “We ought always to pray and not lose heart”? He did so by presenting the example of a widow who wished to obtain justice against her adversary. By repeatedly appealing to an unjust judge, she moved him to hear her—not because he was moved by justice or mercy, but because he was overcome by weariness. Thus we were to learn how much more certainly the merciful and just Lord God hears us when we pray without ceasing, since she could not be ignored even by an unjust and ungodly judge through her persistent appeals; and how willingly and graciously he fulfills the good desires of those whom he knows forgive the sins of others, if that widow attained what she desired when she wished to be avenged (Luke 18:1–8).

Likewise, when a friend had come to a man from a journey and he had nothing to set before him, the man wished to borrow three loaves from another friend—perhaps the Trinity of one substance was represented by these. Although the friend was already sleeping with his servants, the petitioner, most persistent and troublesome, woke him so that he would give him as many as he wanted, more from a desire to avoid annoyance than from consideration of benevolence. From this we understand that if someone who is sleeping is compelled to give because a petitioner unwillingly wakes him, how much more generously does he give who neither knows sleep nor sleeps, and who awakens us when we sleep so that we may ask (Luke 11:5–13).

### 16

Hence also the words:

“Ask, and you shall receive; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it shall be opened. Or what person is there among you who, if his son asks him for bread, would give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, would give him a serpent? Or if he asks for an egg, would give him a scorpion? If you, then, although you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give good things to those who ask him?” (Luke 11:5–13).

Since the Apostle commends three things, faith may be signified by the fish—either because of the water of Baptism or because faith remains whole amid the waves of this age. Opposed to it is the serpent, which by poisonous deceit persuaded humanity not to believe God.

Hope may be signified by the egg, because the life of the chick is not yet present but will be, and is not yet seen but still hoped for; “for hope that is seen is not hope” (Rom. 8:24). Opposed to it is the scorpion, because the person who hopes for eternal life forgets what lies behind and reaches forward to what lies ahead; looking backward is harmful. The scorpion is to be feared from the part that it has poisonous and stinging behind it.

Charity may be signified by the bread: “The greatest of these is charity” (1 Cor. 13:13), and among foods the usefulness of bread surpasses the others. Opposed to it is the stone, because hard hearts reject charity.

Whether these things signify something else more appropriately, nevertheless the one who knows how to give good things to his children compels us to ask, seek, and knock.

### 17

Why does he do this, when he knows what we need before we ask him? This may trouble us unless we understand that our Lord and God does not wish us to inform him of our will—something he cannot fail to know—but wishes our desire to be exercised through prayer, so that we may be capable of receiving what he prepares to give.

That gift is very great, but we are small and narrow in our capacity to receive it. Therefore we are told: “Be enlarged; do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers” (2 Cor. 6:13–14).

The greater our faith in that exceedingly great reality—which no eye has seen, because it is not a color; no ear has heard, because it is not a sound; and which has not entered the human heart (1 Cor. 2:9), because the human heart must ascend to it—the more firmly we hope for it and the more ardently we desire it, the greater will be our capacity to receive it.

## CHAPTER IX

### 18

In faith, hope, and charity, therefore, we always pray with continuous desire. But at fixed intervals of hours and times we also ask God in words, so that by these signs of realities we may remind ourselves how much we have advanced in this desire, and stir ourselves more vigorously to increase it. A more worthy result follows when a more ardent affection precedes it.

Accordingly, what else does the Apostle’s command mean—“Pray without ceasing” (1 Thess. 5:17)—than this: “Desire without ceasing the blessed life, which is eternal and which only he can give”?

Let us therefore always desire this from the Lord God and always pray for it. But because other cares and activities somehow check this desire, at fixed hours we recall our minds from them to the task of prayer, admonishing ourselves through the words of prayer to concentrate on what we desire. Otherwise what has begun to grow lukewarm may grow entirely cold and be completely extinguished unless it is more frequently rekindled.

Hence also what the same Apostle says—“Let your requests be made known to God” (Phil. 4:6)—is not to be understood as though they become known to God, who certainly knew them before they existed, but as becoming known to us in the presence of God through endurance, not to human beings through boastfulness.

Or perhaps they may also become known to the angels who are with God, so that in some way they may offer them to God, consult him about them, and bring us openly or secretly what they learn must be fulfilled at his command, just as they learn that it ought to be fulfilled there. For an angel said to a man: “And now, when you and Sarah were praying, I offered your prayer in the presence of the glory of God” (Tob. 12:12).

## CHAPTER X

### 19

Since these things are so, even when we have time to pray for a long while—that is, when the duties of other good and necessary actions do not prevent it—it is neither improper nor useless to do so. For, contrary to what some think, praying for a longer time is not praying with many words.

A lengthy speech is one thing; a prolonged affection is another. For it is also written of the Lord himself that he spent the night in prayer (Luke 6:12) and that he prayed at greater length (ibid. 22:43). In this, what else was he offering us than an example, being, at the appropriate time, a petitioner, while with the Father he is the eternal hearer?

### 20

It is said that the brethren in Egypt do indeed offer frequent prayers, but that these are very brief and, as it were, cast out rapidly, lest the alert attention—which is exceedingly necessary to one who prays—should disappear and grow dull through excessively prolonged duration.

By this they also show clearly enough that, just as this attention must not be dulled if it cannot continue, so, if it does continue, it ought not to be broken too quickly. Let there be no many-worded speech in prayer, but let there be abundant petition if the attention remains fervent.

To speak much is to burden prayer with superfluous words concerning a necessary matter. To pray much is to knock at the one to whom we pray through a prolonged and devout awakening of the heart. Often this activity is carried on more through groans than through words, more through tears than through speech.

He places our tears in his sight, and our groaning is not hidden from him who created all things through the Word and who does not seek human words.

## CHAPTER XI

### 21

Words are therefore necessary for us, so that we may be reminded and examine what we are asking—not because we think that the Lord must either be instructed or persuaded.

When we say, “Hallowed be your name,” we remind ourselves to desire that his name, which is always holy, may also be held holy among human beings—that is, may not be despised. This benefits not God but human beings.

When we say, “Your kingdom come,” which will come whether we wish it or not, we arouse our desire for that kingdom, so that it may come to us and we may deserve to reign in it.

When we say, “Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven,” we ask him for the obedience by which his will may be done by us as it is done in heaven by his angels.

When we say, “Give us this day our daily bread,” the word “today” signifies the present time. By “bread” we may either ask for that sufficiency, representing the whole by the superior part, or for the Sacrament of the faithful, which is necessary in this present time—not, however, to attain the happiness of this present time, but eternal happiness.

When we say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors,” we remind ourselves both of what we are asking and of what we must do in order to deserve to receive it.

When we say, “Do not bring us into temptation,” we remind ourselves to ask that, deprived of his help, we may neither consent to some temptation after being deceived nor yield to it after being afflicted.

When we say, “Deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6:9–13), we remind ourselves to consider that we are not yet in that good state where we shall suffer no evil. This final petition in the Lord’s Prayer is so comprehensive that a Christian placed in any tribulation may utter his groans in it, pour out his tears in it, begin from it, linger in it, and end his prayer with it.

For these words ought to entrust the realities themselves to our memory.

## CHAPTER XII

### 22

Whatever other words we may say—words which the affection of the person praying either forms beforehand so that it may be made clear, or attends to afterward so that it may grow—we say nothing other than what is contained in the Lord’s Prayer, if we pray rightly and appropriately.

But whoever says something that cannot belong to this evangelical prayer prays carnally, even if he does not pray unlawfully. Indeed, I do not know how such prayer can fail to be called unlawful, since those who have been born again by the Spirit ought to pray only spiritually.

For example, whoever says, “Glorify yourself among all the nations as you have been glorified among us,” and, “May your prophets be found faithful” (Sir. 36:4, 18), what else does he say than, “Hallowed be your name”?

Whoever says, “God of hosts, restore us, and show your face, and we shall be saved” (Ps. 79:4), what else does he say than, “Your kingdom come”?

Whoever says, “Direct my steps according to your word, and let no iniquity rule over me” (Ps. 118:133), what else does he say than, “Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven”?

Whoever says, “Do not give me poverty or riches” (Prov. 30:8), what else does he say than, “Give us this day our daily bread”?

Whoever says, “Remember, Lord, David and all his meekness” (Ps. 131:1), or, “Lord, if I have done this, if there is iniquity in my hands, if I have repaid those who repaid me with evil” (Ps. 7:4), what else does he say than, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors”?

Whoever says, “Take away from me the desires of the belly, and do not let the desire for intercourse seize me” (Sir. 23:6), what else does he say than, “Do not bring us into temptation”?

Whoever says, “Deliver me from my enemies, O God, and free me from those who rise up against me” (Ps. 58:2), what else does he say than, “Deliver us from evil”?

And if you run through all the words of the holy prayers, you will find, I think, nothing that is not contained and included in the Lord’s Prayer. It is therefore permissible to say the same things in prayer in various words, but it is not permissible to say different things.

### 23

These things should be prayed for without wavering or doubt—for ourselves, for our own people, for strangers, and even for our enemies. Nevertheless, affection for one person or another may arise or predominate in the heart of the one praying, according to the closeness or remoteness of their relationships.

But someone who says in prayer, for example, “Lord, increase my riches,” or, “Give me as much as you have given that person or that person,” or, “Increase my honors; make me powerful and illustrious in this world,” or anything of this kind, and says it while desiring these things, without considering how he might use them to benefit people according to God—such a person, I think, cannot find in the Lord’s Prayer anywhere to fit these wishes.

Therefore, let him at least be ashamed to ask for what he is not ashamed to desire. Or, if he is ashamed even of this but desire overcomes him, how much better would it be to ask that he from whom we say, “Deliver us from evil,” would also deliver him from this evil of desire?

## CHAPTER XIII

### 24

You now have, I think, not only what kind of prayer you should offer but also what you should pray for—not because I teach you, but because he has deigned to teach all of us.

The blessed life must be sought, and it must be requested from the Lord God. Many people have argued at length about what it means to be blessed; but why should we go to many people and many things? Scripture has stated briefly and truthfully: “Blessed is the people whose God is the Lord” (Ps. 143:15).

That we may belong to this people and be able to reach the contemplation of him and live with him without end—this is the goal of the commandment: “love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. 1:5). In these same three, hope is included in place of a good conscience.

Faith, hope, and charity therefore lead the one who prays to God—that is, the one who believes, hopes, desires, and considers what he should ask of the Lord in the Lord’s Prayer.

Fasts, restraint of carnal desire from other pleasures without neglecting bodily health, and especially almsgiving, greatly aid prayer, so that we may say: “In the day of my tribulation I sought God, with my hands by night before him, and I was not deceived” (Ps. 76:3).

For how can an incorporeal and intangible God be sought with hands unless he is sought through works?

## CHAPTER XIV

### 25

Perhaps you still ask why the Apostle said, “For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought” (Rom. 8:26). For there is no reason at all to believe that either he himself or those to whom he was speaking did not know the Lord’s Prayer.

Why, then, do we think he said this—a statement he could make neither rashly nor falsely? Because temporal troubles and tribulations often benefit us, either to heal the swelling of pride, to test and exercise patience, for which a brighter and more abundant reward is reserved once it has been tested and exercised, or to scourge and remove whatever sins need to be scourged and removed. Yet, because we do not know how these things benefit us, we desire to be freed from every tribulation.

The Apostle himself does not show that he was free from this ignorance, unless perhaps he knew what to pray for as he ought when, to prevent him from being exalted by the greatness of his revelations, a thorn in the flesh was given him, an angel of Satan to strike him. For this reason he pleaded with the Lord three times that it might be taken away from him—clearly not knowing what he ought to pray for.

Finally, he heard God’s answer as to why what so great a man prayed for was not done and why it was not expedient that it should be done: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:7–9).

### 26

In these tribulations, therefore, which may either benefit or harm us, we do not know what we should pray for as we ought. Nevertheless, because they are harsh, burdensome, and contrary to the feeling of our weakness, we pray, in accordance with the universal human will, that they be taken away from us.

But we owe this devotion to our Lord God: if he does not take them away, we must not therefore think that he is neglecting us. Rather, through devout endurance of evils, we should hope for greater goods; for power is made perfect in weakness.

In anger, the Lord God granted some impatient people what they asked for, just as in kindness he refused it to the Apostle. We read what the Israelites asked for and how they asked for it, and that they received it; but once their desire had been fulfilled, their impatience was severely punished (Num. 11).

He also gave those who asked for a king one according to their heart, as it is written—not according to his own heart (1 Sam. 8:5, 7). He even granted what the devil requested, so that his servant might be tempted in order to be tested (Job 1:12; 2:6). He heard the unclean spirits when they asked that the legion of demons be sent into a herd of many pigs (Luke 8:32).

These things have been written so that no one may think too highly of himself if he is heard when he impatiently asks for something which it would benefit him more not to obtain, or may cast himself down and despair of divine mercy toward him if he is not heard when perhaps he asks for something which, upon receiving it, would afflict him more grievously or, corrupted by prosperity, overthrow him completely.

In such matters, therefore, we do not know what we should pray for as we ought. If something happens contrary to what we pray for, then, by bearing it patiently and giving thanks in everything, we should have no doubt that what ought to have happened was what God’s will—not ours—ordained.

The mediator himself also gave us an example of this. After saying, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me,” transforming the human will in himself through the assumption of human nature, he immediately added: “Nevertheless, not what I will, but what you will, Father” (Matt. 26:39).

Therefore, not without reason, “through the obedience of one, the many will be made righteous” (Rom. 5:19).

27. Whoever, however, asks the Lord for that one thing and seeks it (Ps. 26:4), asks with certainty and confidence, and does not fear that it may harm him when he receives it—for without it, whatever else he may have received by praying as he ought is of no benefit. For it is the one true and only blessed life: to contemplate the Lord’s delight forever, immortal and incorruptible in body and spirit. Everything else is sought and rightly requested for the sake of this one thing. Whoever possesses it will have everything he wishes, and there he will not be able to wish for anything that would be unfitting.

For there is the fountain of life, which we must now thirst for in prayer, as long as we live in hope and do not yet see what we hope for, under the protection of his wings. Before him is all our desire, so that we may be intoxicated by the abundance of his house and drink from the torrent of his delight; for with him is the fountain of life, and in his light we shall see light (Ps. 35:8–10). Then our desire will be satisfied with good things, and there will be nothing more for us to seek with groaning, but only something to possess with rejoicing.

Nevertheless, because that peace surpasses all understanding, even when we ask for it in prayer we do not know what we ought to pray for. For we cannot conceive of it as it truly is, and therefore we do not know it. Whatever comes before the mind in thought, we reject, repudiate, and disapprove, knowing that it is not what we seek, although we do not yet know what that reality itself is like.

## CHAPTER FIFTEEN

28. There is therefore within us, so to speak, a kind of learned ignorance—yet one taught by the Spirit of God, who helps our weakness. For after the Apostle had said, “But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience,” he immediately added: “Likewise the Spirit also helps our weakness; for we do not know what we ought to pray for, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings. And he who searches the hearts knows what the Spirit intends, because he intercedes for the saints according to God” (Rom. 8:25–27).

This is not to be understood as though we should suppose that the Holy Spirit of God—who in the Trinity is the immutable God, and with the Father and the Son is one God—intercedes for the saints as though he were someone who is not what God is. It is said, “He intercedes for the saints,” because he causes the saints to intercede, just as it is said, “The Lord your God tests you, to know whether you love him” (Deut. 13:3), that is, to make you know.

He therefore causes the saints to intercede with inexpressible groanings, inspiring in them a desire even for that great reality which is still unknown, which we await with patience. For how can one describe what one desires when one does not know it? [Col. 0506] Indeed, if it were completely unknown, it would not be desired; and again, if it were seen, it would not be desired or sought with groanings.

## CHAPTER SIXTEEN

29. Considering all these things—and whatever else the Lord may suggest to you concerning this matter, whether it has not occurred to me or whether it was too lengthy for me to state—strive in prayer to overcome this world. Pray in hope; pray faithfully and lovingly; pray persistently and patiently; pray as Christ’s widow.

Although it belongs to all his members—that is, to all who believe in him and are joined to his body—to pray as he taught, nevertheless the Scriptures are found to have imposed a special and more diligent care of prayer upon widows. For there were two women honorably named Anna: one married, who gave birth to the holy Samuel; the other a widow, who recognized the Holy of Holies while he was still an infant.

The married woman also prayed in anguish of spirit and distress of heart because she had no children. At that time she obtained Samuel himself and returned him, once received, to God, because when she asked for him, she made a vow (1 Sam. 1). But how her prayer pertains to that dominical prayer is not easily discovered, except that in the petition set down there, “Deliver us from evil,” it seemed no small evil both to be married and to be deprived of the fruit of marriage, since the sole justification for marriage is the purpose of bearing children.

But concerning the widow Anna, see what is written: “She did not depart from the temple, serving with fastings and prayers night and day” (Luke 2:36–37). The Apostle likewise says—and I mentioned this above: “She who is truly a widow and desolate has placed her hope in the Lord and persists in prayers night and day” (1 Tim. 5:5). And when the Lord exhorted us always to pray and not grow weary, he mentioned the widow who, although the judge was unjust and impious, and despised both God and human beings, turned him toward hearing her case by continually appealing to him.

It can therefore be understood sufficiently from this that widows ought to devote themselves to prayers above others: an example of encouragement to undertake the practice of prayer has been set before everyone in the person of widows.

30. What, then, has been chosen in widows as the character of this calling except abandonment and desolation? Therefore, if every soul understands itself to be abandoned and desolate in this world, for as long as it is away from the Lord, it certainly commends a kind of widowhood of its own to God its defender through constant and most earnest prayer.

Pray, then, as Christ’s widow, not yet possessing the sight of him whose help you implore. And although you are extremely wealthy, pray as a poor woman; for you do not yet possess the true riches of the future age, where you will fear no losses. Although you have children and grandchildren, and a large household, pray as one desolate, as was said above; for all temporal things are uncertain, even those that remain with us for our consolation until the end of this life.

But if you seek and set your mind on the things above, and desire what is eternal and certain, then, so long as you do not yet possess them, you ought to consider yourself desolate, even though all your dependents are safe and obedient. And if you are so, then surely your deeply religious daughter-in-law by your own example, as well as the other holy widows and virgins more securely placed under your care, should be so also. [Col. 0507] For the more devoutly you manage your household, the more earnestly you ought to persist in prayers, not being occupied with the affairs of the present except insofar as the cause of piety requires.

31. Be sure also to remember to pray for us without negligence. For we do not wish you to show us the honor—which we bear perilously—in such a way as to deprive us of the assistance we know to be necessary. The household of Christ prayed for Peter; it prayed for Paul. And we rejoice that you [Note: Seven manuscripts, and Am., Bad., and Er., read “we”] are members of his household, while we need the help of the prayers of our brothers and sisters incomparably more than Peter and Paul did.

Pray eagerly, in a united and holy contest. For you are not contending against one another, but against the devil, who is the enemy of all the saints. Prayer is greatly aided by fasts, vigils, and every form of bodily discipline (Tob. 12:8). Let each of you do what she can. The one who can do less does what she can, if she loves in the other what she herself does not do because she cannot. Therefore, let the weaker not hinder the stronger, and let the stronger not pressure the weaker.

For you owe your conscience to God; but none of you owes anything to another except to love one another. May the Lord hear you, who is able to do more than we ask or understand (Eph. 3:20).

## LETTER 131

[Note: This was collated with manuscripts a, bg, bl, bn, c, cc, cb, ff, g, gv, n, r, s, t, two sb manuscripts, two vc manuscripts, four v manuscripts, and with Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: Elsewhere 156; what was 131 is now 101. Written at approximately the same time.]

Augustine replies to Proba and gives thanks that she was concerned for his welfare.

To the distinguished lady, illustrious in merit, and most excellent daughter, PROBA, AUGUSTINE sends greeting in the Lord.

It is indeed as you say: when the soul is placed in a corruptible body, it is constrained by a kind of earthly contagion and, weighed down and bent by a certain burden, more easily desires and thinks of many things below than of one thing above. For Holy Scripture says this as well: “For the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. 9:13).

But for this reason our Savior came: he raised up by the word of salvation that woman in the Gospel who had been bent over for eighteen years—perhaps signifying this very condition (Luke 13:11–13)—so that the Christian soul might not hear “Lift up your hearts” in vain, nor reply in vain that it has them directed toward the Lord.

With this in view, you are right to regard the evils of this world as bearable through hope for the future. For by a good use they are turned toward good, when they do not increase our desire but exercise our patience. Concerning this the Apostle says: “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God” (Rom. 8:28). “All things,” he says: therefore not only those that are sought as pleasant, but also those that are avoided as burdensome—when we take some things in such a way that we are not captured by them, and endure others in such a way that we are not broken by them, giving thanks to him in all things according to the divine commands, of whom [Col. 0508] we say: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise is always in my mouth” (Ps. 33:2); and, “It is good for me that you have humbled me, so that I may learn your statutes” (Ps. 118:71).

For if the tranquility of deceptive prosperity always smiled upon us here, the human soul would not seek that harbor of true and certain security, distinguished lady, illustrious in merit, and most excellent daughter.

Therefore, in return for the duty of greeting owed to your Excellence, and giving thanks because you exercise a most devout concern for our welfare, I ask the Lord to grant you the rewards of the future life and consolations in the present. I commend myself to the love and prayers of all of you, in whose hearts Christ dwells through faith.

And in another hand:

May the true and truthful God truly console your heart and protect your salvation, distinguished lady, illustrious in merit, and most excellent daughter.

## LETTER 132

[Note: Revised against manuscripts a, bg, bl, c, cc, ff, g, gv, j, l, n, r, s, t, tt, vc, vd, two bn manuscripts, two sb manuscripts, five v manuscripts, and against Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: Elsewhere 1; what was 132 is now 266. Written around the beginning of the year 412.]

Augustine to Volusianus, exhorting him to devote himself to reading the sacred Scriptures and to write back if any difficulty occurs to him while reading them.

To the distinguished and most excellent son, illustrious in merit, VOLUSIANUS [Note: Volusianus is believed to have been the maternal uncle of the younger Melania, that is, the brother of her mother Albina; not her paternal uncle, because Publicola, Melania’s father, had no surviving brother, as is shown by Letter 94. Therefore *theios*, a word common to both paternal and maternal uncles, is not correctly translated “paternal uncle,” both in Photius, 53, and in the Metaphrast, in the Life of Melania. Verses of Rutilius concerning this same Volusianus, as is thought, are extant, and show that he held the office of proconsul of Africa. Furthermore, Photius and the Metaphrast report that Volusianus was brought, through the care of his niece Melania and of Proclus, bishop of Constantinople, to profess the Christian religion at the point of death.], AUGUSTINE, bishop.

Concerning your welfare—which I desire to be found both in this world and in Christ—I am perhaps no less aligned with the prayers of your holy mother. Therefore, returning the duty of greeting owed to your merits, I exhort you as best I can not to hesitate to devote yourself diligently to the study of truly and certainly holy writings.

It is a sincere and solid matter. It does not court the soul with embellished expressions, nor does it produce anything empty and unstable with any verbal covering. It deeply moves one who hungers not for words but for realities, and it greatly terrifies while making one secure.

I particularly exhort you to read the writings of the Apostles. From them you will be stirred to know the Prophets, whose testimonies the Apostles employ. If, whether while reading or while thinking, some question arises for you in whose resolution I may seem necessary, write so that I may reply.

For perhaps, with the Lord’s help, I can do this more effectively than by discussing such matters with you in person—not only because of the various occupations of both you and me, since the time is not always free for me when it happens to be free for you, but also because of the intrusion of those who are often not suited to such a task and take more pleasure in contests of language than in the illumination of knowledge.

But what has been written is always available for reading whenever the reader is available; nor is what is present burdensome [Col. 0509], since you take it up when you wish and set it down when you wish.

## LETTER 133

[Note: We collated this with manuscripts a, bg, bl, c, cc, ff, g, gv, n, r, s, t, vc, two v manuscripts, and with Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: Elsewhere 159; what was 133 is now 99. Written at approximately the same time.]

Augustine to Marcellinus, tribune, asking him to punish the Donatists, who confessed atrocious crimes in the investigation, without capital punishment, as accords with the Church’s gentleness.

To the distinguished lord, illustrious in merit, and dearest son, MARCELLINUS, AUGUSTINE [Note: The manuscripts read “Augustine, bishop.”] sends greeting in the Lord.

1. I have learned from your Nobility that those Circumcellions and clergy of the party of Donatus whom concern for public discipline had brought from Hippo [Note: Lov. reads “from the church of Hippo.” The word “church” is absent from the manuscripts; Augustine often leaves a word or a similar expression to be supplied.] before the court on account of their deeds have been heard by you, and that many of them confessed both to the murder they committed against Restitutus, a Catholic presbyter, and to the killing of Innocentius, another Catholic presbyter, as well as to gouging out his eye and cutting off his finger.

This has caused me the greatest anxiety, lest your Sublimity should judge that they ought to be punished with such severity of law that they should suffer what they inflicted. Therefore, in this letter I appeal to your faith in Christ, and by the mercy of the Lord Christ himself, asking that you neither do this nor permit it to be done at all.

Although we might have remained unconcerned about their death, since they appear to have been brought to trial not by our accusers but by their own *Notoria* [Note: Three manuscripts read *Notaria*; two others, *Notatoria*], by those whose duty was to watch over the public peace, nevertheless we do not wish the sufferings of God’s servants to be avenged, as though by the law of retaliation, through equivalent punishments.

This is not because we wish the power to restrain crimes to be taken away from wicked men. Rather, we want it to be sufficient that they remain alive and are not mutilated in any part of their bodies, and that through legal restraint they are either redirected from insane unrest to the leisure of health, or assigned from wicked works to some useful task.

This too is indeed called condemnation. But who does not understand that it ought rather to be called a benefit than a punishment, where neither the license for savagery is released nor the remedy of repentance withheld?

2. Fulfill, Christian judge, the office of a merciful father. Be angry at iniquity in such a way that you remember to care for humanity. Do not exercise a desire for vengeance upon the atrocities of sinners; rather, apply a willingness to heal the wounds of sinners.

Do not abandon the paternal diligence that you preserved during the investigation itself, when you extracted a confession of such great crimes not by stretching them on the rack, not by tearing them with claws, and not by burning flames, but by blows with rods. This method of coercion is often employed by teachers of the liberal arts, by parents themselves, and even by bishops in judicial proceedings.

Do not therefore avenge more harshly what you discovered more gently. The need to investigate is greater than the need to punish. For this reason even the gentlest people diligently and persistently examine a concealed crime: so that they may discover [Col. 0510] those whom they should spare. Hence it is often necessary for the investigation to be conducted more rigorously, so that once the crime has been disclosed there may be a place for mercy to appear.

All good works love to be brought into the light—not for human glory, but, as the Lord says, “so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16). For this reason the Apostle did not think it enough to advise us to preserve gentleness; he also instructed us to make it known to everyone: “Let your gentleness be known to all” (Phil. 4:5); and elsewhere, “Showing gentleness to all people” (Tit. 3:2).

Thus the most illustrious gentleness of holy David, when he mercifully spared the enemy who had been delivered into his hands (1 Sam. 24:7), would not stand out if power had not appeared at the same time. Therefore, let the power to punish not exasperate you, since the necessity of investigating did not drive mercy from you. When you have discovered the crime, do not seek an executioner whom you were unwilling to employ in discovering it by torture.

3. Finally, you were sent for the benefit of the Church. I testify that this is beneficial and expedient for the Catholic Church—or, so that I may not seem to exceed the measure of my administration, for the Church belonging to the diocese of Hippo Regius.

If you do not listen to a friend making a request, listen to a bishop offering counsel. Since I am speaking to a Christian, especially in such a matter, I would not say arrogantly that it is fitting for you to listen to a bishop who gives an order, distinguished lord, illustrious in merit, and dearest son.

I know, of course, that ecclesiastical cases have principally been entrusted to your Excellence. But because I believe this particular concern belongs to the most illustrious and distinguished proconsul, I have also sent him a letter. I ask that you not consider it burdensome to deliver it to him yourself and, if necessary, to cite it. I beseech you both not to regard our intercession, suggestion, or concern as intrusive.

Do not disfigure the sufferings of Catholic servants of God—which ought to be useful for the spiritual edification of the weak—with the reciprocal punishment of their enemies, by whom they suffered. Rather, by checking judicial severity, do not neglect to commend both your own faith, because you are sons of the Church, and the gentleness of that mother herself.

May almighty God increase your Excellence in every good thing, distinguished lord, illustrious in merit, and dearest son.

## LETTER 134

[Note: We reviewed this against manuscripts a, bg, bl, c, cc, cb, ff, g, gv, n, r, s, sb, t, vc, four v manuscripts, and against Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: Elsewhere 160; what was 134 is now 58. Written at the same time as the preceding letter.]

Augustine asks and admonishes Apringius, the proconsul, to punish more gently the Circumcellions who confessed atrocious crimes, remembering the Church’s gentleness.

To the distinguished lord, exalted in merit, and most excellent son, APRINGIUS, AUGUSTINE.

1. I do not doubt that, in this power which God has given you—a human being over human beings—you think about the divine judgment, where judges themselves will stand to give an account of their judgment. I know that you are imbued with Christian faith. Hence I have greater confidence in your Excellence, not only to ask but also to admonish, because of that [Col. 0511] Lord in whose household we are counted with you by heavenly right, in whom we have equal hope of eternal life, and whom we invoke for you in the sacred mysteries.

Therefore, distinguished lord, exalted in merit, and most excellent son, first I ask that you not regard me as intruding improperly upon your duties with the concern that I ought especially to bear for the Church entrusted to me, whose interests I serve and over which I desire not so much to preside as to be useful. Then I beg you not to disdain to receive what I advise or ask, and not to hesitate to comply.

2. Certain Circumcellions and Donatist clergy were brought before courts and laws by the care of those who serve public discipline, after a *Notoria* had been issued. When they were heard by your brother, my son Marcellinus, the distinguished and eminent tribune and notary, they were restrained not by the torture of claws and flames but by rods, and confessed that they had perpetrated horrifying crimes against brothers and my fellow presbyters. Specifically, they ambushed and killed one of them, and dragged another from his house, gouged out his eye, and cut off his finger.

When I learned that they had confessed, and therefore had no doubt that they would come under the jurisdiction of your axe, I hastened this letter to your Nobility. In it I beg and, by the mercy of Christ, beseech you: let us rejoice in your greater and more certain happiness in such a way that equivalent penalties are not inflicted upon them. The laws cannot punish them by cutting off a finger and tearing out an eye with blows of stones, although these men were able to do so in their savagery.

I am therefore confident concerning those who confessed that they will not receive this retaliation. But I fear that either they themselves, or those whose murder has been disclosed, may be punished by the sentence of your authority. I ask you as a Christian judge not to let this happen, and I admonish you as a Christian bishop.

3. We read that the Apostle said of you that you do not bear the sword without reason, and that you are God’s ministers, avengers against those who do evil (Rom. 13:4). But the province has one reason, and the Church another. The administration of the province must be exercised with terror; the Church’s gentleness must be commended with mercy.

If I were speaking before a non-Christian judge, I would act differently. Even then, however, I would not abandon the Church’s case, and insofar as he allowed it, I would persist in asking that the sufferings of Catholic servants of God—which ought to contribute examples of patience—not be stained by the blood of their enemies. If he refused to comply, I would suspect that he was resisting with a hostile mind.

But now, since the matter is being conducted before you, my approach and counsel are different. We see you as the ruler of exalted power, but we also recognize you as a son of Christian piety. Let your Sublimity yield; let your faith yield. I am dealing with a common cause alongside you, but you can do in it what I cannot. Take counsel with us, and extend your aid.

4. Care was taken to ensure that the enemies of the Church—who customarily trouble the minds of the uneducated with deceptive empty talk, boasting as though they were suffering the persecution they claim to endure—would admit the horrifying crimes they had perpetrated against Catholic clergy and be caught by their own words. [Col. 0512]

The records should be read for the healing of the souls whom they poisoned by their pestilential persuasion. Would you be pleased if, at the end of the records, where they contained the bloody punishment of these men, we were afraid to proceed in reading, placing even our own conscience at risk, lest they who suffered should appear to have repaid evil with evil?

If therefore nothing else could be established to restrain the wickedness of these ruined men, extreme necessity might perhaps compel their execution. Yet as far as we are concerned, if nothing gentler could be done to them, we would prefer that they be released free rather than that the sufferings of our brothers be avenged by shedding their blood.

But now, since something can be done by which both the Church’s gentleness may be commended and the boldness of the harsh restrained, why do you not incline toward the more prudent and merciful sentence—which judges are permitted to impose even in cases not belonging to the Church?

Fear with us, then, the judgment of God the Father, and commend the gentleness of the mother. For when you act, the Church acts, because of whom you act and whose son you are.

Contend in goodness with the wicked. They tore limbs from a living body with monstrous crime; by an act of mercy, make those very limbs—which they employed in their wicked deeds—serve some useful task while remaining whole. They did not spare the servants of God who preached correction to them; spare those who have been arrested, spare those who have been brought before the court, spare those who have been convicted. They shed Christian blood with impious iron; for Christ’s sake, restrain even the judicial sword from their blood. They took away the time of life from a minister of the Church by killing him; grant the enemies of the Church, while they live, time for repentance.

Such a Christian judge you ought to be in a case of the Church, while we ask, admonish, and intercede. When convicted enemies are treated more gently, people generally appeal from the more lenient sentence. But we love our enemies so greatly that, unless we rely upon your Christian obedience, we would appeal from your severe sentence.

May almighty God preserve your Excellence ever greater and happier, distinguished lord, exalted in merit, and most excellent son.

## LETTER 135

[Note: This letter is extant together with Letter 132 in the same manuscripts identified above.]

[Note: Elsewhere 2; what was 135 is now 110. Written at the beginning of the year 412.]
