Volusianus to Augustine, presenting him with questions: how the immeasurable God could have been enclosed in a virgin’s womb and in an infant’s little body; whether meanwhile he had abandoned his care of the world; whether his divinity had been sufficiently manifested even by miracles; and related matters.

To the truly holy and deservedly venerable father, Augustine, bishop, VOLUSIANUS.

1. You ask me, a man who is a testimony of integrity and justice, to put questions about certain ambiguities from which a learned reader may learn something. I embrace with gratitude the favor of the task imposed upon me, and willingly offer myself to your instruction, following the authority of the old saying that no age is too advanced for learning completely.

Nor without reason did the wise man set no limits or end to the pursuit of wisdom, since virtue, remote at its beginnings [Note: One Vatican manuscript, contrary to the others, prefers “truth, remote at its beginnings.”], is never so fully opened to those who approach it that [Col. 0513] everything immediately lies open to understanding.

Truly holy and deservedly venerable father, it is worthwhile to report the conversation we recently had among ourselves. We were present at certain gatherings of friends, where opinions were frequently put forward according to the participants’ abilities and interests. Yet the conversation was a rhetorical exercise in division. I am speaking to one who recognizes this, for you taught these things only a little while ago.

The discussion maintained what invention was, what sharpness belonged to invention [Note: Seventeen manuscripts read: “What the sharpness of invention was being developed.”], how great the labor of arrangement, what grace belonged to metaphor (*translatio*), what beauty belonged to images or figures of speech, and what power of expression was suited to the subject according to its character and the speaker’s talent.

Others in turn praised poetry in their enthusiasm. You do not leave this part of eloquence unmentioned or dishonored, so that the poet might say:

> May ivy creep for you among the victorious laurels.  
> (Virgil, *Eclogues* 8.)

The conversation therefore turned to the great adornment of arrangement, the elegance of metaphors, the sublimity of comparison, and then to light, smooth verses and, so to speak, the measured variation of their pauses.

Then the discussion turned toward your familiar philosophy, which you yourself customarily fostered in an Aristotelian manner, as though it were Isocratic. We asked what the teacher from the Lyceum had accomplished; what the Academy’s many-sided and continuous hesitation meant; what that debater from the Stoa had contributed; what belonged to knowledge of natural philosophy; what belonged to Epicurean pleasure; and what was the meaning of the endless desire for disputation among them all—at which point truth was even more ignored, after it had been assumed that it could be known.

2. While our conversation lingered on these matters, one of the group said: “Who is so perfectly trained in the wisdom of Christianity that he can open up the ambiguities in which I am entangled, and strengthen my doubtful convictions with true or at least probable belief?”

We sat astonished and silent. Then he burst out spontaneously with the following:

“I wonder whether the Lord and ruler of the world filled the body of an undefiled woman; whether the mother endured that long ten-month burden; whether she nevertheless gave birth as a virgin through the ordinary process of childbirth; and whether after this her virginity remained untouched.

“Within the little body of a crying infant lies hidden one to whom the universe is scarcely thought equal [Note: The editions read, “to whom the little universe is thought equal.” But twenty-three manuscripts, both here and in Letter 137, consistently read, “to whom the universe is scarcely thought equal.”]. He undergoes the years of childhood, grows into adolescence, and is strengthened by youth. For so long that ruler is absent from his dwelling, and the care of the entire world is transferred to one little body.

“Then he is dissolved in sleep, nourished by food, and experiences all the feelings of mortals. Nor do any corresponding signs make the indications of such great majesty shine forth, since that deliverance from demons (*larvalis purgatio*) [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads, “that carnal purification.” But all the others have *larvalis*, that is, liberation from demons, who are called *larvae*], care for the weak, and the restoration of life to the dead—these are small things for God, if you also consider others [Note: Lov. and other editions read, “if you consider these and other things.” But in the manuscripts, here and below in Letter 137, the reading is, “these, if you also consider others.”].”

We interrupted him as he continued to inquire. When the gathering broke up, we deferred the matter [Col. 0514] to someone of greater expertise, lest, while sacred secrets were rashly violated, harmless error should turn into guilt.

You have received, man capable of every glory, the confession of ignorance; you recognize what is being sought from your side. It concerns your reputation that we should learn the answers to these questions. Ignorance is tolerated in other priests, without detriment to divine worship; but when one comes to Bishop Augustine, whatever happens to be unknown is a deficiency in the law.

May the supreme divinity protect your Veneration unharmed, truly holy and deservedly venerable father.

## LETTER 136

[Note: Revised against manuscripts a, bg, bl, bn, c, cc, ff, g, gv, j, l, n, r, sb, s, t, vc, vd, two a manuscripts, five v manuscripts, and against Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: Elsewhere 6; what was 136 is now 77. Written at the same time.]

Marcellinus to Augustine, asking him to satisfy Volusianus, and reporting that some people bring accusations: that God abolished the old Law either from weariness or because of inconsistency in his plans; that the evangelical teaching is useless to the state; and, finally, that Christian rulers have brought great evils upon the state.

To the excessively venerable father, whom I uniquely honor in every duty, AUGUSTINE, MARCELLINUS.

1. The distinguished Volusianus read me the letter of your Beatitude—indeed, at my urging he read it to several people. I was astonished throughout at everything you said, since it is truly worthy of wonder. The grace of your divine speech, humbly swelling with dignity, easily earned approval.

What pleased me most was that you strive to steady and strengthen the somewhat faltering steps of a man of good purpose by the encouragement of your exhortation. For we have a daily exchange with him, as far as our abilities and the poverty of our talent permit.

Urged on by the prayer of his holy mother, I make a point of visiting him frequently to greet him, although he himself is also gracious enough to return the favor. After receiving the letter of your Venerability, this man—who is being drawn away from the stability of faith in the true God by the persuasion of many people, of whom there is an abundance in this city—was so moved that, if he had not feared the length of a letter, he would have laid before your Beatitude every ambiguity he might have had, as he himself asserts.

Nevertheless, as you yourself will perhaps deign to approve, he has asked that certain matters be resolved for him at some expense of carefully polished speech and in the clear brilliance of Roman eloquence.

This question has been thoroughly worn over, and the cleverness of those who defame the dispensation of the Lord’s incarnation is sufficiently well known. Yet because I trust that whatever you write on this matter will benefit many, I too have come as a petitioner, asking you to deign to answer more attentively those claims in which they say that the Lord did nothing more than other human beings were able to do.

For they bring forward their own Apollonius and Apuleius, as well as other practitioners of magic, and assert that their miracles were greater.

2. The distinguished man mentioned above said, in the presence of several people, that there were many matters that could reasonably be joined to this question [Note: Eleven manuscripts read, “He said that there were many matters that could reasonably be joined to these questions”], if, as I said earlier, he had not considered the brevity appropriate to a letter from his [Col. 0515] side.

Although he did not wish to write them down, he could not keep silent about them. For he said that even if the basis of the Lord’s incarnation were explained to him today, it could scarcely be made completely clear why this God—who is affirmed also to be the God of the Old Testament—rejected the ancient sacrifices and took pleasure in new ones.

He maintained that nothing can be corrected unless what was done previously is shown not to have been right; or that what was once rightly done ought not to be changed in any way. He said that rightly performed actions could be changed only unjustly, especially because such variation could accuse God of inconsistency.

Then, secondly, he argued that the preaching and teaching of Christ in no respect accords with the customs of the state. For, as many people say, it is evidently his command that we must return no evil for evil (Rom. 12:17), offer the other cheek to one who strikes us, give our cloak to one who persists in taking our tunic, and go twice the distance with anyone who compels us to serve him (Matt. 5:39, 41). He asserts that all these principles are contrary to the customs of the state.

For who would tolerate having something taken from him by an enemy, or be unwilling to return evil by the right of war to a plunderer of a Roman province? And he understands that other matters could be raised concerning the remaining points, as your Venerability does.

He therefore believes that all these matters can be joined to the question, to such an extent that it is manifest that, through Christian rulers who observed the Christian religion to a considerable degree—even if he himself says nothing about this point—so many evils have come upon the state.

Hence, as Your Beatitude deigns to acknowledge with me, in response to all these matters—for without doubt Your Holiness’s desired reply will be placed in the hands of many—a complete and carefully elaborated exposition of the solution ought to be displayed. This is especially so because, while these things were taking place, an eminent proprietor and master of the region of Hippo was present; he praised Your Holiness with flattering irony and insisted that, when he raised these questions, he had not been adequately satisfied. For my part, not forgetful of your promise but pressing you to fulfill it, I beg that you compose books on all these matters, books that will be of incredible benefit to the Church, especially at the present time.

## LETTER CXXXVII

[Note: [Col. 0515] It was corrected against the manuscripts noted above, which contain Letter CXXXII.]

[Note: [Col. 0515] Formerly number 3; the letter that was 137 is now 78. Written shortly after the preceding letter.]

Augustine responds to the individual questions previously proposed by Volusianus.

To the illustrious man, deservedly distinguished and most excellent son, VOLUSIANUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

## CHAPTER ONE

### 1

I have read your letter, in which I saw the outline of a certain extensive dialogue, compressed with commendable brevity. I therefore ought to reply and not offer any excuse on account of delay. It happened opportunely that I had a little leisure from other people’s business. I had intended to devote this leisure to dictating other works, but I postponed that task for a little while, judging it wholly unjust that I should delay someone whom I myself had encouraged to inquire.

When one of us who, as best we can, administers the grace of Christ reads your words, who would wish you to be instructed in Christian doctrine in such a way that it should merely suffice for your salvation—not the salvation of this life, which the divine word has reminded us is very like vapor, appearing for a little while and then immediately vanishing and passing away (James 4:15), but that salvation for the sake of attaining and possessing eternally which we are Christians?

It is therefore not enough for us that you be instructed so as to have sufficient knowledge merely for your own deliverance. Your intellect and eloquence are so excellent and brilliant that they ought also to benefit others. Against their slowness or perversity, the dispensation of so great a grace must be defended with the greatest appropriateness—a grace that proud little souls consider worthless, although they are excessively eager to be very powerful and are powerless to heal or even restrain their own vices.

### 2

You therefore ask whether the Lord and ruler of the world filled the body of an undefiled woman; whether that mother endured the long distastefulness of ten months and yet, while remaining a virgin, gave birth with the normal solemnity of childbirth; and whether, after this, her virginity remained inviolate.

You ask whether, within the tiny body of a crying infant, there was concealed the one to whom the universe is scarcely thought equal; whether he was able to pass through the years of childhood, grow to maturity, and be strengthened by youth; whether that ruler was absent from his dwelling places for so long, and whether the governance of the whole world was transferred into one tiny body; whether he was then overcome by sleep, nourished by food, and experienced all the sensations of mortals; and whether the signs appropriate to such immense majesty failed to become evident.

For, if we consider these and other matters, that cleansing of lepers, the care of the weak, and the restoration of life to the dead are small things for God. You write that at a certain gathering of friends one of the many persons present introduced this question. But you intervened when the inquiry was being pursued further, and the gathering was adjourned, so that the matter might be deferred to the authority of more expert knowledge, lest innocent error, while rashly violating hidden things, should turn into guilt.

### 3

You then direct the purpose of your letter toward me, and, after this confession of ignorance, urge me to recognize what is expected from our side. You also add that it concerns my reputation that you should know the questions raised: for while ignorance in other priests is tolerated without, at any rate, damaging divine worship, whenever someone approaches me as a bishop, anything that has happened to be lacking in learning is considered blameworthy.

First, I ask you to lay aside this opinion of me, too readily assumed, and to release and strip away that disposition, however benevolent toward me it may be. If you return my affection, trust me about myself more than anyone else. For the depth of the Christian Scriptures is so great that I could make daily progress in them if, from earliest childhood to extreme old age, I attempted to learn them alone, with the greatest leisure, the utmost diligence, and the best intellect. This is not because such difficulty is encountered in them concerning what is necessary for salvation; rather, once someone has held the faith without which one cannot live piously and rightly, so many things remain for those who advance to understand, things shaded by so many different coverings of mystery, and such a depth of wisdom lies hidden—not only in the words in which these things were spoken but also in the realities that must be understood—that even the oldest, sharpest, and most ardent lovers of learning experience what the same Scripture says in a certain passage: “When a man has finished, then he begins” (Ecclesiasticus 18:6).

## CHAPTER TWO

### 4

But why say more about this? We should rather come to the matter you are asking about. First of all, I want you to know that Christian doctrine does not teach that God was so infused into the flesh from which he was to be born of a virgin that he either abandoned or lost the care of governing the universe, or transferred it to that tiny body as though matter had been contracted and gathered there.

This is the notion of people capable of thinking of nothing except bodies—whether denser bodies, such as moisture and earth, or subtler ones, such as air and light; bodies nonetheless, none of which can be wholly everywhere, since it must have one part in one place and another elsewhere. However large or small a body may be, it occupies a region of space and fills that region in such a way that it is not wholly present in any part of it. Consequently, being condensed or rarefied, contracted or expanded, reduced into fragments or increased into a mass, belongs only to bodies.

The nature of the soul is very different from that of the body; how much more different, then, is God’s nature, since he is the creator of both soul and body? God is not said to fill the world like water, air, or light, so that a smaller part of him fills a smaller part of the world and a larger part a larger part. He knows how to be wholly everywhere and contained by no place; he knows how to come without departing from where he was; he knows how to depart without abandoning the place to which he came.

### 5

The human mind marvels at this, and because it does not comprehend it, perhaps does not even believe it. Let it first marvel at itself, though ungratefully; let it raise itself a little above the body, if it can,

[Note: [Col. 0517] Nine manuscripts read: “Let it first marvel at itself, having marveled wonderfully.”] and above those things it is accustomed to perceive through the body; and let it see what it is that makes use of the body.

But perhaps it cannot. For, as someone says, it is the mark of a great intellect to separate the mind from the senses and withdraw thought from habit (Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, book 1). Let it therefore examine the bodily senses themselves with somewhat greater unfamiliarity and vigilance.

There are certainly five distinct bodily senses, which cannot exist without the body or without the soul. For only what is alive can perceive, and life is imparted to the body by the soul; nor can we see, hear, or use the other three senses without bodily instruments, as it were vessels and organs.

Let the rational soul attend to these things and consider the bodily senses, not through the bodily senses, but through the mind and reason itself. Certainly a human being cannot perceive unless he is alive; yet he lives in the flesh before death separates the two. How, then, does the soul perceive things that are outside its flesh, when it lives only in its flesh?

Are the stars in heaven not very far from its flesh? Does it not see the sun in the sky? Or is seeing not perceiving, although sight is superior to the other four senses? Does it also live in heaven, because it perceives in heaven, and can there be no sense where there is no life? Or does it perceive where it does not live, because, although it lives only in its own flesh, it also perceives in those places that contain, apart from its flesh, the things it touches with its sight?

Do you see how obscure this is even in so conspicuous a sense as sight? Consider hearing as well. For hearing too, in a certain way, extends outward from the flesh. Why do we say “It sounds outside” unless we perceive it where it sounds? Therefore we also live there, outside our flesh. Or can we perceive where we do not live, when a sense cannot exist without life?

[Note: [Col. 0517] Erasmus considered the negation here superfluous, and the Louvain editors omitted it. But all the manuscripts contain it, and it is judged wholly necessary to the sense.]

### 6

The other three senses perceive within themselves, although smell may to some extent be open to question. Concerning taste and touch there is no controversy: we perceive the things we taste and touch nowhere except in our flesh. These three senses should therefore be set aside from the present consideration.

Sight and hearing raise a remarkable question: either how the soul perceives where it does not live, or how it lives where it is not. For it is nowhere except in its own flesh, yet it perceives even beyond its flesh. It perceives where it sees, because seeing is also perceiving; it perceives where it hears, because hearing too is perceiving. Either, then, it also lives there and consequently is also there; or it perceives where it does not live; or it lives where it is not.

All these alternatives are astonishing. None can be asserted without a certain appearance of absurdity. And we are speaking about a sense belonging to a dying creature. What, then, is the soul itself, apart from bodily sensation—that is, in the mind by which it considers these things? For it is not through bodily sensation that it judges bodily sensations themselves.

Yet we think it incredible when something is said about the omnipotence of God—when it is said that the Word of God, through whom all things were made, assumed a body from a virgin and appeared to mortal senses without corrupting his immortality, changing his eternity, diminishing his power, or abandoning his administration of the world; without departing from the bosom of the Father—that is, from the secret place in which he is with the Father and in the Father.

### 7

Understand the Word of God, through whom all things were made, in this way: do not imagine that any part of him passes away, or that what is future becomes past. He remains as he is, and is wholly everywhere.

He comes when he is manifested, and departs when he is hidden. Yet he is present whether hidden or manifest, just as light is present to the eyes both of one who sees and of one who is blind: to the seeing person it is present, but to the blind person absent. A voice is present to ears that hear, and also to ears that are deaf; but to the former it is open, while to the latter it is hidden.

What is more marvelous than what occurs in our voices and sounding words—in a thing that is manifestly fleeting? When we speak, there is not even room for the second syllable unless the first has ceased to sound. Yet if one listener is present, he hears everything we say; and if two are present, both hear the same whole thing that each hears as a whole. If a silent multitude listens, they do not divide the sounds among themselves in fragments like food; rather, everything that sounds is whole for everyone and whole for each individual.

Is it not therefore more incredible that the passing word of a human being, which presents itself to the ears, should not present the abiding Word of God to created things—so that, just as the former is heard simultaneously and wholly by each individual, the latter might likewise be wholly present everywhere at once?

[Note: [Col. 0518] Earlier editions read: “What is presented to the ears … is not presented to created things.” But nearly all manuscripts read: “What presents itself to the ears … would not present itself to created things.”]

[Col. 0519]

### 8

There is therefore no reason to fear that, in the tiny body of infancy, God may be thought to have suffered such confinement.

[Note: [Col. 0519] Nineteen manuscripts read *tantus* (“so great”).]

God is not great by mass but by power. By his providence he gave ants and bees a better sense than asses and camels. From a very small seed he creates so large a fig tree, although from much larger seeds many things of far smaller size are born. He endowed so tiny a pupil of the eye with visual power that, flashing through the eyes, it might in an instant survey nearly half the heavens. From a point and, as it were, the center of the brain he diffuses all the senses through a fivefold distribution. Through the heart, so small a member, he dispenses vital movement throughout the entire body.

By these and similar things he teaches that great things proceed from small ones, he who is not small in small things.

His very greatness of power, which experiences no confinement in a narrow space, fertilized the virgin womb by a birth that was not adventitious but native. Without itself undergoing any change for the worse, that power united to itself a rational soul, and through that soul also a human body—the whole human being, entirely destined to be changed for the better. It honorably assumed from him the name of humanity and generously bestowed divinity upon him.

That same power brought forth the infant’s limbs through the inviolate mother’s virgin organs, and later brought the young man’s limbs through closed doors (John 20:26).

If an explanation is sought here, the event will not be astonishing; if an example is demanded, it will not be unique. Let us grant that God can do something which we admit we cannot investigate. In such matters, the entire explanation of what has been done is the power of the one who does it.

## CHAPTER THREE

### 9

The fact that he is overcome by sleep, nourished by food, and experiences all human sensations persuades human beings that he is human—one whom these things did not consume, but whom he assumed.

This is how it happened. Yet certain heretics, perversely marveling at and praising his power, refused altogether to acknowledge human nature in him, precisely where the whole commendation of grace is found: the grace by which he saves those who believe in him, containing deep treasures of wisdom and knowledge and filling minds with faith, so that it may raise them to the eternal contemplation of unchangeable truth.

What if the Almighty had not created a human being, formed anywhere else, from a mother’s womb, but had suddenly brought him before human eyes? What if he had not passed through any stages from infancy to youth, and had taken no food or sleep? Would he not have confirmed the mistaken opinion and would no one have believed that he had assumed a true human being? While doing everything marvelously, he would have removed what he did mercifully.

But now he appeared as mediator between God and human beings, joining both natures in the unity of one person. He elevated the customary through the uncustomary and tempered the uncustomary through the customary.

### 10

What does God not do marvelously in all the movements of creation, if familiarity through daily repetition had not made such things seem worthless? Indeed, how many ordinary things, when considered, astonish us!

Consider the very power of seeds: who can approach in thought or express in words how many properties they possess, how alive they are, how effective, how secretly powerful, and how they accomplish great things in small spaces?

He therefore fashioned a human being for himself without seed, he who operates without seeds and produces seeds throughout the order of nature.

He preserved in his own body the measures of time and the stages of life, he who, without any change in himself, wove together the succession of the ages through changing things. For what began from time grew within time. But the Word, in the beginning, through whom times were made, chose the time at which to assume flesh; he did not yield to time by being changed into flesh. Humanity approached God; God did not depart from himself.

### 11

Some people demand an explanation of how God was mixed with a human being so that Christ became one person, even though this was supposed to happen only once—as though they were demanding an explanation of something that happens every day: how the soul is mixed with the body so that a human being becomes one person.

For just as the soul is united with the body in the unity of one person, so that the result is a human being, God is united with a human being in the unity of one person, so that the result is Christ.

In that person, therefore, there is a mixture of soul and body; in this person, a mixture of God and human being—provided that the listener withdraws from the customary notion of bodies, in which two liquids are usually mixed in such a way that neither preserves its own integrity. Yet even among bodies, light is mixed with air without being corrupted.

The person of a human being, then, is a mixture of soul and body; the person of Christ is a mixture of God and human being. For when the Word of God was mixed with a soul possessing a body, he assumed both soul and body at once.

The former occurs daily to bring human beings into existence; the latter occurred once to set human beings free. Nevertheless, a mixture of two incorporeal things ought to have been more readily believed than that of one incorporeal thing with another corporeal thing.

For if the soul is not deceived concerning its own nature, it understands that it is incorporeal. The Word of God is much more incorporeal; therefore the mixture of the Word of God and the soul ought to have been more credible than that of soul and body.

But we experience the latter in ourselves; concerning the former we are commanded to believe in Christ. If, however, we were commanded to believe both as equally unfamiliar to us, which would we believe more readily? How could we fail to admit that two incorporeal things could be mixed more easily than one corporeal and one incorporeal thing?

This is so only if the terms “mixture” or “mingling” may appropriately be applied to these matters, because of their customary use for corporeal things, which are constituted and perceived in a very different way.

### 12

The Word of God, therefore—the Son of God, coeternal with the Father, the very Power and Wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24)—reaching strongly from the highest limit of rational creation to the lowest limit of corporeal creation and ordering all things sweetly (Wisdom 8:1), present and hidden, enclosed nowhere, divided nowhere, swollen nowhere, but wholly everywhere without mass, assumed a human being in a manner entirely different from that in which he is present to other creatures.

He made himself and that human being one, Jesus Christ, the mediator between God and human beings (1 Timothy 2:5),

[Note: [Col. 0520] Seventeen manuscripts read “and himself with that man”; all editions read “and himself and that man.”] equal to the Father according to divinity but less than the Father according to the flesh—that is, according to his humanity; unchangeably immortal according to the divinity equal to the Father, yet the same person changeable and mortal according to the weakness akin to ours.

[Note: [Col. 0521] The editions read *cognitam* (“known”); eight manuscripts more aptly read *cognatam* (“akin”).]

In this Christ, at the time that he himself knew to be most suitable and had ordained before the ages, instruction and assistance came to human beings for attaining eternal salvation.

Instruction came so that the truths profitably proclaimed earlier—not only by the holy Prophets, who spoke everything truthfully, but also by philosophers, poets, and writers of every kind, whom no one doubts mixed many truths with falsehoods—might be confirmed by the authority of that same Truth made present in the flesh, for the sake of those unable to see and distinguish them in Truth’s own innermost reality. That Truth was present even before assuming a human being, to all who were able to share in it.

Above all, by the salutary example of his incarnation he persuaded human beings of this: since most people, eager for divinity, thought they should approach God through heavenly powers whom they considered gods and through various rites—not of lawful worship but of sacrilege—and sought to reach him more proudly than piously, through a kinship of pride demons insinuate themselves to such people in place of holy angels.

[Note: [Col. 0521] The Badian, Erasmus, and Louvain editions read “of proud thought”; some manuscripts, “by thought of pride”; four, “kinships.” The reading adopted here, found in five other manuscripts, was judged preferable.]

Human beings were therefore to know that God was so close to human piety—the God whom they sought as though he were far away, approaching through intermediary powers—that he deigned to assume a human being and unite himself with him in a certain way. Thus the whole human being was joined to him as the body is joined to the soul, except for the mutable composition into which God is not transformed, and which we see to possess both body and soul.

Assistance came through grace, without which no one can conquer vicious desires; and if some of them remain unconquered, they can be cleansed by the remission granted for venial sins.

As far as his instruction is concerned, what utterly uneducated man today, or what utterly insignificant woman, does not believe in the immortality of the soul and in a life after death? Among the Greeks, Pherecydes of Assyria was the first to argue for this; the novelty of his argument moved Pythagoras of Samos to turn from an athlete into a philosopher.

Now, as Maro says, and as we all see, “Assyrian amomum grows everywhere”:

> Under whose guidance, if any traces of our guilt remain,  
> They will be annulled and release the earth from everlasting fear.  
> (Virgil, *Eclogue* 4)

## CHAPTER FOUR

### 13

“But no indications appropriate to such immense majesty became evident,” they say, “because that cleansing of lepers, the care of the weak, and the restoration of life to the dead, if other examples are considered as well, are small things for God.””

We too admit that the Prophets performed certain such deeds. For among these signs, what is more remarkable than the raising of the dead? Elijah did this (1 Kings 17:22), and Elisha did this (2 Kings 4:35).

As for the miracles of magicians, whether they also raised the dead, let those decide who try to defeat Apuleius—even though he most abundantly defended himself against accusations of magical arts—not by accusing him but by praising him.

We read that the Egyptian magicians, the most skilled practitioners of these arts, were defeated by Moses, the servant of God, when they performed certain marvels by wicked arts, while Moses, simply calling upon God, overthrew all their contrivances (Exodus 7–8).

[Note: [Col. 0522] The Louvain, Badian, and Erasmus editions read, “God having been supplicatingly invoked”; the manuscripts prefer the reading translated here.]

Moses himself and the other most truthful Prophets foretold the Lord Christ and bestowed great glory upon him. They announced that he would come, not as their equal or as one superior to them in the same power of miracles, but plainly as the Lord God of all, made human for the sake of human beings.

For that reason he too wished to perform such deeds, lest it seem absurd that he did not perform what he had done through them. Yet he also had to perform something distinctive: to be born of a virgin, to rise from the dead, and to ascend into heaven.

I do not know what more someone who considers this too little could expect from God.

### 14

I think they demand the kind of deeds that, while wearing human form, he ought not to have performed.

[Note: [Col. 0522] The editions read, “which, while acting as a human being, he ought not to have done”; but the negative particle is absent from most manuscripts.]

For “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God, and all things were made through him” (John 1:1).

After assuming a human being, ought he to have made another world so that we would believe him to be the one through whom the world was made? But neither a greater world nor one equal to this world could have been made within this world. If he made a smaller one below this world, that too would likewise be considered too little.

Since, therefore, it was not fitting that he make a new world, he did new things within the world. A human being produced from a virgin, raised from the dead into eternal life, and exalted above the heavens is perhaps a more powerful work than the world itself.

Here they may reply that they do not believe this was done. What, then, is to be done with people who despise small things but do not believe greater things?

The restoration of life to the dead is believed because others performed it, and is considered too little for God. Flesh created from a virgin and raised from death into eternal life above the heavens is not believed because no one else did it, and is considered fitting for God.

Thus each person calmly accepts what he judges easy—not to perform, but to comprehend—and considers whatever surpasses his own capacity as though it were invented and therefore false. Do not be like them, I beg you.

### 15

These matters are discussed at greater length, and all the recesses of necessary questions are searched out, examined, and opened. Faith opens a way for understanding; unbelief closes it.

Who would not be moved to believe by the immense order of events itself from the beginning, and by the connection of the times—the past establishing faith in the present, and earlier things confirming ancient things through later and more recent events?

One man is chosen from the Chaldean people, endowed with most faithful piety. Divine promises are disclosed to him, to be fulfilled in the last times after so long a succession of ages, and it is foretold that all nations will have a blessing in his offspring (Genesis 12:2).

While worshiping the one true God, creator of the universe, he begets a son in old age from a wife whom infertility and age had rendered utterly incapable of hoping for childbirth.

From him a very numerous people is propagated. It multiplies in Egypt, where divine providence—growing more prominent through promises and fulfillments—had brought that stock from the eastern regions.

A strong nation is led out of Egyptian slavery amid dreadful signs and miracles. After wicked nations have been driven out, it is brought into and established in the promised land, and even undertakes to establish a kingdom.

Then, as sin grows stronger, it repeatedly offends the true God, who had bestowed such great benefits upon it, through sacrilegious presumption. It is chastised by various disasters and consoled by prosperity, and is brought onward until the incarnation and manifestation of Christ.

All the promises made to that nation and all the prophecies, priesthoods, sacrifices, the Temple, and absolutely all the sacred rites resounded with the proclamation that Christ—the Word of God, the Son of God, God who would come in the flesh, die, rise again, and ascend into heaven—would have peoples dedicated to him among all nations through his supreme name, and that those who believed in him would have forgiveness of sins and eternal salvation.

### 16

Christ came, and all the Prophets’ proclamations were fulfilled in his birth, life, words, deeds, passion, death, resurrection, and ascension (Matthew 1:25).

He sent the Holy Spirit and filled the faithful gathered together in one house (Acts 2:2), who had been awaiting this very promise through prayer and desire.

Filled with the Holy Spirit, they suddenly spoke in the languages of all nations, boldly rebuked errors, proclaimed saving truth, urged repentance for their former sinful life, and promised forgiveness through divine grace.

Signs and corresponding miracles followed the preaching of true piety and religion. Fierce unbelief was stirred against them. They endured what had been foretold, hoped for what had been promised, and taught the commandments.

Few in number, they were scattered throughout the world. With astonishing ease they converted peoples; they increased among their enemies and grew through persecutions. Through the narrow passages of affliction they spread to the ends of the earth.

From the most uneducated, the most despised, and the fewest in number, the most illustrious intellects were enlightened, ennobled, and multiplied, together with the most cultivated eloquence. They subjected to Christ the astonishing expertise of the keen-minded, eloquent, and learned, and turned it toward preaching the way of piety and salvation.

Through alternating adversities and prosperities in worldly affairs, they vigilantly practiced patience and self-restraint. As the world declines toward its end, and exhausted circumstances announce the final age, they await with much greater confidence—because this too was foretold—the eternal happiness of the heavenly city.

Amid all these things, the unbelief of wicked nations rages against the Church of Christ. The Church overcomes it by suffering and professing unshaken faith amid the fury of those who resist.

When the sacrifice of revealed truth, formerly veiled by mystical promises, takes the place of the earlier sacrifices, those sacrifices by which this truth was symbolized are abolished through the destruction of the Temple itself.

The Jewish nation, rejected through unbelief and uprooted from its dwelling places, is scattered everywhere throughout the world, so that it may carry the holy Books everywhere. Thus the testimony of the prophecy by which Christ and the Church were foretold is produced by the very adversaries themselves, lest it be thought to have been fabricated by us at a later time; and it was also foretold there that they themselves would not believe.

The temples and images of demons, together with sacrilegious rites, are gradually and successively overthrown in accordance with the prophetic predictions.

Heresies arise against the name of Christ, though under the cover of Christ’s name, for the exercise of the teaching of holy religion, just as they were foretold.

All these things are seen to have been fulfilled just as they are read in the prophecies, and from them the fulfillment of the many great things that remain is now awaited.

What mind, eager for eternity and stirred by the brevity of the present life, could contend against the light and summit of this divine authority?

## CHAPTER FIVE

### 17

What discussions by any philosophers, what writings by any philosophers, what laws of any states, could in any way be compared with the two commandments on which Christ says that the whole Law and the Prophets depend:

“You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind”; and, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 22:37, 39)?

Here is physics, because all the causes of all natures are in God the Creator.

Here is ethics, because a good and honorable life is formed from nothing else than loving what ought to be loved, in the manner in which it ought to be loved—that is, God and one’s neighbor.

[Note: [Col. 0524] The editions omit “in the manner in which it ought to be loved”; these words occur in five Vatican and seventeen Gallican manuscripts.]

Here is logic, because God alone is the truth and light of the rational soul.

Here too is the praiseworthy security of the state. For a city is neither founded nor preserved in the best manner except on the foundation and bond of faith and firm concord, when the common good is loved—which is God, the highest and truest good—and when people sincerely love one another in him, since they love one another for the sake of him from whom they cannot hide the spirit in which they love.

### 18

As for the very manner of expression with which Holy Scripture is woven together, how accessible it is to all, although penetrable by very few!

What it contains openly speaks to the hearts of the uneducated and the educated alike, without affectation, like an intimate friend. What it conceals in mysteries does not itself raise up in proud eloquence, so that my rather slow and uneducated mind would not dare approach it, like a poor person approaching a rich one. Rather, it invites everyone in humble speech—those whom it not only feeds with what is manifest but also exercises with the truth that is hidden—possessing in what is plain what it possesses in what is concealed.

Yet, lest the open passages be despised, the same passages are once again desired when hidden, and, once desired, are in a certain way renewed; once renewed, they are gently brought inward.

Through these things, corrupt minds are profitably corrected, small minds are nourished, and great intellects are delighted. The mind hostile to this teaching is one that either, through error, does not know that it is supremely salutary, or, because it is sick, hates the medicine.

### 19

You see how lengthy I have made this letter. Therefore, if anything moves you and you consider it important enough to discuss between us, do not let the customary limits of letters constrain you, as though they had to be observed. You know very well how long the letters of the ancients were when they were dealing with something they could not explain briefly.

And if the custom of authors belonging to other kinds of literature were different, the authority of our own writers would more properly provide an example for us in this matter. Examine the manner of the Apostolic Letters and also of those who interpreted those divine utterances. Do not hesitate either to put forward many questions if many things disturb you, or to spend more time at some point turning over what you are asking, so that, as far as this can be achieved by people such as ourselves, no cloud of doubt may remain to obstruct the light of truth.

### 20

For I know that Your Excellence has to endure the most stubborn contradictions of certain people who think—or wish others to think—that Christian doctrine is incompatible with the welfare of the state. They do so because they do not want the state to stand through the firmness of virtues, but through the impunity of vices.

Yet what many people commit with impunity is not unpunished by God, as it may be by a human king or by any ruler of a state.

His mercy and grace, proclaimed to human beings through the human Christ, but bestowed through God and through Christ himself, the Son of God, do not abandon those who live by faith in him and worship him piously—whether they patiently and courageously endure the evils of this life, or make merciful and temperate use of its goods.

For both they will receive an eternal reward in the heavenly and divine city, where there will no longer be any calamity to endure with distress, nor any desire to restrain with labor, but only the love of God and neighbor to be retained without difficulty and in perfect freedom.

May the most merciful omnipotence of God protect you safe and prosperous, illustrious man, deservedly distinguished and most excellent son.

I offer my most dutiful greetings to your holy mother, most worthy of honor in Christ, whose prayers for you may God hear according to your merits.

My holy brother and fellow bishop Possidius sends Your Excellence his warmest greetings.

## LETTER CXXXVIII

[Note: [Col. 0525] Corrected against the same manuscripts as Letter CXXXVI, and in addition against another manuscript designated *bn.* and against the sixth manuscript designated *V*.]

[Note: [Col. 0525] Formerly number 5; the letter that was 138 is now 122. Written at the same time.]

Augustine to Marcellinus, replying to Letter 136, in which Marcellinus had asked him to satisfy Volusianus and had reported that certain people criticized the fact that God had abolished the ancient Law. They also asserted that evangelical doctrine was harmful to the state; finally, there were some who preferred the magical tricks of Apollonius and Apuleius to the miracles of Christ.

To the distinguished man, deservedly eminent, beloved and most dearly desired son, MARCELLINUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

## CHAPTER ONE
1. To the illustrious, most eloquent, and dearest to us Volusianus [Note: The editions add “son Volusianus.” The manuscripts lack the word “son”], it was necessary to reply only to that which he thought should be investigated. As for the matters which you yourself sent to me in your letter for consideration and resolution, whether they were suggested or pressed upon you by him or by others, they ought rather to be sent to you, considered and resolved to the best of our ability—not in the manner appropriate to a book, but in the manner sufficient for an exchange of letters—so that, if you think fit, these letters may also be read to them, since you experience their agitation in daily discussions. But if this discourse is insufficient for ears inadequately prepared by the piety of faith, first let us accomplish among ourselves what you think will suffice for them, and only then convey to them what has been accomplished. For there are many matters by which, if their minds still recoil and shrink back, they may perhaps eventually be persuaded, either by fuller or subtler reasoning, or at least by an authority which they would consider it disgraceful to resist.

2. Accordingly, you wrote in your letter that some people are troubled as to why this God, who is also affirmed to be the God of the Old Testament, after rejecting the ancient sacrifices, has taken pleasure in new ones. They assert that nothing can be corrected unless it is shown to have been previously done wrongly; or that what was once rightly done ought in no way to have been altered. They say that rightly performed actions cannot be changed except unjustly. I have transferred these words from your letter into mine. If I wished to answer them at length, time would run out sooner than examples—examples showing that nature itself and human works are changed, by a definite principle, as circumstances and times require, while the principle by which these things are changed does not itself change.

Let me therefore mention a few examples, so that from them our attention, as though awakened, may run alertly through many similar cases. Does summer not succeed winter, warmth gradually increasing? Do not the hours of night turn into those of day? How often our own ages change! Childhood yields to adolescence, never to return; youth succeeds adolescence, though it will not remain; old age, bringing youth to an end, is itself ended by death. All these things change, yet the divine providential order by which they change does not change. Nor, I think, when a farmer orders one thing in summer different from what he ordered in winter, does the principle of agriculture change. When the person who rested through the night rises in the morning, he has not changed his plan of life. A teacher imposes upon an adolescent something different from what he used to impose upon a child. Thus, while the teaching remains constant, a changed command changes instruction without changing the teaching [Note: The editions read, “a changed command does not change instruction.” Twenty manuscripts, however, read, “a changed command changes instruction without changing the teaching.” We have preferred the latter reading].

3. For that great physician of our times, Vindicianus, when consulted by someone, ordered that a remedy be applied to his pain which seemed appropriate to the occasion; when it was applied, health followed. Then, several years later, when the same bodily condition had again arisen [Note: The editions read, “having been moved by the bodily condition, this”; we have restored “the same bodily condition having again arisen” from the manuscripts, which omit the word “applied” shortly afterward.], the man thought that this same remedy should be applied. When applied, it made the condition worse. Astonished, he returned to the physician and reported what had happened. The physician, as sharp-witted as ever, replied: “You were harmed because I did not order it”—with the result that everyone who heard him but did not know the man well might think that he did not trust medical skill, but some kind of unlawful power.

Later, when certain people, astonished, questioned him, he explained what they had not understood: namely, that for a person of that age he would no longer have ordered that remedy. So much depends on determining, by unchanging reason and arts [Note: Five manuscripts read, “reason is so powerful in the arts.” Others read, “by reason and arts.”], what must be changed according to the variation of circumstances.

4. It is therefore not true that what has once been rightly done must in no way be changed. When the circumstances of the time have changed, true reason often requires that what was previously rightly done be changed in such a way that, although they say it is not rightly done if it is changed, truth cries out on the contrary that it is not rightly done unless it is changed. For both things will then be right, if they differ according to the variation of circumstances.

What can happen at one time in the case of different persons—namely, that one person may do something with impunity while another may not, not because the act is different but because the person who does it is different—can likewise happen with one and the same person at different times: something ought to be done at one time and not at another, not because the person who does it is different from himself, but because the time at which he does it is different.

5. Anyone who can perceive, and does not neglect to contemplate, how widely this question extends—how the distinction between beauty and suitability is scattered throughout the universe—will certainly see the point. Beauty is considered and praised in itself; its opposite is ugliness and deformity. Suitability, however, whose opposite is unsuitability, depends as though bound to something else. It is judged not from itself but from that to which it is connected. “Becoming” and “unbecoming” either mean the same thing or are understood in the same way.

Now apply what we have said to the matter under discussion. The sacrifice which God had commanded was suitable in the earliest times; now it is not so. For he commanded something else that would be suitable to this time—he who knows far better than a human being what is appropriately applied to each time, what he should bestow, add, remove, take away, increase, or diminish: unchanging amid changing things, both their creator and their governor. Thus the beauty of the entire age, whose parts are the things suitable to their respective times, proceeds like a great song of some ineffable composer, until those who rightly worship God, even while the time of faith lasts, pass from it into the eternal contemplation of beauty.

6. Those who think that God commands these things for his own advantage or pleasure are mistaken; and they are rightly troubled that God has changed them, as though, moved by a changing delight, he had commanded one thing to be offered to him at an earlier time and another now. But this is not so. God commands nothing for his own benefit, but for the benefit of the one to whom he gives the command. He is therefore truly Lord, since he does not need a servant, while the servant needs him.

For in that Scripture called the Old Testament, and at the time when those sacrifices were still being offered which are not offered now, it is said: “I said to the Lord, ‘You are my God, for you have no need of my goods’” (Psalm 15:2). God therefore did not need those sacrifices, nor has he ever needed anything from anyone. Rather, they are signs of things divinely bestowed, whether for forming the soul in virtues or for attaining eternal salvation; through their celebration and performance, acts of piety useful not to God but to us are carried out.

7. It would take too long to discuss suitably the variety of signs which, because they concern divine realities, are called sacraments. Just as a human being is not therefore changeable because he does one thing in the morning and another in the evening, one thing this month and another the next, or does not do this year what he did last year, so God is not therefore changeable because, in the earlier volume of the whole age, he commanded one thing to be offered to him and, in the later volume, another, so that he might arrange, through changing times without any change in himself, the signs appropriately related to the wholesome teaching of religion.

To make clear to those troubled by this that this was already present in the divine plan, and that when the new things were established the former things did not suddenly become displeasing, as though by a changeable will, but that this had already been fixed and ordained in the very wisdom of God—to which the same Scripture says, even concerning greater changes among things: “You will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same” (Psalm 101:27–28)—it should be pointed out to them that this change of the sacraments of the Old and New Testaments was also foretold by prophetic utterances.

They will thus see, if they are able, that what is new in time is not new to him who created time and possesses, outside time, all the things which he distributes according to the variation of their respective times. For in that psalm from which I quoted something to show that God has no need of our sacrifices, where it says, “I said to the Lord, ‘You are my God, for you have no need of my goods,’” we read shortly afterward, in the person of Christ: “I will not gather their assemblies from blood,” that is, from the victims of animals by which the assemblies of the Jews were formerly gathered. Elsewhere he says: “I will not accept calves from your hand, nor goats from your flocks” (Psalm 49:9). Another prophet says: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will confirm a new covenant over the house of Jacob, not like the covenant which I established with their fathers when I led them out of the land of Egypt” (Jeremiah 31:31–32). There are many other testimonies on this matter, in which it was foretold that God would do this; to recount them now would take too long.

8. If it has now been sufficiently established that what was rightly established at one time can rightly be changed at another, through a change in the work rather than in the arrangement—which arrangement is contained in intelligible reason, where, outside time, things that cannot occur simultaneously within time exist together, because times do not proceed together—someone may perhaps expect us to explain the reasons for this particular change, though you know how lengthy that undertaking would be.

Nevertheless, it can be said briefly—perhaps enough for an intelligent person—that Christ ought to have been foretold by one set of sacraments when he was going to come, and announced by another when he had come. Just as, in speaking of this very matter now, the difference between the realities has compelled us also to change the words: for “to be foretold” is one thing, and “to be announced” another; “when he was going to come” is one thing, and “when he had come” another.

## CHAPTER II

9. Let us now examine what follows in your letter. You added that they say the preaching and teaching of Christ are in no respect compatible with the customs of the state. They point especially to his command that we must not repay anyone evil for evil (Romans 12:17), that we must offer the other cheek to one who strikes us, give our cloak to one who persists in taking our tunic, and go twice the distance with one who wishes to press us into service (Matthew 5:39–41).

All these things, they assert, are contrary to the customs of the state. “For who,” they ask, “would tolerate having something taken from him by an enemy, or not wish to repay the plunderers of the Roman provinces with the evils permitted by the law of war?”

I might perhaps refute these and similar words of those who criticize—or who speak in this way not to criticize but to inquire—at greater length, if these debates were being held with men trained in liberal studies. Why, then, should we labor longer instead of asking them how those who, having suffered injury, preferred to forgive rather than to pursue, were able to govern and enlarge the state which they made great and wealthy from a small and impoverished beginning (Sallust, *The War with Catiline*)?

How could Cicero, praising Caesar, who was certainly administering the state, say of his character that he used to forget nothing except injuries (*Oration for Quintus Ligarius*)? He said this either as a great praiser or as a great flatterer. If as a praiser, he knew Caesar to be such; if as a flatterer, he was showing that the head of state ought to be such as he falsely claimed Caesar to be.

What is “not repaying evil for evil,” then, except recoiling from the desire for vengeance? It means preferring to forgive a received injury rather than pursue it, and forgetting nothing except injuries.

10. When these principles are read in the writings of their own authors, people shout and applaud. They seem to see customs being described and praised by which a state ruling so many nations ought to arise: customs according to which, after receiving an injury, they preferred to forgive rather than to pursue.

But when divine authority is read commanding that evil must not be repaid with evil; when this wholesome admonition resounds from a higher place to assemblies of peoples, as though in public schools for both sexes and all ages and ranks, religion is accused as an enemy of the state!

If it were heard as it deserves, it would establish, consecrate, strengthen, and enlarge the state far better than Romulus, Numa, Brutus, and the other illustrious men of the Roman people. For what is a state except the affair of the people? It is therefore a common affair, plainly the affair of a civic community. And what is a civic community except a multitude of human beings brought into a certain bond of concord?

In their writers one reads: “In a short time, a scattered and wandering multitude became a state through concord.” What commands of concord did they ever judge ought to be read in their temples? Indeed, the unfortunate people were forced to ask how they could worship, without offending anyone, gods who were themselves at odds with one another. If they wished to imitate those gods in discord, the bond of concord would be broken and the state would collapse. Later, as their customs were gradually discolored and corrupted, this process began through civil wars.

11. Who, even if alien to that religion, is so deaf as not to know how many commands of concord are repeatedly read in the churches of Christ—not devised by human disputation but written by divine authority?

To this also belong those teachings which they prefer to attack rather than learn: that the other cheek should be offered to the one who strikes, that a cloak should also be given to the one who wishes to take a tunic, and that the journey should be doubled with the one who presses us into service.

This is done so that the evil person may be overcome by good—or rather, so that evil may be overcome by good in the evil person—and so that the human being may be freed from evil, not from something external and belonging to another, but from something inward and his own, by which he is devastated more grievously and harmfully than by the savagery of any external enemy.

The person who conquers evil by good therefore patiently loses temporal advantages in order to teach how lightly those things should be valued for the sake of faith and justice—things which the other, by loving them excessively, becomes evil. Thus the wrongdoer may learn from the very person whom he has injured what sort of things were worth committing an injury for, and may be brought repentant into concord, than which nothing is more useful to a state—not conquered by the strength of someone raging against him, but by the goodwill of the person who endures.

This is rightly done when it appears likely to benefit the person for whose sake it is done, in order to work correction and concord in him. It must certainly be done with this intention, even if another outcome follows and the person for whose correction and reconciliation this remedy was applied, as though for treatment and healing, is unwilling to be corrected and reconciled.

12. Otherwise, if we attend to the words and think we must be slaves to their literal precision, the right cheek should not be offered if the left has been struck. For he says: “If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the left also” (Matthew 5:39). Yet the left cheek is more readily struck, since the blow of someone striking with the right hand falls more easily upon it.

The saying is therefore usually understood as though it meant: “If anyone has pursued what is better in you, offer him what is inferior, lest, being intent upon vengeance rather than patience, you despise eternal things for the sake of temporal things, when temporal things ought rather to be despised for the sake of eternal things, as the left is despised in comparison with the right.”

This was always the intention of the holy martyrs. Final vengeance is justly demanded when no opportunity for correction remains—namely, at the final and supreme judgment. But now we must take care lest, through the desire for vengeance, we lose—not to mention anything else—the very patience which ought to be valued more highly than anything an enemy can take away, even against our will.

Another evangelist, in stating the same teaching, made no mention of the right cheek, but named only the cheek and the other one (Luke 6:29), so that it might be understood somewhat more distinctly in one account, while he himself simply commended the same patience [Note: The editions read: “so that in the other account the other cheek might be understood to be commended as the same patience.” All the manuscripts, however, read: “so that it might be understood in one account, while he himself simply commended the same patience”—that is, so that in Matthew it might be understood more distinctly that temporal things must be despised for eternal things, as the left is despised for the right, and that care must be taken lest patience be lost through the desire for vengeance].

The just and devout person must therefore be prepared patiently to endure the wickedness of those whom he seeks to make good, so that the number of the good may rather increase, instead of his adding himself to the number of the wicked through an equal wickedness.

13. Finally, that these commands relate more to the inward preparation of the heart than to the outward action; that patience together with goodwill is to be maintained in the secret recesses of the soul, while in public one should do what appears capable of benefiting those toward whom we ought to have goodwill—this is clearly shown by the Lord Jesus himself.

When he was struck in the face, he gave the unique example of patience by replying: “If I have spoken evil, reproach me for the evil; but if I have spoken well, why do you strike me?” (John 18:23). If we look merely at the words, then, he did not fulfill his own command. He did not offer the other cheek to the one who struck him; rather, he prevented the person who had inflicted the injury from increasing it.

And yet he had come prepared not only to be struck in the face, but also to be crucified and killed for the sake of those by whom he suffered these things. While hanging on the cross, he said of them: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

Nor does the apostle Paul seem to have fulfilled the command of his Lord and teacher when, after being struck in the face, he said to the high priest: “God will strike you, whitewashed wall! You sit judging me according to the Law, and contrary to the Law you order me to be struck!”

When those standing nearby said, “Do you insult the high priest?” he wished, mockingly [Note: The editions of Amerbach, Badonius, and Erasmus, and manuscript A, read “high priest, incidentally admonishing them.”], to remind them of what he had said, so that those who had understanding might realize that, at Christ’s coming, the whitewashed wall—that is, the hypocrisy of the Jewish priesthood—was already to be destroyed [Note: Lovanius reads “had already been destroyed.” Other witnesses read “was to be destroyed”].

For he said: “I did not know, brothers, that he is the high priest; for it is written, ‘You shall not speak evil of the ruler of your people’” (Acts 23:3–5). Yet plainly, having grown up among that people and been educated there in the Law, he could not have failed to know that he was the high priest; nor could he in any way have deceived those to whom he was so well known by claiming ignorance.

14. These commands of patience must therefore always be retained in the preparation of the heart, and that goodwill, so that evil may not be repaid with evil, must always be fulfilled in the will.

Many things must nevertheless be done, including the punishment, with a certain benevolent severity, of people who are unwilling to be punished; one must care more for their welfare than for their wishes. The writings of those earlier authors praised this most brilliantly in the case of a ruler of the state. For when correcting a son, however harshly, paternal love is certainly never lost. Yet something is done against his will and to his distress when, even unwillingly, he appears to need to be healed through distress.

Accordingly, if this earthly state observed Christian commands, even its wars would not be waged without goodwill, so that the defeated might more easily be helped toward a peaceful fellowship of piety and justice. For the person from whom the freedom to do wrong is taken away is beneficially defeated. Nothing is more miserable than the prosperity of sinners, by which punitive impunity is nourished and an evil will, like an internal enemy, is strengthened.

But human beings with perverse and alienated hearts [Note: The editions read “perverse, alienated, and hostile hearts.” Manuscript SB reads “alienated.” We have preferred the latter reading] consider human affairs prosperous when the splendor of buildings is noticed but the corruption of souls is ignored; when the massiveness of theaters is constructed while the foundations of virtue are excavated; when the madness of bloodshed is glorious and works of mercy are mocked; when actors luxuriate in what the rich possess in abundance while the poor scarcely have necessities; when God, who publicly cries out against this public evil through the public proclamation of his teaching, is blasphemed by impious peoples, and gods are sought whose honor is celebrated by those very theatrical disgraces of body and soul.

When God permits these things to flourish, he is then more gravely angry. When he leaves them unpunished, he then punishes more fiercely. But when he overturns the support of vices and makes abundant lusts powerless, he opposes them mercifully. Indeed, if it were possible, good people would even wage wars mercifully, so that, once licentious desires had been subdued, these vices might be destroyed—vices which ought to have been either eradicated or suppressed by a just authority [Note: The editions read “or brought low.” Four manuscripts read “destroyed.” Sixteen others read “suppressed.”].

15. For if Christian discipline condemned all wars, the advice given in the Gospel to soldiers seeking a rule for salvation would rather have been that they should throw away their weapons and withdraw entirely from military service. But they were told: “Do violence to no one, accuse no one falsely; be satisfied with your pay” (Luke 3:14).

By commanding them to be satisfied with their own pay, he certainly did not prohibit military service. Therefore, those who say that Christ’s teaching is opposed to the state should provide an army such as Christ’s teaching commanded soldiers to be; provide provincials, husbands, wives, parents, children, masters, servants, kings, judges, and, finally, collectors and payers of the imperial treasury’s taxes such as Christian teaching commanded them to be. Then let them dare to say that it is opposed to the state. Rather, let them not hesitate to confess that, if obeyed, it is a great salvation for the state.

## CHAPTER III

16. Why should I answer the claim that many evils have befallen the Roman empire through certain Christian emperors? This general complaint is slanderous [Note: *The City of God*, book 4, chapter 2]. If they would speak more openly about certain emperors of the past, I too could recall similar, or perhaps even more serious, examples among non-Christian emperors, so that they might understand either that these are vices of human beings, not of the teaching, or that they belong not to the emperors but to others without whom emperors can do nothing.

It is sufficiently clear from what time the Roman state began to decline; their own writings testify to it [Note: The same work, book 2, chapter 18]. Long before the name of Christ had shone upon the earth, it was said: “O city for sale, and destined soon to perish if it finds a buyer!” (Sallust, *The Jugurthine War*).

In his book on the Catilinarian war, that same most distinguished historian of theirs, certainly writing before Christ’s coming, does not conceal when the army of the Roman people first began to love, drink, admire statues, painted panels, and chased vessels, to seize them privately and publicly, to strip temples, and to pollute everything sacred and profane.

When, then, neither human beings nor even those whom they thought to be gods were spared by the avarice and rapacity of corrupt and depraved morals, at that time the celebrated glory and welfare of the state began to perish. It would now take too long to say what results their worst vices subsequently produced, and with what harm to human affairs that injustice prospered.

Let them listen to their own satirist, who speaks truth while chattering:

> Humble Fortune once preserved the chaste Latian homes,  
> Nor did harsh labor permit their small houses  
> To be touched by vice; nor sleep was long, nor the hands  
> Were soft, but worn by Tuscan wool; and nearby stood  
> Hannibal, while husbands stood watch upon the Colline tower.  
>   
> Now we suffer the evils of a long peace; more savage than arms,  
> Luxury has settled upon us and avenges the conquered world.  
> No crime is absent, no act of lust is lacking, since  
> Roman poverty has perished.  
>   
> (Juvenal, *Satires* 6)

What, then, should you expect me to do—exaggerate how many evils were brought in when injustice was lifted up by success and prosperity—when even those who considered the matter somewhat more wisely saw that it was more lamentable for Roman poverty to have perished than for Roman wealth? In poverty, integrity of character was preserved; through wealth, dreadful wickedness invaded not the city walls but the minds of the civic community itself, worse than any enemy.

17. Thanks be to the Lord our God, who sent us a singular aid against these evils. What would this river of the human race’s dreadful wickedness not carry away, what would it not entangle, into what depths would it not plunge us, unless the cross of Christ had been set more prominently and firmly in place amid such a vast mass of authority? By grasping its strength, we would stand firm, lest we be swept away and swallowed in the enormous whirlpool of this world by those who give evil advice or drive people into evil.

In this foul accumulation of depraved morals and the ruin of the ancient discipline, heavenly authority especially had to come and bring help. It had to commend voluntary poverty, continence, goodwill, justice, concord, true piety, and the other radiant and powerful virtues of life—not merely so that this life might be conducted with the greatest honor, nor merely for the most harmonious fellowship of the earthly state, but also for attaining eternal salvation and the heavenly and divine commonwealth of an eternal people.

Faith, hope, and love enroll us as citizens of that commonwealth. Therefore, as long as we are exiles from it, we endure those people, if we cannot correct them, who wish to maintain the state through unpunished vices—the state which the first Romans established and enlarged by their virtues, although they lacked true piety toward the true God, a piety which could also have led them, through a saving religion, into the eternal city. Nevertheless, they preserved a certain integrity of their own kind, sufficient to establish, enlarge, and preserve an earthly state.

For God showed, in the wealthy and distinguished Roman empire, how powerful even civic virtues can be without true religion, so that it might be understood that, when true religion is added, human beings become citizens of another city—whose king is truth, whose law is love, and whose measure is eternity.

## CHAPTER IV

18. Who would not consider it laughable that they attempt to compare Apollonius, Apuleius, and the other most skilled practitioners of magical arts with Christ, or even to prefer them to him?

It is nevertheless more tolerable when they compare these men with Christ rather than with their own gods. For Apollonius was, as must be admitted, much better than that author and perpetrator of so many acts of sexual violence whom they call Jupiter.

“These things,” they say, “are fabulous.” Let them therefore continue praising the luxurious, licentious, and plainly sacrilegious happiness of the state which invented these disgraces of the gods, which not only placed them in stories to be heard but also displayed them in theaters to be watched—where there were more crimes than gods, and where the gods themselves were said to enjoy having such things presented to them, although they ought to have punished their worshipers for even watching them patiently.

“But they themselves,” they say, “are not the ones celebrated by the falsehood of such stories.” Who, then, are the beings appeased by the celebration of such obscenities? The perversity and deceit of these demons, through whom magical arts also deceive human minds, has been exposed by Christian teaching. That teaching has revealed it to the whole world, distinguished the holy angels from their wickedness, and warned people that these beings must be avoided and how they are to be avoided. Yet Christian teaching is called an enemy of the state—as though, if temporal happiness were to be obtained through such beings at all, any kind of unhappiness would not rather have been preferable.

Nor did God wish this matter to remain doubtful. For, during the period when the Old Testament—under which the New Testament was veiled—was to remain in shadow, he honored the first people, who worshiped the one true God and despised the most false gods, with such great earthly happiness that anyone can understand that even this happiness is not in the power of demons, but in the power of that one God whom the angels serve and before whom the demons tremble.

19. Apuleius, to speak especially of him—an African who is better known to us Africans—could not, with all his magical arts, attain not only a kingdom but even any judicial office in the state, although he was born in an honorable position in his homeland, liberally educated, and endowed with great eloquence.

Or did he perhaps despise these things willingly, as a philosopher, when, as priest of the province, he considered it a great honor to give public shows and provide clothing for the hunters [Note: Badonius and Erasmus read “and clothe the worshipers.” Lovanius and the manuscripts, more correctly, read “the hunters”—namely, those who took part in the spectacles which Apuleius presented.
