Such spectacles were called *munera*, not only those of gladiators but also those involving hunters, that is, fighters against wild beasts. “The hunts,” Lactantius says in book 6, chapter 20, of the *Divine Institutes*, “which are called *munera*, were attributed to Saturn.”], and to litigate against the opposition of certain citizens over the erection of a statue of himself among the Coans [Note: Eleven manuscripts read “among the Oceans”; five others “among the Oeans”; two others “among the Ceans.”], in whose city he had a wife? So that this matter would not escape the knowledge of posterity, he committed the speech of that same lawsuit to writing for remembrance.

As far as this earthly happiness is concerned, that magician achieved whatever he was able to achieve [Note: This is the reading of Badonius, Erasmus, and most manuscripts. Lovanius reads “as far as he was able.”]. It is therefore clear that he was nothing more—not because he did not wish to be, but because he could not be.

He also defended himself most eloquently against certain people who accused him of magical practices. I am therefore astonished at his admirers, who proclaim that he performed certain miracles by those arts and try to make him a witness against his own defense. Let them see whether they themselves are giving true testimony and he offered a false defense.

If they have any wisdom, let them notice that those who seek magical arts seek them either for earthly happiness or from a curiosity that deserves condemnation; or, though innocent of using them, they praise them with a dangerous admiration. Let them also see that our David, without any such arts, rose from being a shepherd of sheep to royal dignity. Faithful Scripture concealed neither his sins nor his merits, so that we might know both how God is not offended and how an offended God is appeased.

20. As for miracles displayed to human senses in ways that astonish them, those who compare magicians with the holy prophets—who surpass them in the renown of great miracles—are greatly mistaken. How much more mistaken are they if they compare magicians with Christ, whom those prophets, to whom no magician can in any way be compared, foretold as destined to come, both according to the flesh which he assumed from the Virgin and according to the divinity by which he is never separated from the Father!

I see that I have made this letter extremely long, and yet I have not said everything about Christ that might in some measure suffice either for those whose slower minds cannot grasp divine matters, or for those whom, although they are moved by their sharp intelligence, contentious zeal and long-standing preoccupation with error prevent from understanding [Note: All the editions read “those who,” plainly corruptly. Manuscript M reads the better form].

Nevertheless, learn what troubles them against these things, and write back, so that, with God’s help, we may undertake to answer everything either in letters or in books. May you be happy in the Lord, through his grace and mercy, illustrious and deservedly distinguished lord, most dear and most longed-for son.

# LETTER CXXXIX

[Note: We collated this with a, bg, bl, bn, c, cc, cb, ff, g, gg, gv, n, r, s, sb, two vc, four v, and with the editions of Amerbach, Badonius, Erasmus, and Lovanius.] [Note: Formerly 158; what was 139 is now 259. Written in 412, near the end of the month.] That the proceedings drawn up against the Donatists should be published, and that the defendants should be punished more mildly and without the death penalty.

To his deservedly distinguished lord, most dear and most longed-for son MARCELLINUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

1. I eagerly await the proceedings which Your Excellency promised, and I now very much desire that they be read in the church at Hippo and, if possible, also in all the churches established in the diocese. Thus people may hear and fully recognize those confessors of iniquity—not penitence extorted by fear of God, but the hardness of their most cruel hearts laid open by judicial diligence: whether those who confessed the homicide and the blinding and maiming of the priest’s body [Note: Nearly all the manuscripts omit “who confessed”]; or those who did not dare deny that they could have known these things, although they said that they displeased them, while fleeing Catholic peace as though to avoid being polluted by others’ crimes, and persisting in that sacrilegious schism among so great a multitude of such monstrous criminals; or even those who said that they would not withdraw from it even when Catholic truth and Donatist perversity had been demonstrated to them. It is no small thing that God has willed to accomplish through your service. Would that you might hear such cases of theirs frequently in this way, that their crimes and insane obstinacy might so often be exposed, and that the published proceedings might be brought to everyone’s notice! As for what Your Excellency wrote—that you are uncertain whether you ought to order the same proceedings to be displayed in Theoprepia [Note: The editions read “Theopropia.” But the better manuscripts have “Theoprepia.” So too the third Carthaginian conference, no. 5, from which it is clear that this was the name of a church at Carthage then belonging to the Donatists.]—do so, if a large crowd can gather there. Otherwise, another more frequented place must be provided; but in no case should it be omitted.

2. As for their punishment, although they have confessed such great crimes, I ask you that it be something other than the penalty of death—both for the sake of our conscience and in order to commend Catholic gentleness. For the fruit of their confession has come to us: the Catholic Church has found an occasion to preserve and display her mildness toward the most atrocious enemies. In such cruelty, whatever punishment proceeds apart from bloodshed will appear great gentleness. Although this now seems unworthy to some of our people, stirred by that atrocity, and almost like dissolution and negligence, nevertheless, once the passions of men have subsided—for recent events commonly arouse them with greater turbulence—an exceptionally clear goodness will appear. For this reason it will be all the more pleasing to read and exhibit the same Proceedings, my lord, deservedly distinguished, and greatly beloved and longed-for son.

The holy brother and my fellow bishop Boniface is there, and through the deacon Peregrinus, who went with him, I sent a memorandum [Note: The manuscripts lack the word *quod* (“which”); three of them read, “Thus regard it as.”]; regard it as my own presence. Whatever you jointly decide for the welfare of the Church, may it be done with the Lord’s assistance; he is powerful enough to help mercifully amid such great evils.

At present Macrobius, their bishop, accompanied by bands of the lost of both sexes, goes about here and there, and has opened for himself the basilicas which the slightest fear on the part of their owners had closed. While the agent of the illustrious Celer, Spondeus, whom I commended—and continue strongly to commend—to your Affection, was present, their boldness was somewhat broken. But now, after he has departed for Carthage, Macrobius has also opened the basilicas on Spondeus’s estates and is gathering the people.

With him too is that deacon Donatus, rebaptized although he had been a tenant of the Church [Note: The printed editions read, “rebaptized, who, although he had been a tenant of the Church, was involved.” But the manuscripts have a somewhat different word order, restored here.], who played a leading part in that slaughter. What men of such a character are not with him, when even that man is with him?

If the Proconsul—or both of you together—are going to pronounce sentence against them, and if he perhaps persists in wishing to punish them with the sword, although he is a Christian and, as far as we have been able to observe, not inclined to such tortures, nevertheless, if it should prove necessary, order my letters to be cited in the Proceedings [Note: Six manuscripts read *alligari* (“to be bound”), rather than *allegari* (“to be cited”).], each of which I thought ought to be sent to you on this matter. For I often hear that it lies within a judge’s power to soften a sentence and to punish more mildly than the laws command.

But if he should not consent to this even because of my letters, let him at least grant that they be taken into custody. We shall endeavor to obtain this through the clemency of the emperors [Note: The printed editions have *Imperatoris* (“of the emperor”); the manuscripts have *Imperatorum* (“of the emperors”).], so that the sufferings of God’s servants, which ought to be glorious in the Church, may not be dishonored by the blood of enemies.

For I know that, in the case of the clergy of Anaunia [Note: Three Vatican manuscripts read *Anannensium*; the Corbie and German manuscripts, *Anabnensium*; other codices, *Anaunensium*. He is evidently speaking of the holy martyrs Sisinnius, Martyrius, and Alexander, who were killed by pagan peasants in the valley of Anaunia, not far from the city of Trent, at the end of May in the year 397—or, as Paulinus writes in his Life of Saint Ambrose, after Saint Ambrose’s death.], who were killed by pagans and are now honored as martyrs, the emperor, when petitioned, readily granted that those who had killed them and were already being held captive should not be punished with a similar penalty.

3. I have forgotten why I received the books *On the Baptism of Infants* from you again, although I had already sent the codex itself to Your Excellence. Unless perhaps, when I examined them, I found them defective and wished to correct them—but, being wonderfully hindered, I have still not done so.

You should also know that the letter I had begun dictating while I was there, to be written to you and attached to these books, remains unfinished because I added only a little to it. If I could give you an account of all the days and nightly labors spent on other necessities, you would be deeply saddened and astonished at how many things occupy me—things that cannot be postponed at all and do not allow me to undertake those matters to which, by asking and reminding me, you urge me, though I am willing and grieve ineffably because I cannot act.

For whenever I obtain even a little respite from the needs of those people who press me so hard that I can in no way avoid them, nor ought I to disregard them, there is no lack of matters which I must dictate first, fixed as they are at particular moments so that they do not tolerate delay.

Thus it was with the abridgment of the Proceedings of our conference, which cost me considerable labor, when I saw that no one wished to undertake the task of reading so great a mass of writing. So too with the letter to the Donatist laity themselves concerning this same conference of ours, which I have just completed after several nights of labor. So too with two not-short letters: one to Your Affection, the other to the illustrious Volusianus, which I believe you have already received. And now I have in hand a book for our Honoratus concerning five questions that he proposed to me and communicated by letter; you can see how little it would be proper not to answer him immediately.

For the love that, like a nurse, cherishes her children does not place the stronger before the weaker according to the order of loving, but according to the order of helping. It puts the weaker first, wishing them to become such as those already are whom, not despising them but trusting in what they may become, it temporarily passes by.

Such necessities of dictating something that prevents me from dictating those works for which I burn with greater eagerness cannot fail to arise, when scarcely any space is granted between the heaps of occupations by which the desires or needs of others drag us along under compulsion. And I simply do not know what to do.

4. You have heard what you should ask of the Lord together with me. But I also do not want you to cease reminding me so insistently and so frequently; you are not doing nothing by doing so.

I also commend to Your Excellence the Church established in Numidia, on account of whose needs the holy brother and my fellow bishop Delphinus has been sent by my brothers and fellow bishops who are laboring and facing danger there. I do not write more about this matter, since you will hear him in person.

You will find the rest in the memoranda that I sent to the presbyter, either now or through the deacon Peregrinus, so that I may not have to repeat these matters to you so often.

May your heart always thrive in Christ, my lord, deservedly distinguished, and greatly beloved and longed-for son. I commend to Your Excellence our son Ruffinus, the chief magistrate of Cirta [Note: Bad., Am., Er., and three manuscripts have *Circensem*. All the other books have *Cirtensem Principalem*, that is, “the chief magistrate of the city of Cirta,” as it seems to us.].

## Concerning the following letter  
*(Book II of the Retractions, chapter 36)*

At the very time when we were being vigorously engaged against the Donatists, and had already begun to be engaged against the Pelagians [Note: The African bishops began to be engaged against the Pelagians in 411 or 412. By that time, Coelestius, a disciple of Pelagius, had already been tried at the Council of Carthage, as the fathers of another Carthaginian synod in 416 report in the letter published here as Letter 175. There they write to Innocent: “Hence it happened that we thought we should review what had been discussed here in the Church of Carthage concerning Coelestius nearly five years ago,” and so forth. Augustine did not attend that earlier council, as appears from *Retractions* II.33 and from the book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*.], a certain friend sent me from Carthage five questions and asked me to explain them to him in writing. They were these:

What is intended by the Lord’s saying, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46)? What does the Apostle mean when he says, “That, being rooted and grounded in love, you may have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth” (Ephesians 3:17–18)? Who are the five foolish virgins and who are the wise (Matthew 25:2)? What are the outer darknesses (Matthew 22:13)? And how is the statement “The Word became flesh” to be understood (John 1:14)?

But, having regard to the aforementioned heresy, a new enemy of God’s grace, I proposed a sixth question to myself, concerning the grace of the New Testament. In discussing this, after inserting an exposition of the twenty-first Psalm—at whose beginning is written what the Lord cried out on the cross, and which that friend had first asked me to explain—I resolved all five questions, not in the order in which they had been proposed, but as they could appropriately arise in their places while I was discussing the grace of the New Testament.

This book begins as follows: “You proposed five questions for me to discuss” [Note: Augustine seems to have quoted the opening words of Letter 140 less faithfully. Although all the printed editions have *tractandas* at the passage cited here in the *Retractions*, they give *pertractandas* at the beginning of the following letter.].

## Book on the Grace of the New Testament, or Letter 140

[Note: In correcting this text we used manuscripts bg, bl, bn, cc, ff, g, m, sb; three manuscripts designated cb; three designated r; two designated vc; two designated v; and the editions of Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: Elsewhere numbered 120; the letter that was 140 is now numbered 260. It was written immediately after the preceding letter.]

Augustine to Honoratus, replying to his five questions; in addition to these, he proposes for himself a sixth question, concerning the grace of the New Testament, to be discussed against the Pelagians, and interprets the twenty-first Psalm in its entirety for that purpose.

### 1.

You proposed five questions for me to investigate thoroughly and solve, my dearest brother Honoratus [Note: Honoratus had not yet been initiated into baptism, as is clear from chapter 19, section 48, of this book. Later he was raised to the office of presbyter—unless Cassiodorus is mistaken, for in *On Divine Reading*, chapter 16, he says that this work was written to Honoratus the presbyter.], questions gathered from here and there, as they may have troubled you while reading or occurred to you while reflecting, and somehow poured into my view.

If I wished to arrange their solution through discussion—not speaking of each one piecemeal, as they were proposed, but joining and weaving them together into one continuous discourse—the task would seem difficult. Nevertheless, I think they will be solved more easily if I do this. They will assist one another if one depends upon another, until all enter into the sequence of the discussion—not separated individually into distinct places, as though each occupied its own private concern, but contemplating one thing and working together toward one thing through a shared relation and undivided truth.

## CHAPTER ONE

### 2.

You therefore wished, and reminded me in writing, that I should explain and make clear to you what is intended by the Lord’s saying, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”; what the Apostle means by saying, “That, being rooted and grounded in love, you may have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth, length, height, and depth” (Ephesians 3:17); who the five foolish virgins are and who the wise (Matthew 25:2); what the outer darknesses are (Matthew 22:15); and how the statement “The Word became flesh” is to be understood (John 1:14).

These are certainly the five questions you proposed, mentioned by me as briefly as you proposed them. Therefore, if you agree, let us add a sixth and seek above all what the grace of the New Testament is. Let all the others look toward this, and let each contribute its own work to it as opportunity allows—not in the order in which you proposed them and I recalled them, but let each answer when it is needed, as though summoned, and fulfill the task belonging to it.

Let the beginning therefore be as follows.

## CHAPTER TWO

### 3.

There is a certain life of man entangled in bodily senses, devoted to bodily pleasures, avoiding bodily pain, and pursuing enjoyment. The happiness of this life is temporal. To begin from this life is necessary; to persist in it is a matter of will.

For into this life the infant is poured from its mother’s womb. As far as it can, it avoids its pains and seeks its pleasures; it is capable of nothing more. But after it reaches an age at which the use of reason awakens within it, then, aided by God, it can choose another life, whose joy is in the mind and whose happiness is inward and eternal.

A rational soul is present in man, but it makes a difference how he turns the will through the use of that reason [Note: Most manuscripts read: “It makes a difference toward what he turns the use of that reason by his will.”]—whether toward the goods of an exterior and lower nature or toward the goods of an interior and higher nature; that is, whether to enjoy body and time, or to enjoy divinity and eternity.

The soul is placed, as it were, in a middle position: beneath it is bodily creation, while above it is the Creator of both itself and the body.

### 4.

A rational soul can therefore make good use even of temporal and bodily happiness, provided that it does not surrender itself to the creature while neglecting the Creator, but rather makes that happiness serve the Creator, who also bestowed it through the abundant generosity of his goodness.

For just as all things God created are good, from rational creation itself down to the lowest body, so the rational soul acts well in relation to them if it preserves their order and, by distinguishing, choosing, and assigning value, subjects lesser things to greater, bodily things to spiritual, lower things to higher, and temporal things to eternal. Otherwise, by neglecting higher things and desiring lower ones—for by this it itself becomes worse—it sends both itself and its body into a worse condition [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “changes them for the worse.”]. Rather, through ordered love, it turns both itself and its body toward what is better.

Since all substances are naturally good, the order among them is honored with praise, while perversity is condemned with blame. The soul, by using creatures perversely, does not cause itself to escape the Creator’s ordering. For if the soul uses good things badly, the Creator uses even bad things well. Thus the soul becomes evil by using good things perversely, while the Creator remains good by using even evil things in an ordered way. Whoever orders himself unjustly in sins is justly ordered in punishments.

### 5.

Therefore, wishing to show that earthly and temporal happiness is also his gift, and that it ought not to be hoped for from anywhere except him, God judged that in the earlier ages of the world the Old Testament should be administered, pertaining to the old man, from whom this life necessarily begins.

Those fathers’ happinesses are proclaimed as granted by God’s benefit, although they belonged to this passing life. Those earthly gifts were promised and bestowed openly; but, secretly, the New Testament was figuratively foretold through all those things, and its meaning was grasped by the few whom the same grace had deemed worthy of the prophetic gift.

Those holy men therefore administered the Old Testament in keeping with the suitability of the time, but they belonged to the New Testament. For even when they were engaged with temporal happiness, they understood eternal happiness as true and preferable; and they administered the former in mystery so that they might attain the latter as a reward.

And whenever they suffered adversity, they suffered it for this purpose: that, delivered by the most evident divine assistance, they might glorify God, the giver of all good things—not only of the eternal things they devoutly hoped for, but also of the temporal things they prophetically governed.

## CHAPTER THREE

### 6.

When the fullness of time came, so that the grace hidden in the Old Testament might now be revealed in the New, God sent his Son, made from a woman (Galatians 4:4). In accordance with the usage of the Hebrew language, this term designates every female, whether untouched by a man or already joined to one.

But to recognize what Son he sent and wished to be made from a woman, and how great the God is who deigned to undertake this humility for the salvation of believers, now attend to the Gospel:

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made. What was made in him was life, and the life was the light of men; and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:1–5).

This God, therefore, the Word of God through whom all things were made, is the Son of God, remaining immutable, present everywhere, confined by no place, and not distributed piecemeal throughout all things, as though he occupied a smaller part in a smaller place and a larger part in a larger place. Rather, he is wholly present everywhere.

Thus he is not absent even from the minds of the ungodly, although they do not see him—just as this light, when presented to the eyes of the blind, is not seen by them. He therefore shines even in such darknesses as the Apostle signifies when he says, “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5:8); but such darknesses did not comprehend it.

### 7.

He therefore assumed man, whom human beings could see, so that, healed through faith, they might later see what at that time they could not see.

But lest Christ the man, precisely because he appeared visibly, should not be believed to be God as well, and lest he should be credited with no more than the excellence of a man endowed with extraordinary grace and wisdom, a man was sent by God whose name was John.

He came for testimony, to bear witness to the light, so that all might believe through him. He was not the light, but came to bear witness to the light (John 1:6–8).

So great a man had to bear witness to him who was not merely man but also God, so that it might be said of John [Note: So the manuscripts read. The printed editions omit *majori* (“greater”).] the Baptist that among those born of women none had arisen greater than he (Matthew 11:11). Thus the one to whom John bore witness would be understood to be greater than John, because he was not merely man but also God.

John, therefore, was also a light—but a light of the kind concerning which the Lord himself bears witness when he says, “He was a burning and shining lamp” (John 5:35). He also said to his disciples, “You are the light of the world.” And to show what kind of light he meant, he immediately added, “No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house. Let your light so shine before men” (Matthew 5:14–16).

These comparisons were given so that, insofar as we can, we may understand—or, if we cannot yet do so, believe without any doubt—that a rational soul is not God’s nature. For God’s nature is immutable. Yet the soul can be illuminated by participating in it. Lamps need to be lit, and they can be extinguished.

Therefore, when it is said of John, “He was not the light,” this refers to that light which is not illuminated by participation, but by whose participation those whom it illuminates are themselves illuminated.

### 8.

Finally, the text continues: “He was the true light” (John 1:9). And as though we were asking how the true light could be distinguished from an illuminated light—that is, Christ from John—it says, “He was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into this world.”

If every man, then John also. And to show still more clearly, by a far greater distinction, the divinity of this one, it says: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him.”

It is not the world that was made through him that did not know him—for it has no power to know him except rational creation, although this visible world too, namely heaven and earth, was made through him. Rather, by reproving the world that did not know him, he signified unbelievers established in the world.

### 9.

Then it adds: “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him.” This may mean that even the unbelievers, insofar as they are human beings, belong to him through whom they were created. Or he may have wished the Jews to be understood as his own in a special sense, since he assumed the nature of flesh from them. Yet not all of them failed to receive him.

For the text continues: “But to all who received him he gave the power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name, who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (John 1:9–13).

This is the grace of the New Testament, which lay hidden in the Old Testament, yet did not cease to be foretold and proclaimed through shadowing figures, so that the soul might recognize its God and be reborn through his grace.

This birth is spiritual. Therefore it is not from bloods, nor from the will of man, nor from the will of the flesh, but from God.

## CHAPTER FOUR

### 10.

This is also called adoption. Before we were children of God, we were something; and we received the benefit of becoming what we were not. So too, when someone is adopted, before he is adopted he is not yet a son of the one who adopts him, yet he already exists as the one to be adopted.

This generation of grace is distinguished from that Son who, although he was the Son of God, came to become the son of man and to grant to us, who were sons of men, the power to become sons of God.

He became what he was not, yet he was something else; and that very something was the Word of God, through whom all things were made, and the true light that enlightens every man coming into this world, and God with God.

We too, through his grace, have become what we were not—that is, sons of God. Yet we were something, and that something was much lower: sons of men.

He therefore descended so that we might ascend. Remaining in his own nature, he became a participant in our nature, so that, while remaining in our nature, we might become participants in his nature.

Yet not in the same way: participation in our nature did not make him worse, whereas participation in his nature makes us better.

### 11.

Therefore God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the Law (Galatians 4:4). He received the sacraments of the Law in order to redeem those who were under the Law—that is, those whom the Law held guilty through the letter that kills, because the commandment was not fulfilled before the Spirit gave life.

For “the love of God, which fulfills the commandment, has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5).

Accordingly, after saying, “In order to redeem those who were under the Law,” he immediately added, “So that we might receive adoption as sons” (ibid. 5). In this way he distinguished the grace of this benefit from the nature of that Son who was sent as Son—not made so through adoption, but eternally begotten as Son—in order that, having shared in the nature of the sons of men, he might adopt the sons of men so that they too might share in his nature.

Therefore, after saying, “He gave them the power to become children of God,” and adding the manner in which this was to occur, lest a fleshly birth be understood—namely, that he granted this to those who believe in his name and are spiritually reborn by grace, “not of bloods, nor of the will of man, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God”—he immediately commended, as it were, the sacrament of this exchange [Note: So the printed editions read. The Corbie manuscript and others of good quality have *necessitudinis* (“relationship” or “connection”) instead of *vicissitudinis* (“exchange”).]

For, as though we were astonished at so great a good and did not dare to hope for it, he immediately added: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14)—one of the five matters you wished me to explain—as though he were saying:

“O human beings, do not despair of being able to become children of God, because the Son of God himself, that is, the Word of God, became flesh and dwelt among us. Return the exchange: become spirit and dwell in him who became flesh and dwelt among you.

For we must no longer despair that human beings can become children of God through participation in the Word, when the Son of God became the son of man through participation in flesh.”

### 12.

We, therefore, having been changed for the better, become participants in the Word. The Word, however, immutable, underwent no change for the worse when he became a participant in flesh through the mediation of a rational soul.

For Christ the man did not, as the heretics called Apollinarists thought, lack a soul or lack a rational soul. Rather, Scripture, according to its customary manner, used “flesh” for “man,” in order to display Christ’s humility more fully, lest he should seem to have shrunk from the term “flesh” as though it were something unworthy.

For when it is written, “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Isaiah 52:10), souls are not thereby to be excluded from the meaning.

Accordingly, “The Word became flesh” means nothing other than if it were said, “The Son of God became the son of man.”

Although he was in the form of God, as the Apostle says, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized—for it was not an act of usurpation, which could be called seizure, but belonged to his nature that he should be equal—yet “he emptied himself,” not by losing the form of God, but by taking the form of a servant. “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:6–8).

You see how he commends the same one as both man and God [Note: The excellent Corbie manuscript reads: “He commends the same one as man and God, so that…”], so that there might be one person [Note: The printed editions add after *una sit*: “and also profess him to be the son of man.” These words are absent from the manuscripts.] and not a quaternity rather than a Trinity.

For just as the number of persons is not increased when flesh is added to a soul so that there is one man, so the number of persons is not increased when man is joined to the Word so that there is one Christ.

Thus it is written, “The Word became flesh,” so that we may understand the singularity of this person, not suppose that divinity was changed into flesh.

## CHAPTER FIVE

### 13.

Christ the man, therefore, who is also Christ God, was to reveal through himself the grace of the New Testament, which pertains not to temporal life but to eternal life. He was certainly not to be commended by earthly happiness.

Hence submission, hence suffering, hence scourges, spittle, insults, the cross, wounds, and death itself, as though conquered and subdued—all so that his faithful might learn what kind of reward of devotion they ought to seek and hope for from the one whose children they had become.

They were not to serve God for this great purpose: to seek earthly happiness as the reward of serving him, casting aside and trampling upon their faith by judging it a worthless payment.

For this reason almighty God, in his most beneficent providence, granted earthly happiness even to the ungodly, so that the good would not seek it as something of great worth.

This is why the seventy-second Psalm introduces a repentant man who had once served God with a disordered heart for the sake of this reward. When he saw the ungodly enjoying and excelling in it, he was disturbed and began to think that God did not care about human affairs.

When the authority of the saints who belong to God recalled him from this thought, he undertook and devoted himself to recognizing so great a secret—a secret that was not disclosed to him in his distress until he entered the sanctuary of God and understood the final destiny [Note: The printed editions have “in the final thing”; the manuscripts have “in the final things.”]. That is, once he had received the Holy Spirit, he learned to desire better things and looked ahead to the punishment that would come upon the ungodly, even those who had flourished temporarily with a certain hay-like happiness.

Read this seventy-second Psalm, which was expounded through our ministry on the night when the feast of the blessed Cyprian was dawning, and consider it carefully.

### 14.

Therefore Christ the man, who is also God, through whose most merciful humanity and in whose servant-form we ought to learn what should be despised in this life and what should be hoped for in the next, took upon himself, in the very passion in which his enemies seemed to themselves to be great and victorious, the voice of our weakness.

In this voice our old man too was being crucified [Note: Am., Bad., and Er. read: “in the very passion in which our old man was crucified by his enemies.”], so that the body of sin might be destroyed (Romans 6:6). And he said:

“My God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?” (Psalm 21:2).

This is one of the five questions you proposed. Thus begins the twenty-first Psalm, which was sung in prophecy long beforehand concerning his passion and the revelation of the grace he brought for making believers and delivering them.

## CHAPTER SIX

### 15.

I shall therefore proceed through this same Psalm, whose prophecy the Lord showed to pertain to himself when, hanging on the wood, he cried out its first verse, explaining and traversing it by recalling each part. From this you will understand how the grace of the New Testament was not silent even at the time when it was veiled in the Old Testament.

The Psalm is spoken in the person of Christ insofar as he bears the form of a servant, in which our weakness was carried. Isaiah also said of him: “He bears our weaknesses, and for us he is in anguish” (Isaiah 53:4).

From the voice, therefore, of this weakness—concerning which Paul, when his request was not heard and he was therefore in a certain sense forsaken, nevertheless heard from the Lord, “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9)—from the voice, then, of this weakness of ours, which our Head transformed into himself, the Psalm says:

“My God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?”

The one who prays is forsaken precisely in that his prayer is not heard. Jesus transformed this voice into himself: the voice of his body, that is, of his Church, which was to be reformed from the old man into the new; the voice of his human weakness, to which the goods of the Old Testament had to be denied so that it might now learn to desire and hope for the goods of the New Testament.

### 16.

Among those goods of the Old Testament belonging to the old man, what is chiefly desired is the prolongation of this present life, so that it may be held a little longer, since it cannot be held forever.

Therefore everyone knows that the day of death will come, yet everyone—or almost everyone—tries to delay it, even those who believe that after death they will live more happily. So powerful is the sweetness of the union of flesh and soul.

For no one has ever hated his own flesh (Ephesians 5:29). Therefore the soul does not wish even temporarily to depart from the weakness of the flesh, although it trusts that at the end it will receive the flesh again forever without weakness.

Thus, while serving the law of God with the mind but dragging along the desires of sin with the flesh (Romans 7:25)—desires which the Apostle forbids it to obey—the devout person desires, by the reasoning of the mind, to be dissolved and to be with Christ (Philippians 1:23). Yet by the sensation of the flesh he refuses and recoils from this. If it were possible, he would not wish to be stripped off, but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal might be swallowed up by life (2 Corinthians 5:4)—that is, so that the body itself might be transferred from weakness to immortality without passing through death.

### 17.

But these words, by which human life and the lengthening of this present existence are desired, are words of sins [Col. 0545], and they are far from that salvation of which we do not yet possess the reality but already possess the hope. Of this salvation it is written, “For by hope we were saved; but hope that is seen is not hope” (Romans 8:24).

Therefore, in this Psalm too, after saying, “My God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?” he immediately adds, “The words of my sins are far from my salvation.”

That is: these are the words of my sins, and they are far from that salvation which the grace not of the Old but of the New Testament promises me.

The passage can also be punctuated in this way: “My God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me, far from my salvation?”—as though he were saying: “By forsaking me, that is, by not hearing me, you have become far from my salvation,” namely, from the present salvation of this life.

Then the meaning of “the words of my sins” would be: these things I have said are the words of my sins, because they are the words of fleshly desires.

### 18.

Christ says these things in the person of his body, which is the Church. He says them in the person of the weakness of sinful flesh, which he transformed into the likeness of sinful flesh that he assumed from the Virgin.

The Bridegroom speaks in the person of the bride, because in a certain way he united her to himself. In Isaiah too, where he says, “He bound a turban around me like a bridegroom, and adorned me with an ornament like a bride” (Isaiah 61:10), “he bound around me” and “he adorned me” seem to be the voice of one person; yet we understand Christ and the Church as bridegroom and bride.

“But the two shall become one flesh; this is a great mystery,” the Apostle says, “in Christ and in the Church” (Ephesians 5:31–32). Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh (Matthew 19:6).

If they are one flesh, then surely one voice is also fitting.

What are you seeking here, human weakness, the voice of the Word through whom all things were made? Listen instead to the voice of the flesh that was made among all things, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

Listen instead to the voice of the medicine by which you are healed so that you may see God—the God whose vision he postponed for you, while he brought you a man to see, offered him to be killed, presented him to be imitated, and transferred him to be believed, so that through this faith the eye of the mind might be healed for seeing God.

Why, then, do we disdain to hear the voice of the body from the mouth of the Head? The Church was suffering in him when he suffered for the Church; and likewise he himself was suffering in the Church when the Church suffered for him.

For just as we heard the voice of the Church suffering in Christ—“God, my God, look upon me,” and so forth—so we also heard the voice of Christ suffering in the Church: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4).

## CHAPTER SEVEN
### 19

Therefore, when we are not heard in our prayers that temporal goods be retained or acquired, then, when we entreat God for these things, he abandons us precisely by not hearing us; but he does not abandon us with regard to better things, which he wishes us to understand, prefer, and desire. Hence the Psalm continues and says: “I cried to you by day, and you will not hear” (Ps. 21:3); and by night—the same words, “you will not hear,” are understood here as well. But see what he adds: “and not to my foolishness.” This, then, is what he says: “You will indeed not hear me when I cry by day,” that is, amid prosperous circumstances, so that I may not lose them; “and by night,” that is, amid adversity, so that the prosperity I have lost may return. “But you will do this not to my foolishness; rather, you will do it so that I may understand what, through the grace of the New Testament, I ought now to expect from you, desire, and ask for.”

For I cry that temporal goods may not be taken away from me; but “you dwell in the holy place, the praise of Israel” (ibid. 4). I do not want you to abandon my desire by which I seek carnal happiness. Yet this desire is in the filth of the old condition, whereas you seek the purity of newness. By not hearing this desire, you do not abandon me, because you seek the love in which you may dwell; “but the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). Therefore, “you dwell in the holy place, the praise of Israel”: the praise of those who see you, because they are not praised in themselves but in you. “For what do they have that they did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4:7), so that “the one who boasts may boast in the Lord” (ibid. 1:31).

### 20

This is the grace of the New Testament. For in the Old Testament, when you taught that even earthly and temporal happiness ought to be sought and hoped for from you alone, it was said: “In you our fathers hoped; they hoped, and you delivered them. To you they cried, and they were saved; in you they hoped, and they were not put to shame” (Ps. 21:5–6). For those fathers, living amid their enemies, you filled with riches, rescued from their foes, enabled to win glorious victories, and delivered from various deaths. For one of them you substituted a ram so that he might not be struck (Gen. 22:13). You healed another of his corruption and restored to him double what he had lost (Job 42:10). You preserved another unharmed and uninjured among hungry lions (Dan. 14:30–40). You were praised by the pleasing voice of others walking amid flames (ibid. 3:23–90).

The Jews expected something of this kind to happen to Christ, so that they might test whether he was truly the Son of God. In their person, the Book of Wisdom says: “Let us condemn him to a most shameful death, for there will be regard for his words. For if he is the true Son of God, he will receive him and deliver him from the hands of his adversaries.” [Editorial note: Col. 0546. Editions: “for if he is truly of God”; all manuscripts: “true.”] Then it says: “Thus they thought, and they went astray, for their wickedness blinded them” (Wis. 2:18–21).

For they were attentive to the time of the Old Testament and to the temporal happiness of those fathers, in which God showed them, by granting such gifts, that these too were his gifts. They did not see that the time had now come for it to be revealed that, in Christ, God was properly granting eternal goods to the righteous—he who grants temporal goods even to the wicked.

### Chapter VIII

### 21

Finally, after saying, “In you our fathers hoped; they hoped, and you delivered them. To you they cried, and they were saved; in you they hoped, and they were not put to shame,” see what he added: “But I am a worm and not a man.”

This seems to have been said simply to commend humility, so that he might show himself, in the eyes of his persecutors, to be something utterly lowly and contemptible. But we must not disregard the height and depth of the mystery, especially in words that are applied, through prophetic proclamation, to so great a Savior.

Our predecessors offered a most elegant interpretation of this expression [Orig. Hom. 15 on Luke; Ambrose, on this Psalm]: that he wished Christ to be foretold under this name because a worm is born from flesh without sexual intercourse, just as he was born from a virgin.

But in his book Job, when speaking of heavenly creatures—that even they are scarcely clean in God’s sight—he says: “How much more is man corruption, and the son of man a worm!” (Job 25:5–6). He used “corruption” for mortality, which already bears within itself, as it were, the conceived necessity of dying, into which man was driven by sin; and he called the son of man a worm born from corruption, that is, a mortal born from mortality.

Accordingly, through these words of the Psalm he admonished us to seek another meaning, while preserving and not rejecting that earlier one: so that we should examine not only what he says, “I am a worm,” but also what he adds, “and not a man.” This accords with what I recalled from the Book of Job, as though he were saying: “But I am the son of man, and not man”—not because Christ is not man, of whom the Apostle says, “There is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2:5). For every son of man is a man; but this meaning looks toward one who was man in such a way that he was not the son of man, that is, of Adam.

Perhaps, then, it was said in this way: “But I am a worm, and not a man,” that is, “I am the son of man, and not man.” It would be as though he were saying: “I am Christ, in whom all are made alive—not Adam, in whom all die” (1 Cor. 15:22).

### 22

Accordingly, human beings, learn through the grace of the New Testament to desire eternal life. Why do you wish so greatly to be delivered by the Lord from death in the same way as your fathers were delivered, when God was teaching that, apart from himself, there was no other giver even of earthly happiness?

That happiness belongs to the old man; and that old condition began with Adam: “But I am a worm, and not a man”—Christ, not Adam. From the old man you were old; from the new, be new. From Adam, be men; from Christ, be sons of men.

For it is not without reason that the Lord, in the Gospel, most familiarly calls himself “the son of man” (Matt. 17:9, 12), rather than “man.” Nor is it without reason that he says in another Psalm: “You will save men and beasts, Lord; how abundant is your mercy, O God” (Ps. 35:7–10). For from you comes even this salvation that is common to men and beasts.

But new men have another salvation of their own, one that separates them from the fellowship of beasts and belongs to the New Testament [Corbie Manuscript: “Sacrament”]. They certainly have it, for the Psalm continues there: “But the sons of men will hope under the shelter of your wings. They will be intoxicated with the abundance of your house, and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delight. For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Ps. 35:7–10).

He said afterward, “the sons of men,” as though distinguishing the sons of men from men. In that happiness of salvation which is common to men and beasts, he wished to call them by the name that would show them to belong to that first man with whom the old condition and death began—who was man in such a way that he was not the son of man.

But to those later ones who hope for another happiness, the ineffable delight of the fountain of life, and the light of eternal light, he gave the name by which their Lord wished to be called most familiarly, when such grace was revealed to them. Thus he called them sons of men rather than men.

### 23

You must not, however, suppose that a rule of expression has been established which must be observed by an unchanging law, so that wherever you read “men” or “sons of men,” you always understand the terms according to this distinction. Rather, consider the surrounding context: from it the meaning is drawn when it is clear and extracted when it is hidden.

As in this passage of the Psalm, who would not be struck by the intention of the distinction? The one who had said, “In you our fathers hoped, and you delivered them. To you they cried, and they were saved; in you they hoped, and they were not put to shame,” adds, “But I.” He does not say, “And I,” but “But I.”

What, then, is this one who distinguishes himself in this way? “But I am a worm,” he says, “and not a man”—as though he were commending to those whom you heard and delivered that happiness which belonged to the Old Testament and was to be granted to the old man, who began with Adam. “But I am a worm,” that is, the son of man, not man, like that man who was not the son of man.

### Chapter IX

### 24

Accordingly, the words that follow are also: “The reproach of men and the outcast of the people. All who saw me mocked me, spoke with their lips, and shook their heads. He hoped in God; let him deliver him, let him save him, since he desires him.”

They said this with their lips, not in their hearts, taunting him because it was not happening, not believing that it would happen. Yet this too happened—but it had to happen in the Son of Man, in whom the hope of eternal life belonging to the New Testament was to be revealed, not as they expected. Because they did not see it happening, they mocked him as though he had been overcome, belonging as they did to the Old Testament and to the man in whom all die, not to the Son of Man in whom all will be made alive.

Man brought death upon himself and upon the son of man; but the Son of Man, by dying and rising again, brought life to man—“the reproach of men and the outcast of the people”—even unto death. [Editorial note: Col. 0548. Editions: “For this even unto death”; manuscripts: “even unto death. For this,” etc.] For this he wished to suffer in the sight of his enemies, so that they might think him abandoned and so that the grace of the New Testament might be commended. Through this grace we learn to seek another happiness, which is now present in faith but afterward will be present in sight.

“For as long as we are in the body,” the Apostle says, “we are away from the Lord; for we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Cor. 5:6–7). Therefore it is now in hope, but then in reality.

### 25

Finally, he did not wish to reveal his resurrection—which, unlike ours, was not to be delayed for a long time, so that in the example of his flesh we might learn what we ought to hope for in our own—to strangers, but to his own. I call them “strangers” not by nature but by vice, which is always contrary to nature.

He died, therefore, in the sight of men, but rose again in the sight of the sons of men: death belonged to man, but resurrection to the Son of Man. “For as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ.”

Thus, to exhort his faithful by the example of his flesh to despise temporal happiness for the sake of eternal happiness, he endured his persecutors’ violence and savagery even unto death, while they arrogantly mocked him as though he had been conquered and crushed.

But when he raised his flesh from the dead, restored it to the sight and touch of his disciples, and ascended into heaven before their eyes, he strengthened them and demonstrated with the clearest truth what they ought to expect and proclaim.

Those from whom he had endured such evils even unto death, however, he left in the opinion that they gloried in having overcome and destroyed him. Anyone among them who wished to be saved with eternal salvation would have to believe the resurrection of that dead man, as those who had seen it proclaimed with supporting signs—and for the sake of that proclamation did not hesitate to endure similar sufferings.

### Chapter X

### 26

For this reason James, one of his Apostles, also wrote in his Epistle to the faithful who, after Christ’s passion and resurrection, were still held in this life. Distinguishing the dispensation of the Old Testament from that of the New, he says: “You have heard of Job’s endurance, and you have seen the Lord’s end” (James 5:11).

He does not say this so that they might patiently endure temporal evils in order that what we read was restored to Job might likewise be restored to them (Job 42:10). For Job was healed from that wound and corruption, and everything he had lost was restored to him twofold. There too the faith of the resurrection was commended. His sons were not doubled but restored in equal number, signifying that those whom he had lost would rise again; thus, joined to the earlier sons, they too would not be found excluded from the restoration of the double portion.

Therefore, so that we would not hope for such a reward when suffering temporal evils, James did not say, “You have heard of Job’s endurance and end,” but, “You have heard of Job’s endurance, and you have seen the Lord’s end.” It was as though he were saying: “Endure temporal evils as Job did; but for this endurance do not hope for temporal goods, which returned to him increased. Hope rather for eternal goods, which went before in the Lord.”

Job, then, belonged to those fathers who cried out and were saved. For when Christ says, “But I,” he sufficiently indicates what sort of salvation he wishes them understood to have received—the salvation in which he himself was abandoned. This does not mean that they were excluded from eternal salvation; rather, what was to be revealed in Christ was then hidden.

For in the Old Testament there is a veil that will be removed when each person passes from it to Christ. When Christ was crucified, the veil of the Temple was also torn (Matt. 27:51), signifying what the Apostle said about the veil of the Old Testament: “It is abolished in Christ” (2 Cor. 3:14).

### 27

Among those fathers, too, although exceedingly rare, there were examples of endurance even unto death, from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah (Luke 11:51). The Lord Jesus says that their blood will also be required of those who persisted in the wickedness of their fathers, by whom those men were killed.

Nor in the New Testament has there been, or is there lacking, a multitude of faithful and good people who even surpass others in temporal happiness and experience in it the goodness and mercy of God, the giver of all things. Yet they hold fast to what the Apostle, the steward of the New Testament, commanded the rich of this age: “not to be haughty, nor to place their hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who gives us all things abundantly for enjoyment; to do good, to be rich in good works, to be generous in giving, to share, storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of the true life” (1 Tim. 6:17–19).

This true life was manifested in Christ not only in spirit but also in flesh, when he rose from the dead. It was not the kind of life the Jews destroyed in him when God did not rescue him from their hands and seemed to have abandoned him as he cried, “My God, my God, why have you abandoned me?”

He did this in order to transfigure in himself his martyrs, who, even if they did not wish to die—of which he also said to Peter, “Another will gird you and carry you where you do not wish,” signifying by what death he would glorify God (John 21:18)—might appear for a time to have been abandoned by their God, when he refused to grant them what they wanted. They would then utter that voice of the heart and show that devout affection which the Lord himself expressed with his own mouth when his passion was imminent, repeatedly transfiguring them in himself: “Nevertheless, not what I will, but what you will, Father” (Matt. 26:39).

### Chapter XI

### 28

For in whom should this first have appeared, if not in our very Head, on account of the life for which we are Christians? [Edd.: “on account of the reason for which Christians are”; all manuscripts: “on account of the life.”]

For this reason he did not say, “My God, my God, you have abandoned me,” but indicated that a reason was to be sought when he added, “Why have you abandoned me?” That is: Why? For what purpose? For what reason?

There certainly was a reason—and not a small one—for rescuing Noah from the flood, Lot from the heavenly fire, Isaac from the imminent sword, Joseph from the woman’s accusation and the prison, Moses from the Egyptians, Rahab from the destruction of the city, Susanna from false witnesses, Daniel from the lions, the three men from the fires, and the other fathers who cried out and were saved; yet Christ was not rescued from the hands of the Jews, but was abandoned to the power of those raging against him until death’s end.

Why was this? For what reason, unless on account of what he says a little later in the same Psalm: “not to my foolishness”—that is, to my body, my Church, my least ones? For in the Gospel also he says, “Whatever you did for one of my least ones, you did for me” (Matt. 25:40).

Thus “not to my foolishness” was said in the same way as “you did it for me”; and “Why have you abandoned me?” was said in the same way as “Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever rejects you rejects me” (Luke 10:16).

Therefore, it is not for our foolishness, but so that we may become wise. It is not on account of this life, in which God sometimes abandons us to the hands of our persecutors even unto death, but on account of that eternal life that we ought to be Christians. For we see that this preceded in him, from whose name we are so called.

### 29

Behold, this is what happened. Yet so many people wish to be Christians for no other reason than to enjoy the happiness of this life; and therefore, when that happiness fails, they fail as well.

What if such a striking example had not been established in our very Head, teaching us to despise earthly things for the sake of heavenly things, “not looking at what is seen but at what is not seen”? For “what is seen is temporal, but what is not seen is eternal” (2 Cor. 4:18).

He deigned to transfigure us in himself through those words. For as far as he himself is concerned, how could he have wished to be delivered from that hour when he had come for that very hour (John 12:27)? Or how could he have spoken as though something he did not want were happening to him, when he had the power to lay down his life and to take it up again, and no one could take it from him, but he himself laid it down and took it up again, as he says in the Gospel (ibid. 10:18)?

Without doubt, we were present in those words, and the Head was speaking on behalf of his body—not with a division of meaning in the voice, where the connection of unity is not divided.

### Chapter XII

### 30

Finally, the Psalm continues. Notice what he says while praying: “For you drew me out of the womb; my hope from my mother’s breasts. Upon you I was cast from the womb; from my mother’s womb you have been my God” (Ps. 21:10–11).

It is as though he were saying: “You transferred me from one condition to another, from one thing to another, so that you might be my good in place of the temporal goods of this mortality, which I received in my mother’s womb and whose breasts I suckled. This is the old condition from which you drew me; and those are the goods of carnal birth, from which you are my hope. From there I turned to you.

“And from the womb”—that is, “I who began in these things in the womb was cast upon you”: passing to you, I committed my whole self to you. Therefore, ‘from my mother’s womb’—that is, from the goods of the flesh that I took on in my mother’s womb—‘you have been my God,’ so that you might be my good in place of these things.”

This expression is like saying, for example, “From earth I inhabit heaven,” meaning, “From here I have moved there.” This is our transfiguration into him: through the grace of the New Testament we change our life, passing from the old to the new.

He signified this reality through the sacrament of his passion and resurrection when he changed his flesh from mortality to immortality. But he did not change his life from oldness to newness, since he was never in impiety, from which he would have had to pass into piety.

### 31

Nevertheless, some have understood the words “From my mother’s womb you have been my God” as referring to our very Head, because the Father is his God insofar as he is man in the form of a servant, but not insofar as he is equal to him in the form of God [Ambrose, *On the Faith*, book 1, chapter 6]. Thus, “From my mother’s womb you have been my God” would mean: “From the time I became man, you have been my God.”

But what does “You drew me out of the womb” mean if it refers to Jesus, born from the Virgin? Does God not draw out others as well, since the whole order of birth is within his providence? Or did he wish to signify the Virgin’s childbirth, miraculously preserving the integrity of her virginity, when he said, “You drew me out of the womb,” so that what happened there miraculously, when it is said to have been done by God, might seem incredible to no one?

What, then, is meant by “My hope from my mother’s breasts”? How can this too refer to the Head of the Church, as though his hope, which is in God, began for him at his mother’s breasts and not earlier in the womb?

For no other hope is to be understood here than that by which God was destined to exalt him from the dead. All of this is said according to the fact that he became man.

Or perhaps, because women’s breasts are brought from conception itself to fullness, he wished “from the breasts” to be understood in this way, as though he were saying: “From the time I assumed flesh, to which immortality was to be hoped for.” Thus he did not have hope earlier, when he was in the form of God, in which there was nothing that needed to be changed for the better; but he had hope “from his mother’s breasts,” that is, from the very assumption of flesh, which was conceived in hope, and whose hoped-for reality would come when it passed from death to immortality.

### 32

But how can the statement “Upon you I was cast from the womb” be applied to the Head? Surely, while he was in the womb, he was also in God, “in whom we live and move and have our being” (Acts 17:28). Or did his rational soul begin to hope in God only when, from the womb, the flesh proceeded?

Unless perhaps one must believe that a rational soul came to him after he had been born, although it had still been lacking while he was within his mother’s womb. And since that same soul, added to the flesh after birth, clung to God, perhaps one should therefore understand the words according to that same flesh: “Upon you I was cast from the womb,” as though he were saying, “From the womb I received a soul that would cling to you.”

But who would dare rashly throw himself into this opinion, when the question of the soul’s arrival or origin lies so deeply hidden in nature that it is better to continue seeking it for as long as we remain in this life than to presume that we have found it?

How these words can be understood through our transfiguration into him has been stated. If anything more suitable has been, or can be, said, we do not prejudice anyone’s judgment, nor do we begrudge anyone’s learning.

### Chapter XIII

### 33

Now consider how what follows illuminates the meaning of “Why have you abandoned me”: “Do not depart from me, for tribulation is near.”

How did he abandon the one to whom it is said, “Do not depart from me,” unless he abandoned the temporal happiness of the old life? Yet he is asked not to depart from or abandon the hope of eternal life.

But what does “for tribulation is near” mean? It sounds as though his passion were still imminent, even though he is understood to have said these things in the very midst of his passion, which the Psalm prophetically foretold concerning him.

For here he is also going to say what is written most explicitly in the Gospel: “They divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots” (Matt. 27:35). This happened when he was already hanging on the cross.

What, then, does “Tribulation is near” mean, when he was speaking in the midst of it? Surely it means that when the flesh is in pain and suffering, the soul then undergoes a great struggle of endurance. One must labor and pray so that the soul may not fail.

Nothing is closer to the soul than its flesh. Therefore, when any great and perfect despiser of this world suffers elsewhere, he suffers nothing. He can employ vigilant reason when he loses external goods, since these are undoubtedly far from the mind of the wise person who is not attached to them by desire. He does not care about what he suffers, because he does not suffer it inwardly.

But when he loses the principal goods of the body, namely, the body’s life and health, then tribulation is near the goods of the soul, over which the soul itself presides within as the body’s master. What can reason do to prevent him from feeling pain when the body is wounded or burned, since he is so closely joined to it that he can suffer but cannot fail to feel?

### 34

For this reason the devil, following this order of harming, first received power over the external goods of that great man whom he had requested to test. When those goods had been taken away and destroyed, and he saw Job remaining unshaken—for he had said, “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21)—he also asked that his flesh be tormented with a wound.

He engaged Job in such a struggle because he was attacking the nearer goods, that is, the goods of the body. If Job, after losing these, should perhaps succumb and incline his heart toward impiety, the goods of the soul would also perish; and the tempter, already raging against the body, was pressing more closely toward their destruction.

Finally, although that man speaks many things prophetically in the midst of such temptation, when the tribulation near to the goods of the soul had arrived he nevertheless speaks quite differently from the time when those external goods had perished (ibid. 1:11)—in which he had not lost his children but had sent them ahead.

### 35

The soul of the martyr, therefore, transfigured into Christ, cries out when it has begun to suffer in the flesh and says to God—by whom it has been abandoned with respect to earthly happiness, but who remains with it in the hope of eternal life:

“Do not depart from me, for tribulation is near. It is not in my field, nor in my gold, nor in my livestock, nor in my houses and walls; it is not in the bereavement of my loved ones. It is in my flesh, to which I am joined and bound, whose sensation I cannot lack. From nearby it presses upon me, so that I may fail in the virtue of endurance.

“Do not depart from me, for there is no one to help: neither friend, nor relative, nor human praise, nor the memory of former pleasure, nor anything by which the collapse of earthly happiness is supported, nor even the human virtue that is in my soul. For if you abandon me, what virtue does man have?”

### Chapter XIV

> For what is man except that you remember him?

### 36

“Many young bulls surrounded me”—that is, the lesser people among the populace. “Fat bulls besieged me”—that is, the proud and the rich, the leaders of the people.

“They opened their mouth against me,” crying, “Crucify him, crucify him!” (Luke 23:21).

“Like a lion ravening and roaring”: they seized him after he had been arrested and brought him before the governor, and they roared as they demanded his death.

“I have been poured out like water,” as though my persecutors might slip and fall upon me.

“All my bones have been scattered.” What are bones except the supports of the body? The body of Christ is the Church; and who are the supports of the Church except the Apostles, who elsewhere are also called pillars? They were certainly scattered when he himself was led to his passion, or when he had suffered and died.

“My heart has become like melting wax in the midst of my belly.” It is difficult to discover how this can be applied to our Head, the Savior of his own body. For a human heart does not melt like wax except under great fear. How could this have happened in him, who had the power to lay down his life and take it up again?

Yet surely he transferred into himself the condition of his weaker members: either of those who tremble before the fear of death, as Peter himself did, who from an outstandingly presumptuous man became a frequent denier; or of those who waste away in salutary grief, as that same Peter did when he wept bitterly.

For grief also dissolves the heart; hence it is said in Greek that it was called λύπη (*lypē*, “grief” or “sorrow”).

Or perhaps he wished us to understand a profound mystery, so that by “his heart” he might signify his Scriptures, in which his counsel was hidden. This was opened when, by suffering, he fulfilled what had been prophesied about him.

His Scriptures, then, were dissolved in those things completed by his coming, birth, passion, resurrection, and glorification. Who can now fail to understand them in the Prophets, when they have reached even the understanding of the carnal multitude?

Perhaps he signified that multitude by “the midst of his belly,” so that in his body, which is the Church, the carnal and weaker multitude might occupy, as it were, the place of the belly.

Or, if “belly” more properly refers to the inner parts, it has been shown that the understanding of the Scriptures belongs rather to those who are more perfect: his heart—that is, his Scriptures, which contain his counsel—melts like wax in their midst, that is, in their thoughts. This means that, through the fervor of the Spirit, they are opened, discussed, and expounded.

### Chapter XV

### 37

“My strength has dried up like a potsherd.” A potsherd is hardened by fire; so too the strength of Christ’s body is not consumed by fire like hay, but is hardened by his passion as by fire, like a potsherd.

“For the furnace tests the potter’s vessels,” as Scripture says elsewhere, “and trial tests righteous people” (Sir. 27:6).

“And my tongue has cleaved to my jaws.” This can certainly be understood as signifying his silence, which another prophet also commends when he says, “Like a lamb before its shearer, he was without a voice” (Isa. 53:7).

But if we understand his tongue as those members of his body, which is the Church, through whom he speaks his Gospel, then they cleave to his jaws when they do not depart from his commandments.

### 38

But how can what follows—“And you have brought me down into the dust of death”—be applied to the Head, since his body, which rose on the third day, was certainly not dissolved into dust?

Nor did the Apostles interpret the statement made in another Psalm—“You will not allow your holy one to see corruption”—in any other way than that his flesh did not become corrupt, since he rose so quickly (Ps. 15:10; Acts 2:24–32).

Thus, in another Psalm, he says: “What profit is there in my blood, when I descend into corruption? Will the dust give thanks to you, or proclaim your truth?” (Ps. 29:10). He says this because, if he had been left to dissolve into dust in the same way as others, and his flesh had been reserved for the final resurrection, there would have been no profit in his blood. His death would have benefited no one, and the truth of God would not have been proclaimed—the truth that had foretold that he would rise immediately.

What, then, does he mean here by saying, “And you have brought me down into the dust of death”?

Perhaps we should understand his body to be the Church, in which those who have suffered or suffer for his name do not rise as quickly as he did, but are brought down into the dust of death. They will rise when that time comes of which he says in the Gospel: “The hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come forth” (John 5:28–29).

Or perhaps, figuratively, he wished the Jews themselves to be understood as “the dust of death,” into whose hands he was brought. For it is written: “Not so the wicked, not so; but they are like dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth” (Ps. 1:4).

### Chapter XVI

### 39

Finally, the Psalm continues: “For many dogs surrounded me; the assembly of the wicked besieged me.” It is as though he had called those into whose hands he was brought “the dust of death,” and then called them “many dogs” and “the assembly of the wicked.”

He called them dogs because dogs often bark against those with whom they have no familiarity, whether those persons are good or evil. Their nature is such that they do not bark at those with whom they are accustomed to associate, whether good or bad; but when they see unfamiliar persons, they become provoked even against the innocent.

In the words that follow, the Gospel is recited, as it were. His crucifixion is expressed when he says: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they numbered all my bones. But they watched and looked upon me.” For his hands and feet were pierced with nails, and when he was stretched out upon the wood, his bones were in some sense numbered. Moreover, they watched and looked to see what would happen to him, and whether Elijah would come and deliver him (Matt. 27:49).

What follows needs no exposition: “They divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots.” The words then appended are those of one praying, both in the person of the Head—that is, the man who is Mediator—and in the person of the body, which is the Church and which he also calls his only one. “But you, Lord,” he says, “do not put your help far from me”: this pertains to his flesh, whose resurrection was not delayed for a long time as that of others is. “Look to my defense,” so that the enemies who imagine that they have accomplished something by killing mortal flesh may do no harm. Yet they do no harm if, through the defending grace of God, the conquered soul does not consent to them for evil; for thus it was prophesied elsewhere: “The earth has been delivered into the hand of the wicked,” that is, earthly flesh.

“Deliver my soul from the sword.” A *framea* is a sword. Christ was certainly not killed by such an iron weapon but by the cross, nor did they strike his side with a sword but with a lance. Thus, using the word figuratively, he called the tongue of his persecutors a sword, as another Psalm says: “Their tongue is a sharp sword” (Ps. 56:5). Therefore, because the tongue of evildoers prevailed against his flesh, he prays that it may do no harm to his soul when he says, “Deliver my soul from the sword.” If you refer this prayer in prophecy to the Head of the body, it should be seen not as the request of one in need, but rather as a figurative prediction of what was to come.

Or, since his body, that is, his Church, was to endure grievous persecutions, he called *framea* the weapon by which martyrs were chiefly slaughtered. He wishes their souls to be delivered from it, so that they may not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul (Matt. 10:28), and consent to what is unlawful. Or again, in their very sufferings he calls the tongue of their enemies a *framea*, from which he wishes his soul—that is, the soul of his body, the souls of his saints—to be delivered.

What follows—“And my only one from the hand of the dog”—can most fittingly be understood as referring to the one Church. By “dog” he meant the world, barking not by reason but by habit against unfamiliar truth. For it is the nature of dogs not to bark at those with whom they are familiar, whether they are good or bad; but when they see unfamiliar persons, even innocent ones, they are provoked. The hand of the dog signifies the power of the world. He also represented the kingdom of the world, which would be hostile to his body—that is, to his Church—under the name of a lion, when he added: “Save me from the lion’s mouth.”

Hence it is written: “There is no difference between a king’s threats and a lion’s anger” (Prov. 19:12). The Apostle Peter, moreover, compares the devil to a roaring lion, going about and seeking whom he may devour (1 Pet. 5:8).

Showing that the proud of this world would oppose humble Christians, he consequently says: “And from the horns of unicorns, my humility.”

The proud are understood by “unicorns” because pride hates fellowship, and every proud person wishes, as far as he can, to stand out alone.

### Chapter XVII
43. Now consider where the fruit lies: either in the fact that he was forsaken, so that he would not be heard concerning earthly happiness—not in order that we might be foolish, but that we might understand what we ought to desire through the grace of the New Testament—or in the fact that he was not forsaken, but was heard in what he said, “Do not depart from me,” although he had said, “Why have you forsaken me.” These statements are certainly contradictory unless the former is referred to one matter and the latter to another.

Consider and hear how much you understand; draw in as much as you grasp, and as much as I myself am able to express of so great a matter—or rather, as much as he grants who hears us, both in Christ, insofar as he is human and mediator between us and God, and with Christ, insofar as he is God, equal to God and able to do, as the Apostle says, “far more than we ask or understand” (Ephesians 3:20). See in this psalm the grace of the New Testament; see what is accomplished, suggested, commended, and illuminated through the fruit of that forsakenness, tribulation, and prayer.

Observe what we read as prophesied so long beforehand and what we now see fulfilled: “I will declare your name,” he says, “to my brothers; in the midst of the Church I will sing to you.” Those brothers are the ones of whom he says in the Gospel, “Go and tell my brothers” (John 20:17).
