That Church is the one he has just called his only Church: it is the one Catholic Church, spread abundantly throughout the whole world and extending as it grows to the furthest nations. Hence he says in the Gospel, “And this Gospel will be preached throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations; and then the end will come” (Matthew 24:14).

44. When he says, “I will sing,” this is the “new song” of which another psalm says, “Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth” (Psalm 95:1). Here you have both matters: the song with which he says he will sing, and the Church in whose midst he will sing. The former pertains to the new song, the latter to the whole earth.

For it is he himself who sings in us, whose grace enables us to sing, as the Apostle says: “Or do you wish to receive proof that Christ is speaking in me?” (2 Corinthians 13:3). You should understand “in the midst of the Church” as referring to eminence and manifestation, since things are said to be in the midst the more clearly they are known; or, certainly, as referring to the Church’s interior, since the interior is its midst. For not everyone who sounds forth with his lips sings a new song, but the one who sings in the manner urged by the Apostle when he says, “Singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord” (Ephesians 5:19).

This joy is within, where the voice of praise is both sung and heard; by this voice he is praised who is to be loved freely with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole mind, and it kindles his lover within himself through the grace of his Holy Spirit. For what else is the new song than the praise of God?

CHAPTER XVIII

45. Finally, what follows demonstrates this still more clearly. After saying, “I will declare your name to my brothers”—for “no one has ever seen God, but the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared him” (John 1:18)—and adding, “In the midst of the Church I will sing to you,” he immediately made clear how he sang: namely, that he sang in us as we advance in the knowledge of the name he declared to his brothers. And because he sang the praise of God in us, he immediately continued: “You who fear the Lord, praise him.”

But who praises him truthfully except the one who loves him sincerely? It is therefore as though he had said: “You who fear the Lord, love him.” For it was said to humanity, as it is written: “Behold, piety is wisdom” (Job 28:28, according to the Septuagint). Now piety is the worship of God, and he cannot be worshiped except through love. Therefore the highest and true wisdom is contained in that first commandment: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul” (Matthew 22:37). Accordingly, wisdom is the love of God; and it is poured into our hearts only through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Romans 5:5).

“ The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord” (Psalm 110:10); yet fear is not in love, for perfect love casts out fear (1 John 4:18). Thus the fear first introduced into our hearts drives out the habit of evil works and preserves a place for love. When love comes as mistress, so that she may dwell there, fear departs.

46. Therefore, “you who fear the Lord, praise him”: in order that you may worship God not slavishly but freely, learn to love the one whom you fear, and you will be able to praise what you love.

Those who feared God under the Old Testament, because of the terrifying and deadly letter, not yet possessing the life-giving Spirit (2 Corinthians 3:6), ran with sacrifices to the temple. Although these sacrifices were figures of the future blood by which we were redeemed, they sacrificed bloody victims without knowing what was prefigured through them.

Now, however, under the grace of the New Testament: “You who fear the Lord, praise him.” In another psalm, foretelling the changes that would come to those offerings then presented as shadows of the future, he says: “I will not accept calves from your hand, nor goats from your flocks.” Shortly afterward, to show the sacrifice of the New Testament, when those former sacrifices were to cease, he says: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and fulfill your vows to the Most High.” And at the end of the same psalm: “The sacrifice of praise will glorify me; and there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God” (Psalm 49:9, 14, 23).

Christ is the salvation of God. When the old Simeon recognized him in the Spirit and took him into his arms, he said: “Now dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace; for my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:29–30).

CHAPTER XIX

47. “You who fear the Lord, therefore, praise him; all the seed of Jacob, magnify him.” It is not without purpose that he does not merely say “the seed of Jacob,” but adds “all,” lest he be understood to mean only those Israelites who would come to believe.

The seed of Jacob is itself the seed of Abraham. But to all who believe in Christ—not only to the faithful who came from Israel—the Apostle says: “Then you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise” (Galatians 3:29).

There he recalled the prefiguration of the New Testament in what is written: “In Isaac shall your seed be called” (Romans 9:7)—not in Ishmael, the son of the slave woman. Writing to the Galatians about Abraham’s two sons, one a slave and the other free, and about the two women, one a slave and the other free, he says that the two Testaments were prefigured allegorically in them (Galatians 4:22–24). Hence he says: “Not the children of the flesh are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as seed.” For the word of promise is this: “At this time I will come, and Sarah shall have a son” (Romans 9:8; Genesis 18:10).

48. It would be exceedingly long to explain carefully why the children of the promise, who belong to Isaac, are reckoned among the grace of the New Testament. I shall nevertheless touch on it briefly; and the more fruitfully you will consider it, the more devoutly you consider it.

God does not promise everything that he foretells. He foretells even what he himself does not do, because he knows beforehand all future things. Thus he foretells human sins, which he could foresee without causing them. But he promises what he himself will do—and not evil things, but good ones. For who promises evil? Although he inflicts evils upon the wicked, they are not sins but punishments; even so, he threatens them rather than promises them.

He bestows and foreknows everything; but he foretells sins, threatens punishments, and promises benefits. The children of the promise, therefore, are children of the benefit. This is grace, which is given freely—not according to the merits of the one who works, but through the mercy of the giver.

For this we give thanks to the Lord our God. This is the great sacrament in the sacrifice of the New Testament; where, when, and how it is offered, you will discover once you have been baptized.

CHAPTER XX

49. Then it follows and says: “Let all the seed of Israel fear him.” Jacob and Israel were one man with two names—not without a significant mystery. But everything cannot be said in a single book, in which we have already made considerable progress and have not yet said anything about three other questions: namely, about the outer darkness; about breadth, length, height, and depth; and about the five and five virgins.

What he said above, “all the seed of Jacob,” he now consequently expresses as “all the seed of Israel.” But why above does he say, “Magnify him,” and afterward, “Let all Israel fear him”? Magnification belongs to praise, of which he had said, “You who fear the Lord, praise him”; and I have already discussed this at length. There, indeed, the love or charity of God is in view, and perfect love casts out fear.

Why, then, does he again say, “Let all Israel fear him”? “For you have not received,” the Apostle says, “the spirit of slavery again into fear” (Romans 8:15). Yet the same Apostle commands fear when the wild olive is grafted into the olive tree—that is, when the Gentiles are added to the root of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, so that they too become Israel, belonging to the seed of Abraham (Romans 11:17–20).

50. The Lord himself also foretold this grafting of the wild olive, after the natural branches had been cut off because of the pride of unbelief, in the Gospel, on the occasion of the centurion who believed in him as a Gentile.

For then he said: “Truly I tell you, I have not found such faith in Israel.” And he added: “Therefore I tell you, many will come from the east and the west and will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven; but the children of the kingdom will go into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

Thus he signified that the wild olive is grafted in because of humility. For that centurion had said: “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; but only say the word, and my boy will be healed” (Matthew 8:8–12). He signified also the breaking off of the natural branches because of pride—namely, those who, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, were not subject to God’s righteousness (Romans 10:3).

Of those swollen with empty self-exaltation it was said that they would go into the outer darkness. Boasting of the seed of Abraham, they refused to become Abraham’s seed, so that they might be children of the promise. They did not receive the faith of the New Testament, in which God’s righteousness is commended; instead, they wished to establish their own righteousness. That is, relying as though upon their own merits and works, they rejected being children of the promise—children of grace and children of mercy—so that “the one who boasts might boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31), believing in him who justifies the ungodly, that is, who makes the ungodly godly, so that his faith may be reckoned as righteousness (Romans 4:5). Thus what is fulfilled in him is not what his merit demanded, but what the Lord promised as a benefit.

51. Addressing those who were being grafted into the olive tree by grace, the Apostle says: “You will say, ‘Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.’ Good; they were broken off because of unbelief. But you stand by faith. Do not become proud, but fear” (Romans 11:19–20).

It is God’s benefit, not your merit. The Apostle says the same elsewhere: “By grace you have been saved through faith; and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand for us to walk in” (Ephesians 2:8–10).

In this understanding of grace there is the fear of which it is said: “Do not become proud, but fear” (Romans 11:20). But this fear is of another kind. It is not the slavish fear that love casts out. Through the former one fears falling into the torment of punishment; through the latter one fears losing the benefit of grace.

CHAPTER XXI

52. Therefore, although the Apostle says to the faithful who belong to the New Testament—as I recalled shortly before—“You have not received the spirit of slavery again into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans 8:15), that is, so that there may be in us the faith that works through love (Galatians 5:6), not so much fearing punishment as loving righteousness, nevertheless the soul is not made righteous except through participation in the one who is better and justifies the ungodly. For what does anyone have that he has not received?

Therefore, one must not assign to oneself what belongs to God and boast as though one had not received it (1 Corinthians 4:7). For this reason it is said: “Do not become proud, but fear.” This fear is commanded even to those who live by faith, are heirs of the New Testament, and have been called into freedom.

“To become proud” means to exalt oneself. The Apostle makes this sufficiently clear elsewhere by contrast, when he says: “Not aspiring to high things, but associating with the humble” (Romans 12:16). By saying “associating with the humble,” he plainly showed that by “aspiring to high things” he meant nothing other than becoming proud.

53. Fear, then, is not in love, because perfect love casts out fear—but it casts out slavish fear: the fear by which a person abstains from an evil deed because punishment terrifies him, not because he delights in righteousness. Love casts out this fear, since it is not pleased by iniquity even when impunity is offered.

Love does not cast out the fear by which the soul fears losing the very grace that has made it dislike sin; by which it fears that God may abandon it, even if he does not punish it with any bodily torments. This is chaste fear. Love does not expel it but takes it up.

For it is written: “The fear of the Lord is chaste, enduring forever and ever” (Psalm 18:10). It would not call this fear enduring unless it knew of another that would not endure. And rightly does it call this one chaste, for it is not without love—the love by which the soul clings to God and says in another psalm: “You have destroyed everyone who commits fornication away from you; but for me it is good to cling to God” (Psalm 72:27–28).

A wife who harbors an adulterous intention may refrain from adultery out of fear of her husband, yet what is absent from the deed is present in the will. The chaste wife fears differently. She too fears her husband, but chastely. The former fears that her husband may arrive hostile; the latter that he may depart offended. For the presence of the husband is burdensome to the woman who does not love him, while his absence is burdensome to the one who does.

Therefore, with chaste fear, enduring forever and ever, let all the seed of Israel fear God. Let them fear the one they love—not by aspiring to high things, but by associating with the humble—and let them work out their salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in them both to will and to work, according to his good pleasure (Philippians 2:12–13).

CHAPTER XXII

54. This is the righteousness of God; this is what God gives to a human being when he justifies the ungodly. Ignorant of this righteousness of God, and wishing to establish their own, the proud Jews were not subject to God’s righteousness (Romans 10:3). [Note: The editions read “and by pride”; the Vatican manuscripts and two of our manuscripts read “by this pride”; several other Gallic manuscripts read “by this [reading uncertain: superbi].”] Through this pride they are cast down, so that the humble wild olive may be grafted in.

And they will go into the outer darkness—those about whom you asked, among other things—while many come from the east and the west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 8:11–12).

For they are now in outer darkness, from which correction is not to be despaired of. If they despise correction, they will go into the outer darkness where there will be no opportunity for correction. “For God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all” (1 John 1:5)—but this means the light of the heart, not the light seen by these bodily eyes; nor is it at all like the appearance imagined from this visible light. Yet there is sight there also, though in a far different and dissimilar way.

For what kind of light love itself is, who can explain in words? What example drawn from things accessible to the bodily senses could demonstrate it? Or perhaps love is not light? Hear the Apostle John. He said what I have just recalled: “God is light, and there is no darkness in him at all” (1 John 1:5). He also says: “God is love” (1 John 4:8). Therefore, if God is light and God is love, love is certainly that very light which is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Romans 5:5).

He also says: “Whoever hates his brother is in darkness until now” (1 John 2:11). These are the darknesses into which the devil and his angels advanced through great pride. For “love does not envy and is not puffed up” (1 Corinthians 13:4). It does not envy because it is not puffed up; wherever inflation comes first, envy immediately follows, because pride is the mother of envy.

55. The devil and his angels, therefore, turned away from the light and warmth of love and advancing too far into pride and envy, became numb, as though hardened by ice. Hence, figuratively, they are placed in the north.

When the devil oppressed the human race, the grace of the Savior that was to come is spoken of in the Song of Songs: “Rise up, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden, and let its spices flow” (Song of Songs 4:16).

“Rise up”—you who have rushed upon them, who press upon your subjects, who weigh down those you possess. Rise up, so that those whose souls you have bent by pressing upon them may be raised when they are relieved of your burden.

“And come, south wind,” he says, invoking the Spirit of grace, blowing from the south as though from a warm and luminous region, so that the spices may flow. Hence the Apostle says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place” (2 Corinthians 2:15).

For this reason it is also said in a certain psalm: “Restore our captivity, Lord, like streams in the south” (Psalm 125:4)—that captivity, namely, in which they were held under the devil as under the north wind. There, as iniquity abounded, they had grown cold and had, in a sense, frozen.

For this reason the Gospel also says: “Because iniquity will abound, the love of many will grow cold” (Matthew 24:12). But when the south wind blows, the ice melts and streams flow: that is, when sins are forgiven, peoples hasten to Christ in love.

Hence it is written elsewhere: “As ice melts in fair weather, so your sins will be dissolved” (Sirach 3:17).

CHAPTER XXIII

56. Rational creation—whether in the angelic spirit or in the human soul—was made in such a way that it cannot itself be the good by which it becomes blessed. But if its mutability turns toward the immutable good, it becomes blessed; if it turns away, it becomes miserable. Its turning away is its vice, and its turning toward God is its virtue.

Nature, therefore, is not evil. The spiritual creature is a rational life [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “a rational spirit is life.”] which, even when deprived of the good through participation in which it is blessed—that is, even when vicious—is better than the highest body, namely, this light perceived by the eyes of the flesh, since that too is a body. Every incorporeal nature is superior to every body—not in mass, since mass belongs only to bodies, but by a certain power through which it surpasses every image that the mind turns over after drawing it from bodily senses.

Yet just as among bodies those that are lower—such as earth, water, and air itself—become better through participation in what is better, namely, when they are illuminated by light and invigorated by warmth, so incorporeal rational creatures become better through participation in the Creator himself when they cleave to him in the purest and holiest love. When they are wholly deprived of this love, they grow dark and, in a certain sense, harden.

57. Unbelieving human beings, therefore, are darkness; when they turn to God through faith, they become light after a certain preliminary illumination. If, progressing in this light, they pass from faith to sight, so that they deserve to behold what they believe—as far as such a great good can be seen—they will receive the perfect image of God. To such people the Apostle says: “Once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5:8).

The devil and his angels, however, are outer darkness to unbelieving human beings [Note: The printed editions read “worse than unbelieving human beings.” The manuscripts of better authority read “outer.” Two handwritten copies of Eugippius likewise have “outer.”]. For they have turned farther away from love and advanced into their own arrogance and obstinacy.

And because at the final judgment Christ will say to those whom he separates to the left, “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41), he says that these evil spirits will go into the outer darkness, that is, into the punitive fellowship of the devil and his angels, to be joined with them and condemned together with them.

Opposed to this punishment is what is said to the good servant: “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew 25:23), so that, to the extent that those darknesses are outer, this light may be inner.

These things must not be imagined as intervals of place through an empty fantasy. Spatial extensions occupy only bodily masses. This is not true of the spirit of life, nor of the rational soul, and much less of God, the most benevolent Creator and most righteous Organizer of all things. Things are said to approach or become distant, to enter or depart, according to wills and affections.

58. But because they delight in evil works—that is, in works of darkness—and because punishment that torments them will follow, the Lord, after saying “the outer darkness,” added: “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” He did this so that they would not foolishly imagine that, in that punishment also, they would enjoy the pleasures by which the wicked here delight themselves when they grow dark through unbelief and injustice.

For because they willingly use good things unjustly, they will justly be tormented against their will by evil things. Thus the outer darkness may also be understood as bodily punishments. The body is external to the soul; the soul’s evils, in which the mind turned away from the light of love delights through sins, are therefore outer darkness, while the body’s evils, by which it will be tortured eternally to the end, are external darkness. These latter alone are feared by those who are still held by slavish fear.

For if they were permitted forever to roll and wallow with impunity in those external things that consist in sins, they would never wish to approach God, to be illuminated, and to cling to him through love, where there is chaste fear enduring forever and ever. This fear does not torment; rather, it makes the soul cling more firmly to that good which, if it abandons it, will fall.

CHAPTER XXIV

59. “Let all the seed of Israel fear him.” Observe the reason he joins to this: “For he has not despised,” he says, “nor disregarded the prayer of the poor.” By “poor” he means humble; hence: “Do not become proud, but fear.” Therefore let all the seed of Israel fear him, because he has not disregarded the prayer of the one who was not proud but feared.

This may also be appropriately understood in another way: the Savior himself became poor for us in the flesh, although he was rich, so that we might be enriched by his poverty (2 Corinthians 8:9). In the form of a servant he became poor, and in that form he poured out his prayer; for in it he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death (Philippians 2:8).

Observe, then, what he says: “For he has not despised nor disregarded the prayer of the poor, nor turned his face away from me.” Where, then, is “Why have you forsaken me,” if he did not turn his face away from him? The answer is that even when he forsakes, he does not forsake: he does not hear us concerning temporal goods, not to make us foolish, but so that we may understand what he removes from us and what he offers us.

“He has not despised nor disregarded the prayer of the poor, nor turned his face away from me; and when I cried to him, he heard me.” Therefore he did what he had been asked shortly before, when the petitioner said to him: “Do not depart from me.” For if he heard him, he certainly acted accordingly; he did not depart.

Thus he did not forsake in the manner in which he had forsaken in another way, so that we might understand how much more we ought to desire not to be forsaken by him.

60. “My praise is from you.” What harm, then, do those do who insult me as though I had been defeated because you have forsaken me in temporal things?

“In the great Church I will confess to you”—not in that synagogue, however great it is, which mocks the death of the forsaken one, but in the great Church spread throughout all nations, which believes in the resurrection of the one who was not forsaken.

This is that one Church which he asks to be rescued from the hand of the dog, and of which he also said shortly before: “In the midst of the Church I will sing to you.” And now, when he says, “I will confess to you,” he means those in whom confession will be made, in whom he also speaks.

Confession is not only confession of sins but also praise of God. Thus he himself says in the Gospel: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matthew 11:25).

Therefore he continues: “I will fulfill my vows before those who fear him. The poor will eat and be satisfied, and those who seek him will praise the Lord.” These are the little ones of whom he said, “You have revealed them to little ones”: those who fear him, and the poor—that is, the humble—who do not aspire to high things but fear with that chaste fear, not the fear by which punishment is dreaded but the fear by which grace is preserved [Note: Bad., Am., Er. read “commended.”].

61. He wishes his vows to be understood as the sacrifice of his body, which is the sacrament of the faithful. Therefore, after saying, “I will fulfill my vows before those who fear him,” he immediately added: “The poor will eat and be satisfied.”

They will be satisfied with the bread that came down from heaven. Clinging to him and preserving his peace and love, they imitate his humility; for this reason they are called poor.

The Apostles especially shone in this poverty and satisfaction. “And they will praise the Lord,” he says, “who seek him,” understanding that their being satisfied is due not to their own merits but to his grace. For they seek him because they are not among those who seek their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ (Philippians 2:21).

Finally, even if the flesh of those who praise him suffers temporal tribulation or death, their hearts will live forever and ever. This life of the heart is not found in bodily senses. It is hidden in the light that is within, not in the darkness that is without; in the fulfillment of the commandment, not in the beginning of sin.

“The fulfillment of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (1 Timothy 1:5). Love does not envy and is not puffed up (1 Corinthians 13:4), because it does not aspire to high things but fears; and therefore it clings to chaste fear, enduring forever and ever.

The beginning of every sin is pride. Through it the devil advanced irrevocably into the outer realm, and by envying the human being and persuading him to something similar, cast him down. To this human being it is said in a certain Scripture: “Why are earth and ashes proud? For in his life he cast away his inner things” (Sirach 10:9–10, 15).

“In his life” means as though in his own life [Note: Bad., Am., Er. read “as though in his own person”], as though in a private life of his own—the condition in which all pride delights.

CHAPTER XXV

62. Hence love, which is concerned more with the common good than with private advantage, is said “not to seek what is its own” (1 Corinthians 13:5). By this love hearts live forever and ever, as though satisfied with heavenly bread. Of this love the one who satisfies them says [Note: Bad., Am., and Er. read “Of this satisfaction”; three manuscripts read “Of which the Savior himself says.”]: “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54).

Rightly, therefore, the hearts of those who are satisfied will live forever and ever. For Christ is their life, dwelling in their hearts first through faith and afterward through sight. Now they see “through a mirror in an enigma,” but then “face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12).

Accordingly, love is now exercised in good works of affection, extending itself in every direction as far as it can to provide assistance; this is breadth. Now it patiently endures adversity and perseveres in what it has truly held fast; this is length. It does all this in order to obtain the eternal life promised to it on high; this is height.

This love arises from the hidden depth in which we have been founded and rooted, in a certain sense (Ephesians 3:17)—where the reasons for God’s will are not investigated, by whose grace we have been saved, not from works of righteousness that we have done, but according to his mercy (Titus 3:5).

For he begot us willingly by the word of truth (James 1:18), and this will of his is hidden. The Apostle, as though fearing the depth of this mystery, cries out: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and inscrutable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord?” (Romans 11:33–34). This is depth.

“Height” is a common term for what is high and what is deep. When it is used of what is high, the eminence of exaltation is commended; when used of what is deep, it refers to the difficulty of investigation and knowledge. Hence it is also said to God: “How great are your works, Lord! Your thoughts have become exceedingly deep” (Psalm 91:6). And again: “Your judgments are like a great abyss” (Psalm 35:7).

This, then, is the passage of the Apostle that you placed among the matters requiring investigation: “For this reason I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named, that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person, and that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts, so that, rooted and founded in love, you may have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the length and breadth and height and depth, and to know the surpassing knowledge of the love of Christ, so that you may be filled with all the fullness of God” (Ephesians 3:14–19).

CHAPTER XXVI

63. Consider everything carefully. “For this reason,” he says, “I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named.”

You ask, “For what reason?” He had said above: “For this reason I ask that you not grow faint in my tribulations for you.” He therefore desires that they not grow faint in the tribulations that the Apostle endured for them, and for this reason he bent his knees before the Father.

He then follows by explaining how they would not grow faint: “That he may grant you to be strengthened with power through his Spirit, according to the riches of his glory.” These are the riches of which he says: “O the depth of riches!” They have hidden causes, where, without any preceding merits, we have what do we have that we have not received?

Then he continues and adds what he desires: “That Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts in the inner person.” This is the life of the heart, by which we live forever and ever, from the beginning of faith until the end of sight.

“So that,” he says, “rooted and founded in love, you may have strength to comprehend with all the saints.” This is the fellowship of a certain divine and heavenly commonwealth. Here the poor are satisfied—not seeking their own interests but those of Jesus Christ; that is, not pursuing private advantages but caring for the common good, where the salvation of all is found. For concerning the bread by which such people are satisfied, the Apostle says in one place: “Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body” (1 Corinthians 10:17).

What, then, are they to comprehend? “What is the breadth,” he says—as I have already explained, in good works by which benevolence extends even to the love of enemies; “and the length,” so that, for the sake of this breadth, troubles may be endured with patience; “and the height,” so that for these things an eternal reward in heaven, rather than some vain temporal possession, may be hoped for; “and the depth,” from which the free grace of God arises according to the secret and hidden nature of his will.

There we have been rooted; there we have been founded: rooted with reference to cultivation, founded with reference to construction. Since this is not from humanity, the same Apostle says elsewhere: “You are God’s cultivation, God’s building” (1 Corinthians 3:9).

All this takes place while, in our pilgrimage here, faith works through love. But in the future age, love will be perfect and complete, without any endurance of evils. It will not believe through faith what it does not see, nor desire through hope what it does not possess; rather, it will contemplate forever the unchangeable appearance of truth. Its peaceful work, without end, will be to praise what it loves and love what it praises.

Concerning this he next says: “And to know the surpassing knowledge of the love of Christ, so that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.”

64. In this mystery the figure of the cross is displayed. Since he died because he wished to, he died in the manner he wished. He did not therefore choose this kind of death without reason, unless he intended also through it to be the teacher of breadth, length, height, and depth.

Breadth is represented by the wood fixed transversely at the top, for it pertains to good works, because the hands are extended there. Length is represented by what is visible from that wood down to the earth; for there one stands, in a certain sense—that is, one persists and perseveres—and this is attributed to patience.

Height is represented by the part of the wood left above the transverse beam, extending upward toward the head of the crucified one; for the expectation of those who hope for good things is directed toward what is above.

Finally, the part of the wood that does not appear, fixed and hidden beneath the ground, from which the whole structure rises, signifies the depth of free grace. In attempting to investigate this depth, the reasoning of many is crushed, until at last they hear: “O human being, who are you to answer back to God?” (Romans 9:20).

65. The hearts of the satisfied poor, therefore, will live forever and ever—that is, the hearts of the humble, burning with love, who do not seek their own interests but rejoice in the fellowship of the saints.

This first took place among the Apostles. But observe what peoples they won through praising God—that is, preaching the grace of God—for it is said: “Those who seek him will praise the Lord.” See this in what follows.

CHAPTER XXVII
66. “All the ends of the earth,” he says, “will remember and turn to the Lord, and all the countries of the nations will worship in his presence; for the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he himself will rule the nations.” He who was mocked, he who was crucified, he who was abandoned, acquires this kingdom. And at the end he will hand it over to God and the Father—not so that he himself may lose it, but so that what he sowed in faith, when he came in a state lower than the Father, he may bring to the vision in which, as the equal one, he never departed from the Father.

“All the rich of the earth have eaten and worshiped.” By “the rich of the earth” we must understand the proud, if previously we rightly understood “the poor” as the humble—those of whom the Gospel says, “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” For they are the meek, those who mourn, those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, and those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake; to each of these he added blessedness in his preaching (Matt. 5:3–12).

Accordingly, in this passage “the rich of the earth” must be understood as the proud. For they were not distinguished without reason, so that above it was said of the poor, “The poor shall eat and be satisfied,” whereas here it says, “All the rich of the earth have eaten and worshiped.” They too have been brought to Christ’s table and receive something of his body and blood; but they worship only, and are not satisfied, because they do not imitate him. For while they eat the Poor One [Note: [Col. 0566] The Badian, Amerbach, and Erasmus editions omit “the Poor One”; all the manuscripts inspected by us and the Louvain edition contain it.], they disdain to be poor, since Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example [Col. 0567] so that we might follow his footsteps (1 Pet. 2:21).

Yet they reject the fact that he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross—and they refuse to suffer similar things: through swelling pride [Note: [Col. 0567] This is the reading of the better manuscripts; the printed editions have “through fear.”], not greatness; through weakness, therefore, not health. But because God raised him from the dead and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Phil. 2:8–10), they are moved by the fame of his exaltation and the glory of his name, spread everywhere throughout the Church. They too come to the table, eat, and worship; yet they are not satisfied, because they do not hunger and thirst for righteousness—for those who do so will be satisfied.

Although perfect satisfaction will be in that eternal life, when we have come from this pilgrimage from faith to vision, from the mirror to face-to-face sight, from the enigma to manifest truth, nevertheless one who is satisfied with the poverty [Note: [Col. 0567] The Regius Codex has *the poor man*.] of Christ is not improperly called satisfied: for the sake of his righteousness—that is, for the sake of participation in the eternal Word, which he has meanwhile begun through faith—he not only temperately despises all temporal goods but also patiently endures temporal evils.

67. Such were the fishermen and the tax collectors, because he chose the despised things of this world in order to confound the strong (1 Cor. 1:27). Of them it was said, “The poor shall eat and be satisfied.” But because they did not keep this satisfaction to themselves—for in a certain manner they belched forth praise of the Lord, that is, they proclaimed him while seeking him, meaning that they did not seek their own interests but burned with love for him—the world was moved by their preaching, so that “all the ends of the earth” might remember and turn to the Lord, and “all the countries of the nations” might worship in his presence; for “the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he himself will rule the nations.”

Through this expansion of the Church, the proud also—that is, the rich of the earth—were brought to eat; and although they were not satisfied, they nevertheless worship. This is the order the prophecy of the Psalm maintains here, and we see it being fulfilled.

He adds, “In his presence all who go down into the earth will fall”—that is, all who love earthly goods and do not ascend into heaven. For they do not do what the Apostle says: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God; set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are upon the earth” (Col. 3:1–2). Rather, the happier they think themselves in earthly goods, the more they descend into the earth—that is, the more deeply they are pressed down into earthly things. And therefore they will fall in his presence, that is, where he sees them, not where human beings see them, who consider them lofty and exalted.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

68. “And my soul,” he says, “shall live for him”—for him, certainly, not for itself, as do the proud who rejoice in their private good and, in empty exaltation, recoil from the common good of all, which is God [Note: [Col. 0567] The Badian, Amerbach, and Erasmus editions, together with most manuscripts, read “the common good of all goods”; shortly below they read “the true common good of all goods.”]. Let us avoid this, then, and seek rather to enjoy the true common good of all than to rejoice in our private good, so that [Col. 0568] “those who live may no longer live for themselves,” as the Apostle says, “but for him who died and rose again for them” (2 Cor. 5:15).

For this reason he became mediator, in order to reconcile us to God through humility, from whom we had departed far through impious pride. For not only is that saying written which I quoted above, “The beginning of every sin is pride,” but this too is read there: “The beginning of human pride is apostasy from God” (Sir. 10:14–15).

Let no one, therefore, live for himself but for Christ, doing not his own will but Christ’s and remaining in his love, just as Christ himself did the Father’s will and remains in the Father’s love. Advising us of this and exhorting us by his example, he spoke in his Gospel (John 15:10).

But if he, although equal to the Father in the form of God, nevertheless, in the form of a servant which he assumed for our sake, commended himself as doing not his own will but the Father’s, how much more ought we, having rejected our own private will by which we have been darkened, to approach that common light so that we may be illumined and our faces may not be ashamed—the light “which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9)—so that our soul may live for him!

He adds this consistently concerning us when he says, “And my seed shall serve him.” For “the one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man,” and “the good seed—these are the children of the kingdom.”

## CHAPTER XXIX

69. Since all these things said in this Psalm referred not to the present time but to the prophecy of future events, as the events themselves also show, he wished to conclude it in such a way as to demonstrate that he was neither displaying present things nor narrating past things, but prophesying the future:

“An account will be given to the Lord,” he says, “of the generation to come, and the heavens will proclaim his righteousness to the people who will be born, whom the Lord has made.”

He does not say, “The Lord will be proclaimed to the generation to come,” but, “The generation to come will be proclaimed to the Lord.” This must not be understood as though something were announced to one who does not know it, so that he may come to know it. Rather, just as the angels announce to us the benefits of God, so also they announce our prayers to him. For it is written where the angel says to human beings, “I offered the remembrance of your prayer” (Tob. 12:12)—not so that God might then learn what we want or what we need. “Your Father,” the Lord says, “knows what you need before you ask him” (Matt. 6:8). Rather, a rational creature, in obeying God, necessarily refers temporal causes to eternal truth, whether by asking that something be done for it or by seeking guidance about what it should do. This is a pious disposition of mind, by which the creature itself is formed, not by which God is instructed.

For this too is a kind of testimony of the rational creature: that the good by which it becomes blessed is not itself, but the unchangeable good by participation in which it also becomes wise.

70. Alternatively, “The generation to come will be proclaimed to the Lord” may have been said as though it meant that those who proclaim will please the Lord, not themselves—so that “to proclaim to the Lord” is like “to live for the Lord.” Thus it is said, “The one who eats, eats for the Lord; and the one who does not eat, does not eat for the Lord.” He added, “And he gives thanks to God,” to show what it means to do something “for the Lord” (Rom. 14:6): namely, to do it to his praise.

An action is rightly, [Col. 0569] justly, and piously performed when a good work is done to the praise of the one by whose grace it is granted that the work be done.

Accordingly, even if someone wishes to understand these words in such a way that their order is this—“The generation to come will be proclaimed to the Lord,” that is, the generation that is to come to the Lord—the meaning does not depart from the same interpretation: the generation of the godly and holy is meant, because the generation of the ungodly and wicked is coming not to the Lord but to itself.

The same meaning remains: the rational creature, although mutable, does not become blessed except by turning from its own mutable state toward the unchangeable good, which is also the common good, namely God. From him it had withdrawn through proud impiety; converted by humble piety, it remains with him. As it advances in this disposition, whatever good it does, it does for the Lord—that is, to his praise—for it has received his grace in order to do it. From this comes the giving of thanks celebrated in the innermost mystery of the faithful.

## CHAPTER XXX

71. What follows—“And they will proclaim his righteousness to the people who will be born, whom the Lord has made”—confirms the preceding sense. For what was said there, “The generation to come will be proclaimed to the Lord,” is said here as, “They will proclaim his righteousness.” [Note: [Col. 0569] This is the reading of the better manuscripts; the printed texts have, “this is said, this will proclaim his righteousness.”]

That generation of the godly and holy, prophesied as coming, is itself the righteousness of God [Note: [Col. 0569] Most manuscripts read, “of the godly and holy [ones] is the righteousness of God.”], not their own, lest they be among those who, “being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, have not submitted to the righteousness of God” (Rom. 10:3).

It is this righteousness of God that is commended in the words “being ignorant of God’s righteousness”: the righteousness by which we are made righteous through his grace, so that we ourselves are his righteousness when we live righteously, believing in the one who justifies the ungodly (Rom. 4:5)—not the righteousness by which he himself is righteous through his own eternal and unchangeable righteousness.

This righteousness, then, by which we are made righteous through God’s gift, is signified in that Psalm where it is written, “Your righteousness is like the mountains of God” (Ps. 35:7). The mountains of God are his saints, of whom it is said elsewhere, “Let the mountains receive peace for your people” (Ps. 71:3). Much has been written about these mountains in figurative language, but it would take too long to mention it now.

Yet because God justifies human beings by a judgment that is exceedingly hidden—for he does so by free grace, and “if by grace, then not from works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace” (Rom. 11:6)—and because good works begin from the moment we are justified, rather than our being justified because they preceded us; and because this is the depth about which we have already said much above, immediately in the same Psalm, after saying, “Your righteousness is like the mountains of God,” he added, “Your judgments are like a great abyss.”

From there he proceeds to the salvation common to human beings and animals, because this too comes from God’s mercy, and says, “You will save humans and beasts, Lord; how abundant is your mercy, God.” Thus we understand that even that everlasting and immortal salvation of which the Apostle says, “For in hope we were saved” (Rom. 8:24), is received freely by us, just as this salvation common to human beings and animals is—not from works, lest anyone should boast, since we perform good works [Col. 0570] as a result of his justification.

“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand so that we should walk in them” (Eph. 2:8–10). That salvation, therefore, is also free, of which it is said in another Psalm, “Salvation belongs to the Lord, and your blessing is upon your people” (Ps. 3:9).

72. Therefore, just as when we read, “Salvation belongs to the Lord,” we do not understand the salvation by which the Lord himself is saved, but the salvation by which those whom he saves are saved, so when we read of “the righteousness of God” in the words, “Being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own,” we must not understand the righteousness by which God is righteous, but that by which human beings are righteous—those whom he justifies by his grace.

They are saved from the same source from which they are made righteous. For when he says, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick,” he explains this in what follows, saying, “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matt. 9:12–13).

Therefore, “not according to works of righteousness that we ourselves have done, but according to his mercy he saved us through the washing of regeneration” (Titus 3:5). “In this grace we have been saved in hope” (Rom. 8:24).

Hence that Psalm continues: “But the children of human beings will hope under the shelter of your wings. They will be intoxicated with the abundance of your house, and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delight; for with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light. Extend your mercy to those who know you, and your righteousness to those who are upright in heart.” Pride is therefore contrary to this righteousness of God—the pride that trusts as though in its own works. Hence it follows there: “Let not the foot of pride come against me” (Ps. 35:8–12).

73. This righteousness, by which his faithful are righteous while meanwhile living by faith, until they are brought to the vision by perfect righteousness, just as by perfect salvation they are brought to the immortality of the body itself, is the grace [Note: [Col. 0570] The manuscripts read, “the grace of the New Testament.” In the printed editions *est* was missing, and this important passage had been marred by faulty punctuation.] of the New Testament.

Therefore the Apostle says elsewhere, “We are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us; we beseech you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.” Then he adds, “He who knew no sin he made sin for us”—that is, a sacrifice for sins. For in the Law too the offerings made for sins were themselves called “sins”—“so that we might be the righteousness of God in him” (2 Cor. 5:20–21).

That is, in his body, which is the Church and of which he is the head, we might be the righteousness of God. Those who are ignorant of this righteousness and wish to establish their own—that is, who boast as though it came from their own works—have not submitted to the righteousness of God.

Accordingly, in this Psalm too, after saying, “They will proclaim his righteousness,” he continues and adds, “To the people who will be born, whom the Lord has made.”

For what people has the Lord not made, considered simply according to the fact that they are human beings? He also created animals; from him come all life and every nature that has been made and created. But “whom the Lord has made” must be understood to mean that not only the fact that they are human beings, but also the fact that they are righteous, is understood to have been made by him, according to what I have already more than once recalled as said by the Apostle: “We are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand so that we should walk in them.”

## CHAPTER XXXI

74. The mutability of the rational soul [Col. 0571] is therefore brought to its attention, so that it may know that, unless it participates in the unchangeable good, it cannot be righteous, saved, wise, or blessed; nor can it be a good to itself by its own will, but rather an evil.

By its own will it turns away from the unchangeable good, and by that turning it is corrupted. Nor can it heal itself, but only through the free mercy of its Creator, who establishes it in this life, living by faith, in the hope of eternal salvation.

Therefore it must not be proud, but fear; and through that chaste fear it must cling to God, who cleansed it from its own impurity—by which it loved inferior goods in a disordered manner—as though from a kind of spiritual fornication.

Nor must it be exalted by human praise, lest it [Note: [Col. 0571] The printed editions read, “lest it be”; the manuscripts read, “lest it be.”] be among the foolish virgins (Matt. 25:1–13), rejoicing in praise from others—and this is the last matter remaining from your questions—and doing good works for the sake of that empty praise, not for the sake of its conscience, where God is its witness.

Rather, it must be among the wise virgins, where it may say what the Apostle says: “For our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12). This is to carry oil with oneself, rather than to buy it from those who sell it—that is, from flatterers.

For flatterers sell their praise to fools as though it were oil. Of this oil it is said in the Psalm: “Let the righteous correct me in mercy and reprove me; but let the oil of the sinner not fatten my head” (Ps. 140:5). He chose to be mercifully reproved by the righteous and, in a certain sense, struck on the face rather than to have his head grow in pride [Note: [Col. 0571] Erasmus thought *grow fat* should be read. But all the books have *grow*, a word by which Augustine alludes to the proverb he cites above in Epistle 33.3: “Of a man whom false flatteries make arrogant, it is rightly said in common speech, ‘His head has grown.’”] through the praise of a sinner’s flattery.

75. Their response seems to me to be one of mockery when the wise virgins say to them, “Go instead to those who sell, and buy for yourselves,” just as it is written in a certain book of Wisdom, where Wisdom says to the despisers, “I too will laugh at your destruction” (Prov. 1:26).

But the response made to those asking for oil—“Perhaps there will not be enough for us and for you”—was spoken not in despair but in humility. For who can presume so much upon his conscience as to be certain that it will be sufficient for him at God’s judgment, unless the merciful Judge [Note: [Col. 0571] The Vatican manuscripts and nearly all of ours read “unless the merciful [ones] judge mercifully”; the printed editions have the singular.] judges mercifully? “For judgment is without mercy to the one who has not shown mercy” (Jas. 2:13).

The lamps themselves are burning lamps, namely good works, of which the Lord says, “Let your good works shine before human beings [Note: [Col. 0571] Six manuscripts read: “Let your works shine before human beings, so that they may see your good deeds and glorify.”] and let them glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16).

The intention of the wise virgins extends this far: they wish their good works to be seen by human beings not so that human beings may praise them, but so that God may be glorified, from whom they have received the ability to do good works.

Thus they rejoice in the inner good that exists before God, where the almsgiving is done in secret, so that the Father, who sees in secret, may repay it [Note: [Col. 0571] This is the reading of most manuscripts. The printed editions have: “where the Father who sees in secret may repay almsgiving in secret.”]. Therefore their lamps do not fail, because they are nourished by the inner oil [Col. 0572]—that is, by the good intention of conscience, through which whatever shines before human beings in good works is done before God for his glory.

But the lamps of the foolish virgins, who do not carry this oil with them, fail: their good works do not shine perseveringly once human praise has been withdrawn, because they performed them for the sake of that praise, directing their intention only so far as to be seen by human beings, not so that the Father who is in heaven might be glorified.

The intention of the wise is a perpetual orientation toward glory: the soul knows that it owes to God the fact that it has been justified for the doing of good works, and therefore loves to be praised in him, not in itself. Hence the man of God sings elsewhere, “In the Lord my soul shall be praised” (Ps. 33:2), so that “the one who boasts may boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:31).

## CHAPTER XXXII

76. But what does it mean that, in the same Gospel reading, all are said to have fallen asleep while the bridegroom was delayed?

If we understand this sleep as meaning that, as though judgment were delayed—the judgment for which Christ will come—love grows cold because iniquity abounds, how shall we place the wise virgins among those who experience it, when rather the following applies to them: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 24:12)?

It is therefore said, “They all fell asleep,” because not only the foolish, who do good works before human beings for the sake of human praise, but also the wise, who do this so that God may be praised, experience this death: people of both kinds die.

This death is often called sleep in Scripture, because of the future resurrection, as though it were an awakening. Hence the Apostle says, “Concerning those who are asleep, brothers, I do not want you to be ignorant” (1 Thess. 4:12); and elsewhere, “Of whom the greater part remain until now, but some have fallen asleep” (1 Cor. 15:6). Countless other testimonies to this meaning are found plainly throughout the Scriptures of both Testaments.

Hence that poet also says:

> “Sleep, akin to death” (Virgil, *Aeneid* 6).

And if you pay attention, you will find much even in secular literature where death is compared to sleep.

The Lord therefore signified that a time would come when, amid the tribulations and temptations of this world, his coming would already be expected and hoped for as near and imminent, and those who seemed to belong to his household would prepare themselves for it.

This is what is meant by “going out to meet the bridegroom and the bride.” The bridegroom is the Son of God; the bride is so called either because he will come in the body he assumed from the Virgin, or because the Church herself will then appear more glorious, so that the members may hasten together into the gathering of the whole body, and when they have come together its greatness may be displayed.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

77. He called them virgins because of their continence. Ten—that is, five and five—because of the number by which the bodily senses are reckoned, in which continence dwells when one abstains from disgraceful and unlawful pleasures.

The lamps, as has been said, are good works, especially those pertaining to mercy, and that praiseworthy way of life which also shines before human beings. But it makes a great difference with what intention of mind this is done. Therefore he calls some wise and others foolish [Col. 0573].

He distinguishes them by this: the foolish did not take oil with them, whereas the wise took oil in their vessels—that is, in their hearts, where participation in the intimate and heavenly good takes place.

Hence in a certain Psalm, after it had said, “Offer the sacrifice of righteousness and hope in the Lord,” it continues: “Many say, ‘Who will show us good things?’” Then, to make clear by love of what good we ought to perform righteousness—that is, to offer the sacrifice of righteousness [Note: [Col. 0573] The printed editions add after *righteousness*, “and hope”; this is absent from the manuscripts.]—it says, “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, Lord; you have given gladness in my heart” (Ps. 4:6–7).

One who performs good works and conducts himself laudably even in the sight of human beings, with the intention of participating to some degree in this good and of participating in it more fully and perfectly, carries oil with him. Through it his good works, even when shining before human beings, are not extinguished, because his love does not grow cold when iniquity abounds, but perseveres to the end.

The foolish virgins do not have this oil with them. Since they attribute whatever good work they perform to themselves, they necessarily become swollen with pride and take such delight in human praise, because of this vice, that when they do something good they seem to burn and shine with the joy of that praise.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

78. “While the bridegroom was delayed, they all fell asleep.” He will not come when he is expected, but at midnight, when it will be exceedingly dark—that is, hidden—whether he is coming.

Hence he says that at midnight a cry was made: “Behold, the bridegroom is coming; go out to meet him.” This cry is clearly that trumpet of which the Apostle speaks when he says, “The trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible” (1 Cor. 15:52).

By the name “trumpet” he wishes some especially evident and glorious sign to be understood. Elsewhere he calls it the voice of an archangel and the trumpet of God (1 Thess. 4:15). In the Gospel this is also called the voice of the Lord Jesus Christ, which those who are in the tombs will hear, and they will come forth (John 5:28–29).

All those virgins therefore rise—the wise and the foolish—and prepare their lamps, that is, they prepare to give an account of their works.

79. But then, when the clarity of that cry and the resurrection of the dead make it impossible to doubt that judgment is already imminent and present, every support of human praise will be withdrawn.

There will be no opportunity to dispute about another, or judge another, or show favor and give support to another, when each person will bear his own burden and consider that an account must be given for his own deeds. Accordingly, the minds of the foolish virgins will be carried along by their habitual disposition, but, since human praises are not found, they will fail.

They did not truly say, “With you is my praise,” or, “In the Lord my soul shall be praised”; nor did they glory in the Lord, since, being ignorant of God’s righteousness, they established their own righteousness.

Accordingly, they ask the wise for oil—that is, for some consolation—but they neither find nor receive it. The wise reply that they do not know whether even their own conscience will be sufficient, since they await mercy under that Judge who, when he has sat upon his throne, [Col. 0574] who will boast of having a pure heart, or who will boast of being clean from sin, unless mercy triumphs over judgment (Jas. 2:13)?

Mercy will be upon those who performed works of mercy with the intention that the one from whom they knew they had received what they possessed might have mercy on them. They did not boast as though they had not received, or as though they had through themselves possessed the means of pleasing him, as do the foolish, who please themselves as though with a good prepared by themselves for themselves, and who are praised by flatterers or the mistaken as though they themselves were something.

“But the one who thinks he is something, when he is nothing,” as the Apostle says, “deceives himself. Let each one test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself alone, and not in another” (Gal. 6:3). This is to carry oil with oneself, not to depend upon another’s praise.

But what glory will he have in himself unless he has the one [Note: [Col. 0574] The printed editions have “unless it”; the manuscripts have “unless him.”] to whom it is said, “My glory and the one who lifts up my head” (Ps. 3:4)? For, as must often be said, “The one who boasts, let him boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:31).

80. Accordingly, the wisdom that dwells in the wise virgins, in accordance with what he had said earlier when speaking to despisers and to those who refused to receive sound teaching—“I too will laugh at your destruction” (Prov. 1:26)—says to the foolish virgins, “Go instead to those who sell, and buy for yourselves.”

It is as though it were saying: Where are those who deceived you with their most false praises, when you were also deceived by yourselves because you gloried in yourselves and not in the Lord?

When he says, “And while they went to buy, the bridegroom came; and those who were ready entered with him,” this seems to me to mean that they would yearn for empty glory with the vicious affection of the heart with which they had pursued it in the elation of an empty mind.

That desire itself is signified in the words, “While they went to buy, the bridegroom came.” And those who were ready entered with him into the wedding feast: that is, those who carried true faith and true piety in their hearts, by which they could be joined to the number and fellowship of the saints who glory not in themselves but in the Lord, entered with them into that joy of which it is said, “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25:23).

There will be perfect participation in the unchangeable good there, whereas now a kind of pledge of it is held through faith, so that we may live according to this grace, insofar as we live for God and not for ourselves.

## CHAPTER XXXV

81. Accordingly, what follows—“Finally the remaining virgins came, saying, ‘Lord, Lord, open to us’”—does not say that they bought oil and then came, for by that time there was no opportunity to do so. Rather, it means that they sought mercy too late, when the time for judging and separating the righteous from the reprobate had already arrived.

They are rightly answered, “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you.” He says this who is not unaware of anything. But “I do not know you” means nothing other than, “You do not know me,” since you choose to trust in yourselves rather than in me [Note: [Col. 0574] The Badian, Amerbach, and Erasmus editions have “to be considered”; the other books have “to trust.”].

When Scripture says that God knows us, he grants us knowledge of himself, so that we may understand that not even the fact that we know God is to be attributed to ourselves, but that knowledge too must be attributed to his mercy.

Thus, when the Apostle once said, “But now, knowing God,” he corrected himself and said, “Rather, being known by God” [Col. 0575] (Gal. 4:9). What else did he wish to be understood but that God himself had made them knowers of him?

No one knows God except one who understands that he is the supreme and unchangeable good, by participation in which a person becomes good. This is what is placed at the conclusion of this Psalm: “They will proclaim his righteousness to the people who will be born, whom the Lord has made.”

Hence also the saying in another Psalm, “He himself made us, and not we ourselves” (Ps. 99:3). This must not be referred to the nature by which we are human beings—for the creator of that nature is also the creator of heaven and earth, the stars, and all living creatures—but rather to what the Apostle says: “We are his workmanship, created in Jesus Christ for good works, which God prepared beforehand so that we should walk in them” (Eph. 2:10).

## CHAPTER XXXVI

82. I think your five questions have now been sufficiently answered, while I lingered over this, as it were, sixth question of my own, which I proposed concerning the grace of the New Testament. For its sake the Word became flesh: that is, he who was the Son of God became human by assuming our nature, not by abandoning his own.

Through him, when we receive him, power is also given to us, so that we who were human beings may become children of God (John 1:14, 12), changed for the better through participation in the unchangeable good—not adopted for temporal happiness, but for eternal life, which alone is blessed.

For this reason I also chose to work through the prophetic Psalm whose first verse he recalled in his Passion, showing how God abandons us and in what other way he does not depart from us: gathering us toward eternal goods, while at times beneficially granting temporal things and at times beneficially withdrawing them, so that we may learn not to cling to them.

Otherwise, by despising the inner light that belongs to the new life—for this reason the Psalm itself also received the title *for the reception of the morning*, as though for a new light—we might willingly dwell in external darkness. From there those who do not turn from these outer things to the inner are sent into the outer darkness, lest, joined to the devil and his angels, we be punished with the final condemnation.

Understanding, then, our pilgrimage in this life, let us be crucified to the world, stretching out our hands in the breadth of good works and persevering with long-suffering to the end, while keeping our hearts above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God (Col. 3:1–2). Let us attribute all this not to ourselves but to his mercy, whose profound judgments exhaust every investigator.

For this is the breadth, length, height, and depth—not an empty fable, but usefully true—from which we may attain even the surpassing knowledge of Christ’s love and be filled with all the fullness of God (Eph. 3:19).

## CHAPTER XXXVII

83. I know how far from superfluous my concern has been in using this opportunity, provided by the questions you proposed to me, to commend the grace of the New Testament to you at greater length.

It has adversaries who, disturbed by its depth, wish not to attribute their goodness to God but rather to claim it for themselves. They are not people whom you can easily dismiss: they live continently and are praiseworthy in good works. They do not believe in a false Christ, as do the Manichaeans and many other heretics [Col. 0576], but believe in the same true Christ, equal and coeternal with the Father, truly made human, and believe that he came and await his coming. Yet they are ignorant of God’s righteousness and wish to establish their own.

For it was not without reason that the Lord, when he mentioned both those who entered the wedding feast with him and those against whom he shut the door and to whom he replied, “I do not know you,” called both groups virgins, because of their continence.

He called them five because of the fleshly desire subdued through the five senses; he adorned both with lamps because of the brilliant praise of good works and a good way of life before human beings; and both went out to meet the bridegroom because they awaited the coming of Christ.

Yet he called some wise and others foolish, because the wise took oil in their vessels, whereas the foolish did not carry this with them. Though equal in so many respects, they are shown to differ in this one matter; this alone gives them different and opposed names.

84. For what could be more closely joined than virgins and virgins, five and five adorned with lamps, both groups going out to meet the bridegroom? And what could be more opposed than wise and foolish?

The reason is clearly that the wise carry oil in their vessels—that is, an understanding of God’s grace in their hearts. They know that no one can be continent unless God grants it, and they count it as part of wisdom to know whose gift it is (Wis. 8:21).

The foolish, however, do not give thanks to the giver of all good things. They became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools (Rom. 1:21–22).

Of these we must certainly not despair yet, before we fall asleep. But if they should sleep in this way, and when that cry is made by which the bridegroom’s presence will already be announced, they awaken—that is, rise again—and remain outside, this will not be because they are not virgins. Rather, because they do not know from where they have what they are, they are foolish virgins, and rightly they will be outside, because they do not carry with them the inward disposition of grace.

85. When, then, you come upon such people, let them not persuade you of the emptiness of their vessels; rather, persuade them of their fullness. Hence the Apostle says, “If anyone thinks that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know.” And immediately, showing what he meant, he says, “But if anyone loves God, this person is known by him” (1 Cor. 8:2–3). He did not wish to say, “He has known him”; rather, by saying “he is known by him,” he wished more explicitly to commend the fact that even our loving him comes from him. For “God’s love has been poured into our hearts,” not through ourselves, “but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

Someone necessarily loves God only a little if he considers himself to have been made good not by him but by himself. How, then, can such a person fail to glory in himself rather than in the Lord? Whoever glories in being good ought to glory in the one by whom he was made good. Consequently, whoever thinks that he was made good by himself must glory in himself, not in the Lord.

The whole purpose of the grace of the New Testament, by which we “lift up our hearts” (because “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above” [James 1:17]), is to keep us from being ungrateful. In the very act of giving thanks, nothing else is being done except that “whoever glories may glory in the Lord.” You have the book, even if it is lengthy; nevertheless, as I think, it is not superfluous. But love also to read ecclesiastical writings, and you will not find many things that you need to seek from me. By reading and pondering them—and by also praying purely to the Lord, the giver of all good things—you will learn, with his inspiration rather than through any human instructor, everything, or at least very many things, that ought to be known. Indeed, by the very fact that we approve, with sound judgment, someone who admonishes us well from outside, what else do we testify than that we have an inner light as our teacher?

## Letter 141

[Note: We were assisted in correcting this by a. bg. bl. c. cc. ff. g. gv. n. s. sb. t. vc.; two copies marked r.; four marked v.; and Am. Bad. Er. Lov.]

[Note: Elsewhere 152; the letter that was 141 is now 264. Written on 14 June 412.]

To the people of the Donatist faction, explaining how their bishops were convicted at the Carthaginian Conference. They should therefore now at last return to communion with the Catholic Church.

Silvanus the Elder, Valentinus, Aurelius [Note: The name Aurelius is found here in the copies of this letter. But all the manuscripts omit it in Book 2 of the *Retractions*, chapter 40, where Augustine acknowledges that he wrote this same letter, although it was not sent under his private name: “because,” he says, “in the council of Numidia it pleased all of us who were there that this should be done”—namely, that the Donatists should be informed by a very brief letter of what had taken place at the Carthaginian Conference, so that they would no longer be deceived by their own bishops, who reported the matter differently from what had actually occurred.] Innocentius, Maximinus, Optatus, Augustine, Donatus, and the other bishops of the Council of Zertum [Note: Lov. has “of the Council of Cirta.” Two Vatican manuscripts have “of Xersum.” But nearly all the other manuscripts, as well as the editions of Bad., Am., and Er., read “of the Council of Zertum.” We understand this reading to have been approved by certain learned men who infer from the Carthaginian Conference that there was one city in Numidia called Cirta, which was called Constantina, and another called Zertum. At the Conference, besides Fortunatus, the bishop of Constantina, two other bishops of Zertum, Caddentius and Salustius, are listed.], to the Donatists.

### 1

When the report was growing more insistent in our ears that your bishops were saying to you, “The Investigator [Note: Marcellinus.] was bribed by a reward so that a judgment might be pronounced against us,” while you readily believed these things and for that reason many of you still refused to submit to the truth, it pleased us, compelled by the love of the Lord, to send you this letter from our council. Through it you would first be warned that those who are defeated and convicted are spreading these lies to you.

They were also exposed and convicted in their own *Mandate*, which they composed and confirmed with their names and signatures for that Conference. There they called us their betrayers and persecutors, yet they were caught in the most manifest falsehood and lying. Wishing to boast of the number of their fellow bishops, they even inserted among the names of certain absent men the name of someone who was dead. When it was asked where he was, they were suddenly blinded by confusion and themselves admitted that he had died on the journey. When they were asked how he could have signed at Carthage if he had already died on the journey, they were thrown into still greater confusion and bound themselves by another lie, replying that he had died while returning from Carthage. They were completely unable to escape from this lie.

These are the men whom you believe concerning either the ancient betrayal or the corruption of the Investigator—men who could not compose their *Mandate*, in which they charged us with the crime of betrayal, without committing the crime of falsehood themselves. Accordingly, we have collected and inserted in this letter, as in a summary, the matters we judged most necessary, lest you should perhaps be unable to reach the great volumes of the Acts with ease, or should consider reading them laborious.

### 2

We came to Carthage, both we and your bishops. Although previously they had been unwilling to do so and had declared it unworthy, we met together. From among us and from among them, seven from each side were chosen to speak on behalf of all. Another seven from each side were chosen to consult with them whenever the need arose. Four from each side were chosen to supervise the writing of the Acts, so that nothing might be falsely stated by anyone.

Four notaries were also appointed by us and by them, four from each side, so that two at a time would alternate with the judge’s recorders, lest any one of us claim to have said something that had not been recorded. To such great care this too was added: both we and they, like the judge himself, were to sign our words, so that no one could say that anything in those Acts had later been altered.

Since the same Acts will become known, while those who signed them are still alive, in all the places where they ought to become known, the confirmed truth will likewise endure for posterity. Do not, then, be ungrateful for such great mercy from God, which has been made available to you through this diligence. No excuse remains. The hearts of those who still resist such a clear manifestation of the truth are excessively hard—excessively hard, and excessively devilish.

### 3

Look: the bishops of your party, whom all of you chose to speak on behalf of everyone, tried as hard as they could to prevent the very case from being heard—the case for which so great a number of bishops from both parties, from all over Africa and from such distant places, had come to Carthage. While every soul anxiously awaited what would be done at such a gathering, they pressed with all their force for nothing to be done.

Why did they do this, unless they knew that their case was bad and could not doubt that, if it were heard, they would very easily be defeated? Their very state of mind, by which they feared that the case would be heard, already showed that they had been defeated.
