For if they had obtained what they wanted—namely, that the Conference itself should not take place and that the truth should not appear through our debates—what would they have had to answer you when they returned from Carthage? What would they have been able to demonstrate? I suppose they would have produced the Acts and said to you: “We insisted that the case should not be heard; they insisted that it should be heard. You are waiting to see what we did. Read here how we defeated them, so that we did nothing.”

Perhaps you would have replied, if you had any sense: “If you were going to do nothing, why did you summon these men? Or rather, since you did nothing, why did you return?”

### 4

Finally, after they had been unable to accomplish what they had attempted—namely, to prevent the case from being heard—the proceedings themselves showed what they had feared, since they were defeated in every respect.

They confessed that they had nothing to say against the Catholic Church, which is spread throughout the whole world, because they had been overwhelmed by the divine testimonies of the holy Scriptures. These testimonies show that the Church began at Jerusalem and grew throughout the places where the Apostles preached, and that the names of those same places were recorded in their Letters and Acts; from there the Church spread among the other nations.

They openly declared that they had no case against this Church. Here our victory is most evident in the name of God. For when they confirm the Church with which it is manifest that we are in communion, while they are not, they testify that they were defeated long ago. If you are wise, they also make it perfectly clear to you what you ought to abandon and what you ought to retain—not through the falsehood with which they still do not cease to deceive you, but through the truth which, once defeated, they were forced to confess.

### 5

Whoever, then, is separated from this Catholic Church, however commendably he may think he lives, will not possess life because of this one crime: that he has been separated from the unity of Christ. The wrath of God remains upon him.

But whoever lives well in this Church is not harmed by the sins of others, because each person will bear his own burden in it, as the Apostle says (Gal. 6:5). And whoever eats the body of Christ unworthily in it “eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11:29). The Apostle himself also wrote this. When he says, “He eats judgment upon himself,” he sufficiently shows that he does not eat judgment upon someone else, but upon himself.

This is what we argued, demonstrated, and established: the communion of the wicked does not defile anyone through participation in the Sacraments, but through consent to their deeds. For if someone does not consent to wicked deeds, the wicked person bears his own case and his own person, and does not prejudice another whom he does not have as a partner in the consent to the evil deed.

### 6

They too were forced to confess this in the clearest possible terms—not when we were saying these things, but afterward, when something else was being dealt with.

When the case of Caecilian was also reached—a case that we distinguished from the case of the Church, so that, if he should happen to be found wicked, we would anathematize him, but would not on his account abandon the Church of Christ, against which he could not prejudice by his own bad case—when, therefore, the case of Caecilian himself was reached, their council at Carthage was read to them [Note: Held by the faction in 311.]. There they recited the opinions of approximately seventy bishops pronounced against Caecilian in his absence.

We replied that this council of bishops did not harm Caecilian in his absence, just as the council of the Donatist party at Cabarsussa [Note: Held in 393; its synodical letter is found in the *Exposition on Psalm 36*.] had not harmed Primian in his absence, when approximately one hundred bishops had condemned him in the case of Maximian.

Then, when the case of Maximian was mentioned—a case in which they know that they received back into full honor even those whom they had condemned, and that they confirmed rather than destroyed the baptism given in Maximian’s sacrilegious schism; and when they know that in their sentence at Bagai [Note: Pronounced in 394; it is found in Book 3 against Cresconius, chapter 53.], by which they condemned them, they granted a postponement to certain people who had been in that very schism and said that the sacrilegious shoots of Maximian had not polluted them—when, then, this case struck their ears, they became frightened and confused, forgetting the basis on which they had previously argued against us. At once they said, “Neither does one case prejudice another case, nor one person another person.”

By these words they confirmed what we had previously been saying about the Church: not only could the case and person of Caecilian, whatever he may have been, not prejudice the transmarine Catholic Church—against which they confessed that they had nothing to say—but neither could they prejudice the African Catholic Church, which is joined to it in the communion of unity.

For if Maximian, who condemned Primian together with his other associates, does not prejudice the Donatist party; if Felicianus, who likewise condemned Primian and was afterward condemned by the party of Donatus in the case of Primian, does not prejudice the Donatist party, to which he is now attached as a bishop, having been received back, as he had been before; and if Maximian does not prejudice even those of his own associates to whom they granted a postponement, saying that they had not been polluted by him with whom they had been—because neither does one case prejudice another case, nor one person another person.

### 7

What more, then, are you looking for? They burdened the Acts with many superfluous words. Since they were unable to prevent the case from being heard, they did this by talking at great length, so that what had been done would be difficult to read.

But even these few words of theirs ought to be sufficient for you, lest, because of the crimes of I know not what people, you should hate the unity of the Catholic Church. For, as they themselves said, they reread and signed the statement: “Neither does one case prejudice another case, nor one person another person.”

Moreover, even in the case of Caecilian—which, although it did not belong to the case of the Church, we nevertheless undertook to defend so that their calumnies might also be exposed there—they were most clearly defeated, and were unable to prove any of the charges they brought against Caecilian.

In addition, we produced the episcopal Acts concerning the crimes of betrayal [Note: The Council of Cirta, held in 305; its proceedings are extant in Book 3 against Cresconius, chapter 27.]. From them we read that some of their bishops who had pronounced judgments against Caecilian in his absence had been manifest betrayers. Against these very Acts they said, because they had nothing to say, that they were false; but they could not prove this in any way.

### 8

Furthermore, they confessed—or rather, they proclaimed it as a matter of great glory—that Caecilian had been accused before the emperor Constantine by their predecessors. They added a lie: that he had been condemned by the Emperor when those men accused him.

Here too they were defeated, in the very matter from which they habitually spread clouds of error over you, stirring up resentment against us and leading us into your hatred because we conduct the case of the Church before emperors.

Look: their elders, whose names they boast of, conducted the case of the Church before the Emperor. By accusing Caecilian before the Emperor, they persecuted him and said that he had been condemned. Let them no longer deceive you with their utterly empty and lying words. Return to your hearts; fear the Lord; consider the truth; abandon falsehood.

Whatever you may now suffer through imperial laws—what you suffer not for justice but for iniquity—you cannot say that we are unjust because you should not have been treated in this way, or that the Emperor should not have restrained you from this iniquity. Your bishops have confessed that their predecessors treated Caecilian in precisely the way you do not wish to be treated.

Yet it was sufficiently established, even by their own confession and proclamation, that they had persecuted Caecilian before the Emperor. But that Caecilian had been condemned by the Emperor was not established at all. On the contrary, it was established that, although their predecessors accused and persecuted him, he was acquitted twice by bishops [Note: First at the Roman Council, then at the Council of Arles.] and afterward by the Emperor himself.

They themselves also confirmed this when they later produced such material, supposedly on behalf of their own case, that it turned out to be more strongly against them; and what they produced was read in support of Caecilian’s case.

Thus, whatever persons they wished to accuse, they were unable to prove with any reliable evidence. But whatever we said both for the case of the Church and for the case of Caecilian, they themselves confirmed through their own words and through the documents they produced and read.

### 9

First, they produced a copy of Optatus, as though it would prove that Caecilian had been condemned by the Emperor. When this copy was read against them and showed more clearly that Caecilian had been acquitted, everyone laughed at them. But because the laughter itself could not be recorded by the court recorders, they testified in the Acts, in their own words, that they had been laughed at.

Again, they read and produced a petition given to the Emperor Constantine by their predecessors. There they complained that the aforesaid Emperor was severely persecuting them. In this same petition they plainly showed that they had been defeated by Caecilian before the Emperor, and that what they had said—that Caecilian had been condemned by the Emperor—was false.

Third, they produced a letter from Constantine himself to the vicar Verinus. In it he strongly condemns them and for that reason says that they should be released from exile and abandoned to their own madness, because God had already begun to avenge himself upon them.

Thus, by this letter of the Emperor too, they confirmed that they had falsely said that Caecilian had been condemned by the Emperor. Rather, the Emperor showed that they had been defeated by Caecilian when, after vehemently cursing them, he ordered them to be released from exile so that, under God’s judgment, they might be punished—as indeed they had already begun to be punished.

### 10

Afterward they brought forward the case of Felix of Aptunga, the ordaining bishop of Caecilian, saying that this Felix had been a betrayer and that Caecilian had been ordained by him. They produced letters of the same Emperor Constantine written against themselves in support of Caecilian, in which he wrote to the proconsul that Ingentius should be sent to his court.

This Ingentius had confessed in the investigation conducted by the proconsul Aelianus [Note: Most manuscripts have *falsam fecisse*; supply “a letter.” See above, Letter 83, section 4.] that he had fabricated a falsehood against Felix, the ordaining bishop of Caecilian.

They therefore said that the Emperor would not have wished Ingentius to be sent to him without reason, unless Caecilian’s case were still pending. They tried to insinuate the utterly groundless suspicion that, after Ingentius had been sent to the Emperor’s court, the Emperor could then have judged against Caecilian and revoked by a later sentence the judgment we had read, in which he had heard the case between the parties and acquitted Caecilian.

But they were told to read this instead, and they produced nothing at all. The Emperor’s letters [Note: They are extant in Letter 88, section 4.] ordering Ingentius to be sent to him—which they themselves read against themselves in support of Caecilian—state that the proconsul Aelianus had granted a proper hearing in Felix’s case and that Felix had been shown to be innocent of the crime of betrayal. But they also state that he ordered Ingentius to be sent to his court so that he could appear before those who were there and who did not cease to bring charges against him day after day, and so that it might be made clear to them that they had attempted in vain to stir up hatred against Caecilian and to rise violently against him.

### 11

Who would believe that they had read these things against themselves in our favor, unless it had happened by the will of almighty God, so that not only their words would be preserved in the Acts, but the hands of those who signed them would also be read?

If anyone now carefully considers the sequence of the consuls and dates expressed in the Acts, he will find first that Caecilian was acquitted by episcopal judgment. Then, not long afterward, the case of Felix of Aptunga was examined by the proconsul Aelianus, where Felix was shown to be innocent; in that case Ingentius was ordered to be sent to the Emperor’s court.

Much later, the Emperor himself heard and settled the case between the parties. In that hearing he judged Caecilian innocent and them utterly calumnious.

The sequence of the consuls and dates clearly demonstrates that they falsely and calumniously said that, after Ingentius had been sent to the Emperor’s court, the Emperor changed his judgment and later condemned Caecilian, whom he had previously acquitted.

Not only were they unable to read anything about this matter, while they read so much against themselves; they are also more plainly convicted by the sequence of the consuls. After Felix’s case had been settled by the proconsular judgment, in which it was ordered that Ingentius be sent to the Emperor’s court, and not after a short interval but much later, Caecilian was acquitted by the judgment of the aforesaid Emperor, rendered after the case between the parties had been heard.

### 12

Let them not, then, say to you that we corrupted the judge with a bribe. What else do defeated men usually say? Or if we gave something to the judge so that he would pronounce judgment in our favor against them, what did we give them so that they would say—and not merely say, but even read—so many things in our favor against themselves?

Perhaps they want us to thank them before you because, although they say that the judge was bribed by us, they themselves freely provided us with so many things that they said and read in our favor against themselves?

Or if they say that they defeated us because they handled Caecilian’s case better than we did, then believe them completely. We had thought that two readings on his behalf would be sufficient; they produced four.

### 13

But why burden the letter with more? If you wish to believe us, believe us, and let us hold together the unity which God commands and loves.

If you do not wish to believe us, read the Acts themselves, or permit them to be read to you, and determine for yourselves whether what we have written to you is true.

But if you wish to do none of these things, and still desire to follow the falsehood of the party of Donatus, which has been convicted by the most manifest truth, we are free from responsibility for your punishment, when you later repent too late.

If, however, you do not despise what God has granted you, and, after a case conducted and made manifest with such care, you abandon your perverse custom and consent to the peace and unity of Christ, we shall rejoice in your correction. The Sacraments of Christ, which you possess for judgment while in sacrilegious schism, will be useful and salutary for you when, in Catholic peace, you have Christ as your head—where “love covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8).

We wrote this to you on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July [Note: One Vatican manuscript has “the nineteenth day before the Kalends of July.” In the editions, the reading was formerly “in the eighth consulship of the most devout Augustus Honorius,” erroneously, as Baronius observed. For Honorius’s eighth consulship fell in the year of Christ 409. But this letter was written in the year immediately following the Carthaginian Conference, namely in 412, which was the ninth consulship of Honorius. Eight manuscripts support this; some have “eighth consul,” others “ninth consul.”], in the ninth consulship of the most devout Augustus Honorius, so that these letters might reach each one of you wherever possible.

## Letter 142

[Note: Elsewhere 257; the letter that was 142 is now in the Appendix as 17. Written around the same time.]

Augustine to the presbyters Saturninus and Eufratas, and to the other clergy, rejoicing over their return to the Church, confirming them in its communion, and exhorting them faithfully to carry out ecclesiastical duties, each according to his rank.

To his most beloved lords, the presbyter-brothers Saturninus and Eufratas, and to the clergy who are with you, converted to the unity and peace of Christ, Augustine the bishop sends greetings in the Lord.

[Note: It has been found only in the Vatican manuscript and in Lov.]

### 1

Your arrival has made us glad; but let our absence not make you sad. For we are in that Church which, by God’s favor, although it extends everywhere and is spread throughout the whole world, is nevertheless one great body under one great head. Its head is the Savior himself, as the Apostle says (Eph. 5:23; Col. 1:18).

Long before the glorification of this head, which was to take place after his resurrection, the prophet foretold it: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God.” And because, when he had been exalted above the heavens, his Church was to fill the whole earth with abundant fruitfulness, the same psalm immediately added: “And your glory is over all the earth” (Ps. 56:12).

Therefore, beloved, let us remain with steadfast mind and most firm heart under so exalted a head, in so glorious a body, in which we are members of one another. Even if my absence were far away in the most distant lands, we would still be together in him, from whose bodily unity we must not withdraw.

For if one house contained us, we would certainly be said to be together. How much more are we together when we are together in one body! Indeed, the Truth itself also testifies that we are in one house, since holy Scripture, which says that the Church is the body of Christ, likewise says that this same Church is the house of God.

### 2

This house, however, is not built in one corner of the world, but throughout the whole earth. Hence that psalm whose title reads, “When the house was being built after the captivity,” begins in this way: “Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth” (Ps. 95:1).

In the oldness of the old human being, the devil had taken the whole world captive. After this captivity, when the house is built, the renewal of the faithful in the new human being is signified.

Hence the Apostle says, “Put off the old human being, and put on the one who has been created according to God” (Eph. 4:22, 24). And because this takes place throughout the whole earth in Catholic unity, just as it is said in another psalm, “Your glory is over all the earth,” so here, after it had said, “Sing to the Lord a new song,” to show when the house is being built—in this new song—it immediately adds, “Sing to the Lord, all the earth.”

The same psalm exhorts the workers through whom this great house is built when it goes on to say: “Announce his salvation from day to day; proclaim his glory among the nations, his wonders among all peoples.” A little later it says: “Bring to the Lord, families of the nations, bring to the Lord glory and honor.”

What this house is—that is, the Catholic Church—I said elsewhere [Note: In Lov. it was read as follows: “Elsewhere, that is, in the first reply against Petilianus, I said: ‘For the peace of Christ, return to the Church, which did not condemn what it did not know, if, for the peace of Donatus, it pleased you to recall what had been condemned.’” These words, taken incorrectly from Book 1 against the Letters of Petilianus, chapter 13, ought to have been removed here.].

### 3

The enemies of this great house, whose many testimonies are found throughout the whole of Scripture, yielded to such testimonies to the extent that they admitted that they had no case against the transmarine Church, although they confessed that it was Catholic.

We are in communion with this Church so that we may deserve to be joined to the members of Christ and embrace the structure of his body with the devoted affection of the most faithful love.

For in the unity of this Church, whoever lives wickedly “eats and drinks judgment upon himself,” as the Apostle says (1 Cor. 11:29). But whoever lives well is not prejudiced by another’s case or another’s person.

Thus, when they were pressed concerning the case of Maximian, they too were forced by their own mouths to confess that neither does one case prejudice another case, nor one person another person.

Nevertheless, we are concerned for one another as members of one body, so that all of us who, with God’s help, belong to the future granary may meanwhile endure the chaff together on the threshing floor, lest, because of the chaff destined for future fire, we abandon the Lord’s threshing floor.

### 4

Carry out faithfully and cheerfully the ecclesiastical duties that belong to you, each according to your rank, and sincerely fulfill your ministry for the sake of that God under whom we are fellow servants and to whom we consider that we shall render an account of our actions.

For this reason, the bowels of mercy ought to abound in you, because “there will be judgment without mercy for the one who has not shown mercy” (James 2:13).

Therefore pray with us also for those who are still grieving, so that the weakness of their carnal mind, gathered and contracted through long habit, may be healed.

For who does not understand how good and pleasant it is “for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132:1), if this pleasantness touches a sound throat, so that it rejects the bitterness of division—a mind that loves the sweetness of love?

God is powerful and merciful. We pray to him for them, so that through whatever opportunities he may also draw them to salvation. May the Lord preserve you in peace.

## Letter 143

[Note: Corrected with the help of a. bg. bl. c. cc. ff. g. gv. j. n. r. s. t. vd.; two copies marked a.; two marked bn.; two marked vc.; five marked v.; and Am. Bad. Er. Lov.]

[Note: Elsewhere 7; the letter that was 143 is now 187. Written in 412.]

He gives a brief response to a question proposed by Marcellinus from the divine books. Then he explains a passage criticized from his books *On Free Choice of the Will*, declaring first how much authority he wishes to be attributed to his writings. On the same occasion he touches upon various questions concerning the origin of souls. Finally, he rejects the doubt of a certain person—presumably Volusianus—who did not believe that Mary had given birth as a virgin because such a thing had never happened before.

To the eminent lord, distinguished in merit and greatly beloved son Marcellinus, Augustine sends greetings in the Lord.

### 1

When I was writing back, I searched for the letter of yours that I received through the holy brother and my fellow bishop Boniface, but I did not find it. I nevertheless remembered that in it you had asked how Pharaoh’s magicians, after all the water of Egypt had been changed into blood, found water from which they could make something similar.

This question is usually answered in two ways: either that water from the sea could have been supplied, or—and this is more credible—that these plagues did not occur in the region where the children of Israel were. Certain passages of that Scripture make this very clear, even where they do not say explicitly what ought to be understood.

### 2

The letter of yours that the presbyter Urbanus brought contains a question proposed to me from books not divine but mine—the books I wrote *On Free Choice of the Will*.

In questions of this kind I do not labor greatly. For even if my opinion cannot be defended by clear reasoning, it is still mine, not the opinion of an author whose meaning it is not permissible to disapprove, even when, because we have not understood him, we take from it something that ought to be rejected.

I therefore confess that I am trying to belong to the number of those who write by making progress and make progress by writing. Thus, if I have stated something either incautiously or in an unlearned manner—something that deserves to be criticized not only by others who are able to see it, but also by me myself, since, if I make progress, I ought eventually to see it—there is neither cause for surprise nor for sorrow. Rather, there should be pardon and rejoicing: not because an error has been made, but because it has been rejected.

For a person loves himself very perversely if he wants others to err so that his own error may remain hidden. How much better and more useful it is that, where he himself has erred, others should not err, so that through their admonition he may be free from error! If he is unwilling to be corrected, at least let him not have companions in error.

For if God grants me what I wish—that I may gather together and point out, in some work undertaken for this very purpose, whatever in all my books rightly displeases me—then people will see how little I favor my own person.

### 3

But you who love me greatly, if you defend me against those whose malice, incompetence, or understanding leads them to criticize me, by saying that I have never erred in my writings, you labor in vain. You have undertaken a bad case, and with me as judge you are easily defeated in it.

For I do not like to be regarded by my dearest friends as someone I am not. Indeed, they love not me but another in my place, under my name, if they love not what I am but what I am not.

To the extent that they know me or believe what is true about me, I am loved by them. But to the extent that they attribute to me what they do not recognize in me, they love in my place another person who is such as they suppose me to be.

The greatest Roman authority in eloquence, Tullius, said of a certain man: “He never uttered a word that he would wish to retract.” Although this praise may appear most splendid, it is nevertheless more believable of someone excessively foolish than of a perfect wise man.

For even those whom people commonly call simpletons—the more they depart from common sense and the more absurd and tasteless they are—the more they utter no word that they would wish to retract. To regret a bad, foolish, or ill-considered statement is, of course, characteristic of sensible people.

But if the saying is taken in a favorable sense, so that we believe someone to have been such that, while speaking wisely about everything, he never uttered a word that he would wish to retract, this should be believed with the most salutary piety of the men of God who spoke under the sharp impulse of the Holy Spirit, rather than of the man whom Cicero praises in this way.

I am so far from that excellence that, if I have uttered no word that I would wish to retract, I would seem more like a fool than a wise man. For those writings are supremely worthy of the highest authority whose author uttered no word—not one that he would wish to retract, but one that he ought to retract.

Whoever has not yet attained this should make modesty his second choice, since he could not make wisdom his first. Since he was unable to speak carefully about everything that ought not to be regretted, let him regret whatever he discovers ought not to have been said.

### 4

Since, then, I have uttered—not, as some of my dearest friends think, no words or only a few, but perhaps more than even malicious people suppose—which I would rather recall, if I could, Cicero’s celebrated saying does not flatter me: “He never uttered a word that he would wish to recall.” Rather, Horace’s saying troubles me deeply: “A spoken word does not know how to return.”

This is why I am holding on longer than you wish and expect to the books on the most perilous questions—namely, *On Genesis* and *On the Trinity*—so that, if they must contain some things rightly subject to criticism, there may at least be fewer of them than there could be if they were published in hasty and ill-considered haste.

For you, as your letters indicate—for this was also written to me by the holy brother and my fellow bishop Florentius—are pressing for their publication so that they may be defended by me, while I live in this flesh, if they should perhaps begin to be attacked either by biting enemies or even by friends who understand them inadequately. You say this, of course, because you do not think that there is anything in them that could rightly be censured; otherwise you would urge me not toward their publication, but rather toward more careful correction.

I, however, look more toward true judges, judges strict in accordance with truth, among whom I wish first of all to place myself, so that only those matters may reach them for criticism which, although I examined them diligently, I was entirely unable to see.

### 5

Since this is so, let those who think that I established and fixed something certain about the human soul—whether it comes by descent from parents, or whether it sinned in an earlier and heavenly life, so that it deserved to be enclosed in corruptible flesh—carefully observe what I wrote in the third book of *On Free Choice*, when I was discussing rational substance. I put it this way:

> “In lower bodies, however, after sin the soul, having been assigned its place, rules its own body, not entirely according to its will, but as the laws of the universe permit.”

Let them see how carefully I weighed these words, so that, while retaining what I hold as certain—namely, that after the sin of the first man all other human beings were and are born in the flesh of sin, for whose healing the likeness of the flesh of sin came in the Lord—all my words might sound in such a way as to prejudice none of the four opinions which I later set out and distinguished.

I did not affirm any one of them, but, setting aside their discussion for the time being, I determined the matter on which I was engaged in such a way that, whichever of those opinions might be true, God would undoubtedly be praised.

### 6

For whether all souls are propagated from that one soul, or are individually made in each person, or are created elsewhere and sent here, or descend spontaneously into bodies—in any case, without doubt, this rational creature, that is, the nature of the human soul, having been assigned its place in lower, that is, earthly, bodies after sin, rules its own body, not entirely according to its will, while it remains established that this occurred after the sin of the first man.

> **Note:** The Gallican manuscripts have: “According to its will, while it remains established that after sin …” The same is found in four Vatican manuscripts, except that two of these lack the word *interim* (“while”). Some codices have: “while it remains established that by sin …” Others, omitting the remaining words, have only: “not entirely according to its will.” For it was not said, etc.

For it was not said, “After its own sin,” or, “After it sinned,” but “After sin,” so that, if at some later time an examination of the matter should make it possible, whether this refers properly to its sin or to the sin of the parent of its flesh, what was said might be understood correctly: “After sin, having been assigned its place in lower bodies, it rules its own body, not entirely according to its will.”

For “the flesh desires against the spirit” (Galatians 5:17), “we groan, being burdened” (2 Corinthians 5:4), and “the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wisdom 9:15). And who could recount all the troubles of bodily weakness? These will certainly not exist when “this corruptible body has put on incorruption” (1 Corinthians 15:53), so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.

Then, therefore, the spiritual body will rule entirely according to its will. But now it does not rule entirely according to its will, but as the laws of the universe permit—laws by which it has been established that bodies, once brought forth, die, and, once grown, grow old.

For the soul of that first man, before sin, even though it did not yet possess a spiritual body but an animal one, nevertheless ruled according to its will. After sin, however—that is, after sin had been committed in the flesh from which the flesh of sin would thereafter be propagated—the rational soul was assigned its place in lower bodies in such a way that it does not rule its body entirely according to its will.

If those who do not yet accept this in the case of infants—who have as yet committed no sins of their own—nevertheless admit that they already possess the flesh of sin, since even for its healing, when they are baptized, the likeness of the flesh of sin is necessary, then they still have no grounds for being angry with these words of ours. For it is established, unless I am mistaken, that this same flesh, even if it is weak by nature rather than through fault, nevertheless began to be born after sin, since Adam was not created in this condition, nor did he beget anyone before sin.

### 7

Let them therefore seek other matters that they may rightly criticize, not only in other works published too hastily, but also in these very books of mine, *On Free Choice*. I do not deny that they will find something by which they may confer a benefit on me; for if those books, which have already passed into the hands of many people, cannot be corrected, I certainly can be corrected, since I am still alive.

But let only those criticize these words, which I placed with such caution that I prescribed nothing to any of the four opinions or arguments concerning the origin of the soul, who think that my own hesitation about so obscure a matter ought itself to be criticized.

I do not defend myself against them by claiming that I am right to hesitate in this question, since I have no doubt at all that the soul is immortal—not in the same way as God, who alone possesses immortality (1 Timothy 6:16), but in a manner proper to its kind—and that it is a creature, not the substance of the Creator, together with whatever else I hold most certainly concerning its nature.

But since the extreme obscurity of the question concerning the soul’s origin compels me to do this, let them rather extend a hand to one who confesses his ignorance and desires to know what the truth is. Let them teach me, if they can, or show me, if they have learned anything about this matter either by certain reasoning or by believing the clearest divine utterance.

For if a reason is offered against the authority of the divine Scriptures, however subtle it may be, it deceives by a resemblance to truth; for it cannot itself be true. Again, if the authority of the holy Scriptures is set against a most manifest and certain reason, the person who does this does not understand that he is setting against the truth not the meaning of those Scriptures, which he was unable to penetrate, but rather his own meaning; nor does he oppose what he finds in them, but what he has found, as though on their behalf, within himself.

### 8

For example, attend carefully to what I shall say. Near the end of the book called *Ecclesiastes*, when Scripture was speaking about the dissolution of the human being that takes place through this death by which the soul is separated from the body, it says:

> “And the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it” (Ecclesiastes 12:7).

The statement of this authority is undoubtedly certain, and it deceives no one by falsehood. But if someone wishes to interpret it in such a way as to try to establish from it the propagation of souls—that all the others proceed from that one soul which God gave to the first man—it seems to support him that the flesh is mentioned there under the name “dust.”

For surely in this passage “dust” and “spirit” are understood to mean nothing other than flesh and soul. Thus he may assert that the soul returns to God because it is descended from that soul which God gave to the first man, just as the flesh returns to the earth because it too is descended from that flesh which was made from the earth in the first man. In this way he may argue that, on the basis of what is well known concerning the flesh, we ought to believe what is hidden concerning the soul.

There is no uncertainty concerning the descent of the flesh, but there is uncertainty concerning the soul. Yet both are set forth in this testimony as though each were assigned to its counterpart by a similar reasoning: the flesh returns to the earth, as it was, since it was taken from the earth when the first man was made; and the spirit returns to God who gave it when, after breathing into the face of the man whom he had formed the breath of life, “the man became a living soul” (Genesis 2:7), so that thereafter the offspring of each thing would proceed from both.

### 9

Nevertheless, if it is true that souls are not propagated from that one soul, but that God creates them elsewhere and gives one to each person, this too agrees with the statement: “The spirit returns to God who gave it.”

Thus only the other two opinions seem to be excluded. For if individual souls were made in each person when they are created, it would not seem that one ought to say, “The spirit returns to God who gave it,” but rather, “to God who made it.” For “gave” sounds as though what could be given already existed elsewhere.

Moreover, they insist upon and press the word “returns,” saying: “How will it return to a place where it has never previously been?” They maintain that it ought rather to have been said, “And let it go,” or “proceed” or “go to God,” rather than “let it return to God,” if this spirit is not to be believed to have previously been there.

Likewise, how souls spontaneously descend into bodies is not so readily explained when Scripture says that he “gave it.” Thus, as I said, these two opinions struggle against the words of this testimony: one, according to which each soul is made in its own body; the other, according to which souls spontaneously descend into bodies.

But the words fit the other two opinions without difficulty, whether souls come by descent from that one soul or, having already been created and established with God, are given individually to individual bodies.

### 10

And yet, if the advocates of the opinion according to which souls are made in their individual bodies assert that it was said of the spirit—which is used here for the soul—“God gave it,” in the same way that we rightly say that he gave us eyes, ears, hands, or anything else, they may argue as follows:

These bodily members had not already been made outside the body and stored somewhere, to be given—that is, added and joined—when needed. Rather, God made them there within the body to which he is said to have given them.

I do not see what answer can be given to this, unless perhaps other testimonies are produced, or some certain argument by which this opinion can be refuted.

Likewise, those who think that souls spontaneously descend into bodies understand the statement “God gave it” in the same way as the statement, “God gave them over to the desires of their hearts” (Romans 1:24).

Accordingly, one word remains—the word “returns”—which must be explained: how can a soul return to a place where it has not previously been, if souls are made in their respective bodies? By this one word alone, one of the four opinions is placed under pressure.

Yet I do not rashly think that the opinion should be rejected because of this one word, lest it perhaps be shown that, by some manner of expression of the kind ordinarily used by holy Scripture, this too could rightly have been said, so that a created spirit may be understood to “return” to God as its creator, from whom it was created, and not as to one with whom it previously existed.

### 11

I have written these things so that anyone who wishes to establish and defend one of the four opinions concerning the soul may produce evidence of the following kind: either passages from Scriptures received into ecclesiastical authority which cannot be understood in any other way, such as the statement that God made the human being; or reasoning so certain that contradiction is either impossible or rightly judged similar to insanity.

For example, someone might say that no one can know the truth or be deceived except one who is alive. We do not need the authority of Scripture in order to see how true this is; common sense itself proclaims it with such evident reasoning that anyone who contradicted it would be regarded as utterly insane.

If anyone can provide such proof in this extremely obscure question concerning the soul, let him assist my ignorance. But if he cannot, let him not criticize my hesitation.

### 12

As for the virginity of holy Mary: if what I wrote does not persuade anyone that this could have happened, then everything that has happened wondrously in bodily matters must be denied.

But if it is not believed for the reason that it happened only once, ask the friend who is still troubled by this whether anything can be found in secular writings that happened only once and yet is believed—not with the vain credulity of fable, but, as they suppose, with historical faith. Ask him, I beg you.

If he denies that anything of this kind can be found in those writings, he must be admonished. But if he admits it, the question is settled.

## LETTER CXLIV

> **Note:** Corrected according to manuscripts and editions designated a, bg, bl, bn, c, cc, ff, g, gv, j, n, r, s, t, vc, two sb manuscripts, four v manuscripts, and according to the editions of Amerbach, Bad., Erasmus, and Louvain.  
> **Note:** Elsewhere numbered 130; the letter that was 144 is now 145. Written around the year 412.

Augustine congratulates the people of Cirta who had converted from the Donatist faction to communion with the Catholic Church, exhorting them to attribute this to the divine gift.

**To the honorable lords, deservedly worthy of welcome, dearest and most longed-for brothers in every rank of honor, the people of Cirta, Augustine, bishop.**

> **Note:** Amerbach, Bad., and Erasmus read *Circensibus* (“to the Circenses”).

### 1

If what was seriously troubling us in your city has been removed; if the hardness of the human heart, resisting the most manifest and, in a certain sense, public truth, has been overcome by the power of that same truth; if the sweetness of peace is now savored, and the love of unity no longer strikes wounded eyes but enlightens and strengthens healthy ones—these are not our works, but God’s.

I would not attribute these things wholly to human works even if, while we were with you, such a great conversion of the multitude had resulted from our speaking and exhorting. He accomplishes and effects this who, through his ministers, gives outward admonition by signs, but inwardly teaches by the realities themselves through his own action.

Nor should we be slower to hasten to visit you because whatever has been accomplished laudably in you has been done not by us but by him “who alone works wonders” (Psalm 71:18). We ought much more eagerly to hurry to behold divine works than our own, because if we are in any respect a good work, we are his work, not the work of human beings. Hence the Apostle said: “Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:7).

### 2

You write—and from those writings we too remember—that Xenocrates, by discussing the fruit of temperance, suddenly converted Polemo, not merely a drunkard but actually drunk at that moment, to different habits.

Although, therefore, as you wisely and truthfully understood, he was not thereby won for God but merely freed from the domination of luxury, I would still attribute even this improvement in him not to human work but to divine work.

For even whatever good qualities belong to the body itself, which is the lowest part of us—such as form, strength, health, and anything of that kind—come only from God, the creator and perfecter of nature. How much more can no one else bestow the good qualities of the soul!

What could human folly imagine more proudly or ungratefully than that, although God makes a human being beautiful in the flesh, a human being could make him chaste in soul?

This is written in the book of *Christian Wisdom*:

> “When I knew that no one could be continent unless God gave it, and that it was itself wisdom to know whose gift this was” (Wisdom 8:21).

Therefore, if Polemo, having been made continent from a life of luxury, had known whose gift this was in such a way that, after abandoning the superstitions of the nations, he piously worshiped him, he would have become not only continent but also truly wise and salutarily religious. This would have benefited him not only for the moral goodness of the present life but also for the immortality of the future life.

How much less, then, ought I to claim for myself the conversion of you or of your people, which you have just announced to us, and which, without doubt, was brought about by divine action when I was neither speaking nor even present—at least wherever it truly occurred!

Know this above all; think about it with pious humility. Give thanks to God, brothers—give thanks to God. Fear God, lest you fail; love him, that you may advance.

### 3

But if the love of human beings still secretly separates some, and fear of human beings deceitfully gathers others together, let those who are such observe that they neither deceive God, before whom the human conscience lies naked, nor escape him as judge.

If anything concerning the question of unity troubles them out of concern for their salvation, let them impose upon themselves, as I think is most just, the obligation to believe concerning the Catholic Church—that is, the Church spread throughout the whole world—what the divine Scriptures say, not what human tongues utter in their curses.

As for the very dispute that has arisen among human beings—whatever sort of people they may have been, they certainly do not prejudice the promises of God, who said to Abraham, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Genesis 26:4), a promise believed when it was heard as prophecy and denied when it is seen as fulfilled—let them for the moment consider this one brief and, unless I am mistaken, invincible point:

Either this case was tried in an ecclesiastical judgment overseas, or it was not.

If it was not tried there, the fellowship of Christ throughout all the overseas nations is innocent, and we rejoice in communion with that fellowship. Therefore those people are certainly separated from the innocent by a sacrilegious division.

But if this case was tried there, who does not understand, who does not feel, who does not see that those whose fellowship was separated from it were defeated in the case?

Let them therefore choose whether they prefer to believe what the ecclesiastical judges pronounced or what the defeated litigants mutter.

In view of this argument—which is exceedingly brief in wording and very easy to understand—consider carefully, with the prudence you possess, how nothing sober can be answered to it. And yet the wicked Polemo is overthrown even more by the drunkenness of long-established error.

> **Note:** The editions read: “He is turned more by the drunkenness of long-established error.” The manuscripts, however, read: “He is overthrown.” We suspect that this passage was abbreviated by scribes; this may even be inferred from the particle “more.”

Forgive, perhaps, this longer letter rather than a more pleasant one; nevertheless, as I think, it is more useful than flattering, honorable lords, deservedly worthy of welcome, dearest and most longed-for brothers.

As for our coming to you, may God fulfill the desire of both sides. We cannot express in words how ardently the fire of love kindles us to visit you, but we have no doubt that you will kindly believe this.

## LETTER CXLV

> **Note:** Revised according to manuscripts and editions designated a, bg, bl, c, cc, ff, g, gv, l, n, r, s, t, two sb manuscripts, two vc manuscripts, four v manuscripts, and according to the editions of Amerbach, Bad., Erasmus, and Louvain.  
> **Note:** Elsewhere numbered 144; the letter that was 145 is now 248. Written around the year 412 or 413.

Replying to Anastasius, Augustine teaches that righteousness is fulfilled not through the law but through grace, and not through fear but through love.

**To the holy and desirable brother Anastasius, Augustine sends greetings in the Lord.**

### 1

A most trustworthy opportunity has presented itself for greeting your sincerity through the honorable servants of God, our brothers Lupicinus and Concordialis. Through them, even if I did not write, Your Charity could learn everything that is happening among us.

For I know how deeply you love us in Christ, just as you know how deeply we in turn are loved by you in him. Therefore I did not doubt that you might be saddened if you saw them, who have departed from us and are joined to us by such close familiarity, arrive without a letter from me, especially since I was also in your debt for a reply.

For since I received your letter, I do not know that I have replied until now. We are so bound and burdened by many cares that I am even unaware of this.

### 2

We very much wish to know how things are with you and whether the Lord has granted you some rest, insofar as rest is possible in this land. For “if one member is glorified, all the members rejoice together” (1 Corinthians 12:26). It often happens that, while we think of some of our brothers established in even the smallest measure of rest amid our anxieties, we are ourselves refreshed to no small degree, as though we too were living more quietly and peacefully in them.

Yet when troubles multiply in the fragility of this life, they compel us to desire eternal rest. For this world is more dangerously pleasing than troublesome, and it must be feared more when it invites us to love it than when it warns and compels us to despise it.

For since everything in it consists of “the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the world” (1 John 2:16), the affection for earthly sweetness often insinuates itself even into those who prefer spiritual, invisible, and eternal things to such objects. It accompanies our duties with its pleasures.

The better future things are for charity, the more forcefully present things assail our weakness. Would that those who know how to see and lament these things might deserve to overcome and escape them! The human will can accomplish this in no way without the grace of God; nor can it be called free so long as it is subject to desires that conquer and enslave it.

“For by whatever anyone is overcome, by this he is enslaved” (2 Peter 2:19). And the Son of God himself says: “If the Son makes you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8:36).

### 3

The law, therefore, by teaching and commanding what cannot be fulfilled without grace, demonstrates to a human being his weakness, so that the weakness thus revealed may seek the Savior, by whom the healed will can do what, while weak, it could not do.

The law leads to faith; faith obtains a more abundant Spirit; the Spirit pours out love; love fulfills the law.

For this reason the law is called a pedagogue (Galatians 3:24). Under its most threatening severity, “whoever calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Joel 2:32). But “how will they call upon him in whom they have not believed?” (Romans 10:14).

Therefore, lest the letter kill without the Spirit, “the Spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6), and is given to those who believe and call upon God. “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5), so that what the same Apostle says may come to pass: “Love is the fullness of the law” (Romans 13:10).

Thus the law is good for the one who uses it lawfully (1 Timothy 1:8). A person uses it lawfully when, understanding why it was given, he takes refuge through its threats in the grace that sets him free.

Whoever is ungrateful toward this grace, by which the ungodly are justified, and trusts in his own powers as though he were to fulfill the law, “not knowing the righteousness of God and seeking to establish his own, is not subject to the righteousness of God” (Romans 10:3). Thus the law becomes for him not assistance toward absolution but a bond of guilt.

This is not because the law is evil, but because, as it is written, “sin, through what is good, works death” in such people (Romans 7:13). For through the commandment the person who knows by the commandment how evil the act is commits a more serious offense.

### 4

The person who does not sin out of fear of punishment vainly thinks that he has conquered sin. For even if the outward act of evil desire is not carried out, evil desire itself remains an enemy within.

Who is found innocent before God if, once what is feared is removed, he wishes what is forbidden to be done? Thus he is guilty in his very will: he wishes to do what is not permitted, but does not do it only because it cannot be done with impunity.

Insofar as it lies within him, he would prefer that there were no justice prohibiting and punishing sins. And if he would prefer that justice did not exist, who could doubt that, if he were able, he would remove it?

How, then, is he just—being such an enemy of justice that, if power were given him, he would remove the justice that commands, so that he would not have to endure it threatening or judging?

He is therefore an enemy of justice who does not sin out of fear of punishment. But he will be a friend of justice if he does not sin out of love for it; then he will truly fear sinning.

For the person who fears hell does not fear sinning, but burning. The person fears sinning who hates sin itself as he hates hell.

This is “the pure fear of the Lord, enduring forever and ever” (Psalm 18:10). The fear of punishment, however, contains torment and is not in love; perfect love casts it out (1 John 4:18).

### 5

Everyone hates sin only to the extent that he loves justice. This cannot be brought about by the law, which terrifies through the letter, but by the Spirit, who heals through grace.

Then what the Apostle urges comes to pass:

> “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. For just as you presented your members as slaves to impurity and lawlessness for lawlessness, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness for sanctification” (Romans 6:19).

What does “just as this, so also that” mean except this: just as no fear compelled you to sin, but the lust and pleasure of sin itself did so, so fear of punishment should not drive you to live justly, but the delight and love of justice should lead you?

This, as I see it, is not yet perfect justice, but justice that has in some way reached maturity. For the Apostle would not have prefaced his statement with “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh” unless something more remained to be said, if they had already been able to bear it.

For a greater service is owed to justice than human beings are accustomed to offer to sin. Bodily punishment, even if it does not arise from the will, nevertheless restrains a person from the act of sin. There is scarcely anyone who would openly commit an act by which he might obtain unlawful and impure pleasure if it were certain that the torment of punishment would immediately follow.

Justice, however, must be loved in such a way that even bodily punishments should not restrain us from its works. Even among the hands of cruel enemies, our works should shine before human beings, so that those who are able to be pleased by them may “glorify our Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16).

### 6

This is why that most courageous lover of justice cries out:

> “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? As it is written: ‘For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are reckoned as sheep for slaughter’” (Psalm 44:22).

> **Note:** Two Vatican manuscripts read “because of him” instead of “through him.”

> “But in all these things we overwhelmingly conquer through him who loved us. For I am certain that neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:35–39).

Observe how he does not simply say, “Who will separate us from Christ?” Rather, showing from what source we cling to Christ, he says, “Who will separate us from the love of Christ?”

We therefore cling to Christ through love, not through fear of punishment.

Then, after recalling those things that appear to possess force but do not possess the power to separate us, he concluded by calling it the love of God, the same love he had called the love of Christ.

And what is “from the love of Christ” except “from the love of justice”? For it was said of him:

> “He was made for us by God wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption, so that, as it is written, ‘Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord’” (1 Corinthians 1:30–31; Jeremiah 9:24).

Therefore, just as the person is utterly unjust whom even bodily punishments do not deter from the impure works of sordid pleasure, so the person is most just who is not recalled from the holy works of radiant love even by fear of bodily punishments.

### 7

This love of God—which must be held in mind through continual reflection—is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Romans 5:5), so that “the one who boasts may boast in the Lord.”

When, therefore, we feel ourselves poor and needy in that love by which the law is most truly fulfilled, we must not try to draw its riches from our own poverty, but must ask for them by praying, seeking, and knocking.

Then may he with whom is the fountain of life give us to drink deeply from the abundance of his house and from the torrent of his delight (Psalm 36:9–10). Overflowing and strengthened by this, we shall not merely avoid being swallowed up by sorrow, but shall even glory in tribulations, knowing that “tribulation produces endurance, endurance character, and character hope; and hope does not disappoint” (Romans 5:3–5).

This is not because we can do it through ourselves, but because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

### 8

I was glad to speak with you at least by letter about these matters, since I could not do so when I was present. I did not do this on your account—for you do not seek lofty things but consent to the lowly (Romans 12:16)—but on account of certain people who attribute too much to the human will.

They think that, once the law has been given, the human will can be sufficient by itself to fulfill it, without any grace of holy inspiration assisting the teaching of the law. Through their argument, miserable and needy human weakness is persuaded that we ought not even to pray that we may not enter into temptation.

They do not dare to say this openly, but their opinion, whether they wish it or not, necessarily leads to this conclusion. For why are we told, “Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation” (Matthew 26:41)? Why, in accordance with this exhortation, did he command us, when teaching us to pray, to say, “Do not bring us into temptation” (Matthew 6:13), if this is not fulfilled by the assistance of divine grace but depends entirely upon the freedom of the human will?

What more need I say? Greet the brothers who are with you, and pray for us, so that we may be saved according to that salvation of which it is said:

> “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matthew 9:12–13).

Pray, therefore, for us, that we may be righteous. Certainly a human being cannot be righteous unless he knows and wills it, and whoever wills it fully will immediately be righteous. But this will itself will not exist in him unless the grace of the Spirit heals and assists him so that he may be able to do so.

## LETTER CXLVI

> **Note:** Transferred here from the book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*.  
> **Note:** From the book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*. The letter that was numbered 146 is now 205. Written around the year 413.

Augustine replies to Pelagius and expresses gratitude for his courteous letter.

**To the most beloved and most longed-for brother Pelagius, Augustine sends greetings in the Lord.**

I give you very great thanks because you have graciously refreshed me with your letter and informed me of your good health. May the Lord repay you with good things, so that you may always be good and live with him forever and ever, my most beloved and most longed-for lord and brother.

Although I do not recognize in myself the praises of me contained in your letter of kindness, I nevertheless cannot be ungrateful for your goodwill toward my insignificance. At the same time, I urge you rather to pray for me, so that the Lord may make me such as you already think me to be.

**In another hand:** Remember us; may you remain safe and please the Lord, my most beloved and most longed-for lord and brother.

> **Note:** Pelagius produced this letter, together with others addressed to him by orthodox bishops, in order to prove the integrity of his faith at the Synod of Diospolis, held toward the end of the year 415, as Augustine relates in his book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*. See that work, sections 50–53.

## CONCERNING THE TWO LETTERS THAT FOLLOW IMMEDIATELY  
### Book II of the *Retractions*, chapter 41

I wrote a book *On Seeing God*, in which I postponed a more careful investigation of the spiritual body that will exist in the resurrection of the saints—namely, whether, or in what manner, God, who is spirit, may also be seen through such a body.

But afterward I explained this very difficult question, sufficiently, as I think, in the final book, that is, in the twenty-second book of *The City of God*.

I also found in one of our codices, in which this book too is contained, a short memorandum written by me on this subject to Fortunatianus, bishop of Sicca. It is not recorded in the index of my shorter works either among the books or among the letters.

This book begins as follows: “Mindful of my obligation.” The other begins: “Just as I asked when I was present.”

## *ON SEEING GOD*, OR LETTER CXLVII

> **Note:** Corrected according to manuscripts and editions designated a, a, bg, bl, c, cc, cb, g, gv, j, n, r, s, vc, two bn manuscripts, two t manuscripts, three sb manuscripts, five v manuscripts, and according to the editions of Amerbach, Bad., Erasmus, and Louvain.  
> **Note:** Elsewhere numbered 112; the letter that was 147 is now 33. Apparently written in the year 413.

It teaches that God cannot be seen with bodily eyes.

**Augustine sends greetings to Paulina.**

> **Note:** The manuscripts entitle it: “A book addressed to Paulina concerning seeing God.” They do not contain the words “Augustine sends greetings to Paulina,” although Augustine is named beforehand.

### 1

Mindful of the obligation created by your request and my promise, I ought not, religious servant of God Paulina, to neglect fulfilling it as well.

When you had asked me to write to you at length and in detail about invisible God—whether he can be seen through bodily eyes—I could not refuse, lest I offend your holy eagerness. But I postponed fulfilling my promise, either because of my other occupations or because you were asking me to undertake something that required somewhat longer reflection.

Yet since this was a matter whose difficulty lay not so much in considering what ought to be thought or said about it as in determining how to persuade those who thought differently, I eventually decided that an end must be put to the delay. I hoped that divine assistance would be more readily present to me while writing than while postponing the task.

Accordingly, it first seems to me that, in this inquiry, a way of life is more powerful than a way of speaking. Those who have learned from the Lord Jesus Christ to be gentle and humble in heart (Matthew 11:29) make greater progress through reflection and prayer than through reading and hearing.

Nevertheless, speech will not for this reason cease to perform its part. But once the planter and the waterer have performed the duty of their office, speech leaves the rest to him who gives the growth. For he himself formed even the planter and the waterer.

2. Understand the words of this discussion according to the inner man. For he is renewed day by day, even while this outward man is being corrupted (II Cor. IV, 16), whether by the discipline of abstinence, some bodily illness, or any other accident—or certainly by the advance of age itself, which must also affect those who remain long in sound bodily health. Raise, then, the spirit of your mind, which is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of him who created it (Col. III, 10), where Christ dwells in you through faith (Eph. III, 17); where there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female (Gal. III, 28); where you will not die when you begin to be released from the body, since there too you have not withered, although you are weighed down by years. With this inner part of you raised up, pay attention and see what I am saying. I do not want you to follow my authority and therefore think that you must believe something merely because I say it. Rather, believe either the canonical Scriptures, if you do not yet see that something is true, or the truth itself as it demonstrates inwardly, so that you may clearly see it.

3. By way of example I shall say something that may prepare you more securely for these matters, especially for the very point on which the task of discussion in this work has been assigned to us. We believe that God can be seen—not because we see him either through the bodily eyes, as we see this sun, or through the gaze of the mind, as each person inwardly sees himself living, willing, seeking, knowing, or not knowing.

After reading these very words, you remember that you have seen the sun through your bodily eyes; you can also see it immediately, if it is the appropriate time and you are in a place where the sky is open to your eyes in the direction of the sun. But for seeing those things which I said are perceived by the mind—that you are alive, that you want to see God, that you seek this, and that you know yourself to be alive, willing, and seeking, while you do not know how God is seen—you do not employ the bodily eyes, nor do you perceive or seek any spatial interval through which your gaze must be extended in order to reach and discern them.

Thus you see your life, your will, your seeking, your knowledge, and your ignorance, since the very sight of seeing that you do not know is not itself to be despised. Thus, I say, you see all these things: you see them in yourself and possess them within yourself, without any outlines of shapes or brilliance of colors—more clearly and certainly in proportion as you perceive them more simply and inwardly. Since, then, we do not now see God either with the bodily eyes, as we see bodies, whether heavenly or earthly, or with the gaze of the mind, as we see those things—some of which I have mentioned—which you contemplate with complete certainty within yourself, why do we believe that he is seen? Only because we give credence to Scripture, where it is written, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V, 8), and to whatever else has been written in this sense with the same divine authority—which we consider it sacrilegious not to believe, while we have no doubt that believing it is an act of piety.

4. Hold fast, then, to this distinction: if, in the course of discussion, I point out something to you which you see with the eyes of the flesh or perceive through any other bodily sense, or which you remember having perceived in the manner in which colors, noises, smells, tastes, heat, and whatever else we apprehend through the body by seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, or touching are perceived; or if you see it with the mind’s intuition in the way you see your life, will, thought, memory, understanding, knowledge, faith, and whatever else you perceive with the mind, and of whose existence you are certain not merely by believing but by plainly living—judge that I have demonstrated it.

But if I have not demonstrated something in such a way that it can be held as seen and apprehended either by bodily or by mental sense, and yet have said something that must necessarily be either true or false, although it is not seen in either of those two ways, then it remains only to believe it or not to believe it. If, however, its authority is firmly established by the divine Scriptures—namely, those which are called canonical in the Church—it must be believed without any doubt. As for other witnesses or testimonies by which one is persuaded that something should be believed, you may believe or not believe them, according to the weight you judge them to possess—or not to possess—for producing faith.

5. For if we had believed nothing that we had not seen—that is, that we had not perceived in the present appearance [Note: [Col. 0598] Lov., “in the present” (*in praesentia*). But all the other books have “in present appearance” (*in praesenti apparentia*).] either with mind or body, and had not learned from the holy Scriptures by reading or hearing, how would we know that there are cities where we have never been; that Rome was founded by Romulus; or, to speak of places nearer to us, that Constantinople was founded by Constantine? Finally, how would we know which parents had begotten us, from which fathers, grandfathers, and ancestors we were born?

Although we know very many such things, we did not learn them either through some present sense, as we learn the sun or the will of our own mind, or through the authority of canonical writings, as we learned that Adam was the first human being, or that Christ was born, suffered, and rose again in the flesh. Rather, we learned them from other people’s reports, whose testimony we judged should not be doubted, at least in this kind of matter. If we are mistaken in any of these things—by believing that something is so when it is not, or that it is not so when it is— we judge that there is no danger, provided it is not contrary to the faith by which piety is formed.

This preliminary statement of mine does not yet address the question proposed. It prepares you, however, and others who will read these things, to understand what sort of judges you should be of my writings or of those of anyone else: lest you either suppose that you know what you do not know, or rashly believe what you have not apprehended as evident in the thing to be known, either through bodily sensation or mental perception, nor learned from the authority of the canonical Scriptures—although it was not present to your bodily or mental senses—as something that ought nevertheless to be believed.

# CHAPTER I

6. Have we now, then, arrived at the subject itself? Or must the reader still be prepared? Some people think that believing the very thing we are discussing, when the thing believed is true, is nothing other than contemplating it with the mind.

If that is so, our preceding preliminary statement is mistaken. There we distinguished between sensing something through the body—for example, the sun in the sky, or a mountain, a tree, or any other body on earth—and contemplating with the mind something that is nevertheless evident, such as our will, which we inwardly observe when we want something; or thought, when we think; or memory, when we remember; or something of that kind in the soul without the body. We distinguished these from believing something that is neither present nor remembered as having been present to bodily or mental sight, such as Adam’s having been created without parents, and Christ’s having been born from a Virgin, suffered, and risen again.

These things did take place bodily, and, if we had been present at the time, could certainly have been seen by the body. But now they are not present, as this light is present to our eyes, or as the will by which we now want something is present to the mind. Since this distinction is not false, the preliminary explanation evidently lacked only this: the difference between believing and mentally contemplating something present had not been expressed with sufficient clarity to prevent their being considered wholly one and the same.

# CHAPTER II

7. What, then, shall we say? Is it sufficient to say that the difference between seeing and believing is that present things are seen, while absent things are believed? It may indeed be sufficient, if by “present things” here we understand those which are at hand to the senses, whether of mind or body—whence they are also called “present.” Thus I plainly see this bodily light through bodily sensation, and likewise my will, because it is at hand to the senses of the mind and is inwardly present to me.

If, however, someone tells me his will, while his mouth and voice are present to me, nevertheless, because the will itself which he discloses to me is hidden from my bodily and mental senses, I believe it; I do not see it. Or, if I think that he is lying, I do not believe it, even if what he says happens to be true.

Things absent from our senses are therefore believed, provided the witness borne to them appears reliable. Things present to the senses, on the other hand, are seen, and for this reason are called “present” to the senses either of mind or of body.

There are five bodily senses: seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching. Sight, strictly speaking, is especially assigned to the eyes; nevertheless, we use the word “see” with respect to the other senses as well. For we do not say only, “See what is shining,” but also, “See what is sounding,” “See what smells,” “See what tastes,” and “See what is hot.”

When I said that things absent from our senses are believed, this must not be understood to include things that we once saw and remember having seen with certainty, even though they are not present when we recall them. [Col. 0600] They are not counted among things believed, but among things seen. They are known, therefore, not because we trusted other witnesses, but because we unquestionably remember and know that we ourselves saw them.

# CHAPTER III

8. Our knowledge, then, consists of things seen and things believed. In the things we have seen or see, we ourselves are witnesses; in the things we believe, however, we are moved to faith by other witnesses, when signs are given of things that we neither remember having seen nor see—whether in spoken words, letters, or whatever documents cause unseen things to be believed when they are seen.

It is not without reason that we say we know not only what we have seen or see, but also what we believe because suitable testimonies or witnesses for each matter have moved us to faith. Further, if it is not improper to say that we know even what we believe with the greatest certainty, this is why things rightly believed may also be said to be seen with the mind, even though they are not present to our senses.

Knowledge is attributed to the mind, whether it retains something perceived and known through the bodily senses or through the mind itself. Faith itself is certainly seen by the mind, although by faith we believe what is not seen. Hence the apostle Peter says, “In whom now, though you do not see him, you believe” (I Pet. I, 8); and the Lord himself says, “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John XX, 29).

9. When someone is told, “Believe that Christ rose from the dead,” if he believes, observe what he sees and what he believes, and distinguish the two. He sees the person whose voice he hears; and the voice itself belongs among bodily things seen, according to what we said above.

These are two things: the witness and the testimony. One belongs to the eyes, the other to the ears. But perhaps the authority of other testimonies confirms this witness—namely, of the divine Scriptures or of whatever other sources moved him to faith.

The Scriptures belong to the things seen by the bodily eyes if he reads them, or by the ears if he hears them. With the mind he sees whatever he understands to be signified by the forms of the letters or by the sounds. He sees his own faith, by which he answers without hesitation that he believes. He sees the thought by which he considers what benefit his belief may bring him. He sees the will by which he approached to embrace the religion. He also sees a certain image of the resurrection itself formed in his mind, without which he cannot understand anything said to have taken place bodily, whether it is believed or not believed.

# CHAPTER IV

But, I think, you distinguish how he sees his faith, by which he believes, and how he sees that image of the resurrection formed in his mind—an image which even one who does not believe sees if he hears about it.

10. He sees all these things, then, partly with the body and partly with the mind. But he does not see the will of the person from whom he hears the command to believe, nor Christ’s resurrection itself; he believes them. Nevertheless, he is said in a certain way to see them with the mind’s gaze, more on the basis of the faith of the testimonies than through the presence of the things believed.

The things he sees are present to the senses either of mind or of body; the things he believes are absent from the senses both of mind and of body. Although the will of the person from whom he hears the command to believe is not past but remains in the speaker—the speaker himself sees it within himself—the hearer does not see it, [Col. 0601] but believes it.

Christ’s resurrection, however, is past. Even those human beings who were present at the time did not see the resurrection itself as it occurred. Those who saw the living Christ, whom they had seen dying, did not see the resurrection itself while it was taking place; rather, they believed it with complete certainty by seeing and touching alive the one whom they had known to be dead.

We believe everything: that he rose, that he was then seen and touched by human beings, that he now lives in heaven, that he no longer dies, and that death no longer rules over him. The reality itself is present neither to the senses of our body, as this heaven and earth are present, nor to the gaze of our mind, as the faith itself by which we believe this is present.
