11. But by this preliminary explanation of mine, I think you have now sufficiently recognized what it is to see either with mind or body, and how believing differs from both. Believing occurs in the mind and is seen by the mind, since our faith is visible to our mind. Yet what is believed by that same faith is absent from the sight of our body, as the body in which Christ rose is absent; and it is absent from the sight of another person’s mind, as your faith is absent from the sight of my mind, although I believe that it exists in you.

I do not see your faith with the body—which you cannot see either—nor with the mind, which you can, as I see my own faith, but you cannot see mine. “No one knows what is in a person except the spirit of the person which is in him” (I Cor. II, 11), until the Lord comes, “and will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and disclose the thoughts of the heart” (I Cor. IV, 5), so that each person may see not only his own thoughts but also those of others.

The Apostle said that no one knows what is in a person except the spirit of the person who is in him in accordance with what we see in ourselves. For, according to what we believe but do not see, we know that many are faithful, and we are known to many.

# CHAPTER V

12. If these distinctions have now been made, let us come to the matter itself. We know that God can be seen, because it is written: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V, 8).

Or perhaps I should not have said, “We know,” but “We believe,” since we have never seen God either bodily, as we see this light, or mentally, as we see within ourselves the faith by which we believe this. We are certain only because it is written in that Scripture whose faithful adherents we are, and we have no doubt that it is true.

Yet when the apostle John said something of this kind, he said, “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (I John III, 2). See: he said that he knew something that had not yet happened and that he had learned not by seeing but by believing.

We were therefore right to say, “We know that God can be seen,” even though we have not seen him but have believed the divine authority contained in the holy Books.

13. What, then, are we to make of the statement of that same authority, “No one has ever seen God” (John I, 18; I John IV, 12)? Perhaps it may be answered that those testimonies speak of seeing God in the future, not of having seen him. For it says, “They shall see God,” not “They saw”; and not “We have seen him,” but “We shall see him as he is.”

Accordingly, the statement “No one has ever seen God” is not contrary to these passages. Those who have wished to be pure in heart as children of God will see the one whom they have not seen.

What, then, of the statement, “I saw God face to face, and my life was preserved” (Gen. XXXII, 30)? Is this also not contrary to the statement, “No one has ever seen God” (John I, 18)?

And what of what is written about Moses, that “he spoke with God face to face, as one speaks with his friend” (Exod. XXXIII, 11)? What of the prophet Isaiah, speaking of himself, who says, “I saw the Lord Sabaoth sitting upon a throne” (Isa. VI, 1)? And if other similar testimonies are customarily produced from the same authority, how are they not contrary to the statement, “No one has ever seen God”?

Indeed, even the Gospel itself may seem to contradict itself. For how is the statement “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John XIV, 9) true if no one has ever seen God? How is the statement “Their angels always see the face of my Father” (Matt. XVIII, 10) true if no one has ever seen God?

14. By what rule of interpretation, then, shall we prove that these apparently contrary and conflicting passages are neither contrary nor conflicting? It is wholly impossible for the authority of Scripture to lie in any respect.

If we say that in the statement “No one has ever seen God” only human beings are meant, just as in the statement “No one knows what is in a person except the spirit of the person who is in him” (I Cor. II, 11), “no one” obviously means no human being—for this cannot be understood of God, since it is written of Christ that he did not need anyone to testify to him about a person, “for he himself knew what was in a person” (John II, 25)—then the Apostle explains the matter more clearly when he says, “Whom no human being has seen or can see” (I Tim. VI, 16).

If, therefore, “No one has ever seen God” was said as though it meant “No human being has ever seen God,” the question will seem to have been settled to this extent: the Lord’s statement, “Their angels always see the face of my Father,” is not contrary to it, since we would understand that the angels see God, whom no human being has ever seen.

How, then, did Abraham see God (Gen. XVIII, 1), Isaac (Gen. XXVI, 2), Jacob (Gen. XXXII, 30), Job (Job XXXVIII, 1), Moses (Exod. XXXIII, 11), Micaiah (III Kings XXII, 19), Isaiah (Isa. VI, 1), and all the others of whom Scripture, which speaks the truth, testifies that they saw God, if no human being has ever seen God or can see him?

15. Some people, wishing even to prove that the impious will see God, think that the devil himself saw God, interpreting the statement in the Book of Job that the devil also came with the angels “into the presence of God” (Job I, 6; II, 1) in this way.

Then the question also arises how it was said, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V, 8), and, “Pursue peace with all people, and holiness, without which no one will see God” (Heb. XII, 14).

I am greatly surprised if those who think that the impious will see God, and that the devil saw God, go so far as to assert that the impious are pure in heart and pursue peace and holiness with all people.

16. The Lord’s statement, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John XIV, 9), may, on closer consideration, not appear contrary to what he said, “No one has ever seen God” (John I, 18).

For he did not say, “Because you have seen me, you have seen the Father,” but, by saying, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father,” he wished to show the unity of the Father’s and the Son’s substance, so that they would not think them in any respect unlike one another.

Accordingly, since the statement “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” is true, and since no human being has ever seen God, no one should be thought to have seen either the Father or the Son insofar as he is God and Son, and insofar as he is, with the Father, one God.

Insofar as he is human, however, he was certainly seen on earth and lived among human beings (Baruch III, 38; John I, 14).

# CHAPTER VI

17. But there is a great question: how can it not be contrary to the statement that so many people of ancient times saw God, if no one has ever seen God—if no human being has seen him or can see him? You see how difficult a question you have proposed to me, since you wished me to write at length and in detail on this matter on the occasion of a brief letter of mine, which seemed to you to require more careful and fuller explanation.

Would you therefore like to attend to what I have meanwhile found in the writings of other distinguished interpreters of the divine Scriptures, and to what they thought about the vision of God, in case it may satisfy your desire, although perhaps you already know it? Pay attention, then, to the following few points, if you please.

When the blessed Ambrose, bishop of Milan, was explaining the Gospel and came to the passage where the angel appeared in the Temple to Zechariah the priest, observe how much and how important a discussion of the vision of God he introduced on this occasion.

18. “The angel,” he says, “not without reason appears in the Temple, because the coming of the true priest was already being announced and a heavenly sacrifice was being prepared, in which angels would minister. And he is rightly said to have appeared to the one who suddenly caught sight of him.

“Divine Scripture has especially adopted this usage, whether with respect to angels or to God: what cannot be foreseen is said to appear. Thus you read: ‘God appeared to Abraham at the oak of Mamre’ (Gen. XVIII, 1). Because he is not perceived beforehand but is seen by a sudden glance, he is said to appear.

“For sensible things are not seen in the same way as one whose being seen depends upon his will and whose nature is not to be seen, but whose will allows him to be seen. If he does not wish it, he is not seen; if he wishes it, he is seen.

“God appeared to Abraham because he wished to; to others, because he did not wish to, he did not appear. It was also seen by Stephen, when he was being stoned by the people, that heaven was opened [Note: [Col. 0603] Bad., Am., Er., and fourteen manuscripts: “Stephen was also seen opening heaven.”]; Jesus was also seen standing at the right hand of God (Acts VII, 55), and he was not seen by the people.

“Isaiah saw the Lord Sabaoth (Isa. VI, 1), but another person could not see him, because he appeared to whomever he pleased. Why speak of human beings, when we have even read concerning the heavenly Virtues and Powers themselves that ‘no one has ever seen God’? And Scripture adds, beyond the heavenly Powers: ‘The Only-Begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him.’

“We must therefore accept that, if no one has ever seen God the Father, the Son was seen in the Old Testament. Let heretics cease to give him a beginning from the Virgin’s womb, since he was seen before he was born from the Virgin.

“Or certainly it cannot be refuted that either the Father, or the Son, or at least the Holy Spirit—if indeed there is a vision of the Holy Spirit—is seen in whatever form the will chooses, not in one formed by nature, since we have also received the account that the Spirit was seen in the form of a dove (Matt. III, 16).

“And therefore ‘no one has ever seen God,’ because no one has perceived or grasped with mind or eyes the fullness of divinity that dwells in God [Note: [Col. 0604] Lov. reads, “the fullness of divinity that dwells in Christ.” But the earlier editions and fourteen manuscripts have “that dwells in God,” etc.]. The word ‘seen’ must be referred to both matters. Finally, when it is added, ‘The Only-Begotten Son himself has declared him,’ a vision of minds rather than of eyes is indicated. Form is seen, but power is declared: the former is grasped by the eyes, the latter by the mind.

“But what shall I say about the Trinity? The Seraphim appeared when he wished, and Isaiah alone heard his voice. The angel appeared and is now present, but is not seen. For it is not in our power to see, but in his power to appear.

“Nevertheless, although the power to see is not ours, there is a grace by which we may merit to be able to see. Therefore, whoever has received grace has merited the opportunity. We do not merit the opportunity, because we do not have the grace of seeing God.

“And what wonder is it if, in the present age, the Lord is not seen unless he wishes? Even in the resurrection itself it is not easy to see God except for those who are pure in heart; therefore, ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God’ (Matt. V, 8).

“How many blessed people had he already counted, and yet he had not promised them the ability to see God! If, then, those who are pure in heart will see God, obviously the others will not see him. For those who are unworthy will not see God; nor can one who does not wish to see God see God.

“God is not seen in a place, but by the pure in heart. God is neither sought with bodily eyes, nor bounded by sight, nor held by touch, nor heard by speech, nor perceived by movement. When he is thought absent, he is seen; when he is present, he is not seen.

“Finally, not all the Apostles saw Christ; therefore he said, ‘I have been with you so long, and you have not yet known me’ (John XIV, 9). For whoever has understood the breadth, length, height, and depth, and the surpassing knowledge of the love of Christ, has seen Christ and has seen the Father.

“For we no longer know Christ according to the flesh (II Cor. V, 16), but according to the spirit. ‘The Lord Christ is the Spirit before our face’ (Lam. IV, 20); may he deign in his mercy to fill us with the whole fullness of God (Eph. III, 18–19), so that he may be seen by us” (Ambrose, *On Luke*, book I, chapter I, section 11).

# CHAPTER VII

19. If you understand these words, what more remains to be asked of me, since the question that seemed difficult has now been resolved? It has been distinguished how it was said, “No one has ever seen God,” and how the righteous of ancient times saw God.

The former statement was made because God is invisible by nature. Those who saw God saw him because he appears to whomever he wishes, in whatever form he wishes, in the form chosen by his will, while his nature remains hidden.

For if, when the fathers saw God, his very nature appeared to them—although, if he had not wished it, he certainly would not have appeared—how could it be said that no one has ever seen God, when by his will his very nature was seen by so many fathers?

If, however, it is said that the Son was seen by the fathers, so that the statement that no one ever saw God is understood of God the Father, Ambrose did not indeed miss the opportunity to refute certain heretics, namely the Photinians, who assign the beginning of God’s Son to the Virgin’s womb and refuse to believe that he existed beforehand.

But because he saw that others—namely, the Arians—were laying a more dangerous trap, and because their error is undoubtedly strengthened if the Father’s nature is believed invisible but the Son’s visible, he asserted that the nature of both was equally one and invisible, adding the Holy Spirit as well.

He expressed this briefly but wonderfully when he continued: “Or certainly it cannot be refuted that either the Father, or the Son, or at least the Holy Spirit—if indeed there is a vision of the Holy Spirit—is seen in whatever form the will chooses, not in one formed by nature.”

He could have said, “not in one displayed by nature,” but he preferred to say “formed,” so that no one would think that God formed from his own nature the form in which he chose to appear, and so would be compelled to conclude that his substance was changeable and mutable. May God himself, merciful and kind, avert this from the faith of the devout!

# CHAPTER VIII

20. God’s nature, then, is invisible—not only the Father’s, but that of the Trinity itself, the one God. And because it is not only invisible but also unchangeable, he appears to whomever he wishes and in whatever form he wishes, while his invisible and unchangeable nature remains intact with him.

The true desire of the devout, by which they long and burn eagerly to see God, does not, I think, burn to contemplate that form in which he appears as he wishes—a form which is not himself—but that substance by which he is what he is.

The holy Moses, his faithful servant, revealed the flame of this desire when he said to God, with whom he spoke face to face as a friend: “If I have found favor before you, show me yourself” (Exod. XXXIII, 13, according to the Septuagint).

What, then? Was the one who appeared not himself? If he had not been himself, Moses would not have said to him, “Show me yourself,” but, “Show me God.” And yet, if Moses had been contemplating God’s nature and substance, he would have been even less likely to say, “Show me yourself.”

He was therefore himself in the form in which he had wished to appear; but he was not appearing as himself in his own nature, which Moses desired to see. That nature is promised to the saints in the life to come.

Accordingly, what was answered to Moses is true: no one can see the face of God and live—that is, no one can see him in this life, living, as he is. Many did see him, but they saw what the will chose, not what nature formed.

And if John’s statement is rightly understood—“Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (I John III, 2)—this does not mean as human beings saw him when he wished, in the form he wished, not in the nature in which, even when he was seen, he remained hidden in himself. Rather, it means “as he is,” which was requested of him when Moses, who spoke with him face to face, said, “Show me yourself.”

[Col. 0606] 21. Not because anyone has ever comprehended the fullness of God—not only with the eyes of the body, but even with the mind itself.

# CHAPTER IX

For it is one thing to see and another to comprehend the whole by seeing. What is present in some manner is seen; but the whole is comprehended by seeing when it is seen in such a way that nothing of it is hidden from the one seeing, or when its boundaries can be surveyed.

For example, I have given two illustrations: in the one, nothing about your present will is hidden from you; in the other, you can survey the limits of your ring. One belongs to the mind’s gaze, the other to the bodily eyes. Sight, as he said, must be referred to both—that is, to the eyes and to the mind.

22. If, then, the reason no one has ever seen God is that, as the disputant whose words we are considering says, no one has perceived the fullness of his divinity, and no one has comprehended it with mind or eyes—and the word “seen” must be referred to both—it remains to inquire how the angels see God, in view of the Gospel statement that “their angels always see the face of my Father” (Matt. XVIII, 10).

If God appears even to them not as he is, but in a form chosen by his will while his nature remains hidden, then we must inquire all the more how we shall see him as he is, as Moses desired when he asked God—who was present before him—to show himself to him.

For this is promised to us as the highest reward in the resurrection: that we shall be equal to the angels of God (Luke XX, 36). If even they do not see him as he is, how shall we see him in this way when we have become equal to them in the resurrection?

But observe what our Ambrose says next: “Finally,” he says, “when it is added, ‘The Only-Begotten Son himself has declared him,’ a vision of minds rather than of eyes is indicated. Form is seen, but power is declared: the former is grasped by the eyes, the latter by the mind.”

A little earlier he had said that vision must be referred to both; now he assigned it not to the mind but to the eyes. He did not, I think, do this carelessly or without regard for his own words, but because in ordinary speech we more commonly attribute vision to the eyes, just as we attribute form to the body.

This manner of speaking is also more frequently used concerning things contained in places and varied by colors. But if there were no form to be contemplated by the mind, it would not be said that he was “fairer in appearance than the sons of men” (Ps. XLIV, 3). For this was not said according to the flesh, but according to spiritual form.

Form, therefore, can also refer to what belongs to the mind’s gaze. But because the word is more commonly used of bodies, or of likenesses of bodies, he said: “Form is seen, but power is declared: the former is grasped by the eyes, the latter by the mind.”

Accordingly, when the Only-Begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, declares him by an ineffable declaration, the rational, pure, and holy creature is filled with the ineffable vision of God. We shall attain this vision when we have become equal to the angels.

For, just as these visible things, known through bodily senses, are seen, no one has ever seen God. For if he was ever seen in that manner, he is not seen by nature, as these things are, but is seen by will—appearing in the form he wished while his nature remained hidden and unchangeably abiding in itself.

In the manner in which he is seen as he is, he may perhaps now be seen by certain angels; but we shall see him in that way when we have become equal to them.

# CHAPTER X

23. Then, after adding that even the Powers of heaven, like the Seraphim, are not seen unless they wish and in whatever way they wish—so that from this too the invisibility of the Trinity might be inferred—he says: “Nevertheless, although the power to see is not ours, there is a grace by which we may merit to be able to see. Therefore, whoever has received grace has merited the opportunity. We do not merit the opportunity, because we do not have the grace of seeing God.”

Since Ambrose is not teaching these things on his own authority but is explaining the Gospel, he did not mean by these words that some of those who believe—those to whom he gave the power to become children of God—will see God while others will not. The statement “We shall see him as he is” applies to all of them.

Rather, by saying, “We do not merit the opportunity, because we do not have the grace of seeing God,” he indicated that he was speaking of this present age. In it, God has deigned to appear to some, although not in his own nature but in whatever form he wished, as to Abraham, Isaiah, and others like them. To the countless others, however, although they belong to his people and to the eternal inheritance, he does not manifest himself even in such a form.

In the age to come, all who will receive the kingdom prepared for them from the beginning will see him with pure hearts; and none will be in that kingdom except such people.

# CHAPTER XI

24. Pay attention, then, to what he adds as he begins to speak of that age: “And what wonder is it,” he says, “if, in the present age, the Lord is not seen unless he wishes? Even in the resurrection itself it is not easy to see God except for those who are pure in heart; therefore, ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.’

“How many blessed people had he already counted, and yet he had not promised them the ability to see God! If, then, those who are pure in heart will see God, obviously the others will not see him. For those who are unworthy will not see God; nor can one who does not wish to see God see God.”

You see how carefully he speaks now of those who will see God in the age to come: not everyone, but those who are worthy. For both the worthy and the unworthy will rise; but only the worthy will rise for that kingdom in which God will be seen, because “all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come forth,” but with a great distinction: “those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment” (John V, 28–29).

Here “judgment” signifies eternal punishment, as in the statement, “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John III, 18).

25. Therefore, when Saint Ambrose says that neither can one who has been unwilling to see God see God, what else did he intend us to understand except that the person who is unwilling to devote to the purification of the heart the care worthy of so great a matter is unwilling to see God? Consider, then, what he adds: “God is not seen in a place, but by the pure in heart.” What could have been said more plainly or explicitly? The devil, therefore, and his angels, and all the ungodly with them, are excluded from this vision without any cloud of doubt, because they are not pure in heart. Accordingly, although it is written in the Book of Job that the angels came into the presence of God, and that the devil came with them [Col. 0608] (Job 1:6; 2:1), we should not for that reason believe that the devil saw God. For they are said to have come into the presence of God, not that God came into their presence. What we see comes into our presence, not that by which we are seen. Therefore they came, as many manuscripts read, “to stand before God,” not so that God might stand before them. Nor is it necessary to linger here and try, as far as our powers allow, to explain how this too takes place temporally, since everything is always in God’s presence.

26. What is now being asked is how God is seen—not in the form in which, even in this present age, he sometimes wished to appear to certain people, when he spoke not only with Abraham and other righteous persons but also with Cain, the murderer of his brother (Gen. 18:1; 4:6–15), but how he is seen in that kingdom where his children will see him as he is. Then their desire will be satisfied with good things—the desire with which Moses burned, for speaking with God face to face was not enough for him, and he said, “Show yourself to me plainly, so that I may see you” (Exod. 33:13)—as though he were saying what is sung in the Psalm out of that same desire: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. 16:15). Philip too burned with this desire and wished to be satisfied in this way, saying, “Show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John 14:8).

Speaking of this vision, Ambrose himself, its lover and desirer, says: “God is not seen in a place, as at the oak of Mamre, or as on Mount Sinai, but by the pure in heart.” And he continues, knowing what he desires, what he longs for, and what he hopes for: “God is not sought with bodily eyes,” he says, “with which he showed himself to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and others in this age; nor is he circumscribed by sight,” because of what was said, “You shall see my back” (Exod. 33:23); “nor is he grasped by touch,” as when he even wrestled with Jacob (Gen. 32:24–30); “nor is he heard in speech,” as he was heard not only by so many saints but also by the devil; “nor is he perceived in his walking,” as when he once walked in paradise toward evening (Gen. 3:8).

27. You see how this holy man strives to withdraw our minds from all the senses of the flesh, so as to make them fit for seeing God. Yet what does such an external planter and waterer accomplish unless God, who gives the growth, works inwardly (1 Cor. 3:7)? For who, without the help of God’s Spirit, could conceive that there is something—and something greater than all the things perceived through the body—which is not seen in a place, should not be sought with the eyes, is not heard in speech, is not grasped by touch, is not perceived in walking, and yet is seen by the pure in heart?

He was not speaking of this life when he said this. For he clearly distinguished the life of the future age from this age, in which God appeared—not as he is, but in the form in which he wished to appear to those to whom he wished to appear—when he said: “And what wonder is it if, in the present age, the Lord is not seen except when he wishes? Even in the resurrection itself, it is not easy to see God except for those who are pure in heart; and therefore, ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.’”

Here he began to speak of that age in which they will see God—not all who rise, but those who rise to eternal life; not the unworthy, of whom it was said, “Let the impious be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of the Lord” [Col. 0609] (Isa. 26:10, according to the Septuagint), but the worthy, of whom the Lord himself spoke when he was not seen in the present age: “Whoever loves me keeps my commandments”; and, “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and show myself to him” (John 14:21, 23).

Nor will it be those to whom it will be said, “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels,” but those to whom it will be said, “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” For the former will go into eternal burning, but the righteous into eternal life (Matt. 25:41, 34, 46). And what is eternal life except what Life itself says elsewhere: “This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3)? Yet this is how he promised to show himself to those who love him, as the one God with the Father—not as he was seen in bodily form in this age by the good and the wicked alike.

28. Even in the future judgment, when he will come in the same manner as he was seen going into heaven—that is, in the same form of the Son of Man—those to whom he will say, “I was hungry, and you did not give me food” (Matt. 25:42) will see that form (for the Jews too will see him whom they pierced [Zech. 12:10]); they will not see that form of God in which he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized (Phil. 2:6). In that form of God, those who will see him as he is will then see him.

Nor will they see him because in this life they were poor in spirit, or meek, or mourning, or hungering and thirsting for righteousness, or merciful, or peacemakers, or persecuted for righteousness—although the same people may indeed have possessed all these qualities—but because they are pure in heart. For this reason, among those beatitudes, although those who have a pure heart do all these things, it is nowhere stated that they will see God except where it says, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” The pure in heart will see him who is not seen in a place, is not sought with bodily eyes, is not circumscribed by sight, is not grasped by touch, is not heard in speech, and is not perceived in walking.

“For no one has ever seen God,” either in this life as he is, or even in the life of the angels as they see visible things through bodily vision; “because the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has made him known.” Hence what he makes known is to be understood as pertaining not to the vision of bodily eyes but to the vision of the mind.

## CHAPTER XII

29. But again, lest our desire should pass from one bodily sense to another—from the eyes, that is, to the ears—for this reason, after saying, “God is not sought with bodily eyes, nor circumscribed by sight, nor grasped by touch,” he also added, “nor heard in speech.” Thus, if we are able, we may understand the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, as making him known in the manner proper to the Word: not as a sound striking the ears, but as an image becoming known to minds, so that there, in an inward and ineffable light, what was said may shine forth: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). This was said here to Philip, when he was seeing and yet not seeing.

Ambrose, an exceptional lover and desirer of this vision, continues: “Even when he is thought to be absent, he is seen; and when he is present, he is not seen.” He did not say, “When he is absent,” but “when he is thought to be absent.” For he is nowhere absent who fills heaven and earth; he is not enclosed within small spaces or spread throughout great ones, but is wholly everywhere and contained by no place.

Whoever understands this with a mind that has transcended such things sees God even when he is thought to be absent. Whoever cannot do so should pray and act so as to become worthy of being able to do it. Let him not knock at the door of a human disputant, so that he may read what he has not read, but at the door of God the Savior, so that he may be enabled to do what he cannot do.

He then explained why he had said, “and when he is present, he is not seen,” by adding: “Finally, not all the Apostles saw Christ; and therefore he said, ‘For so long a time I have been with you, and still you have not known me!’” Behold how God was present and was not seen.

30. But why did he not dare to say, “Finally, the Apostles did not see Christ,” but said, “not all the Apostles,” as though some of them at that time saw him with the vision in which he and the Father are one? Perhaps he had in mind the fact that when Peter said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” he received the answer, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.”

Yet whether that revelation was made in his mind through faith in so great a reality, or through the vision of what he saw, does not seem clear to me, since Peter himself showed that he was still so little advanced in relation to him that he feared losing him in death, even though shortly before he had confessed him to be the Son of the living God—that is, the source of life (Matt. 16:16–17, 21–22).

## CHAPTER XIII

31. Next, a question may arise about how the very substance of God could have been seen by certain people living in this life, in view of what was said to Moses: “No one can see my face and live” (Exod. 33:20). The answer may be that the human mind can, by divine power, be carried away from this life into the life of the angels before it is released from the flesh through the common death.

Thus was carried away the man who heard ineffable words that it is not permitted to a human being to speak. There was such a withdrawal of attention from the senses of this life that, whether he was in the body or outside the body—that is, whether, as can happen in a more intense ecstasy, his mind had been removed from this life into that life while the bond with the body remained, or whether a complete dissolution had occurred, of the kind that happens in full death—he said that he did not know (2 Cor. 12:2–4).

Thus both statements are true: “No one can see my face and live,” because the mind must be withdrawn from this life when it is taken up into the ineffability of that vision; and it is not unbelievable that certain saints who had not yet died in such a way that their bodies remained to be buried were nevertheless granted this exceptional revelation.

I think that this is what the man we are discussing had in mind when he did not say, “The Apostles did not see Christ,” but said, “Not all the Apostles saw Christ.” He believed that some of them might even then have been granted the vision of the divinity itself of which he was speaking—certainly because of blessed Paul, who, although he was the last, was nonetheless an apostle and did not remain silent about his own ineffable revelation.

32. Indeed, it would be surprising if the faithful ancient servant of God, Moses, who was still laboring on this earth and ruling that people, was not granted what he asked: to see the glory of the Lord. He had said, “If I have found favor before you, show yourself to me plainly.”

He received an appropriate answer for the present circumstances: he could not see the face of God, which no one could see and live. In this way God signified that such a vision belongs to another and better life.

Moreover, in the words of God the mystery of the future Church of Christ was symbolically represented. Moses bore the type of the Jewish people, who would afterward believe in Christ who had suffered. Therefore it was said to him, “When I have passed by, you shall see my back”; and the other things said there prophetically announce, through a marvelous sacrament, the Church that would come afterward. It would take too long to discuss this now.

But what I had begun to say—that, in accordance with his desire, Moses was granted even what he had asked—was demonstrated later in the Book of Numbers. There the Lord rebukes his sister’s insolence and says that he appears to other prophets in a vision and in a dream, but to Moses by an appearance, not through riddles. There he also adds: “And he saw the glory of the Lord” (Num. 12:6–8).

What, then, caused Moses to be so singled out, unless it was perhaps that even then he had a ruler of his people and a faithful minister over his whole house who was worthy of that contemplation, so that he might see God as he is, as he had desired? This contemplation is promised to all his children at the end.

## CHAPTER XIV

33. I believe that the holy man whose words we are examining was considering these matters when he said, “Not all the Apostles saw Christ,” because perhaps some of them had even at that time seen him in accordance with what I have said.

To prove his statement that not all saw him, he immediately added: “And therefore he said, ‘For so long a time I have been with you, and still you have not known me.’” Then, going on to indicate by what kind of people God is seen in that contemplation in which he is seen as he is, he says: “Whoever has understood what is the breadth, length, height, and depth, and the surpassing love of Christ that exceeds knowledge, has seen Christ and has seen the Father.”

34. I am accustomed to understand these words of the Apostle Paul in this way: in breadth, good works of love; in length, perseverance to the end; in height, hope of heavenly rewards; in depth, the inscrutable judgments of God, from which this grace comes to human beings.

I also apply this interpretation to the mystery of the cross: breadth is understood as the transverse wood on which the hands are extended, signifying works; length, as extending from that wood down to the earth, where the whole crucified body appears to stand [Note: [Col. 0611] One Vatican manuscript reads: “From the transverse wood down to the earth, where the whole body of the crucified one appears to stand.”], signifying persistence—that is, remaining with patience; height, as extending upward from the transverse wood to the part that rises toward the head, signifying expectation of heavenly things, so that these good works and perseverance in them may not be thought to be performed for the sake of earthly and temporal benefits from God, but rather for the sake of what faith, working through love, hopes for from above as everlasting.

Depth, however, is that part of the wood which is fixed and hidden in the depths of the earth, yet from which all that rises above the earth emerges. It signifies how, from God’s hidden will, one person is called to share in such great grace in one way and another person in another way [Col. 0612].

But the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge is surely that love in which there is the peace that surpasses all understanding [Note: [Col. 0612] See Letter 140, ch. 26, §§62–64.]. Whether that evangelizing disputant also understood these things in those apostolic words, or perhaps something else more fitting, you nevertheless see, I think, that this interpretation too is not contrary to the rule of faith.

35. Since we are now dealing with spiritual vision, after saying, “Whoever has understood what is the breadth, length, height, and depth, and the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, has seen Christ and has seen the Father,” Ambrose did not want anyone especially slow to understand him to think that he was speaking of bodily vision. He therefore says: “For we no longer know Christ according to the flesh, but according to the spirit.” “For the Spirit is before our face: Christ the Lord.”

When he says here, “we know,” he speaks of the faith that exists now, not of the contemplation that will exist then. For we know whatever, through an unfeigned faith, we already hold firmly by believing, even though we do not yet contemplate it in its actual form.

Finally, after saying, as the Apostle says, that he no longer knew Christ according to the flesh, and after adding the prophetic testimony, “For the Spirit is before our face: Christ the Lord,” he immediately continued: “May he deign in his mercy to fill us with all the fullness of God, so that he may be seen by us.”

It is certainly clear that he placed the knowledge of which he had said, “we know,” in the category of faith, by which the righteous now live (Heb. 10:38), not in the category of contemplation, through which we shall see God as he is. For he subsequently desired this contemplation for himself and for us, and indicated that it is future, by saying: “May he deign in his mercy to fill us with all the fullness of God, so that he may be seen by us.”

## CHAPTER XV

36. Some have understood this fullness of God in the Apostle’s statement in such a way that they thought we would become wholly what God is. The Apostle, as you recognize, used these words when he said: “To know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, so that you may be filled with all the fullness of God” (Eph. 3:19).

“Therefore,” they say, “if we possess anything less than God and are in any respect lesser than God, how shall we be filled with all the fullness of God? But since we shall be filled, surely we shall be equal.”

I know that you reject and detest this error of the human mind, and rightly so. But how this fullness is to be understood—the fullness with which we are said to be filled in every respect with the fullness of God—we shall discuss later, if God wills, to the extent of the powers he grants.

37. Now consider carefully whether the matter you had proposed to me, which seemed difficult to explain, has been explained, by recalling what has been said.

If you ask whether God can be seen, I answer: He can.

If you ask how I know this, I answer: Because the most truthful Scripture says, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God,” and other things of the same kind.

If you ask how he can be called invisible if he can be seen, I answer: He is invisible by nature, but is seen when he wishes and in the manner in which he wishes. For he has been seen by many, not as he is, but in whatever form he was pleased to appear [Col. 0613].

If you ask how the wicked Cain saw him when he was questioned and judged by him concerning his crime (Gen. 4:6), or how the devil himself saw him when he came with the angels to stand before him, if the pure in heart are blessed because they shall see God, I answer: It does not follow that those who sometimes hear voices produced by him also see God. For those who heard him say to the Son, “I have glorified, and I will glorify again” (John 12:28), did not see him.

Nevertheless, it should not be surprising if some who are not pure in heart also see God in the form produced by his will, while his invisible nature remains hidden and unchangeably present in itself.

If you ask whether he can ever be seen as he is, I answer: This has been promised to his children, of whom it was said, “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.”

If you ask by what faculty we shall see him, I answer: By that by which the angels see him, for then we shall be equal to them.

For just as the things called visible are seen, “no one has ever seen God, nor can see him,” because he dwells in inaccessible light and is invisible by nature, just as he is incorruptible. The Apostle placed these qualities together when he said, “To the King of the ages, invisible, incorruptible” (1 Tim. 1:17), and, “whom no human being has seen nor can see” (1 Tim. 6:16). For just as he is incorruptible now and will not become corruptible later, so he is not only invisible now but invisible forever.

He is not seen in a place, but by the pure in heart; he is not sought with bodily eyes, is not circumscribed by sight, is not grasped by touch, is not heard in speech, and is not perceived in walking.

The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, makes known the nature and substance of the Godhead without sound and therefore invisibly displays it to eyes worthy and capable of so great a vision. These are the eyes of which the Apostle says, “the eyes of your heart having been enlightened” (Eph. 1:18), and of which it is said, “Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death” (Ps. 12:4).

“For the Lord is Spirit” (2 Cor. 3:17); hence “whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17). Therefore the person who can see God invisibly can cling to God incorporeally.

## CHAPTER XVI

38. I think that, concerning the question you proposed, there is now nothing further that you need to ask. But throughout this entire discussion of ours, consider what you have seen, what you have believed, and what you still do not know—whether because I did not say it, because you did not understand it, or because you did not judge it worthy of belief.

As for the things you have seen to be true, distinguish further how you saw them: whether you remember seeing them through the body, as with heavenly or earthly bodies, or whether you never touched them with bodily sight but, contemplating them with the mind alone, perceived them to be true and certain, as with your own will. I can believe you when you speak of your will, but I cannot see it myself in the way it appears to you.

When you have distinguished these two things, consider also by what means you distinguish them. Although we see some things with the body and others with the mind, the distinction between these two kinds is itself seen by the mind, not by the body. The things perceived by the mind do not require any bodily sense for us to know that they are true.

Things seen through the body, however, cannot be retained in knowledge unless the mind is present to receive the reports brought to it. What is said to receive these reports as though it received the things themselves leaves the things outside, but preserves their images—that is, incorporeal likenesses of bodies—incorporeally in the memory. Whenever it wishes and is able, it judges these images as though brought out from custody and displayed before the gaze of thought.

When it is able [Note: [Col. 0614] The editions and most manuscripts read, “and when it wishes”; but the Sorbonne codex reads better, “and when it is able.”], it also distinguishes these two things: what it has left outside in bodily form and what similar to it it sees within. It recognizes the former as absent and the latter as present. Thus, when I am absent, you can think of the appearance of my body: the image is present to you, while the face of which it is the image is absent. The one is a body; the other is an incorporeal likeness of a body.

39. Having carefully and confidently examined and distinguished the things you see, consider what you believe in this entire discourse, from the time I began speaking to you through these letters. In matters you have not seen and to which you give faith, weigh the authority of the witnesses by distinguishing their respective weight.

For you do not believe me in the same way as Ambrose, from whose books I have cited those many testimonies. Or if you think that both of us should be believed with equal confidence, surely you will not in any way compare either of us with the Gospel or equate our writings with the canonical Scriptures. If you judge rightly, you certainly see that we are far below that authority. I am farther below it, but however much you may believe either of us, you do not compare either of us with that excellence.

Therefore you believe more firmly what is written—“No one has ever seen God”; “He dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen nor can see”; “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God”—and whatever else I have recalled from those holy books, than what Ambrose said: “God is not seen in a place, nor sought with bodily eyes, nor circumscribed by sight, nor grasped by touch, nor heard in speech, nor perceived in walking.”

He either understood or believed God to be such that he is seen by the pure in heart; I confess that this is also my own position.

40. You therefore receive these divine words in one way and those in another. For, concerning us, some scruple perhaps remains in you, lest we understand something in these divine utterances less clearly than we should, and explain them not as they were spoken but as we merely suppose them to mean.

Perhaps you say to yourself: “What if God is seen by the pure in heart and yet is seen in a place? Or what if those who are pure in heart will see God with bodily eyes as well, when this corruptible body has put on incorruption and we have become equal to the angels of God?”

You may therefore be uncertain how much you ought—or ought not—to believe us. You are careful not to be deceived by believing us either more or less than you should. But you do not doubt that the divine Scriptures must be believed even when their meaning has not yet become clear.

You observe and see within your mind this attitude toward belief and unbelief, this difficulty of knowledge, this turmoil of doubt, and this pious faith owed to divine utterances, just as they are. Nor do you doubt at all that these things are present in you, whether in the way I have described them or in the way you yourself know them more directly.

You see, therefore, your faith; you see your doubt; you see your eagerness and your desire to learn. Though divine authority moves you to believe what you do not see, you nevertheless see without hesitation that you believe these things. You distribute and distinguish them all.

## CHAPTER XVII

41. Will you then in any way compare the bodily eyes with the eyes of your heart by which you contemplate all these things as true and certain, and discern them invisibly as present to you? Even with regard to visible things themselves, which in some manner shine before the sharpness of bodily eyes, and with regard to bodily eyes themselves and their acuity, whatever its quality and extent, consider how far they are removed from invisible things—not from those more excellent things to which you owe faith even though you do not see them, but from the things I have mentioned, which you do not believe to be absent but contemplate mentally as present [Note: [Col. 0615] The printed editions read, “to which we also [owe faith], though not seen”; we have deleted the word nobis (“we/us”), which is absent from some manuscripts].

You judge these things not with those same eyes of the flesh but with those inward eyes. Since the inward eyes are judges of the outward eyes, while the outward eyes serve the inward ones in a certain function and ministry of reporting; since the inward eyes see many things that the outward eyes do not see, while the outward eyes see nothing about which the inward eyes, as governors, do not judge—who would not rank the inward eyes above the outward ones by an incomparable measure?

42. Since this is so, I ask you: when this great matter is being accomplished within you; when you distinguish inward things from outward things and place the former ineffably above the latter; when, leaving the outward things behind, you dwell inwardly among the inward ones and judge them by their own incorporeal boundaries—do you think that you are situated in no light, or in some light?

I think that such great and such true, clear, and certain things cannot appear to you without light. Look, then, upon the light in which you see all those things, and consider whether any ray of bodily eyes can approach it. Surely it cannot.

Consider also and answer whether in that light you see any spaces or intervals of places. If you vigilantly remove from your inward sight every bodily image introduced by the senses of the outward person, you will find, I think, nothing of that kind there. But perhaps this is difficult. From habit of bodily life, a crowd of phantasms in the likenesses of bodies rushes even upon the inward eyes.

As I tried to resist this, I cried out at least by the authority of God, grieving in that brief letter, and said: “Let the flesh, drunk with fleshly thoughts, hear: ‘God is Spirit’” (Letter 92, §5). By that rebuke I restrained not only someone else’s mind but also my own from such vanity.

We are more easily inclined toward familiar things, and it is agreeable to the weakness of the human soul either to send bodily intercourse inward or to admit it there—not where the soul stands in health, but where, in a certain weakness, it leans or lies.

43. Therefore, if you cannot clearly clear the gaze of your mind of the cloud, as it were, of bodily likenesses, observe those likenesses themselves attentively within yourself. Think of heaven and earth as you have become accustomed to seeing them with bodily eyes [Col. 0616], and observe that the images of heaven and earth brought before the eyes of your thought are likenesses of bodies, not bodies themselves.

Thus judge against yourself on behalf of yourself, if you cannot in every way drive the imaginative forms of bodily qualities away from the gaze of your mind; overcome them at the very point at which they overcome you. For I do not think that anyone is so devoted even to such imaginings as to believe that the sun, moon, stars, rivers, seas, mountains, hills, cities, walls of his house, or even those of his bedroom, and whatever else he has learned and retains through the eyes of the body, exist in his memory or before the gaze of his thought in such a way that they stand or move with spatial dimensions and intervals.

If the things in our mind that are most like bodies and places are nevertheless not contained by the spaces and boundaries of places, nor stored in our memory through spatial intervals, how much more do things that bear no likeness to bodies—love, joy, long-suffering, peace, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control—occupy no spatial dimensions, are separated by no interval, and seek no spaces for the eye of the heart to send out its rays so that it may see them!

Are not all these things in one without confinement, and known within their own boundaries [Note: [Col. 0616] Thus all manuscripts; the printed editions have, “And they are known without boundaries.”], without the circuit of regions? Or tell me in what place you see love, which is nevertheless known to you to the extent that you can contemplate it with the gaze of your mind. You do not know it to be great because you have surveyed some enormous mass by looking at it; nor, when it speaks inwardly to you so that you may live according to it, does it make any sound; nor do you raise the light of bodily eyes in order to see it; nor do you prepare the strength of bodily arms in order to hold it firmly; nor, when it comes to mind, do you sense its walking.

44. Behold, then, even love, however small it may be in our will, exists within us and is visible to us, yet it is not seen in a place, is not sought with bodily eyes, is not circumscribed by sight, is not grasped by touch, is not heard in speech, and is not perceived in walking. How much more is this true of God himself, whose pledge this is in us!

For if our inward person, however slight an image of God it may be—an image not begotten from him but created by him—which, although still being renewed day by day, already dwells in such a light that no bodily sense of the eyes approaches it; if the things we contemplate in that light with the eyes of the heart are distinguished from one another and are separated by no spatial dimensions, how much more is this true of God, who dwells in inaccessible light and to whom no bodily sense has access—access possible only to the pure in heart?

When, therefore, we have preferred this light to every bodily light, not only by the judgment of reason but also by the desire of love, the more we are able to do so, the better we shall be able to do so, until all the sicknesses of our soul are healed by him who forgives all our iniquities.

For when we have become spiritual in this more vigorous life, we shall be able to judge all things, while we ourselves are judged by no one. “The natural person does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God; for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are spiritually judged. But the spiritual person judges all things and is himself judged by no one” (1 Cor. 2:14–15).

## CHAPTER XVIII

45. If we are not yet able to prefer the judging light to the light that is judged; to prefer the life that understands to the life that merely senses; to prefer a nature that possesses all it has simultaneously in one place—not having one thing here and another there, as our understanding itself does—to a nature constituted in parts, so that half of it is less than the whole, as is the case with every body, then we are arguing about such great and such important matters to no purpose.

But if we are now able to do this, let us believe God to be something better than our understanding, so that his peace, which surpasses all understanding, may guard our hearts and our understandings in Christ Jesus (Phil. 4:7).

That peace which surpasses all understanding is certainly not less than our understanding, so that, while the latter is invisible to bodily eyes, the former might be thought visible. Or are the peace of God and the splendor of God different things, when the only-begotten Son himself is both—the Son whose love surpasses knowledge, through knowledge of whom we shall be filled with all the fullness of God? That love is not inferior to the light of our mind, which is granted when it is illuminated by him.

If our mind is inaccessible to the eyes of the flesh, how much more is the divine light, which surpasses it incomparably, inaccessible! Since, therefore, one thing belonging to us is visible, such as this body, and another is invisible, such as the inward person; and since the best thing belonging to us, namely the mind and understanding, is invisible to the eyes of the body, how could that which is better than our best be visible to what is inferior in us?

## CHAPTER XIX

46. I think that, after considering all these matters, you now grant that it was rightly said that God is not seen in a place but by the pure in heart; that he is not sought with bodily eyes, is not circumscribed by sight, is not grasped by touch, is not heard in speech, and is not perceived in walking.

If we understand anything in these matters less fully or think about it differently, God will also reveal that to us, provided that we walk in what we have attained (Phil. 3:13, 16).

We have attained this: that we believe God is not a body but Spirit (John 4:24); that “no one has ever seen God” (John 1:18); that God is light and there is no darkness in him at all (1 John 1:5); that with God there is no change or shadow caused by turning (James 1:17); that he dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen nor can see (1 Tim. 6:16); that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, without any diversity or separation of nature (1 John 5:7); that the pure in heart will see him (Matt. 5:8); that we shall be like him because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2); that God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him (1 John 4:16); that we must pursue peace and holiness, without which no one will see God (Heb. 12:14); that this corruptible and mortal body of ours will be changed in the resurrection and will put on incorruption and immortality; and that, since an animal body is sown, a spiritual body will rise (1 Cor. 15:53, 44), as the Lord transforms the body of our humiliation so that he may make it conform to the body of his glory (Phil. 3:21).

We have also attained this: that God made the human being in his own image and likeness (Gen. 1:27); and that we are renewed in the knowledge of God through the spirit of our mind, according to the image of him who created us (Col. 3:10).

Walking by faith in these and similar authoritative passages of the holy Scriptures, those who have advanced spiritually through an intellect granted or divinely assisted, and who have been able to compare spiritual things with spiritual, have seen that the mind sees better than the body; that the mind sees things which are not contained in places, are not separated from one another by spatial intervals, and are not smaller in a part than in the whole.

47. Hence it is that he confidently says that God is not seen in a place, but by the pure in heart; that he is not sought with bodily eyes, nor bounded by sight, nor grasped by touch, nor heard by speech, nor perceived by his walking. Therefore, since his substance is commended in the holy Scriptures as invisible, while in those same authorities he is found to have been seen by many through the body and in bodily places, or by the spirit through which bodily images are perceived, by means of some likeness—incorporeal, certainly, yet still a likeness of body, as in dreams or ecstasy—the holy man distinguished God’s nature from such visions and said that they were forms which God’s will had chosen, not forms which nature had fashioned. For God produces these forms so that, as he wills, to whom he wills, and when he wills, he may appear, while his substance remains hidden and unchangeable in itself. For if our will, remaining and hidden within us without any change in itself, expresses voices by which it makes itself known in some fashion, how much more easily can almighty God, while his nature remains hidden and unchangeable, appear to whomever he wills in whatever form he wills—he who created all things from nothing and, while remaining in himself, renews all things?

## CHAPTER XX

48. With regard to that vision in which we shall see God as he is, he admonished us to purify our hearts. Since bodies are called “visible” by customary usage, God is therefore called invisible, lest he be believed to be a body—not because he will deprive pure hearts of the contemplation of his substance, since this is promised as the great and supreme reward to those who worship and love God. The Lord himself said this when he appeared visibly to bodily eyes and promised that he would be contemplated as invisible by pure hearts: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father; and I will love him, and I will show myself to him” (John XIV, 21).

His nature is invisible equally with the Father, just as it is equally incorruptible. As stated above, the Apostle placed these two qualities together, commending the divine substance to human beings as far as he could by preaching (I Timothy I, 17). If bodily eyes, after the bodies have been transformed, will behold it in the resurrection, let those who can establish this prove it. I am more moved by the judgment of the one who attributes this even in the resurrection not to bodily eyes, but to pure hearts.

## CHAPTER XXI

49. As for the nature of the spiritual body promised to those who will rise, I do not refuse either to learn something further or to inquire into it—provided that, when we discuss this matter, we can remain free from those faults that are often aroused by human studies and controversies, when one person is puffed up against another beyond what is written. For while we argue in our search to discover how God can be seen, we might lose that peace and sanctification without which no one will be able to see God. May he himself avert this from our hearts, so that he may make and preserve them pure for his contemplation.

Yet there is one thing about which I have no doubt and which I do not inquire: God’s nature is never seen in a place. Whether something that is not seen in a place can be seen by the eyes of this body, I am prepared to hear from those who can demonstrate this by their reasoning, in the peace of charity, and to discuss with them what troubles me.

There are some who presume that God himself is altogether a body, thinking that whatever is not a body has no substance at all. I consider such people to be avoided in every way. There are others who have no doubt that God himself is not a body, but nevertheless think that those who rise to eternal life will see God even through the body, because they hope for such a quality in the spiritual body that what was flesh itself will become spirit.

If this is so, how far it differs from the former opinion, and how much more tolerable it is—even if it is not true—I think can readily be judged. First, because it makes a great difference whether something contrary to the truth is thought about the Creator or about the creature. Next, because one can to some extent tolerate the effort of a mind wishing to convert the body into spirit, rather than into God’s body. Finally, because what I said in that letter about the eyes of this flesh of ours—that they can neither now see God nor then be able to see him (Letter 92, §3)—is true even in this sense. For it was said only of bodily eyes, which will not then exist if the body itself will be spirit. Consequently, bodily eyes will never see God, because when he is seen, spirit, not body, will see him.

50. The whole question, therefore, now concerns the spiritual body: to what extent this corruptible and mortal body will put on incorruption and immortality, and to what extent it will be changed from an animal body into a spiritual one. This must be treated with greater care and diligence, especially because of the body of the Lord himself, who “transfigures the body of our humiliation to conform it to the body of his glory” (Philippians III, 21), so that he may subject all things to himself.

Since God the Father sees the Son, and the Son sees the Father, those who are unwilling to attribute vision except to bodies certainly must not be heeded. For it is not permissible to say that the Father does not see the Son; nor, if seeing belongs only to the body, that the Father is clothed with a body in order that he himself may see.

What of the fact that, at the very beginning of the world, before the Son had assumed any form of a servant, God saw the light, that it was good; and the firmament, the sea, and the dry land; every herb and every tree; the sun, the moon, and the stars; creeping creatures possessing living souls; the birds of heaven; and the living soul? Finally, “God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Genesis I, 4–31).

Since Scripture repeated this so many times with regard to each of the creatures, I am astonished at the origin of the opinion that vision pertains only to bodies. Whatever manner of speech may have produced this opinion, the holy Scriptures nevertheless do not customarily speak in that way. If they did not attribute vision not only to the body but also to the spirit—and more to the spirit than to the body—they would not have called the prophets properly “Seers” (I Kings IX, 9), since they saw future things not with the body but also with the spirit.

## CHAPTER XXII

51. We must take care lest we venture upon something presumptuous if we say that, through the glory of the resurrection, the body will lose not only mortality and corruptibility but even this very quality of being a body, and become spirit. For in that case either the substance of the spirit would be doubled, if the body too were spirit; or, if there will be one human spirit, so that when the body is changed and converted into spirit it is doubled neither by duplication nor by increase, nor enlarged at all by the addition of any quantity, we must fear that this will seem to mean nothing other than that the bodies will not remain immortal through that transformation but will rather not exist at all and will perish altogether.

Therefore, until careful inquiry—if the Lord helps us—discovers what should more probably be thought according to the Scriptures about the spiritual body promised in the resurrection, let it suffice for the present that the only-begotten Son, who is also the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (I Timothy II, 5), sees the Father just as he is seen by the Father.

As for that vision of God promised to us in the resurrection, let us not try to transfer to it from this world the desire of the eyes, but let us devote ourselves with devout affection to purifying our hearts. Nor should we think of a bodily face when the Apostle says, “Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma; but then face to face,” especially since the Apostle said more explicitly, “Now I know in part; but then I shall know even as I am known” (I Corinthians XIII, 12).

If, then, we shall know God with a bodily face, we have now been known with his bodily face, for he says, “Then I shall know even as I am known.” Who, therefore, would not understand that in this passage he also wished to signify our face of which he says elsewhere: “But we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (ibid. III, 18)—that is, from the glory of faith into the glory of eternal contemplation?

This is what that transformation accomplishes, by which “the inner person is renewed day by day” (II Corinthians IV, 16). The Apostle Peter also spoke of this person when he urged that he be adorned: “Let them not be adorned outwardly with the braiding of hair, or with gold, or pearls, or expensive clothing; but with the hidden person of the heart, who is rich before God” (I Peter III, 3).

The face on which the Jews have a veil because they do not pass over to Christ is the same face that is unveiled in us and transformed into the same image when anyone passes over to Christ, for the veil is then removed. He says most plainly: “The veil is placed over their hearts” (II Corinthians III, 15–18). There, therefore, is the face which, once unveiled, we now contemplate in faith, although through a mirror and in an enigma; but then, face to face.

## CHAPTER XXIII

52. If you approve these things, hold with me the judgment of the holy man Ambrose, now confirmed not by his authority but by the truth itself. It is not that I approve it merely because, chiefly through his mouth, the Lord freed me from error, and through his ministry granted me the grace of saving baptism, as though I were excessively partial to my planter and waterer. Rather, it is because in this matter he himself said what speaks also to anyone who thinks devoutly and understands rightly—he who is God, who gives the increase (I Corinthians III, 7).

In the resurrection itself, therefore, it is not easy to see God except for those who are pure in heart; and therefore it is written: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” How many blessed people had he already counted, and yet he had not promised them the ability to see God! If, then, those who are pure in heart will see God, evidently others will not see him. For the unworthy will not see God; nor can one who does not wish to see God see him.

God is not seen in a place, but by the pure in heart; God is not sought with bodily eyes, nor bounded by sight, nor grasped by touch, nor heard by speech, nor perceived by his walking. When he is thought absent, he is seen; and when he is present, he is not seen.

Finally, not even all the Apostles saw Christ; and therefore he says: “For so long a time I have been with you, and still you have not known me!” Whoever has understood “the breadth and length and height and depth, and the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge,” has seen Christ and has seen the Father. For we no longer know Christ according to the flesh, but according to the spirit. “The spirit before our face is Christ the Lord,” who in his mercy may deign to fill us with all the fullness of God, so that he may be seen by us.

53. To the extent that you understand these words of the holy man—which are spiritual, not carnal—you recognize that they are true, not because he said them, but because the truth cries out without noise. To that extent you understand where you should cling to the Lord, and prepare within yourself an incorporeal place for his dwelling, in order to hear the silence of his narration and behold his invisible form.

“For blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” He will not appear to them like a body from some interval of place, but he will come to them and make his dwelling with them; for they will thus be filled with all the fullness of God—not when they themselves become fully God, but when they have been perfectly filled with God.

[Note: [Col. 0621] Thus in fifteen manuscripts. But the editions read: “when they have been made perfect.”]

But if we think only of bodies, and cannot even think worthily of that, from which we might think of bodies themselves, let us not seek what we may say against ourselves. Rather, by praying and stretching ourselves toward what lies ahead, let us cleanse our hearts from this carnal habit.

To say not only what blessed Ambrose said, but also what the holy Jerome said (Book 3 on Isaiah 6): not only the divinity of the Father, but neither that of the Son nor of the Holy Spirit—for there is one nature in the Trinity—can be looked upon by the eyes of the flesh, but only by the eyes of the mind. Of these the Savior himself says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” For, as the same Jerome briefly and truthfully defined elsewhere, an incorporeal thing is not seen by bodily eyes.

[Col. 0622] 54. I wished to insert these judgments of such great men on so great a matter not so that you would regard the opinion of any human being as something to be followed like the authority of canonical Scripture, but so that those who think otherwise might strive mentally to see what is true and seek God in simplicity of heart, lest they rashly criticize such learned interpreters of the divine utterances.

Nor should you be disturbed by what some people say without sufficient consideration: “What, then, will bodily eyes see, if they will not see God? Will they perhaps be blind, or will they exist without purpose?” Those who say this fail to attend to the fact that, if there will be no bodies, there will certainly be no bodily eyes either; but if there will be bodies, there will be something that bodily eyes can see.

But let this now suffice. If you carefully read and reread what I have set out from the beginning of this little work, you will perhaps see without any doubt that, in order to see God through his help, you must prepare a pure heart. As for the spiritual body, if the Lord helps us, we shall try in another work to determine what we are able to discuss concerning it (The City of God, Book 22, chapter 29).

[Note: [Col. 0622] Several manuscripts present the preceding little work twice: first in full, as it stands here, with the religious servant of God Paulina named at the beginning; and afterward in a shortened form, as a very brief epitome containing scarcely an eighth of it and written in the form of a letter, beginning: “When you had asked that I speak about the invisible God,” etc.]

# LETTER CXLVIII

[Note: [Col. 0622] Collated with a, bg, bl, c, cc, g, gv, l, n, r, s, vc; two manuscripts designated sb; two designated t; four designated v; and with the editions of Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0622] Elsewhere numbered 111; the letter that was 148 is now numbered 21. Written no later than the year 413.]

Augustine to Fortunatianus, bishop of Sicca, asking him to reconcile him with a certain bishop whom he had offended by a rather harsh letter, especially by writing that “we shall not see God with these bodily eyes.” In the meantime he carefully explains how and to what extent God is seen. It appears that the unnamed bishop favored the Anthropomorphites.

## Memorandum to the holy brother FORTUNATIANUS

[Note: [Col. 0622] Fortunatianus of Sicca took part in the Conference of Carthage. He is listed sixth among the seven bishops chosen to dispute against the Donatists. We believe that he was succeeded by Urbanus, who is praised as bishop of Sicca in Fragment 1, volume X. He was raised to this dignity around the year 413, as can be understood from the following letter, §34.]

## CHAPTER I

1. As I asked you when I was present, so now I remind you to be willing to visit and ask our brother about whom we spoke, that he forgive me if he took anything said about him in that letter as too harsh or severe. I do not regret having written it, because I said that the eyes of this body neither see God nor will see him.

I added the reason why I said this: namely, lest God himself be believed to be corporeal and visible within the extent and interval of a place, since the eye of this body can see nothing otherwise; and lest what is said, “Face to face” (I Corinthians XIII, 12), be understood as though God were bounded by bodily limbs.

I therefore do not regret having said it, lest we think so impiously about God himself as to suppose that he is not wholly everywhere, but divisible through local spaces. We know such things through these eyes.

2. But if someone, holding no such opinion of God, believes him to be an unchangeable and incorporeal spirit, wholly present everywhere, and nevertheless thinks that this body will undergo so great a transformation when it changes from an animal body into a spiritual one that we shall be able through such a body to see an incorporeal substance—not divisible by intervals or spaces of place, nor bounded by the outlines and limits of limbs, but wholly present everywhere—then I want him to teach me, if he thinks rightly.

If he is mistaken in this, it is far more tolerable to attribute something to the body than to detract something from God. And if this judgment is true, it will not contradict my words in that letter. For I said that the eyes of this body would not see God, considering that the eyes of this body can see only bodies separated from them by some interval of place; for if there is no interval, we do not see bodies themselves through them.

3. But if our bodies will be changed into such profound dissimilarity from what they now are that they will have eyes through which that substance may be seen which is neither spread out nor bounded through spaces of place—having one part in one place and another part elsewhere, smaller in a smaller place and larger in a larger one, but wholly incorporeal everywhere—then these bodies will be something entirely different and will not be the same bodies. They will not differ merely because mortality, corruption, and heaviness have been removed; they will in some fashion be converted into the power of the mind itself, if they will be able to see what then even the mind is allowed to see, though now not even the mind is allowed to see it.

If we say that a person is no longer the person he was when his character has changed, and finally say that, when ages have changed, the body itself is no longer what it was, how much more will it no longer be the same body when transformed by so great a change that it not only lives immortally but also sees the invisible?

Therefore, if they will see God, it will not be the eyes of this body that see him, because in this respect the body itself will no longer remain the same, having been changed into such force and power. This opinion, then, is not contrary to the words of my letter.

But if it will no longer be the same body only in this respect—that now it is mortal, then immortal; now it weighs down the soul, then, burdened by no weight, it will be exceedingly agile for every movement—then, if it is nothing other than the same body, it will in no way see an incorporeal substance that is wholly present everywhere, when it sees things perceived through spaces and intervals of place.

Whether, therefore, the one or the other is true, in either case it is true that the eyes of this body will not see God. For either they will belong to this body and will not see him, or they will not belong to this body if they will see him, since through so great a transformation they will belong to a body altogether different.

4. But if this brother knows something better about the matter, I am prepared to learn it either from him or from the one from whom he learned it. If I were speaking mockingly, I would also say that I was prepared to learn about a corporeal God whose members are divided by places. But I do not say this, because I am not speaking mockingly. I have no doubt at all that God is not such, and I wrote that letter so that he would not be believed to be such.

In that letter, while I was carefully engaged in admonition—which I composed without naming anyone—I was excessive and thoughtless in reprimanding.
