I did not consider the fraternal and episcopal person as a brother and bishop, as was fitting. I do not defend this but criticize it; I do not excuse it but accuse it.

I ask forgiveness. Let him remember our former affection and forget the new offense. Let him certainly do what he blamed me for not doing; let him show the gentleness in granting pardon that I did not show in writing that letter.

Through your charity I ask this, which I wished to ask him in person if I had had access to him. When I attempted to do so, he would not come, although a venerable man, to be preferred in honor to all of us, was writing to him. He perhaps suspected some deception on my part, as human beings often do, so far as I can judge. Assure him, as far as you can, that I am far from such deception; you can do this more easily because you are present with him.

Tell him with what great and genuine sorrow I spoke with you about the offense to his mind. Let him know how far I am from despising him, how deeply I fear God in him, and how I consider our head, in whose body we are brothers.

I thought that I should not come to the place where he lives, lest we provide a spectacle to be laughed at by outsiders, mourned by our own people, and regarded by us with shame. Through your holiness and charity everything can be properly settled. It is he who acts through you, dwelling in your heart by faith; and I believe that he does not reject him in you when he recognizes him in himself.

5. Certainly, in this matter I have found no better course than to ask pardon of the brother who complained that he had been wounded by the harshness of my letter. I hope that he too will do what he knows has been commanded by the one who speaks through the Apostle:

“Forgiving one another, if anyone has a complaint against another, just as God in Christ forgave you” (Colossians III, 13). “Therefore be imitators of God, as dearly loved children, and walk in love, just as Christ loved us” (Ephesians V, 1–2).

Walking in this love, let us inquire together, if we can, more carefully into the spiritual body that we shall have in the resurrection. For if we think differently about something, God will also reveal this to us, if we remain in him (Philippians III, 15–16).

“Whoever remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him,” because “God is love” (I John IV, 16)—either by existing ineffably as its source, or by bestowing it upon us through his Spirit.

If it can be taught that love will at some time be seen by bodily eyes, perhaps God too will be able to be seen. But if love will never be seen in this way, much less will its very source—or whatever more excellent and appropriate expression can be used concerning so great a matter—be seen in this way.

## CHAPTER II

6. Certain great men, deeply learned in the holy Scriptures, who greatly aided the Church and the faithful’s good studies through their writings, said whenever the opportunity arose that the invisible God is invisibly seen—that is, through that nature which is also invisible in us, namely, by a pure mind or heart.

When the blessed Ambrose was speaking about Christ according to what he is as the Word, he said: “For Jesus is seen not with bodily but with spiritual eyes.” A little later he said: “The Jews did not see him, for their foolish heart was blinded” (Book 1 on Luke 1), thereby showing by what means he is seen.

Likewise, when speaking about the Holy Spirit, he inserted the words of the Lord: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, to be with you forever: the Spirit of truth, whom this world cannot receive, because it does not see him or know him” (John XIV, 16–17).

“Therefore,” he says, “he rightly manifested himself in the body, because in the substance of divinity he is not seen. We saw the Spirit, but in a bodily form. Let us see the Father too; but because we cannot see him, let us hear him.”

A little later he says: “Let us therefore hear the Father, for the Father is invisible; but the Son too is invisible according to his divinity. For no one has ever seen God” (I John IV, 12). Since the Son is God, therefore, in that in which the Son is God, he is not seen (Book 2 on Luke III, 22).

7. The holy Jerome says: “The human eye cannot see God as he is in his own nature—not only human beings, but neither angels, nor Thrones, nor Powers, nor Dominations, nor any name that is named. For no creature can look upon its Creator.”

In these words the learned man sufficiently showed what he also thought concerning the future age, insofar as it concerns this matter. However much the eyes of our bodies may be changed for the better, they will be made equal to the eyes of angels. Yet here he said that the Creator’s nature is invisible even to them and to the entire heavenly creation.

But if this too becomes a matter of dispute, and someone raises the question whether we shall not be superior to the angels, the Lord himself gives a clear answer when he says concerning those who rise into the kingdom: “They will be equal to the angels of God” (Luke XX, 36).

Therefore the same holy Jerome says elsewhere: “A human being cannot see the face of God; but the angels even of the least in the Church always see the face of God” (Matthew XVIII, 10). “Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma; but then face to face” (I Corinthians XIII, 12), when we have advanced from human beings into angels and have been able to say with the Apostle: “But we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (II Corinthians III, 18), although no creature sees the face of God according to the distinctive property of his nature. He is then perceived by the mind, when he is believed to be invisible (Book 1 on Isaiah 1).

8. Much must be considered in these words of the man of God. First, according to the Lord’s most explicit judgment, Jerome himself believes that we shall see the face of God when we have advanced into angels—that is, when we have become equal to the angels—which will certainly occur in the resurrection of the dead.

Next, through the testimony of the Apostle he made sufficiently clear that, when we see face to face, the face meant is not that of the outward but of the inward person. The Apostle was speaking of the face of the heart when he said what Jerome has just recalled: “But we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image.”

If anyone doubts this, let him review the same passage and attend to what the Apostle was discussing: namely, the veil that remains in the reading of the Old Testament until each person passes over to Christ, so that the veil may be removed.

There he says: “But we, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord.” This face was not unveiled among the Jews, of whom he says: “A veil is placed over their heart,” showing that the face of the heart is revealed to us when the veil is removed.

Finally, lest anyone who considers and distinguishes these matters insufficiently should believe that God is visible either to angels or to human beings—whether now or in the future, when we have become equal to the angels—Jerome expressed his view most clearly by saying that no creature sees the face of God according to the distinctive property of his nature, and that he is then perceived by the mind when he is believed to be invisible.

To whom is he invisible, except to bodily perceptions, including those of the heavenly beings, just as he said above concerning angels, Powers, and Dominations? How much more, then, is he invisible to earthly beings!

9. Elsewhere he says still more clearly: “Not only the divinity of the Father, but neither that of the Son nor of the Holy Spirit—for there is one nature in the Trinity—can be looked upon by the eyes of the flesh, but only by the eyes of the mind.” Of these the Savior himself says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Book 3 on Isaiah 1).

What could be clearer than this statement? If he had said only, “The divinity of neither the Father, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit can be looked upon by the eyes of the flesh,” and had not then added, “but by the eyes of the mind,” someone might perhaps say that flesh should no longer be called flesh when the body has become spiritual. By adding and saying, “but by the eyes of the mind,” he excluded this kind of vision from every sort of body.

But lest anyone think that he was speaking only of the present time, he added the testimony of the Lord, wishing to show which eyes of the mind he meant. That testimony declares not a promise of present vision but of future vision: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew V, 8).

10. The most blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, when arguing against the Arians—who say that only God the Father is invisible but think that the Son and the Holy Spirit are visible—asserted the equal invisibility of the Trinity through the testimonies of the holy Scriptures and the carefulness of his reasoning. He most earnestly urged that God is seen only through the assumption of a creature; according to the distinctive property of his divinity, God is altogether invisible—that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—except insofar as he can be known by the mind and spirit.

Gregory too, the holy eastern bishop, [Note: [Col. 0626] All books read “eastern.” Yet, according to the more probable judgment of scholars, the discourse cited here—number forty-nine among the works of Gregory of Nazianzus—is the work of a Latin writer, perhaps of another Gregory, the bishop of Eliberitanus in Spain, who flourished around the middle of the fourth century.]

says most plainly that God is invisible by nature, and that when he appeared to the fathers, as to Moses, with whom he spoke face to face, he could nevertheless have been seen—while remaining invisible—through the arrangement of some perceptible material that he had assumed.

This is what our Ambrose also says: that both the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are seen in whatever form the will has chosen, not in one fashioned by nature (On Luke, chapter I, §11). Thus both statements are true: “No one has ever seen God” (John I, 18), which is the voice of the Lord Christ himself; and “Whom no human being has seen or can see” (I Timothy VI, 16), which is the voice of the Apostle—or rather, the voice of Christ through the Apostle.

Nor should those testimonies of Scripture be rejected in which God is said to have been seen, because he is invisible according to the proper nature of his divinity, yet, when he wills to be seen, he can be seen through a creature assumed as it pleases him.

## CHAPTER III

11. If invisibility belongs to God’s very nature just as incorruptibility does, that nature will certainly not be changed in the future age so that what is invisible becomes visible, because neither can what is incorruptible become corruptible. It is likewise unchangeable.

The Apostle certainly commended his nature when he placed these two qualities together, saying: “To the King of the ages, invisible, incorruptible, the only God, be honor and glory unto ages of ages” (I Timothy I, 17).

Therefore I do not dare to distinguish the words in this way: “To the incorruptible, unto ages of ages; but to the invisible, not unto ages of ages, but only in this age.”

Yet because these testimonies also cannot be false—“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God”; and “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (I John III, 2)—we cannot deny that the children of God will see God. But they will see him as invisible things are seen, just as the one who appeared visibly in the flesh to human beings promised that he would show himself, when he said: “I will love him and show myself to him” (John XIV, 21), while he spoke visibly before human eyes.

But from where are invisible things seen, if not by the eyes of the heart? Above I have said what Jerome thought concerning these eyes by which God is seen.

12. This is also why the aforementioned bishop of Milan said that in the very resurrection it is not easy to see God except for those who are pure in heart, and that therefore it is written: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.”

“How many blessed people,” he says, “had he already counted, and yet he had not promised them the ability to see God!” Then he adds: “If, therefore, those who are pure in heart will see God, evidently others will not see him.”

And lest we understand those “others” to be the people of whom it was said, “Blessed are the poor,” “Blessed are the meek,” he immediately adds: “For the unworthy will not see God.” By “unworthy” he clearly means those who, although they rise again, will not be able to see God, because they will rise for condemnation, since they were unwilling to purify their hearts through the true faith that works through love (Galatians V, 6).

Therefore he continues and says: “Nor can one who does not wish to see God see God.” Then, because it might occur to us that all the wicked desire to see God, he immediately showed why he had said “one who does not wish to see God.” The wicked certainly do not wish to see God in the manner by which he can be seen, because they do not wish to purify their hearts. He therefore continued:

“God is not seen in a place, but by the pure in heart; God is not sought with bodily eyes, nor bounded by sight, nor grasped by touch, nor heard by speech, nor perceived by his walking” (On Luke, chapter I, §11).

By these words the blessed Ambrose wished to admonish people concerning what they must prepare if they wish to see God: namely, to purify the heart through the faith that works through love, by the gift of the Holy Spirit, from whom we have received the pledge by which we learn to desire that vision (II Corinthians V, 4–8).

## CHAPTER IV

13. As for the members of God that Scripture constantly mentions, lest anyone should believe that we are like God according to the form and shape of this flesh, Scripture itself therefore also said that God has wings (Psalm XVI, 8), which we certainly do not have.

Just as, when we hear of wings, we understand protection, so, when we hear of hands, we should understand activity; when we hear of feet, presence; when we hear of eyes, the vision by which he knows; and when we hear of a face, the knowledge by which he makes himself known. Whatever else Scripture similarly mentions, I think should be understood spiritually.

Nor is this my opinion alone, or something I was the first to say, but the opinion of all who, with whatever degree of spiritual understanding, resist those who for this reason are called Anthropomorphites. To avoid causing greater delay by recalling many of their writings, I shall insert only this one statement from the holy Jerome, so that this brother may know that, if anything troubles him on this matter, he must deal with me no more than with those who preceded me.

14. When that man, highly learned in the Scriptures, was expounding the psalm in which it is said, “Understand, therefore, you who are foolish among the people, and you who are fools, acquire wisdom at last. He who planted the ear—will he not hear? Or he who formed the eye—does he not observe?” among other things he says:

“This passage applies especially against those who are Anthropomorphites, who say that God has the members that we too possess. For example, God is said to have eyes because ‘the eyes of the Lord look upon all things’; ‘the hand of the Lord makes all things’; and, he says, ‘Adam heard the sound of the feet of the Lord walking in paradise’ (Gen. 3:8). They hear these things literally and refer human weaknesses to the majesty of God. But I say that God is wholly eye, wholly hand, wholly foot. He is wholly eye because he sees everything. He is wholly hand because he works everything. He is wholly foot because he is everywhere. Therefore see what he says: ‘He who planted the ear—will he not hear? Or he who formed the eyes—does he not observe?’ He did not say, ‘He who planted the ear, therefore he himself does not have an ear’; he did not say, ‘Therefore he himself does not have eyes.’ Rather, what did he say? ‘He who planted the ear—will he not hear? He who formed the eyes—does he not observe?’ He removed the members and assigned the functions” (*On Psalm* 93:8–9).

15. I have thought it necessary to mention all this from the writings of those Latin and Greek authors who, before us, lived in the Catholic Church and interpreted the divine utterances, so that this brother may know that, if he thinks differently from them, he must seek, learn, or teach the matter with the bitterness of disagreement laid aside and the sweetness of brotherly love preserved and restored intact, through careful and peaceful consideration. For we must not treat the disputations of just anyone—even Catholic and distinguished men—as though they were canonical Scriptures, so that we would be forbidden, while preserving the honor due to those men, to disapprove and reject something in their writings if we happen to find that they have thought differently from the truth, whether that truth has been understood by others through divine assistance or by ourselves.

[Col. 0629] I am like this with the writings of others; I want readers of my writings to be like this with mine. In short, throughout all the things I have cited from the little works of holy and learned men—Ambrose, Jerome, Athanasius, Gregory, and whatever similar passages from others I was able to read but thought it would take too long to cite—I firmly believe, with the Lord’s help, and understand insofar as he grants it, that God is not a body; that he does not have members of human form; that he cannot be divided according to extensions of place; and that by nature he is immutably invisible. I also believe that he appeared to those to whom he appeared not through that same nature and substance, but by assuming a visible form as he willed, whenever Scripture says that he was seen through the eyes of the body.

## CHAPTER V

16. As for the spiritual body that we shall have in the resurrection, how great a transformation for the better will it undergo? Will it pass into the simplicity of spirit, so that the whole human being will now be spirit? Or—and this is what I think more likely, though I do not yet affirm it with complete confidence—will the body then be spiritual in such a way that it is called spiritual because of some ineffable facility, while nevertheless retaining bodily substance, which by itself could neither live nor perceive, but only through the spirit that uses it? For even now, because the body is called “animal,” the nature of the soul is not therefore the same as that of the body.

And if the nature of the body, although by then immortal and incorruptible, is preserved, will it then assist the spirit in seeing visible things—that is, bodily things—as we now cannot see such things except through the body? Or will our spirit even then be able to know bodily things without an organ of the body—for God, too, does not know such things through bodily senses? I confess that I have not yet found anywhere, in this question or in the many other issues it can raise, anything that I considered sufficient either for learning or for teaching.

17. Therefore, if this brother does not disapprove of my caution, however inadequate it may be, let us meanwhile, because it is written, “We shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2), prepare, as far as we can and with his help, a pure heart for that vision. As for the spiritual body, let us inquire more calmly and carefully, lest perhaps God, if he knows this to be useful for us, deign to show us from his Scriptures something certain and clear.

For if more careful inquiry should discover that the body will undergo such a great transformation that it can see invisible things, this bodily capacity will not, I think, take away the vision from the mind, so that the outward human being could see God then, while the inward human being could not—as though God were only outside the human being and not within the human being, when it is written most plainly that “God may be all in all” (1 Cor. 15:28). Nor is he within in such a way—he who is wholly everywhere without any extensions of place—that he can be seen outside only by the outward human being, but cannot be seen within by the inward human being.

If these ideas are recognized as utterly absurd—and surely the saints will be more filled with God, not surrounded externally by him while inwardly empty of him; nor will they, being blind within, fail to see him with whom they will be filled, while seeing only externally with eyes the one by whom they will be surrounded—then it follows that, for now, we should be completely certain about the vision of God according to the [Col. 0630] inward human being. But if the body, too, through a marvelous transformation, should become capable of this, something additional will be gained; the former will not be lost.

18. Let us therefore affirm more confidently what we least doubt: that the inward human being will see God. The inward human being alone can now see love, of which it was said when it was praised, “God is love” (1 John 4:8); and it alone can see peace and sanctification, “without which no one will see God” (Heb. 12:14). For no bodily eye now sees love, peace, sanctification, or anything similar. Yet the eye of the mind already sees all these things, insofar as it can—and the purer it is, the more purely it sees them.

Thus, without hesitation, let us believe that we shall see God, whether or not we discover what we are seeking concerning the nature of the future body. At the same time, we do not doubt that the body will rise and will be immortal and incorruptible, since we hold to the most clear and most authoritative statements of the holy Scriptures on this point. But if this brother has already established for himself as absolutely certain what I am still seeking concerning the spiritual body, then, unless I listen peacefully while he teaches, so that he too listens peacefully while I inquire, he will have just cause for anger. For now, however, I beg you through Christ to obtain his pardon for me concerning the harshness of my letters, by which I have learned that he was understandably offended, and, with the Lord’s help, gladden me by your reply.

## LETTER 149

[Col. 0630]

[Note: We have collated this letter against the manuscripts designated a, bg, bl, c, cc, ff, g, gv, j, n, r, s, vc; two manuscripts designated bn; two designated sb; two designated t; four designated v; and against Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: Elsewhere numbered 59; what was 149 is now 38. It appears to have been written in the year 414.]

He responds to questions proposed above by Paulinus concerning the Psalms, the Apostle, and the Gospel, in Letter 121.

To the most blessed and venerably desirable, and desirably venerable, holy and most holily beloved brother and fellow bishop, PAULINUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

## CHAPTER I

1. The Lord quickly gladdened us with the news of the very prosperous arrival of our brother and fellow presbyter Quintus and those who sailed with him, as your Holiness’s letter reported. Giving thanks to him who refreshes the afflicted and consoles the humble, I now render my reply to your sincere heart, taking the opportunity that has just presented itself through our son and fellow deacon Ruffinus; for he set out from the shore of Hippo.

I approve the merciful plan that the Lord inspired in you and graciously allowed you to disclose to me. May he himself assist and prosper it—he who has already relieved much of our anxiety, since our most beloved brother has arrived safely and has been commended not only by good works but also by your holy prayers.

2. Certainly, the letter of Your Reverence, in which you asked many questions, urged that certain matters be investigated, and taught by your very questioning, reached me. But the reply I immediately sent through the men of those same holy companions who assist us, as I have learned from your more recent letters, was not [Col. 0631] delivered to Your Reverence.

I was unable to recall precisely how far I had answered the questions in it; nor, when I searched for a copy so that I could review the matter, did I find one. Nevertheless, I am entirely certain that I answered some of the questions, and therefore not all of them, because the urgency of the courier pressed me to finish quickly.

At the same time, as you had instructed, I sent a copy of the letter that I had written at Carthage to Your Charity concerning the resurrection of bodies, where the question had arisen about the use of the members.

[Note: Four Vatican manuscripts and three Gallican manuscripts read *scripseram* (“I had written”).]

So now I have sent this as well as a copy of the other letter, because I inferred that the latter itself had not reached your hands, since you again asked certain questions which I read and recognize as having already been answered by me in it. But I do not know through whom I sent this one.

The writings of Your Charity, by which I replied to it—as the letter itself also indicates—were sent to me from Hippo by our people when I was staying with our holy brother and fellow bishop Boniface. I did not see the person who carried them, and I did not delay in sending my reply.

[Note: The editions read *indicant* (“they indicate”); the manuscripts have *indicat* (“it indicates”), namely, the letter returned by Augustine.]

3. Since at that time, as I wrote, I had been unable to consult the Greek manuscripts concerning certain matters in Psalm 16, I later examined those that I found. One had the reading found also in our Latin copies: “Lord, destroying them from the earth, divide them.” Another had the reading that you yourself gave: “From the few, from the earth.”

The first reading has a clear meaning: “Destroying them from the earth that you gave them, divide them among the nations.” This happened to them when they were conquered and overthrown in a severe war.

But how the other reading should be understood does not occur to me, except that, in comparison with their multitude, which was lost, a remnant was saved—namely, among the few from whom Scripture foretold that they would be divided, that is, split apart and separated. Thus Scripture says: “Lord, from the few, from the earth divide them,” meaning: “From the few—that is, from the remnant whom you saved from that people—divide them from the earth.”

By “earth” we may understand the Church, the inheritance of the faithful and the saints, which is also called “the land of the living” and which can rightly be understood in that passage as well: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth as an inheritance” (Matt. 5:4).

When it had said, “From the few, from the earth divide them,” it added, “in their lifetime,” so that it would be understood as something destined to occur openly while they live here. Many are separated from the Church when they die, though while they live they appear to be joined to the Church through participation in the sacraments and in Catholic unity.

These, then, were divided from the few who believed among them, from the earth that the Father, the farmer, cultivates as his field. They were divided in their lifetime—that is, openly here—as we see.

The text continues: “And their belly has been filled from your hidden things.” That is, in addition to being divided openly, their belly has also been filled from your hidden things, which you secretly repay to the conscience of the wicked.

[Note: Bad., Am., and Er., together with two manuscripts, read “for hidden things are misery to them.”]

He uses “belly” for the hidden and inward secrets.

4. As for what follows, “They have been filled with swine”—

[Note: For the Greek *huiōn* (“sons”), the translator seems to have read *huōn*, yielding “swine.”]

—I have already explained what I thought of this. But the other [Col. 0632] manuscripts have a reading that is said to be more accurate, since more carefully prepared copies, by means of accents, remove the ambiguity of the same Greek word according to Greek writing practice. The reading is indeed more obscure, but it seems better suited to the more excellent meaning.

For since he had said, “Their belly has been filled from your hidden things,” words by which the hidden judgments of God are signified—for even those who rejoice in evil are wretched in secret, whom God handed over to the desires of their hearts (Rom. 1:24)—it is as though someone had asked how those who have been filled inwardly with the wrath of God in secret could be recognized. The answer is given in the Gospel: “You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. 7:16).

Immediately, therefore, it is added: “They have been filled with sons,” that is, with fruits—which is expressed more clearly as “with their works.” Hence we read elsewhere: “Behold, he conceived injustice, was pregnant with misery, and gave birth to iniquity” (Ps. 7:15); and elsewhere: “Then desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin” (James 1:15).

Evil sons are evil works, by which those people are recognized who have been filled inwardly, as in a belly, with the hidden judgments of God concerning their thoughts. Good works are good sons.

Hence it is said to the bride, the Church: “Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep ascending from the washing, all of which bear twins, and none among them is barren” (Song 4:2). In this twin offspring the twofold work of love is recognized: love of the Lord God and of one’s neighbor, on which two commandments the whole Law and the Prophets depend (Matt. 22:40).

5. This interpretation—that the words “They have been filled with sons” are explained in this way—had not occurred to me when I replied earlier. But I consulted a very brief exposition of the same psalm that I had dictated long ago, and I found that I had expressed this point quite briefly.

I also examined the Greek manuscripts to determine whether the word “sons” was in the dative case or in the genitive, which that language uses for the ablative, and I found the genitive. If it were translated literally, it would read, “They have been filled with sons’.” But the translator rightly followed the meaning and, according to Latin usage, said, “They have been filled with sons.”

As for what follows, “And they left remnants for their little ones,” I think that “little ones” should be understood as their manifest children of the flesh. Thus, even according to this interpretation—not “swine,” but “sons”—the meaning remains that of the words they said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25). For in this way they left the remnants of their works to their little ones.

6. In Psalm 15, where it is written, “He has made all his wishes wonderful,” or “May he make all his wishes wonderful,” “among them,” nothing prevents us from understanding—and it seems more fitting—that the words are not “among them” but “in them.”

The Greek manuscripts read this way. Frequently, what that language says “in them” our translators render “among them,” where the sense appears to require it.

Let us therefore take the passage as follows: “For the saints who are in his land, he has made all his wishes wonderful in them,” which is the reading found in most manuscripts. Let us understand “his wishes” as gifts of grace, which is given freely—that is, because he willed it, not because it was owed.

Hence we have: “You have crowned us with the shield of your good will” (Ps. [Col. 0633] 5:13); “In your will you have led me” (Ps. 72:24); “He begot us voluntarily by the word of truth” (James 1:18); “Separating the voluntary rain, O God, for your inheritance” (Ps. 67:10); “Distributing his own gifts to each one as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:11); and countless other passages.

Therefore: “He has made all his wishes wonderful in them”—in whom, if not in the saints who are in his land? For if “land,” as we showed above, can be understood in a good sense even where “his” is not added, how much more where it says, “his land”?

He has therefore made all his wishes wonderful in them. He made them altogether wonderful because he marvelously rescued them from despair.

7. From this wonder the Apostle exclaims: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” For earlier he had said: “God has shut up all in unbelief, that he may have mercy on all” (Rom. 11:33, 32).

The same thought follows here: “Their infirmities have been multiplied; afterward they hastened.” He used “infirmities” for sins, just as the Apostle says to the Romans: “For if Christ, when we were still weak, at the appointed time died for the ungodly.” He called those whom he called ungodly “weak.”

Then, shortly afterward, repeating the same meaning, he says: “God demonstrates his love toward us, because while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” Those whom he previously called weak he here calls sinners.

Again, in what follows, expressing the same thought in other words, he says: “For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son” (Rom. 5:6, 8, 10).

Accordingly, in the words “Their infirmities have been multiplied,” we are to understand that their sins have been multiplied. “The Law entered in, so that the offense might abound; but where the offense abounded, grace abounded still more” (Rom. 5:20). Therefore “afterward they hastened.”

For he did not come to call the righteous but sinners, because “those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matt. 9:13, 12). Their infirmities were multiplied so that the medicine of such great grace would be necessary for their healing, and so that the one to whom many sins are forgiven would love much.

8. The ashes of the heifer, the sprinkling of blood, and the multiplication of bloody sacrifices signified this; they did not accomplish it. Therefore he goes on to say: “I will not gather their assemblies from bloods”—that is, from those sacrifices that were offered as a figure of the blood of Christ—“nor will I remember their names through my lips.”

Their names were found in the multiplication of their infirmities: fornicators, idol-servants, adulterers, the effeminate, men who have intercourse with males, thieves, the greedy, robbers, drunkards, revilers, and all others who will not possess the kingdom of God.

But when sin abounded, grace abounded still more; afterward they hastened. And these indeed you were; but you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God (1 Cor. 6:9–11). Therefore he will not remember their names through his lips.

More accurate manuscripts and those of greater authority do not read “his wishes,” but “my wishes.” The meaning is the same, because the words are spoken in the person [Col. 0634] of the Son. It is he himself who is speaking, as is clearly shown by the words also used by the Apostles: “You will not abandon my soul to the underworld, nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption” (Acts 2:31; 13:35).

The gifts of grace belonging to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are the same; therefore the Son can most rightly call them “his wishes.”

9. As for what is understood concerning the Jews in Psalm 58, where it says, “Do not kill them, lest they at some time forget your Law,” I think it was fittingly foretold in this way: even after that nation had been defeated and overthrown, it would not yield to the superstitions of the victorious people, but would remain in the old Law, so that among them there might be testimony from the Scriptures throughout the whole world, from which the Church was to be called.

No more evident proof can be shown to the nations of what is most beneficial to recognize: that the name of Christ has not been established in the hope of eternal salvation by something unexpected and sudden, through the presumptuous spirit of human beings, so that it now prevails with such authority; rather, it was prophesied and written long ago.

For what else would that very prophecy be thought to be fabricated by us if it were not proven from the books of Christ’s enemies? Therefore: “Do not kill them, lest they at some time forget your Law.” That is, do not extinguish the name of that nation, lest they forget your Law. This would certainly have happened if they had been compelled to worship the rites and sacred practices of the Gentiles and had retained no name whatsoever for their own religion.

The same thing is written figuratively about Cain: the Lord set a sign upon him so that no one would kill him (Gen. 4:15).

Finally, after saying, “Do not kill them, lest they at some time forget your Law,” as though someone had asked what should be done with them so that they would not be killed—that is, consumed—and would not forget the Law of God, he immediately added: “Scatter them by your power.”

For if they were in one place on earth, they would not assist by their testimony the preaching of the Gospel, which bears fruit throughout the whole world. Therefore: “Scatter them by your power,” so that everywhere they may be witnesses, through the very Law that they do not forget, to the one whose deniers, persecutors, and killers they were—the one who was prophesied in that Law, though they do not follow him.

Their not forgetting the Law benefits them nothing. For it is one thing to have the Law of God in one’s memory, and another to have it in one’s understanding and practice.

10. In Psalm 67, where you ask about the meaning of, “Yet God will crush the heads of his enemies, the crown of the hair of those who walk in their sins,” I do not think anything else is meant than: “God will crush the heads of his enemies who are excessively proud and who exalt themselves excessively in their sins.”

By hyperbole he signified pride rising so high and advancing with such exaltation that it seemed to tread upon the crown of the head with its hair.

Likewise, in the same psalm, where it is written, “The tongue of your dogs from your enemies, from him,” dogs should not always be understood in an evil sense. Otherwise, the prophet would not rebuke the mute dogs who do not know how to bark and love to sleep (Isa. 56:10). Surely they would be praiseworthy dogs if they knew how to bark and loved to keep [Col. 0635] watch.

And certainly those three hundred men would not have been chosen for victory, in a number made most sacred by the sign of the cross, because they lapped water like dogs (Judg. 7:7), unless they signified something great.

Good dogs keep watch and bark—for the house and for the master, for the flock and for the shepherd. Indeed, here too, when prophecy was being uttered in praise of the Church, the tongue of dogs was mentioned, not their teeth.

But he said, “of your dogs, from your enemies”—that is, so that those who were your enemies might become your dogs and bark for you, those who had raged against you. He added, “from him,” so that they would understand that this had not happened from themselves but from him—that is, from his mercy and grace.

## CHAPTER II

11. Concerning the prophets, where the Apostle says, “God has placed some in the Church as apostles, some as prophets” (Eph. 4:11), I understand it as you yourself have written: that in this passage those are called prophets from whom Agabus was one (Acts 11:27–28), not those who prophesied that the Lord would come in the flesh.

We find evangelists whom we do not read were apostles, such as Luke and Mark. As for pastors and teachers, about which you especially wanted me to make a distinction, I think—as you also have thought—that they are the same people. We should not understand “some pastors” and “other teachers” as different groups. Rather, after saying “pastors,” he added “teachers” to indicate that teaching belongs to the office of pastors.

For this reason he did not say, “Some pastors, others teachers,” although in the preceding expressions he distinguished the offices by the same form of speech, saying, “Some apostles, some prophets, and others evangelists.” Here, as though embracing one thing under two names, he said, “Some pastors and teachers.”

12. The distinctions are especially difficult in the passage where, writing to Timothy, he says: “Therefore, first of all, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made” (1 Tim. 2:1).

They must be distinguished according to the Greek wording. For among our translators scarcely any are found who have taken care to render these terms diligently and knowledgeably.

For example, as you yourself have written them, “I urge that supplications be made,” the Apostle, who certainly wrote that letter in Greek, did not use the same word for both expressions. For the Latin “I urge,” he used the Greek *parakalō* (παρακαλῶ). For what your Latin text has as “supplications,” he used *deēseis* (δεήσεις).

Accordingly, some manuscripts, including some of ours, do not have “supplications” but “entreaties.” The three words that follow—“prayers,” “intercessions,” and “thanksgivings”—are found in most Latin manuscripts in this form.

13. If, then, we wish to distinguish these terms according to the properties of the Latin language and its customary usage, we may perhaps maintain our own understanding, but it would be surprising if we thereby captured the meaning or usage of the Greek expression.

Many of our writers consider “prayer” and “entreaty” to mean the same thing, and this has now become entirely dominant through everyday usage. Those who spoke Latin more precisely, however, used prayers when seeking good things, and entreaties when seeking to avoid bad things.

They said that *precari* meant to seek good things by praying, while *imprecari* meant to seek evil—[Col. 0636] what is now commonly called cursing. They understood *deprecari* as driving away evil by prayer.

But let us follow the customary manner of speech. Whether we find “prayers” or “entreaties,” which the Greeks call *deēseis* (δεήσεις), we should not consider the text in need of correction.

“Prayers,” which the Greek has as *proseuchas* (προσευχάς), are extremely difficult to distinguish from petitions or prayers. Some manuscripts do not have “prayers” but “adorations,” because the Greek does not say *euchas* (εὐχάς) but *proseuchas* (προσευχάς). I do not think this was translated knowingly, for it is very well known among the Greeks that *proseuchas* means “prayers.”

Certainly, to pray is one thing and to adore another. Thus, in the Greek, “You shall adore the Lord your God” (Matt. 4:10) is read with a different word, as is, “I will adore toward your holy temple” (Ps. 5:8), and similar passages.

14. In place of “intercessions,” however, you have written “petitions,” following, I believe, your manuscripts. In these two expressions—“petitions” in some manuscripts and “intercessions” in others—the translators wished to render the single Greek word *enteuxeis* (ἐντεύξεις).

You certainly recognize, and know, that to intercede is one thing and to petition another. We do not usually say, “They petition in order to intercede,” but rather, “They intercede in order to petition.” Nevertheless, a word borrowed from a neighboring expression, whose very proximity supplies its meaning, should not be condemned as though by a censor’s notation.

For it is also said of the Lord Jesus Christ himself that “he intercedes for us” (Rom. 8:34). Surely he intercedes and does not also petition? Indeed, because he petitions, “intercedes” has been used in his case.

For elsewhere it is stated plainly concerning him: “If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the expiation for our sins” (1 John 2:1–2).

Perhaps, however, your manuscripts also read in that passage concerning the Lord Jesus Christ not “he intercedes for us” but “he petitions for us.” For in the Greek, the same word used here for “intercessions,” which you rendered “petitions,” is also found there where the text reads “he intercedes for us.”

15. Since the one who petitions also prays, the one who prays also petitions, and the one who intercedes with God intercedes in order to pray and petition, what does the Apostle intend by setting these terms down in such a way that their distinction is not to be neglected?

Apart from the general term, and without violating customary speech—in accordance with which, whether you say “petition,” “prayer,” “intercession,” or “request,” one and the same thing is understood—we must seek some particular property belonging to each of these terms. Yet it is difficult to arrive at that distinction clearly, for many things can be said about it that should not be rejected.

16. But in these words I choose to understand what almost the whole Church practices: that “petitions” refers to what we do in the celebration of the sacraments, before what is on the Lord’s table begins to be blessed; “prayers,” to what is done when it is blessed and sanctified and broken for distribution. Almost the whole Church concludes this entire petition with the Lord’s Prayer.

The origin of the Greek word also assists us in this interpretation. For the term they call *euchē* (εὐχή) is [Col. 0637] rarely used in Scripture to mean prayer; more often, and much more commonly, it means a vow. But *proseuchē* (προσευχή), the word used in the passage under discussion, always means prayer.

Thus, as I said above, some less learned observers of the origin of the word have wished to say that *proseuchē* means not “prayer” but “adoration.” Adoration is more properly called *proskynēsis* (προσκύνησις). But because prayer is sometimes called *euchē*, *proseuchē* was thought to mean adoration.

Moreover, if, as I have said, *euchē* more commonly means “vow” in the Scriptures, then, apart from the general name “prayer,” the prayer proper is the one that we make toward a vow—that is, *pros euchēn* (πρὸς εὐχήν), “toward a vow.”

Everything that is offered to God is vowed, especially the offering of the holy altar. Through this sacrament our great vow is proclaimed: the vow by which we promise to remain in Christ, that is, in the structure of Christ’s body. The sacrament of this reality is that “we, though many, are one bread, one body” (1 Cor. 10:17).

Therefore, in preparation for this sanctification, I think the Apostle specifically commanded that *proseuchai* (προσευχαί), “prayers,” be made—or, as some less skillful translators rendered it, “adorations.” For this is “toward a vow,” which in the Scriptures is more commonly called *euchē*.

“Intercessions,” or, as your manuscripts have it, “petitions,” are made when the people are blessed. At that time the bishops, as advocates, commend those whom they have received, through the laying on of hands, to the most merciful power.

When these actions have been completed and so great a sacrament has been received, thanksgiving concludes everything. The Apostle also commended this as the final element in these words.

17. The chief reason for saying this was that, after these matters had been touched upon and indicated briefly, no one should think the following words could be neglected: “for all human beings, for kings, and for all who are in positions of authority, so that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all piety and love.”

Because of the weakness characteristic of human thought, someone might suppose that such prayers should not be offered for those by whom the Church was suffering persecution, even though the members of Christ had to be gathered from every kind of human being.

Therefore he adds and says: “For this is good and acceptable before God our Savior, who wants all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.”

And lest anyone say that there could be a way of salvation through good conduct and the worship of the one almighty God without participation in the body and blood of Christ, he says: “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus.”

Thus, the statement that he “wants all human beings to be saved” is not to be understood as being accomplished in any other way than through the mediator—not God, who was always the Word, but the human being Christ Jesus, when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14).

18. Therefore, do not let what the same Apostle says concerning the Jews disturb you: “According to the Gospel, they are enemies for your sake; but according to election, they are beloved for the sake of the fathers” (Rom. 11:28).

That depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God, together with his unsearchable judgments and inscrutable ways, produces great wonder in faithful hearts. They do not doubt what it means that, according to his wisdom, which reaches mightily from one end to the other and [Col. 0638] orders all things sweetly (Wis. 8:1), he wills such people to be born, grow, and multiply—people whom, although he did not himself make evil, he nevertheless foreknew would become evil.

For his plan is exceedingly hidden: he uses even evil people for the advancement of the good, thereby also displaying the marvelous power of his goodness. Just as it belongs to their wickedness to use his good works badly, so it belongs to his wisdom to use their evil works well.

19. The Apostle commends this depth of the mystery in the following way: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, lest you be wise in your own estimation: a partial blindness has happened in Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved” (Rom. 11:25–26).

He said “a partial blindness” because not all had been blinded. There were some among them who recognized Christ.

The fullness of the Gentiles enters in those who have been called according to the purpose; and thus all Israel will be saved, because those from the Jews and from the Gentiles who have been called according to the purpose are the true Israel, of whom the same Apostle says, “And upon the Israel of God” (Gal. 6:16).

But he calls the others Israel according to the flesh: “See Israel according to the flesh,” he says (1 Cor. 10:18).

Then he inserts the prophet’s testimony: “He will come from Zion, the one who delivers and turns impiety away from Jacob; and this will be my covenant with them, when I take away their sins” (Isa. 59:20). This does not mean all the Jews, but the beloved.

[Note: The editions read “the elect”; the manuscripts have “the beloved.”]

20. Hence he adds the matters you set down for inquiry: “According to the Gospel, indeed, enemies for your sake.” For the price of our redemption is the blood of Christ, who could only have been killed by enemies. Here is that use of evil things for the advancement of good things. But when he adds, “According to election, however, beloved for the sake of the fathers,” he shows from this that they are not enemies but elect and beloved. Yet it is the custom of Scripture to speak of a part as though it were the whole. Thus, in the first parts of his Epistle, he praises the Corinthians as though they were all such, although only some of them were praiseworthy; and later, in certain passages of the same Epistle, he reproves them as though all were blameworthy, because some were such. Whoever carefully observes this habit of the divine Scriptures, scattered very frequently throughout the whole body of their writings, resolves many things that appear to contradict one another.

Therefore he calls some enemies and others beloved; but because they belonged to one people, he appears to be calling the very same people by both names. Indeed, even among the enemies who crucified the Lord, many were converted and proved to be elect. They were elect when they were converted, insofar as the beginning of salvation is concerned; but insofar as God’s foreknowledge is concerned, they were not then elect but before the foundation of the world, as the same Apostle says, that he chose us before the foundation of the world (Eph. 1:4). In two ways, then, the same people were both enemies and beloved: either because both groups belonged to one people, or because some of those who had raged as enemies even to the blood of Christ had become beloved according to the election hidden in God’s foreknowledge.

For this reason he added [Col. 0639], “for the sake of the fathers,” because what had been promised to the fathers had to be fulfilled, as he says near the end of the Epistle to the Romans: “For I say that Christ became a servant of circumcision for the sake of the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers, and that the Gentiles might glorify God for mercy” (Rom. 15:8–9). According to this mercy it was said, “enemies for your sake,” which he had also said above: “By their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles.”

21. But after saying, “according to election, beloved for the sake of the fathers,” he added, “For the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable.” You plainly see that those are signified who belong to the number of the predestined. Of these he says elsewhere: “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called according to his purpose” [Note: The printed editions add *sancti* (“holy”) after *vocati sunt*; this word is absent from all the manuscripts and from the Greek text of the Apostle.]. For “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 22:14); and those who are chosen are precisely those who are called according to his purpose. In them, beyond doubt, God’s foreknowledge cannot be mistaken. “Those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. And those whom he predestined, he also called. This calling is according to his purpose; this is irrevocable. And those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified. If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Rom. 8:28–31).

22. Those who, in the faith that works through love (Gal. 5:6), do not persevere to the end—even if they walk in it for some time—do not belong to this calling. Certainly they could have been taken away, lest wickedness change their understanding (Wis. 4:11), if they belonged to that predestination and calling which is according to God’s purpose and irrevocable.

But lest some presumptuous person judge so concerning the hidden matters of others as to say, “They were not taken from this life before they became deserters from the faith because they were not walking faithfully in that same life, and the Lord knew this in their hearts, although they appeared otherwise to human beings”—what will he say about little infants? Many of them, after receiving at that age the sacrament of Christian grace, are allowed to grow up; yet, if they immediately departed this life, they would undoubtedly belong to eternal life and the kingdom of heaven, and some of them even become apostates. Why is this, unless because they do not belong to that predestination and calling which is according to God’s purpose and irrevocable? Why some belong to it and others do not may be a hidden cause, but it cannot be an unjust one. “Is there injustice with God? By no means!” (Rom. 9:14). For this too belongs to that depth of judgments at which the Apostle marveled and, as it were, was overcome with awe. He calls them “judgments” precisely so that no one might think that such things happen either through the injustice or rashness of the one who causes them, or by chance and accident, as though some parts of the ages arranged under God’s great wisdom were simply falling away.

23. As for what is written in the Epistle to the Colossians, “Let no one deceive you, wishing in humility …” (Col. 2:18), and what follows, up to the point that you said remained obscure to you, I too do not yet understand without some darkness. Would that you had asked me about this in person! For, in the sense [Col. 0640] that I seem to discern in these words, a certain expression of the face and manner of voice is needed—something that cannot be represented in writing—in order that it may be disclosed to some extent. This is made more obscure because, as I believe, it is not pronounced correctly.

For when it is written, “Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle,” it is thought to be an injunction of the Apostle forbidding the touching, tasting, or handling of something or other. But the meaning is the opposite, if I am not mistaken amid such great obscurity. For he put down the words of those by whom he did not want them to be deceived and led astray as a mockery. These people, distinguishing foods according to the worship of angels and thus making judgments about this world, say, “Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle,” although “to the pure all things are pure” (Tit. 1:15), and “every creation of God is good” (1 Tim. 4:4). The Apostle himself clearly commends this elsewhere.

24. Let us therefore examine the whole setting of his statement, for when the Apostle’s intention has been perceived, we may perhaps grasp its meaning as far as we are able. He feared that those to whom he was writing would be deceived by the shadows of things, under the pleasant name of knowledge, and turned away from the light of truth that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

He saw that this concern about vain and superfluous observances, under the name of wisdom or knowledge, had to be guarded against—observances arising from pagan superstition, especially from those who were called philosophers, and from Judaism. In Judaism there were shadows of future things that had to be removed, since Christ, their light, had already come.

After he had recalled and commended how great a struggle he had for them, for those in Laodicea, and for all who had not seen his face in the flesh, so that their hearts might be comforted, joined together in love, and in all the riches of the fullness of understanding, for knowing the mystery of God, which is Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, he says: “I say this so that no one may deceive you with plausible speech.” Because they were led by love of truth, he feared that they might be deceived by plausibility. Therefore he commended to them in Christ the treasure they held most dearly: wisdom and knowledge, by whose name and promise they could be drawn into error.

25. “For although I am absent in body,” he says, “I am with you in spirit, rejoicing and seeing your orderliness and what is lacking in your faith in Christ.” He feared for them because he saw what they still lacked. “Therefore, as you received Jesus Christ our Lord, walk in him, rooted and built up in him and confirmed in the faith, as you were taught, abounding in thanksgiving.”

He wants them to be nourished by faith so that they may become capable of sharing in the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden in Christ, lest, before they are fit for these things, they be captured by plausible speech and turn aside from the path of truth.

Then, showing more openly what he feared for them, he says: “See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deception, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ; for in him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily.” He said “bodily” [Col. 0641] because those people were leading them astray through shadows. He uses a transferred expression, just as the term “shadow” in these matters is not a proper word but has been transferred by way of analogy.

“And you,” he says, “have been filled in him, who is the head of every principality and power.” Through principalities and powers the superstition of the Gentiles and of the philosophers was leading them astray, as they proclaimed the theology they called such through the elements of this world. By “head” he wanted Christ to be understood as the beginning of all things, just as, when he was asked, “Who are you?” he answered, “The Beginning, who also speaks to you” (John 8:25). “For all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3).

He wonderfully wants them to be, as it were, despisers of these supposedly marvelous things, when he shows that they have been made the body of that head, saying: “And you have been filled in him, who is the head of every principality and power.”

26. At this point, lest they be led astray by the shadows of Judaism, he adds: “In whom you were also circumcised with a circumcision not made by hand, in the stripping away of the body of the flesh”; or, as some copies read, “in the stripping away of the body of the sins of the flesh, in the circumcision of Christ”; “buried with him in baptism, in which you also rose through faith in the operation of God, who raised him from the dead.”

See how here too he shows them to be the body of Christ, so that they may despise these things, clinging to so great a head of theirs, the mediator between God and human beings, Christ Jesus, and seeking no false or ineffective medium by which to cling to God.

“And you,” he says, “when you were dead in trespasses and in the uncircumcision of your flesh”—he called the uncircumcision what is signified by uncircumcision, namely, the carnal trespasses from which we must be stripped—“he made alive with him, forgiving you all trespasses, blotting out the bond written against us in decrees, which was hostile to us,” because the Law made us guilty, having entered so that trespass might abound.

“Taking it,” he says, “out of the way and nailing it to the cross, stripping off the flesh, he displayed the principalities and powers, triumphing over them openly in himself.” He displayed not good but evil principalities and powers—namely, demonic and diabolical ones [Note: *Edeigmatisen* (“he displayed,” “he exposed as an example”).]—that is, he made an example of them, so that just as he himself stripped off the flesh, he might show that his own followers must likewise be stripped of the carnal vices through which those powers exercised dominion over them.

27. Here pay careful attention to how he introduces the reason for which we have recalled all these things. “Therefore,” he says, “let no one judge you in food,” as though he had said all those things precisely because these people were being led astray from the truth by such observances—the truth by which they were being made free. Of this it is said in the Gospel, “The truth has set you free” (John 8:32), that is, “will make you free.”

“Therefore,” he says, “let no one judge you in food or drink, or in a festival, or a new moon, or sabbaths, which are a shadow of future things.” This refers to Judaism.

Then he proceeds with reference to the superstitions of the Gentiles: “But let no one convict you, who are the body of Christ.” It is shameful, he says, exceedingly incongruous, and alien to the nobility of your freedom, that although you are the body of Christ, you should be led astray by shadows and appear to be convicted as sinners because you neglect to observe these things.

“Therefore, let no one [Col. 0642] convict you, who are the body of Christ, wishing in humility of heart.” If this were expressed by the Greek word, it would sound more familiar even in popular Latin usage. For in common speech one says of someone who pretends to be rich, *thelodives*, and of someone who pretends to be wise, *thelosapiens*, and other expressions of this kind. Thus here too there is *thelohumilis*, more fully *thelon humilis*, that is, “one who wishes to be humble,” “one who affects humility.” This means “one who wishes to appear humble,” “one who affects humility.” Such observances are undertaken so that the human heart may be made humble, as it were, through religion.

He also added “the worship of angels,” or, as your copies have it, “the religion of angels,” which in Greek is called *thrēskeia* (θρησκεία). By “angels” he wants the principalities to be understood—those whom they suppose to preside over the elements of this world and to be worthy of worship through these observances.

28. “Therefore,” he says, “let no one disqualify you, since you are the body of Christ, wishing to appear humble in heart in the worship of angels, insisting on what he has not seen” [Note: *Embateuōn* (“insisting on,” “entering into,” or “dwelling upon”).]—or, as some copies have it, “insisting on what he has seen.”

For either he wished to say “insisting on what he has not seen,” because people undertake these things through suspicions and opinions, not because they have seen that such things ought to be done; or certainly, “insisting on what he has seen,” that is, considering it important because he saw these observances practiced in certain places by people whose authority he trusted, even though no reason was given. Thus he seems important to himself because he happened to see the secrets of certain sacred rites.

But the fuller sense is “insisting on what he has not seen, vainly puffed up by the mind of his flesh.” Wonderfully he says that he is puffed up by the mind of his flesh precisely where he had earlier said *thelohumilis* (“wishing to be humble”). For in marvelous ways it happens in the human soul that a person becomes more puffed up by false humility than if he were openly proud.

“And not holding fast to the head,” which he wants understood as Christ, “from whom the whole body, joined and knit together, supplied and bound together, grows with the growth of God.” Therefore, if you have died with Christ to the elements of this world, why, as though you were still living in the world, do you make judgments about it?

29. After saying these things, he inserts the words of those who make judgments about this world through these observances, as though they were rational, puffed up by an affected vanity of humility: “Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle.”

Let us recall what was said above, so that we may understand this passage. He does not want them to be judged according to these observances, where it is said, “Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle.” “All these things,” he says, “are destined for corruption through misuse.” These things are of greater use for corruption, he says, when people superstitiously abstain from them in order to misuse them—that is, not to use them according to the commandments and teachings of human beings.

This is clear. But you ask at length about what follows: “These things indeed have an appearance of wisdom in the observance, humility of heart, and affliction of the body”; or, as others have interpreted it, “in not sparing the body,” “not in any honor for the satisfaction of the flesh.” Why, you ask, does he say that these things have an appearance of wisdom, when he criticizes them in this way?

30. I shall say what you can also observe in the Scriptures: wisdom is often attributed even to the affairs of this world, which he more explicitly calls “the wisdom of this world.” [Col. 0643] Nor should it trouble us that here he did not add “of this world.” For when elsewhere he says, “Where is the wise person? Where is the scribe?” (1 Cor. 1:20), he did not add “of this world,” as though he were to say, “Where is the wise person of this world?” Yet that is what is understood.

So too here: these things have an appearance of wisdom. For in such superstitious observances they say nothing in which some apparent rationale of wisdom concerning the elements of this world and the natures of things does not seem to be offered. And when he says, “Beware lest anyone deceive you through philosophy,” he does not say “of this world.” What is philosophy in Latin except the pursuit of wisdom?

“Therefore,” he says, “these things do indeed have an appearance of wisdom”—that is, they are things for which some rationale is offered according to the elements of this world and its principalities and powers—“in observance and humility of heart.” For this is what these practices accomplish: through the fault of superstition, the heart is humbled.

“Not sparing the body”: while it is deprived of those foods from which it is compelled to abstain.

“Not in any honor for the satisfaction of the flesh”: not because the flesh is satisfied more honorably by one food than by another, since its need is only to be restored and strengthened by whatever nourishment is suitable to its condition.

## CHAPTER III

31. Your question about the Gospel often troubles many people: how, after the resurrection, when the Lord had risen in the same body, he was both not recognized and recognized by certain people who knew him, men and women alike.

The first question usually raised is whether something happened in his body, or rather in their eyes, so that he could not be recognized. For when we read, “Their eyes were held so that they did not recognize him” (Luke 24:16), some impediment to recognition seems to have been placed in the eyes of those who were looking. But when it is plainly said elsewhere, “He appeared to them in another form” (Mark 16:12), something must have happened in the very body whose form was different, by which their eyes were held back—that is, by which they were delayed in recognizing him.

Yet I am surprised that, since there are two features in the body by which anyone’s appearance is recognized—form and color—no one is troubled by the fact that before the resurrection he was transfigured on the mountain so that his face became exceedingly radiant like the sun (Matt. 17:2), and that he could have changed the color of his body to such an extraordinary brightness and light; whereas after the resurrection people are somewhat troubled by the possibility that his features were changed so that he could not be recognized, and then, by the same power, he restored his former features after the resurrection just as he had earlier restored his former color.

Indeed, the three disciples before whose eyes he was transfigured on the mountain would not have recognized him if someone with such an appearance had come to them from elsewhere. But because they were with him, they retained the absolute certainty that it was he.

But, someone may object, it was the very body in which he rose. What does that have to do with the matter? For it was certainly the same body in which he was transfigured on the mountain, and it was the same body in which he was a young man when he was born. Yet if someone who knew him only as an infant suddenly saw him as a young man, he would not recognize him. Can the power of God not rapidly change facial features, when human age can change them over the course of years?

32. As for what he said to Mary, [Col. 0644] “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father” (John 20:17), know that I have understood it in no other way than you have. For he wished to signify that a spiritual touch was required—that is, an approach through faith by which one believes that he is exalted with the Father.

And no one should doubt that his being recognized by the two disciples in the breaking of bread (Luke 24:30–31) is a sacrament that gathers us into recognition of him [Note: Bad., Am., and Er. read *quo nos* (“by which he gathers us”), supported by four Vatican manuscripts and four of our own, instead of *quod* (“that it is”), the reading of the text.].

33. Concerning the words of Simeon, where he says to the Virgin, the Lord’s mother, “And a sword will pierce your own soul,” I said what I think in another letter, a copy of which I have just sent; and you also seemed to approve this among other things. As for what he added, “so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed” (Luke 2:35), I think this should be understood as meaning that through the Lord’s passion both the plots of the Jews and the weakness of the disciples were exposed.

It is therefore credible that the tribulation was signified by the name of “sword,” by which the mother’s soul was wounded through the experience of grief. He himself was the sword in the mouth of the persecutors, of whom it is said in the Psalm: “And a sword is in their mouth” (Ps. 58:8). They were the sons of human beings “whose teeth are weapons and arrows, and whose tongue is a sharp sword” (Ps. 57:5).

For the iron that passed through Joseph’s soul also seems to me to have been set for severe tribulation. It is plainly said: “Iron passed through his soul until his word came,” that is, he remained in severe tribulation until what he had foretold came to pass. From this he was greatly honored and delivered from that tribulation. But lest what came to pass—namely, the fulfillment of his prediction—be attributed to human wisdom, holy Scripture, in its customary manner, gives the glory to God and immediately adds: “The word of the Lord inflamed him” (Ps. 104:18–19).

34. As far as I was able, I did not fail your questions, aided by your prayers and by the discussions you sent. For when you argue by asking questions, you inquire sharply and teach humbly. It is useful, concerning the obscurities of the divine Scriptures—which God wished to exist for the sake of our exercise—that many interpretations should be found, when one meaning appears to one person and another to another, provided that all agree with sound faith and doctrine.

You will kindly pardon my style, which was in great haste, since I had already boarded the ship in order to meet the bearer. But in this letter I greet again our son Paulinus, most dear in the love of Christ. I exhort him briefly, as I am in haste, to give as many thanks as he can to the mercy of the Lord. The Lord, knowing how to give help in tribulation, sent him through the most turbulent storm into the harbor by which you passed over a calmer sea, placing the least trust in the sea’s tranquility. He should thank the Lord, as much as he can, for having entrusted you with receiving and nourishing his first efforts, and let all his bones say: “Lord, who is like you?” (Ps. 34:10).

He does not read or hear me teaching and discussing, or kindling him through whatever exhortations, with richer fruit than he gains from seeing you live. My fellow servants who are with me greet your holy and most sincere Dignity. Our fellow deacon Peregrinus, who departed from me with our holy brother Urban [Col. 0645] when he went to undertake the burden of the episcopate, has not yet returned to Hippo. Nevertheless, we know from their letters and from reports that they are safe in the name of Christ. We greet with brotherly affection the fellow presbyter Paulinus and all who enjoy your presence in the Lord.

# LETTER 150 [Note: We have collated this letter with manuscripts a, bg, bl, bn, c, cc, ff, g, gv, n, r, s, sb, two manuscripts designated t, four designated v, and with the editions of Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.] [Note: Elsewhere numbered 179; the letter that was formerly 150 is now numbered 242. Written toward the end of 413 or at the beginning of 414.]

Augustine congratulates the noble widows Proba and Juliana on their daughter Demetrias, who had received the veil of virginity; and gives thanks for the little gift they had sent.

To the daughters most worthy of the honor of ladies, deservedly illustrious and most excellent, PROBA and JULIANA, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

You have filled our heart with joy—joy all the more pleasant because it is dear, all the more welcome because it came so quickly. For since the sanctity of virginity belonging to your lineage is proclaimed by the most celebrated fame everywhere that you have become known, and therefore everywhere, you have anticipated its swift flight with the more faithful and certain message of a letter. You made us rejoice before we could doubt what we had heard.

Who could explain in words, who could celebrate with worthy praise, how incomparably more glorious and fruitful it is for Christ to have virgin women from your bloodline than for the world to have men who are consuls? If the records of time regard it as something great and distinguished to mark a person with the dignity of a name, how much greater and more distinguished is it to rise above that dignity through integrity of heart and body!

Let the noble girl therefore rejoice more because she is noble by birth and nobler by holiness, because through divine fellowship she will attain a special eminence in heaven, than if through human marriage she were to produce exalted offspring. For the Anician descendants have chosen more nobly to bless so illustrious a family by knowing nothing of marriage than to multiply it by giving birth; and already to imitate the life of angels in the flesh than still to increase the number of mortals through the flesh.

This is a more abundant and fruitful happiness: not to grow heavy in the womb but to grow great in the mind; not to become milk-filled in the breast but to shine white in the heart; not to bring forth earth from the entrails but to bring forth heaven through prayers.

Daughters most worthy of the honor of ladies, enjoy in her what was lacking to you; may she persevere to the end, clinging to a marriage that has no end. Let many servant girls imitate their mistress, the ignoble the noble, those exalted in fragile things the more exalted in humility. Let virgins who desire for themselves the splendor of the Anicii choose holiness. For when will they attain the former, however great their desire? But if they desire the latter fully, they will have it at once.

May the right hand of the Most High protect you safe and even happier, ladies most worthy of honor and most excellent daughters. We greet, as duty and your merits require, the pledges of your holiness, especially her who is preeminent in holiness herself, with love in the Lord.

We have received with the greatest gratitude the gift accompanying the veiling [Note: Most manuscripts read *apopheretum*.] [Note: This term signifies some customary gift. “On great occasions,” says Ambrose in his *Commentary on Ephesians* 3, “the greatest *apophoreta* are given.” Turnebus thinks that the term referred to gifts given to dinner guests so that they might take them home. With this custom in mind, Ambrose also begins an exhortation to virgins: “Those who are invited to a great banquet are accustomed to take gifts home with them,” and so forth.].

# LETTER 151 [Note: Collated against the Vatican manuscript, in which it alone is found.] [Note: Elsewhere numbered 259; the letter that was formerly 151 is now numbered 3. Written at the end of 413 or the beginning of 414.]

He informs Caecilian of his affection for him and says that his old friendship has not been diminished at all. For he could not possibly suspect that Caecilian himself had been aware of the impious and cruel treachery perpetrated by a powerful man, the Count Marinus, in the killing of two brothers, one of whom, Marcellinus the tribune, possessed an unimpeachable character and was adorned with the splendor of every Christian virtue.

[Col. 0646]

To CAECILIAN, a deservedly illustrious lord and a son worthy, by my duty, of every honor, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

1. The complaint contained in your letter against me is all the more welcome to me because it is fuller of love. If, therefore, I should try to excuse what I left unsaid, what else shall I attempt except to show that you had no reason to be angry with me?
