But since I love in you more the fact that you considered yourself worthy to be offended by my silence than I once believed that, amid your concerns, I had any importance, I would abandon my case if I attempted to excuse myself.

For if you ought not to have been angry because I did not write to you, then you think nothing of me, since you would regard my speaking or remaining silent with indifference. But because you were distressed that I kept silent, that indignation is not really indignation. I therefore grieve less that I did not offer myself than I rejoice that you missed our conversation.

That I was remembered by an old friend—and, what you should not say about yourself but what we must acknowledge, by such a great and distinguished man living abroad and burdened with public affairs—is an honor to me, not a sorrow. Forgive me, then, for giving thanks that you did not think me unworthy of your anger when I remained silent.

For amid so many and such great affairs—not your private affairs but public ones, that is, those of everyone—I believed that my letters could be not only burdensome but also welcome to you because of your goodwill, by which you surpass your own excellence.

2. When I received from the brothers a letter sent by the holy and venerable Pope Innocent, a man of outstanding merits, and when definite indications showed that it had been delivered to me through Your Dignity, I assumed that no page from you had been brought along with it because, occupied with more serious matters, you did not wish to bind yourself with the labor of writing and replying.

For it certainly seemed appropriate that, since you had deigned to send me the writings of the holy man, I should receive them together with something from you. I therefore decided that my letters would not be burdensome to your mind unless it became necessary to commend someone, for whose sake I could not refuse this duty of intercession. This is ordinarily our custom of granting requests to everyone, and a kind of profession—even when somewhat importunate, though not therefore blameworthy.

So I acted. I commended my friend to your kindness, and I have now received his reply, in which he gives thanks; and I too give thanks.

[Col. 0647]

3. But if I had formed some unfavorable opinion of you, especially in that matter [Note: He is speaking of the case of Marcellinus, concerning whom Jerome writes near the end of Book 3 *Against the Pelagians*: “He was killed while innocent by heretics under the suspicion of the tyranny of Heraclianus”; or the man whom, according to Orosius in Book 7, chapter 42, “the Count Marinus killed at Carthage (it is uncertain whether he was goaded by zeal or corrupted by gold).” The Donatists were doubtless behind this, since the unimpeachable judge had incurred their hatred by a sentence delivered against them at the Carthaginian conference. While he was arranging for that sentence to be confirmed by imperial decree, the heretics plotted his death, using this opportunity. Heraclianus, Count of Africa, revolted from Honorius and sailed to Italy with a huge fleet in the year 413. Advancing toward Rome after disembarking his army, he was defeated at Utriculum by the intervention of the Count Marinus and took flight; he returned to Carthage, where he was eventually captured and put to death. Then, when Marinus was pursuing the partners in the rebellion in Africa, Marcellinus was arrested together with his brother and struck down with the sword, falsely accused of having favored Heraclianus, as is sufficiently clear from the Jerome cited above and also from Augustine’s words here, section 4: “Everything at that time conspired so that, even on the testimony of one person, anyone might be removed without distinction by the one who gave the order, on an envious and credible charge.” Marinus, moreover, was immediately recalled from Africa, deprived of every office, and ordered to live an inglorious private life, according to Orosius. On the other hand, Honorius issued a law on August 30, 414, ordering that the proceedings “carried out through the knowledge and diligence of Marcellinus, a man of distinguished memory, against the Donatists, should have perpetual validity,” in Book 16 of the *Theodosian Code*, title 5, *On Heretics*, law 55.], even though your letter did not expressly mention it, I would not have written anything of that sort to you when I was asking for a favor either for myself or for anyone else.

Either I would have remained silent, observing the time when I could have you present; or, if I thought the matter should be handled by letter, I would have dealt with that matter instead, and I would have done so in a way that would scarcely have allowed you to conceal your grief.

For this reason, immediately after his impious and cruel treachery—against which, despite the concern you shared with us, we had vehemently and unsuccessfully pressed our efforts so that it might not strike our hearts with grief or wound his own conscience with so great a crime—I departed from Carthage at once, concealing my departure. I did this lest so many and such important people who feared his sword within the Church should detain me with violent weeping and groaning, thinking that my presence could do something for them, so that I might be forced to plead even for their bodies, since I could not rebuke him for his soul as adequately as was necessary.

Their bodily safety, however, was sufficiently protected by the walls of the church. I myself was being pressed by severe constraints, because he would not allow me to be what I ought to be, and in addition I was compelled to do what was unbecoming.

I also deeply grieved at the situation of my venerable fellow bishop, the ruler of so great a Church, whose duty it was said to be to continue presenting himself humbly after such a wicked deception by that man, so that the others might be spared. I confess that, since I could not endure so great an evil with any strength of heart, I departed.

4. Your action toward him would now be the reason for my silence, just as it was then the reason for my departure, if I believed that you had acted toward him in such a way as to punish such unspeakable wrongs.

Those who do not know how, how often, and what things you said to us when we were anxiously striving to ensure that, the more familiarly he clung to you, the more frequently you visited him, and the more often you conversed with him alone, the more carefully he would protect your reputation—so that he would not give those who were said to be your enemies an ending that would make people think you had done nothing else with him—believe these things.

I, however, do not believe this, nor do my brothers who heard you speak and, through your words and every gesture, saw signs of your kindly heart.

But I beg you to forgive those who believe it. They are human beings, and in human minds there are such hidden places and such recesses that all the suspicious, though rightly blamed, still think they ought to be praised for being cautious.

The circumstances were there. We knew that you had suffered a most serious insult from one of those whom he had suddenly ordered to be held. It was also said that his brother, against whom he had persecuted the Church most severely, had answered you harshly, as though displaying some resentment.

Both were thought to be suspect to you. After the accused had gone away, while you remained there and, as was reported, spoke with him more privately, they were suddenly ordered to be detained.

People spoke of your friendship as not recent but longstanding. The fame of so close an association, and of such constant conversation between you two alone, confirmed it. His power was then great. The ease of slander was shining forth. It was no difficult matter to procure someone who would say what he had ordered him to say, with his safety promised.

Everything at that time conspired so that, even with a single witness, anyone might be removed on an envious and credible charge, without any distinction being made concerning the person who gave the order.

5. Meanwhile, since there was a rumor that ecclesiastical intervention might rescue them, we were being deceived by false promises: namely, that, as though he not merely wished it but even pressed for it, a bishop would be sent to the Court on their behalf, with the promise conveyed to episcopal ears that, until something had been done there for them, no examination of their case would be initiated. Finally, on the day before they were put to death, Your Excellency came to us. You gave us a hope such as you had never given before: that he might grant them to you if you went to him, since you had told him firmly and wisely that all his speaking with you so continually, so familiarly, and so privately did not honor you but rather burdened you [Note: [Col. 0648] Lov., “We might speak,” and “not that you should be honored rather than burdened.”], and that it amounted to this: once the plan of their death had been discussed and considered between you, no one could doubt what would follow after all these things.

When you indicated to us that you had said these things—for while recounting them you were making your way toward the place where the sacraments of the faithful are celebrated—we were astonished that you swore that you had spoken in this way. By swearing that you had said these things, you made me feel that not only then, but even now after such a dreadful and unexpected outcome, when I recall all your gestures, I should be excessively shameless if I believed anything evil about you. You said that he had been so moved by your words that he was about to give you their safety as a kind of familiar provision for your journey.

6. Therefore I testify to Your Affection that on the following day, when the wicked offspring of that labor had been brought forth, we were suddenly informed that they had been led from prison to that judge. Although we were thrown into confusion, I nevertheless considered both what you had told us the day before and what sort of day would dawn after that one. Since the following day was the eve of the feast of blessed Cyprian [Note: [Col. 0648] The killing of St. Marcellinus is assigned to 6 April in the Martyrologies. Yet from this passage it is clear that it occurred in September, one or two days before the feast of St. Cyprian. “And indeed,” says Henricus de Noris in *Historia Pelagiana*, book 1, chapter 5, “that his death did not occur on 6 April is sufficiently established by the fact that in this year, 413, Heraclianus, with so large a fleet, could have set sail from Africa on the open sea only in spring, intending to invade the city; yet Marcellinus’s death followed Heraclianus’s defeat in Italy, the tyrant’s flight, and finally his own killing.”], I thought that he had even chosen that day on which he might grant your requests and, suddenly making the whole Church of Christ rejoice, wished to ascend to the place of so great a martyr—being exalted by the mercy of sparing rather than by the power of killing.

But behold, a messenger burst in upon us, so that we learned that they had already been struck down before we could inquire how their case had been heard. For a place had been prepared nearby, not assigned to the punishment of human beings but rather intended as an adornment of the city. It is rightly believed that he had ordered certain people to be slaughtered there several days earlier, so that this new and hateful act would not appear exceptional: his plan was that these men could be stolen away from the Church if they were ordered to be struck down not only suddenly but also in a nearby place.

Thus he plainly showed that he had not feared inflicting torment upon that mother whose intervention he feared: namely, the holy Church, among whose faithful, baptized in her womb, we knew even him to be numbered. After the outcome of so great an undertaking, then, when everything had been so carefully arranged with us that through you—even though you did not know it—we had nearly become secure and nearly certain of their safety the day before, who, knowing what the mass of human beings is like, would not have considered it beyond doubt that words had also been given to us by you, while their lives were taken from them? Therefore, as I said, good man, even if we do not believe this, forgive those who do believe it.

7. Far be it from my heart and from my life, whatever it may be, that I should intercede with you for anyone or ask you to grant anyone a favor if I believed you to be the author of so great an evil and so criminal a cruelty. But I openly confess that, if you are still on the same terms of intimacy on which you formerly were, then, with your permission, let my grief speak freely: you are compelling us to believe much that we do not wish to believe. Yet it is consistent that I should not believe this either, since I do not believe those other things about you.

Your friend, in the unexpected success of his sudden power, persecuted their lives no more than he persecuted your reputation. In saying this I am not inflaming your hatred against him while forgetting my own character and calling; rather, I am appealing to a more faithful love. For one who deals with the wicked in such a way as to make them repent of their wickedness knows how to benefit them even through indignation: just as the wicked harm by flattering, so the good benefit by opposing.

With the same weapon by which he most insolently killed others, he struck his own soul more gravely and more deeply. If after this life he does not correct it through repentance and make good use of God’s patience, he will be compelled to discover and experience this. Often, however, by God’s judgment even the present life of good people is permitted to be taken away by the wicked, lest undergoing such things be thought an evil. For what harm can dying in the flesh do to those who are going to die? Or what do those who fear death accomplish, except that they die a little later? Whatever harms the dying comes from life, not from death. If, in that life, they possessed souls of the kind that Christian grace assists, their death was not the end of a good life but the beginning of a better one.

8. The character of his elder brother [Note: [Col. 0649] We do not know whether this refers here to Apringius the judge, Marcellinus’s brother, and proconsul in Africa around this time, as we understand from Letter 133, section 3, and Letter 134, section 2 [Col. 0650]. He was also hated by the Donatists because he had imposed punishment upon them for their crimes.] appeared indeed to be more friendly to this world than to Christ, although he too had corrected a considerable part of his earlier worldly life by taking a wife. Yet perhaps merciful God wished him to be his brother’s companion in death only out of compassion.

The other brother, however, lived religiously and was deeply Christian in heart and life. This reputation preceded him, so that he came in the cause of the Church [Note: [Col. 0650] These details fit Marcellinus exceptionally well. He was a tribune and notary sent by Honorius to Africa to serve as mediator in the conference between Catholics and Donatists. He conducted himself energetically in that affair; for that reason Augustine says above, section 4, that the man who killed him especially persecuted the Church in his person.] in such a manner; and this reputation followed him after he had arrived.

What integrity he had in his character, what fidelity in friendship, what zeal in learning, what sincerity in religion, what chastity in marriage, what self-control in judgment; patience toward enemies, courtesy toward friends, humility toward the saints, love toward all; readiness in bestowing benefits, modesty in requesting them, love in doing what was right, grief over sins! What dignity of uprightness, what splendor of grace, what care for piety; what mercy in assisting, what goodwill in forgiving, what confidence in praying! What he knew for his own good, he spoke of with what modesty! What he did not know but which was of no benefit, he investigated with what diligence! How great was his contempt for present things! How great his hope and desire for eternal goods!

The bond of marriage hindered him from abandoning all worldly pursuits in order to take up the belt of Christian service. Already bound by it, he had begun to desire better things, but it was no longer permissible for him to break apart that bond, even though the things it permitted were inferior.

9. One day, when the brothers were already being held together in custody, the elder said to him: “If I am suffering these things for the merits of my sins, then you, whose life we know to be so carefully and fervently Christian [Note: [Col. 0650] Lov., “frequently and fervently”], by what evil merits have you been brought to this?”

But he replied: “Do you think that a small benefit has been divinely conferred upon me, if your testimony about my life is true, namely, that what I am suffering—even if I suffer it to the shedding of blood—is punishment for my sins here, and that they are not reserved for me for the judgment to come?”

At this point someone might perhaps believe that he was conscious of some hidden sins of sexual misconduct. I shall therefore say what the Lord God wished me, to my great consolation, to hear from his own mouth and to know clearly.

Concerned about this very matter, as human beings are, I was speaking with him alone while he was already confined in the same custody, asking whether there was anything for which he ought to make himself pleasing to God through greater and more distinguished repentance. He, being a man of extraordinary modesty, blushed at my suspicion, although it was false, but gratefully accepted the admonition. Smiling modestly and gravely, he took my right hand in both of his and said: “I call to witness the Sacraments that are brought through this hand [Note: [Col. 0650] Elsewhere, “offered.” M.], that I have experienced no sexual intercourse except with my wife, neither before nor afterward.”

10. What evil, then, befell this man in death, and not rather the greatest good, since, possessing these gifts, he departed from this life to Christ, without whom such gifts are possessed in vain? I would not mention these things to you if I believed that you were offended by his praises. But since I do not believe that, neither do I believe that he could have been killed by you—not, I say, because you pressed for it, but even because you wished or desired it.

Therefore you judge with us all the more sincerely and innocently that he dealt more cruelly with his own soul than with this man’s body, when, disregarding us, disregarding his promises, disregarding so many and such great requests and admonitions from you, and finally disregarding the Church of Christ—and in the Church, whom did he disregard except Christ?—he reached the end of his plotting through this man’s death.

Or can his honor really be compared with this man’s imprisonment, when the former raged in exaltation while the latter rejoiced in confinement? The conscience of a wicked man, in its dreadful and punitive darkness, surpasses not only all prisons but even hell itself.

What harm did this do to you? Although he gravely damaged your reputation, he did not destroy your innocence. Indeed, your reputation itself remains unharmed, both among those who know you better than we do and among us ourselves. We saw how deeply you expressed your concern with us, lest so monstrous a crime be committed, and with such feeling that we almost saw with our eyes the things invisible in your heart.

He therefore harmed himself, whatever harm was done: he pierced his own soul, his own life, his own conscience; finally, with that blind cruelty he devastated his own reputation—the good reputation that even the worst people commonly desire. He is all the more hateful to every good person the more he tried to please the impious, or rejoiced that he had pleased them.

11. Where could it have become clearer that he did not have the necessity he pretended to have, in order that under its pretext he might do so great an evil as though he were acting rightly, than from the fact that even the man whose command he dared to invoke as an excuse did not approve of it?

Let the holy deacon who came through N.’s hands report to Your Excellency what happened. He himself had been attached to the bishop whom we sent on their behalf. He will explain how it was not thought that indulgence should be granted them, lest they thereby be marked by some offense, but only that a memorandum should be sent ordering that they be dismissed free from every form of harassment.

Thus, with gratuitous cruelty and without necessity—although there may perhaps have been other reasons that we suspect but need not commit to writing—he grievously distressed the Church. To the bosom of that Church his brother, fearing destruction, had fled, only to find him, alive, an adviser of so great a crime. When he had offended his patron, he himself also sought asylum in that Church, and it could not be denied him.

If you love this man, detest him; if you do not want him to be punished eternally, abhor him. This is how you must care for your reputation and for his life: for one who loves in him what God hates hates not only him but also himself.

12. Since these things are so, I neither believe, given your kindness, that you were the author or accomplice of so great a crime, nor that you were deceived by malicious cruelty [Note: [Col. 0651] The Vatican exemplar from which this letter was recovered reads *credulitate*, “credulity.”]—far be that from your life and character!

Nor do I wish your friendship with him to be of such a kind that he should boast of evil to his own destruction and human suspicion should be confirmed. I wish it rather to be such that he may be prepared for repentance, and for repentance as great and as extensive as the dreadful wounds he has inflicted require as medicine. You will be all the more his friend the more hostile you are to his crimes.

It would be interesting for Your Excellency to inform us by letter where you were on the day when this deed was committed; how you received the news; what you did afterward; and, when you saw him, what you said to him and what you heard from him. For ever since I suddenly departed from there on the following day, I have been unable to hear anything from you concerning this matter.

13. As for what I read in your letter—that you are now being compelled to believe this lest you should appear to me, and that I have been refused at Carthage—you, rather, by these words compel me not to conceal the reasons for my absence.

One reason is that I can no longer endure the labor which must be borne in that city. If I wished to describe it, I would have to say as much again. Added to my own infirmity, which is known to all who know me more intimately, is old age, the common infirmity of the human race.

The second reason is that I have resolved, if the Lord wills, to devote all the time granted me from those occupations demanded by the necessities of the Church, which I serve in my proper office, to the labor of studies relating to ecclesiastical knowledge. In this work I believe that, if it pleases God’s mercy, I may also benefit those who come after us.

14. There is one thing, however, if you want to hear the truth, that I find most troubling in you: although you are both a man of this age and a man of such a life and character, you still wish to remain a catechumen—as though the faithful could not administer the affairs of the state, the more faithfully and better the more faithful and better they were.

What good are you doing amid these great cares and labors of yours except that people may be well? For if this is not what you are doing, it would be better to sleep night and day than to remain awake amid public labors that will benefit no one. I certainly do not doubt Your Excellency … [lacuna]

## LETTER 152

[Note: [Col. 0652] Letters 152 and 154, by Macedonius; and 153 and 155, to Macedonius, were corrected from manuscripts designated a, bg, bl, bn, c, cc, cb, ff, g, gg, gv, j, n, r, s, sb, vd, two copies of a, two copies of t, and four copies of V.]

[Note: [Col. 0652] Elsewhere numbered 53; the letter formerly numbered 152 is now 141. Probably written in 414.]

Macedonius to Augustine, asking whether it is a religious duty for bishops to intercede with judges on behalf of defendants.

Macedonius to Augustine, a lord deservedly venerable and uniquely worthy of honor, father:

1. I received the much-desired letter from Your Holiness through Boniface, the bishop of the venerable law. I loved him all the more warmly because he brought me what I had desired from you: the speech and good health of Your Holiness, my deservedly venerable and uniquely worthy father. Thus, without delay, he obtained what he requested.

But since an opportunity has arisen, I do not wish this small service, whatever its size, which I granted after being asked, to remain without a reward. For I wish to receive a reward that benefits me without disadvantage to the one who depends upon me—indeed, one that benefits me while bringing glory to the dependent [Note: [Col. 0652] Lov. reports that some manuscripts read: “those things that you grant me … indeed … that you grant me.”]

2. You say that it is an obligation of your priesthood to intercede for defendants, and that you are offended if you do not obtain their release, as though you failed to secure what was properly your duty. Here I am very much in doubt whether this proceeds from religion [Col. 0653].

For if sins are so strictly forbidden by the Lord that even an opportunity for repentance is not granted after the first [Note: [Col. 0653] The editions read, “after the first repentance.” All the manuscripts here and in the following letter read “after the first”; supply “opportunity for repentance.”], how can we, on religious grounds, insist that whatever the crime may have been, it be forgiven us? For when we want it to go unpunished, we evidently approve it.

And if it is established that the perpetrator is held no less accountable than the approver in every sin that is committed, it is certain that we become bound in partnership with the guilt whenever we wish the person guilty of wrongdoing to remain unpunished.

Furthermore, there is something more serious. All sins seem more pardonable when the defendant promises correction. But now, as our morals are, people wish both the punishment of their crime to be remitted and to retain the very thing for which the crime was committed. Your priesthood thinks one ought to intercede even for such people, although there is so little hope of their future improvement that the same pattern of crime persists in the present. For whoever clings so stubbornly to the things for which he committed the crime shows that, when he has the opportunity, he will commit similar sins.

3. On these matters, therefore, I consult your wisdom and wish to be freed from the doubt with which I am struggling; do not suppose that I consult you for any other reason.

For the rest, I have resolved to show grace to intercessors, especially to one of such merit as you. There are many things that I do not wish to appear to do voluntarily, lest a relaxation of severity arm others for crimes; yet I desire to remit them when good intercessors plead for them, so that what I willingly grant may, without compromising the severity of judgment, appear to have been granted because of another’s merit.

You had promised me some of your writings, but I have not received them. Please send them now, and reply to this letter of mine, so that, since I am not at present permitted to see Your Holiness, I may at least be nourished by your words.

May eternal divinity protect Your Holiness through a most generous age, my deservedly venerable and truly worthy father.

## LETTER 153

[Note: [Col. 0653] Elsewhere numbered 54; the letter formerly numbered 153 is now 46. Written after the preceding letter.]

Augustine answers the question, incidentally discussing at length the restoration of property taken from one’s neighbor or wrongfully acquired.

Augustine, bishop, servant of Christ and of his household, sends greetings in the Lord to his beloved son Macedonius [Note: [Col. 0653] So Bad., Am., Er., and the manuscripts. Lov.’s edition reads: “Servant of Christ, to Macedonius and his household.”]

### CHAPTER ONE

1. We ought neither to leave without address nor burden with a preface a man exceedingly busy in public affairs and attentive not to his own interests but to those of others—a man such as you are, for which we congratulate both you and human affairs.

Receive, then, what through me you wished either to learn or to test whether I myself knew. If you had judged it small or superfluous, you would by no means have thought it worthy of attention amid your many great and necessary concerns.

You ask me why we say that it is an obligation of our priesthood to intercede for defendants, and that we are offended if we do not obtain their release, as though we failed to secure what was properly our duty. You say that you are very much in doubt whether this proceeds from religion [Col. 0654].

Then you add the reason why you are so moved: “For if sins,” you say, “are so strictly forbidden by the Lord that even an opportunity for repentance is not granted after the first, how can we, on religious grounds, insist that whatever the crime may have been be forgiven?” You press the matter still more strongly and say that we approve what we want to remain unpunished; and, if it is established that the author is held no less accountable than the approver in everything that is sinned, it is certain that we become bound in partnership with the guilt whenever we wish the person liable to guilt to remain unpunished.

2. Who would not be frightened by these words if he did not know your gentleness and humanity? But we who know you, and who have no doubt that you wrote these things in order to inquire rather than to decide, will answer them more quickly by your own words elsewhere.

For it is as though you did not want us to hesitate over this question, or as though you foresaw what we would say, or reminded us what we ought to say. You wrote: “Furthermore, there is something more serious. All sins seem more pardonable when the defendant promises correction.”

Before I examine what that “more serious” point is which follows in your letter, I shall meanwhile accept what you have granted and use it to remove the mass by which our intercessions appeared capable of being suppressed. For this reason, insofar as opportunity is given, we intercede for all sins: because all sins seem more pardonable when the defendant promises correction. This is your judgment, and it is ours as well.

3. We therefore by no means approve the sins that we wish to see corrected. Nor do we wish wrongdoing to remain unpunished because we approve it. Rather, we pity the person while detesting the crime or disgraceful act; and the more the vice displeases us, the less do we wish the vicious person, who is human, to perish without correction.

It is easy and natural to hate the wicked because they are wicked. It is rare and pious to love those same people because they are human: thus, in one and the same person, you condemn the fault and approve the nature, and for that reason hate the fault more justly, because it disfigures the nature that you love.

Therefore, the person who persecutes the crime in order to free the human being is bound not by a partnership in wickedness but rather by a partnership in humanity. The correction of character has no other opportunity than this life; for after it, each person will have what he has acquired for himself in this life.

For this reason we are compelled by love for the human race to intercede for defendants, lest they end this life through punishment in such a way that, once it has ended, they cannot bring their punishment to an end.

### CHAPTER TWO

4. Do not, then, doubt that this duty of ours proceeds from religion. God is one in whom there is no iniquity, whose power is supreme, who sees not only what each person is but also foresees what each person will be, and who alone cannot go astray in judging because he cannot be deceived in knowing. Yet, as the Gospel says, he makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust.

The Lord Christ exhorts us to imitate this wondrous goodness, saying: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you; and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5:44–45).

Who does not know that many abuse this divine indulgence and gentleness to their own destruction? Rebuking and severely reproving them, the Apostle says: “Do you suppose, O man—every man who judges those who do such things and does them himself—that you will escape the judgment of God? Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering? Do you not know that the goodness of God leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of the righteous judgment of God, who will render to each according to his works” (Rom. 2:3–6).

Is it because these people persist in their wickedness that God does not persist in his patience—punishing a few during this age so that divine providence will not be thought nonexistent, but reserving many for the final judgment so that the future judgment may be confirmed?

5. I do not think that that heavenly Teacher commands us to love impiety when he commands us to love our enemies, to do good to those who hate us, and to pray for those who persecute us. For if we worship God piously, we cannot regard as anything but impious our enemies, those stirred against us by the fiercest hatred, and our persecutors.

Are the impious, then, to be loved? Are we to do good to the impious? Are we even to pray for the impious? Certainly. The one who commands this is God. Yet by this command he does not join us to the society of the impious, just as he himself, by sparing them and granting them life and safety, is not thereby joined to them.

The Apostle explains his purpose, insofar as human beings are permitted to know it, by saying: “Do you not know that the patience of God leads you to repentance?” We wish those for whom we intercede to be led to this; we neither spare nor favor their sins.

### CHAPTER THREE

6. For some whose crimes are manifest, after they have been released by your severity, we nevertheless remove from communion at the altar, so that by repenting and punishing themselves they may placate the one whom they had despised by sinning [Note: [Col. 0655] Four manuscripts of good standing, including Corb. and Germ., read: “so that they may be pleasing to him, contemplating his judgment, whom they had despised by sinning,” and so forth.].

For the truly repentant person does nothing other than ensure that he does not allow the evil he has done to remain unpunished. In this way, he spares the one who does not spare himself—the one whose deep and just judgment no contemptuous person escapes.

If, then, God, by sparing the wicked and criminal and granting them life and safety, also shows patience toward many whom he knows will not repent, how much more ought we to be merciful toward those who promise correction, when we are uncertain whether they will do what they promise? We should bend your severity by interceding for them, and we should pray for them to the Lord, who is ignorant of nothing in their character, even what it will be in the future, yet without presumption, since he himself commanded this.

7. Human wickedness sometimes progresses so far that, even after repentance has been performed and reconciliation with the altar has taken place, people commit either similar or more serious sins. Yet God makes his sun rise even upon such people and bestows upon them no less abundantly than before the gifts of life and health.

And although they may not be granted a place in the Church for the humblest repentance [Note: [Col. 0656] Several manuscripts read: “that place for repenting.” Others read: “that place of repentance may not be granted.”], God nevertheless does not forget his patience toward them.

Suppose someone from among them says to us: “Either give me the same opportunity to repent again, or abandon me in despair, so that I may do whatever I please, insofar as my resources assist me and human laws do not restrain me—in prostitution and every kind of luxury, things condemned by the Lord but praised by many human beings. Or, if you turn me back from this wickedness, tell me whether it will benefit me in the future life if in this life I reject the allurements of the most seductive pleasure, restrain the provocations of lust, deprive myself even of many things permitted and granted to me in order to chastise my body, torment myself through repentance more severely than before, groan more miserably, weep more abundantly, live better, support the poor more generously, and burn more fervently with the love that covers a multitude of sins (1 Pet. 4:8).”

Who among us is so foolish as to say to such a man: “None of these things will benefit you hereafter; go and at least enjoy the pleasures of this life”?

May God avert such monstrous and sacrilegious madness! Although it has wisely and beneficially been arranged that the place of that most humble repentance should be granted only once in the Church, lest a medicine become less useful to the sick by being cheap—since it is more healing the less contemptible it is—who nevertheless would dare say to God: “Why do you continue to spare this man, who, after his first repentance, again binds himself in the snares of iniquity?”

Who would dare say that what the Apostle says does not apply to such people: “Do you not know that the patience of God leads you to repentance”? Or that the statement “Blessed are all who trust in him” (Ps. 2:13) has been laid down with such people excluded? Or that what is said, “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord” (Ps. 30:25), does not pertain to them?

8. Since, then, God shows such great patience and such great mercy toward sinners that, if they reform their conduct in this temporal life, they are not condemned eternally—and since he expects no mercy to be shown to himself—for no one is more blessed, more powerful, or more just than he—what kind of people ought human beings to be toward other human beings? We may heap whatever praise we wish upon this life of ours, but we do not say that it is without sin. If we did say this, we would deceive ourselves, as it is written, and the truth would not be in us (1 John 1:8).

Therefore, although one person may be the accuser, another the defender, another the intercessor, and another the judge—and although it would be excessively lengthy and unnecessary to discuss their particular duties in this discourse—divine authority has nevertheless frightened even those who punish crimes—men who are not stirred by their own anger in this office but are ministers of laws not their own, avengers of wrongs examined by others—so that they should consider that, because of their own sins, they need God’s mercy. They should not think that it belongs to the guilt of their office if they act mercifully toward those over whose life and death they possess legitimate authority.

### CHAPTER FOUR

9. When the Jews brought to the Lord Christ a woman caught in adultery, testing him by saying that the Law had commanded her to be stoned, and then asked what he himself commanded concerning her, he answered them: “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her” (John 8:7).

Thus he neither condemned the Law, which commanded that women guilty of such offenses be put to death, nor did he fail to recall to mercy, by frightening them, those whose judgment might have put her to death.

I think that, after hearing this sentence of the Lord, if the husband himself was present—the husband who had demanded that the violation of his marriage bed be avenged—he was terrified and turned his heart from the desire for vengeance toward the willingness to spare.

For how could the accuser not have been warned against pursuing his own injuries, when the judges themselves were thus prohibited from exacting vengeance? In punishing the adulteress, they were not being compelled to serve private grief but the Law.

For this reason Joseph, to whom the virgin Mary, the mother of the Lord, had been betrothed, when he discovered that she was pregnant—although he knew that he had not had intercourse with her, and therefore had believed nothing other than that she was an adulteress—nevertheless did not wish to have her punished. Nor was he an approver of the crime. His intention is even counted as righteousness, for it is written of him: “Since he was a righteous man and did not wish to expose her, he resolved to dismiss her secretly.” While he was considering this, an angel appeared to him and taught him that the event he had thought a crime was divine in origin (Matt. 1:18–20).

10. If, then, when common weakness is taken into account, both the accuser’s grief and the judge’s severity are broken, what do you think the duty of a defender or intercessor ought to be toward defendants? You are good men who are now judges and who at some time practiced in the courts and undertook people’s cases; you know how much more willingly you used to defend than accuse.

Yet a defender is very different from an intercessor. The defender chiefly undertakes to dissolve or conceal crimes; the intercessor, even when guilt is established, takes care to remove or lessen the punishment.

This is what the righteous do before God on behalf of sinners; this is what sinners are admonished to do for one another on their own behalf. For it is written: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another” (James 5:16).

Every human being, wherever possible, claims these duties of humanity before another human being. For what each person would punish in his own house, he wants to remain unpunished in another’s house.

Whether he is called in on behalf of a friend, or someone who has the power of vengeance becomes angry with another in his presence, or he happens upon someone who is angry, he is judged not most just but most inhuman if he does not intervene.

I myself know that you, together with your other friends, interceded in the church at Carthage for a cleric with whom the bishop had good reason to be angry. Certainly, no danger to bodily bloodshed was feared there under bloodless discipline. Nor, when you wished what displeased you as well to remain unpunished, did we judge you approvers of the offense; rather, we listened to you as most humane intercessors.

If, then, it is permissible for you to mitigate ecclesiastical correction by interceding, how should a bishop not intercede against your sword, when the former is exercised so that the person against whom it is exercised may live well, while the latter is exercised so that he may not live? [Note: [Col. 0658] The editions read: “how is a bishop not supposed to intercede with your sword?” The word *non* is absent from the manuscripts, but either reading fits this passage.]

11. Finally, the Lord himself interceded with human beings so that the adulteress would not be stoned, and in this way he commended to us the duty of intercession—except that he accomplished through frightening what we accomplish through asking.

He is the Lord; we are servants. Yet he frightened them in such a way that we ought all to fear. For who among us is without sin?

When he had said this to those who had brought the sinful woman to him to be punished—that whoever knew himself to be without sin should cast the first stone at her—savagery collapsed beneath a trembling conscience. Then, withdrawing one by one from that assembly, they left the wretched woman alone with Mercy.

Let Christian piety yield to this sentence, as Jewish impiety yielded to it. Let the humility of those who obey yield to it, as the pride of those who persecuted yielded to it. Let faithful confession yield to it, as the pretender’s deception yielded to it.

Spare the wicked, good man. The better you are, the gentler you should be; the higher you are in power, the humbler you should become in piety [Note: [Col. 0658] The editions read: “the higher you are in power, the humbler you should become,” and so forth. But the manuscripts have “you are higher” and shortly afterward “you should become humbler.”]

### CHAPTER FIVE
### 12

Indeed, observing your character, I called you a good man; but, observing Christ’s words, say to yourself: “No one is good except one, God” (Mark 10:18). Since this is true—for Truth itself said it—I should not be thought to have said it through deceptive flattery and to have set myself against the Lord’s words, so that, while he says, “No one is good except one, God,” I called you a good man. For the Lord himself did not speak inconsistently when he said: “A good man brings forth good things from the good treasure of his heart” (Luke 6:45).

God, therefore, is good in a unique sense, and he cannot lose this goodness. He is not good through participation in any other good, for the good by which he is good is himself. A human being, however, when good, is good through him; he cannot be good from himself. For all who become good become so through his Spirit, and our created nature was made capable of that Spirit through its own will.

It therefore belongs to us to receive and possess what he gives, since he is good from himself; whoever neglects it is bad from himself. Accordingly, insofar as a person acts rightly—that is, knowingly, lovingly, and devoutly does what is good—he is good; but insofar as he sins—that is, deviates from truth, love, and devotion—he is bad. Yet who in this life is without some sin? We call him good whose good deeds prevail, and best the one who sins least.

### 13

For this reason the Lord himself calls those whom he calls good because they participate in divine grace also bad because of the defects of human weakness, until everything of which we consist has been healed of every defect and passes into that life where there will be no sin at all.

For he was certainly teaching good people to pray, not bad people, when he commanded them to say: “Our Father, who art in heaven.” They are good because they are children of God—not begotten by nature, but made so by grace—like those who, by receiving him, were given power to become children of God (John 1:12). This spiritual generation is also called adoption, in the manner of the Scriptures, so that it may be distinguished from that generation of God from God, coeternal from the eternal, concerning which it is written: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isaiah 53:8).

Having thus shown that those whom he wanted truly to call God’s children were good, he nevertheless commanded them to say, among other things, in that same prayer: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” Although it is clear that these debts are sins, he later made the point still clearer, saying: “For if you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins” (Matthew 6:9, 12, 14).

The baptized pray this prayer, and absolutely no past sin remains that is not forgiven those baptized in the holy Church. But afterward, while living in this mortal weakness, unless they incurred something that needed to be forgiven, they would not truthfully say: “Forgive us our debts.” They are therefore good insofar as they are children of God; but insofar as they sin—as they testify by their own truthful confession—they are certainly bad.

[Note: In earlier printed editions: “They are therefore good insofar as they do not sin, and are children of God.” But the text is more coherent if *do not sin* is rejected, since it is absent from all the manuscripts.]

### 14

Unless, perhaps, someone should say that the sins of good people are one thing and those of bad people another—a claim that is not wholly implausible. Nevertheless, the Lord Jesus unmistakably called the very same people bad whose Father he said God was.

For in the same sermon in which he teaches that prayer, elsewhere exhorting people to pray to God, he says: “Ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives; and whoever seeks finds; and to the one who knocks it will be opened.” A little later he says: “If you, then, although you are bad, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him?” (Matthew 7:7–8, 11).

Is God, then, the Father of bad people? Certainly not. How, then, are they called “your heavenly Father” when they are told, “although you are bad”? The answer is that Truth reveals both things: what we are through God’s goodness [Note: [Col. 0659] Thus the majority of the manuscripts. The printed editions have *through God’s gift*], and what we are through human fault—commending the former and correcting the latter.

Seneca rightly said—he lived in the time of the Apostles, and some letters of his to the Apostle Paul are also read: “I hate all who hate the bad.” Yet bad people should be loved so that they may not remain bad, just as the sick are loved not so that they may remain sick, but so that they may be healed.

### 15

Whatever we sin after the abolition of sins that takes place in Baptism, while we remain in this life—even if it is not such a sin as compels us to be removed from the divine altars—is expiated not by barren grief but by sacrifices of mercy.

Therefore, know that, when we act so that you may act, with us interceding, we offer you to God on your behalf. You need the mercy that you extend; and consider who it was who said: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you” (Luke 6:37–38).

Even if we lived in such a way that there were no reason for us to say, “Forgive us our debts,” the purer the mind was from wickedness, the fuller its clemency ought to be. Thus, if we were not moved by the Lord’s sentence, “Which of you is without sin, let him first cast a stone at her,” we ought to follow the example of the one who spoke those words. Though he was certainly without sin, he said to the woman whom the terrified accusers had left behind: “Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on do not sin.”

The sinful woman could have feared that, once those who had considered their own sins and therefore spared another’s had departed, the one who was without sin would himself condemn her with perfect justice. But he, not frightened by conscience and filled with mercy, said, when she replied that no one had condemned her: “Neither do I condemn you”—as though he were saying: “If wickedness was able to spare you, why do you fear innocence?”

And so that he might not appear to be not the forgiver but the approver of sins, he said: “Go, and from now on do not sin,” thereby showing that he had spared the person, not that the person’s fault had pleased him.

You see, then, that this proceeds from religion: we are not bound by an association in crimes because we often intercede even for criminals; and although we are not criminals, we are nevertheless sinners interceding for sinners. I think you should understand this as said truthfully rather than offensively: as something said, I believe, among sinners.

## CHAPTER VI

### 16

Nor, certainly, were the king’s authority, the judge’s right to wield the sword, the executioner’s claw, the soldier’s weapons, the discipline of the ruler, or even the severity of a good father instituted without reason. All these have their proper limits, causes, grounds, and uses.

When such things are feared, the bad are restrained, and the good live more peacefully among the bad—not because those who refrain from sin out of fear of such things should be pronounced good. No one is good because of fear of punishment, but because of love of justice. Nevertheless, human laws do not uselessly restrain boldness through fear, so that innocence may be safe among the wicked and so that, among the wicked themselves, while their capacity for wrongdoing is curbed by fear of punishment, their will may be healed by calling upon God.

The intercessions of bishops are not contrary to this ordering of human affairs. Indeed, there would be no reason or opportunity for intercession if these institutions did not exist. The benefits of those who intercede and spare are more pleasing in proportion as the punishments of those who sin are more just.

So far as I understand, the only reason that, in the ancient period of the Prophets, the Old Testament’s harsher vengeance through the Law burned so fiercely was to show that punishments had rightly been established for the wicked. Thus, when the leniency of the New Testament teaches us to spare them, this may be either a remedy for salvation, by which their sins and ours are spared, or an encouragement to gentleness, so that through those who spare, the truth that is preached may not merely be feared but also loved.

### 17

It matters greatly, however, with what intention a person spares. For just as there is sometimes a punishing mercy, so there is also a sparing cruelty.

To give an obvious example: who would not more truly call cruel the person who spared a boy obstinately determined to play with snakes? And who would not call merciful the person who forbade such behavior and corrected a despiser of words even with blows? For this reason discipline should not be extended to the point of death, so that there may remain someone whom it can benefit.

Even when one person is killed by another, it makes a great difference whether this is done out of a desire to inflict harm or to take something unjustly—as by an enemy or a robber—or in the course of avenging or obeying authority—as by a judge or an executioner—or from the necessity of escaping or giving aid—as when a traveler kills a robber or a soldier kills an enemy.

Sometimes the person who caused a death is more at fault than the one who killed—for example, if someone deceives his guarantor and the guarantor undergoes the lawful punishment on his behalf. Yet not everyone who causes another’s death is guilty. What if someone demands sexual relations and kills himself when he does not obtain them? What if a son, fearing his father’s loving beatings, dies by throwing himself from a height? What if someone, after another person has been freed—or to prevent another from being freed—inflicts death upon himself?

Are we therefore, because of these causes of other people’s deaths, either to consent to crime, or to remove the punishment of sin—which is imposed not from a desire to harm but from a desire to correct—even when it is paternal, or to restrain works of mercy? When such things happen, we ought to feel human grief for them; but we do not rightly suppress the will to do good merely to prevent such events from occurring.

### 18

So too, when we intercede for a condemned sinner, consequences sometimes follow that we do not want. The person freed through our intercession may become even more savagely audacious with impunity, surrendering to desire and ungrateful toward mercy, so that one person rescued from death kills many others. Or, when someone has been changed for the better and corrected in character through our benefaction, another person may perish through living badly, taking that person’s impunity as a precedent and committing similar or more serious offenses.

These evils, I think, should not be imputed to us when we intercede for you. Rather, we should consider and desire the good things that we seek when we do so: the commendation of gentleness, by which love is won for the word of truth, and that those who are delivered from temporal death may live in such a way that they do not fall into eternal death, from which they will never be delivered.

### 19

Your severity therefore is beneficial; through its ministry peace is strengthened, including our own. Our intercession is also beneficial; through its ministry your severity is moderated.

Do not be displeased that you are asked by good people, since good people are not displeased that they are feared by bad people. The Apostle Paul terrified human wickedness not only with the judgment to come but also with your present swords [Note: Thus nearly all the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “he terrified them with your secular powers,” as does Gratian, who adds “present.”], asserting that these too belong to the administration of divine providence.

“For every soul,” he says, “must be subject to the higher authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been established by God. Therefore whoever resists authority resists what God has appointed; and those who resist will bring judgment upon themselves. For rulers are not a terror to good conduct but to bad. Do you wish not to fear authority? Do what is good, and you will receive praise from it, for it is God’s servant for your good. But if you do what is bad, be afraid, for it does not bear the sword without reason: it is God’s servant, an avenger for wrath against the one who does evil. Therefore you must be subject, not only because of wrath but also because of conscience. For this reason you also pay taxes, since they are God’s ministers, attending constantly to this very task. Render to all what is owed: tax to whom tax is owed, revenue to whom revenue, fear to whom fear, honor to whom honor. Owe no one anything except to love one another” (Romans 13:1–8).

These words of the Apostle show the usefulness of your severity. Therefore, just as those who fear have been commanded to owe love to those who terrify them, so those who terrify have been commanded to owe love to those who fear them.

Let nothing be done from a desire to harm, but let everything be done from a concern for the good; let nothing be done savagely, nothing inhumanely. Let the judge’s punishment be feared in such a way that the intercessor’s religious duty is not despised, because whether by punishing or by forgiving, the only good aim is to correct human life.

But if perversity and impiety are so great that neither discipline nor pardon can benefit their correction, nevertheless, whether through severity or gentleness, the good fulfill only the duty of love, according to the intention and conscience that God sees.

### 20

In the next part of your letter you say: “But now, given the character of our times, people want both the punishment for their crime to be remitted and the possession of the thing for which the crime was committed.” You are referring to the worst kind of people, for whom the medicine of repentance is entirely useless.

If property belonging to another, on account of which the sin was committed, can be returned but is not returned, repentance is not being practiced but feigned. If repentance is genuine, however, the sin will not be forgiven unless what was taken is restored—when it can be restored, as I said.

Often the person who takes something loses it, either by suffering the wrongdoing of others or by living badly himself, and has nothing else from which to make restitution. We certainly cannot say to such a person, “Return what you took,” unless we believe that he has it and is concealing it.

If, while he is thought to possess what he can return, he endures some suffering from the person demanding it, there is no injustice. For even if he has no means of paying back the money he took, he nevertheless justly pays the penalty for the sin by being compelled, through bodily hardships, to return what he wickedly took.

Yet it is not inhuman to intercede even for such people, as for those accused of crimes—not so that what belongs to others should not be restored, but so that one human being may not rage pointlessly against another, especially someone who has already forgiven the fault but seeks the money, and who, if he fears being defrauded, does not seek revenge.

Indeed, in such cases, if we can persuade those for whom we intercede that they do not possess what is being demanded, their sufferings are immediately relaxed for us. Sometimes, however, merciful people do not wish, even in circumstances of uncertainty, to inflict certain punishment on someone for uncertain money.

We ought also to call and exhort you to this mercy. It is better, even if he possesses it, for you to lose the money than, if he does not possess it, to torture or kill him. But in such cases it is more appropriate to intercede with those who demand repayment than with those who judge, lest the person who has the authority but does not compel repayment himself appear to be taking it away. Even when compelling repayment, however, he should exercise such integrity that he does not lose his humanity.

### 21

I would say with complete confidence that the person who intervenes on behalf of someone so that he need not restore what was wrongly taken, and who does not compel the person who has sought refuge with him to make restitution as far as honesty permits, is an accomplice in fraud and crime.

For we withdraw our assistance from such people more mercifully than we provide it. A person does not help someone who assists him in sinning; rather, he overthrows and crushes him.

But does this mean that we either can or ought to demand repayment ourselves, or hand the matter over so that repayment may be demanded? We act insofar as episcopal authority permits, sometimes threatening human judgment, but above all and always divine judgment.

Those whom we know both to have taken something wrongfully and to possess the means of returning it, yet who are unwilling to do so, we accuse, rebuke, and detest—some privately, some publicly—as the differences among persons seem to allow different remedies, lest they be driven into even greater madness to the ruin of others.

Sometimes, too, if no more urgent concern prevents it, we deprive them of communion at the holy altar.

### 22

Often, however, they deceive us, either by denying that they took anything or by asserting that they do not possess the means to make restitution. Often you too are deceived, thinking either that we are not acting to make them return it or that they possess the means to do so.

All, or nearly all, of us like either to call or to regard our suspicions as knowledge when we are moved by credible indications of things, even though some things that seem credible are false and some things that seem incredible are true.

Therefore, when mentioning certain people who want both the punishment for their crime remitted and the possession of the thing for which the crime was committed, you added and said: “Your priesthood also thinks that intercession should be made for such people.”

It may be that you know what I do not know, and that for this reason I think intercession should be made for someone: something may have deceived me, though it could not deceive you, so that I do not believe that he possesses what you know he possesses.

Thus it happens that, although our judgment concerning the accused is not the same, neither of us approves that another person’s property is not returned. As human beings, we judge differently concerning the person; but in justice itself we are united.

Similarly, it may happen that although I know someone does not possess a thing, you do not know with certainty that he possesses it, but suspect credibly that he does. For this reason I may seem to you to be interceding for someone who wants both the punishment for his crime remitted and the possession of the thing for which the crime was committed.

In short, neither before you, nor before people such as we rejoice that you are, nor before those who eagerly seek the property of others—property that will benefit no one and is also highly dangerous and harmful—nor before my own heart, for which God is witness, would I dare to say, think, or decide that intercession should be made for anyone so that he might possess, with impunity for his crime, what he took by crime.

Intercession should be made so that, once the wrong has been forgiven, he may return what he wrongfully took—provided that he has what he took, or something else with which to restore it.

### 23

Of course, not everything taken from an unwilling person is taken wrongfully. Many people are unwilling to pay a physician his fee or a laborer his wages; yet those who receive these payments from unwilling people do not receive them unjustly. Rather, the payments would be unjustly withheld if they were not made.

But a judge should not for that reason sell a just judgment, nor a witness true testimony, merely because an advocate sells just legal representation and a jurist sound advice. The former are appointed to examine the matter between the two parties; the latter stand on one side.

When judgments and testimonies—which ought not to be sold if they are just and true—are sold as unjust and false, money is taken far more criminally, since it is taken criminally even when willingly given.

Nevertheless, the person who bought a just judgment usually seeks to recover his money as though it had been wrongfully taken from him, because it should not have been for sale. The person who paid for an unjust judgment would certainly wish to recover it, if he were not afraid or ashamed that he had bought it.

### 24

There are other persons of lower rank who not improperly receive payments from both sides: officials, the persons by whom they are engaged to perform a service [Note: Lov. has “and the person by whom he is removed.” But the manuscripts have “and the person by whom he is assigned,” that is, the person who hires the official to perform the service], and the persons to whom the service is assigned.

Payments extorted from them through excessive abuse are usually reclaimed; payments given according to a tolerable custom usually are not. We criticize those who unusually reclaim such payments more than those who accept them according to custom, since many necessary persons in human affairs are either invited by such benefits or retained through them.

If these people change their way of life or ascend to a higher degree of holiness, they more readily distribute to the poor as their own what they acquired in this manner than restore it as another’s to those from whom they received it.

But whoever has taken something contrary to the law of human society through theft, robbery, false accusations, oppression, or seizure, we judge that it ought to be restored rather than given away. Such was the evangelical example of Zacchaeus the tax collector, who, after receiving the Lord as his guest and suddenly being changed into a holy life, said: “I give half of my possessions to the poor, and if I have taken anything from anyone, I restore fourfold” (Luke 19:8).

### 25

Nevertheless, if justice is considered more sincerely, it is more just to say to an advocate, “Return what you received,” when you stood against the truth, supported injustice, deceived the judge, crushed a just cause, and won through falsehood—something that you see many highly respectable and eloquent men seeming to do not only with impunity but even with glory—than to say to anyone serving in any office, “Return what you received,” when, at the judge’s command, you detained a person necessary to a particular case, bound him so that he could not resist, imprisoned him so that he could not flee, and finally produced him while the suit continued or released him when it ended.

Why this is not said to the advocate is obvious: a person does not wish to recover what he gave to an advocate so that he might win unjustly in the same way that he does not wish to return what he received from his opponent after winning unjustly.

What advocate—or what outstanding man from among advocates—is so good that he would readily say to his client: “Take back what you gave me when I supported you wrongly, and return to your opponent what you unjustly took while I was acting on your behalf”?

Yet someone who rightly repents of his former unjust life ought also to do this: if the person who litigated unjustly, after being warned, does not wish to correct his injustice, the former advocate should nevertheless not wish to keep the profit of that injustice.

Unless, perhaps, property stolen secretly must be returned, while property obtained in the very forum where sins are punished—by deceiving the judge and circumventing the laws—need not be returned!

What shall I say about interest, which even the laws and judges themselves command to be returned? Is the person who takes or snatches away something from a rich man more cruel than the person who kills a poor man through usury?

These and similar things are certainly possessed wrongly, and I wish they were restored; but there is no judge before whom they can be reclaimed.

### 26

Now, if we carefully consider what is written—“The faithful person possesses the whole world of riches, but the unfaithful person does not possess even a penny” [Note: This saying is written in the Septuagint, Proverbs 17, after verse 6, and is frequently cited by Augustine; also by Jerome in Letter 103 to Paulinus and in his Commentary on Ezekiel 45, by Cassian in Conference 24, chapter 26, and by Bernard in The Life of Saint Malachy, among others]—do we not prove that all those who seem to rejoice in things lawfully acquired, but do not know how to use them, possess what belongs to others?

What is possessed by right is certainly not another’s; but what is possessed by right is what is possessed justly, and what is possessed justly is what is possessed well. Everything, therefore, that is possessed badly is another’s; and a person possesses something badly when he uses it badly.

You see, then, how many people ought to restore what belongs to others, if even a few can be found to whom it should be restored. Wherever such people are, however, they despise these things all the more because they were able to possess them more justly.

No one possesses justice badly, and whoever has not loved it does not possess it. Money, however, is possessed badly by the bad, and is possessed better by the good in proportion as it is loved less.

Meanwhile, the injustice of those who possess things badly is tolerated, and certain rights are established among them that are called civil—not because this makes them good users of their possessions, but so that bad users may be less troublesome.

This continues until the faithful and devout, to whom everything belongs by right—those who either arise from among them or live among them for a time without being bound by their evils but exercised by them—reach that city where the inheritance is eternity [Note: Lov. has “where eternity is.” Bad., Am., Er., and the manuscripts have “where the inheritance is eternity”]; where only the just have a place, only the wise hold authority, and all who are there possess what is truly their own.

Even here, however, we do not intercede so that what belongs to others should not be restored according to earthly customs and laws. We want you to be lenient toward bad people—not so that the bad may please you or remain bad, but because from them all who become good are made, and God is appeased by the sacrifice of mercy. Unless the bad had him as their gracious God, there would be no good people.

It has been a long time since, by speaking, I have seemed burdensome to you in the midst of your occupations, although, as you are an intelligent and learned man, what you asked could have been answered quickly. I should have ended long ago if I had known that you would read only what you requested me to write back.

May you live happily in Christ, dearest son.

## LETTER 154

[Note: Formerly numbered 51; what was formerly number 154 is now 47. Probably written toward the end of 414.]

Macedonius to Augustine, indicating that he had done what Augustine had asked of him with such marked modesty, and also that he had read Augustine’s books with great pleasure and admiration.

**To the deservedly venerable and truly revered father AUGUSTINE, bishop, MACEDONIUS.**

### 1

I am wonderfully moved by your wisdom, both in what you have published and in what you do not hesitate to send when interceding for criminals [Note: Alternatively, “those in difficulty”]. The former possess such keenness, learning, and holiness that nothing could surpass them; the latter possess such modesty that, unless I do what you command, I judge that the blame remains with me and not with the matter itself, deservedly venerable lord and truly revered father.

You do not press me—as many people in this position do—to extort whatever you may anxiously desire. Rather, you indicate what seemed askable of a judge burdened by so many concerns, with the assistance of modesty, which among good people is the most effective instrument in difficult matters.

Accordingly, I immediately fulfilled the wish you entrusted to me, for I had already opened the way for hope.

### 2

I finished reading your books [Note: The first three books of *The City of God*, as appears from the following letter, section 2]. They were not so weak or inert that they would allow me to attend to anything other than themselves. They laid hold of me, tore me away from other causes of anxiety, and bound me with their chains—so may God be gracious to me—that I am uncertain what I should admire more in them: the perfection of the priesthood, the doctrines of philosophy, the full knowledge of history, or the charm of their eloquence.

Their eloquence can entice even the unlearned, so that they do not stop until they have finished reading, and once they have finished, they still seek more.

For the shamelessly obstinate have been convicted of admitting that, even in the prosperous ages they recount, worse things befell because of the obscurity of the nature of events, and that all were deceived by a certain sweetness overlaid upon their prosperity, through which they were led not to blessedness but to ruin.

By contrast, our teachings and the mysteries of the one simple and true God, besides promising eternal life through the purest virtues, also mitigate these worldly events that necessarily befall us because we have been born.

You used a very powerful example from the recent calamity. Although it may have fortified your case most firmly, nevertheless, if either alternative had been possible, I would not have wanted to support you with it. But since a complaint had arisen from that event by which the folly of the others had to be refuted, it was necessary to draw arguments for the truth from it.

### 3

Meanwhile, occupied with other concerns—which, although they are vain, nevertheless seem necessary when we consider how matters turn out, as a condition of being born—I have written this reply.

If I have leisure and life remains to me, I shall also write back from Italy, so that a work of such great learning may be repaid by services that, although they cannot satisfy its worth, are at least appropriate.

May almighty God preserve your Holiness safe and joyful through a very long life, deservedly desirable lord and truly revered father.

## LETTER 155

[Note: Formerly numbered 52; what was formerly number 155 is now 238. Written after the preceding letter.]

Augustine to Macedonius, teaching that the blessed life and true virtue come only from God.

**AUGUSTINE, bishop, servant of Christ and of his household, to his beloved son MACEDONIUS, greetings in the Lord.**

## CHAPTER I

### 1

Although I do not recognize in myself the wisdom that you attribute to me, I nevertheless give and owe you the greatest thanks for your great and sincere goodwill toward me. I rejoice that the labors of my studies have pleased so great a man; but I rejoice much more because I recognize your spirit, affected by love of eternity and truth, and by love itself, yearning for that divine and heavenly commonwealth whose ruler is Christ, in which alone one must live forever and happily if one lives rightly and devoutly here.

I see you drawing near to it, and I embrace you as one burning to possess it. From this indeed true friendship also flows—not to be measured by temporal advantages, but to be valued through disinterested love [Note: The printed editions have *to be possessed*. Thirteen manuscripts have *to be tasted*; eight others have *to be valued*.].

For no one can truly be a friend of a human being unless he has first become a friend of truth itself; and if this does not happen freely, it cannot happen in any way.

### 2

Philosophers have also said much about this matter. But among them true devotion—that is, the true worship of the true God, from which all duties of right living must be derived—is not found.

So far as I understand, the reason is that they wanted in some way to construct the blessed life for themselves, and thought it had to be achieved rather than obtained, although its giver is none but God.

For no one makes a person blessed except the one who made the person. He who bestows so many goods of his creation on good and bad alike—existence, humanity, vigorous senses, bodily strength, and abundant resources—will give himself to the good so that they may be blessed, because it is also his gift that they are good.

But those who, in this life of hardship, in these dying limbs, under the burden of corruptible flesh, wanted to be the authors and, as it were, creators of their own blessed life, pursuing it as though through their own virtues and already possessing it, rather than seeking and hoping for it from that source of virtues, could not fail to experience God resisting their pride.

They therefore fell into an extremely absurd error. For when they assert that the wise person is blessed even in the bull of Phalaris, they are forced to admit that the blessed life must sometimes be fled. When the bodily evils are magnified, they yield and decide that one must depart from this life because of its most grievous torments.

I do not wish to say how great a crime it is for an innocent person to kill himself, since he ought not do so even if guilty. We have already said much about this in the first book of those three books that you read with such kindness and diligence (*The City of God*, book 1, chapters 17 and following). But let us at least consider, and judge soberly rather than proudly, what sort of blessed life this is—one that the wise person does not enjoy when retained, but is compelled to abandon by laying hands upon himself.

### 3

In Cicero, as you know, at the end of the fifth book of the *Tusculan Disputations*, there is a passage that deserves attention for the reason I am giving.

When discussing bodily blindness and asserting that even a blind wise person could be blessed, he said many things that such a person could enjoy by hearing. Likewise, if he were deaf, Cicero transferred to the eyes the things by which he could be delighted.

But if he were deprived of both senses and became blind and deaf, Cicero did not dare to draw a conclusion from this and call him blessed.
