He added even the most severe bodily pains, saying that, if they did not kill him, he should kill himself and, liberated by this virtue, reach the harbor of insensibility.

Thus the wise person yields to and succumbs to monstrous calamities, to the point that he is compelled to commit murder against himself. Who will spare him from those evils when he does not spare himself?

Certainly he is always blessed; certainly he has established the blessed life in his own power and cannot lose it through any force of misfortune. Behold: in blindness, deafness, and the most atrocious bodily torments, he has either lost the blessed life; or, if it remains blessed even amid such afflictions, the disputations of these highly learned men produce the result that there is sometimes a blessed life that the wise person cannot endure—or, more absurdly still, ought not to endure—and that he should flee it, cut it short, cast it away, and remove himself from it by the sword, poison, or some other voluntary death.

Thus he reaches the harbor of insensibility, which is either complete nothingness, as the Epicureans and others of similar folly thought, or else he is blessed because he has been freed from that blessed life as from some plague.

O excessively proud boastfulness! If the blessed life exists amid bodily torments, why does the wise person not remain in it and enjoy it? But if it is miserable, what, I ask you, prevents him—except conceit—from admitting it, praying to God, and entreating the just and merciful one who is powerful either to avert or mitigate the evils of this life, to arm us with courage to endure them, or to free us from them in every way, and afterward to give the truly blessed life in which no evil is admitted and the highest good is never lost?

### 4

This is the reward of the devout. In hope of attaining it, we lead this temporal and mortal life not so much pleasurably as tolerably. We endure its evils courageously through sound judgment and divine gift when we rejoice in the eternal goods promised faithfully by God and awaited faithfully by us.

The Apostle Paul exhorted us to this hope when he said: “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Romans 12:12). By placing “rejoicing in hope” first, he showed why we should be patient in tribulation.

I exhort you to this hope through Jesus Christ our Lord. God himself, our teacher, concealed in the majesty of divinity but revealed in the weakness of flesh, not only taught this by the oracle of his words but also confirmed it by the example of his passion and resurrection. In the one he showed what we must endure; in the other, what we must hope for.

They too would have obtained his grace if, lifted up and inflated by pride, they had not vainly attempted to make the blessed life for themselves—a life that God alone has truly promised to bestow upon his worshipers after this life.

Cicero’s other statement is more sound, where he says: “For this life is indeed death, which I could lament if I wished” (Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*). How, then, if it is rightly lamented, can it be proved blessed? Is it not rather shown to be miserable precisely because it is rightly lamented?

Therefore, I beg you, good man, accustom yourself meanwhile to being blessed in hope, so that you may also be blessed in reality when the reward of eternal happiness is given to steadfast devotion.

## CHAPTER II
5. If I am burdensome because of the length of my letter, you brought this upon yourself by calling me wise. For this reason I have dared to speak to you in this way: not to display to you what sort of wisdom I possess, but to show you what wisdom ought to be. In the present age, this is the true worship of the true God, so that in the age to come it may have a sure and complete fruit. Here there is steadfast piety; there, everlasting happiness. If I possess anything from this wisdom, which alone is true, I have received it from God, not presumed upon it as my own; and I faithfully hope that it will be perfected in me by him from whom I humbly rejoice that it was begun. I am neither unbelieving concerning what he has not yet granted nor ungrateful concerning what he has already granted. For if there is anything praiseworthy in me, I am so not through my own talent or merit, but through his gift. Indeed, certain exceptionally acute and outstanding intellects have fallen into greater errors precisely because they ran more confidently as though relying on their own powers, and did not humbly and sincerely ask God to show them the way. But what are the merits of any human beings, since he who came not with a due reward but with gratuitous grace found all people sinners, and alone set them free and frees them from sins?

6. If, then, true virtue delights us, let us say to it what we read in his sacred Scriptures: “I will love you, Lord, my strength” (Psalm 17:2). And if we truly wish to be blessed—which we cannot possibly fail to wish—let us hold with faithful heart what we have learned in those same Scriptures: “Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord, and who has not turned toward vanities and lying insanities” (Psalm 39:5).

What vanity, what insanity, and what falsehood it is for a mortal human being, leading a troubled life in changeable spirit and flesh, burdened with so many sins, subject to so many temptations, exposed to so many forms of corruption, and destined for the most just punishments, to trust in himself in order to be blessed—when he cannot even reclaim from error what is most excellent in the dignity of his nature, namely, his mind and reason, unless God is present as the light of minds! Let us therefore cast aside, I beg you, the vanities and lying insanities of false philosophers. We shall have no virtue unless he himself is present, by whose help we are aided; nor happiness unless he himself is present, whom we may enjoy; and may he absorb our entire changeable and corruptible nature—which in itself is weak and a kind of material for misery—in the gift of immortality and incorruption.

7. Since we know that you are a lover of the commonwealth, see how clearly those sacred Scriptures show that the human being is not blessed in one way and the state in another. For one who was filled with the Holy Spirit speaks the following words in prayer:

“Deliver me from the hand of foreign sons, whose mouth has spoken vanity, and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity. Their sons are like young plants, firmly established in their youth; their daughters are fashioned and adorned like the likeness of a temple. Their storerooms are full, overflowing from one store to another. Their sheep are fertile, multiplying in their pastures; their oxen are fat. There is no breach in the wall, no passage through it, and no cry in their streets. They called that people blessed which possesses these things; blessed is the people whose Lord is its God” (Psalm 143:11–15).

8. You see that a people is called blessed on account of an exaggeration of earthly happiness only by “foreign sons,” that is, by those who do not belong to the regeneration by which we become sons of God. The one praying asks to be delivered from their hand, lest he be dragged by them into this opinion and into impious sins.

By speaking vanity, they called blessed the people that possesses the things he mentioned above—the things that make up the happiness sought exclusively by lovers of this world. Therefore their right hand is “a right hand of iniquity,” because they have placed first what ought to have been placed last, just as the right hand is placed before the left. If these things are possessed, blessed life must not be placed in them. They ought to be subordinate, not preeminent; to follow, not to lead.

But to this man who prayed in this way and desired to be rescued and separated from the foreign sons who called blessed the people possessing these things—as though we were to say, “What do you yourself think? Which people do you call blessed?”—he did not answer, “Blessed is the people whose strength is its spirit.” Had he said this, he would indeed have distinguished this people from the one that placed blessed life in visible and bodily happiness; but he would not yet have transcended all vanities and lying insanities. For, as the same Scriptures teach elsewhere, “Cursed is everyone who places his hope in man” (Jeremiah 17:5). Therefore no one ought to place his hope even in himself, since he too is a human being. Accordingly, to pass beyond the limits of every vanity and lying insanity, and to place blessed life where it truly is, he says: “Blessed is the people whose Lord is its God.”

## CHAPTER III

9. You see, then, from whom what all educated and uneducated people desire must be sought, though many, through error and pride, neither know from whom it should be sought nor where it is received. Both groups are censured together in a certain divine psalm: those who trust in their own strength and those who glory in the abundance of their riches (Psalm 48:7). That is, both the philosophers of this age and those who recoil from such philosophy while calling blessed the people to whom earthly wealth is available.

Therefore let us ask from the Lord our God, by whom we were made, both for the strength by which we may overcome the evils of this life and for the blessed life in which, after this life, we may enjoy his eternity, so that both in strength and in the reward of strength, as the Apostle says, “the one who glories may glory in the Lord” (2 Corinthians 10:17). Let this be what we desire for ourselves and for the state whose citizens we are. For the blessed city is not one thing and the blessed human being another, since a city is nothing other than a harmonious multitude of human beings.

10. If all your prudence, by which you strive to care for human affairs; all your courage, by which you are not terrified when confronted by anyone’s injustice; all your temperance, by which amid such a plague of wicked human custom you hold yourself back from corruption; and all your justice, by which through right judgment you distribute to each person what is his—if all these labor and strive merely so that those whom you wish to prosper may be bodily safe and secure and peaceful from every wrongdoing, may have sons like young plants firmly established, daughters adorned like the likeness of a temple, full storerooms overflowing from one store to another, fertile sheep, fat oxen, and a country estate not disfigured by the collapse of its wall, while no litigants’ cry resounds in their streets—then your virtues will not be true, any more than their happiness is true.

Here my modesty—the modesty which in your letter you praised with kindly words—must not prevent me from speaking the truth. If, I say, any administration of yours, equipped with the virtues I have mentioned, is directed toward this sole end: that human beings according to the flesh suffer no unjust troubles, and if you do not consider it your concern to what purpose they refer the peace you strive to provide—that is, to put the matter plainly, how they worship the true God, in whom is found the whole fruit of peaceful life—then all this great labor does nothing for true blessed life.

11. I may seem to say this with insufficient modesty, and to have in some way forgotten the customary restraint of my intercessions. But if modesty is nothing other than a certain fear of displeasing, then in this matter I do not fear while fearing. For I fear that I should rightly displease God first, and then the friendship which you have graciously chosen to enter with me, if I were less free in offering admonition—something I believe it is most salutary for me to offer.

I am certainly more modest when I intercede with you for others; but when I intercede for you yourself, I am freer in proportion as I am more your friend, because I am more your friend in proportion as I am more faithful. Indeed, I would not say even these things unless I were acting with restraint. If, as you yourself have written, this is the greatest efficacy among good men in difficult matters, may it assist me with you and for you, so that I may enjoy you in him who has granted me this access and confidence toward you—especially since I think that what I suggest is now easy for your mind, supported and equipped as it is by so many divine gifts.

12. If, recognizing from whom you received the virtues you possess and giving thanks to him, you devote them to his worship even amid your secular honors; if by the example of your religious life and by the very zeal with which you care for them—whether by encouraging or by restraining—you raise up and lead the people subject to your authority toward worshiping him; and if, in the fact that through you they live more securely, you desire nothing else except that by this means they may become worthy of him with whom they will live in blessedness—then those virtues will truly be virtues.

Through the help of him by whose generosity they were given, they will grow and be perfected in such a way that they will lead you without any doubt to the truly blessed life, which is eternal and nothing else. There, no prudence will distinguish evils from goods, because evils will not exist; no courage will endure adversities, because there will be nothing there except what we love, not also what we endure; no temperance will restrain desire, because we will feel none of its provocations; and no justice will assist the needy, because we will have no poor or needy person.

There virtue will be one, and that same thing will be both virtue and the reward of virtue, of which the man who loves it says in the sacred utterances: “But for me, it is good to cling to God” (Psalm 72:28). There will be complete and everlasting wisdom, and truly blessed life itself. For it is arrival at the eternal and supreme good, and to cling to it forever is the end of our good.

It may be called prudence, because it will cling with perfect foresight to a good that cannot be lost; courage, because it will cling most firmly to a good from which it cannot be torn; temperance, because it will cling most chastely to a good in which it cannot be corrupted; and justice, because it will cling most rightly to a good to which it is rightly subject.

## CHAPTER IV

13. Yet even in this life virtue is nothing other than loving what ought to be loved. To choose that is prudence; to be turned away from it by no troubles is courage; by no allurements, temperance; by no pride, justice.

What should we choose to love above all except that than which we find nothing better? This is God. If, by loving something, we either place it before him or make it equal to him, we do not know how to love ourselves. For we are better in proportion as we move more deeply toward him than whom nothing is better. We move toward him not by walking but by loving. We shall have him more present to us in proportion as we are able to have purer the very love by which we strive toward him; for he is neither extended nor enclosed by bodily places.

Therefore it is permissible to go to him who is present everywhere and wholly everywhere, not on foot but by our conduct. Our conduct, however, is usually judged not by what each person knows but by what each person loves. Conduct is made good or bad only by good or bad loves. Through our perversity, then, we are far from God’s rectitude; hence by loving what is right we are corrected, so that, made upright, we may cling to what is upright.

14. Therefore, with all the effort we can, let us act so that those whom we love as ourselves may also reach him, if through loving him we have already learned to love ourselves. For Christ, that is, Truth, says that the whole Law and the Prophets depend upon these two commandments: that we love God with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our mind, and that we love our neighbor as ourselves (Matthew 22:37–40).

Here “neighbor” is to be understood not by blood relationship but by participation in reason, in which all human beings share. For if a financial relationship makes people partners, how much more does the commonality of nature—not the law of doing business but the law of birth—make them partners!

Thus that comic poet—just as truth’s radiance is not absent from brilliant minds—when composing a line spoken by one old man to another,

> Are you so free from concern for your own affairs

> that you attend to matters belonging to another, which have nothing to do with you?

had the other reply:

> I am a human being; I consider nothing human foreign to me.  
> (Terence, *The Self-Tormentor*, act 1, scene 1.)

They say that the entire theater, filled with foolish and uneducated people, applauded this sentiment. For it touched so naturally upon the fellowship of human hearts that no human being there failed to feel himself the neighbor of every other human being.

15. Since by that love which the divine law commands a person ought to love God, himself, and his neighbor, nevertheless three commandments were not given on this account. It was not said, “On these three commandments,” but “On these two commandments the whole Law and the Prophets depend”: namely, on loving God with all one’s heart, with all one’s soul, and with all one’s mind, and one’s neighbor as oneself.

This was said so that it might be understood that there is no other love by which anyone loves himself except the love by which he loves God. For whoever loves himself in another way ought rather to be said to hate himself. He becomes unjust and is deprived of the light of justice when, turning away from the higher and more excellent good and thence turning toward himself, he necessarily turns toward lower and needy things. In him is fulfilled what is most truly written: “But the one who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Psalm 10:6).

Therefore, since no one loves himself except by loving God, it was unnecessary, once the commandment to love God had been given, also to command a person to love himself, since he loves himself precisely in loving God. He must therefore love his neighbor as himself, so that, by whatever means he can—by the consolation of benevolence, by instruction in teaching, or by the correction of discipline—he may lead that person to worship God, knowing that the whole Law and the Prophets depend on these two commandments.

16. Whoever chooses this with sober discernment is prudent; whoever is turned away from it by no affliction is courageous; whoever is turned away by no other pleasure is temperate; whoever is turned away by no elation is just.

Through these virtues, divinely bestowed through the grace of Jesus Christ, the mediator who is God with the Father and human with us, through whom, after the enmity of iniquity, we are reconciled to God in the Spirit of love—through these divinely bestowed virtues, I say, the good life is now lived, and afterward its reward, the blessed life—which cannot be anything other than eternal—is bestowed.

Here these virtues exist in action; there, in effect. Here, in work; there, in reward. Here, in duty; there, in the goal. Therefore all good and holy people, even when supported by divine assistance amid whatever torments, are called blessed because of the hope of that end by which they will be blessed. For if they were to remain forever amid those same torments and most savage pains, no sound reasoning would doubt that they were miserable, whatever virtues they possessed.

17. Piety, therefore—that is, the true worship of the true God—is profitable for all things: both for turning away or lessening the troubles of this life and for leading us to that life and salvation where we will suffer no evil and will enjoy good in the supreme and everlasting good.

I exhort you to attain this more perfectly and to hold it with the greatest perseverance, just as I exhort myself. If you were not already a participant in it, and if you did not judge that your temporary honors ought to serve it, you would not have said to the Donatist heretics, in order to bring them back into the unity and peace of Christ, in an edict:

> “This is being done for you; for you, priests of incorrupt faith; for you, the Emperor Augustus; for you also, we who are his judges, are laboring.”

And you placed many other statements in the same edict in such a way that it is evident that, while wearing the belt of an earthly judge, you were thinking in no small measure about the heavenly commonwealth.

Therefore, if I have wished to speak with you at length about true virtues and the truly blessed life, I beg you not to consider me burdensome to your occupations. Indeed, I am confident that I am not burdensome, since you possess so great and wonderfully praiseworthy a mind that you neither abandon those concerns nor devote yourself to these matters with greater willingness and familiarity.

## LETTER 156

[Note: Columns 673–674: Letters 156 and 157 were corrected with the aid of manuscripts aa, cc, ff, vv, *vetus* 3, *V*, and the editions of Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.; to these was added the manuscript of the Cistercian monastery of Saint-Sulpice.]

[Note: Formerly Letter 88; what was 156 is now 131. It appears to have been written in the year 414.]

Hilary to Augustine, presenting several questions on which he wishes to be instructed.

To the holy lord, rightly and deservedly venerable, and in every respect worthy of worship, Augustine, bishop, Hilary.

[Note: In the Cistercian manuscript, and likewise below in the Victorine manuscript, the name is written *Hilarus*. We do not know whether this is the same man who later wrote to Augustine the letter against the Semi-Pelagians that is numbered here 219, where he professes that he had enjoyed the delights of Augustine’s presence and had been nourished by his salutary breasts.]

The grace of your holiness, which is known to all, persuaded my smallness to send these letters to your venerability by those returning from Syracuse to Hippo.

[Note: Four manuscripts read “our” instead of “your.”]

I ask the most holy Trinity to grant that, by the favor of our God, you may receive this writing of mine for review in safety and strength, holy lord, rightly and deservedly venerable and in every respect worthy of worship.

Accordingly, I ask that you deign to remember me in your holy prayers and to instruct our ignorance concerning what certain Christians at Syracuse expound. They say:

- That a human being can be without sin and can easily keep God’s commandments if he wishes.
- That an unbaptized infant who is overtaken by death cannot justly perish, since he is born without sin.
- That a rich person who remains in his riches cannot enter the kingdom of God unless he sells everything he owns, and that it cannot benefit him if he happens to fulfill the commandments from those riches.
- That one ought never to swear.
- Concerning the Church, which is the one of which it is written that it has neither wrinkle nor blemish (Ephesians 5:27): whether this is the Church in which we are now gathered, or the one that we hope for. Some, however, think that this is the Church now frequented by crowds and that it can be without sin.

[Note: Three manuscripts read “placed” instead of “think.”]

Concerning all these matters, I ask your holiness with all the urgency of which I am capable to command that we be instructed more clearly, so that we may know how far we ought to understand these things.

I pray that the mercy of our God preserve your holiness unharmed for countless years, holy lord, rightly and deservedly venerable and in every respect worthy of worship.

## LETTER 157

[Note: Jerome, writing against the Pelagians in the year 415, testifies in book 3 that books to Marcellinus on the baptism of infants had long before been published by Augustine, but that the letter—or “book,” as he calls it—to Hilary had appeared recently. Orosius read this same letter, recently sent to Sicily, as he says in his *Apology*, at the Palestinian council held in July of the year 415. Finally, Augustine himself reports that the same work was discussed at the Diospolitan synod held in December of that year, 415, in his book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chapter 11; there he calls it a book, not a letter.]

[Note: Formerly Letter 89; what was 157 is now 190. Written after the preceding letter.]

Augustine to Hilary, answering his questions.

Augustine, bishop, servant of Christ and of his Church, to his beloved son Hilary, greeting in the Lord.

## CHAPTER I

1. From your letter I learned not only that you are safe but also that you are devoted to the word of God and concerned in a pious way for your salvation, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. Therefore, giving thanks to God, I did not delay in sending my reply.

2. If, then, you ask whether in this life anyone can advance so far in perfection of righteousness as to live here entirely without any sin, consider what the Apostle John said, whom the Lord especially loved among his disciples:

> “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

If, then, those about whom you wrote to me say that they are without sin, you see that they deceive themselves and that the truth is not in them. But if they confess that they are sinners so that they may be able to obtain God’s mercy, let them restrain themselves from deceiving others as well, by trying to persuade them of this pride.

Everyone needs the Lord’s Prayer, which the Lord gave even to the rams of his flock—that is, to his Apostles—so that each person may say to God:

> “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12).

Whoever has no need of these words in prayer must be declared to live here without sin. If the Lord foresaw that some such people would exist, people better than his Apostles proved to be, he would have taught them another prayer in which they would not ask that their sins be forgiven, since all their sins had already been forgiven in Baptism.

For if holy Daniel, not before human beings through deceptive humility but before God—that is, in the prayer by which he entreated God—confessed not only the sins of his people but also his own, as is expressed by his truthful mouth (Daniel 9:20), I do not see that anything else should be said to these people except what the Lord commands a certain proud man through the prophet Ezekiel:

> “Are you wiser than Daniel?” (Ezekiel 28:3).

3. Certainly, however, a person who, aided by God’s mercy and grace, has abstained from those sins that are also called crimes, and who has not neglected to cleanse those sins without which no one lives here through works of mercy and devout prayers, will deserve to depart from this life without sin, even though while living here he possessed some sins. For just as these sins were not absent, so remedies by which they could be cleansed were present.

But whoever, having discovered this as though it were an excuse, hears that no one lives here without sin by his own choice, gives himself over to lust, binds himself to unspeakable crimes, and persists in these criminal and wicked ways until his final day—whatever alms he may give amid all this—leads a miserable life and ends it even more miserably.

## CHAPTER II

4. These people are at least tolerable when they say that there either is or has been here someone, apart from the one Holy of holies, who had absolutely no sin.

But what they say—that free choice is sufficient for a human being to fulfill the Lord’s commandments, even without being helped toward good works by God’s grace and the gift of the Holy Spirit—must be altogether anathematized and condemned with every possible execration.

Those who assert this are completely alienated from God’s grace. For, as the Apostle says concerning the Jews, “being ignorant of God’s righteousness, and seeking to establish their own, they have not submitted to the righteousness of God” (Romans 10:3). The fullness of the law is nothing other than love (Romans 13:10); and certainly “God’s love has been poured into our hearts,” not through ourselves or the powers of our own will, but “through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5).

5. Free choice is therefore effective for good works if it is divinely helped, and this happens by humbly asking and acting. But when abandoned by divine assistance, however excellent its knowledge of the law may be, it will in no way possess the solidity of righteousness; it will possess only the inflation of impious pride and a destructive swelling.

The Lord’s Prayer itself teaches this. For we ask God in vain, “Do not bring us into temptation” (Matthew 6:13), if this lies so completely within our power that we are able to fulfill it without any assistance from him. “Do not bring us into temptation” means, “Do not permit us to be brought into it by abandoning us.”

“For God is faithful,” says the Apostle, “and he will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation he will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure it” (1 Corinthians 10:13). Why does he say that God does this, if it lies within our own power alone, without his assistance?

6. The law itself was given as assistance to those who use it lawfully, so that through it they may know either what righteousness they have already received, for which they should give thanks, or what they still lack, which they should earnestly ask for.

But those who hear what the law says, “You shall not covet” (Exodus 20:17; Romans 7:7), in such a way that, because they have learned this, they think it is sufficient for them, and do not believe or ask that the power to do what was commanded be given to them through God’s grace—upon them the law entered so that the offense might abound (Romans 5:20). This was said concerning the Jews.

For it is not merely that they fail to fulfill what the law commands, “You shall not covet”; they also grow proud. Ignorant of God’s righteousness—that is, the righteousness God gives when he justifies the ungodly—and wishing to establish their own righteousness as though it were made by the powers of their own will, they have not submitted to God’s righteousness.

“For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10:4). He came so that, where sin abounded, grace might abound still more.

If the Jews were enemies of this grace because they were ignorant of God’s righteousness and wished to establish their own, why are these people also its enemies if they have believed in the one whom the Jews killed? Is it so that those who, after killing Christ, condemned their impiety and submitted themselves to his known grace may receive the reward, while these people bear judgment because they wish to believe in Christ in such a way as to try to kill his very grace?

7. Those who believe rightly believe in him for this purpose: that they may hunger and thirst for righteousness and be filled by his grace. For, as it is written, “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved” (Joel 2:32; Romans 10:13). This does not mean bodily health, which many possess who do not call upon the name of the Lord, but that salvation of which he himself says, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick.” Explaining what he meant, he continued: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matthew 9:12–13).

Thus he called the righteous healthy and sinners sick. Therefore the sick person must not presume upon his own powers, because “by the abundance of his strength he will not be saved.” If he presumes upon it, let him see whether these powers are not the kind possessed by healthy people but rather the kind possessed by the frenzied. Though insane, they think themselves so healthy that they neither seek a physician nor refrain from striking him as though he were troublesome.

In this way these people, through insane pride, somehow strike Christ, whose gracious assistance is necessary for doing righteousness, though they contend that it is not necessary once the commandment of the law has been given. Let them therefore stop raging in this way and understand that they possess free choice to the extent that they can—not so that they reject assistance through proud willing, but so that through devout willing they call upon the Lord.

8. This free will will be freer in proportion as it is healthier, and healthier in proportion as it is more subject to divine mercy and grace. It faithfully prays and says:

> “Direct my paths according to your word, and let no iniquity rule over me” (Psalm 118:133).

For how is it free when iniquity rules over it? To see whom it invokes so that iniquity may not rule over it, observe its prayer. It does not say, “Direct my paths according to free choice, so that no iniquity will rule over me.” Rather, it says, “Direct my paths according to your word, and let no iniquity rule over me.”

It prays; it does not make a promise. It confesses; it does not make a profession. It desires complete freedom; it does not boast of its own power. For it is not everyone who trusts in his own strength who will be saved, but everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord.

“But how,” he says, “will they call upon him in whom they have not believed?” (Romans 10:14). Those who believe rightly believe for this purpose: that they may call upon the one in whom they have believed and be able to do what they have received in the lawful commandments, because what the law commands, faith obtains.

9. Let us for the moment set aside the law’s many commandments and recall from it what the Apostle chose to mention. When the law says, “You shall not covet,” what else does it seem to command except restraint from unlawful desires? The mind is carried by love wherever it is carried, as though by a weight. We are therefore commanded to remove from the weight of desire whatever may be added to the weight of love, until the former is consumed and the latter perfected. For the fullness of the law is love.

Yet concerning this very restraint, see what is written:

> “And when I knew that no one could be continent unless God granted it, and that this itself was wisdom—to know whose gift it was—I approached the Lord and entreated him” (Wisdom 8:21).

Did he say, “When I knew that no one could be continent except through his own free choice, and that this itself was wisdom—to know that this good came from myself”? He certainly did not say what some people assert in their vanity, but what had to be said in accordance with the truth of sacred Scripture: “When I knew that no one could be continent unless God granted it.”

God therefore commands continence and gives continence. He commands through the law and gives through grace; he commands through the letter and gives through the Spirit. For the law without grace makes sin abound, and the letter without the Spirit kills (2 Corinthians 3:6).

He commands for this reason: so that, attempting to do what is commanded and wearied under the law by our weakness, we may learn to ask for the help of grace; and if we are able to do any good work, we may not be ungrateful to the one who helps us. This is what that man did; wisdom taught him whose gift it was.

10. Free choice is not taken away because it is helped; rather, it is helped because it is not taken away. Whoever says to God, “Be my helper” (Psalm 26:9), confesses that he wishes to fulfill what God has commanded, but asks for help from the one who commanded it so that he may be able to do so.

Thus, when this man knew that no one could be continent unless God granted it, he approached the Lord and entreated him. He approached willingly and entreated willingly; he would not have asked unless there had been a will. But if he had not asked, how much could his will have accomplished?

Even if he is able before asking, what benefit is that unless he gives thanks to him, from whom he must ask for what he is not yet able to do, for what he is able to do? For even the person who is already continent certainly does not possess continence unless the will is present. But if he had not received it, what would the will possess?

“What do you have,” he says, “that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

[Note: Two manuscripts read “what you wanted” instead of “what you received.”]

That is: “Why do you boast as though you possess from yourself what, if you had not received it, you could not possess from yourself?”

This was said so that “the one who glories may glory in the Lord” (2 Corinthians 10:17), and so that the one who does not yet have grounds for glorying may not hope in himself but may pray to the Lord.

It is better for someone to possess less that he must ask from God than to possess more that he attributes to himself, because it is better to rise from below than to fall from above. For it is written: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6).

The law therefore teaches us, through the abundance of sins, what we ought to will, unless grace helps us so that we may be able to do what we will and fulfill what we have been able to do.

[Note: Two manuscripts read “what we will have wanted” instead of “what we have been able to do.”]

It will help us if, rather than presuming upon our own powers and setting our minds on high things, we associate with the humble (Romans 12:16); if we give thanks for what we can already do; and if, for what we cannot yet do, we ask God with a devout and longing will. Let us support our prayer with fruitful works: giving, so that it may be given to us; forgiving, so that we may be forgiven.

[Note: Bad., Am., Er., and two Vatican manuscripts read: “supporting our prayer now with fruitful works,” and so forth.]

## CHAPTER III

11. As for what they say—that an infant overtaken by death, unbaptized, cannot perish because he is born without sin—the Apostle does not say this. I think it better that we believe the Apostle rather than them.

That teacher of the Gentiles, in whom Christ was speaking, says:

> “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned.”

A little later he says:

> “Judgment indeed came from one offense to condemnation, but grace came from many offenses to justification” (Romans 5:16).

Therefore, if these people happen to find an infant who was not conceived from the desire of that one man, let them say that this infant is not subject to that condemnation and does not need to be freed from it through Christ’s grace.

For what is “from one offense to condemnation” except the offense by which Adam sinned? And what is “from many offenses to justification” except that Christ’s grace not only removes that one offense by which infants born from that one man are bound, but also removes the many offenses that people add to their evil condition when they grow up and acquire wicked habits?

Yet he says that even that one offense by which the carnal offspring descending from the first man is bound is sufficient for condemnation. Therefore the baptism of infants is not superfluous: those who are bound by generation to that condemnation are released from the same condemnation through regeneration.

For just as no human being is found who is carnally generated apart from Adam,

[Note: Bad., Am., and Er. read: “are freed through regeneration. And just as no human being is found who is released from that same condemnation, so no human being is found,” and so forth.]

so no human being is found who is spiritually regenerated apart from Christ.

Carnal generation is subject to that one offense and to its condemnation; spiritual regeneration, however, causes not only that one offense—for which infants are baptized—but also the many offenses that people add, by living wickedly, to that condition in which they were born, to be abolished.

Therefore he continues and says:

> “For if, because of one man’s offense, death reigned through that one man, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the gift of righteousness reign in life through the one Jesus Christ. Therefore, just as through one offense condemnation came upon all human beings, so through one act of righteousness justification leading to life came upon all human beings. For just as through the disobedience of one man the many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:12–19).

## 12

What will they say in response to these things? Or what remains for them except to maintain that the Apostle was mistaken? The chosen vessel, the teacher of the nations, the trumpet of Christ, cries out, “Judgment from one [offense] unto condemnation”; and these men protest, asserting that infants—whom they admit derive their lineage from that one man of whom he speaks—do not go into condemnation, even if they have not been baptized in Christ.

“Judgment,” he says, “from one unto condemnation.” What does “from one” mean, except “from one offense”? For he continues: “But the gift is from many offenses unto justification.” Therefore judgment derives from one offense unto condemnation, whereas grace derives from many offenses unto justification.

Accordingly, if they do not dare resist the Apostle, let them explain to us why judgment derives from one offense unto condemnation, when people who are to be condemned come to judgment because of many offenses. Or if they think that it was said in this way because the beginning of sin was made by Adam, whom the others imitated, so that they were drawn from that one offense into judgment and condemnation—those who, by imitation, committed many sins—why was the same not said about grace and justification? Why did he not likewise say, “And grace is from one offense unto justification”?

For just as many offenses of human beings are found between that one offense which they imitated and the judgment by which they are punished—for they came from one offense to many, so that they might be led from many offenses to judgment and condemnation—so those same many offenses lie between that one offense itself, by imitation of which they were committed, and the grace by which they are forgiven. For they came from that one offense to many, so that they might come from many offenses to grace and justification.

Since, therefore, in both cases—that is, in judgment and in grace—the same principle applies with regard to one and many offenses, let these men tell us why he said that judgment derives from one offense unto condemnation, but grace from many offenses unto justification. Or let them accept that it was said in this way because two men are established in this matter: Adam, from whom carnal generation proceeds, and Christ, from whom spiritual regeneration proceeds.

But because the one is merely man, whereas the other is both God and man, regeneration does not release only one offense, namely the offense that comes from Adam, in the same way that generation binds us to that one offense. For that generation is sufficiently condemned by the connection with one offense; whatever people subsequently add by their evil works does not belong to that generation, but to human conduct. This regeneration, however, is not sufficient merely to release the offense that is drawn from Adam; it must also release whatever is subsequently added through the wicked works of human conduct. Therefore: judgment is from one offense unto condemnation, but grace is from many offenses unto justification.

## 13

For “if, because of one offense, death reigned through one”—from which offense infants are cleansed through Baptism—“much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and righteousness reign in life through the one Jesus Christ.” Much more, certainly, will they reign in life, because eternal life will be their kingdom, whereas death passes through them temporally and will not reign forever.

**Note [Col. 0680]:** One of the Vatican manuscripts reads, “because eternal life will be the kingdom.”

“Therefore, just as through one offense there came condemnation to all people”—from which condemnation infants are to be delivered through the sacrament of Baptism—“so through one act of justification there came justification of life to all people.” Here too he said “all,” and there he said “all”; not because all people come to the grace of justification in Christ, since so many, alienated from it, die eternally, but because all who are reborn unto justification are reborn only through Christ, just as all who are born into condemnation are born only through Adam.

For no one exists in that generation apart from Adam, and no one exists in this regeneration apart from Christ. Therefore “all” and “all”; yet he later calls those same “all” “many,” adding: “For just as through the disobedience of one man the many were constituted sinners, so also through the obedience of one man the many will be constituted righteous.” Who are these “many,” except those whom he had just called “all”?

## 14

See how he commends “one and one”—that is, Adam and Christ—the former unto condemnation and the latter unto justification, although Christ came in the flesh so long after Adam. This is so that we may know that even the ancient righteous, whoever they may have been, were delivered only through the same faith by which we too are delivered: namely, faith in the incarnation of Christ, which was foretold to them just as it is announced as accomplished to us.

For this reason he calls Christ a man, although he is also God, so that no one might suppose that the ancient righteous could have been delivered through Christ as God alone—that is, through the Word who was in the beginning—and not also through faith in his incarnation, by which Christ is also called man.

This statement cannot be overturned. Elsewhere he says of it: “Through one man came death, and through one man the resurrection of the dead. For just as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive” (1 Cor. 15:21). Certainly he is speaking of the resurrection of the righteous, where there is eternal life, not of the resurrection of the wicked, where there will be eternal death. Therefore he says, “they will be made alive,” because the others will be condemned.

For this reason, even in the ancient sacraments, circumcision was commanded to be performed on infants on the eighth day (Lev. 12:3), because Christ—in whom the stripping away of carnal sin takes place, which circumcision signifies—rose on the Lord’s Day, which is the eighth day after the seventh day, the Sabbath.

This, then, was also the faith of the ancient righteous. Hence the Apostle says: “But possessing the same spirit of faith, according to what is written, ‘I believed, and therefore I spoke’; we also believe, and therefore we speak” (2 Cor. 4:13). He would not have said “the same spirit of faith” unless he were also reminding us that the ancient righteous possessed that very spirit of faith—that is, faith in the incarnation of Christ.

But because what was to come was foretold to them, whereas what has already happened is announced to us; and because what is revealed in the time of the New Testament was veiled in the time of the Old Testament, its sacraments were varied, so that some belonged to the Old Testament and others to the New. The faith itself, however, is not varied but one, because “just as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive.”

## 15

But when he adds to the words we were discussing, “The law entered in beside, so that the offense might abound,” this no longer pertains to that offense which is drawn from Adam, about which he had said above, “Death reigned through one.”

By “law” we may understand either the natural law, which appears in those stages of life when people are already able to use reason, or the written law, which was given through Moses. For even the written law could not give life or free people from the law of sin and death, which was drawn from Adam; rather, it increased transgressions. “Where there is no law,” the same Apostle says, “there is no transgression” (Rom. 4:15).

Accordingly, because there is also a law written naturally in the reasoning of a human being who already exercises free choice—a law written on the heart, by which each person is warned not to do to another what he does not wish to suffer himself—all are transgressors according to this law, even those who did not receive the law given through Moses. Of them it is written in the Psalm: “All the sinners of the earth have been regarded as transgressors” (Ps. 118:119).

For not all the sinners of the earth transgressed the law given through Moses; nevertheless, unless they had transgressed some law, they would not be called transgressors. “Where there is no law, there is no transgression.”

Having therefore transgressed the law given in paradise, a human being is born from Adam with the law of sin and death, concerning which it is said: “I see another law in my members, opposing the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin which is in my members” (Rom. 7:23). Yet unless this law is later strengthened by evil habit, it is more easily conquered—though not without the grace of God.

When the other law is transgressed, the law that exists in the exercise of the reason of the rational soul at the stage of life when a person already uses reason, all the sinners of the earth become transgressors. But when even the law given through Moses is transgressed, the offense abounds much more.

“For if a law had been given that could give life, righteousness would truly be from the law. But Scripture confined all things under sin, so that the promise might be given to believers through faith in Jesus Christ.” If you recognize these words, they are apostolic.

Concerning this law he says again: “The law was established because of transgressions until the offspring should come to whom the promise was made, ordained through angels in the hand of a mediator” (Gal. 3:19–21).

**Note [Col. 0681]:** The Cistercian manuscript reads *dispositum* (“ordained”).

He is commending Christ, through whose grace all are saved: infants, from the law of sin and death with which we were born; adults, who, by using the power of their will badly, transgressed the natural law of reason itself; and those who received the law given through Moses and, by transgressing it, were killed by the letter.

But when a person also transgresses the evangelical commandments, let him be regarded as a man four days dead; yet even then one must not despair of him because of the grace of Christ, who did not speak softly but cried out with a loud voice: “Lazarus, come forth!” (John 11:43).

## [Col. 0682] 16

The law, then, entered in so that the offense might abound: whether when people neglect what God commands, or when, trusting in their own strength, they do not seek the help of grace and add pride to weakness.

But when, through divine calling, they understand why they ought to groan, and invoke the one in whom they rightly believe, saying, “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy” (Ps. 50:1); and, “I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” (Ps. 40:5); and, “In your righteousness give me life” (Ps. 30:2); and, “Remove from me the way of iniquity, and have mercy on me according to your law” (Ps. 118:29); and, “Let not the foot of pride come against me, and let not the hand of sinners move me” (Ps. 35:12); and, “Direct my steps according to your word, and let no iniquity rule over me” (Ps. 118:133)—“for the steps of a man are directed by the Lord, and he wills his way” (Ps. 36:23)—and many other such prayers, which were written for this reason: to remind us that, in order to fulfill what is commanded us, we must seek help from the one who commands us—

when, therefore, a person stretches himself toward God and groans in this way, what follows will come to pass: “Where the offense abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. 5:20); and, “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7:47). The love of God is poured into the heart, from which the fulfillment of the law comes—not through the power of the will that is in us, but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

That man knew the Law who said: “I delight in the law of God according to the inner man”; yet he added: “But I see another law in my members opposing the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin which is in my members. Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

Why did he not instead say, “Through my free will,” except because freedom without grace is not freedom but defiance?

## 17

After the Apostle had said, “The law entered in so that the offense might abound; but where the offense abounded, grace abounded all the more,” he continued by adding: “So that, just as sin reigned in death, so also grace might reign through righteousness unto eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

Now, when he said, “so that, just as sin reigned in death,” he did not say “through one man,” or “through the first man,” or “through Adam,” because he had already said, “The law entered in so that the offense might abound.” This abundance of offense does not pertain to the propagation of the first man, but to the transgression of human conduct, which was added, in the later stages of life, to that one offense by which infants alone are held bound.

But because the Savior’s grace is also able to release all of this—even what does not pertain to the origin of that one offense—therefore, after saying, “so also grace might reign through righteousness unto eternal life,” he added, “through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

## 18

Therefore, let no arguments brought forward against these apostolic words prevent infants from attaining the salvation that is in Christ Jesus our Lord. Indeed, we ought to speak on their behalf all the more because they cannot speak for themselves.

“Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death; and so it passed into all people, in whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12). Just as infants cannot be free from that one man, so they cannot be free from that sin, unless they are released from its guilt through Christ’s Baptism.

“For until the law, sin was in the world.” This was not said because sin was in no one thereafter, but because what could be removed only by the Spirit of grace could not be removed through the letter of the law.

Thus, lest anyone, trusting in his own strength—not, I say, in the strength of his will, but rather in his vanity—should think that the law could suffice through free choice and should mock the grace of Christ, the Apostle says: “For until the law, sin was in the world; but sin was not reckoned when there was no law.”

He did not say, “It was not there,” but “it was not reckoned,” because there was no law by which it might be exposed and demonstrated—whether the law of reason in the infant or the law of the letter in the people.

**Note [Col. 0683]:** Lov. reads *imputabatur* (“was imputed”); but Bad., Am., Er., and most manuscripts read *deputabatur* (“was reckoned”), that is, “it was not thought to be sin,” as he says in *On Merit and the Forgiveness of Sins*, book 1, chapter 10.

## 19

“But death reigned,” he says, “from Adam to Moses,” because even the law given through Moses could not remove the reign of death, which only the grace of Christ removed.

Now observe over whom it reigned: “even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression.” Death therefore reigned even over those who did not sin. But why it reigned he shows when he says, “in the likeness of Adam’s transgression.”

This is the better interpretation of these words: after saying that death reigned over those who did not sin, he adds—as though reminding us why it reigned over those who did not sin—“in the likeness of Adam’s transgression,” that is, because the likeness of Adam’s transgression was present in their members.

The passage may also be understood in this way: death reigned from Adam to Moses even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, because, once they had been born, they did not yet use the reason that Adam used when he sinned, nor had they received the commandment that he transgressed, but were held bound solely by original fault. Through this fault the dominion of death holds them, except for those who, reborn by Christ’s grace, belong to his kingdom.

**Note [Col. 0683]:** Nearly all manuscripts read *renovata* (“renewed”) instead of *renata* (“reborn”). For temporal death, although it too was propagated from original sin, kills the body in them but does not drag the soul into punishment. It is there that he wished the reign of death to be understood: so that the soul reborn by grace would no longer die into Gehenna—that is, would not be alienated from or separated from the life of God.

Temporal death of the body, however, is left even in those redeemed by Christ’s death, for the time being, as an exercise of faith and a struggle in the present contest, in which the martyrs also contended. It too will be consumed in the renewal of the body promised by the resurrection. For there death will be utterly swallowed up in victory (1 Cor. 15:54), whereas now the grace of Christ removes its dominion, so that it does not drag the souls of his people into the punishments of Tartarus.

Some manuscripts do not read, “over those who did not sin,” but rather, “over those who sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression.” By these words, however, this interpretation is in no way removed. For according to this they are understood to have sinned “in the likeness of Adam’s transgression,” in accordance with what was said above: “in whom all sinned.”

Nevertheless, the Greek manuscripts from which Scripture was translated into Latin have, for the most part, the reading we have stated.

## 20

As for what he added about Adam, “who is a type of the one to come,” this too is not understood in only one way.

Either Adam is a type of Christ by contrast, so that just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ; and just as through his disobedience the many were constituted sinners, so through Christ’s obedience the many will be constituted righteous.

Or he called Adam “a type of the one to come” because Adam himself inflicted upon his descendants the type or pattern of death.

The former interpretation is better: Adam is understood to be a type by contrast, a contrast that the Apostle strongly emphasizes.

Finally, lest these contrary patterns be thought entirely equal in every respect, he adds: “But the gift is not like the offense. For if the many died through the offense of one, much more will the grace of God and the gift in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ abound unto the many.””

This is to be understood not as “among more people,” since the wicked who will be condemned are more numerous, but as “abound all the more”: the pattern of death from Adam has temporal force in those who are redeemed through Christ, whereas the pattern of life through Christ will have eternal force.

“Therefore,” he says, “although Adam is a type of the one to come by contrast, Christ nevertheless provides more for those who are regenerated than Adam harmed those whom he generated.”

“And the gift is not like what happened through one sin”—Bad., Er., and the Cistercian manuscript read, “through one who sinned,” corresponding to the Greek *di’ henos hamartēsantos* (δι’ ἑνὸς ἁμαρτήσαντος, “through one who sinned”); Lov. likewise reads this in book 1 of *On the Merits of Sinners*, chapter 12—“for judgment indeed came from one offense unto condemnation, but grace from many offenses unto justification.”

He says that the pattern is not equal in this respect alone: Adam harmed temporally those whom Christ redeemed eternally. It is also unequal because, through Adam’s one offense, his descendants are handed over to condemnation unless they are redeemed by Christ; whereas Christ’s redemption also dissolves the many offenses that the abundance of transgressive wickedness added to that one offense. We have discussed this above.

## 21

If you wish to live for Christ and in Christ, do not yield to anyone who opposes these words of the Apostle and a sound understanding.

For if, as they say, the Apostle mentioned these matters so that we might understand sinners to belong to the first man because we did not draw sin from him by being born, but sin by imitating him, then he ought rather to have named the devil. The devil was the first to sin, and the human race derived no propagation of substance from him; it followed him only by imitation. Hence he is called the father of the wicked, just as Abraham is called our father because of the imitation of faith, not because of the origin of the flesh (John 8:38).

For this reason it is said of the devil: “But those who are on his side imitate him” (Wis. 2:25). Moreover, if the Apostle mentioned the first man here because he was the first human sinner, so that he said all human beings belonged to him as sinners by imitation, why did he not name the holy Abel, who was the first righteous human being, so that all the righteous might belong to him through imitation of righteousness?

But he named Adam, and set no one against him except Christ, because just as that man corrupted his posterity by his offense, so that God-man saved his inheritance by his righteousness: the former by transmitting the uncleanness of the flesh, which the impious devil could not do; the latter by giving the grace of the Spirit, which righteous Abel could not give.

## 22

We have said many things about these questions in other short works of ours and in ecclesiastical sermons, since there were also among us certain people who, wherever they could, scattered the novel seeds of this error of theirs. The Lord’s mercy healed some of them from that plague through the ministry of myself and our brothers.

Nevertheless, I think that some are still not lacking here, especially around Carthage. They now mutter secretly, fearing the Church’s deeply founded faith. For one of them, named Celestius, had already begun to insinuate himself into the honor of the presbyterate in the church of that same city. But through the most faithful freedom of the brethren, he was brought to episcopal judgment because of these very arguments against the grace of Christ.

**Note [Col. 0685]:** Celestius devoted so much effort and zeal to spreading the teaching of Pelagius that the followers of this heresy were also called Celestians, according to Augustine in *On Heresies*, chapter 88. Nor are they recorded as having been condemned by the Council of Ephesus in 431 under any other name. He was first brought to episcopal judgment at Carthage toward the end of 411 or at the beginning of 412, as is understood from a letter of another Council of Carthage held in 416, in which Innocent is informed that judgment had already been rendered there concerning Celestius “nearly five years earlier.” What was then brought against him by the deacon Paulinus is reported by Augustine in *On Original Sin*, chapters 3 and 4, and especially in *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chapter 11, where he writes that the following propositions were found in Celestius’s teaching:

1. Adam was created mortal and would have died whether he sinned or did not sin.
2. Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone and not the human race.
3. The law leads to the kingdom in the same way as the Gospel.
4. Before Christ’s coming there were people without sin.
5. Newly born infants are in the same condition in which Adam was before his transgression.
6. The whole human race neither dies through Adam’s death or transgression nor rises through Christ’s resurrection.

Augustine says that Aurelius and the bishops assembled with him condemned all these propositions. He also says that the proceedings, which had been completed in his absence, were later reviewed by him after he came to Carthage.

Nevertheless, Celestius was compelled to confess that redemption was necessary even for infants who were to be baptized. Although he was unwilling to say anything more explicit about original sin, by the very term “redemption” he nevertheless committed himself substantially. From what, after all, would they need to be redeemed except from the power of the devil—a power under which they could not be unless bound by the obligation of original sin? And by what price are they redeemed except by the blood of Christ, concerning which it is most clearly written that it was poured out for the remission of sins (Matt. 26:28)?

But because he departed more convicted and detested by the Church than corrected and reconciled, I feared that he himself might be the one who is trying to disturb your faith. For that reason I thought his name should be mentioned.

But whether it is he himself or others who share his error—for there are more of them than we might hope, and when they are not refuted they seduce others into their sect as well, multiplying until I do not know where they will break out—we nevertheless prefer that they be healed within the structure of the Church rather than cut away from its body as incurable members, if necessity itself permits this.

For it must be feared that more parts may decay while the decayed are spared. Yet the mercy of our Lord is powerful, and may it rather free them from this plague. Without doubt it will do so if they faithfully attend to and hold fast what is written: “Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved” (Joel 2:32).

# CHAPTER IV

## 23

Now hear a little concerning the rich, which, as your letter continues, must be examined.

For you stated that they say this: “A rich person who remains in his riches cannot enter the kingdom of God unless he has sold everything he possesses, and it does him no good if he happens to fulfill the commandments from those riches.”

Our fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who departed from this life so long ago, escaped these men’s arguments. All of them possessed no small wealth, as the most faithful Scripture testifies. Yet the one who became poor for our sake, although he was truly rich, foretold with the most truthful promise that many would come from east and west and recline in the kingdom of heaven not above or outside them, but together with them (Matt. 8:11).

And although the proud rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day died and was tormented in the underworld, if he had shown mercy to the poor man covered with sores who lay despised before his gate, he too would have deserved mercy.

And if that poor man’s merit had been poverty rather than righteousness, he certainly would not have been carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom, since Abraham had been rich in this life. But in order to show us that poverty was not in itself divinely honored in the one, nor riches condemned in the other, but that piety in the one and impiety in the other brought about their respective ends, the bosom of the rich man received the pious poor man, while fiery torment received the impious rich man (Luke 16:19–22).

Indeed, while he lived here as a rich man, he possessed his riches in such a way, and valued them so little in comparison with God’s commandments, that he was unwilling to offend God, who commanded him, even by the sacrifice of his own son—although he hoped and desired that son to be the heir of his riches (Gen. 22:1–10).

## 24

They certainly say that the reason the ancient fathers did not sell everything they possessed and give it to the poor was that the Lord had not commanded this of them. For the New Testament had not yet been revealed, which could not take place except in the fullness of time; nor had their virtue been revealed, although God knew that they could very easily do this because of the virtue in their hearts. He bore such distinguished testimony to them that, although he is the God of all the saints, he deigned to speak of them as his chief friends: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob; this is my name forever” (Exod. 3:15).

But after the great mystery of piety had been manifested in the flesh (1 Tim. 3:16), and the coming of Christ had dawned for the calling of all nations—the Christ in whom those fathers too had believed, but whose olive of this faith, destined to be manifested in its own time, they preserved as though in the root of the tree of which the Apostle speaks (Rom. 11:17)—it was said to the rich man: “Go, sell everything you possess, give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21).

## 25

If they say this, they seem to be saying something reasonable. But let them hear everything and attend to everything. Let them not open their ears on one side and become deaf on the other.

To whom did the Lord give these commands? Certainly to the rich man who was seeking to receive advice about obtaining eternal life. For he had said to the Lord: “What shall I do to obtain eternal life?”

But the Lord did not answer him, “If you wish to come to life, go, sell everything you possess.” Rather, he said, “If you wish to come to life, keep the commandments.”

When the young man said that, according to the Lord’s reminder from the Law, he had kept these commandments, and asked what he still lacked, he received the answer: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you possess and give to the poor.”

And lest he think that in this way he would lose the things he loved so greatly, the Lord added: “And you will have treasure in heaven.” Then he added: “And come, follow me,” so that no one might think that doing these things would benefit him if he did not follow Christ.

But that man departed sad. Consider how he had kept those commandments of the Law. I think he had answered that he had kept them with greater arrogance than truth.

Nevertheless, the good Teacher distinguished the commandments of the Law from this higher perfection. There he said, “If you wish to come to life, keep the commandments”; here, “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you possess,” and so forth.

Why, then, do we deny that rich people, although they fall short of that perfection, may nevertheless come to life if they keep the commandments, give so that it may be given to them, and forgive so that they may be forgiven (Luke 6:37–38)?

## 26

For we believe that the Apostle Paul was a minister of the New Testament when, writing to Timothy, he said:

“Command the rich of this world not to be high-minded, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who provides us abundantly with all things for enjoyment. Let them do good, let them be rich in good works, let them give readily, let them share, storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of eternal life” (1 Tim. 6:17–19).

This is the life of which it was also said to that young man, “If you wish to come to life.” I think that, by giving these commands, the Apostle was instructing the rich, not deceiving them.

He did not say, “Command the rich of this world to sell everything they possess, give it to the poor, and follow the Lord.” Rather, he said, “not to be high-minded, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches.”

It was that pride that led the rich man, who despised the righteous poor man lying before his gate, and that hope in the uncertainty of riches, by which he considered himself blessed because of his purple, fine linen, and splendid feasts—not riches themselves—that brought him to the torments of the underworld.

**Note [Col. 0687]:** Bad., Am., Er., and the Vatican manuscripts read *veram vitam* (“true life”); the same reading is found below in all editions.

## 27

Or perhaps because the Lord added and said, “Amen, I say to you, a rich man will enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty”; and again, “I say to you, it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven,” these men think that a rich person cannot enter the kingdom of heaven even if he does what the Apostle wrote must be commanded to the rich?

What, then, is the case? Is the Apostle speaking against the Lord, or do these men not know what they are saying? Let the Christian choose which of these he should believe. I think it is better for us to believe that these men do not know what they are saying than that Paul is speaking against the Lord.

Moreover, why do they not listen to the Lord himself in what follows, when he says to the disciples, who were distressed at the plight of the rich: “What is impossible for human beings is easy for God”?

## [Col. 0688] 28

“But,” they say, “this was said because it was going to happen that, after hearing the Gospel, the rich would sell their estates, distribute the proceeds to the poor, follow the Lord, and enter the kingdom of heaven; thus what seemed difficult would come to pass.

It was not said so that those who remained in their riches, keeping the Apostle’s commands—that is, not being high-minded and not hoping in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, doing good, giving readily, and sharing with the needy—might take hold of true life. Rather, they too would fulfill these apostolic commands by selling all their possessions.”

## 29

If they say this—and I know that they do say it—they fail first of all to notice how the Lord proclaimed his grace against their doctrine.

For he did not say, “What seems impossible to human beings is easy for human beings if they wish.” Rather, he said, “What is impossible for human beings is easy for God,” showing that when these things are rightly done, they are not accomplished by human power but by God’s grace.

Let these men attend to this. And if they criticize those who glory in their riches, let them themselves beware of trusting in their own strength. For both groups are reproved together in the Psalm: “Those who trust in their own strength, and those who glory in the abundance of their riches” (Ps. 48:7).

Let the rich therefore hear: “What is impossible for human beings is easy for God.” Whether they remain in their riches and do good works from them, or sell them and distribute them among the necessities of the poor, let them enter the kingdom of heaven by attributing their good to God’s grace, not to their own powers.

For what is impossible for human beings is easy not for human beings but for God.

Let these men also hear this. If they have already sold everything they possess and given it to the poor, or are still doing and arranging this, thereby preparing to enter the kingdom of heaven, let them not attribute it to their own strength, but to that same divine grace.

For what is impossible for human beings is easy not for them—for they too are human beings—but for God.

The Apostle says this to them as well: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you both to will and to work according to his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:12–13).

Certainly, they say that they received from the Lord the counsel of perfection concerning the sale of their possessions so that they might follow the Lord, because the words “and come, follow me” were added there. Why, then, do they presume that the good things they do proceed only from their own will, and not listen to the Lord whom they say they follow, when he reproves and testifies: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5)?

## 30

But if the Apostle said, “Command the rich of this world not to be high-minded, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches,” in order that they might sell everything they possess and, distributing the proceeds to the needy, do what follows—give readily, share, and store up for themselves a good foundation for the future—and if he does not believe that they can enter the kingdom of heaven in any other way, then he deceives those whose households he so carefully orders through the soundness of his teaching, warning and commanding what kind of people wives should be to their husbands, husbands to their wives, children to their parents, parents to their children, slaves to their masters, and masters to their slaves.

For how can these duties be carried out without a household and without some family property?

31. Does what the Lord said move them: “Whoever has left everything of his own for my sake will receive a hundredfold in this age and will possess eternal life in the age to come” (Matthew XIX, 29)? To leave is one thing; to sell is another. For among the things he commanded to be left, a wife is also mentioned—yet no human law permits her to be sold, while Christ’s laws do not even permit her to be dismissed, except on account of fornication (ibid., V, 32). What, then, do these commandments mean—for they cannot contradict one another—unless an occasion of necessity sometimes arises in which either the wife must be dismissed or Christ? To mention other cases, suppose the Christian husband displeases his wife, and she proposes either divorce from him or separation from Christ. What should he choose in such a case except Christ, and whom should he laudably leave for Christ’s sake except his wife? For the Lord commanded both Christian spouses that neither should dismiss the other, except on account of fornication.

But where one of them is an unbeliever, the Apostle’s counsel should be observed: “If the unbeliever consents to live with the believing husband, the husband should not dismiss his wife. Likewise, if the believing wife’s husband consents to live with her.” But if the unbeliever departs, he says, “let him depart: for the brother or sister is not subject to servitude in such circumstances” (I Corinthians VII, 12, 15). That is, if the unbeliever does not wish to remain with the believing spouse, let the believer recognize his or her freedom, and not consider himself or herself so subject to servitude that, in order not to lose an unbelieving spouse, he or she would abandon the faith itself.

32. The same is to be understood of sons and parents, and the same of brothers and sisters: all are to be left for Christ’s sake when the condition is proposed that one must leave Christ in order to keep them. The same, then, is to be understood here of a house and fields, and of those possessions held by pecuniary right. For concerning these also he does not say, “Whoever sells, for my sake, whatever it is lawful to sell,” but, “Whoever leaves.” It can happen that some authority says to a Christian: “Either you will not be a Christian, or, if you wish to remain so, you will have no house or possessions.” Then even those rich people who had resolved to remain in possession of their riches in such a way as to earn God’s favor by good works from them should leave these things for Christ’s sake rather than leave Christ for the sake of these things. Thus they may receive in this age a hundredfold—the perfection of that number signifying everything—for “the whole world is the wealth of the faithful person,” and in this way they become “as having nothing, yet possessing everything” (II Corinthians VI, 10)—and in the age to come possess eternal life, lest, by leaving Christ for these things, they be hurled into eternal death.

33.
