Under this law and condition, therefore, not only those who, through the excellence of their minds, have received the counsel of perfection—to distribute what they sell to the poor and, with shoulders freed from every burden of this age, to carry Christ’s light burden—but also anyone weaker and less suited to that glorious perfection, who nevertheless remembers that he is truly a Christian, when he hears it proposed that unless he leaves all these things he will be leaving Christ, will grasp instead “the tower of strength in the presence of the enemy” (Psalm LX, 4). For when he was building it upon his faith, he counted the cost by which it could be completed (Luke XIV, 28). That is, he approached the faith with the intention of renouncing this age not merely in words; for “if he bought something, it was as though he did not possess it, and if he used this world, it was as though he did not use it” (I Corinthians VII, 30–31), placing his hope not in the uncertainty of riches but in the living God.

34. For since everyone who renounces this age undoubtedly renounces all that belongs to it, so that he may be Christ’s disciple—for after giving the comparisons concerning the expense required for building a tower and preparing for war against another king, he added: “Whoever does not renounce all that is his cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV, 33)—he certainly renounces his riches also, if he possesses any. Either he does so by not loving them at all, distributing them wholly to those in need and freeing himself from burdens that are superfluous; or he does so by loving Christ more, transferring his hope from them to him, and using them in such a way that, readily giving and sharing, he stores up treasure in heaven. He must be prepared to leave these things, just as he would leave parents, children, brothers, and wife, if such a condition were imposed that he could not possess them without leaving Christ.

For if he renounces this age in any other manner when he approaches the sacrament of faith, he does what blessed Cyprian deplores concerning the fallen, saying: “Renouncing the age in words alone, and not in deeds.” It is of such a person that this is said, when temptation comes and he fears losing these things more than denying Christ: “Behold the man who began to build and was unable to finish.” He is also the one who, while his adversary was still far away, sent ambassadors to seek peace; that is, while temptation had not yet afflicted him but was still threatening and looming over him, he agreed to abandon and deny Christ so as not to be deprived of what he loved more. And there are many such people who even think that the Christian religion ought to support them in increasing their wealth and multiplying their earthly pleasures.

35. Yet those rich Christians are not of this kind who, although they possess these things, are not so possessed by them that they place them before Christ; for with a truthful heart they have renounced the age, so that they place no hope in such things. They instruct their wives and children and entire households with sound discipline to hold fast to the Christian religion. Their houses, burning with hospitality, receive the righteous in the name of the righteous, so that they may receive the reward of the righteous (Matthew X, 41). They break their bread for the hungry, clothe the naked, and redeem the captive (Isaiah LVIII, 7; Matthew XXV, 35–36); they store up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of the true life.

And if, perhaps, financial losses must be endured for the faith of Christ, they hate their riches. If this world threatens bereavement or separation from their own for Christ’s sake, they hate parents, brothers, children, and wives. Finally, if they must negotiate even concerning the life of this body with the adversary, lest Christ, once abandoned, abandon them, they hate even their own life. For concerning all these things they have received the command that otherwise they cannot be Christ’s disciples (Luke XIV, 26–27).

36. Yet because they have been commanded to hate, for Christ’s sake, even their own lives, this does not mean that they should sell them or pour them out by laying violent hands upon themselves. Rather, they are prepared to lose them by dying for Christ’s name, lest, though dead, they live by denying Christ. Likewise, although they were not prepared to sell their riches when Christ admonished them, they ought to be prepared to lose them for Christ, lest they perish with them after Christ has been lost.

We have examples of this in rich men and women of the highest distinction, raised to the glory of martyrdom. Thus many whom it had displeased to be perfected beforehand by selling their possessions were suddenly perfected by imitating Christ’s passion; and those who had used their riches to indulge some weakness of flesh and blood suddenly fought against sin for the faith, even unto bloodshed.

But those who have not received the crown of martyrdom, nor received that great and glorious counsel of perfection concerning the sale of their possessions, and yet, free from damnable crimes, have fed the hungry Christ, given drink to the thirsty, clothed the naked, and welcomed the stranger, will not indeed sit with Christ to judge in exalted places; but they will stand at his right hand to be judged mercifully (Matthew XXV, 34–40). “Blessed are the merciful, for God will show mercy to them” (ibid., V, 7). “Judgment without mercy will be upon the one who has shown no mercy; but mercy triumphs over judgment” (James II, 13).

37. Therefore let such people cease speaking against the Scriptures, and in their exhortations to greater things let them stir people up in such a way that they do not condemn lesser things. Can they not persuade people to holy virginity by exhorting them in another way, unless they condemn the marriage bond, when the Apostle teaches that “each person has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that” (I Corinthians VII, 7)?

Let them therefore walk the way of perfection, selling all their possessions and distributing them mercifully. But if they are truly Christ’s poor, and gather not for themselves but for Christ, why do they punish his weaker members before they have received judicial seats? For if they are to be of the kind to whom the Lord says, “You will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew XIX, 28), and of whom the Apostle says, “Do you not know that we will judge angels?” (I Corinthians VI, 3), let them rather prepare themselves to receive not criminal but religious rich people into eternal dwellings—people by whom they have been made friends “through the mammon of unrighteousness” (Luke XVI, 9).

For I think that some of those who babble these things shamelessly and imprudently are supported in their necessities by rich and devout Christians. The Church has, in a certain sense, her soldiers and, in another sense, her provincials. Hence the Apostle says, “Whoever serves as a soldier at his own expense?” She also has a vineyard and cultivators; she has a flock and shepherds. Hence he goes on to say, “Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Who tends a flock and does not receive milk from the flock?” (I Corinthians IX, 7).

Although to argue such things as these people argue is not to serve as a soldier but to rebel; not to plant a vineyard but to uproot one; not to gather those who are to be fed but to separate from the flock those who are to be destroyed.

[Col. 0692] 38. Just as those who are fed and clothed by the religious services of the rich—for they receive nothing for their necessities except from those who sell their possessions—are nevertheless not judged and condemned by the more excellent members of Christ, who, with the greater virtue highly commended by the Apostle, support themselves by the work of their own hands (Acts XX, 34), so these people ought not to condemn Christians of lesser merit, by whose resources they are supported—*[Note: [Col. 0692] The editions read “works” (*operibus*), in place of which one Vatican manuscript substitutes “resources” (*opibus*).]*—rather, by living and teaching rightly, they should say to them: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your material things?” (I Corinthians IX, 11).

Indeed, the servants of God who live by selling the honest work of their hands condemn these people with far less impudence, since they receive nothing from them, than these people condemn those from whose resources they live, because of some bodily weakness that prevents them from working with their hands.

39. I who write this have ardently loved the perfection of which the Lord spoke when he said to the rich young man, “Go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matthew XIX, 21), and, with the assistance of his grace rather than my own strength, I acted accordingly. Nor, because I was not rich, will it therefore be counted against me to a lesser degree; for the Apostles themselves, who did this first, were not rich. But the person who leaves both what he possesses and what he desires to possess leaves the whole world.

How far I have progressed along this path of perfection I know better than any other human being; but God knows it better than I do. To this purpose I exhort others with all the strength I can, and in the Lord’s name I have companions to whom this has been commended through my ministry. Yet this is so only if sound doctrine is held above all, and we do not judge those who do not do these things through empty obstinacy, saying that it benefits them nothing that they live chastely, though in marriage; that they govern their houses and households as Christians; and that through works of mercy they store up treasure for themselves in the future. Otherwise, in arguing such things, we may be found not interpreters of the holy Scriptures but their accusers.

I have mentioned this because, when these people are forbidden to say such things by those who have not undertaken this counsel of the Lord, they reply that the others are unwilling to discuss such matters because they favor their own vices and refuse to fulfill the Lord’s commandments. This is as though—even leaving aside those who, though weaker, nevertheless use their riches religiously—even those who use them badly, being greedy and avaricious and fixing their hearts of clay upon an earthly treasure, must necessarily be carried by the Church to the end, just as those bad fish were carried in the nets to the shore (ibid., XIII, 47–48). Such people are more tolerable within her than those who, by speaking and spreading such things, want to appear great because they have sold their riches or however small their patrimonies may be in obedience to the Lord’s command, and who therefore attempt by this unsound teaching to disturb and overthrow his inheritance, which is extended and spread to the ends of the earth.

## CHAPTER V

40. Since on this occasion I have already said briefly what I also think about Christ’s Church in this age—that is, that she must carry both the good and the wicked to the end of this age, since you also asked about this among your questions—I shall finally bring this lengthy letter to a conclusion.

Avoid oaths as much as you can. It is better not to swear even what is true than, through the habit of swearing, to fall often into perjury and always to approach it. But those people, as far as I have heard some of them, have no idea at all what it means to swear. They think they are not swearing when they have in their mouths, “God knows” (II Corinthians XII, 2), and “God is my witness” (Romans I, 9; Philippians I, 8), and “I call God as witness upon my soul” (II Corinthians I, 23), because the phrase “by God” is not used and because such expressions are found in the Apostle Paul.

Yet even there an expression has been found against them which they admit is an oath—*[Note: [Col. 0693] The Louvain edition and most manuscripts read “do not admit”; Bad., Am., Er., and the Cistercian manuscript lack the negation.]*—where the Apostle says: “I die daily, by your glory, brothers, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord” (I Corinthians XV, 31). For in the Greek manuscripts this is plainly found to be an oath, lest anyone in the Latin language understand “by your glory” in the same way as “by my coming again to you,” and many similar expressions in which something is said to be “by” another thing without being an oath.

But because the Apostle, a man most steadfast in truth, swore in his writings, an oath should not therefore become a game for us. Much safer for us, as I have said, is never to swear, so that “Yes, yes; no, no” may be in our mouths, as the Lord commands (Matthew V, 37). This is not because it is a sin to swear truly, but because it is a very grave sin to swear falsely; and the person accustomed to swearing falls into it more quickly.

41. You have received what seems to me the case. Let better people explain these matters better—not those whose opinion I already know must be rejected, but others who are genuinely able to do so. For I am more ready to speak than to teach; and you will confer a great benefit on me if you do not let me remain unaware of what the holy brothers there say against the empty talk of these people.

May you live rightly and faithfully in the Lord, my most beloved son.

## LETTER CLVIII

*[Note: It was collated against the Vatican codex, in which it is found in only one manuscript, and against Lovaniensis.]*

*[Note: Formerly 258; the letter that was 158 is now 139. Written approximately in the year 414.]*

Evodius, bishop of Uzalis, after praising the conduct and blessed death of a certain young man, and recounting apparitions of him and of other dead persons, asks whether the soul, released through death, is entirely without a body by which it might be carried from place to place. Then he wishes to be instructed about the various ways in which wisdom is spoken of with reference to God and human beings.

To the venerable and dearly beloved lord, brother and fellow priest AUGUSTINE, and to the brothers who are with you, EVODIUS and the brothers who are with me, greetings in the Lord.

1. I claim the debt owed by the letter I sent; and I wanted first to learn the matter about which I asked, and afterward to inquire about this. Listen, if you are willing, to the matter that has made me impatient, so that I might hasten to know it, if possible, in this life.

I had a certain boy, the son of the presbyter Armenius Melonitanus, serving as a notary. He was already plunging himself into the age—for he was serving the proconsul’s legal secretary—but through my humility God rescued him. As is natural at a boy’s age, he was ready and somewhat restless; but as he grew older—for he died in his twenty-second year—he was so adorned by seriousness of character and the guardian of a good life that it is a great pleasure to remember him.

He was skillful with shorthand and very diligent in writing. He had also begun to be devoted to reading, so that he encouraged my slowness by reading at night. For some time he himself read to me during the night, when everything had fallen silent. He did not want to pass over a passage until he understood it; he repeated it a third and fourth time, and did not lay it aside until the answer he sought had become clear to him. I had begun to regard him not as a boy and notary, but as a quite indispensable and delightful friend. His stories gave me pleasure.

2. He also desired what was granted to him: “to depart and be with Christ” (Philippians I, 23). He was ill for sixteen days at his parents’ home, and throughout almost the whole illness he spoke from memory about the Scriptures. But when he began to approach the end of his life, he sang in the hearing of everyone: “My soul longs for and hastens toward the courts of God” (Psalm LXXXIII, 3). After this he sang again: “You have anointed my head with oil; and how glorious is your cup, making me drunk!” (Psalm XXII, 5). He remained occupied with this; he found his delight in this consolation.

Then, when he began to be released, he began to make the sign of the cross on his forehead, moving his hand downward toward his mouth, which he desired to sign, when the inner man, renewed day by day, had already laid aside its house of clay. Such joy came to me that I think he entered my soul after leaving his own body, and there granted me a certain brightness of his presence, because my joy at his liberation and security is beyond telling.

I had indeed shown great concern for him, fearing for his youth. I took care to ask him whether perhaps he had been polluted by contact with a woman. He testified that he was free from this, increasing our joy still further. Thus he was released. We provided a sufficiently honorable funeral, worthy of so great a soul; for three days we praised the Lord with hymns over his tomb, and on the third day we offered the sacraments of redemption.

3. But behold: two days later a respectable widow, Urbica of the Figentes, who said that she had been a widow for twelve years and was a servant of God, saw the following dream.

She saw a certain deacon, who had been freed from the body four years earlier, preparing a palace with servants and maidservants of God—virgins and widows. It was being adorned, and, as the brilliance of the place shone forth, the whole place seemed to be made of silver. When she asked more carefully for whom this was being prepared, the deacon replied that it was being prepared for the boy who had died the day before, the son of the presbyter.

In the same palace, she said, a certain old man in white appeared, ordering two men in white to proceed and carry the body, taken from the tomb, up to heaven. “And when,” she said, “the body had been taken from the tomb and lifted into heaven, branches of roses of virgins—for this is what enclosed virgins are commonly called—rose up from that same tomb.”

4. I have told you what happened. Now kindly hear my question and teach me what I ask. The departure of this soul compels me to inquire into such matters.

While we are in the body, we possess an alert inner sense, proportionate to the energy of our study; and the more studious we have been, the more vigilant and ardent it is. It seems probable that we are still held back by the body as an impediment. Who, however, could recount all that the mind undergoes through the body?

Amid these disturbances and troubles, arising from suggestions, temptations, necessities, and various calamities, the mind does not abandon its strength: it resists and conquers, though sometimes it is conquered. Yet because it remembers itself, it becomes more agile and watchful, aroused by such labors; it breaks the various knots of wickedness and passes on to better things. Your Holiness understands what I mean.

While we are in this life, then, we are hindered by such wretchedness, and yet, as it is written, “we conquer through him who loved us” (Romans VIII, 37). When we leave the body and escape both every burden and agile sin, what are we?

5. First I ask whether there is some body that does not abandon an incorporeal thing—that is, the substance of the soul—when it leaves this earthly body. Perhaps it is one of four kinds: aerial or ethereal, or one of the others. Since the soul is incorporeal, if it is entirely without a body, then all souls are already one.

And where will be the rich man dressed in purple and Lazarus covered with wounds? How will they be distinguished according to their merits, so that one has punishment and the other joy, if one incorporeal soul appears to have arisen from all—assuming, of course, that those things are not meant figuratively? It is certain, however, that things held in places are held by bodies, as that rich man is in the flame and that poor man in Abraham’s bosom (Luke XVI, 19, 22). If there are places, there are bodies, and souls are in bodies; and in the body are punishments or rewards in the consciences.

Whatever this one soul may be, formed from many souls, let it be afflicted and rejoice in one, so that a substance collected from many souls may appear. Or, if this is said of how one incorporeal mind is one thing, while memory, will, and understanding are in it, and all these faculties are incorporeal and possess a fitting share of their functions—*[Note: The Vatican codex has “proportion” instead of “share.”]*—yet none obstructs another, I think it can somehow be answered that some punishments and some rewards accompany a substance gathered from many souls.

6. Or, if this is not so, what prevents each soul, when it is without this solid body, from having another body, so that the soul always animates some body? Or to what does it make its passage, if there is some region to which necessity compels it to go?

For even the angels themselves cannot be said to be many if they are not counted by bodies, as Truth itself says in the Gospel: “I could ask my Father to send me twelve legions of angels” (Matthew XXVI, 53).

Furthermore, it is clear that Samuel was seen in a body when he was summoned at Saul’s request (I Samuel XXVIII, 14); and it is manifest from the Gospel that Moses, whose body was buried, came in a body to the Lord on the mountain (Matthew XVII, 3), when they stood there.

Moreover, in the apocryphal writings and in the secret writings of Moses—which Scripture does not authorize—when he ascended the mountain to die, the power of the body is said to have brought it about that one thing was entrusted to the earth, while another accompanied the attending angel. But I am not sufficiently compelled to prefer the opinion of the apocryphal writings to the matters established above. What is being asked must therefore be examined, and investigated either by authority or by reason.

But it is said that the future resurrection shows that the soul has been entirely without a body. This is not a sufficient objection, since those angels who are invisible and who wished to appear and be seen with bodies—and whatever the nature of those bodies may be, they are fitting for their spirits—nevertheless appeared to Abraham (Genesis XVIII, 2) and to Tobias (Tobit XII, 15).

Thus it can happen that, although this resurrection of the flesh, which is rightly believed to be future, will take place, the soul may nevertheless be restored in such a way that it is found never to have been without some body.

Since the body itself consists of the four elements, it seems to lose one of them, namely the hot element, when it appears to depart from this body. For what is earthly remains, and liquid is not absent; nor is the element of cold matter lacking. Only the hot element is removed from it. Perhaps the soul itself draws this along with it if it passes from place to place. This is what I would say for now concerning the body.

7. It also seems to me that if, while placed in the body, as I have said, the soul uses a vigorous and strenuous concentration of mind, how much more will it be freed, agile, vigorous, ardent, strenuous, and attentive, and become more receptive and better, since it has tasted virtue while placed in the body?

Once the body has been laid aside, the cloud is more thoroughly cleared away; the soul becomes wholly serene, placed in tranquility without temptation. It sees what it desired and embraces what it loved. It may also remember its friends, recognize those whom it had sent on ahead, and recognize those whom it left behind. Perhaps this is so; I do not know—I am seeking to learn.

But I am greatly troubled if the soul itself falls into some kind of sleep, so that it is like one sleeping in the body, as though buried and living only in hope, but otherwise possessing and knowing nothing—especially if it is stirred by no dream. This prospect greatly terrifies me and seems to indicate a soul that has been extinguished.

8. I also ask, if it is found to possess a body, whether it is not also without some sense. Certainly, if, as I think, it cannot be given the need to smell, nor to taste, nor even to touch, I doubt that sight and hearing remain.

For what does it mean that demons are said to hear—not in all those whom they torment, since that too is a question—but also when they appear in their own bodies? As for sight, how do they pass from place to place if they have bodies but lack the guidance of visual perception?

Do you think human souls are not like this when they depart from their bodies: that they possess some body and are not without some sense? What also is the meaning of the fact that many dead people have been seen entering houses in the way they were accustomed to, either by day or by night, by those who were awake and walking about?

I have not heard this only once. Nor do I forget what is usually said to occur during some particular part of the night, in places where bodies have been buried, and especially in basilicas: disturbances and prayers. I do not remember hearing this from only one person. A certain holy presbyter was a witness to such a vision: he saw a multitude of such persons leaving the baptistery in luminous bodies and afterward observed them praying in the middle of the church.

All these things either support our inquiry, or, if they are fables, they are astonishing. Yet I would like to know something about this, because these persons come, visit, and appear, apart from dreams.

9. From this another question arises. I am not concerned merely with the phantasy that an unlearned heart invents for itself; I am speaking of visitations. How did Joseph appear in a dream (Matthew I, 20), and how were many others visited?

Thus, too, our own dead whom we have sent on ahead sometimes come and appear in dreams and speak. I myself remember that Profuturus, Privatus, and Servilius—holy men whom I remember as having gone before us from the monastery—spoke to me, and what they said came to pass. Or, if some better spirit assumes their appearance and visits the mind, let the one to whom all things are naked from the highest neck see to that.

If, therefore, the Lord should deign to speak to Your Holiness by reason concerning all these matters, I beg you to make me a participant in this knowledge. I did not want to pass over this matter either, for perhaps it pertains to my inquiry.

10. The boy in question himself, at the time when he was being released, seems in a certain way to have been escorted on his way.

For his fellow student and fellow reader, with whom he served as a secretary for me, and who had himself been freed from the body eight months earlier, appeared in a dream to one who saw him at that time. When he was asked why he had come, he replied: “I have come to lead this friend of mine.” And so it happened.

Moreover, in the very same house, a man carrying laurel in his hand appeared to an elderly man who was almost awake; something was written on the laurel. After this vision, it was added that, following the boy’s death, his father the presbyter had begun staying in the monastery with the old man Theasius in order to console themselves. But on the third day after the boy’s death, the boy appeared to have entered the monastery and, in a certain dream, was asked by one of the brothers whether he knew that he had died. He said that he knew. He was asked whether he had been received by God. He said that he had, and reported this with great rejoicing.

When he was asked why he had come, he then replied: “I have been sent to bring my father.” The person to whom these things were shown awoke and reported them. The matter reached the ears of Bishop Theasius. He was disturbed and rebuked the one who had spoken, lest the report easily reach the presbyter’s ears and he be troubled by such a message.

What more need be said? Perhaps four days after the visitation, the presbyter was speaking—he had felt a slight fever, but there was no danger, and the physician was absent, though he would have declared that there was absolutely no cause for concern. But when he reclined on his bed, that same presbyter was released.

Nor should I remain silent about this: on the very day on which the boy was released, he asked his father for peace, and asked a third time; at each kiss he said to his father, “Father, let us give thanks to God.” He compelled his father to say it with him, as though exhorting him to depart from this life together with him. For seven days are counted between their deaths.

What is to be made of such great events? Who will be the most faithful teacher of these hidden causes? The heat of my heart pours itself out to you in this time of distress. The providential ordering of the boy’s death and that of his father is clear, because “two sparrows will not fall to the ground without the will of the Father” (Matthew X, 29).

11. That the soul cannot be entirely without every body is shown, I think, by this fact, since God alone is always without every body.

After the soul’s departure, the laying aside of so great a bodily burden shows that it will be more vigilant; for then, freed in action and knowledge from so great a bond, it appears, I think, to be more excellent. All that spiritual rest demonstrates it to be free from every disturbance and error; it does not make it withered, sluggish, torpid, or entangled. It is enough for it to enjoy the very freedom it has obtained when it is without the world and the body.

For you wisely said that the intellect is nourished by this, and that it places its spiritual mouth at the fountain of life, where it possesses the happy and blessed property of its own mind. Once, after his departure, I saw our brother Servilius in a dream, while I was still living in the monastery. He said that we labor through reason to reach understanding, whereas he and others like him remain in the very delight of contemplation.

12. I also ask you to show me in how many ways wisdom is spoken of: how God is called wisdom; how a wise soul is called wisdom; how it is spoken of as light; how Beseleel, who constructed the Tabernacle, or the maker of ointments, is said to possess wisdom; how Solomon’s wisdom is understood; and whether there is any other kind. Also explain how these differ from one another.

And is that one eternal wisdom with the Father to be understood in these degrees, just as the diverse gifts of the Holy Spirit are spoken of—the Spirit who distributes to each person his own gift as he wills? Or, apart from that one wisdom which was not made, were these others made and do they possess their own substance? Or were they produced and received their character from the definition of their work?

I ask many things. May the Lord grant you the grace to discover, the wisdom to dictate, and the speed to write to us. I have written incompetently and crudely; but because you deign to know what I am asking, I entreat you through Christ our Lord to correct me in these matters and teach me what you understand me to desire to know.

## LETTER CLIX

*[Note: Collated against bl. cc. cb. ff. gg. r. sb. vc., two copies of t., three of v., and against Am. Bad. Er. Lov.]*

*[Note: Formerly 100; the letter that was 159 is now 133. Written after the preceding letter.]*

Augustine’s reply to Evodius concerning questions about the soul released from the body and about extraordinary apparitions.

To the most blessed, venerable, and desired lord, my brother and fellow priest EVODIUS, and to the brothers with you, AUGUSTINE and the brothers with me, greetings in the Lord.

1. This brother Barbarus has long been established at Hippo as a servant of God, and is a fervent and devoted hearer of the word of God. He desired letters from us to Your Holiness; in them we commend him to you in the Lord and, through him, offer you the greeting owed to you.

It is an exceedingly laborious task to answer the letters of Your Holiness, in which you have woven together immense questions—even for people at leisure, and much more for those endowed with less ability to discuss matters and less sharpness of understanding than we possess.

Of the two letters of yours in which you gather many great questions, one somehow went astray and, although sought for a long time, could not be found. The other, which was discovered, contains a most delightful commendation of a good and chaste servant of God, describing how the young man departed from this life and by what testimonies of fraternal visions his worth could be made known to you.

Then, on this occasion, you propose and turn over the extremely obscure question concerning the soul: whether it departs from the body with some body by which it can be carried to bodily places or contained in bodily places.

The treatment of this matter, if indeed it can be examined to the point of clarity by people such as we are, requires the most demanding care and labor, and therefore a mind entirely free from other occupations. But if you wish to hear briefly what I think, I believe in no way that the soul leaves the body together with a body.

### 2

As for how those visions and predictions of future things come about, let the person explain it who knows by what power such great things are produced in each soul when it thinks. For we see—and plainly perceive—that innumerable images of many visible things, and of things belonging to the other bodily senses, are produced within it. It makes no difference whether these images are formed in an orderly or confused manner; but since it is evident that they are formed, whoever can explain by what power and how they are formed—and these experiences are certainly daily and continuous—may dare to presume to say something and even to define something about those exceedingly rare visions.

I dare this all the less because I am even less capable of explaining how that which we experience continuously, whether awake or asleep, comes about within us. When I dictated this letter to you, was I not contemplating you in my mind—although you were absent and unaware—and imagining, according to the knowledge of you that I possess, how you might be moved by these words? Yet I could not grasp or investigate how this was happening in my mind. I was nevertheless certain that it was not produced by bodily masses or bodily qualities, although it became very similar to a body. For the moment, accept this as dictated by one who is occupied and in haste.

In the twelfth book of those which I wrote on Genesis this question is treated at length, and the discussion grows out of many examples of things experienced and credibly heard about. When you have read it, you will judge what we were able to accomplish there, or what we may have accomplished—provided that the Lord deigns to grant me permission to publish those books, corrected as consistently as I can make them, and no longer to keep the expectation of many brothers suspended by a long delay.

### 3

I shall briefly relate one matter from which you may form a judgment. Our brother Gennadius, well known to almost everyone and a physician very dear to us, who now lives at Carthage and excelled at Rome in the practice of his profession—as you know, a religious man, and toward the care of the poor tireless in mercy and exceedingly kindhearted—nevertheless once doubted, as he has recently told us, when he was still a young man and most fervent in these acts of almsgiving, whether there was any life after death.

Since God would in no way abandon this man’s disposition and works of mercy, a conspicuous young man, worthy of attention, appeared to him in a dream and said to him: “Follow me.” As he followed him, he came to a certain city, where he began to hear, on the right-hand side, the sounds of exceedingly sweet singing, sweeter than the customary and familiar sweetness. When he asked attentively what it was, the young man said that they were hymns of the blessed and the saints. What he reported seeing on the left-hand side I do not remember sufficiently.

He awoke, and the dream fled.

[Note: In nearly all manuscripts, “and the dream as it was”; perhaps for “and the dream fled away.”]

He thought about it only as much as one thinks about a dream.

### 4

On another night, behold, the same young man appeared to him again and asked whether he recognized him. Gennadius replied that he recognized him very well and clearly. Then the young man asked where he had come to know him. Gennadius did not fail to remember what he repeatedly answered; and he related the entire vision, and the hymns of the saints which he had gone to hear under the young man’s guidance, with the ease with which he recalled recent events.

Then the young man asked whether what he had related he had seen in sleep or while awake. Gennadius replied: “In sleep.” The other said: “Good; you remember correctly. It is true: you saw those things in sleep. But know that even now you are seeing me in sleep.”

When Gennadius heard this, he believed that it was so and confirmed it by his reply. Then the one who was teaching him added:

“Where is your body now?”

He replied: “In my bedroom.”

“Do you know,” the young man said, “that your eyes are now bound, closed, and inactive in that same little body, and that with those eyes you see nothing?”

He replied: “I know.”

Then the young man said: “Who, then, are these eyes with which you see me?”

Unable to find what to answer, Gennadius fell silent. As he hesitated, the young man disclosed what he was trying to teach him by these questions:

“Just as the eyes of your flesh are now inactive while you are asleep and lying on your bed, and perform no action, yet they are the eyes with which you look at me and use this vision, so when you have died, although the eyes of your flesh will be doing nothing, you will still possess the life by which you live and the sense by which you perceive. Therefore, from now on, take care that you do not doubt that life remains after death.”

Thus, this faithful man says that his doubt about the matter was taken away. And who was it that taught him this, if not the providence and mercy of God?

### 5

Someone might say that by this narrative we have not resolved such a great question, but rather bound it more tightly.

[Note: The editions read “increased it.” But the better manuscripts read “bound it.”]

Nevertheless, since each person is free either to believe or not to believe these words, each person has within himself something to turn his attention toward in this most profound question. A human being is awake, a human being sleeps every day, and a human being thinks. Let him say from what these things arise—things resembling forms, qualities, and movements of bodies, yet not being bodily matter. Let him say, if he can. But if he cannot, why does he rush to pronounce a supposedly definitive judgment about exceedingly rare or unexperienced matters, when he cannot resolve what is continuous and daily?

Although I cannot explain in words at all how these things that resemble bodily things come about without a body, nevertheless, just as I know that they are not produced by a body, so I wish I knew how to distinguish the things that are sometimes seen through the spirit and are thought to be seen through the body; and how to distinguish the visions of those whom error or impiety commonly deceives, when so many similar visions are reported among the visions of the pious and the saints. If I had wished to recall examples of these, I would have lacked time rather than material.

May you flourish through the mercy of the Lord, [Col. 0701], most blessed lord, venerable and much-desired brother.

---

## LETTER CLX

[Col. 0701]

[Note: Letters CLX and CLXI have been corrected with the aid of manuscripts cb, gg, r, sb, t, vc, three V manuscripts, and the editions of Louvain.]

[Note: Elsewhere 246; the letter formerly numbered 160 is now 134. Written about the year 414.]

Evodius to Augustine, raising a question concerning reason and God.

### EVODIUS TO AUGUSTINE, BISHOP, GREETINGS

[Note: The salutation formula is lacking in the manuscripts; they contain only “The Letter of Saint Evodius,” or, as it is consistently written in most codices, “of Eubodius.”]

### 1

Perfect reason is that which possesses knowledge of all things, and especially of eternal things that are grasped by the intellect. Reason itself teaches and demonstrates that this reason is eternal and must have been eternal, and that the eternal is what neither began nor changes nor varies. Reason must be eternal, not only because it teaches and demonstrates eternal things, but much more because eternity itself cannot exist without reason. For, I think, there would be no eternity if reason itself had not been eternal.

Furthermore, reason demonstrates that God exists—or that God must have existed—and that things could not have happened otherwise than in such a way that God existed. Whether or not there were beings who knew this, nevertheless, since God is eternal, there can be no doubt that the reason which declares that God must have existed is eternal, and that it thereby demonstrates itself to be coeternal with him.

### 2

There are, however, certain things which are compelled by reason to exist, so that reason is prior, and the effect is posterior to that which reason shows will exist. For example, when the world was made, reason determined that the world should be made. Reason, therefore, is prior to the world.

Thus, the things which reason knew would exist followed, so that reason is first and the operation of the world afterward. Now, since reason demonstrates that God exists, or that it was necessary for God to exist, what shall we place before what? Shall we place reason before God, or reason before the world, or God before reason, without which it is in no way probable that God could exist?

For if “God’s being eternal” means “being eternal by reason,” what is this reason? Therefore, either God is reason, or reason belongs to God, as reason itself teaches. If reason itself is God, reason demonstrates that God is reason, and these things can be coeval and coeternal. But if this reason is God’s likeness, it demonstrates likewise that reason belongs to God; and this too will be coeval and coeternal.

Reason itself shows that God could not similarly come to be unless he were God. If reason is removed—which it is sacrilegious to say—God will not exist, if reason has not demonstrated that it is necessary for God to exist. God, therefore, exists when his reason demonstrates that he should be God. Since God exists, there is without doubt a reason which taught that he exists.

### 3

What, then, if it may be said, is first in God: reason or God? But God will not exist unless there has been reason teaching that God ought to exist. Nor will reason exist unless God exists. Therefore, there is neither a first nor a last there. This divine nature, then, in some manner possesses both reason and God simultaneously.

But one generates the other: either reason generates God, or God generates reason. The subject, perhaps, may be said to be reason and God, or reason and God may be said to exist in a subject. God and reason are one in one.

God, however, rightly generates reason, because reason demonstrates that God exists. God is understood by reason as the Son is understood by the Father, and reason by God as the Father is understood by the Son. For reason itself, together with God, is God. God was never without reason, nor reason without God. God exists when reason exists, and the Son exists when the Father exists; for if reason were removed—as has been said, though it is not lawful to say so—even God himself would not exist, since through his reason there is the act and operation by which he is God.

Let us say the same thing again: if reason did not exist, God did not exist; and if God does not exist, reason did not exist. Reason and God, therefore, are an everlasting reality; and God and reason are likewise an everlasting reality.

The connection and union of reason with God, and of God with reason, of the Father with the Son, and of the Son with the Father, provide for each other, in some manner, principles and causes of existence, because one cannot exist without the other.

Words fail us, and whatever is said is said for this purpose: that we may not remain silent. But should we call God the seed of reason, or reason the seed of God? For neither can the fruit exist without the root, nor is the root anything without fruit.

(The comparison is introduced so that some understanding of God may be indicated. For a fertilizing principle lives even in a grain of wheat, by which it is not permitted to be sterile. But, again, if there were no grain of wheat, the principle would have no material from which to produce these things.)

### 4

Since, therefore, reason, which is God, either shows that God is reason or that reason is God—one in some way showing the other—the Father is not shown except through the Son, nor is the Son shown except through the Father. And the Son is, as it were, in silence when one comes to the Son through the Father, so that one is in some manner hidden while the other is revealed. Thus, by revealing himself, one reveals the other, and one cannot be known while the other remains hidden.

For he says: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father,” and “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:9, 6); and, “No one comes to me unless the Father has drawn him” (John 6:44).

We have undertaken an extremely difficult and arduous task: to understand something about God when we do not understand him. Nevertheless, just as nothing that exists is understood without some form, and things without form are unknowable, so God is much more unknowable without the Son—that is, without reason.

For what? Was the Father ever without reason—alogos, without the Word? Who would dare to say this? Therefore, God must be known through reason as one from one, or one in one, and at the same time as one: for God is one, and it is necessary that there be in him that love which reason itself teaches must always be possessed, or which God commands to be offered.

---

## LETTER CLXI

[Col. 0702]

[Note: Elsewhere 247; the letter formerly numbered 161 is now 49. It appears to have been written in 414.]

Evodius to Augustine, concerning what is written in Letter 137 to Volusianus—“If reason is sought, it will not be miraculous,” and so forth. Evodius shows that those who would claim that God could be seen by Christ with bodily eyes might abuse this statement, contrary to what Augustine taught in Letter 92 to Italica.

To the holy lord, venerably beloved brother and fellow priest Augustine, and to the brothers who are with you, Evodius and the brothers who are with me send greetings in the Lord.

### 1

Through Jobinus,

[Note: In ancient manuscripts, “through Jovinus.”]

who had been sent to the Marcian estate,

[Col. 0703]

I long ago sent you a letter asking one question concerning reason and God, but I have not yet deserved to receive an answer. Since, however, we have had in our hands and have been reading letters of Your Holiness, one to the illustrious Volusianus and another to Italica, an illustrious woman in Christ, something occurred to me in the earlier letter.

Concerning the carnal conception of our Lord Jesus Christ, our God, in the Virgin, and his birth from her, you wrote: “If reason is sought, it will not be miraculous; if an example is demanded, it will not be unique.”

It seemed possible to say something similar about every birth, whether of a human being, of any living creature, or of seed. For if the reason for such a thing were sought, it would not be discovered, and it would certainly be miraculous; and if an example were demanded, since nothing of the kind exists among examples, it would be unique.

For no intercourse of man and woman, nor any conception whatever, which is formed in secret, can ever be explained by reason. Nor can any reason be found for seeds arising from the earth, first rotting and afterward bearing fruit.

Is it not also miraculous to find, within an apple formed by a virginal conception, a single worm, without any parent at all, if uniqueness is required? This, I think, is why it was said as an example: “I am a worm and not a man” (Psalm 22:6).

Concerning conceptions, then, whether joined or solitary, I do not know what sort of reason can be offered. The reason for the Virgin’s conception, therefore, is not merely unavailable; I think that no conception at all can have its reason fully explained.

### 2

If an example is demanded, mares are said to conceive from the wind, hens from ashes, ducks from water, and certain other animals to produce their young without male seed. Certainly, even if they do not give birth while remaining entirely intact, they may conceive without being violated. How, then, can it be said, “If an example is demanded, it will not be unique,” when so many examples present themselves?

It is also known to everyone that certain animals are born within bodies—not only female bodies but even, I mean, within men. Does seed produce conception there as well? Behold examples; behold miracles for which no explanation can be given at all.

Or if an explanation is offered on the ground that nothing of this kind has ever happened in a human virgin, nevertheless there are examples in other kinds of things, since things are born and conceived without seeds, and no explanation for them can be given in any way.

Yet even in generation one can find something of this sort, which produces offspring in such a way that the integrity of nature is not violated. I often hear that a spider, without any male conception or corruption in giving birth, wonderfully produces, according to the mode of its nature, all those threads by which it usually hangs suspended in its web, and that this has been granted to it alone, as something unique.

Therefore, if this too is examined, it is not merely miraculous, but no such examples can in any way be supplied. For I fear that these examples may have preceded the argument for this very reason: so that those who would not believe that a virgin could conceive might be refuted by them and shown that the event is indeed miraculous but nevertheless not unique. For all God’s works are miraculous, because they were made in wisdom.

If this objection is brought against us, what shall we answer?

### 3

There is another matter which presses me most forcefully: the same argument can be made concerning the substance of the Lord’s glorified body, since it too might be able to see the substance of God. You said in your letter to Italica that it cannot do so—and this is certain.

Thus, [Col. 0704]

when we begin to give a reason why it cannot, someone may object that if what was accomplished in that conception and birth is miraculous and unique, and neither the reason they demand nor an example is supplied,

[Note: Thus read three Vatican manuscripts and several of our own. The editions have: “Nor was it sought by reason, nor by example; because …”]

because this was granted to one person alone, then just as no reason is given for conception and generation, but uniqueness is found in him alone, so no reason should be given for his vision, nor should an example be demanded; rather, it should be permitted to him alone, uniquely, to see the substance of divinity with his body.

If it is answered that a reason can be given, because a corporeal thing cannot in any way see an incorporeal thing, I fear that someone may answer that the conception too can be explained by reason and confirmed by examples.

Either reason will fail among human beings and examples will cease, and they will confirm that the Only-Begotten can see God with his body; or, if a reason is supplied here, it will follow that certain men who are excessively wise could also give a reason for that conception and the subsequent birth.

What answer should be given to such people, I ask. I am not sowing disputes; I am asking how one should answer those who lay snares.

For my part, I believe in the Virgin’s conception and childbirth as I have always believed; and I conclude, by whatever reasoning I can, that God cannot be seen even with a glorified body. Nevertheless, I think that one must confront people who either habitually stir up seditions from questions or awaken to learning with fervent zeal.

Pray for us. May the peace and love of Christ make Your Holiness mindful of us, holy lord and most venerably blessed brother.

---

## LETTER CLXII

[Note: Compared with manuscripts bl, cb, ff, gg, r, vc, two sb manuscripts, two t manuscripts, three V manuscripts, and the editions of Ambrosius, Badius, Erasmus, and Louvain.]

[Note: Elsewhere 101; the letter formerly numbered 162 is now 43. Perhaps written in 415.]

Augustine replies to Evodius that the solution of the question proposed in Letter 160 should be sought in other writings of his. He confirms the opinion he had touched upon in Letter 159 concerning the soul separated from the body and concerning extraordinary visions. Finally, he defends the statement criticized in the preceding letter: “If reason is sought, it will not be miraculous,” and so forth.

To the most blessed lord, venerable brother and fellow bishop Evodius, and to the brothers with you, Augustine and the brothers with me send greetings in the Lord.

### 1

You ask many things of a man who is greatly occupied; and, what is more serious, you think that matters so difficult that, even when dictated or written with great care, they can scarcely be brought to the understanding of people such as yourself ought to be rushed through dictation.

Moreover, it is not only you and people like you who are to be considered as readers of what we write. Certainly those also who possess a less acute and less practiced intellect are carried by such zeal toward knowing our writings—whether with friendly or hostile intent—that they cannot be excluded from consideration altogether.

When you reflect on this, you see how much care must be taken in writing, especially about matters so important that even great minds labor over them. But if, whenever I have something in hand, it must be interrupted and postponed so that I may answer whatever new matters are [Col. 0705]

demanded, what will happen if, while those too are being answered, other matters arise? Would you like us, leaving even those aside, to take up the new ones, so that the later matters that arise are always dealt with first, and we can complete only those matters which, while they are being written, are not interrupted by something else being asked?

It is very difficult for this to happen to me, but I do not think you would approve of it. Therefore, I ought not to have interrupted other matters when yours arrived, just as I ought not to interrupt yours if other matters should press upon me again. Yet I am not allowed to preserve this justice.

For behold, in order to write this very reply to you, by which I might bring this matter to your attention, I interrupted what I was doing and turned my mind away from another matter requiring great concentration toward this letter.

### 2

It was easy, I think, to send you this excuse, written into the letter, and not an unjust one. But it is not equally easy to respond to your inquiries. I think that in the very little works which now occupy me so intensely there will be certain passages in which I shall resolve the matters you ask about, if the Lord favors me.

Many of the questions you have just sent have already been resolved in those books which I have not yet published, whether in the books on the Trinity or those on Genesis.

Even if you reread those works which have long been known to you—or, if I am not mistaken, were known to you, since perhaps you have forgotten what I wrote when you discussed and conversed with me—whether concerning the Quantity of the Soul or Free Will, you will find there the means of dissolving your doubts even without my assistance, provided that you apply a certain amount of the labor of thought, joining together the consequences of what has been brought there to clear and certain understanding.

You also have the book On True Religion. If you were to recall and examine it, you would never think that God is compelled by reason to exist, or that by reasoning it is brought about that God must exist.

For in the case of the reasoning involved in numbers, which we certainly use in daily life, if we say, “Seven and three ought to be ten,” we speak less carefully. They ought not to be ten; they are ten.

Concerning the matters about which it is rightly said that they ought to be, whether they already exist or ought to exist, we have discussed sufficiently, I think, in the books I mentioned. A human being ought to be wise—if he is wise, so that he may remain so; if he is not yet wise, so that he may become wise. But God ought not to be wise; he is wise.

### 3

Review again and again those matters concerning visions which I wrote to you most recently and which you mention as subtly expressed but as having entangled you in greater questions. Think about them more carefully. Do not let your consideration pass over them; let it dwell in them. From them you may perhaps form some conception of how the soul is present or absent.

In these visions the soul lingers in sleep when it is absent from the sense and presence of seeing which, while awake, it provides to the eyes. But if this absence of the soul from the eyes—that is, from what are like the lights of the body—were increased by a greater force, so that the whole of it were withdrawn, this would be death.

Therefore, just as the soul does not depart from the sense of seeing into dream visions with some body—unless perhaps we are going to suppose that the things which appear in dreams are bodily, and that we ourselves are carried here and there among them with some body, which I think you no longer believe—

[Col. 0706]

so, if the soul is completely withdrawn and absent, as happens in death, it should not be thought to carry away with it some body from the body.

For if it carried one away, then even when we sleep and it withdraws from the eyes, to the extent that it leaves them it would carry away the eyes with it, however subtle they might be, though still bodily. But it does not do this.

Nevertheless, it carries away with it certain eyes very similar to them, but not bodily, by which it sees visions very similar to bodies in dreams—but the visions themselves are not bodily either.

### 4

If someone insists that even dream visions, which appear similar to bodies, are nothing other than bodily things, he seems to himself to be saying something; and this slowness of understanding is not easily refuted, since it is shared even by many people of no ordinary sharpness.

They pay too little attention to the power of images of bodies which are formed in the spirit and are not bodies at all. But when they are compelled to look at these images, if they observe correctly and discover that they are not bodily but very similar to bodies, they are nevertheless not immediately able to explain by what causes and in what manner they are formed, or finally by what nature they subsist, or in what subject they exist.

Are they formed in the soul as letters made from ink on parchment, where both substances exist—the parchment and the ink? Or are they formed like a seal in wax, or like any figure for which wax is the subject, the figure existing in the subject? Or do these things come about in our spirit in both ways, sometimes in one way and sometimes in the other?

### 5

For not only do those things move us which are absent from the bodily senses and are found in our memory, or which we ourselves make, arrange, enlarge, and diminish at will, varying them in position, appearance, movement, and innumerable qualities and forms.

[Note: Louvain reads: “not only so that we may think about things that are absent, but also in position, appearance, and so forth.” Badius, Erasmus, and most manuscripts lack the words “so that we may think” and “but also.”]

Perhaps those things by which we are deceived while sleeping, when we are not divinely admonished, are of the same kind—except that we perform the former willingly, whereas we suffer the latter against our will.

It is not only these things that move us—things which one might reasonably think are produced in the soul by the soul itself, although even this occurs through more hidden causes, by which it is brought about that this rather than that comes into the soul’s view. It is also what the prophet says: “And the angel who spoke in me said to me” (Zechariah 1:9).

For we should not believe that external voices came to the prophet’s bodily ears when he says “who spoke in me,” not “to me.” Were they voices made from the spirit, similar to bodily voices, such as those we produce when, silently within ourselves, we run through many things from memory, often even by singing them, but nevertheless voices uttered by the angel who was suggesting them to him?

And what is written in the Gospel: “Behold, an angel of God appeared to him in a dream, saying” (Matthew 1:20)—how did he appear? Was it an angelic body to closed eyes, as angels appeared to Abraham while he was awake, so that he even felt them by touch when he washed their feet (Genesis 18:4)? Or was it a spirit appearing to the spirit of the sleeping person in some form similar to a body, just as we ourselves seem to ourselves, when dreaming, to move through places in such a form, in a manner far different from the way our limbs lie and move on our beds?

[Col. 0707]

### 6

These things are marvelous because they possess a more hidden reason than can be seen or explained by one human being to another. For the causes of wonder are either that the reason for a thing is hidden, or that the thing itself is unusual, being unique or rare.

For the first cause—the hiddenness of the reason—I said in the letter which you mention having read (Letter 137 to Volusianus), when I was replying to those who deny that one should believe that Christ was born of a virgin and that she remained a virgin:

“If reason is sought, it will not be miraculous.”

This was not said because the matter lacks a reason, but because its reason is hidden from those to whom God wished it to be miraculous.

For the other cause of wonder, which exists because something unusual occurs, it is written concerning the Lord that he marveled at the centurion’s faith. The reason for no matter could have been hidden from him; rather, wonder was used as praise for one whose equal had not appeared among the people of Israel. Hence this wonder is sufficiently explained when the Lord says: “Truly I tell you, I have not found such great faith in Israel” (Luke 7:9).

### 7

But when I added in the same letter, “If an example is demanded, it will not be unique,” you seemed to yourself, wrongly, to have found examples in the little worm that is born in an apple and the spider that gives birth to the thread of its web from its apparently intact body.

Some things are said for the sake of an ingenious resemblance, others more remotely, others more appropriately. But Christ alone was born from a virgin. Hence, as I think you now understand, you see why I said that this occurred without an example.

Everything, therefore, has its own causes and right, blameless reasons, by which God brings about both customary and unusual things. But when these causes and reasons are hidden, we marvel at what happens; when they are evident, we consequently say that things happen rightly or appropriately, and that what reason required to happen is not marvelous because it has happened.

Or, if we marvel, we do not marvel by being astonished at something unexpected, but by praising its excellence. It was in this kind of wonder that the centurion was praised.

Nor is the statement, “If reason is sought, it will not be miraculous,” to be rejected on this account, since there is another kind of wonder even when the reason is evident to the one who wonders.

For the statement “God tempts no one” (James 1:13) is not thereby to be condemned, since there is another kind of temptation on account of which it is likewise rightly said: “The Lord your God is testing you” (Deuteronomy 13:3).

### 8

No one should suppose that, for this reason, it may rightly be said that the Father can be seen by the Son with bodily eyes, rather than in the manner in which the Son is seen by the Father. Those who think this, when they fail to provide a reason, may themselves say: “If reason is sought, it will not be miraculous.” This was said not because there is no reason, but because the reason is hidden.

Whoever undertakes to refute those who hold this opinion must demonstrate that there is no reason for it—not that it is a miracle, but that it is an error.

For just as there is no reason by which God’s nature could die, be corrupted, or sin, and when we say that God cannot do these things we do not detract from his power but praise his eternity and truth, so, when we say that he cannot be seen with bodily eyes, the reason is not hidden but evident to those who understand correctly.

It is clear that God is not a body, and that nothing can be perceived by bodily eyes unless it is seen through the interposition of some interval. But only a body can be seen in this way, and a substance which is smaller in a part than in the whole. Even those who are not yet able to understand this ought to regard it as impious to believe such a thing of God.

### 9

The reason for different changes is hidden, and from this arises the entire forest of miracles among visible things. But does it follow that it is therefore hidden that bodies exist, that we have a body, that there is no body, however small, which does not occupy a space according to its own mode, and that in the space it occupies it is not wholly present everywhere, but is smaller in a part than in the whole?

Since these things are not hidden, they must be connected with the consequences which should be drawn from them. To do this now would take too long. Those consequences would show that it is not the reason that is hidden, but that there is absolutely no reason by which one ought to believe—or can understand—that God, who is wholly present everywhere and is not spread out through spatial intervals by a bodily mass, so that he must consist of larger and smaller parts, can be seen by bodily eyes.

I would say more if I had undertaken this in the present letter. I have advanced in its length without realizing it, almost forgetting my occupations, so that perhaps—contrary to what I expected—I have sufficiently satisfied your intention. You can, after a brief admonition, think through more matters that are relevant; but this will not likewise be true of those into whose hands these writings may come profitably, if they are discussed more carefully and at greater length.

People labor in learning: they cannot understand brief treatments, and they do not like to read lengthy ones. Likewise, those who teach labor, since they uselessly pour little into the minds of the slow and much into those of the lazy.

Send also a copy of that letter which, having gone astray among us, could not be found.

---

## LETTER CLXIII

[Col. 0708]

[Note: Revised with the aid of manuscripts gg, r, two sb manuscripts, two t manuscripts, two V manuscripts, and the editions of Ambrosius, Badius, Erasmus, and Louvain.]

[Note: Elsewhere 98; the letter formerly numbered 163 is now 44. Written shortly after the preceding one.]

Evodius presents several questions to Augustine.

### EVODIUS, BISHOP, TO AUGUSTINE, BISHOP

I previously sent questions to Your Holiness: one concerning reason and God, I think through Jobinus, who serves the maidservants of God.

[Note: The Vatican manuscripts lack the words “who serves the maidservants of God.”]

Another concerned the body of the Savior, which is thought to see the substance of God.

I now state a third question: Does the rational soul which the Savior assumed together with the body belong to one of those opinions proposed when the origin of the soul is investigated, if any truth can support one of them there? Or, although it is rational, does it not belong to those kinds of souls which are spoken of in the case of animals, but exist in another category?

I ask a fourth question: Who are those spirits concerning whom Peter, in his Letter, bears witness about the Lord, saying: “Put to death in the flesh, made alive in the spirit; in which also he came and preached to the spirits who were in prison” (1 Peter 3:18–19), and so forth? I add this: that they were in hell, and that Christ, descending, evangelized all of them and freed them all by grace from darkness and punishments, so that, from the time of the Lord’s resurrection, judgment might be awaited, the realms of hell having been emptied.

I wish to know what Your Holiness thinks about this matter.

---

## LETTER CLXIV

[Note: Corrected with the aid of manuscripts a, bg, bl, ff, g, gv, j, n, s, vc, vd, two a manuscripts, two bn manuscripts, two sb manuscripts, four t manuscripts, four V manuscripts, and the editions of Ambrosius, Badius, Erasmus, and Louvain.]

[Note: Elsewhere 99; the letter formerly numbered 164 is now 87. Written at the same time.]

Augustine replies to Evodius concerning two questions, one about an obscure passage in the third chapter of the First Letter of Peter, the other about the soul of Christ.

[Col. 0709]

To the most blessed lord, brother and fellow bishop Evodius, Augustine sends greetings in the Lord.

### CHAPTER ONE

#### 1

The question which you proposed to me from the Apostle Peter’s Letter—a question which, as I do not think is hidden from you, usually troubles us exceedingly—concerns how those words are to be understood as having been spoken about the lower regions (inferis).

I therefore repeat the same question to you, so that either you may be able to remove and resolve my doubt yourself, or may find someone who can do so. But if I should be able to do this first, when the Lord grants it, and should be able to share the result with you, I will not withhold it from Your Love.

For the present, however, I shall explain what troubles me in that passage, so that, in accordance with these points, you may either consider those apostolic words yourself or consult someone whom you find capable of doing so.

2. When he had said that Christ was put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit, he immediately added: “In which spirit he also came and preached to those spirits imprisoned in the prison, who had once been unbelieving, when the patience of God was waiting in the days of Noah, while the ark was being built, in which a few—that is, eight souls—were saved through water.” Then he continued and said: “And now baptism, in a similar form, saves you also” (1 Peter 3:18, 21). It is therefore troubling that, if the Lord, when he died, preached in hell to the spirits confined in prison [Note: [Col. 0709] The older editions here insert the passage found below in §7, “That only these two … bears such distinguished witness.” Following the example of the Louvain editors, the Benedictine Fathers removed the whole passage as a repetition carelessly introduced. M.], what good had those alone done to deserve that the Lord should descend into hell, who were unbelieving at the time when the ark was being built? For after the time of Noah many thousands of people from so many nations died before Christ’s passion, whom he could have found in hell—not, certainly, those who had believed in God, such as the prophets and patriarchs descended from Abraham, and Noah himself in earlier times, together with his entire household, which was saved through the water, except perhaps one son who was later rejected; nor, again, only the descendants of Jacob, since there were others who believed in God, such as Job, the city of Nineveh, and any others who either appear in Scripture or remain hidden within the human race. Rather, I mean the many thousands of people who, ignorant of God and devoted to the worship of demons or images, departed this life from the time of Noah until Christ’s passion. When Christ found them in hell, why did he not preach to them, but only to those who had been unbelieving in the days of Noah, while the ark was being built? Or, if he preached to everyone, why did Peter mention only those, leaving aside the innumerable multitude of the others?

## CHAPTER II

3. That the Lord, having been put to death in the flesh, [Col. 0710] came into hell is sufficiently established. For one cannot contradict either the prophecy that said, “For you will not abandon my soul in hell”—a passage which Peter himself explains in the Acts of the Apostles, lest anyone dare to understand it otherwise—or those words of Peter himself in which he asserts that Christ released the pains of hell, in which it was impossible for him to be held (Psalm 15:10; Acts 2:24, 27). Who, then, except an unbeliever, would deny that Christ was in hell?

If it troubles anyone how the statement that he released the pains of hell should be understood—for he had not begun to be in those pains as though in chains, and did not release them as someone releases chains with which he had been bound—it is easy to understand that they were released in the manner in which hunters’ snares can be released, so that they no longer hold someone, not because they had held him. It can also be understood in this way: we may believe that he released those pains by which he himself could not be held, but by which others were held—others whom he knew were to be liberated.

4. But who these people were, it is rash to determine. For if we say that all without exception who were found there were then liberated, who would not rejoice if we could demonstrate this? This is especially so on account of certain people who have become familiarly known to us through their literary labor, whose eloquence and intelligence we admire—not only poets and orators, who in many passages of their shorter works showed those very false gods of the nations to be despised and ridiculed, and at times even confessed the one true God, although they continued to worship those superstitious deities along with the others, but also those who expressed such views not by singing or declaiming, but by philosophizing.

There are also many whose writings we do not possess, but whose lives we have learned from the writings of others to have been praiseworthy in a certain respect. Apart from the worship of God, in which they went astray by worshiping vain things that had been officially established for worship, and by serving the creature rather than the Creator, they may rightly be set before us as examples for imitation in their other conduct: frugality, self-restraint, chastity, sobriety, contempt for death for the sake of their country’s safety, and the keeping of faith not only with fellow citizens but also with enemies.

Yet when these things are not referred to the end of true and rightly ordered piety, but to the empty display of human praise and glory, they too become empty in a certain sense and are rendered barren. Nevertheless, they please us by a certain natural disposition of the soul, so that we would especially wish those in whom these qualities existed to be liberated from the torments of hell, either alone or together with the others—unless human sentiment were one thing and the justice of the Creator another.

5. If, then, these things are so—if the Savior liberated everyone from there and, as you wrote in asking me, emptied hell so that thereafter only the final judgment was to be awaited—these are the matters that, as I consider them for the moment, reasonably trouble me.

First, on what authority is this opinion established? For what is written about Christ’s death, that the pains of hell were released, may be understood as referring to Christ himself: he released them in the sense that he rendered them ineffective, so that he himself would not be held by them, especially since what follows says that it was impossible for him to be held by them.

Or, if the reason is sought why he wished to come into hell, where there were those pains by which he could not possibly [Col. 0711] be held—for, as it is written, he was “free among the dead” (Psalm 87:6), and in him the prince and ruler of death found nothing deserving punishment—then the statement that the pains of hell were released can be understood as referring not to everyone but to certain people whom he judged worthy of that liberation. Thus he is not thought to have descended there in vain, as though he would benefit none of those who were held there in confinement; yet it does not follow that what divine mercy and justice granted to some must be considered granted to all.

## CHAPTER III

6. As for that first man, the father of the human race, nearly the whole Church agrees that Christ liberated him from there. We should believe that the Church did not hold this belief without reason, whatever the tradition from which it was derived, even if no explicit authority from the canonical Scriptures is produced on the matter. Nevertheless, what is written in the Book of Wisdom seems to support this opinion more than any other interpretation:

> “She guarded the first-formed father of the world, when he alone had been created, and delivered him from his sin, and gave him strength to rule all things” (Wisdom 10:1–2).

Some add that this benefit was also granted to the ancient saints—Abel, Seth, Noah and his household, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and the other patriarchs and prophets—so that when the Lord came into hell, they would be released from those pains.

7. But how Abraham could have been in those pains, when even that pious poor man was received into Abraham’s bosom, I do not see. Perhaps those who are able can explain it.

That only two persons, namely Abraham and Lazarus, were in that memorable bosom of rest before the Lord descended into hell, and that only these two were meant when the rich man was told, “Between us and you a great chasm has been fixed, so that those who wish to cross over from here to you cannot, nor can anyone cross over from there to us” (Luke 16:26)—I do not know whether this does not seem absurd to anyone.

Moreover, if more than two were there, who would dare say that the patriarchs and prophets were not there, to whom Scripture bears such distinguished witness concerning God’s justice and piety? What benefit, then, did the one who released the pains of hell confer upon these people, when they were not in those pains? I still do not understand this, especially since I have nowhere been able to find hell itself called good in Scripture.

If this is nowhere read in the divine authorities, then Abraham’s bosom—that is, the dwelling place of a certain hidden rest—should certainly not be considered a part of hell. Indeed, even in the words of that great teacher himself, where Abraham is said to have declared, “Between us and you a great chasm has been fixed,” it seems sufficiently clear, in my opinion, that this bosom of such great blessedness is not some part or, as it were, member of hell. For what is a great chasm except a kind of gulf that greatly separates things between which there is not merely a separation but one that has also been firmly established?
