Therefore, if Holy Scripture had said that the dead Christ came into Abraham’s bosom, without mentioning hell and its pains, I wonder whether anyone would dare assert that he descended into hell.

[Col. 0712] 8. But because clear testimonies mention both hell and its pains, no reason presents itself for believing that the Savior came there except that he might save people from its pains. Whether he saved all whom he found in them, or only certain ones whom he judged worthy of that benefit, I am still investigating. Nevertheless, I do not doubt that he was in hell and granted this benefit to those who were situated in its pains.

As for those righteous people who were in Abraham’s bosom, I have not yet discovered what he conferred upon them when he descended into hell. I do not see how he could ever have withdrawn from them according to the blessed presence of his divinity. Likewise, on that very day on which he died, he promised the thief that he would be with him in paradise (Luke 23:43), at the time when he was going to descend to release the pains of hell.

Therefore, even before that time, he was certainly in paradise and in Abraham’s bosom through his wisdom, which bestows blessedness, and in hell through his power of judgment. For where is the divinity not present, being confined by no place?

Nevertheless, according to the creature which, by assuming it at a particular time, he—remaining God—became man, Scripture clearly declares that he was in hell according to his soul. This is stated beforehand in prophecy and sufficiently explained through the apostolic interpretation: “You will not abandon my soul in hell” (Psalm 15:10).

9. I know that some think that, at the death of the Lord Christ, the righteous were granted a resurrection of the kind promised to us at the end. For it is written that, in the earthquake at the time of his passion, when the rocks were split and the tombs opened, many bodies of the saints rose and appeared with him when he rose in the holy city (Matthew 27:51–53).

If, of course, they did not again sleep after their bodies had been restored to the tombs, we must consider how Christ can be understood as “the firstborn from the dead” (Revelation 1:5), if so many preceded him in that resurrection.

If it is answered that this was said by anticipation—so that the tombs are understood to have been opened in that earthquake while Christ hung on the cross, but that the bodies of the saints rose not then but when Christ had first risen—then, although, as I said, the matter may have been added by anticipation, so that Christ might without ambiguity be believed to be the firstborn from the dead and that those righteous people might immediately be granted resurrection, with him going before them, into eternal incorruption and immortality, there remains another matter that troubles me.

How could Peter have said—and said most truly—that, through that prophecy, it had been foretold not of David but of Christ that his flesh would not see corruption, and then have added concerning David that his tomb was among them (Acts 2:27, 29)? This would not have convinced them if his body were no longer there, because, if he too had risen earlier, shortly after his death, and his flesh had not seen corruption, his tomb could nevertheless have remained.

It seems difficult, moreover, to suppose that David was not among those righteous people in that resurrection, if eternal life [Note: [Col. 0712] Four manuscripts: “if eternal life has been granted to them.”] had already been granted to them—David, whose descendant Christ is so frequently, so clearly, and with such great honor commended.

The statement made in Hebrews concerning the ancient righteous would also be [Col. 0713] endangered: “Because God had provided something better for us, so that they should not be made perfect without us” (Hebrews 11:40), if they had already been established in that incorruptible resurrection which is promised to us for our perfection at the end.

## CHAPTER IV

10. You see how obscure it is why Peter wished to mention only those to whom the Gospel was preached while they were confined in prison—those who had been unbelieving in the days of Noah, when the ark was being built—and what troubles me, so that I dare not make any assertion on the basis of this passage.

Moreover, after the apostle had said, “And now baptism, in a similar form, saves you also—not the removal of the filth of the flesh, but the appeal of a good conscience to God through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who is at the right hand of God, having swallowed up death so that we might be made heirs of eternal life, having gone into heaven, with angels and authorities and powers subjected to him,” he immediately added:

> “Therefore, since Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same understanding, because whoever has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sins, so that he may live the remaining time in the flesh no longer for human desires but for the will of God.”

Then he said:

> “For the past time is sufficient, when you walked according to the will of human beings, in lusts, desires, drunkenness, revelries, drinking parties, and unlawful worship of idols. In these things they are astonished that you do not run with them into the same flood of debauchery, and they blaspheme. They will give an account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead.”

After these words he adds:

> “For this is why the Gospel was preached even to the dead, so that, although they might be judged in the flesh according to human standards, they might live in the spirit according to God.”

11. Who would not be troubled by this profundity? He says that the Gospel was preached to the dead. If we understand these as people who have departed from the body, they will, I think, be the people of whom he said above, “who had been unbelieving in the days of Noah,” or certainly all those whom Christ found in hell.

What, then, does it mean that “they might be judged in the flesh according to human standards, but live in the spirit according to God”? How are they judged in the flesh if they do not have the flesh because they are in hell, or have not yet received it if they have also been released from the pains of hell?

For even if, as you suggest in your inquiry, hell was emptied, we are not thereby to believe that everyone who was then there rose again in the flesh. Nor did those who appeared when the Lord rose receive flesh for the purpose of being judged in it according to human standards. I do not see how this can be understood even of those who were unbelieving in the days of Noah. It is not written that they lived in the flesh, nor can it be believed that the pains of hell were released for the purpose of restoring flesh to those liberated from there so that they might suffer punishment in it.

What, then, does it mean that they might be judged in the flesh according to human standards but live in the spirit according to God? Perhaps this was granted to those whom Christ found in hell: that they might be made alive in spirit through the Gospel, although at the future resurrection they are to be judged in the flesh, so that through some punishment of the flesh they may pass into the kingdom of God.

But if this is so, why is it said only of those who once did not believe in the days of Noah, and not also of the others whom Christ’s visitation found there, [Col. 0714] who were revived in spirit through the preaching of the Gospel and later were to be judged in the flesh through a temporary punishment?

If we understand it of everyone, the question remains why Peter mentioned only those who were unbelieving at the time when the ark was being built.

12. It is also troubling that those who try to give an account of this matter say that, when Christ descended into hell, those who were found there and had not heard the Gospel had those punitive places emptied as prisons. While they were alive, the Gospel had not yet been preached throughout the whole world, and they had just reasons for not believing, since it had not been announced to them.

Afterward, however, those who despise the preaching of the Gospel celebrated and spread among all nations will have no excuse. Therefore, once those prisons were emptied, only the just judgment remains, by which the disobedient and unbelieving will also be punished with eternal fire.

Those who hold this view do not consider that all who departed this life after Christ’s resurrection, before the Gospel reached them, could have the same excuse. For after the Lord returned from hell, no one was permitted to go into hell again without having heard the Gospel—yet so many people died throughout the world before this proclamation reached them. All of them will have the excuse that is said to have been removed from those to whom the Lord came, because they had not previously heard, and to whom he is said to have preached in hell.

13. Unless perhaps it is said that those who died, or die, after the Lord’s resurrection without the Gospel yet having been announced to them could have heard, or could still hear, the message in hell, so that there they might believe what must be believed concerning the truth of Christ, and they too might receive the remission and salvation that those deserved to whom Christ was announced there.

For the fact that Christ ascended again from hell does not mean that his fame was extinguished there. He also ascended from here into heaven, and yet those who believe in him will be saved through the announcement concerning him.

For this reason he was exalted and was given the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—not only of those in heaven and on earth, but also of those in hell (Philippians 2:9–10).

But if we admit this opinion, by which it may be thought that people who, while alive, did not believe at all can believe in Christ in hell, who could tolerate the absurdities that follow, which are contrary to faith?

First, we would seem to grieve needlessly over those who departed from the body without this grace, and to take care needlessly, and exhort people urgently, that they receive it before they die, lest they be punished with eternal death.

Or, if only those believe uselessly and fruitlessly in hell who refused to believe here after the Gospel had been announced to them, while belief there will benefit those who did not despise here what they were unable to hear at all, another and even more absurd consequence follows: the Gospel should not be preached here, since everyone will certainly die and, without any guilt for having despised the Gospel, ought to come into hell, where it can benefit them once they believe there. To hold this opinion is impious folly.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0715]

14. Therefore, let us hold most firmly what faith, established upon the strongest authority, teaches: “That Christ died according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, and that he rose on the third day according to the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:3–4), together with the other matters concerning him that have been written down with the fullest certainty.

Among these matters is also this: that he was in hell and, having loosed its pains, by which it was impossible for him to be held, is rightly understood also to have loosed and liberated from them those whom he wished; and that he received again the body which he had left on the cross and which had been placed in the tomb.

As for the question you proposed concerning the words of the apostle Peter, since you see what troubles me—and since other matters might perhaps also cause difficulty if they were examined more carefully—let us investigate them, either by considering them among ourselves or by consulting those whom it is appropriate and possible for us to consult.

15. Consider, nevertheless, whether perhaps everything that the apostle Peter says about the spirits confined in prison who had not believed in the days of Noah has nothing at all to do with hell, but rather with those earlier times whose pattern he transferred to the present.

For that historical event had been a pattern of things to come: those who now do not believe the Gospel, while the Church is being built among all nations, are understood to resemble those who did not believe at the time when the ark was being built. Those who believed and are saved through baptism are compared with those who were then saved through water in the same ark. Hence he says, “So baptism also saves you in a similar form.”

Let us therefore adapt the other statements concerning the unbelievers to this similarity of the pattern, and let us not suppose that the Gospel was preached in hell to make believers and liberate them, or that it is still preached there, as though the Church had also been established there.

16. The people who have believed that Peter understood the passage in the way that troubles you seem to have been led to this interpretation because he said that preaching was addressed to spirits confined in prison, as though souls could not be understood as spirits—souls that were then in the flesh and were shut up, as it were, in a prison of ignorance.

It is from such a prison that the one who says, “Bring my soul out of prison, so that I may confess your name” (Psalm 141:8), desires to be released. Elsewhere this prison is called the shadow of death. Those who have been liberated from it are not liberated in hell but here, as it is written: “Those who sat in the shadow of death, light has risen for them” (Isaiah 9:2).

The preaching to those people in the days of Noah was fruitless because they did not believe, while the patience of God was waiting for them during the many years [Note: [Col. 0715] Bad., Am., and Er.: “during the hundred years.”] in which that same ark was being built. For its construction too was, in a certain sense, a proclamation.

In the same way, those who resemble them now do not believe. Under the same pattern, they are confined, as it were, in a prison of ignorance, looking in vain upon the Church being built throughout the world, while judgment approaches like the flood in which all the unbelievers then perished.

For the Lord says:

> “As it was in the days of Noah, so will it be in the days of the Son of Man. They were eating, drinking, marrying, and giving in marriage, until Noah entered the ark; the flood came and destroyed them all” (Luke 17:26).

But [Col. 0716] because that historical event also signified a future event, the flood there signified both baptism for the faithful and punishment for the unbelieving.

Similarly, in the figure—not of an event that occurred, but merely of something spoken—which says what is written about the stone (Psalm 117:22; Isaiah 8:14 and 28:16; Daniel 2:34, 45; Matthew 21:44; Luke 20:17; Acts 4:11; Romans 9:33, etc.), by which Christ was signified, two things were foretold: a stumbling block for the unbelieving and a building stone for the faithful.

Sometimes, however, within the same figure—whether enacted or spoken—two things signify one reality. Thus the faithful signified the pieces of wood fitted together for the construction of the ark, and those same faithful also signified the eight souls who were saved in that ark. In the Gospel’s analogy of the sheepfold, Christ himself is both the shepherd and the door (John 10:1–2).

## CHAPTER VI

17. Nor should it prevent this interpretation that the apostle Peter said that the same Christ preached to those confined in prison who had once not believed in the days of Noah, so that we might consequently think this interpretation impossible because Christ had not yet come at that time.

He had not yet come, certainly, in the flesh, as he came when afterward he was seen on earth and lived among human beings (Baruch 3:38). Nevertheless, from the beginning of the human race, whether to rebuke the wicked—as he did Cain, and earlier Adam and his wife—or to console the good, or to admonish both groups, so that some might believe for their salvation and others might refuse to believe to their punishment, he himself was certainly coming—not in the flesh but in the spirit—addressing those whom he wished, through appearances suited to them, in whatever way he wished.

When I said, “He was coming in the spirit,” the Son himself, in the substance of his divinity, is spirit, since he is not a body. But what does the Son do without the Holy Spirit or without the Father, since all the works of the Trinity are inseparable?

18. The very words of Scripture under discussion also indicate this sufficiently, as I think, to those who pay careful attention:

> “Because Christ,” he says, “died once for our sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, so that he might bring us to God, being put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit, in which spirit he came and preached also to those spirits who had once been unbelieving, when the patience of God was waiting in the days of Noah, while the ark was being built.”

Now, I think, the order [Note: [Col. 0716] Thus the manuscripts; the editions read “pattern.”] of the words is apparent: “Christ, put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit.” In that spirit he came and preached to those spirits who had once been unbelieving in the days of Noah.

Before he came in the flesh to die for us—the one time when he did so—he had often previously come in the spirit to those whom he wished, admonishing them through appearances in whatever way he wished, certainly in the spirit by which he was also made alive when he had been put to death in the flesh during his passion.

For what does it mean that he was made alive in the spirit except that the same flesh, which alone had been put to death, rose again through the life-giving spirit?

## CHAPTER VII

19. As for the claim that Jesus’ soul was put to death—that is, the spirit belonging to a human being—who would dare make it, since the death of the soul is nothing other than sin, from which he was entirely free when he was put to death in the flesh for us?

If all human souls derive from that one soul which was breathed into the first man, through whom sin entered the world, and through sin death, and thus passed into all human beings [Col. 0717] (Romans 5:12), then either Christ’s soul did not derive from that source, since he had no sin at all—neither original nor personal—for which death could be considered owed to him, and he paid on our behalf a debt he did not owe, in whom the prince and ruler of death found nothing (John 19:30); nor is it absurd that the one who created a soul for the first man also created one for himself.

Or, if Christ’s soul too derived from that source, he cleansed it by assuming it, so that he might come to us and be born from a virgin without any sin whatsoever, whether committed or transmitted.

But if souls are not propagated from that one soul, and only the flesh derives original sin from Adam, then the Son of God created a soul for himself just as he creates one for the others, but did not join it to sinful flesh, rather to “the likeness of sinful flesh” (Romans 8:3).

For he took from the Virgin a truly material substance of flesh, but not sinful flesh, since it was neither sown nor conceived through carnal desire. It was certainly mortal and subject to change through the stages of life, resembling sinful flesh in every respect except sin.

20. Accordingly, whatever opinion concerning the soul is true—I still do not dare rashly affirm any of them, except that I reject the opinion according to which souls are believed to be thrust individually into individual bodies as into prisons on account of the merits of some unknown prior acts—Christ’s soul was certainly not only immortal according to the nature shared by other souls, but also was not put to death by any sin or punished by condemnation. Death of the soul can be understood on the basis of these two causes. Therefore Christ could not be said to have been made alive in the spirit according to his soul.

For he was made alive in that in which he had been put to death. Therefore the statement was made concerning the flesh. The flesh itself came back to life when the soul returned, because it itself had died when the soul departed.

Thus he is said to have been put to death in the flesh because he died according to the flesh alone; but he was made alive in the spirit because, through the operation of that spirit in which he came and preached to those whom he wished [Note: [Col. 0717] Nearly all manuscripts: “to those to whom he came, he preached.”], the same flesh was also made alive and rose again—the flesh in which he now comes to human beings.

21. Accordingly, it does not follow from the later statement concerning the unbelievers—“who will give an account to him who is ready to judge the living and the dead”—that we must understand the dead here as those who have departed from the body.

For he may have called the unbelievers dead—that is, dead in soul—of whom it is said, “Let the dead bury their dead” (Matthew 8:22). The living, however, are those who believe in him, not without reason hearing the words, “Awake, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ will shine upon you” (Ephesians 5:14). Of such people the Lord himself also says, “The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live” (John 5:25).

Likewise, what Peter says next—“For this is why the Gospel was preached even to the dead, so that, although they might be judged in the flesh according to human standards, they might live in the spirit according to God”—does not compel us to understand the passage as referring to hell. [Col. 0718]

For this reason the Gospel was preached in this life also to the dead, that is, to unbelievers and unrighteous people, so that, when they believed, they might indeed be judged in the flesh according to human standards—that is, through various tribulations and through the death of the flesh itself. Hence the same apostle says elsewhere that it is time for judgment to begin from the household of the Lord (1 Peter 4:17).

But they might live in the spirit according to God because they too had been put to death in that respect, being held by the death of unbelief and impiety.

22. Whoever is dissatisfied with this exposition of Peter’s words—or to whom, even if it is not displeasing, it is nevertheless insufficient—should seek to understand them with reference to hell. If such a person can resolve the matters that I mentioned above as troubling me, removing the doubt they cause, let him share the solution with me.

If this is done, those words may be understood in both ways. But this interpretation is not proved false by anything.

As for the questions you sent earlier, apart from the matter of seeing God through the body, which requires a greater work to be undertaken, I have answered as well as I could and sent the answers through the deacon Asellus, which I think you have by now received.

In your recent memorandum, to which I am now replying, you had asked two questions. Both have been treated—one at greater length, the other more briefly—namely, the words of the apostle Peter and the soul of the Lord.

I also remind you not to hesitate to send again a copy of your letter containing the question whether the substance of God can be seen bodily, as though in a place. Somehow that letter went astray among us, and although it was sought for a long time, it could not be found.

## LETTER CLXV

[Col. 0718]

**[Note: Revised with the assistance of manuscripts bl. bn. tt. vc. quinque. v., and of Am. Bad. Er. Lov.]**

**[Note: Elsewhere 27; the letter that was 165 is now 53. Written not long after the year 410.]**

Jerome to Marcellinus and Anapsychia, explaining various opinions concerning the origin of the soul, urging them to seek the remaining answers from Augustine, and indicating the studies with which he himself is occupied.

To the truly holy lords and sons worthy of veneration for every affection of service, MARCELLINUS **[Note: This Marcellinus is the tribune who was killed by the heretics under suspicion of Heraclianus’ tyranny, as we observed above in connection with Letter 151. Although this letter to Marcellinus was written not long after the year 410, it should not have been published separately from the following letter, since it has thus far been placed among Augustine’s letters in order to illuminate that letter.]** and ANAPSYCHIA, JEROME sends greetings in Christ.

## CHAPTER I

1. At last I have received from your Africa a letter from your Unity. I do not regret the boldness with which, although you remained silent, I repeatedly pressed my letters upon you, so that I might earn a reply and learn that you were safe—not from reports by others, but chiefly from your own words.

I remember your little question—or rather, your very great ecclesiastical question—concerning the condition of the soul:

Whether it fell from heaven, as the philosopher Pythagoras, all the Platonists, and Origen believe;

or whether it is from God’s own substance, as the Stoics, Mani, and the Spanish heresy of Priscillian suspect;

or whether souls are kept in God’s treasury, having been created long ago, as certain churchmen trust through foolish persuasion;

or whether they are made by God each day and sent into bodies, according to what is written in the Gospel: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17);

or, finally, whether they are propagated, as Tertullian, Apollinaris, and the greater part of the Westerners maintain—so that just as body comes from body, soul is born from soul, and exists in the same condition as the souls of irrational animals.

Concerning this matter, I know that I wrote what I thought in the short works against Rufinus, directed against the book that he gave to Anastasius of holy memory, bishop of the Roman Church. In that book, through a slippery and deceptive—or rather foolish—confession, while he tried to mock the simplicity of his listeners, he mocked his own faith—or rather his faithlessness.

I think that your holy father Oceanus has these books. They were published long ago, answering in many books Rufinus’ calumnies.

Certainly, you have there the holy and learned bishop Augustine, who, as they say, will be able to teach you by the living voice and explain his own opinion—or rather, our opinion through him.

## CHAPTER II

2. Long ago I wished to undertake the volume of Ezekiel and to fulfill my repeated promise to diligent readers. But at the very beginning of dictating it, my mind was so disturbed by the devastation of the western provinces, and especially of the city of Rome, that, according to the common proverb, I no longer knew even my own name. I remained silent for a long time, knowing that it was a time for tears.

This year, when I had explained three books, a sudden assault by the barbarians—of whom your Virgil says, “The Barcaeans wander far and wide” (Virgil, *Aeneid* 4)—and whom Holy Scripture describes in the case of Ishmael: “He shall dwell opposite all his brothers” (Genesis 16:12), swept along the border of Egypt, Palestine, Phoenicia, and Syria like a torrent, dragging everything with it, so that we scarcely managed to escape their hands through the mercy of Christ.

And if, according to the famous orator, “In times of war the laws are silent” (Cicero, *Pro Milone*), how much more do the studies of Scripture fall silent, since they require both a multitude of books and silence, the diligence of scribes, and—what is particularly necessary—security and leisure for those who dictate?

I have therefore sent two books to my holy daughter Fabiola. If you wish to have copies of them, you can borrow them from her. Because of the pressure of time, I could not have others transcribed. Once you have read them and seen the vestibules, you will easily infer what the house itself is going to be like.

But I trust in the mercy of God, who aided us at the most difficult beginning of the work mentioned above, that he will also aid us in the penultimate parts of the prophet, where the wars of Gog and Magog are narrated (Ezekiel 38–39), and in the final parts, where the construction, variety, and measurements of the most sacred and ineffable temple are described (ibid. 40–43).

## CHAPTER III
### 3

Our holy brother Oceanus, to whom you wish to be commended, is so great and distinguished, and so well instructed in the law of the Lord, that without our urging he can instruct you and, according to the measure of our common intelligence, explain our view concerning all the questions of Scripture. May Christ our almighty God preserve you safe and flourishing in a long life, truly holy lords.

### Concerning the Two Letters That Follow Immediately  
*(Book II of the Retractions, Chapter XLV)*

I also wrote two books to the presbyter Jerome, residing at Bethlehem: one on *The Origin of the Human Soul*; the other on *The Statement of the Apostle James*, where he says, “Whoever [Col. 0720] keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all of it” (James 2:10), consulting him about both matters. In the former, I myself did not solve the question that I had proposed; in the latter, however, I did not conceal what seemed to me to be its solution, but consulted him as to whether he approved it as well. He replied, praising the same consultation of mine, but answered that he had no leisure to respond.

While he was still alive, I did not wish to publish these books, lest perhaps he should at some time reply and they should be published more appropriately together with his reply. After his death, however, I published the former so that whoever reads it may be warned either not to ask at all how the soul is given to those who are born, or, at least, to accept concerning this most obscure matter a solution of the question that is not contrary to the clearest truths that the Catholic faith knows concerning original sin in infants, who, unless they are regenerated in Christ, are without doubt condemned. I published the latter so that the solution of the question discussed there which seemed satisfactory to us might itself become known. This work begins as follows: “Our God, who called us…”

## Book on the Origin of the Human Soul, or Letter 166

[Note: In preparing this recension, the following witnesses were collated: b. bl. c. ct. s. i. l. mr. r. sh. t. tt. vc.; two bn.; two th.; ten v.; and Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: Elsewhere numbered 28; what was formerly 166 is now 105. Written in the year 415, in the spring.]

Augustine to Jerome, reviewing the various opinions concerning the origin of the soul and wishing to be taught which should chiefly be held, and how the view that Jerome had, in the preceding letter, almost indicated as his own—namely, that individual souls are newly made for those who are born—can be defended against the doctrine of the Pelagians.

## Chapter I

### 1

I have prayed, and I continue to pray, that our God, who called us into his kingdom and glory (1 Thess. 2:12), may will that what I am writing to you, holy brother Jerome, consulting you about matters I do not know, may be fruitful for us. [Note: Lov. reads “may you will” (*velis*); Bad., Er., and the manuscripts read “may will” (*velit*).] Although you are much older in age than I am, I too am already an old man when I consult you. Yet, for learning what is necessary, no age seems late to me; for although it is more fitting for old men to teach than to learn, it is still more fitting to learn than to be ignorant of what they should teach.

Indeed, amid all the difficulties I suffer in dealing with the most difficult questions, I bear nothing more heavily than the absence of your Charity at so great a distance, so that I can scarcely send you my letters or receive yours, and then only at intervals not of days or months but of several years. If it were possible, I should wish to have you present every day, so that I might speak with you about whatever I wished. Nevertheless, I ought not for that reason to have failed to do what I could, merely because I could not do everything I wished.

### 2

Behold, there has come to me the religious young man Orosius, a brother in Catholic peace, a son in age, and our fellow presbyter in honor: alert in intelligence, ready in speech, burning with zeal, and desiring to be a useful vessel in the house of the Lord, [Col. 0721] for refuting the false and destructive doctrines that have slaughtered the souls of the Spaniards far more unhappily than the barbarian sword has slaughtered their bodies.

For this reason he hastened to us from the shore of the ocean, prompted by the report that from me he could hear whatever he wished to know. Nor did his arrival yield him no benefit. First, I prevented him from believing too much of the reputation he had heard about me. Then I taught the man what I could; and for what I could not, I pointed out where he might learn it, and urged him to go to you.

Since he willingly and obediently accepted my advice and instruction in this matter, I asked him, when he had come from you, to return through us to his own country. Holding fast to this promise of his, I believed that the Lord had granted me an opportunity to write to you about the things I desire to know through you. I had been looking for someone to send to you, but it was not easy for me to find a person suitable in fidelity of conduct, eagerness to obey, and experience of travel. When, therefore, I had tested this young man and found him to be the very kind of person I had been asking from the Lord, I could not doubt it.

## Chapter II

### 3

Receive, then, the matters that I ask you not to disdain to open and discuss for me. The question of the soul troubles many people, and I confess that I am among them. I will not conceal what I hold most firmly about the soul; then I will add what I still wish to have clarified.

The human soul is immortal in a certain respect of its own. For it is not immortal in every respect as God is, of whom it is said that he alone possesses immortality (1 Tim. 6:16). Holy Scripture, after all, mentions many deaths of the soul; hence the saying, “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Matt. 8:22). Yet the soul dies in such a way, when alienated from the life of God, that it nevertheless does not entirely cease to live in its own nature. Thus it is found to be mortal for some reason, while it is also reasonably called immortal.

The soul is not a part of God. For if it were, it would be wholly unchangeable and incorruptible. If that were so, it would neither decline for the worse nor advance for the better; nor would anything in itself begin to possess what it had not possessed, or cease to possess what it had possessed, insofar as its own affections are concerned. That it is otherwise needs no external testimony: whoever turns attention to himself recognizes it.

Those who wish the soul to be a part of God say in vain that the stain and disgrace we see in the most wicked human beings, and finally the weakness and sickness that we feel in all human beings, do not arise from the soul itself but from the body. What difference does it make from where the soul becomes sick, if, were it unchangeable, it could not become sick from any source? For what is truly unchangeable and incorruptible cannot be changed or corrupted by the addition of anything else. Otherwise not only Achilles, as the myths relate, but all flesh would be invulnerable if no accident could befall it.

Therefore a nature that is changeable in some way, for some reason, or in some respect is not unchangeable. But it is impious to believe that God is anything other than truly and supremely unchangeable. The soul, therefore, is not a part of God.

### 4

I am also convinced that the soul is incorporeal, although this can be difficult to persuade those who are slower to understand. But lest I either needlessly [Col. 0722] provoke a dispute about a word or rightly suffer one, since when the matter is clear there is no need to quarrel about the name: if every substance or essence—or whatever more suitable term may now be used for that which in some way exists in itself—is a body, then the soul is a body.

Likewise, if one wishes to call only that nature incorporeal which is supremely unchangeable and wholly present everywhere, then the soul is a body, since it is not such a thing.

Further, if a body is only that which is established or moved through the extension of a place, with some length, breadth, and height, so that the greater part of it occupies a greater place and the smaller part a smaller one, and so that it is less in a part than in the whole, then the soul is not a body.

For the soul extends through the whole body that it animates, not by local diffusion but by a certain vital tension. It is wholly present at once through all its parts; it is not less in smaller parts or greater in larger ones, but is more intensely present in some places and less intensely in others, while it is wholly present both in all parts together and in each individual part.

Otherwise, although something is perceived in only a part of the body, the whole soul would not perceive it as a whole. [Note: Several manuscripts read: “although something occurs in a part of the body, nevertheless the whole soul perceives it,” etc.] When some small point in living flesh is touched, even though that place is not merely less than the whole body but scarcely visible as part of the body, the whole soul is nevertheless not unaware of it. Nor does what is sensed travel through the entire body; it is sensed only where it occurs.

How, then, does what does not occur throughout the body immediately reach the whole soul, unless the soul is wholly present there where the event occurs, without abandoning the other parts in order to be wholly present there? For the other parts remain alive because the soul is present in them, even where nothing of this kind has happened. If such an event were occurring there too, and both events occurred simultaneously, the whole soul would be equally unaware of neither.

Accordingly, the soul could not be wholly present simultaneously in all the parts and in each individual part of its body if it were diffused through them in the way we see bodies diffused through spatial regions, occupying smaller spaces with their smaller parts and larger spaces with their larger parts.

Therefore, if the soul is to be called a body, it certainly is not a body of the kind that is earthly, nor one that is watery, airy, or ethereal. All such bodies are greater in larger places and smaller in smaller places, and none of them is wholly present in any one of its parts. Their parts occupy places in proportion to the parts of the bodies themselves.

From this it is understood that the soul, whether it is to be called a body or incorporeal, has a nature of its own. It was created as a substance superior to all these elements of the world’s mass. It cannot truly be conceived through any image of bodily forms that we perceive by the senses of the flesh; rather, it is understood by the mind and experienced through life.

I do not say these things, therefore, in order to teach you what is already known to you, but to disclose what I hold most firmly about the soul, lest anyone, when I come to the matters I am asking about, suppose that I hold nothing about the soul either by knowledge or by faith.

### 5

I am also certain that the soul fell into sin neither through any fault of God, nor through any necessity imposed by God or by itself, but through its own will. Nor can it be freed from this body of death by the power of its own will, as though that were sufficient for it, nor by the death of the body itself, but only by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord (Rom. 7:24–25).

Nor is there any soul at all in the human race for whose liberation [Col. 0723] the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, is not necessary.

Whatever soul, at whatever age of the body, departs from the body without the grace of the Mediator and his sacrament will enter future punishment and, at the last judgment, will receive a body for punishment. But if, after human generation—which came from Adam—it is regenerated in Christ and belongs to his fellowship, it will have rest after the death of the body and will receive the body for glory.

These are the things I hold most firmly about the soul.

## Chapter III

### 6

Now receive, I ask, what I am seeking, and do not despise me. [Note: Four manuscripts read: “if he does not despise you.” Bad. and Er. read: “lest he despise you.”] May he who deigned to be despised for us not despise you. I ask where the soul contracted the guilt by which it is dragged into condemnation, even in the case of an infant overtaken by death, if the grace of Christ does not come to its aid through the sacrament by which infants too are baptized.

For you are not among those who have recently begun to chatter out some novel doctrine, saying that no guilt derived from Adam is absolved through baptism in an infant. If I knew that you held this view—or rather, if I did not know that you did not hold it—I would certainly not ask you about it or think that it needed to be asked.

But because we know your opinion on this matter to agree with the deeply grounded Catholic faith, by which, when refuting the empty talk of Jovinian, you also brought forward testimony from the Book of Job: “No one is clean in your sight, not even an infant whose life upon the earth is but one day” (Job 15:4, according to the Septuagint), and then added, “And we are held guilty in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (Jerome, *Against Jovinian*, Book 2); and because your book on the prophet Jonah makes this sufficiently and remarkably clear, where you said that infants were rightly compelled to fast on account of that very original sin (Jerome, *On Jonah*), I ask you without impropriety where the soul contracted this guilt, on account of which it is necessary for it to be freed even at that age through the sacrament of Christian grace.

### 7

Some years ago, when I was writing certain books on Free Will, which circulated among many people and are now possessed by a great number, I treated four opinions concerning the soul’s incarnation as follows: whether all other souls are propagated from the one soul that was first given to the first human being; whether new souls are now made individually for each person; whether souls already existing somewhere are either sent by God or spontaneously fall into bodies.

I thought that these views should be discussed in such a way that, whichever of them might be true, it would not impede the purpose for which I was then contending with all the strength I possessed against those who attempt to introduce a nature of evil endowed with its own principle, in opposition to God—that is, against the Manichaeans [Note: Lov. reads *editam* (“set forth”); the older editions and manuscripts read *praeditam* (“endowed”).] (*On Free Will*, Book 3, chapter 21). At that time I had still heard nothing about the Priscillianists, who invent blasphemies not very different from those of the Manichaeans.

For this reason I did not add a fifth opinion, which you mentioned among the others in your letter, so that you would omit none when replying to the question put to you by Marcellinus, a man of revered memory and most dear to us in the love of Christ. You wrote that the soul is a part [Col. 0724] of God [Note: The editions read “that the soul is not a part of God.” The negation has been removed, since it is absent from the better manuscripts; for the Manichaeans held that the soul is a part of God.]: first, because when this question is asked, the issue concerns not its incarnation but its nature; and second, because this is what those against whom I was arguing believe. My chief purpose was to distinguish the blameless and inviolate nature of the Creator from the faults and corruption of the creature, whereas they maintain that the very substance of the good God, insofar as it has been captured, has been corrupted and oppressed by the substance of evil, to which they assign its own principle and rulers, and has been brought into the necessity of sinning.

Apart from this error of heretical opinion, I desire to know which of the remaining four opinions should be chosen. Whatever is to be chosen, may it not oppose this faith of which we are certain: that every soul, even that of a little infant, needs liberation from the obligation of sin, and that such liberation exists only through Jesus Christ, and him crucified.

## Chapter IV

### 8

Therefore, to be brief, you certainly hold that God now makes individual souls for individual persons who are born. If it is objected to this view that God completed all creatures on the sixth day and rested on the seventh, you cite the testimony of the Gospel: “My Father is working until now” (John 5:17).

This is what you wrote to Marcellinus. In that letter you also most kindly deigned to mention me, saying that he had me here in Africa, so that I could more easily explain the matter to him (Sap., Letter 165). If I had been able to do so, he would not have inquired of you, situated so far away—provided, that is, that he wrote to you about this from Africa. I do not know when he wrote; I know only that he was well aware of my hesitation about this matter. That is why he wished to act without consulting me.

Even if he had consulted me, I would have been more inclined to urge him and to give thanks that something could be contributed [Note: The editions read “contribute” (*conferre*).] for the benefit of us all, unless you preferred to reply briefly rather than answer fully. I suppose you did so lest you labor needlessly, since I was here, whom you thought knew best what he had asked.

Behold, I wish that this opinion were mine as well, but I do not yet affirm that it is.

### 9

You sent disciples to me so that I might teach what I myself have not yet learned. Teach me, then, what I am to teach. Many demand that I teach it, and I confess to them that I am ignorant of this just as of many other things. Perhaps, although they are ashamed to say it to my face, they nevertheless say among themselves, “You are the teacher of Israel, and you do not know these things?” (John 3:10).

The Lord said this to one of those who delighted in being called “Rabbi.” He had therefore come by night to the true teacher, perhaps because he was ashamed to learn after having been accustomed to teach.

As for me, I prefer to hear a teacher rather than to be heard as though I were a teacher. I remember what he said to those whom he chose above the others: “Do not allow yourselves to be called Rabbi by human beings; for one is your teacher, Christ” (Matt. 23:8).

It was no other teacher who taught Moses even through Jethro (Exod. 18:14–23), nor Cornelius even through the earlier Peter (Acts 10:25–48), nor Peter even through the later Paul (Gal. 2:11–21). For whoever speaks the truth speaks it by the gift of him who is Truth itself. [Col. 0725]

What if we still do not know these things for this reason: so that we may be tested not only in how lovingly we teach the unlearned, but also in how humbly we learn from the learned?

### 10

Teach me, then, I ask, what I am to teach; teach me what I am to hold; and tell me this: if souls are made individually for each person who is born today, where do they sin in infants, so that they require the forgiveness of sin in Christ’s sacrament, as those who sinned in Adam, from whom the sinful flesh has been propagated?

Or, if they do not sin, by what justice of the Creator are they so bound by another’s sin, when they are inserted into mortal members propagated from that source, that condemnation overtakes them unless the Church comes to their aid, even though it is not within their power to obtain the assistance of baptismal grace?

How, then, are the many thousands of souls who depart from the bodies of infants at death without the pardon of the Christian sacrament condemned justly, if, newly created [Note: In a considerable number of manuscripts, “creatures” (*creaturae*).] and without any preceding sin of their own, they were individually joined to each individual born by the will of the Creator, who created and gave them in order to animate each person—although he certainly knew that each of them would depart from the body without the baptism of Christ through no fault of its own?

Since, therefore, we can neither say of God that he compels souls to become sinful or punishes the innocent, nor may we deny that those who depart from their bodies without Christ’s sacrament—even infants—are drawn into condemnation, I beg you: how is this opinion defended, according to which souls are believed not all to be made from that one soul of the first human being, but, just as that one was made for one person, so individual souls are made for individual persons?

## Chapter V

### 11

I think I can easily refute the other arguments brought against this opinion, such as the one by which some seem to press it: how did God complete all his works on the sixth day and rest on the seventh (Gen. 2:2), if he is still creating new souls?

If we answer them with what you included from the Gospel in the letter mentioned above—“My Father is working until now”—they reply that “working” means administering established things, not establishing new natures, lest this contradict the text of Genesis, where it is stated most plainly that God completed all his works.

And when Scripture says that he rested, they say that this must be understood as his resting from creating new creatures, not from governing them. For at that time he made things that did not exist, and from making them he rested, because he had completed everything that, before it existed, he saw needed to be made. Thereafter he created and made whatever he made not from things that did not exist but from things that already existed.

Thus both statements are shown to be true: that he rested from his works, and that he is working until now, since the Gospel cannot contradict Genesis.

### 12

But to those who say these things in order to prevent belief that God now makes new souls, as he made that one soul which did not exist, and instead creates them from that one which already existed—or sends them from some fountain or treasury that he made at that time—it is easily replied that during those six days God also created many things from natures he had already created, such as birds and fish from the waters, and trees, grass, and animals from the [Col. 0726] earth.

Yet it is clear that at that time he made things that did not exist. There was no bird, no fish, no tree, and no animal. It is therefore rightly understood that he rested from creating those things which did not exist and were created—that is, that he ceased creating things that did not previously exist.

But now, when it is said that he does not send souls already existing in some unknown fountain, nor sprinkle them from himself as though they were his own parts, nor derive them originally from that one soul, nor fetter them with bodily bonds on account of sins committed before the flesh, but creates new souls individually for each person born, this is not said to be something he had not done before.

For on the sixth day he had already made the human being in his own image. This is understood to have been done according to the rational soul. [Note: Five Vatican and six French manuscripts add after this: “At last, after a long discussion, you confirmed the ecclesiastical opinion. This he does even now,” etc.]

This is what he does now as well—not establishing what did not exist, but multiplying what did exist. Hence it is true both that he rested from establishing things that did not exist and that he continues to work, not only by governing what he made but also by creating more abundantly something that he had already created, not something that did not yet exist.

Thus, either in this way or in any other, we escape the objection concerning God’s rest from his works, so that it does not prevent us from believing that new souls are still being made—not from that one soul, but in the same manner as that one.

### 13

As for the question, “Why does he make souls for those whom he knows will die soon?” we can answer that in this way the sins of the parents are either exposed or chastised.

We can also rightly leave such matters to the governance of the one whom we know to give to all temporal things that pass away—including the births and deaths of animals—a course of the greatest beauty and order, although we are unable to perceive these things. If we could perceive them, we would be soothed by ineffable delight.

For it was not without reason that the prophet, who had learned these matters by divine inspiration, said of God: “He brings forth the world according to number” [Note: The Septuagint reads, in Isaiah 40:26, *ho ekpherōn kat’ arithmon ton kosmon autou*—“he who brings forth his world according to number.”]

Hence music—that is, the art or sense of arranging sounds harmoniously—was granted by God’s generosity even to mortal beings who possess rational souls, as a reminder of a great truth.

If a human being who is skilled in composing a song knows what durations to assign to which sounds, so that what is sung may proceed and pass beautifully through sounds that depart and follow one another, how much more does God, whose wisdom, through which he made all things, surpass all arts by far, permit no intervals of time in things that come into being and pass away—intervals that are like syllables and words belonging to the parts of this age—to pass either more briefly or at greater length than the previously known and determined harmony requires, in this wondrous song of transient things?

I have said this even about the leaf of a tree and the number of the hairs on our heads. How much more does it apply to the coming into being and passing away of a human being, whose temporal life is extended for a shorter or longer duration only as God, the disposer of times, knows to be consonant with the ordering of the whole?

### 14

Nor does the argument that everything that begins to exist in [Col. 0727] time cannot be immortal move our faith. They say that everything born dies and everything that grows oldens, and thus attempt to compel belief that the human mind is immortal because it was created before all times.

To say nothing of other matters, the immortality of Christ’s flesh began in time, yet it no longer dies, and death will no longer rule over him (Rom. 6:9).

### 15

Nor am I troubled by what you wrote in your book against Rufinus: that some people slander this opinion because it seems unworthy of God to give souls to adulterous conceptions, and that they therefore attempt to establish that, on account of merits acquired in a life lived before the flesh, souls may justly be brought into such prisons (*Against Rufinus*, Book 3).

I think of many considerations by which this slander can be refuted. Your own answer is an elegant comparison: the fault does not lie in the seed of wheat, although it is said to have been stolen, but in the person who stole the grain; nor should the earth therefore have failed to warm the seeds in its womb because the sower cast them forth with an unclean hand.

Even before I read this, the objection concerning adulterous offspring caused me no difficulty in this question, since I considered generally that God makes many good things even from our evils and our sins.

The creation of any animal, if it has a pious and prudent observer, awakens ineffable praise of the Creator. How much more does the creation not of just any animal but of a human being do so!

If the reason for creating is sought, no answer can be given more quickly or more suitably than this: every creature of God is good. And what is more worthy than that a good God should make good things, which no one but God can make?

## Chapter VI

### 16

These and other arguments that I can make, insofar as I can, I set forth against those who try to undermine the opinion according to which souls are made individually for individuals, as that one soul was made for one person.

But when we come to the punishments of infants, believe me, I am pressed by great difficulties and find absolutely no answer. I mean not only the punishments they suffer after this life, the condemnation into which they must be drawn if they depart from the body without the sacrament of Christian grace, but also the very sufferings that pass before our eyes in this life and afflict us. If I wished to enumerate them, time would run out before the examples: they languish in sicknesses, are tortured by pains, tormented by hunger and thirst, weakened in their limbs, deprived of their senses, and harassed by unclean spirits.

It must surely be shown how they justly suffer these things without any evil cause of their own. For it is not permissible to say either that these things occur without God’s knowledge, or that he is unable to resist those who cause them, or that he either does or permits them unjustly.

Can we rightly say, as we say of irrational animals, that human beings are given for the use of superior natures, even when those natures are vicious, just as we plainly see in the Gospel that the swine were granted to the demons for the use they desired (Matt. 8:32)? Can we rightly say this about a human being as well? A human being is an animal, but a rational one, even though mortal.

The soul is rational in those members that pay the penalty through such great afflictions. God is good, God is just, God is almighty; it is utterly insane to doubt this. Let the just cause, then, of the many evils inflicted on infants be stated.

When adults [Col. 0728] suffer such things, we usually say either that their merits are being tested, as in Job, or that their sins are being punished, as in Herod. From certain examples that God wished to make clear, human beings are permitted to infer other matters that remain obscure. But this applies to adults.

What answer are we to give concerning infants? Explain it, if no sins are being punished in them by such great sufferings. For certainly at those ages there is no righteousness being tested.

### 17

What shall I say about the diversity—or rather, the absurdity [Note: Bad., Am., Er., and eleven manuscripts omit “or rather, the absurdity.”]—of intellectual capacities? It is hidden in infants, but, deriving from their very natural beginnings, it becomes visible in adults. Some are so slow and forgetful that they cannot learn even the first elements of the letters; others are so foolish that they differ little from cattle. Such people are commonly called idiots.

Perhaps the answer is made: “The bodies cause this.” But according to the opinion we wish to defend, did the soul choose its body and, being deceived in its choice, make a mistake? Or, when it was compelled to enter a body by the necessity of birth, did it find no other body because crowds of souls had already occupied them, and so, just as at some spectacle it takes whatever seat it can, did it occupy not the flesh it wished but the flesh it was able to obtain?

Can we either say or think such things? Teach us, then, what we ought to think and say, so that the rationale of newly made souls, individually assigned to individual bodies, may become clear to us.

## Chapter VII

### 18

In those books on Free Will I did say something about the punishments that infants suffer in this life, although not about their intellectual capacities. I will explain what it was, and why it does not suffice for me in the question now before us; I will also insert here the passage itself, excerpted from the third book.

It reads as follows:

“Concerning the bodily sufferings by which infants are afflicted—who, by reason of their age, have no sins—if the souls by which they are animated did not exist before the human beings themselves began to exist, a greater complaint, a kind of merciful protest, is usually made when it is said, ‘What evil have they done that they should suffer these things?’ as though there could be a merit of innocence before anyone is able to do harm.

“But when God accomplishes something good in correcting adults, when they are chastised through the sufferings and deaths of their little ones, who are dear to them, why should these things not occur, since, once they have passed away, they will be as though they had not occurred to those in whom they occurred? Those for whose sake they occurred will either become better, if, corrected by temporal hardships, they choose to live more rightly; or they will have no excuse at the punishment of the future judgment if, through the anguish of this life, they were unwilling to turn their desire toward eternal life.

“Who knows what God reserves in the secrecy of his judgments as a good compensation for the infants whose sufferings either break the hardness of adults, exercise their faith, or test their mercy? Who, then, knows what good compensation God reserves for the infants themselves? Although they have done nothing rightly, they have nevertheless not suffered these things as sinners.

“For it is not without reason that the Church commends those infants who were killed when Herod sought to kill our Lord Jesus Christ, receiving them into the honor of the martyrs [Col. 0729]” (*On Free Will*, Book 3, chapter 23, section 67).

### 19

I said these things at that time because I wished to reinforce the very opinion now under discussion. As I mentioned shortly before, whichever of those four opinions concerning the soul’s incarnation was true, I was striving to demonstrate that the Creator’s substance was blameless and as far removed as possible from participation in our sins.

Therefore, whichever of them could be shown by the truth to be defeated and rejected was irrelevant to the purpose I then had. Once all had been examined through a careful discussion, whichever of them rightly overcame the others would have left me entirely secure, since I was demonstrating that, according to all of them, the position I was defending remained undefeated.

Now, however, I wish, if I can, to choose one of them by sound reasoning. For that reason, when I look more attentively at my words in the passage I have quoted from that book, I do not see a strong and firm defense of the very opinion now under discussion.

### 20

For its apparent foundation is what I said there:

“Who knows what God reserves in the secrecy of his judgments as a good compensation for the infants whose sufferings either break the hardness of adults, exercise their faith, or test their mercy? Who, then, knows what good compensation God reserves for the infants themselves?”

But I see that this can rightly be said of those who either suffer something of this kind, even without knowing it, for the sake of Christ’s name and true religion, or who have already been imbued with Christ’s sacrament. For they cannot be freed from condemnation without fellowship with the one Mediator, so that this compensation may also be granted to them for the evils they endured here amid various afflictions.

But now, since the question cannot be resolved unless we also answer concerning those infants who die after the most grievous sufferings without the sacrament of Christian fellowship, what compensation can be conceived for them, when condemnation has additionally been prepared for them?

In the same book I also gave an answer concerning the baptism of infants—not indeed sufficiently, but as far as seemed adequate for that work—insofar as baptism benefits even those who are unaware and do not yet possess their own faith. At that time, however, I did not think that anything needed to be said about the condemnation of those infants who depart from this life without baptism, because the issue then being treated was not the issue now before us.

21. But even if we set aside and disregard those things that are suffered for a short time and which, once past, cannot be recalled, can we likewise disregard that “through one man there is death, and through one man the resurrection of the dead. For just as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Cor. 15:21–22)? Through this apostolic, divine, and clear pronouncement it shines forth plainly enough that no one enters death except through Adam, and no one enters eternal life except through Christ. For this is the meaning of “all” in both places: just as all human beings belong to Adam through the first, that is, carnal, generation, so all human beings come to the second, that is, spiritual, generation—those, namely, who come to Christ. Therefore it is said both here “all” and there “all”: just as all who die die only in Adam: [Col. 0730] so all who will be made alive will be made alive only in Christ.

Accordingly, whoever tells us that anyone can be made alive in the resurrection of the dead except in Christ must be detested as a pestilence [Note: Thuanus Manuscript: “enemy”] of the common faith. Likewise, whoever says that even infants who depart this life without participation in his Sacrament will be made alive in Christ is plainly contradicting apostolic preaching and condemning the whole Church, where people hasten and run to have infants baptized precisely because it is undoubtedly believed that they cannot be made alive in Christ in any other way.

But whoever is not made alive in Christ must remain in that condemnation of which the Apostle says: “Through one offense [judgment came] upon all human beings to condemnation” (Rom. 5:18). That infants are born subject to this offense is believed by the whole Church; and you yourself, when disputing against Jovinian and expounding the prophet Jonah, as I recalled shortly before, have already defined this with the most certain faith. I believe that you have done so also in other places among your shorter works, which I have either not read or do not presently remember.

I therefore seek the cause of this condemnation in infants, because, if souls are newly created individually for each person, I see no sin in them at that age, nor do I believe that God condemns any soul which he sees to possess no sin.

## CHAPTER VIII

22. Or should it perhaps be said that, in an infant, the flesh alone is the cause of sin, while a new soul is made for the child? If that soul lives according to God’s commandments, with the help of Christ’s grace, and is able to tame and subjugate the flesh itself, it can acquire the merit of incorruption. But because, in an infant, the soul is not yet able to do this unless it has received Christ’s Sacrament, through this grace the flesh acquires what the soul’s conduct could not yet obtain. If, however, the infant’s soul departs without that Sacrament, would the soul itself indeed be in eternal life, from which no sin could separate it, while its flesh would not rise in Christ because it had not received the Sacrament before death?

23. I have never heard or read this opinion. But I have plainly heard and believed the following, on account of which I also have said: “The hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice; and they will come forth, those who have done good, to the resurrection of life” (John 5:28–29). This is the resurrection of which it is said, “through one man, the resurrection of the dead”; this is the resurrection in which “all will be made alive in Christ.” “But those who have done evil” will rise “to the resurrection of judgment.”

What, then, are we to understand here about those infants who, before they were able to do either good or evil, were deprived of their bodies without Baptism? Nothing is said here about such persons. But if their flesh will not rise for this reason—that they did neither good nor evil—then neither will the flesh of those rise who died at that age after receiving the grace of Baptism, when they could do neither good nor evil.

If, however, the latter will rise among the saints, that is, among those who did good, among whom will those others rise, unless it is among those who did evil? Are we then to believe that certain human souls will not receive their bodies, whether for the resurrection of life or for the resurrection of judgment?

Before this opinion is refuted, it already displeases us by its very novelty [Col. 0731]. Moreover, who could tolerate the belief that those who hurry with their infants to Baptism are hurrying for the sake of their flesh, not their souls? Blessed Cyprian, preserving the Church’s most firmly established faith rather than formulating any new decree, was correcting those who thought that an infant should not be baptized before the eighth day after birth. He said that it was not the flesh but the soul that must not be lost, and maintained, with some of his fellow bishops, that a newborn could rightly be baptized immediately (Cyprian, Letter 59, to Fidus).

24. Let everyone think what he wishes concerning some opinion of Cyprian, where perhaps he did not see what needed to be seen. Only let no one think contrary to the unmistakably clear apostolic faith, which proclaims that, because of one offense, all are led into condemnation, and that no one is freed from this condemnation except by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, in whom alone all are made alive who are made alive.

Let no one think contrary to the Church’s most firmly established practice. If people ran to Baptism only for the sake of infants’ bodies, then dead infants would be brought forward for baptism.

25. Since this is so, we must seek and provide the reason why souls newly created individually for each person are condemned if infants die apart from Christ’s Sacrament. That they are condemned if they depart the body in this condition is attested both by Holy Scripture and by the holy Church.

Therefore, if that opinion concerning the creation of new souls does not oppose this most firmly established faith, let it also be mine; but if it opposes it, let it not be yours.

26. I do not want it said to me that this opinion ought to be supported by what is written: “He who formed the spirit of the human being within him” (Zech. 12:1), and, “He who formed their hearts individually” (Ps. 32:15). Something utterly powerful and unconquerable must be sought—something that does not compel us to believe that God condemns any souls without some fault of theirs.

For creating perhaps has equal force with forming, or perhaps even greater force. Yet it is written: “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Ps. 51:12). It cannot therefore be supposed that the soul is here wishing to be made before it existed. Thus, just as an already existing soul is created through renewal in righteousness, so an already existing soul is formed through the shaping influence of teaching.

Nor does the statement written in Ecclesiastes confirm the opinion we wish to make our own: “Then the dust will return to the earth as it was, and the spirit will return to God who gave it” (Eccles. 12:7). Indeed, this supports more strongly those who think that all souls come from one soul. For, they say, just as the dust returns to the earth as it was, although the flesh of which this was said does not return to the human being from whom it was propagated, but to the earth from which the first human being was made, so the spirit propagated from that one spirit does not return to him, but to the Lord by whom it was given to him.

But because this testimony sounds so much in their favor that it does not appear wholly opposed to the opinion I wish to defend, I have thought it sufficient merely to call your prudence to mind, lest you try to rescue me from these difficulties by means of such testimonies. For although no one can make something true by wishing it true when it is not true, nevertheless, if it could be so, I would wish this opinion to be true; just as I wish that, if it is true, you would defend it with the utmost clarity and invincibility [Col. 0732].

## CHAPTER IX

27. This difficulty also confronts those who think that souls already existing elsewhere, prepared by God from the beginning of his works, are sent by him into bodies. For they too must answer the same question: if souls without guilt obediently come to the places to which they are sent, why are they punished in infants if the infants end this life without Baptism?

The difficulty is precisely the same in both opinions. Those who assert that souls are individually joined to individual bodies according to the merits of a former life seem to themselves to escape this question more easily. They think that “dying in Adam” means suffering punishment in the flesh propagated from Adam. From this guilt, they say, Christ’s grace frees the little along with the great.

This is correct, true, and entirely sound: Christ’s grace frees the little along with the great from the guilt of sins. But I do not believe, accept, or agree that souls sinned in another, earlier life and were then thrust into bodily prisons. First, because these people say [Note: Fifteen manuscripts: “These people bring this about through I know not what cycles.”] that this happens through I know not what cycles, so that after I know not how many ages have passed, one must return again to this burden of corruptible flesh and undergo punishment. I do not know what more horrible notion could be imagined.

Furthermore, what righteous person has ever died concerning whom we should not be anxious—if these people are right—that, while sinning in Abraham’s bosom, he might be cast into the flames of that rich man (Luke 16:22–23)? Why should he not be able to sin after this body if he was able to sin before it?

Finally, it is one thing to have sinned in Adam, of whom the Apostle says, “in whom all sinned,” and another thing to have sinned somewhere outside Adam and therefore to be thrust into Adam—that is, into the flesh propagated from Adam—as into a prison.

As for the opinion that all souls come from one soul, I do not wish to examine it unless necessity requires it. And would that the opinion we are now discussing, if it is true, were defended by you in such a way that this necessity no longer existed.

28. Although I desire, ask, ardently pray, and await that the Lord, through you, remove my ignorance of this matter, nevertheless, if—God forbid—I should not have deserved this, I shall ask our Lord God for patience. We believe in him in such a way that, even if he does not reveal certain things to us when we knock, we must in no way murmur against him.

[Note: Thirteen manuscripts: “Let us remember [what was said] to the Apostles themselves,” etc.] I remember that the Apostles themselves were told beforehand: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16:12). As far as I am concerned, I should count this matter among them. Nor should I be indignant that I am unworthy to know it, lest by this very reaction I prove myself even more unworthy.

I am similarly ignorant of many other matters, which I can neither recall nor enumerate. I would endure this ignorance tolerably enough if I did not fear that some one of these opinions might steal into unwary minds against that which we hold with the firmest faith.

But before I know which of them ought rather to be chosen, I openly declare that I do not rashly think this: whichever opinion is true cannot be opposed to that strongest and most firmly grounded faith by which Christ’s Church [Col. 0733] believes that even infants, human beings most recently born, cannot be freed from condemnation except by the grace of Christ’s name, which he has commended in his Sacraments.

# A BOOK ON THE STATEMENT OF JAMES, OR LETTER 167

[Note: Corrected by collation with manuscripts bl, c, fs, mr, tt, vc; two manuscripts designated e; two sb; eight v; and editions Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: Elsewhere numbered 29; what was formerly 167 is now 89. Written at the same time.]

Augustine to Jerome, concerning the passage in James 2:10, “Whoever stumbles in one point has become guilty of all”: with much discussion of the Stoics, who taught that all sins are equal, and that whoever possessed one virtue possessed them all, while whoever lacked one possessed none.

## CHAPTER I

1. What I wrote to you, my honored brother in Christ, Jerome, asking about the human soul—whether, if new souls are still made individually for each person at birth, they acquire the bond of sin that, as we do not doubt, must be loosed even in newly born infants through the Sacrament of Christ’s grace—was becoming a work of considerable length. I therefore did not wish to burden it with any other question. But what presses more urgently must even less be neglected. Therefore I ask and implore you by God to explain to me—for I think it will benefit many—how we are to understand what is written in the Epistle of the Apostle James: “Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all.” Or, if you already have an exposition of it, whether by yourself or by someone else, send it to us. The matter is of such a kind and importance that I greatly regret not having written to you about it long ago.

2. The question concerns the conduct of our present life and how we may attain eternal life, not the investigation of a past life that oblivion has completely engulfed—as in the question I thought should be raised concerning the soul.

A saying is elegantly reported that fits this matter very well. When someone had fallen into a well in which there was enough water to receive him and keep him from dying rather than to suffocate him and prevent him from speaking, another person approached. Seeing him, the newcomer asked in astonishment [Note: Ten manuscripts: “asked compassionately”], “How did you fall in here?” The man replied, “Please consider how you may get me out; do not ask how I fell in.”

Thus, since we confess and hold by catholic faith that even the soul of an infant must be freed by Christ’s grace from the guilt of sin as from a well, it is enough for that infant that we know the way by which it is saved, even if we never know how it entered that evil condition.

I nevertheless thought the question ought to be raised, lest we inadvertently hold one of those opinions about the soul’s incarnation that altogether contradicts the need to free the infant’s soul by denying that it is in this evil condition.

Let us therefore hold with the utmost firmness that an infant’s soul must be freed from the guilt of sin, and that it can be freed in no other way than by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord. [Col. 0734] If we can also know the cause and origin of this evil, we shall be better and more fully equipped to resist not disputants but empty talkers and contentious people. If we cannot, however, the fact that the beginning of misery is hidden must not make the work of mercy grow sluggish.

Against those who seem to themselves to know what they do not know, we are safer because we are not ignorant of our own ignorance. For it is one thing not to know something whose ignorance is harmful; it is another not to know something that either cannot be known, or need not be known, or is irrelevant to the life we seek. But the matter I now inquire into from the writings of the Apostle James concerns the very conduct of life in which we live and strive to please God so that we may live forever.
