3. How, then, I beg you, are we to understand this statement: “Whoever keeps the whole Law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all”? Does someone who commits theft—or indeed someone who says to a rich man, “Sit here,” but to a poor man, “Stand there”—thereby become guilty of murder, adultery, and sacrilege?

If not, how has the person who stumbles in one point become guilty of all? Or does what he said about the rich and poor not belong with these matters—so that whoever stumbles in one of them becomes guilty of all?

We must recall where that statement came from, what preceding words produced it, and to what words it is connected and from which it depends.

“My brothers,” he says, “do not hold the faith of our glorious Lord Jesus Christ with partiality. For if a man wearing a gold ring in splendid clothing enters your assembly, and a poor man in filthy clothing also enters, and you look upon the one wearing the splendid clothing and say to him, ‘You sit here in a good place,’ while you say to the poor man, ‘You stand there,’ or, ‘Sit under my footstool,’ are you not judging among yourselves and becoming judges with evil thoughts?

“Listen, my beloved brothers: has not God chosen the poor of this world, rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom which God promised to those who love him? But you have dishonored the poor”—the one, evidently, to whom it was said, “Stand there,” while the man wearing the gold ring was told, “You sit here in a good place.”

Then he continues, developing and explaining the same point at greater length:

“Do not the rich oppress you by their power and drag you before the courts? Do they not blaspheme the good name that has been invoked over you? If you fulfill the royal law according to Scripture, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself,’ you do well. But if you show partiality, you commit sin, being convicted by the law as transgressors.”

Observe how he calls those who say to the rich man, “Sit here,” and to the poor man, “Stand there,” transgressors of the law. Observe also that, lest they should think it a trivial sin to transgress the law in this one matter, he immediately adds: “Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all.”

For he who said, “You shall not commit adultery,” also said, “You shall not kill.” If you do not kill but do commit adultery, you have become a transgressor of the law”—because of what he had said, “being convicted by the law as transgressors.”

Since this is so, it appears to follow—unless some other interpretation is demonstrated—that whoever says to the rich man, “Sit here,” and to the poor man, “Stand there,” while giving the former honor, must be judged guilty of every crime: of idolatry, blasphemy, adultery, [Col. 0735] murder, and, not to list everything at length, all the rest. For “he who stumbles in one point has become guilty of all.”

## CHAPTER II

4. But, someone may object, does not the person who has one virtue possess them all, while the person who lacks one possesses none? If this is true, it confirms the present interpretation. But I want this statement explained, not confirmed; for in itself it is firmer among us than all the authority of the philosophers.

Even if what is said about virtues and vices is true, it does not follow that all sins are therefore equal. As for the inseparability of the virtues, although I may be mistaken—and if I remember correctly, which I scarcely do—it pleased all philosophers who said that those same virtues are necessary for the conduct of life.

But only the Stoics dared to argue that sins are equal, against the entire common sense of the human race. You most clearly convicted this folly in that Jovinianus who was a Stoic in this doctrine but an Epicurean in pursuing and defending pleasures, using the Holy Scriptures (Jerome, *Against Jovinianus*, Book 2).

In that delightful and distinguished work of yours it became sufficiently clear that our authorities—or rather the truth that spoke through them—did not approve the claim that all sins are equal.

I shall try, with the Lord’s help, to explain as far as I can how it is possible that, even if this is true of the virtues, we are nevertheless not compelled to admit the equality of all sins. If I succeed, you will approve; where I fall short of the argument, you will supply what is lacking.

5. Those who persuade us that whoever possesses one virtue possesses them all, and that whoever lacks one lacks them all, certainly argue that prudence cannot be idle, unjust, or intemperate. For if it were any of these, it would not be prudence.

Moreover, if prudence exists only when it is courageous, just, and temperate, then wherever prudence is present it certainly has the other virtues with it. Similarly, courage cannot be imprudent, intemperate, or unjust. Temperance must likewise be prudent, courageous, and just; and justice is not justice unless it is prudent, courageous, and temperate.

Thus, wherever one of these virtues is genuine, the others are present as well. Where the others are absent, the one in question is not genuine, even if in some manner it appears similar to it.

6. As you know, some vices are plainly opposed to virtues, such as imprudence to prudence. Others are opposed simply because they are vices, while nevertheless resembling the virtue in a deceptive form—for example, not imprudence but cunning as opposed to prudence.

By “cunning” I mean here what is more commonly understood and called cunning in malicious people, not the way our Scripture customarily speaks, since it often uses cunning in a good sense: “Be cunning as serpents” (Matt. 10:16), and, “That he may give cunning to the innocent” (Prov. 1:4).

Even among the Romans, the most eloquent speaker of their language said, “Yet neither deception nor cunning was lacking in him for taking precautions” (Sallust, *The War with Catiline*), placing cunning in a good sense. But this usage is very rare among them and very common among our writers.

Likewise, among the parts of temperance, extravagance is plainly opposed to frugality. What is commonly [Col. 0736] called stinginess is also a vice, but it resembles frugality not by its nature, but by a most deceptive appearance.

Injustice is manifestly opposed to justice. Yet the desire for revenge often imitates justice, although it is a vice.

Cowardice is plainly opposed to courage; hardness, however, differs from it by nature but deceives by its resemblance.

Constancy is a part of virtue. Inconstancy is far removed from it and plainly opposed to it. Obstinacy, however, wants to be called constancy, but is not, because the former is a virtue and the latter a vice.

7. To avoid having to repeat the same things, let us offer one example from which the others may be understood.

According to those who were able to know him and wrote about him, Catiline could endure cold, thirst, and hunger. He was more capable of bearing fasting, cold, and sleeplessness than anyone could believe; and therefore he appeared to possess great courage, both for himself and for his followers (Sallust, *The War with Catiline*).

But this courage was not prudent, for he chose evil things instead of good. It was not temperate, for he was defiled by the most shameful corruptions. It was not just, for he had conspired against his fatherland.

Therefore it was not courage either. Rather, hardness assumed the name of courage in order to deceive fools. For if it had been courage, it would have been a virtue, not a vice; and if it had been a virtue, it would never have been abandoned by the other virtues as inseparable companions.

8. When, therefore, the question is also raised whether all vices are similarly present wherever one is present, or whether none are present wherever one is absent, the matter is difficult to demonstrate. The reason is that two vices are usually opposed to one virtue: one that is openly contrary to it, and another that is shaded by a semblance of likeness.

Thus it was easier to see that Catiline’s hardness [Note: Two manuscripts: “That hardness of Catiline, since it was not courage …”] was not courage, since it did not possess the other virtues with it. But it is difficult to persuade people that it was cowardice, when he possessed such extraordinary endurance in exercising and bearing every kind of severe hardship.

Yet perhaps, to those who look more sharply, cowardice itself appears in that hardness, because he had neglected the labor of good pursuits by which true courage is acquired.

Nevertheless, because there are bold people who are not timid, and again timid people who lack boldness, although both are vices—for one who is courageous with true virtue neither dares rashly nor fears recklessly—we are compelled to admit that vices are more numerous than virtues.

9. Therefore sometimes one vice is removed by another, as love of money may be displaced by love of praise. Sometimes one gives way and several take its place, as when someone who had been a drunkard drinks moderately but learns both stinginess and ambition.

Vices can therefore give way to vices that succeed them, not to virtues; and for that reason they are more numerous.

But wherever one virtue enters, it brings the others with it, and therefore all the vices that were present certainly give way. For they were not all present at once: sometimes an equal number succeeded an equal number, sometimes more succeeded fewer, or fewer succeeded more.

## CHAPTER III

10. Whether matters stand this way must be investigated more carefully. For this too is not a divine pronouncement: “Whoever possesses one virtue possesses them all, [Col. 0737] and whoever lacks one possesses none.” It was the opinion of human beings—highly gifted and diligent, certainly, but still human beings.

I do not know how I could say that a man—after whom virtue is said to take its name—or even a woman who preserves fidelity to her husband’s marriage bed, if she does so because of God’s command and promise, and is first faithful to him [Note: The editions read, “and who first …” But the better reading in the Casal and Vatican manuscripts is “and is first faithful to him”; or, as three other Vatican manuscripts have it, “and to whom she is first faithful,” namely, to God]—does not possess chastity, or that chastity is no virtue or only a small one.

The same applies to a husband who preserves this fidelity toward his wife. Yet there are many such people, and I would not say that any of them is without some sin; and certainly whatever that sin may be comes from some vice.

Therefore, although marital chastity in devout men and women is undoubtedly a virtue—for it is neither nothing nor a vice—it does not nevertheless have all the virtues with it. For if all were present, there would be no vice; if there were no vice, there would be no sin at all.

But who is without some sin? Who, then, is without some vice—that is, without some fuel, or as it were root, of sin—when the one who reclined upon the Lord’s breast cries out: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8)?

This need not be pursued at greater length with you. I say it for the sake of others who may perhaps read this. You yourself, in that distinguished work against Jovinianus (Book 2), carefully demonstrated this from the Holy Scriptures. There you also cited from this very Letter, whose words we are now seeking to understand: “For in many things we all stumble” (James 3:2).

The Apostle of Christ did not say, “You stumble,” but “we stumble.” And in the passage under discussion he says, “Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all”; there he says not “in one,” but “in many,” and he says that all, not merely some, stumble.

11. Far be it from any believer to think that the many thousands of Christ’s servants who truthfully say that they have sin—lest they deceive themselves and the truth be absent from them—possess no virtue, since virtue is great wisdom.

Wisdom itself said to the human being, “Behold, piety is wisdom” (Job 28:28, according to the Septuagint).

Far be it, then, from us to say that so many and such great faithful and devout people of God do not possess piety, which the Greeks call either εὐσέβεια (*eusebeia*) or, more expressly and fully, θεοσέβεια (*theosebeia*). For what is piety except the worship of God? And by what is he worshiped except by love?

Love, therefore, proceeding from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith, is a great and true virtue, because it is itself “the end of the commandment” (1 Tim. 1:5).

It is rightly said to be “strong as death” (Song of Songs 8:6): either because no one conquers it, just as no one conquers death; or because, in this life, the measure of love extends to death, as the Lord says, “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13); or rather because, just as death tears the soul away from the senses of the flesh, so love tears it away from carnal desires.

Knowledge serves love when it is useful; for without it knowledge “puffs up” (1 Cor. 8:1). But once love has built up, [Col. 0738] knowledge will find nothing empty there with which to inflate itself.

He demonstrated what useful knowledge is by defining it. After saying, “Behold, piety is wisdom,” he immediately added, “But to abstain from evil is knowledge.”

Why, then, do we not say that whoever possesses this virtue possesses them all, since “love is the fullness of the law” (Rom. 13:10)? Or is it rather that the more love there is in a person, the more virtue that person possesses; and the less love, the less virtue, because love itself is virtue? And the less virtue there is, the more vice there is?

Where love is full and perfect, therefore, nothing of vice will remain.

12. The Stoics therefore seem to me to be mistaken because they refuse to admit that a person progressing in wisdom possesses wisdom at all. They say that he possesses it only when he has become entirely perfect in it.

They do not deny that he has advanced; but unless, emerging suddenly from some deep abyss, he bursts forth into the free air of wisdom, they say that he is wise in no respect.

For, just as it makes no difference to suffocating a person whether the water above him is many stades deep, one palm deep, or one finger deep, so they say that those who strive toward wisdom do indeed make progress, as though they were rising from the bottom of a whirlpool into the air. But unless, by progressing and emerging, they escape all folly—the water, as it were, that presses upon them—they do not possess virtue and are not wise.

Once they have escaped, however, they immediately possess the whole of wisdom, and no folly remains from which any sin could arise.

13. This comparison, in which folly is represented as water and wisdom as air, so that the mind, emerging from the suffocation of folly, suddenly breathes into wisdom, does not seem sufficiently suited to the authority of our Scriptures.

A better comparison is to liken vice or folly to darkness, and virtue or wisdom to light, insofar as such comparisons drawn from bodily things can be applied to intelligible realities.

The person does not rise from water into air, suddenly breathing as much as is needed once he has passed above the water’s surface. Rather, like someone proceeding from darkness into light, he is illuminated gradually as he advances.

Until this process is complete, we nevertheless say that he is like someone emerging from the deepest cavern, touched by the nearness of the light, increasingly so the closer he comes to the exit. What shines in him is from the light toward which he advances; what remains dark is from the darkness from which he is emerging.

Thus, “no living person will be justified in your sight” (Ps. 143:2), and yet “the just person lives by faith” (Hab. 2:4). The saints are clothed with righteousness (Job 29:14), one more and another less; and no one here lives without sin, one more and another less. The best person, however, is the one who has the least.

## CHAPTER IV

14. But what am I doing? Have I forgotten whom I am addressing and made myself resemble a teacher, when I had proposed to learn from you what I want to know?

Since I had decided to lay before you my opinion for examination concerning the equality of sins—the question that led me into the present discussion—I shall finally bring it to a conclusion.

Even if it is true that whoever possesses one virtue possesses them all, while whoever lacks one possesses none, [Col. 0739] sins are not thereby equal. For where there is no virtue at all, nothing is indeed right; but it does not follow that one crooked thing is not more crooked than another, or one distorted thing more distorted than another.

If, however, which I think more true and more consistent with the Holy Scriptures, the soul’s dispositions are like the members of the body—not in their spatial locations but in their affective tendencies—and one is illuminated more, another less, while another altogether lacks light and is overshadowed by a dark obstruction, then, according to the degree to which each person is moved by the illumination of devout love, more in one action, less in another, and not at all in some, one virtue may be said to be present and another absent, one present more and another less.

We can rightly say, “There is greater love in this person than in that one”; and, insofar as love is piety, “There is some love in this person and none in that one.” In the same person we can say that he has greater chastity than patience, greater chastity today than yesterday if he is progressing, and that he does not yet possess continence but does possess considerable mercy.

15. To state generally and briefly what I understand virtue to be: insofar as it concerns right living, virtue is love, by which what ought to be loved is loved.

In some people this love is greater, in others less, and in others absent. But no one living here possesses love in its fullest measure and perfection, such that it could not increase further. As long as it can increase, whatever is less than it ought to be derives from vice.

Because of this vice, “there is no righteous person on earth who does good and does not sin” (3 Kings 8:46); because of this vice, “no living person will be justified in the sight of God.”

Because of this vice, “if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). Because of it, however much progress we may have made, we must still say, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12), even though everything said, done, and thought has already been forgiven in Baptism.

Anyone who sees rightly therefore sees where, when, and in what condition that perfection is to be hoped for to which nothing can be added.

If there were no commandments, a person would have no certain place in which to examine himself, to see from what he should turn away, toward what he should strive, for what he should give thanks, and what he should pray for.

The commandments are therefore of great benefit, provided that free will is granted only so much that the grace of God may be honored more greatly.

## CHAPTER V

16. If this is so, how does the person who has kept the whole law become guilty of all if he stumbles in one point?

Is it perhaps because the fullness of the law is love, by which God and one’s neighbor are loved, and because the whole law and the Prophets depend upon these commandments of love (Matt. 22:40)? The person who acts against love, upon which everything depends, is therefore rightly made guilty of all.

No one sins except by acting against love. For “You shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill, you shall not steal, you shall not covet,” and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

Love does no harm to one’s neighbor. Therefore love is the fullness of the law (Rom. 13:9–10).

No one loves his neighbor unless he loves God, and unless, as far as he is able, he bestows upon his neighbor—whom he loves as himself—that which may lead the neighbor also to love God. If he himself does not love God, [Col. 0740] he loves neither himself nor his neighbor.

Accordingly, whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point becomes guilty of all because he acts against love, upon which the whole law depends. He therefore becomes guilty of all by acting against that upon which everything depends.

17. Why, then, are the sins not said to be equal? Perhaps because the one who sins more seriously acts more gravely against charity, while the one who sins less seriously acts less gravely? By the very fact that he commits a sin, he does indeed become guilty of all; but the one who sins more seriously, or sins in more matters, is more guilty, whereas the one who sins less seriously, or in fewer matters, is less guilty: his guilt is greater in proportion as he has sinned more, and less in proportion as he has sinned less. Nevertheless, even if he offends in one matter, he is guilty of all, because he acts against charity, on which everything depends. If this is true, then in the same way that statement is explained which the man of apostolic grace says: “For we all offend in many ways” (James 3:2). We all offend, but one more seriously and another less seriously, according as each has sinned more or less [Note: Eleven manuscripts read: “more or less he may have sinned.”]. The greater one is in committing sin, the less he is in loving God and neighbor; and, conversely, the less one is in committing sin, the greater he is in loving God and neighbor. Thus one is fuller of iniquity in proportion as he is emptier of charity. We are perfect in charity when nothing remains of weakness.

18. Nor, as I believe, should it be thought that it is a slight sin to hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ while showing partiality, if we refer that distinction between sitting and standing to ecclesiastical honors. For who could tolerate a rich man’s being chosen for the seat of honor in the Church while a poorer man, better instructed and holier, is despised? But if he is speaking of ordinary seating arrangements, who does not sin in this way? Yet he sins only if he inwardly judges the matter in such a way that the richer person seems to him correspondingly better than the poorer one. For this is what he appears to have meant when he says: “Are you not judging among yourselves, and have you not become judges with evil thoughts?”

CHAPTER VI

19. The law of liberty, then, is the law of charity, of which he says: “If, however, you fulfill the royal law according to the Scriptures, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself,’ you do well.” “But if you show partiality, you commit sin, being convicted by the law as transgressors.” And after that exceedingly difficult statement, concerning which I have said enough of what I thought ought to be said, he recalls the same law of liberty: “So speak and so act as those who are beginning to be judged by the law of liberty.” Since he knows what he said shortly before—namely, “We all offend in many ways”—he offers the Lord’s medicine, as it were, for daily wounds: daily wounds, though lesser ones. “For judgment,” he says, “is without mercy to the one who has shown no mercy.” Hence also the Lord says: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you” (Luke 6:37–38). But mercy exults over judgment. He did not say, “Mercy conquers judgment,” for mercy is not opposed to judgment; rather, it “exults,” because more people are gathered through mercy—but those who have shown mercy. “Blessed are the merciful, for God will have mercy on them” (Matthew 5:7).

20. It is certainly just that they should be forgiven because they have forgiven, and that it should be given to them because they have given. For in God there is both mercy when he judges and judgment when he shows mercy. Therefore it is said to him: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Psalm 100:1). Whoever, as though excessively righteous, confidently awaits judgment without mercy provokes the most just anger—an anger feared by the one who said: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant” (Psalm 143:2). Hence it is said to the rebellious people: “Why do you wish to contend with me in judgment?” (Jeremiah 2:29).

For when the just King sits upon the throne, who will boast that he has a pure heart? Or who will boast that he is clean from sin? What hope, then, is there unless mercy exults over judgment? Yet this is true concerning those who have shown mercy, sincerely saying, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive,” and giving without complaint—for “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).

Finally, holy James now speaks from this point about works of mercy, so that he may console those whom that severe statement had greatly frightened. He reminds them how even daily sins, without which no one lives here, are expiated by daily remedies, lest a person who, when he offends in one matter, becomes guilty of all—because “we all offend in many ways”—should, by offending in many ways, reach the tribunal of so great a Judge because of the great accumulation of his guilt, gathered little by little [Note: Several manuscripts, omitting the word *propter* (“because of”), read as follows: “May he bring the great accumulation of his guilt, gathered little by little, to the tribunal of so great a Judge.”], and fail to find the mercy he did not show; but rather, by forgiving and giving, may he deserve to have his sins forgiven and the promises returned to him.

21. I have said many things which may perhaps cause you weariness, although you do not expect to learn these matters—which you nevertheless approve—from me, since you are accustomed to teaching them. If there is anything in them that bears upon the matter itself—for I do not greatly concern myself with the eloquence in which they have been expressed—if, then, there is anything in them that offends your learning, I ask you to advise me by writing back, and not to consider it burdensome to correct me. For he is unfortunate who neither honors as they deserve the great and holy labors of your studies nor gives thanks for them to our Lord and God, by whose gift you are such a person.

Since, therefore, I ought more willingly to learn from anyone what I ignorantly fail to know than readily to teach anyone what I do know, how much more justly do I ask this debt of charity from you, whose teaching, in the name and by the help of the Lord, has so greatly assisted ecclesiastical literature in the Latin language—so greatly that it had never before been able to do so! Above all, however, concerning this statement—“Whoever keeps the whole law but offends in one point has become guilty of all”—I earnestly beseech Your Love, by the Lord, that if you know of any other way in which it can be better explained, you would kindly share it with us.

EPISTLE 168

[Note: This has been transferred here from the book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*.]

[Note: From the book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*: what was formerly numbered 168 is now 34. Probably written in the year 415.]

Timasius and James to Augustine, giving thanks for the book written for them, *On Nature and Grace*, against Pelagius’ treatise, in which he defended nature while not without detriment to grace.

[Col. 0742]

To the truly most blessed Lord and deservedly venerable father and bishop AUGUSTINE, TIMASIUS and JAMES send greetings in the Lord.

Your word, through which the grace of God was administered, has so restored and revived us that we can say, in the fullest sense, “He sent his word and healed them” (Psalm 107:20), most blessed Lord and deservedly venerable father. We have found that Your Holiness examined the text of that treatise with such care that we are astonished to see answers supplied to every detail, whether in those matters which a Christian ought to refute, condemn, or avoid, or in those where the author is not found to have erred sufficiently—although, by some unknown cunning, he nevertheless believed that God’s grace should be suppressed even in those matters.

There is, however, one thing that troubles us amid so great a benefit: that this so splendid a gift of God’s grace has shone forth so late. For it happened that some people were absent whose blindness ought to have been enlightened by this illumination of such evident truth [Note: Timasius and James were thinking especially of Pelagius when they said that they were troubled because I had written the book late. “They also thought that the name, or names, ought still to be withheld, so that while friendship remained, the error rather than the friends might die.” These words are Augustine’s in the book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, chapter 25, immediately after the example of the preceding letter quoted there.]. Nevertheless, we do not despair that, although later, the same grace will reach them by God’s favor—for he wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2:4).

As for us, although long ago instructed by the spirit of illumination that is in you and having rejected the subjection imposed by that error, we now give thanks also for this: that we have learned to open to others what we previously believed, as Your Holiness’ fuller discourse has opened a way of easier access. And in another hand: May the mercy of our God glorify Your Blessedness forever, preserving you in safety and mindful of us.

EPISTLE 169

[Note: This has been corrected against bl., ff., vc., three v., Am., Bad., Er., and Lov., to which was added a manuscript of the Sulpician monastery, of the Cistercian order.]

[Note: Formerly numbered 102; what was numbered 169 is now 35. Written toward the end of the year 415.]

Augustine to Evodius, replying to two questions, concerning the Trinity and the dove in which the Holy Spirit was manifested; teaching that understanding questions of this kind, which are difficult, is by no means necessary for salvation.

AUGUSTINE, bishop, to EVODIUS, bishop.

CHAPTER ONE

1. If Your Holiness considers it important to know the matters that occupy me most, and from which I do not wish to be diverted to something else, send someone to copy them for you. Several works have now been completed which we had begun during the approaching Lenten season before Easter this year. For, in addition to those three books on the City of God against its enemies, the worshipers of demons, we have added two others. In these five books I believe that enough has been argued against those who think that the gods should be worshiped for the sake of the happiness of the present life, and who, supposing that we obstruct that happiness, are hostile to the Christian name.

Next we must speak, as we promised in the first book (*City of God*, book 1, chapter 36), against those who consider the worship of their gods necessary for the life that is to follow death—the life for whose sake we Christians exist. I have also dictated expositions of three psalms, in sizeable volumes: the sixty-seventh, the seventy-first, and the seventy-seventh. The remaining psalms, not yet dictated or treated, are being eagerly awaited and insistently demanded of us.

I do not wish to be called away from or delayed in these works by whatever questions may burst in from the side. Thus I do not presently wish to attend even to the books on the Trinity, which I have long had in hand and have not yet completed, because they are excessively laborious and, I think, can be understood by only a few. Those matters which we hope will be useful to more people press upon us more urgently.

For the Apostle did not say, as you write, “The one who is ignorant will be ignored” (1 Corinthians 14:38), concerning this matter—as though the person who cannot, by intellectual understanding, distinguish the ineffable unity of the Trinity in the way that memory, understanding, and will are distinguished in our mind were to be punished for that reason. The Apostle was speaking about something else. Read the passage, and you will see that he was speaking of things that would build up the faith or conduct of many, not of things that would reach only a few—and even then only the small degree of understanding that can be attained in this life concerning so great a matter. He was saying that prophecy should be placed above tongues, that those activities should not be carried on in disorder, as though the spirit of prophecy compelled people to speak even against their will, that women should be silent in church, and that everything should be done honorably and according to order.

While dealing with these matters he says: “If anyone thinks that he is a prophet or spiritual, let him recognize that what I am writing to you is a command of the Lord. But if anyone is ignorant, he will be ignored.” By these words he restrains and recalls to peaceful order those who were restless, all the more prone to sedition because they seemed to themselves to excel in the Spirit, while in their pride they were throwing everything into confusion.

“If anyone thinks that he is a prophet or spiritual,” he says, “let him recognize that what I am writing to you is a command of the Lord.” He says “thinks that he is,” and plainly he is not; for the person who is truly such recognizes this without hesitation and has no need of admonition or exhortation, because “he judges all things, and is judged by no one” (1 Corinthians 2:15). Those, then, who caused seditions and disturbances in the Church were people who seemed to be in the Church but were not. He teaches them to recognize that the command is the Lord’s, because God is not a God of sedition but of peace.

“But if anyone is ignorant, he will be ignored”—that is, he will be rejected. For God does not, if you refer the matter to knowledge, fail to know those to whom he will say, “I do not know you” (Luke 13:27); rather, their rejection is indicated by this expression.

3. Since the Lord says, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8), and since that vision is promised to us at the end as the highest reward, we need not fear that, because we are now unable to behold with complete clarity what we believe concerning God’s nature, this is the meaning of the statement, “The one who is ignorant will be ignored.” Because the world did not know God through the wisdom of God, “it pleased God through the folly of preaching to save those who believe.” This folly of preaching, and the “foolishness of God” that is wiser than human beings (1 Corinthians 1:21, 25), draws many to salvation. Thus not only those who are not yet able, with certain understanding, to behold the nature of God—which they hold by faith, but also those who have not yet learned, even in their own soul, to distinguish incorporeal substance from the generality of bodies, as certainly as they know that they live, know, and will, are not thereby excluded from the salvation that this foolishness of preaching grants to believers.

4. For if Christ died only for those who can distinguish these matters with certain understanding, we are laboring in the Church almost in vain. But if, as the truth teaches, the weak among the believing people run to the physician to be healed through Christ—and Christ crucified—so that where sin abounded, grace might abound all the more (Romans 5:20), then, through the depth of the riches of God’s wisdom and knowledge and through his judgments, which are unsearchable (Romans 11:33), remarkable things occur.

Some people, distinguishing incorporeal things from bodies, come to think highly of themselves on account of this and mock the foolishness of preaching through which believers are saved; yet they wander far from the one way that alone leads to eternal life. Many others glory in the cross of Christ and do not depart from that same way. Even if they are ignorant of the matters discussed with the greatest subtlety, because not one of those for whom he died perishes [Note: Two manuscripts marked V. read: “Not one of the little ones perishes.” The Sulpician manuscript comes close to this, reading: “Not one little one perishes,” in place of the transmitted wording.], they reach the same eternity, truth, and love—that is, stable, certain, and complete happiness—where, for those who remain, see, and love, all things are clear.

CHAPTER II

5. Let us therefore firmly and devoutly believe in one God, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, in such a way that the Son is not believed to be the Father, nor the Father the Son, nor the Father or the Son the Spirit belonging to both. Nothing in this Trinity should be thought to differ in time or place; rather, these three are equal and coeternal, and altogether one nature.

No creature was created by the Father as one nature, by the Son as another, and by the Holy Spirit as another; rather, all things and each individual thing that has been created or is being created subsist through the Trinity as Creator. No one is freed by the Father without the Son and the Holy Spirit, or by the Son without the Father and the Holy Spirit, or by the Holy Spirit without the Father and the Son, but by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—the one true and truly immortal God, that is, the only God who is wholly unchangeable.

Scripture nevertheless speaks of the individual persons separately in many passages, so that it may make known that, although the Trinity is inseparable, it is still a Trinity. Just as the three cannot be spoken of simultaneously when they are recalled by bodily sounds, although they exist simultaneously and inseparably, so in certain passages of Scripture and through certain creatures they are shown individually and in turn: the Father in the voice that sounded, “You are my Son” (Luke 3:22); the Son in the human being whom he assumed from the Virgin (Luke 2:7); and the Holy Spirit in the bodily form of a dove (Matthew 3:16). These three, shown separately but in no way separated, are thereby manifested.

6. To gain some understanding of this, we take memory, understanding, and will as an analogy. Although we state these one by one, each at its own time and separately, we nevertheless do or say none of them without the other two. They must not, however, be thought to be compared with the Trinity in such a way that the comparison corresponds in every respect. For what likeness in an argument can be granted such complete correspondence that it fits the thing to which it is applied in every respect? Or when is anything resembling the Creator taken from a creature in every respect?

First, then, this likeness is found to be unlike the reality in that these three—memory, understanding, and will—are present in the soul, whereas the Trinity is not present in anything, but is itself God. Hence an astonishing simplicity is affirmed there, because in God being is not one thing and understanding another, nor is anything else that is said of God’s nature distinct from his being. The soul, however, although it exists even when it does not understand, is one thing in respect of what it is and another in respect of what it understands.

Moreover, who would dare to say that the Father does not understand through himself but through the Son, as memory does not understand through itself but through understanding—or rather, as the soul itself, in which these faculties exist, understands only through understanding, remembers only through memory, and wills only through will?

This analogy is therefore introduced so that, in some fashion, we may understand the following: although, when the three individual names are pronounced, each name indicates one of the three, each name is nevertheless pronounced with all three cooperating, since it is spoken through remembering, understanding, and willing. In the same way, no creature by which the Father alone, the Son alone, or the Holy Spirit alone is manifested is produced without the Trinity working together, since the Trinity works inseparably. Consequently, neither the Father’s voice, nor the Son’s soul and flesh, nor the Holy Spirit’s dove was made without the same Trinity cooperating.

7. That sound of the voice, which immediately ceased to exist, was not joined to the unity of the Father’s person; nor was the bodily form of the dove joined to the unity of the Holy Spirit’s person. For the dove itself, like the luminous cloud that covered the Savior on the mountain with the three disciples (Matthew 17:5), or rather like the fire that manifested the same Holy Spirit (Acts 2:3), ceased to exist as soon as it had fulfilled its function of signification.

Only the human being, because all those things were done for the sake of liberating human nature itself, was joined, through a marvelous and unique assumption, to the unity of the person of the Word of God—that is, of the only-begotten Son of God. The Word nevertheless remained unchangeably in its own nature, in which no phantasy of the human mind should suspect any composite element with which it might subsist.

It is indeed written, “The Spirit of wisdom is manifold” (Wisdom 7:22), but he is rightly also called simple. He is manifold because he possesses many things, yet simple because he is not other than what he possesses. Thus the Son is said to have life in himself (John 5:26), and he is himself that same life.

The human being was joined to the Word; the Word was not convertibly changed into the human being. Thus the Son of God is spoken of together with the human being whom he assumed. The same Son of God, therefore, is unchangeable and coeternal with the Father, but in the Word alone; and the Son of God was buried, but in the flesh alone.

8. Accordingly, when words are spoken about the Son of God, we must consider in what respect they are spoken. The number of persons was not increased by the assumption of the human being; the same Trinity remained. For just as in any human being, apart from that one who was uniquely assumed, soul and body constitute one person, so in Christ the Word and the human being constitute one person.

And just as, for example, a human being is called a philosopher only according to the soul, yet we nevertheless say, quite properly and in the most customary manner, that the philosopher was beaten, the philosopher died, and the philosopher was buried—although all of this happened according to the flesh and not according to that by which he is a philosopher—so Christ is called God, the Son of God, the Lord of glory, and whatever else is said according to the Word. Yet it is rightly said that God was crucified, since it is beyond doubt that he suffered this according to the flesh and not according to that by which he is the Lord of glory [Note: See Epistle 187, chapter 3, sections 8 and 9.].

9. The sound of that voice, the bodily form of the dove, and the divided tongues like fire that rested upon each of them, like the things that occurred in terrifying form on Mount Sinai (Exodus 19:18), and like the column of cloud by day and of flame by night (Exodus 13:21), were produced and completed through a symbolic operation. Above all, we must take care that no one believe the nature of God—whether of the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit—to be changeable or convertible.

Nor should it trouble us that sometimes the thing that signifies receives the name of the thing it signifies. The Holy Spirit was said to have descended and remained upon him in bodily form as a dove. In the same way, Christ is called “the rock” (1 Corinthians 10:4), because the rock signifies Christ.

CHAPTER III

10. I am surprised that it seems to you that the sound of the voice by which it was said, “You are my Son,” could have been produced by divine command through the bodily nature alone, without the mediation of a soul, while it does not seem to you that in the same way the bodily form and movement resembling those of any living creature could have been produced by divine command without the intervention of an animal spirit.

For if a bodily creature obeys God without the ministry of a life-giving soul, so that sounds are produced of the kind ordinarily produced from an animate body, and the form of articulated speech is brought to the ears, why should it not obey him so that, by the same power of the Creator, the shape and movement of a bird might be presented to the eyes without the ministry of a life-giving soul?

Can the sense of hearing merit this, while the sense of sight cannot, when both bodies are formed from adjacent matter [Note: Thus the Vatican manuscript; others read “body”]—both what resounds in the ears and what appears to the eyes, both the articulations of the voice and the outlines of the limbs, both audible and visible movement—so that what is perceived by the bodily sense is truly a body, and nothing more is present than what is perceived by the bodily sense? For the soul is not perceived by any bodily sense in any living creature.

There is therefore no need to ask how the bodily form of the dove appeared, just as we do not ask how the sounds of an articulated body were produced. If the soul could be absent where a voice—not something merely like a voice—is said to have been made, how much more could it be absent where something is said to be “like a dove,” when by this expression a mere bodily form, signified by the word, was presented to the eyes, and not the nature of a living animal reproduced?

In the same way, it is said: “Suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a rushing mighty wind, and there appeared to them divided tongues as if of fire.” There, a certain form resembling wind and a sensible fire resembling familiar and well-known natures seem to be signified, not those familiar and well-known natures themselves temporarily made.

11. But if a subtler reasoning or a more excellent investigation of the matter demonstrates that a nature which is moved neither temporally nor locally is moved only through that which can be moved temporally but not locally, it will follow that all those things were produced through the ministry of a living creature, as things are done through angels. To discuss this more carefully would therefore be both lengthy and unnecessary.

Furthermore, there are visions that appear to the spirit as bodily things appear to the bodily senses—not only to people who are asleep or delirious, but sometimes to those who are awake and sound-minded. These visions do not arise through the deception of mocking demons, but through some spiritual revelation produced by incorporeal forms resembling bodies. They cannot be discerned at all unless they are more fully revealed by divine assistance and judged by the understanding of the mind—only rarely while they are occurring [Note: Two manuscripts read *fierent* (“were occurring”)], but generally afterward, once they have passed.

Since this is so, whether these things seem to appear to our spirit as bodily senses perceive them through bodily natures, or through bodily form alone while the nature itself is spiritual, when sacred Scripture recalls them we must not rashly judge which of these two kinds they belong to, nor whether, if they occur bodily, they are produced through a living creature’s mediation.

We must nevertheless believe without any doubt—or grasp with whatever understanding we can attain—that the invisible and unchangeable nature of the Creator, that is, of the supreme and ineffable Trinity, is remote and distinct both from the mortal bodily senses and from every kind of convertibility, whether into something better, something worse, or anything else whatsoever.

CHAPTER IV

12. I have written these things to you about the two questions—concerning the Trinity and concerning the dove in which the Holy Spirit was manifested, not in its own nature but in a symbolic form. Similarly, the Son of God was crucified by the Jews not in his own birth, about which the Father said, “Before the morning star I begot you” (Psalm 110:3), but in the human being assumed from the Virgin’s womb. You can see how, although extremely occupied, I was nevertheless able to write to you at leisure. I did not think that everything you set out in your letter had to be treated. Rather, I believe that I have answered the two things you wished to hear from me—not sufficiently for your eagerness, perhaps, but obediently to your charity.

13. Besides the two books which I mentioned above that I had added to the three, and the exposition of the three psalms (above, chapter 1, section 1), I also wrote a book to the holy presbyter Jerome concerning the origin of the soul [Note: This book is Epistle 166.]. I consulted him about how that position could be defended which he had written to the holy memory of Marcellinus as his own: that individual souls are newly created for those being born. The purpose was that the firmly established faith of the Church should not be shaken, by which we unshakably believe that “in Adam all die” (1 Corinthians 15:22), and that, unless they are freed through the grace of Christ—which operates even in infants through his sacrament [Note: Lovaniensis reads, “who through his sacrament,” etc.; all the manuscripts prefer our reading.]—they are drawn into condemnation.

I also wrote another letter to the same man [Note: Epistle 167], asking how he thought the statement written in the Epistle of James should be understood: “Whoever keeps the whole law but offends in one point has become guilty of all” (James 2:10). In this letter I also stated what I think; but in the matter of the soul’s origin I merely asked what he thought, in a consultative sort of discussion.

I did not wish to lose the opportunity presented by a certain most holy and zealous young presbyter, Orosius, who came to us from the farthest part of Spain—that is, from the shores of the ocean—kindled solely by zeal for the holy Scriptures. I persuaded him to go to Jerome as well. To Orosius himself I also replied in one not very large book, with as much brevity and clarity as I could, concerning certain questions that troubled him about the heresy of the Priscillianists and some opinions of Origen that the Church has not accepted.

I have also written a fairly large book against Pelagius’ heresy [Note: The book *On Nature and Grace*, addressed to Timasius and James.], compelled by certain brothers whom he had persuaded to hold an exceedingly harmful opinion against the grace of Christ.

If you wish to have all these works, send someone to you who can copy everything for you. As for me, allow me to devote myself to seeking and dictating the works that are useful to many, since I think they ought to take precedence over investigations that concern very few.

EPISTLE 170

[Note: Corrected against a., bl., cc., cb., ff., gg., mr., two vv., vc., two t., and two v.]

[Note: Formerly numbered 66; what was numbered 170 is now 52. Probably written in the year 415.]

Alypius and Augustine to Maximus, a physician recently converted from the Arian heresy to the Catholic faith, exhorting him to strive to bring others to the same faith, especially since he had led some into error by his authority; and instructing him against those who impiously dispute concerning the one essence of the three persons.

To the excellent, deservedly honorable, and religious brother MAXIMUS [Note: The manuscripts consistently prefer the name *Maximi* here and in the following letter, except that the older manuscripts of Corbie, Germanus, and others place this heading before the letter: “Of the holy Alypius and Augustine to Maximus, physician of Thenita, an Eunomian.” Nevertheless, in Possidius’ Index, chapter 5, this letter is said to have been written to Maximinus. In manuscript C., Maximus is called a physician and citizen of Thenita.], ALYPIUS and AUGUSTINE send greetings in the Lord.

1. When we were asking our holy brother and fellow bishop Peregrinus especially about the spiritual, not bodily, salvation of you and your people, his answers made us glad concerning you but sad concerning your people, because they have not been joined to the Catholic Church through a salutary correction. Since we were hoping that this would happen soon, we are still very much grieved that it has not yet occurred [Note: Four manuscripts read: “We grieve that it has not yet happened,” and so forth.], excellent, deservedly honorable, and religious brother.

2. Therefore, greeting Your Charity in the peace of the Lord, we both command and ask you not to delay teaching them what you have learned: namely, that there is one God alone, to whom the service called by the Greek word *λατρεία* (*latreia*) is owed.

For the very word occurs in the Law, where it is written: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve” [Note: *Latreuseis* (“you shall serve with latreia”).] (Deuteronomy 6:13). If we say that he is God the Father alone, the response will be: “Then *latreia* is not owed to the Son”—which it is impious to say. But if it is owed to the Son, how is it owed to God alone, if it is owed both to the Father and to the Son? It is so because there is one God, to whom alone we have been commanded to render service through *latreia*; and he is called the one God in such a way that the Father and the Son are understood—indeed, also the Holy Spirit.

For concerning the Holy Spirit the Apostle says: “Do you not know that your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own? For you were bought with a great price. Glorify God and bear him in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). Which God does he mean, if not the Holy Spirit, whose temples he had said our bodies were? *Latreia*, therefore, is owed to the Holy Spirit. For if we were commanded to build him a temple, as Solomon built one of wood and stone, then by building a temple we would plainly be shown to render *latreia* to him. How much more do we owe *latreia* to the one for whom we do not build a temple but are ourselves the temple!

3. Therefore, if *latreia* is owed to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and is rendered by us to them—the service concerning which it was said, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve”—then without doubt the Lord our God, whom alone we must serve through *latreia*, is not the Father alone, nor the Son alone, nor the Holy Spirit alone, but the Trinity itself, the one God alone: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

This does not mean that the Father is himself the Son, or that the Holy Spirit is himself either the Father or the Son, since within that Trinity the Father is the Father of the Son alone, the Son is the Son of the Father alone, while the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of both the Father and the Son. Rather, because they have one and the same nature and inseparable life, the Trinity itself, as far as human beings can understand, is apprehended—with faith preceding understanding—as the one Lord our God.

Of him it was said, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve,” and the Apostle proclaims him when he says: “For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen” (Romans 11:36).

4. The only-begotten Son is not from God the Father in the same way that the whole creation is from him, since God created the creation from nothing. He begot the Son from his own substance; he did not make him from nothing. Nor did he beget him in time, since through him he created all times.

For just as a flame does not precede in time the radiance that it generates, so the Father was never without the Son. The Son is the Wisdom of God the Father, concerning whom it is written: “For she is the splendor of eternal light” (Wisdom 7:26). She is therefore unquestionably coeternal with the light whose brightness she is—that is, with God the Father.

For this reason, just as “in the beginning God made heaven and earth,” he did not make the Word in the beginning; rather, “in the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1). The Holy Spirit, too, was not made from nothing like a creature; rather, he proceeds from the Father and the Son in such a way that he was made neither by the Son nor by the Father [Note: The words “and the Son” are absent from the Corbie, Germanus, Regius, and Victor manuscripts. Some other manuscripts, as well as the editions of Badius, Ambrosius, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis, omit the entire sentence: “But he proceeds from the Father and the Son in such a way that he was made neither by the Son nor by the Father.”].

5. This Trinity has one and the same nature and substance. It is no less in each individual person than in all three together, nor greater in all three than in each individual person. It is as great in the Father alone or in the Son alone as it is in the Father and Son together; and it is as great in the Holy Spirit alone as it is in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together.

The Father did not diminish himself in order to have the Son from himself; rather, he begot another self from himself in such a way that he remained wholly in himself and was as great in the Son as he is alone. Likewise, the Holy Spirit is wholly from the Whole: he does not precede the one from whom he proceeds, but is as great with him as he is from him; by proceeding, he neither diminishes him nor, by abiding in him, increases him.

All these things are neither confused into one nor divided into three [Note: The editions read “distinctly”; the manuscripts read “not divided.”]. Rather, although they are one, they are three; and although they are three, they are one. Therefore, the one who has granted so many hearts of his faithful people to be one heart preserves all the more within himself that these three should be each God individually and, together, not three gods but one God.

This is the one Lord our God, whom we serve with complete devotion, to whom alone that *latreia* is owed.

### 6

Although, in things that come into being in time, by his goodness he has brought it about that each thing begets offspring of its own substance—for example, a human being begets a human being, not something of another nature, but something of the nature that he himself possesses—consider how impiously it is said that he himself did not beget what he himself is. These are names of relationship, not of nature [Col. 0750], and therefore they are called ad aliquid, or relational terms; sometimes the relations are the same, sometimes different.

They are the same when a brother is related to a brother, a friend to a friend, a neighbor to a neighbor, a kinsman to a kinsman, and in any similar cases—it would be endless to go through them all. In these cases, what one person is in relation to the other, the other is in relation to the first. They are different, however, in cases such as father to son, son to father, father-in-law to son-in-law, son-in-law to father-in-law, master to servant, servant to master. What this person is in relation to that one is not what that one is in relation to this person; yet both are human beings: the relation is different, not the nature.

For if you consider what one is in relation to the other, this person is not in relation to that one what that one is in relation to this person, because one is father and the other son; or one father-in-law and the other son-in-law; or one master and the other servant. But if you consider what each is in himself or with respect to himself, the one is what the other is, because the one is a human being just as the other is.

Hence your prudence understands that those persons, from whose error the Lord has delivered you, do not reasonably say that the nature of God the Father and God the Son is different because one is Father and the other Son; nor that God the Father did not beget what he himself is because he did not beget the Father of his Son, who is himself in relation to that Son. For who does not see that these terms do not reveal natures in themselves, but signify the persons of one in relation to another?

### 7

The same applies to what they say in a similar error: that the Son is of another nature and a different substance because God the Father is not from another God, whereas the Son is indeed God, but is from God the Father. Here too substance is not indicated, but origin—that is, not what each is, but from whom each is or is not.

For Abel and Adam were not, for that reason, of different nature and substance because the one was a human being from that human being, while the other was from no human being. If, then, the nature of both is asked, Abel is a human being and Adam is a human being; but if their origin is asked, the first human being is the one from whom Abel came, while no human being is the one from whom Adam came.

Thus, in the case of God the Father and God the Son, if the nature of both is asked, both are God, and neither is more God than the other. But if their origin is asked, the Father is God from whom the Son is God; but as for the one from whom the Father is, there is no God.

### 8

Therefore, when they try in vain to answer this by saying, “A human being begets with passion, whereas God begot the Son without passion,” this not only does them no good, but greatly assists us. For if God has granted temporal and passible things that they beget what they are, how much more did he himself, eternal and impassible, beget nothing other than what he himself is—the one Father, his only-begotten Son—something that fills us with indescribable wonder because it was without passion and with such equality to himself that he did not precede the Son either in power or in age!

Yet the Son attributes to the Father everything that he has and can do, because he is not from himself but from the Father. He is equal to the Father, but he also received this from the Father. Nor did he receive from him the source of his equality as though he had previously been unequal; rather, he was born equal, and, just as he was always born, so he was always equal.

He did not therefore beget one who was unequal and then add equality to him after he had been born. Rather, by begetting him he gave him equality, because he begot one who was equal, not unequal. Therefore, to be equal to God in the form of God was not robbery for him (Philippians 2:6), but nature, since by being born he received what he was, and did not presumptuously seize it through pride.

### 9

He says that the Father is greater because he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant without losing the form of God. On account of this form of a servant he was made lower not only than the Father, but also than himself and the Holy Spirit; and not only lower than this most exalted Trinity, but also “a little lower than the angels” (Hebrews 2:9). He was lower than human beings as well, when he was subject to his parents (Luke 2:51).

It was on account of this form of a servant, which he received when he had emptied himself at the fullness of time, that he said, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28). But on account of that form which he did not lose even when he emptied himself, he said, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30): he became human while remaining God. For humanity was assumed by God; God was not consumed in humanity.

Therefore Christ as human is rightly lower than the Father, while that same Christ as God is equal to the Father.

### 10

Since, then, we rejoice that you are united with us in this true and catholic faith, in our presence and amid the great exultation of God’s people, why are we still saddened by the sluggishness of your people? We implore you, by the mercy of God, with his help to remove this sorrow from our hearts.

For we must not believe that your authority could have had great power to lead your people into perversity, yet have no power at all to correct them. Or do they perhaps despise you because you came to participate in the Catholic Church only in your later years, when they ought rather to admire and venerate you because, with a kind of youthful vigor in old age, you overcame an error [Col. 0751] of the greatest antiquity?

Far be it from them to resist you when you speak the truth, though they had consented to you when you were straying from the truth. Far be it from them to refuse to think rightly with you, when they took pleasure in erring with you.

You, therefore, pray for them and urge them. Indeed, bring them with you to the house of God, since those who are in your house are with you; or do not hesitate to come with them to the house of God, since they were accustomed to assemble in your house with you.

Especially since the Catholic mother asks some of them from you and asks others back: she asks for those whom she finds with you; she asks back those whom she lost through you. Let her not be tormented by losses, but rather rejoice in gains; let her acquire sons whom she did not have, rather than mourn those whom she had.

We pray to God that you may do what we urge, and we hope in his mercy that, through the letter of our holy brother and fellow bishop Peregrinus and through the reply of Your Love, our heart will soon be filled with joy concerning this matter, and our tongue with exultation (Psalm 125:2).

## LETTER 171

[Note: [Col. 0751] Revised against manuscripts cb, gg, gv, n, r, sb, vc, two t manuscripts, two v manuscripts, and Lovaniensis.]

[Note: [Col. 0751] Formerly Letter 220; what was numbered 171 is now 76. Written after the preceding letter.]

Augustine excuses the form of the preceding letter addressed to Maximus.

To the most blessed Lord, and venerably beloved brother and fellow bishop, PEREGRINUS, ALYPIUS and AUGUSTINE send greetings in the Lord.

We sent a letter to our honorable brother Maximus, believing that he would receive it gladly. Whether, however, we have accomplished anything, kindly let us know by reply at the earliest opportunity you can find.

You should know that we are accustomed to write lengthy letters to our most intimate friends—not only laymen but also bishops—in the same manner in which this one was written, so that they may be composed quickly and the page may be held [Note: The manuscripts of the best quality read this way. Lovaniensis has: “so that they may be written quickly and be held securely.”] more conveniently while they are being read. Otherwise, if he did not know our custom, he might think that an affront had been committed against him.

## FRAGMENT

[Note: This fragment of St. Augustine’s letter to Maximus is found, inappropriately relegated, in the third volume of the Benedictine Fathers and in the eighth volume of the GG edition. Since we had followed their footsteps too closely, we had initially fallen unwarily into the same error; but once we had the matter clearly before us, it seemed to us that our expense and labor would not be wasted if that precious fragment were restored to its proper place—namely, to this second volume. M.]

LETTERS OF AUGUSTINE TO MAXIMUS HITHERTO UNPUBLISHED.

Found in Primasius’s Commentary on the Apocalypse, book 2, at the words, “These seven degrees, moreover . . .”; the same outstanding teacher, Augustine, mentions them often. Finally, writing to Maximus [Note: There can scarcely be doubt that this is Maximus the physician of Thenis, who, after renouncing the Arian heresy, received the letter now numbered 170, written in the names of Alypius and Augustine to strengthen him in the faith of the Trinity. We suppose that this is why Augustine mentions the Trinity once and again here, although the matter itself does not at all require it. Compare this fragment with On Christian Doctrine, book 2, chapter 7, and with On the Sermon on the Mount, book 1, chapter 3.], he says as follows:

Conform your life and conduct to the commandments of God, which we have received in order that we may act rightly, beginning with religious fear. “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Psalm 110:10), and in it human pride is broken and weakened.

Second, so that, made gentle and mild by piety, you may not resist with contentious obstinacy even those things that you do not yet understand, and that seem absurd and contradictory to the inexperienced in the Holy Scriptures; nor impose your own meaning upon the meanings of the divine Books. Rather, yield and defer your understanding in gentleness, instead of accusing the secret things with harshness.

Third, when human weakness begins to be disclosed to you for the knowledge of yourself, and you learn where you lie, what penal bonds of mortality, propagated from Adam, you drag along with you, and how far you wander from the Lord; and when you perceive another law in your members warring against the law [Col. 0752] of your mind and taking you captive under the law of sin that is in your members, cry out: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Romans 7:24). Then the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord will console you in your mourning, promising that very deliverance.

Fourth, desire already to fulfill righteousness much more intensely and fervently than the most wicked people ordinarily desire the pleasures of the flesh. In this desire, however, the ardor is tranquil and the flame more secure because of hope in divine assistance.

At this fourth degree of life, one applies oneself earnestly to prayers, so that fullness of righteousness may be granted to those who hunger and thirst for it; so that abstaining from the pleasure of every corruption—whether one’s own or another’s, or by resisting it—may not only be free from burden but even delightful.

To make this readily granted by God, a fifth degree is added: the counsel to show mercy, so that in what you can do, you may help the needy, because in what you cannot yet do, you desire to be helped by the Almighty.

The gift of mercy is twofold: when punishment is remitted and when kindness is shown. The Lord briefly gathered these two together: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you” (Luke 6:37–38).

This work also serves the cleansing of the heart, so that, insofar as is possible in this life, we may be able to behold the immutable substance of God with a pure understanding. For something is held against us that must be released, so that our vision may break forth into the light. Hence the Lord himself says: “But give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41).

Therefore the sixth degree follows: the very cleansing of the heart. But so that a straight and pure gaze may be directed toward the true light, neither the things we do well and laudably, nor the things we perceive keenly and intelligently, should be referred to the goal of pleasing human beings or of relieving the needs of the body.

God wishes to be worshiped freely, because there is nothing for which he himself ought to be desired. When we have reached this purity of understanding through the degrees of a good life—whether more slowly or more quickly—then we may dare to say that we have attained, to some extent in mind, the unity of the supreme and ineffable Trinity.

There will be supreme peace there, because there is nothing further to be awaited, when the sons of God, transformed from human beings into the image of their own kind, enjoy the Father’s unchangeableness.

First: “Blessed are the poor in spirit,” where there is fear of God.

Second: “Blessed are the meek,” where there is teachable piety.

Third: “Blessed are those who mourn,” where there is knowledge of one’s own weakness.

Fourth: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness,” where there is the strength to strive to keep desires subdued.

Fifth: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy,” where there is the counsel to help, so that you may deserve to be helped.

Then one reaches the sixth degree, in which it is said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:3–8). There the pure and capable understanding cannot behold the Trinity, however partially, unless we also do not desire human praise, even when we do what deserves praise.

Accordingly, at the seventh degree we arrive at the tranquility of that peace which the world cannot give.

For even with those four virtues which philosophers, by their memorable diligence, were once able to investigate—prudence, courage, temperance, and justice—if we add these three to the perfect worship of religion, namely faith, hope, and love, we certainly find the number seven. These three are rightly not omitted, since without them we know that no one can worship God or be pleasing to him.

## LETTER 172

[Note: [Col. 0752] Revised against manuscripts a, b, bl, bn, c, cc, fs, j, l, mr, sb, t, tt, vc, ten v manuscripts, and the editions of Ambrosius, Lyon, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis.]

[Note: [Col. 0752] Formerly Letter 30; what was numbered 172 is now 51. Written at the beginning of the year 416.]

Jerome to Augustine, praising his two little books On the Origin of the Soul and On the Sentence of James, but excusing why he had not replied.

To the truly holy lord, and pope Augustine, venerable to me with every affection, JEROME sends greetings in Christ.

### 1

I received my honorable brother, the presbyter Orosius, son of Your Dignity, both because of his own merits and because you instructed me to do so. But an extremely difficult time intervened, when it was better for me to keep silent than to speak, so that our studies came to an end and, in Appius’s phrase, “canine eloquence” was practiced.

Thus I was unable for a time to reply to your two little books, which you dedicated to my name, books of great learning and shining with every splendor [Col. 0753] of eloquence. This was not because I think there is anything to criticize in them, but because, according to the blessed Apostle, “Let each one abound in his own opinion; one indeed in this way, another in that” (Romans 14:5).

Certainly, whatever could be said, and whatever could be drawn by a lofty intellect from the fountains of the Holy Scriptures, has been set forth and explained by you. But I ask Your Reverence to permit me for a little while to praise your intellect. We discuss these matters among ourselves for the sake of learning. But our rivals, and especially the heretics, if they see different opinions between us, will slander them as arising from resentment of spirit.

For my part, I have resolved to love you, esteem you, venerate you, admire you, and defend your words as though they were my own. Indeed, in the dialogue that I recently published—Book 3 Against the Pelagians—I remembered Your Blessedness as was fitting.

Let us rather devote ourselves to removing from the churches the most destructive heresy, which always pretends to repentance so that it may have the opportunity to teach in the churches; for if it were to reveal itself in the open light, it would be expelled and perish.

### 2

Your holy and venerable daughters Eustochium and Paula are advancing worthily both by their lineage and by your exhortation, and they greet Your Blessedness especially, as does all the brotherhood that strives with us to serve the Lord and Savior.

Last year we sent the holy presbyter Firmus [Note: [Col. 0753] The Sorbonne manuscript has Firminus twice, while the other witnesses disagree.] to Ravenna, and from there to Africa and Sicily, on their business. We think that he is now staying somewhere in the regions of Africa.

I ask you to greet as a service to me the holy men who cling to your side. I have also sent a letter of mine to the holy presbyter Firmus; if it comes to you, do not hesitate to forward it to him.

May Christ the Lord preserve you safe and mindful of me, truly holy lord and most blessed pope.

And below [Note: [Col. 0753] The editions omit “and below,” which appears in most manuscripts.]:

We suffer from a great scarcity of notaries in this province who know the Latin language. For this reason we cannot comply with your instructions, especially concerning the edition of the Septuagint, which is marked with asterisks and obeli; for we have lost much of our earlier work through someone’s deceit.

## LETTER 173

[Note: [Col. 0753] Compared with manuscripts a, bg, bl, c, cc, ff, g, gv, j, n, r, s, vd, two bn manuscripts, two s manuscripts, two t manuscripts, four v manuscripts, and the editions of Ambrosius, Badius, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis.]

[Note: [Col. 0753] Formerly Letter 204; what was numbered 173 is now 66. Written around the year 416.]

Augustine to Donatus, a presbyter of the Donatist party at the estate of Mutugenna in the diocese of Hippo. Donatus, ordered to be arrested and brought to the church, attempted to do himself violence. Augustine urges him, after sober consideration of the matter, to come to his senses, teaching that a perverse will may rightly be compelled toward better things.

To Donatus, presbyter of the party of Donatus, AUGUSTINE, bishop of the Catholic Church.

### 1

If you could see the pain of my heart and my concern for your salvation, perhaps you would have pity on your soul, pleasing God (Ecclesiasticus 30:24) by listening to the word—not ours, but his—and by not fixing his Scriptures in your memory in such a way that you close your heart against them.

You are displeased because you are being dragged toward salvation, although you have dragged so many of our people [Col. 0754] toward destruction [Note: The manuscripts read this way. The editions have “you have dragged.”].

What did we want, except that you should be arrested, brought before us, and kept safe lest you perish? As for the fact that your body was injured, you did it to yourself: you refused to use the animal that had immediately been brought for you, and you threw yourself heavily to the ground. Certainly, the other man who was brought with you, your colleague, came unharmed; he did not do such things to himself.

### 2

But you also think that this ought not to have been done to you because you believe that no one should be compelled toward what is good. Consider what the Apostle said: “Whoever desires the office of bishop desires a good work” (1 Timothy 3:1). Yet many are held unwilling, led away, confined, guarded, and made to endure many things they do not want until they acquire the will to undertake the good work.

How much more, then, must you be dragged away from a destructive error in which you are enemies to yourselves and led toward the truth, either to recognize it or to choose it—not merely so that you may possess honor in a healthy manner, but also so that you may not perish most disastrously!

You say that God gave free choice, and therefore that a human being should not be compelled even toward what is good. Why, then, are those whom I mentioned above compelled toward good?

Consider, then, what you refuse to consider. A good will is mercifully bestowed so that the human being’s evil will may be directed. For who does not know that a person is condemned only on account of an evil will, and liberated only if he has a good will?

Nevertheless, those who are loved must not on that account be left with cruel impunity to their evil will. Wherever power is given, they must be restrained from evil and compelled toward good.

### 3

For if an evil will must always be left to its freedom, why were the Israelites, when they refused and murmured, restrained from evil by such harsh scourges and compelled toward the promised land?
