If an evil will must always be left to its freedom, why was Paul not permitted to use the evil will with which he persecuted the Church, but was thrown down so that he might be blinded, blinded so that he might be changed, changed so that he might be sent, and sent so that he might suffer for the truth what he had done in error?

If an evil will must always be left to its freedom, why is a father instructed in the Holy Scriptures not merely to correct a stubborn son with words, but also to strike his sides, so that, compelled and subdued, he may be directed toward good discipline (Ecclesiasticus 30:12)? Hence the same Scripture says: “You indeed strike him with the rod, but you deliver his soul from death” (Proverbs 23:14).

If an evil will must always be left to its freedom, why are negligent shepherds rebuked, and why is it said to them: “You did not bring back the wandering sheep; you did not seek the lost” (Ezekiel 34:4)?

You are Christ’s sheep, and you bear the Lord’s mark in the sacrament that you received; but you wander and perish. Therefore do not be displeased with us because we bring back those who wander and seek those who are lost.

For we do better when we obey the will of the Lord, who commands us to compel you to return to his sheepfold, than when we consent to the will of wandering sheep and allow you to perish.

Do not continue to say what I constantly hear you saying: “This is how I want to wander; this is how I want to perish.” We are doing everything we can to prevent this entirely [Col. 0755].

### 4

Just now, when you threw yourself into a well so that you might die, you certainly acted by free choice. But how cruel would God’s servants have been if they had permitted you to follow this evil will and had not delivered you from that death! Who would not rightly have blamed them? Who would not rightly have judged them impious?

And yet you willingly threw yourself into the water to die; they lifted you unwillingly from the water so that you would not die. You acted according to your will, but to your destruction; they acted against your will, but for your salvation.

If, then, this bodily salvation must be guarded in such a way that those who love people preserve it even against their will, how much more must that spiritual salvation be guarded, the abandonment of which threatens eternal death!

Moreover, in the death that you yourself wished to inflict upon yourself, you would have died not only for a time but also forever. For even if you were being compelled—not toward salvation, not toward the peace of the Church, not toward the unity of Christ’s body, not toward holy and undivided love, but toward some evil—you still ought not to have inflicted death upon yourself.

### 5

Consider the divine Scriptures, examine them as much as you can, and see whether any of the righteous and faithful ever did this when they had suffered such great evils at the hands of those who were driving them toward eternal destruction rather than eternal life—the destination toward which you are being compelled.

I have heard that you said the Apostle Paul indicated that this ought to be done when he said, “Even if I hand over my body so that I may be burned” (1 Corinthians 13:3). You apparently think that he was listing every good thing that is of no benefit without love, such as the tongues of human beings and angels, all the sacraments, all knowledge, all prophecy, and all faith “so as to move mountains,” as well as the distribution of one’s possessions to the poor [Note: The editions add “that it may benefit the poor.”]. Therefore it seems to you that he also included among good things the act of inflicting death upon oneself.

But pay close attention and recognize how Scripture says that someone hands over his own body to be burned. It does not mean that he himself throws himself into the fire when he suffers a persecuting enemy. Rather, when he is offered the choice either of doing something evil or of suffering something evil, he chooses not to do evil rather than not to suffer evil. Thus he hands over his body to the power of the executioner, as did those three men who were compelled to worship the golden statue. If they did not do so, the man who compelled them threatened them with a burning furnace.

They refused to worship the idol; they did not throw themselves into the fire. Yet it is written of them that they handed over their bodies so that they would neither serve nor worship any god [Note: Four manuscripts read “that god.”], but their own God (Daniel 3:14–95). This is how the Apostle’s words are to be understood: “Even if I hand over my body so that I may be burned.”

### 6

Now consider what follows: “If I do not have love, it profits me nothing.”

You are being called to this love; by this love you are not permitted to perish. And yet you think it benefits you to throw yourself into destruction, although it would benefit you nothing even if another person killed you as an enemy of love!

Established outside the Church [Col. 0756] and separated from the structure of unity and the bond of love, you would be punished with eternal suffering even if you were burned alive for the name of Christ. This is what the Apostle says: “Even if I hand over my body so that I may be burned, but do not have love, it profits me nothing.”

Therefore recall your mind to sound consideration and sober thought. Pay close attention to whether you are being called to error and impiety, and endure whatever hardships may come for the sake of truth.

But if you are instead living in error and impiety, while where you are being called there are truth and piety, because there are Christian unity and the love of the Holy Spirit, why do you continue trying to be your own enemy?

### 7

For this reason the mercy of God brought it about that both we and your bishops should come to Carthage in such a frequent and numerous gathering and discuss the very disagreement among us in the most orderly manner.

The proceedings were written down, and our signatures are preserved. Read them, or allow them to be read to you, and then choose what you wish.

I have heard that you said you could do something with us concerning the proceedings themselves if we omitted the words of your bishops: “Neither one case prejudges another case, nor one person another person.”

You want us to omit these words, although through them, without knowing it, the truth itself spoke. But you will say that they were mistaken here and fell incautiously into a false opinion.

We, however, say that they spoke the truth, and we prove this very easily through your own position. For if your bishops, chosen by the entire party of Donatus to sustain the cause of all, were such that the others would regard whatever they did as agreeable and acceptable, yet you do not want them to prejudice your case in what you think they said rashly and wrongly, then they spoke the truth: neither one case prejudges another case, nor one person another person.

And here you ought to recognize that if you do not want the person of so many of your bishops, assembled among those seven, to prejudice the person of Donatus the presbyter of Mutugenna, how much less should the person of Caecilian—even if something evil had been found in him—prejudice the whole unity of Christ, which is not confined to one estate at Mutugenna but is spread throughout the entire world?

### 8

But look: we will do what you wished. We will deal with you as though your people had not said, “Neither one case prejudges another case, nor one person another person.”

You discover what they ought to have said when the case and person of Primianus were brought before them. Primianus condemned his condemners along with the rest, yet again received those whom he had condemned and rejected into their former honors. He preferred to acknowledge and accept the baptism that those dead men had administered—for in that celebrated judgment it had been said of them that “the shores are filled with the funerals of the dead” [At the council of Bagai]—rather than blow it away and annul it.

In this way he dissolved everything that you customarily say in your misunderstanding: “What benefit is there to one who is baptized by a dead man from his washing?” (Ecclesiasticus 34:30).

If, then, they had not said, “Neither one case prejudges another case, nor one person another person,” they would have been held liable in the case of Primianus. But by saying this, they exempted the Catholic Church from the case of Caecilian, just as we maintained.

[Col. 0757]

### 9

But read the rest and examine the rest. See whether they were able to prove anything evil against Caecilian himself, whose person they were trying to use to prejudice the Church.

See whether they did not rather do much on his behalf and, through the many readings that they produced and recited against themselves, establish his case as entirely sound.

Read these proceedings, or have them read to you. Consider everything, review it carefully, and choose what you will follow: whether you will rejoice with us in the peace of Christ, in the unity of the Catholic Church, and in fraternal love, or whether, on account of this wicked disagreement, the party of Donatus, and this sacrilegious division, you will continue to endure the persistence of our love for you.

### 10

You pay attention, and often repeat, as I hear, that it is written in the Gospel that seventy disciples departed from the Lord and were left to the choice of their own evil and impious departure, while the remaining twelve received the answer: “Do you also wish to go away?” (John 6:68).

But you do not pay attention to the fact that at that time the Church was first beginning to sprout as a new growth, and the prophecy had not yet been fulfilled in it: “All the kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations shall serve him” (Psalm 71:11).

The more this is fulfilled, the greater the authority the Church exercises, so that she not only invites people to what is good but also compels them.

This is what the Lord then wished to signify. Although he possessed great power, he first chose to commend humility. He also demonstrated this clearly enough in the likeness of the banquet, where he sent to those who had been invited, but they refused to come, and he said to the servant:

“Go out into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in here the poor, the weak, the blind, and the lame.”

And the servant said to his master, “It has been done as you commanded, and there is still room.”

And the master said to the servant, “Go out into the roads and hedges, and compel them to enter, so that my house may be filled” (Luke 14:21–23).

Now observe how it is said of those who came first: “Bring them in here.” It does not say, “Compel them.” In this way the beginnings of the Church are signified as growing toward the point at which she would possess the strength even to compel.

Therefore, since it was necessary that, strengthened by her power and greatness, she should also compel people to the banquet of eternal salvation, after it had been said, “It has been done as you commanded, and there is still room,” he said: “Go out into the roads and hedges, and compel them to enter.”

Accordingly, if you were walking peacefully outside this banquet of eternal salvation and the holy unity of the Church, we would find you, as it were, on the roads [Note: Lovaniensis reads this way. Fifteen manuscripts and the older editions omit “of eternal salvation and.”].

But now, because through the many savage evils that you commit against our people you are, as it were, full of thorns and roughness, we find you in the hedges, and we compel you to enter.

One who is compelled is forced to go where he does not wish; but once he has entered, he is fed willingly.

Therefore restrain such an unjust and unpeaceful spirit, so that you may find the saving banquet in the true Church of Christ.

## LETTER 174

[Note: [Col. 0757] Transferred here from Volume 4, where it had formerly been published before the books On the Trinity.]

[Note: [Col. 0757] From Volume 3, prefixed to the books On the Trinity; what was numbered 174 is now 238. Written around the year 416.]

Augustine to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, sending him the books On the Trinity, finally completed according [Col. 0758] to the desire of Aurelius and others and corrected.

To the most blessed lord, and venerable with the purest love, holy brother and fellow priest, Pope AURELIUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

I began the books On the Trinity, who is the supreme and true God, as a young man, and published them as an old man.

For I had set the work aside after I learned that they had been taken from me—or stolen—before I had completed them and revised and polished them as I had intended. I had decided not to publish them one by one, but all together, because the later books are joined to the earlier through the progress of inquiry.

Since, however, through those men—for the books were able to reach some of them before I wished it—my plan could not be fulfilled, I abandoned the interrupted dictation. I was considering complaining about this very matter in some of my writings, so that those who could know would understand that the same books had not been published by me but taken away before they seemed worthy of publication in my edition.

Yet, compelled by the most urgent requests of many brothers, and especially by your command, I took care, with the Lord’s help, to bring this laborious work to completion. I sent the corrected books to Your Reverence through our most beloved son and fellow-deacon, not as I wished but as I was able, so that they might not differ too greatly from those that had already been stolen and circulated among people.

I permitted anyone who wished to hear, copy, or read them to do so. If my plan could have been preserved in them, they would certainly have been much more fully elucidated and clearer, even though they contained the same ideas, insofar as the difficulty of explaining such great matters and our ability permitted.

There are copies that contain the first four, or rather the first five, books even without the prefaces, and the twelfth without a considerable final portion. But if this edition becomes known to them, they will correct everything, if they wish and are able.

I ask you to order that this letter be placed separately, but nevertheless at the beginning of those same books.

Farewell. Pray for me.

## LETTER 175

[Note: [Col. 0758] Revised against manuscripts cb, ff, gg, rm, th, vc, two v manuscripts, and the editions of Ambrosius, Badius, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis.]

[Note: [Col. 0758] Formerly Letter 90; what was numbered 175 is now 239. Written in the year 416.]

The fathers of the Council of Carthage to Pope Innocent of Rome concerning the proceedings against Pelagius and Caelestius.

[Col. 0758] To the most blessed and most honored lord, holy brother Innocent, Aurelius, Numidius, Rusticianus, Fidentianus, Evagrius, Antonius, Palatinus, Adeodatus, Vincentius, Publianus, Theasius, Tutus, Pannonius, Victor, Restitutus, Rusticus, Fortunatianus, another Restitutus, Ampelius, Ambivius, Felix, Donatianus, Adeodatus, Octavius, [Col. 0759] Serotinus, Majorinus, Posthumianus, Crispulus, Victor, another Victor, Leucius, Marianus, Fructuosus, Faustinianus, Quodvultdeus, Candorius, Maximus, Megasius, Rusticus, Rufinianus, Proculus, Severus, Thomas, Januarius, Octavianus, Praetextatus, Sixtus, Quodvultdeus, Penthadius, Quodvuldeus, Cyprianus, Servilius, Pelagianus, Marcellus, Venantius, Didymus, Saturninus, Bizacenus, Germanus, Germanianus, Inventius, Majorinus, Inventius, Candidus, Cyprianus, Aemilianus, Romanus, Africanus, Marcellinus, and the others who were present at the council of the Church of Carthage.

[Note: The editions of Badius, Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain read *Mundius, Rusticanus, Fidentius*. But the Vatican and Gallican manuscripts, as well as the editions of the Councils, read *Numidius, Rusticianus, Fidentianus*. They do not agree entirely concerning *Rusticianus*: for most manuscripts have *Rusticus* here, but later, in Innocent’s Rescript—our Epistle 181—they read *Rusticiano*.]

[Note: The Gallican manuscripts and one of the Vatican manuscripts read *Antoninus* here. But in Epistle 181, *Antonio*.]

[Note: The editions of the Councils read *Publicanus*.]

[Note: So consistently in the manuscripts. The editions, however, read *Panthonius*.]

[Note: Badius, Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain read *Animus*. The editions of the Councils read *Avinius*. Moreover, the manuscripts omit this bishop’s name here, but restore it in Epistle 181 as *Ambivio* or *Ambibio*.]

[Note: The editions of Badius, Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain read *Posthumanus*. In Victor’s manuscript, *Postumianus*; in one Vatican manuscript, *Pontinianus*; in other manuscripts, *Posthumianus*.]

[Note: So in the manuscripts. But the editions print *Trispulus*.]

[Note: One of the Vatican manuscripts consistently reads *Leontius*. The German manuscript has only *Eleutius* here. Soon afterward all the manuscripts read *Marianus*, whereas the editions have *Macianus* or *Macinus*.]

[Note: So consistently in all the manuscripts. But Badius, Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain read *Megarius, Rusticus, Rufianus, Proculianus, Thomas*, omitting the name *Severus*, which appears in all the manuscripts. Some of these also have *Rusticius* here; but in Epistle 181, *Rustico*.]

[Note: The Gallican manuscripts have *Praetextius, Sextius* here. But in Epistle 181 they agree with the editions.]

[Note: So consistently in the manuscripts, except for the manuscript of the church of Reims, which reads *Pelaianus*. In the printed editions, however, *Pelagius*.]

[Note: The editions read *Tiazacenus*. One Vatican manuscript has *Bizatenus*. Another, together with our Gallican manuscripts, has *Bizacenus*.]

[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read *Viventius*. Three Gallican manuscripts have *Invenitus, Majorinus, Inventinus*; yet in both places in Epistle 181 they read *Invenito*. In the editions of the Councils, *Juventius* is printed twice.]

[Note: The words *and the others* are absent from the editions, but are found in the Vatican and Gallican manuscripts.]

1. When we had solemnly come, as is customary, to the Church of Carthage, and a synod had been convened from among us for various reasons, our fellow presbyter Orosius delivered to us letters from our holy brothers and fellow priests Heros and Lazarus, a copy of which we have decided to append below.

[Note: The Vatican manuscripts have *Anerotis*. The editions of the Councils, *Averothis*. Badius, Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain, *Herodis*. But the Gallican manuscripts more correctly have *Herotis*. He was from Arles; Lazarus was bishop of Aix in Gaul. Both of them, driven from their sees, came to Palestine and delivered a written petition against Pelagius and Caelestius to the Primate, namely Eulogius of Caesarea, by whose authority the Synod of Diospolis was held in 415.]

After these documents had been read, we recognized that Pelagius and Caelestius, the authors of an utterly impious error, were to be accused and anathematized by all of us.

[Note: So in all the Gallican manuscripts. The editions omit *argui* (“were to be condemned”).]

[Note: The editions read *anathematizandi* (“to be anathematized”), and below *anathematizaverint*, *ipsos anathematizari*, and so forth. But the Gallican manuscripts consistently have *anathemandi*, *anathemaverint*, and *anathemari*. This ancient reading is approved by Claudius Salmasius in his note on Tertullian’s *De Pallio*, chapter 3, at the words “you will turn the animated threads,” where he wishes to restore *nemata* from the verb *nemare*, which derives from the Greek *nēma*, just as *plasma* gives *plasmare*, *chrisma* gives *chrismare*, and *sagma* gives *sagmare*. In the same way, he observes that the ancients said *anathemare* from *anathema*. Elsewhere Louvain, Erasmus, and others retained this reading.]

We therefore asked that what had been done nearly five years earlier concerning Caelestius at Carthage be reviewed. Once it had been read out, as Your Holiness will be able to perceive from what follows, although the judgment was plainly established and it seemed that at that time this wound had been cut away from the Church by episcopal judgment, nevertheless we judged by common deliberation that the authors of such a persuasion—even though Caelestius is said afterward to have attained the presbyterate—ought themselves to be anathematized unless they most clearly anathematized these doctrines. Thus, even if their own health could not be secured, at least the healing of those who had been or might be deceived by them could be procured once the sentence passed against them had become known.

2. We have therefore thought it necessary, brother lord, to report this action to Your Holy Charity, so that the authority of the Apostolic See may be added to the decrees of our mediocrity, for the protection of the salvation of many and also for the correction of certain people’s perversity.

For these men, by their damnable disputations, strive—not by defending free will, but rather by exalting it to sacrilegious pride—to leave no place for the grace of God by which we are Christians and by which even the freedom of our will truly becomes free, when it is liberated from the domination of carnal desires. The Lord says: “If the Son sets you free, then you will be truly free” (John 8:36). This help is obtained by faith, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

[Note: The Corbie and German manuscripts omit the sentence: “This help is obtained by faith, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.”]

But they assert—as we have learned from brothers who have also read their books—that God’s grace consists in the fact that he established and created human nature in such a way that, through its own will, it can fulfill God’s law, whether that law was naturally written on the heart or given in written form. They also say that this same law belongs to God’s grace because God gave it to human beings as a help (Isaiah 8:20, according to the Septuagint).

3. They absolutely refuse to acknowledge that grace by which, as has been said, we are Christians, and of which the Apostle is the preacher.

[Note: Three Gallican manuscripts read *witness*.]

He says:

“I delight in the law of God according to the inner person; but I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin which is in my members. Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7:22–25).

Yet they do not even dare openly to oppose this grace. But what else are they doing when they continually persuade animal human beings, who do not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God (1 Corinthians 2:14), that human nature alone is sufficient for working and perfecting righteousness and fulfilling God’s commandments?

They pay no attention to what is written: “The Spirit helps our weakness” (Romans 8:26); and, “It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Romans 9:16); and that “we are one body in Christ, but individually members of one another, having different gifts according to the grace that has been given to us” (Romans 12:5–6); and, “By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not empty, but I labored more abundantly than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me”; and, “Thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:10, 57); and, “Not that we are competent to think anything as from ourselves, but our competence is from God” (2 Corinthians 3:5); and, [Col. 0761] “We have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing greatness of the power may be God’s and not from us” (2 Corinthians 4:7); and countless other passages of this kind. If we wished to gather them from all the Scriptures, time would not suffice.

[Note: Badius, Amerbach, Erasmus, and the editions of the Councils read *tomus* (“volume”) instead of *tempus* (“time”).]

We are concerned that, by recalling these very things to Your Holiness—things that you proclaim from the Apostolic See with still greater grace—we may seem to act improperly. But we do so because the weaker we are, the more each of us is thought, wherever he may be, to be attentive in preaching the word of God, the more frequently and boldly we suffer these men to rise up against us.

[Note: One Vatican manuscript reads *quo inferiores sumus* (“insofar as we are inferior”) rather than *quo infirmiores sumus* (“insofar as we are weaker”).]

4. Therefore, even if Pelagius appeared to Your Veneration to have been justly acquitted in the episcopal proceedings said to have been conducted in the East,

[Note: The proceedings of the Synod of Diospolis.]

nevertheless that error and impiety, which already has many scattered supporters, must also be anathematized by the authority of the Apostolic See.

Let Your Holiness consider—and, with pastoral compassion, suffer with us—how pestilential and destructive to the sheep of Christ is what necessarily follows from these men’s sacrilegious arguments: that we ought not to pray that we enter not into temptation, although the Lord both admonished his disciples to do so (Matthew 26:41) and placed this petition in the prayer he taught (Matthew 6:13); nor that our faith should fail, although he himself testified that he had prayed this for the Apostle Peter (Luke 22:32).

For if these matters have been placed within the power of nature and the choice of the will, who would not see that they are vainly requested and deceptively prayed for when, in prayer, we ask for things that the already-established powers of our nature obtain by their own sufficiency? Should the Lord Jesus then not have said, “Watch and pray,” but merely, “Watch, lest you enter into temptation”? And should he not have said to the most blessed Peter, the first of the Apostles, “I have prayed for you,” but rather, “I warn and command you that your faith must not fail”?

5. Their contention also contradicts our blessings, making us seem to say over the people in vain whatever we ask from the Lord on their behalf—that by living rightly and devoutly they may please him—or what the Apostle prays for believers when he says:

“I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit” (Ephesians 3:14–16).

If, then, in blessing the people we wish to say, “Grant them, Lord, to be strengthened with power through your Spirit,” their argument contradicts us, asserting that free will is denied if we ask God for what lies within our own power. “If we wish to be strengthened with power,” they say, “we can do so by that possibility of nature which we do not now receive, but received when we were created.”

6. They also deny that infants should be baptized on account of the salvation given through Christ the Savior, and thus, through this deadly doctrine, they kill them eternally, promising that even if they are not baptized they will possess eternal life. They claim that infants do not belong among those of whom the Lord says, “The Son of Man came to seek and save what was lost” (Luke 19:10), because, they say, “these had not been lost, and there is nothing in them to be saved or redeemed at so great a price.” Nothing in them, they say, has been corrupted; nothing is held captive under the devil’s power; and no blood was shed for them, though that blood is read to have been shed for the remission of sins (Matthew 26:28).

Caelestius, however, has already confessed in his written petition at the Church of Carthage that the redemption even of infants takes place through Christ’s baptism. Nevertheless, many who are said to be, or to have been, their disciples do not cease affirming by every means available these evils by which they attempt to overthrow the foundations of the Christian faith.

Therefore, even if Pelagius and Caelestius have been corrected—or say that they never held these views, and deny that any writings produced against them are theirs, so that there is no way to convict them of falsehood—nevertheless, whoever teaches and asserts that human nature is sufficient for avoiding sins and fulfilling God’s commandments, and is thereby found to oppose the grace of God, which is more clearly revealed in the prayers of the saints; and whoever denies that infants are liberated from perdition through Christ’s baptism and receive eternal salvation: let that person be anathema.

[Note: The editions read *ad vincenda* (“for overcoming”), while the manuscripts read *ad vitanda* (“for avoiding”).]

As for whatever other charges are brought against them, we do not doubt that, when Your Veneration has examined the episcopal proceedings said to have been conducted in the East in this same matter, you will judge in such a way that we may all rejoice in God’s mercy.

Pray for us, most blessed lord Pope.

[Note: The Gallican manuscripts lack these final words, “Pray for us,” and so forth.]

## Epistle 176

[Note: Revised according to manuscripts a, bg, bl, c, cb, ff, g, gv, n, s, sb, t, th, vc, two r manuscripts, four v manuscripts, and the editions of Amerbach, Badius, Erasmus, and Louvain.]

[Note: Formerly numbered 92; what was 176 is now 240. Written shortly after the preceding letter.]

### The Fathers of the Council of Milevis to Innocent, concerning the restraint of the Pelagian heretics

To the most blessed lord, deservedly venerable and honored in Christ, Pope Innocent, Silvanus, Valentinus, Aurelius, Donatus, Restitutus, Lucianus, Alypius, Augustine, Placentius, Severus, Fortunatus, Possidius, Novatus, Secundus, Maurentius, Leo, Faustinianus, Cresconius, Malchus, Littorius, Fortunatus, Donatus, Ponticanus, Saturninus, Christonius, Honorius, Lucius, Adeodatus, Processus, Cresconius, Secundus, Felix, Asiaticus, Rufinianus, Faustinus, Servus, Terentius, Cresconius, Sperantius, Quadratus, Lucillus, Sabinus, Faustinus, Cresconius, Victor, Gignantius, Possidonius, Antoninus, Innocentius, Praesidius, Crescentius, Felix, Antonius, Victor, Honoratus, Donatus, Petrus, Praesidius, Cresconius, Lampadius, Delphinus, from the Council of Milevis, greetings in the Lord.

[Note: The editions of the Councils have *Silvanus Senex* (“Silvanus the Elder”).]

[Note: Eight Gallican manuscripts omit *Placent ius*.]

[Note: The Gervasian and Gemblacian manuscripts have *Fortunus*.]

[Note: Five manuscripts have *Litorius*. The Casalensis manuscript has *Lictorius*. The editions of the Councils have *Victorius*.]

[Note: Seven manuscripts and the editions of the Councils have *Cresconius*. The Casalensis manuscript has *Crisconius*.]

[Note: The editions of the Councils have *Rufinus*; and below, in place of *Servus*, they read *Servius*.]

[Note: The editions of the Councils omit *Faustinus* here and put *Sabinus* in its place as a second occurrence.]

[Note: Three Vatican manuscripts, seven Gallican manuscripts, and the editions of the Councils have *Gigantius*.]

[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts have *Possidius, Antonius*.]

[Note: The editions of the Councils and seven Gallican manuscripts omit *Crescentius*. Praesidius is named only once, namely after Petrus.]

[Note: The editions of the Councils and several manuscripts consistently have *Antoninus*.]

1. Because the Lord has placed you in the Apostolic See as a special gift of his grace, and has granted you to our times in such a way that, if we were silent before Your Veneration about matters that ought to be brought forward for the Church, our silence would count against us as negligence more than you could receive them with either disdain or carelessness, we ask you to apply pastoral diligence to the great dangers threatening the weak members of Christ.

2. For a new and exceedingly harmful heresy has begun to arise among the enemies of Christ’s grace, who are even trying, through impious arguments, to take away from us the Lord’s Prayer.

[Note: Badius, Amerbach, and Erasmus read: “And a most harmful storm has begun to arise among the enemies of Christ’s grace.”]

For when the Lord taught us to say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors,” they say that in this life a person, once acquainted with God’s commandments, can attain such perfection of righteousness without the help of the Savior’s grace, through the mere freedom of the will, that it is no longer necessary for him to say, “Forgive us our debts.”

Nor, they say, should what follows—“Do not bring us into temptation” (Matthew 6:12–13)—be understood as though we ought to ask for divine help lest, when tempted, we fall into sin. Rather, they claim that this lies within our power, and that the human will alone is sufficient to fulfill it. It would therefore have been pointless for the Apostle to say, “It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Romans 9:16), and, “God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation will also provide the way out, so that you may be able to endure it” (1 Corinthians 10:13).

It would likewise have been pointless for the Lord to say to the Apostle Peter, “I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:32), and to all his disciples, “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matthew 26:41), if all this lies entirely within human power.

They also wickedly insist that little children will possess eternal life even if they are not renewed by any sacraments of Christian grace, thereby nullifying what the Apostle says: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans 5:12); and elsewhere: “As all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:22).

3. To omit the many other things they argue against the holy Scriptures, how can faithful hearts endure these two doctrines, by which they attempt entirely to overthrow everything that makes us Christians: that we should not ask God to be our helper against the evil of sin and for the working of righteousness, and that the sacrament of Christian grace does not assist infants in attaining eternal life?

By bringing these matters to your apostolic heart, we need not say much or enlarge upon such great impiety in words. Without doubt, they will move you so greatly that you will be unable to ignore the need to correct them, lest they spread more widely and contaminate—or rather destroy—many while, under the name of Christ, completely alienating them from the grace of Christ.

4. Pelagius and Caelestius are said to be the authors of this most destructive error. We would rather see them healed within the Church than cut off from the Church as men whose salvation is hopeless, if no necessity compels the latter course.

One of them, namely Caelestius, is also said to have attained the presbyterate in Asia. Your Holiness is better informed by the Church of Carthage about what happened concerning him a few years ago.

Pelagius, however, as letters sent by certain of our brothers report, is said to be deceiving some while established at Jerusalem. Nevertheless, many more who have been able to investigate his views more carefully are fighting against him on behalf of Christ’s grace and the truth of the catholic faith—especially your holy son, our brother and fellow presbyter Jerome.

5. But we believe that, with the help of the mercy of our Lord God, who may deign both to guide you when you deliberate and to hear you when you pray, those who hold such perverse and destructive opinions will more readily yield to the authority of Your Holiness, drawn from the authority of the holy Scriptures, so that we may rejoice in their correction rather than grieve over their destruction.

Whatever they themselves may choose, Your Venerability certainly sees that immediate and prompt action is needed to prevent them from ensnaring in their traps even others—whom they can number in great numbers—if they are allowed to go unchallenged.

We have sent this letter to Your Holiness from the Council of Numidia, following the example of our fellow bishops of the Church of Carthage and of the province of Carthage. We have learned that they have written to the Apostolic See, which you blessedly illuminate, concerning this matter.

[Note: So in the manuscripts. The printed editions omit the words *Carthaginensis Ecclesiae*, and so forth.]

[Note: The remaining words are absent from the Vatican and Gallican manuscripts. They are found in all the editions. Badius, Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain read: “May you increase in the grace of God.” The editions of the Councils have: “in the grace of the Lord,” or “in the grace of God.”]

In another hand:

Remember us, and may you increase in the grace of God, most blessed and deservedly venerable lord, honored holy Father in Christ.

## Epistle 177

[Note: In correcting this letter we used manuscripts ff, th, two v manuscripts, and the editions of Amerbach, Badius, Erasmus, and Louvain. In the manuscripts and the editions of the Councils, the following title is placed before it: “A personal letter of five bishops to Pope Innocent.”]

[Note: Formerly numbered 95; what was 177 is now 241. Written at approximately the same time.]

### Aurelius and three others, together with Bishop Augustine, to Innocent, exposing Pelagius’ heresy and requesting that it be proscribed by the Apostolic See

To the most blessed and deservedly most honored brother, Pope Innocent, Aurelius, Alypius, Augustine, Evodius, and Possidius, greetings in the Lord.

1. We have sent to Your Holiness letters signed by a considerable number of bishops from the two councils of the province of Carthage and of Numidia, against the enemies of Christ’s grace. They trust in their own strength and in a certain sense say to our Creator: “You made us human beings; we made ourselves righteous.”

They say that human nature is free for the purpose of avoiding the need to seek a Liberator; they say that it is sound so that they may judge a Savior superfluous. For they claim that it is so powerful that, through free will, by its own strength once received at the beginning of its creation, and with no further assistance from the grace of him who created it, it can subdue and extinguish every desire and overcome every temptation.

Many of them rise up against us and say to our soul, “There is no salvation for it in its God” (Psalm 3:3).

The household of Christ, therefore, which says, “When I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Corinthians 12:10), and to which its Lord says, “I am your salvation” (Psalm 34:3), awaits, with anxious heart and with fear and trembling, the Lord’s help also through the charity of Your Veneration.

2. We have heard that in the city of Rome, where Pelagius lived for a long time, there are some who favor him for various reasons: some, it is said, because he persuaded them of such things;

[Note: Badius, Amerbach, Erasmus, Louvain, and the editions of the Councils have: “because he is said to have persuaded you of such things.” A Vatican manuscript has: “because he is said to have persuaded us.” Perhaps the reading should be “because he is said to have persuaded you.” Certainly, as Possidius relates in chapter 18, the Pelagians “were attempting through their ambition to persuade the holy See of their perfidy”; and it is not implausible that they themselves claimed to have actually persuaded him. Nevertheless, we adopt another reading, taken from the Oxford manuscript and substituted by R. P. Quesnel, to whom the common reading seemed insulting to the Roman pontiff.]

but more numerous are those who do not believe that he holds such views, especially because, in the East, where he resides, ecclesiastical proceedings are said to have taken place

[Note: The proceedings of the Synod of Diospolis.]

by which he is thought to have been cleared.

If the bishops there declared him a catholic, this must be believed to have happened for no other reason than that he said he confessed God’s grace and that a person could live righteously through his own labor and will, while not denying that God’s grace assists him in this.

When the catholic bishops heard these words, they could understand no other grace of God than that which they were accustomed to read in the books of God and preach to the people of God—the grace of which the Apostle says, “I do not nullify the grace of God. For if righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing” (Galatians 2:21). This is unquestionably the grace by which we are justified from iniquity and saved from weakness, not the grace by which we were created with a will of our own.

For if those bishops had understood him to be speaking of the grace that we possess even with the impious, with whom we are human beings, while denying the grace by which we are Christians and children of God, what Catholic priest would—not merely patiently listen to him, as we do not say—but even bear him before his eyes?

Therefore the judges are not to be blamed, because, according to ecclesiastical custom, they heard the word “grace” without knowing what such men customarily spread either in the books of their doctrine or into the ears of their followers.

3. The issue is not one Pelagius, who perhaps has already been corrected—would that it were so!—but so many people who contend noisily, drag weak and uneducated souls along as though bound, and weary those who are firm and steadfast in the faith by their very contention, that everything everywhere is already full of them.

Either he must be summoned to Rome by Your Veneration and carefully questioned about what grace he means, so that—if he now admits it—he may confess that grace assists human beings in not sinning and in living righteously; or this same matter must be taken up with him by letter.

When it has been discovered that he means the grace taught by ecclesiastical and apostolic truth, he must then be acquitted without any scruple on the part of the Church and without any hiding-place of ambiguity; then we may truly rejoice at his purification.

4. For whether he says that grace is free will, or that grace is the remission of sins, or that grace is the commandment of the law, he is saying none of the things that, through the provision of the Holy Spirit, pertain to overcoming desires and temptations. God poured out this Spirit upon us most richly (Titus 3:6), he who ascended into heaven and, taking captivity captive, gave gifts to human beings (Ephesians 4:8).

For this reason we pray that we may be able to overcome the temptation of sins, and that the Spirit of God, from whom we have received the pledge (2 Corinthians 2:22), may help our weakness (Romans 8:26).

But whoever prays and says, “Do not bring us into temptation,” is certainly not praying to be human, which he is by nature; nor is he praying to possess free will, which he already received when nature itself was created; nor is he praying for the remission of sins, since that was said above: “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:13, 12); nor is he praying to receive a commandment. Rather, he is plainly praying that he may fulfill the commandment.

[Note: The words “Rather, he is plainly praying that he may fulfill the commandment” were absent from Badius, Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain, but have been restored from the Vatican manuscripts.]

For if he is brought into temptation—that is, if he fails in temptation—he certainly commits the sin that is contrary to the commandment.

He therefore prays that he may not sin, that is, that he may do nothing evil. This is what the Apostle Paul prays for the Corinthians when he says: “We pray to the Lord that you do nothing evil” (2 Corinthians 13:7).

It is therefore sufficiently clear that, although the choice of the will unquestionably exists for not sinning—that is, for not doing evil—its power is nevertheless insufficient unless weakness is assisted.

The prayer itself, therefore, is a most evident testimony to grace. Let Pelagius confess this, and we shall rejoice in him, whether he is upright or corrected.

5. Law and grace must be distinguished. The law knows how to command; grace knows how to help. The law would not command unless there were a will, and grace would not help if the will were sufficient.

We are commanded to possess understanding where it says, “Do not be like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding” (Psalm 32:9); yet we pray to possess understanding where it says, “Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments” (Psalm 119:125).

We are commanded to possess wisdom where it says, “Fools, come at last to wisdom” (Psalm 94:8); yet we pray to possess wisdom where it says, “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach, and it will be given to him” (James 1:5).

[Note: Both this sentence and the following one, which had previously been printed in mutilated form at their beginning, are restored in full by the Vatican and Fuxensis manuscripts.]

We are commanded to possess self-control where it says, “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12:35); yet we pray to possess self-control where it says, “When I knew that no one could be self-controlled unless God gave it, and that it was itself a mark of wisdom to know whose gift it was, I approached the Lord and pleaded with him” (Wisdom 8:21).

Finally, lest it take too long to go through everything, we are commanded not to do evil where it says, “Turn away from evil”; yet we pray not to do evil where it says, “We pray to the Lord that you do nothing evil.”

We are commanded to do good where it says, “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 37:27); yet we pray to do good where it says, “We do not cease praying and asking for you,” and, among the things he prays for them, he says, “That you may walk worthily of God in every pleasing thing, in every good work and word” (Colossians 1:9–10).

Therefore, just as we recognize the will when these things are commanded, so let him also recognize grace when they are requested.

6. We have sent Your Reverence a book that certain religious and honorable young servants of God delivered to us; we do not conceal their names, for they are called Timasius and James.

As we have heard—and as you also know—at Pelagius’ exhortation they abandoned the hope they had placed in the world and now serve God in continence.

When, at last, through some effort of ours, with the Lord’s inspiration, they had been freed from the same error, they produced this book, saying that it belonged to Pelagius, and earnestly requested that a reply be made to it.

This was done; the reply itself was sent back to them.

[Note: The book *On Nature and Grace*.]

They replied with thanks.

[Note: Epistle 168.]

We have sent both works: the one to which the reply was made and the reply itself. And, so as not to burden you excessively, we have marked the passages where we ask you not to hesitate to examine how, when challenged with the question of whether he denied God’s grace, he answered in such a way that he did not say grace was anything except the nature in which God created us.

7. But if he denies that this book is his, or denies that the passages in the book are his, we do not contend over the matter. Let him anathematize them and openly confess that grace which Christian teaching demonstrates and proclaims to be proper to Christians: it is not nature, but that by which nature is saved.

It does not sustain nature by a doctrine sounding in the ears or by some visible assistance, like a planter and waterer acting externally; rather, it sustains it by the provision of the Spirit and by hidden mercy, as God does when he gives the growth (1 Corinthians 3:7).

[Note: Louvain reads: “Let nature be saved, not by a doctrine sounding in the ears or by some visible assistance, as it is somehow planted and watered externally.” Badius, Amerbach, and Erasmus have: “Nature is saved, not by the ears, and so forth.” But the better reading is that of the Vatican manuscript, according to which we have corrected this passage.]

For although, in a certain unobjectionable sense, the grace of God by which we were created may be called grace, so that we might be something rather than nothing, and not something like a corpse that does not live, a tree that does not perceive, or an animal that does not understand, but human beings who exist, live, perceive, and understand, and who are able to give thanks to our Creator for so great a benefit—so that this too may rightly be called grace, since it was granted not on account of the merits of any preceding good works but through God’s free goodness—nevertheless there is another grace by which we are called according to predestination, justified, and glorified, so that we may say, “If God is for us, who is against us? He who did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Romans 8:31–32).

8. This was the grace at issue when those whom Pelagius seriously offended and disturbed told him that he opposed it in his arguments, by which he asserted that human nature, through free will, was sufficient not only for doing but also for perfecting the divine commandments.

Apostolic teaching rightly calls this grace by that name: through it we are saved and justified by the faith of Christ.

Of this grace it is written: “I do not nullify the grace of God. For if righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing” (Galatians 2:21).

Of this grace it is written: “You have been severed from Christ, you who are justified in the law; you have fallen away from grace” (Galatians 5:4).

Of this grace it is written: “But if it is by grace, it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace” (Romans 11:6).

Of this grace it is written: “To the one who works, the reward is not counted according to grace but according to obligation; but to the one who does not work, yet believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness” (Romans 4:4–5).

There are many other passages that you yourself can remember more fully, understand more wisely, and proclaim more clearly.

As for the grace by which we were created as human beings, although we understand that it may rightly be called grace, it is nevertheless remarkable if we read it called by this name in any authentic prophetic, evangelical, or apostolic writings.

9. When, therefore, he was challenged concerning this grace, which is so well known to faithful and catholic Christians, so that he might cease opposing it, what is the meaning of his having raised the same objection against himself in his book, as though from an opponent, and then, in order to clear himself by his reply, answered nothing other than by attributing the grace of the Creator to the nature of created humanity?

Thus he says that righteousness can be fulfilled without sin through free will with the help of divine grace, because God gave this to human beings in the very possibility of their nature.

He is rightly answered: “Then the scandal of the cross has been abolished” (Galatians 5:11). Then Christ died for nothing.

For if he had not died on account of our sins and risen on account of our justification (Romans 4:25), and had not ascended on high, taking captivity captive and giving gifts to human beings, would this possibility of nature that he defends not have existed in human beings?

10. Or was God’s command lacking, and therefore did Christ die? On the contrary, this too was already holy, just, and good (ibid. VII, 12); it had already been said, “You shall not covet” (Exod. XX, 17); it had already been said, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Lev. XIX, 18), and the Apostle says that the whole Law is fulfilled in this commandment (Rom. XIII, 9). And since no one loves himself unless he loves God, the Lord says that the whole Law and the Prophets depend on these two commandments (Matt. XXII, 37–40)—and these two commandments had already been divinely given to humanity. Or had the eternal reward of righteousness not yet been promised? He himself does not say this, since in his writings he even stated that the kingdom of heaven was promised in the Old Testament as well (Heb. XI). If, then, the possibility belonging to nature through free will already existed for producing and perfecting righteousness; if God’s holy, just, and good commandment of the Law already existed; if the eternal reward had already been promised—then Christ died for nothing.

11. Therefore righteousness comes neither through the Law nor through the possibility belonging to nature, but from faith and the gift of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, the one mediator between God and human beings (I Tim. II, 5). If he had not died in the fullness of time for our sins and risen for our justification, then certainly the faith both of the ancients and of us would be made void. But once faith is made void, what righteousness remains for a human being, since “the just shall live by faith” (Hab. II, 4)? For since through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned (Rom. V, 12), unquestionably no one has been or is liberated from this body of death—where another law wars against the law of the mind—by his own possibility, which has been lost, needs a Redeemer, and, wounded, needs a Savior. Rather, liberation comes through the grace of God by faith in the one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus (ibid. VII, 21–25): who, although he was God, made himself human; and, remaining God, became human and himself remade what he had made.

12. I think he is unaware that the faith of Christ, which later came into revelation, was hidden in the times of our fathers; yet through it they too were liberated by the grace of God—all who, throughout the ages of the human race, were able to be liberated by God’s hidden judgment, though that judgment was not blameworthy. Hence the Apostle says, “But possessing the spirit of faith”—obviously the same spirit as they possessed—“according to what is written: I believed, and therefore I spoke; and we also believe, and therefore we speak” (II Cor. IV, 13). From this comes the statement of the Mediator himself: “Abraham your father rejoiced that he was to see my day; he saw it and was glad” (John VIII, 56). From this also Melchizedek, having brought forth the sacrament of the Lord’s table, knew how to prefigure his eternal priesthood [Note: [Col. 0769] In the Vatican Manuscript, “sacrifice.”] (Gen. XIV, 18).

13. But when the Law given in the Scriptures had entered—the Law which the Apostle says came in so that transgression might abound, and of which he says, “If the inheritance is from the Law, it is no longer from the promise. But God granted it to Abraham through the promise”—what, then, is the Law? “It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator. Now a mediator is not of one party; but God is one. Is the Law, then, against the promises of God? Certainly not. For if a law had been given that could give life, righteousness would truly have come from the Law. But Scripture shut up everything under sin, so that the promise might be given to believers through faith in Jesus Christ” (Gal. III, 18–22). Is it not sufficiently shown that this was accomplished through the Law: that sin might be recognized and increased through transgression—for “where there is no law, neither is there transgression” (Rom. IV, 15)—and that thus, against sin’s victory, recourse might be had to divine grace, which is contained in the promises [Col. 0770]? In this way the Law would not be against the promises of God, since through it the knowledge of sin comes about, and through transgression of the Law sin’s abundance, so that God’s promises might be sought for liberation—which is the grace of God—and righteousness might begin to exist in a human being, not his own righteousness but God’s, that is, righteousness given by God’s gift?

14. Even now, certain people, ignorant of God’s righteousness—as it was also said then concerning the Jews—and wishing to establish their own, “are not subject to the righteousness of God” (ibid. X, 3). They too suppose that they are justified through the Law, since free will is sufficient for them to keep it—that is, by their own righteousness produced from human nature, not bestowed by divine grace, which is why it is called God’s righteousness. Hence it is likewise written: “Through the Law comes knowledge of sin. But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the Law, attested by the Law and the Prophets” (ibid. III, 20–21). When he says, “has been manifested,” he shows that it existed then also, but was at that time hidden as the rain obtained by Gideon was hidden, as it were, in the fleece, whereas now it is manifest as upon the threshing floor (Judg. VI, 36–40). Since, therefore, without grace the Law could not have been the death of sin but rather its strength—for it is written, “The sting of death is sin, and the strength of sin is the Law” (I Cor. XV, 56)—just as many now flee from the face of reigning [Note: [Col. 0770] One Vatican manuscript reads “resisting.”] sin to grace, now manifest as upon the threshing floor, so few then fled to it when it was hidden as in the fleece. This distribution of the times, however, refers to the depth of the riches of God’s wisdom and knowledge, concerning which it is said: “How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways” (Rom. XI, 33)!

15. Therefore, if both before the time of the Law and during the time of the Law the righteous fathers, living by faith, were justified not by the possibility of their weak, needy, corrupted nature, sold under sin [Note: [Col. 0770] Bad., Er., etc., read “unworthy.” But Lov. and the manuscripts have “needy,” or, according to an ancient spelling, “indiguae.”], but by the grace of God through faith—and if that same grace, now brought into the open and revealed, justifies even now—then let Pelagius anathematize his writings, in which he argues against this grace, not indeed through defiance but through ignorance, by defending the possibility of nature for conquering sins and fulfilling the commandments. Or, if he denies that those writings are his, or says that writings inserted by his enemies have been attributed to him although he denies that they are his, nevertheless let him anathematize and condemn them, at the fatherly urging and by the authority of Your Holiness.

If, then, he wishes to remove this scandal, burdensome to himself and harmful to the Church, let him learn to do so. His hearers and those perversely devoted to him do not cease to spread this scandal everywhere. For if they learn that the same book which they either think or know to be his has been anathematized and condemned by the authority of Catholic bishops, and especially by that of Your Holiness—which we have no doubt carries the greatest weight with him—we do not think they will thereafter dare, by speaking against the grace of God revealed through Christ’s passion and resurrection, to disturb faithful and sincerely Christian hearts. Rather, with the Lord’s mercy assisting them, and with your prayers—burning with charity and piety and contending together with us—they will trust not in their own strength but in that same grace, so that they may be not only blessed forever but also righteous and holy [Col. 0771].

For this reason we have thought it better to send Your Beatitude the letter written to him by one of us, to whom, through a certain Eastern deacon who was also a citizen of Hippo, he sent certain writings as a kind of defense of himself. We judged it better, and request, that you yourself deign to send it to him; for in that way he will be less unwilling to read it, paying greater attention to the person who sent it than to the person who wrote it.

16. As for what they say—that a human being can be without sin and easily keep God’s commandments if he wishes—although, when this is said together with the help of grace, which was nevertheless revealed and bestowed through the incarnation of God’s Only-Begotten Son, it may seem more tolerable to say, it can nonetheless reasonably cause concern: where and when does this same grace bring it about in us that we are entirely without any sin? Is it in this life, when the flesh desires against the spirit (Gal. V, 17), or rather in that life when the saying written in Scripture will be fulfilled: “Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting? For the sting of death is sin” (I Cor. XV, 54–56)?

This must be examined more carefully on account of certain others who have held, and committed to memory in their writings, that even in this life a human being can be without sin—not from the beginning of his birth, but by conversion from sins to righteousness and from a wicked life to a good life. For thus they understood what is written about Zechariah and Elizabeth: that they walked in all the Lord’s commandments blamelessly. They took the phrase “blamelessly” to mean “without sin,” not denying—indeed, piously confessing, as is also found elsewhere in their writings—the help of the grace of our Lord, not through the natural spirit of a human being but through the ruling Spirit of God (Ambrose, Commentary on Luke I, 6).

They seem, however, to have paid insufficient attention to the fact that Zechariah himself was certainly a priest; and that at that time all priests necessarily had first to offer a sacrifice for their own sins according to God’s Law, and then one for the people (Lev. IX, 7; Heb. VII, 27). Just as now, through the sacrifice of prayer, we are convicted of not being without sin, since we have been commanded to say, “Forgive us our debts,” so then, through the sacrifices of animal victims, the priests were convicted of not being without sin, since they were commanded to offer sacrifices for their own sins.

17. If, then, the matter stands as follows—that through the grace of the Savior we make progress in this life, desire diminishing and charity increasing, but are perfected in the life to come, desire being extinguished and charity completed—then surely what is written, “Whoever is born of God does not sin” (I John III, 9), is spoken with reference to charity itself, which alone does not sin.

For charity belongs to the birth that is from God, as something to be increased and perfected; not the desire that must be diminished and consumed. Yet as long as this desire remains in our members, by a certain law of its own it wars against the law of the mind. But one born of God, neither obeying its desires nor presenting his members as weapons of iniquity to sin, can say, “It is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me” (Rom. VII, 20) [Col. 0772].

18. However this question may stand—for even if a human being is not found to be without sin in this life, it is nevertheless said that this can be achieved through the help of grace and the Spirit of God, and one must strive and pray that it may be achieved—anyone who affirms and desires this, even though he cannot demonstrate that what he affirms is possible, is tolerably mistaken; this is not diabolical impiety but human error. For he believes that what it is certainly praiseworthy to wish for can be accomplished.

For us, however, it is enough that no one is found in the Church of God, at whatever degree or excellence of righteousness, who dares say that he does not need to pray the Lord’s Prayer, “Forgive us our debts,” or who says that he has no sin, lest he deceive himself and the truth not be in him (I John I, 8), even if he is already living blamelessly. For what comes under accusation is not some ordinary human temptation, but grave sin.

19. As for the remaining matters objected to him, Your Beatitude will unquestionably judge them as you have seen them defended in the Proceedings. The gentle kindness of your heart will grant us pardon for having perhaps sent Your Holiness a longer letter than you wished. For we are not pouring our little stream back into your abundant spring to enlarge it; but in this not insignificant trial of the times—from which may the One whom we address with “Do not bring us into temptation” deliver us—we wish you to approve whether our stream, however small, flows from the same source from which your abundant streams flow, and to be consoled by your replies concerning our common participation in the one grace.

## LETTER CLXXVIII [Note: [Col. 0772] We corrected this according to bl. cb. ff. gg. rm. vc. four manuscripts, and according to Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.] [Note: [Col. 0772] Elsewhere 94; the letter that was numbered 178 is now in the Appendix as 19. Written at the same time.]

Augustine to Hilary, concerning the Pelagian heresy condemned in two councils in Africa.

To the most blessed lord, and venerable brother and fellow priest in the truth of Christ, HILARY [Note: [Col. 0772] This Hilary, to whom he sends greetings as a fellow priest—that is, a fellow bishop—according to the heading of the Corbie Manuscript, and who appears from other words of Augustine to have held this office overseas, may reasonably be suspected to be the same as Hilary of Narbonne, to whom Zosimus wrote in the year 417. We believe him, moreover, to be different both from Hilary of Arles, who did not assume the episcopate before the year 428, and from Hilary, a layman, who informed Augustine by letter about the Pelagian heresy emerging in Sicily, around the year 414; for this man to whom the present letter is written appears hitherto not to have known of the Pelagian heresy.], AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

1. When our honorable son Palladius was sailing from our shore, he conferred a favor by asking that I commend not only him to Your Goodness but also myself to your prayers, most blessed lord and venerable brother in the charity of Christ. In doing this, I am certain that Your Holiness will also do what we both anticipate concerning the matter. Since I know that your affection is concerned for us, just as ours is for you, Your Holiness will hear from the aforementioned bearer what circumstances surround us [Col. 0773].

Nevertheless, I shall briefly state what is most necessary. A certain new heresy hostile to the grace of Christ is attempting to rise up against the Church of Christ, but it has not yet openly separated itself from the Church: namely, the heresy of people who dare attribute so much power to human weakness [Note: [Col. 0773] In most manuscripts, “to attribute power to human infirmity.”] that they maintain that only this belongs to God’s grace: that we were created with free will and the possibility of not sinning, and that we received God’s commandments, which we could fulfill; but that, for keeping and fulfilling those commandments, we need no divine assistance.

They hold that remission of sins is necessary for us only because we cannot undo the evil deeds we have committed in the past. But for avoiding and conquering future sins, and overcoming every temptation by its own strength, they hold that human will is sufficient by natural possibility, without any further assistance from God’s grace. They also hold that infants do not need the grace of the Savior by which, through his baptism, they may be delivered from perdition, because they have not contracted from Adam any contagion of condemnation.

2. Your Venerability sees with us how hostile these teachings are to the grace of God, which has been granted to the human race through Jesus Christ our Lord, and how they endeavor to overturn the foundations of the entire Christian faith. We ought not to have kept silent before you, so that in your pastoral care you might guard against such people—people whom we desire and wish rather to be healed within the Church than cut off from it.

For already, as I was writing this, we had learned that in the Church of Carthage an episcopal council had issued a decree against them, to be sent by letter to the holy and venerable Pope Innocent [Note: [Col. 0773] Lov. reads “to be sent to Innocent”; so do we. But the older editions and three Vatican manuscripts read “to be sent,” masculine, agreeing with “decree.”]. We too had already written in a similar manner from the council of Numidia to the same Apostolic See.

3. For all who have our hope in Christ must resist this deadly impiety and condemn and anathematize it in harmony. It even contradicts our prayers, granting that we may say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI, 12), but granting this in such a way as to assert that a human being can, by his own powers, attain such righteousness in this corruptible body, which weighs down the soul, that it is not necessary for him to say, “Forgive us our debts.”

As for what follows, “Do not bring us into temptation” (ibid. 12–13), they do not understand it as a prayer that God should be asked to help us overcome the temptations of sins, but as a prayer that no bodily accident should assail us by falling upon us as a human calamity. For they hold that conquering the temptations of sins has already been placed in our power, through the possibility of nature, so that we regard it as useless to seek this in our prayers.

In one short letter we cannot collect all, or even most, of the arguments of such great impiety, especially since, as I was writing these things, the bearers, who were preparing to sail, would not allow me to delay longer [Col. 0774]. I think I have not been burdensome to your holy understanding by refusing to remain silent concerning so great an evil, which must be avoided with every vigilance, with the Lord’s help [Note: [Col. 0774] Am., Bad., Er., and several manuscripts read “with the vigilance of all.”].

## LETTER CLXXIX [Note: [Col. 0774] Published by Lov. from the Vatican Manuscript, in which alone we found it.] [Note: [Col. 0774] Elsewhere 252; the letter numbered 179 is now 150. Written at approximately the same time.]

Augustine to John, bishop of Jerusalem, exposing the Pelagian heresy contained in his book, which he sends him together with his own book, *On Nature and Grace*, composed against Pelagius; requesting in turn that he send the ecclesiastical Proceedings of the Council of Diospolis, by which Pelagius is said to have been cleared.

To the most blessed lord, and deservedly venerable brother and fellow bishop JOHN, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

1. I dare not be angry that I have not deserved writings from Your Holiness. I think it more likely that a bearer failed to come than that I was despised by Your Veneration, most blessed lord and deservedly venerable brother. But now, since I have quickly learned that God’s servant Luke, through whom I sent these things, will soon be returning, I shall give abundant thanks to the Lord and to your kindness if you deign to visit me by letter.

As for our brother Pelagius, your son, whom I hear that you love greatly, I suggest that you show him this love in such a way that people who know him and have listened to him carefully will not think that Your Holiness has been deceived by him.

2. For certain young men among his disciples, born of highly respectable families and educated in the liberal disciplines, abandoned, at his exhortation, the hope they had placed in the world and devoted themselves to God’s service. Yet in them certain views appeared that opposed the sound doctrine contained in the Savior’s Gospel and declared in the apostolic writings: namely, they were found to argue against God’s grace, through which we are Christians and in which, by faith, we await the hope of righteousness; and they were beginning to be corrected by our admonitions.

They gave me a book which they said belonged to Pelagius himself, asking me to answer him instead. After I saw that I ought to do so, in order that the wicked error itself might be more completely removed from their hearts in this way, I read the book and replied to it.

3. In this book he calls God’s grace nothing other than the nature with which we were created by free will. But the grace that Holy Scripture commends through innumerable testimonies—the grace by which Scripture teaches that we are justified, that is, made righteous, and that in every good work, whether in undertaking or completing it, we are assisted by God’s mercy, as the prayers of the saints most openly show, since they ask from the Lord the things that the Lord commands—this grace he not only leaves unmentioned but speaks much against it.

For he asserts, and vehemently insists, that by free will alone human nature is sufficient for itself to perform righteousness and keep all God’s commandments. Who, then, after reading the same book, would not see how God’s grace is attacked—the grace of which the Apostle says, “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. VII, 24–25)? No place is left for divine assistance, which is why we ought to say in prayer, “Do not bring us into temptation” (Matt. VI, 13). And the Lord would seem to have said to the Apostle Peter without reason, “I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (Luke XXII, 32), if all this is accomplished in us without any help from God, solely by the power of the will.

4. These perverse and impious arguments therefore contradict not only our prayers, in which we ask from the Lord whatever we read and understand the saints to have asked, but also resist our blessings, when we say over the people, wishing and asking the Lord to make them abound in charity toward one another and toward all (I Thess. III, 12), and to grant them, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit (Eph. III, 16), and to fill them with all joy and peace in believing, so that they may abound in hope through the power of the Holy Spirit (Rom. XV, 13).

Why do we ask these things for them, which we know the Apostle asked from the Lord for the peoples, if our nature, created with free will, can already provide all these things for itself by its own will? Why does that same Apostle say, “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God,” if we are led by the spirit of our nature so as to become sons of God? Why does he likewise say, “The Spirit helps our weakness” (ibid. VIII, 14, 26), if our nature was created in such a way that it does not need to be assisted by the Spirit for works of righteousness? Why is it written, “God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure it” (I Cor. X, 13), if we were already created in such a way that by the strength of free will we could overcome every temptation by enduring it?

5. Why should I say more to Your Holiness, when I feel that I am being burdensome—especially since you hear my letter through an interpreter? If you love Pelagius, let him also love you, or rather, let him love himself more, and let him not deceive you.

When you hear him confessing the grace and assistance of God, you think that he means what you mean, since you understand according to the Catholic rule; but you do not know what he has written in his book. For this reason I sent both the book itself and my reply to him, so that Your Venerability may see what grace or assistance of God he means when he is accused of contradicting God’s grace and assistance.

Therefore show him, by teaching, exhorting, and praying for his salvation—which must be found in Christ—that he should confess the grace of God which God’s saints are shown to have confessed when they asked the Lord for the very things he commanded them to do. For they would not be commanded unless our will were to be revealed; nor would they be asked unless the weakness of the will were to be assisted by the One who had commanded.

6. Let him be openly asked whether he approves of praying to the Lord that we may not sin. If he disapproves, let the Apostle be read in his hearing: “We pray to God that you may do no evil” (II Cor. XIII, 7). But if he approves, let him openly proclaim the grace by which we are helped, lest he himself do much evil [Note: [Col. 0776] Lov. reads “so that he himself may not.” But the Vatican manuscripts read “lest he himself.”].

For through this grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord, all who are liberated are liberated; for no one can be liberated in any other way apart from this grace. Therefore it is written, “As all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ” (I Cor. XV, 22): not because no one will be condemned, but because no one will be liberated in any other way [Note: [Col. 0776] These words were absent from the printed editions: “not because no one will be condemned, but because no one will be liberated in any other way”; we have restored them from the Vatican manuscripts.].

For just as no one becomes a son of man except through Adam, so no one becomes a son of God except through Christ. Thus all human beings can become sons of man only through Adam, and all who are descended from them can become sons of God only through Christ.

Let him therefore also state clearly here what he thinks: whether he approves that even infants, who are not yet able either to will or not to will righteousness, are nevertheless liberated by the grace of Christ because of the one human being through whom sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned (Rom. V, 12). Let him say whether he believes that Christ’s blood was shed also for them on account of original sin—blood which was certainly shed for the remission of sins (Matt. XXVI, 28). Above all, we want to know from him what he believes, holds, and certainly confesses and proclaims concerning these matters. In the other things objected to him, even if he is proved to be in error, he is nevertheless tolerated more readily until he is corrected.

7. I also ask that you deign to send us the ecclesiastical Proceedings by which he is said to have been cleared. I ask this at the desire of many bishops who, together with me, are disturbed by uncertain reports concerning the matter. But I alone have written this because I did not wish to miss the opportunity afforded by the bearer’s haste—someone whom I heard could soon return to us.

Instead of these Proceedings, he has already sent us not any part of the Proceedings, but a kind of defense written by himself, in which he said that he had answered the objections of the Gauls [Note: [Col. 0776] Heros and Lazarus, concerning whom see Letter 175, no. 1.]. In it, to omit other matters, when responding to the objection that he had said a human being could be without sin and keep God’s commandments if he wished, he says: “We said that God gave him this possibility. We did not say that someone can be found who has never sinned from infancy to old age; but that, once converted from sins through his own labor and assisted by God’s grace, he can be without sin and, because of this, will not thereafter be incapable of conversion.”
