8. In this response of Pelagius, Your Reverence sees that he confessed that the earlier life of a human being, which extends from infancy, is not without sin, but that a person can be converted to a life without sin through his own labor and with the help of God’s grace.

Why, then, does he say in the book to which I replied that Abel lived in this way—without committing any sin at all? These are his words on the matter:

“This can rightly be said,” he says, “of those whose good or evil deeds Scripture does not mention. But concerning those whose righteousness it mentions, it would undoubtedly also have mentioned their sins if it had perceived them to have sinned. But let us suppose,” he says, “that at other times, because of the great multitude of the people, it concealed and passed over everyone’s sins. At the very beginning of the world, however, when there were only four human beings, what shall we say? Why did it not wish to mention the deeds of all? Was it because of the great multitude, which did not yet exist? Or because it remembered only those who had committed sin, while it could not remember the one who had committed none?

“Certainly,” he says, “at the first time Adam and Eve, from whom Cain and Abel were born, are reported to have been only four human beings. Eve sinned; Scripture made this known. Adam also transgressed; the same Scripture did not remain silent. Cain also sinned, and Scripture itself bore witness to it. It indicates not only their sins but also the character of their sins. If Abel too had sinned,” he says, “Scripture would undoubtedly have said so. If it did not say so, then neither did he sin.”

9. I have excerpted these words from his book; Your Holiness will also be able to find them in that same volume, so that you may understand how you ought to believe him when he denies the other matters as well.

Unless perhaps he says that Abel committed no sin, but that he was nevertheless not without sin—and therefore could not be compared with the Lord, who alone in mortal flesh was without sin—because there was original sin in Abel, which he had drawn from Adam but had not himself committed. Would that he at least say this, so that for the present we might be able to hold a definite view of his position concerning the baptism of infants!

Or perhaps, since he said “from infancy to old age,” he might say that Abel did not sin because he is not shown to have grown old. His words do not indicate this. He said that the earlier life, from the beginning, was sinful, but that the later life could be without sin. For he says that he did not say that someone could be found who had not sinned from infancy to old age, but that, once converted from sins through his own labor and assisted by God’s grace, he could be without sin.

When he says “converted from sins,” he shows that the earlier life is lived in sins. Let him therefore admit that Abel sinned, whose first life was in the world, which he admits is not without sins; and let him look again at his book, where it is clear that he said what he says in this defense: “We did not say.”

10. But if he denies that this book, or this passage in the book, is his, I have suitable witnesses: honorable and faithful men, and unquestionably his friends, who can testify that they themselves gave me the book, that this passage is read in it, and that they said it belonged to Pelagius. Let this at least be sufficient for me, so that he cannot say that I either wrote or falsified it.

Let each person now choose whom he wishes to believe; it is not my task to argue the matter any longer. We ask that you at any rate send the book to him if he denies holding these views, which are objected to him as hostile to the grace of Christ.

His defense is so carefully concealed that, if no ambiguity in his words has deceived your holy prudence—which does not know his other writings—we shall rejoice and give great thanks. We shall not be greatly concerned whether he has never held those perverse [Col. 0778] and impious views or whether he has at some time corrected himself concerning them.

## LETTER CLXXX [Note: [Col. 0778] It was not found in the manuscripts except in the Vatican Manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 0778] Elsewhere 260; the letter numbered 180 is now 228. Written toward the end of the year 416.]

Augustine to Oceanus, briefly replying about the origin of the soul and about a useful lie, and asking him to send Jerome’s book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*.

To the deservedly dear lord and venerable brother among the members of Christ, OCEANUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings.

1. I received two letters from Your Affection at the same time. In one of them you mention a third and recall that you sent it earlier; I do not remember receiving it—or rather, I seem to remember well that I did not receive it.

For the letters I did receive, however, I give abundant thanks to your kindness toward us. The reason I did not answer immediately is that I was swept away amid one storm after another of various occupations. Now, having found a drop of free time, I preferred to answer something rather than maintain a prolonged silence toward your most sincere affection and become more troublesome through silence than through speaking.

2. I already knew what the holy Jerome thought concerning the origin of souls, and I had already read these very words that you placed in your letter from his book. But the difficulty of the question does not lie in what troubles some people: how God can justly bestow souls even upon adulterous conceptions. For sins cannot harm those who live well and turn to God in faith and piety—not even their own sins, much less the sins of their parents.

The question is rightly asked, however, whether it is true that new souls are individually made from nothing for each person who is born: how can the countless souls of infants—whom it is certain will leave their bodies without baptism before they reach rational years, before they are able to know or grasp anything just or unjust—be justly handed over to condemnation by him with whom there is no injustice (Rom. IX, 14)?

There is no need to say more about this matter, since you know what I wish, or rather what I do not wish, to say. I think that what I have said should be enough for a wise person. Nevertheless, if you have read anything bearing on this from which the question might be resolved, or heard anything from his own mouth, or if the Lord has granted you knowledge of something while you were reflecting on it yourself, I beg you to share it with me, so that I may give more abundant thanks.

3. As for what you thought could be resolved concerning a useful and beneficial lie, using the Lord’s example when he said that the Son does not know the day and hour at which this age will end (Mark XIII, 32): as I read it, I was delighted by the effort of your ingenuity, but it seems to me in no way correct to call a figurative expression a lie.

It is not a lie when we call a day “joyful” because it makes people joyful, or a lupine “sad” because, when tasted, its bitter flavor makes the taster’s face sad; nor is it a lie when we say that God knows because he makes a human being know. You yourself recalled this statement addressed to Abraham: “Now I know” (Gen. XXII, 12).

These are certainly not lies, as you very easily perceive. Therefore blessed Hilary, when he explained an obscure question through this obscure kind of figurative expression, so that we might understand that he had evidently said that Christ did not know in the sense that he makes others not know by concealing the matter, did not excuse a lie but showed that it was not a lie—not only in the more customary figures of speech but also in that figure called metaphor, which is familiar to everyone through ordinary speech (Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book 9).

For someone might insist that it is a lie to say that vines are “gemmed,” crops “wave,” and young men “blossom,” since in these things one sees neither waves, stones, herbs, nor trees where these words are used literally.

4. Moreover, with your intelligence and learning you readily perceive how different from these is what the Apostle says: “When I saw that they were not walking uprightly according to the truth of the Gospel, I said to Peter before them all: If you, though you are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?” (Gal. 2:14). There is no figurative obscurity here; the words are literal and plainly expressed. The Apostle to the Gentiles certainly either spoke the truth or spoke falsely to those whom he was travailing over until Christ should be formed in them (Gal. 4:19), and to whom he had declared under divine attestation: “What I am writing to you, behold, before God, I do not lie” (Gal. 1:20). If he spoke falsely—which God forbid—you see what follows; and the testimony of truth and the remarkable example of humility in the Apostle Peter admonish you to shudder at both alternatives. [Note: Lov. reads, “removes from you the truth, which you should shudder at.” The Vatican manuscript reads, “warning you, as you shudder,” etc. We suspect that the dilemma proposed here—namely, “Either he spoke the truth or he spoke falsely,” etc.—has been shortened by the loss of some clause. For what follows does not immediately state, “If he spoke the truth,” etc.]

5. But why say more about this, when I and the aforesaid venerable brother Jerome have already dealt sufficiently in letters with this question between us? In his most recent work, which he has just published under the name of Critobulus against Pelagius (Book 1 against Pelagius), he likewise maintained concerning this matter the same judgment about the event and words of the Apostles that we too have followed from the blessed Cyprian (Epistle 71 to Quintus).

Rather, concerning the origin of souls—not because of adulterous births, but because of the condemnation, God forbid, of the innocent, a question which, in my opinion, is not foolishly raised—if you have learned anything from so great and eminent a man that could properly be answered to those who are uncertain, I ask you not to refuse to share it with us. For you appeared to me in your letters so learned and agreeable that it is worthwhile to converse with you by letter.

I do not know whether the book of that same man of God, which the presbyter Orosius brought and gave to Your Dilection to copy, and in which he is praised for having argued splendidly concerning the resurrection of the flesh, has already been sent to us; I ask you not to delay sending it. We did not request it earlier precisely because we intended that it should be copied and corrected; and we now think that ample time has been granted for both tasks. May you live mindful of us in God.

## LETTER CLXXXI

[Note: Reviewed against the manuscripts bl. cb. ff. gg. rm. th. vc., and against Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]  
[Note: Also numbered 91. The letter that was numbered 181, bearing an Italian heading, is contained in Letter 147 to Paulina. Written after the preceding letter.]

Innocentius to the Fathers of the Council of Carthage, confirming their teaching and judgment against the Pelagians.

[Col. 0780]

INNOCENTIUS to Aurelius, Numidius, [Note: Thus in the Vatican and Gallic manuscripts. In the printed editions, after Aurelius alone there follows: “And to all the holy bishops, and to the others,” etc.] Rusticianus, Ridentianus, Evagrius, Antonius, Palatinus, Adeodatus, Vincentius, Publianus, Theasius, Tutus, Pannonius, Victor, Restitutus, the other Restitutus, Rusticus, Fortunatianus, Ampelius, Ambivius, Felix, Donatianus, Adeodatus, Octavius, Serotinus, Majorinus, Posthumianus, Crispulus, Victor, the other Victor, Leucius, Marianus, Fructuosus, Faustinianus, Quodvultdeus, Candorius, Maximus, Megasius, Rusticus, Rufinianus, Proculus, Severus, Thomas, Januarius, Octavianus, Praetextatus, Sixtus, Quodvultdeus, Pentadius, Quodvultdeus, Cyprianus, Servilius, Pelagianus, Marcellus, Venantius, Didymus, Saturninus of Byzacena, Germanus, Germanianus, Inventius, Majorinus, Inventius, Candidus, Cyprianus, Romanianus, Aemilianus, Africanus, Marcellinus, [Note: Thus in the manuscripts, except the Vatican, which after the name Marcellinus inserts: “and to all the holy bishops”] and to the other most beloved brothers who were present at the Council of Carthage: greetings in the Lord.

### 1

In seeking guidance concerning matters which ought to be treated with every diligence by priests, and especially by a true, just, and Catholic council, while preserving the examples of ancient tradition and mindful of ecclesiastical discipline, you have now confirmed the strength of our religion by your sound judgment no less in consulting us than previously when you issued your decision. You approved that judgment should be referred to us, knowing what is owed to the Apostolic See, since all of us placed here desire to follow the Apostle, from whom the episcopate itself and the whole authority of this title arose. Following him, we know how both to condemn what is evil and to approve and praise what deserves approval.

You also rightly judge that the institutions of the Fathers, which you preserve in priestly duty, must not be trampled upon: namely, that whatever was done, even in separate and distant provinces, should not be considered concluded before it came to the knowledge of this See, so that by the full authority of this See whatever judgment was just might be confirmed. From here the other Churches were to receive their directives—as though all waters flowed from their source, and pure streams from an uncorrupted head flowed through the various regions of the whole world—whom they should instruct, whom they should cleanse, and whom the water worthy of clean bodies should avoid as stained with filth that could not be washed away.

### 2

I therefore rejoice, dearest brothers, that you sent letters to us through our brother and fellow bishop Julius, and that, together with the Churches over which you preside, you show your concern for the welfare of all. You ask that throughout all the Churches of the entire world there should be one common decision about what is beneficial to all, so that the Church, established upon its own regulations and strengthened by a decree of a just judgment that protects it from such men, may not be compelled to fear them. [Note: Thus in the Gallic manuscripts. One Vatican manuscript reads: “So that, with the Churches established by their regulations and these men guarded against by firm decretal ordinances, and others whose perfidy has not yet become evident, who, instructed in perverse doctrines,” etc. Bad., Am., Er., and Lov. read: “So that the Church, established upon its regulations, may be strengthened by decretal ordinances through this very judgment by which it is protected from them.”]

These men, instructed—or rather destroyed—by the sophistries of perverse words, disputing under the appearance of Catholic faith and breathing out a poisonous venom in order to corrupt the hearts of right-thinking people toward the worse, seek to overthrow the whole discipline of true doctrine.

### 3

The disease must therefore be healed without delay, lest the accursed sickness creep farther into people’s minds. When a physician sees that some illness has affected this earthly body, he considers it a great proof of his art if, through his timely intervention, one who seemed hopelessly ill quickly recovers. Or when he sees a putrid wound, he applies poultices and other remedies by which the wound that has arisen may be covered over; but if, remaining as it is, it cannot be healed, then, lest it infect the rest of the body with its corruption, he cuts away with the knife what is harmful, so as to preserve the remainder whole and untouched.

That wound, therefore, which has crept into an otherwise pure and healthy body must be cut away, lest, when it is cleansed too slowly, the sediment of this evil settle almost in the very vitals, where it cannot be drained out.

### 4

For what sound judgment can we henceforth have concerning men who think that they owe their goodness to themselves and do not consider the One whose grace they receive every day? Yet these men, being what they are, receive no grace from God, because they trust that they can attain without Him as much as even those who ask it from Him scarcely deserve to receive.

What can be so unjust, so barbarous, so ignorant of the whole of religion, so hostile to Christian minds, as to deny that you owe to Him whatever you obtain through daily grace, when you yourself confess that you owe to Him the fact that you were born? Will you therefore be more capable of providing for yourself than He can be within you—He who made you exist?

And when you think that you owe Him the fact that you live, how can you not think that you owe Him the manner in which you live, through obtaining His daily grace? And when you deny that we need divine assistance, as though we were made perfect in every respect by our own power, how can we not call His assistance upon us, since we are nevertheless able to be such by ourselves? [Note: Bad., Am., Er., and Lov. read, “how, then, can we not?” But the Gallic and Vatican manuscripts read, “how can we not?” This is evidently the correct reading from what follows, since Innocentius wishes to prove that a just person should call upon God’s help in order to live more holily. A little later the same manuscripts read, “whether we live well, we call upon him,” where most printed editions have, “we pray.”]

### 5

Whoever denies the assistance of God—I would like to ask what he means: that we do not deserve it, or that God cannot provide it, or that there is nothing for which anyone ought to request it? That God can provide it is demonstrated by the works themselves, and we cannot deny that we need daily assistance.

Whether we live well, we call upon it so that we may live better and more holily; or whether, thinking wrongly, we turn away from good things, so that we may return to the right path, we need His assistance all the more.

For what could appear more deadly, more precipitous toward ruin, or more exposed to every danger than this: if, thinking that the only thing sufficient for us is what we received when we were born, namely free will, we seek nothing further from the Lord? That would mean forgetting our Creator and, to show ourselves free, renouncing His power, as though He had nothing more that He could give—He who made you free at your birth.

We do not know that unless God’s grace, implored with great prayers, descends upon us, we cannot even attempt to overcome the errors of earthly corruption and the worldly body; for it is not free will, but God’s assistance alone, that can make us equal to resisting them.

### 6

If the one who cries out that he needs divine assistance does so, although he would not seek it if free will were more beneficial to him—for although he was a blessed man and already chosen by the Lord, he needed nothing—yet he thus beseeches God, saying: “Be my helper; do not abandon me or despise me, O God my Savior” (Ps. 26:9), then we say that what we received at birth is sufficient for us as free will, while he asks God to be his helper. We say that we can suffice by ourselves; he begs God not to abandon him.

Do we not plainly learn what we ought to pray for, when that man, blessed to such a degree, as we said above, earnestly asks not to be despised? Those who affirm the former propositions must necessarily condemn this one. Should David be accused as ignorant of prayer and unaware of his own nature, when, though he knows how much is present in his own nature, he asks God to be his helper and constant helper—and, not content with that constant help, earnestly begs in prayer that He never despise him—and proclaims and cries this throughout the whole Psalter?

If, therefore, that great man confessed this to be necessary, just as he continually said it, and taught it by his example, how do Pelagius and Celestius, setting aside the whole testimony of the Psalms and rejecting such teaching, expect to persuade anyone that we neither ought to seek God’s assistance nor need it, when all the saints testify that they can do nothing without it?

### 7

Long ago, free will, by using its own goods without due caution, fell and sank into the depths of transgression; it found no way by which it could rise from there. Deceived by its own freedom, it would have lain crushed forever beneath this ruin, had not Christ’s coming, according to His grace, raised it up.

Through the cleansing of the new birth, He purged every former fault by the washing of His baptism. Strengthening its condition so that it might proceed more rightly and securely, He nevertheless did not deny His grace for the future. For although He had redeemed the human being from former sins, He knew that the person could sin again, and He preserved many means of restoration, by which He might correct him after those sins as well.

He provides daily remedies. Unless we rely upon them and strive with confidence in them, we shall in no way be able to overcome human errors. For it is necessary that by the help of the One with whose aid we conquer, we should again be conquered if He does not assist us. But I could say more, were it not clear that you have said everything.

### 8

Therefore, whoever appears to agree with the opinion that we do not need divine assistance confesses himself an enemy of the Catholic faith and ungrateful for God’s benefits. For they are not even worthy of our communion, since by preaching such doctrines they have polluted it. By following of their own accord the things they teach, they have withdrawn farther from true religion.

Since the whole of our profession consists in this, and since in our daily prayers we do nothing except seek how we may obtain God’s mercy, how can we tolerate men who boast such things? What error, I ask, so blinds their hearts that, if they themselves feel no grace of God because they are neither worthy of it nor deserve it, they do not consider what divine grace bestows every day upon each of the others?

These men are entirely deserving of such blindness, since they have not even left themselves the belief that they can be recalled from errors by divine assistance. By denying assistance, they have taken it away completely—not from others, but from themselves. They must be removed farther away and kept far from the inner life of the Church, lest an error that has occupied much ground for a long time without punishment should afterward grow incurable. For if they remain long under this impunity, they will necessarily lead many into the perversity of their own minds and deceive the innocent—or rather the unwary—who follow the Catholic faith. They will think that those men are right-minded whom they continue to see remaining in the Church.

### 9

Let the incurable wound therefore be separated from the healthy body. When the breath of the raging disease has been removed, let what is sound endure with greater caution, and let the purer flock be cleansed from the contagion of this diseased sheep.

Let the perfection of the whole body remain undefiled. We have learned that you follow and maintain it by this judgment against those men, and together with you we preserve it with equal agreement.

If, however, they should call upon some assistance of God—which up to now they have denied—and recognize that they need His help in order to be freed from the stain into which they fell through the crookedness of their hearts, and if, as though dragged into the light from foul darkness, they should condemn what they have hitherto believed, after removing and rejecting everything by which their entire vision was defiled and darkened so that they could not see the truth; if they should at last submit their minds to sound arguments and, corrected to some extent from this stain, entrust and subject themselves to true counsel, then it will lie within the power of the bishops to help them to some degree and to provide such wounds with the care which the Church customarily does not deny to the fallen when they have come to their senses.

Thus, recalled from their precipices, they may be brought back within the Lord’s fold, lest, remaining outside and excluded from the great protection of the fortress of faith, they be exposed to every danger, to be devoured and tormented by the teeth of wolves—against which, because of the perverse teaching by which they provoked them against themselves, they would be unable to resist.

But your admonitions have provided a sufficient answer, since examples from our law abound so fully. We have judged that nothing remains for us to say, since it is clear that you omitted nothing and suppressed nothing by which those men might be refuted and shown to be utterly convicted.

For this reason we set out no testimonies, because your report is full of them, and it is sufficiently clear that so many highly learned priests have said everything. Nor is it proper to believe that you overlooked anything that could contribute to the case.

And in another hand: Farewell, brothers.

And at the side: Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, after the consulship of Theodosius Augustus, seven times consul, and Junius Quartus, a man of clarissimus rank. [Note: Thus in the manuscripts. The printed editions read “on the fifth day before the Kalends,” omitting the consuls, whom we have supplied from the Vatican, Corbie, and Germain manuscripts, although in the Corbie manuscript one of the consuls is called Lunus or Lunius. In the Vatican manuscript he is called Lucius, as also in the Germain manuscript, where, through an incorrect interpretation of the abbreviations v. c., it is written “with Lucius Quartus V as consuls.”]

## LETTER CLXXXII

[Note: Reviewed against bl. ff. th., two Vatican manuscripts, Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]  
[Note: Also numbered 93. The letter that was numbered 182 is now Appendix 1. Written at the beginning of 417.]

Innocentius, Roman pontiff, to the Fathers of the Council of Milevis, approving their proceedings against the Pelagians.

[Col. 0784]

INNOCENTIUS to Silvanus the elder, Valentinus, and the other most beloved brothers who were present at the Council of Milevis: greetings in the Lord.

### 1

Among the other concerns of the Roman Church and the occupations of the Apostolic See, in which we carefully and moderately deliberate upon the petitions of different persons, our brother and fellow bishop Julius unexpectedly brought me your letters, which you sent from the Council of Milevis with an especially zealous concern for the faith. He appended as well writings of equal character containing the complaints of the Council of Carthage.

The Church certainly rejoices that pastors show such concern for the flocks entrusted to them that they not only do not allow any of them to fall into error, but, if some sheep have been led astray by the grass of a more baneful pleasure and persist in error, either wish them to be entirely separated or, avoiding things long since unlawfully sought, wish to protect them by the vigilant circumspection of their former guardianship. In both respects they are acting for the good of the Church: lest either, by receiving such people, the others should be led astray by their example, or, by rejecting those who return, they should seem to have delivered them to the bites of wolves.

This is a very prudent consultation, full of Catholic faith. [Note: The Vatican manuscripts and the editions of the councils read, “full of the will of consultation.” Bad., Am., Er., and Lov. read, “full of consolation.” Some manuscripts have “consultation.”]

For who could tolerate someone who remains in error, or fail to receive someone who corrects himself? For just as I consider it harsh to show indulgence to sinners, so I judge it impious to deny a hand to those who have been converted.

### 2

You therefore consult carefully and appropriately the mysteries of the apostolic honor—of that honor, I mean, whose concern extends to all the Churches beyond those matters that are external (II Cor. 11:28)—about anxious questions concerning what judgment ought to be upheld, following the pattern of the ancient rule which, as you know, has always been observed with me throughout the whole world.

But I pass over this; I do not think your prudence is unaware of it. What did you establish by your action except this—that you know that answers are always sent from the apostolic source to those who seek them throughout all the provinces?

Especially whenever the faith is at issue, I think all our brothers and fellow bishops ought to refer the matter only to Peter, that is, to the author of their name and honor, just as Your Dilection has now referred this matter, so that it may benefit all the Churches throughout the whole world in common.

They will necessarily become more cautious when they see that the inventors of evils have been separated from ecclesiastical communion by the decrees of our judgment, after the report of the two councils.

### 3

Your charity will therefore enjoy a twofold benefit. You will possess the grace of preserved canons, and the whole world will make use of your benefit.

For what Catholic man would wish to continue conversation with the adversaries of Christ? Who would wish even to share the very light of life with them in communion? The authors of this new heresy must certainly be avoided.

For what could they have devised more bitterly against God than to nullify divine assistance and remove the reason for daily prayer? This is to say: “Why do I need God?”

Hymnidicus rightly says against them: “Behold, men who did not set God as their helper” (Ps. 52:9).

Therefore, while denying God’s help, they say that a human being can be sufficient for himself and does not need divine grace. Deprived of this, he must necessarily perish, entangled in the snares of the devil, while he attempts to fulfill all the commandments of life by freedom alone.

O perverse doctrine of utterly depraved minds! Let it finally recognize that freedom itself deceived the first human being in such a way that, while using its reins too indulgently, he fell through presumption into transgression. He could not be rescued from it until the coming of Christ the Lord, through the providence of regeneration, restored his former state of freedom.

Let it hear David saying: “Our help is in the name of the Lord” (Ps. 123:8); and: “Be my helper; do not abandon me or despise me, O God my Savior” (Ps. 26:9). He would have spoken these words in vain if what he was asking from the Lord in mournful speech had depended solely upon his own will.

### 4

Since these things are so, and since throughout all the divine Scriptures we read that nothing but God’s assistance is to be joined to free will, and that free will can do nothing when deprived of heavenly protection, how do Pelagius and Celestius stubbornly defend this possibility as belonging to free will alone, as you report, and persuade themselves—or, what is more grievous to the common sorrow, already persuade many others?

We could employ many examples to destroy such teaching, if we did not know that Your Holiness fully understands all the divine Scriptures. Especially since your report is filled with such abundant and powerful testimonies that by these alone the present doctrine can be overthrown, there is no need for hidden proofs, since they neither dare nor are able to oppose the passages you have set out, which are obvious and readily available.

They therefore attempt to take away God’s grace, which we must seek even after the former state of our freedom has been restored; for we cannot otherwise avoid the devil’s schemes unless He assists us in the same way.

### 5

But what your fraternity says they preach—that infants can be granted the rewards of eternal life even without the grace of Baptism—is utterly foolish.

“For unless they eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, they shall not have life in themselves” (John 6:54).

Those who defend for infants a life without regeneration seem to me to wish to abolish Baptism itself, since they preach that infants possess what, according to the belief concerning them, is conferred only through Baptism. If, therefore, they do not wish non-regeneration to cause any harm, they must admit that the sacred waters of regeneration are also of no benefit.

But so that the perverse doctrine of these superfluous men may be swiftly cut off by the reasoning of truth, the Lord proclaims this in the Gospel, saying: “Let the children come to me, and do not prevent them; for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these” (Luke 18:16).

### 6

We therefore decree, by the authority of apostolic vigor, that Pelagius and Celestius—that is, the inventors of new expressions which, as the Apostle said, customarily produce no edification but rather utterly empty questions—be deprived of ecclesiastical communion until they recover their senses from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive according to his will (II Tim. 2:23, 26).

Meanwhile, they are not to be received into the Lord’s fold, which they themselves chose to abandon by following the path of a perverse way. “Those who trouble you and wish to pervert the Gospel of Christ must be cut off” (Gal. 1:7).

At the same time we command that whoever attempts to defend this position with similar obstinacy be restrained by an equal punishment. For not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to those who do them, are worthy of death (Rom. 1:32). I do not think there is much difference between the intention of the one who commits an act and the favor of the one who consents to it. I add something further: often the person who errs ceases to err when no one agrees with him.

Let this judgment therefore remain fixed against the aforesaid men, dearest brothers. Let them be absent from the courts of the Lord; let them lack pastoral protection, lest the dreadful contagion of two sheep perhaps spread through the unwary populace, and the wolf rejoice in his predatory heart within the Lord’s fold at seeing so great a mass of sheep laid low, while the wound of two is negligently tolerated by the guardians.

Care must therefore be taken lest, by permitting wolves, we appear to be hirelings rather than shepherds.

### 7

Because Christ the Lord Himself declared in His own voice that He does not desire the death of the dying, but only that he turn back and live (Matt. 9:13), we command that if they should ever return to soundness, abandoning the error of their perverse doctrine, and should condemn the things by whose transgression they condemned themselves, the Church must not deny them its customary medicine—that is, its shelter.

Otherwise, while perhaps preventing them from returning, we may leave them truly outside the fold, where they remain awaiting the enemy and are swallowed by his ravenous jaws, which they armed against themselves with the weapons of their evil disputation. [Note: Thus in the Vatican manuscript. The printed editions read: “Remaining outside and awaiting the jaws of the enemy.”]

Farewell, brothers. Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Honorius and Constantius.

## LETTER CLXXXIII

[Note: Corrected against cb. ff. th., two Vatican manuscripts, Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]  
[Note: Also numbered 96. The letter that was numbered 183 is now Appendix 2. Written at the beginning of 417.]

A rescript of Innocentius to five bishops, rejecting the teaching of Pelagius and declaring that he must be condemned unless he renounces the heresy.

To the most beloved brothers, the bishops Aurelius, Alypius, Augustine, Evodius, and Possidius: Innocentius sends greetings.

### 1

We received with great pleasure the letters of Your Fraternity, full of faith and strengthened throughout by the whole force of Catholic religion. They were sent from two councils through our brother and fellow bishop Julius. Their entire tenor and composition consist in a sound consideration of God’s daily grace and in the correction of those who hold the contrary view, so that they may both remove every error from those men and, by providing whatever example of our law may be needed, offer them a worthy teacher whom they ought to follow.

But concerning these matters we have already said enough above, I think, when in reply to your reports we sent our rescript expressing what we thought both of their perfidy and of your judgment.

Nevertheless, something further continually presents itself that may be said against them, and what can overcome them cannot ever be lacking, since their position is so wretched and impious that it is overcome by the power of our faith and by truth itself in even fuller measure.

For whoever rejects and despises every hope of life, confusing his heart by an argument hostile and deserving of condemnation, believing that there is nothing to receive from God and nothing left to request for his healing—what has he left for himself thereafter, since he has taken this away from himself?

### 2

If, therefore, there are some whom such great perversity has bound in its own defense, who surrender and attach themselves to this doctrine, hoping that what is in fact utterly abhorrent and completely opposed belongs to Catholic teaching, then, infected by their warnings and words and led astray by them, they should hasten to return to the straight path, lest error, occupying their minds for too long and nourished as though by their own senses, invade them.

For wherever Pelagius took his stand, he deceived by this assertion the minds of those who readily or simply believed him as he argued—whether they are in this city (whom, since they are unknown to us, we can neither expose nor deny, for even if they exist they remain hidden, and they would never dare either to defend him when he preaches these things or to boast such doctrines in the presence of one of our number; nor could anyone easily be detected amid so great a multitude of people or be recognized anywhere), or whether they live in any place throughout the world.

We trust in the mercy and grace of our God that they will readily be corrected when they hear the condemnation of the man who is found to be obstinate and resistant, the author of this doctrine. It makes no difference where these people are, provided that wherever they can be found, they can be healed.

### 3

Yet we cannot be persuaded that he has been cleared, although Acts have been brought to us by certain laymen unknown to me, in which he was supposedly heard and acquitted. We doubt whether these are genuine, because they did not come with any formal presentation of that council, nor have we received any letters from those before whom he pleaded the case.

If he could have trusted in his own acquittal, we believe he would have done what would have been much more appropriate and much truer: he would have compelled those who judged him to announce it in their letters.

But since the Acts themselves contain certain matters which he partly suppressed by avoiding the charges brought against him, and partly confused in complete obscurity by turning many words back upon himself; since he cleared himself in some matters by arguments that were more false than sound, as it might appear for the moment, denying some things and changing others through a false interpretation—

### 4

Would that, as is more greatly to be desired, he might now turn from the error of his own path to the true way of the Catholic faith, and desire and wish to be cleared by considering God’s daily grace and recognizing His assistance! Then he might be seen to be genuinely corrected and approved by all through manifest reasoning—not by the evidence of the Acts, but by a heart converted to the Catholic faith.

Therefore we can neither condemn nor approve the judgment of those men, since we do not know whether the Acts are genuine; or, if they are genuine, it is clear that he evaded the matter rather than cleared himself in complete truth.

If he trusts and knows that he is not worthy of condemnation by us, and that he has now refuted everything he previously said, he ought not to wait to be summoned by us; rather, he himself should hasten so that he may be acquitted.

For if he still holds these opinions, when he knows that he must be condemned, how will he submit himself to our judgment upon receiving any letters whatsoever? If he had to be summoned, it would be better done by those who are nearer and not separated by so great a distance.

Yet care will not be lacking if he provides an opportunity for healing. He can condemn the opinions he held and, by sending letters concerning his error, ask forgiveness from us—as is fitting for one returning—dearest brothers.

### 5

We carefully read the book said to be his, which Your Charity sent to us. In it we found many things written against God’s grace, many blasphemies, nothing pleasing, and almost nothing that would not be utterly displeasing—something to be condemned and trampled upon by anyone. No one except the person who wrote such things would receive or hold their like in his mind.

We did not think it necessary here to discuss the Law at greater length, as though Pelagius were present and resisting, since we are speaking with you, who know the whole matter and rejoice with us in equal agreement. [Note: The Vatican manuscripts read, “knowing the whole matter.” Most printed editions read, “knowing the whole,” while Quesnel reads, “knowing the whole,” referring it to the Law. There is an allusion to Romans 7:1, “I speak to those who know the Law.”]

These examples are better set out when we are dealing with people who are known to be ignorant of such matters. For to whom who thinks rightly would discussion of the possibility of nature, free will, the whole grace of God, and daily grace not be an especially abundant subject?

Let him therefore anathematize the opinions he held, so that those who collapsed under his speeches and instructions may learn what the true faith contains. They will more easily be recalled when they perceive that these things have been condemned by their own author.

But if he stubbornly wishes to persist in this impiety, action must be taken so that help may at least be provided for those whom not their own error but rather his has led astray. [Note: Thus in the manuscripts. Lov. and several other printed editions read: “those whom not crime brought here, but rather error led astray.”] Otherwise they too may lose the benefit of this medicine, which he himself neither accepts nor seeks.

(And in another hand:) May God keep you safe, dearest brothers. Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, after the consulship of the most glorious Theodosius Augustus, seven times consul, and Junius Quartus Palladius, a man of clarissimus rank. [Note: Bad., Am., Er., and Lov. note “on the fifth day before the Kalends of February.” But the Vatican manuscript and the editions of the councils have “on the sixth day,” omitting the consuls, who are identified in the Corbie manuscript—not, as Noris reports from Sirmond in *History of the Pelagians*, Book 1, chapter 11, namely, “Given on the day before the Kalends of February, after the consulship of the most glorious,” etc., but as follows: “Given on the day before the Kalends of February, with the most glorious Theodosius Augustus and Junius Quartus Palladius, men of clarissimus rank, as consuls.” The copyist appears to have made two errors: first, he moved the abbreviation P. C., which signified “after the consulship,” and interpreted it as “on the day before the Kalends”; second, from the abbreviation VII he made the word *qui*.]

## LETTER CLXXXIV

[Note: Collated with cb. ff., two Vatican manuscripts, Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]  
[Note: Also numbered 97. The letter that was numbered 184 is now Appendix 3. Written at approximately the same time.]

INNOCENTIUS to Aurelius and Augustine, bishops.

The return of our most beloved Germanus the fellow presbyter ought not to have been fruitless for the duties of our office. For it seems somehow natural and appropriate to us to greet the dearest through those who are dear.

We therefore earnestly desire that Your Germanitas may rejoice in the Lord, and we ask you to return like prayers to God on our behalf, because, as you well know, we accomplish more through prayers offered jointly and reciprocally than through prayers made singly or privately.

# LETTER CLXXXIV BIS

[Note: This letter, which is absent from B., was taken from a single Gottweig manuscript, as is noted in the preface, col. XXXVIII and following.] [Note: See the preface, cols. 49–50, where the two recently discovered letters of Augustine are discussed. They were written at the beginning of the year 417. M.] Praising Peter’s and Abraham’s zeal, he incidentally mentions the Pelagians and approves the view that infants dying without baptism are condemned, since they are conceived through concupiscence; but unbelievers, whose kinds are many, are not corrected by the authority of Sacred Scripture but converted through suppliant prayers. The plan and arrangement of the books of *The City of God*.

[Col. 0789]

To my most beloved lords and holy sons, Peter and Abraham, Augustine sends greetings in the Lord.

## CHAPTER I

### 1

Your holy zeal, by which you think that many things must be asked of me so that you may be able to resist contentious impieties without being unarmed, justice ought not to despise, nor can charity do so. But a single letter, however lengthy, cannot contain a careful response to everything. You should know that in many of my shorter works I have already answered, insofar as I could, everything—or nearly everything—you ask. [Note: Augustine uses almost the same opening in *Book to Orosius against the Priscillianists*, chapter 1, §1: “In answering you, dearest son Orosius, I ought neither to respond to everything that you have set down in your memorandum, nor ought I wholly fail to respond, lest I seem to have despised your zeal, which is most pleasing to me, and thereby give unintended offense. For in certain of our short works, which you have either read or will be able to read, much has been said that can serve against the Priscillianist heresy,” etc. We have transcribed this merely as an example; henceforth it will be sufficient to indicate similar and parallel passages.]

If you read these works—for I hear that you have ordered your lives in service to God in such a way that you have leisure for reading—either the whole of your instruction will be laid open to you, or, at least, I do not think much will be lacking, especially since you possess within you the Teacher through whose grace you are what you are. For what does one human being contribute to another’s learning if we are not teachable by the Lord (John 6:45)? Nevertheless, in this letter too, with the Lord’s help, I shall not defraud your expectation, at least not with a brief reply.

### 2

The Lord says: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16:16). Therefore, when infants are baptized, it is not said without meaning but is truly enacted that they are counted among believers. [Note: See *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book 1, §24, and book 3, §2; Letter 98, §10; Sermon 294, §14; *Unfinished Work against Julian*, book 6, chapter 3.] Hence newborn offspring are now called by the mouths of all Christians. Clearly, then, if they do not believe, they will be condemned; and since they have added nothing by living badly to original sin, it may rightly be said that their punishment in that condemnation is minimal, though not nonexistent. [Note: *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book 1, §21.]

Anyone who thinks that there will be no diversity of punishments should read what is written: “It will be more tolerable for Sodom on the day of judgment than for that city” (Matthew 10:15). Therefore, infants should not be assigned by deceivers a place midway between the kingdom and punishment. [Note: The Pelagians constructed for unbaptized infants a “place of second happiness,” as Augustine says in *Unfinished Work*, book 1, chapter 130; in the same work, chapter 50, the pious Bishop wittily calls it a “third place.”] Rather, let them pass from the devil to Christ—that is, from death to life—so that the wrath of God may not remain upon them; for only the grace of God delivers from this wrath of God. What, then, is the wrath of God except the punishment and vengeance deserved from the just God? For God is not thrown into turmoil by any agitation, as a changeable mind becomes angry; rather, what is called the wrath of God is nothing other than the just punishment of sin—a punishment that is not surprising to find transmitted to descendants.

### 3

Carnal concupiscence, through which they are sown and conceived, did not exist before sin, nor would it have existed at all unless the disobedience of the human being had been followed by the reciprocal punishment of the disobedience of his flesh. Although the good of marriage makes good use of this evil, even lawful and honorable intercourse for the sake of marriage—that is, for the begetting of children—cannot take place without it. It could take place without it if human nature had remained without sin in the condition in which it was created. For the genital members too could have been moved, like the other members, by the command of the will to perform their proper work, rather than aroused by the heat of lust.

Who would deny that God’s words, “Increase and multiply” (Genesis 1:22), were not a curse upon sinners but a blessing upon marriage? Therefore, because Christ was neither sown nor conceived through this concupiscence [Note: Perhaps “through which.”], since the Virgin’s childbirth occurred in an entirely different manner [Note: *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 10, §§32, 35, and Letter 202*, §20.], whatever human beings are sown, conceived, and born through this concupiscence must be reborn if they are not to be punished. For although a child is born of parents who have been reborn, carnal generation cannot confer upon the child what spiritual regeneration alone conferred upon the parents. Just as not only from the seed of a wild olive but also from the seed of a cultivated olive there grows only a wild olive, although the cultivated olive is not a wild olive. [Note: Letter 194, §44; and *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book 1, §11.]

I have said much about these matters in other letters of mine as well; I would rather that you read them than compel us to repeat the same things.

## CHAPTER II

### 4

A more laborious response is required for unbelievers, who are bound by no authority of the Christians’ books. Their perversity cannot be corrected by the weight of divine Scripture; rather, Scripture itself—which they attack more openly—must be defended against them. Even if the Lord helps you so that you are able to do so, you accomplish little among those whom you wish to become Christians if you overcome their unbelief with truthful arguments, unless you also ask for faith for them through suppliant prayers.

For faith itself, as you know, is a gift of God, who apportions to each person a measure of faith, and it is such a gift that it must precede understanding. The prophet does not err when he says: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isaiah 7:9). And since the Apostle was praying that the Jews might believe—not as though they were already faithful, but because they were still unbelievers—when he said: “Brothers, the good desire of my heart and my prayer to God for them is for salvation” (Romans 10:1), he was praying for those, namely, who had killed Christ and who would certainly have killed this man also if power had been given to them. [Note: Thus the Gottweig manuscript. Later editions read, “whom surely these men would have killed,” incorrectly. Augustine does not say that unbelievers would also have killed Christ if power had been given to them; rather, he says that the Jews, after killing Christ, would also have killed Paul unless they had been prevented by the centurion. Nevertheless, the Apostle prayed for the Jews, just as the Lord did while hanging on the cross and being mocked, and blessed Stephen did while being stoned, as is stated immediately afterward.]

For such people the Lord prayed while he was mocked as he hung upon the cross (Luke 23:34), and blessed Stephen prayed while he was being stoned (Acts 7:59).

## CHAPTER III

### 5

These unbelievers, whom we customarily call either Gentiles or, in the now ordinary term, pagans, are of two kinds: one consists of those who prefer the superstitions they regard as important [Note: Perhaps, “which they regard as important.”] to the Christian religion; the other consists of those who are bound by no name of religion.

In certain books that I titled *The City of God*, and whose existence I expect has already become known to you—and the remaining books of which I am still laboring, amid my many occupations, to complete if the Lord wills—I have composed ten substantial volumes against the first of these groups, which the Apostle censures when he says: “What the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God” (1 Corinthians 10:20); or again when he says: “They worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator” (Romans 1:25).

The first five of these volumes refute those who maintain that, in order to obtain or preserve this earthly and temporal happiness in human affairs, it is necessary to worship not one supreme and true God but many gods. The other five are directed against those who, raising themselves up with excessive arrogance and conceit against the doctrine of salvation, think that the blessedness hoped for after this life can also be attained through the worship of demons and many gods. In the final books of these five, their distinguished philosophers are also refuted by us. [Note: Perhaps, “of these five.”]

The remaining books, beginning with the eleventh, however many there may be, will contain what we hold and believe concerning *The City of God*. I have already completed three, and I have the fourth in hand, so that we may not appear to have wished in this work merely to refute what belongs to others and not also to affirm what belongs to us. This book, the fourth after the ten—and likewise the fourteenth book of the entire work—will, if the Lord wills, resolve all the questions you posed to me in your letter.

### 6

As for the other kind of unbelievers—those who either believe that there is no divine power or do not believe that human affairs pertain to it—I do not know whether one should discuss with them any question of religion. Yet in our times scarcely anyone is found so foolish as to dare to say even in his heart: “There is no God” (Psalm 13:1). There are, however, other fools who have said: “The Lord will not see” (Psalm 94:7)—that is, “His providence does not extend to earthly affairs.” [Note: Perhaps, “does not direct its attention to them.” Thus Sermon 69, chapter 2, §3, treating the same argument, says: “Would he who made your eye not direct his eye toward you?”]

Nevertheless, in these books, which I wish your Charity to read, *The City of God* affirms not only that God exists—something that scarcely any impiety ever eradicates, since it is implanted in nature—but also that he cares for human affairs, from the very creation of humankind until he makes the righteous blessed with the holy angels and condemns the impious with the evil angels. If God wills, and to whomever he wills, this will become credible.

[Col. 0792]

### 7

This letter must not be burdened any further, most beloved. We have said enough about where you may hope to learn through our ministry what you wish to know. We have taken care, insofar as our limited ability permits, to ensure that you may obtain these same books—if you do not yet possess them—through my holy brother and fellow presbyter Firmus, who loves you greatly and has informed us more fully about you, thereby expressing his gratitude for your mutual affection. [Note: Firmus, mentioned here, was an African. Augustine was deeply attached to him. He lived a monastic life, if he is the same person whom Jerome mentions in his letter to Augustine, Letter 81; for a time he lived with Jerome, Paula, Eustochium, and the other saints at Bethlehem. Certainly his manner of life can be amply confirmed by this letter itself and by Letter 248.]

# CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING LETTER  
*(Book II of the Retractions, chapter XLVIII)*

At the same time I also wrote a book *On the Correction of the Donatists*, for those who did not want them to be corrected by the imperial laws. This book begins as follows: “I praise, and rejoice, and marvel.”

# BOOK ON THE CORRECTION OF THE DONATISTS, OR LETTER CLXXXV

[Note: In preparing this recension, the following manuscripts and editions were collated: a, bg, bl, bn, c, cc, ff, g, gv, j, s, t, vc, two copies of sb, five copies of v, Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: Formerly numbered 50; what was Letter 185 is now Appendix 4. Written around the year 417.]

Augustine to Boniface—tribune and eventually count in Africa, according to Letter 220—showing him that the Donatist heresy has nothing in common with the Arian heresy, and explaining how, through fear of the imperial laws, heretics can be restored to communion with the Church. He also discusses at some length the savagery of the Donatists and Circumcellions, and finally the sin against the Holy Spirit, which is not forgiven. He treated the same subject in Letter 93.

## CHAPTER I

### 1

I praise, and rejoice, and marvel, dearest son Boniface, that amid the cares of wars and arms you ardently desire to know the things that belong to God. From this it is clear that even your military valor serves the faith that you have in Christ.

To explain briefly to Your Charity the difference between the error of the Arians and that of the Donatists: the Arians say that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have different substances; the Donatists do not say this, but confess one substance of the Trinity. And although some of them have said that the Son is lesser than the Father, they have nevertheless not denied that he is of the same substance. Indeed, most of them say that they believe concerning the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit precisely what the Catholic Church believes.

Nor is their dispute with us about this; rather, they quarrel unhappily over communion alone and, in the perversity of their error, exercise rebellious hostility against the unity of Christ. At times, however, as we have heard, some of them, wishing to win over the Goths when they see that the Goths possess some power, say that they believe what the Goths believe. But they are refuted by the authority of their predecessors, since even Donatus himself is not said to have believed in this way, although they boast that they belong to his party.

### 2

Do not let these things disturb you, dearest son. Heresies and scandals were foretold as things that would come, so that we might be instructed among our enemies and thus both our faith and our love might become more proven: our faith, so that we are not deceived by them; our love, so that we may care for their correction as far as we can—not only by taking measures to prevent them from harming the weak and to free them from their wicked error, but also by praying for them, so that the Lord may open their understanding and they may comprehend the Scriptures.

For in the holy books, wherever the Lord Christ is revealed, there his Church too is declared. Yet these men, in their astonishing blindness, although they know Christ himself only from the Scriptures, do not recognize his Church by the authority of the divine writings; instead, through the emptiness of human accusations, they fabricate a church of their own.

### 3

They acknowledge Christ with us in the passage that reads: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones. They observed and looked upon me; they divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots.” Yet they refuse to acknowledge the Church in what follows shortly afterward: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship before him; for the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he shall rule the nations” (Psalm 22:16–18, 27–28).

They acknowledge Christ with us in the passage that reads: “The Lord said to me, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you.’” Yet they refuse to acknowledge the Church in what follows: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Psalm 2:7–8).

They acknowledge Christ with us in what the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “It was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day.” Yet they refuse to acknowledge the Church in what follows: “and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:46–47).

There are countless other testimonies in the holy books, which I ought not to compress into this book. In them the Lord Christ appears—whether according to his divinity, by which he is equal to the Father, who in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; or according to the humility of the flesh he assumed, by which the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:1, 14). In the same way his Church also appears, not confined to Africa alone, as these men rave with the most shameless folly, but spread throughout the whole world.

### 4

They prefer their disputes to the divine testimonies because, in the case of Caecilianus, once bishop of the Church of Carthage, they brought accusations against him that they neither could nor can prove, and thereby separated themselves from the Catholic Church—that is, from the unity of all nations.

Even if the charges they brought against Caecilianus had been true and could at some point have been demonstrated to us, we would have anathematized Caecilianus himself, since he was already dead. [Note: This letter was produced at the Fifth Synod, session 5, when the case of Theodore of Mopsuestia was being discussed and the question was raised whether a person could be condemned after death.] Nevertheless, we must not abandon the Church of Christ—which is not fabricated by contentious opinions but established by divine attestations—for the sake of any individual, because “it is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in a human being” (Psalm 118:8).

I say this without doing injury to Caecilianus’s innocence: even if Caecilianus sinned, Christ did not thereby lose his inheritance. It is easy for one human being to believe either true or false things about another human being; but it is criminally shameless to wish to condemn the communion of the whole world on account of a person’s crimes that you cannot demonstrate to the whole world.

### 5

Whether Caecilianus was ordained by traditors—those who handed over the divine books—I do not know. I did not see it; I heard it from his enemies. No passage from God’s Law, no proclamation of the prophets, no sanctity of the Psalms, no statement from Christ’s Apostle, no word of Christ is recited to me concerning it.

But the Church spread throughout the whole world, with which the party of Donatus does not communicate, is proclaimed with unanimous voice by the testimonies of all the Scriptures.

“In your seed all nations shall be blessed,” says the Law of God (Genesis 26:4).

“From the rising of the sun to its setting, a pure sacrifice is offered to my name; for my name is glorified among the nations,” the Lord says through the prophet (Malachi 1:11).

“He shall rule from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the earth,” the Lord says through the Psalm (Psalm 72:8).

“Bearing fruit and growing throughout the whole world,” the Lord says through the Apostle (Colossians 1:6).

“You shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and throughout all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth,” the Son of God said with his own mouth (Acts 1:8).

Caecilianus, bishop of the Church of Carthage, is accused in human disputes; the Church of Christ, established among all nations, is commended by divine voices. Piety, truth, and charity themselves do not permit us to accept against Caecilianus the testimony of those whom we do not see in the Church to which God bears witness. Those who do not follow the divine testimonies have forfeited the weight of human testimony.

## CHAPTER II

### 6

I add that they themselves sent the case of Caecilianus, by accusing him, to the judgment of the emperor Constantine. Indeed, after the episcopal tribunals [Note: The Roman and Arles tribunals.] where they were unable to crush him, they brought Caecilianus himself, through their most persistent persecutions, before the examination of the aforesaid emperor.

What they now criticize in us, in order to deceive the uninformed—saying that Christians ought not to ask Christian emperors for anything against the enemies of Christ—they themselves did first. They were not even bold enough to deny this at the conference we held together at Carthage. Indeed, they dared to boast that their predecessors had criminally pursued Caecilianus before the Emperor, adding the lie that they had defeated him there and had caused him to be condemned. [Col. 0795]

How, then, are they not persecutors? They pursued Caecilianus by accusing him, were defeated by him, and nevertheless wished, with the most shameless lie, to claim a false glory for themselves—not merely failing to regard this as a fault but boasting of it as their praise, if they could prove that Caecilianus had been condemned when their predecessors accused him.

As for how completely they were defeated at that very conference: the official proceedings are extremely lengthy, and since you are occupied with other matters necessary for the peace of Rome, it would be too much to ask you to read them. Perhaps a summary of the conference could be read to you. I believe that my brother and fellow bishop Optatus possesses it; or, if he does not, it can easily be obtained from the Church of Sitifis. [Note: The editions read “Sitivensis.” Thirteen manuscripts, however, read “Sitifensis.”] This book itself has perhaps already become burdensome to your cares because of its length.

### 7

What happened to the Donatists happened also to the accusers of holy Daniel. Just as the laws were turned against those men like the lions were turned against them (Daniel 6:24), so the laws that they wished to use to crush the innocent have been turned against these men. The difference is that, through Christ’s mercy, these laws are more beneficial to them, although they appear adverse: for many have been corrected through them and are corrected every day, and they give thanks that they have been corrected and freed from that frenzied destruction.

Those who hated now love; and as much as, in their madness, they detested the laws as troublesome, so much do they rejoice in their recovery, recognizing that the laws were salutary. Toward those who remain, with whom they would have perished, they are now stirred, together with us, by a similar love, so that we may work together to prevent them from perishing.

A physician is troublesome to a raging madman, and a father to an undisciplined son—the one by binding him, the other by beating him—but both do so out of love. If they neglected such people and allowed them to perish, that supposed gentleness would instead be false and cruel.

If a horse and a mule, which have no understanding, resist with bites and kicks the people who handle the wounds that need to be treated, and although people are often endangered and sometimes injured between their teeth and hooves, nevertheless do not abandon them until, through medicinal pain and distress, they recall them to health, how much more must one human being not abandon another human being, or one brother another brother, lest he perish eternally—especially when, once corrected, he can understand what benefit was being provided to him when he complained of suffering persecution?

### 8

As the Apostle says: “While we have opportunity, let us work what is good toward all without weariness” (Galatians 6:10). Let all be called to salvation and all be recalled from destruction—those who can be reached by the preaching of Catholic preachers [Note: The editions read “Catholic teachers.” Most manuscripts, however, read “Catholic preachers.”], and those who can be reached by the laws of Catholic rulers: some through those who obey divine admonitions, others through those who obey imperial commands.

For when emperors establish bad laws against the truth on behalf of falsehood, those who believe rightly are tested and those who persevere are crowned. But when they establish good laws on behalf of the truth against falsehood, the violent are terrified and the understanding are corrected.

Whoever refuses to obey the emperors’ laws that are issued against God’s truth gains a great reward; whoever refuses to obey the emperors’ laws that are issued for God’s truth gains a great punishment. For even in the times of the prophets, all the kings among God’s people who neither prohibited nor destroyed institutions contrary to God’s commandments are blamed; those who prohibited and destroyed them are praised above the others.

King Nebuchadnezzar, although he was a servant of idols, established a sacrilegious law that an image should be worshiped; those who refused to obey that impious decree acted piously and faithfully. Yet the same king, corrected by a divine miracle, established a pious and praiseworthy law on behalf of the truth: whoever spoke blasphemy against the true God of Sidrac, Misac, and Abdenago was to perish utterly together with his household (Daniel 3:5, 96).

If anyone despised this law and deservedly suffered what had been decreed, they ought to have said what these men say: that they were righteous because they were suffering persecution under the king’s law. They would indeed have said this if they had been mad in the same way as these men, who divide Christ’s members, spit upon Christ’s sacraments, and boast about persecution because the emperors’ laws—established for Christ’s unity—prohibit them from doing these things. They falsely proclaim their innocence and seek from human beings the glory of martyrs that they cannot receive from the Lord.

### 9

But those are true martyrs of whom the Lord says: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matthew 5:10). Therefore, those who suffer persecution for iniquity and for the wicked division of Christian unity are not true martyrs; those who suffer persecution for righteousness are.

Hagar too suffered persecution from Sarah (Genesis 16:6), and the woman who inflicted it was holy, while the woman who suffered it was wicked. Can holy David, whom the wicked Saul persecuted, be compared with the persecution Hagar suffered (1 Samuel 18–19 and following)? There is an immense difference—not because one suffered, but because one suffered for righteousness.

The Lord himself was crucified with thieves (Luke 23:33), but although suffering joined them, their cause separated them. Therefore, in the Psalm we should understand the voice of true martyrs, who wish to be distinguished from false martyrs: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation” (Psalm 43:1). He did not say, “Distinguish my punishment,” but “Distinguish my cause.”

The punishment of the impious can be similar, but the cause of the martyrs is dissimilar. Their voice also says: “They persecuted me unjustly; help me” (Psalm 119:86). He considered himself worthy to be helped justly because they persecuted him unjustly; for if they had persecuted him justly, he should not have been helped but corrected.

### 10

If they think—as they said at the conference—that no one can justly persecute another, and that the true Church is the one that suffers persecution, not the one that inflicts it, I shall pass over what I mentioned above: if things are as they say, then Caecilianus belonged to the true Church when their predecessors pursued him by accusation as far as the emperor’s judgment.

We say that he belonged to the true Church not because he suffered persecution, but because he suffered persecution for righteousness; and that they were alienated from the Church not because they persecuted, but because they persecuted unjustly. This is what we say.

But if they do not ask the reasons why someone inflicts or suffers persecution, and think that this alone is a sign of a true Christian—that he does not inflict persecution but suffers it—then, without doubt, they place Caecilianus within that definition, since he did not inflict persecution but suffered it; while they exclude their predecessors from that definition, since they inflicted persecution and did not suffer it.

### 11

But, as I said, I shall pass over this and say the following: if the true Church is the one that suffers persecution, not the one that inflicts it, let them ask the Apostle what Church Sarah signified when she persecuted her maidservant.

For he says that our free mother, the heavenly Jerusalem—that is, the true Church of God—was prefigured in the woman who afflicted her maidservant (Galatians 4:22–31). If we examine the matter more carefully, Hagar persecuted Sarah more by her pride than Sarah persecuted Hagar by restraining her. Hagar was injuring her mistress; Sarah was imposing discipline upon a proud woman.

Next I ask: if good and holy people persecute no one but merely suffer persecution, whose voice do they think is heard in the Psalm where we read: “I will pursue my enemies and overtake them, and I will not turn back until they fail” (Psalm 18:38)?

If we wish to speak or acknowledge the truth, there is an unjust persecution inflicted by the impious upon Christ’s Church, and there is a just persecution inflicted by Christ’s Church upon the impious.

The Church, therefore, is blessed when it suffers persecution for righteousness; but those who suffer persecution for injustice are wretched. Accordingly, the Church persecutes by loving, while they persecute by raging; the Church does so to correct, while they do so to overthrow; the Church does so to call people back from error, while they do so to plunge them into error.

Finally, the Church pursues and overtakes its enemies until they fail in vanity, so that they may advance in truth. But they, repaying evil for good, because we care for their eternal salvation, also try to take our temporal lives. They love murder so much that they carry it out upon themselves when they cannot perpetrate it upon others.

For just as charity labors to rescue them from that destruction, so that none of them may die, their fury labors either to kill us, so that they may feed the desire of their cruelty, or even to kill themselves, lest they appear to have lost the power of killing others.

## CHAPTER III

### 12

Those who do not know their custom think that they now kill themselves when, through the opportunity provided by these laws established for unity, so many people are being freed from their utterly insane domination.

But those who know what they used to do even before these laws do not marvel at their deaths; they remember their customs. Especially when idolatry was still practiced, enormous crowds came to the most famous pagan festivals—not to break the idols but to be killed by the idol-worshipers.

If they had wished to do this after receiving lawful authority, and something had happened to them, they might have had at least some semblance of the name of martyrs. But they came solely so that, while the idols remained intact, they themselves might be killed. For the most vigorous young men among the idol-worshipers were accustomed to vow to the idols how many of these people each of them would kill.

Some even thrust themselves upon armed travelers to be slaughtered, threatening them terribly that they would strike the travelers unless the travelers killed them. Sometimes they violently extorted from passing judges that they should be struck by executioners or by official personnel.

Accordingly, one man is said to have mocked them in this way: he ordered them to be bound and released as though they were to be beaten, and thus escaped their attack without bloodshed or injury.

Moreover, killing themselves by throwing themselves over steep precipices, into water, or into flames was their daily sport. The devil taught them these three kinds of death, so that when they wanted to die and could not find someone whom they could terrify into striking them with his sword, they would hurl themselves upon rocks or give themselves over to fire and water.

But whom should we believe to have taught them these things, possessing their hearts, except the one who also suggested to our Savior, as though from the Law, that he throw himself down from the pinnacle of the temple (Luke 4:9)? They would certainly have barred that suggestion from themselves if they carried Christ the teacher in their hearts.

But because they gave the devil greater room within themselves, either they perish in the manner of that herd of pigs which a crowd of demons drove from the mountain into the sea (Mark 5:13), or, rescued from those deaths and gathered into the pious bosom of the Catholic mother, they are freed in the manner of the man whom the Lord delivered when his father offered him for healing from a demon, saying that the boy sometimes fell into water and sometimes into fire (Matthew 17:14).

### 13

Therefore great mercy is shown toward them when, even through these imperial laws, they are first forcibly rescued from the sect where they learned these evils through the teachings of lying demons, so that afterward they may be healed within the Catholic Church and accustomed to good instruction and conduct.

Many of them, whose pious fervor of faith and remarkable charity within Christ’s unity we now admire, give great thanks to God that they escaped the error in which they regarded these evils as good. They would not now give these thanks willingly unless they had first been compelled to leave that wicked society against their will.

What shall we say about those who confess to us every day that they long ago wished to be Catholics, but lived among people among whom, because of the weakness produced by fear, they could not become what they wished? If they said a single word on behalf of the Catholic Church, both they and their households would have been utterly destroyed.

Who is so mad as to deny that imperial commands ought to have come to the aid of such people, so that they might be rescued from so great an evil—while those whom they feared are compelled to fear, and through that same fear are either corrected themselves or, at least, pretend to have been corrected and spare those whom they formerly caused to fear?

14.
