But if they should wish to kill themselves, so that those who are to be rescued may not be rescued, and in this way terrify the compassion of those rescuing them—so that, while it is feared that certain lost people may perish, those are not snatched from destruction who either no longer wished to perish or, if restrained, could avoid perishing—[Col. 0799] what does Christian charity do here, especially since those who threaten their own voluntary and frenzied deaths are very few in comparison with the populations to be rescued? What, then, does fraternal love do? Does it, while fearing for a few the passing fires of furnaces, abandon everyone to the eternal fires of Gehenna, and leave so many—either already willing, or later unable, to come through Catholic peace to everlasting life—to eternal destruction, taking care lest certain people die a voluntary death, although they live only to impede the salvation of others, whom they do not allow to live according to Christ’s teaching, so that they may teach them, at whatever time, according to the custom of the devil’s doctrine, to hasten toward those voluntary deaths which are now feared in them? Or does it rather preserve those whom it can, even if those whom it cannot preserve perish willingly?

For it ardently desires that all may live; but it labors still more earnestly that all may not perish. Thanks, however, be to the Lord, because among us also—not indeed everywhere, but in very many places—and throughout other parts of Africa, Catholic peace has spread, and is spreading, without any deaths at all among these madmen. Those fatal events occur where there is such a frenzied and useless class of people, who have been accustomed to do the same things at other times as well.

## CHAPTER IV

15. Indeed, before these laws were sent by the Catholic emperors, the teaching of the peace and unity of Christ was gradually growing, and each person was crossing over to it from that faction as he learned, wished, and was able to do so. Meanwhile, however, among them the utterly mad bands of ruined men were disturbing the peace of the innocent in various ways.

What master was not compelled to fear his slave if the slave had fled to their protection? Who dared even threaten a destroyer? [Note: Am., Bad., Er., and most manuscripts: “Who dared [to threaten] the author, the plunderer?” Perhaps for: “Who dared either to threaten or restrain the plunderer?” And shortly afterward the manuscripts have “shopkeeper.”] Who could bring to account a plunderer of shops, or anyone who was demanding aid and defense from them as a debtor? Out of fear of clubs, fires, and immediate death at the hands of the worst slaves, documents were broken so that free people might depart. Promissory acknowledgments extorted from debtors were returned. Whoever had disregarded their harsh words was compelled by harsher beatings to do what they ordered. The houses of innocent people who had offended them were either razed to the ground or burned with fire. Certain heads of households, born in honorable circumstances and raised in noble refinement, were removed scarcely alive after their massacres; or, bound to a mill, they were driven by blows to turn it around like contemptible beasts of burden.

For what assistance from the laws, through the civil authorities, was of any value against them? What official dared draw breath in their presence? What tax collector exacted what they did not want? Who attempted to avenge those who had been killed by their violence, except that their own madness demanded punishment from them: some by provoking against themselves the swords of men whom they terrified with death so that they would strike them; others by throwing themselves from various precipices; others into the waters; others into fires; and everywhere casting away their savage souls [Col. 0800] through punishments inflicted by themselves upon themselves?

16. Very many people who remained within that heretical superstition shuddered at these things. And when they thought that the fact that such deeds displeased them was sufficient proof of their innocence, Catholics said to them:

“If these evils do not stain your innocence, how can you say that the Christian world has been polluted by the sins of Caecilianus, whether false or at least unknown? How can you separate yourselves by a wicked crime from Catholic unity, as though from the Lord’s threshing floor, which until the time of winnowing must necessarily contain both grain to be stored in the granary and chaff to be consumed by fire (Matthew 3:12)?”

In this way an explanation was given to some, and certain people crossed over to Catholic unity, prepared even to endure the hostility of the ruined men. But more people, although they wished to do so, did not dare to make enemies of those men who had been granted such license to rage against them. Indeed, some who crossed over to us suffered extreme cruelty from them.

17. It also happened that, at Carthage, certain bishops of that faction ordained their own deacon, Maximianus, as bishop against his bishop, after he had arrogantly set himself against his bishop and they had created a schism by dividing the Donatist party among the people of Carthage.

When this displeased many of them, they condemned Maximianus himself, together with twelve others who had been present at his ordination; but to the rest who belonged to the same schismatic association they granted, on a fixed date, the opportunity to return. Later, however, they received certain of those twelve, and also some of those to whom an extension had been granted who returned after the appointed date, back into their offices for the sake of peace. And they did not dare rebaptize anyone whom those condemned men had baptized outside their communion.

This action of theirs began to have great force against them in support of the Catholic Church, so that their mouths were completely closed. When this matter—as was appropriate—was more insistently disseminated for the healing of people’s schismatic minds, and was demonstrated everywhere possible in Catholic speeches and disputations—namely, that for the sake of Donatist peace they had received their own condemned men back with full honor, and had not dared to rescind the baptism that the condemned men, or even those granted an extension, had administered outside their Church; and that they nevertheless charged the whole world with pollution of Christ’s peace because of the sins of I know not whom, while invalidating the baptism given even in those Churches from which the Gospel itself had come into Africa—very many people were confounded, and, ashamed before the manifest truth, were corrected, more frequently than usual and much more wherever some degree of freedom from their savagery could be enjoyed.

18. Then they blazed up in such a way and were driven on by such goads of hatred that, in the face of their plots, violence, and utterly blatant brigandage, scarcely any Church of our communion could be secure, and scarcely any road was safe for those who traveled while preaching Catholic peace against their fury and convicting their madness by evident truth.

So severe, indeed, was the situation that not only laypeople and ordinary clergy, but even Catholic bishops themselves, were placed in a kind of harsh dilemma. Either [Col. 0801] the truth had to be silenced, or their brutality had to be endured. But if the truth were silenced, not only would no one have been rescued by that silence, but many would also have been lost through their deception. If, on the other hand, the preaching of truth provoked their fury to violence, then, although some of our people would be rescued and strengthened, fear would again prevent the weaker from following the truth.

Since the Church was therefore afflicted by these straits, whoever thinks that everything ought rather to be endured than that God’s aid should be sought so that it might be brought through Christian emperors pays too little attention to the fact that no good account could be given of such negligence.

## CHAPTER V

19. Those who do not want just laws to be established against their impieties say that the Apostles did not ask such things of the kings of the earth. They fail to consider that the time then was different, and that everything takes place in its proper times.

For what emperor had then believed in Christ, so that he might serve Him out of devotion by issuing laws against impiety, when the prophetic passage was still being fulfilled:

“Why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise vain things? The kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against His Christ”?

What is said shortly afterward in the same psalm was not yet taking place:

“And now, O kings, understand; be instructed, you who judge the earth. Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice before Him with trembling” (Psalm 2:1–2, 10–11).

How, then, do kings serve the Lord with fear, unless by religious severity they prohibit and punish what is done against the Lord’s commands? For a king serves in one way because he is a human being, and in another because he is also a king. Because he is a human being, he serves Him by living faithfully; but because he is also a king, he serves Him by enacting with appropriate vigor laws that command what is right and prohibit what is contrary to it.

Thus Hezekiah served Him by destroying the sacred groves and temples of the idols, and the high places that had been constructed against God’s commands (2 Kings 18:4). Josiah served Him by doing the same things (ibid. 23:4–5). The king of the Ninevites served Him by compelling the whole city to appease the Lord (Jonah 3:6–9). Darius served Him by handing over the idol to Daniel’s authority so that it might be destroyed, and by throwing its worshipers to the lions (Daniel 14:21, 41). Nebuchadnezzar, whom we have already mentioned, served Him by forbidding through a terrible law everyone in his kingdom to blaspheme God (ibid. 3:96).

In this way kings serve the Lord, insofar as they are kings, when they do for His service what only kings can do.

20. Since, then, in the time of the Apostles kings did not yet serve the Lord but were still devising vain things against the Lord and against His Christ, so that all the predictions of the Prophets might be fulfilled, impieties could not then be prohibited by laws but rather were practiced. For the sequence of times was unfolding in such a way that the Jews would kill the preachers of Christ, thinking that they were performing a service to God, just as Christ had foretold (John 16:2); the Gentiles would rage against Christians; and all would be overcome by the patience of the martyrs.

But after what is written began to be fulfilled—“All the kings of the earth shall adore Him; all nations shall serve Him” (Psalm 71:11)—what person of sound judgment would say to kings:

“Do not concern yourselves in your kingdom with who holds or attacks [Col. 0802] the Church of your Lord; it is none of your concern, within your kingdom, whether anyone wishes to be religious or sacrilegious”?

No one could say to them:

“It is none of your concern, within your kingdom, who wishes to be chaste or unchaste.”

For why, when free will has been divinely given to human beings, should adulteries be punished by law while sacrileges are permitted? Or is failure to keep faith with God a lighter matter than failure to keep faith with a woman or a man? Or, if offenses committed not through contempt but through ignorance of religion ought to be punished more mildly, should they for that reason be neglected?

## CHAPTER VI

21. It is certainly better—and who would doubt it?—that people be led to worship God by teaching rather than compelled by fear or pain of punishment. But because some are better than others, those who are not of this kind must not therefore be neglected.

For it has benefited many—as we have proved and continue to prove by experience—to be compelled first by fear or pain, so that afterward they might be taught, or might practice in deed what they had already learned in words.

Some people quote to us the opinion of a certain secular author, who said:

> “I believe it better to retain free people through modesty and generosity than through fear.”  
> (Terence, *Adelphoe*, act 1, scene 1.)

This is indeed true. But just as those whom love directs are better, so there are more whom fear corrects. For, to answer them from that very author, they also read in him:

> “Unless compelled by punishment, you do not know how to do right.”

Moreover, divine Scripture spoke, on behalf of those who are better, in these words:

> “There is no fear in love; but perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18).

But on behalf of those who are inferior—and they are more numerous—it says:

> “A stubborn servant will not be corrected by words; for even if he understands, he will not obey” (Proverbs 29:19).

When it says that he is not corrected by words, it does not command that he be abandoned; rather, it silently indicates by what means he ought to be corrected. Otherwise it would not say, “He will not be corrected by words,” but merely, “He will not be corrected.”

Elsewhere it says that not only a servant but also an undisciplined son must be restrained by blows, and with great benefit:

> “You indeed strike him with the rod, but you will deliver his soul from death” (ibid. 23:14).

And elsewhere it says:

> “Whoever spares the rod hates his son” (ibid. 13:24).

Produce, then, someone who says with correct faith and true understanding, with all the strength of his soul:

> “My soul has thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Psalm 41:3).

For such a person, fear of temporal punishments or imperial laws is not necessary; indeed, even fear of Gehenna is unnecessary. Union with God is so desirable a good to him that he not only dreads separation from that blessedness as a great punishment, but also bears delay with distress.

Nevertheless, before good sons can say, “We desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23), many are first recalled to their Lord, like bad servants and, in a sense, wicked runaways, by the blows of temporal scourges.

22. Who could love us more than Christ, who laid down His life for His sheep (John 10:15)? And yet, when He called Peter and the other Apostles by word alone, He first restrained Saul—later the great builder of His [Col. 0803] Church, but previously its terrible devastator—not merely by a voice but also by power, striking him down. To urge him, raging in the darkness of unbelief, to desire the light of the heart [Note: Ten manuscripts: “And raging in the darkness of unbelief, so that he might rise to desire the light of the heart.”], He first struck his body with blindness.

If that punishment had not occurred, he would not afterward have been healed of it. And when, with his eyes open, he could see nothing, if his eyes had remained sound, Scripture would not relate that, at the laying on of Ananias’s hands, his sight was restored, as though scales that had covered his eyes fell away (Acts 9:1–18).

Where is the claim that these people habitually shout: “It is free to believe or not to believe”? Whom did Christ use force against? Whom did He compel? Behold the Apostle Paul. Let them recognize in him Christ first compelling, and afterward teaching; first striking, and afterward consoling.

It is remarkable, moreover, that the man who entered the Gospel after being compelled by bodily punishment labored in the Gospel more than all those who had been called by word alone (1 Corinthians 15:10). The one whom greater fear compelled to love was released from fear by perfect love.

23. Why, then, should the Church not compel lost sons to return, if lost sons have compelled others to perish? Even those whom they did not compel but merely deceived, if they are brought back into her embrace by terrifying but health-giving laws, the devout mother embraces more tenderly and rejoices over them far more than over those whom she had never lost.

Does it not belong to pastoral care to recall even those sheep that have wandered from the flock—not violently seized, but gently and softly led astray—and have begun to be possessed by strangers, bringing them back to the Lord’s fold by the terrors or even the pains of blows if they resist? This is especially so because, if they multiply prolifically among runaway slaves and brigands, the fact that the lordly mark is recognized in them has the stronger claim—a mark not at all violated in those whom we receive but nevertheless do not rebaptize.

Thus error must be corrected in the sheep without corrupting in it the seal of the Redeemer. For if someone is marked with a royal mark by a deserter who bears that mark, and both receive pardon—one returning to military service, the other beginning to serve in the army although he had not previously done so—is that mark erased from either of them? Rather, it is recognized in both and approved with the honor due to it, because it is royal.

Since, therefore, they cannot show that the thing to which they are compelled is evil, neither do they contend that they ought to be compelled to what is good. But we have shown that Paul was compelled by Christ. The Church therefore imitates her Lord in compelling these people. She first waited without compelling anyone, so that the prophetic proclamation concerning the faith of kings and nations might be fulfilled.

24. This can also be understood, not implausibly, from that apostolic statement in which the blessed Paul says:

> “Ready to avenge every disobedience, when your obedience has been fulfilled” (2 Corinthians 10:6).

For this reason the Lord Himself first orders guests to be brought to His great banquet [Col. 0804], and afterward to be compelled. When His servants replied, “Lord, what you commanded has been done, and there is still room,” He said:

> “Go out into the roads and hedges, and compel them to enter, whoever you find” (Luke 14:22–23).

In those who were first brought gently, the prior obedience was fulfilled; but in those who are compelled, disobedience is restrained. For what does “compel them to enter” mean, when He had first said, “Bring them in,” and the reply had been, “What you commanded has been done, and there is still room”?

If He had wished them to understand that people were to be compelled by the terrors of miracles, many more divine miracles were performed for those who had first been called—especially for the Jews, of whom it is said, “Jews demand signs” (1 Corinthians 1:22). Among the Gentiles as well, such miracles commended the Gospel in the time of the Apostles. Thus, if people were commanded to be compelled by such means, the earlier guests would more justly be considered to have been compelled, as I have said.

Therefore, if by the authority that the Church received as a divine gift, through the religion and faith of kings, at the time appointed, those who are found on the roads and in the hedges—that is, in heresies and schisms—are compelled to enter, they should not complain that they are compelled; rather, they should consider what they are being compelled to enter.

The Lord’s banquet is the unity of Christ’s body, not only in the sacrament of the altar but also in the bond of peace. Of these people themselves we can most truly say that they compel no one to what is good: for everyone whom they compel, they compel only to evil.

## CHAPTER VII

25. Nevertheless, before the laws by which they are compelled to enter the holy banquet were sent into Africa, it seemed to certain brothers—including me—that, although the Donatists’ fury raged everywhere, we ought not to ask the emperors to command that the heresy itself cease entirely, by establishing a penalty for those who wished to remain in it. Rather, we thought that they should establish that those who did not tolerate Catholic truth—whether by preaching it in speech or by promulgating it in writing—should not be subjected to the frenzied violence of the Donatists.

We thought that this could be accomplished to some extent if the law of Theodosius, of most blessed memory, which he had issued generally against all heretics, were applied more explicitly to the Donatists. The law stated:

> “Whoever among them is found anywhere to be a bishop or cleric shall be fined ten pounds of gold.”

Since the Donatists denied that they were heretics, we thought the law should be confirmed in such a way that not all of them would suffer the fine, but only those in whose regions the Catholic Church suffered some act of violence from their clergy, Circumcellions, or people. Thus, after a protest by Catholics who had endured such treatment, the bishops or other ministers would then be held responsible by the authorities for paying the fine.

We thought that, once they were terrified and dared to do nothing of the kind, Catholic truth could be freely taught and maintained. No one would be compelled to embrace it; whoever wished to follow it without fear could do so, and we would not have false and pretended Catholics.

Although other brothers had a different opinion—men more advanced in age, or those who had seen the examples of many cities and regions [Note: Thus one Vatican manuscript; another has “relating”; the printed editions, “running.”] where we observed a firm and genuine Catholic Church established and strengthened [Col. 0805] by such benefits of God, since people had been compelled to Catholic communion through the laws of earlier emperors—we nevertheless succeeded in having what I have described requested from the emperors instead. It was decreed in our council [Note: Carthage, A.D. 404, June 26.], and envoys were sent to the imperial court.

26. But God’s greater mercy, knowing how necessary the terror of these laws and a certain medicinal discomfort would be for the perverse or cold minds of many, and for that hardness which cannot be corrected by words but can nevertheless be corrected by some degree of disciplinary severity, brought it about that our envoys could not obtain what they had undertaken.

For already very serious complaints from other places had reached us from certain bishops who had suffered many evils at their hands and had been driven from their sees. Above all, the horrible and incredible massacre of Maximianus, the Catholic bishop of the Church of Bagai [Note: In the printed editions, *Vagiensis*; in some manuscripts, *Vaginensis*; in most others, *Vagaiensis*—that is, with B changed to V. The form should be *Bagaiensis*. See the note on Epistle 88, section 8, and book 3 against Cresconius, chapter 43.] caused our embassy to have nothing further to do.

A law had already been promulgated so that the Donatist heresy, guilty of such savagery and seemingly treated more leniently than it itself raged, would not merely be forbidden to commit violence but would be prohibited from existing with impunity at all. This was not done by capital punishment, because Christian gentleness was to be preserved even toward the unworthy, but by imposing financial penalties and assigning exile for bishops and their ministers.

27. The aforementioned bishop of Bagai [Col. 0805] had obtained the basilica [Note: The estate of Calvianus: book 3 against Cresconius, chapter 43.] before the ordinary judge, after judgment had been rendered between the parties. They had seized it when it was Catholic. While he was standing at the altar, they rushed upon him with horrifying force and savage fury, and beat him savagely with clubs and weapons of every kind, finally using pieces of the broken altar itself. They also struck him in the groin with a dagger. The wound caused blood to flow and would have left him lifeless, had their greater savagery not benefited him by preserving his life.

For while they dragged him severely wounded along the ground, dust blocked the vein from which the blood was pouring and stopped the bleeding [Note: Lov., “the blood prevailed”; Bad., Am., and Er., “the blood prevailed.” But nearly all the manuscripts read, “stopped the blood.”], which otherwise was carrying him toward death.

Then, when our people at last tried to carry him away after the attackers had abandoned him, the Donatists, inflamed by even fiercer anger, seized him from the hands of those carrying him. They badly injured and put to flight the Catholics, whom they greatly outnumbered and easily terrified by their violence.

From there they carried him up to a certain tower and, thinking that he had already died, threw him down, although he was still alive. But he was caught by a soft mound of earth. Some people passing by at night saw him by lamplight, recognized him, gathered him up, and carried him to a religious house. After great care had been applied, he recovered from the point of death after many days.

Nevertheless, news of his death had already been carried even across the sea by the report of the Donatists’ crime. When he later arrived and his utterly unexpected survival became evident, his scars—so numerous, so enormous, and so recent—showed [Col. 0806] that the report had not without reason announced him dead.

28. He therefore sought assistance from a Christian emperor, not so much to avenge himself as to protect the Church entrusted to him. If he had neglected to do so, his patience would not have deserved praise; rather, his negligence would rightly have been blamed.

The Apostle Paul, too, was not looking after his passing life but after the Church of God when, against those who had conspired to kill him, he arranged through the tribune that their plot should be disclosed. As a result, an armed soldier escorted him to the place to which he was to be taken, so that he would not fall victim to their ambush (Acts 23:17–32).

He did not hesitate to appeal to Roman laws either, proclaiming that he was a Roman citizen, whom at that time it was unlawful to subject to scourging (ibid. 22:25). Likewise, so that he would not be handed over to the Jews who desired to kill him, he appealed for the assistance of Caesar (ibid. 25:11)—a Roman ruler, certainly, but not a Christian.

Thereby he showed clearly enough what the ministers of Christ ought afterward to do when they found Christian emperors while the Church was in danger. Thus it happened that a devout and pious emperor, once such matters had been brought to his attention, preferred by most pious laws to correct the error of that impiety entirely, and, by frightening and restraining those who bore Christ’s insignia against Christ, to bring them back to Catholic unity, rather than merely removing their license to rage while leaving them free to err and perish.

29. Once the laws themselves had arrived in Africa, especially those who were seeking an opportunity, or fearing the fury of the violent, or ashamed to offend their own people, immediately crossed over to the Church.

Many others had been held there merely by the custom handed down to them by their parents. They had never previously considered what basis the heresy itself possessed, nor had they wished to investigate or reflect upon it. But as soon as they began to pay attention and found nothing in it worthy of suffering such losses for its sake, they became Catholics without difficulty. Concern taught those whom security had made negligent.

Many followed the authority and persuasion of all these earlier converts—people who were less capable on their own of understanding the difference between the Donatist error and Catholic truth.

30. Thus, while the true mother joyfully received great crowds of people into her embrace, there remained hard-hearted groups who persisted in that wretched obstinacy. Many of these too communicated while pretending; others concealed themselves because they were few.

But those who were pretending gradually became accustomed to Catholic communion and, by listening to the preaching of truth—especially after the conference and disputation that took place between us and their bishops at Carthage—were corrected for the most part.

In certain places, however, where a more obstinate and disorderly multitude prevailed, and where the smaller number, whose judgment concerning communion was better, could not resist it, or where crowds submitted in the wrong way to the authority of a few more powerful men, the work continued for somewhat longer.

Among these are places where the work is still continuing. In that labor Catholics [Col. 0807], especially bishops and clergy, have suffered many horrible and harsh things, which it would take too long to recount. The eyes of some were put out; the hands and tongue of one bishop were cut off; and some were even slaughtered.

I say nothing of the most savage massacres and the plundering of houses through nighttime attacks and fires—not only of private dwellings but also of churches. There were even people who threw the Lord’s books into the flames.

31. But the fruit that followed consoled us, as was fitting, in our affliction by such evils. For wherever these deeds were committed by the lost, Christian unity made more vigorous and more perfect progress there, and the Lord was praised more abundantly, because He had deigned to grant that His servants should gain their brothers through their sufferings, and that His sheep, scattered by deadly error, should be gathered by their blood into the peace of eternal salvation.

The Lord is powerful and merciful. We ask Him daily to grant repentance also to the others, so that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive according to his will (2 Timothy 2:26). They seek only grounds on which to slander us and repay evil for good, because they neither know how to understand what love and disposition we maintain toward them, nor how we wish, according to the Lord’s command given through the prophet Ezekiel to the shepherds, to recall the wandering and find the lost (Ezekiel 34:4).

## CHAPTER VIII

32. They do not attribute to themselves what they do to us, as we have said elsewhere at another time; but they attribute to us what they do to themselves.

For which of us would wish not only for any one of them to perish but even for any of them to lose anything? But if the house of David could not otherwise obtain peace than by the death in battle of its son Absalom, who was waging war against his father—although David had carefully commanded his men to preserve him alive and safe as far as they could, so that there might be someone to whom a repentant father’s affection could grant forgiveness—what remained for David but to mourn the lost son and console his grief with the peace acquired for his kingdom (2 Samuel 18–22)?

So too the Catholic mother, while those who fight against her are none other than her sons—for this branch in Africa was broken from that great tree which spreads throughout the whole world by extending its branches—gives birth to them in love so that they may return to the root, without which they cannot possess true life. If, by the loss of some, she gathers so many others, especially since these people perish not through the chance of war, as Absalom did, but rather through voluntary destruction, she alleviates and heals the sorrow of her maternal heart through the liberation of so many peoples.

If you could see their joy in the peace of Christ, their crowds and celebrations, their lively and cheerful gatherings to hear and sing hymns and to receive the word of God; if you could see how many of them remember their former error with great sorrow, consider the truth they have come to know with joy, and express indignation and abhorrence at the falsehood of their teachers now that they know how falsely those teachers had boasted about our sacraments; if you could hear the confessions of many among them that they had long wished to be Catholics but had not dared to do so among people of such great fury—if you could see, gathered together in one view, the assemblies of these peoples liberated from destruction throughout the many regions of Africa [Col. 0808], then you would say that it would have been extreme cruelty if, while it was feared that desperate people—who cannot be compared in any calculation with this innumerable multitude—might burn themselves in their own voluntary fires, these others had been left to eternal destruction and torment in everlasting fires.

33. For suppose two people lived in one house which we knew with complete certainty was about to collapse. We warned them of this, but they refused to believe us and persisted in remaining there. If we could rescue them from it even against their will, and afterward show them the collapse that had threatened them, so that they would not dare to return again to its danger, I think that, if we did not do so, we would rightly be judged cruel.

But suppose one of them said to us, “When you enter to rescue us, I shall immediately kill myself,” while the other did not wish either to leave or to be rescued, but also did not dare to kill himself. What would we choose: to leave both to be crushed by the collapse, or, after at least one had been saved through our merciful efforts, to allow the other to perish—not through our fault but rather through his own?

There is no one so unfortunate that he could not very easily judge what ought to be done in such circumstances. I have proposed this comparison concerning two people, one lost and one rescued. What, then, should we think about a few lost people and an innumerable multitude of peoples rescued?

Those who perish by their own will are not even as numerous as the estates, villages, hamlets, fortified settlements, towns, and cities that through these laws are rescued from that pestilential and eternal destruction.

34. But if we consider more carefully the matter of which we are speaking, I think that, if many people were in a collapsing house and at least one of them could be rescued, and if, as we tried to do so, others killed themselves by leaping from it, we would console ourselves for the others’ loss through the rescue of even one. Nevertheless, we would not, in order to prevent the others from destroying themselves, allow everyone to perish with no one rescued.

What, then, should be judged concerning the work of mercy that we ought to perform for people so that they may obtain eternal life and avoid eternal punishment, if sound and compassionate reasoning compels us to help people in this way for the sake of preserving not only a temporal salvation but even a brief one, for only a short time?

## CHAPTER IX

35. They accuse us of coveting and taking away their property. Would that they become Catholics, and possess with us, in peace and charity, not only what they call theirs but also what is ours!

They are so blinded by their desire to slander that they fail to notice how contradictory are the things they say. They themselves certainly say—and appear to complain most resentfully—that we constrain them into our communion by the violent authority of the laws. We would assuredly never do this if we wished to possess their property. What miser seeks a co-owner? Who, inflamed by the desire to rule or lifted up by the arrogance of domination, wishes to have a partner?

Let them look at their own former associates, now our associates and joined to us in brotherly love, and observe how they hold what is theirs—not only what they possessed but also what is ours [Col. 0809], which they did not possess. Yet, if we are fellow-poor with the poor, these things are both ours and theirs. If, on the other hand, we possess privately what is sufficient for us, those things are not ours but belong to the poor, whose administration we in some sense undertake, without claiming ownership for ourselves through a damnable appropriation.

36. Whatever, therefore, was possessed under the name of the Churches of the party of Donatus, the Christian emperors ordered by religious laws to pass, together with those Churches themselves, to the Catholic Church [Note: [Col. 0809] Cod. Theod. book 16, title 5, *On Heretics*]. Since, then, the poor of those same Churches, who were supported by those same little properties, are with us, let those who remain outside rather cease coveting what belongs to others; let them enter into the fellowship of unity, so that together we may administer not only what they call theirs, but also what is called ours. For it is written: “All things are yours; but you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s” (1 Cor. 3:22–23). Under that head, in his one body, let us be one, and concerning such things let us do what is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “They were of one soul and one heart; and no one called anything his own, but all things were common to them” (Acts 4:32). Let us love what we sing: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132:1)! Thus let them experience and know how truthfully the Catholic mother cries out to them what the blessed Apostle writes to the Corinthians: “I do not seek what is yours, but you” (2 Cor. 12:14).

37. But if we consider what was said in the Book of Wisdom, “Therefore the righteous took the spoils of the ungodly” (Wis. 10:19), and likewise what is read in Proverbs, “The riches of the ungodly are treasured up for the righteous” (Prov. 13:22, according to the Septuagint), then we shall see that we ought not to ask who possess the property of heretics, but who are in the fellowship of the righteous. We know, indeed, that they arrogate such righteousness to themselves that they boast not only of possessing it but also of giving it to other people. For they say that the person whom they baptize is justified by them. Nothing remains for them except to tell the one baptized by them to believe in his baptizer. Why should he not do so, when the Apostle says, “To the one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness” (Rom. 4:5)? Let him therefore believe in him, if that person himself justifies him, so that his faith may be reckoned as righteousness.

But I think that they themselves would shudder at this, if only they were willing even to consider it. For no one is righteous and justifying except God. What the Apostle says about the Jews can also be said about them: “Being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, they have not submitted to the righteousness of God” (Rom. 10:3).

38. Far be it from any of us to call himself righteous in such a way that he wishes either to establish his own righteousness—that is, one supposedly given to him by himself—when it is said to him, “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4:7), or to dare boast that he is without sin in this life, as they said in our conference that they belonged to the Church which already “has no spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind” (Eph. 5:27). They do not know that this is fulfilled in them who depart from this body either immediately after Baptism or after the remission of the debts whose remission is sought in prayer; but that it will be fulfilled in the whole Church only then, when it will be possible to say, “Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting? For the sting of death is sin” (1 Cor. 15:55–56).

39. But in this life, where “the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul” (Wis. 9:15), if their Church is already such, then let them not say to God what the Lord taught us to pray: “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12). Since everything was forgiven in Baptism, why does the Church ask this if, even in this life, it has no spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind? Let them disregard the apostle John, crying out in his Epistle: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity” (1 John 1:8–9).

Because of this hope the whole Church says, “Forgive us our debts,” so that, not growing proud but confessing, we may be cleansed by him from all iniquity. Thus the Lord Christ may present to himself on that day a glorious Church having no spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind, which he now cleanses “by the washing of water in the word.” For in Baptism nothing remains unforgiven of all past sins—provided that Baptism itself is not held outside in vain, but is either received within, or, if it has already been received outside, one does not remain outside with it—and whatever faults are contracted through human weakness by those who live here after receiving Baptism are forgiven because of that washing [Note: [Col. 0810] Most manuscripts: “Whatever faults are contracted, through it.”].

For it does no good for one who has not been baptized to say, “Forgive us our debts.”

40. Thus he now cleanses his Church by the washing of water in the word, so that then he may present it to himself without spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind—that is, wholly beautiful and perfect—when “death will be swallowed up in victory” (1 Cor. 15:54). Therefore, insofar as what we have been born from God is vigorous in us, and we live by faith, we are righteous; but insofar as we draw from Adam the remnants of mortality, we are not without sin. Both statements are true: “Whoever is born of God does not sin” (1 John 3:9), and, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

The Lord Christ, therefore, is both righteous and justifying; but we are justified freely by his grace (Rom. 3:24). He justifies only his own body, which is the Church. And so, if the body of Christ takes the spoils of the ungodly, and the riches of the ungodly are treasured up for the body of Christ, the ungodly ought not to remain outside and slander us, but should rather enter so that they may be justified.

41. Accordingly, what is written concerning the day of judgment—“Then the righteous will stand with great confidence against those who afflicted them and took away their labors” (Wis. 5:1)—must not be understood to mean that the Canaanite will stand against Israel because the Canaanites took away Israel’s labors. Rather, Naboth will stand against Ahab because Ahab took away Naboth’s labors: the Canaanite was ungodly, whereas Naboth was righteous.

In the same way, the pagan will not stand against the Christian who took away his labors when the temples of idols were stripped or destroyed [Note: [Col. 0811] Elsewhere: “given away”]; rather, the Christian will stand against the pagan who took away his labors when the bodies of the martyrs were laid low. Thus the heretic will not stand against the Catholic who took away his labors when the laws of the Catholic emperors prevailed; rather, the Catholic will stand against the heretic who took away his labors when the frenzies of the ungodly Circumcellions prevailed.

Scripture itself resolves the question. It does not say, “Then human beings will stand,” but, “Then the righteous will stand.” Therefore they will stand with great confidence, because they will have a good conscience.

42. No one here is righteous through his own righteousness—that is, as though it had been made for him by himself—but, as the Apostle says, “As God has apportioned to each a measure of faith.” He continues and adds: “For just as in one body we have many members, and all the members do not have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ” (Rom. 12:3–5).

Accordingly, no one can be righteous so long as he has been separated from the unity of this body. For just as a member, if cut off from the body of a living human being, cannot retain the spirit of life, so a person cut off from the body of righteous Christ can in no way retain the spirit of righteousness, even if he retains the form of the member that he received in the body.

Let them therefore enter into the structure of this body and possess their labors, not through a desire to dominate, but through the piety of making good use of them. As already stated, we purge our own intention of the filth of this desire, regardless of whatever enemy may judge it, when we seek as far as we can to have those whose labors are in question use them together with us—for themselves, for us, and for ours—in the Catholic fellowship.

## CHAPTER X

43. “But this,” they say, “is what troubles us: if we are unjust, why do you seek us?”

We answer: We seek you as unjust, so that you may not remain unjust; we seek the lost, so that we may rejoice over those who have been found, saying, “The brother was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found” (Luke 15:32).

“Why, then,” he says, “do you not baptize me, so that you may wash me from my sins?”

I reply: Because I do not violate the emperor’s mark when I correct the deserter’s error.

“Why,” he says, “do I not even do penance among you?”

Rather, unless you do penance, you cannot be saved. For how will you rejoice that you have been corrected unless you grieve that you were perverse?

“What, then,” he says, “do we receive from you when we pass over to you?”

I reply: You do not receive Baptism, certainly, since the Baptism that could exist in you outside the structure of Christ’s body could not benefit you. But you receive “the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4:3), without which no one will be able to see God, and charity, which, as it is written, “covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8).

The Apostle testifies that, without this great good, neither tongues of human beings and angels, nor knowledge of all the mysteries, nor prophecy, nor such faith as could move mountains, nor the distribution of everything a person possesses to the poor, nor the body’s suffering in the flames is of any benefit (1 Cor. 13:1–3). If, therefore, you regard this great good as small or as nothing, you are rightly and unhappily in error; and rightly, if you do not pass over into Catholic unity, you perish.

44. “If, then,” they say, “we must repent of having been outside the Church and opposed to the Church, so that we may be saved, how can we remain among you after this repentance as clergy or even as bishops?”

This would not happen—or rather, as must be admitted, it ought not to happen—unless it were healed by compensation for peace itself. But let those who lie in so great a death of separation say this to themselves and grieve with profound humility, so that through this wound of the Catholic mother they may come back to life.

When a severed branch is grafted in, another wound is made in the tree, by which it can be received, so that the branch which was perishing without the life of the root may live. But when, once received, it has grown together with the one receiving it, both vigor and fruit follow. If it does not grow together, it withers, but the life of the tree remains.

There is also a kind of grafting in which the branch outside is grafted in without any branch inside being cut off; nevertheless, this is not done without a wound to the tree, even if the wound is slight. Thus, when these people come to the Catholic root, and the honor of clergy or episcopate is not taken away from them even after their repentance for their error, something does indeed occur, as it were, in the bark of the mother tree, contrary to the integrity of strictness. Yet because “neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters” (1 Cor. 3:7), when the peace of the grafted branches grows together through poured-out prayers to God’s mercy, charity covers a multitude of sins.

45. The rule established in the Church—that no one, after doing penance for a crime, should receive clerical office, return to clerical office, or remain in clerical office [Note: [Col. 0812] Pope Innocent I, in Letter 6 to the bishops of Apulia, Agapitus, Macedonius, and others, writes: “The canons established at Nicaea exclude penitents even from the lowest offices of the clergy”—was established not through despair of pardon, but through the strictness of discipline. Otherwise an argument would be raised against the keys given to the Church, concerning which it was said, “Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven” (Matt. 16:19).

But lest perhaps, even after crimes had been exposed [Note: [Col. 0812] Editions: “even concerning other crimes.” Manuscripts: “after crimes had been exposed.”], a mind swelling with the hope of ecclesiastical honor should perform penance arrogantly, it was decided with the greatest strictness that after penance had been done for a damnable crime, no one should be a cleric. Thus, through despair of temporal elevation, the remedy of humility would be greater and more genuine.

The holy David also did penance for deadly crimes, and yet remained in his honor. Blessed Peter, when he shed the bitterest tears, certainly repented of having denied the Lord, and yet remained an Apostle. But for this reason the later diligence of those who, where nothing was taken away from salvation, added something to humility should not be considered superfluous. They had learned, I believe, from the affected exercise of honors and power that some people’s penances were feigned, and they wished salvation to be more securely fortified.

For the experience of many diseases compels people to discover many remedies. But in such cases, when through grave breaches of disagreement it is not the danger of this or that individual that is at issue, but the slaughter of peoples lies before us, something must be taken away from strictness so that sincere charity may come to the aid of healing greater evils.

46. Let these people, then, have bitter grief over their former detestable error, as Peter had over his deceitful fear, and let them come to the true Church of Christ, that is, the Catholic mother. Let those who were hostile against her become usefully her clergy; let them be bishops. We do not begrudge them this; rather, we embrace them, desire it, exhort them, and compel those whom we find on the roads and in the hedges to enter—even if we do not yet persuade some that we seek not their property but them [Note: [Col. 0813] Thus several manuscripts. Editions instead: “and thus some must be brought in.” The manuscript of the Augustinians: “And thus some must be brought in, etc.”].

When the Apostle Peter denied the Savior, he wept and remained an apostle; he had not yet received the promised Holy Spirit. But these people have received him much less, since, separated from the structure of the body—which alone the Holy Spirit gives life to—they have held the Church’s Sacraments outside and against the Church, and, as in a civil war, have fought with our own banners and weapons raised against us.

Let them come. Let there be peace in the strength of Jerusalem, and that strength is charity. To this holy city it was said: “Let peace be in your strength, and abundance in your towers” (Ps. 122:7).

Let them not exalt themselves against the mother’s solicitude, which she has had and continues to have for gathering them, and so many peoples whom they deceive or deceived. Let them not grow proud because she receives them in this way; let them not turn to the harm of their arrogance what she does for the good of peace.

47. In this way she has always been accustomed to help multitudes perishing through schisms and heresies. This displeased Lucifer [Note: [Col. 0813] Bishop of Cagliari. See *On Christian Combat*, chapter 30], because it was done in receiving and healing those who had perished through the poison of the Arian disease; and the one whom this displeased fell into the darkness of schism, having lost the light of charity.

The African Catholic Church has observed this practice toward these people from the beginning, following the judgment of the bishops who adjudicated in the Roman Church between Caecilian and the party of Donatus. After condemning one Donatus [Note: [Col. 0813] Donatus of Casae Nigrae], who was shown to have been the author of the schism, they decided that the others, even if they had been ordained outside the Church, should be received in their offices once corrected—not because they could possess the Holy Spirit while outside the unity of Christ’s body, but especially because of those whom, while remaining outside, they could deceive and prevent from receiving that gift. In addition, it was done so that their own weakness, received more gently within, might become healable, since no obstinacy now closed the eyes of their hearts against the evidence of truth.

What else were they themselves considering when, after condemning the Maximianists in a sacrilegious schism, as their council [Note: [Col. 0813] The council of Bagai] makes clear, and after ordaining others in their place, they later saw that the peoples did not depart from them and therefore, lest they lose everyone, received them in their offices? They raised no opposition or question concerning the Baptism which those condemned by them had administered outside.

Why, then, do they wonder, complain, or slander us because we receive them in this way for the sake of the true peace of Christ, and do not remember what they themselves did for the sake of Donatus’s false peace, which is opposed to Christ? If their action is held against them and intelligently maintained, they will have no answer at all.

## CHAPTER XI

48. They say, “If we have sinned against the Holy Spirit because we blew upon your Baptism, why do you seek us, since this sin absolutely cannot be forgiven, as the Lord says, ‘Whoever sins against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come’ (Matt. 12:32)?”

They do not attend to the fact that, according to this interpretation, no one should be liberated. For who does not speak against the Holy Spirit and sin against him—whether one who is not yet a Christian, or an Arian, Eunomian, or Macedonian heretic, who say that he is a creature; or a Photinian, who entirely denies that he has any substance and says that there is only one God, the Father; or the other heretics, whom it would take too long to enumerate?

Are none of these, then, to be liberated? Or were the Jews themselves, against whom the Lord made this charge, not to be baptized if they believed in him? The Savior did not say, “It will be forgiven in Baptism”; rather, he said, “It will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come.”

49. Let them understand, therefore, that not every sin, but a particular sin, is meant by sin against the Holy Spirit—a sin that will absolutely not be forgiven. Just as he said, “If I had not come, they would not have sin” (John 15:22), he certainly did not mean every sin, since they were full of many great sins. Rather, he meant a particular and distinctive sin: if they did not have that sin, everything else they had could be forgiven—that is, their failure to believe in him when he came. They would not have had this sin if he had not come.

So also, when he said, “Whoever sins against the Holy Spirit,” or, “Whoever speaks a word against the Holy Spirit,” he did not mean every sin committed against the Holy Spirit in deed or word, but wished a particular and definite sin to be understood.

This is hardness of heart to the end of this life, by which a person refuses to receive the remission of sins within the unity of Christ’s body, which the Holy Spirit gives life to. For when he had said to the disciples, “Receive the Holy Spirit,” he immediately added, “If you forgive anyone’s sins, they are forgiven; if you retain anyone’s sins, they are retained” (John 20:22–23).

Whoever, therefore, resists and opposes this gift of God’s grace, or in any way remains alienated from it until the end of this temporal life, will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come. This is the great sin by which all sins are held fast; and it is not shown to be committed by anyone unless he departs from the body.

As long as he lives here, God’s patience, as the Apostle says, leads him to repentance. But if, through the most persistent iniquity, he stores up wrath for himself—as the Apostle goes on to say—“according to the hardness of his heart and his unrepentant heart, on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God” (Rom. 2:4–5), he will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come.

50. These people with whom we are dealing, or about whom we are speaking, are not to be abandoned to despair; for they are still in the body. But let them not seek the Holy Spirit except in the body of Christ. Outside they possess the sacrament, but inwardly they do not possess the reality of which it is the sacrament; and therefore they “eat and drink judgment upon themselves” (1 Cor. 11:29).

For the one bread is the sacrament of unity, since, as the Apostle says, “Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body” (1 Cor. 10:17). Accordingly, the Catholic Church alone is the body of Christ, whose head is the Savior of his body (Eph. 5:23).

Outside this body the Holy Spirit gives life to no one, because, as the Apostle himself says, “God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). But one who is an enemy of unity does not share in divine love.

Therefore those who are outside the Church do not have the Holy Spirit. For it is written of them, “It is they who separate themselves, sensual, not having the Spirit” (Jude 19). Nor does the person who is false within the Church receive him, since it is also written, “For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from deceit” (Wis. 1:5).

Whoever, therefore, wishes to have the Holy Spirit must beware of remaining outside the Church; he must beware of entering it under false pretenses. Or, if he has already entered in such a condition, he must beware of persisting in that pretense, so that he may truly grow together with the tree of life [Note: [Col. 0815] Editions: “enter under false pretenses.” But manuscripts: “having entered under false pretenses.”].

51. I have sent you a lengthy book, perhaps burdensome for your occupations. If it can be read by you, even in parts, the Lord will grant you understanding, so that you may have what to answer those whom the mother Church, as to a faithful son, commends to you for correction and healing wherever and however you can—whether by speaking and answering yourself, or by leading them to the teachers of the Church—with the Lord’s help.

## LETTER 186 [Note: [Col. 0815] Two distinguished men, C. F. V. and two others—A. M., B., E., and Lov.—were used for the correction of this text; the manuscript of Sulpicius was also added.] [Note: [Col. 0815] Elsewhere numbered 106; what was 186 is now in the Appendix as 5. Written around the middle of the year 417.]

Alypius and Augustine to Bishop Paulinus, instructing him more fully against the heresy of Pelagius.

To the most blessed lord, and brother more than can be expressed in words, embraced with genuine affection in the innermost being of Christ, most earnestly desired, and fellow bishop, PAULINUS [Note: [Col. 0815] Not to Boniface, as Erasmus and the Louvain scholars report that some manuscripts had it; but that this letter was given to Paulinus, bishop of Nola, is entirely clear—not only from *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 21, and from Prosper’s *Against the Collator*, chapter 43, but also from what Augustine here, in section 40, recalls concerning the statements about original sin made by the person to whom he is writing. Those words are taken from Paulinus’s eighth letter to Severus.], ALYPIUS AND AUGUSTINE.

## CHAPTER I

1. At last God has provided us with a most trustworthy bearer of letters, our brother Januarius, deservedly dear to all of us. Through him, even if we did not write, Your Sincerity could learn everything concerning us as though through a living and intelligent letter. We know that you loved Pelagius—the one whom, we believe, is called a Briton in order to distinguish him from the Pelagius who is said to be from Tarentum [Note: [Col. 0816] Manuscripts C. C. and Sulpicius: “the one said to be from Terentius.”]—as a servant of God; but now we do not know how you love him.

For we not only loved him, but still love him; yet we love him now in one way, whereas we once loved him in another. At that time, it was because he appeared to us to hold the right faith; now it is so that, by God’s mercy, he may be freed from those views which he is said to hold that are hostile and opposed to God’s grace.

When rumor had been spreading this about him for some time, it was certainly not easy to believe, since rumor is accustomed to lie. But what brought us nearer to belief was that we read a certain book of his, handed to us by servants of Christ who had heard him teach such things most zealously and had followed him. The book was plainly attempting to persuade people of positions that would erase from the hearts of the faithful belief in the grace of God bestowed upon the human race through the one Mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ.

At the request of those same people, because we saw that this ought to be done, one of us replied to that book in a discussion without naming its author, lest he be offended and thereby rendered more difficult to heal [Note: [Col. 0816] In the book *On Nature and Grace*].

That book contains—and asserts at length and abundantly—the following position [Note: [Col. 0816] So the manuscript of Sulpicius: “a reply was made, which the book contains.”]: in certain letters addressed to Your Reverence [Note: [Col. 0816] See *On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 35], he says that he should not be thought to defend free will without God’s grace, since he says that the capacity for willing and acting, without which we could not will or do anything good, has been implanted in us by the Creator. Thus, according to the teacher himself, this is understood to be the grace of God which is common to pagans and Christians, ungodly and godly, believers and unbelievers.

2. We refuted as best we could these pernicious views, by which the coming of the Savior would be emptied of its force, using what the Apostle says concerning the Law: “If righteousness comes through nature, then Christ died for nothing” (Gal. 2:21). We did so in the hearts of those who held such views, so that, once they recognized them, Pelagius himself, if possible, might correct them without being provoked. In this way both the destructive error would be overthrown and the man’s embarrassment spared.

But after letters came to us from the East openly debating the same matter, we could no longer, in any way, fail the Church in the exercise of our episcopal authority. Reports were therefore sent concerning this matter from two councils, Carthaginian and Milevitan, to the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0816] Letters 175 and 176], before the ecclesiastical proceedings in which Pelagius is said to have been acquitted before the bishops of the province of Palestine had reached either our hands or Africa.

We also wrote to Pope Innocent of blessed memory, in addition to the reports of the councils, a personal letter in which we dealt at somewhat greater length with the matter itself [Note: [Col. 0817] Letter 177]. He replied to all our communications in the manner that was proper and fitting for a bishop of the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0817] Letters 181, 182, and 183].

3. You can now read all these documents, if perhaps none or not all of them have reached you. There you will see that, while the moderation that was owed to the man was preserved, lest he be condemned if he condemned what was wrong [Note: [Col. 0817] Vatican manuscripts: “moderation toward the men, lest they be condemned if they condemned what was wrong”], the novel and pernicious error itself was so suppressed by ecclesiastical authority that we are greatly surprised that there are still some who attempt, through any error, to resist the grace of God.

This is so, if they have learned that these proceedings took place: that the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord—which the true and Catholic faith of the Church has always held—transfers the weak along with the strong from the death of the first human being to the life of the second human being; and that it assists those who are already able to use free will, not only by leading them to grieve over their sins, but also by enabling them not to sin and to live rightly, so that, unless he assists us, we can possess no piety or righteousness, either in action or even in the will itself. “For God is the one who works in us both to will and to act, for his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:13).

## CHAPTER II

4. For who, except the one who came to seek and save what was lost, distinguishes us from that mass and lump of perdition? Hence the Apostle asks, saying, “Who distinguishes you?” If a person answers, “My faith, my will, my good work,” the reply is made to him: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

All this is said not so that the human being may not boast, but so that “the one who boasts may boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:31); not “from works, lest anyone should boast” (Eph. 2:9)—not because good works are rendered fruitless, since God will repay each person according to his works and “glory and honor and peace” belong to everyone who does good (Rom. 2:6, 10)—but because works arise from grace, not grace from works. For faith, which works through love (Gal. 5:6), would accomplish nothing unless the love of God were poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5). Nor would faith itself exist in us unless God apportioned to each a measure of faith (Rom. 12:3).

5. It is therefore good for a person, with all the strength of his free will, truly to say, “I will guard my strength toward you” (Ps. 59:10). For the one who thought that he could guard what had been given without God’s help went off into a distant country and, living prodigally, squandered everything. Worn down by the misery of harsh servitude, he came to himself and said, “I will arise and go to my father” (Luke 15:12–18).

When would he have had this good thought unless the most merciful Father had secretly inspired it in him as well? Understanding this, that minister of the New Testament says, “Not that we are competent of ourselves to think anything as though from ourselves; but our competence is from God” (2 Cor. 3:5).

Thus, after he had said, “I will guard my strength toward you,” lest he arrogate even this very act of guarding to his own powers—as though it had come into his mind that “unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it watch in vain” (Ps. 127:1), and that “he who guards Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps” (Ps. 121:4)—he added the reason by which he becomes competent to guard, or rather the guardian by whom he is preserved: “For you, O God,” he says, “are my protector.”

6. Let this person, then, recall, if he can, his merits—what caused God to deign to be his protector, as though God had been received by him. Let him recall whether he sought God or was sought by him who came to seek and save what was lost (Luke 19:10).

For if a person wishes to ask what he deserved before grace, he can find his evils, not his good things, even if the Savior’s grace found him possessing only a single day of life on earth. If a person does something good in order to merit grace, the reward is not reckoned to him according to grace but according to debt.

But if he believes in the one who justifies the ungodly, so that his faith may be reckoned as righteousness (Rom. 4:4–5)—for “the righteous person lives by faith” (Hab. 2:4)—then, before he is justified by grace, that is, before he is made righteous, what is the ungodly person except ungodly? If debt followed him, what would be repaid to him according to his merit except punishment?

If, therefore, it is by grace, it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace (Rom. 11:6). For debt is repaid according to works, whereas grace is given freely; hence it is even called *grace*.

## CHAPTER III

7. But if someone says that faith merits the grace of doing good, we cannot deny it; indeed, we gladly acknowledge it. This is the faith we wish our brothers who boast greatly of their works to possess, so that they may obtain love, which alone truly does good. Love is so completely a gift of God that God is said to be love (1 John 4:8).

Those who have faith by which they obtain justification have, through God’s grace, reached the law of righteousness. Hence it is said, “At an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you” (Isa. 49:8).

Accordingly, in those who are saved by the election of grace, God the helper works both to will and to act for his good pleasure, because “all things work together for good for those who love God” (Rom. 8:28). If all things do so, then certainly love itself, which we obtain through faith, also works together for good, so that we may love by his grace the one who first loved us so that we might believe in him, and may be loved although we ourselves have not performed these works.

8. Those, however, who expect rewards as debts owed to them on the basis of their merits, and attribute even their merits not to God’s grace but to the powers of their own will, are like carnal Israel, of whom it was said that, “pursuing the law of righteousness, they did not attain the law of righteousness.” Why? “Because it was not from faith, but as though from works.”

For this is the righteousness that comes from faith, which the Gentiles apprehended. Concerning them it is said: “What shall we say, then? That the Gentiles, who did not know righteousness, attained righteousness—the righteousness that comes from faith. But Israel, pursuing the law of righteousness, did not attain the law of righteousness. Why? Because it was not from faith, but as though from works. For they stumbled over the stumbling stone, as it is written: ‘Behold, I place in Zion a stumbling stone and a rock of offense; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame’” (Rom. 9:30–33).

This is the righteousness that comes from faith, by which we believe that we are justified—that is, made righteous—by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, so that we may be found in him, not having our own righteousness that comes from the Law, but that which comes through faith in Christ. This righteousness that comes from God is in faith, certainly in faith [Note: [Col. 0819] Thus the manuscripts and the first editions. The Louvain edition reads: “The righteousness that is from God is in faith, certainly in faith by which, etc.”], by which we believe that righteousness is given to us by God, not made by ourselves within ourselves through our own powers.

### 9

For why did the Apostle call that righteousness which is from the Law his own, and not from God—as though the Law were not from God? Who but an impious person would think this? But because the Law commands through the letter and does not help through the Spirit, whoever hears the letter of the Law in such a way that it seems sufficient to him merely to know what it commands or forbids, trusting that he will fulfill it by the power of his own free choice, and does not in faith flee for help to the life-giving Spirit, lest the letter, having made him guilty, kill him—such a person certainly has zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.

For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness—that is, the righteousness given by God—and wishing to establish his own, so that it might be righteousness from the Law alone, he is not subject to God’s righteousness. For Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes (Rom. X, 2–4), just as the same Apostle says, so that we might be the righteousness of God in him (II Cor. V, 21). Therefore, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ (Rom. V, 1); but having been justified freely by his grace (ibid. III, 24), so that faith itself may not become proud.

### 10

Nor should a person say to himself, “If it is by faith, how is it free? For if faith earns it, why is it not rather paid back than given?” Let the believer not say this, because when he says, “I have faith in order that I may earn justification,” the answer is made to him: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (I Cor. IV, 7).

Therefore, when faith obtains justification, just as God has apportioned to each person the measure of faith itself, no human merit precedes the grace of God. Rather, grace itself merits increase, so that, once increased, it may merit completion—with the will accompanying, not leading; following, not going before.

Hence the one who said, “I will keep my strength for you,” and gave the reason by saying, “For God is my protector,” as though asking by what merits he had obtained this and finding nothing in himself prior to God’s grace, says, “My God, his mercy will go before me.” However much, he says, I consider my preceding merits, his mercy will go before me. Accordingly, preserving for God the strength which he attributed to him, he did not lose it through the same Savior through whom he had received it from the Giver.

Nor does he merit greater gifts for any other reason than by piously and faithfully knowing from whom all good things come to him—and by knowing this, not from himself, lest even this should be something in him that is not from God.  
[Note: [Col. 0820] The Vatican manuscripts and cc. read, “lest even this not be in him.” Not a bad reading.]

Hence the Apostle says most aptly: “We have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things granted to us by God” (I Cor. II, 12).

Accordingly, even human merit itself is a free gift. No one merits receiving anything good from the Father of lights, from whom every good and perfect gift descends (James I, 17), except by receiving what he does not merit.

## CHAPTER IV

### 11

But what God’s grace, through Jesus Christ our Lord, provides for infants is much more merciful, and beyond all doubt more freely given: that generation from Adam should not harm them, while regeneration in Christ benefits them. In them, too, God’s mercy anticipates by so long a time even the capacity to receive. Certainly, if they should depart from the body at this tender age, they knowingly receive eternal life and the kingdom of heaven, by the merit of that gift which, although it has benefited them here, they did not know.

Certainly, in these matters, after the teaching concerning older persons, these are the first gifts alone. In bestowing them, God’s grace works in such a way that the will of those receiving them is neither first, nor joined to, nor subsequent to the gift. For so great a benefit is given not only to those who do not desire it, but even to those who resist; and it would be counted against them as a great sacrilege if, at that age, the exercise of free choice had any power.

### 12

We have said this because those who, unable to search out the inscrutable judgments of God in the matter of grace—why, from the mass of Adam, which certainly fell wholly into condemnation through one man, he makes one vessel for honor and another for dishonor—nevertheless dare to make infants guilty of their own sins, so that those who cannot think either good or evil are thought capable, by free choice, of deserving either punishment or grace.

Yet apostolic truth, by saying, “From one came condemnation for all” (Rom. V, 16), sufficiently shows that they are born into punishment, so that they are reborn into grace not by merit but by mercy. Otherwise grace is no longer grace, if it is given freely through divine works but repaid according to human merits.

Grace alone distinguishes in such a way from punishment that, whereas punishment is owed to all through Adam, grace through the one Jesus Christ is owed to no one but is freely given. Thus, if it is truly grace,  
[Note: [Col. 0820] Three manuscripts read, “that it may be true.”]

the inscrutable judgments of God can exist—as befits God—when he himself distinguishes among infants whom no merits distinguish. Yet they cannot be unjust, because “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV, 10).

Therefore, when the grace of mercy is granted to one person, he has no ground for boasting in human merit, since it is “not from works, lest anyone should boast.” But when truth in the form of retribution is returned to another, he has no reason to complain justly: what is returned is what sin rightly deserves. For the one in whom all sinned is certainly punished in each individual also. In their punishment it is shown more clearly what is bestowed upon the vessels of mercy through grace that is not owed but true—that is, freely given.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 0821]

### 13

But how they argue against the Apostle, who says most plainly, “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. V, 12), while also saying that infants have sins of their own through free choice—it is wearisome to consider and burdensome to state, but we are compelled to do so.

For whatever great and subtle intellects have been able to devise must either be avoided by silence because of poverty of thought, or passed over with contempt because of arrogance. “Look,” they say, “Esau and Jacob wrestle within their mother’s womb; and as they are being born, one is supplanted by the other, and the hand of the one who follows and holds the heel of the one preceding is found upon that preceding foot.  
[Note: [Col. 0821] Thus the Vatican manuscript: *manus* (“hand”).]

Thus the struggle, as it were, persists and is confirmed. How, then, when infants are doing these things, can there be no exercise of their own will, either toward good or toward evil, from which rewards or punishments might follow upon preceding merits?”

### 14

To this we reply that those movements, and what appeared to be a quarrel between the infants, were signs of great realities precisely because they were not an exercise of free choice but a portent. For we are not going to grant free choice of the will even to asses, because the prophet says that an animal of this kind, “a beast of burden without a voice, answering with a human voice, restrained the prophet’s madness” (II Pet. II, 16).

But those who insist that these were not portentous movements but voluntary acts, and that they were not performed concerning infants but by infants, what will they answer to the Apostle? Seeing that these twins also were to be recalled as evidence of freely given grace, he says: “For when they had not yet been born and had done nothing good or evil, so that God’s purpose according to election might remain—not from works but from him who calls—it was said, ‘The elder shall serve the younger’” (Rom. IX, 11–13).

Then he adds the testimony of the prophet, who spoke these things much later but nevertheless declared God’s ancient purpose concerning this matter: “As it is written,” he says, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. I, 2, 3).

### 15
