Indeed, the Teacher of the Gentiles testifies in faith and truth that these twins, not yet born, had done nothing good or evil, so that grace might be commended; so that what was said, “The elder shall serve the younger,” might be understood to have been said not from works but from him who calls; and so that God’s purpose according to election might remain, without human merit preceding it.

For he does not speak of an election of human will or nature, since the condition of death and condemnation was equal in both; rather, there is unquestionably an election of grace. Grace does not find those who are to be chosen; it makes them. Speaking of this later in the same Epistle, he says: “So also at the present time a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace. But if by grace, then it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace” (Rom. XI, 5, 6).

This passage is fully consistent with the present one, where it is recalled that “The elder shall serve the younger” was said not from works but from him who calls. Why, then, is such shameless resistance offered to this most glorious commendation of grace concerning the free choice of infants and the acts of those not yet born? Why is grace said to be preceded by merits, when it would not be grace if it were reckoned according to merit? Why is there contention, in a Christian disputation, against the salvation sent to the lost and coming to the undeserving—however acute, abundant, and adorned the argument may be?

## CHAPTER VI

### 16

“But how,” they say, “is there no injustice with God, if, by loving, he distinguishes those whom no merits of works distinguish?”

This is said to us as though the Apostle himself had not seen, proposed, and answered this question. He certainly saw what human weakness or ignorance might think upon hearing these things. Proposing the same question to himself, he says: “What shall we say, then? Is there injustice with God?” He immediately answers: “Certainly not.”

And when giving the reason why there is no injustice—that is, why there is no injustice with God—he does not say, “For he judges the merits or works even of infants, although they are still established in their mother’s womb.” How could he say this, when he had already said concerning those not yet born, and concerning those who had not yet done anything good or evil, that “The elder shall serve the younger” was said not from works but from him who calls?

Rather, wishing to show why there is no injustice with God in these matters, he says: “For he says to Moses, ‘I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion.’”

What did he teach us here except that, from the mass of the first man, to whom death is rightly owed, the fact that anyone is delivered belongs not to human merits but to God’s mercy? Thus there is no injustice with God, because whether by remitting or by exacting what is owed, he is not unjust.  
[Note: [Col. 0822] The printed editions read, “nor by permitting.” One of the Vatican manuscripts instead reads, “nor by remitting”; Lov. had arrived at this reading by conjecture.]

For there grace is forgiveness where punishment could justly have been exacted. From this it becomes still more evident how great a benefit is conferred upon one who is delivered from deserved punishment and freely justified, while another, equally guilty, is punished without any injustice on the part of the punisher.  
[Note: [Col. 0822] Bad., Am., Er., and the Fuxensis manuscript read *grata* (“pleasing”) rather than *gratia* (“grace”).]

### 17

Finally, he adds and says: “Therefore it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy.” This was said concerning those who are delivered by grace and justified.

But concerning those upon whom God’s wrath remains—because God also makes good use of them to instruct others whom he deigns to deliver—he adds and says: “For Scripture says to Pharaoh, ‘For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed throughout the whole earth.’”

Then, concluding with respect to both, he says: “Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills”—certainly neither through any injustice, but both through mercy and truth.

And yet bold human weakness is still stirred up—namely, the weakness of those who attempt to ponder the inscrutable depth of God’s judgments according to the conjectures of the human heart.

### 18

Putting this question to himself by way of opposition, the Apostle says: “You will say to me, then, ‘Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?’”

Let us suppose that this is said to us. What else should we answer than what the Apostle answered? Or, if such things also trouble us—for we too are human—then all of us ought together to hear him saying: “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Shall what is formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me like this?’ Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (ibid. IX, 14–21).

If this mass were so neutral that, just as it deserved no good, it also deserved no evil, it would rightly appear unjust for vessels to be made from it for dishonor. But since, through the free choice of the first man, the whole human race flowed into condemnation, there is no doubt that the fact that vessels are made from it for honor is to be attributed not to its own righteousness—for no grace preceded it—but to God’s mercy; while the fact that vessels are made for dishonor is to be attributed not to any injustice in God—far be it that such a thing should exist with God—but to judgment.

Whoever understands this with the Catholic Church does not argue against grace on the basis of merits, but sings to the Lord of mercy and judgment, so that he neither refuses mercy in ingratitude nor accuses judgment of injustice.  
[Note: [Col. 0823] Elsewhere, *invitus* (“unwilling”).]

### 19

For there is another lump, of which the same Apostle says: “If the first portion is holy, so is the lump; and if the root is holy, so are the branches” (Rom. XI, 16). That lump is from Abraham, not from Adam—that is, from communion in the sacrament and likeness of faith, not from mortal propagation.

But this lump—or, as it is read in most books, this mass (*massa*)—  
[Note: [Col. 0823] Phurama.]

is wholly subject to death: “When through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned.” From that lump, mercy makes one vessel for honor, while judgment makes another for dishonor.

Neither there do merits precede the grace that delivers; nor here do sins escape the justice that punishes. This is not so evident in older persons, where, by the merits of human beings, they take refuge as though under the protection of some obscurity against those who argue contentiously. For this reason the Apostle brings forward, against their contention, those who had not yet been born and had done nothing good or evil, concerning whom it was said not from works but from him who calls: “The elder shall serve the younger.”

### 20

Since in this matter God’s judgments are exceedingly deep and inscrutable, and his ways unsearchable (ibid. 33), let a person meanwhile hold that there is no injustice with God. But let him confess that he, as a human being, does not know by what equity God has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills.

Let him do so in such a way that, because he firmly holds that there is no injustice with God, although no one is justified by preceding merits, he nevertheless knows that no one is hardened except by merit.

For it is piously and truthfully believed that God, by justifying the guilty and ungodly, delivers them from deserved punishments. But if it is believed that God condemns someone who is undeserving and subject to no sin, he is not believed to be free from injustice.

Where, then, the undeserving person is delivered, the greater the punishment that would justly have been owed, the greater the thanksgiving that is due. But where the undeserving person is condemned, neither mercy nor truth is upheld.  
[Note: [Col. 0823] The editions read, “nor is truth condemned.” All the manuscripts read, “neither mercy nor truth is upheld.” Immediately before Er. and Lov. read, “where the deserving person is condemned.” Bad., Am., and two manuscripts, however, read *indignus* (“undeserving”), and this is better; the argument is pressing the question, “How is Esau not condemned undeserving?”—with “of condemnation” understood.]

### 21

“How,” they ask, “is Esau not condemned undeserving, if ‘not from works but from him who calls’ it was said, ‘The elder shall serve the younger’?”

Just as no good works had preceded Jacob, so that he might belong to grace, so no evil works of Esau had preceded him, so that he ought to belong to punishment. In both there were plainly no works, good or evil, but works of their own.

Yet both were subject to that one man in whom all sinned, so that all might die in him. For all who were to come from that one man, many as they would be in themselves, were then one in him. Therefore, that sin would belong to him alone if no one had come forth from him. But since the common nature was in him, no one is free from his fault.

If both, who had not yet performed any works of their own, whether good or evil, were nevertheless born guilty through their origin, let the one who is delivered praise mercy, and let the one who is punished not accuse judgment.

## CHAPTER VII

### 22

If here we were to say, “How much better it would be if both were delivered,” nothing more appropriate could be said to us than: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?”

For he knows what he is doing, and how great the number ought to be—first of all of human beings, then of the saints—as of the stars, as of the angels; and, to speak of earthly things, as of cattle, fish, birds, trees and grasses, and finally of the leaves and hairs of our heads.

For even with human reasoning we can say: Since all these things he made are good, how much better it would be if he had doubled and multiplied them, so that there would be many more than there are. If the world could not contain them, could he not also have made the world itself as much larger as he wished?

Yet however much he made either the things themselves more numerous or the world more capacious and larger, the same question could nevertheless be raised concerning multiplying them, and there would be no excessive limit.  
[Note: [Col. 0824] Perhaps, “moderate.”]

### 23

For this too can be said: whether it is grace by which the unjust are justified—a matter about which we are not permitted to doubt—or, as some wish, free choice always precedes, with either punishment or reward following upon its merit, why were those people created at all whom God certainly foresaw would sin in such a way that they would be condemned to eternal fire?

Although he did not make the sins, who but God created the natures themselves, which are undoubtedly good in themselves, but which, by the choice of the will, were destined to become the vices of sinners—many of them such that eternal punishment would be repaid to them? Why, except because he willed it? But why he willed it—“O man, who are you to answer back to God?” Does what is formed say to the one who formed it, “Why did you make me like this?” Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?

### 24

And would that we learn what follows: “But if God, wishing to show his wrath and demonstrate his power, endured with great patience the vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory upon the vessels of mercy.”

Now an answer has been given to human beings, as much as an answer could be given to them—if, indeed, the person who contends for the freedom of his own choice in such great weakness can grasp even this. The reasons have been stated.

Who, then, are you to answer back to God, if God, wishing to show his wrath and demonstrate his power, since the all-good God can also make good use of evil people—evil not by divine creation, but by the corrupted wickedness of the will, while the nature created by God the Creator was good—endured with great patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction?

This was not because he needed either angelic or human sins—for he does not need the righteousness of any creature—but so that he might make known the riches of his glory upon the vessels of mercy. Thus they would not exalt themselves over good works as though they possessed them by their own powers, but would humbly understand that, unless God’s grace—which was not owed but freely given—came to their aid, what would have been repaid to them was what they saw repaid to others in the same mass.

### 25

Therefore the number and multitude of the saints is fixed by God’s foreknowledge. For those who love God, all things work together for good through what he has given them by the Holy Spirit poured out into their hearts—those who are called according to his purpose.

“For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers and sisters. Those whom he predestined, he also called”—here we must understand, “according to his purpose.” For there are others who are called but not chosen, and therefore are not called according to his purpose.

“Those whom he called”—that is, according to his purpose—“he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. VIII, 28–30).

These are the children of promise; these are the elect who are saved through the election of grace, where it was said: “But if by grace, then it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace.”

These are the vessels of mercy, in whom God also makes known the riches of his glory through the vessels of wrath. Through the Holy Spirit they become “one heart and one soul” (Acts IV, 32), blessing God and not forgetting all his rewards—him who is gracious to all their iniquities, who heals all their diseases, who redeems their life from corruption, who crowns it with mercy (Ps. CII, 2)—because it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy.

### 26

But the other human beings, who do not belong to this fellowship, nevertheless have both soul and body made by God’s goodness, as well as whatever nature itself possesses apart from the fault inflicted upon it by the audacity of a proud will.

They were created by God’s foreknowledge for this purpose: that in them he might show what the free choice of the deserter could accomplish without his grace; and that, through their just and deserved punishments, the vessels of mercy—separated from that mass not by the merits of their own works but by God’s freely given grace—might learn what had been bestowed upon them.

Thus “every mouth may be stopped” (Rom. III, 19), and “whoever boasts may boast in the Lord” (I Cor. I, 31).

## CHAPTER VIII

### 27

Whoever teaches otherwise, and does not assent to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ, who said, “The Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost” (Luke XIX, 10)—for he did not say, “What was going to be lost,” but “What was lost”—what does this show except that, through the sin of the first man, the nature of the entire human race was lost?

Whoever, therefore, teaches otherwise, and does not assent to the doctrine that accords with piety (II Tim. VI, 3), defending human nature against the grace of the Savior and against the blood of the Redeemer as though it were safe and free, while nevertheless seeking to be regarded as a Christian—what will he say concerning the distinction among infants? Why is one taken into the life of the second man while another is left in the death of the first man?

If he says that the merits of free choice preceded, the Apostle answers him with what we said above concerning those not yet born and having done nothing good or evil.

But if he says what is defended in the books that Pelagius is said to have published most recently—although he now appears to have anathematized, in the episcopal judgment at Palestine, those who say that Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone and not the human race—if you say that both were born without judgment and drew nothing from the condemnation of the first man, then, since he does not dare deny that the person regenerated in Christ is adopted into the kingdom of heaven, let him answer what will become of one who, through no fault of his own, was not baptized and was overtaken by this temporal death.

If we do not suppose that he will say that God will condemn to eternal death an innocent person who has no original sin before reaching the years in which he could have his own sin, he is compelled to answer what Pelagius was forced to anathematize in the ecclesiastical judgment in order to be pronounced Catholic in some fashion: that infants, even if they are not baptized, have eternal life. For if this is denied, what remains except eternal death?

### 28

Thus he will argue against the Lord’s statement: “Your fathers ate manna in the wilderness, and they died. This is the bread that came down from heaven, so that if anyone eats of it, he may not die.” He was certainly not speaking of this death, which even those who eat that bread must necessarily suffer.

And shortly afterward: “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John VI, 49, 50, 54)—clearly, the life that is to come after this death.

He will also argue against the authority of the Apostolic See, where, when this very matter was being discussed, this evangelical testimony was brought forward so that infants who have not been baptized might not be thought capable of possessing life (Innocent, Epistle 182, no. 5).

And he will argue against Pelagius’ own words, expressed before the bishops by whom he was heard, where he anathematized those who said that unbaptized infants have eternal life.

### 29

We have recalled this because, among you—or rather, in your city, if what we have heard is true—some people are striving with such obstinacy on behalf of this error that they say it would be easier for them even to abandon and despise Pelagius, who anathematized those holding these views, than to depart from what they regard as the truth of this opinion.

But if they yield to the Apostolic See—or rather, to the very teacher and Lord of the Apostles, who says that they will not have life in themselves unless they eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, which the unbaptized certainly cannot do—then at some point they will confess that unbaptized infants cannot have life. Consequently, although they are punished with eternal death more tolerably than all those who also commit their own sins, they are nevertheless so punished.

### 30

Since this is so, let them debate and strive to persuade as many as they can that the just God, with whom there is no injustice, will condemn infants who are innocent of their own sins to perpetual death, if they are not also bound and held guilty through Adam.

But if this is utterly absurd and wholly alien to God’s justice, and yet no one who remembers that he is a Christian of the Catholic faith denies or doubts that infants who have not received the grace of regeneration in Christ, without eating his flesh and drinking his blood, do not have life in themselves, and consequently are subject to eternal punishment, then it certainly remains that, since they themselves have done nothing good or evil, the punishment of their death is just because they die in him in whom all sinned.

Hence they are justified in this one alone, from whom neither original sin could be contracted nor personal sin committed.  
[Note: [Col. 0827] The Sulpician manuscript reads, “made alive.”]

### 31

He called us not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles. For he himself gathered the children of that Jerusalem which killed the Prophets and stoned those sent to her, although she herself was unwilling, gathering whom he willed (Matt. XXIII, 37). He gathered them both before his incarnation, as he gathered the Prophets, and afterward, when the Word became flesh, as he gathered the Apostles and the thousands of people who placed the prices of their possessions at the Apostles’ feet (Acts II, 41; IV, 4, 34, 35).

All those people are children of Jerusalem, which was unwilling that they should be gathered, yet they were gathered despite her unwillingness—  
[Note: [Col. 0827] The Vatican manuscripts read, “while he willed it.”]

Concerning them he says: “If I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your children cast them out? Therefore they shall be your judges” (Matt. XII, 27).

It had been foretold concerning them: “Though the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved” (Isa. X, 22; Hos. I, 10; Rom. IX, 24–27).

The word of God cannot fail, nor has he rejected his people whom he foreknew; yet a remnant has been saved through the election of grace. But if by grace—as must often be said—it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace. These are not our words but the Apostle’s (Rom. XI, 2, 5, 6).

Therefore, what he cried out concerning Jerusalem unwilling that her children should be gathered, we cry out against those who do not want willing children to be gathered into the Church. They are not corrected even after the judgment that was held concerning Pelagius himself in Palestine—  
[Note: [Col. 0827] The Council of Diospolis.]

He would have emerged from it condemned unless he himself had condemned the statements brought against him concerning God’s grace—statements that he could not obscure.

## CHAPTER IX

### 32

Besides those matters which he dared to defend, as best he could, by whatever sort of reasoning, certain charges were brought against him which, unless he had anathematized them after removing every evasion, would have resulted in his own anathematization.

It was alleged that he said:

- Adam would have died whether he sinned or did not sin;
- Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone and not the human race;
- infants newly born are in the same condition in which Adam was before his transgression;
- neither through Adam’s death or transgression does the whole human race die, nor through Christ’s resurrection does the whole human race rise;
- infants, even if they are not baptized, have eternal life;
- baptized rich people, unless they renounce everything, are not credited with any good they may appear to do, and cannot possess the kingdom of God;
- God’s grace and help are not given for individual acts, but consist in free choice or in the Law and teaching;
- God’s grace is given according to our merits;
- no one can be called a child of God unless he has become entirely free from sin;
- free choice would not exist if it needed God’s help, since each person has it in his own will to do something or not to do it;
- our victory comes not from God’s help but from free choice;
- forgiveness is not given to the penitent according to God’s grace and mercy, but according to the merit and labor of those who have become worthy of mercy through repentance.

### 33

Pelagius anathematized all these propositions, as the Acts themselves sufficiently attest, without offering any argument whatsoever in any way to defend them.

It follows that whoever follows the authority of that episcopal judgment and Pelagius’ own confession must hold what the Catholic Church has always held:

Adam would not have died unless he had sinned;

Adam’s sin harmed not Adam alone but also the human race;

infants newly born are not in the condition in which Adam was before his transgression, so that what the Apostle briefly says also pertains to them: “Through one man came death, and through one man the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (I Cor. XV, 21, 22).

Hence unbaptized infants cannot possess not only the kingdom of heaven but even eternal life.

He must also confess that baptized rich people, even if they do not abandon their riches and are such as the Apostle describes to Timothy when he says, “Command the rich in this present world not to be proud, nor to place their hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who gives us all things abundantly for enjoyment; let them be rich in good works, generous and sharing, storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of the true life” (I Tim. VI, 17–19), cannot be deprived of the kingdom of God.

Let him confess that God’s grace and help are also given for individual acts, and that grace is not given according to our merits, so that it may truly be grace—that is, freely given through the mercy of him who said, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion” (Exod. XXXIII, 19).

Let him confess that those who say every day, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. VI, 12), can be called children of God. They would certainly not say this truthfully if they were entirely without sin.

Let him confess that free choice exists even when it needs divine help.

Let him confess that when we fight against temptations and unlawful desires, although we also have our own will in that struggle, our victory nevertheless proceeds not from that will but from God’s help. Otherwise what the Apostle says would not be true: “It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy.”

Let him confess that forgiveness is given to the penitent according to God’s grace and mercy, not according to their merits, since the Apostle also called repentance itself a gift of God when he said concerning certain people: “Lest perhaps God may grant them repentance” (II Tim. II, 25).

Let anyone who assents to Catholic authority and to Pelagius’ own words explicitly recorded in the ecclesiastical Acts confess all these things plainly, without any evasions. For one cannot truly believe that the propositions contrary to these were anathematized unless the propositions to which they are contrary are held in a faithful heart and proclaimed in open confession.

## CHAPTER X

### 34

Nor is it sufficiently clear what the same Pelagius thinks about this matter in the more recent books which he is said to have published after that judgment, although he appears to agree with the help of divine grace.

At one point he weighs the power of the will with equal force and on an even balance, defining it to be as effective for not sinning as for sinning—  
[Note: [Col. 0829] According to the Sulpician manuscript and Lov., “so that it is also somewhat effective.” The older editions and four manuscripts read, “so that it is also as effective.”]

If this is so, no place is left for the help of grace, whereas we say that, without it, the exercise of free choice has no power at all to prevent sin.

At another point he admits that we are fortified by the daily help of God’s grace, although we may have a strong and firm free choice not to sin. Yet he ought to have confessed that this free choice is ineffective and weak until all the diseases of our soul are healed.

For the person who said, “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak; heal me, Lord, for my bones are troubled; and my soul is greatly troubled” (Ps. VI, 3, 4), was not praying on account of bodily weakness. To show that he was asking on behalf of his soul, he immediately added, “And my soul is greatly troubled.”

### 35

He therefore seems to think that the help of grace is granted as something additional—that is, that even if it were not granted, we would nevertheless possess a strong and firm free choice not to sin.

So that we may not seem to suspect him rashly, and so that someone might perhaps say that he regards free choice as strong and firm for not sinning in the sense that, although it cannot accomplish and fulfill this without God’s grace, we call healthy eyes firm for seeing even though they can in no way see if the aid of light is absent, he shows elsewhere what he says or thinks on this point. He states that God’s grace is given to human beings so that what they are commanded to do through free choice they may fulfill more easily through grace.

When he says “more easily,” what can he intend to be understood except that, even if grace is absent, it is possible through free choice—either easily or even with difficulty—to fulfill what God commands?  
[Note: [Col. 0829] See *On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 7 and following.]

36. Where, then, is the statement, “What is man, unless [Note: [Col. 0829] The editions read, “man, that.” But the manuscripts read, “man, unless that.”] you are mindful of him” (Ps. 8:5)? And finally, where are those testimonies which the bishop of the Jerusalem Church [Note: [Col. 0829] John.] recalls, as we read in the same Acts, having spoken to Pelagius himself when it had been reported to him that Pelagius said that a human being could exist without sin apart from the grace of God? For these are the three very weighty testimonies he cited against such impious presumption: the Apostle’s words, “I labored more abundantly than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15:10); and, “It depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9:16); and, “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Ps. 126:1).

How, then, is what God commands fulfilled without his help, even with difficulty, when Scripture says that, unless the Lord builds, the builder has labored in vain? It does not say, “It does indeed depend on the one who wills and runs, but it is accomplished more easily through the mercy of God”; rather, it says, “It depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy.” This is not because there is no human willing and striving [Note: [Col. 0830] Thus the better manuscripts. Bad., Am., and Er. read: “Not because there is no cooperation of the human will and striving.” Lov.: “Not because there is no human will and striving.” Two manuscripts: “will and cooperation.”], but because it can accomplish nothing unless he shows mercy. Nor did the Apostle say, “And I,” but, “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me.” This is not because he himself did nothing good, but because he would have done nothing if grace had not assisted him.

Moreover, the supposed equal capacity of free choice for good and evil leaves no room even for this “facility”—which he at least seems to have admitted when he said, “They can fulfill more easily through grace”; good is fulfilled more easily through grace [Note: [Col. 0830] Two manuscripts omit “good through grace.” The printed edition of Louvain, 1647, reads: “They can fulfill more easily. For if the law is fulfilled more easily through grace,” etc.], whereas evil is done most easily without grace. Clearly, then, this capacity is not weighed in an even balance.

## CHAPTER XI

37. But why say more? We must not only be on our guard against such persons, but neither should we grow weary of teaching or warning them, if they will bear it. Yet we undoubtedly do them a greater service if we pray that they may be corrected, lest, with such great abilities, they either perish or destroy others by damnable presumption. For they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge; that is, being ignorant of the righteousness that is from God, and wishing to establish their own, they are not subject to the righteousness of God (Rom. 10:2–3). Since they call themselves Christians, they must certainly be watched more carefully than the Jews, of whom the Apostle said this, lest they stumble on the stone of stumbling (Rom. 9:32), as though cleverly defending nature and free choice, like the philosophers of this world, who labored hard to be thought—or thought themselves—to attain the blessed life by the strength of their own will [Note: [Col. 0830] See above, Letter 155, no. 2 and following.]. Let these persons therefore beware lest through the wisdom of words they make the cross of Christ void (1 Cor. 1:17), and thus stumble on the stone of stumbling. For even if human nature had remained in the integrity in which it was created, it could by no means preserve itself without the help of its Creator. Therefore, since without God’s grace it cannot keep the salvation which it received, how can it without God’s grace restore that which it lost?

38. Yet we ought not for that reason refrain from praying for them: if they are not corrected, this must indeed be imputed to the will of those who refuse to believe that even for this very thing they need the grace of the Savior—although they suppose it to consist in the powers of the will alone. For those to whom these people are altogether similar in this matter, of whom the Apostle said that, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own, they were not subject to God’s righteousness, certainly did not believe through the fault of their own will. They were not compelled into the fault of unbelief in order that they might be unbelievers; but by refusing to believe, they were not free from the guilt of unbelief. And yet, because the will is not sufficient of itself to be moved to believe true things unless God helps through grace—as the Lord himself said when speaking of those who did not believe, “No one comes to me unless it has been given him by my Father” (John 6:66)—the Apostle, though he preached the Gospel to them earnestly, nevertheless judged this too little unless he also prayed that they might believe. For he says: “Brothers, the good will indeed of my heart, and my prayer to God, is for them unto salvation”; and then he added the words we have cited: “For I bear them witness that they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge,” etc. Let us therefore pray for them, holy brother.

## CHAPTER XII

39. For you see with us how grievous is the error by which they are held. Your letters breathe the most sincere fragrance of Christ, in which you appear as a most devoted lover and confessor of his grace. But we have thought it right to speak with you at length on this matter: first, because it is most delightful—for what ought to be more delightful than the grace by which the weak are healed, the slothful aroused, and the willing helped?—and secondly, that, if by God’s help our discussion can do anything, not your faith but the confession of your faith may support it against such people, just as we too are assisted in this ability by the letters of Your Brotherliness.

40. For what could be richer or fuller of a most true confession than what occurs in one of your letters, where you humbly lamented that our nature did not remain as it was created, but was corrupted through that father of the human race, saying: “Poor and sorrowful man that I am, still encrusted with the squalor of the earthly image, and bearing, in the perceptions of the flesh and earthly acts, more from the first Adam than from the second—how shall I dare portray myself to you, when I am proved to be a defacer of the heavenly image through earthly corruption? Shame hems me in on both sides. I blush to portray what I am; I dare not portray what I am not. I hate what I am, and I am not what I love. But what will it profit me in my misery to hate iniquity and love virtue, when I do instead what I hate, and, being slothful, do not labor to do instead what I love? I am divided against myself and torn apart by inward warfare, while spirit fights against flesh, flesh against spirit, and the law of the body, by the law of sin, attacks the law of the mind. Unhappy man that I am, who have not digested within myself the poisonous taste of the hostile tree even by the wood of the cross! For that paternal poison from Adam [Note: [Col. 0831] In Paulinus it reads, “from Adam.”] endures in me, by which the father, having transgressed, infected the whole of his race” (Paulinus, Letter 8, to Severus); and you continue [Note: [Col. 0831] Three manuscripts read, “you weave together.”] many further expressions of groaning over this misery, awaiting the redemption of your body and knowing that you are saved not yet in reality but in hope (Rom. 8:23–24).

41. But perhaps, when you said these things, you transformed another person into yourself, and yourself suffer none of the unwelcome and hateful troubles arising from the flesh’s desire against the spirit, though you do not consent to it. Nevertheless, both you and whoever suffers these things and awaits the grace of Christ by which he may be delivered from this body of death, were not yet manifestly in themselves, but were there secretly in that man when the forbidden food was touched and the destruction, soon to spread far and wide through all, was conceived [Col. 0832]. And concerning prayer and the groanings by which one begs for the help needed to make progress and live rightly, what letter of yours does not glow [Note: [Col. 0832] The editions read, “Whom would not your letter strike?” But the manuscripts better read, “what letter of yours does not glow,” that is, which of your letters, etc.]? What part of your discourse, however slight, is there in which is not scattered, with mournful piety, that which we say in prayer: “Lead us not into temptation” (Matt. 6:13)? Let us therefore comfort one another in all these matters, exhort one another, and help one another as far as the Lord grants. But Your Holiness will hear from our common friend matters which we greatly grieve over and are reluctant readily to believe; through God’s mercy, when he returns safely, we hope to be able to become fully certain concerning all of them.

## CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING LETTER  
*(RETRACTIONS, BOOK II, CHAPTER XLIX.)*

I wrote a book *On the Presence of God*, in which our attention is especially alert against the Pelagian heresy, though it is not expressly named. In it there is also a careful and subtle discussion of the presence of that nature which we call the true and supreme God, and of his temple. This book begins: “I confess, most beloved brother Dardanus.”

## BOOK ON THE PRESENCE OF GOD, OR LETTER CLXXXVII

[Note: [Col. 0832] Corrected from manuscripts a, bg, bl, c, cc, ff, g, gv, j, n, s, vc, vd, two bn, two sb, two t, five v; and from Am., Bad., Er., Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0832] Formerly 57; the letter which was 187 is now Appendix 6. Written about the middle of 417.]

He answers two questions of Dardanus. The first asks concerning Christ: how he is now believed to be in heaven, when, hanging on the cross and about to die, he said to the believing thief that he would be with him that day in paradise; whether perhaps this is because Christ exists everywhere, or because paradise is situated in heaven. The second asks concerning infants: whether they do not know God even while in the womb, since John leaped in the womb at the presence of the Lord’s mother.

## CHAPTER I

1. I confess, most beloved brother Dardanus [Note: [Col. 0832] It is understood almost from the gifts of mind which he recognizes in this man as joined with high rank that he is the very Dardanus distinguished by the prefecture of Gaul, to whom Jerome also wrote, about A.D. 414, in reply to a question concerning the promised land: “You ask, Dardanus, noblest of Christians and most Christian of nobles,” etc. And ending the letter he says: “To you, most eloquent man, now more honorable in Christ after the honor of a double prefecture, I dictated these words in a hurried and brief night’s work.”], that I replied to your letter later than I ought. I would not have you inquire into the reasons, lest you bear it more impatiently while I make a longer excuse than you endured while I delayed in answering; for I would rather have you readily forgive my offense than judge my defense. Whatever those reasons were, believe that there could have been no contempt of you in me. Indeed, I would have replied most swiftly had I despised you. Nor, merely because I have at last replied, have I at last produced something worthy of you as reader [Col. 0833], something which I could deservedly mark with your name; but I have preferred somehow to reply now rather than allow this summer [Note: [Col. 0833] The editions read “life”; sixteen manuscripts read “summer.”] also to pass while I remain debtor for this duty. Nor did your rank frighten me and make me hesitate, since your humanity is more welcome than that rank is intimidating. But the very reason why I love you more makes it harder for me to discover how I may satisfy so great an eagerness in your religious affection.

2. In addition to the flame of our mutual charity—by which we love even persons whom we have never seen, when we believe them to possess what we love, and in this respect you have certainly anticipated me and made me fear lest your opinion and expectation of me be deceived—you proposed in your letter questions of such a kind that, if proposed by anyone at all, they would make no small task even for my leisure, which I lack [Note: [Col. 0833] Thus all the manuscripts; Er. and Lov. read, “which I lack, would make no small task.”]. But when they are proposed by you, for whom, in searching deeply, the surface of their solution is by no means enough, and when they are proposed to one very busy, beset and bound by the burdens of other cares, it belongs to your prudence and kindness to consider how patient you ought to be with me, whether because I have answered late or because even now I may not answer in proportion to the greatness of your inquiry.

## CHAPTER II

3. You ask, then, how Christ Jesus, the man who is Mediator between God and men, is now believed to be in heaven, when, hanging on the wood and already about to die, he said to the believing thief: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). From this you perhaps say that paradise should be understood as situated in some part of heaven; or that, because God is everywhere, that man also, who is in God, is spread everywhere—wishing thereby, of course, to infer that he who is everywhere could also have been in paradise.

4. Here I ask—or rather recognize—how you understand Christ as man. Certainly not as certain heretics understand him: the Word of God and flesh, that is, without a human soul, so that the Word was to the flesh in place of a soul; or the Word of God and soul and flesh, but without a human mind, so that the Word of God was to the soul in place of a human mind [Note: [Col. 0833] The Arians, from the book *On Heresies*, chapter 49; and the Apollinarians, ibid., chapter 55.]. You certainly do not understand Christ as man in that way, but as you said above, when you declared that you receive Christ as almighty God on this ground of faith: you would not believe him to be God unless you also believed him to be a perfect man. Certainly, when you say “perfect man,” you mean the whole human nature there; but a man is not perfect if either a soul is lacking to the flesh or a human mind to the soul itself.

5. Therefore, if we suppose that “Today you shall be with me in paradise” was said according to the man whom God the Word assumed, paradise is not on the basis of these words to be thought in heaven. For Christ Jesus as man was not to be in heaven that day, but in hell according to his soul and in the tomb according to his flesh. The Gospel makes it perfectly clear that his flesh was laid in the tomb that day; and apostolic teaching proclaims that that soul descended into hell, since blessed Peter applies to this matter testimony from the Psalms, where he shows it was foretold: “For you will not abandon my soul in hell, nor give your Holy One to see corruption” (Acts 2:27; Ps. 15:10). The former was said of the soul, because it was not abandoned there, whence it returned so quickly; the latter of the body, because in the tomb it could not decay on account of the swift resurrection. But no one understands paradise to be in the tomb. And if anyone were so absurd as to try to think this, because that tomb was in a garden, he would surely be recalled from this opinion by the fact that the person to whom it was said, “Today you shall be with me in paradise,” was not with Christ in that tomb on that day. Nor would burial of the flesh, which feels neither joy nor pain in death, be offered as a great reward for his faith, when he was thinking of a rest in which there is sensation.

6. It remains, then, that if “Today you shall be with me in paradise” was said according to the man, paradise must be understood to be in hell, where Christ was to be that day according to his human soul. But whether that bosom of Abraham, where the impious rich man, while in the torments of hell, saw the poor man at rest, should be reckoned under the name of paradise or thought to belong to the lower regions, I would not readily say. For we read that it was said of the rich man: “And the rich man also died and was buried in hell”; and, “when he was in torments among the lower regions.” But neither hell nor the lower regions are named in connection with the poor man’s death or rest; rather, it says: “And it came to pass that that poor man died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom.” Then Abraham says to the burning rich man: “Between us and you a great chasm has been fixed” (Luke 16:22–26), as though between hell and the abodes of the blessed. For it is not easy to find anywhere in the Scriptures the name of hell used in a good sense. Hence the customary question: if hell is rightly understood only as a place of punishment, how can we piously believe that the soul of the Lord Christ was in hell? The answer is good: he descended in order to help those whom it was proper to help. Thus blessed Peter says that he loosed the pains of hell, in which it was impossible for him to be held (Acts 2:24). Further, if both regions, that of those in pain and that of those at rest—that is, both where that rich man was tormented and where that poor man rejoiced—are to be believed to be in hell, who would dare say that the Lord Jesus came only to the penal regions of hell and was not among those who rest in Abraham’s bosom? If he was there, that is to be understood as the paradise which he deigned to promise that day to the thief’s soul. If these things are so, “paradise” is a general name for a place where one lives happily. For the fact that paradise was the name of the place where Adam was before sin does not prohibit Scripture from also calling the Church a paradise bearing the fruit of trees.

## CHAPTER III

7. But there is a much simpler sense, free from all these ambiguities, if Christ is understood to have said, “Today you shall be with me in paradise,” not according to that by which he was man, but according to that by which he was God. For Christ as man was to be that day in the tomb according to the flesh and in hell according to the soul; but the same Christ as God is always everywhere. For he is the light which shines even in darkness, though the darkness does not comprehend it (John 1:5) [Col. 0835]. He is the Power and Wisdom of God, of whom it is written that he reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly (Wis. 8:1); and that, because of his purity, he reaches everywhere and nothing defiled comes upon him (Wis. 7:24). Therefore, wherever paradise may be, whoever of the blessed is there is there with him who is everywhere.

8. For since Christ is God and man—God, according to which he says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); man, according to which he says, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28)—and since he is at once the only-begotten Son of God from the Father and the son of man from David’s seed according to the flesh, both must be observed in him when he speaks, or when Scripture speaks concerning him, and one must see according to which nature each statement is made. For just as one human being is rational soul and flesh, so one Christ is Word and man. Accordingly, as regards the Word, Christ is Creator: “For all things were made through him” (John 1:3); but as regards the man, Christ was created [Note: [Col. 0835] The editions read “Christ is a creature”; seventeen manuscripts read “Christ was created.”]: “For he was made from David’s seed according to the flesh” (Rom. 1:3), and “made in the likeness of men” (Phil. 2:7). Again, since there are two things in a human being, soul and flesh, according to the soul he was sorrowful unto death (Matt. 26:38), and according to the flesh he suffered death (Acts 3:18).

9. Yet when we call Christ Son of God, we do not separate the man; nor, when we call that same Christ son of man, do we separate God. According to the man, he was on earth, not in heaven where he now is, when he said: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13); although, according to that by which he was Son of God, he was in heaven, while according to that by which he was son of man, he was still on earth and had not yet ascended into heaven. Likewise, although according to that by which he is Son of God he is the Lord of glory, and according to that by which he is son of man he was crucified, the Apostle nevertheless says: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8). Thus the son of man was in heaven according to God, and the Son of God was crucified on earth according to man. Therefore, just as the Lord of glory could rightly be called crucified, although that suffering belonged to the flesh alone, so it could rightly be said, “Today you shall be with me in paradise,” although according to human lowliness he was to be that day in the tomb through the flesh and in hell through the soul, while according to divine immutability he had never departed from paradise, because he is always everywhere.

10. Therefore do not doubt that the man Christ Jesus is now where he is to come from; remember and faithfully hold the Christian confession: he rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father, and will come from no other place than there to judge the living and the dead. And, as the angelic voice testified, he will come in the same way as he was seen going into heaven (Acts 1:10–11), that is, in the same form and substance of flesh. To this flesh he certainly gave immortality; he did not take away its nature. According to this form he must not be thought spread everywhere. For we must beware of so affirming the divinity of the man [Col. 0836] that we take away the reality of the body. It does not follow that what is in God is everywhere as God is. For the most truthful Scripture says even of us that “in him we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28); yet we are not everywhere as he is everywhere. But that man is in God in one way, since that God is in man in another, by a certain proper and singular mode. For God and man are one person, and both are the one Christ Jesus: everywhere according to that by which he is God, but in heaven according to that by which he is man.

## CHAPTER IV

11. Even in saying that God is spread everywhere, however, we must resist a carnal thought and draw the mind away from bodily senses, lest we suppose God to be spread through all things by spatial magnitude, as earth, moisture, air, or this light is spread (for every magnitude of this kind is less in its part than in its whole). Rather, we should understand him as great wisdom is, even in a human being whose body is small. If there are two wise persons, one of whom is larger in body, while neither is wiser, wisdom is not greater in the larger and smaller in the smaller, nor smaller in one than in two. It is as great in this person as in that, and as great in each one as in both; for if they are equally wise in every respect, the two are not wiser than either singly, just as, if they are equally immortal, the two do not live more than either singly.

12. Finally, the very immortality of the body, which has preceded us in Christ’s flesh and is promised to us at the end, though it is a great thing, is certainly not great in bulk. Though possessed bodily, it is a certain incorporeal excellence. For although the immortal body itself is less in a part than in the whole, its immortality is as complete in a part as in the whole; and although some limbs are larger than others, they are not more immortal than others. So now, when we are healthy in every part according to the measure of present bodily health, we do not say that, because the whole hand is larger than a finger, the health of the whole hand is greater than that of the finger. Rather, health itself is equal in those unequal members, when smaller are compared with larger so that what cannot be as large as another may nevertheless be as healthy. Health would be greater in the larger members if the larger were healthier; but since this is not so, and larger and smaller are equally healthy, the quantity in the bulk of the limbs is indeed unequal, but health is equal amid the inequalities.

13. Therefore, since body is a substance, its quantity lies in the magnitude of its bulk; but its health is not its quantity, but its quality. Thus bodily quantity could not achieve what quality could achieve. In parts separated from one another, which cannot all be together because each occupies its own spatial extent—the smaller occupying smaller, the larger larger—quantity cannot be whole or as great in each several part. Rather, it is greater in greater parts, smaller in smaller, and in no part as great as throughout the whole. But the quality of body called health, when the whole body is healthy, is as great in greater as in smaller parts [Col. 0837]. The less large parts are not therefore less healthy, nor the larger more healthy. Far be it, then, that what the quality of a created body can do should not be possible in the very substance of the Creator.

14. God, then, is spread throughout all things. For he himself says through the prophet: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23:24); and, as I set forth a little before concerning his wisdom, “It reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1). Again it is written: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world” (Wis. 1:7); and in a psalm he is addressed: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” [Note: [Col. 0837] After “you are present,” the printed editions add: “Because God is substantially spread everywhere.” These words are absent from nineteen manuscripts and seem to have been transferred here from the margin.] (Ps. 138:7). But God is so spread throughout all things that he is not a quality of the world, but the substance that creates the world, governing it without toil and sustaining it without burden. Yet he is not spread through spaces of place, as though diffused in bulk, so that he should be half in one half of the world’s body and half in the other, and thus whole throughout the whole. Rather, he is whole in heaven alone, whole in earth alone, whole in heaven and earth, contained by no place, but everywhere whole in himself.

15. So is the Father, so the Son, so the Holy Spirit, so the Trinity, one God. For they have not divided the world among themselves into three portions, each filling a separate portion, as though the Son or the Holy Spirit would have nowhere to be in the world if the Father occupied it all. The true, incorporeal, immutable divinity is not so constituted. They are not bodies, whose magnitude is greater in three than in each singly; nor do they occupy places by their bulk so that they cannot be together in spaces that are apart. For if the soul placed in a body finds not only no confinement but even a kind of breadth—not of bodily places, but of spiritual joys—when what the Apostle says comes to pass, “Do you not know that your bodies are the temple in you of the Holy Spirit, whom you have from God?” (1 Cor. 6:19), it can only be said most foolishly that the Holy Spirit has no place in our body because our soul has filled it all. How much more foolishly is it said that the Trinity is hindered by any constraints so that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit cannot all be everywhere together!

## CHAPTER V

16. But this is much more wonderful: though God is everywhere whole, he does not nevertheless dwell in all. For not to all can what the Apostle says be said—what I have already quoted—or also this: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 3:16). Hence he says conversely of some: “But whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ is not his” (Rom. 8:9). Who, moreover, unless wholly ignorant of the inseparability of the Trinity, would dare suppose that the Father or the Son can dwell in someone in whom the Holy Spirit does not dwell, or that the Holy Spirit can dwell in someone in whom the Father and the Son do not also dwell? We must therefore confess that God is everywhere through the presence of divinity [Col. 0838], but not everywhere through the grace of indwelling. Because of this indwelling, where the grace of his love is undoubtedly recognized, we do not say, “Our Father who are everywhere,” though that too is true, but, “Our Father who are in heaven” (Matt. 6:9), so that in prayer we may rather recall his temple, which we ourselves ought to be and, insofar as we are, thereby belong to his fellowship and household of adoption. For if God’s people, not yet made equal to his angels and still in this pilgrimage, are called his temple, how much more is his temple in heaven, where the people of angels are, to whom we are to be joined and made equal when, our pilgrimage ended, we receive what has been promised!

17. Therefore, although he who is everywhere does not dwell in all, neither does he dwell equally in those in whom he dwells. For why did Elisha ask that the Spirit of God which was in Elijah might be in him twofold (2 Kings 2:9)? And why are some saints holier than others, except because they possess God their indweller more abundantly? How, then, was what we said above true, that God is everywhere whole, when he is more in some and less in others? But we must attend carefully to what we said: that he is everywhere whole in himself. Therefore he is not in them according as some contain more of him and others less [Note: [Col. 0838] With substantial manuscript agreement: “Some things contain more of him, others less.”]. For this reason he is said to be everywhere, because he is absent from no part of things; and for this reason whole, because he does not present one part of himself to one part of things and another part to another, equal to equal, a smaller part to the smaller and a greater to the greater. Rather, he is present whole alike not only to the whole creation but to each part of it. Those are said to be far from him who by sinning have become most unlike him; those to draw near to him who by pious living receive his likeness. Thus eyes are rightly said to be farther from this light in proportion as they are blinder. For what is so far from light as blindness, even if the light is at hand and floods extinguished eyes? But eyes that make progress by receiving sight through the advance of health are deservedly said to draw near to the light [Note: [Col. 0838] Thus fifteen manuscripts. The editions read, “by receiving sight, they receive light.”].

## CHAPTER VI

18. Moreover, I see that what we thought could be understood insufficiently distinctly when we said that God is everywhere whole, unless we added “in himself,” must be explained more carefully. For how is he everywhere if in himself? Everywhere, certainly, because he is absent nowhere. But in himself, because he is not contained by those to whom he is present, as though he could not exist without them. Take spatial extension away from bodies and they will be nowhere; and because they will be nowhere, they will not exist. Take bodies themselves away from the qualities of bodies and there will be nowhere for them to be, and therefore they must not exist. For when a body is equally healthy or equally white throughout its whole bulk, its health or whiteness is not greater in one part than another, nor greater in the whole than in a part, because the whole is not found to be healthier or whiter than a part. But if it is unequally healthy [Col. 0839] or unequally white, health or whiteness may be greater in a smaller part, when smaller limbs are healthier or whiter than larger ones. Thus what is called great or small in qualities does not at all depend on bulk. Nevertheless, if the bodily bulk itself, however great or small, is entirely removed, its qualities will have nowhere to be, although they are not to be measured by bulk. But God is not himself smaller because he is less comprehended by one to whom he is present. For he is whole in himself, and he is not in those in whom he is as though he needed them, as though he could not exist except in them. And just as he is not absent from one in whom he does not dwell, but is wholly present although that person does not have him, so he is wholly present to one in whom he dwells, though that person does not comprehend him wholly.

19. For he does not divide himself in order to dwell in human hearts or bodies, allotting one part of himself to this person and another to that, as this light does through the openings and windows of houses. Rather, if any sound—which is a bodily and transient thing—is not apprehended by a deaf person, is not wholly apprehended by one hard of hearing, and among those who hear and approach it together one apprehends it more than another in proportion as his hearing is sharper, and less in proportion as it is duller, while the sound itself does not resound more or less variably but is equally at hand to all in the place where they are: how much more excellently can God, who is by nature incorporeal and immutably living, neither be extended and divided like a sound through intervals of time nor need airy space as though it were his place, in which he may be at hand to those present, but, abiding in himself with eternal stability, be wholly present to all things and wholly to each, although those in whom he dwells possess him according to the diversity of their capacity, some more, some less—those whom he by the grace of his goodness builds up as his most beloved temple!

20. Divisions of gifts are indeed spoken of, as though they were parts and members of one body, in which all together are one temple and each one a separate temple; for God is not greater in all than in each. And it often happens that many comprehend him less and one more. But after the Apostle had said, “There are divisions of gifts,” he immediately added, “But the same Spirit.” Likewise, after he had enumerated those divisions of gifts, he said: “But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each his own as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:4, 11). He distributes, then, without himself being divided, because he is one and the same. But these are called divisions, like the divisions of members in a body, because ears do not have the same power as eyes, and thus the remaining members are harmoniously apportioned among diverse functions. Yet, when we are healthy, they rejoice in one health, neither diverse nor greater in one place and less in another, but common and equal, although the members themselves are unequal. Christ is the head of this body; the unity of this body is commended by our sacrifice. The Apostle briefly signified this when he said: “We who are many are one bread, one body” (1 Cor. 10:17). Through our head we are reconciled to God, because in him the divinity of the Only-begotten became a participant in our mortality, so that we also might become participants in his immortality [Col. 0840].

21. This sacrament is far removed from the hearts of proud wise men, and therefore from the hearts of Christians—and consequently from those of the truly wise. I mean even those wise men who came to know God; for although they knew God, as the Apostle says, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks to him (Rom. 1:21). You know, moreover, in what sacrifice it is said, “Let us give thanks to the Lord our God.” From the humility of that sacrifice their arrogance and tragic grandiloquence are far removed. It is therefore a most astonishing thing how God can dwell in some who do not yet know him, while he does not dwell in some who do know him. For those who, although they knew God, did not glorify him as God or give thanks to him do not belong to the temple of God; whereas the little ones sanctified by the sacrament of Christ and regenerated by the Holy Spirit do belong to the temple of God, although plainly, because of their age, they cannot yet know God. Thus the former could know but not possess the one whom the latter could possess before knowing him. But those are most blessed for whom possessing God is the same as knowing him; for that very knowledge is altogether complete, true, and blessed.

## CHAPTER VII

22. We must now examine also the question that you added after the subscription to your letter: If little children still do not know God, how could John, even before he was born, leap for joy in his mother’s womb at the coming and presence of the mother of the Lord? For after mentioning that you had read my book *On the Baptism of Little Children*, you added and said: “I wish to know what you think about pregnant women, since the mother of John the Baptist answered with the faith of belief on behalf of the child.”

23. These are certainly the words of Elizabeth, John’s mother: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb. And from where does this happen to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me? For behold, as the voice of your greeting came into my ears, the infant leaped for joy in my womb” (Luke 1:42–44). But, as the Evangelist had stated beforehand, she said this after being filled with the Holy Spirit; and, plainly by his revelation, she understood what that leaping of the infant signified: namely, that the mother of the one had come whose forerunner and herald he himself was to be.

This, then, could have been a sign of so great a reality, meant to be recognized by adults rather than recognized by the little child. For when this event was previously narrated in the Gospel, it was not said, “The infant believed in her womb,” but “He leaped”; nor did she herself say, “The infant leaped in faith in my womb,” but “He leaped for joy.” Yet we see that not only little children but also animals leap—not, of course, from any faith, religion, or rational knowledge of any kind. But this leaping was plainly extraordinary and unprecedented, because it occurred in the womb and at the coming of the woman who was to give birth to the Savior of humanity. Therefore it was marvelous and was to be counted among great signs. Thus this leaping, like a greeting returned to the mother of the Lord, occurred divinely in the infant, as miracles usually occur, not humanly by the infant.

24. Yet even if the use of reason and will had been so greatly hastened in that child that, while still within his mother’s womb, he could already recognize, believe, and consent to what age is awaited in other little children before they can do so, this too must be regarded as a miracle of divine power and must not be made into a rule for human nature. For when God willed it, even a mute beast spoke rationally (Num. 22:28); but human beings were not thereby instructed to await the counsel of asses in their deliberations.

Accordingly, I neither disregard what happened in John, nor establish from it a rule concerning what should be thought about little children. Indeed, I declare it marvelous in him precisely because I do not find it in others. Something similar is found in the struggle of the twins in Rebekah’s womb; but this too was so extraordinary that the woman therefore sought a divine oracle and heard that two peoples had been represented by those two infants (Gen. 25:22–23).

25. If we wished to demonstrate in words that little children who do not yet know even human things are ignorant of divine things, I fear that, by arguing the point, we might seem to do violence to our own senses, when the evidence of truth so easily surpasses every power and function of speech. Do we not see that, even when they begin to produce whatever signs of articulated speech they can and pass from infancy toward the beginning of speaking, they still feel and say things such that, if they remained at that stage and continued to be like that as the years advanced, no one—not even a complete fool—would doubt that they were foolish?

Unless, perhaps, we are to believe that in the crying of infancy, or even in the silence still present in the womb, little children were wise, but that after they began to speak with us they gradually arrived at the ignorance we see in them. You see how absurd this is, since the understanding expressed by children in whatever words they burst forth—an understanding that is certainly almost nonexistent in comparison with what adults know—can nevertheless be called understanding when compared with the state in which they are born.

And why, in that very great provision for their salvation, when Christian grace comes to their aid, are the cries and movements by which they resist not counted against them, and all their resistance regarded as nothing until the sacraments are performed in them, by which what they have drawn from original condemnation is cleansed? Is it not because they are so ignorant of what they are doing that they are not even judged to be doing it? Moreover, if they already possessed the exercise of reason and the choice of will by which consent ought to be given to that sanctification, what an evil it would be to resist so great a grace, and how resisting it would not merely fail to benefit them but would increase their guilt—what Christian does not know?

## CHAPTER VIII

26. We therefore say that the Holy Spirit dwells in baptized little children, although they do not know it. They are ignorant of him, although he is in them, just as they are ignorant of their own mind. In them there is the faculty of reason, which they cannot yet use, like a certain dormant spark awaiting awakening as age advances.

Nor should this seem astonishing in little children, since the Apostle says even to some older people, “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 3:16). Of such people he had said shortly before, “The natural person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God.” He also calls them little children—not in bodily age but in mind (1 Cor. 2:14; 3:1–2). They therefore did not perceive by knowledge the Holy Spirit who dwelt in them; and although the Holy Spirit dwelt in them, they were still natural, not yet spiritual, because they were not yet able, through knowledge, to perceive their indwelling Spirit.

27. He is said to dwell in such people for this reason: he works secretly in them so that they may be his temple, and he brings this work to completion in those who advance and persevere in advancement. “For by hope we were saved,” as the Apostle says; while elsewhere he says, “He saved us through the washing of regeneration” (Titus 3:5). When he says here, “He saved us,” as though salvation had already been given, he explains how this is to be understood where he says, “For by hope we were saved.” But hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience (Rom. 8:24–25).

Many things are spoken of in Scripture as though they had already happened, although they are understood to remain in hope. Thus the Lord also said to his disciples, “Everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:15). Yet this was said according to the hope of future things to such an extent that he later said to them, “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16:12).

He therefore works in those mortals in whom he still dwells, building his dwelling itself—a dwelling that he completes not in this life but in another life after this one, when “death will be swallowed up in victory” and it will be said to death: “Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O death?” For what is the sting of death except sin? (1 Cor. 15:54–56).

28. Therefore, although we have now been reborn of water and the Spirit, and all sins have been erased in the cleansing of that washing—whether sins of origin, from Adam in whom all sinned, or sins of our deeds, words, and thoughts—nevertheless, because we remain in this human life, which is a time of testing upon the earth, we rightly say, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12).

The whole Church says this prayer. The Savior cleanses the Church by the washing of water with the word, so that he may present it to himself glorious, “without spot or wrinkle” (Eph. 5:26–27), or anything of that kind—certainly when it will be perfected in reality, whereas now it advances by walking in hope.

For how can it now be without spot or wrinkle, or anything of that kind, when either all the human beings who belong to it and already exercise the reason of mind and the choice of will while carrying the burden of mortal flesh, or at least—as even the contentious must admit—in many of its members it truthfully says, “Forgive us our debts”?

29. Since, then, he increasingly justifies those who advance, in whom he dwells as mortals being renewed from day to day; since he hears those who pray and cleanses those who confess, so that he may present to himself a temple undefiled forever, he is rightly said not to dwell in those who, although they know God, have not glorified him as God or given thanks.

By worshiping and serving the creature rather than the Creator (Rom. 1:21, 25), they did not wish to be the temple of the one true God. Thus, while they wanted to possess him together with many others, they more easily brought it about that they did not possess him than that they should mingle him with many false gods.

And he is rightly said to dwell in those whom, called according to his purpose, he has received in order to justify and glorify them, even before they are able to know his incorporeal nature, which is wholly present everywhere, to the extent that it can be known by a human being in this life—partially, through a mirror and in a riddle—when he has made very great progress (1 Cor. 13:12).

Among those in whom he dwells are many like those to whom the Apostle says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal people, as little children in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food, for you were not yet able; indeed, even now you are not able” (1 Cor. 3:1–2). To such people he also says: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 6:19).

If the final day of this life should find such people before they reach the spiritual age of mind, where they are nourished not by milk but by solid food, their indwelling inhabitant will complete in them whatever understanding they lacked here, because they have not withdrawn from the unity of the body of Christ, who became our way, or from fellowship with the temple of God.

To keep them from withdrawing, they hold steadfastly in the Church to the common rule of faith shared by the little and the great. They walk in what they have attained until God reveals to them if they think anything otherwise. They do not turn their carnal thoughts into dogmas, because they do not harden themselves by persisting in contentious defenses. [Note: Lovaniensis reads “are not hardened”; Badius, Ambrosianus, Erasmus, and most manuscripts read “harden themselves.”] Rather, they labor, as it were, by walking—that is, by advancing—and obtain clarity of understanding through the devotion of faith.

## CHAPTER IX

30. Since these things are so, the two events that occur in one human being—birth and rebirth—belong to two human beings: one to the first Adam, the other to the second, who is called Christ.

“But the spiritual was not first,” says the Apostle, “but the natural; afterward the spiritual. The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly, so are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, so are the heavenly. Just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the one who is from heaven.” He likewise says, “Through one man came death, and through one man the resurrection of the dead. For just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ” (1 Cor. 15:46–49, 21–22).

He said “all” and “all” for this reason: no one comes into death except through the one, and no one comes into life except through the other. In the first it became clear what human choice could accomplish with respect to death; in the second, what God’s help could accomplish with respect to life.

Finally, the first man was merely man; the second, God and man. Sin came about through abandoning God; righteousness does not come about without God. Consequently, we would neither die unless we came from his members through carnal descent, nor live unless we were members of this one through spiritual connection.

Therefore we needed to be born and reborn, while he needed only to be born for our sake. We pass from sin to righteousness by being reborn; he passed from no sin to righteousness. But by being baptized he commended, through his humility, the sacrament of our regeneration in a higher way, signifying our old self by his passion and our new self by his resurrection.

31. The disobedience of desire dwelling in mortal flesh, by which even the members of the body are moved apart from the will’s choice, is brought under the order of conjugal righteousness so that children are born from parents lawfully joined together—children who must themselves be regenerated.

Christ, however, did not wish to take his flesh through such a union of male and female. Rather, from a virgin, who in conceiving him was untouched by any such desire, he took the likeness of sinful flesh for us, so that sinful flesh might be cleansed in us (Rom. 8:3–4).

“For just as,” says the Apostle, “through one trespass condemnation came upon all human beings, so through one act of justification justification of life came upon all human beings” (Rom. 5:18). No one is born except through the operation of carnal desire, which was drawn from the first man, Adam; and no one is reborn except through the operation of spiritual grace, which was given through the second man, Christ.

Therefore, if by being born we belong to the one, and by being reborn to the other—and no one can be reborn before being born—then he alone was born in a singular manner, for whom rebirth was unnecessary. He did not pass from sin, in which he never was, nor was he conceived in iniquity, nor did his mother nourish him in the womb amid sins. For the Holy Spirit came upon her, and the power of the Most High overshadowed her; therefore the holy one who was born from her is called the Son of God.
