The good of marriage does not extinguish the evil of disobedient members, but moderates it, so that carnal desire, limited in a certain way, may at least become conjugal chastity. But the virgin Mary, to whom it was said, “The power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35), in conceiving a holy offspring, did not burn with any heat of this desire under such a shadow.

Except, then, for this cornerstone, I do not see how human beings are built into the house of God so that God may dwell in them, unless they have been reborn; and they cannot be reborn before they have been born.

## CHAPTER X

32. Whatever opinion we may still hold concerning pregnant women—or rather, concerning human beings still enclosed within their mothers’ wombs—whether we think that they can or cannot be granted some form of sanctification, either because of John, who, before being brought forth into this light, nevertheless leaped for joy (which surely no one would believe could have happened except through the operation of the Holy Spirit), or because of Jeremiah, to whom the Lord says, “Before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you” (Jer. 1:5), nevertheless that sanctification by which each of us becomes a temple of God, and all of us together become one temple of God, belongs only to those who have been reborn; and human beings cannot be reborn unless they have been born.

No one will bring the life in which he was born to a good end unless he has been reborn before bringing it to an end.

33. But if someone says that a human being is already born while still in his mother’s womb, and brings as evidence from the Gospel the statement made to Joseph concerning the pregnant Virgin, the mother of the Lord, “For that which has been born in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1:20), does a second birth follow this birth? Otherwise it will no longer be a second birth but a third.

But when the Lord spoke of this, he said, “Unless someone is born again” (John 3:3), counting as the first birth that which occurs when the mother gives birth, not when she conceives and is pregnant; that is, the birth that occurs from her, not the one that occurs in her.

For we do not say that a person has been reborn when his mother gives birth to him, as though he had been born a second time after already having been born once in the womb. Rather, without counting the conception that makes a woman pregnant, a person is called born at delivery, so that he may be reborn of water and the Spirit.

It is according to this birth from his mother that the Lord himself is also said to have been born in Bethlehem of Judea (Matt. 2:1). If, therefore, a human being can be regenerated by the grace of the Spirit in the womb, since birth still remains for him, he is reborn before being born—which cannot happen in any way.

Accordingly, human beings who have been born are transferred into the framework of Christ’s body, as into the living structure of the temple of God, which is his Church—not on account of works of righteousness that they have performed, but by being reborn through grace, as though from a mass of ruin into the foundation of a building.

Apart from this building, which is being constructed for blessedness as the eternal dwelling of God, the whole life of a human being is miserable and should rather be called death than life.

Therefore, whoever is to be inhabited by God will not be alien to this body, this temple, this city, lest the wrath of God remain upon him.  
[Note: Four Vatican manuscripts and several Gallican manuscripts read “from this life” instead of “from this city”; this is not unsuitable if one refers it back to the preceding words, “as into the living structure.”]

Every person who has not been reborn, however, is alien.

## CHAPTER XI

34. The Mediator, once manifested, wished the sacrament of our regeneration to be made manifest. For the ancient righteous possessed something hidden, although they too were saved by the same faith that was to be revealed in its own time.

We do not dare to place the believers of our time above the friends of God through whom these things were prophesied to us, since God commends himself as the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, declaring that this is his name forever (Exod. 3:15).

But if circumcision is believed to have been baptism for the ancient saints, what answer will be given concerning those who pleased God before this commandment existed, although not without faith? For, as it is written to the Hebrews, “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6).

“Having,” says the Apostle, “the same Spirit of faith, according to what is written, ‘I believed, and therefore I spoke’; we too believe, and therefore we speak” (2 Cor. 4:13). He would not have said “the same” unless the very same Spirit of faith also belonged to them.

Just as they, when the same sacrament was hidden, believed that Christ’s incarnation would occur, so we believe that it has occurred. Both they and we await his coming for judgment. For there is no other mystery of God than Christ, in whom the dead who died in Adam must be made alive; for just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ (1 Cor. 15:22), as we explained above.

## CHAPTER XII

35. Therefore God, who is present everywhere and wholly present everywhere, does not dwell in everyone, but only in those whom he makes his most blessed temple—or his most blessed temples—rescuing them from the power of darkness and transferring them into the kingdom of the Son of his love (Col. 1:13), which begins with regeneration.

His temple is called such in a figurative sense when it is made by human hands from inanimate materials, as with the tabernacle, made of wood, curtains, skins, and other movable things of that kind, and with the temple constructed by King Solomon from stones, wood, and metals. It is called his temple in another sense in the true reality prefigured by those symbols.

Hence it is said, “You yourselves, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house” (1 Pet. 2:5). And hence it is also written, “For we are the temples of the living God,” as God says: “I will dwell in them and walk among them; I will be their God, and they will be my people” (2 Cor. 6:16).

36. Nor should it trouble us that through certain people who do not belong—or do not yet belong—to this temple, that is, in whom God does not dwell or does not yet dwell, he nevertheless performs some work of power. Thus he ordered that the man who cast out demons in Christ’s name, although he did not follow Christ, be permitted to do so, because the commendation of his name was beneficial to many (Mark 9:37–39).

He also says that many will say to him on the last day, “In your name we performed many mighty works.” He would certainly not answer them, “I do not know you” (Matt. 7:22–23), if they belonged to the temple of God, which he blesses by dwelling in it.

The centurion Cornelius, too, before being incorporated by regeneration into this temple, saw an angel sent to him and heard the angel say that his prayers had been heard and his alms accepted (Acts 10:4). God performs such works as one who is present everywhere, or through his holy angels.

37. As for Jeremiah’s sanctification before he came forth from the womb, although some understand it as a type of the Savior, who had no need of regeneration, nevertheless, even if it is understood of the prophet himself, it can appropriately be interpreted according to predestination.

The Gospel calls people sons of God even before they have been regenerated. When Caiaphas said of the Lord, “It is better for you that one man should die for the people, rather than that the whole nation should perish,” the Gospel immediately added: “He did not say this on his own, but, being high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus was going to die for the nation—and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad” (John 11:50–52).

He called “children of God” those established not only among the Hebrew people but also among all the other nations—people who were not yet believers and had not yet been baptized. How, then, could they be called children of God except according to predestination, according to which the Apostle also says that God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world (Eph. 1:4)?

That gathering into one was to make them children of God. The phrase “into one” does not mean one physical place, since the prophet, speaking of such a calling of the nations, had foretold, “All the islands of the nations will worship him, each from his own place” (Zeph. 2:11). Rather, “he would gather them into one” means into one spirit and into one body, whose one head is Christ.

Such a gathering is the building of the temple of God. Such a gathering is brought about not by carnal generation but by spiritual regeneration.

## CHAPTER XIII

38. God therefore dwells in each person as in his temples, and in all those gathered together into one as in his temple. As long as this temple is tossed about in this world like Noah’s ark, what is written in the Psalm comes to pass: “The Lord dwells over the flood.” This may also appropriately be understood because of the many peoples of the faithful among all nations, whom the Apocalypse signifies under the name of waters (Rev. 17:15): “The Lord dwells over the flood.”

The Psalm continues, “And the Lord will sit as king forever” (Ps. 28:10)—plainly in his temple, once it has been established in eternal life after the tossing of this world.

God, then, is present everywhere, wholly present everywhere; yet he does not dwell everywhere, but in his temple, toward which he is gracious and propitious through grace. When he dwells in people, he is received more fully by some and less fully by others.

39. Concerning our head the Apostle says: “In him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily.” He does not say “bodily” because God is corporeal. Rather, he either used a transferred expression, as though God had dwelt in a temple made by hands not bodily but figuratively—that is, through signs prefiguring what was to come. For he calls all those observances “shadows of future things” (Col. 2:9, 16–17), using the word metaphorically. The Most High God, as it is written, does not dwell in temples made by hands (Acts 17:24).

Or “bodily” was said because God dwells in the body of Christ, which he assumed from the Virgin, as in a temple. This is why, when the Jews asked for a sign and he had said, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up,” the Evangelist, explaining what he meant, added: “He was speaking about the temple of his body” (John 2:19, 21).

40. What, then, is the distinction? Do we think that the difference between the head and the other members is that, although divinity dwells in any particular member, however distinguished—such as a great prophet or apostle—the whole fullness of divinity does not dwell in it as in the head, which is Christ?

In our own body, too, sensation is present in each member, but not as fully as in the head, where all five senses are present: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. In the other members there is only touch.

Or, in addition to the fact that the whole fullness of divinity dwells in that body as in a temple, is there something else that distinguishes that head from the excellence of any member? Certainly there is: through a singular assumption of that man, one person was made with the Word.

Of no saint could it be said, or can it be said, or will it be possible to say, “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14). No saint, however eminent in grace, received the name of the Only-Begotten, so that, together with the assumed man, he might be called what the Word of God itself was before the ages.

That assumption, therefore, is singular, and it cannot in any way be shared with any holy human being, however outstanding in wisdom and holiness. Here there is a sufficiently clear and unmistakable proof of divine grace.

For who could be so sacrilegious as to dare to assert that, through the merit of free choice, some soul could be made another Christ? How, then, could one soul, through free choice—a gift given commonly and naturally to all—have merited being joined to the person of the Only-Begotten Word, unless this had been granted by a singular grace? It is right to proclaim that grace; it is wrong to wish to judge it.

41. If, according to our abilities and insofar as the Lord has helped us, we have treated these matters properly, then when you extend your thought toward God as present everywhere—not spread out through intervals of space as though by some mass or extension, but wholly present everywhere—turn your mind away from all images of bodies, which human thought is accustomed to roll about within itself.

Wisdom is not conceived in that way; neither is justice, nor finally love, of which it is written, “God is love” (1 John 4:8).

When you think of his dwelling, think of the unity and gathering of the saints—especially in heaven, where he is said particularly to dwell because there his will is perfectly accomplished through the obedience of those in whom he dwells. Then think of him on earth, where he dwells as he builds his house, which is to be dedicated at the end of the age.

Do not doubt that Christ our Lord, the Only-Begotten Son of God, equal to the Father, and likewise the Son of man, in which respect the Father is greater, is wholly present everywhere as God; that he is in that same temple of God as God dwelling within it; and that he is in some place in heaven according to the mode of his true body.

But since I enjoy speaking with you, I do not know whether I have kept within the proper measure of a sufficient discourse, as though I were compensating for a long silence by talking at length. Yet because, through the devotion and affection with which you anticipated me, you have become so deeply rooted in my heart that I speak with you as with a true friend, give thanks to God for whatever you recognize as having been usefully accomplished in the work of my pen. If you perceive any faults of mine, forgive them as a dearest friend—wishing me healing with the same sincerity of love with which you grant pardon.

# LETTER 188

[Note: Corrected with the aid of manuscripts a, bg, bl, c, cc, ff, j, g, gv, n, r, s, sb, t, vc, four v manuscripts, and the editions of Ambrose, Badius, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis.]

[Note: Elsewhere numbered 143; the letter that was 188 is now in the Appendix as no. 7. Written at the end of 417 or the beginning of 418.]

Augustine and Alypius to Juliana, widow and mother of the virgin Demetrias, lest she or her household absorb the poison administered in the book written to Demetrias; they wish to know who wrote that book.

To the lady Juliana, honored in Christ with the duties owed to her and illustrious by her merits, Alypius and Augustine send greetings in the Lord.

## CHAPTER I

1. It happened most agreeably and pleasantly for us that, while we were together at Hippo, your letter reached us, so that we might return this reply jointly. We rejoice to have learned of your safety, and in return, through our mutual affection, we announce our own, which we trust is dear to you, lady honored in Christ with the duties owed to her and illustrious by her merits.

We know very well how much religious affection we owe you, and how great a concern we have for you both before God and among human beings. Although our insignificance first came to know you through letters and afterward also through bodily presence, as pious and Catholic—that is, true—members of Christ, nevertheless, through our ministry, when you received the word of God that you heard, you received it, as the Apostle says, not as the word of human beings but, as it truly is, the word of God (1 Thess. 2:13).

With the help of the grace and mercy of the Savior, such fruit arose from this ministry of ours in your household that, although a human marriage had already been arranged, the holy Demetrias preferred the spiritual embrace of that bridegroom who is more beautiful than the sons of men, to whom virgins are wedded in order to bear richer fruit in spirit without losing bodily integrity.

We would not have known how our exhortation at that time had been received by the faithful and noble virgin if, after we had departed, she had shortly afterward professed virgin consecration, and we had not learned through the most joyful message and truthful testimony of your letters that this great gift of God—who plants and waters through his servants but gives the growth through himself (1 Cor. 3:6–7)—had come to fruition through us, his laborers.

2. Since these things are so, no one should call us wrongdoers if, in admonishing you to avoid teachings contrary to the grace of God, we are moved by an especially strong obligation to be concerned for you.

Although the Apostle commands us to insist on proclaiming the word not only at a convenient time but also at an inconvenient one (2 Tim. 4:2), we do not count you among those to whom our speech or writing would seem unwelcome, since we urge you to avoid vigilantly what does not belong to sound doctrine.

This is why you received our admonition with such gratitude that, in your letter to which we are now replying, you said: “Indeed, I give abundant thanks for such a pious admonition, since your Reverence urges me not to lend my ears to those people who often corrupt the venerable faith through their perverse treatises.”

3. You then add and say: “But let your priesthood know that I and my little household are entirely separated from such people; and our whole household follows the Catholic faith so faithfully that it has never strayed into any heresy or ever fallen into one—not, I do not say, into those sects whose errors can scarcely be expiated, but not even into those that seem to have small errors.”

This is precisely what increasingly compels us not to remain silent with you concerning those who try to corrupt even what is sound. For we count your household as no small Church of Christ.

Nor is the error of those people small who think that, if we possess any righteousness, continence, piety, or chastity, we have it from ourselves. They say that God created us in such a way that, beyond revealing knowledge to us, he gives us no further help enabling us to do, through love, what we have learned by instruction ought to be done.

Thus they define nature and teaching alone as the grace of God and his assistance for living rightly and justly. But when it comes to possessing a good will—the very thing by which we live justly—and to possessing love, which surpasses all God’s gifts to such an extent that it is even called God (1 John 4:8), and by which alone whatever we fulfill of the divine law and commandment is fulfilled in us, they do not wish us to be divinely assisted. Instead, they say that we ourselves are sufficient for these things through our own choice.

Do not regard this error as insignificant: they profess a desire to be Christians, yet refuse to listen to Christ’s Apostle. After saying, “The love of God has been poured into our hearts,” he immediately added, lest anyone think that he possesses it solely through his own choice, “through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

You understand how greatly and disastrously anyone errs who still does not confess that this is the great grace of the Savior, who, when he ascended on high, led captivity captive and gave gifts to human beings (Ps. 67:19; Eph. 4:7).

## CHAPTER II

4. How, then, could we refrain from admonishing you—people to whom we owe such great affection—to avoid such teachings, when we had read the book written to the holy Demetrias? We want to learn from your reply who wrote it, or whether it even reached you.

In that book, if it is permissible to say so, the virgin of Christ is instructed to believe that her virginal holiness and all her spiritual riches come from herself alone, and thus, before she is perfectly blessed, to learn—God forbid—to be ungrateful to God.

The words written to her in that book are these:

“You have, therefore,” he says, “even here the means by which you may rightly be placed above others—or rather, especially here. For bodily nobility and wealth are understood to belong to your family, not to you; but no one except yourself can confer spiritual riches upon you. In these, therefore, you are rightly to be praised; in these you deservedly take precedence over others, since they cannot exist except from you and in you” (*Letter to Demetrias*, chapter 11).

5. You see, of course, how great a danger must be guarded against in these words. For what was said—“These things cannot be good except in you”—was said very well and most truly; this, plainly, is wholesome food. But what he says, “only from you,” is altogether poison. Far be it that the virgin of Christ should gladly hear this—she who piously understands the poverty proper to the human heart and therefore knows that she can be adorned there only by the gifts of her Bridegroom.

Let her rather hear the Apostle saying: “I betrothed you to one man, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ. But I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the chastity that is in Christ” (II Cor. 11:2–3). And therefore, concerning these spiritual riches also, let her hear not the one who says, “No one can confer them upon you except yourself,” and, “They cannot exist except from you and in you,” but the one who says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing power may be of God and not from us” (ibid. 4:7).

6. Concerning that sacred virginal continence also—namely, that it is not from herself, but is God’s gift, although bestowed upon one who believes and wills—let her hear the same truthful and devout teacher, who, when speaking of this, says: “I wish that all were as I myself am; but each has his own gift from God, one in this way, another in that” (I Cor. 7:7).

Let her also hear Christ himself, not merely her own Bridegroom but the one Bridegroom of the whole Church, speaking of such chastity and integrity: “Not all can receive this saying, but those to whom it has been given” (Matt. 19:11). Thus she should understand that, for possessing so great and excellent a good, she ought rather to give thanks to God and our Lord than to listen to the words of some person who says that she possesses it—as it were—from herself [Col. 0851]; not that we should call him an obsequious flatterer, lest we seem rashly to judge the hidden things of human beings, but certainly an erring praiser.

“For every good gift and every perfect gift,” as the Apostle James also says, “is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1:17). Hence also comes holy virginity, by which your daughter surpassed you while you were willing and rejoicing: younger by birth, earlier in conduct, sprung from you by descent, before you in honor, later in age, but preceding you in holiness. [Note: Lov.: “greater”; but the other editions and manuscripts, better: “less.”] In her, what could not have been in you began also to be yours. For she did not marry carnally, so that she might be spiritually increased beyond you not only for her own sake but also for yours; for you are less than she in this respect, that you married so that she might be born.

These are God’s gifts. They are indeed yours, but not from you; for you have this treasure in earthly and still fragile bodies, as in earthen vessels, “so that the surpassing power may be of God and not from you.” Nor should you be surprised that we say both that these things are yours and that they are not from you. For we also call daily bread ours, yet we add, “Give it to us” (Luke 11:3), lest it be thought to be from us.

7. Therefore, as it is written, “Pray without ceasing; give thanks in all things” (I Thess. 5:17–18). You pray so that you may possess these things with perseverance and make progress; you give thanks because you do not possess them from yourselves. For who distinguishes you from that mass of death and perdition descended from Adam? Is it not the one who came “to seek and to save what was lost” (Luke 19:10)?

Or, when a person hears the Apostle saying, “Who distinguishes you?” will he answer, “My good will, my faith, my righteousness,” and not immediately hear what follows: “What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (I Cor. 4:7).

Therefore we do not wish the sacred virgin, when she hears or reads, “No one can confer spiritual riches upon you except yourself; in these you are rightly praised and deservedly preferred to others, for they can exist only from you and in you,” to boast as though she had not received them.

Let her indeed say: “In me are your vows, O God, which I shall render to you as a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 55:12). [Note: Editions: “I shall render praises to you”; manuscripts: “a sacrifice of praise to you,” following the Greek text of the Septuagint, αἰνέσεώς σου, “of your praise.”] But because they are in her, and not also from her, let her remember to say: “Lord, in your favor you established strength for my beauty” (Ps. 29:8). For although they are also from her, because of the exercise of her own will, without which we do not do good, they are nevertheless not—as this man said—only from her.

For one’s own free will, unless it is aided by God’s grace, cannot even be good will in a human being. “It is God,” says the Apostle, “who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:13). He does not, as these people think, assist us merely by revealing knowledge, so that we may know what we ought to do; he also inspires charity, so that what we have learned by learning we may do by loving.

8. For that man certainly knew how great a good continence was when he said: “And since I knew that no one can be continent unless God grants it.” Thus he knew not only how great this good was and how earnestly [Col. 0852] it ought to be desired, but also that it could not exist unless God granted it. Wisdom had taught him this, for he says: “And this itself was wisdom: to know whose gift it was.”

Yet knowledge alone did not suffice him. He says: “I approached the Lord and entreated him” (Wis. 8:21). God therefore helps us not only to know what must be done, but also to do by loving what we already know through learning. No one, then, can be not merely knowledgeable but also continent unless God grants it.

Hence, although that man already possessed knowledge, he prayed that he might also possess continence, so that what he knew was not from him might also exist in him—or, if on account of free will it was in some measure proper to him and from him, nevertheless not only from him, because “no one can be continent unless God grants it.”

But this man, concerning spiritual riches—which certainly include that luminous and beautiful continence itself—did not say, “They can exist in you and from you.” Rather, he said, “They cannot exist except from you and in you,” so that, just as they exist for her nowhere except in herself, they might be believed to exist for her from nowhere except herself; and consequently—may the merciful Lord turn this away from his heart!—she might boast as though she had not received them.

## CHAPTER III

9. As for us, concerning the discipline of the holy virgin and her Christian humility, in which she was nourished and educated, we suppose that, when she read those words—if indeed she read them—she groaned, humbly struck her breast, and perhaps even wept. She confidently prayed to the Lord, to whom she has been dedicated and by whom she has been sanctified, that, just as those were not her words but another’s, so her faith might not be of such a kind that she believed herself to possess something about which she would glory in herself rather than in the Lord.

For her glory is indeed in herself, not in another’s words, as the Apostle says: “Let each person test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself and not in another” (Gal. 6:4). But far be it that she herself should be her glory, and not the one to whom it is said: “My glory and the one who lifts up my head” (Ps. 3:4)!

Her glory is therefore beneficially in her when the God who is in her is himself her glory—the God from whom she has all the good things by which she is good, and will have all the things by which she will become better, insofar as she can become better in this life, and by which she will be perfected when she has been perfected by divine grace, not by human praise.

“For in the Lord her soul will be praised” (Ps. 33:2), who “satisfied her desire with good things” (Ps. 102:5). For he himself also inspired that desire, lest his virgin should glory in some good as though she had not received it.

10. Whether we are mistaken, then, about this disposition of hers, make us more certain by writing back. For we know very well that you have been and are, together with all your household, worshipers of the undivided Trinity. But human error does not creep in only when something else is thought concerning the undivided Trinity. There are also other matters in which people err most disastrously, as in this matter, about which we have perhaps spoken at greater length in this letter than was necessary for your faithful and chaste prudence.

Yet when someone denies that the good which is from God is from God, we do not know whom he injures except God, and consequently that Trinity. May such an evil be far from you, as we believe it is! Far be it entirely that this book should have produced anything of that sort in the mind—not, I say, of you or of your sacred virgin daughter, but of any servant or maidservant of yours, however insignificant in merit. For this reason we thought it appropriate to set down some words from it that might more easily be understood. [Col. 0853]

11. But if you examine more carefully even those passages in which he appears to speak of God’s grace or assistance, you will find them so ambiguous that they can be referred either to nature, to instruction, or to the remission of sins.

For even what they are compelled to confess—namely, that we ought to pray lest we enter into temptation—they can interpret as meaning that we are assisted only to the extent that, when we pray and knock, the understanding of truth is opened to us, where we learn what we ought to do, and not that our will receives the strength by which we do what we learn.

And what they call the Lord Christ’s example of right living, given to us in God’s grace or assistance, they refer to the same instruction, since we learn from his example how we ought to live. But they do not wish us to be assisted so that what we come to know by learning we may also do by loving.

12. Or else, if you can, find something in that same book where, apart from nature; apart from what belongs to that same nature, namely, the exercise of the will; apart from the remission of sins; and apart from the revelation of instruction, he confesses such assistance from God as does the one who said: “Since I knew that no one can be continent unless God grants it, and this itself was wisdom, to know whose gift it was, I approached the Lord and entreated him.”

For he was not praying to receive the nature in which he had been created; nor was he striving after the natural exercise of the will with which he had been created; nor was he seeking remission of sins, since he desired continence precisely so that he would not sin; nor did he desire to know what ought to be done, since he already confessed that he knew whose gift this was. Rather, he certainly wished to receive from the Spirit of wisdom such strength of will and such ardor of love as would suffice to fulfill the greatness of continence.

If, therefore, you can find anything of this kind there, we shall give abundant thanks if you deem it worthy to disclose it to us in your reply.

13. It is impossible to say how earnestly we desire to find, in the writings of those men who are read by many because of their forcefulness and eloquence, an open confession of that grace which the Apostle strongly commends. He says that even “the measure of faith”—without which it is impossible to please God (Heb. 11:6), by which the righteous person lives (Rom. 1:17), and which works through love (Gal. 5:6), before and without which no one’s good works should be considered good, since “whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23)—is apportioned by God to each person (ibid. 12:3).

He does not say that we are divinely assisted only by the revelation of knowledge, so that we may live piously and justly—which, without charity, puffs up (I Cor. 8:1)—but also by the inspiration of charity itself, which is “the fullness of the law” (Rom. 13:10), and which builds up our heart so that knowledge may not puff it up.

Yet so far we have been unable to find anything of this kind in their writings.

[Col. 0854] 14. Above all, we would wish this to be present in that book from which we quoted those words: the book in which, while praising the virgin of Christ as though no one except herself could confer spiritual riches upon her, and as though they could exist only from her, he does not wish her to glory in the Lord, but to glory as though she had not received them.

Although in that book he did not expressly mention either her name or that of Your Reverence, he nevertheless records that her mother had asked him to write to her. In one of his letters, however, the same Pelagius, where he most plainly gives his own name and does not suppress the name of the sacred virgin, says that he wrote to her; and he tries, by the testimony of that same work of his, to prove that he openly confesses the grace of God, which he is accused either of keeping silent about or denying.

But whether this is the book in which he placed those words about spiritual riches, or whether it reached Your Holiness, we ask that you kindly make us more certain by your reply.

## EPISTLE CLXXXIX

[Note: “Corrected from a, bg, c, cc, ff, g, gv, j, l, n, s, two sb, two t, two vc, four v; Lov.”]  
[Note: “Formerly 205; what was 189 is now in Appendix 8. Written around A.D. 418.”]

He prescribes for Boniface, serving honorably in the army, a rule of life; incidentally showing that a Christian may bear arms for the public peace.

To the eminent lord, deservedly distinguished and honorable son BONIFACE, AUGUSTINE sends greeting in the Lord.

1. I had already written back to Your Charity, but while an opportunity was being sought to dispatch the letter, my most beloved son Faustus arrived, proceeding to Your Eminence. When he received the letter I had already written, so that he might deliver it to Your Benevolence, he told me that you greatly desired me to write something to you that might build you up toward eternal salvation, in which you have hope through our Lord Jesus Christ. Although I was occupied, he pressed me so insistently that I did not delay, as much as you know that he sincerely loves you. Therefore, hastening to meet your request, I preferred to write something hastily rather than delay your religious desire, eminent lord and deservedly distinguished and honorable son.

2. What I can say briefly is this: “Love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength”; and, “Love your neighbor as yourself.” For this is the word that the Lord abbreviated upon the earth, saying in the Gospel: “On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 22:37, 39–40).

Make progress, therefore, in this love every day, both by praying and by doing good, so that, with the help of him who commanded and granted it to you, it may be nourished and grow until it makes you perfect. For this is the charity which, as the Apostle says, “has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). This is what he likewise says: “The fullness of the law is charity” (ibid. 13:10). This is what makes faith operative; hence he says again: “Neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love” (Gal. 5:6).

3. In this love all our holy fathers, Patriarchs, Prophets, and Apostles pleased God. In this love all true martyrs fought against [Col. 0855] the devil even unto blood; and because it neither cooled nor failed in them, they conquered.

In this love all good believers make daily progress, desiring to attain not the kingdom of mortals but the kingdom of heaven; not a temporal but an eternal inheritance; not gold and silver but the incorruptible riches of the angels; not any goods of this age, in which one lives with fear and which no one can take away with him when he dies, but the vision of God. His sweetness and delight surpasses the beauty not only of earthly but also of heavenly bodies; it surpasses the beauty of souls, however just and holy; it surpasses the splendor of the heavenly angels and Powers; it surpasses whatever is not only said but even thought about him.

Nor should we despair of receiving so great a promise because it is very great; rather, because the one who promised it is very great, we should believe that we shall receive it. For, as the blessed Apostle John says: “We are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (I John 3:2).

4. Do not suppose that no one who serves in military arms can please God. Saint David was among such men, and the Lord bore witness to him in so great a manner; many righteous men of that time were also among them.

Among them was also the centurion who said to the Lord: “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; but only say the word, and my servant will be healed. For I too am a man placed under authority, having soldiers under me, and I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.” Of him the Lord also said: “Amen, I say to you, I have not found such faith in Israel” (Matt. 8:8–10).

Among them was also Cornelius, to whom the angel sent said: “Your almsgiving has been accepted, and your prayers have been heard.” He instructed him to send for the blessed Apostle Peter and hear from him what he ought to do; and, so that he might come to him, Cornelius sent a devout soldier to that Apostle (Acts 10:4–8).

Among them were also those who, when they came to John to be baptized—the holy forerunner of the Lord and friend of the bridegroom, of whom the Lord himself said, “Among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist” (Matt. 11:11)—asked him what they should do. He answered them: “Do violence to no one, accuse no one falsely; let your pay be sufficient for you” (Luke 3:14). He certainly did not forbid them to serve under arms; he commanded them to regard their pay as sufficient.

5. Those who, having abandoned all these secular occupations, serve God in the highest continence of chastity do indeed hold a higher place with God. But, as the Apostle says, “each has his own gift from God, one in this way, another in that” (I Cor. 7:7).

Some fight on your behalf against invisible enemies by praying; you labor on their behalf by fighting against visible barbarians. Would that there were one faith in all, because there would then be less labor and the devil with his angels would more easily be defeated!

But since in this age it is necessary that the citizens of the heavenly kingdom be harassed by temptations [Col. 0856] among the erring and impious, so that they may be exercised and tested like gold in a furnace (Wis. 3:6), we ought not prematurely wish to live with the saints and righteous alone, so that in its proper time we may deserve to receive this.

6. Therefore, first consider this when you arm yourself for battle: your bodily strength itself is also God’s gift. In this way you will consider the gift of God and not act against God.

For when a pledge is made, it must be kept even toward an enemy against whom war is being waged; how much more toward a friend for whom one fights! The will ought to have peace, and war ought to be a necessity, so that God may free us from necessity and preserve us in peace. Peace is not sought in order to provoke war; rather, war is waged in order to obtain peace.

Be peaceful, therefore, even while fighting, so that by conquering you may lead those whom you defeat toward the benefit of peace. “Blessed are the peacemakers,” says the Lord, “for they shall be called children of God” (Matt. 5:9).

If human peace is so sweet for the temporal safety of mortals, how much sweeter is divine peace for the eternal salvation of angels! Therefore, let necessity, not your will, destroy the enemy who fights. Just as violence is returned to one who rebels and resists, so mercy is already owed to one who has been defeated or captured, especially when no disturbance of peace is feared from him.

7. Let conjugal chastity adorn your conduct; let sobriety and frugality adorn it also. For it is very shameful that one whom a human being cannot conquer should be conquered by lust, and that one who cannot be defeated by iron should be overwhelmed by wine.

If secular riches are lacking, let them not be sought in the world through evil deeds; but if they are present, let them be preserved in heaven through good works. They ought neither to lift up a manly and Christian spirit when they arrive nor break it when they depart.

Let us rather consider what the Lord says: “Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matt. 6:21). And certainly, when we hear the command that we should lift up our hearts, we ought not to respond falsely—as you know that we do respond.

8. I have learned that you are diligent in these matters, and I take great pleasure in your reputation and rejoice greatly in you in the Lord, so that this letter may be more a mirror in which you see what kind of person you are than a place where you learn what kind of person you ought to be.

Nevertheless, whatever you find either in this letter or in the Holy Scriptures that you still lack for a good life, strive to acquire it both by acting and by praying. For what you possess, give thanks to God as the fountain of goodness from whom you have received it; and in all your good deeds give him glory and yourself humility.

For, as it is written: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1:17).

However much you may progress in love of God and neighbor and in true devotion, do not believe yourself to be without sin so long as you live in this life. For concerning this life it is written in the Holy Scriptures: “Is not human life upon the earth a temptation?” (Job 7:1).

Therefore, since, as long as you are in this body, it is always necessary for you in prayer to say what the Lord taught: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12), remember to forgive quickly if [Col. 0857] someone sins against you and asks your pardon, so that you may pray truthfully and obtain forgiveness for your own sins.

I have written this hastily to Your Charity because the haste of the messenger pressed me. But I give thanks to God that, in some manner, I have not failed your good desire. May the mercy of God always protect you, eminent lord and deservedly distinguished and honorable son.

## EPISTLE CXC

[Note: “Corrected from a, bg, bl, bn, c, cc, cb, ff, g, gg, gv, n, r, s, two e, two sb, two t, two vc, five v; Am., Bad., Er., Lov.”]  
[Note: “Formerly 157; what was 190 is now in Appendix 9. Written a little after the middle of A.D. 418.”]

It shows Optatus what is certain concerning the origin of the soul, what may rightly be questioned, and that in this inquiry one must above all preserve the faith by which we believe that no one is born from Adam except bound by the bond of condemnation, and that no one is freed from it except by being reborn through Christ.

To the most blessed lord, brother and fellow bishop OPTATUS, desired in sincere love, AUGUSTINE sends greeting in the Lord.

## CHAPTER I

1. Although I have received no letter addressed to me personally by Your Holiness, nevertheless the letters which you sent to Caesarean Mauretania arrived while I was present at Caesarea, whither an ecclesiastical necessity imposed upon us by the venerable Pope Zosimus, bishop of the Apostolic See, had drawn us. Thus it came about that I too read what you wrote, when my dearest brother in Christ, the holy servant of God Renatus, gave me that same letter of yours. At his request—and though I was occupied with other matters, he urged me strongly—I was compelled to reply to it.

There was added also the arrival, while we were staying in the aforesaid town, of another holy brother of ours, to be named with due honor, and, so far as I learned from him, an intimate friend of yours, Muressis. [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “Maurensis”; another Vatican manuscript and four French manuscripts, “Murensis”; two other French manuscripts, “Murusis.”] He told me that letters from Your Veneration on this subject had also been sent to him, and consulted me on this very question, so that he might communicate to you, either in my reply or in his own, what I thought: namely, whether souls, like bodies, are born by propagation and derive from the one soul created for the first human being, or whether the almighty Creator, who certainly works even now, without any propagation makes new individual souls for each person.

2. Before I offer Your Sincerity any admonition on this question, I want you to know that in my many writings I have never dared to pronounce a definite judgment upon it, or presumptuously set down in writing for the instruction of others what had not been resolved in my own mind. It would take too long to set out in this letter the considerations and reasons which move me not to incline my assent to either assertion, but still to deliberate between the two. Nor is it so necessary that, without doing so, we cannot discuss sufficiently what concerns this question—not indeed so as to [Col. 0858] remove hesitation, but certainly so as to avoid rashness.

3. For that on which the Christian faith especially depends—that “through a human being came death, and through a human being the resurrection of the dead; for as all die in Adam, so all shall be made alive in Christ” (I Cor. 15:21–22); and that “through one human being sin entered into this world, and through sin death; and so death passed upon all human beings, in whom all sinned”; and that “judgment indeed came from one offence unto condemnation, but grace from many offences unto justification of life”; and that “through the offence of one came condemnation upon all human beings, and through the justification of one came justification of life upon all human beings” (Rom. 5:12, 16, 18); and whatever other testimonies declare that no one is born from Adam except bound by the bond of guilt and condemnation, and that no one is freed from it except by being reborn through Christ—we must hold so unshakably that we know anyone who denies it has no part whatever in the faith of Christ or in the grace of God, bestowed through Christ upon little and great alike.

Therefore, if the origin of the soul is unknown while redemption is clear, there is no danger; for we believe in Christ not in order to be born, but in order to be reborn, however we may have been born.

4. We say that the origin of the soul may safely remain unknown only provided that we do not believe it to be a part of God, but a creature: not born from God, but made by him; to be adopted into his kind through the wonderful condescension of grace, not through an equal dignity of nature. Nor is it a body, but a spirit; certainly not Creator, but created.

Nor did it come into this corruptible body, by which it is weighed down, because the merits of an earlier evil life, whether in heaven or in any other regions of the world, compelled it to do so. For the Apostle, speaking of Rebecca’s twins before they were born, says that they had done neither good nor evil, so that it might be said, not on account of works—by which, when neither had done any, one was not distinguished from the other—but on account of him who calls, that the elder should serve the younger (Rom. 9:11–13).

## CHAPTER II

5. With these points therefore most firmly established, if it is so hidden and stored away among God’s secret works that it is not disclosed even by the plain utterance of the divine Scriptures, whether we should believe that those not yet born have done neither good nor evil because each person receives a soul not propagated from others but immediately created from nothing; or because, though they existed originally in their parents, they as yet did not exist as persons living their own individual lives—let that faith nevertheless remain safe by which we believe that no human being, whether old or a child of however small and recent an age, is freed from the contagion of ancient death and the obligation of sin which he contracted in his first birth, except through the one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (I Tim. 2:5).

6. By the most saving faith in this man, who is also God, those righteous persons too were saved who, before he came in the flesh [Note: Most manuscripts consistently read “into flesh.”], believed that he would come in the flesh. For their faith and ours are the same, since they believed as future what we believe as accomplished. [Col. 0859]

Hence the Apostle Paul says: “Having the same Spirit of faith, according to that which is written, ‘I believed; therefore I spoke,’ we also believe; therefore we also speak” (II Cor. 4:13). If, then, those who foretold Christ’s coming in the flesh had the same Spirit of faith as those who proclaimed that he had come, the sacraments could differ according to the diversity of times, yet converge in fullest harmony upon the unity of the same faith.

It is written in the Acts of the Apostles that the Apostle Peter said: “Why therefore do you tempt God by placing upon the neck of the disciples a yoke which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But we believe that through the grace of the Lord Jesus we shall be saved, in the same manner as they” (Acts 15:10–11).

If, therefore, they too—that is, the fathers, unable to bear the yoke of the old law—believed that they would be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, it is manifest that this grace also caused the righteous of old to live by faith: “the righteous lives by faith” (Hab. 2:4).

7. “The Law entered in so that offence might abound; that grace might superabound” (Rom. 5:20), by which the abundance of offence might be healed. For if a law had been given which could make alive, righteousness would indeed be from the law.

The Apostle then added, explaining the good purpose for which the Law was given [Note: Most better manuscripts, as also Bad., Am., and Er.; Lov. reads: “But why the good Law was given.”]: “But Scripture shut up all things under sin, so that the promise from faith in Jesus Christ might be given to believers” (Gal. 3:21–22).

The Law therefore had to be given, so that the human being might show himself more clearly to himself, lest the proud human mind should suppose that it could be righteous by itself; and, ignorant of God’s righteousness—that is, the righteousness which comes to a human being from God—and wishing to establish its own, that is, a righteousness supposedly acquired by its own powers, should fail to be subject to the righteousness of God (Rom. 10:3).

It was necessary, therefore, that when the commandment was added, whose utterance is “You shall not covet” (Exod. 20:17), the charge of transgression should be added also to the proud sinner; and thus weakness, not healed by the Law but convicted by it, should seek the medicine of grace.

8. Accordingly, since all righteous persons—that is, true worshippers of God, whether before or after Christ’s incarnation—have neither lived nor live except by faith in Christ’s incarnation, in whom is the fullness of grace, what is written, “There is no other name under heaven in which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12), has been effective for the salvation of the human race from the time when the human race was corrupted in Adam.

For as all die in Adam, so all shall be made alive in Christ: just as no one is in the kingdom of death without Adam, so no one is in the kingdom of life without Christ; just as all people are unrighteous through Adam, so all people are righteous through Christ; just as through Adam all, made mortal in punishment, become children of this age, so through Christ all, made immortal in grace, become children of God.

## CHAPTER III

9. Why even those whom the Creator foreknew [Note: The Victorinus manuscript reads “willed”; the German and Corbie manuscripts, “knew.”] not to belong to grace but to condemnation are created, the blessed Apostle states with a brevity proportionate to his greater authority. [Col. 0860]

He says that God, “willing to show wrath and make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy”; above he had said that God, like a potter, makes from the same lump of clay one vessel for honor and another for dishonor (Rom. 9:22, 21).

It would rightly seem unjust that vessels of wrath are made for destruction if the whole mass were not itself condemned in Adam. Thus their being born from it as vessels of wrath belongs to deserved punishment; but their being reborn as vessels of mercy belongs to undeserved grace.

10. God therefore showed his wrath—not a disturbance of mind, such as is called human anger, but a just and fixed retribution—because the offspring of sin and punishment is derived from the stock of disobedience. And a human being born of a woman, as is written in the book of Job, “is short-lived and full of wrath” (Job 14:1, according to the Septuagint).

For he is a vessel of that with which he is full; hence they are called vessels of wrath.

He also showed his power, by which he makes good use even of the evil, granting them many natural and temporal goods and adapting their malice for the exercise of the good and for admonishing them by comparison, so that in them the good may learn to give thanks to God because they have been distinguished from them, not by their own merits, which were equal in that same mass [Note: One Vatican manuscript: “who were equal in the same mass”; another Vatican manuscript: “which … equally,” etc.; editions: “which … equal.” But very many manuscripts read better: “which … equal,” namely, merits.], but by God’s mercy.

This is especially evident in little children: when through Christ’s grace they are reborn and, ending this life at that tender age, pass into eternal blessedness, it cannot be said that they are distinguished by free choice from other infants who die without this grace in the condemnation of that same mass.

11. But if only those who would be recreated through grace were created from Adam, and no other human beings were born besides those adopted as children of God, the benefit bestowed on the undeserving would remain hidden, because no one coming from the same condemnable stock would receive the punishment due.

But when God endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, he not only showed wrath and made known his power by exacting retribution and by making good use of those who are not good; he also made known the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy.

For the person justified freely thus says what has been granted to him, while he is distinguished from one condemned—not by his own merit, but by the glory of God’s most abundant mercy—although by the same justice he too was to be condemned with him.

12. Yet he willed that so many should be born, whom he foreknew would not belong to his grace, that by an incomparable multitude they should outnumber those whom he deigned to predestine as children of promise for the glory of his kingdom. Thus, even by the multitude of the rejected, it would be shown how little importance, before the just God, belongs to any number, however great, of those most justly condemned. And so those who are redeemed from that very condemnation may understand that this was owed to the whole mass: they see it returned to so great a portion of it—not only in those who, by the free choice of an evil will, add many evils to original sin, but also in so many infants who, bound only by the chain of original sin, are snatched from this light without the grace of the Mediator.

For the whole of this mass would receive the due of just condemnation, unless the just and merciful Potter made from it other vessels for honor according to grace, not according to what was owed—helping infants, whose merits cannot be mentioned, and going before adults, so that they might be able to acquire some merits.

## CHAPTER IV

13. Since this is so, if your assertion is not directed toward saying that new souls, on account of the innocence of their newness, before they make use of free choice in order to sin, cannot be subject to original condemnation, but if you confess according to the Catholic faith that, even if they depart from the body at that tender age, they will go into the condemnation of perdition unless they are freed by the sacrament of the Mediator, who came to seek and save what was lost (Luke 19:10), then ask where, or from what source, or when they began to possess the merit of condemnation, if they are new—provided, of course, that you do not make God, nor any nature that God did not create, the author either of their sin or of the condemnation of the innocent.

And if you discover what I have urged you to seek—what, I confess, I myself have not yet discovered—defend and assert it as vigorously as you can. Maintain that the souls of infants are so new that they are derived through no propagation, and share with us, in brotherly love, whatever you discover.

14. But if you do not discover why or how the souls of infants become sinful, possessing no evil in themselves, and are compelled to draw from Adam that by which they are condemned—while you believe that they were not propagated from that first sinful soul, but are new and innocent souls enclosed in sinful flesh—then do not rashly let your assent be diverted to the contrary position, so as to believe that they are transmitted by propagation from that one soul. Perhaps someone else may discover what you cannot, or perhaps you may at some time discover what you cannot now.

Those who assert that souls are propagated from the one soul which God gave to the first man, and thus say that they are drawn from their parents, if they follow Tertullian’s opinion, plainly contend that souls are not spirits but bodies, and that they arise from bodily seeds. What could be said more perversely? Nor is it surprising that Tertullian dreamed this, since he also supposes that God himself the Creator is nothing but a body [Note: [Col. 0861] Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, ch. 7. See Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 10, ch. 25.].

15. Once such madness has been driven from the heart and mouth of a Christian, whoever confesses that the soul, as it is, is not a body but a spirit, and nevertheless is conveyed into children from their parents, is certainly not constrained by any difficulty insofar as the true faith proclaims that all souls, including those of infants whom the Church baptizes not into a false but into a true remission of sins, draw original sin, committed by the will of the first man and transmitted by generation to all his descendants, to be cleansed only by regeneration.

But when one begins to consider and investigate what is being said, it is astonishing if any human understanding can grasp how, as a lamp is kindled from a lamp and one fire proceeds from another without detriment to the other, a soul is made from the soul of its parent in the offspring, or is transmitted into the offspring. Does the incorporeal seed of the soul, by some hidden and invisible route of its own [Note: [Col. 0862] Seven manuscripts: *animae suae, quadam*, etc.], pass separately from the father into the mother when conception takes place in the woman? Or—something still more incredible—is it concealed in the bodily seed?

When seeds flow fruitlessly, without any conception, does the seed of the soul not go out at the same time? Or does it return with the greatest speed, in an atom of time, to the place from which it emerged? Or does it perish? And if it perishes, how is the soul itself, whose seed is mortal, immortal? Or does it receive immortality when it is formed so as to live, just as it receives righteousness when it is formed so as to understand?

And in what manner does God fashion it in the human being—even if the soul is drawn seminally from a soul—as he fashions the limbs of the body in the human being, although the body is drawn seminally from a body? For if the spiritual creature were not also fashioned by God, it would not be written, “He who fashions the spirit of man within him” (Zechariah 12:1). And in the passage, “He who fashioned the hearts of them all individually” (Psalm 32:15), if “hearts” signifies souls, who would doubt that they can be fashioned? The question, however, is whether they are fashioned from the one soul of the first man, just as he fashions the faces of human beings individually, though they nevertheless derive from the one body of the first man.

## CHAPTER V

16. Since many questions of this and similar kinds are raised about this matter—questions that cannot be investigated by any bodily sense, that lie far beyond our experience, and that are hidden in the most secret recesses of nature—one ought not to be ashamed to confess that one does not know what one does not know, lest, while pretending to know, one never become worthy to know.

Who, then, denies that God is the creator and maker not merely of one soul but of every soul, except one who most openly resists his utterances? For through the prophet he says without any ambiguity, “I made every breath” (Isaiah 57:16), plainly wishing souls to be understood, as the words that follow make clear. Therefore he himself made, and he still makes, not merely the one breath that he breathed into the first man whom he had formed from the earth, but every breath.

Yet the question remains whether he makes every breath from that one breath, just as every human body is made from that one body, or whether he indeed makes new bodies from the one, but new souls from nothing. For who makes kinds of things corresponding to their origins, even from seeds, except the one who made the seeds themselves without seeds?

But when a matter naturally obscure surpasses our limited capacity, and clear divine Scripture does not come to our aid, human conjecture rashly presumes to define something on the basis of it. According to the lives they begin to possess as their own, we say that new human beings are born, whether in soul or in body. But according to original sin, they are born old; therefore they are renewed by Baptism.

17. I have not yet found anything certain in the canonical Scriptures concerning the origin of the soul. For those who assert that souls are made new, without any propagation, place among the testimonies by which they strive to prove this the two passages I mentioned shortly before: “He who fashions the spirit of man within him,” and “He who fashioned the hearts of them all individually.” You see how those who resist them can answer: when he fashions, it is uncertain whether he fashions from something else or from nothing.

One testimony, however, among the others appears especially important, that which is read in Solomon’s book, Ecclesiastes: “And the dust will return to the earth as it was, and the spirit will return to God who gave it” (Ecclesiastes 12:7).

But the response is very easily made: the body returns to the earth from which the body of the first man was initially made, and the spirit returns to God by whom the first soul of man was made. For, they say, just as our body, although propagated from that first body, nevertheless returns to the place from which that first body itself was formed, so our soul, although propagated from that soul, does not return to nothing—for it is immortal—but returns to the one from whom that first soul itself was made.

Consequently, what is written about the spirit of each human being—that it returns to God who gave it—does not resolve this exceedingly obscure question, because whether he gives it from that one soul or from no other source, God certainly gave it.

18. Likewise, those who defend the propagation of souls with inconsiderate rashness believe that among the other testimonies which they suppose support their cause, none can be produced that is more manifest and explicit on their behalf than what is written in Genesis: “All the souls, moreover, who entered Egypt with Jacob, who came out from his thighs” (Genesis 46:26).

By this apparently most evident testimony, souls may be believed to be propagated into children from their parents, since it seems to say quite openly that souls too, and not merely the bodies of the children, came out from Jacob’s thighs. In the same way they wish to understand, as a part standing for the whole, what Adam said when his wife was shown to him: “This now is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh” (Genesis 2:23). For he did not say, “And soul from my soul.” Yet it is possible for both to be understood when flesh is named, just as here he named souls and nevertheless wished bodies also to be understood in the children.

19. But this testimony, however clear and manifest it may seem, would certainly not suffice to resolve this question—not even if it were read in the feminine gender, “who came out from his thighs,” so that we understood it to mean souls who came out [Note: [Col. 0863] So read Bad., Am., Er., and several manuscripts. At. and Lov. have *intellegeremus usquequaque exire*, “we should understand that they came out in every respect.”].

The reason it would not suffice is that the word “soul” can also signify the body alone, by a certain manner of speech in which what contains is signified by what is contained. Thus someone says, “The wines crown” (Virgil, *Aeneid* 7), when it is the wine vessels that are crowned: the wine is contained, while the vessel contains it.

Just as, therefore, we call a basilica a church—the people contained within it being properly called the Church—and by the name “church,” that is, by the name of the people contained, signify the place that contains them, so, since souls are contained in bodies, the bodies of the children can be understood by the souls that are named.

In this way the passage in which the Law says that a person who enters upon “a dead soul” is defiled (Numbers 9:10) is better understood to mean “upon the corpse of the dead,” so that by “dead soul” the dead body that contained the soul is understood. For even when the people, that is, the Church, are absent, that place is nevertheless still called a church.

This would be the response if, as I said, the feminine gender had been used: “who came out from Jacob’s thighs,” that is, “which souls.” But since the masculine gender is used—“who came out from Jacob’s thighs”—who would not prefer to understand it as meaning, “all the souls of those who came out from his thighs,” that is, the souls of human beings? In this way, too, the human beings may be understood to have come out from the father’s thighs only according to the body, while the souls belonged to them; and by the number of those souls the total number of human beings is indicated.

## CHAPTER VI

20. I should like to read the little book of yours that you mentioned in your letters, lest perhaps you have set down in it some unambiguous testimonies. When a most dear friend of mine, deeply devoted to the divine Scriptures, asked me what I thought about this question, and when, without embarrassment, I had confessed to him both my perplexity and my ignorance [Note: [Col. 0864] In *Epistle* 143e, to Marcellinus.], he wrote across the sea to a most learned man. That man replied that he should rather consult me [Note: [Col. 0864] Jerome, above, in *Epistle* 165.], unaware that he had already done so and had been unable to hear anything certain and definite from me.

Nevertheless, in the same brief letter he indicated that he himself believed souls to be made rather than propagated, while also observing that the propagation of souls was commonly held by the Western Church—for he himself is in the East. Taking advantage of this greater opportunity, I wrote him a lengthy book, consulting him and asking him first to teach me and then to send me those whom I might teach [Note: [Col. 0864] *Epistle* 166.].

21. In my own judgment, this book of mine may be read as the work not of a teacher but of an inquirer, and indeed of one eager to learn. It ought not, however, to be sent anywhere or given to anyone outside, except after I have received a reply, with the Lord’s help. I would most readily and willingly defend what he thinks, if he could teach me how souls do not come from Adam and yet find in him a just share of condemnation unless they are reborn for the remission of sins.

For far be it from us to believe either that the souls of infants receive in the bath of regeneration a false cleansing from sins, or that God, or any nature God did not create, is the author of the defilement from which they are cleansed.

Until he replies, or until I myself, if God wills, learn in some way what the cause is of the soul’s incurring original sin—which must be present in all infants—if it derives no origin from that sinful soul, I dare not proclaim anything of this kind. For God does not compel the innocent soul to bear it, since he is not the author of sin; nor can any evil nature do so, since no such nature exists.

22. But if you willingly or patiently accept it, dearest brother, I warn you not to incur through insufficient caution a new heresy that seeks, by disputing against the grace of God, to tear down the foundations established by the most ancient faith. This grace the Lord Christ bestows with ineffable goodness upon the little and the great.

Its authors, or at least its most vigorous and notorious advocates, Pelagius and Caelestius, were condemned throughout the Christian world by the vigilance of episcopal councils, with the help of the Savior who protects his Church, and also by two venerable bishops of the Apostolic See, Pope Innocent and Pope Zosimus—unless, after correction, they also performed penance.

We have taken care to have sent you copies of the recent letters concerning them, both those addressed specifically to the Africans and those that proceeded universally to all bishops from the aforementioned See, lest they may not yet have reached Your Holiness. They were sent by those brothers to whom we entrusted these letters as well, so that they might forward them to Your Reverence.

These men are not heretics merely because they say that souls do not derive their origin from that first sinful soul—a claim that may perhaps be true for some reason, or may be unknown without any violation of the faith. But from this they endeavor to establish—and for this they are judged altogether manifest heretics—that the souls of infants draw nothing evil from Adam that must be expiated by the bath of regeneration.

Pelagius’s argument on this matter, which, among his other condemnable statements, was also included in the letters of the Apostolic See, runs as follows: “If the soul is not derived by transmission, but only the flesh possesses the transmission of sin, then only the flesh deserves punishment. For it is unjust that a soul born today, not from Adam’s mass, should bear an ancient sin belonging to another; since it is in no way permissible that God, who forgives personal sins, should impute another’s sin.”

23. If, then, you can assert the newness of souls without any propagation in such a way that, by a just argument not foreign to the Catholic faith, they can nevertheless be shown to be subject to the sin of the first man, assert what you think as best you can.

But if you cannot make them foreign to propagation in any other way than by making them free from every bond of sin at the same time, refrain entirely from such an argument. The remission of sins in the baptism of infants is not false; it is not said merely in words, but truly effected.

To use now the words found in the letter of the blessed bishop Zosimus: “The Lord is faithful in his words, and his baptism, both in reality and in words—that is, in deed, confession, and the true remission of sins—holds the same fullness in every sex, age, and condition of the human race. For no one is made free except one who is a slave of sin, nor can anyone be called redeemed unless he was truly held captive beforehand by sin, as it is written: ‘If the Son makes you free, you will be truly free’” (John 8:36).

“Through him we are reborn spiritually; through him we are crucified to the world. By his death, the document of death introduced and transmitted from Adam to us all, contracted by every soul through propagation, is torn up. No one whatsoever among those born is not held liable by it before being freed through Baptism” [Note: [Col. 0865] Zosimus, who succeeded Pope Innocent in 417, was for a time misled by the Pelagians. But after receiving the replies of the African Fathers and finally conducting a more rigorous investigation, he became convinced of their heresy and pronounced judgment against them before the middle of 418, issuing the *Tractoria*, as Mercator calls it in *Commonitorium*, ch. 3, throughout the Christian world. Here you have a fragment of that *Tractoria*, apart from another very brief portion reported by Prosper in the appendix to Celestine’s letter to the bishops of Gaul; the rest is no longer extant.].

In these words of the Apostolic See, the Catholic faith is so ancient, so firmly founded, certain, and clear that it is impious for a Christian to doubt it.

24. Since, therefore, by Christ’s death the document of death contracted through the propagation of not one soul or a few souls but of the entire human race is torn up, if you can defend souls as foreign to propagation while nevertheless demonstrating by the most correct reasoning that they are bound by this document—which can be torn up only by Christ’s death—and that they are justly bound by this debt not through their own propagation but through the flesh, then defend this position, no one forbidding you; indeed, show us how we can defend it with you.

But if what you think about the newness of souls cannot be asserted in any other way than by saying that they are not held by the sin of the first man, or that, through a propagation not of their own but of the flesh, with God as author—or through some nature of evil, I know not what—they are made sinners though utterly innocent, then it is better for the origin of the soul to remain hidden, provided that we do not doubt that it is God’s creature, than either to call God the author of sin, or to introduce against God a foreign nature of evil, or to render the baptism of infants ineffectual.

25. Yet, so that Your Love may also hear from me something definite about this question—something not to be valued lightly, but especially necessary and to be retained—whatever the origin of souls may be, whether they are propagated from that one soul or from no other source, there can be no doubt that the soul of the Mediator drew no sin from Adam.

For if no soul is propagated from another, while all are bound by the propagated flesh of sin [Note: [Col. 0866] Seven manuscripts read *propagatae carne peccati*, “propagated by the flesh of sin,” which is less satisfactory, although the received reading itself does not seem entirely sound. Perhaps *reae*, “liable,” should be supplied after *tenentur*.], how much less should we believe that a soul could come by propagation from a sinful soul when his flesh came from a virgin—not conceived by lust but by faith—so that he might be “in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Romans 8:3), not in sinful flesh?

But if the other souls are held liable because of the sin of the first sinful soul precisely because they were propagated from it, then plainly the soul which the Only-Begotten united to himself either did not draw sin from it or was not drawn from it at all. For the one who removed our sins could surely draw a soul for himself without sin; nor could the one who created a new soul for that flesh which he made from earth without a parent fail to create a new soul for the flesh which he took from a woman without a man.

26. As I have been able, I have answered these matters—not indeed in response to letters addressed to me, but nevertheless in letters addressed to our dearest brothers concerning Your Holiness—not with the expertise you desired, but with concerned affection.

If you gratefully accept this as a brotherly and useful admonition, and preserve it—not by erring but by prudent reflection—in peace with the Church, thanks be to God. But if you are surprised that I do not yet know these things—or even if you are not surprised—and do not refuse, in mutual charity, to teach me something certain about the origin of souls while preserving this faith, which is most certain and clear, then thanks be to God all the more abundantly.

Remember us, and may you always live in the Lord, most blessed lord, brother desirable in sincere affection.

# LETTER CXCI

[Note: [Col. 0867] Compared with bl. ff. m. r. sb. two v. Am. Bad. Er. Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0867] Elsewhere 104; the letter that was numbered 191 is now in the Appendix as 10. Written toward the end of 418.]

To the presbyter Sixtus, later Roman pontiff, who had undertaken the defense of God’s grace against the Pelagians, concerning whom there had been a rumor that he favored them. Augustine congratulates him and urges him to continue restraining the shameless and healing those who dissemble.

[Col. 0867]

To the venerable lord, holy brother and fellow presbyter SIXTUS, to be embraced in the love of Christ, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

1. When the letters of Your Benevolence, sent to Hippo through our holy brother Firmus the presbyter, arrived during my absence, I was able to read them only after I had returned, although the bearer of them had already departed. This first and most welcome opportunity to reply has now presented itself through our dearest son Albinus the acolyte.

The reason you did not receive letters from both of us together was that we were not together at that time; thus you received separate letters from each of us rather than one letter from both. The bearer of this letter left me in the company of my venerable brother and fellow bishop Alypius, who was passing on to send another reply to Your Holiness. He himself also carried to Alypius the letters from you which I had already read.

What joy those letters poured over us—what can a person strive to say that he cannot express? Nor do I think you yourself sufficiently know it; but believe us, and see how much good you did by sending us such letters.
