For just as you are a witness to your own state of mind, so we are witnesses to our own, to how it has been affected by the exceptionally clear sincerity of those letters.

When we copied out your very brief letter on this same matter, which you sent through the acolyte Leo to the blessed old man Aurelius [Note: [Col. 0867] They suppose this to be the same Leo the Great who later succeeded Sixtus in the Roman See, in the year 440. Consult the Quesnel edition of Leo’s works, vol. 2, dissertation 1.], with exultant eagerness, and read it with great zeal to as many as we could, in which you explained what you thought of that most pernicious doctrine and, in opposition to it, what you thought of the grace of God, which he bestows upon little and great alike and which that doctrine most bitterly opposes—how much exultation do you think we felt when reading these longer writings of yours, and how eagerly we have offered them to others to read, as far as we have been able, and continue to offer them?

For what can be more pleasant to read or hear than so pure a defense of God’s grace against its enemies from the mouth of one who was formerly being proclaimed as a patron of those same enemies of considerable importance? Or from what source ought we to give fuller thanks to God than that his grace is thus defended by those to whom it is given, against those to whom it is either not given or what is given is unwelcome—for, by God’s hidden and just judgment, it is not given to them so as to be welcome?

2. Therefore, venerable lord and holy brother, to be embraced in the love of Christ, although you do very well when you write about this matter to the brothers among whom they are accustomed to boast of your friendship, a greater responsibility still remains for you: not only must those who dare to chatter too freely about that error, so hostile to the Christian name, be punished with salutary severity, but pastoral vigilance must also be most carefully on guard against those who, for the sake of the Lord’s weaker and simpler sheep, do not cease to insinuate it to them more closely indeed and more timidly, while entering houses, as the Apostle says, and doing the other things that follow with practiced impiety [Note: [Col. 0868] Five manuscripts read: “They must be guarded against most vigilantly with pastoral care.”] (2 Timothy 3:6 and following). Nor are those to be neglected who suppress what they think out of fear, even to the point of profound silence, but nevertheless do not cease to hold the same perversity.

Some of them may have become known to you before this plague was condemned by the most manifest judgment of the Apostolic See; now you see that they have suddenly become silent. Whether they have been healed cannot be known unless they not only fall silent about those false doctrines but also defend the true doctrines opposed to them with the zeal they customarily gave to the false ones.

Nevertheless, such people should certainly be treated more gently. Why should those need to be frightened whom their very silence shows to be sufficiently frightened? Yet they should not be passed over as though they were healthy, without the diligence of medical care, since their wound is hidden.

Although they should not be frightened, they must still be taught. In my judgment, they can more easily be brought to reject by speech what they no longer dare to speak, while the fear of severity assists the teacher of truth in them, so that, with the Lord’s help, once his grace has been understood and loved, they may overcome it.

# LETTER CXCII

[Note: [Col. 0868] Revised against bl. cb. ff. gg. r. two sb. two t. two v. Am. Bad. Er. Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0868] Elsewhere 62; the letter that was numbered 192 is now in the Appendix as 11. Written at the same time.]

Augustine to the deacon Caelestine, later Roman pontiff, concerning mutual goodwill.

To the venerable and greatly desired lord, holy brother and fellow deacon COELESTINE, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

1. Although I was far away when the writings of Your Holiness, sent to me at Hippo through the cleric Projectus [Note: [Col. 0868] Four Gallican manuscripts have *Prolectus*. In the same manuscripts, and also in two Vatican manuscripts, *Alvini* is written shortly afterward instead of *Albini*.], arrived, after I came back and, having read them, recognized that I had become obligated to reply, I was waiting for an opportunity to do so. And now, suddenly, the most welcome opportunity has arisen through our dearest brother Albinus the acolyte, who is about to leave us.

Having therefore rejoiced at your health—which is most desirable to me—I return the greeting owed to Your Holiness. But I always owe love, which alone, even when repaid, always keeps one in debt. It is repaid when it is bestowed, yet it remains owed even after it has been repaid, because there is never a time when it ought no longer to be bestowed.

When it is repaid, it is not lost but rather multiplied: it is repaid by possessing it, not by lacking it. And since it cannot be repaid unless it is possessed, nor possessed unless it is repaid, indeed, when it is repaid by one person it grows in that person; and the more people to whom it is repaid, the greater the love acquired.

How, moreover, can what is owed to enemies be denied to friends? Toward enemies it is bestowed cautiously; toward friends it is returned securely. Yet it works as far as it can to receive from those to whom it returns good for evil what it itself has bestowed. For we desire the one whom we truly love as an enemy to become a friend, because we love him only if we wish him well; and he will not be well until he has lost the evil of enmity.

2. Love, then, is not bestowed in the same way as money. Apart from the fact that money is diminished by being spent while love is increased, the two also differ in this: toward someone to whom we have given money, we are more benevolent if we do not seek to receive it back; but no one can be a true giver of love unless he is also a kindly demander of it.

For when money is received, it comes to the one to whom it is given but departs from the one who gives it. Love, however, not only grows in the person who demands it from the one he loves, even if he does not receive it; the person from whom he receives it also begins to possess it precisely when he returns it.

Therefore, brother and lord, I willingly return mutual love to you, and I receive it with joy. What I receive, I still ask for; what I return, I still owe. For we must hear obediently from the one teacher under whom we are fellow students, through his Apostle, who commands and says: “Owe no one anything except to love one another” (Romans 13:8).

# LETTER CXCIII

[Note: [Col. 0869] Here it is published for the first time from a manuscript of the monastery of Saint Bertin in Belgium.]

[Note: [Col. 0869] It is now published for the first time from a very ancient codex of the monastery of Saint Bertin in Belgium. The letter that was numbered 193 is now in the Appendix as 12. Written at the same time.]

Augustine to Mercator, explaining why he has not yet replied to his earlier letters, and showing that the Pelagians are nearly refuted in the question of the baptism of infants precisely because they admit that infants in some manner believe through those by whom they are brought to be baptized. He then shows that they argue in vain, on the basis of the translation of Enoch and Elijah before their death, or of the living faithful being snatched away at Christ’s coming, that death is not the punishment of sin.

To his beloved son MERCATOR, who is to be proclaimed in the members of Christ with the sincerest love, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord [Note: [Col. 0869] This is undoubtedly the same man whose first name was Marius, the author of the recently published short works against the Pelagians. Possidius also lists this letter in his *Index*, ch. 4. Augustine translated the third part of it into *The Eight Questions of Dulcitius*, immediately before these words in question 3: “But concerning those who will be snatched up in the clouds, in a certain letter which I wrote to my son named Mercator, undoubtedly well known to you” (so it is read in all the manuscripts, not as the printed editions have hitherto had it: “which begins, ‘Undoubtedly well known to you,’” and so on), “when he consulted me about certain questions of the Pelagians, who deny that death is repaid for sin, I argued as follows, in the passage below. ‘But those,’ I said, concerning whom,” and the rest, which is reproduced here from chapter 4 to the end of the letter.]

## CHAPTER I

1. The letters of Your Love, which I received from you at Carthage, affected me with such joy that I even received with great pleasure your later letters in which you were angry that I had not written back to you. For your indignation was not the beginning of hostility but an indication of affection.

The reason I did not reply from Carthage was not a lack of bearers; rather, other matters that were more urgent kept us extremely occupied and intent until we departed. When we left there, we continued as far as Caesarean Mauritania [Note: [Col. 0869] Augustine mentions the journey he undertook to Caesarean Mauritania above, at the beginning of Letter 190, and in *Retractions* 2.51, as well as Possidius, ch. 14. From these passages it can be established that this letter was sent toward the end of 418.]. Ecclesiastical necessity drew us there.

As we traveled through all those lands, our attention was repeatedly snatched here and there by the various matters presented to our senses. No persistent reminder came from anyone to prompt me to write to you, and no suitable bearer presented himself.

When I returned, I found among our people another letter from Your Sincerity, already sharpened by complaint, together with another book against the new heretics, filled with testimonies from the holy Scriptures. After reading and examining these, as well as those you had sent first, the most opportune occasion for writing back arose through our dearest brother Albinus, the acolyte of the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0870] This is the same man who carried the earlier letters to Sixtus and Caelestine; from this one may infer that Mercator was at that time staying in Rome with them.].

2. Therefore, dearest son, far be it from me to receive carelessly or dismiss with proud disdain your writing to me, or your sending me writings for my consideration, especially since my joy over you is all the greater because your progress has come so unexpectedly and unforeseeably. I confess that I did not know you had advanced so far.

And what could we desire more than that there should abound people who everywhere expose the errors that attack the Catholic faith and lie in wait for uneducated and weaker brothers, and who vigorously and faithfully defend Christ’s Church against profane novelties of speech (1 Timothy 6:20), since, as it is written, “The multitude of the wise is the health of the world” (Wisdom 6:26)?

I have therefore examined your heart as far as I could in your writings, and I found it worthy of embrace. I urge you to extend yourself forward with the most persistent diligence, with the Lord’s help, who has given you the strength that he would nourish in you.

## CHAPTER II

3. In the question of the baptism of infants, those whom we are trying to bring back from error into the way came not a little near to the truth when they confessed that any infant, however recently expelled from its mother’s womb, believes through those by whom it is brought to be baptized [Note: [Col. 0870] See below, Letter 194, chapter 10, no. 45.].

For, as you write, when they say that infants do not believe in the remission of sins in such a way that sins are remitted to them—for they think that infants have no sin—but because they themselves also receive the same washing in which remission of sins takes place wherever it takes place, they believe that this remission takes place in others, though it does not take place in them, then, when they say, “They do not believe in that way, but they believe in this way,” they plainly do not doubt that they believe.

Let them therefore hear the Lord: “He who believes in the Son has eternal life; but he who is unbelieving toward the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him” (John 3:36).

Accordingly, because infants become believers through others by whom they are brought to be baptized, through those others they are certainly unbelievers if they are among people who, because they believe baptism to be of no benefit, do not believe that the infants should be brought for baptism. Consequently, if they believe through believers, they have eternal life; plainly, if they are through unbelievers, they are unbelievers, and they will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon them.

For it is not said, “It came upon them,” but “It remains upon them,” because it was already in them by origin, and it is removed from them altogether only by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

This wrath is also read of in the Book of Job: “A human being born of woman is short-lived and full of wrath.” From where, then, does the wrath of God rest upon the innocence of an infant, except from the lot and defilement of original sin? Concerning this it is likewise written in the same book that not even an infant, whose life is but one day upon the earth, is clean from it (Job 14:1, 5, according to the Septuagint).

4. Therefore, what is being argued against them with the greatest urgency, and what Catholic voices resound around their ears from every side, has not accomplished nothing in them, since, although they wished to argue against the Sacraments of the Church, they nevertheless admitted that infants believe. Let them therefore not promise infants life even if they have not been baptized—for of what other life is it said, “Whoever is unbelieving toward the Son will not see life”? Nor should they acknowledge that infants are excluded from the kingdom of heaven in such a way as nevertheless to defend them from condemnation; for what is signified by the wrath which the Lord testifies remains upon the unbeliever, if not condemnation? Much ground has truly been gained, and the case has been settled without a contentious struggle. For if they grant that infants believe, then undoubtedly, just as that saying applies to them, “Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5), so too does this saying of the same Lord apply: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16:16). Therefore, since these people admit that infants are believers when they are baptized, let them not hesitate to say that unbelievers are condemned; and let them now dare to say, if they can, that by the just God those are condemned who draw no evil from their origin and have no contagion of sin.

## CHAPTER III

5. But as for what you mentioned in your letter—that they object to us the cases of Enoch and Elijah, because they did not die but were transferred from human society with their bodies—how this helps them in the matter under discussion, I do not understand. To pass over the fact that they too are said afterward to be destined to die, as many interpret the Apocalypse of John concerning those two prophets of whom it speaks without naming them: namely, that those two holy men will then appear with the bodies in which they now live, so that they too, like the other martyrs, may die for the truth of Christ (Apocalypse 11:3–7)—to pass over this, then, and postpone that question, whatever the case may be, how, I ask you, does this help them? For they do not thereby show that human beings do not die bodily on account of sin. For if God, who forgives those very sins to so many of his faithful, also wished to forgive this punishment of sin to certain persons, who are we to answer God, asking why one person is thus and another otherwise?

6. We therefore say what the Apostle states most plainly: “The body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness. But if the Spirit of him who raised Christ from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Romans 8:10–11). Yet we do not say this in such a way as to deny that God can now cause those whom he wishes to pass without death into what we undoubtedly believe he will cause so many to attain after death. Nevertheless, it will not for that reason be false that “through one man sin entered into this world, and through sin, death, and thus passed into all human beings.” This was said because, unless death had entered through sin, there would be no death at all.

For when we say, “All are sent into Gehenna because of their sins,” do we therefore say something false because not all human beings are sent into Gehenna? That statement is true not because every human being is sent there, but because no one is sent there except on account of the merits of sins. The contrary statement has the same character: “Through the justification of one, justification of life came to all human beings” (Romans 5:12, 18). Not all human beings, indeed, belong to the justification of Christ; but this was said because no one is justified except through Christ.

7. The more legitimate question, therefore, is why the punishment of sin remains when the sin itself does not remain; that is, if bodily death is also the punishment of sin, the question should rather be why an infant dies after having been baptized than why Elijah did not die after having been justified. In the infant’s case, since his sin has ended, the question is why the punishment of sin followed; in Elijah’s case, since his sin has likewise ended, there ought to be no question if the punishment of sin does not follow.

If, then, in the books *On the Baptism of Infants*, which I know are thoroughly familiar to you, we have resolved, with the Lord’s help and as far as we were able, the question of baptized people’s death—why, once sin has been abolished, some punishment of sin nevertheless follows [Note: [Col. 0872] Book 2, chapter 30 and following]—how much less should the question trouble us when it is asked, “Why did righteous Elijah not die, if death is the punishment of sin?” It is as though one were saying, “Why did sinful Elijah not die, if death is the punishment of sin?”

8. Unless, perhaps, they derive one question from another and say: If Enoch and Elijah were so free from sin that they did not even suffer death, which is the punishment of sin, how does no one here live without sin? As though they could not be answered more plausibly: Precisely because the Lord wished certain people to live after their sins had been brought to an end, they were not permitted to live here, since no one can live here without sin.

But these and similar arguments could be made against them if they could establish from some other source with certainty that those men would never die. Since they cannot demonstrate this, and since it is more credible that they will eventually come to death, there is no reason why they should bring them forward against us, when in no respect will they benefit their case.

## CHAPTER IV

9. As for those of whom the Apostle said, when he was speaking about the resurrection of the dead, “Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air; and thus we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thessalonians 4:16), they do indeed raise a question, but one concerning themselves, not because of these others. For even if they too are not going to die, I do not see how they help these people at all, since things can be said about them such as were said about those two.

Yet, as far as the words of the blessed Apostle are concerned, he seems to assert that, when the Lord comes at the end of the age and the resurrection of the dead is to take place, some will not die but, having been found alive, will suddenly be changed into that immortality which is also given to the other saints, and will be caught up together with them, as he says, in the clouds. Whenever I have wished to reflect on these words, nothing else has seemed possible to me.

10. But I would rather hear more learned people on this matter, lest the Apostle should be found to say even to those who think that some will pass into everlasting life without death preceding: “Fool! What you sow is not made alive unless it first dies.” For what else can be the meaning of the reading found in most manuscripts, “We shall all rise again” (1 Corinthians 15:36, 51), unless we all die? Resurrection, unless death has preceded, is no resurrection at all.

And the reading found in some manuscripts, “We shall all sleep,” makes this much easier and clearer to understand. If anything else of this kind is found in the sacred Scriptures, it seems to press toward the conclusion that no human being is thought to attain immortality unless death has first occurred.

Therefore, when the Apostle said, “We who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, shall not precede those who have fallen asleep. For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God; and the dead in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air; and thus we shall always be with the Lord,” I would like, as I said, to hear more learned people on this matter. And if these words can be explained in such a way that it may be understood that all human beings who are alive, or who will live after us, will die, I would be willing to correct what I may once have thought otherwise.

For we must not be unwilling to learn from teachers. Certainly, it is better for a person to be corrected while still pliable than to be broken when stubborn, provided that, through what we or others have written, our weakness may be exercised and educated, without any of it being established as though it possessed canonical authority.

11. For if no other meaning can be found in these words of the Apostle, and it becomes clear that he intended what the words themselves seem to proclaim—that there will be people at the end of the age, at the Lord’s coming, who will not be stripped of the body but clothed over with immortality, “so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (2 Corinthians 5:4)—then this opinion will undoubtedly agree with what we confess in the rule of faith: that the Lord will come to judge the living and the dead.

By “the living” we should not then understand righteous people and by “the dead” unrighteous people, although both the righteous and the unrighteous will be judged; rather, the living are those whom his coming will find not yet departed from their bodies, while the dead are those whom it will find already departed from their bodies.

If this is established as the case, then those words will have to be examined: how are we to understand, “What you sow is not made alive unless it first dies,” and “We shall all rise again,” or “We shall all sleep,” so that they do not conflict with the opinion according to which some are believed to live eternally with their bodies, without tasting death?

12. But whichever of these interpretations proves more truthful and more perceptive, what does it have to do with the case of these people—whether all are punished by the death they owe, or whether some are spared this condition? It nevertheless remains certain that death—not only of the soul but also of the body—would not have followed if sin had not preceded; and that, by the more wondrous power of grace, the righteous are restored from death to eternal blessedness rather than escaping the experience of death.

Let this suffice concerning those about whom you wrote to me, although I now do not think that they would maintain that, even if Adam had not sinned, he would have died bodily.

13. As for the question of the resurrection, however, on account of those who are believed not to die but to pass from this mortality into immortality without an intervening death, a more careful investigation is required. If you have heard, read, or even been able to consider anything on this subject that has been settled and defined through a reasonable and complete argument—or if you can still hear, read, or consider anything of the sort—I ask that you not hesitate to send it to me.

For I, as I must confess to Your Charity, love learning more than teaching. We are also admonished of this by the Apostle James, who says: “Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak” (James 1:19).

Thus, the sweetness of truth ought to invite us to learn; but the necessity of charity ought to compel us to teach. In this respect, it is preferable to hope that the necessity by which one human being teaches another will pass away, so that we may all be teachable by God—although we are teachable even when a human being appears to teach us those things that pertain to true piety.

For “neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:7). Since, if God did not give the growth, the Apostles who plant and water would be nothing, how much more am I, or you, or any human beings of this age, when we imagine ourselves to be teachers?

## LETTER CXCIV

[Note: [Col. 0874] We have reviewed this letter against the manuscripts b. bl. cb. ff. gg. m. rm. vc. vv.; two manuscripts of sb.; two of t.; four of v.; and the editions Am., Bad., Er., Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0874] Elsewhere numbered 105; the letter that was numbered 194 is now in the Appendix as 13. Written somewhat after the preceding letters.]

Augustine to Sixtus, Roman presbyter (and later bishop of Rome), instructing him against the arguments of the Pelagians.

To his most beloved lord in the Lord of lords, the holy brother and fellow presbyter SIXTUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

## CHAPTER I

1. Letter [Note: [Col. 0874] Editions: “In the letter which.” The particle *in*, absent from the manuscripts, ought to have been deleted. Indeed, nothing of the longer letter which Augustine says he promised is found in that which was transmitted through Albinus [“in the letter”].] that I sent through our most beloved brother Albinus, the acolyte, I promised that I would send a longer one through our holy brother and fellow presbyter Firmus, who had brought us a letter from Your Sincerity, filled with the sincerity of your faith. That letter brought us as much joy as we are capable of possessing rather than expressing.

For—I must confess this to Your Charity—we were exceedingly sad when rumor spread that you favored the enemies of Christian grace. But, so that this sadness might be wiped from our hearts, rumor did not fail first to report that you had pronounced an anathema against them before a very large gathering. Then, when the letters of the Apostolic See condemning them had been sent to Africa [Note: [Col. 0874] Zosimus’s letters], your own letter also followed, addressed to the venerable old man Aurelius. Although it was brief, it nevertheless sufficiently indicated your firmness against their error.

But now, when, in your letters, the very faith of the Roman Church was speaking with us more openly and fully concerning what you thought about and against that doctrine—the Church to which the blessed Apostle Paul spoke much and in many ways concerning the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord— Not only did every cloud of sadness flee from our hearts, but so great a light of joy shone upon them that our sorrow and fear seemed to have accomplished nothing in us except to prepare the way for a greater ardor of joy to follow.

2. Therefore, dearest brother, although we do not see you with the eyes of the flesh, in the faith of Christ, in the grace of Christ, and among the members of Christ we hold you, embrace you, and kiss you in spirit. And now that our most holy and faithful messenger has returned from us to you—the one whom you wished to be among us not only as the bearer of your writings but also as the narrator and witness of your actions—we send you our reply and converse with you at somewhat greater length.

We urge you to persist in teaching those whom, as we have learned, you have persisted sufficiently in terrifying. For there are some who still think that impieties justly condemned ought to be defended more freely. There are others who enter houses secretly and, although they fear to proclaim openly what they now fear to shout, do not cease to sow it in private. Others have fallen completely silent, overcome by great fear, but still retain in their hearts what they no longer dare to utter with their mouths. Yet they may be well known to the brothers from their earlier defense of that very doctrine.

Accordingly, some must be restrained more severely, others investigated more watchfully, and others treated more gently but taught no less diligently, so that, even if they are not feared lest they cause loss, they may nevertheless not be neglected lest they perish.

## CHAPTER II

3. They think that free will is taken away from them if they admit that a human being cannot possess even a good will without God’s assistance. They do not understand that they are not strengthening human choice but driving it [Note: [Col. 0875] Three manuscripts read *infirmare*, “to weaken.” Three others read *inflare*, “to inflate.”], so that it is carried along by empty things rather than placed in the Lord as upon a firm rock. “The will is prepared by the Lord.”

4. They imagine that they would be acknowledging God as a respecter of persons if they believe that, without any preceding merits, he has mercy on whom he wills, calls those whom he deigns to call, and makes religious whomever he wills. They pay little attention to the fact that a deserved punishment is rendered to the condemned, while an undeserved grace is given to the liberated, so that the former may not complain that he is unworthy, and the latter may not boast that he is worthy.

Rather, there is no respect of persons precisely where one and the same mass of condemnation and offense envelops everyone, so that the person who has been freed may learn from the person who has not been freed that the same punishment would also have been appropriate for him, unless grace had come to his aid. And if it is grace, then it is certainly not rendered on account of any merits, but bestowed through gratuitous goodness.

5. “But it is unjust,” they say, “for one person to be freed and another punished in one and the same evil condition.”

Then, surely, it is just for both to be punished. Who would deny this? Let us therefore give thanks to the Savior, while we see that what we recognize as having been due even to us, in the condemnation of those like us, has not been repaid to us.

For if everyone were freed, it would remain hidden what is owed to sin through justice; if no one were freed, it would remain hidden what grace bestows. Thus, in this most difficult question, let us rather use the words of the Apostle: “God, desiring to show wrath and to make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath, fitted for destruction, and to make known the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy.” The thing fashioned cannot say to him, “Why have you made me thus?” when he has power from the same mass to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor (Romans 9:20–23). Since this entire mass was deservedly condemned, justice returns the dishonor that is owed, while grace bestows the honor that is not owed—not by any privilege of merit, not by the necessity of fate, and not by the randomness of fortune, but by the depth of the riches of God’s wisdom and knowledge.

The Apostle does not open this depth but marvels at it as closed, crying out: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how untraceable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, so that he might be repaid? For from him, and through him, and in him are all things. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen” (Romans 11:33–36).

## CHAPTER III

6. These people do not wish God to receive glory in the justification of the ungodly through gratuitous grace. “Because they do not know the righteousness of God, they wish to establish their own” (Romans 10:3). Or, already overwhelmed by the repeated cries of religious and devout people, they admit that they are divinely helped to possess or accomplish righteousness, but in such a way that some merit of their own precedes—as though they first wished to give something so that it might be repaid to them by the one of whom it was said, “Who has first given to him, so that he might be repaid?”

They think that their own merit goes before the one of whom they hear—or rather, refuse to hear—“For from him, and through him, and in him are all things.” But the depth of his wisdom and knowledge belongs to these riches: the riches of his glory are in the vessels of mercy, whom he calls into adoption. He wishes these riches to be made known even through the vessels of wrath, which are prepared for destruction.

And what are the untraceable ways except those of which the Psalm sings: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Psalm 24:10)? His mercy and truth, therefore, are untraceable, because he has mercy on whom he wills—not through justice but through the grace of mercy [Note: [Col. 0876] So Bad., Am., and Er. Lov. has: “not of justice, but by the grace of mercy.” Most manuscripts: “not justice, but mercy”]; and he hardens whom he wills—not through wickedness but through the truth of punishment.

Yet mercy and truth meet one another in such a way—as it is written, “Mercy and truth have met one another” (Psalm 84:11)—that neither does mercy hinder the truth by which the deserving person is punished, nor does truth hinder the mercy by which the undeserving person is freed.

What merits, then, will the person who has been freed boast of, when, if what was deserved according to his merits were repaid, he would be condemned? Are there, then, no merits of the righteous? There certainly are, because they are righteous. But they were not merits by which they became righteous. They became righteous when they were justified; yet, as the Apostle says, they were “justified freely by his grace” (Romans 3:24).

7. Although these people are hostile and opposed to this grace, Pelagius nevertheless, in the ecclesiastical judgment held in Palestine [Col. 0877] [Note: [Col. 0877] Diospolis]—for otherwise he would not have departed from it unpunished—anathematized those who say that God’s grace is given according to merits.

But nothing else is found in his later arguments either than the claim that grace is given according to merits—the very grace about which the Apostolic Letter to the Romans speaks most emphatically, so that from there its proclamation might spread, as from the head of the world, throughout the whole world. For this is the grace by which the ungodly is justified, that is, by which the person who was previously ungodly is made righteous.

Therefore, no merits precede the reception of this grace, because the merits of the ungodly deserve not grace but punishment. Nor would it be grace if it were not given freely but were rendered as something owed.

8. But when these people are asked what grace Pelagius thought was given without any preceding merits, when he anathematized those who say that God’s grace is given according to our merits, they answer that, without any preceding merits, grace itself is the human nature in which we were created. For before we existed, they say, we could not have merited anything in order to exist.

Let this deception be banished from the hearts of Christians. For the Apostle is not at all commending the grace by which we were created so that we might be human beings, but the grace by which we were justified when we were evil human beings [Note: [Col. 0877] Manuscripts: “Not at all this grace”; “not this”]. This is the grace through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Indeed, Christ did not die for those who did not yet exist, so that they might be created as human beings; he died for the ungodly, so that they might be justified. The person who said, “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7:24–25), was already a human being.

9. They can indeed say that the remission of sins is grace, since it is given without any preceding merits—for what good merit can sinners possess? But even the remission of sins is not without some merit if faith obtains it. For faith has merit; it was by such faith that the man said, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner,” and went down justified through the merit of faithful humility [Note: [Col. 0877] Bad., Am., and Er. read *fidelis humiliatus*, “having been humiliated in faith”; seven manuscripts agree with them], since “whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 18:13–14).

It remains, therefore, that we must not attribute faith itself—the faith from which all righteousness takes its beginning, which is why it is said to the Church in the Song of Songs, “You will come and pass over from the beginning of faith” (Song of Songs 4, according to the Septuagint)—to human choice, which these people exalt [Note: [Col. 0877] So read most manuscripts. The editions have *quo isti extolluntur*, “by which these people are exalted”], nor to any preceding merits, since all merits that are good begin from it.

Rather, if we are thinking of true grace—that is, grace without merits—we must confess that faith is God’s gratuitous gift, because, as we read in the same Epistle, “God apportions to each the measure of faith” (Romans 12:3).

Good works are performed by a human being, but faith is produced in a human being; without faith, no good works are performed by anyone. For “whatever is not from faith is sin” (Romans 14:23).

10. Therefore, lest even the merit of prayer itself exalt itself—although assistance is given to the person praying so that he may overcome desires for temporal things, love eternal goods, and love God himself, the source of all good—it is faith that prays, and faith was given to one who was not yet praying. If it had not been given, he could not pray.

“For how will they call upon him in whom they have not believed? And how will they believe in him of whom they have not heard? And how will they hear without someone preaching? Therefore faith is from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Romans 10:14, 17).

Accordingly, the minister of Christ, the preacher of this faith, according to the grace given to him (Romans 15:15–16), is a planter and a waterer. “Yet neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:5–8), who apportions to each the measure of faith.

Hence it is also said elsewhere, “Peace to the brothers, and charity with faith”; and, so that they would not attribute this to themselves, he immediately added, “from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ” (Ephesians 6:23). For not everyone who hears the word has faith, just as not everything that is planted and watered produces growth; rather, growth is given by God.

But why does one person believe and another not believe, when both hear the same thing and, if a miracle occurs before their eyes, both see the same thing? This is the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God, whose judgments are unsearchable and with whom there is no injustice, while he has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills (Romans 9:14, 18). These things are not unjust merely because they are hidden.

11. Furthermore, after the remission of sins, if the Holy Spirit does not inhabit the cleansed house, does not the unclean spirit return with seven other spirits, and do not the last condition of that person become worse than the first (Matthew 12:44–45)?

But for the Holy Spirit to inhabit the person: does he not breathe where he wills (John 3:8)? And is not the love of God, without which no one lives well, poured into our hearts—not by us, but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Romans 5:5)?

The Apostle defined this faith when he said: “Neither circumcision is anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6). This is the faith of Christians, not of demons. For “the demons also believe and tremble” (James 2:19); but do they also love? If they did not believe, they would not say, “You are the Holy One of God,” or, “You are the Son of God” (Luke 4:41). But if they loved him, they would not say, “What have we to do with you?” (Matthew 8:29).

12. Faith, therefore, draws us to Christ. Unless it were given to us from above as a gratuitous gift, Christ himself would not have said: “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him.”

A little later he also says: “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life. But there are some of you who do not believe.” Then the Evangelist adds: “For Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who believed, and who it was who would betray him.”

And lest anyone think that believers belonged to his foreknowledge in the same way as unbelievers—that is, as though faith itself were not given to them from above, but only their will were foreknown—he immediately added: “For this reason I told you that no one can come to me unless it has been given to him by my Father.”

This explains why, of those who had heard him speaking about his flesh and blood, some were offended and went away, while others remained by believing (John 6:44–66): no one can come to him unless it has been given to him by the Father, and consequently also by the Son himself and by the Holy Spirit.

For the gifts and works of the inseparable Trinity are not separated. The Son, in honoring the Father in this way, does not offer evidence of any inequality or distance, but provides a great example of humility.

13. Here again these defenders—or rather deceivers—of free will, deceivers because they inflate people, and inflaters because they presume, will speak not against us but against the Gospel. What else do they say than what the Apostle attributed to himself as an objection, as though it were spoken by such people?

“You will say to me, then, ‘Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?’” He set this contradiction against himself as though it were posed by another, as though it came from the voice of those who refuse to accept what he had said above: “Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills.”

Let us therefore say to such people, with the Apostle—for we cannot find anything better to say than what he said: “O human being, who are you to answer back to God?” (Romans 9:18–20).

14. We ask what the merit of hardening is, and we find it. The entire mass was condemned on account of the merit of sin. God does not harden by imparting wickedness, but by not imparting mercy. Those to whom he does not grant mercy are neither worthy nor deserving of it; rather, they are worthy of and deserving the very fact that mercy not be granted to them.

But when we ask what the merit of mercy is, we find none. Otherwise grace would be emptied of its meaning if it were not given freely but repaid according to merits.

15. For if we say that faith preceded, and that in faith there was a merit deserving grace, what merit did a person possess before faith by which he might receive faith? “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

Just as a human being would not possess wisdom, understanding, counsel, strength, knowledge, piety, or fear of God unless, according to the prophetic utterance, he had received “the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, and the Spirit of the fear of God” (Isaiah 11:2–3); and just as he would not possess virtue, love, or self-control unless he had received the Spirit of whom the Apostle says, “You have not received the spirit of fear, but of power, and love, and self-control” (2 Timothy 1:7)—so he would not possess faith unless he had received the Spirit of faith.

Of this Spirit the same Apostle says: “Having the same Spirit of faith, according to what is written, ‘I believed, and therefore I spoke’; we also believe, and therefore we speak” (2 Corinthians 4:13).

That he received this not through merit but through the mercy of him who has mercy on whom he wills, he shows most clearly when he says of himself: “I obtained mercy so that I might be faithful” (1 Corinthians 7:25).

## CHAPTER IV

16. If we say that a merit of prayer precedes, so that the gift of grace may follow, prayer itself clearly shows, by obtaining whatever it obtains, that the gift is from God. Thus a person cannot think that he has from himself what, if it were in his own power, he would not ask for.

Nevertheless, lest people should think that even merits of prayer precede, so that grace is not given freely but is owed—and therefore is no longer grace, because it would be rendered as a debt—even prayer itself is found among the gifts of grace.

“For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought,” says the Doctor of the Gentiles, “but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings.” What does “he intercedes” mean except “he causes us to intercede”? For to intercede with groanings is the clearest sign of someone in need. Yet it is not right to believe that the Holy Spirit is in need of anything.

The expression “he intercedes” is therefore used because he causes us to intercede and inspires in us the disposition to intercede and groan, just as it is said in the Gospel: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:20).

This does not happen through us as though we were doing nothing. The assistance of the Holy Spirit is expressed in such a way that he is said to do what he causes us to do.

17. That the “spirit” of which it is said that he intercedes with inexpressible groanings is not our spirit but the Holy Spirit, by whom our weakness is assisted, the Apostle himself demonstrates sufficiently. He began by saying, “The Spirit helps our weakness”; then he continued: “For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought,” and so forth.

Elsewhere he speaks more plainly of this Spirit: “You have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans 8:26, 15).

Here he did not say that the Spirit himself cries out in prayer, but “in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’” Yet elsewhere he says: “Because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Galatians 4:6).

Here he did not say “in whom we cry,” but preferred to say that the Spirit himself cries out—the Spirit by whom we are enabled to cry out. The same is true of the statements, “The Spirit himself intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings,” and “It is the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.”

18. Therefore, just as no one possesses right wisdom, right understanding, or right counsel and strength; no one is knowingly pious or piously knowledgeable; and no one fears God with chaste fear unless he has received the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, counsel and strength, knowledge and piety, and the fear of God; and just as no one possesses true virtue, sincere love, or religious self-control except through the Spirit of virtue, love, and self-control—so no one will believe rightly without the Spirit of faith, nor pray for salvation without the Spirit of prayer.

This is not because there are many spirits, but because the one and same Spirit accomplishes all these things, distributing to each person his own gifts as he wills (1 Corinthians 12:11), because “the Spirit breathes where he wills” (John 3:8).

But—and this must be acknowledged—the Spirit assists in one way when he does not yet inhabit a person, and in another way when he inhabits that person. When he does not yet inhabit someone, he assists so that the person may become faithful; when he inhabits someone, he assists those who are already faithful.

## CHAPTER V

19. What, then, is a person’s merit before grace, by which merit he may receive grace, when grace alone makes every good merit of ours exist in us, and when God, in crowning our merits, crowns nothing other than his own gifts?

For just as from the beginning of faith we obtained mercy—not because we were faithful, but so that we might become faithful—so at the end, when eternal life will be given, he will crown us, as it is written, “with compassion and mercy” (Psalm 102:4).

It is therefore not without reason that we sing to God, “His mercy will go before me” (Psalm 58:11), and, “His mercy will follow me” (Psalm 22:6).

Hence eternal life itself—which will certainly be possessed at the end, without end, and is therefore rendered on the basis of preceding merits—nevertheless is also called grace. The merits by which it is rendered were not prepared by us through our own sufficiency, but were produced in us through grace. It is called grace for no other reason than that it is given freely—not because it is given without merits, but because the merits by which it is given were themselves given.

Where do we also find eternal life called grace? We have the Apostle Paul, that magnificent defender of grace: “The wages of sin is death, but the grace of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 6:23).

20. Consider, I ask you, how watchfully he placed his words in such a brief statement. If they are carefully considered, the obscurity of this question will become somewhat clearer.

When he had said, “The wages of sin is death,” who would not judge that it would be most appropriate and logical for him to add, “But the wages of righteousness are eternal life”? And this is true: just as death is rendered as the wages owed for the merit of sin, so eternal life is rendered as the wages owed for the merit of righteousness.

Or, if he did not wish to say “of righteousness,” he could have said “of faith,” since “the righteous person lives by faith” (Habakkuk 2:4 and Romans 1:17).

For this reason it is also called a reward in many places in the sacred Scriptures. But righteousness or faith is nowhere called a reward, as though a reward were rendered to righteousness or faith. What a reward is for one who works, a wage is for one who serves as a soldier.

### 21

But the blessed Apostle, combating the pride that attempts to insinuate itself even into such great matters that, because of it, he says an angel of Satan was given to him to buffet him, lest he should lift up the summit of presumption (2 Cor. 12:7)—combating, then, this plague of pride with the utmost vigilance—says: “The wage of sin is death.” Properly called a wage, because it is owed, because it is deservedly repaid, because it is rendered according to merit. Then, lest righteousness should exalt itself on account of good human merit, just as evil human merit is unquestionably sin, he did not state the contrary by saying, “But the wage of righteousness is eternal life”; rather, he says, “the grace of God is eternal life.” And lest any other way should be sought apart from the Mediator, he added, “in Christ Jesus our Lord.” It is as though he were saying:

Having heard that the wage of sin is death, what are you preparing to exalt, O human being—not righteousness, but plainly pride under the name of righteousness? What are you preparing to exalt, and to demand eternal life, contrary to death, as a wage owed to you? The one to whom eternal life is owed possesses true righteousness. But if it is true righteousness, it is not from you; it is from above, descending from the Father of lights (James 1:17). If you have it—provided, indeed, that you have it—you certainly received it. For what do you have that you did not receive (1 Cor. 4:7)? Therefore, O human being, if you are to receive eternal life, it is indeed the wage of righteousness, but for you it is grace, just as righteousness itself is grace for you. For it would be returned to you as something owed if righteousness, to which it is owed, came from you for yourself.

But now, from his fullness we have received not only grace—the grace by which we now live justly amid labors to the end—but also grace in exchange for this grace (John 1:16), so that afterward we may live without end in rest. Faith believes nothing more salutary than this, because understanding finds nothing truer; and we must hear the prophet saying: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. 7:9, according to the Septuagint).

## CHAPTER VI

### 22

“But,” they say, “people who do not wish to live rightly and faithfully will excuse themselves by saying: ‘What have we done, we who live badly, since we have not received the grace by which we might live well?’”

Those who live badly cannot truthfully say that they have done nothing evil. For if they do nothing evil, they live well; but if they live badly, they live badly from what is their own—whether from what they originally inherited or from what they subsequently added.

But if they are vessels of wrath, prepared for destruction, and what is owed to them is repaid, let them attribute this to themselves, since they were made from that mass which, because of the sin of one in whom all sinned, God justly and deservedly condemned. But if they are vessels of mercy, and God did not wish to repay them, though made from the same mass, the punishment they deserved, let them not inflate themselves; rather, let them glorify him who bestowed upon them a mercy not owed. And if they understand anything otherwise, he will reveal this also to them (Phil. 3:15).

### 23

Finally, in what way will these people excuse themselves? Surely in the manner which the Apostle briefly placed before himself as though in their own voice, so that they might say: “Why does he still complain? For who can resist his will?” For this is what they are saying:

Why is complaint still made against us because we offend God by living badly, when no one can resist his will—he who hardened us by not granting mercy?

If, then, they are not ashamed to contradict not us but the Apostle with this excuse, why should we hesitate to say to them what the Apostle said, again and again:

“O man, who are you to answer back to God? Shall what is formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me like this?’ Does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same mass—which was certainly justly and deservedly condemned—to make one vessel for an undeserved honor, because of the grace of mercy, and another for deserved dishonor, because of the justice of wrath, and to make known the riches of his glory in the vessels of mercy, thereby showing what he bestows upon them, while the vessels of wrath receive the punishment that was owed equally to all?”

For the time being, it should be enough for the Christian who still lives by faith and does not yet see what is perfect, but knows only in part (1 Cor. 13:9–10), to know—or to believe—that God liberates no one except by gratuitous mercy through our Lord Jesus Christ, and condemns no one except by the most equitable truth through that same Lord Jesus Christ.

But why he liberates one person rather than another, or does not liberate him, let the one who can search out the great depth of his judgments investigate—yet let him beware of the precipice. For is there injustice with God? By no means. But his judgments are inscrutable, and his ways unsearchable.

### 24

And, at least in the case of those of more mature age, it can rightly be said: “They did not wish to understand, so that they might do good” (Ps. 35:4). What is more serious, they understood and did not obey; for, as it is written: “A stubborn servant will not be corrected by words; even if he understands, he will not obey” (Prov. 29:19).

From what will he refuse to obey, except from his own most evil will? To such a person a heavier condemnation is owed according to divine equity, for “from everyone to whom much has been given, much will be required” (Luke 12:47–48).

Scripture calls those people inexcusable who are not ignorant of the truth, yet persist in iniquity. “The wrath of God,” the Apostle says, “is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of people who suppress the truth in unrighteousness; because what can be known about God is manifest among them. For God has manifested it to them. For his invisible attributes, from the creation of the world, are understood and perceived through the things that have been made—both his eternal power and divinity—so that they are inexcusable” (Rom. 1:18–20).

### 25

If, then, he calls those people inexcusable who were able to perceive, through the things that have been made, his invisible attributes, yet did not obey the truth but remained unrighteous and ungodly—for they did not fail to know, but, as he says, “although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks” (Rom. 1:21)—how much more inexcusable are those who, instructed from his law, trust that they themselves are guides of the blind, and teach others while not teaching themselves; who preach that one must not steal, yet steal; and the other things the Apostle says about them!

To them he says: “Therefore you are inexcusable, O every person who judges; for in judging another you condemn yourself, since you do the same things that you judge” (Rom. 2:1).

### 26

The Lord himself also says in the Gospel: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” (John 15:22).

Certainly, they would not have had no sin at all, since they were full of other great and numerous sins. Rather, he wishes this sin to be understood as one they would not have had if he had not come—a sin consisting in this: that, after hearing him, they did not believe in him. He asserts that they do not have this excuse by which they could say: “We did not hear, and therefore we did not believe.”

Human pride, presuming as it does upon the strength of free choice, thinks itself excused when what it does wrong appears to arise from ignorance rather than from the will.

[Note: [Col. 0883] Lov. reads, “it is the will that sins.” But the older editions and nine manuscripts have, “what sins appears to arise from ignorance rather than from the will.”]

### 27

According to this excuse, divine Scripture calls all those inexcusable whom it proves to sin knowingly. Yet God’s just judgment does not spare even those who have not heard: “For all who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law” (Rom. 2:12).

And although they may appear to excuse themselves, the one who knows that he made the human being upright and gave him a command of obedience does not admit this excuse. He also knows that sin passed even to subsequent generations only through the free choice of the will, which the human being used wrongly.

For those who did not sin are not condemned, since that sin passed from one person to all, in whom all had already sinned collectively before their own individual sins were committed (Rom. 5:12).

Accordingly, every sinner is inexcusable, whether through the guilt of origin or through the addition of personal will; whether he knows or is ignorant, whether he judges or does not judge. For ignorance itself is unquestionably sin in those who did not wish to understand, but in those who were unable to understand it is the punishment of sin. Therefore, in both groups there is not a just excuse, but a just condemnation.

### 28

For this reason the divine utterances call those who sin knowingly, not in ignorance, inexcusable, so that, according to the judgment of their pride—by which they place great confidence in the powers of their own will—they may see themselves to be inexcusable. They no longer have the excuse of ignorance, and they do not yet possess the righteousness which they presumed their will could supply.

[Note: [Col. 0884] Thus Bad., Am., Er., and manuscripts of better authority. Lov. reads: “and while there is not yet righteousness,” etc.]

But the one to whom the Lord has granted the grace both of knowing and of obeying says: “Through the law comes knowledge of sin” (Rom. 3:20); and: “I would not have known sin except through the law. For I would not have known covetousness unless the law said, ‘You shall not covet.’”

He does not wish the human being to be understood as ignorant of the law that commands, but as in need of the grace that liberates, when he says: “I delight in the law of God according to the inner person.” And after speaking not only of knowledge but also of delight in the law, he later says: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:7, 22, 24–25).

Therefore no one delivers from the wounds inflicted by that slaughterer except the grace of this Savior. No one releases those sold under sin from the bonds of the one who holds them captive except the grace of the Redeemer.

### 29

Accordingly, all who wish to be excused for their wickedness and iniquities are punished most justly, because those who are liberated are liberated only by grace. For if an excuse were just in that matter, they would no longer be liberated by grace but by justice.

But since grace alone liberates, it finds nothing just in the one whom it liberates: neither the will, nor the deed, nor even the excuse itself. For if the excuse is just, whoever uses it is liberated by merit, not by grace.

We know that by the grace of Christ some even of those who say, “Why does he still complain? For who can resist his will?” are liberated. If this is a just excuse, then they are no longer liberated by gratuitous grace, but because of the justice of this excuse. But if it is by grace that they are liberated, then this excuse is certainly not just.

For grace is truly grace by which a human being is liberated if he is not repaid according to the debt of justice.

Therefore nothing occurs in those who say, “Why does he still complain? For who can resist his will?” except what is read in the book of Solomon: “The folly of a man perverts his ways, but in his heart he blames God” (Prov. 19:3).

### 30

Although, then, God makes vessels of wrath for destruction, so that he may show his wrath and demonstrate his power, by which he also makes good use of the wicked, and so that he may make known the riches of his glory in the vessels of mercy, which he makes for honor—not an honor owed to the condemnable mass, but one bestowed by the generosity of his grace—nevertheless, in those same vessels of wrath, made for deserved dishonor because of the merit of the mass—that is, in human beings created indeed for the goods of nature, but destined for punishment because of their vices—he himself knows how to condemn the iniquity which truth most rightly reproves; he does not make it.

For just as human nature is attributed to his will, with no one doubting that it is worthy of praise, so guilt is attributed to the human will, with no one refusing to condemn it.

The human will either transmitted hereditary vice to subsequent generations, whom it contained within itself when it sinned, or acquired other vices as well, when each person lived recklessly in himself.

But no one is liberated or justified either from what is originally inherited, or from the evils which each person accumulates in his own life, whether by failing to understand or by refusing to understand, or which, even after being instructed by the law, he increases by adding transgression—except by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

This occurs not only through the remission of sins, but first through the very inspiration of faith and fear of God, through the health-giving gift of a disposition and effect of prayer, until he heals all our diseases, redeems our life from corruption, and crowns us with compassion and mercy (Ps. 103:3–4).

## CHAPTER VII

### 31

But those who think that God is a respecter of persons, if his mercy comes upon some in one and the same situation while his wrath remains upon others, lose the entire force of their human argument when they consider little children.

For, to say nothing for the moment of the fact that no one, however recently born from the maternal womb, is exempt from that punishment of which the Apostle says, “Through one trespass condemnation came upon all people,” from which only that one liberates us of whom he likewise says, “Through one act of righteousness justification leading to life came upon all people” (Rom. 5:18)—to omit this for the moment, and to speak only of little children: even they, terrified by the authority of the Gospel, or rather shattered by the most harmonious consensus of Christian peoples in the faith, concede without any resistance that no child enters the kingdom of heaven unless reborn of water and the Spirit (John 3:5).

What reason, I ask, will they offer here for one child being so governed that he leaves this life baptized, while another, handed over to the hands of unbelievers—or even dying among believers before being brought by them to baptism—expires? Will they attribute this to fate or to fortune? I do not think they will break out into such madness, however slight a claim they wish to retain to the Christian name.

### 32

Why, then, will no child enter the kingdom of heaven without receiving the bath of regeneration? Did the child choose for himself unbelieving or negligent parents from whom he would be born?

What shall I say about the countless unexpected and sudden deaths by which the infants even of devout Christian parents are often overtaken and snatched away from baptism, while, on the contrary, the children of sacrilegious people and enemies of Christ, somehow coming into the hands of Christians, depart this life not without the sacrament of regeneration?

What will those who contend that certain human merits must precede grace, lest God be a respecter of persons, say here? What merits preceded in this case?

If you consider the children themselves, they have no personal merits; the same mass is common to both. If you consider the parents, good are the parents whose children perished through sudden deaths without Christ’s baptism, while evil are those whose children, through some Christian authority, reached the sacraments of the Church.

And yet the providence of God—to whom our hairs are numbered, without whose will not even a sparrow falls to the ground (Matt. 10:29–30), who is neither constrained by fate, hindered by accidental events, nor corrupted by any injustice—does not provide for all the infants of his own children to be reborn to a heavenly inheritance, while it provides for some infants of the impious.

This child, born of married believers and received with the joy of his parents, becomes an exile from and stranger to the faith of his own people when he is suffocated by the sleepiness of his mother or nurse. That child, born of sacrilegious fornication, is exposed by his mother in cruel fear, taken up by the merciful piety of strangers, baptized through their Christian care, and becomes a companion and participant in the eternal kingdom.

Let them consider these things; let them reflect upon them. Here let them dare to say either that God is a respecter of persons in his grace or that he rewards preceding merits.

[Note: [Col. 0885] All manuscripts have this reading, except Lov., which has “and why nevertheless?”]

### 33

For even if they attempt to imagine some merits—whether good or evil—in people of mature age, what will they say about these infants? This one could not have acquired for himself, by any evil personal merits, the violence of the one who suffocated him; nor could that one, by good merits, have acquired the care of the one who baptized him.

They are guilty of excessive vanity and blindness if, even after considering these things, they do not deign to cry out with us:

“O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11:33).

Let them not oppose the gratuitous mercy of God with the most stubborn madness. Let them allow the Son of Man to seek and save, at whatever age, what had perished (Luke 19:10). Let them not dare to judge his inscrutable judgments concerning why, in one and the same situation, his mercy comes upon one person while his wrath remains upon another.

## CHAPTER VIII

### 34

For who are these people who would answer back to God, when he said concerning Rebecca, who had conceived twins by Isaac our father in a single act of intercourse, while they had not yet been born and had done neither good nor evil, that his purpose according to election might remain—namely, the election of grace, not of debt; the election by which he himself makes people chosen, rather than finding them so—that the elder would serve the younger?

In support of this interpretation the blessed Apostle also took up the testimony of a much later prophet: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. 1:2–3). Thus it was to be understood that what the prophet later made explicit had already existed, before they were born, in God’s predestination by grace.

For what did he love in Jacob before Jacob had done anything good, except the gratuitous gift of his mercy? And what did he hate in Esau before Esau had done anything evil, except original sin?

For he would not have loved righteousness in Jacob, since Jacob had performed none; nor would he have hated nature in Esau, since God himself had made that nature good.

### 35

It is astonishing, when they are pressed by these difficulties, into what precipices they hurl themselves while fearing the nets of truth.

“Therefore,” they say, “he hated one and loved the other before they were born because he foresaw their future works.”

Who would not be astonished that the Apostle lacked this exceptionally acute insight? For he did not see this when, as though a question opposed to him had been raised, he could have given precisely this brief, obvious, and—so they think—true and complete answer.

For after he had proposed the astonishing question of how it could rightly be said of those not yet born and having done neither good nor evil that God loved one and hated the other, he expressed the movement of the hearer by putting the very question to himself:

“What then shall we say?” he says. “Is there injustice with God? By no means.”

Here, then, was the place to say what they think: “For God foresaw their future works when he said that the elder would serve the younger.”

But the Apostle does not say this. Rather, lest anyone dare to glory in the merits of his own works, he wished what he said to serve the commendation of God’s grace and glory.

When he had said, “By no means is there injustice with God,” it is as though we were saying to him: “How do you demonstrate this, when you assert that it was said not from works but from him who calls, ‘The elder will serve the younger’?”

“For he says to Moses,” he continues: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion. So then it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy.”

Where now are the merits? Where are the works, whether past or future, accomplished or to be accomplished as though through the powers of free choice?

Did the Apostle not bring forth an open declaration in commendation of gratuitous grace—that is, true grace? Did God not make the wisdom of the heretics foolish?

### 36

What, then, was being done when the Apostle said this, when he recalled the example of these twins? What was he trying to persuade them of? What did he wish to impress upon them?

Precisely what their madness attacks, what the proud fail to grasp, what those who do not wish to understand refuse to accept: that, “being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they were not subject to the righteousness of God” (Rom. 10:3).

The Apostle was dealing sufficiently with grace itself, and for that reason he commended the children of promise. For what God promises, God alone accomplishes. It has a certain reason and truth to it that a human being should promise and God should accomplish; but for a human being to claim that he accomplishes what God has promised is the perverse judgment of proud impiety.

### 37

In commending the children of promise, therefore, he first displayed what was signified through Isaac, the son of Abraham.

For the work of God appears more evidently in one whom the ordinary order of nature did not beget from sterile wombs worn out by old age, so that in the children of God who were foretold as future, this might be a sign of divine rather than human action.

“In Isaac,” he says, “your offspring shall be called.” That is: it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God; rather, the children of promise are counted as offspring.

For the word of promise is this: “At this time I will come, and Sarah shall have a son.”

“And not only this,” he says, “but Rebecca also, having conceived by one act of intercourse with Isaac our father.”

Why did he add “by one act of intercourse” unless to prevent Jacob from boasting not only of his own merits, or of those of his parents, but even of the merits of that one father, as though his will had perhaps been changed for the better? He might otherwise have said that he was loved by the Creator because his father, when he fathered him, possessed better and more praiseworthy morals.

“By one act of intercourse,” he says: at that time there was one merit of the father in begetting them and one merit of the mother in conceiving them. For although their mother carried them enclosed in her womb until she gave birth, and perhaps changed her wills and affections, she changed them not for one but certainly for both, whom she carried together in her womb.

[Col. 0888]

### 38

The Apostle’s intention must therefore be observed: in commending grace, he does not wish the one of whom it was said, “Jacob I loved,” to glory except in the Lord.

When, from the same father and the same mother, by one act of intercourse, before they had done anything good or evil, God loves one and hates the other, Jacob should understand that, from that mass of original iniquity in which he sees his brother—who shared the same condition with him—deserving condemnation by justice, he himself could have been distinguished only by grace.

For, before they were born and before they had done good or evil, so that God’s purpose according to election might remain, it was said to him not from works but from him who calls: “The elder will serve the younger.”

### 39

The same Apostle most clearly demonstrates elsewhere that the election of grace is made without any preceding merits of works:

“So then,” he says, “at the present time there is a remnant according to the election of grace. But if it is by grace, it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace” (Rom. 11:5–6).

According to this grace, therefore, he consequently takes up the prophetic testimony as well: “As it is written,” he says, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”

And immediately he adds: “What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God? By no means.”

But why “By no means”? Was it because of the works which he foresaw both of them would perform? Rather, even that must be rejected:

“For he says to Moses: I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion. So then it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy.”

And so that, in the vessels prepared for destruction—the destruction owed to the condemned mass—they may recognize what mercy has bestowed upon the vessels made from the same mass for honor, he says:

“For Scripture says to Pharaoh: For this very purpose I raised you up, so that I might show my power in you, and so that my name might be proclaimed throughout all the earth.”

Finally, he concludes concerning both: “Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills.” This is done by one with whom there is no injustice. He therefore has mercy by a gratuitous gift, but he hardens by the most just merit.

### 40

But let the proud elevation of an unbeliever, or the condemnable excuse of one being punished, still say: “Why does he still complain? For who can resist his will?”

Let him say it, and let him hear what is fitting for a human being:

“O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (Rom. 9:20), and the rest, about which I have already discussed as much and as often as I could.

Let him hear these words and not despise them. If he despises them, let him discover that he was hardened even so that he might despise them. But if he does not despise them, let him believe that he was helped even so that he might not despise them—hardened according to what was owed, helped by grace.

[Note: [Col. 0888] Twelve manuscripts read: “hardened according to what was owed, helped gratuitously.”]

## CHAPTER IX

### 41

For even if God foresaw the future works of the two twins born to the patriarch Isaac—although we have already shown how blind such a statement is—who lived and grew old, and for that reason loved Jacob but hated Esau, no one can therefore say of infants who are to die that God foresaw their future works in deciding not to provide baptism for one but to provide it for another. For how can things that will not exist be called future?

### 42

“But,” they say, “in those whom he takes from this life, God foresees how each one would have lived if he had lived. Therefore, knowing that one would have lived wickedly, he causes him to die without baptism, punishing in him the evil works not that he committed but that he would have committed.”

If, then, evil works that have not even been committed are punished by divine judgment, let them first consider how falsely they promise that infants who die without baptism will not go to condemnation because they are not baptized on the grounds that they would have lived badly if they had lived. For if the bad life that would have occurred is punished, they will unquestionably be condemned precisely because of that bad life.

Next, if baptism is provided to those whom God knows would have lived well if they had lived, why are they not all preserved in the life which they would adorn with good works? Why do some of those who are baptized live very wickedly for a long time, and sometimes even proceed to apostasy?

Why did he not cast the first married pair of sinners out of paradise beforehand, since God certainly knew that they would sin, so that they might not commit there what would be unworthy of so holy a place—if sins not yet committed are justly punished?
