Finally, what is granted to the one who is snatched away, “lest wickedness change his understanding and deceit beguile his soul” (Wis. 4:11), if those things too are justly punished which, although he did not commit them, he would nevertheless have committed in living?

Finally, why is the sacrament of the bath of regeneration not provided more readily for one who is about to die, if he would have lived badly had he lived, so that the sins he would have committed might be forgiven him in baptism?

For who is so senseless as to deny that baptism can remit sins which, he says, can be punished without baptism?

## CHAPTER X

### 43

But in arguing against those who, although convicted on every side, still try to persuade people that God is the avenger even of sins not committed, we must fear that we may appear to be inventing these arguments against them, while they may be thought not so dull as to hold or attempt to persuade anyone of such views.

Nevertheless, unless I had heard them say these things, I would not have thought that they needed to be refuted.

For they are hemmed in both by the authority of the divine readings and by the ancient and steadfast rite of the Church, handed down and preserved in the baptism of infants. In that rite infants are most clearly shown to be liberated from the dominion of the devil, both when they are exorcized and when they answer through those by whom they are carried that they renounce him.

Finding no way out, they rush headlong into folly because they refuse to change their opinion.

### 44

They think they make one particularly acute point:

“How does sin pass into the children of believers, when we do not doubt that it was forgiven in their parents through baptism?”

As though, for that reason, carnal generation could not possess what only spiritual regeneration removes! Or as though, in baptism, the weakness of the desire of the flesh were immediately healed, just as its guilt is immediately abolished—by the grace of being reborn, not by the condition of being born.

Therefore whoever is born through this desire, even from one who has been reborn, will unquestionably bring harm to the one born, unless he too is similarly reborn.

But whatever difficulty there may be in this question, it does not prevent the workers in Christ’s field from baptizing infants for the remission of sins, whether they have been born of believers or of unbelievers, any more than it prevents farmers from transforming wild olive trees into cultivated olives by the work of grafting, whether the shoots arise from wild olives or from cultivated ones.

If this matter were put to a farmer in a way that demanded an answer—what causes it that, although an olive and a wild olive are different, nevertheless nothing but a wild olive grows from either seed—he would not abandon the work of grafting even if he could not solve the question. Otherwise, while he supposed that shoots arising from the seed of an olive could be nothing other than olives, his idle foolishness would cause the entire field to grow wild in bitter sterility.

### 45

As for what they devised when they were being crushed by the weight of truth—since the faithful Lord is in his words, and therefore his Church in no way deceitfully baptizes infants for the remission of sins, but, so that what is done may be done in faith, what is said is certainly done—who would not laugh at what they devised when this most evident mass of truth pressed upon them, however clever he might regard them?

For they say:

“Infants truly answer through the mouths of those who carry them that they believe in the remission of sins, but not because sins are remitted to them personally. Rather, they believe that remission takes place in the Church or in baptism, in which those are found who have sins, not those in whom there are none.”

Accordingly, they do not wish infants to be baptized for the remission of sins as though remission itself took place in them, since they maintain that they have no sin. Rather, although they are without sin, they are baptized in that baptism in which the remission of sins takes place in those who have sins.

### 46

It may be possible to refute this crafty subtlety more fully and sharply in a work undertaken at leisure. Nevertheless, according to their own cleverness, they find nothing to answer concerning the fact that infants are exorcized and exsufflated.

For this is unquestionably done deceitfully if the devil does not rule over them. But if he rules over them, and therefore they are not deceitfully exorcized and exsufflated, through what does he rule except through sin, since he is the prince of sinners?

Therefore, if they now blush and dare not say that these things are deceitfully performed in the Church, let them acknowledge that what had perished is sought even in infants. For what had perished had perished only because of sin, and it can neither be sought nor found except by grace.

But thanks be to God that, although they argue against the remission of sins so that it may not be believed to take place in infants, they nevertheless now confess that infants believe, though through the hearts and mouths of adults.

Therefore, just as they hear the Lord saying, “Whoever is not reborn of water and the Holy Spirit will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5), on account of which they concede that infants must be baptized, so let them hear the same Lord saying, “Whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16:16). For just as they confess that infants are reborn through the ministry of those who baptize, so they also confess that they believe through the hearts and mouths of those who profess the faith.

Let them therefore dare to say that an innocent person will be condemned by a just God if he is bound by no bond of original sin.

### 47

If this letter is long and burdensome amid your occupations, forgive me. For, in writing these things to you, and in conversing with you—even though I was occupied with your letters, signs of your goodwill toward us—I too have forced myself to interrupt my own occupations.

If you know of anything else they devise against the Catholic faith, and whatever you, with faithful and wholly pastoral love, discuss against them so that they may not devastate the weak members of the Lord’s flock, make it known to us.

Through the restlessness of heretics, our diligence is, as it were, awakened from the sleep of indolence, so that we may search the Scriptures more vigilantly and find means of confronting them before they harm Christ’s fold. Thus, through the manifold grace of the Savior, God turns even what the enemy contrives for destruction into assistance, because “all things work together for good for those who love God” (Rom. 8:28).

May you always live in God, remembering us, dearest brother.

## LETTER CXCV

[Note: [Col. 0891] Compared with c. mr. tt., two vd., six v., Am., Bad., Er., Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0891] Elsewhere numbered 25; the letter that was numbered 195 is now in the Appendix as 14. Probably written in the year 418.]

Jerome to Augustine, congratulating him that he had deserved the hatred of all heretics; he rejoices that this hatred is shared with him.

To the holy and most blessed Pope Augustine, Jerome.

At all times I have venerated Your Beatitude with the honor that is fitting, and I have loved the Lord Savior dwelling in you. But now, if possible, we add something in abundance and bring our tribute to fullness, so that we may not allow even a single hour to pass without mentioning your name—you who stood firm against the blowing winds with the ardor of faith and preferred, insofar as it lay within you, to be liberated alone from Sodom rather than remain among those who were perishing.

Your prudence knows what I mean. Well done for your courage! You are celebrated throughout the world. Catholics venerate and honor you as once again the founder of the ancient faith. And what is a sign of greater glory, all heretics detest you—and they persecute me with the same hatred, so that those whom they cannot kill with swords they may kill by their wish.

May the clemency of Christ the Lord preserve you unharmed and mindful of me, my venerable and most blessed lord and pope.

## LETTER CXCVI

[Note: [Col. 0891] Reviewed against a. bg. bl. c. cc. ff. g. gv. l. n. r. rm. s. vc.; two sb.; two t.; four v.; Am., Bad., Er., Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0891] Elsewhere numbered 200; the letter that was numbered 196 is now in the Appendix as 15. Written toward the end of the year 418.]

Augustine to Bishop Asellicus, explaining the usefulness of the Mosaic law, which Christians are not permitted to observe according to the custom of the Jews. He teaches that Christians are truly Israelites in the spiritual sense; nevertheless, this name should not commonly be applied to them. He briefly notes that the Pelagians have fallen into condemnable Judaism.

To the most blessed lord, brother, and fellow bishop Asellicus, Augustine sends greetings in the Lord.

## CHAPTER ONE
1. The letter of Your Holiness which you sent to the venerable old man Donatianus [Note: [Col. 0891] Primate of the province of Byzacena.] concerning the controversy over avoiding Judaism, he himself graciously sent on to me and urgently commanded me to answer it. Fearing to disregard him, I shall answer as best I can with the Lord’s help. I consider it pleasing also to Your Charity that, by writing to you, I have not refused to obey him who ordered me to do so, and whom both of us venerate for his merits.

2. The apostle Paul teaches that Christians, especially those coming from the Gentiles, ought not to judaize, when he says: “I said to Peter before everyone: If you, though you are a Jew, live as a Gentile and not as a Jew, how can you compel the Gentiles to judaize?” And he continued: “We are Jews by nature, and not sinners from the Gentiles. Yet, knowing that a person is not justified by works of the Law but through faith in Jesus Christ, we too have believed in Christ Jesus, so that we might be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the Law; for by works of the Law no flesh shall be justified” (Gal. 2:14–16).

3. But it is not only those works of the Law that belong to the former sacraments and that Christians no longer observe after the New Testament was revealed—such as circumcision of the foreskin, bodily cessation from work on the Sabbath, abstinence from certain foods, the sacrifice of animals, new moons, unleavened bread, and other things of this kind. Even what was said in the Law, “You shall not covet” (Exod. 20:17)—which, of course, no one doubts must also be said to Christians—does not justify a person except through faith in Jesus Christ and the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

The same apostle himself says: “What then shall we say? Is the Law sin? Certainly not. Yet I did not know sin except through the Law; for I would not have known covetousness unless the Law said, ‘You shall not covet.’ But sin, taking an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me every kind of covetousness. For apart from the Law sin is dead. Once I was alive without the Law; but when the commandment came, sin revived, and I died. And the commandment that was meant for life was found by me to be for death. For sin, taking an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me. Therefore the Law is indeed holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous, and good. Did then what is good become death to me? Certainly not. Rather, sin, so that it might appear as sin, worked death in me through what is good, so that through the commandment sin might become exceedingly sinful. For we know that the Law is spiritual; but I am carnal, sold under sin. For I do not understand what I do; for I do not do what I want, but I do what I hate. But if I do what I do not want, I agree with the Law, that it is good” (Rom. 7:7–16).

4. Thus, in these apostolic words we see that the Law is not only not sin, but is also holy, and that the commandment is holy, righteous, and good—the commandment that says, “You shall not covet.” But sin deceives through what is good and through it kills those who, although carnal, think that they can fulfill the spiritual Law by their own powers. Consequently, they become not only sinners—which they would be even if they had not received the Law—but also transgressors, which they would not be unless they had received the Law. For he says elsewhere: “Where there is no Law, neither is there transgression” (Rom. 4:15). Thus the Law entered in, as he himself testifies elsewhere, “so that the trespass might increase.” But where trespass increased, grace abounded all the more (Rom. 5:20).

## CHAPTER II

5. This, then, is the usefulness of the Law: it reveals a person to himself, so that he may recognize his weakness and see how, through prohibition, carnal desire is increased rather than healed. For the things that are forbidden are desired more ardently, while the person who is carnal is compelled to observe what is commanded spiritually.

But a person who fulfills the spiritual Law does not become spiritual through the Law itself, but through grace: that is, not through command, but through gift; not through the letter commanding, but through the Spirit assisting. A person begins, according to grace, to be renewed in the inner person (2 Cor. 4:16), so that he may do with his mind what he loves and not consent to the flesh when it does what he hates. This means not that he does not covet at all, but that he does not follow his covetous desires.

This is indeed so great a thing that, if it were accomplished in every respect, and although the desires of sin remain while we are in this body of death, we nevertheless gave assent to none of them, we would have no reason to say to our Father who is in heaven, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12). Yet even then we would not already be what we shall be when this mortal nature has put on immortality. For then we shall not only obey no sinful desire; there will be no such desires at all, to which we might be commanded not to give obedience.

6. When it is said, “It is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me” (Rom. 7:17), this refers to the desire of the flesh, which produces its movements in us even when we do not obey them, so long as sin does not reign in our mortal body, causing us to obey its desires, and so long as we do not present our members as weapons of unrighteousness to sin (Rom. 6:12–13).

In this righteousness, which has not yet been brought to completion, we must persevere and make progress until eventually we arrive at its completion, where the desire of sin will not need to be restrained or curbed, but will not exist at all. This is what the Law established by saying, “You shall not covet”—not because we are capable of achieving it here and now, but because it is toward this that we are to advance.

Yet this comes about not through the Law, which commands it, but through faith, which obtains it; not through the letter, by which it is commanded, but through the Spirit, by whom it is given. It therefore comes not through the merits of the person who works, but through the grace of the Savior who bestows.

The usefulness of the Law, then, is to convict a person of his weakness and compel him to implore the medicine of grace that is in Christ. For “everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved” (Joel 2:32; Acts 2:21). “How then shall they call upon him in whom they have not believed?” And how shall they believe in him whom they have not heard? Hence shortly afterward he says: “Therefore faith is from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ.”

7. Since this is so, those who delight in being Israelites according to the flesh and boast in the Law apart from the grace of Christ are the ones of whom the apostle also says that, “being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they have not submitted to God’s righteousness” (Rom. 10:3, 14, 17).

He calls God’s righteousness that which comes from God to a person; but he calls “their own” that which they think sufficient for themselves to carry out the commandments without the help and gift of the one who gave the Law.

Those who profess to be Christians but oppose the grace of Christ in such a way that they think they can fulfill the divine commandments by human powers are like them. Thus they too, “being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, have not submitted to God’s righteousness,” and, although not in name, nevertheless judaize in their error.

This class of people had found Pelagius and Celestius as its leaders, the most vigorous defenders of this impiety. By a recent judgment of God, through his diligent and faithful servants, they have been deprived even of communion with the Catholic Church, and because of their unrepentant hearts they still persist in their condemnation.

8. Whoever seeks to remain separate from this carnal and animal—and therefore not unjustly reprehensible and damnable—Judaism must not only keep himself apart from those ancient observances which, after the New Testament had been revealed and the things that they signified as future had come, unquestionably ceased to be necessary, so that no one may be judged concerning food and drink, or a festival, new moon, or Sabbaths, “which are a shadow of things to come” (Col. 2:16–17).

He must also understand, embrace, and observe those things commanded in the Law that serve to shape the conduct of the faithful—that is, so that “having denied impiety and worldly desires, we may live temperately, righteously, and devoutly in this age” (Tit. 2:12). Among these is the commandment that the apostle especially chose to commend from the Law: “You shall not covet,” together with all that is commanded in the Law concerning love of God and neighbor without any symbolic sacraments. Upon these two commandments, the Lord Christ himself says, the whole Law and the Prophets depend (Matt. 22:40).

A person must receive and embrace these commandments, and must not doubt that they are to be observed, in such a way that whatever progress he makes in them he attributes not to himself but to the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

## CHAPTER III

9. Nevertheless, when someone has become in this way a true and genuine Christian, it is rightly asked whether he should also be called a Jew or an Israelite.

If this is understood not according to the flesh but according to the spirit, he ought not to apply that name to himself in ordinary speech, but should retain it in spiritual understanding, lest, because of the ambiguity of the term—which everyday speech does not distinguish—he appear to profess something hostile to the Christian name.

The blessed apostle himself clarifies and resolves this question for us—namely, whether a person who is a Christian can also be understood as a Jew or Israelite—when he says:

“Circumcision indeed profits you if you keep the Law; but if you are a transgressor of the Law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision. Therefore, if the uncircumcised person keeps the righteous requirements of the Law, will not his uncircumcision be counted as circumcision? And will not the uncircumcision which is by nature, fulfilling the Law, judge you who, with letter and circumcision, are a transgressor of the Law? For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is that circumcision which is outward in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter. His praise is not from human beings but from God” (Rom. 2:25–29).

When, therefore, we hear the apostle of Christ commending to us a Jew inwardly—not by circumcision of the flesh but of the heart, and in the spirit rather than the letter—who is this except a Christian?

10. Thus we are Jews not carnally but spiritually, just as we are Abraham’s offspring not according to the flesh, as are those who boast proudly in that carnal name, but according to the spirit of faith, which they do not possess.

For we know that we were promised when God said to him, “I have appointed you the father of many nations” (Gen. 17:4). We know how much the apostle says about this matter.

“For we say,” he writes, “that faith was counted to Abraham as righteousness. How then was it counted? When he was circumcised, or while he was uncircumcised? Not while circumcised, but while uncircumcised. And he received the sign of circumcision, the seal of the righteousness of the faith he had while uncircumcised, so that he might be the father of all who believe while uncircumcised, so that righteousness might be counted to them also; and the father of circumcision—not only to those who are of the circumcision, but also to those who follow the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had while uncircumcised.”

And shortly afterward:

“Therefore it is by faith, so that the promise may rest on grace and be secure for all the offspring—not only for the one who is of the Law, but also for the one who is of the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all, as it is written: ‘I have appointed you the father of many nations’” (Rom. 4:9–17).

Likewise, in the Letter to the Galatians:

“Just as Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness, understand therefore that those who are of faith are sons of Abraham. And foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, Scripture announced the Gospel beforehand to Abraham: ‘In you all the nations shall be blessed.’ Thus those who are of faith are blessed with faithful Abraham.”

And somewhat later in the same Letter:

“Brothers, I speak in human terms: even a humanly ratified covenant no one annuls or adds conditions to. The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his offspring. He does not say, ‘And to offsprings,’ as though referring to many, but as referring to one: ‘And to your offspring,’ who is Christ.”

And shortly afterward:

“For you are all one in Christ Jesus. And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to the promise” (Gal. 3:6–29).

11. According to this apostolic understanding, then, Jews who are not Christians are found, although they derive their origin from Abraham’s flesh, not to be Abraham’s sons. For when he says, “Understand therefore that those who are of faith are sons of Abraham,” he clearly indicates that those who are not of faith are not Abraham’s sons.

Accordingly, unless Abraham is the father of the Jews in the same way as he is ours, what benefit do they gain from having arisen from his flesh and retained the name without its power [Note: [Col. 0895] One of the Vatican manuscripts reads “truth” instead.]?

When they pass over to Christ and begin to be Abraham’s sons by faith, then they will be Jews not outwardly but inwardly, through circumcision of the heart; in the spirit, not in the letter; and their praise will be not from human beings but from God.

Separated from this faith, they will be reckoned among the broken branches of that olive tree into whose root, as the same apostle says, the wild olive—that is, the Gentiles—is grafted (Rom. 11:16–25). This grafting is certainly not accomplished through the flesh but through faith; not through the Law but through grace; not through the letter but through the spirit; not through circumcision of the flesh but of the heart; not outwardly but inwardly; and not through praise from human beings but from God.

Thus every Christian is not a carnal but a spiritual son of Abraham, and likewise not a carnal but a spiritual Jew, and not a carnal but a spiritual Israelite.

For the apostle also speaks of this name in the following way:

“For not all who are from Israel are Israel; nor because they are Abraham’s offspring are they all sons. Rather, ‘In Isaac shall your offspring be called.’ That is, it is not the children of the flesh who are children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring” (Rom. 9:6–8).

Are these not great wonders and a profound mystery: that many born from Israel are not Israel, and that many are not sons although they are Abraham’s offspring?

How are they not, and how are we [Note: [Col. 0896] Bad., Am., Er.: “How then are they not, and how are we?”]? They are not children of the promise belonging to the grace of Christ, but children of the flesh bearing an empty name. Accordingly, they are not Israel as we are, nor are we Israel as they are. We are Israel according to spiritual regeneration; they according to carnal generation.

12. We must observe and distinguish that one Israel is the Israel who received the name because of the flesh, while another is the Israel who, because of the spirit, obtained the reality signified by that name.

Were Israelites born from Hagar, Sarah’s slave woman? Was not Ishmael born from her, and did he not propagate by his offspring the nation not of the Israelites but of the Ishmaelites? For Israel came from Sarah through Isaac, who was born to Abraham according to the promise.

Yet, although the matter stands thus according to the succession of the flesh, when we arrive at spiritual understanding, carnal Israelites who derive their origin from her flesh are found not to belong to Sarah, while Christians belong to her instead. They are not, like Ishmael, sons of the flesh according to the flesh, but, like Isaac, sons of the promise, belonging not to Isaac’s carnal offspring but to the spiritual mystery.

Thus the apostle speaks to the Galatians:

“Tell me, you who desire to be under the Law, do you not hear the Law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman. But the one by the slave woman was born according to the flesh, while the one by the free woman was born through promise. These things are spoken allegorically. For these women are two covenants: one from Mount Sinai, bearing children for slavery, which is Hagar. For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia, corresponding to the present Jerusalem, and it is in slavery with her children. But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother. For it is written:

‘Rejoice, barren woman who does not give birth; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of the woman who has a husband.’

Now we, brothers, like Isaac, are children of promise. But just as at that time the one who was born according to the flesh persecuted the one born according to the spirit, so it is now. But what does Scripture say? ‘Cast out the slave woman and her son; for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman.’

Therefore, brothers, we are not children of the slave woman but of the free woman—the freedom with which Christ set us free” (Gal. 4:21–31).

13. Behold: according to this spiritual and apostolic understanding, we belong rather to the free Sarah, although we derive no carnal descent from her. The Jews, however, who derive carnal descent from her, are shown rather to belong to the slave woman Hagar, from whom they do not derive their carnal descent.

The same great and profound mystery is found in the grandsons of Abraham and Sarah, that is, in the sons of Isaac and Rebekah, the twins Esau and Jacob, who was afterward called Israel.

Speaking of this, the same apostle, after recalling through Isaac the children of promise who belong to the grace of Christ, says:

“And not only that, but Rebekah also, having conceived by one man, Isaac our father—for although they had not yet been born and had done nothing good or evil, so that God’s purpose according to election might stand, not because of works but because of him who calls—it was said to her, ‘The elder shall serve the younger’; as it is written, ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated’” (Rom. 9:10–13).

This apostolic and catholic teaching clearly indicates to us that, according to the origin of the flesh, the Jews—that is, the Israelites—belong to Sarah, while the Ishmaelites belong to Hagar; but according to the mystery of the spirit, Christians belong to Sarah and Jews to Hagar.

Likewise, according to the origin of the flesh, the nation of the Idumaeans belongs to Esau, who was also called Edom, while the nation of the Jews belongs to Jacob, who was also called Israel. But according to the mystery of the spirit, the Jews belong to Esau, and Christians to Israel.

Thus what is written is fulfilled: “The elder shall serve the younger”—that is, the people of the Jews, born first, shall serve the later-born people of the Christians.

Behold how we are Israel by divine adoption, not boasting in human kinship; Jews not outwardly but inwardly; not by the letter but by the spirit; not by circumcision of the flesh but of the heart.

## CHAPTER IV

14. Although these things are so, we must not confuse the usage of human speech through foolish talk, nor mix commonly used terms with confused meanings when distinguishing realities. Thus no one should attempt, by an unusual term, to call those who are Christians and are called Christians by the most customary designation “Jews”; nor, while being and being called a Christian, should anyone take pleasure in the name “Israelite.”

What must always be understood as a mystery, but expressed more sparingly with the lips, should not be preferred in everyday speech through foolish eccentricity—or, if one may say so, through ignorant knowledge.

Did the apostles, through whom we learned these things, not know that we are rather Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to Isaac and the promise; Jews in spirit, not in the letter; circumcised in heart, not in the flesh; and Israel not according to the flesh, but the Israel of God?

They certainly knew these matters much more wisely and surely than we do. Nevertheless, in ordinary speech they called Jews and Israelites those who, coming according to the flesh from Abraham’s stock, were universally called by that name.

15. “Jews ask for signs,” says the apostle Paul, “and Greeks seek wisdom; but we preach Christ crucified: to the Jews a stumbling block, but to the Gentiles foolishness; yet to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the Power of God and the Wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:22–24).

Those whom he called Greeks he also designated by the name “Gentiles,” because this language is especially prominent among the Gentiles. Yet he called Jews those whom everyone calls by that name.

For if Christians themselves are Jews, then Christ crucified is a stumbling block to Christians, concerning whom it was said, “To the Jews a stumbling block.” Who except a completely insane person could think this?

Again he says: “Be without offense to Jews and Greeks and the Church of God” (1 Cor. 10:32). How could he distinguish these groups if, in ordinary speech, he ought also to call the Church of God “Jews”?

Again he says: “Those whom he also called, not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles.” How did he call them from the Jews if he rather called them from those who were not Jews, so that they might become Jews?

And concerning the Israelites:

“What then shall we say? The Gentiles, who did not pursue righteousness, have attained righteousness—the righteousness that comes from faith. But Israel, pursuing a law of righteousness, did not attain the law of righteousness. Why? Because it was not from faith but as though from works; for they stumbled over the stone of stumbling” (Rom. 9:30–32).

Again:

“But to Israel he says: ‘All day long I stretched out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people’” (Rom. 10:21).

And he continues:

“I ask, then, has God rejected his people? Certainly not. For I too am an Israelite, from the offspring of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew” (Rom. 11:1–2).

How did the apostle here call Israel disobedient and contrary if Christians are Israel? Or how did he call himself an Israelite? Was it because he had become a Christian? Certainly not, but because according to the flesh he had come from Abraham’s offspring, from the tribe of Benjamin. We are not so according to the flesh, although according to faith we are Abraham’s offspring and therefore also Israel.

One thing is what a higher understanding of the mystery recognizes; another is what the everyday usage of the term requires.

16. Finally, this Aptus [Note: [Col. 0898] The editions read *Aptius*. But the Vatican manuscripts and nearly all the others have *Aptus*.]—I do not know who he is—about whom you wrote that he teaches Christians to judaize, calls himself, as Your Holiness indicated, a Jew and an Israelite in such a way that he forbids the foods from which, as suited that time, the Law given through God’s holy servant Moses forbade people to eat, and urges the observance of the other practices of that period, now abolished and removed from among Christians.

The apostle calls these practices “shadows of things to come” (Col. 2:16–17), so that prophecy may be understood in them and their observance shown to have now been annulled.

From this it is evident why this Aptus wishes to be called an Israelite and a Jew: not spiritually, but entirely carnally.

We, however, are not bound by those observances that were annulled after the New Testament was revealed. At the same time, we have learned and teach that the commandments of the Law still necessary for the present age—such as, “You shall not commit adultery,” “You shall not commit murder,” and “You shall not covet” (Exod. 20:13–17), and any other commandment summed up in this saying, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Rom. 13:9)—must be observed not by human powers, as though we were establishing our own righteousness, but by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, in that righteousness which comes to us from him.

Yet for this reason we do not deny that we are Abraham’s offspring, to whom the apostle says, “You are therefore Abraham’s offspring” (Gal. 3:29); nor that we are Jews inwardly, of whom the same apostle says:

“For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is that circumcision which is outward in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter, whose praise is not from human beings but from God” (Rom. 2:28–29).

Nor do we deny that we are spiritual Israelites, belonging to the one to whom it was foretold that the younger would be served by the elder.

But we do not improperly apply these names to ourselves; we retain them as an understanding of mysteries, not parade them with an insolent use of words.

## LETTER CXCVII

[Note: [Col. 0899] Corrected against manuscripts bl. cb. ff. r. vc.; two sb.; two t.; two v.; Am., Bad., Er., Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0899] Formerly 78; the letter that was numbered 197 is now 16 in the Appendix. It appears to have been written toward the end of 418 or at the beginning of 419.]

Augustine to Hesychius, bishop of Salona, concerning the final day of the world, which should not be investigated, and concerning Daniel’s Weeks.

To the most blessed lord HESYCHIUS [Note: [Col. 0899] He was bishop of Salona, as is shown by our German and Corbie manuscripts, and also by Augustine in *The City of God*, book 20, chapter 5. He was not among the Africans, as is sufficiently clear from Letter 199, section 46: “For there are among us, that is, in Africa,” etc., but among the Dalmatians; and, we think, he was the same man to whom Pope Zosimus wrote in 418.] AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

1. When your son, our fellow presbyter Cornutus, returned, he brought me the letter of Your Veneration, by which you graciously visited my lowliness. At last I am paying my debt by replying, and offering the service of a return greeting. I commend myself greatly to your prayers, which are most acceptable to the Lord, most blessed brother.

Concerning the prophetic sayings, or prophecies, about which you wished me to write something, I thought it better to send Your Beatitude the explanations of those same passages by the holy Jerome, a most learned man, excerpted from his works—perhaps you do not have them.

But if you already had them and they did not satisfy your inquiry, please do not hesitate to write back to me with your opinion of them and with your own understanding of those prophetic oracles.

For my part, I think especially that Daniel’s Weeks are to be understood in relation to the time that has already elapsed. As for the Savior’s coming, which is awaited at the end, I do not dare to calculate its time. Nor do I think that any prophet set a number of years for this matter. Rather, what the Lord himself said prevails: “No one can know the times which the Father has placed in his own authority” (Acts 1:7).

2. Concerning what he says elsewhere, “But of that day and hour no one knows” (Matt. 24:36), there are people who understand it in such a way that they think they can calculate the times, while no one knows only the day and the hour themselves.

I shall pass over how Scripture commonly uses “day” or “hour” also to mean a period of time. But certainly the statement about ignorance of the times was made with the greatest clarity.

When the Lord was asked about this by his disciples, he said: “No one can know the times which the Father has placed in his own authority.” He did not say “the day” or “the hour,” but “the times,” which ordinarily do not refer to a brief span such as a day or an hour—especially if we consider the Greek expression. We know that this book, where these words are written, was translated into our language from Greek, although the meaning could not be expressed fully in Latin.

For the Greek reads: *χρόνους ἢ καιρούς*—“times or appointed seasons.” Our translators call both words *tempora*, “times,” whether *χρόνους* or *καιρούς*, although the two terms have a distinction between them that should not be neglected.

The Greeks call *καιροί* certain times—not those that pass in extended periods of duration, but those perceived as opportune or inopportune in relation to circumstances, such as harvest, vintage, heat, cold, peace, war, and similar things. They call *χρόνοι* the durations of time themselves.

3. The apostles themselves certainly did not ask the question as though they wished to know one final day or hour—that is, a small portion of a day—but whether the time had already arrived when the kingdom would be restored to Israel.

Then they heard: “No one can know the times which the Father has placed in his own authority”—that is, *χρόνους ἢ καιρούς*. If this were rendered in Latin as “times or opportunities,” the statement would still not be fully expressed, because whether the times are opportune or inopportune, they are called *καιροί*.

To calculate the times—that is, the *χρόνοι*—so that we may know when the end of this age or the Lord’s coming will occur seems to me nothing other than a desire to know what he himself said no one could know.

4. That time will certainly not be opportune before the Gospel has been preached throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations. For the Savior’s statement on this matter is read with complete clarity:

“This Gospel of the kingdom shall be preached throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come” (Matt. 24:14).

What does “then it will come” mean except that it will not come before then? How long afterward it will come is uncertain to us; but we must certainly not doubt that it will not come before then.

If the servants of God undertook the task of traveling through the world and gathering, as far as they could, information about which nations remain where the Gospel has not yet been preached, we could in some measure infer from this how far the time is from the end of the age.

But if, because of certain inaccessible and inhospitable regions, it is not believed possible for the servants of God to travel through the world and reliably report how many and what nations still lack the Gospel of Christ, I consider it even less possible to determine from Scripture how many periods of time will remain until the end, since we read in it: “No one can know the times which the Father has placed in his own authority.”

Therefore, even if it had already been reported to us with complete certainty that the Gospel was being preached among all nations, we still could not say how much time remained until the end. We could only rightly say that it was drawing nearer and nearer.

Unless someone perhaps replies that, because the Gospel was preached with such speed among the Roman peoples and among most of the barbarians, and because some peoples were converted to the faith of Christ not gradually but suddenly, it is not incredible that within a few years—not necessarily within the lifetime of those of us who are already old, but within the lifetime of young people who will come to old age—the Gospel could fill all the nations that remain.

But if this will happen, it can more easily be proved by experience after it has occurred than discovered by reading before it occurs.

[Col. 0901] 5. The opinion of a certain person compelled me to say this—one whom the presbyter Jerome also marks as rash [Note: [Col. 0901] Jerome, on Daniel, chapter 9.] because he dared to interpret Daniel’s Weeks as referring to Christ’s future coming rather than to his past coming.

If, in view of your greater merits, the Lord has revealed or should reveal something better to the holy humility of your heart, I ask you to grant us a share in it and to communicate it to us. Receive this reply of mine as coming from a man who would certainly rather possess knowledge than ignorance concerning what you asked me, but who, because I have not yet been able to obtain it, prefer to confess cautious ignorance rather than profess false knowledge.

## LETTER CXCVIII

[Note: [Col. 0901] Corrected against the same manuscripts, except one sb., and additionally against gg.]

[Note: [Col. 0901] Formerly 79; the letter that was numbered 198 is now 148. It was written shortly after the preceding letter.]

Hesychius to Augustine, indicating that, after considering the divine testimonies concerning the end of the age, he thinks that the day and hour are sought in vain; nevertheless, he teaches that it is possible to recognize from the signs whether the time of Christ’s coming is already at hand, and that this coming should be piously awaited as soon.

To the most blessed lord, and most sincerely beloved and venerable brother and fellow bishop AUGUSTINE, HESYCHIUS sends greetings in the Lord.

1. As I longed for and awaited him, our holy fellow presbyter Cornutus brought me the letter you sent. It made me rejoice that you graciously retain a good memory of us, and that, in a few words of your own, spoken from your holy mind, you briefly indicated to me what I had asked.

You also appended several passages from the works of the holy fellow presbyter Jerome, so that by reading his work on the Holy Scriptures I might resolve my question.

Since you graciously asked us to communicate by letter what we thought about these questions, I have written below concerning the matters about which I read in your letter, insofar as the limited understanding of my mediocrity has been able to perceive or comprehend them.

2. Since everything is accomplished by the judgment and power of God Almighty, the creator of the whole creation—both what has already happened and what is still to happen—are made known through the voices of the holy Prophets, who, before the things that were to happen occurred, spoke to human beings by the divine will, it is sufficiently astonishing if God determined that those things which he wished to be foretold could not at all reach human understanding.

This seems to follow from the passage in which the Lord spoke to the blessed apostles, saying: “No one can know the times which the Father has placed in his own authority.”

First, however, in the most ancient books of the churches it is not written, “No one can”; rather, it is written: “It is not yours to know the times or moments which the Father has placed in his own authority.” The logic of the statement is properly completed by the following words: “But you shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in Judea, and in Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (Acts 1:7–8).

Thus he did not intend the apostles to be understood as witnesses of the consummation of the world, but of his name and resurrection.

3. For the Lord himself gives instruction concerning the recognition of the times: “Who, then, is the faithful and wise servant whom [Col. 0902] the master appointed over his household, to give them food at the proper time? Blessed is that servant whom his master, when he comes, finds doing so.” Christ’s household is nourished by the word of preaching, and the faithful servant is found to be the one who, at the proper time, supplies necessary food to believers awaiting the Lord. For the wicked servant is reproved in this way: “But if that wicked servant says, ‘My master is delaying his coming,’ his master will come on a day on which he does not expect him and at an hour of which he is unaware”; and so forth. Again, he rebukes them for failing to recognize the time, saying: “Hypocrites, you know how to assess the appearance of the sky; why do you not recognize this time?” (Luke 12:42–43, 45, 56). The Apostle likewise says: “In the last days perilous times will come” (2 Tim. 3:1); and so forth. Again, the Apostle says: “Concerning the times and seasons, brothers, we have no need to write to you. For you yourselves know very well that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night. When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them, like labor pains upon a pregnant woman, and they will not escape” (1 Thess. 5:1–3). Again, the Apostle says: “Do you not remember that when I was still with you I used to tell you these things? And now you know what restrains him, so that he may be revealed in his own time. For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work; only let the one who now restrains it continue to restrain it, until he is removed from the midst. And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth” (2 Thess. 2:5–8). Again, in the Gospel the Lord reproves the Jews: “And you too, if you had recognized the time of your visitation, perhaps you would have remained; but now these things have been hidden from your eyes” (Luke 19:42). And the Lord thus preaches to the Jews: “Repent; the times have been fulfilled; believe the Gospel” (Mark 1:15). He rightly said to the Jews that their times had been fulfilled, because their times ended thirty-five or forty years after his preaching. And in Daniel: “Until the beast was killed and perished, and its body was given to be burned; and the dominion of the other beasts was taken away, while an extension of life was granted to them for a time and a time”—which in Greek is called ἕως χρόνου καὶ καιροῦ, “until a time and a season.” And it continues: “And behold, one like a Son of Man came with the clouds of heaven” (Dan. 7:11–13). The mystery of the beast and the transfer of the dominion of the other beasts is clear to those who understand Scripture.

4. The Lord’s coming must be loved and awaited. For there is great blessedness for those who love his coming, as the blessed Apostle Paul testifies: “For the rest,” he says, “the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day—and not only to me, but also to those who love his coming” (2 Tim. 4:8). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13:43). Likewise the prophet says: “For behold, darkness and gloom will cover the earth over the nations; but the Lord will appear upon you, and his majesty will be seen upon you” (Isa. 60:2). Again the prophet says: “But those who wait for the Lord will rejoice with strength; they will grow wings like eagles, they will run and not grow weary, they will walk and not hunger” (Isa. 40:31). Many such passages are found to pertain to the blessedness of those who love the Lord’s coming.

5. That no one can calculate the measures of the times is clear [Col. 0903]. The Gospel indeed says, “No one knows that day or hour”; but, insofar as my understanding permits, I say that neither the day, nor the month, nor the year of his coming can be known. I ought, however, to see and believe the signs that accompany his coming, to await it, and to give this food to believers, so that those who await his coming may love it—he who said, “When you see all these things, know that he is near, at the doors.”

The Gospel and prophetic signs that have been fulfilled among us therefore make the Lord’s coming known. For those who seek, or those who criticize, seek in vain to include days and years within a calculation, since it is written: “Unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved; but for the sake of the elect those days will be shortened” (Matt. 24:36, 33, 22). It is certain that the time which the Lord, who established the times, is to shorten cannot be calculated. Yet that his coming has drawn near is shown by the fact that we see some of the signs of his coming fulfilled in the things that have taken place. He also says again: “When these things begin to happen, straighten up and lift up your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.”

The signs he said were to be seen are clearly set out in the Gospel of Saint Luke: “Jerusalem will be trampled by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled.” This has happened, and no one can doubt that it is happening. It continues: “And there will be signs in the sun, and in the moon, and in the stars, and on earth distress among the nations.” The things we suffer are forced upon us to confess, even if the will should perhaps not care; for it is clear that at one and the same time signs in heaven and the distress of the nations on earth are seen and endured by human beings [Note: Perhaps he is referring to that notable eclipse of the sun which, historians report, occurred on 19 July 418, and which was followed by such great drought—so Philostorgius writes—that it brought about everywhere the unusual death of many people and other animals.]. And it continues: “People fainting from fear and expectation of what is coming upon the whole world.” It is certain that in our times no country and no place is free from affliction or humiliation, as it was said, “from fear and expectation of what is coming upon the whole world” (Luke 21:24–28). All the signs which the Gospel above makes clear to its readers have, for the most part, been fulfilled.

6. As for what was said, “This Gospel will be preached throughout the whole world, and then the end will come” (Matt. 24:14): first, the Lord’s own promise was that his Apostles would become witnesses to his name and resurrection in Jerusalem, in Judea, in Samaria, and to the ends of the earth. The Apostle teaches this with that authority: “But I ask: Have they not heard? Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Rom. 10:18). Again: “Because of the hope laid up for you, which you heard before in the word of truth, the Gospel that has come to you, just as in the whole world it is bearing fruit and growing” (Col. 1:5–6).

But the faith announced among the nations by the Apostles [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts and all the Gallican manuscripts except one read “initiated.”] had many persecutors, so that, though held back, it might grow strong more slowly, and so that the following might be fulfilled: “Before all these things, they will lay their hands on you and persecute you, handing you over to synagogues and prisons and bringing you before kings and governors for the sake of my name” (Luke 21:12). This too was fulfilled, as it had been written: “You will be rebuilt swiftly by those who destroyed you” [Col. 0904]. For from the time when, by the will of God, the most merciful emperors began to be Christians, although faith had been growing gradually in the world because of persecution, once Christian kings had come to power the Gospel of Christ penetrated everywhere in a short time.

7. The exposition of the blessed Daniel’s prophecy of the Weeks, which our holy fellow-presbyter Jerome expounded—namely, how the teachers of the Churches had handed it down—leaves the reader in suspense. For if that most learned man, our fellow-presbyter, says that it is dangerous to judge the opinions of the teachers of the Churches and to prefer one to another, how much less can a reader do what a teacher hesitated to do!

We believe, however, what the Lord said: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but not one iota or one stroke of the Law will pass away until all things have taken place” (Matt. 5:18). How, then, can the mystery of the Weeks have been fulfilled up to the birth and passion of Christ, I wonder, when the Prophet spoke of it as occurring in the middle of the week, saying: “In the middle of the week my sacrifice and supplication will be taken away, [followed by] the destruction of desolations and an abomination at the sacrifice” (Dan. 9:27)? If, then, this abomination had already been fulfilled, how does the Lord warn and say: “When you see the abomination of desolation, spoken of through Daniel the prophet, standing in the holy place—let the reader understand” (Matt. 24:15)?

I did not wish to be contemptuous of Your Beatitude’s request; therefore I have written to Your Charity what I have understood in this matter. Be pleased, however, to instruct and gladden us more fully by writing back with the word of your grace.

## LETTER 199 [Note: We have emended this according to a, bg, bl, c, cc, cb, ff, g, gg, gv, j, n, r, s, sb, vc; two bn manuscripts; two c manuscripts; four v manuscripts; Am., Bad., Er., Lov.] [Note: Elsewhere numbered 80; what was formerly 199 is now 262. Written after the preceding letter, in the year 419.]

### ON THE END OF THE AGE [Note: When he published the twentieth book of *The City of God*, chapter 5, he recalled this letter: “which I wrote in reply,” he says, “to the blessed man of sacred memory, Hesychius, bishop of Salona, whose letter bears the title ‘On the End of the Age.’”]

Augustine to Hesychius, showing how the passages of Scripture that speak in different ways about the end of the age are to be understood, and that it is better not to inquire into the time of Christ’s coming, but to work so that each person may be prepared to receive him.

To the most blessed Lord, and venerably revered brother and fellow bishop, HESYCHIUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

## CHAPTER ONE

1. I have received the letter of Your Veneration, in which you very beneficially exhort us to love and desire the coming of our Savior. You do this as a good servant of that same master of the household, eager for gains for your Lord and wishing to have many companions in the love with which you yourself are especially and perseveringly inflamed.

Considering, then, what you recalled from the Apostle—that he said the Lord would give the crown of righteousness not only to him but also to all who love his manifestation (2 Tim. 4:8)—we live rightly and conduct ourselves in this world as pilgrims when our heart extends itself progressively in this love, whether he comes sooner or later than is thought, whose manifestation is loved with faithful charity and desired with devout affection [Col. 0905].

For that servant who says, “My master is delaying,” and beats his fellow servants, eats and drinks with drunkards (Luke 12:45), certainly does not love his master’s manifestation. His character reveals the disposition of his soul. The good teacher took care to express these traits, though briefly—namely, pride and indulgence—so that no one would think that when he said, “My master is delaying,” he was saying it out of longing for his master, with which the one who said, “My soul thirsts for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” was aflame (Ps. 41:3).

By saying, “When shall I come?” he was distressed by delay; for even what is hastened by time appears slow to desire. How, then, is his coming slow, or how can it still be far off, when the Apostles themselves, while they were still in the flesh, said, “It is the last hour” (1 John 2:18), although they had heard from the Lord, “It is not yours to know the times”?

They did not know what we also do not know—I speak for myself and for those who, with me, do not know it. Yet those to whom it was said, “It is not yours to know the times which the Father has placed in his own authority” (Acts 1:7), loved his manifestation, gave food to their fellow servants at the proper time, did not beat them by lording it over them, and did not indulge themselves with lovers of the world by saying, “My Lord is delaying.”

2. Ignorance of the times is one thing; moral corruption and love of vices are another. When the Apostle Paul said, “Do not be quickly shaken in mind or alarmed, either by a spirit or by a word or by a letter supposedly from us, as though the day of the Lord were imminent” (2 Thess. 2:2), he certainly did not want them to believe those who already thought that the Lord’s coming was near. Yet neither did he want them, like that servant, to say, “My master is delaying his coming,” and surrender themselves to be destroyed by pride and indulgence.

He did not want them to listen to false reports about the approaching last day, but he did want them to await the coming of their Lord prepared, with their loins girded and their lamps burning (Luke 12:35–36). To them he says: “But you, brothers, are not in darkness, so that that day should overtake you like a thief. For you are all sons of light and sons of the day; we are not of night or darkness” (1 Thess. 5:4–5).

The one who says, “My master is delaying his coming,” so that he may beat his fellow servants and feast with drunkards, is not a son of light but of darkness. Therefore that day will overtake him like a thief. Every person ought also to fear this concerning the final day of his own life. For on whatever day his own last day finds him, on that day the world’s last day will overtake him; for as each person dies on this day, so he will be judged on that day.

3. This is relevant to what is written in the Gospel according to Mark: “Therefore keep watch, because you do not know when the master of the house will come—whether in the evening, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or in the morning—lest, when he comes suddenly, he find you sleeping. And what I say to you I say to all: Keep watch” (Mark 13:35, 37).

To whom does he say “to all” except his elect and beloved, who belong to his body, which is the Church? He therefore spoke not only to those who were listening to him at that time, but also to those who came after them and before us, and to us ourselves, and to those who will come after us until his final coming.

But will that day find everyone still in this life? Or will someone say that what he says, “Keep watch, lest when he comes suddenly he find you sleeping,” also applies to the dead? Why, then, does he say it to all if it applies only to those who will be alive then, unless it applies to all in the manner I have explained? That day will come to each person when the day comes for him to depart from this life in the condition in which he is to be judged on that day.

Thus every Christian ought to keep watch, lest the Lord’s coming find him unprepared. That day will find a person unprepared if the final day of this life finds him unprepared. At least this was clear to the Apostles: the Lord would not come during their own time, while they were living here in the flesh. Yet who would doubt that they especially kept watch and observed what he said to all, lest he come suddenly and find them unprepared?

## CHAPTER TWO

4. I do not yet understand in what way what Your Holiness wrote should be accepted—namely, that the Lord said to the Apostles, “It is not yours to know the times or seasons which the Father has placed in his own authority,” because he immediately added, “But you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in Judea, and in Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (Acts 1:7–8).

You explain the meaning of Scripture in such a way as to say: “He therefore intended the Apostles to be understood not as witnesses of the consummation of the world, but of his name and resurrection.” He did not say, “It is not yours to preach the times,” but, “It is not yours to know.” But if you wish what he said, “It is not yours to know,” to be understood as though he had said, “It is not yours to make others know”—that is, “It is not yours to teach this”—who among us would dare to teach, or presume that he knows, what that divine Teacher did not teach even those disciples who were present when he was asked, and what those holy and great teachers could not teach the Church?

5. Will the answer be that the Apostles did not teach these things, but the Prophets did? You said this, and it is true: future things are known through the voices of the holy Prophets, who, before they happened, spoke to human beings by the divine will of the things that were going to happen.

But if Your Veneration says that it is a matter of great wonder if God determined that the things he wished to be foretold could not at all reach human understanding, how much greater would be the wonder if the Apostles were either forbidden to know or to teach the things that the Prophets had spoken to human beings!

How would the Apostles fail to understand these times under discussion, if we understand them? Or if the Apostles understood them—the Prophets—as they prophesied this measure of time, how could they not teach what they understood, when through their proclamation the Prophets themselves became known—the very men who had taught them these things in their books?

Therefore, through the same writings by which the Apostles themselves had learned these things, others too could learn them among the nations where the Apostles commended prophetic authority. Why, then, was it said to them, “It is not yours to know”—or, if it is to be understood in this way, “It is not yours to teach the times which the Father has placed in his own authority”—when they were teaching these things by making known through themselves the writings in which they were learned?

It is therefore more credible that God did not wish what he wanted proclaimed to remain unknown [Note: Lov. reads, “what he did not wish to be proclaimed.” Several manuscripts more correctly read, “what he wished.”], but that he did not wish what he saw could not profitably be known to be proclaimed.

6. “Why, then,” you ask, “does the Lord himself give instruction concerning the recognition of the times, when he says: ‘Who, then, is the faithful and wise servant whom the master appointed over his household, to give them food at the proper time?’” and so forth.

Rather, he gives instruction not so that the good servant may know the end of the times, but so that at every time he may keep watch in good works, because he does not know the end of the times. He does not instruct us to attain, beyond the Apostles, the times which the Father has placed in his own authority; he instructs us, because we do not know when the Lord will come, to imitate the Apostles in preparing our hearts. I have already spoken sufficiently about this above.

He rebukes the Jews for failing to recognize the time, saying: “Hypocrites, you can assess the appearance of the sky,” and so forth (Luke 12:42, 56), because they did not recognize the time which he already wished to be recognized—namely, the time of his first coming, so that they might believe in him and wish to await his other coming in watchfulness, whenever it might occur.

For whoever has not recognized the Lord’s first coming will not be able to prepare himself for the second by believing in him and keeping faithful watch, lest it overtake him like a thief in the darkness, whether he comes later or sooner than expected.

## CHAPTER THREE

7. As you remind me, the Apostle Paul also says: “In the last times perilous times will come,” and so forth (2 Tim. 3:1). But does he thereby teach the times which the Father has placed in his own authority? Or does anyone thereby know how long or how short those very times are, which we must acknowledge to be the last? We ought to consider how long ago it was said: “Little children, it is the last hour” (1 John 2:18).

8. Again, you recall that the same Apostle said: “Concerning the times and seasons, we have no need to write to you. For you yourselves know very well that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night. When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them, like labor pains upon a pregnant woman, and they will not escape” (1 Thess. 5:1–3).

Here too he did not say after how much time this would happen, but how it would happen—that is, not how short or how long the span of the age would be, but that, however great the interval and span of time, this final evil would not come upon them until they said, “Peace and security.”

By these words the Apostle seems to have removed either the hope or the fear of this final day from our present time. For we do not see those lovers of this age, upon whom sudden destruction will come, already saying, “Peace and security.”

9. What, then, is sufficient to know? The Apostle himself shows this clearly when he says: “Concerning the times and seasons, we have no need to write to you”—or, as other manuscripts read, “You have no need to have this written to you.” He did not then add: “For you yourselves know very well how much time remains,” but said: “For you yourselves know very well that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night.”

This, then, is what must be known: that the children of light should take care to be such and keep watch with prepared hearts, if they do not wish that hour to overtake them like a thief in the night.

For if, in order to avoid this evil—that is, lest the Lord’s hour find us unprepared like a thief—it were necessary to know the spans of time, the Apostle would not have said that there was no need for him to write this; rather, as the most provident teacher, he would have judged that this was precisely what ought to be written to them.

Instead, he showed that even they had no need of this knowledge. It was enough for them to know that the Lord’s hour would come like a thief upon the unprepared and sleeping, and by knowing this to be watchfully prepared, however long a time might pass before it came. He also maintained the proper measure: although he was an Apostle, he did not presume to teach others what he knew the Lord had said to the Apostles: “It is not yours to know.”

10. You also set out what the same Apostle said: “Do you not remember that when I was with you I used to tell you these things? And now you know what restrains him, so that he may be revealed in his own time. For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work; only let the one who now restrains it continue to restrain it, until he is removed from the midst. And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth” (2 Thess. 2:5–8; see *The City of God*, book 20, chapter 19).

Would that you were willing not merely to quote these apostolic words but also to explain them! They are indeed so obscure and mystically expressed that nevertheless it is clear that he said nothing about fixed times, and disclosed no interval or span of them.

He says, “so that he may be revealed in his own time,” but he did not say after how much time this would happen. Then he added: “For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work.” However this mystery of lawlessness is understood—by one person in one way, by another in another—it is nevertheless hidden how long it will be at work.

Nor did the Apostle make this explicit, as a human being belonging to the number of those to whom it was said, “It is not yours to know the times.” Although he was not yet among them when this was said to them, we do not doubt that he too belonged to their fellowship and company.

11. The following words likewise—“Only let the one who now restrains it continue to restrain it, until he is removed from the midst; and then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth”—teach us that the Antichrist will be revealed. For he seems to have touched on him with somewhat clearer indication, as one who is to be killed by the breath of the Lord Jesus Christ. But after how much time this will occur, he did not state even obscurely.

Who the one is who now restrains, or what he restrains, or what is meant by “until he is removed from the midst,” anyone may constrain himself to understand, or may suspect to some extent, since he reads the passage in whatever way he can. But how long the restrainer will restrain, and after how great a span of time he will be removed from the midst, is entirely left unstated.

## CHAPTER FOUR

12. “Again,” you say, “the Lord reproves the Jews in the Gospel, saying: ‘And you too, if you had recognized the time of your visitation, perhaps you would have remained; but now these things have been hidden from your eyes’” (Luke 19:42).

But this concerns the time of the Lord’s first coming, not [Col. 0909] the second, which is now under discussion. For concerning his second coming he said, “It is not yours to know the times,” not concerning the first. The disciples asked him about the coming they hoped for, not about the one they were already seeing.

If the Jews had recognized his first coming, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor. 2:8), and therefore they could have remained, rather than being overthrown.

As for what he said to them, “Repent; the times have been fulfilled; believe [Note: The editions read, “Believe the Gospel.” The manuscripts have, “believe in the Gospel,” in accordance with the Greek πιστεύετε ἐν τῷ Εὐαγγελίῳ.] in the Gospel” (Mark 1:15), you yourself have rightly affirmed that this was said of the times of the Jews, which were to pass away shortly afterward, after a few years, and which we now know have already passed away—namely, when the city in which their kingdom had been established was overthrown.

13. Therefore, concerning what Your Veneration set out from Daniel about the slain beast, the kingdom of the other beasts, and, in the midst of these things, the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven, you said that it was clear to those who understand Scripture.

But if you would kindly explain how these things pertain to knowing the length of time after which the Savior’s coming will occur, so that they may be found to be clear without any ambiguity, I too will confess, with great thanksgiving, that what the Lord said, “It is not yours to know the times,” was said only to the Apostles and not to their successors, who were going to learn these things.

## CHAPTER FIVE

14. The Lord’s coming, then, must be loved and awaited, as you devoutly exhort us. You say that there is great blessedness for those who love his coming, and you bring forward the Apostle’s testimony, whose words you quote as follows: “For the rest, the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day—not only to me, but also to those who love the Lord’s coming” (2 Tim. 4:8).

Then, as you recall from the Gospel, “The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13:43). And as the prophet says: “For behold, darkness and gloom will cover the earth over the nations; but the Lord will appear upon you, and his majesty will be seen upon you” (Isa. 60:2). Likewise it is written: “But those who wait for the Lord will rejoice with strength; they will grow wings like eagles, they will run and not grow weary, they will walk and not hunger” (Isa. 40:31).

15. You speak in an entirely devout and truthful manner, commending the blessedness of those who love the Lord’s coming. But those to whom the Apostle said, “Do not be quickly shaken in mind, as though the day of the Lord were imminent,” certainly also loved the Lord’s coming.

When the Teacher of the Gentiles said this to them, he was not breaking them away from that love with which he wanted them to be inflamed. He therefore did not want them to believe those from whom they heard that the day of the Lord was imminent, lest, when the time they had believed it would come had passed and they did not see it arrive, they should conclude that the other promises made to them were likewise deceptive and despair of the reward of faith itself.

The one who asserts that the Lord’s coming is near does not therefore love it, nor does the one who asserts that it is not near. Rather, the one who loves it is the person who, whether it is near or far, awaits it with sincerity of faith, steadfastness of hope, and ardor of charity.

For if the Lord is loved more the more strongly it is believed and preached that he will come soon, then those who said that his coming was already imminent loved him more than those whom the Apostle forbade them to believe—or than the Apostle himself, who certainly did not believe this.

## CHAPTER SIX

16. If the weakness of my understanding is not burdensome to Your Holiness, I ask you not to hesitate to explain more clearly how you said that no one can calculate the measures of the times. Otherwise, I may perhaps seem to understand this in the same way that Your Charity does, and any one of us may wait in vain to be instructed by the other.

After saying this, you went on and stated: “The Gospel indeed says, ‘No one knows the day or the hour’” (Matt. 24:36); but, you say, “insofar as my understanding permits, I say that neither the month nor the year of his coming can be known.”

This seems to mean that the year in which he will come cannot be known, but that the week of years or the decade might be known—as though it could be stated and defined that he will come within this or that seven-year period, or within this or that ten-year period.

If even this cannot be determined, I ask whether the time of his coming can at least be defined in this way: that we say he will come within, for example, fifty or one hundred years, or within any number of years, whether greater or smaller, while not knowing in which of those years he will come.

If you have already understood this, then you have understood a great deal. This is precisely what I ask you kindly to grant us, bringing forward suitable proofs by which you were able to investigate it. But if you do not presume to have understood even this, then you understand the matter as I do.

17. All of us who believe these things see that the present times are the last, as is apparent from the many signs of events which we read that the Lord foretold. Yet even a period of one thousand years, if its end were the end of the age, could be called the whole of the last time, or even the last day, because it is written: “A thousand years in your sight are like one day” (Ps. 89:4). Thus whatever might be done throughout those thousand years could be said to be done in the last time or on the last day.

I say again what must often be said in this matter: let us consider how many years ago the blessed Evangelist John said, “It is the last hour.” If we had been living at that time and had heard this, when would we have thought that so many years would pass afterward? Would we not rather have expected the Lord to come while John himself was still living in the body?

For he did not say, “It is the last time,” or “the last year,” or “the last month,” or “the last day,” but, “It is the last hour.” And behold how long this hour has been! Yet he did not lie. Rather, he must certainly be understood to have used “hour” for “time.”

Some understand this by assigning six thousand years as one day and dividing it into twelve parts, as though into hours, so that the final hour would appear to contain the final five hundred years. They say that John was already speaking in those years when he said that it was the last hour.

18. But knowing something is one thing, and suspecting it is another. For if six thousand years are to be reckoned as one day, why should one hour be a twelfth rather than a twenty-fourth part of it [Col. 0911]—that is, two hundred and fifty years rather than five hundred?

The whole day, the entire circuit of the sun, is more correctly named not from sunrise to sunset but from sunrise to sunrise, since, after the entire day has passed—that is, after twenty-four hours—it rises again. Accordingly, this final hour, counting from the time when John spoke those words, is found already to have elapsed nearly seventy years ago, at the least, and yet the end of the age has not come.

Moreover, on careful examination of ecclesiastical history, it is found that the Apostle John died long before five thousand five hundred years had been completed from the beginning of the human race. Therefore the final hour had not yet arrived, if a twelfth part of six thousand years—namely, five hundred years—is reckoned as the span of one hour.

But if, according to the Scriptures, we posit that one day consists of one thousand years, then the final hour of so long a day passed long ago—not merely if it is reckoned as its twenty-fourth part, which is a little more than forty years, but even if it is reckoned as its twelfth part, which contains twice that number of years.

Therefore that Apostle is more appropriately understood to have used “hour” for “time.” How long this hour is, we do not know, because it is not ours to know the times which the Father has placed in his own authority. Yet we do know that it is the final hour—indeed, we know this all the more than those who lived before us, from the time when this hour began to exist or to be called the final hour.

## CHAPTER SEVEN

19. Your Veneration seems to think that the measures of the times cannot be understood as defining the year in which the end will occur because, according to the Lord’s promise, those days will be shortened. I do not understand this at all.

For if they will be shortened so that many become fewer, I ask: according to what truth were they going to be more numerous unless they were shortened? You think that the Weeks of the holy Daniel pertain not to the Lord’s first coming, as many have thought, but rather to his second.

Will they therefore be shortened so that one of the Weeks will be lacking from them, and the prophecy will prove false—a prophecy that took such care to define the number of the Weeks that it even said something would be fulfilled in the middle of a Week? I wonder whether the prophecy of Daniel is being destroyed by Christ’s prophecy.

Furthermore, how can we suppose that Daniel—or rather the angel through whom he spoke these things—did not know that the Lord would shorten those days, and therefore was mistaken in saying this; or that he knew it but lied to the one whom he was teaching?

If that is absurd, why do we not rather believe that Daniel prophesied that number of years, according to the fact that the Lord will shorten those days? This is so, at least if that number refers to the Lord’s second coming—which I do not know how it can be demonstrated.
