20. Finally, if these Weeks foretell the Lord’s coming, it is stated much more certainly and safely that the Lord’s coming will occur within seventy years, or at most within one hundred years.

For the seventy Weeks contain four hundred and ninety years. From the Lord’s birth, approximately four hundred and twenty years are now reckoned; from his resurrection or ascension, approximately three hundred and ninety years. Accordingly [Col. 0912], if the calculation begins from his birth, seventy years remain; if from his passion, approximately one hundred remain. Within these periods all Daniel’s Weeks will be fulfilled, if they were prophesied concerning his final coming.

Whoever says, “It will occur within this many years,” is speaking falsely if it occurs later. But because the days will be shortened, they may be fewer, not more. It is therefore correctly said, “It will occur within these years,” because however much they are shortened, this will remain true. For if the shortening is to be understood in such a way that they become fewer, it does not permit the day of the Lord to come beyond those years, but rather places it increasingly within them as they become fewer.

This shortening therefore does not disturb the calculator who defines the matter by saying that the day of the Lord will come within this many years. Rather, it helps him, since the more the days are reduced in number, the more certainly it will be within them and cannot be beyond them. Thus what is defined by saying, “It will occur within this many years,” will be true, even though the particular year in which it will occur is unknown.

21. Accordingly, the whole question is whether Daniel’s Weeks were fulfilled at the Lord’s first coming, or whether they prophesied the end of the age, or whether they pertain to both. There have indeed been men of insight who said that they were completed at the time of Christ’s first coming and that from then until the end of the age an equal number would once again have to be completed. I certainly see that, if the first coming did not complete them, the second must complete them, since that prophecy cannot be false. But if it was fulfilled at the time of the first coming, that does not compel us to understand that it will also be fulfilled concerning the end of the age. Consequently, even if the claim is true, it remains uncertain; it should neither be denied nor presumed that this will happen. It therefore remains for anyone who wishes to compel belief that this prophecy will be fulfilled at the end of the age to argue as strongly as possible and, if he can, to show that it was not completed at the Lord’s first coming—contrary to so many interpreters of the divine words, who demonstrate that it was completed there not only by calculating the times but also by the events themselves, especially because it is written there, “And the Holy of holies will be anointed”; or because in the Hebrew manuscripts the same prophecy states more explicitly, “The Christ will be killed, and he will have nothing” (Dan. IX, 24, 26), that is, he will have nothing of that city. For he was thus alienated from the Jews, who therefore believed that he was not their Savior and Redeemer, because they were able to kill him. Christ will not be anointed or killed at the end of the age, so that this prophecy of Daniel should then be expected to be fulfilled, as though it had not yet been fulfilled.

## CHAPTER VIII

22. Who denies that, in view of the evangelical and prophetic signs which we see taking place, we ought to hope that the Lord’s coming is near? Every day, indeed, it becomes nearer and nearer. But by what interval it is near, this, as has been said, is not yours to know. Consider when the Apostle said, “For now our salvation is nearer than when we believed. The night has passed, but the day has drawn near” (Rom. XIII, 11–12)—and see how many years have passed! Yet what he said is not false. How much more should it now be said that the Lord’s coming is near, when such great progress has been made toward the end! Certainly the Apostle says, “The Spirit expressly says that in the last times some will depart from the faith” (I Tim. IV, 1). Those times had not yet arrived—namely, the times of heretics and of such people as he describes in the same passage—but they have now come. Accordingly, even through these people we seem to be warned about the end of the age.

Likewise, elsewhere he says, “But know this, that in the last days difficult times will come,” or, as some manuscripts read, “dangerous times.” Then, describing what they will be like, he says: “For people will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, irreligious, without affection, slanderers, intemperate, ruthless, without kindness, traitors, reckless, blinded, lovers of pleasures rather than of God, having an appearance of piety but denying its power.” It is astonishing if such people have ever been absent. Finally, because they already existed then, he adds and says, “Avoid these people. For among them are those who creep into houses and take captive little women” (II Tim. III, 1–6). He does not say, “They will creep in,” as though here too he were announcing something future, just as above he had said, “Difficult times will come”; rather, he says, “They creep into houses and take captive little women.” He does not say, “They will take captive,” or “They are going to take captive,” but “They already take captive.”

23. We should not suppose that here he used present-tense verbs in place of verbs referring to the future, since he was warning the person to whom he was writing to avoid them. Yet he did not say without reason, “In the last days dangerous times will come,” and, demonstrating from this that they would be dangerous, he predicted that such people would exist—unless it is because they will be more numerous and will abound more greatly as the end draws nearer. We therefore see that such people now abound. But what if they will abound more after us, and be most abundant when the end itself is already imminent, although we do not know how long it will remain distant?

The last days were spoken of even in those first days of the Apostles, when the Lord had recently ascended into heaven and, on the day of Pentecost, sent the promised Holy Spirit. Some were astonished, marveling that they were speaking in languages they had not learned; others, however, mocked them and said that they were full of new wine. On that day Peter spoke to those who were variously disturbed by this matter: “For these men are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is the third hour of the day. But pay attention: this is what was spoken through the prophet: ‘It will be in the last days, says the Lord, that I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh,’” and so forth (Acts II, 1, 17).

24. Even then, therefore, the last days were already present. How much more so now—even if as many days remain until the end as have passed from the Lord’s ascension to this day, or whether fewer or more remain! We certainly do not know this, because it is not ours to know the times or the moments which the Father has placed in his own power. Yet we know that we are living in the last times, in the last days, in the last hour, just as the Apostles did—although those who lived after them and before us knew this much more, and we know it more than they did, and those who will come after us will know it more than we do, until we arrive at those who will be, if one may put it so, the last of the last, and finally at the very last day, which the Lord intends when he says, “And I will raise him up on the last day” (John VI, 40). How far away that day is cannot be grasped.

## CHAPTER IX

25. The signs foretold as future in the Gospel, as Your Holiness recalls, are the same according to Luke (Luke XXI, 7–33), Matthew (Matt. XXIV, 1–44), and Mark (Mark XIII). These three relate what the Lord said when his disciples asked him when the things he had foretold concerning the destruction of the temple would happen, and what sign would indicate his coming and the consummation of the age.

They do not differ in substance merely because one says something another omits, or says it in another way. Rather, when they are compared with one another, they assist the reader’s understanding and guide it. But it would now be too long to discuss everything. In response to the disciples’ questions, the Lord spoke about events that would follow from that time onward: whether concerning the destruction of Jerusalem, which gave rise to the question itself; or concerning his coming through the Church, in which he does not cease to come until the end—for he is recognized as coming among his own when his members are born daily. Concerning this coming he said, “From now on you will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds” (Matt. XXVI, 64). Of these clouds it was said through the prophet, “I will command my clouds not to rain upon it” (Isa. V, 6). Or he spoke concerning the very end, when he will appear to judge the living and the dead.

26. Since, then, he mentions signs that pertain to these three things—that is, to the destruction of that city; to his coming in his body, which is the Church; and to his coming in the head of the Church, which is himself—we must discern through careful consideration which of these signs should be referred to which of the three. Otherwise, we may perhaps think that what pertains to the overthrow of Jerusalem should be referred to the end of the age; or conversely affirm that what pertains to the end of the age belongs to the destruction of that city; or say that what pertains to his coming in his body, which is the Church, belongs to his final coming in his body, which is the head of the Church; or again assert that what pertains to his final coming in person belongs to the coming that takes place through the Church.

Among all these matters, some are clear, while others are so obscure that it is either laborious to distinguish them or rash to make any judgment about them so long as they are not understood.

27. Who, for example, does not see that the statement, “When you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army, then know that its desolation has drawn near” (Luke XXI, 20), pertains to that city? Likewise, who does not see that the statement, “When you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near,” pertains to the Lord’s final coming?

But the statement, “Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing infants in those days. Pray that your flight may not take place in winter or on the Sabbath. For then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world and will never be,” is placed according to Matthew and Mark in such a way that it is uncertain whether it should be understood of the destruction of that city or of the end of the age.

For this same passage is read in Mark as follows: “Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing infants in those days. Pray that it may not happen in winter. For those days will be tribulation of such a kind as has not been from the beginning of the creation which God made until now, nor ever will be. And unless the Lord had shortened those days, no flesh would have been saved; but for the sake of the elect whom he chose, he shortened the days.” Matthew says substantially the same.

Luke, however, presented the matter in such a way that it appears to pertain to the destruction of that city. For he reads as follows: “Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing infants in those days. For there will be great distress upon the earth and wrath against this people. They will fall by the edge of the sword and will be led captive among all the nations, and Jerusalem will be trampled by the nations until the times of the nations are fulfilled.”

28. As for the point at which this matter is reached, Matthew writes as follows: “Therefore, when you see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet, standing in the holy place—let the reader understand—then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains; and let the one who is on the roof not come down to take anything from his house; and let the one who is in the field not return to take his cloak. Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing infants in those days,” and so forth.

Mark, however, has it this way: “When you see the abomination of desolation standing where it ought not to be—let the reader understand—then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains; and let the one who is on the roof not come down into the house, nor enter in to take anything from his house; and let the one who is in the field not turn back to take his garment. Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing infants in those days,” and the rest.

Luke, in order to show that the abomination of desolation foretold by Daniel had taken place when Jerusalem was conquered, recalls at this point these words of the Lord: “When you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army, then know that its desolation has drawn near.” It therefore appears that the abomination of desolation spoken of by those two evangelists was then placed there.

Finally, Luke too continues in a similar way: “Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains.” In place of what the other evangelists said—“and let the one who is on the roof not come down into the house, nor enter in to take anything from the house”—he says, “and let those who are in its midst depart,” thereby showing that the words placed in the other evangelists prescribe a hurried flight.

In place of what they said—“and let the one who is in the field not turn back to take his garment”—Luke says more explicitly, “and let those who are in the countryside not enter it,” because “these are the days of vengeance, so that all things that are written may be fulfilled.”

Then Luke likewise continues, so that it is altogether clear that this passage of the Gospel belongs to all three evangelists and concerns this very matter: “Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who are nursing infants in those days,” along with the other statements pertaining to it, which I have already mentioned above.

29. Luke therefore made clear that what had been said about the abomination of desolation, and what had been said about the shortening of the days for the sake of the elect, could be understood as pertaining not to the end of the age but to the conquest of Jerusalem. For although he did not say those things himself, he did say other matters concerning the same event more explicitly, and thereby showed that those statements too pertained to it.

We should not doubt that, when Jerusalem was overthrown, there were among that people elect of God who had believed, or were going to believe, from the circumcision—those elected before the foundation of the world. For their sake those days would be shortened, so that the evils might become bearable.

Some seem to me to have understood the matter more appropriately by taking the evils themselves to be signified by the name “days,” just as “evil days” are mentioned in other passages of divine Scripture (Eph. V, 16). The days themselves are not evil, but the things that take place in them. It is therefore those things that are said to be shortened, so that, by God’s gift of endurance, they might be felt less severely, and thus what was great might be made brief.

30. But whether that shortening of the days is to be understood in this way, or as their being reduced in number, or as their being shortened by the sun’s moving more swiftly—for there are also those who think this, namely, that the days will be called shorter in the same way that the day was made longer when Joshua prayed (Josh. X, 12–14)—nevertheless the evangelist Luke taught that both this shortening of the days and the abomination of desolation, neither of which he himself mentioned but which Matthew and Mark mentioned, pertain to the overthrow of Jerusalem. Along with them, he said other things more explicitly about this same matter, which they had stated more obscurely.

For Josephus, who wrote a history of the Jews, says that such evils befell that people at that time that they scarcely seem credible. Hence it was not without reason that it was said that such tribulation had neither occurred from the beginning of creation nor would ever occur.

But even if such tribulation, or something greater, will perhaps occur in the time of Antichrist, we must understand the statement as referring to that people: such a tribulation will not happen to them again. For if they are going to receive Antichrist first and above all, that people will then cause tribulation rather than suffer it.

31. There is therefore no reason for us to think that the Prophet Daniel’s Weeks were disrupted because of the shortening of the days, or that they had not already been completed at that time but were to be completed at the end of the age. They were not completed before the Lord’s Passion.

Those who think they were should be refuted most appropriately by your judgment, in which you said: “If this abomination had already been completed, how does the Lord warn us and say, ‘When you see the abomination of desolation, spoken of through Daniel the prophet, standing in the holy place—let the reader understand’?” (Matt. XXIV, 15).

By these words of Your Beatitude those people are rightly corrected who say that, when the Lord spoke these things, the abomination had already been completed, either before his Passion or before his resurrection. Those who say—as the evangelist Luke also most explicitly testifies—that it took place when Jerusalem was overthrown must consider what answer should be given to those who think that these events will occur at the end of the age or near its end. Yet, because of the obscurity of the saying, the abomination of desolation itself may have been understood in more than one way by different people.

32. The statement, “Let the one who is on the roof not come down to take anything from his house, and let the one who is in the field not return to take his cloak,” can more appropriately be understood spiritually as a warning concerning every tribulation: one must beware lest anyone, overcome by it, descend from spiritual elevation to carnal life, or lest someone who had made progress by stretching toward what lies ahead turn back in failure toward what is behind.

If this had to be guarded against in every tribulation, how much more in that tribulation which was foretold as destined to befall that city in such a way as had not occurred from the beginning and would never occur! And if it had to be guarded against in that tribulation, how much more in the final tribulation destined for the world—that is, for the Church spread throughout the whole world!

Luke himself, not in the passage where the Lord was questioned by his disciples about his coming, which Matthew and Mark record, but elsewhere, where the Pharisees asked him when the kingdom of God would come, reports that he said something similar: “In that hour, let the one who is on the roof, with his possessions in the house, not come down to take them; and let the one who is in the field likewise not return” (Luke XVII, 20–31).

33. But the present issue concerns the calculation of the times relating to Daniel’s Weeks. If they were not completed around the time of the Lord’s first coming but are to be completed at the end, who could believe that the Apostles did not know this, or that they knew it but had been forbidden to teach it?

Yet if this is so, it is beneficial that the nations do not know what the Lord forbade those whom he intended to be teachers of the nations to teach. But if the Weeks have already been completed—because the Holy of holies has already been anointed, Christ has already been killed so that he would have nothing of that city, and the sacrifice has already been removed from that temple, with the anointing removed as well—then the Apostles’ question about the end was rightly answered: “It is not yours to know the times which the Father has placed in his own power.” For the times that they could know through Daniel’s prophecy did not pertain to the end of the age, about which they had asked.

## CHAPTER X

34. As for the signs in heaven and on earth, have we seen anything greater than those who lived before us? If the history of the nations is read, are not so many extraordinary events found to have occurred in heaven and on earth that some of them are not even believed?

But, to omit many matters whose pursuit would take too long, when have we seen two suns, as those who lived at that time recorded in writing before the Lord came in the flesh? When have we seen the sun darkened in the way it was darkened when the Light of the world hung upon the wood? Unless perhaps we count among heavenly prodigies the eclipses of the sun and moon which astronomers are accustomed to record and predict. For we have seen the moon eclipsed more often when full, and the sun more rarely, but nevertheless eclipsed at the end of the lunar cycle, according to their calculations.

The solar eclipse that occurred when Christ was crucified was not of this kind, and therefore it was truly marvelous and prodigious. It was the Passover of the Jews, which is celebrated only at the full moon. According to the calculations of astronomers, it is certain that when the moon is full the sun cannot be eclipsed, but only when the moon is at the end of its cycle—not always, indeed, but never at any other time, according to those calculations, does it undergo an eclipse.

What such thing, then, has anyone ever remembered appearing in heaven after the Lord foretold those events, like what appeared when he suffered? Therefore, if such signs will appear again—unless they are to be understood spiritually—they will appear when the end draws so near that they ought to appear.

35. As for wars, at various intervals of time and in various places, when has the earth not been devastated? To pass over extremely ancient events, under the emperor Gallienus, when barbarian forces invaded the Roman provinces everywhere, how many of our brothers who were then in the flesh might we suppose were able to believe that the end was near, since this occurred long after the Lord’s ascension!

Accordingly, we do not know what such events will be like when the end is altogether near—provided, that is, that these predictions are not to be understood as referring instead to the Church.

There are two peoples and two kingdoms: one belonging to Christ and the other to the devil. Of these it could be said, “Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom.” This has not ceased to happen since it was said, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. III, 2). Consider when this was said and how many years have passed since then; yet it was said with complete truth.

For the Lord came through a virgin in the last days. This hour would not be called the last unless the kingdom of heaven were drawing near. Throughout this entire hour the things that the Lord foretold would happen as his kingdom drew near are taking place. But if the Apostles were told how long this hour would extend, “It is not yours to know,” how much more must any human being, such as I am, recognize his own measure, lest he be wiser than he ought to be wise (Rom. XII, 3).

## CHAPTER XI

36. “But,” you say, “our suffering compels us to confess that the end is already here, since what was foretold is being fulfilled: ‘People will wither away from fear and from expectation of what is coming upon the whole world.’ No homeland, no place,” you say, “is certainly free in our times from affliction or tribulation, just as it was said, ‘From fear and from expectation of what is coming upon the whole world.’”

If, then, these evils which the human race now suffers are certain signs that the Lord is already about to come, what does the Apostle mean when he says, “When they say, ‘Peace and security’” (I Thess. V, 3)? For after the Gospel had said, “People will wither away from fear and from expectation,” it immediately added, “For the powers of heaven will be shaken; and then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with great power and majesty.”

37. Let us therefore see whether it may be better understood, not that the things foretold in these words are now being fulfilled, but rather that they will occur then, when such tribulation will affect the whole world that it pertains to the Church, which will be afflicted throughout the whole world, rather than to those who will afflict it.

For those people themselves will say, “Peace and security,” so that sudden destruction may come upon them and the Lord’s coming may overtake them like a thief in the night. In contrast, those who love the Lord’s manifestation will rejoice and exult.

At present, however, we see that these evils—which are believed to be supreme and final—are common to both peoples and both kingdoms, that is, to Christ’s and the devil’s. Good and evil alike are afflicted by them, and no one says, “Peace and security,” wherever such things occur or are feared.

Yet amid these evils luxurious banquets continue to be held everywhere, drunkenness rages, greed runs rampant, wanton songs resound, along with organs, flutes, lyres, citharas, dice, and many varied kinds of sounds and games. Is this to wither away from fear, or rather to become drenched in lust? But the children of darkness will possess and practice these things more abundantly when they say, “Peace and security.”

38. What of the children of light and the children of the day, who are not in darkness, so that that day may overtake them like a thief? Do they not still use this world as though they did not use it? For although it was said many years ago, in the time of the Apostles, they nevertheless consider with devout concern what was said: “The time is short” (I Cor. VII, 29).

Are not most of them still planting, building, buying, possessing, holding offices, and taking wives? I am speaking of those who await their Lord, wondering when he will come from the wedding feast (Luke XII, 36), yet do not abstain from earthly marriages. Rather, with the greatest obedience and charity, they listen to the Apostle’s instructions about how wives should live with husbands, husbands with wives, children with parents, parents with children, slaves with masters, and masters with slaves.

Do not all these people use this world in all these matters? They plow, sail, trade, beget children, serve in the army, and administer affairs. I think they will not be living in this way when the signs foretold in the Gospel appear—signs in the sun, moon, and stars, and upon the earth distress among the nations because of the confusion caused by the roaring of the sea and the waves; people withering away from fear and from expectation of what is coming upon the whole world. For the powers of heaven will be shaken.

39. I think these matters are better understood as referring to the Church, lest the Lord Jesus, as his second coming draws near, appear to have foretold as extraordinary things that had commonly happened to this world even before his first coming, and lest we be mocked by those who have read in the history of the nations about events which we dread as though they were final and the greatest of all, and even about events much greater.

The Church is the sun, moon, and stars, to which it was said, “Beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun” (Song VI, 9). In this world, as in Egypt, our Joseph is worshiped after being raised from the lowest condition to the highest. For Joseph’s mother certainly could not worship him, since she had died before Jacob came to his son (Gen. XXXV, 19; XLVI), so that the truth of that prophetic dream (XXXVII, 9) might be reserved for fulfillment in Christ the Lord.

When the sun is darkened, the moon does not give its light, the stars fall from heaven, and the powers of heaven are shaken—as this passage is recalled by the other two evangelists—the Church will not be visible. At that time, impious persecutors will rage beyond measure, and, with fear removed, will say “Peace and security,” as though the prosperity of the world were smiling upon them.

Then the stars will fall from heaven and the powers of heaven will be shaken, because many who appeared to shine with grace will yield and fall before their persecutors, and even the strongest of the faithful will be shaken.

According to Matthew and Mark, this is said to occur after the tribulation of those days—not because these events will happen only after the entire persecution has ended, but because the tribulation will come first, followed by the falling away of some. Since this will happen throughout all those days, it is therefore said to occur after the tribulation of those days, though it will nevertheless occur during those same days.

40. Accordingly, when Luke says, “And upon the earth distress among the nations,” he wished “nations” to be understood as those who do not belong to the seed of Abraham, in whom all nations will be blessed (Gen. XXII, 18), but those nations that will stand on the left when all nations are gathered before the Judge of the living and the dead.

Both parties will exist among all nations: one that causes distress and another that suffers distress; one that says, “Peace and security,” and another in which the sun is darkened, the moon does not give its light, the stars fall, and the powers of heaven are shaken.

41. “And then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with great power and majesty.” I see that this can be understood in two ways: either as his coming in the Church, as in a cloud, just as he does not cease to come even now, in accordance with the statement, “From now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming in the clouds of heaven.”

But he will then come with great power and majesty because his greater power and majesty will appear to the saints, to whom he will give great strength so that they may not be overcome by such great persecution.

Or it may be understood as his coming in his body, in which he sits at the right hand of the Father, in which he also died, rose again, and ascended into heaven, according to what is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “When he had said these things, a cloud received him, and he was lifted up from them.”

And because the angels also said there, “He will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts I, 9, 11), he should rightly be believed to come not only in the same body but also in a cloud, since he will come as he departed, and a cloud received him as he departed.

42. But which of these two interpretations should be preferred here is difficult to judge. The more immediate sense, certainly, is that anyone who hears or reads, “And then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with great power and majesty,” should understand this plainly as his coming—not through the Church but in person—when he will come to judge the living and the dead.

Yet because the Scriptures must be searched, and we ought not to be content with their surface, since they have been composed in such a way for our exercise that they desire to be penetrated more deeply, the subsequent passages must be examined carefully.

After saying, “And then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with great power and majesty,” he added: “But when these things begin to happen, look up and lift up your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.”

And he told them a parable: “Look at the fig tree and all the trees. When they already put forth fruit from themselves, you know that summer is near. So also, when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near.”

When he says, “When you see these things happening,” what can we understand except the things mentioned above? Among them is also what he says: “And then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with great power and majesty.” Therefore, when this too has been seen, the kingdom of God will not yet be present, but it will be near.

43. We see the other two evangelists maintain this same order. In Mark, after it had been said, “And the powers that are in heaven will be shaken,” he says, “And then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory.”

Then he adds what Luke did not say: “And then he will send his angels and gather his elect from the four winds, from the end of the earth to the end of heaven.”

At that point, where Luke speaks of the fig tree and the other trees, Mark mentions only the fig tree: “From the fig tree,” he says, “learn the parable. When its branch has already become tender and leaves have grown, you know that summer is near. So also, when you see these things happening, know that he is near, at the doors.”

What does “When you see these things happening” mean except the things he mentioned above? Among them is also the statement, “And then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory.” And then he will send his angels and gather his elect.

The end, therefore, will not yet be present; rather, it will then be near.

44. Or should we say that not everything mentioned above is to be understood where he says, “When you see these things happening,” but only some of those things—specifically excluding the statement, “And then they will see the Son of Man coming,” and so forth? For that will itself be the end, not something near the end.

But Matthew made clear that the statement, “When you see these things happening,” should be understood without excluding anything. For in his account, after it had been said, “And the powers of heaven will be shaken,” he says, “Then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven, and then all the tribes of the earth will mourn. And they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty. And he will send his angels with a trumpet and a great voice, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from the highest heavens to their limits.”

“From the fig tree,” he continues, “learn the parable. When its branch has already become tender and its leaves have grown, you know that summer is near. So also, when you see all these things, know that he is near, at the doors.”

45. We therefore know that he is near when we see not some of these things but all of them, including the appearance of the Son of Man coming, his sending of his angels, and his gathering of his elect from the four parts of the world—that is, from the whole earth.

He does this throughout the whole final hour, coming in his members as in clouds, or in the whole Church itself, which is his body, as in a great cloud that bears fruit and grows throughout the whole world. This has occurred from the time when he began to preach and say, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.”

Thus it may perhaps be discovered, when the statements of all three evangelists concerning his coming are more carefully compared and examined together, that they pertain to the fact that he comes daily in his body, which is the Church. Concerning this coming he said, “From now on you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming in the clouds of heaven.”

The exceptions are those passages in which his final coming in person, when he will judge the living and the dead, is promised in such a way that it is said to be near, and the passage at the end of Matthew’s discourse in which that coming itself is clearly expressed, with its nearness shown above through certain signs.

For Matthew concludes the discourse in this way: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then he will sit upon the throne of his majesty. Then all nations will be gathered before him,” and so forth, up to the statement, “And these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. XXV, 31–46).

No one doubts that this was foretold concerning Christ’s final coming and the end of the age. Yet there have also been people who, in a disputation not without merit, wished to teach that those five and five virgins (Matt. XXV, 1–13) pertain to his coming which now takes place through the Church.

But these claims should not be made rashly, lest something arise that strongly contradicts them—especially since, in such obscurities of the divine words, by which God has been pleased to exercise our understanding, not only is one person among those who treat the Holy Scriptures in a reasonably sound manner moved more perceptively than another, but even one and the same person understands sometimes less well and sometimes better.

## CHAPTER XII

46. Nevertheless, I do not know whether we could discern something more certain in this question if by any means or capacity we could determine when the whole world would be filled with the Gospel. In my earlier letter I already addressed this matter.

You think that this has already been accomplished through the Apostles themselves, but I proved with reliable evidence that this is not so. For among us—that is, in Africa—there are countless barbarian peoples among whom the Gospel has not yet been preached. We can readily learn this every day from those who are captured there and are now being mixed among the services of the Romans.

It has nevertheless been only a few years since some of them—the rarest and very few [the text reads *pucati*, perhaps an OCR corruption]—who live close to the Roman frontiers, so that they have no kings of their own but have prefects appointed over them by the Roman government, both they and their prefects began to become Christians.

As for those farther inland, who are subject to no Roman authority, absolutely none of them are held, even in some part of their people, by the Christian religion; nor can it rightly be said that these people do not belong to God’s promise.

47. For it was not to the Romans, but to all nations, that the Lord promised the seed of Abraham, confirmed also by an oath (Gen. 22:16–18). From this promise it has already come about that certain nations not subject to Roman rule have received the Gospel and have been joined to the Church, which bears fruit and grows throughout the whole world.

It still has room to grow, until what was prophesied concerning Christ in the figure of Solomon is fulfilled: “He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 71:8). The river, of course, where he was baptized, since from there he began to preach the Gospel; and from sea to sea means the whole world with all its nations, since the entire world is surrounded by the ocean.

How else, moreover, can that prophecy be fulfilled: “All the nations that you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord” (Ps. 85:9)? They will not come by migrating from their own lands, but by believing where they are. For the Lord said of believers: “No one can come to me unless it has been given to him by my Father” (John 6:66). The prophet, however, says: “And they shall worship him, each one from his own place, all the islands of the nations” (Zeph. 2:11). He said “all the islands,” as though he had said, “even all the islands,” thereby showing that no part of the earth is left without the Church, since no islands are left without it—some of them, moreover, being situated even in the Ocean—and we have learned that some of these have already received the Gospel.

Thus, on each individual island also, what was said is fulfilled: “He shall rule from sea to sea,” since each island is surrounded by sea. The same is true of the whole inhabited earth, which is in a certain sense the greatest of all islands, because it too is encircled by the Ocean. We already know that the Church has reached its shores in the western regions; and wherever along those shores it has not yet arrived, it will certainly arrive, bearing fruit and growing.

48. Therefore, since the prophecy of truth cannot lie, it is necessary that all the nations that God has made worship him. How, however, will they worship him unless they call upon him? And how will they call upon one in whom they have not believed? Or how will they believe in one of whom they have not heard? And how will they hear without someone preaching? And how will they preach unless they are sent (Rom. 10:14)?

For he sends his angels and gathers his elect from the four winds (Matt. 24:31), that is, from the whole inhabited earth. Therefore, in whatever nations the Church does not yet exist, it must come to exist—not so that everyone who is there will believe. For all nations have been promised, not all the people of every nation; “for faith does not belong to all” (2 Thess. 3:2).

Thus every nation believes in all those who were chosen before the foundation of the world (Eph. 1:4); it does not believe in the others, and it hates those who do believe. For how else will this also be fulfilled: “You will be hated by all nations for my name’s sake” (Matt. 24:9), unless in all nations there are both those who hate and those whom they hate?

49. In what sense, then, was this preaching completed by the Apostles, when there still remain nations—and this is absolutely certain to us—in which it has only now begun, and in which it has not yet begun to be fulfilled?

Thus it was not said to the Apostles, “You shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and throughout all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (Acts 1:8), as though they alone, to whom he was then speaking, were to fulfill so great a task. Nor was it said to them alone, “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20), although who does not understand that he promised this to the whole Church, which will remain here until the consummation of the age, with some dying and others being born?

Similarly, he said to them something that does not pertain to them at all, though it was expressed as though it concerned them alone: “When you see all these things, know that he is near, at the gates” (Matt. 24:33). For to whom does this apply except to those who will then be alive in the flesh, when all these things are fulfilled? How much more was it said to them in this manner concerning what was for the most part to be accomplished through them, although the same work was also reserved for their successors?

50. As for what the Apostle said, “Have they not heard? Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Rom. 10:18; Ps. 18:5): although he spoke in words belonging to the past, he referred to what was to happen, not to what had already been accomplished and completed. Thus the prophet whom he used as his witness does not say, “Their sound will go out into all the earth,” but says, “Their sound has gone out”—something that had certainly not yet happened. [Col. 0924] The same is true of: “They pierced my hands and feet” (Ps. 21:17), which we know was fulfilled only very long afterward.

But lest we think that such expressions were found only among the prophets and not also among the Apostles, did not that same Apostle say: “Which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth. And undoubtedly great is the mystery of piety: it was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, was preached among the nations, was believed in the world, was taken up in glory” (1 Tim. 3:15–16)?

It is surely evident that what he placed last—“was taken up in glory”—has not yet been fulfilled, even now; how much less was it fulfilled when he was saying these things? For the Church will be taken up in glory when it is said, “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matt. 25:34). Yet what was certainly known to be future was spoken of as though it had already happened.

51. It is far less surprising, then, that he also used the present tense in the passage which you repeatedly recalled him saying: “Because of the hope laid up for us, which you heard before in the word of the truth of the Gospel, which has come to you, just as it is in the whole world, bearing fruit and growing” (Col. 1:5–6), although the Gospel did not yet possess the whole world. He said that it was bearing fruit and growing in the whole world in order thereby to signify how far it would extend as it bore fruit and grew.

Therefore, if it is hidden when the whole world, from sea to sea, will be filled through the fruitfulness and growth of the Church, then without doubt it is hidden when the end will be; for the end will not come before that.

## CHAPTER XIII

52. To disclose to you, as a holy man of God and most sincere brother, what I think about this question: error is to be avoided on both sides, insofar as a human being can avoid it—whether one believes that the Lord will come sooner or later than he actually will. But it seems to me that a person does not err when he knows that he does not know something; rather, he errs when he thinks that he knows what he does not know.

Let us therefore remove from our midst that evil servant who says in his heart, “My master is delaying his coming,” and who then lords it over his fellow servants and joins the drunken in feasting (Matt. 24:48–49; Luke 12:45). For this servant undoubtedly hates the coming of his master.

With that evil servant removed, let us place before our eyes three good servants, carefully and soberly managing their master’s household, ardently desiring, watchfully awaiting, and faithfully loving the coming of their master. One of them thinks that the Lord will come sooner, another later, while the third confesses his ignorance on the matter. Although all agree with the Gospel, because they all love the manifestation of the Lord and await it eagerly and watchfully, let us nevertheless see which of them agrees with it more fully.

53. One says, “Let us watch and pray, because the Lord will come sooner.” Another says, “Let us watch and pray, because this life is brief and uncertain, although the Lord will come later.” The third says, “Let us watch and pray, because this life is both brief and uncertain, and we do not know when the Lord will come.”

The Gospel says: “See, watch, and pray, for you do not know when the time is” (Mark 13:33). [Col. 0925] I ask you: what else do we hear this third servant saying than what we hear the Gospel saying?

All of them, out of desire for the kingdom of God, want what the first says to be true. But the second denies it, while the third denies none of these things and instead confesses that he does not know which of the others is speaking the truth.

Accordingly, if what the first predicted comes to pass, the second and the third will rejoice with him; for all of them love the manifestation of the Lord. They will therefore rejoice that what they love has come sooner. But if it does not happen, and what the second said begins to appear true, there is reason to fear that those who believed what the first said may become troubled during the delay and begin to think that the Lord’s coming is not merely delayed but nonexistent. You can see how great the destruction of souls would be.

If, however, they possess such great faith that they turn to what the second predicted and faithfully and patiently await the Lord even while he delays, there will nevertheless be abundant reproaches, insults, and mockery from enemies, which will turn many weak people away from the Christian faith. They will say that the kingdom was promised to them as falsely as it was falsely said that the Lord would come soon.

But those who believe what the second says—that the Lord will come later—if this proves false and the Lord comes sooner, will in no way be disturbed in their faith. Rather, they will enjoy an unexpected joy.

54. Therefore, the one who says that the Lord will come sooner speaks in a more desirable manner, but if he is mistaken, his error is more dangerous. Would that it were true! For it will be grievous if it is not true.

But the one who says that the Lord will come later, while nevertheless believing, hoping for, and loving his coming, even if he is mistaken about the delay, is happily mistaken. For if it is so, he will have greater patience; if it is not so, greater joy.

Accordingly, among those who love the manifestation of the Lord, the former is heard more pleasantly, while the latter is believed more safely. But the one who confesses that he does not know which of these is true desires the one and endures the other; he errs in neither, because he neither affirms nor denies either of them.

I ask you not to reject me as such a person. I too love you when you affirm what I desire to be true; and the more I love what you promise, and the more I see how dangerous it would be if you were mistaken, the more I do not want you to be mistaken.

Forgive me if I have been burdensome to your holy sentiments. For the rarer such an opportunity is, the more it has pleased me to speak with you at least through letters for a longer time.

## LETTER 200

[Note: This has been incorporated into this volume from volume 7, where it is prefixed to Book 4 of *On Marriage*.]

[Note: In volume 7 it was prefixed to Book 1 of *On Marriage*. What was formerly numbered 200 is now 196. It appears to have been written toward the end of 418 or at the beginning of 419.]

Augustine to the Count Valerius, now sending him the book dedicated to him, Book 1 of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*.

To the illustrious and deservedly outstanding lord, and most beloved son in the love of Christ, VALERIUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

1. I had long been troubled that, although I had written several times, I had not received any reply from Your Sublimity. Then suddenly I received three letters from Your Goodness: one [Col. 0926] addressed not to me alone and sent through my fellow bishop Vindemialis, and two others sent shortly afterward through my fellow presbyter Firmus.

This holy man, united to us by a most familiar affection—as you could learn from him—and who, in speaking much with us about your excellence and truthfully conveying the kind of man he knows you to be in the heart of Christ, surpassed not only the letters which the aforesaid bishop had brought, or which he himself brought, but also those letters whose non-arrival we had been lamenting.

For this reason his account of you was more pleasing to us: he said things which you could not write back, even if I had asked you, lest you become, contrary to what holy Scripture forbids (Prov. 27:2), a herald of your own praises. Although I too am afraid to write these things to you, lest I incur the suspicion of flattery, illustrious and deservedly outstanding lord, and most beloved son in the love of Christ.

2. Consider, then, what pleasure and joy it was for me to hear from him your praises in Christ—or rather, Christ’s praises in you—since he could not deceive me because of his faithfulness, nor fail to know them because of your friendship.

We have also heard from others, though not as much or with equal certainty, how sound and Catholic your faith is; how devoutly you await the future; how great is your love of God and of the brethren; how you are not proud in your exalted honors, nor place your hope in uncertain riches, but in the living God, and are rich in good works; how your household is a refuge and consolation for the saints and a terror to the impious; how great your concern is that no one should lie in wait for the members of Christ, whether concealed beneath the name of Christ among his former enemies or his more recent ones; and how carefully you seek the salvation of these same enemies while opposing their error.

These and similar things, as I said, we usually hear from others; but now, through the brother mentioned above, we have learned them in greater number and with fuller testimony.

3. As for conjugal chastity—which would enable us also to praise and love this virtue in you—would we have heard of it unless from some close member of your household who knew your life not superficially but thoroughly?

About this good of yours, therefore, a gift of God, I too am pleased to speak with you more familiarly and at somewhat greater length. I know that I will not be a burden to you if I send something lengthy, so that by reading it you may remain with us longer.

For I have also learned that, amid your many and great cares, you readily and gladly read, and take considerable pleasure in our little works, even those which we have written for others, whenever any of them have come into your hands. How much more, then, will you enjoy what is written to you, where I shall speak as though you were present, and where you will deign to pay closer attention and receive it more graciously?

From this letter, then, proceed to the book which I have sent along with it. Its opening will explain more conveniently both why it was written for Your Reverence and why it was sent especially to you.

## LETTER 201

[Note: This letter is included in this volume in an edition corrected against various editions and manuscripts.]

[Note: What was formerly numbered 201 is now 90. It was written in June 416.]

The Emperors, having issued a new sanction against the Pelagians and their supporters, instruct Aurelius—and Augustine as well, by a letter separately addressed to him in identical terms—to require the other bishops to subscribe against the condemned heresy.

[Col. 0927]

The Emperors HONORIUS and THEODOSIUS Augusti, to Bishop AURELIUS, greetings.

1. It had previously been decreed that Pelagius and Celestius, the discoverers of an infamous doctrine, should be expelled from the city of Rome as certain contagions threatening Catholic truth, lest they corrupt the minds of the ignorant through a savage persuasion. In this matter our clemency followed the judgment of Your Holiness, by which it is established that they were condemned by all after a proper examination of the sentence.

But because the persistent evil of an obstinate crime required that the constitution be strengthened, we have also decreed by a recent sanction that if anyone knowingly allowed them to lie concealed in any part of the provinces, and delayed either expelling or exposing them, he should, as their accomplice, be subjected to the prescribed penalty.

2. Above all, however, in order to correct the obstinacy of certain bishops who either support their perverse arguments by silent consent or fail to destroy them by public opposition, it will be appropriate, dearest and most beloved father, for the authority of Your Holiness to intervene, so that the Christian devotion of all may agree in abolishing this perverse heresy.

Let Your Religiousness therefore cause everyone to be warned by appropriate writings. They are to know, by the definition of Your Sanctity, that this decree has been prescribed for them: whoever, through impious obstinacy, neglects to subscribe to the condemnation of the persons mentioned above, thereby failing to show a pure mind, shall be punished by the loss of his episcopate, expelled forever from the cities under prohibition, and deprived of communion.

For since, in accordance with the Council of Nicaea, we ourselves venerate with sincere confession God, the Creator of all things and the author of our empire, Your Holiness will not permit men of a detestable sect, devising novel and unheard-of things to the injury of religion, to conceal by secret machinations a sacrilege once condemned by public authority.

For the guilt of those who either connive by dissembling or offer harmful support by failing to condemn is one and the same, dearest and most beloved father.

(And in another hand:) May the Divinity preserve you unharmed for many years. Given on the fifth day before the Ides of June at Ravenna, in the consulship of Monaxius and Plinta. A letter in the same terms was also given to the holy Bishop Augustine.

[Note: These words are appended in all the ancient manuscripts. Here one sees that what was granted to Aurelius of Carthage on account of the dignity of his See was also extended by the Emperors to Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, because of his personal merit and renown. Hence again in 430, when Theodosius was writing “a Sacred Letter,” as Liberatus says in *The Breviary*, chapter 5, “to all the bishops, so that they might assemble at Ephesus and deliberate about the books of Nestorius and the judgment of Cyril, the Emperor wrote a Sacred Letter also to the blessed Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, through Ebagnius the *Magistrianus*, so that he might lend his presence to the council.” Aurelius promptly obeyed the command of the Emperors, as is confirmed by the encyclical letter of his that survives, addressed to the bishops of the provinces of Byzacena and Arzugitana and dated on the Kalends of August. Along with it he arranged to send a copy of the imperial letter, saying: “When your Love has read the accompanying copy, you will learn how each of you ought to subscribe.” This letter has been published by the Magdeburg Centuriators, Baronius, and others.]

## LETTER 202

[Note: Collated with mr. tt., six v., Am., Bad., Er., Lov.]

[Note: Formerly numbered 24; what was numbered 202 is now 91. Written toward the end of 419.]

Jerome congratulates Alypius and Augustine, through whose efforts the Celestian heresy has been extinguished; and excuses himself for not yet having refuted the books of Annianus the Pelagian.

[Col. 0928]

To the truly holy lords, deserving of every affection and honor, the bishops ALYPIUS and AUGUSTINE, JEROME sends greetings in Christ.

## CHAPTER I

1. The holy presbyter Innocentius, who is the bearer of this letter, last year, when he seemed unlikely ever to return to Africa, did not take with him my writings to Your Dignity. Nevertheless, we give thanks to God that it happened in such a way that you overcame my silence with your letters.

Every occasion is exceedingly welcome to me by which I write to Your Reverence. I call God to witness that, if it could be done, I would take the wings of a dove and embrace you—always, indeed, because of the merit of your virtues, but now especially because, with you as cooperators and authors, the Celestian heresy has been slaughtered.

It infected the hearts of many so thoroughly that, even though they know themselves to have been defeated and condemned, they nevertheless do not abandon the poison of their minds. They hate us—the only thing they can do—because they think that through us they have lost the freedom to teach their heresy.

[Note: Lov. reads “with you as helpers.” The older editions and six Vatican manuscripts, however, have “as authors”; two of those manuscripts preface it with “because you acted as cooperators.”]

## CHAPTER II

2. As for your question whether I have written a reply against the books of Annianus [Note: Here he translated into Latin several homilies of John Chrysostom. From the preface to Orontius, that Pelagian bishop who was condemned at the Council of Ephesus, you will understand that he undertook this work with a thoroughly heretical intention; likewise from his letter to Evangelus, preserved in Bede, volume 6. In that letter he seems to designate Augustine—or Jerome—as “the Traducian.” There is no slight conjecture that this is the same blabberer whose tongue and pen Pelagius abused. Jerome indicates this in the words: “who is fed most abundantly so that he may supply frivolous words of another’s blasphemy.”], the pseudo-deacon of Celeda, who is fed most abundantly so that he may supply frivolous words of another’s blasphemy, know that I received the books themselves, sent on sheets by the holy brother Eusebius the presbyter, not long ago.

From that time onward, either because illnesses pressed upon me or because of the death of your holy and venerable daughter Eustochium, I was so grieved that I almost thought them unworthy of attention. For he flounders in the same mud and, apart from tinkling and beggarly words, says nothing else.

Nevertheless, we achieved a great deal: while attempting to answer my letter, he exposed himself more openly and made his blasphemies plain to everyone. Whatever he denies having said at that miserable Synod of Diospolis, he professes in this work; and it is no great task to answer the most foolish fables.

If the Lord grants me life and we have enough copyists, I shall reply in a few little nocturnal labors—not in order to convict a dead heresy, but to refute its ignorance and blasphemy in my own words. Your Holiness would do this better, so that we are not forced to praise our own work against a heretic.

Our holy sons, Albina, Pinianus, and Melania, greet you warmly. I have given these little letters at holy Bethlehem to the holy presbyter Innocentius to deliver.

[Col. 0929] Your niece Paula earnestly begs that you remember her and sends you many greetings. May the clemency of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve you unharmed and mindful of me, truly holy lords and venerable fathers, deserving of every affection.

## LETTER 202 BIS

[Note: This letter, which is absent from B, was taken from a single manuscript at Göttweig, as noted in the preface, columns 49–50.]

[Note: See the preface, columns 49–50, where the discussion concerns two letters of Augustine recently discovered. Written toward the end of 419 or, more probably, at the beginning of 420.]

He informs Optatus that Jerome did not respond to his inquiry concerning the origin of the soul, and that he himself has not yet dared to assert anything on this question. He urges Optatus to imitate him, not only by his example but also in the method and manner of Optatus’s own letter. He again asks him to send the *Book of Faith* and not, as a new and inexperienced teacher, to undertake to corrupt the traditions of learned bishops. Finally, he briefly explains what faith teaches concerning the soul and incidentally resolves several questions that arise.

To the most blessed, sincerely beloved and greatly desired brother and fellow bishop OPTATUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

## CHAPTER I

1. Through the religious presbyter Saturninus I received a letter from Your Veneration, earnestly requesting from me something which I do not yet possess. You explained why you had done this: namely, because you believed that a response had already been given to the inquiry that you had made of me concerning this matter.

Would that it were so! Far be it from me to defraud you—whose most eager expectation I know—of the sharing of such a gift. But, if you can believe it, dearest brother, nearly five years have now passed since I sent to the East a book [Note: Marcellinus, who presided over the Carthaginian Conference in 412, asked Augustine what should be held concerning the origin of souls. In his reply the holy Doctor related four different opinions commonly expressed on this question, yet did so in such a way that, according to Fulgentius, “he did not wish to put forward a definite judgment on this matter.” Marcellinus, displeased by this, wrote to Jerome in the same year, asking him to remove his doubt and ignorance. At the beginning of 413, as was noted somewhat earlier, Jerome replied that he stood with those who held “that souls are daily made by God and sent into bodies,” and urged him to “consult the holy and learned Bishop Augustine, who, as they say, could teach him by living speech and explain his own—or rather Jerome’s own—opinion.” These last words moved Augustine to send Jerome a letter, or rather a treatise of inquiry, concerning the origin of the human soul; this is the treatise chiefly at issue here. See Augustine, Letters 163 and 166.] not as an act of presumption but of inquiry; and I have still not deserved a reply that would unravel this question, on which you wish me to bring you a definite opinion.

I would have sent both, if I had both.

2. As for what I possess, it does not seem that I ought to send or publish it to anyone without the other work, which I do not yet possess [Note: He says the same in Letter 190, section 21: “This book of mine,” he says, “can be read by me as the work not of a teacher but of an inquirer, and rather of one eager to learn; but it ought not to be sent anywhere or given out to anyone.” Yet Augustine seems to have thought otherwise earlier, as the same Letter 169, section 13, shows.]

For the one who may perhaps respond to me, as I desire, might rightly be angry that my question, elaborated through a very laborious disputation, should be circulated among people’s hands and knowledge without his response—which is not yet to be despaired of—and might judge that I had done this more boastfully than usefully, as though I had been able to ask what he had been unable to unravel, when perhaps he is able to do so and we ought to await his doing it.

[Note: Augustine retained deeply in mind what Jerome had once reproached him with in these words: “Some of my friends and vessels of Christ, of whom there is a very great abundance at Jerusalem and in the holy places, suggested that you had not acted toward me with a simple intention, but were seeking praise, branches of renown, and a little popular glory, so that you might grow at our expense: so that many might learn that you challenge me while I fear; that you write as a learned man while I keep silent as an ignorant one; and that at last you had found someone to impose a limit on my loquacity.” In Augustine, Letter 72, section 2.]

For I know that he is occupied with other matters that ought by no means to be delayed and that deserve greater weight.

3. So that Your Holiness may also know this, attend for a little to what he wrote to me another year through the bearer [Note: Orosius. See Letters 166, 169, and 172.] through whom I had written to him when he was returning. I transferred this passage from his letter into this one [Note: This passage and what follows through the end of section 3 are found in Jerome, Letter 79, and also in Augustine, Letter 172, section 1; but in the former, “it begins” is read, not “a difficult time has arisen.”]: “A very difficult time has come,” he says, “when it was better for me to be silent than to speak, so that our studies ceased, lest, as Appius says, a doglike eloquence be exercised.

“Therefore, I was unable for a time to respond to your two little books, dedicated to my name, most learned and shining with every splendor of eloquence—not because I think that anything in them deserves criticism, but because, according to the blessed Apostle, ‘Let each person abound in his own opinion: one indeed in this way, another in that’ (Rom. 14:5).”

[Note: In the cited passages of Augustine and Jerome, “and” is read—incorrectly, for thus Jerome’s meaning and the sequence of the sentence are inverted and confused.]

“Certainly, whatever could be said and drawn from the fountains of the holy Scriptures by a lofty intellect has been set forth and discussed by you. But I ask Your Reverence to bear with me somewhat while I praise your intellect. We discuss these matters among ourselves for the sake of learning.

“Moreover, rivals, and especially heretics, if they see that we hold different opinions, will allege that they arise from bitterness of spirit. But I have resolved to love you, receive you, honor you, admire you, and defend your words as though they were my own. [Note: The editions, and Augustine and Jerome in the cited passages, read “esteem”; but the reading of the Göttweig manuscript seems more Jerome’s.]

“Certainly, in the dialogue which I recently published [Note: Book 3 *Against the Pelagians*, near the end.], I remembered Your Beatitude as was fitting. Let us rather work to remove from the Churches that most pernicious heresy, which always pretends to repentance so that it may have the opportunity to teach in the Churches; for if it revealed itself in the open light, it would be expelled and perish.”

## CHAPTER II

4. You see, venerable brother, that these words of my most beloved friend, returned in answer to my inquiry, did not deny a response but excused the delay on the grounds that he was compelled to devote his attention to matters that were more urgent.

You also see how benevolent an attitude he has toward me, and what he warns against: namely, that rivals, and especially heretics, should not slander what we do for the sake of learning, with our affection and the sincerity of our friendship preserved, as though it arose from bitterness of spirit.

Accordingly, if people read both of our works—both the one in which I inquired and the one in which he answered my questions [Note: See Letter 190, section 21.]—then, since I ought also to give thanks if the same question has been sufficiently explained according to his opinion and I have been instructed, there will be no small benefit when this becomes known to many.

Our successors will thereby learn not only what they ought to think about this matter, which has been examined among us by careful disputation, but also, by our example, with God’s mercy and favor, how disputation in the spirit of mutual inquiry can exist between most beloved brothers while love nevertheless remains inviolate.

5. But if my writing, in which the most obscure matter is merely read as having been investigated, should circulate without his reply, in which perhaps the answer will appear to have been found; if it should spread further and reach even those who, “comparing themselves with themselves,” as the Apostle says (2 Cor. 10:12), do not understand the spirit in which we act because they do not know how to act in that spirit themselves; if they explain my attitude toward a friend whom I love and honor for his immense merits—not as they see it, since they do not see it, but as they please and as their hatred dictates that they suspect it—then we must certainly guard against this as far as lies within us.

6. But if, despite our unwillingness, what we do not wish to become known through us should nevertheless become known to those to whom we do not wish it known, what will remain except to accept the Lord’s will with an even temper?

For I ought not to have written this to anyone if I had wished it always to remain hidden. Yet if, God forbid, through some accident or necessity he should never reply, our inquiry, which we sent to him, will undoubtedly one day become known.

It will not be useless to those who read it. For even if they do not find what they seek, they will certainly learn how such matters ought to be investigated, and that what they do not know must not be rashly affirmed. According to what they read there, they will also take care to consult those whom they can, with diligent charity and not contentious disagreement, until either they find what they seek or, through the inquiry itself, exercise the mind’s vision so that they recognize that nothing further needs to be investigated.

For now, however, while a response from the friend whom we have consulted is not yet to be despaired of, I think I have persuaded Your Love that our inquiry should not be published, insofar as this lies within us. You yourself, moreover, did not ask for it alone, but wished to have sent to you together with it the response of the man whom I consulted; I would certainly do this if I had it.

But if, to use the words of Your Holiness which you placed in your letter, by “the lucid demonstration of my wisdom,” which, as you write, “the author of my life, the source of light, has attributed to me according to my merit,” you do not mean my inquiry and investigation itself, but think that I have already discovered the matter I sought and ask that I send you that discovery instead, I would do so if matters were as you think.

For I confess that I have still not discovered how the soul derives sin from Adam—for there is no legitimate doubt that it does—and yet is itself not derived from Adam. This is something that ought to be investigated more carefully than asserted rashly.

## CHAPTER III

7. Your letter mentions I do not know how many old men, men instructed by learned priests, whom you were unable to recall to an understanding suited to your modesty and to an assertion completely full of truth. Yet you do not state what your assertion, completely full of truth, actually is, to which you could not recall those old men and men instructed by learned priests.

For if these old men held, or hold, what they received from learned priests, how had a rustic and less-instructed crowd of clerics caused you trouble in matters about which they had been instructed by learned priests?

But if these old men, or the crowd of clerics, had deviated through their own perversity from what they had received from learned priests, they should rather have been corrected by the authority of those priests and restrained from their extremely contentious tumult.

But again, when you say that you, a new and inexperienced teacher, feared corrupting the traditions of so many and such great bishops, and feared turning people toward a better understanding because of the injury to the dead, what do you imply except that those whom you wished to correct refused to abandon the traditions of learned and great bishops who had already died, and declined to yield to a new and inexperienced teacher?

For the moment I say nothing about them. But I greatly desire to know your assertion, which you say is completely full of truth—not the opinion itself, I mean, but its assertion.

## CHAPTER IV
8. For you have sufficiently brought to our notice your disapproval of those who maintain that all human souls are propagated and transmitted by succession through the generations from that one soul which was given to the first-created man. But by what reasoning, or by what testimonies of the divine Scriptures, you have shown this to be false, we do not know, since your letter does not contain it. Furthermore, what you yourself hold in place of what you disapprove is not clearly apparent to me as I read both the letter you previously sent to the Caesareans and the one you most recently sent to me—except that I see you believe, as you write, that God has made, is making, and will make human beings, and that nothing exists or has existence in heaven or on earth without having been established and being sustained by him as author. This is indeed so true that no one ought to doubt it.

But you must still explain from what source God makes the souls which you deny are made by propagation: whether from some other source—and, if so, what that source is—or entirely from nothing. May you be far from holding the view of Origen and Priscillian, or of anyone else who thinks something of this sort: that, on account of merits from a former life, earthly and mortal bodies are assigned [Note: [Col. 0932] The editions read *in*: “very well.”] to them. For apostolic authority utterly contradicts this opinion, saying that Esau and Jacob, before they had been born, had done nothing either good or evil (Rom. 9:11). Thus your opinion on this matter is known to us not in its entirety but only in part; but its assertion—that is, the grounds by which what you think is taught to be true—remains entirely hidden from us.

9. For this reason I had asked in my earlier letter [Note: [Col. 0933] Epistle 190, §20.] that you kindly send me the *Book of Faith* which you say you wrote, and which you complain that some priest falsely subscribed; and I ask this again now, together with whatever divine testimonies you were able to bring forward for resolving this question.

For in your letter to the Caesareans you say that it seemed good to you that even secular judges should investigate every matter relevant to establishing the truth. When they had taken their seats at your common request and examined everything relating to the faith, Divinity, as you write, granted this by an infusion of his mercy: that they should put forward a stronger affirmation and assertion in support of their views than your moderation toward them had been able to maintain with the authority of immense testimonies. I therefore greatly desire to know these immense authorities of testimony.

10. For you appear to have pursued only one argument by which to refute your opponents: namely, that they denied our souls to be God’s work. If they hold this, their opinion is rightly judged worthy of condemnation. For if they said this about the bodies themselves, they would undoubtedly need correction—or condemnation. What Christian, after all, would deny that the bodies of every human being who is born are God’s works? Yet we do not for that reason deny that they are begotten by their parents, because we acknowledge that they are fashioned by God.

When, therefore, it is said that certain incorporeal seeds of our souls, each of their own kind, are likewise drawn from their parents, and that souls are nevertheless made from them by God’s work, this must be refuted not by human conjecture but by the testimony of divine Scripture. For the canonical books of holy Scripture could provide us with an abundance of testimonies proving that God makes souls. But such testimonies refute those who deny that each individual soul in human beings who are born is God’s work—not those who confess this and nevertheless maintain that souls, just as bodies, are formed by God’s activity but arise through propagation from their parents.

To refute these people you must seek certain divine testimonies; or, if you have already found them, you must send them, in mutual love, to us who have not yet found them, while we inquire as earnestly as we can.

## CHAPTER V

11. For your brief and final consultation in the letter which you sent to the Caesarean brethren [Note: [Col. 0933] Caesarea of Mauretania Caesariensis was the more distinguished city. Pliny, *Natural History* 5.2: “There is there the very celebrated town formerly called Caesarea, formerly Jol, the royal residence of Juba, granted colonial status by the deified Claudius, who sent veterans there by his command.” Whether it still survives under the name of Algiers, as some think, is uncertain; but Sanson, the celebrated geographer of the immediately preceding century, disagrees.] runs as follows:

“I earnestly beg you to instruct me, your son and disciple, who have only recently and very lately, with God’s help, come to these mysteries, by the kind of instruction that is proper and fitting, and by which wise priests ought to reply. Is it rather the opinion to be maintained that says the soul is derived from another soul, and that, by a certain hidden origin and secret order, all the other souls of the human race flow forth from the transfusion of Adam, the first-created man [Col. 0934]; or should that definition instead be chosen and that belief retained which all your brethren and the priests stationed here maintain and affirm—namely, that God both was, is, and will be the author of all things and of all human beings?”

Of these two alternatives, then, which you proposed in your consultation, you wish one to be selected and an answer given to you in favor of one or the other. This would be proper if the two were known to be contrary to one another, so that, once one had been chosen, the other would consequently have to be rejected.

12.
