But now, if someone does not choose one of these two alternatives, but answers that both are true—that is, both that all the other souls of the human race flow forth by the transfusion of Adam, the first-created man, and that God nevertheless was, is, and will be the author of all things and of all human beings—what do you think should be said against him?

Are we perhaps to say: “If souls are propagated from their parents, God is not the author of all things, because he does not make souls”? For if we say this, the reply will be: “Then, because bodies are propagated from their parents, God is not the author of all things, if for this reason he is said not to make bodies.”

Who, however, would deny that God is the author of all human bodies, while saying that this applies only to the body which he first formed from the earth—or certainly also to that of the man’s wife, since he himself formed her from the man’s side—but not also to the bodies of other people, because we cannot deny that the remaining human bodies flowed forth from them?

## CHAPTER VI

13. Accordingly, if those with whom you are in conflict on this question assert that souls are propagated by descent from that one soul in such a way that they now deny God makes and forms them, persist in refuting, convicting, and correcting them as far as, with the Lord’s help, you can.

But if they affirm that certain beginnings are drawn from that one soul and thereafter from parents, while nevertheless maintaining that each individual soul in each individual human being is created and formed by God, the author of all things, inquire from the sacred Scriptures what should be answered to them—something that is unambiguous and cannot be understood in another way [Note: [Col. 0934] See *On the Soul and Its Origin*, book 2, chapter 14, §20.]. Or, if you have already found such an answer, as I requested above, send it to us.

But if, like me, you still do not know it, persist with all your strength in refuting those who say that souls are not God’s work. In your first letter you said that they had murmured this among their more private tales and that, on account of this foolish and impious opinion, they had withdrawn from your fellowship and from the service of the Church. Against them, therefore, defend and uphold by every means what you stated in that same letter: that God has made, is making, and will make souls, and that nothing exists or has existence in heaven or on earth without having been established and being sustained by him as author.

For this is most truly and rightly believed, said, defended, and confirmed concerning every kind of creature without exception. God was, is, and will be the author of all things and of all human beings. You included this in your final consultation to our fellow bishops of the province of Caesarea, and you urged them in some fashion to choose it instead, following the example of all the brethren and fellow priests who are with you and who retain this belief [Col. 0935].

14. But one question is whether God is the author and maker of all souls and bodies, which is true, or whether some natures arise which he does not make, which is altogether an error. Another question is whether God makes human souls by propagation or without propagation, although there can be no legitimate doubt that they are made by him.

In this question I want you to be sober and vigilant. Do not destroy the propagation of souls in such a way that, through carelessness, you fall into the Pelagian heresy. For if, concerning human bodies—whose propagation is known to everyone—we say, and rightly say, that God is the creator not only of the first human being or of the first couple, but of all those propagated from them, I think it can easily be understood that those who defend the propagation of souls do not intend, on this account, to deny that God makes souls, since he also makes bodies, whose arising through propagation we cannot deny.

Rather, other proofs must be sought by which those who hold that souls are propagated may be refuted, if truth declares them to be in error. Concerning this matter, they themselves ought to have been questioned—if this had been possible—on whose account, as you write in the later letter you sent to me, you feared to turn people toward a better view, because of the injury that might be done to the departed.

For you said that these departed men were such and so great, and such learned bishops, that you feared, as a new and inexperienced teacher, that you might appear to corrupt their traditions. Thus, if I could know by what—or by what testimonies—such, so great, and so learned men asserted this opinion concerning the propagation of souls [Note: [Col. 0935] In the editions *vel* (“or”) is omitted as superfluous. Perhaps the text should read *qualibus, quibusve testimoniis* (“by what kinds of testimonies, and by which testimonies”), or rather *qua ratione, quibusve testimoniis* (“by what reasoning, or by which testimonies”); compare above, §8.]: although in your letter to the Caesareans, without at all considering their authority, you called it a new invention and an unheard-of doctrine; whereas we certainly know that, even if it is an error, it is nevertheless not a new one, but an old and ancient one [Note: [Col. 0935] Tertullian in many places, and Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* 2.34, teach that souls are made by propagation.].

## CHAPTER VII

15. When certain circumstances rightly compel us to doubt in some question, we ought not therefore to doubt whether we ought to doubt. For concerning doubtful matters we must doubt without hesitation.

You see how the Apostle does not hesitate to doubt concerning himself whether he was caught up into the third heaven in the body or outside the body: “Whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows” (2 Cor. 12:2–3) [Note: [Col. 0935] The same or similar points are repeated concerning the origin of the soul, book 1, chapter 15.].

Why, then, should I not be permitted, as long as I do not know, to doubt whether my soul came into this life by propagation or without propagation, since I do not doubt that, in either case, it was made by the supreme and true God? Why should I not be permitted to say: “I know that my soul exists by God’s work, and is altogether God’s work; whether it comes by propagation like the body, or outside propagation like the soul given to the first human being, I do not know; God knows”?

Which of these alternatives do you wish me to confirm [Col. 0936]? I could do so if I knew. But if you yourself know it, then you have in me someone more eager to learn what I do not know than to teach what I do know [Note: [Col. 0936] He bears witness to the same in Epistle 148, §4; Epistle 157, §41; and *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis* 12.18.39.].

But if you do not know, as I do not, pray as I do that the Teacher who said to his disciples, “Do not wish to be called rabbi by men; for one is your teacher, Christ” (Matt. 23:8), may teach us, whether through any servant of his [Note: [Col. 0936] See the final number of the book *Against the Priscillianists*], or through himself—if he knows that it is beneficial for us to know such things. For he knows not only what he should teach but also what it is beneficial for us to say.

16. For I confess to your Affection my desire. I do indeed wish to know what you ask; but I would much more wish, if it were possible, to know when the One desired by all nations will appear [Note: [Col. 0936] Perhaps one should read *praesentiatur*, “is perceived as present.” Thus in *Confessions* 11.18: “Whether the same is true also of the prediction of future things, so that images of things which do not yet exist are perceived as present—this, my God, I confess, I do not know.” And shortly afterward: “However the secret anticipation of future things may be situated,” and so forth. Earlier editions had *praesententur* corruptly instead of *praesentiantur*, and *praesentia* instead of *praesentio*.], and when the kingdom of the saints will come, than from where I began to come into this earth. Yet when the disciples—our Apostles—asked him who knows all things about the former, they received this answer: “It is not for you to know the times or seasons which the Father has placed in his own power” (Acts 1:7).

What if he also knows that it is not for us to know this, since he certainly knows what it is useful for us to know [Note: [Col. 0936] He raises the same question in *On the Soul and Its Origin* 4.4.5.]? I know through him that it is not for us to know the times which the Father has placed in his own power.

But whether it is for us to know the origin of souls, which I do not yet know—that is, whether knowing it pertains to us—I do not even know this. For if I knew at least that it was not for us to know, I would cease not only to affirm it while I remain ignorant but also to seek it. As things stand, although it is so obscure and profound that in this matter I am more careful to avoid the rashness of teaching than eager to learn, I nevertheless wish to know it, if I can.

And although what that holy man says is much more necessary—“Make known to me, Lord, my end” (Ps. 38:5), for he did not say “my beginning” [Note: [Col. 0936] Perhaps one should read: “I would not wish that,” and so forth.]—as far as this question is concerned, I wish that my beginning were not hidden from me.

## CHAPTER VIII

17. Yet even concerning my beginning I am not ungrateful to my Teacher. I know that the human soul is spirit, not body, and that it is rational or intellectual. I know that it is not God’s nature but rather a creature that is in some respect mortal [Note: [Col. 0936] Consult *Against the Priscillianists* 1.1.1 and *Against Maximinus* 2.12.2.], inasmuch as it can be changed for the worse and alienated from the life of God, by participation in which it is blessed; and in some respect immortal, since it cannot lose the capacity by which, after this life, it experiences either good or evil.

I also know that it did not merit being enclosed in the flesh because of deeds performed before the flesh; but neither does that mean that it is in a human being without the stain of sin, even if, as it is written, his life upon the earth should be of one day (Job 14:5, according to the Septuagint) [Col. 0937].

Accordingly, I know that no one is born from Adam through the succession of generation without sin. Hence even infants need to be born again through the grace of regeneration in Christ.

I rejoice that I have learned, and I affirm that I know, these many and not insignificant things concerning the beginning or origin of our souls—things in which there is much that belongs to the knowledge established by faith. Therefore, if I do not know whether, in the origin of souls, God makes them for human beings by propagation or without propagation, although I do not doubt that they are made by him, I choose to know this also rather than not know it. But as long as I cannot, it is better for me to doubt concerning it than rashly to affirm as certain something that might be contrary to that matter concerning which I ought not to doubt.

18. Therefore, my good brother, since you consult me and wish me to define one of these alternatives—whether the other souls are made from that one human being by propagation, as bodies are, or without propagation, as that one soul was made by the Creator, each soul individually for each person—for we do not deny that they are made by him in either way—allow me also to ask how the soul can derive original sin from the source from which it is not itself originally derived.

For we likewise do not deny that all souls derive original sin from Adam, lest we fall into the detestable Pelagian heresy. If you do not know what I am asking, let me patiently remain ignorant of both matters: the one you ask about and the one I ask about. But if you already know what I ask, then, once you have taught me this also, I will answer what you wish me to answer, since I will then have nothing further to consider there [Note: [Col. 0937] This is an obscure passage, which some think should be read conjecturally as: “Fearing nothing further there, I will answer.”].

I therefore ask you not to be angry because I was unable to confirm what you ask, but was able to show you what you ought to ask. When you have found it, do not hesitate to confirm what you were asking.

19. I considered that this, indeed, ought to be written to Your Holiness, since you think that the propagation of souls, as though you were already certain, must be rejected. But if I had to write back to those who assert it, perhaps I would show how they are ignorant of what they think they know, and how greatly they ought to fear daring to assert it.

20. Certainly, in the reply of our friend which I inserted into this letter, do not be disturbed by the fact that he mentioned two books sent by me and replied that he had not had leisure to answer them: only one of them concerns this question, not both. In the other I asked him about another matter and sought his consideration of it [Note: [Col. 0937] One should certainly read “another matter from him.” What that other matter was may be learned from Augustine himself, *Revisions* 2.45: “I also wrote two books to Jerome, who was staying at Bethlehem: one concerning the origin of the soul, the other concerning the saying of James, ‘Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all of it’; I consulted him about both. In the former, I did not myself resolve the question I had proposed; in the latter, I did not remain silent about what seemed to me to be its solution, but I consulted him whether he too approved it. He replied, praising the consultation I had made, but said that he did not have leisure to answer.”].

As for his warning and exhortation that we should work more diligently to remove the most pernicious heresy from the Churches, he means that very Pelagian heresy. I warn you, brother, as carefully as I can to avoid it when you think or debate about the origin of souls, lest you come to believe that no soul at all, except that of the one Mediator, derives from Adam the original sin to which it is bound by generation and released by regeneration [Col. 0938].

[Note: [Col. 0938] Perhaps one should read *subrepat*, “creep in”; thus, in exactly the same sense, *Tractates on the Gospel of John* 51.10: “But see that it does not creep in upon you, so that you wish to destroy yourself.” And *On the Soul* 2.6.10: “You rashly believed what you gladly heard, and false speech crept in upon you through pleasant speech.” Likewise Gregory the Great, *Homilies on the Gospels* 1.12.1: “Let the desire for praise not creep in”; although some manuscripts have *subripiat*.]

# EPISTLE 203

[Note: [Col. 0938] Revised according to manuscripts bl. cb. ff. gg. r. sb. vc., two t. and two v., Am. Bad. Er. Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0938] Elsewhere numbered 82; what was 203 is now 23. Probably written around the year 420.]

Augustine to Largo, urging him, having experienced the vanity of the goods of this world, to despise them, and to emerge better from having endured evils.

To the distinguished, excellent, and most dearly desired son LARGO, Augustine sends greetings in the Lord.

I have received the letter from Your Eminence in which you asked me to write to you. You would not have desired this unless you also regarded as welcome and pleasing what you thought I could write. It is this: if you desired the vanities of this world while you had not experienced them, then, having experienced them, you should despise them.

Their sweetness is deceptive, their labor fruitless, their fear perpetual, and their exaltation dangerous. Their beginning is without foresight, and their end is accompanied by repentance. Such is everything that is pursued in this mortal misery with more eagerness than prudence.

The hope of the devout, however, is different; different is the fruit of their labor, and different the reward of their dangers. For in this world it is impossible not to fear, not to grieve, not to labor, or not to be in danger. But it makes a very great difference for what reason, with what expectation, and toward what end each person endures these things.

When I look at those who love this world, I do not know when a suitable opportunity for healing their minds might arise. For when they possess what appear to be prosperous circumstances, they reject salutary warnings in their arrogance and regard them as though they were an old woman’s tale. But when they are living amid adversity, they think more about escaping what presently troubles them than about accepting what might heal them and lead them to a place where they could not be troubled at all.

Sometimes, nevertheless, some lend their hearts’ ears and give heed to the truth—more rarely amid prosperity, more frequently amid adversity. Yet they are few, for so they were foretold. I wish you to be among them, because I sincerely love you, my distinguished, excellent, and most dearly desired son.

Let this admonition be my greeting to you. For although I do not wish you henceforth to endure such things as you have endured, I nevertheless grieve more that you endured these very things without any change of life for the better.

# EPISTLE 204

[Note: [Col. 0939] Corrected according to manuscripts ff. vc. v., Am. Bad. Er. Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0939] Elsewhere numbered 61; what was 204 is now 173. Written approximately at this time.]

Augustine to Dulcitius, tribune and notary, and executor of the imperial orders issued against the Donatists, from book 2 of the *Revisions*, chapter 59. He indicates that he had already abundantly answered the complaints of the Donatists and exposes the madness of those who voluntarily brought about their own deaths.

[Col. 0939]

To the distinguished and honorable son DULCITIUS, Augustine sends greetings in the Lord.

1. I ought not to have disregarded your request, by which you wished me to instruct you how you ought to answer heretics, whose salvation is sought through the Lord’s mercy and through the persistent zeal of your energetic service.

Although great numbers of them—and we rejoice greatly at this—understand what benefit is being conferred upon them, some nevertheless, driven by a pitiable madness and ungrateful toward God and human beings, when they cannot devastate us by their own slaughter, think that they can terrify us by their own destruction, either seeking their own joy in our deaths or our grief in theirs.

But the salvation of so many and such great peoples ought not to be obstructed by the mad error of a few. What we wish for them is perceived not only by God and wise people but also by the very men who are our bitterest enemies. For when they think that they must terrify us by their own destruction, they do not doubt that we fear their perishing.

2. But what are we to do, seeing that many, with the Lord’s help, find the way of peace through your efforts? Can or ought we to prevent you from pursuing this unity because we fear that some of the most stubborn and most cruel toward themselves may destroy themselves—not by our will but by their own?

Certainly we would wish all those who bear the sign of Christ against Christ, and who boast against the Gospel about Christ from the Gospel they do not understand, to abandon their perversity and rejoice with us in his unity.

But since God, by a sufficiently hidden yet nevertheless just disposition, has predestined some of them to ultimate punishments, it is undoubtedly better that, after an incomparably greater number have been restored and gathered from that pestilential division and dispersion, some should perish in their own fires than that all alike should deservedly burn in the everlasting fires of hell because of their sacrilegious dissension.

The Church grieves over these perishing people as the holy David grieved over his rebellious son, concerning whose preservation he had given anxious instructions motivated by love. For when he had been deservedly killed on account of his unspeakable impiety, David nevertheless lamented him with the testimony of a tearful voice. Yet when the proud and wicked man had departed to his own place, the people of God, who had been divided by his tyranny, recognized their king; and the perfection of unity consoled the father’s grief over his lost son (2 Sam. 18–19).

3. We therefore do not criticize you, distinguished and honorable son, for thinking that such men at Thamugadi should first be admonished by an edict. But when you said there, “Know that you are to be handed over to the death you deserve,” they thought, as their replies indicate, that you had threatened to kill them after apprehending them [Col. 0940]. They did not understand that you were speaking of the death which they themselves wished to inflict upon themselves.

For you had received from no law the right of the sword against them, nor had you been instructed by the imperial enactments whose execution was entrusted to you to have them killed. In the second edict of Your Affection you explained more clearly what you intended.

You also thought it appropriate to address their bishop himself [Note: [Col. 0940] Gaudentius of Thamugadi.] in the most humane terms. This showed how gently those in the Catholic Church temper even the men who, by the authority of the Christian emperor, are placed in charge of correcting errors, whether by intimidation or by punishment—except that you treated him in more honorific language than was appropriate for a heretic.

4. But since you wished me to answer his reply, I think you judged that this too ought to be provided for the people of Thamugadi: that the false teaching of the man by whom they were being deceived should be refuted with somewhat greater care. We, however, are extremely occupied, and in many other little works of ours we have already refuted such empty talk.

For already, I do not know how many times, in argument and writing, we have shown that they cannot have the death of martyrs, because they do not have the life of Christians; it is not punishment but the cause that makes a martyr.

We have also taught that free will was given to human beings in such a way that, nevertheless, both divine and human laws have rightly established severe punishments for serious sins. It belongs to religious kings of the earth to restrain not only adulteries, murders, and other such crimes and offenses, but also sacrileges, with appropriate severity [Note: [Col. 0940] In Epistle 185.].

They are greatly deceived if they think that we receive such people as they are because we do not rebaptize them. For how are they received as they are when they are heretics and become Catholics by passing over to us? It does not follow that depraved hearts may not be corrected because the Sacraments once given may not be repeated.

5. We have often answered, according to the Scriptures and the reasoning of Christians, concerning the frenzied deaths which some of them inflict upon themselves—deaths which are usually detestable and abhorrent even to many of their own people, whose minds have not been so thoroughly possessed by madness.

For it is written: “He who is wicked to himself, to whom is he good?” (Sir. 14:5). Or, if they wish to die amid the very temptations in which they are placed, let the one who thinks it useful and permissible to kill himself kill his neighbor as well, since Scripture says: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Lev. 19:18; Mark 12:31).

That it is not permissible to kill another person, even one who wishes and asks for it and is no longer able to live, unless commanded by laws or legitimate authorities, is sufficiently indicated by the Book of Kings. There we read that King David ordered the man who had killed King Saul to be killed, although the man said that Saul, already wounded and half-dead, had asked him to do this, so that with one blow he might free him from those tortures by releasing the soul struggling against and wishing to escape the bonds of the body (2 Sam. 1:1–16).

Therefore, since anyone who kills another human being without the authority of legitimate power is a murderer, whoever kills himself is not a murderer only if he is not a human being. [Col. 0941] We have said all this in many ways in many other sermons and letters of ours.

6. Yet, as must be acknowledged, concerning that elder Razias—whom, because they are constrained by an extreme lack of examples, they boast that they finally found, after searching through all the ecclesiastical authorities, in the books of the Maccabees, as though for an authority supporting the crime by which they destroy themselves—I do not recall having answered them before.

But this should suffice for Your Charity and for all prudent people to refute them: if they are prepared to transfer to Christian life examples of all deeds from the Jewish people and from those Scriptures, then let them transfer this example as well.

But if among those books there are many deeds also of people who are praised for the truth of those Scriptures, which are either unsuitable for the present time or were not rightly done even then, this deed committed by Razias is of that kind.

For although this Razias was noble among his people and had advanced greatly in Judaism—things which, in comparison with Christian righteousness, the Apostle says were losses and refuse to him (Phil. 3:8)—and for this very reason Razias was called the father of the Jews, what wonder is it if pride, like a human impulse, crept upon him, so that he preferred to perish by his own hand rather than, after having stood so exalted in the eyes of his own people, endure dishonorable servitude in the hands of his enemies?

7. Such things are commonly praised in the writings of the Gentiles. But in the books of the Maccabees, although the man himself is praised, his deed is narrated, not praised; it is set before our eyes to be judged rather than imitated.

It should not, however, be judged by our own judgment—the judgment which we too might possess as human beings—but by the judgment of sober teaching, which is clear even in those ancient books themselves.

This Razias was far removed from the words that we read: “Accept whatever happens to you, and endure in pain, and in your humiliation have patience” (Sir. 2:4). This man, therefore, was not wise in choosing death; he was impatient of enduring humiliation.

8. It is written that he wished to die nobly and manfully. But does that mean wisely? Nobly, supposedly, so that as a captive he would not lose the freedom of his people; manfully, because he possessed such strength of spirit as to be capable of killing himself. When he could not accomplish this with the sword, he threw himself headlong from the wall, and while still alive ran upon the rock below. There, already drained of blood, he pulled out his entrails and scattered them among the people with both hands; afterward, exhausted, he died (2 Macc. 14:37–46).

These are great deeds, but they are not good. For not everything that is great is good, since great evils also exist.

God said: “Do not kill the innocent and the righteous” (Exod. 23:7). If, then, this man was not innocent and righteous, why is he proposed for imitation? But if he was innocent and righteous, why is the killer of the innocent and righteous man—that is, Razias himself—thought worthy of additional praise?

9. For the present, so that this letter may not become excessively long, let these points suffice to complete it.

I owe this kind of service of charity to the people of Thamugadi [Col. 0942], since they have been well commended to me both by your wish and by my honorable and dearly loved son Eleusinus, who served as tribune among them. I must therefore answer both letters of Gaudentius, the Donatist bishop, and especially his later letter, which he thinks he composed according to the holy Scriptures, so that no point may be thought to have been omitted.

# EPISTLE 205

[Note: [Col. 0942] We have collated this with manuscripts a. bg. bl. bn. c. cc. ff. g. gv. j. n. r. s. t., two sb., two vc., four v., and with Am. Bad. Er. Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0942] Elsewhere numbered 146; what was 205 is now 189. Written around the year 420.]

Augustine to Consentius, answering his questions about what sort of body Christ now has, and also about what sort of bodies ours will be in the resurrection.

To his most beloved brother CONSENTIUS, Augustine.

## CHAPTER I

1. As far as the bodily eyes are concerned, we see some people whom we do not know; their pursuits and manner of life are unknown to us. We know some whom we do not see; their affection and feeling toward us have become known, and you are among them. For that reason we desire all the more to see you, so that you may be among those whom we both see and know.

Those who, unknown to our eyes, are thrust upon our sight are not merely undesirable but scarcely tolerable, unless the beauty of the inner human being appears in them through certain signs.

But when someone’s mind, like yours, has first become apparent to us through understanding rather than through seeing the body, we already know such people. Yet for that very reason we also desire to see them, so that through what is visible to the eyes we may enjoy much more pleasantly and familiarly the inner friend whom we already know.

Perhaps God will also grant us this concerning you, when human affairs are, as we wish, quieter and more tranquil, so that it may be a matter of honorable affection rather than troublesome necessity.

Now I shall answer, as I am able with the Lord’s help, the questions you sent me on another sheet in addition to your letter.

## 2

You ask whether the Lord’s body now has bones and blood, or the other features of flesh. What if you had added: whether it also has clothing? Would not the question have grown? Why else, except that we can scarcely conceive without corruption those things which we know to be subject to corruption in the ordinary course of this present life, although certain demonstrations of divine miracles have already been given, from which we may infer greater things? For if the clothing of the Israelites could remain unworn for so many years in the wilderness, and if the leather of their sandals lasted so long without decay, God can everywhere preserve the incorruptible condition of any bodies for as long as he wishes.

I therefore believe that the Lord’s body is in heaven as it was on earth when he ascended into heaven. To the disciples who, as we read in the Gospel, were doubting his resurrection and thought that what they saw was not a body but a spirit, he had said: “See my hands and feet; touch me and see, because a spirit does not have bones and flesh as you see me have” (Luke 24:39). Just as, while he was on earth, he was handled by their hands, so, when he was going into heaven, he was conveyed before their eyes. There the angelic voice sounded: “He will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts 1:11). Let faith be present, and no question will remain.

## 3

Unless, perhaps, the question must be asked about blood, because when he had said, “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones,” he did not add “blood.” Let us therefore not add to our inquiry what he did not add to his statement; and, if you please, let the question be ended here in brief.

For perhaps, once an opening has been made concerning blood, a more troublesome investigator will press us and say: “If there is blood, why not also phlegm? Why not yellow bile and black bile, by which medical science likewise testifies that the nature of flesh is tempered through the four humors?” But whatever anyone adds, let him beware of adding corruption, lest he corrupt the soundness and purity of his faith.

## 4

Human weakness measures divine works that it has not experienced by the customary things it has experienced, and thinks itself clever when it chatters: “If it is flesh, it is also blood; if blood, then the other humors as well; if the other humors, then corruption too.”

By the same reasoning it would say: “If there is flame, it burns; if it burns, it scorches; if it scorches, therefore the bodies of the three men whom the impious king cast into the furnace were consumed by the fire.” But if no one who thinks rightly about divine works doubts that this miracle happened to the three men (Dan. 3), why should we not believe that the one who made those bodies unable to be consumed by fire also made that body unable to be corrupted by fire, hunger, illness, old age, or any other force by which corruption usually weakens human bodies?

If someone says that incorruption against the fire was not added to the flesh of those three men, but that the fire itself was deprived of the power to consume, why should we fear that he could not make flesh incapable of corruption, who made fire incapable of consuming? Indeed, if this is understood not as a change in the flesh but as a change in the fire, it is much more marvelous: at the same time it did not burn the human bodies, so that it could not harm them, and it did burn the wood of the furnace, so that it could blaze.

But those who do not even believe these things distrust divine power excessively; our present discussion is neither with them nor for them. Those, however, who believe these things should also infer from them, in whatever way they can, the matters they are faithfully investigating.

Divine power is therefore able, from this visible and tangible nature of bodies, while leaving certain qualities in place, to remove whichever qualities it wishes. Accordingly, it is also able to strengthen mortal members with enduring vigor, while their bodily features remain but the corruption of mortality has been extinguished: so that decay is absent, but form remains; movement is present, but weariness absent; the power to eat is present, but the necessity of hunger absent.

# CHAPTER II

## 5

What is therefore read in the Apostle—“Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 15:50)—can indeed be resolved in the manner you mentioned, by understanding “flesh and blood” to mean the works of flesh and blood. Yet because the Apostle was speaking not about works but about the manner of the resurrection, and was dealing with that question in his argument, it is better understood in that passage that “flesh and blood” stands for the corruption of flesh and blood.

For if the word “flesh” signifies an activity, why should it not also signify corruption, as it is said: “All flesh is grass”? For here too corruptibility itself is signified; the passage continues: “All the glory of flesh is like the flower of grass. The grass withered, and the flower fell” (Isa. 40:6–7).

Does this also apply to that flesh of which it was said: “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have bones and flesh as you see me have”? For how could it wither or fall, when it is written that “Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more, and death will no longer rule over him” (Rom. 6:9)?

## 6

Accordingly, look above at the Apostle’s own statement and consider it in its entirety. When he wished to persuade those who said that there is no resurrection of the dead that the dead are indeed resurrected, he first set Christ’s resurrection before them as an example. Among the other matters he discussed there, he raised this question for himself and said: “But someone will say, ‘How are the dead raised? With what body will they come?’”—that is, with what kind of body?

Then, bringing forward the evidence of seeds, he says: “Fool! What you sow is not made alive unless it first dies; and what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare grain, perhaps of wheat” [Note: Three manuscripts read, “a grain of spelt-wheat.” Twelve others, together with Badius and Erasmus, read, “almost wheat.”], “or of some other kind. But God gives it a body as he has willed, and to each of the seeds its own body.”

It is in this sense, therefore, that he had said, “not the body that is to be.” For it will indeed be wheat from wheat; but because no one sows the blade, or the stalk, or the many coverings of the grains in the chaff—although the seeds rise together with them—he therefore says, “a bare grain.” He wished thereby to show that, if God can add what was not present in the bare seed, he can much more restore what was present in the human body.

## 7

What he adds next concerns the distinction among those who rise, on account of the different glories of the faithful and the saints. “Not all flesh,” he says, “is the same flesh: one kind is the flesh of human beings, another the flesh of animals, another of birds, another of fish. There are also heavenly bodies and earthly bodies; but the glory of heavenly bodies is one thing, and that of earthly bodies another. The glory of the sun is one thing, the glory of the moon another, and the glory of the stars another. For star differs from star in glory: so also is the resurrection of the dead.”

The meaning throughout is this: if kinds of flesh, although all mortal, nevertheless differ among themselves according to the differences among living creatures; and if bodies, although all visible, nevertheless differ according to the differences of their places, so that the glory of heavenly things is one thing and that of earthly things another; and if, in the exalted places, although all are heavenly, they themselves also differ in the brightness of their lights, it is not surprising that in the resurrection of the dead there will be a difference in the glory of merits.

## 8

He then proceeds to what all flesh that rises to eternal life has in common, and says: “It is sown in corruption, it will rise in incorruption; it is sown in dishonor, it will rise in glory; it is sown in weakness, it will rise in power; it is sown an animal body, it will rise a spiritual body.”

In these words of the Apostle, is it permissible to think that our bodies will rise in a better condition than Christ’s, when his body is set forth as the example that we must faithfully contemplate and hope to attain through his grace?

Accordingly, Christ’s body could in no way have risen with corruption if our resurrection is promised in incorruption; nor could his body have risen without glory if ours will rise in glory. But where would there be glory if corruption still remained?

It is therefore exceedingly absurd to believe that his body was sown in weakness—that is, put to death—and rose in weakness, when our body is sown in weakness and rises in power; and when the same Apostle says of Christ: “Although he was crucified in weakness, he lives by the power of God” (2 Cor. 13:4).

Who could think so absurdly as to believe that his body was sown as an animal body and resurrected as an animal body, if ours is sown as an animal body and will rise as a spiritual body?

## 9

It is therefore established, and there is no reason for doubt, that Christ’s body—which, although it did not see the corruption of decay in the tomb, so that it is written, “You will not give your holy one to see corruption” (Ps. 15:10), could nevertheless be pierced by nails and a lance—now exists wholly in incorruption.

What was sown in the dishonor of passion and death now exists in the glory of eternal life; what could be crucified in weakness now reigns in power; and what was an animal body, because it was taken from Adam, is now spiritual, because it has been inseparably joined to the Spirit.

For when the Apostle wished to support his statement about the animal body with testimonies from Scripture, he cited what is read in Genesis: “If there is,” he says, “an animal body, there is also a spiritual one; as it is written, ‘The first Adam was made a living soul,’ or ‘a living being’” (1 Cor. 15:44).

You surely recall how it is written: “And God breathed into his face the breath of life, and the human being became a living soul” (Gen. 2:7). It is also said of the animals: “Let the earth bring forth a living soul” (Gen. 1:24).

An animal body is therefore understood to be called such because it resembles the other animals in its dissolution and corruption through death—it is daily restored by food and afterward, when the organism’s frame has been broken apart [Note: Several manuscripts read, “when the structure of the living being has been overcome”], is dissolved.

A spiritual body, on the other hand, is one that is already immortal together with the spirit.

## 10

Some, however, think that the body then becomes spiritual when the body itself is changed into spirit, and that what was a human being composed of body and spirit will become wholly and entirely spirit—as though the Apostle had said, “The body is sown; the spirit will rise.”

But he said: “An animal body is sown; a spiritual body will rise.” Therefore, just as an animal body is not the soul but a body, so we must not think that a spiritual body is spirit, but a body.

Who would dare to suppose either that Christ’s body did not rise spiritual, or that, if it rose spiritual, it was no longer a body but spirit—when Christ refutes this opinion of the disciples? When they saw him and thought they were seeing a spirit, he said: “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have bones and flesh as you see me have.”

That flesh, then, was already a spiritual body; yet it was not spirit, but body, no longer to be dissolved and separated from the soul by any death. Similarly, the animal body, animated by God’s breath when the human being became a living soul, would itself have become spiritual without the intervention of death, had the transgression of the commandment not first inflicted punishment through sin, before God granted the crown to preserved righteousness.

## 11

This is why the Lord Christ came through us to us, when he found us sinners and himself righteous: as though upon the bed of our humility, but not with the disease of our iniquity.

He appeared to us through an animal—that is, a mortal—body. Yet, if he had wished, he could have come at the outset with an immortal body. But because it was necessary for us to be healed through the humility of the Son of God, he descended to the level of our weakness and, through the power of his resurrection, displayed the merit and reward of our faith.

Therefore the Apostle continues and says: “The last Adam became a life-giving spirit.”

Whether the first Adam is understood as the one formed from dust, and the last Adam as the one born from a virgin; or whether both are fulfilled in each human being, so that the first Adam is the human being in a mortal body and the last Adam is that same person in an immortal body—he nevertheless wished to establish this distinction between a living soul and a life-giving spirit: there the body is animal, here it is spiritual.

For the soul does live in an animal body, but it does not give life so as to remove corruption. In a spiritual body, however, because it adheres perfectly to the Lord and is “one spirit” with him (1 Cor. 6:17), it gives life in such a way as to make the body spiritual, consuming all corruption and fearing no separation.

## 12

He therefore continues: “But not first the spiritual, but the animal; afterward the spiritual. The first human being was from the earth, earthly; the second human being was from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly, so also are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, so also are the heavenly. And just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the one who is from heaven.”

What does “As was the earthly, so also are the earthly” mean except “mortals from a mortal”? And what does “As is the heavenly, so also are the heavenly” mean except “immortals through an immortal”? The former comes through Adam, the latter through Christ.

For the Lord became earthly for this purpose, although he was heavenly: to make those who were earthly heavenly. That is, he became mortal from immortal by assuming the form of a servant, not by changing the nature of the Lord, so that he might make those who were mortal immortal by imparting the Lord’s grace, not by retaining a servant’s indignity [Note: The Cistercian manuscript reads, “and enduring a servant’s indignity.”].

## 13

When, therefore, the Apostle was discussing the resurrection of the body and teaching that our bodies would become incorruptible from corruptible, glorious from contemptible, powerful from weak, spiritual from animal—in other words, immortal from mortal—he added the point under discussion and said: “Now this I say, brothers, that flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God.”

And lest anyone think that the Apostle had defined this according to the substance of flesh, he made clear what he meant by adding: “Nor will corruption possess incorruption.” It is as though he had said: “I said that flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God for this reason: corruption will not possess incorruption” [Col. 0947].

In this passage, therefore, he wished the term “flesh and blood” to be understood as referring to the corruption of mortality.

## 14

Finally, as though someone were to say to him, “How will it be flesh, and yet not be flesh?”—for it will be flesh, since after his resurrection the Lord said, “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have bones and flesh as you see me have”; yet it will not be flesh, since “flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God”—he explains what he has said by adding: “Behold, I tell you a mystery: we shall all rise,” or, as the Greek manuscripts have it, “we shall all sleep, but we shall not all be changed.”

Whether he intended this change to be understood for the worse or for the better is shown by what follows. “In an atom,” he says—that is, in a point of time that cannot be divided—“in the twinkling of an eye,” that is, with the utmost speed—“at the last trumpet,” that is, at the final sign that will be given so that these things may be completed: “for the trumpet will sound,” he says, “and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed.”

This change must therefore without doubt be understood as being for the better, because both the righteous and the unrighteous will rise. But, as the Lord says in the Gospel, “those who have done good will rise to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5:29), calling eternal punishment “judgment,” as he says elsewhere: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18).

Accordingly, those who will rise for judgment will not be changed into that incorruption which cannot suffer even the corruption of pain. That incorruption belongs to the faithful and the saints; the others, however, will be tormented by perpetual corruption, because “their fire will not be quenched, and their worm will not die” (Isa. 66:24).

## 15

What, then, does this distinction mean—“The dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed”—unless it means that all will rise incorruptible, but that among them the righteous will also be changed into that incorruption which absolutely no corruption can harm?

Accordingly, those who will not be changed into it will indeed rise incorruptible in the integrity of their members, yet they will still be corrupted by the pain of punishments, when they hear: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41). “The righteous will not fear that evil report” (Ps. 111:7).

After he had said of the change of the righteous, “We shall be changed,” as though we were asking how this would happen, or what sort of change it would be, he adds: “For this corruptible thing must put on incorruption, and this mortal thing must put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:35–53).

I think it should not be doubted that this is the meaning of the statement, “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God”: corruption and mortality of flesh and blood will not be there. It is with reference to these qualities that he names flesh and blood in this passage.

## 16

Accordingly, to offer an example that occurs to me for the moment: it is written, “Lest the tempter tempt you, and our labor be in vain” (1 Thess. 3:5). Here the tempter is understood to be the devil, as though God did not tempt at all; yet Scripture says elsewhere of God, “He himself tempts no one” (James 1:13).

Nor is this statement contrary to the one that says, “The Lord your God is testing you” (Deut. 13:3). The question is resolved when we recognize that the word “temptation” has different meanings: one kind is the temptation of deception, another the temptation of testing. In the former sense, the tempter is understood to be the devil; in the latter, God tests.

Likewise, when it is said, “Flesh will possess the kingdom of God,” and, “Flesh will not possess the kingdom of God,” the meaning of this term must also be distinguished, and there will be no question. Flesh according to its substance—the sense in which it was said, “A spirit does not have bones and flesh as you see me have”—will possess the kingdom of God. But flesh understood according to corruption will not possess it.

This was explained when it was said, “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God,” in the immediately added statement, “Nor will corruption possess incorruption,” as I believe we have discussed sufficiently.

# CHAPTER III

## 17

As for what you ask—whether the features of bodies are formed individually by God the Creator—you will not be troubled if, so far as the human mind can, you understand the power of divine activity.

How could we deny that God is even now at work in all things that are created, when the Lord says: “My Father is working until now” (John 5:17)? Accordingly, the cessation of the seventh day must be understood as referring to the creation of the natures themselves, not to the administration of those natures, which are said to have been created.

Since, therefore, the nature of things is administered by the Creator, and all things come into being according to their orders, in their appointed places and times, God is working until now.

For if God does not now form these things, how is it written, “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you” (Jer. 1:5)? How can this also be understood: “If God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven” (Matt. 6:30)? Unless perhaps we must believe that the grass is clothed by God, but bodies are not formed by God!

When he said “clothes,” he clearly indicated a present activity, not merely a past ordering. The Apostle’s statement about seeds, which I mentioned above, also belongs here: “You do not sow the body that is to be,” he says, “but a bare grain, perhaps of wheat or of some other kind; but God gives it a body as he wills.”

He did not say, “He gave,” or “He arranged,” but “He gives,” so that you may understand the Creator to apply the efficacy of his wisdom to forming the things that arise daily at their appointed times.

Of this wisdom it is said: “She extends mightily from end to end”; and it does not say, “She arranged,” but “She orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1).

It is a great matter even to have a faint understanding of how changeable and temporal things are created not by changeable and temporal movements of the Creator, but by his eternal and steadfast power.

# CHAPTER IV

## 18

Regarding the matter you thought should be asked—whether all baptized persons who leave the body entangled in various crimes, without repentance, will obtain forgiveness at some time—I have already written a book of considerable length [Note: The book *On Faith and Works*]. If you take care to have it copied, perhaps you will ask nothing further about this matter.

## 19

You also wish to know from me whether that breath of God in Adam is itself the soul. I answer briefly: either it is the soul itself, or the soul was made from it.

But even if it is the soul itself, it was made. For God speaks of the soul through the prophet Isaiah, where he says: “I have made every breath”; the following words sufficiently indicate this, for the passage continues: “Because of sin I afflicted him a little” (Isa. 57:16–17)—that is, the breath itself—and the rest, which cannot be understood except of the human soul.

In this question we must especially beware of believing that the soul is not a nature made by God, but the very substance of God, like the only-begotten Son, who is his Word, or some portion of him—as though that nature and substance by which God is whatever he is could be changeable. Everyone who feels that he has a soul perceives that the soul is changeable.

While I was dictating these things, the courier, already waiting for a favorable wind, was pressing me urgently to sail. Therefore, if you find anything here expressed disorderly or inelegantly, or if you see that the whole thing is so, devote your attention to the teaching and pardon the language.

And in another hand: “May you live for God, dearest son.”

# LETTER 206

[Note: Revised against the Vatican manuscript and against Lovaniensis.]  
[Note: Elsewhere numbered 270; the letter formerly numbered 206 is now 267. Written about A.D. 420.]

Augustine commends Bishop Felix to the count Valerius.

To the deservedly illustrious and most distinguished lord, and most beloved son in Christ, Count VALERIUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

Whenever people ask me to commend them to your kindness and trustworthiness, if I do not do so, I seem to myself to judge incorrectly either your mercy toward those in need of help or your goodwill toward us.

Therefore I do so, and I do not hesitate especially to commend to Your Excellency the ministers of Christ who care for the Church, whose co-heir and son we rejoice that you are—deservedly illustrious and most distinguished lord, and most beloved son in Christ.

When our holy brother and fellow bishop Felix asked me to do this, I certainly ought not to refuse. I therefore commend to you a bishop of Christ who needs the assistance of a man of rank. Do what you can, since the Lord, whose gains we know you to pursue with the greatest eagerness, has granted you very great power.

# LETTER 207

[Note: Taken from volume 7, prefixed to the books containing the controversy with Julian.]  
[Note: From volume 7, prefixed to the books against Julian. The letter formerly numbered 207 is now 70. Written in A.D. 421 or shortly afterward.]

Augustine to Bishop Claudius, sending him the books composed against Julian.

To the most blessed brother and fellow bishop CLAUDIUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

Since, moved by fraternal affection, you sent me Julian’s four books—which he wrote against one book of mine [Note: The first book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*]—before I asked for them, I thought there was nothing more appropriate to do than for you above all to read and judge the things I am answering, and whether I have answered rightly and suitably.

For someone—I do not know who—had written to the illustrious and devout man Count Valerius, against that same book of mine which he knew I had written to him, extracting certain passages from those four books. When these writings came into my hands through the care of that eminent man, I did not delay adding to the first volume a second, in which I refuted all those points as best I could.

But now, when I examined the same books more carefully, I discovered that the person who had selected certain passages from them had not reproduced everything as it is found in those books. Consequently Julian, or any of his associates, may be able to make it appear that I had rather lied, because those extracts taken from the books and sent to the aforementioned count could not become known in precisely the same form as these four books.

Whoever, therefore, has read that second book of mine, written to Count Valerius as the first likewise was, should know that in some matters I was not answering Julian, but rather the person who selected those passages from his books and did not reproduce them as he found them, but thought that they needed some alteration—perhaps so that, in that form, he might make what was demonstrably another person’s appear almost as his own.

Now, believing the copies sent by Your Holiness to be more accurate, I see that I must answer the author himself, who boasts that he has refuted one book of mine in four of his own and does not cease scattering the poisons of his faith everywhere.

I have therefore undertaken this work with the help of the Savior of the weak and the strong. I know that you prayed for me, that I might complete it, and for those whom we believe and hope will benefit from labors of this kind.

Attend, then, to my response, the beginning of which will follow this letter. Farewell in the Lord, remembering us, most blessed brother.

# LETTER 208

[Note: Revised against two Vatican manuscripts, two others, and Lovaniensis.]  
[Note: Elsewhere numbered 209; the letter formerly numbered 208 is now 218. Perhaps written about A.D. 423.]

Augustine to the virgin Felicia, who bore with excessive displeasure the bad life of certain pastors of the Church—perhaps that of Antony of Fussala, mentioned in the following letter—admonishing her not to withdraw from the Catholic Church because she was offended by scandals.

To the deservedly respected daughter and one to be honored among the members of Christ, FELICIA, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

## 1

I do not doubt that your spirit has been troubled both on account of your faith and because of the weakness or wickedness of others, since the holy Apostle, full of the depths of charity, confesses and says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not on fire?” (2 Cor. 11:29).

Accordingly, I too have been pierced with concern and, anxious for your salvation, which is in Christ, have thought that these letters should be sent to Your Holiness either for consolation or for exhortation. For in the body of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is his Church and the unity of his members, you have become a most genuine sister to us: you are loved as an honorable member in its structure, and with us you live by its Holy Spirit.

## 2

Therefore I warn you not to be more deeply disturbed by these scandals, which were foretold as destined to come precisely so that, when they came, we might remember that they had been foretold and might not be greatly shaken by them.

The Lord himself foretold these things in the Gospel: “Woe to the world because of scandals! Scandals must come; but woe to that person through whom the scandal comes!” (Matt. 18:7).

Who are these people except those of whom the Apostle says: “Seeking their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Phil. 2:21)?

There are some who occupy pastoral thrones in order to care for Christ’s flocks; there are others who sit in them in order to enjoy their temporal honors and worldly advantages. These two kinds of pastors must necessarily remain in the Catholic Church until the end of the age and the judgment of the Lord, with some dying and others being born.

For if there were such people in the times of the Apostles, among whom the Apostle would lament over false brothers and say, “Perils among false brothers” (2 Cor. 11:26), and if he did not separate them through pride but endured them with patience, how much more must they exist in our times, since the Lord speaks most clearly about the period of this age, which is approaching its end: “Because iniquity will abound, the charity of many will grow cold”?

But what follows ought to console and exhort us: “The one who perseveres to the end,” he says, “will be saved” (Matt. 24:12–13).

## 3

Just as there are good and bad pastors, so among the flocks themselves there are both good and bad. The good are signified by the name “sheep,” while the bad are called “goats.” But they feed together in a mixture until the prince of shepherds comes, who is called the one Shepherd (John 10:16), and, as he himself promised, separates the sheep from the goats as a shepherd does (Matt. 25:32).

He commanded us to gather; he reserved separation for himself, because the one who does not know how to err ought to separate.

For the proud servants who rashly dared to separate before the time that the Lord reserved for himself were themselves separated from Catholic unity. For, being unclean through schism, how could they possess a clean flock?

## 4

Therefore, so that we may remain in unity and, though offended by the scandals of the chaff, not abandon the Lord’s threshing floor, but rather persevere as grains until the end of the winnowing (John 3:12), and endure the crushed straw with the firm weight of charity, our shepherd himself warns us in the Gospel about good pastors.

He teaches us that, because of their good works, we should not place our hope even in them, but should glorify the Father who is in heaven, who made them such. He also speaks of bad pastors, whom he intended to signify by the name of the scribes and Pharisees: they teach good things and do evil things.

## 5

For he speaks of the good pastors in this way: “You are the light of the world. A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden; nor do they light a lamp and put it under a measure, but on a lampstand, so that it may shine for all who are in the house. Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:14–16).

He warns the sheep about bad pastors, saying: “They sit on Moses’ seat. Do what they say, but do not do what they do; for they say things and do not do them” (Matt. 23:2–3).

When they hear this, Christ’s sheep hear his voice even through bad teachers and do not abandon his unity, because the good things they hear them say do not belong to those teachers but to him. Thus the sheep feed securely, because even under bad pastors they are nourished in the Lord’s pastures.

They do not imitate the deeds of the bad pastors, because such works do not belong to him but to the pastors themselves. When they see good pastors, however, they not only hear the good things they say but also imitate the good things they do.

The Apostle was such a pastor, saying: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. 11:1). He was a light illuminated by the eternal Light, the Lord Jesus Christ himself, and he had been placed on a lampstand because he gloried in Christ’s cross. Thus he says: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6:14).

And because he did not seek his own interests but those of Jesus Christ, although he urges those whom he had begotten through the Gospel to imitate him (1 Cor. 4:15), he nevertheless severely rebukes those who created schisms under the names of the Apostles. He reproves those who were saying, “I belong to Paul”: “Was Paul,” he says, “crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (1 Cor. 1:12–13).

## 6

From this we understand that good pastors seek not their own interests but those of Jesus Christ. We also understand that good sheep, although they imitate the actions of good pastors, nevertheless do not place their hope in those through whose ministry they have been gathered, but rather in the Lord, by whose blood they have been redeemed.

Thus, if they happen to encounter bad pastors who preach his teaching but practice their own evil works, they should do what the pastors say but not do what they do; and, because of the children of iniquity, they should not abandon the pastures of unity.

For in the Catholic Church—which is not confined to Africa, like the party of Donatus, but, as it was promised, expands and spreads among all nations, bearing fruit and growing throughout the whole world, as the Apostle says (Col. 1:6)—there are both good and bad.

But those who are separated from it cannot be good so long as they think against it. Even if the conduct of some of them appears to show them to be good and worthy of praise, division itself makes them bad, since the Lord says: “Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters” (Matt. 12:30).

## 7

Therefore I exhort you, deservedly respected lady and daughter honored among the members of Christ, to hold faithfully what the Lord has granted you, and to love with your whole heart both him and his Church. He did not allow the fruit of your virginity to be lost or to perish with the lost.

For if you were to depart from this world separated from the unity of Christ’s body, the preservation of your bodily integrity would profit you nothing.

But God, who is rich in mercy, brought about for you what is written in the Gospel. When those invited to the banquet excused themselves, the master of the household said among other things to his servants: “Go out into the roads and hedges, and compel them to enter, whoever you find” (Matt. 22:9).

Therefore, although you owe the most sincere love also to his good servants, through whose ministry you were compelled to enter, you must place your hope in the one who prepared the banquet and for whom you are concerned to attain blessed eternal life.

When you entrust to him your heart, your purpose, your holy virginity, your faith, hope, and charity, you will not be shaken by the scandals that will abound until the end. Rather, preserved by the steadfast strength of devotion, you will be saved and glorious in the Lord by persevering in his unity to the end.

Let me know by your reply how you have received this concern of mine for you, which I have taken care to make known to you in such words as I could. May God’s mercy and grace always protect you.

# LETTER 209

[Note: Purged of many errors in accordance with the Vatican exemplar.]  
[Note: Elsewhere numbered 261; the letter formerly numbered 209 is now 208. Perhaps written at the beginning of A.D. 423.]

Augustine congratulates Pope Celestine of Rome on his peaceful election, which may be assigned to the end of A.D. 422. He then explains the case of Bishop Antony of Fussala, who, deprived of the administration of his church because of his crimes, had appealed to the Apostolic See; and he earnestly begs that the sentence passed against him be allowed to stand.

To the most blessed lord and holy pope COELESTINE, deservedly venerated with due charity, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

1. First, I return congratulations for your merits, because our Lord God has established you in that See without any division, as we have heard, among his people. Next, I make known to Your Holiness what circumstances concern us, so that you may assist us not only by praying for us, but also by advising and helping us. For, placed in great tribulation, I have directed this letter to Your Beatitude, because, wishing to benefit certain members of Christ in our vicinity, I imprudently and incautiously brought upon them a great disaster.

2. Fussala [Note: Certain miracles divinely wrought in the territory of Fussala are related in Book 22, chapter 8, of *The City of God*. From that passage it appears that the same territory belonged to the care of the bishop of Hippo, still at the time when those events occurred—that is, when Maximinus of Sinitum, mentioned there with praise, had already entered into communion with the Church; and therefore after the year 405, when he was converted from a Donatist bishop to a Catholic.] is said to be a fortified town bordering the territory of Hippo. Previously there had never been a bishop there, but, together with the adjoining region, it belonged to the parish of the Church of Hippo. That land had few Catholics; the remaining populations there, composed of a great multitude of people, were miserably held by the error of the Donatists, so that in the town itself there was absolutely no Catholic.

It came about, by God’s mercy, that all those places adhered to the unity of the Church. It would take too long to explain through how many labors and dangers of ours this was accomplished, so that the presbyters whom we first appointed to gather them together were stripped, beaten, maimed, blinded, and killed. Yet their sufferings were not useless or fruitless, since the security of unity was established there.

But because the town mentioned was separated from Hippo by forty miles, and because, in governing them and gathering together their remnants—although they were few, and those of either sex who had gone astray were by then no longer threatening but fleeing—I saw that I was extending myself more widely than was proper and that I could not provide the diligence which I clearly recognized ought to be provided, I arranged for a bishop to be ordained and appointed there.

3. To accomplish this, I was seeking someone suitable and appropriate for that place, who was also versed in the Punic language. I had a presbyter ready, the one I was considering; and, in order that he might be ordained, I obtained by letter a request that a holy old man who at that time held the primacy of Numidia [Note: Unless we are mistaken, Silvanus of Zama is to be understood here, the predecessor in the primacy of Numidia of Valentinus of Baia. But below, section 6, Valentinus himself seems to be indicated, since he held the primacy in the year 419, as is clear from the synodal letter of the African fathers to Boniface.] come from far away. When he was already present, and everyone’s minds were anxious about so serious a matter, the man who had seemed ready to me abandoned me at the decisive moment by resisting in every possible way.

But I, who—as the outcome showed—ought certainly rather to have postponed than rashly hurried this dangerous business, did not want the most venerable and holy old man, who had traveled all the way to us, to return home without accomplishing what had brought him from so far away. Therefore, although no one had asked for him, I offered them a certain young man named Antonius [Note: Perhaps this is the same man who is named above among the fathers of the Council of Milevis in Letter 176.], who was then with me. He had indeed been raised by us in the monastery from early childhood, but, apart from the duty of reading, he was unfamiliar with any clerical rank or labor.

Those poor people, not knowing what was going to happen, accepted him obediently when I offered him. What more is there to say? It was done: he began to be their bishop.

4. What am I to do? I do not wish to burden Your Veneration with one whom I gathered in order to nurture; I do not wish to abandon those whom I brought forth through fears and pains so that they might be gathered together; and I cannot discover how to do both.

The matter has indeed reached such a scandal that here among us they brought charges against him—those very people who had obeyed us in accepting his episcopate, as though we were advising them well. In those proceedings, the capital crimes of sexual violation, which had been brought forward not by the people over whom he was bishop but by certain others, could in no way be proved; and he appeared to have been cleared of the allegations that had been spread most maliciously.

He therefore became so pitiable to us and to others that whatever was alleged by the townspeople and by the inhabitants of that region—concerning intolerable domination, plunder, and various forms of oppression and crushing—did not seem to us sufficient reason for depriving him of the episcopate, whether on account of those matters individually or of all of them heaped together. Rather, whatever was proved to have been taken away ought to be restored.

5. In the end, we tempered our judgments in such a way that, while his episcopate was preserved, the acts which ought neither to be done again by him nor proposed for imitation by others would nevertheless not be left altogether unpunished. We therefore preserved the young man’s full honor, while correcting him; but by reprimanding him we diminished his power, so that he would no longer preside over those with whom he had acted in such a way that, in their justified grief, they could not bear him as their superior at all, and lest their impatience under that grief should perhaps erupt into some crime, to the danger of both themselves and him.

Their disposition was already clearly apparent when the bishops dealt with him before them, although the distinguished man Celer—whose powerful administration against him he had complained of—now held no authority either in Africa or anywhere else.

6. But why delay with many words? Work together with us, I beg you, venerable and most blessed lord, and holy Pope, worthy of our dutiful affection. Order everything that has been sent to you to be read aloud. See how he administered the episcopate; how he agreed so completely with our judgment that, after being deprived of communion unless all things were first restored to the people of Fussala, he later set aside a sum of money, once the matter had been settled and the property assessed, so that communion might be restored to him; and how, by crafty persuasion, he induced our holy primate, that most venerable man, to entrust everything to him and recommend him to the venerable Pope Boniface as one wholly without fault.

Why do I need to recall the other matters, when the venerable old man already mentioned has reported everything to Your Sanctity?

7. In those numerous official proceedings containing our judgment concerning him, I ought rather to fear that we may appear to you to have judged less severely than was fitting, if I did not know that you are so inclined toward mercy that you would think not only that we ought to be spared because we spared him, but that he himself ought also to be spared.

But he attempts to turn what we did either kindly or leniently into a precedent and to claim it for himself. He cries out, “Either I ought to have sat in my own chair, or I ought not to have been a bishop,” as though he now sits anywhere except in his own. For this reason those places were left and permitted to him in which he had previously been bishop, so that he would not be said to have been illicitly transferred to another’s chair contrary to the decrees of the Fathers [Note: Council of Nicaea, canon 16; Council of Sardica, canon 1; Council of Antioch, canon 21, and others.].

Or is anyone to be so exacting, whether in severity or in leniency, that those who are not judged worthy of being deprived of the honor of the episcopate may in no way have anything exacted from them, or that those from whom something is judged to be exacted must be deprived of the honor of the episcopate?

8. There are examples, with the Apostolic See itself passing judgment or confirming the judgments of others, of men who, on account of certain offenses, were neither stripped of their episcopal honor nor left altogether unpunished.

I will not seek examples from times so distant from our own, but will mention recent ones [Note: Examples from earlier times, even those sought outside Africa, would have been sufficient for the matter. But the examples he produces were especially near at hand if, as is probable, those bishops, like Antonius himself, had been prompted by the case of the presbyter Apiarius and had likewise fled to the Roman bishop so that they might be restored in full by his authority.].

Let Priscus, bishop of the province of Caesarea, cry out: “Either a place in the primacy ought to have been open to me as to the others, or my episcopate ought not to have remained.”

Let another, Victor, bishop of the same province, cry out. He was left under the same penalty as Priscus, and no bishop anywhere communicated with him except in his own diocese. Let him cry out, I say: “Either I ought to have been admitted to communion everywhere, or I ought not to have been admitted to communion even in my own places.”

Let a third bishop of the same province, Laurentius, cry out, and let him cry out precisely in these words: “Either I ought to have sat in the chair to which I was ordained, or I ought not to have been a bishop.”

But who would condemn these things except someone who pays insufficient attention to the fact that not everything should be left unpunished, nor should everything be punished in the same way?

9. Since, therefore, the most blessed Pope Boniface, with pastoral and vigilant care, wrote in his letter, speaking about the bishop Antonius, “If he has faithfully reported the order of events to us,” receive now the order of events that he omitted in his memorandum, and then what was done after the letters of that holy man [Col. 0956]—now deceased—were read in Africa.

Come to the aid, in Christ’s mercy, of people who seek your help much more eagerly than he does, and who desire to be freed from his agitation. For he himself, or the frequent rumors, threatens them with judgments, public authorities, and military assaults as though these were going to execute the sentence of the Apostolic See [Note: These rumors were spread among the people because during that period the African fathers had more than once deliberated against appeals by African bishops to the Roman See. On this matter they later wrote to Caelestine himself: “We earnestly beg that in future you do not too readily admit to your ears those who come from here, nor wish to receive into communion those whom we have excommunicated; for Your Veneration will readily observe that this too was defined by the Council of Nicaea. For even if it appears that provision was made there concerning inferior clerics or laymen, how much more did it wish this to be observed concerning bishops, lest those suspended from communion in their own province appear to be restored to communion by Your Sanctity either hastily, prematurely, or improperly?” Later they finally ask: “Do not send your clerics as executors to anyone who asks, and do not authorize them to do so, lest we appear to introduce into the Church of Christ the notorious arrogance of the world, whereas she displays the light of simplicity and humility to those who desire to see God.” In fact, Caelestine did not undertake anything of the kind that Augustine feared. For there is no indication that the administration of the Church of Fussala was ever restored to Antonius; Augustine himself continued to exercise it until near the end of his life, as is understood from the Letter to Quodvultdeus, here numbered 224, in which he commends to him a presbyter of Fussala and indicates that the man belonged to his care. After Antonius’s death, it is reasonable to believe that another was appointed in his place. Certainly, in the *Notitia Africae*, Melior of Fussala is counted among the Numidian bishops. These observations may be noted to reconcile confidence in this Letter, which, as we understand, has been suspected by some learned men.].

Do not allow this to happen, I beg you, by the blood of Christ and by the memory of the apostle Peter, who warned the overseers of Christian peoples not to dominate their brothers violently (1 Peter 5:3). I commend to the kindness of Your Sanctity’s charity the Catholic people of Fussala, my children in Christ, and the bishop Antonius, my son in Christ, because I love both and commend both to you.

Nor am I angry with the people of Fussala because they bring a just complaint against me to your ears: that I imposed upon them a man whom I had not yet tested, nor even sufficiently strengthened by age, and by whom they were so afflicted.
