Nor do I wish harm to this man, for the more sincerely I cherish him, the more firmly I resist his perverse desire.

May both receive your mercy: the people of Fussala, so that they may not suffer evil; Antonius, so that he may not inflict it. Let the former not come to hate the Catholic Church if they are not helped against a Catholic bishop by Catholic bishops, and especially by the Apostolic See itself. Let the latter not bind himself by so great a crime that, while he attempts to make those people his unwilling subjects, he makes them strangers to Christ.

10. Indeed, as I must confess to Your Beatitude, such fear and grief torment me amid the danger of both parties that I am considering withdrawing from the office of administering a bishopric and giving myself over to lamentations suited to my error, if I should see the Church of God laid waste through the man whose episcopate I imprudently supported, and—God forbid—even him who lays waste the Church perish with it.

Recalling what the Apostle says, “If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged by the Lord” (1 Corinthians 11:31), I will judge myself, so that he may spare me who is going to judge the living and the dead.

But if you restore the members of Christ who are in that region from their destructive fear and grief, and console my old age through this merciful justice, he will repay you, both in the present life and in the life to come, with good for good—the one who through you comes to our aid in this tribulation and who established you in that See.

## LETTER 210

[Note: Corrected from manuscripts bl., cb., ff., gg., r., sb., two t., two vc., three v., Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: Formerly numbered 87; what was 210 is now 57. Written around the year 423.]

Augustine to Felicitas and Rusticus, concerning the evils that must be endured and fraternal correction; perhaps prompted by the disturbance that arose in a community of consecrated women, discussed in the letter immediately following this one.

To the most beloved and holy mother FELICITAS, and to the brother RUSTICUS, and to the sisters who are with you, AUGUSTINE and those who are with me send greetings in the Lord.

1. The Lord is good, and his mercy is poured out everywhere; through it, in its inmost depths, he consoles us concerning your love. How much he loves those who believe and hope in him, who love him and one another, and what he has prepared for them in the future, he shows especially by this: that even in this present age he lavishes such great blessings upon the faithless, the despairing, and the perverse [Note: So all the manuscripts. “[Upon the faithless and despairing, to whom…”], although he threatens those who persist in evil will to the end with eternal fire together with the devil. He makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45). A brief statement has been made, so that more may be considered.

For who can enumerate how many gifts and gratuitous benefits the wicked possess in this life from the one whom they despise? Among them is this great benefit: by the examples of tribulations which, like a good physician, he mixes into the sweetness of this age, he warns them—if they are willing to pay attention—to flee from the coming wrath and, while they are on the way, that is, in this life, to be reconciled with the word of God, whom they have made their adversary by living badly.

What, then, is not mercifully granted to human beings by the Lord God, from whom even tribulation is a benefit? Prosperity is the gift of the God who consoles; adversity is the gift of God who warns. If he grants these things, as I have said, even to the wicked, what does he prepare for those who endure him? You rejoice that, by his grace, you have been gathered among them, bearing with one another in love and striving to preserve the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace (Ephesians 4:3).

For there will not fail to be things that you must bear with in one another, until the Lord has so purified you, with death swallowed up in victory, that God may be all in all (1 Corinthians 15:54, 28).

2. Dissensions, however, should never be loved; yet sometimes they either arise from charity or test charity. For who is easily found who wishes to be reproved? And where is that wise person of whom it is said, “Reprove a wise man, and he will love you”?

Nevertheless, should we therefore not reprove and correct a brother, lest he proceed securely toward death? It commonly happens, and frequently occurs, that for a time he is saddened when reproved, resists, and argues; yet afterward he considers the matter with himself in silence, where there is no one but God and himself. He does not fear displeasing human beings because he is reproved, but fears displeasing God because he is not corrected. Thereafter he does not do the thing for which he was justly reproved; and to the extent that he hates his own sin, he loves the brother whom he has recognized as the enemy of his sin.

But if he belongs to the number of those of whom it is said, “Reprove a fool, and he will add to his hatred of you” (Proverbs 9:8), the dissension does not arise from his charity; nevertheless, it exercises and tests the charity of the one who reproves him, because hatred is not repaid to him, but the love that compels correction endures undisturbed even when the one who has been reproved hates him.

If, however, the one who corrects wishes to repay evil for evil to the person who is angry at the correction, he was not worthy to correct, but was plainly worthy himself to be corrected.

Act so that indignation either does not arise among you or, once it has arisen, is immediately destroyed by the swiftest peace. Take greater care to reconcile yourselves than to rebuke one another. For just as vinegar corrupts a vessel if it remains there too long, so anger corrupts the heart if it lasts into another day.

Act accordingly, and the God of peace will be with you. Pray together also for us, that we may eagerly fulfill what we rightly teach.

## LETTER 211

[Note: Corrected from the manuscripts Sulpitian, bl., ff., vc., two v., Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: Formerly numbered 109; what was 211 is now 247. Written around the year 423.]

Augustine recalls to concord the nuns who, while attempting to change their superior, had caused an unbecoming disturbance, and prescribes for them a rule of life.

[Note: In the manuscripts it is entitled, “Rebuke concerning the dissension of the consecrated women,” and in some copies there is added, “And after the rebuke of them, a regular instruction.” In Possidius’s index, and in ours, chapter 7, it is likewise listed in these words: “Rebuke and rule for the consecrated women.”]

1. Just as severity is ready to punish the sins it finds, so charity does not wish to find what it may punish. This is why I did not come to you when you were seeking my presence—not for the joy of your peace, but for the increase of your dissension.

For how could I have overlooked it and left it unpunished if, in my presence, such a great disturbance had arisen among you as arose in my absence—although it escaped my eyes, it nevertheless struck my ears through your voices? Perhaps your sedition would even have been greater in my presence, since it would have been necessary to refuse you the things you were asking for, which would have set a most pernicious example against sound discipline and would not have benefited you.

Thus I would have found you as I do not wish you to be, and I myself would have been found by you to be as you did not wish me to be.

2. Since the Apostle therefore writes to the Corinthians, saying, “I call God to witness upon my soul, that to spare you I have not yet come to Corinth—not that we lord it over your faith, but that we are fellow workers for your joy” (2 Corinthians 1:23), I also say this to you: to spare you, I did not come to you.

I also spared myself, so that I would not have sorrow upon sorrow. I chose not to show my face to you, but to pour out my heart to God for you and to plead before God with tears, rather than with words before you, the cause of your great danger, lest he turn my joy into mourning—the joy with which I ordinarily rejoice over you and, amid the many scandals with which this world everywhere abounds, sometimes find consolation when I think of your numerous congregation, chaste love, holy manner of life, and the more abundant grace of God that has been given to you, so that you not only despised carnal marriage but also chose to live together unanimously in one household, so that you might be one soul and one heart directed toward God.

3. When I consider these good things in you, these gifts of God, my heart, shaken by many storms arising from other evils, is accustomed to find some rest. You were running well; who bewitched you? That persuasion is not from God, who called you (Galatians 5:7).

“A little leaven” (1 Corinthians 5:6)—I do not wish to say what follows. I desire, pray, and exhort this even more: that the leaven itself be changed for the better, lest the whole lump, as it had almost already done, be changed for the worse.

If, then, you have begun again to think soundly, pray that you may not enter into temptation, nor again fall into contentions, rivalries, resentments, dissensions, slanders, seditions, and whisperings. For we did not plant and water the Lord’s garden in you so that we might reap these thorns from you.

But if your weakness is still in turmoil, pray that you may be rescued from temptation. Whatever it is that troubles you—if it still troubles you—unless those responsible correct themselves, they will bear judgment.

4. Consider how great an evil it is that, while we rejoice in the Donatists’ unity, we should mourn internal schisms in the monastery.

Persevere in your good purpose, and you will not desire to change your superior, under whom you have grown for so many years in number and in age. She received you as a mother, not bodily but in spirit.

All of you who came there found her either serving and pleasing my holy sister, the superior, or already herself the superior who received you. Under her you were instructed; under her you were veiled; under her you multiplied. Yet you are making such a disturbance that she should be changed, when you ought to mourn if we wished to change her for you.

She is the one you know; she is the one to whom you came; she is the one under whom, by having her for so many years, you have grown. You have received nothing new except a male superior. Or if you are seeking novelty on his account, and have rebelled against your mother in such a way out of hostility toward him, why did you not rather ask that he himself be changed for you?

But if you shrink from this because I know how reverently you love him in Christ, why do you not shrink still more from having her changed? For in governing you, the beginnings of the superior’s office are so disturbed that he would rather abandon you himself than endure this reputation and hostility directed against him—that people should say you would not have sought another superior unless you had first begun to have him as your superior.

May God therefore calm and settle your minds. May the work of the devil not prevail in you, but may the peace of Christ triumph in your hearts. Do not, out of inward grief because what you want is not done, or because you are ashamed to have wanted what you ought not to have wanted, rush shamefacedly toward death. Rather, by repenting, recover your strength. Do not have the repentance of Judas the betrayer, but rather the tears of Peter the shepherd.

5. These are the things which we command you, established in the monastery, to observe.

First, the reason for which you have been gathered together: live unanimously in the house, and let your heart and soul be one in God. Do not call anything your own; rather, let everything be common to you. Your superior is to distribute food and clothing to each of you—not equally to all, because you are not all equally strong, but to each according to her need.

For this is what you read in the Acts of the Apostles: “They had everything in common, and it was distributed to each according to what each needed” (Acts 4:32, 35).

Those who possessed something in the world when they entered the monastery should willingly wish it to be held in common. Those who possessed nothing should not seek in the monastery what they were unable to possess outside it. Nevertheless, what is necessary should be given to their weakness, even if, when they were outside, their poverty could not find even those necessities. They should not now think themselves happy merely because they have found food and clothing of a kind they could not find outside.

6. Let them not hold their heads high because they associate with women whom they did not dare approach outside; rather, let them set their hearts on things above and not seek earthly goods, lest monasteries begin to be useful to the rich rather than the poor—if the rich are humbled there while the poor are puffed up.

Again, those who seemed to be somebody in the world should not despise their sisters who came from poverty into that holy fellowship. Rather, let them strive to glory not in the dignity of wealthy parents but in the company of poor sisters.

Nor should they become proud if they have contributed something of their possessions to the common life, lest they become more proud of sharing their wealth with the monastery than they would have been of enjoying it in the world.

Every other kind of iniquity is practiced in evil works so that they may be done; but pride also lies in wait for good works so that they may perish. What benefit is there in scattering one’s possessions by giving to the poor and becoming poor, if the wretched soul becomes more proud through despising than it had been through possessing?

Therefore, live unanimously and harmoniously, and honor God in one another, whose temples you have become.

7. Persevere in prayer at the appointed hours and times. In the oratory no one should do anything except what it was made for and from which it received its name, so that if some wish to pray even outside the appointed hours, when they have leisure, they may not be hindered by those who wish to do something else there.

When you pray to God with psalms and hymns, let what is spoken be present in your heart. Do not sing anything except what you read is to be sung [Note: Several manuscripts have “what you have read.”]. Anything that is not written to be sung should not be sung.

8. Discipline your flesh by fasting and abstinence from food and drink, insofar as health permits. When, however, someone is unable to fast, she should nevertheless not take any food outside the hour of the meal, unless she is ill.

When you come to the table, listen without disturbance or quarrels to what is customarily read to you until you rise from it. Let it not be only your throats that receive food; let your ears also receive the word of God.

9. Those who are weak because of their former habits, if they are treated differently in their diet, should not trouble the others, nor should this seem unjust to those whom a different habit has made stronger.

The stronger should not consider the weaker happier because they receive what they themselves do not receive. Rather, let them rejoice for themselves because they possess the strength that the others do not.

If something is given to those who came to the monastery from more delicate habits—some food, clothing, bedding, or covering—which is not given to the others who are stronger and therefore happier, those to whom it is not given should consider how far the women who receive it have come down from their worldly life into this one, even though they have not been able to attain the frugality of those who are physically stronger.

Nor should those women be disturbed when they see that they themselves receive more—not because they are honored, but because they are being tolerated—lest the detestable perversion occur that in the monastery, where industrious women become rich insofar as they can, delicate women become poor.

Certainly, just as the sick necessarily have to receive less so that they are not burdened, so after illness they should be treated in such a way that they recover more quickly—even if they came from the humblest poverty of the world—as though their more recent illness had conferred upon them what an earlier habit had conferred upon the rich.

But when they have recovered their former strength, let them return to their more fortunate way of life, which is more fitting for servants of God the less they need. Let not the will of those who are now vigorous hold them in the place to which necessity had raised them when they were weak.

Let those consider themselves richer who have been stronger in enduring frugality. For it is better to need less than to have more.

10. Your clothing should not be conspicuous. Do not seek to please by your garments, but by your conduct. Nor should your head coverings be so delicate that the hairnets beneath can be seen.

Do not have your hair bare at any part, nor should negligence scatter it outside, nor skill arrange it. When you go out, walk together; when you arrive where you are going, stand together.

In your walking, standing, clothing, and all your movements, let nothing be done that might incite anyone’s lust, but only what is fitting for your holiness.

Even if your eyes fall upon someone, let them be fixed on no one. For when you go out, you are not forbidden to see men, but you are forbidden to desire them or to wish to be desired by them.

A woman is desired, and desires, not only through touch but also through affection and sight. Do not say that you have chaste minds if you have immodest eyes, because an immodest eye is the messenger of an immodest heart.

When, even while the tongue is silent, immodest hearts communicate themselves to one another through mutual glances, and they delight in each other’s passion according to the desire of the flesh, chastity itself departs from their conduct even though their bodies remain untouched by an unclean violation.

Nor should the woman who fixes her eyes on a man and delights in his fixed gaze upon herself think that no one else sees her doing this. She is certainly seen even by those whom she does not think are watching.

But suppose she remains hidden and is seen by no human being: what will she do about that heavenly observer from whom nothing can be hidden? Is he therefore to be thought not to see because, in his wisdom, he sees with such patience?

Let the holy woman therefore fear displeasing him, lest she wish to please a man wrongly. Let her think that he sees everything, lest she wish to look wrongly upon a man.

For his fear is also commended in this matter, where it is written: “An eye fixed upon another is an abomination to the Lord” (Proverbs 27:20, according to the Septuagint).

Therefore, whenever you are together in church, and wherever men are also present, guard one another’s chastity. For God, who dwells in you, will also in this way guard you through yourselves.

11. If you notice in any one of you the wantonness of the eyes of which I am speaking, warn her immediately, so that what has begun may not advance but may be corrected at once.

If, after the warning, you again see her doing the same thing, either then or on any other day, let the woman who was able to discover it report her as someone already wounded and in need of healing—but first let the matter be shown to another or a third woman, so that she may be convicted by the testimony of two or three (Matthew 18:16) and restrained with appropriate severity.

Do not think yourselves malicious when you report this. You are rather not innocent if, by remaining silent, you allow your sisters—whom you could correct by reporting them—to perish.

If your sister had a wound on her body that she wished to conceal because she feared being cut, would it not be cruel of you to remain silent about it, and merciful to report it? How much more, then, ought you to reveal her fault, lest it grow more disastrously rotten in her heart?

Before she is shown to others, through whom she is to be convicted if she denies it, she should be brought before the superior if, after being warned, she has neglected to correct herself, so that perhaps, being corrected more privately, she may not become known to the others [Note: The printed editions lacked the negation here; it has been restored from the manuscripts.].

But if she denies it, then other women are to be brought in against the woman who denies it [Note: The manuscripts read, “against the woman who lies.”], so that before everyone she may now be accused not by a single witness but convicted by two or three.

Once convicted, she must, at the discretion of the superior or presbyter, undergo corrective punishment [Note: All the manuscripts read “discipline.”]. If she refuses to endure it, and does not depart of her own accord, she is to be expelled from your fellowship.

This too is not done cruelly but mercifully, lest through a deadly contagion she destroy many.

What I have said about not fixing the eyes is likewise to be carefully observed in discovering, prohibiting, reporting, proving, and punishing all other sins, with love for persons and hatred of vices.

If any woman has progressed so far into evil that she secretly receives letters or any little gifts from someone, if she confesses this voluntarily, let her be spared, and let prayers be offered for her. But if she is caught and convicted, let her be corrected more severely, according to the judgment of the superior, the presbyter, or even the bishop.

12. Keep your clothing in one place, under one custodian, or two, or as many as may suffice to shake it out, lest it be damaged by moths; and just as you are fed from one storeroom, so let yourselves be clothed from one wardrobe. And, if it can be done, it should not be your concern what is brought out for you to wear as the season requires—whether each of you receives what she had taken off, or something else that another had worn—provided that what each one needs is not denied her.

If disputes and murmuring arise among you on this account, and one complains that she has received something worse than what she had previously had, and judges herself unworthy to be dressed in the way in which another sister was dressed, then test yourselves by this: how greatly you are lacking in that inner, holy disposition of heart, when you quarrel over bodily clothing.

Nevertheless, if your weakness is tolerated so that you receive what you had put away, still keep what you put away in one place, under common custodians. Let no one procure anything for herself—whether something to wear, something on which to lie, something with which to gird or cover herself, or something to cover her head—but let all your work be done in common, with greater zeal and more frequent cheerfulness than if each of you were making things for herself.

For the love of which it is written that “it does not seek its own” (1 Cor. 13:5) is understood in this way: it prefers what is common to what is private, not what is private to what is common. Therefore, the more you care for the common good than for your own, the more you should know that you have made progress, so that in all things subject to passing necessity, the love that endures may take precedence.

It follows, then, that whatever any man or woman may have given to her own people, daughters, or others related to her who are established in the monastery—whether clothing or anything else that must be counted among necessities—must not be received secretly. Rather, it must be in the power of the superior, so that, once placed in common, it may be given to the one who needs it.

[Note: [Col. 0962] Thus in the manuscripts. But in the Rule adapted for men it reads: “you shall have them in one place.”]

[Note: [Col. 0963] Thus the Vatican manuscripts. But the editions and the Rule for men have: “let her not be dressed in this way.”]

[Note: [Col. 0963] The editions read: “when it is necessary.” But the manuscripts read better: “to whom”; and undoubtedly Saint Benedict read it this way, for he transferred several precepts from here—and this very one in this form—into his Rule, chapter 54: “Let it be in the abbot’s power to order to whom that thing is to be given.”]

If any woman conceals something given to her, let her be condemned under the judgment for theft.

[Note: [Col. 0963] This sentence is absent from some manuscripts.]

13. Let your garments be washed according to the judgment of the superior, whether by you or by launderers, lest excessive concern for clean clothing bring uncleanness upon the inner soul. Nor should bathing the body and the use of baths be frequent; rather, it should be granted at the customary interval, namely once a month.

But if the necessity of an illness compels someone to wash her body, it should not be postponed for long. Let it be done without murmuring, on the advice of the physician, so that even if she does not wish to do so, she may, at the superior’s command, do what must be done for her health. If she wishes to bathe but it is perhaps not expedient, her desire must not be indulged; for sometimes what pleases is believed to be beneficial even when it is harmful.

Finally, if a servant of God has a hidden pain in her body, whatever she says is hurting her must be believed without hesitation. Nevertheless, if it is uncertain whether what pleases her is beneficial for treating that pain, let the physician be consulted.

Nor should fewer than three go to the baths, or wherever else it is necessary to go. Nor may a woman who has some necessity for going somewhere go with whomever she wishes, but she must go with those whom the superior orders.

Care of the sick—whether of those recovering after illness or of those suffering from some weakness even without fever—must be assigned to someone, so that she herself may request from the storeroom whatever she sees each person needs. Those placed in charge of the storeroom, the clothing, or the books must serve their sisters without murmuring.

Books may be requested at a fixed hour each day; outside that hour, those requested must not be given. Clothing and footwear, whenever they are necessary for someone in need, must not be withheld by those under whose custody the requested items are kept.

14. Either have no quarrels, or settle them as quickly as possible, lest anger grow into hatred, make a beam out of a splinter, and make the soul murderous. For what is written—“Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15)—does not pertain to men alone. The female sex also received this command, although the male sex was created first by God.

Whoever has injured another by insult, curse, or even accusation of a crime must remember to remedy what she has done by making satisfaction as quickly as possible. The woman who has been injured must forgive without argument.

If they have injured one another, they must mutually forgive one another what is owed, for the sake of your prayers. And clearly, the more frequent your prayers are, the holier they ought to be.

The woman who, although often tempted by anger, nevertheless hastens to obtain forgiveness from the one whom she acknowledges having wronged is better than the woman who is slower to become angry but more reluctant to bend toward seeking pardon.

She who does not wish to forgive her sister should not hope to receive the effect of prayer. She who never wishes to ask forgiveness, or does not ask it sincerely, is in the monastery without purpose, even if she is not expelled from it.

Therefore, spare one another harsher words. If such words escape from your mouths, do not be reluctant to bring forth remedies from the very mouths from which the wounds were made.

When the necessity of discipline compels you to speak harsh words in correcting those who are junior, if you also feel that you have exceeded proper measure in those words, you are not required to ask forgiveness from them, lest, among those who ought to be subject, excessive humility weaken the authority of governance. Nevertheless, forgiveness must be sought from the Lord of all, who knows with what affection you love even those whom you perhaps correct more severely than is just.

Your love for one another must not be carnal but spiritual. For actions performed without regard for modesty—even women with women—through indecent joking and play are not to be done not only by widows and untouched maidservants of Christ established in a holy vocation, but absolutely not even by married women or by virgins intending marriage.

15. Obey the superior as a mother, while preserving the honor due to her, lest God be offended in her; and obey the presbyter much more, since he has care for all of you.

Therefore, so that all these things may be observed, and so that if anything has not been observed it may not be passed over negligently but may be corrected and amended, this pertains especially to the superior: she must report to the presbyter who watches over you whatever exceeds her measure or strength.

She herself should not consider herself blessed because she exercises dominating power, but because she serves in love. Let her be set above you in honor before human beings; in fear before God, let her lie prostrate at your feet.

In all things, let her offer herself as an example of good works (Titus 2:7). Let her rebuke the unruly, comfort the fainthearted, support the weak, and be patient toward all (1 Thess. 5:14). Let her willingly maintain discipline, but impose it with fear.

Although both are necessary, let her desire to be loved by you more than feared, always considering that she will have to render an account to God for you. Thus, by obeying, you show mercy not only to yourselves but also to her, because the higher her position among you, the greater her danger.

[Note: [Col. 0964] The editions omit “in fear.” We have restored the word from one of the Vatican manuscripts and from the Rule adapted for men.]

16. May the Lord grant that you observe all these things with love, as lovers of spiritual beauty, fragrant with the good odor of Christ through a good manner of life—not as maidservants under the law, but as free women established under grace.

So that you may be able to look at yourselves in this little book as in a mirror, and not neglect anything through forgetfulness, let it be read to you once a week. Whenever you find yourselves doing what is written, give thanks to the Lord, the giver of every good. But whenever one of you sees that something is lacking in her, let her grieve over the past, beware of the future, and pray that both her debt may be forgiven and that she may not be led into temptation.

# LETTER 212

[Note: [Col. 0965] Collated with the manuscripts designated bl, cb, ff, gg, r, t, vc, and three designated v, and with the revised editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0965] Formerly 103; what was 212 is now 251. Written about the year 425.]

Augustine commends to Quintilian a widowed mother with her virgin daughter, who were carrying relics of the martyr Stephen.

To the most blessed Lord, and deservedly venerable brother and fellow bishop, QUINTILIAN, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

I commend to Your Reverence, in the love of Christ, the honorable servants of God and precious members of Christ, Galla, a widow of holy purpose, and her daughter Simpliciola, a consecrated virgin, subject to her mother in age but superior to her in holiness. We have nourished them in the word of the Lord as best we could. Through this letter I hand them over, as though with my own hand, to be consoled and assisted in every way that their benefit or necessity may require—something Your Holiness would undoubtedly do even without my recommendation.

For if, because of the heavenly Jerusalem, whose citizens we all are and in which they have desired to possess a place of greater holiness, we owe them not only civic affection but also brotherly affection, how much more do you owe it to them, since their earthly homeland is also among you, where those ladies despise secular nobility for the love of Christ?

I also ask that you deign to accept from them my duty of greeting with the same affection with which I have sent it, and that you remember us in your prayers.

They are indeed carrying with them relics of the most blessed and glorious martyr Stephen. Your Holiness knows, as we too have done, how fittingly you ought to honor them.

# ECCLESIASTICAL ACTS, OR LETTER 213

[Note: [Col. 0966] Collated with the manuscripts designated b, bl, cb, f, ff, gg, m, r, vc, two copies designated s, two designated t, and four designated v; and with the editions of Amerbach, Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0966] Formerly 110; what was 213 is now 1. Completed on September 26, 426.]

Ecclesiastical proceedings conducted by Blessed Augustine in designating Eraclius to succeed him in the episcopate and meanwhile to relieve the old man of part of his burdens.

[Col. 0966]

## 1

In the consulship of the most glorious Theodosius for the twelfth time and Valentinian Augustus for the second time, on the sixth day before the Kalends of October, when Bishop Augustine had taken his seat in the Church of Peace at Hippo Regius together with his fellow bishops Religianus and Martinianus, in the presence of the presbyters Saturninus, Leporius, Barnabas, Fortunatianus, Rusticus, Lazarus, and Eraclius, with the clergy and a large crowd standing by, Bishop Augustine said:

“What I promised your Charity yesterday, and on account of which I wanted you to assemble more frequently—and I see that you have assembled more frequently—must now be done without any further delay. For if I wished to speak about something else, you would listen less attentively, being suspended in expectation of that matter.

“We are all mortal in this life, and the final day of this life is always uncertain for every human being. Nevertheless, childhood is expected to reach boyhood, boyhood to reach adolescence, adolescence to reach youth, youth to reach maturity, and maturity to reach old age. Whether this happens is uncertain, but there is nevertheless something to be hoped for.

“Old age, however, has no other age to hope for. It is also uncertain how long old age itself will last for a person; yet this is certain: no age remains that can succeed old age.

“Because God willed it, I came to this city with the strength of adulthood. Yet I was young, and I have grown old. I know that after the deaths of bishops, Churches are often disturbed by ambitious or contentious men. Since I have often experienced and lamented this, I must do what lies within my power to ensure that it does not happen to this city.

“As your Charity knows, I was recently in the Church of Milevis. The brothers there, and especially the servants of God who are there, asked me to come because some disturbance was feared after the death of blessed memory, my brother and fellow bishop Severus.

“I came, and as the Lord willed, in his mercy he helped us so that they received in peace the bishop whom their bishop had designated while still alive. Once this became known to them, they willingly embraced the wishes of their preceding and departing bishop.

“Yet something had been left undone, which saddened some people. Brother Severus had thought it sufficient to designate his successor among the clergy; he had not addressed the people about it, and therefore there was some sadness among certain people.

“What more can I say? It pleased God: the sadness was driven away, and joy took its place. The bishop whom the preceding bishop had designated was ordained.

“Therefore, so that no one may complain about me, I bring my wish—which I believe to be God’s wish—to the knowledge of all of you: I wish the presbyter Eraclius to be my successor.”

The people acclaimed: “Thanks be to God; praises to Christ.” This was said twenty-three times.

“Hear us, O Christ; life to Augustine.” This was said sixteen times.

“You are father; you are bishop.” This was said eight times.

[Note: [Col. 0966] The editions have “Eradius.” But all the manuscripts consistently have “Eraclius,” or “Heraclius.” Shortly afterward, two manuscripts have “presbyter” instead of “presbyters.”]

## 2

When silence had been restored, Bishop Augustine said:

“There is no need for me to say anything in praise of him. I defer to his wisdom and spare his modesty. It is enough that you know him; and I say that I wish what I know you wish. Even if I had not known it before, I would have learned it today.

“This, then, is what I wish. From our Lord God, even now in the chill of old age, I ask it with fervent prayers. I exhort, admonish, and beg you to pray with me, so that God may confirm what he has worked in us, when all your minds have been brought together and fused in the peace of Christ (Ps. 67:29).

“May the one who sent him preserve him; may he preserve him safe and blameless, so that the one who brings joy to the living may fill the place of the dying.

“As you see, the Church’s notaries are recording what we say and what you say. My speech and your acclamations do not fall to the ground. To put it more plainly, we are now drawing up ecclesiastical proceedings. For, so far as human beings are concerned, I wish this to be confirmed in this way.”

The people acclaimed thirty-six times: “Thanks be to God; praises to Christ.”

“Hear us, O Christ; life to Augustine.” This was said thirteen times.

“You are father; you are bishop.” This was said eight times.

“He is worthy and just.” This was said twenty times.

“Well deserving, fully worthy.” This was said five times.

“He is worthy and just.” This was said six times.

## 3

When silence had been restored, Bishop Augustine said:

“Therefore, as I was saying, I wish my will and your will to be confirmed in the ecclesiastical proceedings, so far as human beings are concerned. But as regards the hidden will of the Almighty, let us all, as I said, pray that God may confirm what he has worked in us.”

The people acclaimed: “We give thanks for your judgment.” This was said sixteen times.

“Let it be done, let it be done.” This was said twelve times.

“You are father; Eraclius is bishop.” This was said six times.

## 4

When silence had been restored, Bishop Augustine said:

“I know that you also know this, but I do not want what happened in my case to happen to him.

“Many of you know what happened; only those who were then either not yet born or not yet old enough to know are unaware of it. While my father and bishop, Valerius of blessed memory, was still alive and in the body, I was ordained bishop and sat with him. I did not know, nor did he know, that this had been prohibited by the Council of Nicaea.

“Therefore, what was criticized in me, I do not want criticized in my son.”

The people acclaimed: “Thanks be to God; praises to Christ.” This was said thirteen times.

## 5

When silence had been restored, Bishop Augustine said:

“He will remain a presbyter as he is; when God wills, he will become bishop. But plainly, with the help of Christ’s mercy, I am now going to do what I have not yet done.

“You know what I wished to do several years ago, and you did not permit it. It pleased me and you, on account of the care of the Scriptures which my brother and father fellow bishops graciously imposed upon me in two councils, those of Numidia and Carthage, that for five days no one should trouble me.

“Proceedings were drawn up; it pleased you, and you acclaimed. Your decision and your acclamations are being read. This was observed around me for a short time; afterward it was forcibly broken into, and I am not allowed to devote myself to what I wish. Before midday and after midday I am entangled in the affairs of human beings.

“I beg and bind you by Christ to allow me to transfer to this young man—that is, to the presbyter Eraclius, whom today in Christ’s name I designate as bishop and my successor—the burdens of my activities.”

The people acclaimed: “We give thanks for your judgment.” This was said twenty-six times.

## 6

When silence had been restored, Bishop Augustine said:

“I give thanks to our Lord God for your affection and goodwill; indeed, I give thanks to God for them.

“Therefore, brothers, whatever is brought to me must be brought to him. When he needs advice, I will not withhold my assistance; far be it from me to withdraw it. Nevertheless, whatever is brought to me must be brought to him.

“Let him either consult me if perhaps he does not find what he ought to do, or ask as a helper for one whom he knows to be his father. Thus nothing will be lacking for you, and I too, if God grants me even a little time in this life, may at last not give my small life to sloth or idleness, but may devote it to the holy Scriptures insofar as he himself permits and grants. This will benefit him, and through him it will also benefit you.

“Let no one therefore begrudge me my leisure, for my leisure has a great task.

“I see that, concerning the matter for which I invited you, I have done with you everything I ought to do. As a final request, I ask that those of you who can do so deign to subscribe to these proceedings.

“Here I need your response. Let me have your response; acclaim something about this assent.”

The people acclaimed: “Let it be done, let it be done.” This was said twenty-five times.

“It is worthy; it is just.” This was said twenty-eight times.

“Let it be done, let it be done.” This was said fourteen times.

“Long since worthy, long since deserving.” This was said twenty-five times.

“We give thanks for your judgment.” This was said thirteen times.

“Hear us, O Christ; preserve Eraclius.” This was said eighteen times.

## 7

When silence had been restored, Bishop Augustine said:

“It is well, so that we may be able to perform the things of God around his sacrifice. At that hour of our supplication, I especially commend to your Charity that you suspend all your causes and affairs and pour out prayers to the Lord for this Church, for me, and for the presbyter Eraclius.”

# LETTER 214

[Note: [Col. 0968] We have corrected Letters 214 and 215 with the help of the manuscripts designated a, b, bg, bl, c, cc, cb, cl, ff, g, gv, j, m, n, r, s, sb, t, th, vc, two copies designated bn, and four designated v.]

[Note: [Col. 0968] Formerly 46; what was 214 is now 2. It seems to have been written in 426 or 427, before Easter.]

Augustine to Valentinus the abbot and the monks of Hadrumetum, concerning a disagreement that had arisen among them about free will and God’s justice through an incorrect interpretation of the longer letter to Sixtus. He teaches that the Catholic faith defended in that letter is this: it neither denies free will nor attributes so much to it that it can accomplish anything toward the good without God’s grace.

To the most beloved Lord and brother honored among Christ’s members, VALENTINUS, and to the brothers who are with you, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

## 1

Two young men, Cresconius and Felix, came to us, saying that they belonged to your congregation. They reported that your monastery was disturbed by some disagreement because certain members of your community preach grace in such a way as to deny that human beings possess free will; and, what is more serious, they say that on the day of judgment God will not repay each person according to his works (Matt. 16:27; Rom. 2:6).

They also indicated, however, that many of you do not think this way, but acknowledge that free will is assisted by God’s grace, so that we may think and do what is right; and that when the Lord comes to repay each person according to his works, he may find our works good, works that God prepared so that we might walk in them (Eph. 2:10). Those who think this think rightly.

## 2

I therefore beg you, brothers, as the Apostle begged the Corinthians, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing and that there be no divisions among you (1 Cor. 1:10).

First, the Lord Jesus, as it is written in the Gospel of the apostle John, did not come to judge the world but so that the world might be saved through him (John 3:17). Later, however, as the apostle Paul writes, God will judge the world (Rom. 3:6), when he is to come, as the whole Church confesses in the Creed, to judge the living and the dead.

If, then, there is no grace of God, how does he save the world? And if there is no free will, how does he judge the world?

Therefore, understand my book or letter, which the aforesaid men brought with them to us, according to this faith: neither deny God’s grace nor defend free will in such a way as to separate it from God’s grace, as though without that grace we could in any way think or do anything according to God. We absolutely cannot.

For this reason, when the Lord was speaking about the fruit of righteousness, he said to his disciples: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

[Note: [Col. 0969] The editions have “brought to you.” But thirteen manuscripts have “brought to us.”]

## 3

Know, therefore, that the aforementioned letter to Sixtus, presbyter of the Roman Church, was written against the new Pelagian heretics (Letter 194). They say that God’s grace is given according to our merits, so that whoever boasts may boast not in the Lord but in himself—that is, in a human being and not in the Lord.

The Apostle forbids this, saying: “Let no one boast in a human being” (1 Cor. 3:21); and elsewhere: “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord” (ibid. 1:31).

Those heretics, however, thinking that they make themselves righteous by themselves, as though God had not given this to them but they had given it to themselves, boast not in the Lord but in themselves.

To such people the Apostle says: “For who makes you different?” He says this because, from that mass of perdition which arose from Adam, no one distinguishes a human being so as to make him a vessel for honor rather than dishonor except God.

But when a carnal and vainly inflated person hears “For who makes you different?”, he could respond, whether by voice or in thought: “My faith makes me different; my prayer makes me different; my righteousness makes me different.”

The Apostle immediately confronts his thoughts and says: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (ibid. 4:7).

Those who think that they justify themselves by themselves boast as though they had not received these things; and so they boast in themselves, not in the Lord.

## 4

For this reason, in the letter that has reached you, I proved through the testimonies of the holy Scriptures—which you can examine there—that our good works, devout prayers, and right faith could in no way have existed in us unless we received them from the one of whom the apostle James says: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1:17).

This was so that no one might say that God’s grace had been given to him on account of the merits of his works, prayers, or faith, and that what those heretics say might be thought true—namely, that God’s grace is given according to our merits.

This is entirely false—not because there is no merit, whether of the pious as good or of the impious as evil. Otherwise, how would God judge the world? Rather, God’s mercy and grace convert a human being. Of this the Psalm says: “My God, his mercy will go before me” (Ps. 58:11).

Thus the impious person is justified—that is, the unrighteous person is made righteous—and begins to possess good merit, which the Lord will crown when the world is judged.

## 5

There was much that I wished to send you, which, once read, would have enabled you to know more carefully and fully the whole matter that was dealt with in the councils of bishops against those same Pelagian heretics. But the brothers who came to us from your number hurried away, and through them we have not replied to you but written to you.

They brought no letter from your Charity to us. Nevertheless, we received them, since their simplicity sufficiently indicated that they could not have fabricated anything for us.

They hurried because they wanted to celebrate Easter among you, so that, with the Lord’s help, this holy day might find your peace rather than your dissension.

## 6

You will do better—and I strongly ask this of you—if you do not hesitate to send me the very man whom they say caused them to be disturbed.

Either he does not understand my book, or perhaps he himself is not understood when he attempts to resolve and untangle a very difficult question intelligible to only a few.

This is the question concerning the grace of God, which led people who did not understand it to suppose that the apostle Paul was saying: “Let us do evil so that good may come” (Rom. 3:8).

Therefore, in his Second Letter, the apostle Peter says:

“Therefore, beloved, as you await these things, strive to be found by him undefiled and blameless in peace; and consider the patience of our Lord to be salvation, just as our most beloved brother Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given to him, speaking of these things in all his letters. In them there are some matters difficult to understand, which the ignorant and unstable distort, as they do the other Scriptures, to their own destruction” (2 Pet. 3:14–16).

## 7

Beware, therefore, what so great an apostle says with such terror. And wherever you realize that you do not understand, meanwhile believe the divine utterances, because both human free will exists and God’s grace exists, without whose assistance free will can neither turn toward God nor make progress in God.

Pray that what you piously believe you may also understand wisely. For free will exists precisely for this purpose as well—that is, so that we may understand wisely.

For unless we understood and possessed wisdom by free will, Scripture would not command us, saying: “Understand, you who are foolish among the people; and you who are fools, become wise at last” (Ps. 93:8).

By the very fact that we are commanded and ordered to understand and become wise, our obedience is required; and there can be no obedience without free will.

But if this could be done through free will without the assistance of God’s grace—if we could understand and become wise—then we would not say to God: “Give me understanding, and I shall learn your commandments” (Ps. 118:125). Nor would it be written in the Gospel: “Then he opened their minds so that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:45). Nor would the apostle James say: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach anyone, and it will be given to him” (James 1:5).

The Lord is powerful enough to grant this both to you and to us, so that we may rejoice through swift messengers at your peace and devout agreement.

I greet you, not only in my own name but also in the name of the brothers who are with me, and I ask you to pray for us harmoniously and earnestly.

May the Lord be with you.

# LETTER 215

[Note: [Col. 0971] Formerly 47; what was 215 is now 268. Written in the same year, after Easter.]

Augustine to Valentinus and his monks, on the same subject, sending them at the same time his book *On Grace and Free Will*.

To the most beloved Lord and brother honored among Christ’s members, VALENTINUS, and to the brothers who are with you, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

## 1

Your Charity should know that Cresconius, Felix, and another Felix, servants of God who came to us from your congregation, celebrated Easter with us.

We kept them somewhat longer for this reason: so that they might return to you better instructed against the new Pelagian heretics. Whoever thinks that God’s grace—which alone liberates a human being through our Lord Jesus Christ—is given according to some human merits falls into their error.

But whoever thinks that, when the Lord comes to judgment, a person who has already reached an age at which he could use the free choice of his will will not be judged according to his works is likewise in error.

Only infants, who do not yet have works of their own, either good or evil, will be condemned solely on account of original sin, if the grace of the Savior does not come to their aid through the washing of regeneration.

All the others, however, who, already using free will, have added their own sins to original sin, if they are not rescued by God’s grace from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of Christ, will receive judgment not only according to the merits of their origin but also according to the merits of their own will.

The good, too, will obtain a reward according to the merits of their good will; but they have also obtained that very good will through God’s grace.

Thus what is written is fulfilled: “Wrath and indignation, tribulation and distress for every human soul that does evil, for the Jew first and also for the Greek; but glory and honor and peace for everyone who does good, for the Jew first and also for the Greek” (Rom. 2:9–10).

[Note: [Col. 0971] Thus sixteen manuscripts. The printed editions have: “He thinks that God’s grace is given on account of some human merit.”]

## 2

I did not need to argue at greater length in this letter about this very difficult question—that is, concerning will and grace—since I had already given them another letter, as they were returning sooner.

I have also written to you a book [Note: [Col. 0972] The book *On Grace and Free Will*.] which, if you read it carefully with the Lord’s help and understand it attentively, I think will prevent any further disagreements among you on this matter.

They are also carrying other materials which we thought should be sent to you, so that you may learn how the Catholic Church, by God’s mercy, drove back the poisons of the Pelagian heresy.

We have briefly set out against that error what was written to Pope Innocent, bishop of the city of Rome, from the council of the province of Carthage and from the council of Numidia, as well as what was written somewhat more carefully by five bishops, and what he himself wrote in reply to these three documents.

We have also included what was written to Pope Zosimus from the African council, together with his reply sent to all the bishops throughout the world [Note: [Col. 0972] See above, Letter 190, chapter 6, section 22.]

We have included what we briefly established against the same error at the later plenary council of all Africa [Note: [Col. 0972] This plenary council was held at Carthage, in the basilica of Faustus, on May 1, 418, by Aurelius of Carthage and Donatianus of Telepte, primate of the province of Byzacena, together with 203 other bishops from the provinces of Byzacena, both Mauritanias—Sitifensis and Caesariensis—from Tripolitana, Numidia, and Spain, as is reported in the old book of Ghent and in the Code of Canons of the Roman Church. These books attribute to that council the famous eight, or nine, canons established against the heresy of Pelagius, which some have wrongly assigned to the Council of Milevis of 416. The African Code of Canons, as well as Photius in codex 53 and Celestine in the appendix to his Letter to the Bishops of Gaul, also assigns them to this council. In fact, the final three canons condemn the Pelagians’ view of sinlessness (*anamartêsia*) among the righteous; hence Augustine thereafter—that is, after the Carthaginian synod—attacks that view as heretical. Earlier, however, in several short works written after the Council of Milevis—namely, in the letter numbered here 177, sections 16 and 17, and in *The Proceedings of Pelagius*, chapter 30—he spoke about this question as though it had not yet been defined by the Church.]

We have also included the book of mine mentioned above, which I have now written to you. We read all these things with them while they were present, and we sent them to you through them.

## 3

We also read with them the book of the most blessed martyr Cyprian, *On the Lord’s Prayer*, and showed how he taught that everything pertaining to our conduct, by which we live rightly, must be requested from our Father who is in heaven, lest, presuming upon free will, we fall away from divine grace.

There too we demonstrated how that glorious martyr admonished us to pray even for our enemies who do not yet believe in Christ, so that they may believe. This would certainly be done in vain unless the Church believed that even the evil and unbelieving wills of human beings can be converted to good through God’s grace.

But because they said that this book of Saint Cyprian is also present among you, we did not send it.

We also read with them my letter to Sixtus, presbyter of the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0972] Letter 194.], which they had brought with them to us, and we showed that it was written against those who say that God’s grace is given according to our merits—that is, against those same Pelagians.

[Col. 0973]

## 4

Therefore, insofar as we were able, we dealt with these brothers, both yours and ours, so that they might persevere in the sound Catholic faith. This faith neither denies free will, whether toward an evil life or a good one, nor attributes so much to it that it can accomplish anything without God’s grace—whether turning from evil to good, perseveringly advancing in good, or reaching eternal good, where it will no longer fear falling away.

You too, beloved, I exhort in this letter to do what the Apostle exhorts us all to do: not to be wiser than one ought to be, but to be wise with moderation, according to the measure of faith that God has apportioned to each person (Rom. 12:3).

### 5

Consider what the Holy Spirit admonishes through Solomon:

> “Make straight paths for your feet, and direct your ways; do not turn aside to the right or to the left, but turn your foot away from the evil way. For the ways that are on the right the Lord knows; but those on the left are perverse. He himself will make your paths straight, and he will bring your journeys forward in peace” (Prov. 4:26–27).

In these words of Holy Scripture, brothers, consider that, if there were no free will, it would not be said, “Make straight paths for your feet, and direct your ways; do not turn aside to the right or to the left.” And yet, without the grace of God, if this could be done, it would not afterward be said, “He himself will make your paths straight, and he will bring your journeys forward in peace.”

### 6

Therefore, do not turn aside to the right or to the left, although the ways that are on the right are praised and those on the left are condemned. This is why he added, “But turn your foot away from the evil way,” that is, from the left; and he makes this clear in what follows, saying, “For the ways that are on the right the Lord knows; but those on the left are perverse.”

We ought surely to walk in those ways that the Lord knows. Concerning them it is written in the Psalm: “The Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the ungodly will perish” (Ps. 1:6). The Lord does not know this latter way because it is on the left, [Note: [Col. 0973] The manuscripts of the Cluniac recension read: “The Lord does not know it, which is on the left.”] just as he will also say to those placed on the left: “I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12; Luke 13:27).

But what is it that he does not know, who certainly knows all things, whether human goods or evils? What is “I do not know you,” except “I did not make you such”? Likewise, when it is said of the Lord Jesus Christ that he did not know sin (2 Cor. 5:21), what does “he did not know” mean except that he had not made it?

Accordingly, how should the statement “The Lord knows the ways that are on the right” be understood except as meaning that he himself made the ways on the right—that is, the ways of the righteous—which are certainly the good works that God prepared, as the Apostle says, so that we might walk in them (Eph. 2:10)? But he does not know the perverse ways on the left, that is, the ways of the ungodly, because he did not himself make them for humanity; rather, human beings made them for themselves. Hence he says: “But I hated the perverse ways of the wicked; they are on the left.”

### 7

But someone replies to us: Why then did he say, “Do not turn aside to the right or to the left,” when he ought rather to have said, “Keep to the right, and do not turn aside to the left,” if the ways on the right are good?

[Col. 0974] Why, we ask, except because the ways on the right are good in such a way that turning aside to the right is nevertheless not good? For the person who wishes to assign to himself, rather than to God, the good works themselves that belong to the ways on the right is to be understood as turning aside to the right.

Therefore, after saying, “For the ways that are on the right the Lord knows; but those on the left are perverse,” as though someone had said to him, “How, then, do you not want us to turn toward the right?” he immediately added: “He himself will make your paths straight, and he will bring your journeys forward in peace.”

Understand, then, what has been commanded you: “Make straight paths for your feet, and direct your ways.” Understand that, when you do this, it is granted to you by the Lord God that you do it. Thus you will not turn aside to the right, although you walk in the ways on the right, because you do not trust in your own strength. Rather, he himself will be your strength—he who will make your paths straight and bring your journeys forward in peace.

### 8

Therefore, dearly beloved, whoever says, “My will is sufficient for me to perform good works,” turns aside to the right.

But those who think that a good life should be abandoned when they hear God’s grace preached in such a way that it is believed and understood that grace itself makes human wills good from evil ones, and also preserves those whom it has made good—and who consequently say, “Let us do evil so that good may come” (Rom. 3:8)—turn aside to the left.

That is why he said to you, “Do not turn aside to the right or to the left.” That is: do not defend free will in such a way that you attribute good works to it without the grace of God; nor defend grace in such a way that, as though secure because of it, you love evil works. May the grace of God itself turn this away from you.

Presenting the words of such people, the Apostle says: “What shall we say, then? Are we to continue in sin so that grace may abound?” And to these words of people who were wandering and did not understand the grace of God, he replied as he ought: “By no means! For if we have died to sin, how shall we live in it?” (Rom. 6:1–2).

Nothing could have been said more briefly or better. What more useful thing does the grace of God confer upon us in this present evil age than that we should die to sin? Accordingly, the person who wishes to live in sin because of that grace through which we die to sin will be found ungrateful to grace itself.

But may God, who is rich in mercy, grant you both sound understanding and the grace to persevere productively in your good purpose to the end. Pray earnestly and watchfully in fraternal peace for this—for you, for us, for all who love you, and for those who hate you. May you live for God. If I have any claim upon you, let brother Florus come to me.

## LETTER 216

[Note: [Col. 0974] Corrected according to cl. j. sb. v. and Lov.]  
[Note: Elsewhere numbered 256; what was 216 is now 85. Written shortly after the preceding letters.]

Valentinus to Augustine, reporting what had been the cause of the dissension and who had instigated the disturbance in his monastery; then declaring his belief concerning free will and the justice of God who rewards; and finally clearing Florus, whom he sends to Augustine, of suspicion of error.

To the truly holy lord, to the most blessed Pope Augustine, venerably preferred above all others by us and honored with devout exultation: Valentinus, servant of Your Holiness, and the entire congregation which, [Col. 0975] together with me, hopes in the Lord through your prayers, sends greetings.

### 1

We received the venerable writings and the book of Your Holiness with such trembling hearts that, just as blessed Elijah, when he stood at the entrance of the cave and the glory of the Lord passed by, covered his face, so we covered our rebuked eyes, because we were ashamed in our own judgment on account of the rusticity of our brothers, whose disorderly departure caused us to deserve to greet Your Beatitude.

There is a time for speaking and a time for silence, lest, while we were writing through doubt and wavering concerning the truth, we should appear, by doubting together with those who doubt, to doubt the words of your wisdom, which is like the wisdom of an angel of God.

For it was not necessary for us to inquire about your blessedness and wisdom, which by God’s grace is known to us. We rejoiced so eagerly over the most delightful book of Your Holiness that, just as the Apostles, after the resurrection, did not dare to ask the Lord, who was dining with them, who he was—for they knew that it was Jesus (John 21:12)—so we neither wished nor dared to ask whether the book belonged to Your Holiness, since the very grace of the faithful that is so generously commended in it bears vivid testimony to us, through your words, that it is yours, holy lord pope.

### 2

Let us now, most blessed lord pope, set forth the sequence of the disturbance itself.

Our most beloved brother Florus, servant of Your Paternity, had gone to the territory of Uzalis at the prompting of charity. During the intervals of his stay in his own city, he brought us some devotional gifts from the monastery [Note: The Julian manuscript reads “to the monastery.” Immediately afterward the same codex, together with one Vatican manuscript, reads: “brought to us your writings,” etc.] from the works of Your Holiness, accompanied by a brother named Felix, who is known to have come late to Your Holiness after his companions, faithfully dictating the same book.

The book came to the monastery with him, while brother Florus had gone from the city of Uzalis to Carthage. Without showing me the book, they began to read it aloud to the inexperienced brothers. It disturbed the hearts of some who did not understand, because, when the Lord said, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54), those who understood it impiously departed—not because of any fault in the Lord who spoke, but because of the hardness of their most impious hearts. [Note: Thus the Cluniac manuscript; another manuscript reads “because.”]

### 3

The aforementioned brothers, who overturned everything, began to disturb the souls of the innocent, while my own insignificance was entirely unaware of it. I was so unaware of their murmuring assembly that, unless brother Florus, returning from Carthage, had recognized their disturbances and carefully reported them to me, there would have been among them a secret, almost servile dispute about the truth they did not understand. [Note: The Louvain edition reads “repeated,” but the Gallic manuscripts more correctly read “returning.”]

To remove their impious questions, I proposed that we send for the holy lord Father Evodius, so that he might write back to us something more certain concerning this most holy book for the sake of the ignorant. [Note: Evodius did in fact write back. His letter to Valentinus on this very matter was found by Jacques Sirmond in a manuscript of Saint Maximin of Trier; [Col. 0976] from it he transferred this fragment into *The History of Predestination*, chapter 1:

> “Honorable brothers have reported to us that, I do not know what, certain questions have arisen there among you concerning free will and the justice of God. We praise your zeal, but we do not wish it to be contentious; for contention arouses disturbance, whereas zeal requires devotion. The man first created—Adam, I mean—possessed the fullest exercise of free will. But when free will itself was wounded, it became weakened. Therefore there is now free will in humanity, but wounded. Hence it is said: ‘My strength has failed through poverty, and the light of my eyes is not with me’ (Ps. 37:11). For its recovery, the physician Christ the Savior was sent, to save what had perished and heal what had been corrupted.”

> And later:

> “Let them therefore read the sayings of the holy men of God and of the elders, as I have already said—those who possess a devout disposition toward the divine gift. And when they do not understand, let them not quickly criticize, but pray that they may understand.”]

They were unwilling to receive even this patiently. Instead, they undertook a departure that we had not wished for in this manner. Brother Florus was almost thrown into confusion by their fury [Note: Thus the Cluniac manuscript: “thrown into confusion by their fury.”], and they raged against him because, as they thought, he had brought them the wounds inflicted by this book, in which, being infirm, they could not recognize the medicine.

Therefore we also asked the holy presbyter Sabinus, for the sake of greater authority, and His Holiness read the book with clear interpretations. Even then the wounded soul was not healed.

Out of concern for their devotion, we gave them expenses, lest we aggravate their wounds—wounds that the grace of this book could heal, a grace in which your holy presence shines forth. After they had departed, rest and peace rejoiced among all the brothers in the Lord. For this contention arose through the zeal of five brothers, or more.

### 4

But since joy sometimes arises from sorrow, lord pope, we are not excessively saddened, because through the ignorant and the curious we were found worthy to be enlightened by the sweetest admonitions of Your Holiness. Indeed, the doubt of blessed Thomas the Apostle, who sought the marks of the nails (John 20:25), became a confirmation of the universal Church.

Therefore, lord pope, we received the medicine of your devoutly healing letters with their grace, and we struck our breasts [Note: Thus the Cluniac manuscript; the Louvain edition reads “we beat our breasts.”], so that in this way at least our conscience might be healed—our conscience which grace heals and gives life through our free will, a free will bestowed by mercy. Yet this is in the present time, when we still sing of mercy with delay.

For when we begin to sing judgment to the Lord, we shall carry away a reward for our work, because the Lord is merciful and just, compassionate and upright (Ps. 112:4). As Your Holiness teaches us, we must be brought before the tribunal of Christ, so that each of us may receive what belongs to the body according to what he has done, whether good or evil (2 Cor. 5:10). For “the Lord will come, and his reward is with him” (Isa. 40:10); a person will stand, and his work [Note: Thus the Cluniac manuscript; another reading is “his body.”] will stand before him. The Lord will come like a burning furnace, to set the ungodly ablaze like straw (Joel 2:3, 5); and for those who fear the name of the Lord the sun of righteousness will rise, when the ungodly are punished by the judgment of justice (Mal. 4:1–3).

The righteous man, whose friend you are, lord pope, exclaims, trembles, and supplicates:

> “Lord, do not enter into judgment with your servant” (Ps. 143:2).

If grace were what rewards, the righteous man would not fear the secret judgment of majesty.

This, father, is the faith of your servant Florus—not as those brothers spoke. At present they heard him say that the gift of devotion is not given according to our merits, but through the grace of the Redeemer. As for that day, who could doubt that grace will be far removed when justice begins to be angry?

[Col. 0977] This is what we cry out, father; this is what, taught by you, we sing—not confidently, but trembling:

> “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your wrath” (Ps. 6:2).

This is what we say:

> “Correct us, Lord, and instruct us from your law, so that you may moderate us from the days of evil” (Ps. 94:12–13).

We believe this because you teach it, venerable father: God questions the righteous and the ungodly; and, with the good and the evil placed on the right and on the left, he assigns to the works of devotion their rewards and counts out the punishment due to persistence in ungodliness.

Where will grace be, when works—whether good or evil—are weighed according to their quality?

### 5

But why does he not fear that a direct lie is being uttered? We do not deny that free will has been healed by the grace of God [Note: The Louvain edition omits “healed”; the Gallic manuscripts contain it.], but we believe and confidently trust that it makes progress and is helped through Christ’s daily grace.

What do people mean when they say, “It is in my power to do good”—if only people actually did good? O empty boasting of wretched people! They accuse sins every day, yet themselves claim a naked free will, boasting of it, without examining their conscience, which cannot be healed except by grace, so that they might say:

> “Have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” (Ps. 41:5).

What would those who glory in free will do—which is not denied, provided it is understood to exist only with God’s help—if death had already been swallowed up in victory, if our mortal nature had already put on immortality, and our corruptible nature had put on incorruption (1 Cor. 15:53–54)?

Behold, the wounds stink, yet medicine is arrogantly demanded. They do not say, like the righteous man:

> “If the Lord had not helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in hell” (Ps. 94:17).

They do not say, like the holy man:

> “Unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it watches in vain” (Ps. 127:1).

### 6

But pray, most devout father, that we now have no concern except to cleanse our sin with tears and commend the grace of God. Pray, lord father, that the pit may not close its mouth over us (Ps. 69:16), that we may be saved from those who descend into the pit (Ps. 30:4), and that our soul may not perish with the ungodly (Ps. 26:9) through our pride, but may be healed through the Lord’s grace.

As you commanded, lord pope, our brother Florus, servant of Your Holiness, proceeded with complete eagerness. His weariness does not hinder him but benefits him, so that the clarified instruction of his heart may increase. We humbly commend him to Your Holiness, and we likewise earnestly ask that you commend the ignorant to the Lord through your prayers, so that they may be most gently set right.

Pray, lord and sweetest father, that the devil may flee from our congregation, and that, every storm of alien questions having been removed, the ship of our purpose, laden with peaceful passengers [Note: *Epibatai* are soldiers of the fleet who serve aboard ships.], may safely remain within the secure station of the safest harbor while it sails across this great and boundless sea; and that, in that harbor where the voyage of life will no longer be feared, it may receive without distinction the price of the desired cargo.

We trust that we shall obtain this through the help of Your Holiness, through the grace that is in Christ [Col. 0978] Jesus our Lord.

We beg you to greet on our behalf all the children of your apostolate, our lords the clergy, and the holy men serving in the congregation of your purpose, so that, together with Your Beatitude, they may all deign to pray for us.

May the undivided Trinity of the Lord our God preserve your apostolate—which he chose by grace—for us in his Church, and crown you, mindful of us, in the great Church. This is our wish, lord.

And if your servant, our brother Florus, should suggest anything to Your Holiness concerning the rule of the monastery, we ask you, father, graciously to receive it and to instruct us, weak as we are, in all things.

## LETTER 217

[Note: [Col. 0978] Corrected according to a. bl. ff. sb. 2 vc. 3 v. Am. Bad. Er. Lov.]  
[Note: Elsewhere numbered 107; what was 217 is now 59. Written around the year 427.]

Augustine to Vitalis of Carthage, against the report that Vitalis taught that the beginning of faith is not a gift of God; Augustine protests forcefully and refutes him from the prayers of the Church itself. He also proposes twelve principles pertaining to the Church’s faith concerning the question of the grace of God.

Augustine, bishop, servant of Christ and through him servant of his servants, to Vitalis, his brother: greeting in him.

## CHAPTER ONE

### 1

When unfavorable things were reported to me about you, I prayed to the Lord; and, until favorable things are reported to me, I continue to pray that you neither reject my letter with resentment nor fail to read it for your benefit. If he hears this prayer of mine on your behalf, he also grants me the opportunity to offer thanksgiving for you. If I obtain this, you will certainly not contradict the very beginning of my letter.

For this is what I pray for you: that you may be of sound faith. If, then, you do not object to our praying for our loved ones, if you recognize this prayer as Christian, and if you either remember praying such things for your own loved ones or acknowledge that you ought to pray them, how can you say what I hear you say: “That we may rightly believe in God and consent to the Gospel is not a gift of God, but comes from us—from our own will, which he himself has not worked within our hearts”?

And when you hear the question, “What, then, does the Apostle mean by saying, ‘God works in you both to will and to accomplish’?” (Phil. 2:13), you reply: “God works through his law and through his Scriptures, which we either read or hear, so that we may will; but whether we consent to them or do not consent is so much our own affair that, if we wish, it happens, whereas, if we do not wish, we make God’s working have no effect in us.

“You say, God works, insofar as it depends on him, so that we may will, when his words become known to us. But if we do not wish to yield to them, we ourselves make his working unprofitable in us.”

If this is what you say, you are certainly contradicting our prayers.

### 2

Say openly, then, that we ought not to pray for those to whom we preach the Gospel that they may believe, but only to preach to them. Bring your arguments against the prayers of the Church. When you hear a priest of God exhorting the people of God at the altar to pray for unbelievers, that God may convert them to the faith; for catechumens, that he may inspire them with the desire for regeneration; [Col. 0979] and for the faithful, that by his gift they may persevere in what they have begun to be—mock these devout words and say that you do not do what he urges.

That is, say that you do not ask God to make believers out of unbelievers, because these are not benefits of divine mercy but duties of human will.

And, as a man instructed in the Church of Carthage, condemn even the book of the most blessed Cyprian *On the Lord’s Prayer*. When that teacher expounded it, he showed that the things to be requested from God the Father are precisely those that you say come to a person from the person himself—that is, from himself.

### 3
