But if you think that what I have said concerning the prayers of the Church and the martyr Cyprian is insufficient, dare to go further and criticize the Apostle, who said: “We pray to God that you may do no evil” (2 Cor. 13:7).

You will surely not say that the person who does not believe in Christ, or who abandons faith in Christ, does no evil. Therefore the person who says, “that you may do no evil,” does not wish these things to happen either. It is not enough for him to command; he acknowledges that he is asking God that they may not happen, knowing that the human will is corrected and directed by God so that it may not do these things.

“For a person’s steps are directed by the Lord, and he will desire his way” (Ps. 37:23). Scripture did not say, “He will learn his way,” or “He will hold to it,” or “He will walk in it,” or anything similar that you could say is indeed given by the Lord, but given to a person who already wills it. You might thus claim that, before God grants the benefit by which he directs a person’s steps so that he may learn, hold to, and walk in his way, the person advances by his own will and earns this gift of God by his prior will.

But Scripture says, “A person’s steps are directed by the Lord, and he will desire his way,” so that we might understand that the good will by which we begin to wish to believe—for what is God’s way except right faith?—is the gift of the one who first directs our steps for this very purpose: that we may will.

Scripture does not say, “A person’s steps are directed by the Lord because he desired his way.” Rather, it says, “They are directed, and he will desire.” Therefore his steps are not directed because he desired; he will desire because his steps are directed.

## CHAPTER TWO

### 4

Here again, perhaps, you will say that this is done by the Lord while his teaching is read or heard, provided that a person consents by his own will to the truth that he reads or hears.

“For,” you say, “if God’s teaching were hidden from him, his steps would not be directed; once directed, he would desire God’s way.”

Accordingly, you think that the Lord directs a person’s steps toward choosing God’s way only in this sense: without God’s teaching, the truth to which he may consent by his own will cannot become known to him.

“If he consents to it,” you say—and this is established in his free will—“then his steps are rightly said to be directed by the one whose way he desires. He follows that one’s teaching, preceded by persuasion and followed by consent. He does this by natural freedom if he wishes; if he does not wish, he does not do it, and he will receive a reward or punishment for what he has done.” [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts and one Gallic manuscript read: “if he wishes, he does not do it.”]

This is that evil opinion of the Pelagians, rightly defamed and deservedly rejected, and condemned even by Pelagius himself, who feared condemnation in the judgment of the Eastern bishops. [Note: See *On the Proceedings against Pelagius*, chapter 14.] They say that the grace of God is not given for individual acts, but exists in free will or in the law and teaching.

[Col. 0980] Shall we, then, brother, be so dull of heart that, concerning the grace of God—or rather, against the grace of God—we hold that Pelagian opinion which Pelagius himself condemned, though with feigned sincerity, because he feared Catholic judges?

### 5

“But how,” you will say, “is this to be answered?”

How do you think it can be answered more easily and plainly than by embracing what we discussed above concerning praying to God, so that no creeping forgetfulness may remove it from our minds and no clever argumentation wrest it away?

If what is written—“A person’s steps are directed by the Lord, and he will desire his way”; and “The will is prepared by the Lord” (Prov. 8:35, according to the Septuagint); and “God is the one who works in you both to will”—and many similar passages that commend the true grace of God, that is, grace which is not given according to our merits but gives the merits themselves when it is given, because it precedes a person’s good will and does not find it in the heart of anyone but creates it—

if, then, God prepared and worked a person’s will in such a way that he merely offered his law and teaching to that person’s free will, without moving his understanding by that profound and hidden calling so that he would give assent to the same law and teaching, then surely it would be sufficient simply to read, understand by reading, or even expound and preach it. There would be no need to pray that God convert the hearts of unbelievers to his faith and, once converted, grant them persevering progress in that same grace through his generosity.

If, then, you do not deny that these things must be requested from the Lord, what remains, brother Vitalis, except that you confess that they are granted by the one from whom you agree they must be requested?

But if you deny that we ought to ask these things from him, you contradict his own teaching, because in that teaching we have also learned to ask these things from him.

### 6

You know the Lord’s Prayer, and I do not doubt that you say to God: “Our Father, who art in heaven,” and so forth.

Read its most blessed expositor, Cyprian, and carefully attend to how he explained the words, “Thy will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth” (Matt. 6:9–10). Understand them obediently. He will certainly teach you to pray for the unbelieving enemies of the Church, according to the Lord’s command: “Pray for your enemies” (Matt. 5:44).

He will teach you to pray that God’s will may be done in them just as it is done in those who are already faithful and bear the image of the heavenly man, and who therefore deserve to be called “heaven”; and likewise in those who, through unbelief, bear only the image of the earthly man (1 Cor. 15:47–49), and for that reason are rightly called “earth.”

These, then, are the enemies for whom the Lord commanded us to pray; and the most glorious martyr explained that, when we say in the prayer, “Thy will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth,” we are asking that they too may have the faith possessed by the faithful.

These enemies of Christian devotion either utterly refuse to hear the law of God and the teaching by which faith in Christ is preached, or they hear and even read it in order to mock and detest it, and blaspheme against it with every contradiction they can muster.

Therefore, if it does not belong to God’s grace to convert to his faith the wills of human beings who oppose the faith, then we pour out prayers to God for them—asking that, by believing, they may consent to the teaching they resist—in vain and more as a formality than in truth.

[Col. 0981] Likewise, when some of them believe, we offer great thanksgiving to God with rejoicing in vain and more as a formality than in truth, if he himself does not bring this about in them.

### 7

Let us not deceive human beings, for we cannot deceive God. We are certainly not praying to God, but only pretending to pray, if we believe that we ourselves, rather than he, bring about what we pray for.

We are certainly not giving thanks to God, but only pretending to do so, if we do not think that he himself brings about the thing for which we give him thanks.

If lying lips are found in any human conversations, at least let them not be found in prayers. Far be it from us to deny in our hearts that God does what we ask him with our mouths and voices to do. Worse still, let us not keep this hidden in our arguments when we wish to deceive others as well.

While we wish to defend free will before human beings, let us not lose before God the help of prayer, nor fail to offer true thanksgiving by refusing to acknowledge true grace.

## CHAPTER THREE

### 8

If we truly wish to defend free will, let us not attack the source from which free will comes. For whoever attacks the grace by which our will is freed to turn away from evil and do good still wishes his own will to remain captive.

Answer me, I beg you: how can the Apostle say, “Giving thanks to the Father, who has made us fit to share in the inheritance of the saints in light; he has delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love” (Col. 1:12–13), if it is not God himself but free will itself that frees our will?

Then we give thanks to the Father deceitfully, as though he did what he does not do. And the Apostle was mistaken when he said that God made us fit to share in the inheritance of the saints in light, because he himself delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love.

Answer me: how did we possess free will to turn away from evil and do good when we were under the power of darkness? If, as the Apostle says, God delivered us from it, then he himself certainly made our will free.

If he does this great good of ours merely through the preaching of his teaching, what shall we say about those whom he has not yet delivered from that very power of darkness? Is divine teaching merely to be preached to them, or should we also pray for them, so that they may be divinely delivered from the power of darkness?

If you say that it is merely to be preached, you contradict the Lord’s command and the prayers of the Church. But if you acknowledge that we ought to pray for them, then you acknowledge that we ought to pray that, with their will freed from the power of darkness, they may consent to that same teaching.

Thus it comes about that people become faithful neither without free will, and yet become faithful through the grace of the one who freed their will from the power of darkness.

In this way the grace of God is not denied, but is shown to be genuine because it comes without any preceding human merits. And free will is defended in such a way that it is strengthened by humility rather than cast down by pride; so that the one who boasts may boast not in a human being, or in anything else, or in himself, but in the Lord (1 Cor. 1:31).

### 9

For what is the power of darkness except the power of the devil and his angels? Although they had been angels of light, they did not stand in the truth through free will [Col. 0982] (John 8:44); they fell from it and became darkness.

I am not teaching you these things, but reminding you of what you know.

The human race, through the ruin of the one first human being to whom transgression was persuaded by that power and in whom we all fell, was therefore subjected to this power of darkness. For this reason infants too are delivered from the power of darkness when they are reborn in Christ.

This does not become apparent in their liberated will until they reach the years of rational maturity, possessing a will that consents to the saving teaching in which they were nurtured and ending this life in that teaching—if they have been chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless before him in love, predestined for adoption as sons (Eph. 1:4–5).

### 10

This power of darkness—that is, the devil, who is also called “the prince of the power of the air”—works in the sons of disobedience (Eph. 2:2). This prince is also called “the ruler of the darkness” (Eph. 6:12), that is, of the sons of disobedience themselves; he rules them according to his own will.

Yet even he does not possess free will for doing good. His will has been hardened toward the greatest malevolence by the punishment of his crime. Hence no one of sound faith believes or says that these apostate angels will ever be converted again to their former devotion through a corrected will.

What, then, does this power work in the sons of disobedience except its own evil works, and above all their disobedience and unbelief, by which they are enemies of the faith? Through that faith, he knows, they can be cleansed, healed, made perfectly free, and reign in eternity—a destiny he vehemently envies them.

Therefore he allows some of them, through whom he seeks to deceive more extensively, to possess certain works that appear good, in which they are praised—people who lived nobly and most gloriously among various nations, especially among the Roman people.

But since, as the most truthful Scripture says, “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23), and “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6)—not human beings—this ruler does nothing so much as ensure that people do not believe in God and do not come in faith to the Mediator, by whom his works are undone.

### 11

But the Mediator himself enters the strong man’s house (Matt. 12:29)—that is, this age of mortals, established, insofar as it concerns him, under the power of the devil. For it is written of the devil that he has the power of death (Heb. 2:14).

He enters the strong man’s house, that is, the house of the one who holds the human race under his rule. First he binds him—that is, restrains and curbs his power—with the stronger bonds of his own power. Then he carries off his vessels, all those whom he has predestined to rescue, freeing their will from the devil’s power so that, without the devil’s interference, they may believe in Christ with a free will.

Therefore this is the work of grace, not of nature. It is, I say, the work of the grace brought to us by the second Adam—not of the nature that the first Adam wholly lost in himself.

It is the work of grace that removes sin and gives life to the sinner dead through sin; it is not the work of the law, which displays sin but does not give life from sin.

For that great preacher of grace says: “I did not know sin except through the law” (Rom. 7:7). And he says: “If a law had been given that could [Col. 0983] give life, then righteousness would truly have come from the law” (Gal. 3:21).

This is the work of grace: those who receive it, even if they were enemies of the saving teaching of the Holy Scriptures, become its friends. It is not the work of that same teaching when those who hear and read it without the grace of God become worse enemies of it.

## CHAPTER FOUR
12. Therefore the grace of God is not present in the nature of free choice, nor in the law and teaching, as Pelagian perversity foolishly claims; rather, it is given for each individual act by the will of him of whom it is written: “You will set apart, O God, a voluntary rain for your inheritance” (Ps. 67:10). For we lost free choice for loving God through the enormity of the first sin; and the law and teaching of God, although holy and just and good (Rom. 7:12), nevertheless kills if the Spirit does not give life (2 Cor. 3:6). Through the Spirit, the law and teaching are grasped not merely by being heard but by being obeyed, not merely by reading but by loving.

Therefore, that we may believe in God and live piously, it depends “not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9:16)—not because we ought not to will and to run, but because he himself works in us both the willing and the running. Hence the Lord Jesus himself, distinguishing believers from unbelievers—that is, vessels of mercy from vessels of wrath—says: “No one comes to me unless it has been given to him by my Father” (John 6:65). His disciples, moreover, had been scandalized by this teaching when he said it, and afterward they did not follow him.

Let us not, then, say that grace is teaching; rather, let us recognize grace as that which makes teaching beneficial. When this grace is absent, we see that teaching even does harm.

13. Although God foreknew all his future works in predestination, he arranged them in such a way that he converts certain unbelievers to his faith by hearing the prayers of believers on their behalf. Let those who think that God’s grace is the nature of free choice with which we are born—or that God’s grace is teaching, useful though it may be, proclaimed through languages and letters—be refuted and, if he is merciful to them, corrected.

We do not pray for unbelievers that they may become human beings—that is, that they may possess this nature—or that teaching may be proclaimed to them, which they hear to their own harm if they do not believe. Often we pray for those who, though they read or hear, do not wish to believe. Rather, we pray that their will may be corrected, that they may consent to the teaching, and that their nature may be healed.

14. Moreover, the faithful pray even for themselves, that they may persevere in what they have begun to be. It is beneficial for all, or nearly all, as a most salutary exercise in humility, that they should not be able to know what they will become. Hence it is said: “Let the one who thinks he stands take care lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10:12).

For the beneficial purpose of this fear, so that those who have been regenerated and have begun to live piously may not, as though secure, become presumptuous, some who will not persevere are mingled, by God’s permission or providence and arrangement, with those who will persevere. Terrified when these fall, let us walk with fear and trembling along the right path until we pass from this life—which is a time of testing upon the earth (Job 7:1)—to another, where there will no longer be any arrogance to restrain, nor any struggle against its suggestions and temptations.

[Col. 0984] 15. Concerning this matter—that is, why some who will not remain in Christian faith and holiness nevertheless receive this grace for a time and are permitted to live here until they fall, although they could be snatched from this life lest wickedness change their understanding, as is written concerning one who died prematurely in holiness in the Book of Wisdom (Wis. 4:11)—let each person seek as he can. If he finds, in addition to the explanation I have given, another plausible account that does not depart from the rule of right faith, let him hold to it, and I will do so with him, provided it does not escape me.

Nevertheless, let us walk in what we have attained until God reveals to us whether we think otherwise, as we are admonished in the apostolic Letters (Phil. 3:15–16). What we have attained, however, consists in those matters that we know most firmly to belong to the true and catholic faith. With God’s help and mercy, we must walk in them, saying to him: “Lead me, Lord, in your way, and I will walk in your truth” (Ps. 85:11), so that we do not in any way deviate from them.

# TWELVE STATEMENTS AGAINST THE PELAGIANS

## CHAPTER V

16. Since, therefore, by Christ’s favor we are Catholic Christians:

1. We know that the unborn have done nothing good or evil in their own life, and that they could not individually have possessed any previous life of their own [Note: [Col. 0984] Thus two Vatican manuscripts and all the French manuscripts, as well as Bad. and Am.; but Er. and Lov. read: “which no one could have possessed as his own.”] according to whose merits they might come into the miseries of this life. Yet we know that, being born carnally according to Adam, they contract the contagion of ancient death by their first birth, and that they are not freed from the punishment of eternal death—which a just condemnation, passing from one person to all, derives from the one—unless they are reborn in Christ by grace.

2. We know that God’s grace is given neither to infants nor to adults according to our merits.

3. We know that it is given to adults for each individual act.

4. We know that it is not given to all human beings; and that to those to whom it is given, it is given not only apart from the merits of their works, but even apart from the merits of the will of those to whom it is given. This is especially evident in infants.

5. We know that to those to whom it is given, it is given by God’s gratuitous mercy.

6. We know that to those to whom it is not given, it is not given by God’s just judgment.

7. We know that we shall all stand before Christ’s tribunal, so that each person may receive according to what he has done through the body—not according to what he would have done if he had lived longer—whether good or evil.

8. We know that infants too will receive either good or evil according to what they have done through the body. They have done this not by themselves, but through those who, acting as their representatives, are said to renounce the devil on their behalf and to believe in God. Hence they are also counted among the faithful, belonging to the Lord’s sentence: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved.” For this reason, what follows also applies to those who do not receive this sacrament: “But whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16:16).

Thus they too, as I have said, if they die at that tender age, are judged according to what they have done through the body—that is, during the time they were in the body—when they believed or did not believe through the hearts and mouths of those carrying them; when they were baptized or not baptized; when they ate the flesh of Christ [Col. 0985] or did not eat it; and when they drank his blood or did not drink it. According to these things, therefore, which they did through the body, they are judged—not according to what they would have done if they had lived here for a long time.

9. We know that the dead who die in the Lord are blessed, and that whatever they would have done if they had lived longer does not pertain to them.

10. We know that those who believe in the Lord with their own heart do so by their own will and free choice.

11. We know that we who already believe act rightly in praying for those who do not wish to believe, asking God that they may wish to believe.

12. We know that, concerning those among them who have believed, we rightly and truly both ought to give thanks to God and are accustomed to do so, as for benefits received.

17. I think you recognize that, when I said that we know these things, I did not wish to mention everything belonging to the Catholic faith, but only those matters relevant to the question now being discussed between us concerning God’s grace: whether this grace precedes or follows the human will—or, to express it more clearly, whether it is given to us because we wish it, or whether through it God himself also brings about our willing.

If, then, you too, brother, hold with us these twelve statements that I said we know to belong to right and catholic faith, I give thanks to God. I certainly could not give thanks sincerely unless God’s grace brought it about that you held them. Once you hold them, no dispute at all remains between you and us concerning this question.

## CHAPTER VI

18. To run briefly through the same twelve points: how can grace follow the merit of the human will, when it is given even to infants, who are not yet able either to will or not to will this?

How can the merits of the will be said to precede grace even in adults, if grace, in order to be true grace, is not given according to our merits? Pelagius himself feared this Catholic position so much that he unhesitatingly condemned those who say that God’s grace is given according to our merits, lest he be condemned by Catholic judges.

How can God’s grace be said to exist in the nature of free choice or in the law and teaching, when Pelagius himself condemned this position, plainly confessing that God’s grace is given for each individual act—namely, to those who already make use of free choice?

19. How can it be said that all human beings would have received grace if those to whom it is not given did not reject it by their own will, since “God wills all human beings to be saved” (1 Tim. 2:4)? Grace is not given to many infants, and many die without it who possess no contrary will. At times, even when parents desire and hasten to obtain it, and ministers are willing and prepared to administer it, God does not will that it be given: the child suddenly expires before it is given, although people were running to obtain it for the child.

It is therefore clear that those who resist this evident truth do not understand in what sense it was said that God wills all human beings to be saved. So many are not saved, not because they themselves do not wish it, but because God does not wish it; this is revealed without any obscurity in the case of infants.

In the same way, the statement “All will be made alive in Christ” (1 Cor. 15:22) was made although so many are punished with eternal death. It means that all who receive eternal life receive it only in Christ. Likewise, the statement that God wills all human beings to be saved, although he does not will so many to be saved, means that all who are saved are saved only because he wills it. If those apostolic words can be understood in any other way, they must nevertheless be understood so that they cannot contradict this most evident truth: we see so many people not being saved, although human beings desire their salvation, because God does not will it.

20. How can the human will merit the giving of divine grace, if grace is given by gratuitous mercy to those to whom it is given, so that it may truly be grace? How can the merits of the human will be weighed in this matter, when those to whom this grace is not given are often distinguished from those to whom it is given by no merit and no will, but share with them the same condition, and yet, by God’s just judgment, grace is not given to them? “For there is no injustice with God” (Rom. 9:14).

Those to whom grace is given should therefore understand how freely it is given to them, since it is indeed justly not given to others who have the same condition.

21. How can not only the will to believe from the beginning but also perseverance to the end not belong to God’s grace, when the end of this life itself lies not in human power but in God’s, and God can certainly bestow even this benefit on one who will not persevere, snatching him from the body lest wickedness change his understanding?

A person will receive neither good nor evil except according to what he has done through the body, not according to what he would have done if he had lived longer.

22. How can it be said that grace is not given to some, while it is given to certain infants who are going to die, because God foresees the future wills they would have if they lived? Each person receives either good or evil according to what he has done through the body, not according to what he would have done if he had remained longer in the body, as the Apostle establishes (2 Cor. 5:10).

How can people be judged according to their future wills, which they are said to have had if they had been kept longer in the flesh, when Scripture says: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord” (Rev. 14:13)? Their blessedness is certainly not secure and assured if God will judge even those things they did not do but would have done had this life been prolonged for them.

Nor does the one who is snatched away receive any benefit, lest wickedness change his understanding, since he pays the penalty even for that wickedness which perhaps was approaching and from which he was taken away. Nor should we rejoice over those whom we know to have died in right faith and good conduct, lest they be judged according to certain crimes that they might perhaps have committed if they had lived. Nor should we grieve over or detest those who ended this life in unbelief and depraved conduct, because perhaps, if they had lived, they would have repented and lived piously, and according to these hypothetical acts they would have to be judged.

The entire book *On Mortality* by the most glorious martyr Cyprian must therefore be rejected and cast aside, since its whole purpose is that we should know to congratulate good believers when they die, because they are taken away from the trials of this life and will thereafter remain in the most blessed security.

But since it is not false that the dead who die in the Lord are blessed without a doubt, the error must be mocked and detested which supposes that people are to be judged according to future wills that will not be future wills for the dying.

23. How can those who confess that every person who believes in God with his own heart believes only by his own free will be said to deny the free choice of the will? Rather, it is those who attack God’s grace who attack free choice, since grace truly makes it free for choosing and doing good.

How can it be said that what Scripture itself says—“The will is prepared by the Lord” (Prov. 8:35, according to the Septuagint)—comes about through God’s law and the teaching of Scripture, and not rather through the hidden inspiration of God’s grace? For on behalf of those who contradict this teaching and refuse to believe it, we rightly ask God himself that they may be willing to believe.

24. How does God wait for human wills to precede him before he gives them grace, when we rightly give him thanks for those to whom he showed mercy even though they did not believe in him and persecuted his teaching with impious will, converting them to himself with almighty ease and making the unwilling willing?

Why do we give him thanks for this if he did not do it himself? Why do we glorify him all the more the less willing to believe were those whose belief makes us rejoice, if divine grace does not change the human will for the better?

The Apostle Paul says: “I was unknown by face to the churches of Judea that are in Christ; they only heard that the one who once persecuted us now preaches the faith that he once destroyed; and they glorified God in me” (Gal. 1:22–24).

Why did they glorify God if God had not turned that man’s heart to himself by the goodness of his grace, when Paul himself confesses that he obtained mercy so that he might be faithful (1 Cor. 7:25), in the faith that he had once destroyed? Even the word he used clearly declares who performed this great good. For what does “they glorified God in me” mean except that they proclaimed God magnificent in me?

How, however, could they proclaim him magnificent if he himself had not performed that great act in Paul’s conversion? And how had he performed it if he himself had not made the unwilling willing to believe?

25. It is plainly evident from those twelve statements—which you are not permitted to deny belong to the Catholic faith—that each and every one of them establishes that we must confess that human wills are preceded by God’s grace, and that through grace they are prepared rather than grace being given on account of their merit.

Or, if you deny that any one of these twelve statements is true—I emphasize their number so that they may more easily be committed to memory and held more distinctly—do not hesitate to write back and inform me, so that I may answer with whatever ability the Lord grants me.

I do not believe that you are a Pelagian heretic; but I do want you to be such that none of that error passes over to you or remains in you.

## CHAPTER VII

26. Among these twelve statements you may perhaps find something that you think must be denied or doubted, and so compel us to argue at greater length.

Will you also forbid the Church to pray for unbelievers, that they may become believers; for those who do not wish to believe, that they may wish to believe; and for those who dissent from his law and teaching, that they may consent to his law and teaching? Will you forbid her to pray that God may give them what he promised through the prophet: “a heart to know him and ears to hear” (Baruch 2:31)—ears which, of course, they had received, concerning which the Savior himself said: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. 13:9)?

When you hear a priest of God exhorting the people at his altar to pray to God, or praying aloud himself that he may compel unbelieving nations to come to the faith, will you not answer, “Amen”? Or will you argue against the soundness of this faith as well?

Will you loudly or secretly declare that the most blessed Cyprian was mistaken when he teaches us to pray for the enemies of the Christian faith, so that they too may be converted to it?

27. Finally, will you blame the Apostle Paul for expressing such wishes for unbelieving Jews? Concerning them he says: “The good desire of my heart and my prayer to God for them is for salvation” (Rom. 10:1).

He also says to the Thessalonians: “Finally, brothers, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may run and be glorified, as it is also among you, and that we may be delivered from wicked and evil people; for not all possess faith” (2 Thess. 3:1–2).

How would the word of God run and be glorified unless those to whom it was preached were converted to the faith, since he says to those who already believe, “as it is also among you”? He certainly knows that this is brought about by the one whom he wishes to be asked to bring it about, so that he may also be delivered from wicked and evil people—people who, clearly, would not believe even when those believers prayed for them.

For this reason he added, “For not all possess faith,” as though he were saying: “The word of God will not be glorified among everyone, even when you pray for them.” Those who had been appointed to eternal life would certainly believe, having been predestined for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ and chosen in him before the foundation of the world (Eph. 1:4–5). But God makes those who do not yet believe believe through the prayers of believers, in order to show that he himself brings this about.

No one is so ignorant, so carnal, or so dull of understanding that he does not see that God does what he commands people to ask him to do.

28. These and other divine testimonies, which it would take too long to recall, show that God removes the heart of stone from unbelievers by his grace and precedes the merits of good wills in human beings. Thus the will is prepared by preceding grace, rather than grace being given because of a preceding merit of the will.

Both thanksgiving and prayer indicate this: prayer for unbelievers, thanksgiving for believers. The one whom we must ask to do something is the one to whom we must return thanks when he has done it. Hence the same Apostle says to the Ephesians: “For this reason I too, having heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all the saints, do not cease giving thanks for you” (ibid. 1:15).

29. We are speaking now about the very beginnings, when people who were estranged and hostile are converted to God, begin to will what they did not will, and acquire the faith they did not possess. In order that this may occur in them, prayer is made for them, although they do not pray themselves. For “how will they call upon him in whom they have not believed?” (Rom. 10:14).

When what is prayed for has come about, thanks are given to the one who brought it about—both for them and by them.

I do not think that we need to contend with you concerning the prayers already made by the faithful, which they offer both for themselves and for other believers so that they may advance in what they have begun to be, or concerning thanksgiving, since they are advancing. This conflict is one that you and we share against the Pelagians.

They attribute everything belonging to the faithful and pious life of human beings to free choice of the will, so that they think these things must be possessed from ourselves rather than requested from the Lord. You, however, if what I hear about you is true, do not wish the beginning of faith—which is also the beginning of good, that is, pious, willing—to be God’s gift. You insist that we possess it from ourselves, so that we begin to believe. You do concede that God gives the other goods of religious life by his grace to those who already ask, seek, and knock in faith.

But you do not consider that we pray to God on behalf of unbelievers so that they may believe because God also gives faith; and that we give thanks to God on behalf of those who have believed because he has also given them faith.

30. To bring this discourse to a conclusion at last: if you deny that we should pray for those who do not wish to believe, asking that they may wish to believe; if you deny that we should give thanks to God because those who did not wish to believe have wished to believe, then we must deal with you differently, so that you may not continue in such error—or, if you persist in error, so that you may not lead others into error.

But if—as I more strongly believe—you think and agree that we ought and are accustomed to pray to God for those who do not wish to believe, that they may wish to believe, and for those who oppose and contradict his law and teaching, that they may believe it and follow it; and if you think and agree that we ought and are accustomed also to give thanks to God for such people when they are converted to his faith and teaching and become willing instead of unwilling, then you must undoubtedly confess that human wills are preceded by God’s grace; that God brings it about that people wish what they did not wish to wish; and that he is the one whom we ask to do this, and to whom we know it is right and just to give thanks when he has done it.

May the Lord grant you understanding in all things, my lord brother.

# LETTER 218

[Note: We have collated this letter against manuscripts bl. cb. vc., two v. manuscripts, and Lov.]

[Note: Elsewhere numbered 208; the letter that was 218 is now 13. It was perhaps written at approximately the same time.]

Augustine exhorts Palatinus to advance and persevere in Christian wisdom, taking the greatest care not to place his hope of living well in his own strength.

To his most beloved and most longed-for son PALATINUS, AUGUSTINE.

1. Your more resolute and fruitful conversion to the Lord our God has brought us great joy. From your youth you chose instruction, so that you might find wisdom even unto old age (Ecclus. 6:18). The gray hairs, then, are the understanding of a human being, and the age of old age is an unblemished life (Wis. 4:9).

May the Lord grant this to you when you ask, seek, and knock—he who knows how to give good gifts to his children (Matt. 7:11). Although exhorters and exhortations to the way of salvation and eternal glory abound for you, especially Christ’s own grace, which has spoken so beneficially in your heart, nevertheless we too, in fulfillment of the duty of love that we owe you, offer some exhortation in this reply of ours. We do not rouse you as though you were sluggish or asleep, but encourage and urge you onward while you are running.

2. You must be wise, my son, so that you may persevere, because you were wise enough to choose. Let this itself be part of your wisdom: to know whose gift this is.

“Commit your way to the Lord, and hope in him; and he himself will act. He will bring forth your justice like the light and your judgment like midday” (Ps. 36:5–6). He himself will make your courses straight and bring your paths forward in peace (Prov. 4:27).

Just as you despised what you had hoped for in the world, so that you would not glory in the abundance of riches, which you had begun to desire in the manner of the children of this world, so now do not trust in your own strength to remove the Lord’s yoke and his burden. Then it will be easy and this burden light (Matt. 11:29–30).

The Psalm equally condemns those who trust in their strength and those who glory in the abundance of their riches (Ps. 48:7). You no longer possessed the glory of riches; rather, you most wisely rejected the glory you had desired to possess. Take care lest you secretly begin to trust in your own strength. You are a human being, and “cursed is everyone who places his hope in a human being” (Jer. 17:5).

But trust wholly in your God with all your heart, and he will be your strength. Trust in him piously and gratefully, saying to him humbly and faithfully: “I will love you, Lord, my strength” (Ps. 18:2). For even the love of God, which perfect love casts out fear (1 John 4:18), is not poured into our hearts through our own, that is, human, powers, but—as the Apostle says—“through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

3. Therefore keep watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation (Mark 14:38). Prayer itself reminds you that you need the help of your Lord, so that you do not place your hope of living well in yourself.

You pray not now to receive the riches and honors of the present world, or any human vanity, but that you may not enter into temptation. If a person could provide this for himself simply by willing it, it would not be sought through prayer.

Therefore, if our will were sufficient to keep us from entering into temptation, we would not pray; yet if the will were absent, we could not pray either. Let God be present, then, so that we may will; and let us pray that we may have the strength to accomplish what we have willed, once, by his gift, we have come to sound judgment.

Since you have already begun this good, you have reason to give thanks. “For what do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7)—that is, as though you could have it from yourself.

Knowing from whom you received it, ask him to bring it to perfection, since it was he who gave you the beginning. Therefore work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For “God is the one who works in you both to will and to accomplish, for his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:12–13), since “the will is prepared by the Lord” (Prov. 8:35, according to the Septuagint), and human steps are directed by him, and he wills his way (Ps. 36:23).

This holy thought will preserve you, so that your wisdom may be piety—that is, so that you may be good through God and not ungrateful for Christ’s grace.

4. Your parents long for you, faithfully rejoicing in the better hope that you have begun to possess in the Lord. We, however, whether you are bodily absent or present, wish to possess you in one spirit, through whom love is poured into our hearts, so that wherever our flesh may be, our souls may in no way be separated.

We received with great gratitude the hair shirts that you sent, in sending which you first reminded us to practice and preserve humility in prayer.

# LETTER 219

[Note: This letter is appended here to Augustine’s letters because, according to the opinion of scholars, it was dictated by him.]

[Note: The letter that was numbered 219 is now 252. It appears to have been written in 426 or 427.]

Augustine and other African bishops write to the Gallican bishops Proculus and Cillinnius, who had expelled the monk Leporius because he had erred concerning the faith in the incarnation of the Word, urging them to embrace him now that he has repented and been corrected by God’s grace.

To our most beloved and honorable brothers and fellow priests, PROCULUS and CYLINNIUS, Aurelius AUGUSTINE, FLORENTIUS, and SECUNDINUS send greetings in the Lord.

[Note: Sirmond judges from the style that the letter was dictated by Augustine; others likewise make the same judgment concerning the *Book of Leporius’s Correction*. We think that the errors of this monk had not yet come to Augustine’s attention when, in *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 11, he said: “For no one is so blind through ignorance of this matter and faith that he would dare to say that, although the Son of Man was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, he nevertheless merited by living well through free choice and by doing good works without sin to be the Son of God.” Leporius himself also detests this as “the utter blindness of his folly” in the *Book of Correction*. That book was therefore written after the same work, *On Rebuke and Grace*. Gennadius mentions Leporius as “corrected by Augustine” in *On Illustrious Men of the Church*, chapter 59; likewise Cassian in book 1 of *On the Incarnation*, Pope John II in his letter to Avienus, Facundus in book 1, chapter 4, and others.]

1. When our son Leporius came to us after being expelled from your presence, we received him—salutarily shaken by the correction he had deservedly and appropriately received from you—for correction and healing.

For just as you obeyed the Apostle by correcting the disorderly, so we obeyed him by consoling the fainthearted and supporting the weak (1 Thess. 5:14).

He had been caught, as a human being may be, in a certain offense—and no small one. Concerning the only-begotten Son of God, who was “the Word in the beginning,” and “the Word was with God, and the Word was God,” and when “the fullness of time came, the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1, 14), he did not hold a right understanding or entertain the truth.

He denied that God had become human, evidently lest an unworthy change or corruption should affect the divine substance, by which he is equal to the Father. Nor did he see that he was thereby introducing a fourth person into the Trinity, something wholly alien to the soundness of the Creed and to Catholic truth.

With the Lord’s help, we instructed him in the spirit of gentleness as best we could. The Vessel of Election especially admonished us to do this when he added: “Pay attention to yourself, lest you too be tempted” (Gal. 6:1). He did not want certain people to rejoice at having reached spiritual maturity in such a way that they thought they could no longer be tempted as human beings. He added the salutary and peaceful instruction that “we should bear one another’s burdens, for in this way we will fulfill the law of Christ. For whoever thinks he is something, when he is nothing, deceives himself” (Gal. 6:1–3), most beloved and honorable brothers.

2. Yet we perhaps could never have completed his correction unless you had first condemned what was defective in him. Thus our one Lord and physician, using his vessels and ministers—he who said, “I strike, and I heal” (Deut. 32:39)—struck through you what was swollen and healed through us what was suffering.

The same administrator and provider of his household destroyed through you what had been badly constructed and restored through us what had been properly arranged. The same diligent farmer of his estate uprooted through you what was barren and harmful and planted through us what was useful and fruitful.

Let us therefore give glory not to ourselves but to his mercy, in whose hand both we and our words are held. And just as our humility praised your ministry in the case of the son mentioned above, so let your Holiness rejoice in our ministry.

Receive, therefore, with paternal and fraternal affection the man corrected by us with merciful severity. Although one thing was done through us and another through you, one love made both necessary for our brother’s salvation. One God, therefore, accomplished it, because “God is love” (1 John 4:8, 16).

3. Therefore, just as he was received by us through his repentance [Note: Elsewhere, “presence”], so let him be received by you through his letter [Note: Leporius’s *Book of Correction*]. We thought it appropriate to add our own hand and signature to that letter, testifying that it is his.

We have no doubt, your affection, that you will receive his correction gratefully and make it known to those for whom his error was a stumbling block. Those who came with him to us were corrected and healed along with him, as is expressly recorded in their signatures, which were made in our presence.

It remains for you, rejoicing in our brother’s salvation, to deign in turn to gladden us by a reply from your Blessedness. We desire you, most beloved and honorable brothers, to be well in the Lord and mindful of us.

# LETTER 220

[Note: Corrected against manuscripts bl. cb. ff. gg. r. vc., two sb., two t., two v., and the editions of Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: Elsewhere numbered 70; the letter that was numbered 220 is now 171. It appears to have been written toward the end of 427.]

Augustine to Count Boniface, who had first undertaken a vow of monasticism but later, on Augustine’s advice, accepted the office of count; contrary to Augustine’s counsel, he married and committed serious offenses in many matters. Augustine urges him to return to his former purpose if his wife permits it; if she does not, he should use worldly power for good, not evil.

To his lord son BONIFACE, whom God’s mercy protects and governs, for present and eternal salvation, AUGUSTINE.

1. I have never been able to find a more faithful person, or one who could more easily bring my letter to your ears, than the one whom the Lord has now provided: Paul, a servant and minister of Christ, a deacon dear to both of us. Through him I may say something to you—not concerning your power or the honor you hold in this wicked world, nor concerning the safety of your corruptible and mortal flesh, since that too is transitory and it is always uncertain how long it will last, but concerning the salvation Christ promised us.

For this reason he was dishonored and crucified here: to teach us to despise the goods of this world rather than love them, and to love and hope from him what he displayed in his resurrection. For he rose from the dead, “dies no more, and death no longer rules over him” (Rom. 6:9).

2. I know that there is no shortage of people who love you according to the life of this world and who give you counsel according to it—sometimes useful, sometimes useless—because they are human beings and, as best they can, they judge the present, not knowing what will happen on the following day.

But concerning God, and lest your soul perish, scarcely anyone gives you counsel—not because there are none who would do so, but because it is difficult to find a time when they can speak with you about these things.

I have always desired such an opportunity, but I have never found a place or time to do with you what I ought to do with a person whom I greatly love in Christ. You know what condition you saw me in at Hippo when you graciously came to me, for I could scarcely speak, exhausted by bodily weakness.

Now, then, my son, hear me—at least through this letter speaking to you. In your dangers I was never able to send you such a letter, considering the danger to its bearer and taking care lest my letter should reach those to whom I did not wish it to come.

Therefore I ask you to forgive me if you think I feared more than I ought. Nevertheless, I have said what I feared.

### 3

Hear me, then—or rather, hear the Lord our God through the ministry of my weakness. Recall what sort of man you were, while your first wife, of revered memory, was still living; and how, upon her recent death, you came to loathe the vanity of this present age, and how you desired the service of God. We know—we were witnesses—what you said to us at Tubunas about your mind and will. Only Alypius and I were with you. For I do not suppose that the earthly cares with which you have been filled had such power that they could completely erase this from your memory.

Surely you wished to abandon all the public activities with which you were occupied, to withdraw into holy leisure, and to live the life in which the servants of God, the monks, live. But what held you back from doing so except that, when we pointed out to you how greatly what you were doing could benefit the Churches of Christ, you considered doing it for the sole purpose that, once defended from the assaults of the barbarians, they might lead a quiet and peaceful life, as the Apostle says, “in all piety and chastity” (1 Tim. 2:2)? You yourself would seek nothing from this world except what was necessary to sustain this life of yours and that of your dependents, girded with the belt of the most chaste continence, and, amid bodily weapons, more safely and more strongly fortified with spiritual weapons?

[Note: [Col. 0993] In nine manuscripts consistently, *Tubanas*: and below, *Tubanīs*; and *Tubanensia*. Erasmus and the Louvain editions have *Tubunas*.]

### 4

When, therefore, we rejoiced that you were settled in this purpose, you sailed away and took a wife. Your sailing was an act of obedience, which, according to the Apostle, you owed to the higher powers (Rom. 13:1); but you would not have taken a wife unless, abandoning the continence you had undertaken, you had been overcome by desire. When I learned this, I confess, I was astonished and stunned. My grief was consoled to some extent by hearing that you had refused to marry her unless she first became Catholic. Yet the heresy of those who deny the true Son of God prevailed so greatly in your household that your daughter was baptized by them. And now, if what has been reported to us is not false—may it indeed be false!—that even maidservants dedicated to God have been rebaptized by those same heretics, with what floods of tears must so great an evil be lamented? People also say that your wife herself was not enough for you, but that you were polluted by intercourse with certain concubines—though perhaps they are lying.

### 5

What shall I say about these evils, so numerous and so great, which became evident to all after you married?

[Note: [Col. 0994] Thus the manuscripts. The editions have: “These things are evident to all, so many and such great evils as followed you after you married. What, then, shall I say?”]

You are a Christian; you have a heart; you fear God. Consider for yourself what I do not wish to say, and you will discover how many evils you ought to repent of. I believe that for the sake of this repentance the Lord is sparing you and will free you from all dangers, so that you may perform it as it ought to be performed. But hear what is written: “Do not delay turning to the Lord, nor put it off from day to day” (Ecclus. 5:8).

You say, certainly, that you have a just cause. I am not its judge, since I cannot hear both sides. But whatever your cause may be—it is not now necessary to inquire into or debate it—can you deny before God that you would not have come into this necessity unless you had loved the goods of this world? As God’s servant, as we formerly knew you, you ought altogether to have despised them and regarded them as nothing. When they were offered, you ought to have accepted them so that you might use them for piety, but you ought not to have sought what was withheld or assigned elsewhere in such a way that because of them you would be brought into this necessity. Here, when goods are loved,

[Note: [Col. 0994] Thus the manuscripts. The editions have: “when vanities are loved.”]

evils are committed—few by you, but many because of you. And when things that cause harm for a brief time, if indeed they cause harm at all, are feared, people commit those things that truly cause eternal harm.

### 6

To mention one aspect of this: who does not see that many people cling to you to protect your power or safety? Even if all of them are loyal to you and none of them is suspected of plotting against you, nevertheless they desire, through you, to attain those goods which they themselves also love, not according to God but according to the world. Thus, although you ought to restrain and curb your own desires, you are compelled to satisfy the desires of others.

For this to happen, many things displeasing to God must be done. Yet even then such desires are not satisfied; for they are more easily cut off in those who love God than in those who love the world, among whom they are sometimes indulged to satiety. Therefore divine Scripture says:

“Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him; because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age. This is not from the Father but from the world. And the world passes away, and its desire; but whoever does the will of God remains forever, just as God also remains forever” (1 John 2:15–17).

When, then, will you be able to satisfy the desires of so many armed men, whose greed must be indulged and whose ferocity is feared? When, I ask, will you be able—not to satisfy the desires of those who love the world, for that cannot possibly be done—but to feed them even in part, lest everything perish still more, unless you do what God forbids and threatens those who do it?

That is why you see so many things crushed, so that scarcely anything of value remains to be seized.

[Note: [Col. 0995] The editions have: “lest the populace perish.” In their place all the Gallican manuscripts and two Vatican manuscripts have *plus pereant* (“lest more perish”).]

### 7

What shall I say about the devastation of Africa, which the African barbarians are inflicting while no one resists, because you are occupied with such necessities of your own and are making no arrangements by which this calamity might be averted?

Who would have believed, who would have feared, that, with Boniface, commander of the household troops and count of Africa, established in Africa with so great an army and authority—he who, when a tribune with a few federated troops, had pacified all those peoples by defeating and terrifying them—the barbarians would now dare so much, advance so far, devastate so much, carry off so much, and turn so many places formerly filled with inhabitants into deserts?

Did people not say that, whenever you assumed the power of the countship, the African barbarians would become not merely subdued but tributary to the Roman state? And now you see how completely people’s hopes have been turned into their opposite. There is no need to speak with you about this any longer, because you can think more about it than we can say.

### 8

But perhaps you will reply that these matters ought rather to be charged to those who injured you, who repaid your dutiful services not with equal deeds but with their opposites. I cannot hear or judge those causes. Look instead to your own cause, and examine it—your cause, which you know you have not with just any human beings but with God. Since you live faithfully in Christ, you must fear offending him.

For my part, I attend rather to the higher causes, because the fact that Africa is suffering such great evils must be attributed to the sins of its people. Nevertheless, I would not wish you to belong to the number of those through whom God scourges with temporal punishments whomever he wills, though they are wicked and unjust. For the wicked themselves, if they are not corrected, he reserves eternal punishments, while he justly uses their wickedness to inflict temporal evils upon others.

Pay attention to God; consider Christ, who has bestowed such great benefits and endured such great evils. Whoever desires to belong to his kingdom and to live forever blessed with him and under him loves even his enemies, does good to those who hate him, and prays for those by whom he suffers persecution (Matt. 5:44). And if at times such a person applies harsh severity for the sake of discipline, [Note: [Col. 0995] One Vatican manuscript has “moderate.”] he nevertheless does not lose his most sincere charity.

If, therefore, benefits have been bestowed upon you—although they are earthly and transitory, and bestowed by the Roman government, which itself is earthly, not heavenly, and can bestow only what lies within its power—then do not repay good with evil. But if evils have been inflicted upon you, do not repay evil with evil. I neither wish nor am able to investigate or judge which of these two situations is yours. I am speaking to a Christian: do not repay either good with evil or evil with evil.

### 9

Perhaps you say to me: “In such a crisis, what do you want me to do?”

If you are asking me, according to this world, how your transitory safety may be protected, and how your power and wealth may either be preserved as they now are or even increased, I do not know what answer to give you. Things so uncertain cannot have a certain plan.

But if you consult me according to God, lest your soul perish, and if you fear the words of truth that say, “What does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Matt. 16:26), then I certainly have something to say. I have advice for you to hear from me.

What need is there for me to say anything other than what I said above?

Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. For if anyone loves the world, the Father’s charity is not in him, because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age. This is not from the Father but from the world. And the world passes away, and its desire; but whoever does the will of God remains forever, just as God also remains forever (1 John 2:15–17).

There is the advice: seize it and act. Let it now be shown whether you are a strong man. Conquer the desires by which this world is loved. Repent of your past evils, when, overcome by those desires, you were dragged along by unworthy longings.

If you accept, hold fast, and preserve this advice, you will reach those certain goods, and you will pass through these uncertainties with the salvation of your soul.

### 10

But perhaps you again ask me how you can do this while entangled in so many necessities of this world.

Pray fervently, and say to God what you have in the Psalm: “Deliver me from my necessities” (Ps. 24:17). For these necessities end when those desires are conquered.

He who heard you—and us on your behalf—so that you might be freed from so many and such great dangers of visible and bodily wars, in which only this life, which will one day end, is endangered, while the soul does not perish unless it is held captive by wicked desires—he himself will hear you, so that you may invisibly and spiritually conquer your inner and invisible enemies, that is, the desires themselves.

Thus you will use this world as though you were not using it: from its goods you will do good, and you will not become evil. For those goods themselves are good, and they are given to human beings only by him who possesses authority over all heavenly and earthly things. But lest they be thought evil, they are given also to the good; and lest they be thought great or supreme goods, they are given also to the wicked. Likewise, they are taken away from the good so that they may be tested, and from the wicked so that they may be tormented.

### 11

Who does not know this? Who is so foolish that he does not see that the health of this mortal body, the strength of corruptible limbs, victory over human enemies, and temporal honor and power, along with all the other earthly goods of this kind, are given both to the good and to the wicked, and are taken away both from the good and from the wicked?

[Note: [Col. 0996] The Louvain editions have “victory over all enemies.” But the other editions and the manuscripts, “victory over human beings,” are better.]

But the salvation of the soul together with the immortality of the body, the strength of righteousness, victory over hostile desires, and glory, honor, and peace forever are given only to the good.

Love these things, then; desire these things; seek them in every way. To acquire and obtain them, give alms, pour out prayers, and practice fasting as much as you can without harming your body.

But do not love those earthly goods, however abundantly they may overflow to you. Use them in such a way that you do many good things from them, but do no evil for their sake. For all such things will perish; but good works do not perish, including those that are done from perishable goods.

### 12

If you had no wife, I would tell you what we also said at Tubunas: that you should live in the holiness of continence.

[Note: [Col. 0997] Five manuscripts of better quality have: “that you should live in the chastity of continence.”]

I would add what we then forbade you to do: that, insofar as you could do so without disturbing the peace in human affairs, you should now withdraw from these military matters and devote yourself to that life among the company of the saints to which you then desired to devote yourself. There Christ’s soldiers fight in silence—not to kill human beings, but to conquer rulers and authorities and the spiritual forces of wickedness (Eph. 6:12), that is, the devil and his angels.

These are the enemies whom the saints conquer, though they cannot see them. Yet, although they do not see them, they conquer them by conquering the things they do perceive.

But since I am not urging you toward this life, your wife is an impediment; without her consent you may not live continently. For even though, after those words of yours at Tubunas, you ought not to have taken her as your wife, she nevertheless married you innocently and simply, knowing nothing of any of this.

Would that you could persuade her to continence, so that without impediment you might render to God what you recognize that you owe him. But if you cannot deal with her in this way, at least preserve conjugal chastity, and pray to God—who will deliver you from your necessities—that what you cannot do now, you may someday be able to do.

Nevertheless, so that you may love God and not love the world; so that, if you still need to remain involved in those wars, you may keep faith and seek peace; so that you may do good works from the goods of the world and may not do evil works for the sake of the world’s goods—your wife either does not hinder you or ought not to hinder you.

Charity commanded me to write this to you, dearest son: I love you according to God, not according to this present age. For, remembering what is written, “Reprove a wise person, and he will love you; reprove a fool, and he will add to his hatred of you” (Prov. 9:8), I ought certainly to think of you not as a fool but as a wise man.

## LETTER 221

[Note: [Col. 0997] Letter 221 and the following letters, both those from Quodvultdeus and those addressed to Quodvultdeus, have been brought here from volume 6 and collated with various manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0997] From volume 6, before the book *On Heresies*. What was formerly 221 is now 119. Written around A.D. 427.]

Quodvultdeus to Augustine, requesting that he write a catalogue of all the heresies that have arisen against the Christian faith and briefly set forth their errors and rites.

To the deservedly venerable and truly most blessed father, Augustine, bishop, Quodvultdeus, deacon.

### 1

For a long time I was anxious, and repeatedly postponed daring to make this request of mine. But, as the saying goes, the benevolence of Your Blessedness, approved by all, chiefly encouraged me. As I considered it, I became more afraid that, by not asking, I might be judged arrogant by the Lord; by not seeking, lazy; and by not knocking, sluggish.

I would have thought that merely having such a desire would be enough for me, even if I could not obtain its fruit. But since I know for certain that your holy mind, possessed by Christ, is ready to open the door of divine discourse—which heavenly grace has opened to Your Reverence—not only to all who wish to enter, but also to persuade those who do not wish to enter, so that they may not be reluctant to come in, I shall not delay Your Reverence’s occupations with excessive words. I shall briefly indicate the desire expressed in my petition.

### 2

I infer from my own case that some members of the clergy of this very great city are unlearned [Note: [Col. 0998] The manuscripts have “of every [city].”], and I submit for Your Holiness’s consideration how greatly the entire order would benefit from what I am requesting.

By the privilege of all those who deserve to receive something from your spiritual labors, I presume that even I, unworthy as I am, shall obtain such a benefit, deservedly venerable lord and truly most blessed father.

I therefore ask Your Blessedness to explain: from the time when the Christian religion received the name of the promised inheritance, what heresies have existed and now exist; what errors they introduced and now introduce; what they have thought and now think against the Catholic Church concerning the faith, the Trinity, Baptism, Penance, Christ as man, Christ as God, the resurrection, the New and Old Testaments, and absolutely everything by which they dissent from the truth; which of them possess Baptism and which do not; after which of them the Church baptizes, yet does not rebaptize; how she receives those who come to her; and what she answers to each by law, authority, and reason.

### 3

Nor should Your Blessedness think me so foolish as not to realize how many and how enormous volumes would be required to resolve these matters.

But I am not asking you to do that; I have no doubt that it has already been done many times. Rather, I ask that the views of each heresy be set forth briefly, concisely, and in summary, and that what the Catholic Church holds against each be appended insofar as is sufficient for instruction.

Then, as though from a memorandum composed from all these matters, anyone who wishes to know some objection or refutation more fully, extensively, and clearly may be directed to the rich and magnificent volumes which various authors—and especially Your Reverence—have demonstrably labored to produce for this very purpose.

Such a notice, I think, will suffice for the learned and the unlearned, for those at leisure and those occupied, and for persons promoted from every quarter to ministry in the Church at whatever level. The one who has read much will briefly recall the same material, while the uninstructed will be taught by the abridgment, so that he may know what he ought to hold, what he ought to avoid, what he ought to shun and not do, and what he ought to attain in order to do.

Perhaps—and if what I think is true, this too will be the case—this little work will, among the other marvelous testimonies to your crown, not be lacking as a witness against the wicked minds and deceitful lips of slanderers. For those to whom a broader field for slander lies open will find themselves confined by the strong and entirely closed boundaries of the faith and surrounded by every kind of weapon of truth; struck down suddenly by a single many-formed missile, they will not dare to breathe out their death-dealing spirits.

### 4

I see how burdensome I am becoming to a holy old man who is considering better things, arranging greater matters, and enduring the complaints of the body.

But through Christ the Lord I ask you—he who has granted you a share in his wisdom without envy—to bestow this grace upon the unlearned of the Church. You acknowledge that you are debtor to the wise and to the foolish (Rom. 1:14), and you will rightly and justly be able to say: “See that I have not labored for myself alone, but for all who seek the truth” (Ecclus. 24:47; 33:18).

I could still offer suppliant and repeated prayers and enlist with me whole classes of unlearned people; but I preferred already to hear you dictating rather than continue to occupy you while you read.

[Note: [Col. 0999] Thus one Vatican manuscript. The editions have: “to rejoice while you dictate.”]

## LETTER 222

[Note: [Col. 0999] From volume 6, before the book *On Heresies*. What was formerly 222 is now 120. Written shortly after the preceding letter.]

Augustine to Quodvultdeus, excusing the difficulty of the proposed work and noting that others have attempted it.

To his dearest son and fellow deacon, Quodvultdeus, Augustine, bishop.

### 1

When I received your letter, in which you earnestly requested that I write briefly about all the heresies that have sprung up against the teaching of the Lord and Savior after his coming, I immediately replied, when an opportunity arose, through my son Philocalus, the chief citizen of Hippo, explaining how difficult this was. Soon another opportunity presented itself, through which I now write and briefly point out the difficulty of the work.

### 2

A certain Philaster, bishop of Brescia, whom I myself saw at Milan with the holy Ambrose, wrote a book on this subject. He did not omit the heresies that existed among the Jewish people before the Lord’s coming, and he listed twenty-eight of those, followed by one hundred twenty-eight after the Lord’s coming.

On this subject the Cyprian bishop Epiphanius also wrote in Greek; he was honorably renowned for his Catholic teaching. But, gathering together heresies from both periods, he included eighty.

Since both of them wished to do what you ask of me, you see how much they differ from one another, at least concerning the number of sects. This would certainly not have happened unless one of them thought something was a heresy that the other did not.

Nor should we suppose that Epiphanius was ignorant of some heresies known to Philaster, since we found Epiphanius far more learned than Philaster. If the former had included more and the latter fewer, we should rather have said that many had escaped Philaster’s notice.

But without doubt, in the question of what constitutes a heresy, the two did not hold the same view; and in fact it is extremely difficult to define this precisely. Therefore, when we try to reduce them all to a number, we must take care not to omit some that are heresies, or to count some that are not heresies.

Consider, then, whether perhaps I ought to send you the book of Saint Epiphanius. I think that he spoke on this subject more learnedly than Philaster. It could be translated into Latin more easily and conveniently at Carthage, so that you might provide us with what you are asking from us.

### 3

I warmly commend the bearer of this letter. He is a subdeacon from our diocese, and he comes from the estate of the eminent and very dear man Orontius.

[Note: [Col. 1000] The Michaelinus and Becheronensis manuscripts, and one Vatican manuscript, have *Honorati*.]

For his sake, and for the sake of his father, by whom he was adopted, I have also written to that man. When your Christian Kindness has read the letters, I ask you by your intercession to deign to support them with the man mentioned.

I have also sent with him a member of the Church, lest access to Your Holiness prove difficult for him. I am very concerned about him; and, as I hope, through the earnestness of your charity the Lord will free me from this concern.

I also ask that you not hesitate to write back to me concerning how that Theodosius is standing in the Catholic faith, through whom certain Manichaeans were exposed, and also concerning those whom we think were corrected after being exposed by him.

If you have heard anything about the departure of the holy bishops, let me know.

May you live for God.

## LETTER 223

[Note: [Col. 1000] From volume 6, before the book *On Heresies*. What was formerly 223 is now 61. Perhaps written in A.D. 428.]

Quodvultdeus to Augustine, again urgently requesting that he write the little work on heresies.

To the deservedly venerable and most blessed holy father, Augustine, bishop, Quodvultdeus, deacon.

### 1

I received one memorandum from Your Reverence, which you kindly sent through an ecclesiastical intermediary. The one that Your Blessedness indicated had previously been sent through the honorable man Philocalus has not yet reached me.

Although I have always been conscious of my own sins, I now clearly recognize, by attaining the office for which I prayed, that my person is an impediment to the whole Church. [Note: [Col. 1000] Six manuscripts have: “Looking to the gift which I requested.”] Nevertheless, I am wholly confident that he who, through the grace of his Only-Begotten, deigned to blot out the crimes of the human race will not permit mine to prevail to the ruin of all. Rather, where sin abounded, he will cause grace to overflow (Rom. 5:20), deservedly venerable lord and most blessed father.

I did not previously fail to acknowledge the difficulty of the work which, through your kindness, I have humbly begged you to provide for the instruction of the most unlearned among us. But I trusted with a truthful heart in the abundance of the divine spring which the Lord has granted you.

### 2

For although the revered bishops Philaster and Epiphanius are said to have written something of this kind—which, without doubt, is hidden from me among all their other works, indeed as are all of them—I do not think that they took such care and diligence as to append contrary opinions to each individual view and then add the rites associated with them.

Moreover, whatever the work of either of them may be, it perhaps does not possess the brevity I desire.

Nor is Greek eloquence assigned to a person who has not learned Latin to any purpose, because I asked not only for advice but also for assistance. Why should I remind Your Reverence not only of the difficulty but also of the obscurity of translators, when you yourself judge this matter more fully and accurately?

It is also relevant that some heresies are said to have arisen after their deaths, of which they made no mention.

### 3

Therefore I flee to the special protection of your piety, and with my own voice—but with the desire of the whole Church—I appeal to your sacred and holy heart, ready for mercy. Setting aside foreign flavors, considering the text of my earlier letter, do not deny to one who knocks late and suffers hunger the African bread which our province customarily produces of the finest quality, seasoned also with heavenly manna.

For certainly I shall not cease knocking until you yourself grant my request, so that what privilege cannot obtain where there is no merit,

[Note: [Col. 1001] Several manuscripts have *quia* (“because”); or, “because there is no merit.”]

at least unwearied persistence may deserve.

## LETTER 224

[Note: [Col. 1001] From volume 8, before the book *On Heresies*. What was formerly 224 is now 125. Written after the preceding letter.]

Augustine to Quodvultdeus, promising that he will write about heresies when other occupations permit. For the present, he says that Alypius is pressing him to answer Julian’s later books.

To his sincerely beloved lord, brother, and fellow deacon, Quodvultdeus, Augustine, bishop.

### 1

When the Fussalan presbyter, whom I commend to your charity, afforded me an opportunity to write this letter, I reread your letter in which you ask me to write something about the heresies that may have arisen since the Lord’s coming in the flesh began to be proclaimed.

I did this to see whether I ought already to undertake the work itself and send you something, so that you might recognize that it is more difficult in proportion as you wish it to be shorter.

But even this I could not do, prevented by cares that arose and which I could not entirely disregard; for they turned me away even from the work I had in hand.

### 2

That work is my response to Julian’s books. He published eight after the four to which I had previously replied. When our brother Alypius received these in Rome, he had not yet copied all of them. But he did not wish to let an opportunity pass, and he sent me five, promising to send the other three soon and pressing me strongly not to delay my response.

His insistence compelled me to proceed more slowly with what I was doing,

[Note: [Col. 1001] The editions have: “to proceed ever more slowly with what I was doing.” Almost all the manuscripts have: “to proceed more slowly than I had been doing.”]

so that I would not neglect either work: one by day, the other by night, whenever I could be spared from the other occupations that kept coming upon me from every direction without ceasing.
