I had been engaged in a very necessary task, for I was revising my shorter works. If anything in them displeased me or might offend others, I was working partly by censuring it, partly by defending what ought and could be read.

I had already completed two volumes, having revised all my books, whose number I had not known. I discovered that there were 232 of them. The letters remained, and then the popular discourses, which the Greeks call homilies.

I had already read many of the letters, but had dictated nothing from them when these books of Julian also began to occupy me. I have now begun to answer the fourth of them.

When, therefore, I have completed that response and answered the fifth—if the remaining three have not arrived—I plan, God willing, to begin what you request as well, working on both simultaneously: this work, naturally, and the work of revising my shorter writings, assigning each its nighttime and daytime hours.

[Col. 1002]

### 3

I have explained this to Your Holiness so that, in proportion to your desire to receive what you request, you may ask the Lord more fervently to grant me assistance, by which I may serve your praiseworthy zeal and the benefit of those whom you think will profit from it, sincerely beloved lord and brother.

I again commend the bearer of this letter and the business for which he has gone. If you discover with whom it must be conducted, please do not hesitate to help him.

For we cannot abandon the necessities of people who are not our tenants but, what is more, are our brothers and belong to our care in the charity of Christ.

May you live for God.

## LETTER 225

[Note: [Col. 1002] Letters 225 and 226 have been corrected against the manuscripts and editions and transferred here from volume 7.]

[Note: [Col. 1002] From volume 7, prefixed to the book *On the Predestination of the Saints*. What was formerly 225 is now 126. Written in A.D. 428 or 429.]

Prosper to Augustine, informing him that the remnants of the Pelagian heresy are secretly growing in Gaul under the Catholic name, and reporting the complaints of certain people concerning what Augustine had written against the Pelagians about the distinction among human beings, calling according to purpose, and the predestination of the elect, about prevenient grace, and about the fixed number of the elect; asking him to clarify with the clearest explanations whatever is obscure in these questions.

To the most blessed pope, ineffably marvelous, incomparably worthy of honor, and outstanding patron, Augustine, Prosper.

### 1

Although unknown to you in face, I am already known to you to some extent, if you remember, in mind and speech. For through my holy brother the deacon Leontius I sent and received letters. Now too I dare to write to Your Blessedness, not merely with the intention of saluting you, as at that time, but also with affection for the faith by which the Church lives.

Since your most vigilant diligence keeps watch over all the members of Christ’s body, and since you fight against the snares of heretical doctrines with the power of truth, I thought I had no reason to fear being burdensome or importunate to you in a matter that concerns the salvation of many and, consequently, your own piety. Rather, I would have believed myself guilty if I did not refer matters which I understand to be extremely dangerous to the special patron of the faith.

### 2

Many servants of Christ who reside in the city of Massilia think that, in the writings of Your Holiness which you composed against the Pelagian heretics, whatever you have argued concerning the calling of the elect according to God’s purpose is contrary to the opinion of the Fathers and to the ecclesiastical understanding.

For a time they preferred to blame their own slowness rather than criticize what they did not understand. Some of them wished to request a clearer and more explicit explanation from Your Blessedness on this point.

Then, by God’s merciful providence, when certain monks within Africa had raised similar questions, you issued the book *On Correction and Grace*, full of divine authority. When it reached our knowledge at an unexpectedly timely moment, we thought that all the complaints of those who resisted would be silenced, because you answered all the questions on which Your Holiness needed to be consulted so fully and definitively there that it seemed as though you had deliberately labored to settle the disturbances among us.

When this book of Your Blessedness had been read, those who had previously followed the holy and apostolic authority of your teaching became much more enlightened and instructed. But those who were hindered by what was obscure in their own persuasion withdrew more alienated than before.

Their abrupt dissent must first be feared on their own account, lest the spirit of Pelagian impiety deceive men so distinguished and outstanding in their devotion to every virtue. Then it must be feared lest the more simple-minded, among whom these men possess great respect because of their reputation for goodness, should judge that what they hear asserted by persons whose authority they follow without judgment is safest for them.

### 3

For this is their own definition and profession: that every human being sinned when Adam sinned, and that no one is saved by his own works, but by the grace of God through regeneration. Nevertheless, the propitiation that is in the sacrament of Christ’s blood has been offered to all human beings without exception, so that whoever wishes to approach faith and Baptism may be saved.

But those who are going to believe, and those who are going to remain in that faith—which thereafter is to be aided by grace—God foreknew before the foundation of the world; and those whom he foresaw would, once freely called, prove worthy of election and depart this life with a good end, he predestined for his kingdom. Therefore every human being is admonished to believe and to act according to the divine commandments, so that no one may despair of attaining eternal life, since a reward has been prepared for voluntary devotion.

But this purpose of God’s calling—in which, whether before the beginning of the world or at the very creation of the human race, a distinction is said to have been made between those to be chosen and those to be rejected, so that, according to what pleased the Creator, some were created vessels of honor and others vessels of dishonor—both removes from the fallen any concern to rise again and gives the saints an occasion for tepidity. For on either side labor would be superfluous, if neither the rejected could enter by any exertion nor the elect could fall away through any negligence: however they might conduct themselves, nothing other than what God had determined could happen to them. Nor can one’s course be steady under uncertain hope, since, if the choice of the one who predestines has determined something else, the effort of the one who strives is futile.

Thus, they say, all exertion is removed and the virtues abolished if God’s decree precedes human volitions; and under the name of predestination a kind of fatal necessity is introduced. Alternatively, the Lord would be said to be the creator of different natures, if no one could be other than he was made.

To state their opinion more briefly and fully: whatever Your Beatitude opposed to yourself in this book from the position of those who contradict you, and whatever you also most powerfully refuted in the books against Julian that he himself raised under this question—all of it is proclaimed most vehemently by these holy men.

When we present against them your writings, furnished with the strongest and most numerous testimonies of the divine Scriptures, and, following the form of your arguments, establish something by which they too may be brought to a conclusion, they defend their obstinacy by its antiquity. They assert that the passages drawn from the Apostle Paul’s Letter to the Romans, concerning the manifestation [Col. 1004] of divine grace that precedes the merits of the elect, have never been understood by any ecclesiastical writers in the way they are now understood.

When we ask them to explain those passages according to whatever interpretations they please, they declare that they have found nothing satisfactory and demand silence concerning matters whose profundity no one has reached. Finally, their obstinacy descends to this point: they define our faith as contrary to the edification of those who hear it and therefore, even if it is true, as not to be publicly proclaimed, because what is taught without due caution is to be received perniciously, whereas what cannot be understood may be kept silent without danger.

### 4

Some of them, however, depart so little from the paths of the Pelagians that, when they are compelled to acknowledge the grace of Christ that precedes all human merits—for if it were given in response to merits, it would be called grace in vain—they want this condition to belong to every human being: that the Creator’s grace, when the person neither previously deserving anything nor even yet existing, establishes him as a rational creature endowed with free will, so that through the discernment of good and evil he may direct his will toward the knowledge of God and obedience to his commandments, and may reach that grace by which we are reborn in Christ through a natural capacity—by asking, seeking, and knocking.

Thus, they say, he receives, finds, and enters for this reason: because, having made good use of nature’s goodness, he has merited, with the aid of initial grace, to reach this saving grace.

They define the purpose of calling grace entirely in this way: God ordained that no one should be admitted into his kingdom except through the sacrament of regeneration, and that all human beings universally should be called to this gift of salvation, whether through natural law, written law, or evangelical preaching. In this way those who wish may become children of God, while those who refuse to be believers are left without excuse, because God’s justice consists in the fact that those who do not believe perish; and his goodness appears in this, that he rejects no one from life but wishes all alike to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.

At this point they produce testimonies by which the exhortation of the divine Scriptures incites human wills to obey—wills that, by free choice, either do what is commanded or neglect it. They consider it to follow that, just as the transgressor is said not to have obeyed because he did not wish to obey, so the faithful person must be acknowledged to have been devoted because he wished to be. Each person, they say, has as much capacity for good as for evil; and the mind can, with equal momentum, turn itself either toward vices or toward virtues. God’s grace supports the person who desires good, while just condemnation overtakes the person who pursues evil.

### 5

When the countless multitude of infants is set before them in the midst of these arguments—infants who, apart from original sin, under which all human beings are born alike into the condemnation of the first human being, have as yet no wills and no actions of their own, yet are not separated without God’s judgment—some being taken away from the use of this life before discerning good and evil and, through regeneration, made heirs of the heavenly kingdom, while others, without Baptism, pass into perpetual death as its debtors, they say that such infants are lost or saved according to what divine knowledge foresaw they would become in later years if they had been preserved into active adulthood.

They do not consider that, according to their own fancy, they subject the grace of God—which they wish to be an accompanying, not a preceding, grace of human merits—even to those wills which they do not deny were preceded by it. Indeed, they subject God’s election to such fictitious merits [Col. 1005] that, because past merits do not exist, they fabricate future merits that will not be future. In a new form of absurdity among them, things that ought not to be done are foreknown, and things foreknown are not done.

They seem to support this foreknowledge of human merits, according to which the grace of calling operates, with much greater plausibility when they turn to those nations that either in past ages were left to enter upon their own ways or even now perish in the impiety of their former ignorance, with no illumination of either the Law or the Gospel having shone upon them. Yet, insofar as a door has been opened and a way made for preachers, the people of the nations that sat in darkness and in the shadow of death have seen a great light (Isaiah 9:2; Matthew 4:16); those who once were not a people are now God’s people; and those upon whom he once had not mercy now receive mercy (Hosea 2:23–24; Romans 9:25).

They say that the Lord foresaw who would believe, and that times and the ministries of teachers were distributed to each nation in such a way that the belief of good wills would arise. Nor, they say, is the statement that “God wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” unstable (1 Timothy 2:4), since those are without excuse who could have been instructed by natural understanding in the worship of the one true God, yet did not hear the Gospel because they would not have received it.

### 6

They say that our Lord Jesus Christ died for the entire human race, and that absolutely no one was excluded from redemption by his blood, even if that person passed through the whole of this life with a mind utterly alien to Christ, because the sacrament of divine mercy pertains to all human beings. Many are therefore not renewed because they are foreknown not to possess the will to be renewed.

Thus, as far as God is concerned, eternal life has been prepared for everyone; but, as far as freedom of choice is concerned, it is grasped by those who freely believe in God and receive the help of grace as the deserved reward of their belief.

Those whose contradiction troubles us have turned especially to this proclamation of grace, though previously they held better views, because, if they confessed that all good merits are preceded by grace and are granted by grace so that they may exist, they would necessarily have to concede that God, according to the purpose and counsel of his will, by a hidden judgment and manifest work, creates one vessel for honor and another for dishonor. For no one is justified except by grace, and no one is born except in transgression.

But they shrink from confessing this and fear to attribute the merits of the saints to God’s work. They do not accept that the number of the predestined elect can be neither increased nor diminished, lest the exhortations of those who urge the unbelieving and negligent have no place, and the command to exertion and labor prove superfluous, since the effort would be frustrated if election ceased.

They hold, rather, that each person can be called to correction or progress only if he knows that he can become good through his own diligence, and that his freedom should therefore be aided by God if he chooses what God commands. Thus, since in those who have received the time of free will there are two things that bring about human salvation—namely, God’s grace and human obedience—they want obedience to precede grace, so that the beginning [Col. 1006] of salvation should be believed to depend on the one who is saved, not on the one who saves, and so that the human will should produce for itself the assistance of divine grace, rather than grace subject the human will to itself.

### 7

Since, through God’s mercy revealing the truth and Your Beatitude instructing us, we know this to be utterly perverse, we can indeed be steadfast in refusing to believe it, but we are not equal to the authority of those who hold such opinions. They greatly surpass us in the merits of their lives, and some of them are pre-eminent because they have recently attained the highest priestly office. Nor has anyone, except for a few fearless lovers of perfect grace, easily dared to oppose the arguments of such superiors.

Consequently, the danger has increased not only for those who listen to them but also for those who are listened to, together with their dignities. Their reverence either restrains many through an unprofitable silence or leads them, without careful examination, to assent; and what is scarcely criticized by anyone appears to them most wholesome.

Since, therefore, a vein of no ordinary virulence is nourished in these remnants of Pelagian perversity—if the beginning of salvation is wrongly placed in humanity; if human will is impiously preferred to the divine will, so that someone is helped because he wished, rather than wishing because he is helped; if a person who is originally evil is wrongly believed to begin receiving good from himself rather than from the highest good; and if God is believed to be pleased by anything other than what he himself has granted—grant us, most blessed pope and excellent father, in this matter as much of your pious diligence as, with the Lord’s help, you can provide. Deign to disclose, in the clearest explanations, those matters in these questions that are more obscure and more difficult to understand.

### 8

First, since many do not think that the Christian faith is violated by this disagreement, make clear how much danger lies in their persuasion. Next, explain how free choice is not impeded by this grace that works beforehand and works together with us.

Then clarify whether God’s foreknowledge remains according to his purpose in such a way that the very things which are purposed are to be understood as foreknown; or whether these matters vary according to kinds of causes and classes of persons, so that, because the callings differ among those who are saved without doing anything, God’s purpose alone seems to be present, whereas among those who are going to do something good the purpose can stand by means of foreknowledge.

Or is the matter uniform, so that, although foreknowledge cannot be separated from purpose by a temporal distinction, foreknowledge nevertheless rests upon purpose in a certain order? Just as there is nothing in any undertaking that divine knowledge has not preceded, so may there be nothing good that has flowed into our participation without God as its author?

Finally, explain how, through this proclamation of God’s purpose—by which those who have been foreordained to eternal life become believers—none of those who must be exhorted is impeded, nor do they have an occasion for negligence if they despair of being predestined.

We also ask you, by patiently bearing with our ignorance, to show how this matter may be resolved: after the opinions of earlier writers on the subject have been reconsidered, almost all of them are found to share one and the same view, by which they received God’s purpose and predestination according to foreknowledge. They therefore held that God made some vessels of honor and others of dishonor because he foresaw the end of each person and, under the assistance of grace, foreknew what that person’s will and action would be.

[Col. 1007]

### 9

When all these matters, and many others that you can see more profoundly to pertain to this case, have been disentangled and examined, we believe and hope that not only will our weakness be strengthened by the support of your arguments, but that those themselves whose distinction in merit and honor is obscured by the darkness of this opinion will receive the purest light of grace.

Your Beatitude should know that one of them, a man of exceptional authority and spiritual devotion, the holy Hilary, bishop of Arles, is in all other matters an admirer and follower of your teaching, and that for some time he has wished to communicate his view to Your Holiness by letter concerning the matter of which he complains.

[Note: Some thought that Honoratus should be substituted here; but the manuscripts examined by us consistently prefer Hilary. Having been a monk of Lérins, he was made bishop of Arles after Honoratus, who died in the year 428 or certainly at the beginning of 429. For Honoratus, who succeeded Patroclus after his murder in 426, occupied the see of Arles for two years, according to Prosper’s Chronicle, as Honoratus of Marseille attests.]

But since it is uncertain whether he will do this or to what end he will do it, and since, by God’s grace providing for the present age, the weariness of us all now breathes again in the vigor of your charity and knowledge, add instruction to the humble and rebuke to the proud.

It is necessary and useful to write what has been written, lest what is not frequently reproved be considered insignificant. They think something sound if it does not hurt, and they do not feel the wound beneath the skin that has grown over it. But let them understand that what has had a persistent swelling will eventually reach the surgeon’s knife.

May the grace of God and the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ crown you at all times, and may he glorify you eternally as you walk from virtue to virtue, most blessed lord pope, ineffably wondrous, incomparably honorable, and most excellent patron.

## Letter 226

[Note: From volume 7, prefixed to *On the Predestination of the Saints*. What was formerly numbered 226 is now 256. Written at the same period.]

**Hilary to Augustine, on the same subject**

To the most blessed lord, greatly longed for with the whole affection of my heart, and most dearly embraced in Christ as my father, AUGUSTINE, HILARY.

[Note: This Hilary evidently distinguishes himself below, in section 10, from Hilary of Arles, who, as Prosper writes in the preceding letter, “was bringing [Augustine’s] view of predestination into question,” in these words: “I do not want Your Holiness to think that I write this as though I doubted about what you have now published.” He later indicates that he had once enjoyed Augustine’s “delights in his presence” and had been nourished by his “abundant and salutary breasts”; in section 9 he suggests that he is a layman; and finally he calls Augustine “father,” while Augustine in turn calls him “son” in book 1 of *On the Predestination of the Saints*. These details certainly do not suit the bishop of Arles.]

### 1

If, when the questions of those who contradict have ceased, the inquiries of serious students are generally welcome, so that they may learn even those things which could be ignored without danger, I think that the diligence of my report will be even more welcome. For, while it indicates that certain matters are presented by some people as contrary to the truth, it seeks, through the counsel of your holiness, to provide assistance not so much for itself as for those who are disturbed and who disturb others, most blessed lord, greatly longed for with the whole affection of my heart, and most dearly embraced in Christ as my father.

### 2

These, then, are the matters being debated at Marseille and also in other places in Gaul.

They say that it is novel and useless to the preaching [Col. 1008] of the faith that certain people are said to be chosen according to God’s purpose, so that they can neither seize nor retain that purpose unless the will to believe has been granted to them. They think that all force from preaching is excluded if it is said that nothing remains in human beings which preaching can arouse.

They agree that every human being perished in Adam and that no one can be freed from this by his own choice. But they assert that the following is consistent with the truth and appropriate to preaching: when the opportunity of attaining salvation is announced to those who lie prostrate and will never rise by their own strength, they can be healed of their disease by the merit of having wished and believed, and can thereby obtain both an increase of faith itself and the effect of complete health.

For the rest, they agree that no one is sufficient for himself for beginning any work, much less for completing it. They do not think that the terrified and suppliant will of a sick person, by which each person wishes to be healed, should be counted among the works of their healing.

They assert that when it is said, “Believe, and you will be saved,” one thing is demanded and another is offered: once what is demanded has been supplied, what is offered is subsequently bestowed because of it. Hence they think that faith must be exhibited by the person to whom, by the will of the Creator, this capacity has been granted by nature. They think that no nature has been so corrupted or extinguished that a person neither ought nor can wish to be healed. Consequently, a person is either healed from his disease or, if he does not wish to be healed, is punished together with his disease.

They say that grace is not denied if such a will is said to precede it—a will that seeks only the physician and is already capable of nothing else. They want testimonies such as “as God has apportioned to each the measure of faith” (Romans 12:3), and similar passages, to mean that the one who has begun to wish is helped, not that the will to wish is itself granted. Others who are equally guilty are excluded from this gift, although they too could be freed if the will to believe, bestowed equally upon those who are equally unworthy, were likewise bestowed upon them.

If, they say, it is maintained that some capacity of will remains in everyone, by which a person can either despise or obey, they think that the question of the elect and the rejected is conveniently resolved by adding to each person the merit of his own will.

### 3

When they are asked why the Gospel is preached to some people or in some places, not preached to others or elsewhere, or preached now when at one time it was preached to almost everyone, just as now it is not preached to certain nations, they say that this belongs to divine foreknowledge: the truth was or is announced at that time, in that place, and to those people when and where it was foreknown that it would be believed.

They claim to prove this not only from the testimonies of other Catholics but also from an earlier argument of Your Holiness [Col. 1009], in which you nevertheless taught the same grace with no lesser clarity of truth. For example, Your Holiness said in the question against Porphyry, concerning the timing of the Christian religion:

“Christ then wished to appear to human beings and to have his teaching preached among them when and where he knew that there would be people who would believe in him” (*Letter* 102, question 2, section 14).

Or there is the passage from the book on the Letter to the Romans:

“You say to me, then, ‘Why does he still complain? For who resists his will?’” (Romans 9:19).

“To this inquiry,” you say, “he responds in such a way that we understand that, for spiritual people—even those who do not live according to the earthly human being—the first merits of faith and impiety can be evident: how God, by foreknowledge, chooses those who will believe and condemns unbelievers; choosing neither the former on the basis of works nor condemning the latter on the basis of works, but granting to the faith of the former that they may act well, while hardening the impiety of the latter by their abandonment, so that they may act wickedly.”

And again, earlier in the same book:

“All are equal before merit, and election cannot be named among things that are in every respect equal. But because the Holy Spirit is given only to believers, God does not choose the works that he himself bestows when he gives the Holy Spirit so that we may do good works through love. Nevertheless, he chooses faith, because unless someone believes and persists in the will to receive, he does not receive God’s gift, that is, the Holy Spirit, through whom he can do good by the love infused into him.

“Therefore, in his foreknowledge he does not choose anyone’s works, which he himself is going to bestow; rather, he chooses faith in his foreknowledge, so that the person whom he foreknew would believe might be the one whom he chose to receive the Holy Spirit, so that by doing good he might also attain eternal life. For the Apostle says: ‘It is the same God who works all things in all people’ (1 Corinthians 12:6). Nowhere, however, is it said, ‘God believes all things in all people.’ What we believe belongs to us; but what we do belongs to him” (*On the Explanation of Certain Propositions from the Letter to the Romans*, propositions 12 and 60).

They declare that they accept and approve these and the other passages in the same work, as agreeing with evangelical truth.

### 4

For the rest, they insist that foreknowledge, predestination, or purpose means that God foreknew, predestined, or purposed to choose those who would believe. They say that faith cannot be described by the words, “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7), since the same nature remained in human beings, although corrupted, that had previously been given to them sound and perfect.

When Your Holiness says that no one perseveres except by receiving the power of perseverance, they understand this only to mean that, although it is inert, it is nevertheless attributed to the person’s preceding exercise of his own choice. They say that free choice is limited to this: that a person may wish or refuse to admit the medicine.

For the rest, they testify that they themselves abominate and condemn the view that any power remains in a person by which he can progress toward health. They do not want perseverance preached in such a way that it cannot either be obtained by humble supplication or lost through obstinacy. Nor do they want to be led into uncertainty regarding God’s will, since, as they think, it is evident what kind of beginning of the will each person has for obtaining or admitting grace.

They also define the testimony you cited, “He was taken away lest wickedness should change his understanding” (Wisdom 4:11), as noncanonical and therefore to be omitted.

Accordingly, they understand foreknowledge in this way: people are to be understood as foreknown because of their future faith. They deny that anyone is given such perseverance that he is not permitted to transgress; rather, they say that a person can fall away from it and grow weak by his own will.

### 5

They assert that the customary practice of exhortation is useless if nothing is said to remain in a human being which correction can arouse. They acknowledge that this is present in nature, but they say that the very fact that truth is preached to someone who is ignorant must be referred to the benefit of present grace.

“If people,” they say, “are predestined to either outcome in such a way that no one can pass from one group to the other, what is the point of such persistent external correction? Perhaps from a human being there may arise, even if not perfect faith, at least the sorrow of a contrite weakness, or dread of the danger of a death that has been revealed.”

[Col. 1010]

For if a person cannot fear the thing by which he is frightened except through the will that is received, he should not be blamed for not wishing now. Rather, the blame lies in and with the one who at some time refused in such a way that he deserved to incur that condemnation together with his descendants, so that he would always desire what is perverse and never what is right.

But if some kind of sorrow arises from the exhortation of the one who corrects, they say that this very thing is the reason why one person is rejected and another assumed. Thus, they conclude, it is unnecessary to establish separate groups to which nothing can be added and from which nothing can be taken away.

### 6

They are also troubled by the way grace is divided—the grace given either to the first human being at that time or now given to all:

“Adam received perseverance, not by which he would persevere, but without which he could not persevere by free choice. Now, however, the saints who are predestined by grace for the kingdom receive not such assistance for perseverance, but assistance of such a kind that perseverance itself is granted to them: not merely so that without this gift they could not persevere, but also so that through this gift they can do nothing except persevere” (*On Rebuke and Grace*, chapters 11–12).

Your Holiness’s words move them to say that a kind of despair is being presented to human beings. If Adam was helped in such a way that he could both stand firm in righteousness and depart from righteousness, whereas the saints are now helped in such a way that they cannot depart—since they received the perseverance of willing, so that they cannot will anything else—or if some people are abandoned in such a way that they either do not approach or, if they approach, depart again, then they say that the benefit of exhortation and threat belonged to that will which possessed the free power both to persist and to desist, not to this will, for which the inability to refuse righteousness is joined to inevitable necessity.

They except those who were so created together with those who were condemned along with the entire mass of humanity that they might be rescued by grace. Thus, they want the nature of the first human being to differ from that of all others in this one respect: grace helped him, while he was willing, with the full powers of his will, although without grace he could not persevere. But those who believe after losing and destroying their powers are not merely raised when prostrate; they are also supported while walking.

For the rest, they insist that whatever has been given to the predestined can be either lost or retained by their own will. This would be false only if they considered it true that some people had received perseverance in such a way that they could do nothing except persevere.

### 7

This is why they likewise reject the view that the number of those who are to be chosen and rejected has been fixed. They accept an explanation of that statement different from the one you have drawn out: namely, that God wills all human beings to be saved, not only those who will belong to the number of the saints, but absolutely everyone, with no one excepted.

They do not think it necessary to fear the claim that some perish against God’s will. Rather, they say: just as God does not wish anyone to sin or abandon righteousness, yet righteousness is constantly abandoned against his will and sins are committed, so he may wish all human beings to be saved and yet not all human beings be saved.

They think that the testimonies of Scripture which you cited concerning Saul and David (*ibid.*, chapters 13–14) do not pertain to the question under discussion, which concerns exhortation. They refer other passages to this: that they commend the grace by which each person [Col. 1011] is helped after the will has arisen, or to the calling that is granted to the unworthy. They testify that they demonstrate this in those passages of your smaller works and in other writings as well, which it would take too long to pursue.

### 8

They do not allow the case of infants to be brought forward as an example for adults. They say that Your Holiness touched upon it only so far as to leave the matter uncertain and, rather, to prefer that doubt be entertained about the punishments of infants. You remember that this was stated in the third book of *Free Choice* (book 3, chapter 23) in a form that could have provided them with this opportunity.

They do the same with books by other authors that possess authority in the Church. Your Holiness sees that these books can assist those who contradict us considerably unless we produce greater or at least equal authorities. For your most prudent piety is not unaware how many people in the Church are held to a position, or transferred from a position, by the authority of names.

In short, after all of us have been wearied, their argument—or rather their complaint—turns to this. Even those who do not dare to disapprove of this definition agree in saying:

“What need was there to disturb the hearts of so many people of limited understanding with the uncertainty of a discussion of this kind? Without this definition, they say, the Catholic faith was defended no less usefully for so many years by so many interpreters, in so many books written both by you and by others, against various opponents and especially against the Pelagians.”

### 9

My father, I would have preferred to bring these matters and many others of interminable extent before you myself, if I may confess my deepest desire; or, since I have not deserved that privilege, at least to collect and send over a longer period everything that troubles them, so that I might hear what in all that is said against this matter ought to be refuted or, if it cannot be refuted, endured.

But since neither outcome has followed according to my wish, I preferred to send these matters gathered together as best I could rather than remain completely silent about the great contradiction of certain people.

Some of those involved are persons to whom, according to ecclesiastical custom, it is necessary for laymen to show the highest reverence. With God’s help we have taken care to preserve that reverence, while, when necessary, not remaining silent about what the smallness of our powers suggested in defense of this question.

For now, however, I have offered these points summarily, insofar as the haste of the messenger permitted, as reminders. It belongs to your holy wisdom to determine what must be done so that the purpose of such important persons may be overcome or moderated.

I think I would accomplish little by merely giving you an account unless authority were added—authority that contentious hearts, indefatigable in transgression, could not pass beyond. But I must certainly not leave unsaid that they claim to admire Your Holiness in all your deeds and words except in this matter.

It will be yours to decide how their contradiction should be tolerated. Nor should you be surprised that I have added other matters in this letter, or matters which I think I did not mention in the preceding one. Their present definition is of this kind, apart from what I may have passed over through haste or forgetfulness.

### 10

When the books you are preparing on your entire body of work have been published, I ask that we may be worthy to receive them.

[Note: He means the books of the *Retractions*.]

Above all, may we receive them so that, by their authority, if anything in your writings displeases you, we may now, without fear, remove it from the dignity of your name.

We do not possess your book *On Grace and Free Choice*; [Col. 1012] may we be worthy to receive it, since we are confident that it is useful for this question.

I do not want Your Holiness to think that I write these things as though I doubted what you have now published. Let my punishment be sufficient: exiled from the delights of your presence, where I was nourished by your salutary and abundant breasts, I am tormented not only by your absence but also by the obstinacy of certain people who reject not only what is manifest but even criticize what they do not understand.

For the rest, I am so free from this suspicion that I rather regard as noteworthy my own weakness, by which I endure such people with too little patience. As I have said, I leave it to your wisdom to judge how these matters should be addressed.

I believed that it belonged to me, out of the love that I owe to Christ and to you, not to remain silent about matters that have become questions. Whatever you wish or are able to do for the sake of that grace which we, small and great alike, admire in you, we shall receive with the greatest gratitude, as though it were decreed by an authority most dear and reverend to us.

Since, under pressure from the messenger, I feared that, conscious of my own powers, I might be unable to send either everything or even these matters in a sufficiently worthy form, I approached a man distinguished in character, eloquence, and zeal, asking him to communicate in his own letter as much as he could gather.

[Note: Prosper seems to be meant, whose letter precedes this one.]

I have taken care to send that letter together with this one. He is indeed such a man that, even apart from this necessity, he should be considered worthy of Your Holiness’s acquaintance.

The holy deacon Leontius, your devotee, sends you many greetings together with my parents. May the Lord Christ deign to preserve Your Paternity for many years for his Church, my lord and father.

And below:

Your Holiness should know that my brother—the principal reason we departed from here—has, together with his wife, by mutual consent, vowed perfect continence to God. Therefore we ask Your Holiness to deign to pray that the Lord may confirm and preserve this very commitment in them.

## Letter 227

[Note: Reviewed in the manuscripts designated bl. ff. gg. r. sb. vc. v.; two copies marked t.; and the editions of Amerbach, Badianus, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis.]

[Note: Formerly numbered 67; what was numbered 227 is now 124. Probably written in the year 428 or 429, after Easter.]

**Augustine to the elder Alypius, concerning Gabinianus, recently baptized, and Dioscorus, converted to Christianity through miracles**

**AUGUSTINE TO THE ELDER ALYPIUS**
Brother Paul is safe here; he brings the second instalment of his affairs. May the Lord grant that these may also be the last. He sends you many greetings, and reports the joys concerning Gabinianus [Note: [Col. 1012] The Corbie and German manuscripts read *Gaviniano*.], who, having been freed by God’s mercy from that former condition of his, is not merely a Christian but also a very good and faithful one. He was baptized recently at Easter, having in his heart and on his lips the grace that he received. When shall I explain how much I long for him? But you know how I love him.

The chief physician [Note: [Col. 1012] The printed editions read *Architheater*. But the better manuscripts have *Archiater*, that is, “chief physician.”] Dioscorus too is a faithful Christian, having received grace at the same time. Hear also how this happened—for that little neck and tongue of his would not have been subdued except by some miracle. His daughter, in whom alone he placed his satisfaction, fell ill and, according to the report of that very father, reached the point of complete despair of temporal [Col. 1013] recovery. The story is told—and it is confirmed, since the count Peregrinus, an admirable man and a good Christian, who was baptized with them at the same time, related it to me before Brother Paul’s return—that the old man finally turned to imploring Christ’s mercy and bound himself by a vow that he would become a Christian if he saw her restored to health.

It happened. But he delayed fulfilling what he had vowed; and still the hand was raised on high. For he was suddenly overwhelmed by blindness, and at once it came to his mind why this had happened. He cried out in confession and vowed again that, once his sight had been restored, he would fulfil what he had vowed. He recovered it and fulfilled his vow; and still the hand was raised on high. He had not retained the Creed—or perhaps he had refused to retain it and excused himself by saying that he had been unable to do so. God had seen this.

Then, after all the celebrations of his reception [Note: [Col. 1013] The Victor and Vatican manuscripts read, “yet after he had confessed all his deception.” Most of the others read, “yet after all the weariness of his reception.”] he was struck with paralysis in many, indeed almost all, of his limbs, and also in his tongue. Then, warned in a dream, he confessed in writing that this had happened to him because he had not delivered the Creed. After that confession, the functions of all his limbs were restored, except that of the tongue alone. Nevertheless, he wrote that he had learned the Creed and therefore now retained it in his memory, even while undergoing the same trial. Thus all his frivolity was eradicated—frivolity which, as you know, greatly disfigured a certain natural kindness in him and made him, in his mockery of Christians, a very sacrilegious man. What can I say except: let us sing a hymn to the Lord and exalt him above all forever. Amen.

## LETTER CCXXVIII

[Note: [Col. 1013] Revised against manuscripts a, b, bg, bl, c, cc, f, ff, fs, g, gv, n, r, two sb, two t, two vc, four v, and the editions of Amerbach, Badenius, Erasmus, and Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 1013] Formerly 180; the letter that was 228 is now 114. Written around 428 or 429.]

Augustine to Honoratus, explaining when a bishop or clergy may flee when the danger of siege or destruction is imminent.

To his holy brother and fellow bishop HONORATUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 1013] Possidius inserted this entire letter into his Life of Saint Augustine, chapter 30: “Meanwhile, it must by no means be left unmentioned that, when the aforesaid enemies—the Vandals—were threatening, our holy man’s fellow bishop Honoratus of the Church of Thiava consulted him by letter about whether, upon their arrival, bishops or clergy ought to withdraw from the churches or not; and Augustine indicated in his reply what was more greatly to be feared from those destroyers of the Roman lands. I wished to insert that letter into this work, for it is exceedingly useful and necessary for the conduct of the priests and ministers of God.”]

### 1

When I sent Your Charity a copy of the letter that I wrote to our brother and fellow bishop Quodvultdeus, I thought that I had discharged the burden you had laid upon me by asking my advice about what you ought to do amid the dangers that our times have brought upon us. Although I wrote that letter briefly, I nevertheless believe that I omitted nothing sufficient both for one answering to say and for one asking to hear, since I said both that those who desire to migrate to fortified places, if they can, ought not to be prevented, and that we must not break the bonds of our ministry by which Christ’s charity has bound us, so that we abandon the churches that we ought to serve.

These, then, are the words that I placed in that letter [Letter to Bishop Quodvultdeus, which is not extant]:

> It remains, therefore, that we, whose ministry is so necessary to whatever small people of God remains here that it would not be right for them to remain without it, should say to the Lord: “Be for us a God who protects us and a fortified place” (Psalm 30:3).

### 2

[Col. 1014] But, as you write, this advice does not satisfy you, lest we seem to act contrary to the Lord’s command or example, where he teaches that one should flee from city to city. We recall the words of him who says: “When they persecute you in this city, flee into another” (Matthew 10:23). But who could believe that the Lord intended this to mean that the flocks he purchased with his own blood should be abandoned, even though they cannot live without the ministry that is necessary to them?

Did he do this when, carried by his parents into Egypt, he fled as a little child (Matthew 2:14)—he who had not yet gathered churches that we could say had been abandoned by him? Or when the Apostle Paul, so that the enemy might not seize him, was lowered in a basket through a window and escaped his hands (2 Corinthians 11:33), was the church that was there abandoned in the absence of the ministry it needed? Was what was necessary not fulfilled by other brothers who had been established there? The Apostle had done this at their request, so that he might preserve for the Church himself, whom that persecutor was specifically seeking.

Therefore let Christ’s servants, ministers of his word and sacrament, do what he commanded or permitted. Let them flee from city to city when one of them is specifically sought by persecutors, so that the Church is not abandoned by others who are not sought in the same way. Rather, let them provide sustenance for their fellow servants, whom they know cannot live otherwise.

But when the danger is common to all—that is, to bishops, clergy, and laity [Note: The printed editions omit “and laity”; we have restored it from the manuscripts]—those who need others must not be abandoned by those whom they need. Either all should move to fortified places, or those who have an obligation to remain must not be abandoned by those through whom the Church’s ministry to them must be supplied, so that they may either live together or endure together whatever the master of the household wills them to endure.

### 3

If it should happen that some suffer less and others more, or that all suffer equally, it becomes clear which of them suffer on behalf of the others: namely, those who, although they could have freed themselves from such evils by fleeing, preferred to remain rather than abandon the needs of others.

This especially proves the charity that the Apostle John commends when he says: “As Christ laid down his life for us, so we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers” (1 John 3:16). Those who flee—or who cannot flee because they are bound by their own necessities—if they are captured and suffer, suffer for themselves, not for their brothers. But those who suffer because they were unwilling to abandon the brothers who needed them for Christian salvation undoubtedly lay down their lives for their brothers.

### 4

[Col. 1015] This is why what we heard a certain bishop say is true and acceptable: “If the Lord has commanded us to flee in those persecutions in which there can be the fruit of martyrdom, how much more ought we to flee barren sufferings when there is a barbarian and hostile invasion?” Yet this applies to those who are not held by the bonds of ecclesiastical office.

For the person who does not flee hostile disasters, although he could escape, so that he may not abandon Christ’s ministry—without which people cannot become or remain Christians—finds a greater fruit of charity than the person who, not for the sake of his brothers but for his own sake, flees, is captured, does not deny Christ, and accepts martyrdom.

### 5

What, then, is the meaning of what you wrote in your earlier letter? You say:

> If we must remain in the churches, I do not see what benefit we can provide either to ourselves or to the people, except that men may fall before our eyes, women be violated, the churches be burned, and we ourselves perish under torture when they demand from us what we do not possess.

God is indeed powerful enough to hear the prayers of his household and avert these things that are feared. Nevertheless, because of those uncertain events, there ought not to be a certain abandonment of our ministry, without which certain destruction awaits the people—not in the affairs of this life, but in that other life, which must be cared for with incomparably greater diligence and concern.

For if these evils that are feared were certain to occur in the places where we are, then all those for whose sake it is necessary to remain would first flee from there and free us from the necessity of remaining. No one would say that ministers ought to remain where there are no longer any people who need to be ministered to.

Thus certain holy bishops fled from Spain, after their peoples had partly escaped by flight, partly been killed, partly been consumed by siege, and partly been scattered into captivity. But many more remained under the same density of dangers, because those for whose sake they should remain were remaining. If some abandoned their peoples, that is precisely what we say must not happen. Such men were not taught this by divine authority; rather, they were overcome either by human error or by fear.

### 6

Why do they think that the command must be obeyed without distinction wherever they read that one should flee from city to city, while they do not shrink from being hirelings—those who see the wolf coming and flee because they have no concern for the sheep (John 10:12–13)?

Why do they not strive to understand these two dominical and true sayings—the one in which flight is permitted or commanded, and the other in which it is reproved and condemned—in such a way that they are found not to contradict one another, as indeed they do not?

How can this be discovered except by considering what I have already discussed above: that Christ’s ministers are to flee from the places where they are under the pressure of persecution when either Christ’s people are not there to be ministered to, or they are there but the necessary ministry can be fulfilled by others who do not have the same reason for fleeing?

Thus the Apostle fled when he was lowered in a basket, as I mentioned above, because he himself was specifically sought by the persecutor, while the others there plainly did not share the same necessity, and the Church’s ministry was not to be abandoned by them. So too the holy Athanasius [Col. 1016], bishop of Alexandria, fled when the emperor Constantius specifically desired to seize him, while the Catholic people remaining in Alexandria were by no means abandoned by the other ministers.

But when the people remain and the ministers flee, and the ministry is withdrawn, what will this be except the damnable flight of hirelings, who have no concern for the sheep? For the wolf will come—not a human being but the devil, who has often persuaded the faithful to become apostates when the daily ministry of the Lord’s body was lacking; and the weak brother will perish through your not knowing—not through your knowledge—for whom Christ died (1 Corinthians 8:11).

### 7

As for those who are not deceived by error in this matter but overcome by fear, why do they not rather, with the Lord’s mercy and help, fight bravely against their fear, lest evils incomparably more serious—and therefore much more dreadful—befall them?

This happens where the love of God burns, not where desire for the world smokes. For charity says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not on fire?” (2 Corinthians 11:29). But charity is from God. Let us therefore pray that it may be given by him who commands it.

Through this charity, let us fear more that the sheep of Christ may be slaughtered in their hearts by the sword of spiritual wickedness than that they may be slaughtered in their bodies by iron, since they must eventually die, at some time and by some kind of death. Let us fear more that, when their inner understanding has been corrupted, the chastity of faith may perish than that women may be violently violated in the flesh; for violence does not violate modesty if it is preserved in the mind. Indeed, modesty is not violated even in the flesh when the will of the sufferer does not use its own flesh shamefully, but without consent endures what another does.

Let us fear more that the living stones may be extinguished because we abandon them than that the stones and timbers of earthly buildings may be burned while we are present. Let us fear more that the members of Christ’s body, deprived of spiritual nourishment, may perish than that the members of our own bodies may be tortured beneath the assault of the enemy.

This is not because such things are not to be avoided when they can be avoided, but because they must rather be endured when they cannot be avoided without impiety—unless someone should maintain that a minister is not impious when he withdraws the ministry necessary for piety precisely when it is most necessary.

### 8

Do we not consider what usually happens when these dangers reach their extreme and there is no power at all to flee? People of both sexes and every age stream together into the Church. Some demand baptism, others reconciliation, others even the performance of penance; all seek consolation and the preparation and distribution of the sacraments.

If ministers are absent, what destruction follows for those who depart this world either unregenerated or bound! What grief also comes to their faithful people, who will not have them with them in the rest of eternal life! And finally, what groaning from everyone, and what blasphemy from some, because of the absence of ministers and their ministries!

See what fear of temporal evils does, and how great an acquisition of eternal evils there is in it. But if ministers are present, then, according to the strength that the Lord supplies them, [Col. 1017] everyone receives help: some are baptized, others reconciled, no one is deprived of communion in the Lord’s body, all are consoled, built up, and exhorted to pray to God, who is powerful to avert all that is feared. They are prepared for either outcome, so that, if this cup cannot pass from them, the will of him who cannot will anything evil may be done (Matthew 26:42).

### 9

Surely you now see what you wrote that you did not see: how much good the Christian peoples receive if, amid their present evils, the presence of Christ’s ministers is not lacking. You also see how greatly their absence harms them, while the ministers seek their own interests and not those of Jesus Christ (Philippians 2:21), lacking the disposition of which it is said, “It does not seek its own” (1 Corinthians 13:5), and not imitating the one who said, “not seeking what is useful to me, but what is useful to many, that they may be saved” (1 Corinthians 10:33).

He too would not have fled the plots of that persecuting ruler if he had not wished to preserve himself for others who needed him. Therefore he says: “I am hard pressed between the two: my desire is to depart and be with Christ, which is far better; but to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake” (Philippians 1:23).

### 10

Someone may perhaps say that God’s ministers ought to flee when such evils threaten in order to preserve themselves for the Church’s benefit during more peaceful times.

This is rightly done by some when there are others through whom the ecclesiastical ministry can be supplied, so that the Church is not abandoned by everyone. We have already said that Athanasius did this. For how necessary he was to the Church, and how beneficial it was that that man remained in the flesh, is known by the Catholic faith, which was defended against the Arian heretics by his mouth and his love.

But when the danger is common to all, and it is more to be feared that someone may be thought to do this not out of a desire to provide counsel but from fear of dying, and that his example of fleeing may do more harm than his ministry of living does good, then it must be done for no reason at all.

Finally, the holy David, so that he would not expose himself to the dangers of battle and perhaps be extinguished—as the “lamp of Israel” was said to be there (2 Samuel 11:17)—accepted this request from his men; he did not presume to do it himself. Otherwise he would have created many imitators of cowardice, who would have thought that he had done this not from consideration for the usefulness of others but from the disturbance of his own fear.

### 11

Another question arises, which we must not neglect. If this benefit is not to be disregarded—namely, that some ministers should flee when some devastation threatens so that they may be preserved to minister to those whom they might later find surviving the disaster—what will happen when everyone seems destined to perish unless some flee?

What if that calamity rages so far that it pursues only the ministers of the Church? What shall we say? Should the Church be abandoned by ministers who flee, so that it is not abandoned even more miserably by those who die?

But if the laity are not being sought for death, they can somehow conceal their bishops and clergy, with the help of him in whose power all things are and who can preserve by his wondrous power even one who does not flee. Yet we ask what we ought to do precisely so that, by waiting for divine miracles in every circumstance, we may not be judged to be tempting the Lord.

[Col. 1018] This storm is not, in fact, of such a kind that the danger is common to laity and clergy, just as in one ship the danger is common to merchants and sailors. But far be it from us to value this ship of ours so little that the sailors, and especially the pilot, ought to abandon it when it is in danger, even if they could escape by leaping into a small boat or even by swimming.

For those whose destruction we fear through our abandonment, we fear not temporal death, which will come at some time, but eternal death, which can come if it is not guarded against and can also, if it is guarded against, fail to come.

But in a common danger to this present life, why should we suppose that, wherever there is an enemy invasion, all the clergy—but not also all the laity—will die, so that they will all end this life at the same time, even though the clergy are necessary to them? Or why should we not hope that, just as some of the laity remain, some of the clergy will also remain, through whom the necessary ministry may be provided to them?

### 12

Indeed, if only there could be a dispute among God’s ministers about which of them should remain, so that the Church would not be abandoned by everyone fleeing, and which of them should flee, so that it would not be abandoned by everyone dying! Such a contest would take place among them when both sides were burning with charity and both sides were pleasing to charity.

If this dispute could not otherwise be settled, then, as it seems to me, lots should determine who should remain and who should flee. Those who said that they ought rather to flee would either appear cowardly, because they were unwilling to endure the impending evil, or arrogant, because they judged themselves more necessary to the Church than those who were to be preserved.

Furthermore, perhaps those who are better would choose to lay down their lives for their brothers, while those whose lives were less useful because they possessed less ability to give counsel and govern would be preserved by fleeing. Yet, if these latter are piously wise, they will contradict those whom they see ought rather to live and prefer to die rather than flee.

Therefore, as it is written, “The lot puts an end to disputes and decides between the powerful” (Proverbs 18:18). For in such perplexities God judges better than human beings, whether he deigns to call the better men to the fruit of suffering and spare the weak, or to make these latter stronger for enduring evils and remove from this life those whose lives cannot benefit God’s Church as much as the lives of the former.

The practice would be less usual if such a lot were cast; but if it were done, who would dare to criticize it? Who, unless inexperienced or envious, would not praise it with appropriate commendation?

If it is not pleasing to do what has no precedent, let no one’s flight cause the Church’s ministry—especially a ministry so necessary and obligatory amid such great dangers—to be lacking. Let no one exempt his own person [Note: Ten manuscripts read *accipiat*, “let no one accept his own person.”], saying that because he seems to excel in some grace, he is therefore more worthy to live and, for that reason, to flee. Whoever thinks this is excessively pleased with himself; whoever even says it displeases everyone.

### 13

[Col. 1019] There are certainly some who think that bishops and clergy who do not flee in such dangers, but remain, cause the peoples to be deceived, since the people do not flee precisely because they see their superiors remaining.

But it is easy to avoid this objection, or the accusation of envy, by addressing those same peoples and saying:

> Do not let the fact that we are not fleeing from this place deceive you. We are remaining here not for our own sake but rather for yours, so that we may not fail to minister to you whatever we know to be necessary for your salvation, which is in Christ. If, therefore, you wish to flee, you have released us from these bonds by which we are bound.

I think this should be said when it truly seems useful to migrate to safer places. When they hear this, if either all or some say, “We are in the power of him whose anger no one escapes wherever he goes, and whose mercy can be found wherever he is by one who wishes to go nowhere—whether prevented by definite necessities or unwilling to undertake uncertain refuges, thereby not ending but merely changing the dangers,” then without doubt such people must not be abandoned in their Christian ministry.

But if, after hearing this, they prefer to leave, then those who remained for their sake ought not to remain either, because the people for whose sake they should still remain are no longer there.

### 14

Therefore, whoever flees in such a way that the ministry necessary to the Church is not lacking while he flees does what the Lord commanded or permitted. But whoever flees in such a way that the flock of Christ is deprived of the nourishment by which it lives spiritually is that hireling who sees the wolf coming and flees because he has no concern for the sheep.

Because you consulted me, dearest brother, I have written these things to you with the truth and certain charity that I judged appropriate. But I have not prescribed that you must not follow a better opinion if you find one.

Nevertheless, we cannot find anything better to do in these dangers than to offer prayers to the Lord our God, that he may have mercy on us. By God’s gift, some prudent and holy men have deserved both to will and to do precisely this—that they should not abandon God’s churches—and they did not in the least depart from their purpose amid the teeth of their detractors.

## LETTER CCXXIX

[Note: [Col. 1019] Letters CCXXIX and CCXXX have been revised against the Vatican manuscript and the Louvain edition.]

[Note: [Col. 1019] Formerly 262; the letter that was 229 is now 113. Written near the end of Augustine’s life, perhaps in 429.]

Augustine congratulates the count Darius, who has been sent to negotiate peace, and invites him to write in reply.

To the deservedly illustrious and most magnificent, and in Christ most beloved son, DARIUS [Note: [Col. 1019] We do not know whether this is the same Darius who held the office of praetorian prefect in 346], AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

### 1

From my holy brothers and fellow bishops Urbanus and Novatus I learned what kind of man you are and how great a man you are. One of them came to know you at Carthage, in the town of Hilaris, and more recently at Sicca; the other came to know you at Sitifis.

Through them, therefore, it happened that I could not remain entirely unacquainted with you. For although bodily weakness and an innate chill—that is, the condition of my age—do not permit me to converse with you face to face, it does not follow that I have not seen you.

When one of them deigned to come to me, he was present to me; the other, through his letters, showed me not the face of your flesh but that of your heart, so that I might see you more sweetly because I saw you more inwardly.

[Col. 1020] You yourself, by God’s favor, look upon this face of yours with the greatest joy both in the holy Gospel and in us, as in a mirror, where it is written by the Truth who says: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:9).

### 2

Great indeed are those who possess their own glory—not only the bravest but also, which is a truer kind of praise, the most faithful warriors. Through their labors and dangers, with the aid and protection of God, the unconquered enemy is defeated and rest is secured for the state and peace for the provinces.

But it is a greater glory to destroy wars by speech itself rather than human beings by the sword, and to acquire or preserve peace through peace rather than through war. For those who fight, if they are good men, undoubtedly seek peace, but they seek it through blood. You, however, were sent so that no one’s blood would be sought. Thus the former have that necessity, while you have this good fortune.

Therefore, deservedly illustrious and most magnificent lord, and in Christ most beloved son, rejoice in this great and truly good achievement of yours, and enjoy in God the source from which you received the qualities that made you such a man and led you to undertake such tasks.

May God strengthen what he has accomplished for us through you (Psalm 67:29). Receive this greeting of ours and deign to return yours. As Brother Novatus wrote to me, he arranged that your excellence and learning should become acquainted with me through my little works as well. If, therefore, you have read what he gave you, I too have become known to your inmost understanding.

I do not think they displease you greatly, provided that you have read them with a more generous affection than severity. It is not much, but it would be very welcome, if, in return for our writings, both these and those, you were to send us a single letter.

I also greet Verimodus, the pledge of peace [Note: Verimodus, the son of Darius], whom, with the help of the Lord our God, you have happily received, with the affection that I owe.

## LETTER CCXXX

[Note: Formerly 263; the letter that was 230 is now 115. Written after the preceding letters.]

Darius to Augustine, returning thanks for the letter he received from him, asking that the books of the *Confessions* be sent to him, and desiring to be commended to God through Augustine’s prayers.

DARIUS sends greetings to his lord Augustine.

### 1

Would that, holy father and lord, just as my name was carried to your ears through the gracious goodwill toward me of your fellow bishops, as you call them, Urbanus and Novatus, so the God of all things—your God—had presented me in person to your hands and eyes!

I do not mean that he would have shown me to be greater, or perhaps as great as, the benevolent conversation and mention in their letters of such important men had represented me to you, or that he would have proved me better under the refining judgment of your scrutiny. Rather, I wish that I might have received the truest and immortal fruits of your heavenly wisdom from your own mouth, like the sweetness of pure water from the very presence and perpetual flow of its spring.

How blessed I would have been—not merely three or four times, as is said of someone I do not know, but a thousand times and beyond every number—if I had been granted to look upon your truly starry countenance in person, and to hear your divine voice singing divine things, and to receive and drink in not only the fruits of your mind but also the delight of your ears!

I would surely have thought that I was receiving certain laws of immortality, not merely from heaven, but as one established in heaven itself, and hearing certain words of God not far from the temple but near the very tribunal where God stood.

### 2

[Col. 1021] Perhaps I deserved that this should happen to me because of my ardent desire for you; because of my conscience, I confess, I did not deserve it. Yet, even in your absence, I received no small fruits of a good desire, and I possess, among secondary goods, the supreme perfection of good things.

I have been commended to the one to whom I would wish to be commended, by the mouths of holy priests in two places and regions distant from one another. The benevolent speech about me of the one whom I have already mentioned, and his present, so to speak, testimony, have converged with the other’s written words, flying to you with the same meaning and an equal judgment.

Such great and worthy men have woven for me before you a kind of crown—not with the growth of blooming flowers but with the testimony of glorious speech, as with certain jewels of perpetuity.

For this reason I pray to the supreme God on your behalf, and I earnestly request your intercession, holy father, so that, since I am by no means conscious of possessing such a great testimony, I may at some time become such a man.

Have not all those losses of my absence already been overcome by the fact that you deign to speak to us, write to us, and greet us, and that, although I am absent, you do not allow me to be absent?

I grieved that, after God, I had [lacuna] not been seen. Yet you attend not to the face of my flesh—for thus you say—but to what is greater, the face of my heart. Thus I seemed more pleasing to you the more deeply you looked within me.

May God grant that I may correspond to your judgment, my father, and that I may not be guilty before my own conscience when, inwardly, I do not see myself as the person whom you yourself have portrayed.

### 3

In that same divine and heavenly letter of yours, with eloquence—as is your custom—serving you in praising what you wished to praise, you say that I, I repeat, destroy wars by speech.

At this point, holy father, my spirit seemed to emerge from certain shadows of thought, as though it had recognized the genuine praises of itself. To confess the whole matter briefly and simply to Your Beatitude: if we have not extinguished the wars, at least we have postponed them; and, with the help of God, the ruler of all, the evils that had already grown to a certain summit of calamity have been lulled to rest.

Nevertheless, I hope from him—from whom we must hope for everything good—and I even augur from your letter a blessing so abundant and so assured that this very postponement of the wars of which I have spoken may possess and retain the lasting and perpetual stability of peace.

For you said, and fixed it by the perpetual law of God, that I should rejoice in this, as you call it, my great and truly good achievement, and enjoy in God the source from which you say I received the qualities that made me such a man and led me to undertake such tasks.

Then you add: “May God,” you say, “strengthen what he has accomplished for us through you.”

O prayers pronounced not only for me but for the salvation of all! For my glory cannot be separated from the salvation of all; and if I am to be made happy by your prayers, it is necessary that all be happy together with me.

For a long time, father, may you offer and pronounce such prayers for the Roman Empire, for the Roman state, and also for those whom you may encounter as worthy of them. Whenever you raise yourself to heaven, hand them on to posterity and entrust them to those who come after.

### 4

[Col. 1022] Perhaps I have gone on farther than I ought, but certainly I have spoken less than I wished. I confess that, when I write to you, I imagine your faces as though you were present; and although once my unpolished and impoverished speech fails me, still, as though I were conversing and chatting with you face to face, I am not satisfied.

From this, too, measure the longing that we have for you. Since the letter’s page perhaps deserved to come to an end long ago, its tedious verbosity, we put aside modesty while attending to desire, and suspect that to leave off speaking is to withdraw from you.

Therefore I do not wish to continue—but I cannot stop. For if you believe that you have become so fixed in our senses and our hearts that, not content with your very glorious and very great reputation, we preferred to behold you in your writings, consider that this one short letter of yours has stirred up in me such flames and conflagrations of ardor.

Therefore we entreat you and ask with our whole mind that, since by reading you we have despised pagan rites more abundantly and fully than ever before—for although we received the rights of Christ from our parents, grandparents, and all the way down through the final offspring of our race, nevertheless the proud vanity of superfluous superstition sometimes wandered through our minds—you deign also to send and give us the books of the *Confessions* that you composed.

If others too, with willing hearts and benevolent minds, have generously given us your writings, how much more ought you yourself not to withhold from us what is yours?

### 5

There is said to be a letter of some satrap, or rather of a certain king [Note: The letter of King Abgar to Christ, about which Eusebius speaks in book 1, chapter 13], imploring the Lord Christ, while he was still living in the regions of Judaea and had not yet returned to his heaven. Since illness prevented the king from going to him and he did not believe that he could be healed in any other way, he asked that the salvation and healing of the world might come to him, if Christ deigned to do so.

And lest he seem to offer an insult to such majesty—majesty that the ignorant king had conceived with a prudent though imperfect understanding—he is also said to have praised his own city, so that God, attracted by the city’s beauty and the king’s hospitality, might not disdain the prayers of his suppliant.

God was present to the king, and he was healed. And, enlarging the gift of his petition, Christ sent him by letter not only health as to a suppliant but also security as to a king; moreover, he commanded that his city should forever and always be free from enemies.

What can be added to such benefits? I, a humble man and servant of kings, ask you, my lord, not to delay interceding for me every day with that Christ and God the Prince for my sins; pray tirelessly for me and ask for me whatever you yourself wish.

### 6

If my long letter is tedious to you, moderate that feeling through the patience of your greatness, and blame yourself for it, since you yourself commanded me to write.

Yet we pray and repeatedly entreat you to write again; for then we shall be able to suppose that you have willingly received my writings.

May God grant us Your Beatitude for many years, praying for us, truly holy father and lord.

Our son Verimodus greets Your Beatitude. He was exceedingly pleased that, in your letter to us, you deigned to mention him.

We have given to the holy priest Lazapus certain medicines received from the chief physician who is with us, to be brought to Your Beatitude. As that physician affirms, they will be of no small benefit for relieving pain and curing the illness.

## LETTER CCXXXI

[Note: [Col. 1022] Formerly 264; the letter that was 231 is now 116. Written after the two preceding letters.]

[Col. 1023] Augustine to Darius, declaring how exceedingly delighted he was with Darius’s letter and why; incidentally saying much about the love of human praise; and sending him the books of the *Confessions* and certain other little works of his.

AUGUSTINE, servant of Christ and of the members of Christ, to DARIUS, a son and member of Christ, sends greetings in Christ.

1. You wished my reply to be evidence that I had gladly received your letter. Behold, I am replying; yet by this reply I cannot convey what I mean—not by this one, nor by any other, whether I write briefly or at greatest length. For what cannot be conveyed in words cannot be conveyed by either a few words or many. And I, for my part, speak with little eloquence, even if I speak at length; but I would not concede to any eloquent man at all that, in a letter of whatever kind or length, he could explain the affection which your letter produced in your mind, though I myself cannot, even if he could see it in my heart as I do. It remains, then, for me to indicate to you what you wished to know in such a way that, in my words, you may sense even what they do not express. What, then, shall I say except that your letter delighted me—delighted me greatly?
