The repetition of this word is not really repetition, but almost a continuous utterance: since it could not be said always, it was made at least to be repeated; perhaps that is how it can be expressed.

2. If someone should ask what, ultimately, delighted me so greatly in your letter, was it its eloquence? I shall answer, No. And he might perhaps reply, “Then your praises?” But to this also I shall answer, No—not because these things are absent from that letter. For its eloquence is such that it makes it brilliantly evident that you were born with an excellent talent and sufficiently instructed in such disciplines; and it is altogether full of my praises. “Then,” someone may say, “do these things not delight you?” Indeed they do. For, as someone says, I do not have a hornlike fiber—“a heart of horn” (Persius, *Satire* 1)—so as not to feel these things, or to feel them without delight. These things do delight me; but compared with that which, as I said, delighted me greatly, what are they? Your eloquence delights me because it is solemnly sweet, or sweetly solemn; and as for my praises, although I certainly am delighted neither by every kind of praise nor by everyone, I cannot deny that I was delighted by the praises in your letter, since you judged me worthy of such praise and you are the kind of person who loves Christ’s servants for Christ’s sake.

3. Let serious and learned men judge what they think about that Themistocles—if, indeed, I remember the man’s name correctly—who, when at a banquet he refused to sing to the lyre, as the distinguished and educated men of Greece were accustomed to do, and was therefore considered less learned and rejected that entire kind of pleasure, was asked: “What, then, do you enjoy hearing?” He is said to have replied: “My praises.” Let them judge for what purpose and with what intention they believe he said this, or what his own intention was in saying it. For according to the standards of this world he was a magnificent man. Indeed, when he was asked, “What, then, do you know?” he replied, “How to make a small state great.”

But what Ennius says—“All mortals desire to be praised”—I consider partly worthy of approval and partly something to be guarded against. Just as truth is to be desired—truth which undoubtedly exists and is praiseworthy even if it is not praised—so vanity, which easily steals in through human praise, must be avoided. This occurs either when the very good things that deserve praise are not thought worth possessing unless a person is praised by others, or when someone wishes to be greatly praised even for things that deserve little praise or even blame. Hence Horace, more watchful than Ennius, says:

> Are you swollen with love of praise? There are certain expiations  
> That, after thrice reading the little book, can restore you.  
> (*Horace, Book 1, Letter 1*)

4. Thus he thought that the swelling caused by love of human praise—even if it had bitten deeply into him—should be charmed away, as it were, by medicinal words. The good Teacher therefore taught us through his Apostle that we should not do what is right for the sake of being praised by human beings—that is, we should not place the goal of our righteousness in human praise—and yet that, for the sake of those very people, we should seek human praise. For when the good are praised, the benefit goes not to those who are praised but to those who praise them. As far as the good themselves are concerned, the fact that they are good is enough; but those who benefit from imitating the good should rejoice when the good are praised by them, since in this way they show that those whom they praise sincerely please them.

The Apostle therefore says in one place: “If I were pleasing human beings, I would not be Christ’s servant” (Galatians 1:10). And in another place he says: “Please everyone in everything, just as I also please everyone in everything,” adding the reason: “not seeking my own advantage, but that of the many, so that they may be saved” (1 Corinthians 10:32–33). See what he sought in human praise when he also said:

> Finally, brothers, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is chaste, whatever is holy, whatever is most dear, whatever is of good repute—if there is any virtue, if there is any praise—think about these things. What you have learned and received and heard and seen in me, do these things; and the God of peace will be with you (Philippians 4:8–9).

Thus he embraced the other things mentioned above under the name of virtue, saying, “if there is any virtue”; but what he added—“whatever is of good repute”—he expressed in another single, fitting word when he said, “if there is any praise.”

What he says, “If I were pleasing human beings, I would not be Christ’s servant,” must therefore be understood as though he had said: “If I did the good things I do for the sake of human praise, I would be swollen with love of praise.” The Apostle therefore wanted to please everyone and rejoiced that he pleased them—not those whose praises made him swell with pride in himself, but those whom, by being praised, he built up in Christ.

Why, then, should I not be pleased to be praised by you, since you are a good man—unless you deceive me—and praise those things which you love, and which it is useful and salutary to love, even if they are not in me? This is beneficial not only to you but also to me. For if these things are not in me, I am salutarily ashamed and burn with desire that they may be in me. And when I recognize in your praise what is mine, I rejoice that I possess it and that both it and I myself are loved by you on account of it. As for what I do not recognize in myself, I desire not only to attain it so that I may possess it myself, but also that those who sincerely love me may not always be deceived when they praise me.

5. See how much I have said, and yet I have not said what it was that delighted me in your letter far more than your eloquence and far more than my praises. What do you think it was, good man, except that I made a friend of you—a man of such character, though unseen? If I ought to say “unseen,” whose body I had not seen, yet I saw his soul in your very letter, where I came to believe concerning you, not as previously on the testimony of my brothers, but for myself. For I had already learned who you were, but I had not yet grasped what sort of person you were toward me.

I have no doubt that, through this friendship of yours, even my praises—which I have sufficiently explained in what sense they delight me—will be of much greater benefit to the Church of Christ. For you receive, read, love, and proclaim my labors in defense of the Gospel against the remnants of the impious worshipers of demons in such a way that I become better known in proportion as you yourself are more distinguished. You make them illustrious though they are hidden, and make them known though you yourself are renowned; and wherever you see that they can be useful, you do not allow them to remain wholly unknown.

If you ask how I know this, you appeared to me as such a person in your letter. From this you can now see how much that letter could delight me. If you think well of me, consider how much the gains of Christ must delight me.

And now, when you yourself—who, as you write, were able to receive the rights of Christ from your parents, grandparents, and ultimately through the final descendants of your family—indicate that you have nevertheless been assisted by these same labors of mine against pagan rites as never before, do I not consider how much good our writings, commended and disseminated by you, can easily and profitably bring to others, and to many others—distinguished people and people for whom such things are appropriate? And, thinking of this, could I fail to be flooded with the joy of great, rather than small or moderate, happiness?

6. Since, then, I could not express in words how much pleasure I derived from your letter, I have explained what it was in the letter that delighted me. As for what I have been unable adequately to say—that is, how greatly it delighted me—I leave you to infer.

So take them, my son; take them, good man—not superficially, but in Christian love, as a Christian. Take, I say, the books of my *Confessions* that you desired. There examine me, so that you do not praise me beyond what I am. There do not believe others about me, but believe me. There attend to me and see what I was in myself and through myself. And if anything in me pleases you, praise with me there the one whom I wished to be praised concerning me—not me. For “he himself made us, and not we ourselves” (Psalm 99:3); but we had destroyed ourselves, and the one who made us remade us.

When you have found me there, pray for me, so that I may not fail but be perfected. Pray, my son; pray. I know what I am saying; I know what I am asking. Do not think it beneath you, as though it were beyond your merits. You will deprive me of great assistance if you do not do this.

Not only you, but also all who, through your mouth, have come to love me: pray for me. Tell them that I have asked this of them. And if you attribute much to us, consider that we have commanded what we ask; nevertheless, give to those who ask, or obey those who command. Pray for us.

Read the divine Scriptures, and you will find that our own rams—the Apostles—asked this of their children, or commanded it of those who heard them. Certainly, since you asked this of me for your sake, the one who hears sees how much I do for you; he saw that I was already doing it before. But in this also return the favor of love.

We are your superiors; you are God’s flock. Consider and see that our dangers are greater than yours, and pray for us. For it is fitting both for us and for you that we should render a good account of you to the chief Shepherd and Head of us all, and that together we should escape the more dangerous allurements of this world rather than its troubles—unless its peace contributes to that for which the Apostle instructed us to pray: that “we may lead a quiet and tranquil life in all piety and love” (1 Timothy 2:2).

For if piety and love are absent, what is tranquility and repose amid these and the other evils of the world except material for luxury and destruction—whether as an invitation or as an aid? Therefore, that we may lead a quiet and tranquil life in all piety and love, pray for us—for what we do for you—wherever you are. Wherever we are, there is no place where he is not, whose we are.

7. I also sent other books that you did not request, so that I would not do only what you asked: *On Faith in Things Unseen*, *On Patience*, *On Continence*, *On Providence*, and one large work *On Faith, Hope, and Charity*. If you read all these while you are still in Africa, send us your judgment of them—or send it to us, or leave it there so that it may be sent to us through our lord brother Aurelius. Indeed, wherever you may be, we hope for your letters from there, and from here, as long as we are able, for ours.

I received with the greatest gratitude what you sent: through it you were pleased to assist both my health, though bodily—for you wish me to devote myself to God without the hindrance of ill health—and our library, so that we may have the means either to acquire or to restore books. May the Lord repay you, both in this age and in the age to come, with the good things he has prepared for people such as he wished you to be.

I ask that the pledge of peace deposited with you, and so exceedingly dear to both of us, be greeted by you now in return, just as previously I greeted it.

## FOURTH CLASS

Letters written by Saint Augustine the bishop, whose dates are less certainly known.

[Col. 1025]

## LETTER 232

[Note: [Col. 1025] Corrected according to a, bg, bl, bn, c, cc, ff, g, gv, n, r, s, sb, t, vc, four copies of v, and the editions Am., Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 1025] Formerly 42; the letter that was 232 is now 253.]

He exhorts the idolatrous people of Madaura to the true religion, instilling fear by announcing the final judgment, which he persuades them will come—especially since all the other things foretold in Scripture concerning the Christian religion have already occurred. Finally, he touches briefly upon the mystery of the Trinity and the Incarnation.

[Col. 1025]

[Col. 1026] To the honorable lords and most beloved brothers, the people of MADAURA, whose letter I received through our brother Florentinus, AUGUSTINE.

1. If those among you who are Catholic Christians sent me such a letter, I am surprised only that they did not send it in their own name rather than in the name of their order. But if it is truly all, or nearly all, the men of your order who were pleased to write to me, I am surprised that you wrote to “the father” and “eternal salvation in the Lord,” when your superstitious worship of idols is notorious to me with great sorrow. Against these idols your temples are closed more readily than your hearts—or rather, those idols are enclosed no more in your temples than in your hearts—unless perhaps you have at last begun, with prudent reflection, to think about the salvation itself that is in the Lord, through whom you wished to greet me.

For if this is not so, I ask you: what have I injured, what have I offended in your goodwill, that you thought I should be mocked rather than honored by the title of your letter, honorable lords and most beloved brothers?

2. When I read what you had written—“To Father Augustine, eternal salvation in the Lord”—I was suddenly raised up by such hope that I believed you had either already been converted to the Lord himself and to that eternal salvation, or desired to be converted through our ministry. But when I read the rest, my spirit grew cold. Nevertheless, I asked the bearer of the letter whether you were already Christians or wished to become Christians. When I learned from his reply that you had not changed at all, I grieved more deeply that you had thought the name of Christ—which you see has already subjected the whole world—not only to be rejected by you but also mocked in us.

For I could not imagine another Lord according to whom you might call a bishop “father,” apart from the Lord Christ. And if there could be any doubt about the meaning of your words, your signature would remove it, since you openly wrote: “We wish you, lord, in God and in his Christ, to rejoice for many years always in your clergy.”

After reading and examining all this, what else could occur to me—or to anyone—except that these words were written either with a truthful or with a deceitful intention on the part of those who wrote them?

But if you write these things with a truthful intention, who has blocked your path to this truth? Who has placed rough thickets beneath your feet? Who, as an enemy, has set precipitous cliffs in your way? Finally, who has closed the door of the basilica to those wishing to enter, so that you do not wish to have with us the same salvation in the same Lord through whom you greet us?

But if you write these things deceitfully and mockingly, are you really imposing your affairs upon me to manage, so that you dare not raise the name of the one through whom I can do anything with the reverence due to him, but instead toss it about with flattering insult?

3. Know, my dearest brothers, that I say these things with an indescribable trembling of heart on your behalf. For I know how much graver and more dangerous a case you will have before God if I have said these things to you in vain.

Everything that our ancestors remember having happened in former times concerning the human race and handed down to us, and everything that we ourselves see and hand down to posterity—so far as these things pertain to seeking and holding the true religion—divine Scripture has not kept silent about. Rather, all things pass away exactly as they were foretold to pass away.

You certainly see the Jewish people torn away from their settlements and scattered and dispersed throughout almost all lands. The origin of that people, its growth, the loss of its kingdom, and its dispersal everywhere have occurred just as they were foretold.

You certainly see the word of God and the law proceeding from that very people through Christ, who was wondrously born from them, and taking possession of and preserving the faith of all nations. We read all these things as having been foretold in such a way that we see them fulfilled.

You certainly see many who have been cut off from the root of the Christian fellowship, which is spread throughout the world by the established propagation of the Apostolic Sees and the succession of bishops, nevertheless boasting under the Christian name of the mere appearance of their origin, like withering branches. These we call heresies and schisms. All this was foreseen, foretold, and written down.

You certainly see the temples of images partly collapsed beyond restoration, partly demolished, partly closed, and partly converted to other uses. You see the images themselves either broken, burned, enclosed, or destroyed. And you see the very powers of this age—which once persecuted the Christian people on behalf of the images—defeated and subdued, not by Christians who fought back but by Christians who died; you see them turn their assaults and laws against those very images for which they had killed Christians, and the highest summit of the noblest empire, with its diadem lowered, supplicate at the tomb of the fisherman Peter.

4. All these things were attested by the divine Scriptures—which have now come into the hands of everyone—as destined to occur long ages ago. We rejoice that all these things are happening with the stronger faith, the more authoritatively we find them proclaimed in the holy Scriptures.

Shall we, I ask you, shall we suppose that only the judgment of God—which we read in those same Scriptures is to come between the faithful and the unfaithful—will not come, when all those other things have arrived just as they were foretold? Indeed it will come, just as all those things have come.

Nor will any person of our times be able to defend himself in that judgment on the grounds of his unbelief, when the just man sings of Christ for righteousness, the perjurer for fraud, the king for rule, the soldier for battle, the husband for governance, the wife for obedience, the father for command, the son for submission, the master for mastery, the servant for service, the humble for piety, the proud for rivalry, the rich so that he may give, the poor so that he may receive, the drunkard for the cup, the beggar for the door, the good so that he may benefit, and the wicked so that he may deceive.

The Christian sings of Christ in worship, the pagan in flattery. All sing of Christ, and they will undoubtedly render an account to the very one whom they sing of concerning the intention and the mouth with which they sing.

5. There is something invisible from which, as from the Creator and first principle, all the things we see have come: supreme, eternal, unchangeable, and ineffable to anyone except itself.

There is something by which the summit of majesty itself declares and proclaims itself, not unequal to the one who begets and declares the Word, by whom the one who begets the Word is shown.

There is a certain holiness—the sanctifier of all things that become holy—an inseparable and undivided communion of the unchangeable Word itself, through which that first principle is declared, and of that first principle which declares itself through an equal Word.

Who, then, could contemplate this whole reality—which I have attempted to speak by not speaking and not to speak by speaking—with a mind utterly serene and sincere, and derive blessedness from that contemplation, and, in a certain way, forget himself as he is absorbed into what he contemplates, and proceed into that whose vision is invisible to us [Note: [Col. 1029] Bad., Am., and Er.: “by whose vision it is invisible.” Five manuscripts: “by whose vision it is visible.”]—that is, to be clothed with immortality and obtain eternal salvation, through which you deign to greet me?

Who could do this except one who, confessing his sins, has flattened all the empty swellings of his pride and made himself submissive, gentle, and humble, ready to receive God as his teacher?

6. Since, therefore, we must first be brought down from the vanity of pride to humility, so that, rising from there, we may hold a solid exaltation, this could not have been instilled in us more magnificently and more gently—so that our ferocity might be calmed not by force but by persuasion—unless the Word through whom God the Father reveals himself to the angels, who is his Power and Wisdom, and who could not be seen by the human heart blinded by desire for visible things, had deigned to assume and display his own person in a human being. In this way human beings would fear being exalted through human arrogance more than being humbled by the example of God.

Therefore it is not Christ adorned with an earthly kingdom, nor Christ rich in earthly wealth, nor Christ shining with that earthly happiness, but Christ crucified who is proclaimed throughout the whole world.

What the peoples of the proud once mocked—and whose remnants still mock—the few first believed, and now the peoples believe. For then, when Christ crucified was being proclaimed in opposition to the mockery of the peoples and for the faith of the few, the lame walked, the mute spoke, the deaf heard, the blind saw, and the dead rose again.

Thus earthly pride finally perceived that nothing among earthly things is more powerful than divine humility (1 Corinthians 1:23–25), so that human humility, which is most salutary, might also be defended against the pride that insults it by the protection of imitation of the divine.

7. Wake up at last, my brothers and my parents, people of Madaura [Note: [Col. 1029] Because he studied literature and the art of rhetoric among them, as he says in *Confessions* 2.3, he perhaps calls them “parents.”] God has given me this opportunity to write to you.

As far as I could, in the matter of our brother Florentinus, through whom you sent the letter, I was present and helped as God willed. But it was a matter that could easily have been carried through even without my assistance: nearly all the members of his household who are at Hippo know Florentinus and greatly grieve his bereavement.

But a letter was sent to me by you, so that my letter would not be inappropriate when, on an occasion supplied by you, it addressed the worshipers of idols about Christ. I ask you, therefore: if you did not mention him in that letter without purpose, may I not have written these things to you without purpose.

But if you wished to mock me, fear the one whom the proud world once mocked after he had been judged, and whom it now awaits in submission as judge. For this letter, insofar as I have been able, will bear witness before you to the feeling of my heart toward you; and it will bear witness to you at the judgment of the one who will strengthen those who believe in him and put the unbelieving to shame.

May the one and true God, having freed you from all the vanity of this age, convert you to himself, honorable lords and most beloved brothers.

## LETTER 233

[Note: [Col. 1030] Letters 233 and 234 were reviewed according to a, bg, bl, bn, c, cc, ff, g, gv, j, l, n, r, s, t, two copies of a, two copies of vc, six copies of v, and the editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1030] Formerly 20; the letter that was 233 is now 254.]

Augustine to Longinianus, a pagan philosopher, challenging him to write how he believes God should be worshiped and what he thinks about Christ.

[Col. 1030]

LONGINIANUS, AUGUSTINE.

It is said that one of the ancients used to say that those who were sufficiently convinced that they wished to be nothing other than good men had the rest of their education easily available to them. This opinion—for, if I remember correctly, it is Socratic—had been preceded long before by a prophetic one, which briefly and at once commanded a person not only to prefer being good to being anything else, but also taught how one becomes good:

“You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind” (Deuteronomy 6:5); and, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18).

If someone were convinced of this, the rest of the teaching would not merely be easy for him; rather, all of it would be useful and salutary. For there are many teachings—if they are to be called teachings at all—that are either superfluous or harmful.

Christ, bearing witness to the books of the ancients, says: “On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matthew 22:40).

Accordingly, since I seem to have looked into your conversation with me as into a mirror and to have seen that you prefer being nothing other than a good man, I dare to ask you how you believe God should be worshiped—God than whom nothing is better and from whom the human mind draws what makes it good. For I already understand that you believe he should be worshiped.

I also ask what you think about Christ. I have noticed that you do not regard him as insignificant. But I wish to know whether you think that one can reach the blessed life by that path alone which he demonstrated, and that you neglect to follow it for some reason, postponing it; or whether you think there is another path, or other paths, to such a rich possession, desirable above all others, and believe that you are already entering upon one of them. I think it is not impertinent for me to ask this.

I love you for the reason stated above, and I do not rashly suppose that I am loved by you. Among people who know one another with goodwill, no conversation is either more fruitful, more offered, more requested, more received, or more welcomed than conversation about that by which we become good and blessed.

## LETTER 234

[Note: [Col. 1030] Letters 233 and 234 were reviewed according to a, bg, bl, bn, c, cc, ff, g, gv, j, l, n, r, s, t, two copies of a, two copies of vc, six copies of v, and the editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1030] Formerly 21; the letter that was 234 is now 255.]

Longinianus to Augustine, replying that, according to Trismegistus and the Platonists, one reaches the supreme God through lesser gods, but not without sacred purifications.

To the venerable lord, and truly and deservedly revered holy father Augustine, LONGINIANUS.

1. I am blessed, and greatly illuminated by the shining and pure light of your virtue, since you judged me worthy to be honored by your divine address. But you impose upon me a heavy burden and an exceedingly difficult task of replying, venerable lord, especially through your questions and at such a time, when the matters at issue must be explained according to the judgment of my opinion—that is, by a pagan.

For although the questions may abound in matters on which we have either long ago agreed in part or now agree increasingly through our repeated letters—not merely according to Socratic teachings, nor merely according to yours, you truly excellent Roman, or according to the prophetic teachings of the few Jerusalemites, but also according to Orphic and Agetic teachings, and according to Trismegistus, much more ancient than all of them, born when the ages were still almost primitive, with the gods as their authors, and divinely displayed to the whole world, divided into three regions by fixed boundaries, before Europe had a name, Asia had received one, or Libya possessed one—I have heard and read and seen no one, except perhaps the fictional character composed in Xenophon’s stories. Or, after that one, I have seen no one whom, with God as my witness, I could affirm with certainty and without danger to be good, except you.

For you continually recognize God and strive toward him; you can easily pursue him with purity of mind after casting off the burden of the body; and with the hope of a perfected conscience, you hold to him with unwavering belief.

2. But how this can be accomplished by a path, it is more appropriate that you should know and explain to me—not by some external suggestion planted in me—than that you should learn it from me, revered lord. For then, I confess, as I am about to set out toward the dwelling of this good, I am not yet sufficiently equipped with provisions, as my priesthoods require, although I am collecting provisions for the journey, if I am able.

Nevertheless, I shall explain briefly, as best I can, what I have received and have held and preserved as sacred and ancient teaching.

There is a better way to God: the way by which a good man, approved by pious, pure, just, chaste, and truthful words and deeds, without seeking the empty display of changing times, and surrounded by the company of the gods, having duly served the powers of God—that is, filled with the virtues of that one, universal, incomprehensible, ineffable, and tireless Creator whom you rightly call the Angels—hastens with the intention of heart and mind toward whatever exists after God, or with God, or from God, or toward God.

There is, I say, a way by which those purified through the pious instructions and most pure expiations of ancient rites, and refined through abstinent observances, hasten onward steadfast in soul and body.

3. As for Christ—the God in flesh and spirit of your present faith—through whom you go safely to that supreme, blessed, true Father of all [Note: [Col. 1031] Bad. and Er.: “and the Spirit of God”; Lov.: “and by the gift of the Spirit”; manuscripts: “and spirit God.”], revered father, I neither dare nor am able to express what I think, because I believe it exceedingly difficult to define what I do not know.

But since you once deigned to make known to me, who am a worshiper of your virtues, that you love me, I have sufficient testimony to a good life in the fact that I take care not to displease you, since you daily commend both yourself and your soul to God. You understand, without doubt, that I love you with delight, since I accept and hold the rule and standard of your judgment concerning me.

Before everything else, however, I ask you to grant pardon to my very slight opinion and readily forgive my speech to you—perhaps unrestrained and unsuitable—since you compelled me to speak. And, if I deserve it, deign to instruct me, through your holy writings, which, as that man says, are sweeter not now than honey but than nectar (Ovid, *Tristia* 5.5), concerning what you think about these matters, or what your own view is.

May you enjoy the mercy of God, revered father, and please God by perpetual holiness, as you must.

## LETTER 235

[Note: [Col. 1032] Formerly 22; the letter that was 235 is now 64.]

Augustine to Longinianus, asking him to explain why one who is already surrounded by divine virtues should be thought to require purificatory sacrifices.

[Col. 1032]

LONGINIANUS, AUGUSTINE.

1. I have received the fruit of my letter—namely, the reply of Your Benevolence. From this I now see that a seed has arisen and been sown among us for a great discussion of this great matter. This is what I wanted first, and what I still want; God will help us. My desire is that what has been begun may be brought to its proper and salutary conclusion.

Accordingly, I am not unwilling to accept the restraint you exercised in thinking that nothing concerning Christ should be rashly denied or affirmed by you. Nor shall I refuse, or cease to serve, your desire—so good and so dear to me—to be instructed about this matter by my writings.

But first it is necessary, in a sense, to filter your opinion and make it clear concerning the ancient rites. You said that the better way to God is the way by which a good man, approved by pious, just, pure, chaste, and truthful words and deeds, without seeking the empty display of changing times, and surrounded by the company of the gods, having duly served the powers of God—that is, filled with the virtues of that one, universal, incomprehensible, tireless, and ineffable Creator whom you rightly call the Angels—hastens with the intention of heart and mind toward whatever exists after God, or from God, or with God, or toward God. These words you recognize from your letter.

Then you added and said: “There is, I say, a way by which those purified through the pious instructions of ancient rites and their most pure expiations, and refined through abstinent observances, hasten onward steadfast in soul and body.”

2. In these words, unless I am mistaken, I perceive that you think it is not sufficient for the way by which one goes to God that a good man, through pious, just, pure, chaste, and truthful living, should win the favor of the gods, and, surrounded by their company, hasten toward that supreme God, creator of all things, unless he is also purified through the pious instructions and expiations of the ancient rites.

I would therefore like to know what you think must be purified through sacred rites in someone who, by living piously, justly, purely, and truthfully, wins the favor of the gods, and through them of that one God of gods.

For if he still needs to be purified through sacred rites, he is certainly not clean. And if he is not clean, he does not live piously, justly, purely, and chastely. For if he already lives in this way, he is already clean. And if he is already clean and pure, why does he need to be purified by expiatory rites?

This, then, is the knot of our discussion. When it has been untied, we shall see the consequences:

Is a person to live well in order to be purified by sacred rites? Or is he to be purified by sacred rites in order to live well? Or is whatever degree of good living a person can attain not yet sufficient for the blessed life received from God unless the aids of sacred rites are added? Or is receiving sacred rites itself a kind of portion of good living, so that living well is not one thing and living in a sacred manner another, but a sacred life also falls within the limits of good living?

Of these four alternatives that I have proposed, I ask you not to hesitate to make clear in a letter which one you approve most. For it matters greatly to the task we have undertaken and are completing through our conversation, lest, when I attempt to refute many things that are unnecessary—as though you held opinions that perhaps you do not hold—I should spend necessary time on superfluities.

I therefore did not wish to burden you with a long letter, so that, when you reply soon, we may weave together what remains.

## LETTER 236

[Note: [Col. 1033] Corrected according to bl, cb, ff, gg, r, sb, vc, two copies of t, three copies of v, and the editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1033] Formerly 74; the letter that was 236 is now 65.]

Augustine to Deuterius the bishop. He reports that he removed from the clerical order Victorinus, a subdeacon who had secretly taught the Manichaean heresy after being discovered; he warns that Victorinus should not be received there for penance unless he reveals all those whom he knows to be infected with the same error. He also explains who among the Manichaeans are called “hearers” and who are called “the elect.”

To the most blessed lord and venerably beloved brother and fellow bishop Deuterius, AUGUSTINE, greetings in the Lord.

1. I thought I could do nothing better than write especially to Your Holiness, so that through negligence the enemy of our Lord Jesus Christ might not ravage the Lord’s flock in your province [Note: [Col. 1033] Bad., Am., and Er.: “our province.”]. He never ceases to lie in wait in order to destroy souls purchased at so great a price.

It has become clear among us that a certain Victorinus, a subdeacon of Malliana [Note: [Col. 1033] Four manuscripts: “Victorianus.”], is a Manichaean, and that he was hiding in so sacrilegious an error under the name of a cleric. He is also already advanced in age.

He was exposed in such a way that, when questioned by me before he was convicted by witnesses, he could not deny it. For he already knew that there were so many people of such a kind to whom he had incautiously revealed himself that, if he attempted to deny it, he would appear not merely most shameless but completely mad.

He confessed that he was a “hearer” of the Manichaeans, not one of the elect.

2. The hearers, as they are called among them, eat meat and cultivate fields, and, if they wish, have wives; none of this is done by those who are called the elect. Yet the hearers themselves kneel before the elect so that hands may be laid upon them in supplication [Note: [Col. 1033] Bad., Am., Er., and most manuscripts read *imponatur* (“may be laid upon [them]”).]—not only by their presbyters, bishops, or deacons, but by any of the elect. They also worship and pray with them to the sun and moon [Note: [Col. 1033] Lov. omits “and pray,” which is found in the other editions and in the manuscripts.]. On Sundays likewise they fast with them and believe with them all the blasphemies by which the detestable heresy of the Manichaeans is characterized: namely, they deny that Christ was born of a virgin and do not confess that his flesh was real, but rather false; and consequently they maintain that his passion too was false and that there was no resurrection. They blaspheme the patriarchs and prophets. They say that the Law given through God’s servant Moses came not from the true God but from the prince of darkness. They hold that the souls not only of human beings but also of animals are of God’s substance and are, in every respect, parts of God. Finally, they say that the good and true God fought with the race of darkness, mingled his own part with the rulers of darkness, and that this part, defiled and bound throughout the whole world [Col. 1034], is cleansed through the foods of his elect and through the sun and moon. Whatever of that part of God could not be cleansed, they assert, will at the end of the age be bound in an eternal and punitive bond. Thus God is believed not only to be violable, corruptible, and capable of defilement—since a part of him could be brought into such great evils—but even incapable of being entirely cleansed from such defilement, impurity, and misery at the end of the age.

3. These intolerable blasphemies the subdeacon, as though he were a Catholic, not only believed with them but, to the extent of his ability, taught. For he was exposed while teaching, when he entrusted himself to those who seemed to be learning. After he had confessed that he was a hearer of the Manichaeans, he did indeed ask me to recall him to the way of truth, the Catholic doctrine; but, I confess, I was horrified by his pretense under the appearance of a cleric, and I saw to it that, after being restrained, he was expelled from the city. Nor was this enough for me unless I also informed Your Holiness by letter, so that, suitably removed from the clerical rank by ecclesiastical severity, he might become known to all as someone to be avoided. If he asks for an opportunity for penance, let him then be believed, provided that he also reveals to you the others whom he knows to be there—not only in Malliana but throughout the entire province.

# LETTER CCXXXVII

[Note: [Col. 1034] Sought in vain in the Gallican manuscripts. Corrected according to the Vatican manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 1034] Elsewhere numbered 253; formerly 237, now 56.]

Augustine to Ceretius, concerning the Priscillianists’ fraud in interpreting the Scriptures, both sacred and apocryphal, and concerning the hymn which they pretended had been spoken by Christ and set before the canonical Scriptures.

To the most blessed Lord and deservedly venerable brother and fellow bishop Ceretius, Augustine sends greetings in the Lord.

1. Having read what Your Holiness sent, it seems to me that Argirius attacked the Priscillianists either without knowing what he was doing, so that he had no idea at all whether they themselves were Priscillianists, or else he had already become entangled in the snares of that same heresy. I have no doubt that those writings are Priscillianist. I scarcely managed to find enough leisure, with one necessity after another pressing upon me without interruption, for at least one complete text from the two copies themselves to be read to me. For somehow the other copy had gone astray and, although it was sought for most diligently among our people, could not be found at all, most blessed lord and deservedly venerable father.

2. The hymn which they say belongs to our Lord Jesus Christ, and which especially disturbed Your Veneration, is usually found in apocryphal writings. These are not peculiar to the Priscillianists; other heretics too, through the impious vanity of certain sects, make use of them. They hold different views among themselves, and thus each has followed its own diverse heresy, but they possess these writings in common amid their diversity. Those who do not accept the Old Law and the canonical Prophets especially tend to make frequent use of them. For they deny that these belong to the good God and to Christ his Son—Manichaeans, Marcionists, and others who have approved this damnable blasphemy.

[Col. 1035] Such people do not accept everything even in the canonical Scriptures of the New Testament—that is, in the true evangelical and apostolic writings—but only what they want, choosing the books they accept and rejecting others. They also distinguish, within each individual book, passages that they think accord with their errors; the rest they regard as false. Some Manichaeans, for example, reject the canonical book entitled the Acts of the Apostles. They fear the most manifest truth found there, where the Holy Spirit appears as having been sent—the Spirit promised by the Lord Jesus Christ in the evangelical truth (Acts 2:2–4). Under the name of that Spirit, from whom they are wholly alien, they deceive the ignorant hearts of people, asserting with astonishing blindness that the same promise of the Lord was fulfilled in their heresiarch Manichaeus. The heretics called Cataphryges do the same, saying that, through certain mad people—namely Montanus and Priscilla, whom they also regard as their own prophets—the Holy Spirit whom the Lord promised to send had come.

3. The Priscillianists, however, accept everything, both canonical and apocryphal alike. But whatever is directed against them they twist into the meanings of their perversity—sometimes by a crafty and cunning interpretation, sometimes by a ridiculous and foolish one. Nor do they even interpret them in such a way that they believe the very things they expound to people outside their sect to be true. Otherwise they would either be Catholics or would not be far removed from the truth, since they would find—or would appear to wish to find—Catholic meanings even in the apocryphal writings. But although they hold and teach—or learn among themselves—other doctrines that they do not dare to disclose because they are truly wicked and detestable, they preach the Catholic faith to those whom they fear, not the faith they hold but one under which they may conceal themselves.

Perhaps some heretics can be found who are more impure, but none can equal these in deceitfulness. Others, in keeping with human vices, lie about the conduct or weakness of this life; these, however, are said to have in the very doctrine of their wicked heresy a command that, in order to conceal their teachings, they should lie even with a false oath. Those who have had experience of them, who once belonged to them and were freed from them by God’s mercy, also recall the very words of this command:

> Swear, forswear yourself, do not disclose the secret.

4. Accordingly, so that it may plainly be seen that they do not hold about the apocryphal writings what they pretend to expound, one must consider the reasoning they appear to offer for attributing divine authority to those same writings—and, more wickedly, for placing them even before the canonical writings. You have their words set down in that book as follows:

> “The hymn of the Lord, which he spoke secretly to his holy apostles, his disciples, because it is written in the Gospel, ‘After saying the hymn, he went up onto the mountain’ (Matt. 26:30); and which was not placed in the canon, because of those who think according to themselves and not according to the Spirit and truth of God, since it is written, ‘It is good to conceal the king’s secret, but honorable to reveal the works of God’ (Tob. 12:7).”

This is their great [Col. 1036] reason why the hymn is not in the canon: it had to be hidden, like the king’s secret, from those who think according to the flesh and not according to the Spirit and truth of God. Therefore, the canonical Scriptures do not belong to the king’s secret, which these people think ought to be hidden; rather, they were written for those who think according to the flesh and not according to the Spirit and truth of God. What else is this than saying that the canonical holy Scriptures neither have the understanding of the Spirit of God nor belong to the truth of God? Who could hear this? Who could endure the horror of such great impiety? Or, if the canonical Scriptures are understood spiritually by spiritual people and carnally by carnal people, why is this hymn not also in the canon, if spiritual people understand it spiritually and carnal people carnally?

5. Furthermore, why do these people try to expound this same hymn according to the canonical Scriptures? If it is not in the canonical Scriptures because those Scriptures were written for carnal people, whereas this hymn was written for spiritual people, how can the hymn—which does not belong to carnal people—be expounded from Scriptures that belong to carnal people? If, for example, the words “I wish to loose, and I wish to be loosed” are sung and spoken in this hymn because, as they explain them, the Lord Christ looses us from worldly conduct so that we may not again be bound by it, surely we learned in the canonical Scriptures that the Lord looses us from worldly conduct and that we must not again be bound by it. For what else is meant by, “You have broken my bonds” (Ps. 115:16)? What else by, “The Lord looses those who are shackled” (Ps. 145:7)? And the Apostle admonishes those who have already been loosed, saying, “Stand firm, therefore, and do not again submit to the yoke of slavery” (Gal. 5:1). The apostle Peter likewise says, “If, after escaping the defilements of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, the latter condition has become worse for them than the former” (2 Pet. 2:20), thereby showing that, once loosed, we must not again be bound to the world.

Since these matters are plainly found in the canon—whether in the testimonies I have mentioned or in many others—and since they never cease to be read and preached, why do these people say that this hymn is not in the canon lest its words be veiled from carnal people, when we see that they are instead revealed in the canon, while in this hymn they are entirely veiled, as they themselves assert? Indeed, it is more credible that the words are not these at all, but some other words which, by such an interpretation, they veil much more deeply and fear to reveal.

6. For certainly, if those words signify that the Lord looses us from worldly conduct so that we may not again be bound by it, the hymn would not say, “I wish to loose, and I wish to be loosed,” but, “I wish to loose, and I do not wish those whom I have loosed to be bound.” Or, if he transforms his members—that is, his faithful—into himself, just as he says, “I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matt. 25:35), he should rather have said, “I wish to be loosed, and I do not wish to be bound.” Or, if he himself looses and is himself loosed because the head looses and the members are loosed [Col. 1037]—the members whom Saul was persecuting, to whom Christ cried from heaven, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4)—this interpreter of those words did not say so. But even if he had, we would answer him what we answered shortly before: we read these things in the canonical Scriptures; there we understand them, from there we establish them, and from there we preach them every day.

What, then, is the reason for saying that this hymn was withheld from carnal people and therefore not placed in the canon, when what is covered in it is plainly disclosed in the canon? Have they become so foolish—or rather, so insane—that they dare to say that the king’s secret is hidden in this hymn from spiritual people but is revealed in the canon to carnal people?

7. The same may be said of the preceding words of the hymn, where it says, “I wish to save, and I wish to be saved.” If, as they explain it, these words mean that we are saved by the Lord through Baptism and that we save—that is, preserve within us—the Spirit given to us through Baptism, does not the canonical Scripture proclaim this meaning when we read, “He saved us through the washing of regeneration” (Titus 3:5), and when we are told, “Do not quench the Spirit” (1 Thess. 5:19)?

How, then, is this hymn not in the canon for the reason that it should not become known to carnal people, when what is obscure in it shines in the canon? The only explanation is that, under whatever sort of interpretation they offer to others, they are trying to conceal what they themselves understand here. Yet they are so blind that they even employ certain words from the canon itself to expound the hymn which, they say, is not in the canon lest the king’s secret be disclosed to carnal people. What, then, are they doing with the clearer passages placed in the canon, by which the obscure things in this hymn are opened up?

8. For if, as they say, this is what is to be understood in the hymn where it says, “I wish to be generated,” namely what is written in the canonical Epistle of the apostle Paul, “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. 4:19); if this is what is to be understood in the hymn where it says, “I wish to sing,” namely what is written in the canonical Psalm, “Sing to the Lord a new song” (Ps. 95:1); if this is what is to be understood in the hymn where it says, “Dance, all of you,” namely what is written in the Gospel song, “We sang to you, and you did not dance”; if this is what is to be understood in the hymn, “I wish to mourn; strike your breasts, all of you,” namely what is written in the Gospel song, “We mourned for you, and you did not lament” (Matt. 11:17); if “I wish to adorn, and I wish to be adorned” signifies in this hymn what is written in the canon, “That Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts” (Eph. 3:17), and, “You are God’s temple, and the Spirit of God dwells in you” (1 Cor. 3:16); if what he says in the hymn, “I am a lamp for you, you who see me,” signifies what is written in the canonical Psalm, “In your light we shall see light” (Ps. 35:10); if what he says in the hymn, “I am a door for you, whoever knocks at me,” signifies what is read in the canonical Psalm, “Open for me the gates of righteousness; entering through them, I will confess to the Lord” (Ps. 117:19), and in another Psalm, “Lift up your gates, you rulers, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter” (Ps. 23:7); if what he says in the [Col. 1038] hymn, “You who see what I do, keep silent about my works,” signifies what is written in the Book of Tobit, “It is good to conceal the king’s secret” (Tob. 12:7)—why is this hymn said not to be in the canon because the king’s secret is to be hidden from carnal people, when the things expounded in this hymn are also read in the canon and are found there so plainly that through them the obscure passages are explained? The reason can only be that they possess these interpretations as hiding places, while in the words of the hymn—which they pretend to expound—they understand something they fear to explain to others.

9. It would take too long to demonstrate everything by argument. From what we have said, however, it is easy to consider the rest and to see that the good and honorable things they mention in their exposition of this hymn are also found in the canon. Their claim, therefore, is not an argument but an evasion: that the hymn was separated from the canon because the king’s secret had to be hidden from carnal people. Hence they are rightly believed not to wish, through these interpretations, to disclose what they read, but rather to conceal what they understand.

Nor is this surprising, since they believed that the Lord Jesus himself, speaking not through the mouths of prophets, apostles, or angels but through his own mouth, was more a deceiver than a teacher of truth. Since they attribute divine authority to this hymn, in which some author of the same hymn falsely invented that he said, “By a word I deceived all things, and I was not altogether deceived,” let these distinguished spiritual people answer, if they can: where should we go, to whom should we open our ears, whose speech should we believe in any way, and in whose promise should we place our hope, if Christ deceived all things by a word, if the omnipotent teacher deceived all things by a word, if he who is the Only-begotten Word of God the Father deceived all things by a word?

What more can I say about those ruined prattlers and seducers of minds—first of their own, and then of the minds of others whom they have been able to join to themselves, predestined for eternal destruction? I have written back to Your Veneration much later than I wished and at greater length than I had intended. You are doing very well to guard vigilantly against wolves; but also labor, with pastoral diligence and with the help of the Lord of shepherds himself, for the healing of any sheep they may perhaps have violated or already wounded.

# LETTER CCXXXVIII

[Note: [Col. 1038] Letters CCXXXVIII and CCXXXIX have been corrected according to manuscripts a, bg, bl, c, cc, ff, g, gv, n, r, s, sb, t, vc, v, and according to the editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1038] Elsewhere numbered 164; formerly 238, now 69.]

Augustine to Pascentius, an Arian count of the imperial household, who had challenged him to a conference at Carthage (from Possidius, ch. 17), had evaded him in the confession of faith, and afterward boasted that he had defeated Augustine. In writing Augustine gives an account of his faith concerning the three persons and one God, and concerning the word *homoousios* (ὁμοούσιον).

## CHAPTER ONE

1. At your request and insistence—as you will remember—or rather, in view of your age and rank, at your command, I had wished to discuss the Christian faith with you in person, as one present with another, insofar as the Lord might grant me the ability. But because, after lunch, you disliked what had pleased us in the morning—namely, that our words should be recorded by notaries—do not continue to say, as I hear you have not ceased saying, that I did not dare to state my faith to you. In this letter receive what you may read yourself, hand to whomever you wish to read it, and answer in writing as you wish. For it is unjust that anyone should wish to judge another and not wish to be judged himself.

2. As for our previous agreement, which you were unwilling to fulfill at the appointed midday hour, it can easily be judged which of us lacked confidence in his own faith: whether the one who wanted it to be spoken but feared that it might be held against him, or the one who was so unwilling to have it withheld from the judgment of those debating that he wanted it committed to writing and entrusted to the memory of readers—lest anyone, whether through forgetfulness or irritation born of disagreement, should say that one of us had either not said what had been said or had said what had not been said.

Those who are more eager for contention than for truth commonly seek hiding places for their bad defense in such matters. But neither you nor I, and neither about you nor about me, could have said this if you had remained faithful to our agreement that our words should be recorded and written down—especially since you yourself, in the words with which you declared your faith, varied them each time you repeated them. I believe this happened not through fraud but through forgetfulness.

3. At first you said that you believed in God the almighty Father, invisible, unbegotten, incapable of suffering; and in Jesus Christ, his Son, God [Note: [Col. 1039] Lov. has “Lord.” The readings of Bad., Am., Er., and six manuscripts—“God”—are better, as appears from §8], born before the ages, through whom all things were made; and in the Holy Spirit. After hearing this, I replied that you had not yet said anything contrary to my faith and that, if you had written these things, I could subscribe to them as well. Somehow, however, matters proceeded to the point that, after receiving a sheet of paper, you wished to set down in your own hand the very things you had said.

When you gave it to me to read, I noticed that you had written “God almighty, invisible, unbegotten, unborn,” without writing “Father.” When I pointed this out, without much discussion you added “Father.” You had omitted in writing the word “incapable of suffering,” which you had spoken aloud; but I made no mention of this.

4. Then, when I said that I was still prepared to subscribe to those words and that they could also be mine, I first asked—so that what had occurred to me might not slip away—whether “the unbegotten Father” was found anywhere in the divine Scriptures. I did this because, at the beginning of our discussion, when Arius and Eunomius had been mentioned—not by me but by my brother Alypius, who was asking whom Auxentius followed, a man whom you had praised with no small commendation—you anathematized both Arius and Eunomius with an outcry. Immediately afterward you demanded that we too anathematize *homoousios* (ὁμοούσιον), as though it were the name of some human being, like Arius and Eunomius.

Then you vehemently demanded that we show you this word in the Scriptures, so that you might immediately communicate with us. We replied that, since we spoke Latin and it was a Greek word, we first had to ask what *homoousios* meant, and only then demand that it be shown in the sacred books. You, on the other hand, repeatedly recited the word itself, paraded it offensively, and mentioned that it had been written down in the councils of our predecessors. You pressed us insistently to show in the sacred books the very word *homoousios*, while we repeatedly reminded you that our language was not Greek and that the meaning of *homoousios* first had to be translated and explained, and only then sought in the divine writings—for even if the word itself were perhaps not found, the reality itself would be found. What is more contentious than, when the matter is agreed upon, disputing about the name?

5. Since we had already discussed these matters between ourselves, when the point was reached at which you wrote your faith, as I have said, I saw nothing in your words contrary to our faith and therefore said that I was prepared to subscribe to them. Nevertheless, as I said, I asked whether the Scripture of God contained the statement that the Father was unbegotten; and when you replied that it did, I asked more insistently that you show it. Then one of those who were present, evidently a companion in your faith, said to me, “What then? Do you say that the Father is begotten?” I replied, “I do not say that.” And he said, “If he is not begotten, then surely he is unbegotten.”

To him I said, “You see that it can happen that an account may nevertheless be given showing why one may rightly use a word that is not found in the Scripture of God. Likewise, then, with *homoousios*, which we were compelled to show in the authority of the divine books: even if we do not find the word itself there, it may still be possible for us to find that to which the word is rightly judged applicable.”

6. After these remarks, I waited to hear what you thought of them, and you said, “It was rightly done that the Father should not be called unbegotten in the sacred Scriptures, lest he be injured even by such a word.” “Then,” I said, “God has just been injured—and by your own hand.” On hearing this, you began to admit that you should not have said this [Note: [Col. 1040] Bad., Am., Er., and most manuscripts read “he began.”]. But when I urged you, if you considered the word so objectionable that it constituted an injury to God, to erase it from the place where you had written it, you considered, I believe, that it could rightly be said and defended; and again you said, “That is precisely what I say.”

Then I repeated what I had already said: that it could likewise happen that *homoousios*, although not written in the sacred pages, might nevertheless be defended when asserted in a confession of faith—just as we nowhere read “unbegotten” of the Father in those books, yet its use is defended as necessary. At that point you took from me the sheet you had given me and tore it up. We then decided that, after midday, notaries should be present to record our words and that we should discuss these matters between us as carefully as we could.

7. As you know, we came at the appointed hour, brought notaries, and sat down so that your people too might be present. You again recited your faith, and in your words I did not hear “the unbegotten Father.” I believe you had reflected on what had been said in the morning and wished to guard against it. Then you asked me also to state my faith. When I requested—recalling our morning agreement—that you should be so kind as to dictate [Col. 1041] what you had said, you cried out that we were preparing a charge against you and therefore wanted to retain your words in writing.

I do not wish to remember what I answered there; would that you too remembered it no longer. Nevertheless, I preserved the honor due to your rank and did not count as an insult what I deserved to hear not from truth but from power. Yet, since I even repeated the very words, saying in a lowered voice, “Are we then preparing a charge against you?” I ask you to forgive me.

8. But after hearing this, you again repeated your faith in a louder voice, and in your words I did not hear “the Son, God”—something you had never omitted whenever you stated it. Here I suggested, as modestly as possible and without pressing you, that our agreement about having our words recorded should be fulfilled; I even drew from the present experience a useful lesson. I said that you yourself had been unable to retain in memory the words most familiar to you, since we saw that you had never managed to repeat them accurately when you were not preparing something especially necessary. How much less could those listening to us remember our words so accurately that, if either you wished to reconsider and discuss something I had said or I something you had said, they would clearly remember whether it had or had not been spoken? The reading of the notaries’ record would easily assist us in this difficulty.

Then you indignantly said that it would have been better had you always heard my reputation, since you had found me far inferior to what that reputation had proclaimed about me. I then recalled that, when we greeted you before lunch and you had praised that reputation to us, I had said that it had lied about me. Here you said that I had spoken the truth.

Thus, since two different accounts of me had been given to you—one by my reputation and another by me—I ought surely to rejoice more that I, rather than it, had been found truthful. But since it is written, “God alone is true, and every human being is a liar” (Rom. 3:4), I fear that I may have said this rashly even about myself. For we are not truthful in ourselves or through ourselves when we are truthful; rather, we are truthful when he who alone is true speaks through his servants.

9. If you recall that these events occurred as I have related them, you see how little you ought to boast before people that I did not dare to affirm my faith to you, since you were unwilling to stand by our agreement. You are a man of such consequence that, for the faith you owe to the state, you do not fear the insults of the provincials, yet for the faith you owe to Christ, you fear the accusations of bishops.

Furthermore, since you wished distinguished men to attend our discussion, I wonder how, in the very effort to avoid an accusation, you fear having your words written down by notaries, yet do not fear having them heard from your own mouth by illustrious witnesses. Do you not see how difficult it is for people to suppose that you feared any accusation from us and therefore refused to have your words recorded? Rather, when you thought that you had been held to the word written in your own hand before lunch, you may also have thought that you could not erase the notaries’ tablets as easily as you tore up that sheet.

If you say that events did not occur as I have related them, then either you are deceived by forgetfulness—for I do not dare to say that you are lying—or I am similarly mistaken or lying. You see, then [Col. 1042], how rightly I say that the events concerning these matters above all ought to be recorded and written down, and how rightly you too had approved this very practice—unless your afternoon fear had broken your morning agreement.

## CHAPTER TWO

10. Hear my faith now. The mercy of our Lord God is powerful enough to grant that I speak what I believe in such a way that I neither offend his truth nor your humanity. I profess that I believe in God the almighty Father, and I call him eternal with that eternity—that is, immortality—which God alone possesses. I believe the same concerning his only-begotten Son in the form of God, and the same concerning the Holy Spirit, who is the Spirit of God the Father and of his only-begotten Son.

But because that only-begotten Son of God the Father, our Lord and God Jesus Christ, after the fullness of time had come, suitable [Note: [Col. 1042] Bad., Am., and Er. read *opportuni*; one Vatican manuscript reads *opportune*.] for the day of our salvation, took the form of a servant (Gal. 4:4), many things are said of him in the Scriptures according to the form of God, and many according to the form of a servant. By way of example, I mention two things, so that each may be referred to its corresponding form. According to the form of God he said of himself, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); according to the form of a servant, “For the Father is greater than I” (John 14:28).

11. What is written of God—“who alone possesses immortality” (1 Tim. 6:16), and “to the invisible, only God, be honor and glory” (1 Tim. 1:17), and other statements of this kind—we understand not of the Father alone but also of the Son, insofar as the form of God is concerned, and of the Holy Spirit. For Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, the one true God, and the one immortal God according to an entirely unchangeable substance.

If, then, it is said of flesh of different sexes, “He who joins himself to a prostitute is one body,” and if it is consequently written of the human spirit—which is not what the Lord is—“He who joins himself to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:16–17), how much more are God the Father in the Son, God the Son in the Father, and the Spirit of the Father and the Son one God, where there is no difference of nature, when, in the case of distinct things joined together in a certain manner, one spirit or one body is spoken of?

12. And when one human being is spoken of in the case of soul and body joined together, why should the Father and Son not be called one God much more, since they are joined to each other inseparably, unlike body and soul? And when soul and body are one human being, although soul and body are not one thing, why should the Father and Son not be much more one God, since the Father and Son are one, according to the voice of Truth, “I and the Father are one”?

Again, although the inner human being and the outer human being are not one—for the outer is not of the same nature as the inner, since the outer is called “human being” together with the body, while the inner is understood in the rational soul alone—yet both together are called not two human beings but one. How much more, then, are the Father and Son one God, since the Father and Son are one, because they are of the same nature or substance—or, if some other term more suitably expresses what God is, the reality concerning which it was said, “I and the Father are one”? [Col. 1043]

Thus there is one Spirit of the Lord and one human spirit, and yet they are not one; nevertheless, when the human spirit cleaves to the Lord, they are not two but one spirit. There is one inner human being and one outer human being, and they are not one; nevertheless, through the bond of their natural connection, both together are not two but one human being. Much more, therefore, since the Son of God says, “I and the Father are one,” God the Father is one and God the Son is one; yet together they are not two but one God.

13. What one faith, one hope, and one love accomplished in many holy people called to adoption as coheirs with Christ—so that they might have one soul and one heart directed toward God—compels us especially to understand that the nature of the Father and Son is one and the same, if this is the appropriate way to speak of their divinity. Thus the Father and Son, who are one, inseparably one, and eternally one, are not two gods but one God.

Those human beings were one through participation in and communion with the one same nature of which all human beings partook. If at some time they were not one because of differing wills, opinions, judgments, and ways of life, they will nevertheless become fully and perfectly one when they reach that end at which God will be all in all. But God the Father and his Son, his Word, God with God, are always and ineffably one; hence they are not two gods but one God.

14. People who understand less clearly why something is said in relation to something else want to have statements laid open before them. Since they do not scrutinize the Scriptures carefully, when they seize upon a defense of some opinion and either never or only with difficulty turn away from it, they desire more to be thought learned and wise than to be so. They transfer to the form of God what was said according to the form of a servant; and again, what was said so that the persons might be referred to one another, they want to be names of nature and substance.

Our faith, however, is to believe and confess that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, yet not to call the one who is the Son “Father,” nor the one who is the Father “Son,” nor the one who is the Spirit of the Father and Son either “Father” or “Son.” These names signify how they are related to one another, not the substance itself by which they are one. For when “father” is said, it is said only in relation to some son; and “son” is understood only in relation to some father. Likewise, “spirit,” insofar as it is referred to something else, belongs to one who breathes it forth; and one who breathes is certainly one who breathes forth spirit [Note: [Col. 1043] Thus the manuscripts. The editions read, “one who breathes forth with the spirit.”].

15. These things, however, are not perceived bodily, nor understood in God in the customary way—for He is able to do, as the Apostle says, “far more than we ask or understand” (Eph. 3:20). But if He can make [such things], how much more can He be [such]? For the term “spirit,” not according to what it refers to in relation to something else, but according to what signifies a certain nature, is applied in Scripture to every incorporeal nature; hence this term is appropriate not only to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but also to every rational creature and to the soul. [Col. 1044]

Thus the Lord says, “God is spirit; and therefore those who worship God must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:24). It is also written, “He makes his angels spirits” (Ps. 103:4). It was said of certain human beings, “For they are flesh, and a spirit that goes and does not return” (Ps. 77:39). And the Apostle says, “No one knows what is going on in a person except the person’s spirit, which is in him” (1 Cor. 2:11). Likewise it is written: “Who knows whether the spirit of the children of man goes upward, and whether the spirit of the animal goes downward into the earth?” (Eccl. 3:21).

“Spirit” is also used in Scripture according to a certain distinction within the one soul of a single human being. Hence the Apostle says, “May your spirit and soul and body be kept complete for the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thess. 5:23). Elsewhere: “If I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful. What then? I shall pray with the spirit; I shall pray with the mind also” (1 Cor. 14:14–15).

The Holy Spirit, however, is called by a particular manner of expression “Spirit,” insofar as He is related to the Father and the Son, as being their Holy Spirit. But according to substance—for it has once been said, “God is spirit”—the Father is spirit, the Son is spirit, and the Holy Spirit Himself is spirit; yet there are not three spirits, but one spirit, just as there are not three gods, but one God.

16. Why are you surprised? So great is the power of peace—not just any peace, as the term is usually understood, nor the kind praised in this life through the harmony and love of the faithful, but that peace of God which, as the Apostle says, “surpasses all understanding” (Phil. 4:7). What understanding, if not ours—that is, the understanding of every rational creature?

Therefore, considering our weakness and hearing the Apostle confess and say, “Brothers, I do not consider that I have apprehended it” (ibid. 3:13), and, “If anyone thinks that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know” (1 Cor. 8:2), let us converse peacefully with the divine Scriptures, as far as we can, without contention. Let us not strive, through empty and childish zeal, to overcome one another, so that rather “the peace of Christ may prevail in our hearts” (Col. 3:15), insofar as He has granted us to apprehend it even in this life.

Let us consider what that same peace accomplished among the brethren: from so many minds and so many hearts it made one soul and one heart directed toward God. Thus, with due piety, let us believe that much more truly, in that peace of God which surpasses all understanding, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three gods but one God—by as much more excellent as the peace that surpasses all understanding is more excellent than the peace by which the one heart and one soul of all those people were held together in God.

17. We call the same person the Son of Man whom we call the Son of God—not, however, because of the form of God, in which He is equal to God the Father, but because of the form of a servant that He assumed, in which He is less than the Father. [Note: [Col. 1044] Bad., Am., Er., and six manuscripts read, “in which the Father is greater.”]

And because we call Him the Son of Man, for this reason we also confess that the Son of God was crucified—not through the power of divinity, but through the weakness of humanity; not through the continuance of His own nature, but through His assumption of our nature. [Note: [Col. 1044] The editions read *permixtione* (“mixture”); but the Vatican manuscripts and eleven Gallican manuscripts read *permansione* (“continuance”), which, in our judgment, is better. The meaning is that the Son of God was crucified not through His nature, which remained what it was, but through ours, which He assumed.] [Col. 1045]

### CHAPTER III

18. Now consider for a little while what statements of Scripture compel us to confess one Lord God, whether we are asked about the Father alone, the Son alone, the Holy Spirit alone, or the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together.

Certainly it is written, “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord is one” (Deut. 6:4). Of whom do you think this was said? If of the Father alone, then Jesus Christ is not our Lord God. And where is that voice of the one who touched Him and cried out, “My Lord and my God,” which Christ Himself did not rebuke but approved, saying, “Because you have seen me, you have believed” (John 20:28)?

But if the Son is also Lord God, and the Father is Lord God, then there are already two lords and two gods. How, then, will it be true that “the Lord your God, the Lord is one”? Or perhaps the Father is one Lord, while the Son is not one Lord but simply “Lord,” in the manner of which it is said, “There are many gods and many lords,” and not in the manner of that one of whom it is written, “The Lord is one”?

What, then, shall we answer the Apostle when he says: “For although there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many gods and many lords—yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we for Him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through Him” (1 Cor. 8:5–6)?

If what is said about the one God, the Father, compels one to separate the Son from Him, let those who dare do so say that the Father can no longer be understood as Lord, because, he says, “there is one Lord, Jesus Christ.” For if He is one, He is certainly alone; and if He is alone, how can the Father also be Lord, unless both He and the Father are one God and God alone, without the Holy Spirit being separated?

Therefore there is one God, the Father, and with Him the Son is one God, although the Father is not, with Him, one Father. Likewise there is one Lord, Jesus Christ, and with Him the Father is one Lord, although the Father is not, with Him, one Jesus Christ—as though the Father too were Jesus Christ. For this name was assumed as part of the dispensation of mercy and of the humanity He took upon Himself.

19. Or perhaps, when the Apostle says, “one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things,” you do not wish the word “one” to be joined to “Lord,” but to what he says, “through whom are all things,” so that what is understood is not “one Lord” but “one through whom are all things”; and so the Father is not the one through whom all things are, but the Father alone is the one from whom all things are, and the Son alone the one through whom all things are?

If this is so, then at last confess that the Father and the Son are our one Lord and God. For “who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been His counselor? Or who has first given to Him, and it shall be repaid to him? For from Him and through Him and in Him are all things; to Him be glory” (Rom. 11:34–36).

For he did not say, “All things are from the Father and through the Son,” but “from Him and through Him and in Him.” From whom, if not the Lord of whom he says, “Who has known the mind of the Lord?” All things, therefore, are from the Lord, through the Lord, and in the Lord—not from one Lord and through another, but from one Lord, because he did not say, “To them be glory,” but “to Him be glory.”

20.
