But if someone says that when the Apostle writes, “one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things,” the meaning is neither “one Lord” nor “one through whom are all things,” but “one Jesus Christ”—and that this one Jesus Christ is also called Lord, though not so that “one Lord” may be one, but so that “one Jesus Christ” may be one—what will he say when he hears that same Apostle crying out: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all” (Eph. 4:5–6)?

Since he mentions God the Father here, when he says, “one God and Father of all,” there can be no doubt that by what he said there, “one Lord,” he intended Jesus Christ. If, then, they approve this interpretation, let the Father cease to be Lord, because Jesus Christ is one Lord.

But if it is absurd and impious to think so, let us learn to understand the unity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, so that when something has been said of the one God alone, we are not immediately prevented from understanding it of the Son or of the Holy Spirit as well. For the Father is not the Son, the Son is not the Father, and the Spirit of both is neither the Father nor the Son; yet the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together are the one, only, and true Lord God.

### CHAPTER IV

21. For if the Holy Spirit were not God, or true God, our bodies would not be His temples. “Do you not know,” he says, “that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God?” And lest anyone deny that the Spirit Himself is God, he immediately adds, “And you are not your own: for you were bought with a great price.” [Note: [Col. 1046] Many manuscripts omit *magno* (“great”); and later they also omit *et portate* (“and bear”), words that are likewise absent from the Greek text. Chrysostom and others repeatedly quote the passage in this form.]

“Therefore glorify and bear God in your body”—namely, the One whose temple he had declared our bodies to be.

Now this is astonishing, if what I hear you say is true: that the Holy Spirit is less than the Son in the same way that the Son is less than the Father. For since our bodies are members of Christ, as the Apostle says, and our bodies are also the temple of the Holy Spirit, as the same Apostle says (1 Cor. 6:19–20, 15), I am greatly surprised how they can be members of the greater and a temple of the lesser.

Or perhaps you now approve saying that the Holy Spirit is greater than the Lord Jesus Christ? That opinion seems to be supported also by the statement: “Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matt. 12:32). For sin is committed more dangerously against the greater than against the lesser.

Nor is it permissible to separate the Son of Man from the Son of God, because the Son of God Himself became the Son of Man—not by changing what He was, but by assuming what He was not.

But may even such impiety be far from us, that the Holy Spirit should be believed greater than the Son. Therefore let not statements made in such a way that they seem to show one greater than another easily move you into error.

22. For some things are said in such a way that, to people of little understanding, even the Son may seem greater than the Father. Who, when asked which is greater, the true thing or truth, would not rather answer that truth is greater? For by truth all things that are true are true.

But it is not so in God. We certainly do not say that the Son is greater than the Father; yet the Son is called truth: “I am,” He says, “the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

You, however, wish it to be understood of the Father alone when He says, “That they may know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3). We understand Jesus Christ also to be included as true God, so that the meaning is: “That they may know you and Jesus Christ whom you have sent as the one true God.” Otherwise the absurdity would follow that, if Jesus Christ is not true God because it was said to the Father, “you, the one true God,” then the Father is not Lord because it was said of Christ, “one Lord.”

Nevertheless, according to a perverse understanding—or rather, an error—God who is truth is greater than God who is true, because the true God derives from truth. The Son, therefore, would be greater than the Father, because the one is truth and the other is true.

This perversity is driven from the mind of anyone who has learned that the Father is true God by generating truth, not by participating in it. The substance of the one who generates truth and the substance of the truth generated are not different.

23. But since the eye of the human heart is weak for contemplating these things, it is also made turbulent by contention. And when will it behold them?

Scripture calls the Son of God, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, the Word of God, and truth, and wisdom. Yet before the incarnation that He received from the Virgin Mary, without any assumption whatsoever of bodily creature, by the very nature and substance by which He is the Word of God and the Wisdom of God, people say that He was visible and corruptible, while wishing to maintain what they think about the statement that was made of the Father alone: “To the invisible, incorruptible, only God” (1 Tim. 1:17).

I ask you: the word of a human being is not visible, much less the Word of God. And that Wisdom of which it was said, “She reaches everywhere because of her purity,” and, “Nothing defiled enters into her,” and, “Remaining in herself, she renews all things,” together with similar statements too numerous to list—if she is corruptible, I do not know what to say except that I should grieve over human presumption and marvel at divine patience.

24. Since it was said of her, “For she is the radiance of eternal light” (Wis. 7:24–27), your people, I think, no longer say that the light of the Father—what is that except His substance? [Note: [Col. 1047] Lov. reads, “if it is His substance.” But the other editions and manuscripts read more suitably, “what is that except …?”]—once existed without the radiance generated from it, as these things can be believed and in some measure understood in relation to divine, spiritual, incorporeal, and unchangeable realities. For I hear that they have now corrected themselves.

Or is it false that they once said that the Father existed at some time without the Son, as though eternal light existed without the radiance it generated?

What, then, shall we say? If the Son of God was born from the Father, then the Father ceased to beget; and if He ceased, He began. But if He began to beget, He once existed without the Son. Yet He never existed without the Son, because His Son is His Wisdom, and that Wisdom is the radiance of eternal light.

Therefore the Father is always begetting, and the Son is always being born. Here again we must fear that the generation will be thought imperfect if we say not that He has been born but that He is being born.

Have pity on me, I beg you, amid these straits of human thought and language, and let us flee together to the Spirit of God, who speaks through the prophet: “Who will declare His generation?” (Isa. 53:8).

25. For the present I ask only that you carefully inquire whether divine Scripture anywhere says of different substances that they are one. For if the statement is found only concerning things that clearly belong to one and the same substance, why should we rebel against the true and catholic faith?

But if you find it written somewhere also of different substances, then I shall be compelled to inquire further, so that I may show on what grounds the Father and the Son are rightly called *homoousios* (ὁμοούσιον), “of one substance.”

For if those who either do not know our Scriptures or do not painstakingly examine them nevertheless believe that the Son is of the same substance as the Father and equal to Him, let them say to those who do not wish to believe this—while nevertheless believing that God the Father has an only-begotten Son: “Did God not wish to have an equal Son, or was He unable?” If He did not wish to, He is envious; if He was unable, He is weak. But to think either of these things about God is sacrilegious.

I do not know whether they can find anything to say if they do not wish to utter things utterly absurd and foolish.

### CHAPTER V

26. Behold, as far as I could, I have explained my faith to you. More could indeed be said and discussed more carefully, but I fear that even what I have said may be burdensome amid your occupations.

Nevertheless, I wished not merely to have these things written down from dictation, but also took care to sign them with my own hand. I had wished to do this earlier as well, if what had been agreed between us had been observed.

But now, surely, I think you should no longer say that I was afraid to tell you my faith, since I not only stated it but also signed it in writing, so that no one could say either that I had said what I did not say or that I had not said what I did say.

Do the same yourself, if you are seeking judges—not people who, in your presence, show reverence for your person, but people who, in your writings, exercise their freedom.

For if you fear slander—which I would in no way dare to say unless you yourself had said it—you are free not to sign. For this is why I also did not wish your name to be written in these letters of mine: lest perhaps you had not wished it.

27. Anyone can easily defeat Augustine; the question is whether by truth or by shouting. It is not for me to say anything except that anyone can easily defeat Augustine—how much more easily, then, can he appear to have defeated him; or, even if he does not appear to have defeated him, nevertheless be said to have done so?

This is easy. I do not want you to think it a great achievement; I do not. I do not want you to pursue it as something great. For when people perceive the enormous hunger of your heart in this matter, many will rejoice that they have found an opportunity, with a few “Well done! Well done!” to make so powerful a man their friend.

I do not want to say that if they do not support you, or if they express an opposing opinion, they may even fear becoming your enemy—foolishly and stupidly, certainly, but nevertheless many people are like this.

28. Do not therefore consider how Augustine, one human being of whatever sort, may be defeated. Consider rather whether *homoousion* can be defeated—not the Greek word itself, which it is easy for the uninformed to mock, but what is written: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); and, “Holy Father, keep them in your name, whom you have given me, so that they may be one, as we are” [Note: [Col. 1048] The manuscript of Gervasius and several others add here, “from the world.”]

A little later He says: “I do not pray for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word: that all may be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I in you, so that they too may be one in us, that the world may believe that you sent me. And the glory that you gave me I have given them, so that they may be one, just as we are one: I in them and you in me, so that they may be perfected into one” (John 17:11, 20–23).

See how many times He said, “that they may be one, as we are one.” Yet nowhere did He say, “Let them and us be one,” but rather, “As I and you are one, so let them be one in us.” For just as they were of one and the same substance, whom He wished also to make participants in eternal life, so it was said of the Father and the Son, “We are one,” because they are of one and the same substance—not participants in eternal life, but eternal life itself in the primary sense.

He could have spoken according to the form of a servant and said, “I and they are one,” or, “Let us be one.” Yet He did not say this, because He wished to show one substance belonging to the Father and Himself, and another belonging to them.

If He had said, “That you and they may be one, as I and you are one,” or, “That you and I and they may be one, as I and you are one,” none of us would refuse to allow that different substances can be called one. But you see that this is not so, because He did not say it in that way, and by saying what He did repeatedly He strongly commended its meaning.

29. You therefore find in Scripture a case in which different natures are one, as we showed above, but something is added or understood as the thing in which they are one. Thus, from soul and body, we say “one living being,” “one person,” and “one human being,” whether singular or plural in expression.

But if you find in Scripture the expression “they are one” without any addition, and unless it concerns things that are of one substance, you will most justly demand that we produce something else by which we may demonstrate *homoousion*.

There are many other considerations as well. But for the present reflect on this one, setting aside the desire for contention, so that you may have God favorable to you.

For it is not good for one human being to defeat another human being. Rather, it is good for a human being that truth should defeat him willingly; for it is bad for him that truth should defeat him unwillingly. Truth itself must prevail, whether over someone who denies or over someone who confesses.

Forgive me if I have spoken with too much freedom—not to insult you, but to defend myself. I presumed upon your seriousness and prudence, because you can consider how great a necessity of responding you imposed upon me. Or, if I have not acted rightly even in this, forgive me for that as well.

I, Augustine, have signed this letter dictated and reread by me.

## LETTER CCXXXIX

[Note: [Col. 1049] Elsewhere 175; the letter that was 239 is now 83.]

Augustine to Pascentius, insisting on the same matter that he explain his faith.

1. If you say that you told me your faith and that I did not wish to tell you mine—something I hear you do not cease saying—remember, I beg you, that both claims are false.

For you did not wish to tell me your faith, and I did not refuse to tell you mine; rather, I wished to state it in such a way that no one could say either that I had said something I did not say or that I had not said something I did say.

You would have told me your faith if you had stated the point on which you dissent from us—if you had said: “I believe in God the Father, who made the Son the first creature before all the other creatures; and in the Son Himself, who is neither equal nor similar to the Father, nor true God; and in the Holy Spirit, made through the Son after the Son.” For I hear that you say these things.

Or, if it is false that you say these things, I would rather learn that from you. But if it is true that you say them, I wish to know how you defend them from the holy Scriptures.

Instead, you said that you believe in God the almighty Father, invisible and immortal, begotten by no one and from whom all things are; and in His Son Jesus Christ, God born before the ages, through whom all things were made; and in the Holy Spirit.

This faith is not yours but the faith of both of us—just as it would be if you added that the same Son of God, Jesus Christ, was also born from the Virgin Mary, which we equally believe, together with any other matters that we confess in common.

If, then, you had wished to state your own faith, you would not have stated this faith, which is shared by us, but rather the one in which we differ from you.

2. I would have said this and more in person, if our words had been recorded as had been agreed. But because you refused, saying that you feared slander from us, and because after lunch you withdrew from the agreement to which you had consented in the morning, why should I say something in a form that you could report as having been said according to your wishes, while I would have no means of showing what I had said or how I had said it?

Do not therefore continue to boast that you stated your faith while I did not state mine. There are people who may judge that I had greater confidence in my faith, since I wished it to be written down, whereas you did not have such confidence, since you seemed to fear slander.

You were therefore prepared to deny it if you were charged with having said something contrary to my faith. Consider what impression you have caused people to form of you.

But if you were not going to deny the charge, why did you refuse to have what was said written down—especially since you had very much wished that distinguished men should also be present at our conversation?

Why, then, while wishing to avoid slander, did you fear the pens of the notaries but not fear the testimony of distinguished men?

3. But if you want me also to state my faith, just as you say that you stated yours, I can state it more briefly: I believe in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

If, however, you wish to hear something distinctive, in which I differ from you, I believe in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, saying neither that the Son is the Father, nor that the Father is the Son, nor that the Holy Spirit of both is either the Father or the Son; and yet that the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God—one alone eternal and immortal in His own substance, just as God alone is eternal and immortal, in that divinity which exists before the ages.

If this displeases you, and you wish to hear from me how it is asserted from the holy Scriptures, read also the longer work that I sent to Your Goodness.

But if you do not have time to read that, neither do I have time to cast words uselessly into the air. Nevertheless, insofar as the Lord grants me ability, I can respond to whatever you wish, whether you dictate it to me or write it, and whether I respond by dictating or writing myself.

I, Augustine, have signed this letter dictated and reread by me.

## LETTER CCXL

[Note: [Col. 1051] Elsewhere 176; the letter that was 240 is now 63.]

Pascentius addresses Augustine abusively, insisting that he explain how one God is three persons and challenging him to a public disputation before arbiters.

[Col. 1051]

I had hoped, dearest brother, that you would abandon the counsel of your former error. Now I am astonished that you still persist in it, as the letter you sent me cries out.

For Your Dignity is like a thirsty man, inflamed by excessive heat, who, upon finding muddy water, gulps it down and afterward, even if he finds and drinks clear and cold water, cannot make sufficient progress, since his heart and soul have once been overwhelmed by mud.

In short, if I may say so with your permission, the counsel of Your Eminence is like a crooked and knotty tree, which contains nothing straight in itself and distorts the sharpness of the eyes.

Your Holiness writes back to me that the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, but that there is one God. Which of the three is the one God? Or perhaps there is one three-formed person who is called by this name?

If you wished and had confidence in your profession, you would sit with me and your fellow bishops, with a pure and peaceful mind and spirit, and discuss the things that belong to God and that pertain to spiritual glory and grace.

Why, then, is there any need to write and write back about matters that do not edify us?

## LETTER CCXLI

[Note: [Col. 1051] Elsewhere 177; the letter that was 241 is now 62.]

Augustine professes one God and denies a three-formed God; he does not refuse a disputation, provided that what is said is recorded.

1. Your letter could neither provoke me to return insults nor deter me from replying. What you wrote would have moved me if it had been said from the truth of God rather than from human power.

You said that my counsel was a crooked and knotty tree, which contained nothing straight in itself and distorted the sharpness of the eyes.

What would you have said of me if I had withdrawn from the agreement we established between us in the morning, and had placed a crooked resistance and knots of difficulty in the easiest matter on which we had rightly agreed?

You would not have judged me to have gulped down muddy water, but—what is much worse—to have been drowned in the drunkenness of faithlessness, if I had not returned after lunch as I had departed before lunch.

But see: did you not write back what you wished, without fearing any slander? Therefore you too can do the rest, so that there may be something that we ourselves or others can consider and judge.

For when you say that I believe God to be a three-formed person, if you had deigned to read what I sent you, somewhat longer, and had wished to respond to what was written there, perhaps you would not have said this.

Yet here too you have stated it: you dictated and sent in writing that I call God a three-formed person, and you feared no slander. You have shown that what I say is true: you did not refuse, as had been agreed when we were together, to dictate your words because you feared slander, but because you lacked confidence in the truth.

Now that you have chosen to dictate that I believe God to be a three-formed person, I answer that I do not believe this. There is one form, because there is, so to speak, one divinity; and therefore the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God.

[Col. 1052]

2. But please deign to answer briefly how you understand what the Apostle says: “The one who joins himself to a prostitute is one body; but the one who joins himself to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:16–17).

He called bodies of different sexes, joined to one another, one body. And although the human spirit can in no way say, “I and the Lord are one,” nevertheless, when it joins itself to the Lord, it is one spirit.

How much more, then, is the One who most truly said, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), because He is inseparably joined to the Father, Himself and the Father one God?

That is, if this expression can even be admitted in that divinity, so that we say that He “is joined,” when there has never been and never can be any separation from which He would be apart.

Answer this: do you approve of calling the spirit two-formed when the one who joins himself to the Lord is one spirit?

If you do not approve this, neither did I call the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit a three-formed God, but one God.

If you wish us to converse in person, I am indeed grateful for your esteem and goodwill. But just as you have now deigned to write back what you wished, so deign to write back that we shall dictate what we are going to say, and I shall not fail to comply with your wish insofar as the Lord assists me.

For if writing and replying do not edify us, how does saying and replying edify us, when after the clamor of words we have nothing to review by reading?

I, Augustine, dictated this and signed it after rereading it.

Let us abstain from insults, lest we spend our time uselessly, and let us attend rather to the matter being discussed between us.

## LETTER CCXLII

[Note: [Col. 1052] Corrected according to manuscripts a, bg, bl, bn, c, cc, ff, g, gv, n, r, s, sb, t, two vc manuscripts, four v manuscripts, and the editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1052] Elsewhere 150; the letter that was 242 is now 84.]

Augustine to Elpidius the Arian, proving that the Son of God is equal to God and begotten from Him, not made; promising also to respond more fully to a certain Arian’s little book if leisure and opportunity are granted.

To the distinguished, deservedly honorable and beloved lord ELPIDIUS, AUGUSTINE.

[Note: [Col. 1052] Some manuscripts have *Helpidius*; others, *Helvidius*.]

1. Which of us is in error in faith or in knowledge of the Trinity is another question. I am certainly grateful that, although you do not know me personally, you nevertheless believed that I was in error and attempted to call me back from error.

May God repay you for this goodwill and enable you to know what you think you know—for the matter is difficult, as I judge.

And I ask you not to take as an insult the fact that I wished for you the gift of such knowledge. For I fear that the prejudice of supposed knowledge, if it does not repel true instruction—which I would by no means presume to offer you—will at least repel from your ears our good wishes, which I am permitted to have for you even though unlearned (for they ought to be offered not expertly but as a friend). You may instead be angry with me because I have not already congratulated you as wise, rather than give thanks because I have prayed for wisdom for you.

Nevertheless, if I, bearing the burden of the episcopal name, most gladly welcome your goodwill because you deigned, as you write, to send me across the sea to Bonosus and Jason, most learned men, in order that I might bring back abundant fruits from their discussions; and if, finally, with solicitous kindness, you arranged for a little book of one of your bishops, prepared with his intellectual ability and strength, to be brought to me for dispelling the darkness of the whole error—how much more fitting is it for you to receive in good spirit my wish that the Lord God grant you things that no human intellect or power can provide?

For the Apostle says: “We have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things granted to us by God. These things we also speak, not in words taught by human wisdom, but taught by the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual. But the natural person does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him” (1 Cor. 2:12–14).

2. I would therefore rather inquire with you, if it were possible, how long a person should be called “natural,” so that, if we have already transcended that condition, we might perhaps rightly rejoice that we have touched, in some measure, those things that remain unchangeably above the human mind and understanding.

For we must take care lest the Son’s equality with the Father seem foolish to us because we are still living as natural people, of whom it was said that the things of the Spirit of God are foolishness to them.

Although that majesty, exalted above all things, can indeed be conceived by spiritual beings but cannot be expressed by anyone, it is nevertheless easy, as I think, to see that the One through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made, was not made.

For if He was made by Himself, He existed before He was made, so that He could be made by Himself. This is surely said the more absurdly the more vainly it is conceived.

But if He was not made by Himself, He was not made at all, since whatever was made was made through Him: “All things were made through Him, and without Him nothing was made” (John 1:3).

3. I am astonished that insufficient attention is paid to what the Evangelist wished to make so explicit that he allowed no one to evade it. For it was not enough to say, “All things were made through Him,” unless he added, “and without Him nothing was made.”

But although I am slow and still carry an eye of the mind wounded by uncleared darkness for contemplating the incomparable and ineffable excellence of the Father and the Son, I nevertheless grasp with complete ease what was sown beforehand for us in the Gospel—not so that we might comprehend that divinity from this, but so that we might be warned not to boast of a rash comprehension.

For if all things were made through Him, whatever was not made through Him was not made. But He was not made through Himself; therefore He was not made.

And we are compelled by the Evangelist to believe that all things were made through Him; therefore by the same Evangelist we are compelled not to believe that He was made.

Likewise, if nothing was made without Him, then He is nothing, because He was made without Himself.

But if it is sacrilegious to think this, it remains that we must confess either that He was not made without Himself or that He was not made.

We cannot say that He was not made without Himself. For if He made Himself, He already existed before He was made. But if He supplied assistance to another so that He might be made by that other, nevertheless, in order that He might be made with His own assistance, He already existed before He was made.

It therefore remains that He was made without Himself. But whatever was made without Him is nothing.

Either, then, He is nothing, or He was not made. But He is not nothing; therefore He was not made.

And if He was not made, yet is the Son, then without doubt He was born.

### 4

“How,” you ask, “could the Son have been born from the Father alone, equal to him from whom he was born?” I can no longer explain this, and I yield to the prophet who says: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53:8). But if you think this should be understood of the human generation by which he was born of a virgin, examine yourself and ask your soul whether, if it has failed in explaining human generation, it would dare to explain divine generation.

“Then,” you say, “do not call him equal.” Why should I not say what the Apostle said? “He did not regard equality with God as robbery” (Phil. 2:6). For although he did not explain that equality to the human mind, which had not yet been purified, he nevertheless placed it in the Word, where it can be found by a purified mind. Let us therefore devote ourselves to cleansing our heart, so that from it may arise the vision by which we can see these things. “Blessed are the pure in heart,” he says, “for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:7). Thus, rising above the dark images of the animal human being, we shall come to that clarity and purity in which we can see what we recognize cannot be expressed.

### 5

For, if I have leisure and the opportunity is granted me to respond point by point to the little book you have deigned to send me, I think you will learn that the less each person is clothed with the light of truth, the more he seems to himself to bring forth the naked truth. Who could endure—leaving other matters aside and mentioning for the moment only what grieved me most—that, while the apostle Paul says, “Now we see through a mirror in a riddle, but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12), this man should already say that he brings forth the truth naked, with every covering removed? If he had said, “We see the naked truth,” nothing would be blinder than this arrogance of vision. But he did not say, “We see”; he said, “We bring forth,” so that truth seems not merely to lie open already to the mind’s discovery, but also to be subject to the power of the tongue.

Many things may be said concerning the ineffability of the Trinity—not so that it itself may be stated, since then it would not be ineffable, but so that it may be understood that it cannot be stated by those sayings.

But by now, I think, my letter has exceeded the proper length, since through your letter you admonished me to write briefly. Yet because you have deigned to excuse yourself by appealing to the practice of the ancients, you will not think me absurd if you do not object to recalling the length of certain letters of Cicero, whom you also mentioned in your letters.

## LETTER 243

[Col. 1054]

[Note: Collated against a. a. bg. bl. bn. c. cc. cb. ff. g. gg. gv. j. n. s. sb. t. vc. vd., five copies of v., and the editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1054] Formerly 38; the letter that was 243 is now 246.]

Augustine to Laetus, who had undertaken a complete contempt of the world but seemed to be troubled by Satan into reclaiming what he had abandoned. He encourages him to press forward courageously, disregarding the affections of his relatives.

[Col. 1055]

To the most beloved and greatly longed-for brother LAETUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 1055] Erasmus thought that this letter differed greatly from Augustine’s style and should be attributed to Paulinus. The Louvain theologians disagree, since Possidius, in the *Index*, chapter 7, lists a letter sent to Laetus; and Bede the Vulgate, when citing it in his commentary on 1 Timothy 5, recognizes it as Augustine’s.]

### 1

I read the letter you sent to the brothers, desiring to console you because your beginnings as a novice were being shaken by many temptations; in it you also intimated that you desired a letter from me. I grieved with you, brother, and could not refrain from writing, lest I deny not only your desire but also my own, since I saw that charity required this of me.

If, then, you profess to be a novice of Christ, do not abandon the camp. In it you must also build that tower of which the Lord speaks in the Gospel. When you stand in it and serve under the arms of the word of God, no temptations can penetrate you from any side. From there the missiles cast against the enemy come with great force, while those directed against you are avoided by means of a firm defense.

Consider also that our Lord Jesus Christ, although he is our king, nevertheless, in that fellowship by which he also deigned to be our brother, called his soldiers kings; and he warned each one that he must be prepared to wage war against a king who has twenty thousand men with an army of ten thousand.

### 2

But shortly before he set forth these exhortatory comparisons concerning the tower and the king, notice what he said:

“If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father, and mother, and wife, and children, and brothers, and sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple. And if he does not carry his cross and come after me, he cannot be my disciple.”

Then he adds:

“Who among you, wishing to build a tower, does not first sit down and calculate whether he has enough for its completion, lest, after he has laid the foundation, he should be unable to finish it, and all who pass by and see it should begin to say, ‘This man began to build and was unable to finish’? Or what king, going to engage in war with another king, does not first sit down and consider whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand? Otherwise, while he is still far away, he sends an embassy, asking for peace.”

He clearly showed what these comparisons referred to by their conclusion, for he said:

“So therefore, every one of you who does not renounce all that belongs to him cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:26–33).

### 3

Accordingly, both the expense required to build the tower and the strength [Note: [Col. 1055] Most manuscripts omit “of combatants.”] of ten thousand combatants against a king who has twenty thousand mean nothing other than that each person must renounce all that belongs to him.

The opening statement agrees with the final conclusion. For in renouncing all that belongs to him, each person also renounces his father, mother, wife, children, brothers, sisters, and even his own life. All these are his private possessions, [Col. 1056] which often entangle and hinder him from obtaining—not these private things, which pass away in time, but the common things that remain forever.

For the fact that a certain woman is now your mother does not make her my mother as well. Therefore this is temporal and transitory, as you already see has passed away: she conceived you, carried you in her womb, gave birth to you, and nourished you with milk.

But that she is your sister in Christ is true both for you and for me, and for all those to whom one heavenly inheritance, God as Father, and Christ as brother are promised within the same fellowship of charity. These things are eternal; they are not worn away by any corruption of time. They are hoped for and held all the more firmly because they are proclaimed as things to be obtained not by private but rather by common right.

### 4

You can recognize this very easily in your own mother. For what is it that now ensnares and entangles you, turns you back, and bends you away from the course you have undertaken, except that she is your private mother? Since she is the sister of all those for whom God is Father and the Church is mother, she no longer hinders you—nor does she hinder me or all our brothers, who love her with a public love in the house of God, not with the private love you show her in your own home.

Therefore, the fact that you are attached to her by a bodily relationship should serve to make conversation more familiar and counsel more open, so that this very private love with which she loves you may be put to death in her. She must not value more highly the fact that she bore you from her own womb than the fact that she was born with you from the womb of the Church.

What I have said about your mother should be understood also of every other such relationship. Let each person think the same concerning his own life, so that even in it he may hate the private affection that is undoubtedly temporal. Let him instead love that communion and fellowship of which it is said: “They had one soul and one heart directed toward God” (Acts 4:32).

Thus your soul is not your own but belongs to all the brothers; and their souls also belong to you—or rather, their souls together with yours are not many souls but one soul, the one soul of Christ, whose deliverance from the hand of the dog is sung in the Psalms (Ps. 21:21). From this one reaches contempt of death with great ease.

### 5

Let parents not be angry that the Lord commands us to hate them, since the same is commanded concerning our own life. For just as we are now commanded to hate our life, together with our parents, for Christ’s sake, so what the same Lord says elsewhere about life can most appropriately be applied also to parents:

“He who loves his life will lose it” (John 12:25).

I shall say this confidently: he who loves his parents will lose them. There he spoke of the soul with the word “hate”; here, with the word “lose.” But just as this command, by which we are ordered to lose our life, does not mean that anyone should kill himself—for that is an unforgivable crime—yet it does mean that he should kill within himself the carnal affection of the soul by which the present life, with its impediment to the life to come, is pleasing to him, so too this is what is meant by “he should hate his life” and “he will lose it.” Yet this takes place through loving it, since in the same command he most clearly mentions the fruit of recovering that life, saying: “He who loses it in this world will [Col. 1057] find it unto eternal life.”

So it is rightly said concerning parents that he who loves them will lose them—not killing them in the manner of parricides, but striking and putting to death with the spiritual sword of the word of God their carnal affection, by which they try to bind both themselves and those whom they have begotten with the entanglements of this world. He must do this devoutly and courageously, so that in them there may live that by which they are brothers, by which, together with their temporal children, they recognize God and the Church as their eternal parents.

### 6

Behold, zeal for the truth and for knowing and understanding God’s will in the holy Scriptures carries you away; the ministry of proclaiming the Gospel carries you away. The Lord sounds the signal for us to keep watch in the camp and to build a tower from which we may both see and repel the enemy of eternal life.

The heavenly trumpet summons Christ’s soldier to battle, yet his mother holds him back! She is plainly not like the mother of the Maccabees, nor even like the Spartan mothers, of whom tradition has handed down that they roused their sons to military contests much more strongly and ardently, so that they might shed their blood for their earthly country, than the sound of the standards summoned them.

For the mother who does not allow you to withdraw from secular cares in order to learn the way of life sufficiently shows what she would do if necessary: she would allow you to renounce the world completely in order to face death.

### 7

But what does she say, or what does she plead? Perhaps the ten months during which you burdened her womb, the pains of childbirth, and the labors of raising you. Kill this—yes, this—with the saving word; destroy this aspect of your mother, so that you may find her unto eternal life.

Remember this: if you love her, if you are a novice of Christ, if you have laid the foundations of the tower, hate this in her, lest passers-by say, “This man began to build and was unable to finish.”

For this is a carnal affection, and it still sounds like the old person. Christian warfare urges us to destroy this carnal affection both in ourselves and in our relatives. Yet it does not do so in such a way that anyone becomes ungrateful to his parents or mocks the very benefits by which he was brought into this life, received, and nourished, once they have been enumerated. Rather, let him preserve devotion everywhere; let these obligations have their place wherever greater obligations do not summon him.

### 8

The Church, your mother, is also the mother of your mother. She conceived you both from Christ; she gave birth to you through the blood of the martyrs; she brought you forth into everlasting light; she has nourished and continues to nourish you with the milk of faith. Yet, preparing stronger food, she shudders when you, still little and without teeth, want to cry for it.

This mother, spread throughout the whole world, is harassed by such varied and manifold attacks of error that her aborted children now do not hesitate to wage war against her with unbridled weapons. She also grieves that, through the laziness and sluggishness of certain people whom she holds in her bosom, her limbs grow cold in many places and become less capable of warming her little ones.

From whom, except through other children—except through other members, among whose number you are—does she rightly and necessarily seek help? Will you abandon her needs and turn to carnal words? Does she not resound in your ears with more serious complaints? Does she not display more precious entrails and heavenly breasts?

Add to this the taking on of flesh by her husband, so that you would not cling to carnal things; [Col. 1058] and from the eternal Word add all the things that your mother reproaches you with, so that you would not become entangled in those things that he assumed for you: insults, scourges, death—and death on a cross.

### 9

Conceived by such seeds and begotten for new life through such a marriage, are you growing weak and wasting away in the old person?

Did your Emperor not have an earthly mother? Yet when she was announced to him while he was engaged in heavenly matters, he replied: “Who is my mother, or who are my brothers?” And stretching out his hand toward his disciples, he said that no one belonged to his kinship except those who did the will of his Father (Matt. 12:48–50).

In that number, surely, he graciously included Mary herself, for she too did the Father’s will. Thus the excellent and divine Teacher rejected even the maternal name, which they had announced to him as though it were private and proper to him, because it was earthly, in comparison with heavenly kinship. By recalling that same heavenly kinship in his disciples, he showed by what fellowship of lineage that virgin was again joined to himself and to the other saints.

And lest this most salutary teaching—by which he taught that carnal affection toward parents must be despised—provide support for the error of those who deny that he had a mother, elsewhere he warned his disciples not to call anyone on earth their father (Matt. 23:9). Thus, just as it is evident that they had fathers, he made it evident that he had a mother; yet, by despising that earthly kinship, he offered the disciples an example of despising such relationships.

### 10

So these matters are interrupted by the voices of your mother, and amid them there is room for mention of pregnancy and nursing, so that you might be born and nourished as another Adam from Adam and Eve?

Look instead—look at the second Adam from heaven, and now bear the image of the heavenly one, just as you bore that of the earthly one (1 Cor. 15:47–49).

Indeed, let the very maternal benefits that are recited to weaken your heart have their place here; let them have it entirely. Do not be ungrateful: repay your mother with gratitude; repay spiritual things for carnal things, eternal things for temporal things.

But if she does not wish to follow, let her not impede you. If she does not wish to be converted to something better, beware lest she turn and overthrow you for the worse. What difference does it make whether Eve is present in a wife or in a mother, so long as Eve is avoided in whatever woman she appears?

For this shadow of devotion comes from the leaves of that tree with which our first parents clothed themselves in that damnable nakedness. Whatever, in those words and suggestions, she presents to you as though it were a duty of charity, in order to turn you away from the most genuine and sincere charity of the Gospel, belongs to the serpent’s cunning and to the duplicity of that king who has twenty thousand men. We are taught to overcome this with ten thousand—that is, with the simplicity of the heart in which we seek God.

### 11

Attend rather to these things, dearest brother; take up your cross and follow the Lord. For when I observed that you were being held back from divine devotion by domestic concerns, I sensed that you were being carried and led by your cross, rather than carrying and leading it yourself.

For what else does our cross, which the Lord commands us to carry so that we may follow him with complete freedom, signify except the mortality of this flesh? [Col. 1059] It torments us until death is swallowed up in victory (1 Cor. 15:54).

Therefore this very cross must be crucified and pierced through with the nail of the fear of God, lest, once your limbs are loose and free, you be unable to carry it as it resists you. You cannot follow the Lord at all unless you carry it. For how can you follow him if you are not his?

“But those who belong to Jesus Christ,” says the Apostle, “have crucified their flesh with its passions and desires” (Gal. 5:24).

### 12

If your household has any money, with the business of which you ought neither to be entangled nor occupied, it should indeed be given to your mother and your household members. For if, in order to be perfect, you have decided to distribute such possessions to the poor, the need of these people must have first place with you [Note: [Col. 1059] The editions read, “to distribute such possessions, your own people must have first place with you”; we have corrected the passage from the manuscripts and Bede the Vulgate’s commentary on 1 Timothy 5.]:

“If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially for members of his household,” says the Apostle, “he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. 5:8).

If you left us in order to arrange these matters and to free your neck to be clothed with the bonds of wisdom, how do the tears of your mother, flowing from her flesh, or the flight of a servant, or the deaths of maidservants, or the sickness of your brothers harm you or tear you away?

If your charity is properly ordered, you will know how to put greater things before lesser, and to be moved by compassion so that the poor may be evangelized, lest the Lord’s abundant harvest lie exposed as prey to birds because of a shortage of workers. You will also keep your heart prepared to follow the Lord’s will in whatever he has decided to do with his servants, whether by chastising or sparing them.

Meditate on these things; devote yourself to them, so that your progress may be evident in all things (1 Tim. 4:15).

I beg you to take care lest, through your sluggishness, you cause greater sadness to the good brothers than you had already given them joy by your eagerness. To recommend you by letters, as you wished, I considered just as unnecessary as if someone had wished to recommend you to me in the same manner.

## LETTER 244

[Note: [Col. 1059] Corrected according to a. ff. gg. r. vc., two copies of cb., two of sb., two of t., two of v., and the editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1059] Formerly 83; the letter that was 244 is now 79.]

Augustine to Chrisimus, consoling him so that he may not give way under adversity.

To the truly and deservedly beloved brother, worthy of proclamation, CHRISIMUS

[Note: [Col. 1059] The editions have *Chrysinus*. The manuscripts have *Chrisimus* or *Chrissimus*.]

AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

### 1

Rumor has reported to me—may God grant that it be untrue—that you are so disturbed in mind that I am greatly astonished that your prudence and Christian spirit give so little thought to the fact that earthly circumstances can in no way be compared with heavenly things, where our heart and hope ought to be placed.

Courageous man, was all your good contained in those things that you now seem to be losing? Or did you reckon the good there to be so great that, when it was taken away, your mind should become so darkened by excessive sadness, as though its light were earth and not God?

For I have heard—I have already said, may God grant that I heard falsely—that you even wished to lay hands upon yourself. I would rather not believe that this thought entered your heart or came from your mouth. Yet because you have been so disturbed that such a thing could be said of you, I have been deeply saddened on your account and have thought that your Charity should be consoled by this written address.

I do not doubt, however, that our Lord God is speaking better things in your heart; for I know with what devout zeal you have always listened to his word.

### 2

Therefore lift up your spirit, dearest brother in Christ. Our God is neither lost by his own nor will he lose his own. Rather, he wishes to warn us how fragile and uncertain are the things that people love too much, so that we may loosen from them the bond of desire by which they drag us along in entanglement, and accustom all our love to run toward him, in whom we need fear no losses.

He exhorts you through our ministry to think manfully that you are a faithful Christian and have been redeemed by the blood of him who, not only as eternal wisdom but also in his human presence [Note: [Col. 1060] The editions read “but also through present evils.” We prefer the reading found in an old Corbie manuscript and one manuscript of Saint-Omer.], taught us to despise the prosperity of this world temperately and to endure adversity courageously. He promised the reward of that happiness which no one can take from us.

I have also written to the admirable count. It will be up to you whether you wish that letter to be delivered. As for the person through whom it may be delivered, I do not doubt that, with the Lord’s help, a bishop, presbyter, or anyone else will be available.

## LETTER 245

[Note: [Col. 1060] Corrected according to a. bl. c. cc. ff. g. gv. j. n. r. s. t. vc., two copies of sb., four of v., and the editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1060] Formerly 73; the letter that was 245 is now 8.]

Augustine to Possidius, concerning dress, cosmetics, and earrings, and concerning not ordaining someone baptized in the Donatist party.

To the most beloved and venerable brother and fellow priest POSSIDIUS, and to the brothers who are with you, AUGUSTINE, and the brothers who are with me, send greetings in the Lord.

### 1

One must think more about what to do with those who refuse to obey than about how to show them that what they are doing is unlawful. But at present your Holiness’s letter found me extremely occupied, and the very swift return of the messenger allowed me neither to refrain from writing back nor to respond to the matters on which you consulted me as I ought.

Nevertheless, I do not want you to reach a hasty judgment in prohibiting ornaments of gold or clothing, except in the case of those who are neither married nor wishing to marry and who ought to think about how to please God. Married people think about the things of the world, how either husbands may please their wives or wives their husbands (1 Cor. 7:32–34).

Yet it is not fitting even for married women to uncover their hair, whom the Apostle also commands to cover their heads (1 Cor. 11:5–13). To apply cosmetics so that a woman may appear either redder or whiter is an adulterous deception. I have no doubt that husbands themselves do not wish to be deceived by it, since women are permitted to adorn themselves for them alone, according to concession, not according to command.

For the true adornment of Christian men and women is not merely the absence of deceptive cosmetics, but also not the display of gold or clothing; it is good character.

### 2

The execrable superstition of amulets, among which men’s earrings are also counted when they are suspended from the upper part of one ear, [Col. 1061] is practiced not to please human beings but to serve demons.

Who could find specific prohibitions of wicked superstitions in Scripture, when the Apostle says generally, “I do not want you to become partners with demons” (1 Cor. 10:20), and again, “What harmony is there between Christ and Belial?” (2 Cor. 6:15)?

Perhaps, because he named Belial and prohibited partnership with demons in general, Christians are permitted to sacrifice to Neptune, since we do not read that anything specifically concerning Neptune was forbidden!

For the moment, let these wretched people be warned that, if they refuse to obey the more salutary commands, they should at least not defend their sacrileges, lest they entangle themselves in a greater crime.

But what should be done with people who fear removing their earrings yet do not fear receiving the body of Christ with the devil’s sign? Concerning ordaining someone baptized in the Donatist party, I cannot be your adviser. It is one thing to do something if compelled; it is another to advise that you do it.

## LETTER 246

[Note: [Col. 1061] Not found in the manuscripts except for one Vatican manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 1061] Formerly 243; the letter that was 246 is now 160.]

Augustine to Lampadius, showing that fate is wrongly offered as an excuse for sins, since even the astrologers themselves have no such explanation when punishing their subordinates.

AUGUSTINE TO LAMPADIUS.

### 1

Concerning the question of fate and fortune, by which I noticed that your mind was not slightly disturbed when I was present and have now learned more agreeably and certainly from your letters, I owe you a written response of no small length. May the Lord grant that I explain it as he knows to be suitable for the salvation of your faith.

For it is no small evil to be led by perverse opinions not only into committing sin through the seduction of pleasure, but also, while defending sin, to be turned away from the remedy of confession.

### 2

Know this, at least, as quickly and briefly as possible: all laws and all institutions of discipline—praise, blame, exhortations, terrors, rewards, punishments, and everything else by which the human race is administered and governed—would be utterly weakened and overthrown, and no justice whatsoever would remain in them, unless the will were the cause of sinning.

How much more freely and fairly, then, do we condemn the errors of astrologers than we would be compelled to condemn and reject the divine laws, or even the administration of our own households—which the astrologers themselves do not do!

For when one of them has sold foolish destinies to wealthy people, as soon as he turns his eyes from his ivory tablets back to the management and care of his own household, he corrects his wife not only with words but also with blows—not, I do not say, if he catches her joking too wantonly, but if he notices her looking through the window too immoderately.

If she then says to him, “Why are you beating me? Beat Venus, if you can; she is forcing me to do this,” he does not care what empty words he may compose to deceive strangers, but only what just blows he may inflict to correct his own household.

### 3

[Col. 1062]

Therefore, when someone, once he has begun to be reproved, turns the cause over to fate and does not want to be blamed because he says that fate compelled him to do what he is accused of doing, let him return to himself and apply this principle to his own household.

Let him not punish a thieving slave; let him not complain about an insulting son; let him not threaten a wicked neighbor. For how can he act justly in any of these matters if everyone from whom he suffers injury is driven to act not by his own fault but by fate?

But if, with the authority proper to a householder and the diligence of a father, he urges whatever people he temporarily has under his power toward good, deters them from evil, commands them to obey his will, honors those who obey him at his nod, punishes those who despise him, returns thanks to benefactors, and hates the ungrateful—shall I wait for him to argue against fate, when I discover him declaring all this not in words but in deeds, so that he seems almost to break all the astrologers’ hair over their heads with his own hands?

If your eagerness is not satisfied by these few remarks and you desire some book on the subject which you can read at greater length, you must patiently await the periods when we have leisure and pray to God, who may deign to grant your mind both leisure and opportunity to be satisfied concerning this matter.

I shall nevertheless be more eager if you do not find it burdensome often to recall me affectionately in your letters and if you inform me by writing what you think of this letter.

## LETTER 247

[Note: [Col. 1062] This letter was revised according to bl. cb. vc., two copies of v., and Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 1062] Formerly 211; the letter that was 247 is now 161.]

Augustine to Romulus, a powerful man whom he had begotten in Christ, begging him not to be excessively harsh and unjust in exacting from his administrators the taxes that had been paid; threatening him with the final judgment if he continued to exact them tyrannically.

To his most beloved son ROMULUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

### 1

Truth is both sweet and bitter. When it is sweet, it spares; when it is bitter, it heals. If you do not refuse to drink what I offer in this letter, you will prove what I have said.

Would that whatever insults you direct against me harmed you no more than they harm me; and would that the injustice you inflict upon wretched and poor people harmed you as much as it harms those against whom you inflict it!

They suffer for a time. But consider what you are storing up for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s just judgment, who “will repay each person according to his works” (Rom. 2:5–6).

I beseech his mercy to correct you here as he knows best rather than reserve you for that day, when there will no longer be any opportunity for correction. May he who gave you his fear—for which reason I do not despair of you—open your understanding, so that you may see what you are doing, shudder at it, and amend it.

For the things you do seem small and almost insignificant to you, yet they are such great evils that, when your subdued desire allows you to consider them, you will water the earth with tears so that God may have mercy on you.

Or, if I am unjust in taking this matter up with you, so that wretched and needy people do not pay twice what they owe after the tenants have paid it to their agent, obeying the subordinate official set over them and issuing orders, while that agent cannot deny having received it [Note: [Col. 1062] Thus in all manuscripts; the printed editions read “subordinates.”]—if, then, I am unjust because it seems wrong to me that sums should be demanded twice from people who scarcely manage to pay once, [Col. 1063] do whatever you wish.

But if you see that it is unjust, do what is fitting, do what God commands, and what I ask.

### 2

I ask this of you not chiefly for their sake—he knows whom I fear—but for your own sake. I ask you to show mercy to your own soul, as it is written: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Sirach 30:24).

At present, indeed, you should not be asked but rebuked; for this too is written: “Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline” (Rev. 3:19).

If you were to be asked on my own behalf, perhaps I would not ask you. But because you must be asked for your own sake, I ask you, angry man, to spare yourself, to become pleasing to yourself, so that the one whom you entreat may be pleased with you.

On Saturday, while you were still eating, I sent word to you not to depart unless you had seen me; you announced that you would do so. On Sunday you rose and, as I heard, came to the church and prayed, then departed without wishing to see me.

May God forgive you. What else can I say to you except what he himself knows I desire? But I know that unless you correct yourself, he is just.

When you spare yourself, you also spare me. For I am not so wretched or so estranged from the compassion of Christ that my heart is not struck by a most grievous wound when those whom I begot through his Gospel act in this way.

### 3

Again you will say: “I did not command them to give it to Ponticanus.”

The answer is: “But you commanded them to serve Ponticanus,” and they could not distinguish how far they were to serve him and how far they were not, especially since he was asking for things that they knew they owed.

They ought to have had your letters, which they could produce to the administrator if he was exacting anything against your will, and read back to him that they were not to give anything unless they had received your letters.

For if on some occasion you commanded verbally that they give nothing to the administrator, it is asking much that they should remember it. It is asking much that you yourself should remember whether you truly gave the command, whether you gave it to them, to others, or to everyone—especially since even now you heard that the money had been given to another administrator and was safe, and you were not displeased that they had given it.

But when I said, “What if this man too had diverted it? Would it then have had to be demanded from them again?” you once more began to be displeased that they had given it.

And although you had often told me that you had never assigned your responsibilities to Valerius or Aginesis [Note: [Col. 1063] An old Corbie manuscript reads *Agmesis*, here and below.], suddenly, when the matter concerned wine—because they ought to have shown whether it had begun to sour—and you were told that he was absent, I believe you forgot what you had told me so many times. You said that they had to show it to Aginesis and act according to his judgment.

When I then said, “Certainly you do not usually assign your responsibilities to these men,” you replied, “But Aginesis had my letters”—as though those to whom you assign anything always recite your letters to rustic people, so that they may believe that you gave the order.

But because they see that these men are connected with you in this way, they certainly do not believe that they dare to presume anything rashly unless authority has been given by you. Therefore, amid these uncertainties, it is not apparent what you command, nor can they retain anything firmly unless they have your letters, which they can produce to everyone; [Col. 1064] and they must obey only when your letters have been produced, whenever anything is to be given to them.

### 4

But why should I argue with you for so long and burden your occupations with words, so that perhaps, when you become angry at my words, you may wish to rage against wretched people?

It will be reckoned to their credit as a good deed that, for the sake of your salvation—for which I say so much to you—they endure your anger. But I do not wish to say anything harsher to you, lest you think that I say such a thing out of ill will rather than concern.

Fear God if you do not wish to be deceived. I call him as witness over my soul that, when I say these things, I fear for you more than for those on whose behalf I seem to be interceding with you.

If you believe me, thanks be to God. But if you do not believe me, I am consoled by what the Lord says: “Say, ‘Peace to this house.’ And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him; but if not, it will return to you” (Matt. 10:12–13).

May the mercy of God protect you, my most beloved son and lord.

## LETTER 248

[Note: [Col. 1064] Corrected according to a. bg. c. cc. cb. ff. g. gg. gv. j. n. r. sb. t., two copies of vc., four of v., and the editions.]

[Note: [Col. 1064] Formerly 145; the letter that was 248 is now 263.]

Augustine to Sebastianus, concerning the devout sadness that the good suffer because of the wickedness of the evil. Alypius subscribed this letter.

To the holy and desirable brother, most pleasing in the honor of Christ, SEBASTIANUS

[Note: [Col. 1064] In the Royal, Corbie, German, and other manuscripts he is called “Abbot”; in Possidius’s *Index*, “monk.”]

AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

1. Although the sweet bond of charity in no way permits you to be separated from our heart, and although we continually recall your holy conduct and conversations, you have nevertheless done well, and we give thanks that, by sending us written news of your bodily health as well, you have greatly refreshed us. I sensed from your letter that you have been wearied by sinners who abandon God’s law; for you live by that spirit of which it is said: “I saw the senseless, and I wasted away” (Psalm 118 [119]:53, 158). This is a pious sadness and, if one may so call it, a blessed misery: to be troubled by the vices of others without becoming entangled in them; to grieve without clinging to them; to be drawn inward by sorrow, not attracted by love. This is the persecution endured by all who wish to live piously in Christ, according to the Apostle’s pointed and truthful saying (2 Timothy 3:12). For what persecutes the life of the good here more than the life of the wicked—not when it compels them to imitate what displeases them, but when it compels them to grieve over what they see? For one who lives impiously in the presence of a pious person, although he does not bind the one who refuses consent, torments the one who perceives it. Indeed, the bodies of the impious are often and for a long time spared from secular authorities and all manner of harassment; but the hearts of the pious are never spared from the evil conduct of human beings until the end of this age. Thus rather is fulfilled what I recalled the Apostle saying: “All who wish to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution”; and all the more bitterly, the more inwardly, until the flood passes, in which the ark contains both the raven and the dove.

[Note: Some manuscripts and Bede’s commonly circulated text of 2 Timothy 3 have “of the pious” instead of “of the impious.”]

2. But cling, brother, to him from whom you heard: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 24:13); join yourself to the Lord, so that your life may increase in its final days. For I know that the heart does not lack refreshment from good brothers. Add to this the faithful, great, certain, and everlasting promises of God, and the unshaken and unspeakable reward of endurance itself; then see how truly you sing to the Lord: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul” (Psalm 93:19).

Send our letter to our brother Firmus. The brothers and sisters who are with us salute your Holiness and the household of God governed by your ministry, together with us in the Lord.

*(In another hand:)* Pray for us in good health, dearest and holy brothers.

I, Alypius, send the fullest greetings to your Sincerity and to all who are joined to you in the Lord; and I ask that you regard this as my letter as well. For although I could have sent another letter of my own, I preferred to subscribe to this one, so that our unanimity might also be attested by a single page.

## LETTER 249

[Note: Revised according to manuscripts bl. cb. ff. gg. r. sb. vc., two t., two v., and the editions.]

[Note: Formerly numbered 69; what was 249 is now 94.]

Augustine to Restitutus, on the extent to which evil people are to be tolerated in the Church.

To his most longed-for and honorable son, his very dear brother in sincere affection and fellow deacon, RESTITUTUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

The faithful participant in them, our brother Deogratias—as you know—indicated to me the ardor that reveals the pious flame of your heart. Therefore read Tychonius, whom you know well, though you will certainly not approve everything in him; for you know well what must be avoided in him. Nevertheless, it seems to me that he has vigorously treated and resolved this question: how, if we are unable to correct or extinguish something perverse or even criminal in the Church of God, it may be tolerated while the bond of unity is preserved.

Although his treatment is corrected merely in intention, we ought to return to the very sources of the divine Scriptures, so that there we may see how few testimonies of sayings or examples of actions he has set forth concerning this matter—and how no one could set them all forth unless he wished to transfer nearly all the pages of the holy Books into his own writing. There is scarcely a page that does not warn us that, within the very fellowship of the Sacraments by which we are formed for eternal life, we must remain peaceful with those who hate peace until our long pilgrimage has passed with groaning (Psalm 119:5–7); and that, in the strength of Jerusalem, our eternal mother, we may enjoy the most secure peace and abundance of true brothers in her towers (Psalm 122), though at present, amid many false brothers, we groan over their scarcity.

What, however, is the strength of that city except its God, who is our God? You see, then, in whom alone peace is found: both in individual people who wage war against themselves without him, even when no external scandal has arisen, and in all people together who, although they love one another in this life and are held together by the bonds of faithful friendship, are nevertheless not united in body or mind with complete and perfect closeness. Let your heart be strengthened in the Lord, remembering us.

## LETTER 250

[Note: Corrected according to manuscripts bl. ff. vc., three v., the editions, and the collection of Anselm of Lucca.]

[Note: Formerly numbered 75; what was 250 is now 95.]

Augustine, an old man, to Auxilius, a young bishop, urging him either to rescind the sentence of anathema or to explain on what grounds he thinks that an entire household can be excommunicated on account of one person’s sin.

To his most beloved and venerable brother and fellow priest, AUXILIUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

1. Our distinguished son Classicianus [Note: In Anselm of Lucca it reads: “Count Classicianus.”] has complained to me bitterly in a letter that he has suffered the injustice of anathema from Your Holiness. He relates that he came to the church accompanied by a few people appropriate to his rank and authority, and pleaded with you not to favor, to his own harm, those who, by swearing falsely by the Gospel, were seeking in the very house of faith assistance for violating faith. Yet, he says, when they considered what evil they had done, they were not forcibly dragged away from there but departed voluntarily; and that Your Veneration then became so angry with him that, through the formal ecclesiastical Acts, he and his entire household were struck by the sentence of anathema.

After reading his letter, I was considerably agitated, my thoughts tossed by a great storm in my heart, and I could not remain silent before Your Charity. If you have a judgment on this matter established by certain reasons or by testimonies of Scripture, may you deign to teach us as well how it is right for a son to be anathematized for his father’s sin, a wife for her husband’s, a slave for his master’s, or anyone in a household—even one not yet born—if he is born at the very time when the whole household is bound by anathema, so that he cannot be helped by the washing of regeneration in the danger of death.

For this is not the bodily punishment by which we read that certain despisers of God were killed together with all their people, even though those people had not shared in the same impiety. At that time mortal bodies, which were in any case destined to die, were put to death for the terror of the living. But spiritual punishment, by which what is written is brought about—“Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven” (Matthew 16:19)—binds souls, concerning which it is said: “The soul of the father is mine, and the soul of the son is mine; the soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezekiel 18:4).

2. Perhaps you have heard that certain priests of great reputation anathematized someone together with his household for the sins of that person; but perhaps, if they had been questioned, they would have been found able to give an account of the matter. I, however, since I do not know what answer to give if someone asks me whether this is rightly done, have never dared to do it, even when I was profoundly disturbed by crimes monstrously committed against the Church by certain people.

But if the Lord has perhaps revealed to you that it is justly done, I do not in the least despise your youthful age or the beginnings of your ecclesiastical dignity. Behold, I am here: an old man prepared to learn from a young man, and a bishop of so many years from a colleague not yet a year old, how we can render a just account either to God or to human beings if we punish innocent souls with spiritual punishment for another’s crime—one from which they do not derive, as they derive from Adam, in whom all sinned (Romans 5:12), original sin.

Indeed, although Classicianus’s son inherited from his father the guilt of the first human being, to be cleansed in the sacred font of Baptism, who would doubt that whatever sin his father committed after begetting him, in which the son himself did not share, does not pertain to him?

What shall I say of the wife? What of all the souls in the entire household? If, through this severity by which the whole household has been anathematized, one soul should perish by departing the body without Baptism, the death of countless bodies—even if innocent people were forcibly removed from the Church and killed—could not be compared with that loss.

Therefore, if you can give an account of this matter, I hope that by writing back you will provide one for us also, so that we too may be able to do so. But if you cannot, why, in an ill-considered disturbance of mind, do something for which, if questioned, you are unable to find a proper answer?

3. I have said this even if our son Classicianus committed something that, in your judgment, appeared most justly punishable by anathema. But if he sent me a truthful account, he alone in his household ought not to have been restrained by this sentence.

In this matter I am not dealing with Your Holiness except to ask you to forgive the petitioner if he acknowledges his fault. But if you wisely recognize that he has committed no sin, since he was more justly demanding in the house of faith that faith ought to be preserved, so that it would not be broken in the very place where it is taught, do what a holy man ought to do. If, as a human being, what the man of God says in the Psalm has happened to you—“My eye was troubled because of anger”—cry out to the Lord: “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak” (Psalm 6:8, 3). May he extend his right hand to you, restrain your anger, and calm your mind so that you may see and carry out justice. For it is written: “The anger of man does not accomplish the justice of God” (James 1:20).

Nor should you think that unjust agitation cannot steal upon us because we are bishops. Rather, let us consider that we live most dangerously amid the snares of temptation, because we are human beings.

Therefore remove the ecclesiastical Acts that you perhaps drew up in a more disturbed state, and let the charity return between you which you had with him even when he was a catechumen [Note: Anselm of Lucca reads “catechumens.”]. Remove the quarrel and restore peace, lest a friendly human being perish for you and the hostile devil rejoice over you.

The mercy of our God is powerful. May it hear me as I pray, so that my sadness over you may not increase, but rather that the sadness which has arisen may be healed; and may it raise you up [Note: Anselm of Lucca reads “and guide you.”] by its grace and make your youth glad because it does not despise my old age. Farewell.

## FRAGMENT

Found in an old codex of the Church of Troyes containing the collections of Cresconius and Ferrandus, with the title attached here.

### FROM THE LETTER TO CLASSICIANUS

[Note: This fragment was communicated to us from the papers of N. Rigault by D. de Vion San-Victorinus, canon and doctor of Paris.]

He had been excommunicated.

On account of those who, for the sin of one soul, bind his entire household—that is, very many souls—with anathema, especially lest anyone there depart the body without Baptism, and on the question whether those who flee to the Church in order to break faith with their guarantors should not also be expelled from the Church, I wish, with the Lord’s help, to act in our council and, if necessary, to write to the Apostolic See, so that in these cases it may be established and confirmed, by the concordant authority of all, what we ought to follow.

[Note: The following sentence is found in Anselm of Lucca, book 12, chapter 66, and in Gratian, Causa 11, question 3, canon 87.]

This, certainly, I may say without rashness: if any member of the faithful has been unjustly anathematized, it will harm the one who imposes it more than the one who suffers the injustice. For the Holy Spirit dwelling in the saints, through whom each person is bound or loosed, inflicts no undeserved punishment on anyone. Through him, after all, charity is poured into our hearts, and charity does not act wrongly.

## LETTER 251

[Note: Revised according to manuscripts cb. vc., two v., and Lov.]

[Note: Formerly numbered 212; what was 251 is now 269.]

Augustine to Pancarius, concerning the presbyter Secundinus, accused of certain crimes: he does not wish to admit the accusations of heretics against him, but is prepared to hear those of Catholics.

To his most beloved and deservedly honorable son PANCARIUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

Before Your Reverence arrived, the presbyter Secundinus was not displeasing to the people of Germanicianum. I do not know, then, most beloved and deservedly honorable son, what has now happened that, as you have written, they are even prepared to accuse him of I know not what crimes.

Nevertheless, we cannot in any way disregard what they appear to bring against the presbyter, provided only that those who bring the charges are Catholics. For we neither can nor ought to admit the accusations of heretics against a Catholic presbyter.

Therefore let your Prudence first establish that they are not heretics where they were not heretics before your arrival; and we shall hear the presbyter’s case as it ought to be heard.
