I do, however, offer this admonition, since you deign to accept it: your safety and reputation are very dear to us, and the people of Germanicianum also belong to the care of our humility. Deign confidently to present what you obtained from the most glorious emperors and what you pursued before the competent judges, so that it may be clear to everyone that you are doing nothing disorderly. Otherwise, in your case—for which you are contending over possession—those wretched people may again be wearied and perish under still heavier affliction.

I also commend that the house of the same presbyter not be plundered or laid waste. For it has been reported to us concerning his church that certain people—I do not know who—wish to demolish it; but I do not think that this can in any way be permitted by Your Reverence.

## LETTER 252

[Note: Revised according to manuscripts cb. gv. n. vc., two v., and Lov.]

[Note: Formerly numbered 217; what was 252 is now 179.]

Augustine to Felix, concerning a young girl entrusted to the Church’s guardianship.

To his most beloved and deservedly honorable, distinguished brother FELIX, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

Your Reverence knows very well what care the Church, and bishops in particular, ought to exercise in protecting all people, but especially wards. Therefore, after receiving your letters and the sample letter of our distinguished brother [Note: Perhaps Rusticus, to whom Letter 255 is addressed.], I could neither would nor ought to entrust the girl indiscriminately to anyone—especially since she was commended to the Church, most beloved and deservedly honorable brother whom I esteem.

Accordingly, I am waiting for her arrival, so that, if anything ought to be done, I may deliberate in her presence and do what the Lord inspires should be done.

## LETTER 253

[Note: Letters 253 and 254 are found in no manuscripts except cb. and v.]

[Note: Formerly numbered 232; what was the first Letter 253 is now 237, and what was the second Letter 253 is now 103.]

Augustine to Benenatus, concerning the same girl (as it appears), who is not to be given in marriage except to a Catholic man.

To his most blessed, venerable, and desired brother BENENATUS, and to the brothers who are with him, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

Through him I salute Your Holiness, and we rejoice in his faith and good zeal for the Church. He wished to come to Your Benevolence with my letter, most beloved and venerable brother.

Since I have heard that you are considering reaching an agreement concerning that affair—if it is true, which I am astonished to hear—you know how, with episcopal fatherly care, you ought to provide for the Catholic Church. You should not conduct the matter with just anyone, if what I have heard is true, but rather with a Catholic household, from which the Church may receive not only no opposition but also faithful assistance.

## LETTER 254

[Note: Formerly numbered 233; what was 254 is now 104.]

Augustine to the same Benenatus, who is acting as intermediary for the son of Rusticus.

To his most blessed, venerable, and desired brother and fellow priest BENENATUS, and to the brothers who are with him, AUGUSTINE and the brothers who are with me send greetings in the Lord.

The girl about whom Your Holiness wrote to me is resolved that, if she were already of marriageable age, she would marry no one. In fact, she is at an age when, even if she had the desire to marry, she ought not yet to be given or promised to anyone.

Moreover, God so protects her in the Church that he protects her against wicked men—not so that she may be handed over to whomever I wish, but so that she may not be seized by one to whom she ought not be given, most beloved and venerable brother Benenatus.

The condition you have been pleased to suggest therefore does not displease me, if she is to marry. Whether she is in fact going to marry, however, although we now especially desire what she says with her mouth, we do not know; for she is at an age when her claim that she wishes to be a consecrated virgin may be merely the joke of a talkative girl rather than the pledge of one making a profession.

Furthermore, she has a maternal aunt whose husband is our honorable brother Felix. When I discussed this matter with him—for I could neither have done otherwise nor ought I to have done so—he did not receive it unwillingly; indeed, he was even glad. But, by the right of friendship, he was not without proper sorrow that nothing had been written to them about it.

For perhaps her mother, who is not now in view, will appear; and, as I believe, nature gives everyone priority to the mother’s will in giving away a daughter—unless the girl has already reached an age at which she may with greater freedom choose for herself what she wishes.

Your Sincerity should also consider this: if complete and supreme authority over her marriage were granted to me, and if she herself were already mature and willing to marry, entrusting herself to me under the judgment of God to be given to whomever I wished, I say this, and I say it truthfully: I would approve this condition, so that, because of God the judge, I could not reject the better choice. Whether such a situation will arise is, of course, uncertain.

Therefore Your Charity sees how many considerations converge, so that at present it is entirely impossible for me to promise her to anyone.

## LETTER 255

[Note: Letters 255 and 256 were revised according to two manuscripts, cb. and v.]

[Note: Formerly numbered 234; what was 255 is now 108.]

Augustine to Rusticus, concerning a girl sought in marriage for his son.

To his most beloved, deservedly praiseworthy, and venerable son RUSTICUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

Although I wish every good thing for you and your entire household—not only those things belonging to the happiness of the present age, but also those belonging to the future and eternal life, whose truth you have not yet been persuaded to believe—nevertheless, concerning the girl whom you seek, I have not yet dared to promise anything. I have written to my holy brother and fellow bishop Benenatus what seemed sufficient to me, most beloved and venerable son.

For if you, although you know with complete certainty that, even if it were entirely within our power to give any girl in marriage, we could not give a Christian woman to anyone except a Christian, nevertheless did not wish me to promise you anything of the kind concerning your son, whom I hear is still a pagan, how much more ought I, on account of what you will be able to read in the letter of the brother I mentioned, not to pledge anything concerning that girl’s marriage—even if I held what I said about your son not merely as a promise, but rejoiced that it had already been done?

## LETTER 256

[Note: Formerly numbered 226; what was 256 is now 216.]

Augustine writes courteously to Christinus.

To his deservedly praiseworthy, sincerely beloved, and greatly desired brother CHRISTINUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

Your letter informed me that you desired a letter from me. Brother Jacobus came as a richer witness of your desire for us, for he told me more pleasant things about you, things he had experienced in himself, than that little sheet of paper could contain.

Therefore I congratulate your Benevolence and give thanks to our Lord God for your Christian heart, since these are his gifts, most deservedly praiseworthy, sincerely beloved, and greatly desired brother.

As for your request that I seek you out in writing, I seek you with affection, which surpasses every letter; and I know where I should seek you, as you understand well. As far as my being read is concerned, I fear that my loquacity will be criticized in your hands more than I expect eloquence to be sought.

I shall say briefly what you will perceive if you ponder it at length: on God’s road, easier and fruitful things are avoided through cowardly sloth, while on the worldly road, harder and barren things are endured through toil and misery.

May you remain safe in Christ, flourish, and advance, most deservedly praiseworthy, sincerely beloved, and greatly desired brother.

## LETTER 257

[Note: Revised according to manuscripts a. bl. c. cb. ff. g. gv. j. n. r. s. sb., four v., and the editions.]

[Note: Formerly numbered 123; what was 257 is now 142.]

Augustine to Orontius, returning his greetings.

To his distinguished, deservedly honorable, and worthy son ORONTIUS, AUGUSTINE.

I give thanks that you were pleased to anticipate even the arrival of Your Eminence in a letter, and that, before I could behold you, you sent a conversation, so that we might enjoy your words before your appearance and, as it were, previewing through the solace of a letter the acquaintance we had long desired, await you more eagerly and ardently, in order to receive you with greater pleasure and gratitude, most distinguished, deservedly honorable, and venerable son.

I therefore return to your merits and your preceding courtesies the due service of reciprocal greeting, rejoicing that your health has been announced and wishing that it may continue.

You added, in reclaiming a reply from my smallness by right of the benevolence you had shown first, the words: “If only we can deserve this from so great a holiness.” I in no way dare to despair of this. The very source of that holiness from which we have drawn something according to our measure is not only to be praised but also to be shared with us, and it will please your Prudence, so that God, incomparably and unchangeably good, who by his power formed such a good mind in you, may also by his grace restore it.

May almighty God guard you unharmed and make you happier, most distinguished, deservedly honorable, and venerable son.

## LETTER 258

[Note: Revised according to manuscripts a. bg. bl. c. cc. cb. ff. g. gg. gv. n. r. s. sb. t., two vc., four v., and the editions.]

[Note: Formerly numbered 155; what was 258 is now 158.]

Augustine to Martianus, an old friend, congratulating him on becoming a catechumen and exhorting him to receive the Sacraments of the faithful.

To his deservedly welcome lord, and most beloved and greatly desired brother in Christ, MARTIANUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

1. I have snatched—or rather stolen—myself away from my many occupations, in a manner of speaking, in order to write to you, an ancient friend whom I did not possess, however, for as long as I did not possess you in Christ.

You know how the Roman defined friendship, as Tullius, a supreme authority in eloquence, says [Lucan, Book 7]. He said—and said most truthfully: “Friendship is agreement concerning human and divine matters, with benevolence and affection” (Cicero, *Laelius* 20).

But you, my dearest friend, once agreed with me concerning human matters, when I desired to enjoy them in the manner of the crowd; and by favoring my pursuit of those things of which I now repent, you filled my sails—or rather, together with my other friends at that time, you inflated the sails of my desires with the breeze of praise.

But concerning divine matters, whose truth had not yet shone upon me at that time, our friendship was certainly deficient in the greater part of that definition. It was agreement concerning merely human matters, not divine ones, although accompanied by benevolence and affection.

2. And after I ceased to desire those things, while your benevolence continued, you wished me to be safe with a mortal safety and happy with the prosperity of worldly affairs, as the world is accustomed to wish. Thus, to some extent, there was already between us a benevolent and affectionate agreement concerning human matters.

But now, how can I express in words how greatly I rejoice in you, when the man whom I had for a long time as a friend in some fashion I now have as a true friend? For agreement concerning divine matters has also been added, since you who once spent temporal life with me in the most pleasant kindness have now begun, with me, to share the hope of eternal life.

Now there is also no disagreement between us concerning human matters, since we weigh them by the knowledge of divine things, so that we do not assign them more importance than their measure most justly requires; nor, by casting them away in contempt, do we wrong their Creator, the Lord of heavenly and earthly things.

Thus it comes about that among friends in whom there is no agreement concerning divine matters, there cannot be a complete and true agreement concerning human matters either. For one who despises divine things must assess human things otherwise than he ought; and no one knows how to love a human being rightly who does not love the one who made the human being.

Therefore I do not say that you are now more fully my friend, though previously you were my friend in part; rather, so far as reason shows, you were not even my friend in part, since you did not possess a true friendship with me even in human matters. You were not yet my companion in divine matters, by which human things are rightly weighed—whether when I myself was not yet involved in them, or after I had begun, however imperfectly, to understand them, while you were far removed from them.

3. Do not become angry, then, nor think it absurd that, at the time when I was burning with the empty passions of this world, although you seemed to love me greatly, you were not yet my friend—since I myself was not my own friend but rather my enemy. For I loved iniquity; and the true divine judgment is that which is written in the holy Books: “The one who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Psalm 10:6).

Since I hated my own soul, how could I have a true friend who wished for me the things in which I myself was suffering as my own enemy? But when the kindness and grace of our Savior shone upon me—not according to my merits, but according to his mercy—how could you, being estranged from this, be my friend? You had no knowledge at all of the source of my blessedness, and you did not love me in that in which I had already, to some extent, become my own friend.

4. Thanks be to God, then, that at last he deigns to make you my friend. For now we possess in Christ Jesus our Lord, our truest peace, agreement concerning human and divine things, with benevolence and affection.

He included all the divine proclamations in two commandments, saying: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind”; and, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” “On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matthew 22:37–40).

In the first of these there is agreement concerning divine matters; in the second, agreement concerning human matters, with benevolence and affection. If you hold these two most firmly with me, our friendship will be true and everlasting; and it will join not only us to one another but also both of us to the Lord himself.

5. To bring this about, I exhort your gravity and prudence now also to receive the Sacraments of the faithful. For this befits your age and, I believe, accords with your character. Remember what you said to me when I was setting out—a comic verse from Terence, if you recall it, but nevertheless most apt and useful:

> Now this day brings another life; it demands other manners.  
> *(Terence, *Andria*, Act 1, Scene 2.)*

If you spoke truthfully, as I ought not to doubt about you, then surely you are now living in such a way that you are worthy to receive Baptism and obtain remission of your past sins. For the human race has no one else to whom it can say:

> With you as guide, if any traces of our crime remain,  
> You will make them void and release the earth from everlasting fear.  
> *(Virgil, *Eclogue* 4.)*

Virgil admitted that he transferred this from the Cumaean—that is, the Sibylline—poem, since perhaps that prophetess too had heard in the spirit something concerning the one Savior, which she was obliged to acknowledge.

I have written these things to you, deservedly welcome lord and most beloved and greatly desired brother in Christ, whether they are few or perhaps many, while exceedingly occupied. I long to receive your reply and to learn immediately that you have enrolled, or are about to enroll, among the candidates for Baptism.

May our Lord God, in whom you have believed, preserve you both in this age and in the age to come, deservedly welcome lord and most beloved and greatly desired brother in Christ.

## LETTER 259

[Note: Revised according to manuscripts a. bg. bl. c. cc. ff. g. gv. j. n. r. s. sb. t., four v., and the editions.]

[Note: Formerly numbered 125; what was 259 is now 151.]

Augustine to Cornelius, devoted to prostitutes, admonishing him to imitate the chastity of his deceased wife Cypriana if he wishes to obtain her praises.

To his most beloved and honorable brother CORNELIUS, AUGUSTINE.

1. You wrote asking me to send you some lengthy letter of consolation because you were deeply distressed by the death of your excellent wife, as you remember that the holy Paulinus did for Macarius.

That soul, having been received into the fellowship of the faithful and chaste, neither cares for nor seeks human praise. But since these things are done for the sake of those who live, it is first necessary that you, who desire consolation through her praise, live in such a way that you may deserve to be where she is.

For I do not doubt that you do not believe her to be in the place where those women are who either polluted the marriage bed by adultery or, bound by no marriage, flowed into fornication.

Therefore, to wish to drive away grief by praising her to a husband utterly unlike her is flattery, not consolation. For if you loved her as she loved you, you would have preserved for her what she preserved for you. And since, if you had died first, it is in no way to be believed that she would have married anyone, would you not, if you were truly grieving her death and wished to be consoled by her praises, seek not even one lawful wife after her?

2. Here you will say: “Why are you dealing harshly with me? Why do you rebuke me severely? Have we not grown old amid these words, while life is being led that ought to be ended before it is corrected?”

You want me to forgive your ruinous complacency. How much more fitting it is for you to forgive my concern—if not loving, at least compassionate—for you!

Tullius was speaking with a hostile spirit, and the intention of one governing an earthly republic was altogether different; nevertheless he said: “I wish, Conscript Fathers, to be merciful; I wish, amid such dangers to the republic, not to appear negligent” (Cicero, *For Sextus Roscius*).

How much more justly may I speak in this way, since you know what a friendly spirit I bear toward you, established as I am in the service of the eternal city as a minister of the divine word and Sacrament: “I wish, brother Cornelius, to be merciful; I wish, amid such great dangers to you and to me, not to appear negligent”?

3. A crowd of women keeps watch at your sides; the number of your mistresses grows daily. Shall we bishops patiently listen to their master—or rather, their slave—pouring himself out in insatiable lust among so many prostitutes, demanding from us, as though to soothe his grief, the praises of his deceased chaste wife by right of friendship?

When you were, I will not say a catechumen, but a young man standing with us in the most destructive error, you had corrected yourself, by a most temperate resolve, from this vice, and you were younger than we were. Yet, after not a long time, you returned to it in a more sordid form; then, baptized in the final danger of your life—I will not say in your old age, but certainly when we were already old men and, moreover, bishops—you have still not been corrected.

You wish us to console you over the death of a good wife. Who consoles us over this more genuine death of yours? Or, because we cannot forget the great services you once rendered us, must we therefore continue to be tormented by your conduct, despised, and regarded as worthless, when we groan to you about you?

But we confess that we are not sufficient to correct and heal you. Let God be regarded, let Christ be considered, let the Apostle be heard saying: “Taking the members of Christ, shall I make them members of a prostitute?” (1 Corinthians 6:15).

If you disregard in your heart the words of your bishop friend, consider the body of your Lord in your own body. Finally, how can you continue to sin by postponing from day to day, when you do not know your final day?

[Note: Five Gallican manuscripts and two Vatican manuscripts read “since” (*quoniam*); four others read “because” (*quia*).]

4. Now I shall show what praises of Cypriana you desire from our mouth. Certainly, if I were still selling words to students in the school of rhetoric, I would first take payment from them. I wish to sell you praise of your most chaste wife; first give me your payment: your chastity. Give it, I say, and receive.

I speak in human terms, because of your weakness. I think that Cypriana is not worthy in your eyes, since you place the love of your concubines before her praises. You will certainly do this if you prefer to remain in that love rather than attain these praises.

Why do you seek to extort from me by asking for what you see is demanded for your own sake? Why do you plead as a subject for what you could command as a corrected man?

Let us send spiritual gifts to your wife: you, imitation; I, praise. Yet, as I said above, she no longer seeks praise from human beings. But she seeks your imitation, even in death, as much as while alive she loved you despite your dissimilarity to her.

I shall do for her what you wish when you have done what both I and she desire.

5. For if that proud and impious rich man, as the Lord speaks in the Gospel—the man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day—when he was paying the penalty for his evil deeds among the dead and had been unable to obtain even a drop of water from the finger of the despised poor man at his gate, remembered his five brothers and begged that the same poor man, whose repose he saw far off in Abraham’s bosom, be sent to them, lest they too should come to that place of torment (Luke 16:19–28): how much more does your wife remember you? How much more does she, being chaste, not wish you to come to the punishment of adulterers, if even the proud man did not wish his brothers to come to the punishment of the proud? And when a brother did not wish his brothers to be joined with him in misery, how much less does a wife, established among the blessed, wish to have her husband separated from her among the miserable?

Read the passage itself in the Gospel: it is Christ’s merciful voice; believe God. You evidently grieve for your dead wife and think that, if I praise her, you will be comforted by my words. Learn what you should grieve over: that you will not be with her. Is it more grievous to you that she is not yet praised by me than it is to me that she is not loved by you? For surely, if you loved her, you would desire to be with her after death—and you certainly will not be there if you remain what you are. Love, therefore, the one whose praise you demand, lest I justly refuse what you wrongly demand.

*(By another hand:)* May the Lord grant us to rejoice in your salvation, most beloved lord and honorable brother.

## LETTER 260

[Note: Letters 260 and 261 were collated with manuscripts a, bl, c, cc, ff, g, gv, j, n, r, s, sb, t, vc, four manuscripts designated v, and the editions.]

[Note: Elsewhere 139; what was formerly numbered 260 is now 180.]

Audax to Augustine, requesting that a longer letter be sent to him.

To the truly praiseworthy lord, most worthy of veneration, father AUGUSTINE, to be honored with every kind of praise, AUDAX sends greetings in the Lord.

I give thanks to Your Blessedness for having willingly accepted my attempts at speech; for sons of good faith are given boldness when they have been watered by the rains of their father’s fountain. Thus I challenged you, sweet bishop, not that I might receive a little draught from your lavish heart, but that I might drink deeply from the immense and abundant river of your wealth. I desired the treasure of wisdom, but received less than I wished—though it ought not to be called “less,” but rather a gift, since Augustine, the oracle of the Law, the consecrator of justice, the restorer of spiritual glory, and the dispenser of eternal salvation, has bestowed it.

The worldly sphere is as known to you as it is marked out; you are as well known to it as you are approved by it. Therefore I desire to be nourished by the flowers of wisdom and watered by draughts from the living fountain. Grant what will surely benefit the one who longs for it. Even the genital covering of one almost naked in strength can grow green, if it deserves to be increased little by little by your flowing streams.

Therefore I promise the presence of my humility, not so much in writing as in desire, if I reread the writings of Your Venerability in place of your presence. [Note: Three manuscripts read “at your command” instead of “in place of your presence.”] May divine mercy protect you for countless years, venerable lord.

Why has the fountain of the world flowed forth in a little stream?

Has it thought hearts too little suited to its waters?

Since every mind lies open to the waters and beholds the eloquent

aid of religion, grant grateful rains to the senses,

which full faith in Christ, hanging from the stock, awaits.

## LETTER 261

[Note: Elsewhere 140; what was formerly numbered 261 is now 209.]

Augustine excuses his occupations to Audax, advising him either to devote himself to reading Augustine’s books or to hear him speak in person.

To his most beloved brother Audax, praiseworthy in Christ and greatly desired, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

### 1

I received your short letter—plainly a vehement demand for a lengthy letter from me—not unwillingly, but even gladly. This was not because I could easily satisfy your eagerness, but because I rejoiced in your love; for although you seek from one unable to provide it, what you seek is nevertheless good. I lack time more than ability for composing a long letter. I am, of course, extremely occupied with ecclesiastical concerns, from which only a few drops of time scarcely allow me to recover—whether while thinking out something, dictating what seems more urgent and likely to benefit more people, or restoring the bodily strength necessary for our service.

Words, indeed, are not lacking with which many pages could be filled; but as for that abundance of speech which you desire from me, I reply that I am not adequate to it. You said that you desired the treasure of wisdom but received less than you wished, while I myself beg a daily allowance from that treasure with a beggar’s prayer and scarcely obtain it.

### 2

But how am I the oracle of the Law, when from its broad and hidden inner chambers I know far more that I do not know than what I do know, and cannot approach and penetrate its many recesses and shadowy retreats as I wish, recognizing myself to be nothing other than unworthy?

Moreover, who am I to be called the consecrator of justice, when it is already a very great thing for me to be consecrated to it? And when you call me the restorer of spiritual glory, forgive me: you do not know well the one to whom you are speaking. I myself am still being restored in that glory in such a way that I confess I do not know, from day to day, not only how much I am advancing but whether I am advancing at all.

I am plainly a dispenser of eternal salvation together with my countless fellow servants. If I do this willingly, I receive a reward; but if unwillingly, only a stewardship has been entrusted to me. For to be a dispenser of that salvation through word and sacrament does not thereby mean that one is also a participant in it. If it were not dispensed through the good, the Apostle would not rightly say, “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. 4:1, 16). Again, if it were not dispensed through the wicked, the Lord would not say of certain people, “Do whatever they say, but do not do what they do; for they speak but do not act” (Matt. 23:3).

There are therefore many dispensers through whose ministry one reaches eternal salvation. But among dispensers it is required that one be found faithful (1 Cor. 4:2). And among those faithful, in whose number may the One who does not deceive count me, “one is thus, another is thus” (ibid. 7:7), according as God has allotted to each a measure of faith (Rom. 12:3).

### 3

Therefore, dearest and sweetest brother, may the Lord nourish you rather with the flowers of wisdom and water you with draughts from the living fountain. If you think that anything can be contributed to your most religious zeal through my little work—since I understand that you are capable and perceive that you are eager—you should direct your attention more to some of our other works, which are contained in many volumes, than hope for something in letters that could satisfy your desire.

Or else, come in person and receive what I can offer. I think you have not presented yourself to us because you do not wish to. What great thing is it, with the Lord’s help, for a man free from the obligation of any post to come to us, whether you intend to remain with us for a long time or to return after at least a little while?

### 4

Behold, what you placed third among your five lines has almost come to pass: you have obtained a letter from me more loquacious than eloquent. But in the fifth and final line there are seven feet. I do not know whether the number deceived your ear or whether you wished to test whether I still remember how to judge such things—things perhaps already forgotten by those who were once devoted to them and later made great progress in ecclesiastical literature.

### 5

I do not possess the Psalter translated from Hebrew by Saint Jerome. We did not translate it; rather, we corrected some corrupt readings in the Latin manuscripts from Greek exemplars. Thus perhaps we made something more serviceable than it had been, but not yet what it ought to have been. Even now, if, as we read, passages that escaped us at that time draw our attention, we correct them by comparing manuscripts. Thus we too, together with you, continue to seek what has been perfected.

## LETTER 262

[Note: Revised from manuscripts a, bg, bl, c, cc, ff, g, gv, j, n, r, s, sb, vc, two manuscripts designated t, four designated v, and the editions.]

[Note: Elsewhere 199; what was formerly numbered 262 is now 229.]

Augustine sharply corrects Ecdicia, who, without her husband’s knowledge, had distributed her possessions as alms and had assumed widows’ dress, ordering her to make satisfaction to her husband concerning these matters.

To the most religious lady and daughter ECDICIA, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

[Note: Ancient German manuscripts and the Corbie manuscript read “Egdicia.”]

### 1

After reading the letter of Your Reverence and questioning its bearer about what remained to be asked, I grieved profoundly that you had chosen to deal with your husband in such a way that the building of continence, which had already begun to be constructed in him, should, through the loss of perseverance, collapse miserably into adultery.

For he would have been worthy of mourning if, after having vowed continence to God and already undertaking it in conduct and way of life, he had returned to conjugal intercourse. How much more must we mourn this man, now plunged into deeper destruction, who commits adultery through so abrupt a dissolution—angry with you, destructive to himself—as though he would inflict more bitter harm upon you if he himself perished?

This great evil occurred because you did not handle his spirit with the moderation you ought to have shown. Although by mutual agreement you were no longer joined in bodily intercourse, in all other matters you ought nevertheless, as a wife, to have served your husband with conjugal obedience, especially since both of you were members of Christ’s body. And certainly, if, being faithful yourself, you had had an unbelieving husband, you ought to have conducted yourself in submissive behavior so as to win him for the Lord, as the Apostles instructed.

### 2

I pass over the fact that I have learned that you undertook continence, before he was willing, contrary to sound doctrine. He ought not to have been deprived of the debt of your body before, concerning that good which surpasses conjugal chastity, his will had also been added to your will—unless perhaps you had not read, heard, or attended to the Apostle’s words:

“It is good for a man not to touch a woman. But because of fornications, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband. Let the husband render the debt to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; likewise also the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does. Do not defraud one another, except by agreement for a time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer; and come together again, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control” (1 Cor. 7:1–17).

According to these apostolic words, even if he had wished to practice continence and you had not, he would have been compelled to render the debt to you. God would have credited continence to him if, yielding not to his own weakness but to yours, he did not refuse you marital intercourse, lest you fall into the punishable outrage of adultery. How much more ought you, who should have been more submissive, to have obeyed his will in rendering such a debt, lest he too be drawn into adultery by the devil’s temptation, since God would accept your will to practice continence because you would not do so lest your husband perish?

### 3

But, as I said, I pass over this, because afterward, when you were unwilling to consent to render the conjugal debt to him, he himself consented to the same compact of continence, lived with you for a long time in the strictest continence, and by his consent absolved you from the sin whereby you denied him the debt of the flesh.

The question in your case is therefore no longer whether you ought to return to intercourse with your husband. What both of you had vowed to God by mutual agreement, both of you ought to have fulfilled perseveringly to the end. If he has fallen from that resolve, you at least must persevere with complete steadfastness. I would not exhort you to this if he himself had not consented to it with you.

For if you had never obtained his agreement, no number of years would have defended you. Even if you had consulted me after any length of time, I would have answered you nothing other than what the Apostle says: “The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does.” By that authority he had already permitted you to practice continence in such a way that he himself would undertake it with you.

### 4

But this is what I regret you observed too little: the more religiously he had granted you so great a thing by imitating you, the more humbly and obediently you ought to have served him in domestic life.

It was not because you abstained equally from sexual intercourse that he ceased to be your husband. Rather, you remained husbands and wives all the more holily insofar as you jointly observed holier agreements. Therefore you ought not to have done anything concerning your clothing, your gold or silver, your money, or any of your earthly possessions without his decision, lest you scandalize the man who had vowed greater things to God with you and who had continently abstained from what he could lawfully have demanded from your body.

### 5

In the end it happened that contempt caused him to break the bond of continence with which that beloved man had bound himself, and, angry with you, he did not spare himself. For, as the bearer of your letter reported to me, when he learned that you had given away all or nearly all that you possessed to some two wandering monks, as though they were poor men to be assisted, he then detested them along with you. He considered them not servants of God but intruders into another’s household, your captors and plunderers; and in indignation he cast away the holy burden that he had undertaken with you.

He was weak, and therefore you, who seemed stronger in the common undertaking, ought not to have disturbed him by presumption but to have carried him through love. Even if he was perhaps moved somewhat sluggishly to make those very alms more generously, he could have learned this as well if he had not been struck by your unexpected expenditures, but invited by anticipated acts of service. Then even what you rashly did alone could have been done by both of you with far greater deliberation, concordant love, order, and propriety.

Nor would God’s servants have been blasphemed—if indeed these men were God’s servants—when, in the husband’s absence and without his knowledge, they accepted so much from an unknown woman and another man’s wife. God would have been praised in your works, whose fellowship would have been so faithful that you would jointly maintain not only complete chastity but also glorious poverty.

### 6

Now, however, consider in your thoughtless haste what you have done. Even if, concerning those monks, whom your husband complains had not built you up but stripped you, I should form a favorable opinion, and even if I should not readily agree against servants of God with a man whose vision is disturbed by anger, is it really as great a good that you refreshed the bodies of the poor with more generous alms as it is an evil that you destroyed your husband’s mind, which had embraced so good a purpose?

Should the temporal salvation of anyone have been dearer to you than his eternal salvation? If, considering the greater mercy, you had delayed distributing your possessions to the poor so that your scandalized husband would not perish before God, would God not have credited you with more abundant alms?

Therefore, if you recall what you had gained when you had won your husband so that he might serve Christ with you in holier chastity, understand how much more grievously you have been struck by the loss caused by those alms, through which his heart was overturned, than by the gains you imagined to be heavenly.

If broken bread has a great place there when given to the hungry, how great a place must be believed to belong there to the mercy by which a human being is snatched from the devil, like a roaring lion seeking someone to devour?

### 7

We do not say this in such a way as to think that, if someone has been scandalized by our good works, we should cease performing them. But there is one case when the persons involved are strangers, another when they are necessary members of some relationship; one case concerns a faithful person, another an unbeliever; one concerns parents toward children, another children toward parents.

Finally, there is the case that must be considered above all in these matters: husband and wife. A married woman may not say, “I do what I wish with what is mine,” since she herself is not her own but belongs to her head, that is, to her husband (Eph. 5:23).

Thus, as the Apostle Peter recalls, certain holy women who hoped in God adorned themselves while submitting to their husbands. Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord; “you have become her daughters,” he says (1 Pet. 3:5–6)—and he was speaking to Christian women, not Jewish women.

### 8

What wonder, then, if the father did not wish their common son to be deprived by his mother of the means of sustaining this life, since he did not know what the boy would pursue when he reached a more mature age: the monastic profession, ecclesiastical ministry, or the bond of marriage?

Although the children of holy people ought to be directed and instructed toward better things, each person nevertheless has his own gift from God: “one is thus, another is thus” (1 Cor. 7:7). Unless perhaps a father is to be blamed for looking ahead and taking precautions, when the blessed Apostle says: “If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially for his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. 5:8).

When he was speaking about giving alms, he said: “Not that there should be relief for others and hardship for you” (2 Cor. 8:13). You should therefore have taken counsel together about everything and jointly determined what should be stored up in heaven and what should be left for the sufficiency of this life—for yourselves, your household, and your son—lest there be relief for others and hardship for you.

In arranging and carrying out these matters, if something seemed better to you, you should respectfully have suggested it to your husband and obediently followed his authority as your head. Then all who think soundly, to whom the good reputation of your household might reach, would rejoice in the fruitfulness and peace of your home, and the adversary would be put to shame, having nothing evil to say about you.

### 9

If, then, concerning giving alms and spending your possessions on the poor—an excellent and great work concerning which the Lord’s commands are so explicit—you ought to have consulted your faithful husband, who was maintaining with you the holy compact of continence, and ought not to have despised his will, how much more ought you not to have changed or assumed anything concerning your habit and clothing without his decision, since we read of no divine commandment concerning this?

It is indeed written that women should be in becoming attire; but the placing of gold around them, the twisting of their hair, and other such things, which are commonly employed either for empty display or for the enticement of beauty, are rightly condemned (1 Tim. 2:9). [Note: This is the reading of the Bad., Am., and Er. editions, supported by the manuscripts with broad agreement, except that the Gallican manuscripts have “ordered” instead of “becoming.” In Lov.’s edition the passage reads: “It is indeed written that women should not be in becoming attire, with gold arranged around them and hair twisted, and other things of this sort,” and these things are rightly condemned.]

There is, however, a matronly dress appropriate to a person’s station and distinct from widows’ clothing, which can suitably be worn by married Christian women without violating religious observance. If your husband did not wish you to put this aside, lest you behave as though you were a widow while he was alive, I think this matter ought not to have been carried as far as the scandal of disagreement, since the evil of disobedience is worse than the good of any abstinence.

What is more absurd than for a woman to be proud toward her husband because of humble clothing, when it would be more fitting for you to obey him with a bright character than to oppose him with dark garments? Even if the dress of a nun pleased you, it could have been adopted more acceptably by showing due regard for, and obtaining the consent of, your husband than by presuming it without consulting him and in contempt of him.

And if he absolutely refused to permit it, what would your purpose have lost? Far be it from us to suppose that you would displease God because, while your husband was not yet dead, you did not dress like Anna but like Susanna.

### 10

Nor would the man who had already begun with you to preserve so great a good of continence, even if he wished you to wear married rather than widowed clothing, have compelled you to indecent adornment as well. Even if you were compelled by some harsh necessity to do this, you could have a humble heart beneath proud attire.

Indeed, among the fathers, Esther—the queen who feared God, worshiped God, and was subject to God—served submissively under a foreign king who did not worship the same God as she did. When, in the extreme danger not only of herself but also of her nation, which at that time was God’s people, she prostrated herself before the Lord in prayer, she said in that very prayer that her royal adornment was to her like a menstrual cloth (Esther 14:16). The One who searches the heart knew that she spoke truly and immediately heard her prayer.

She had, of course, a husband who was the husband of many women and a worshiper of alien and false gods. But if your husband had persevered in the purpose he had undertaken with you, and if he had not been offended by you and fallen into outrage, you would have had a husband who was not only faithful and a worshiper with you of the true God, but also continent. Certainly, mindful of your shared purpose, even if he compelled you to wear married women’s clothing, he would not have compelled you to wear proud ornaments.

### 11

I have written these things to you because you thought you should consult me—not to break your right resolve by my words, but because I grieved at your husband’s action when you acted disorderly and carelessly. [Note: Perhaps “broken,” namely, the husband’s right resolve.]

You must think most earnestly about repairing it if you truly wish to belong to Christ. Put on humility of mind, therefore, and, so that God may preserve you in perseverance, do not despise your husband as he perishes.

Pour out pious and continual prayers for him; sacrifice tears like the blood of a wounded heart. Write to him making satisfaction and asking forgiveness, because you sinned against him by acting concerning your possessions without his counsel and will—not because you regret giving to the poor, but because you refused to have him share in and regulate your good work.

Promise that henceforth, with the Lord’s help, if he too repents of his disgrace and takes up again the continence he abandoned, you will serve him in everything as is fitting. Perhaps, as the Apostle says, God may grant him repentance so that he may recover from the devil’s snares, by whom he is held captive according to the devil’s will (2 Tim. 2:25–26).

As for your son, since you conceived him from a lawful and honorable marriage, who does not know that he is more under his father’s authority than yours? Therefore he cannot be denied to his father wherever the father learns that he is and lawfully demands him. Consequently, if the child is to be brought up and instructed in the wisdom of God according to your wishes, your concord with one another is also necessary.

## LETTER 263

[Note: Not found in the manuscripts except one Vatican manuscript.]

[Note: Elsewhere 248; what was formerly numbered 263 is now 230.]

Augustine tells the virgin Sapida that he has received the tunic she had woven with her own hands for her brother, whom she was mourning as dead, and that he had already put it on—the comfort she had desired him to provide. He further exhorts her to make use of a fuller and truer consolation drawn from faith in the divine Scriptures.

To the most religious lady and holy daughter SAPIDA, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

### 1

I accepted what you wished me to receive from the just and pious labor of your hands, lest I should grieve you more severely when I ought rather to console you. This was especially because you considered it no small consolation if I wore the tunic you had made for your holy brother, a minister of God, since he had already departed from the land of the dying and had no need of corruptible things.

I therefore did what you desired and did not deny your brotherly affection whatever true or slight comfort you may judge this to be. I received the tunic sent by you, and when I wrote these things to you, I had already begun to wear it.

Be of good courage; but make use of much better and greater consolations, so that the cloudiness contracted in your heart through human weakness may be cleared by divine authority. Live perseveringly in such a way that you may live with your brother, for your brother died in such a way that he lives.

### 2

There is indeed material for tears in the fact that you no longer see your beloved brother, who held you in the greatest respect for your life and profession of sacred virginity, entering and leaving as you were accustomed to see him, the deacon of the Church of Carthage, busied with the vigor of his ecclesiastical office. You no longer hear from him those honorable words that, with a well-mannered, pious, and dutiful affection, he used to offer to the holiness of your sisterly relationship.

When these things are considered and the force of habit demands him back, the heart is pierced and tears burst forth like the blood of the heart. [Note: Perhaps “returns” instead of “demands him back.”] But let the heart be lifted above, and the eyes will be dry.

For although these things that you mourn as having been taken from you have passed away in the temporal course of events, the love with which Timotheus loved and loves Sapida has not perished. [Note: Timotheus the deacon is praised above in Letter 110, section 1; perhaps this is Sapida’s own brother.] It remains preserved in its treasury and is hidden with Christ in God.

Do those who love gold lose it when they store it away? Are they not then more secure concerning it, insofar as possible, when they keep it, removed from their eyes, in safer places? Does earthly desire consider itself more secure if it does not see what it loves, while heavenly love grieves as though it had lost what it has sent ahead into the heavenly storehouses?

Sapida, consider what you are called, and savor the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God (Col. 3:1–3). He deigned to die for us so that we might live even after death, and so that death itself would not be feared by human beings as though it were going to consume them, nor would anyone grieve for the dead, for whom Life itself died, as though they had lost life.

Let these and similar things be your divine consolations, before which human grief may blush and give way.

### 3

There is no need to condemn the grief of mortals over beloved dead persons; but prolonged grief ought not to belong to the faithful. If, then, you have been saddened, let it now be enough. Do not grieve as the Gentiles do, who have no hope. [Note: In Lov.’s edition some words had been omitted here; we restored them from a Vatican manuscript.]

Paul the Apostle did not forbid grief when he said this, but rather grief of the kind experienced by the Gentiles, who have no hope. Martha and Mary, pious and faithful sisters, wept for their brother Lazarus, although at that time they did not know that he would return to this life in the resurrection. The Lord himself wept for that same Lazarus, whom he was going to raise (John 11:19–35). He did this, plainly, so that we too might weep for those dead whom we believe will rise to true life. Although he did not command it by precept, he permitted it by example.

Nor does Scripture say without reason in the book of Ecclesiasticus: “Bring forth tears for the dead, and begin lamentation as one who has suffered dreadful things.” But shortly afterward it says, “And console yourself because of the sorrow; for from sorrow comes death, and sorrow of heart will bend strength” (Ecclus. 38:16–19).

### 4

Your brother, daughter, lives in mind and sleeps in the flesh. “Will not one who sleeps arise again?” (Ps. 40:9). God, who has already received his spirit, will restore to him his body, which he took away not to be lost but deferred for return.

There is therefore no reason for prolonged sorrow, because the reason for everlasting joy is greater. For not even that mortal part of your brother which lies buried in the earth will perish for you—the part in which he presented himself to you, by which he addressed you and conversed with you, from which he brought forth a voice so familiar to your ears, just as he presented his face to your eyes, so that wherever his voice sounded he could usually be recognized even when unseen.

These things are withdrawn from the senses of the living, and therefore the absence of the dead causes pain. But since even the bodies themselves will not perish forever—just as not a hair of the head will perish (Luke 21:18)—and since what has been laid down for a time will be received again in such a way that it will never again be laid down but will be transformed for the better and made firm, the cause for rejoicing in the hope of immeasurable eternity is certainly greater than the cause for sorrow in the reality of an exceedingly brief time.

The Gentiles do not possess this hope, because they do not know the Scriptures or the power of God (Matt. 22:29)—the God who can restore what has been lost, bring the dead to life, restore what has decayed, join together again what has been separated, and thereafter preserve corruptible and finite things without end.

He who established faith through those things which he had already promised and fulfilled promised that he would do these things. Let your faith speak of these matters with you, for your hope will not be disappointed, even if your love is now deferred. Meditate on these things; console yourself more abundantly and more truly with them.

For if it gives you some consolation that I am wearing—for he could not—the garment you had woven for your brother, how much more and more certainly ought you to be consoled because the one for whom it had been prepared, then needing no corruptible garment, will be clothed in incorruption and immortality!

## LETTER 264

[Note: Corrected from manuscripts a, bg, bl, c, cc, ff, g, gv, j, n, r, s, sb, t, two manuscripts designated vc, four designated v, and the editions.]

[Note: Elsewhere 141; what was formerly numbered 264 is now 231.]

He consoles Maxima, a pious woman who was very distressed and somewhat disturbed in mind because she saw her province endangered by harmful errors—perhaps Spain, where “pernicious doctrines were slaughtering souls, much more unhappily than the barbarian sword slaughtered bodies,” when Orosius came from there to Africa, as is said above in Letter 166, section 2, and in Orosius’s *Commonitorium*, volume 6.

To the honorable and excellent handmaid of God MAXIMA, praiseworthy among the members of Christ, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

### 1

As much as your holy zeal gladdens us, so much does it again grieve us that you report your province to be in great danger through harmful and most destructive errors. But since these things were foretold as future, we should not be surprised that they arise; we must be vigilant lest they cause harm.

Our God and Deliverer would not permit these things to arise unless it were useful for his saints to be instructed even through such temptations. By their perverse will, those people are indeed storing up for themselves both the desert of present blindness and the punishment of future eternity, if through obstinacy they remain unwilling to learn and neglect to correct and amend themselves while they are in this life.

Nevertheless, just as they misuse God’s good gifts—he makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and rains upon the just and the unjust (Matt. 5:45), and in his patience calls them to repentance, while they store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath and the revelation of God’s just judgment (Rom. 2:4–5)—so, just as they misuse his kindness and patience, that is, God’s good gifts, by refusing to be corrected, God in turn makes good use even of their evils.

He uses them not only for his own justice, by which he will repay them what they deserve at the end, but also for the exercise and advancement of his saints, so that the good may progress, be tested, and be revealed through the very perversity of the wicked. As the Apostle says: “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (1 Cor. 11:19).

### 2

For if God could make no good use even of the wicked for the benefit of his elect—God who, even through the evil of Judas, provided us with so great a good that we were redeemed by Christ’s blood—he could either have prevented those whom he foreknew would become wicked from being born, or have destroyed them at the very beginning of their wickedness.

But he permits them to exist for as long as he knows to be useful and sufficient for admonishing and exercising his holy household. Therefore he consoles our sadness concerning them, because the very sorrow we feel for them relieves us, while it weighs upon them if they persist in their perversity.

The joy we experience when some of them are corrected, changed for the better, and joined to the fellowship of the saints cannot be compared with any joy in this life. For this reason it is written: “My son, if you are wise, you will be wise for yourself and for your neighbors; but if you become wicked, you alone will bear the evil” (Prov. 9:12).

When we rejoice over the faithful and just, their goodness benefits both them and us. But when we grieve over the unbelieving and wicked, their wickedness and our sorrow harm them alone; we too are greatly helped before God by grieving mercifully for them, groaning and praying because of that grief.

Therefore, honorable and praiseworthy handmaid of God in Christ, I greatly approve and praise both your sorrow over such people and the vigilance and caution against them that you expressed in your letter. So that you may continue to walk steadfastly on this path, insofar as my strength permits, since you require it, I exhort and admonish you to have mercy on them as one who is simple like a dove, but to beware of them as one who is shrewd like a serpent (Matt. 10:16).

And make every effort, as far as you can, so that those who cling to you may remain with you in the right faith—or, if some have been corrupted in some respect, may be corrected and brought to the right faith.

### 3.

As for the human being whom the Word of God assumed when he became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), I would correct something if I found anything false or perverse in what you believe. Believe, then, what you do believe: that in that human being the Son of God assumed our entire nature—that is, both a rational soul and mortal flesh, without sin. He became a participant in our weakness, not in our wickedness, so that through the weakness we share he might dissolve our wickedness and lead us to his righteousness, drinking death from what is ours and offering life from what is his.

But if you have any writing of theirs in which they assert something contrary to this faith, please be so kind as to send it, so that we may, as far as we can, not only state our faith but also refute their faithlessness. Without doubt, they try to support this very thing, which they perversely and impiously think, by certain testimonies of the divine Scriptures. We must show them in these passages how incorrectly they understand the sacred writings composed for the salvation of the faithful—as though someone were to seriously injure himself with surgical instruments that were instituted not for wounding but for healing.

We have worked very hard, and continue to work, insofar as the Lord grants it, to refute various errors. But if you happen to wish to possess the little works of our labors, send someone to copy them for you. For God willed that you should be able to do this very easily, since he gave you the means by which you could do so.

## LETTER 265  
[Note: [Column 1086] Listed as 108 in a. bg. bn. bl. c. ec. cb. ff. g. gg. gv. j. n. r. s. t. tt. vc.; in two copies of e.; in three of sb.; and in the editions.]  
[Note: [Column 1086] Elsewhere 108: the letter that was 265 is now 106.]

Augustine to Seleuciana, concerning baptism and Peter’s repentance, against a certain Novatian.

To the most religious handmaid of God, worthy of honor in the love of Christ, SELEUCIANA, Augustine, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord.

### 1.

After reading your letter, I rejoiced over your salvation and did not delay replying to what you had written. First, I was astonished that this Novatian says that Peter was not baptized, since shortly before you wrote that he had said that the Apostles had been baptized. I do not know why it seems to him that Peter was not among the baptized Apostles. Therefore I have sent you a copy of your letter, in case you do not have one, so that you may examine more carefully my responses to what I found in your letter. If the secretary took down or wrote it without error, I do not know what kind of mind the man has who says that the Apostles were baptized while denying that Peter was baptized.

### 2.

As for the statement that Peter did penance, we must take care not to suppose that he did so in the manner of those who in the Church are properly called penitents. Who could tolerate our thinking that the first of the Apostles should be numbered among such penitents? He repented of having denied Christ, as his tears show; for it is written that “he wept bitterly” (Matthew 26:75). The Apostles had not yet been strengthened by the Lord’s resurrection or by that coming of the Holy Spirit which appeared on the day of Pentecost, or by that inspiration which the Lord displayed after he rose from the dead, when he breathed upon their faces and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22).

### 3.

Therefore it can rightly be said that when Peter denied the Lord, the Apostles had not yet been baptized—not with water, however, but with the Holy Spirit. For after he had risen and had lived among them, he said to them: “John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit, which you will also receive not many days from now” (Acts 1:5). Some manuscripts read: “But you will begin to be baptized with the Holy Spirit.” Whether it is said “you will be baptized” or “you will begin to be baptized” makes no difference to the matter.

In whatever manuscripts one finds “you will baptize” or “you will begin to baptize,” they are corrupt; this is very easily demonstrated from the Greek. But if we say that they were not baptized with water, we must fear that we may seriously err concerning them, by giving people authority to despise Baptism. Apostolic discipline itself commends Baptism as something that must not be despised to such an extent that Cornelius the centurion and those who were with him, even after they had already received the Holy Spirit, were baptized (Acts 10:48).

### 4.

Just as it was not a sin for the ancient righteous not to be circumcised; but after God commanded Abraham and his descendants to be circumcised, failure to do so became a grave sin, so also, after the Lord Christ gave holy Baptism in his Church as the sacrament of the New Testament in place of circumcision of the flesh [Note: [Column 1087] All editions read this way. But the Louvain editors, in their *Castigations*, report that some manuscripts had: “So also, before the Lord Christ instituted the sacrament of the New Testament in his Church, it was not a sin not to be baptized; that is, no one was held guilty if he had not been washed in Baptism, since at that time it was not known whether this would benefit or harm. But after he gave holy Baptism in place of circumcision of the flesh,” and so forth. In the manuscripts examined by us, no more words are found than in the editions, although twelve of them, instead of “so also, after,” have “so also, before.” Unless this is a scribal error, it indicates that something was omitted here.], and most clearly said, “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5), we must no longer ask when each person was baptized. Rather, whenever we read that people belong to the body of Christ, which is the Church, we must understand that they are baptized and belong to the kingdom of heaven—unless perhaps they were overtaken by the crisis of persecution [Note: [Column 1087] In some manuscripts, as the Louvain editors observe, it was read this way: “That is, the Church, to have been taken up, and to understand that they themselves are neither truly united to the body of Christ nor belong to the kingdom of heaven unless baptized with water—unless perhaps those whom the crisis of persecution found unbaptized, and who, unwilling to deny Christ,” and so forth. Nevertheless, all our manuscripts agree with the editions.], and were killed before they were baptized because they were unwilling to deny Christ; for them, that very suffering was reckoned in place of Baptism.

But can we say this of the Apostles, who had so much time in which to be baptized that they even baptized others? Yet not everything that happened is found written down; nevertheless, events are proved to have occurred by other evidence. It is written when the Apostle Paul was baptized (Acts 9:18), but it is not written when the other Apostles were baptized. Nevertheless, we must understand that they too were baptized. Similarly, it is written when the peoples of the Churches in Jerusalem (Acts 2:41) and Samaria (Acts 8:12) were baptized; but when the other peoples of the nations to whom the Apostles sent letters were baptized is certainly not written. Yet we have no doubt that they too were baptized, because of the Lord’s statement: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven.”

### 5.

Both things are written about the Lord: that he baptized more people than John, and that he himself did not baptize, but his disciples did. Thus we understand that he indeed baptized through the presence of his majesty, but did not himself baptize with his own hands. The sacrament of Baptism belonged to him; the ministry of baptizing belonged to the disciples.

Accordingly, when John the Evangelist says in his Gospel, “After this Jesus and his disciples went into the land of Judea, and there he remained with them and baptized” (John 3:22), shortly afterward, speaking of him, he says: “When Jesus therefore learned that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John (although Jesus himself was not baptizing, but his disciples), he left Judea and went again into Galilee” (John 4:1–3).

Therefore, when he left Jerusalem with his disciples and went into the land of Judea, remaining there with them, he was baptizing not through himself but through his disciples. We understand that they had already been baptized, either with John’s baptism, as some suppose, or, what is more credible, with Christ’s Baptism. For he would not have avoided the ministry of baptizing in order to have baptized servants through whom he might baptize others, since he did not avoid that memorable ministry of humility when he washed their feet. When Peter asked him to wash not only his feet but also his hands and head, he replied: “The one who has bathed does not need to wash except his feet, but is entirely clean” (John 13:10). Here it is understood that Peter had already been baptized.

[Note: [Column 1088] Thus the editions and all our manuscripts. In the Louvain *Castigations*, however, some manuscripts are noted as reading: “Whom we understand to have already been baptized in this act; for the unbaptized could not baptize. It is therefore established that those who baptized others had already been baptized, whether,” and so forth.]  
[Note: [Column 1088] The editions read: “For he did not fail in the ministry of baptizing . . . who did not fail . . . in the ministry.” But the manuscript reading that we have restored here is better.]

### 6.

It is not clearly expressed how this man can say what you included in your letter: that the Apostles imposed penance in place of Baptism. If he says this because sins are forgiven through penance, what he says has some rational basis. Such penance after Baptism can indeed be useful if someone has sinned.

But since he denies that there is an opportunity for penance after Baptism—when, as you wrote, he says that penance exists only before Baptism—it appears that he meant that the Apostles imposed penance in place of Baptism in such a way that they imposed it before Baptism, and that those upon whom it was imposed were afterward not baptized because that penance served for them in place of Baptism. I have never heard Novatians say this. Therefore investigate carefully, in case this belongs to some other error and he merely pretends or supposes himself to be a Novatian. Or, if Novatians also say this, I do not know. I do know, however, that whoever says it is entirely alien to the rule of the Catholic faith and to the teaching of Christ and the Apostles.

### 7.

People do penance before Baptism for their former sins, but in such a way that they are also baptized, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles. Peter spoke to the Jews and said: “Do penance, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, and your sins will be forgiven you” (Acts 2:38).

People also do penance if, after Baptism, they have sinned in such a way that they deserve to be excommunicated and afterward reconciled, as happens in all the Churches to those who are properly called penitents. For the Apostle Paul spoke of such penance when he said: “Lest, when I come again, God humble me before you, and I mourn over many of those who sinned previously and did not do penance for the uncleanness, sexual excess, and fornication that they committed” (2 Corinthians 12:21). He would not have written this except to people who had already been baptized.

We also have in the Acts of the Apostles Simon, already baptized, who wished to buy with money the power for the Holy Spirit to be given through the laying on of his hand [Note: [Column 1088] The editions read: “So that the Holy Spirit might be given to him through the laying on of hands,” and so forth.]. Peter admonished him to do penance for this grave sin (Acts 8:18–23).

### 8.

There is also the almost daily penance of good and humble believers [Note: [Column 1089] Bad., Am., Er., and two manuscripts read *poena* (“penalty”) instead of *poenitentia* (“penance”).], in which we beat our breasts, saying: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12). We do not wish to have forgiven us those things that we do not doubt were forgiven in Baptism, but rather those things—however small—that continually slip into human weakness. If these are accumulated against us, they will burden and crush us like one great sin.

For what difference does it make to a shipwreck whether the ship is covered and overwhelmed by one great wave, or whether water gradually enters the bilge, is left there through negligence and disregard, fills the ship, and sinks it? For these things fasting, almsgiving, and prayers keep watch. When we say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors,” we show that we have something to be forgiven; and by humbling our souls in these words, we do not cease, in a certain sense, to do daily penance.

I think I have answered briefly but sufficiently what you wrote. It remains that the man for whose winning over you thought such a letter should be sent to me should not be contentious.

## LETTER 266  
[Note: [Column 1089] Collated with a. bl. c. cc. ff. g. gv. j. n. r. s. sb. t. vc.; with four copies of v.; and with the corrected editions.]  
[Note: [Column 1089] Elsewhere 132: the letter that was 266 is now 107.]

Augustine to Florentina, an earnest young woman, offering his services as a teacher if she states what she wishes explained.

To the distinguished lady, deservedly honorable in Christ and worthy of welcome [Note: [Column 1089] The Louvain edition reads *worthy of admiration*. But Bad., Am., and Er., as well as four Vatican and seven Gallican manuscripts, read *worthy of welcome*. Some of these manuscripts, however, later read *worthy of admiration* where the editions have *worthy of welcome*. The matter is therefore uncertain.], his daughter FLORENTINA, Augustine, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord.

### 1.

Your holy purpose and the chaste fear of the Lord, permanently rooted in your heart for ever and ever (Psalm 18:10), arouse my concern for you—not only in prayers before God, but also, to no small degree, in admonitions addressed to you yourself. I have done this more than once in letters that I gave to your mother, whom I must name with due honor because of her reverence.

But since she deigned to write back to me that you first wished to receive a letter from me, and that afterward, if something should perhaps be needed from my ministry, which I know that I owe in free service to your reverent devotion and to that of all such people insofar as I can, you would not remain silent but would indicate it by writing back—behold, I have done what I learned you wished, although not through you, lest I should seem to close the door of confidence against you in an inhuman way.

It remains for you yourself to state whether you think there is anything you wish to ask of me. Either I know what you will ask, and I will not refuse; or I do not know it in such a way that my ignorance causes no harm to faith or salvation, and, if I can, I will make you secure about this too by giving an explanation. Or, if I do not know but the matter nevertheless ought to be known, I will either obtain from the Lord that I not fail you—for often the duty of giving is itself a merit of receiving—or I will answer you so that you may know whom we ought to approach concerning this very matter, which we equally do not know.

### 2.

I have said this beforehand so that you will not confidently expect to hear from me whatever you ask, and then, when this does not happen, judge that I acted boldly rather than wisely in giving you the opportunity to ask whatever you wish. I did this not as a perfect teacher, but as one who, together with those being taught, still needs to be perfected, distinguished lady, deservedly honorable in Christ and worthy of welcome.

Indeed, even in matters that I know to some extent, I want you to be knowledgeable rather than dependent upon our knowledge. We ought not to wish for the ignorance of others in order to teach what we know. For all of us are much better taught by God. This will be perfected in that heavenly homeland, when what has been promised is fulfilled in us, so that no one will say to his neighbor, “Know the Lord”; for all will know him, from the least to the greatest (Jeremiah 31:34).

In teaching, we must take the utmost care to avoid the vice of pride, which is not present in learning to the same degree. Therefore Holy Scripture admonishes us, saying: “Let every person be swift to hear, but slow to speak” (James 1:19). And the Psalmist says: “You will give joy and gladness to my hearing”; immediately he adds: “And the humbled bones will rejoice” (Psalm 51:10). He saw that humility is very easily preserved in listening, but is difficult in teaching, because a teacher must occupy a higher place, where it is difficult to ensure that elation does not creep in.

### 3.

Do you see how we are endangered by those from whom it is expected that we should not only be teachers but, although we are human beings, teach divine things? Yet our labors and dangers have one extraordinary consolation: you make such progress that you reach the place where you have no need of any human teacher.

But it is not only we who are endangered by this danger—for what are we in comparison with the one of whom I am about to speak? The Apostle to the Gentiles himself testifies that he was endangered by it when he says: “Lest I should be exalted by the greatness of my revelations, a thorn in the flesh was given to me” (2 Corinthians 12:7), and so forth.

Hence the Lord himself, that wonderful physician of this swelling [Note: [Column 1090] The Louvain edition reads “fear.” But Bad., Am., Er., and several manuscripts have the better reading, “swelling.”], says: “Do not allow yourselves to be called Rabbi by human beings; for one is your teacher, Christ” (Matthew 23:8). Keeping this in mind, the same Apostle to the Gentiles says: “Neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:7).

This was also remembered by the one who, the greater he was among those born of women (Matthew 11:11), the more he humbled himself in everything (Sirach 3:20), declaring himself unworthy to carry Christ’s sandals (Luke 3:16). For what else does he show when he says: “The one who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom stands and listens to him, and rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice” (John 3:29)? This is the hearing of which I spoke a little earlier, as it is written in the Psalm: “You will give joy and gladness to my hearing, and the humbled bones will rejoice.”

### 4.

Therefore, know that I rejoice over your faith, hope, and love with greater certainty, greater solidity, and greater soundness the less you need to learn anything—not only from me but from any human being at all.

Nevertheless, because when I was there you were restrained by modesty on account of your age, your good parents, who love your good studies most dearly, deigned to tell me how ardently you burned with true piety and wisdom, and most kindly asked that I not refuse you whatever little assistance of mine might be needed for your instruction. I have therefore thought that these letters should admonish you, in accordance with the alternatives stated above, to ask whatever you wish, lest I be superfluous if I attempt to teach what you already know.

Only hold firmly to this: even if you are able through me to know something beneficially, he will teach you who is the inner teacher of the inner person, who shows you in your heart that what is said is true: “Neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth.”

## LETTER 267  
[Note: [Column 1091] Collated with bl., cb., sb., vc., two copies of v., and the Louvain edition.]  
[Note: [Column 1091] Elsewhere 206: the letter that was 267 is now 50.]

Augustine to Fabiola, distressed by her pilgrimage in this life, concerning the presence of souls bound together by the bond of friendship.

To the most religious and distinguished lady, and daughter praiseworthy in the love of Christ, FABIOLA, Augustine sends greetings in the Lord.

Although you have returned an answer, I nevertheless read your letter in such a way that I thought it my duty to respond to it. You grieved over the pilgrimage by which it is possible to rejoice perpetually with the saints, and you rightly preferred the longing for the heavenly homeland, where we will no longer be separated by earthly distance but will always rejoice in the contemplation of one.

You are blessed to think faithfully about such things; happier to love them; and therefore you will be happiest when you attain them.

But even now consider more carefully what makes us absent from one another: is it that we do not see one another’s bodies, or that we do not give and receive signs of our souls, which is conversation? For I think that, although separated bodily by distant regions, if we could know one another’s thoughts, we would be more truly with one another than if we sat silently in one place, looking at each other but giving no signs of our inner feelings through our voices and indicating nothing of our souls through bodily movements.
