Accordingly, you understand that each person is more present to himself than one person is to another because each is better known to himself than to another—not by contemplating his own face, which, unless a mirror is present, is carried about and remains hidden [Note: [Column 1091] Thus the manuscript of Corbie. The Louvain edition reads “shines.”], but by contemplating his conscience, which he sees even with his eyes closed.

How great, then, is even this life of ours, which is considered so important?

## LETTER 268  
[Note: [Column 1091] Collated with bl., cb., vc., two copies of v., and the Louvain edition.]  
[Note: [Column 1091] Elsewhere 215: the letter that was 268 is now 11.]

A certain Fascius, overwhelmed by debt, had taken refuge in the church. Augustine satisfied his creditors with money borrowed from others; he asks that the money be repaid for Fascius through a public collection among Christ’s faithful.

To the most beloved and longed-for lords, the holy people [Column 1092] whom I serve as minister [Note: [Column 1092] The Louvain edition reads “together with the minister.” But the manuscript of Corbie has “to whom.”], members of Christ, Augustine sends greetings in the Lord.

### 1.

Your devotion in our Lord Jesus Christ is known and highly approved by me. It has given me confidence that, even while absent, I may presume upon what I customarily rejoice in when present: I am always with you in spirit—not only because the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ never ceases to burn with such sweetness, but also because you do not allow me, who serve you in the Gospel, to suffer distress.

When our brother Fascius [Note: [Column 1092] The editions read “Fastius.” The manuscripts have “Fascius.”] was being pressed by those holding his pledge to repay a debt of seventeen solidi, and could find no immediate means of extricating himself, he fled for help to the holy Church so that he would not suffer bodily injury. The collectors, however, were being forced to depart and therefore could not grant a postponement; they burdened me with the most serious complaints, so that I either hand him over to them or provide a way for them to receive what they showed was owed to them.

When I offered Fascius the opportunity for me to address your Holiness concerning his needs, he was deterred by shame and begged me not to do so. Thus, pressed by an even greater necessity, I received seventeen solidi from our brother Macedonius and immediately gave them for Fascius’s case. He promised that he would be able to meet them on a fixed day for their repayment, and agreed that, if he could not do so, his situation would be brought before your mercy, which you are accustomed to extend fraternally to your brothers.

### 2.

Now, therefore, since he is absent, it remains for you to help—not him, whom no one can compel while absent, but my promise, whose reputation is always present to you. The day on which he promised to meet his obligation has already passed, and I do not know what answer to give the man who entrusted his solidi to my word except to do what I promised I would do.

But since I was not informed of this matter in time to address you about it on the holy day of Pentecost, when your attendance was greater, I ask you to regard this letter as my present voice. God and our Lord, in whom you have believed and who never departs from those who fear him and honor his name, admonishes and exhorts you in your hearts.

In him we too are always joined to you, although we appear to have departed from you bodily. He promises you, from the seed of these good works, a harvest of eternal life, as the Apostle says: “In doing good, let us not grow weary; for in due time we shall reap without growing weary. Therefore, while we have the opportunity, let us do good to all, and especially to those who belong to the household of faith” (Galatians 6:9–10).

Since, then, he is a member of the household of faith—a faithful Christian and our Catholic brother—I ask you to do what the Lord commands. Do it without sadness, without murmuring, and with joy and gladness. You believe in God, not in a human being; for he promises that you will lose none of the things you mercifully do, but will receive them on that day with immortal interest (Matthew 25:34–40).

And since the Apostle himself says, “I say this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly” [Column 1093] (2 Corinthians 9:6), you must understand that the time has come for us, while we are still in this life, to acquire the gift [Note: [Column 1093] The manuscripts read *domum* (“house”); this is not inappropriate if what follows is read as “they bought this [house].”] of eternal life eagerly and gladly. For when the end of the age comes, it will be given only to those who purchased it for themselves through faith before they were able to see it [Note: [Column 1093] Thus the better-quality manuscripts. The editions read: “who earned this for themselves through faith.”].

I have also written to the priests that, if anything is lacking after your Holiness’s collection, they should complete it from what the Church possesses, provided that you make your offering gladly, as is fitting. For whether it is given from your resources or from the Church’s, everything belongs to God, and your devotion will be sweeter than the Church’s treasures, as the Apostle says: “Not that I seek the gift, but I seek the fruit” (Philippians 4:17).

### 3.

Therefore gladden my heart, because I desire to rejoice in your fruits. You are God’s trees, which he deigns to water with continual rains even through our ministry.

May the Lord protect you from every evil, both in this age and in the age to come, my most beloved and longed-for lords and brothers.

## LETTER 269  
[Note: [Column 1093] Not found in the manuscripts except one Vatican manuscript.]  
[Note: [Column 1093] Elsewhere 251: the letter that was 269 is now 12.]

Augustine to Bishop Nobilio, explaining that he cannot come for the dedication of a new building.

To the most blessed and venerable brother and fellow priest NOBILIO, Augustine sends greetings.

The solemnity to which the affection of your Fraternity invites me is so great that my little body would be drawn to you by its desire, were it not held back by weakness. I could come if it were not winter; I could disregard winter if I were young. Either the warmth of youth would withstand the severity of the season, or the warmth of summer would temper the cold of age.

But now, in winter, I cannot endure so long a journey with the icy old age that I carry with me, most blessed lord, holy and venerable brother and fellow priest.

I offer you the greeting due to your merits. I commend my well-being to your prayers, asking God the Lord himself that the dedication of so great a building may be accompanied by the prosperity of peace.

## LETTER 270  
[Note: [Column 1094] Added here from the edition of Jerome’s works.]  
[Note: [Column 1094] This edition adds it; the letter that was 270 is now 206.]

An anonymous writer to Augustine—not Jerome, as is clear from the style, although it has been published among Jerome’s letters as Letter 40—explaining that he was deeply saddened not to find Augustine together with Severus in the city of Leges, and expressing the depth of his affection for him.

When I had come to the city of Leges some time ago, I was deeply saddened that I could not find you there in your entirety. I did find Severus, your dearest friend and, so to speak, a part of your soul [Note: [Column 1094] He is speaking of Severus, bishop of Milevis, whom Augustine himself calls above, in Letter 110.4, “most closely and intimately joined to his soul,” and shortly afterward “his other soul”; indeed, he says that “his soul and mine are one.”], and I rejoiced in part.

For I would have rejoiced completely if I had found you entire. Thus, insofar as I found you, I rejoiced; but because I did not see that part of you, I was saddened in every way. Therefore I said to my soul: “Why are you sad, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God” (Psalm 42:6), and he will make present the friend whom you love.

Accordingly, I trust in the Lord and hope that he will make me rejoice in seeing you. If only love could be seen with the eyes! You would certainly see how great our love for you is. Or, by matching your love, it would bring you a great desire to imitate it.

Therefore, because I love you in the Lord, love the one who loves you. And so that others may love you with you, exhort them through ecclesiastical authority.

As for what you ask in your letter—that I pray for you—I would rightly do so if I myself were free from sins, so that I might be permitted to pray for others. Therefore I admonish you to send the constant prayers of your heart to the Lord for me. Remember your profession, and set before your eyes that day on which the righteous will not fear the report of evil (Psalm 112:7). The righteous will not fear because they will not hear, “Go into the eternal fire,” but rather, “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom” (Matthew 25:41, 34).

May he lead us to that kingdom, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

[Column 1093]

# APPENDIX TO VOLUME TWO OF THE WORKS OF SAINT AUGUSTINE, CONTAINING SEVERAL LETTERS ONCE WRONGLY ASCRIBED TO HIM

(C, G, S)

They are:

Sixteen shorter letters of Augustine to Boniface and vice versa; a letter of Pelagius to Demetrias; Augustine’s letter to Cyril and the reply, concerning the praises of Jerome; and the Dispute of Augustine with Pascentius.

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE SIXTEEN LETTERS THAT FOLLOW

The sixteen shorter letters under the names of Augustine and Boniface, as they are headed in very ancient manuscripts, were rejected here, after Erasmus, by the Louvain theologians: first, because they differ greatly from Augustine’s manner and style; next, because they are not listed by Possidius and are not cited by any of the ancients—except the thirteenth, which nearly six hundred years ago Anselm of Lucca included in his collection, book 13, chapter 5, and after him Ivo and Gratian.

They consist of ineptly sewn-together fragments. The first, for example, contains the sentences “May chastity adorn your morals,” and “For it is a grave—or, better, shameful—thing that one whom a human being does not conquer,” which have been copied from Letter 189 to Boniface. They also contain certain statements that do not sufficiently agree with the history of the times or with Boniface’s deeds; such examples are found especially in Letter 10.

Furthermore, Augustine himself testifies in writing to Boniface above, in Letter 220.2, that he was never able to send letters to that commander during his dangers, because he considered the danger to the bearer and took care lest his letter reach people whom he did not wish to receive it.

Thus most learned men judge that these letters were fabricated by an idle writer for the sake of practicing style. Although Baronius opposes their judgment, we think it should be followed.

## LETTER 1  
[Note: [Column 1095] Elsewhere 182.]

To the exalted and ever-magnificent son BONIFACE, Augustine, bishop.

May conjugal chastity adorn your morals; may sobriety and moderation adorn them. For to act well while failing to prohibit what is unlawful is to consent to error.

As a consecrated virgin was leaving the church, she encountered the drunken mind and body of the Goth Herpa. Let the soldier placed under a commander, I ask, possess discipline. It is a grave thing that one whom a human being does not conquer should be conquered by lust, or that one who is not conquered by iron should wallow in wine.

## LETTER 2  
[Note: [Column 1095] Elsewhere 183.]

To the deservedly honorable father AUGUSTINE, supreme among bishops, Boniface.

I received the letter of Your Holiness, which, through its admonition, terrified me. For, venerable pope, if that lawful marriage-bed has timid approaches, with what punishment ought one to be punished who violates divine ordinances? He will therefore certainly be accused who neglected both divine and human matters; and the avenging sword will destroy the man whom lust overcame. The one whom truthful report has proclaimed intemperate amid such great dangers will be held in the custody of prison, where he will perish under whatever punishment is imposed.

## LETTER 3  
[Note: [Column 1095] Elsewhere 184.]

I rebuke and chastise those whom I love; I do not desire them to be killed or thrust into a prison filled with filth. Admonition alone is sufficient.

If time for repentance is granted to him by divine mercy, the man who dared to violate the Lord’s temple may be forgiven. Let the one who did this himself be the judge of his vow; for it is not right that a guilty man should be killed at the urging of a bishop when he is being reserved for pardon if he repents.

For if we wish to exercise vengeance in the errors of the Barbarians, as is fitting, we will find few of them, and those few will not be eager for battle.

## LETTER 4  
[Note: [Column 1095] Elsewhere 185.]

To the exalted and ever-magnificent son BONIFACE, Augustine, bishop.

As I hear, an overseas soldier has reached the African shore; but the commander of this soldier dissents from Catholic truth. I do not know what I ought to pray for.

From Italy, a public enemy has been announced, raising proud spears against the victorious standards. I would wish peace to be made between you, if I knew more fully what I do not know.

A war long prepared in Italy is indeed now come upon Africa; nevertheless, dearest son, I do not envy Roman territory. But I say what I feel: with divine help, a Catholic will not turn his back to a heretic.

Direct the intention of your heart toward God; you will fear neither the soldier, nor the Goth, nor the Hun.

## LETTER 5  
[Note: [Column 1095] Elsewhere 186.]

To the holy father AUGUSTINE, bishop, Boniface.

I know that Your Holiness is anxious about my life, and I knew what that tyrant had arranged and was arranging against me even before he wrote to your Priesthood.

Let us meet those who rush willingly toward death; Christ, as we believe, will make them subject to our victory. But if the divine will should determine something else concerning me and all my men, pray that God may free my soul; and a fitting answer will be given to the adversary a second time.

[Column 1096] In the battle the fury of both sides rages, but God examines the causes. Therefore pray, as I have said, and the one Trinity will conquer for us.

## LETTER 6  
[Note: [Column 1096] Elsewhere 187.]

To his most beloved and distinguished son BONIFACE, Augustine, bishop.

I marvel at how the ram of the enemy has broken through the wall of faith so suddenly; for I know with what devotion you have always revered the Church. At whose instigation, then, and driven by what fury, have you dragged a man from the Church? If your fugitive had perhaps presumed upon your friend, he could undoubtedly obtain pardon through the intervention of a friend; therefore, if friendship is being invoked, why is God offended? But if power is being presumed upon, consider King Nebuchadnezzar, who, because of his pride, was changed from a man into an ox (Dan. 4:30). I do not write this to shame you, but to admonish my dearest son (1 Cor. 4:14). Restore unharmed to the Church the man whom, as a most irreligious person, you carried away. I have ordered that the offering of your household not be accepted by the clergy; and I forbid you communion until, after you have completed the penance which I have determined for your presumption or error, and after the allotted time has been granted, you offer God a fitting sacrifice with a contrite and humbled heart for this deed.

## LETTER VII  
[Note: [Col. 1096] Formerly 188.]

**BONIFACE TO AUGUSTINE.**

I offer a humble greeting, which is the first thing to do; but I received, trembling, the words of Your Holiness, full of blows. I know that pardon is being prepared for the man corrected by Augustine, the most perfect priest; nor should an episcopal pardon be denied for what was done either by intention or by accident: for he denies himself care who does not disclose his case to his physician. Thus, most devout father, my command and fury removed from your holy sight the man who had been snatched from the thresholds of the church. These deeds were not done on another’s counsel; I live under the governance of God and his saints. Therefore, to that man most deserving of death, whom, as I said, my fury dragged away from the church doors, we grant life and safety at your command. I acknowledge my faults: may my unworthy tears be joined to your righteous weeping, so that this mark, written in black on a charred tablet, may be erased. Let me not be denied entrance to the Church: there I hope for pardon, where I committed the fault. As for the offering of my household, as Your Holiness commanded, it shall be presented by his hands at the table of the heavenly King.

## LETTER VIII  
[Note: [Col. 1096] Formerly 189.]

**AUGUSTINE, BISHOP, TO THE EXALTED AND EVER-MAGNIFICENT BONIFACE, HIS SON.**

While I was stationed in a certain place and watching the passage of Your Eminence, your gentle yet formidable stride pleased my eyes. But after that head, smoothed and anointed with sacred chrism, left the city gate with a few companions, suddenly the household pours forth its horsemen, the city disgorges its army, weapons resound, trumpets blare, and tufts of tow, twisted by the wind, hang from the spearheads; iron coats bind the limbs of the strong men; the rider’s and horse’s flanks are clothed in a bristling covering, and the drawn bow is carried ready. I saw everything splendid; I saw nothing better than Count Boniface.

But after Your Eminence came, as I learned, to Palmas, you had ordered that the short passage of sea there—though short, it is full of dangers and can scarcely ever be crossed by ship—be traversed in the morning, lest the darkness of night bring about some misfortune. Gudila, the most faithful servant of Your Eminence, riding on horseback, while swimming across the arm of that very sea, reached the shore of the forbidden coast; and plainly he was not immediately able to return. For the swelling of the sea increased and denied the passage to one attempting to go back. This could not escape your most vigilant senses: reason provoked anger, and guilt urged the young man to flee; but blessed is the flight that runs toward life.

The aforementioned Gudila took refuge with your patron, Saint Stephen the first martyr. He himself commanded me to come as a petitioner on Gudila’s behalf before your devotion. Let him therefore, I beg, have pardon, since neither did the horse, disturbed by the waves, fall, nor did the deep whirlpool swallow the man whom God rescued and the water preserved. May this letter of petition, I ask, have influence with you; for, as I entreat, you will be free from the anger of the Lord whenever Augustine, petitioning you, has not been offended by you.

## LETTER IX  
[Note: [Col. 1097] Formerly 190.]

**BONIFACE TO AUGUSTINE, MOST BLESSED AND VENERABLE HOLY FATHER AND BISHOP.**

Though enraged, I spare, because, even when I stand in the path of battle, I am checked by the command of Your Holiness. I have always wished the very brave man Gudila to live, but I fear that the light-mindedness of his youth may one day cause his death. Girded with arms, he can indeed slaughter however many enemies he encounters. But among warlike men, the man who is killed is called a victor, even when defeated. For when, mounted on horseback, he swam across the arm of the sea, this was not wantonness but courage. I think that he had planned to do something to the enemy during the night; but when the sun appeared, the approach of day removed the plans he had prepared. Yet I grieved over this: in so long a swim he could have been killed both by falling from the horse and by the waters. Therefore, as you command, I carry out your orders, imposed by holy and blessed Stephen. For I promise him and you that, at your command, Gudila has been granted pardon by you.

## LETTER X  
[Note: [Col. 1097] Formerly 191.]

**BONIFACE TO AUGUSTINE, VENERABLE HOLY FATHER AND BISHOP.**

That Castinus, the former consul, persecutor of my life and reputation, as is known to all, committing and fabricating worse factions—as though forgetful of the gifts I had bestowed upon him [Note: [Col. 1097] Several manuscripts: *edatium*.]—fled Italy and put himself into the hands of my supporters in Africa for protection.

I omit, most blessed father, the sufferings formerly inflicted upon me by that same man and the dangers he brought upon me; even now I survive by fleeing him. Born a Thracian, I barely escaped the Scythian; under an envious consul I endured military service. But divine power, which knows how to level the exalted and raise the fallen higher, made of the proud man what it wished; and, while I remained at peace, it subjected my enemy to me by a victory of the kind it knew best.

Such humiliation of the defeated is enough for a funeral: the cloak bowed before the *saraca* [Note: [Col. 1097] *Saraca* is a kind of cloak.]; the senator feared the barbarian head; the commander trembled before the soldier. These things, holy father, are spoken in the tragic buskin of grief; for I honor the most illustrious consul and now behold a foremost senator. But lest his customary wicked deceit toward me, as usual, contrive something, and lest he think that through his frauds he can benefit Roman commanders and be involved in my ruin, let him give Your Blessedness an unreserved oath concerning his intentions, if no deceit is turning in his heart.

For my part, by everything that is holy, I swear that if I find purity of spirit in him, I shall restore him safe and exalted to Italy and Rome, after frustrating and subduing his enemies. But he will be the enemy of his own soul if I find anything of a sinister nature in him.

## LETTER XI  
[Note: [Col. 1097] Formerly 192.]

**AUGUSTINE, BISHOP, TO BONIFACE, HIS SON, ILLUSTRIOUS IN MERIT AND EXALTED.**

The most illustrious Castinus has declared under oath that he is free from every fault and error. He says that the allied Sonia, while you were still stationed at the palace, was stirring him against you by false suggestions. But lest everything that was then being done be brought into the open [Col. 1098], let brevity be imposed upon prolixity.

That shepherd David obtained the kingdom by sparing his enemies. Christ asked the Father not to be angry with the Jews who fastened him to the cross, and in his mercy granted pardon to unworthy men. Therefore believe the man who gave me a faithful oath and seeks, with my promise, the support of life through your protection. For I know that you will fulfill for me the promise made concerning his safety.

## LETTER XII  
[Note: [Col. 1098] Formerly 193.]

**BONIFACE TO AUGUSTINE, VENERABLE HOLY FATHER AND BISHOP.**

The war is severe for us. The enemy’s sword strikes our breasts. Pour out prayers to God, as you are accustomed; let your prayer accompany us. The hoarse trumpet and terrifying bugle—I think they frighten even the stars. The enemy’s shouting is monstrous, but we are not frightened by it; for we have known such things before today. Therefore, venerable priest of Christ, ask God to direct our missiles against the enemy, so that they may slaughter one another in mutual carnage.

## LETTER XIII  
[Note: [Col. 1098] Formerly 194.]

**AUGUSTINE, BISHOP, TO BONIFACE, HIS DEAREST AND ILLUSTRIOUS SON.**

You complain of the severity of the battle. I do not want you to doubt: I shall give you and your men useful counsel. Seize your weapons in your hands; let prayer strike the ears of the Author. For when battle is being fought, God looks down from the opened heavens, and to the side he sees to be just, there he grants the palm of victory.

## LETTER XIV  
[Note: [Col. 1098] Formerly 195.]

**BONIFACE TO AUGUSTINE, VENERABLE HOLY FATHER AND BISHOP.**

The proud hand has fallen, with God’s help—the hand that shortly before carried a sword boldly raised. Many of the enemy have fallen; but of our men, with Christ’s help, no one has been wounded. Therefore pray, venerable pope, that such vengeance may often proceed against the enemy.

## LETTER XV  
[Note: [Col. 1098] Formerly 196.]

**AUGUSTINE, BISHOP, TO BONIFACE, HIS ILLUSTRIOUS AND EXALTED SON.**

I do not believe that it is unknown to Your Nobility that I lie sick in bed, and I desire my final day to come. I rejoice in your victory. I ask you to preserve the Roman city; govern your men as a good commander. Presume nothing upon your own strength; glory in the Author of your virtues, and pay no heed whatever to any enemy. Farewell.

## LETTER XVI  
[Note: [Col. 1098] Formerly 197.]

**BONIFACE TO AUGUSTINE.**

Divinity never despises the prayers and tears of sinners. You yourself desire to depart from this life in safety to the kingdoms of heaven; but we need you, weary as we are and still placed amid such great dangers. Therefore pray with us, that our salvation may be granted a little more time through you.

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING LETTER

This is the very book addressed to Demetrias which, when it formerly came into Augustine’s hands without the author’s name, prompted him to write back at once to Demetrias’s mother Juliana (above, Letter 188), wishing to discover from where this little work had come, since he recognized that Pelagian error was being conveyed in it. Later, however, in his book *On the Grace of Christ*, chapter 20 and following, he identified Pelagius as its author. Indeed, from chapter 37 of that same book Pelagius himself declared this in a letter to Pope Innocent, writing: “Let them read what we composed in the East for the holy virgin of Christ Demetrias, and they will find that we praise human nature in such a way that we always add the help of God’s grace.”

Orosius attributed it to the same Pelagius in his *Apologeticus*, published in the year 415, except that he says the discourse was supplied to Pelagius by someone else, perhaps by that deacon Annianus whom Jerome censures above in Letter 202. After Saint Augustine, Prosper—or rather Pope Leo—in his letter to Demetrias, and Bede in the first book of his commentary on the *Canticles*, wrote against this same letter of Pelagius. Bede noted that some had falsely attributed it to Jerome, though he himself also falsely attributed it to Julian.

It was written either in the year 413, when Jerome, Augustine, and Innocent vied in sending letters to Demetrias as she received the veil of virginity, or certainly in 414, after she had returned to Rome; this is what Pelagius here seems to indicate in chapter 23.

## LETTER XVII  
[Note: [Col. 1099] Formerly 142.]

**PELAGIUS TO DEMETRIAS.** *(C, G, S)*

### CHAPTER I

Even if, relying on exceptional talent and equal learning, I thought that I could easily fulfill the duty of writing, nevertheless I could not undertake so difficult a work without great fear of its difficulty. Yet one must write to Demetrias: a virgin of Christ, a noble virgin, a wealthy virgin, and—greater than these qualities—a virgin who tramples nobility and wealth beneath the ardor of faith.

Because of the distinction of such remarkable virtue, it is certainly easy for everyone to praise her, but difficult to teach her. Who could lack words in celebrating the praise of one who, born in the highest station, raised amid the greatest wealth and pleasures, and entangled as if by the tightest bonds in so many and varied allurements of this life, has suddenly broken free and exchanged all the goods of the body at once for the virtue of the soul; who has cut down the very flower of her still-beginning youth with a certain sword of faith—that is, with her will—and, crucifying her flesh with Christ, has consecrated it to God as a living and holy offering; who has rejected, for love of virginity, the posterity of the noblest blood?

The path of speech, however, is open and easy when the abundance of the subject itself kindles the course of discourse. But we must proceed by another route, since our purpose is to write instruction for a virgin, not praise; to express not so much the virtues she has already prepared as those still to be prepared; and to arrange her remaining life rather than adorn her past.

It is exceedingly difficult to deal with a person in whom there is such a great desire for speaking and such an ardor for perfection that scarcely any teaching, however perfect, could be equal to her. For she remembers—and rightly remembers—which riches and glory of the world she rejected, which pleasures she renounced, and which allurements of the present life she finally despised. Therefore she is not content with this ordinary and average manner of living; and because it would easily become commonplace through association with the many, she seeks something new and unusual, something exceptional and singular. She wants her way of life to be as remarkable as her conversion.

Noble in the world, she desires to be nobler before God; she seeks qualities in her conduct as precious as the possessions she despised. What stream of talent could ever satisfy such ardor of a devoted mind, such thirst for such perfection? What force of speech, what abundance of words, could ever express as much in language as the virgin is prepared to fulfill in deeds?

But pardon must be granted to us, who offer our gift, according to our strength, for the adornment of the Lord’s tabernacle. Nor do we fear that, by rashly writing to a virgin of such nobility, we may voluntarily expose ourselves to the bites of envy. For we write at the request—indeed, at the command—of her holy mother, who has demanded this from us by letters sent across the sea with wondrous eagerness of spirit. She easily shows with what devotion and care she planted the heavenly shoot in her daughter, since she so earnestly desires that it be watered by others.

Therefore, removed from rashness and free from ambition, let us labor at the task we have undertaken; and let us not distrust our modest talent [Col. 1100], which we believe will be assisted both by the faith of the mother and by the merit of the virgin.

### CHAPTER II

Whenever I have to speak about the formation of character and the conduct of a holy life, I usually first display the power and quality of human nature and show what it can accomplish. In this way I stimulate the listener’s mind from the outset toward the forms of virtue, so that it may not be uselessly summoned to things it has perhaps already sensed to be impossible for itself.

For we can never enter upon the way of virtue unless hope leads us as a companion: every effort to seek something perishes through despair of attaining it. This order of exhortation, which I have followed in other little works as well, I think must be observed especially here, where the goodness of nature ought to be declared more fully because a more perfect life is to be formed. Otherwise the mind will be that much more relaxed and slower in pursuing virtue to the degree that it believes itself less capable; and, while it does not know that something exists within it, it will suppose that it does not possess it.

That thing whose use is desired must always be brought to knowledge; and whatever good nature can do must be explained, since whatever it is proved capable of doing must be fulfilled. Let these, then, be laid down first as the foundations of a holy and spiritual life, so that the virgin may recognize her powers, which she will finally be able to exercise well once she has learned that she possesses them.

The best incentives for the soul arise when someone is taught that he can accomplish what he desires. In war, too, the greatest encouragement, and that which possesses the greatest authority, is the one that reminds the fighter of his strength.

First, therefore, you must measure the goodness of human nature by its creator—namely, God. Since he is said to have made all the works of the world and everything within the world good, and very good, how excellent do you think he made the human being himself, for whose sake he is also understood to have created all things?

When he resolved to make the human being in his own image and likeness, before making him he showed what sort of being he was going to make. Then, when he subjected all animals to him and established him as their lord—although he had made some of them far stronger than human beings in bodily mass, in magnitude of strength, or in the weapons of their teeth—he declared how much more beautifully the human being himself had been created. By this he wished him to understand the dignity of his own nature, as he admired the powerful animals subjected to him.

Nor did he leave him naked and without protection, or expose him as weak to various dangers. Rather, although he had made him externally unarmed, he armed him more effectively within, with reason and prudence. Thus, through understanding and strength of mind, by which he surpassed the other animals, he alone might recognize the maker of all things, and serve God by the very faculty through which he ruled over the others.

Yet the Lord wished him to be an executor of justice voluntarily, not under compulsion. Therefore he left him in the power of his own counsel, and placed before him life and death, good and evil; and whatever pleases him will be given to him (Ecclus. 15:14, 13). Hence we also read in Deuteronomy: “I have set life and death before your face, blessing and curse; choose life, that you may live” (Deut. 30:19).

### CHAPTER III

From this point we must take care lest that idea trouble you which rashly offends the uneducated crowd, causing you to think that the human being was not truly made good because he is able to do evil and is not constrained by the very force of nature to an unavoidable necessity of unchangeable good.

For if you reconsider the matter carefully and compel your mind to a more refined understanding, the superior and better condition of the human being will appear to you precisely where it is thought to be inferior. In this division between two paths, in this freedom toward either side, lies the dignity of the rational soul.

Here, I say, lies the whole honor of our nature; here its dignity; here, finally, the praise earned by the best people, and here their reward. There could be no virtue at all in one who perseveres in good if he could not pass over to evil.

Since God wished to endow the rational creature with the gift of voluntary good and the power of free choice, by implanting in the human being the possibility of either side he made it proper to him to be whatever he wished. Thus, capable of good and evil, he could naturally be capable of either, and incline his will toward either one.

For he could not otherwise possess good spontaneously unless the creature could also possess evil. The best Creator wished us to be capable of both, but he commanded us to do one—the good—and gave the capacity for evil only so that we might make his will our own will.

Since this is so, even the fact that we can do evil is itself good. Good, I say, because it makes the better part of good voluntary. It makes it self-governing and its own master, not bound by necessity but free in judgment. We are permitted to choose, reject, approve, and refuse.

Nor is there any reason why the rational creature should be preferred to the others except that, while all other things possess goodness merely by condition and necessity, this creature alone possesses goodness also by will.

Yet many people, impiously no less than ignorantly, when the condition of the human being is questioned—for I hesitate to say it—speak as though they were criticizing the work of the Lord. They say that he ought to have been made such that he could not do evil at all.

Thus the creature says to the one who formed it: “Why have you made me thus?” (Rom. 9:20). And the most wicked of human beings, while concealing their failure to manage well the very thing they were made to be, prefer to have been made otherwise. In this way, since they do not wish to improve their own lives, they seem to wish to improve nature.

The goodness of nature has been so generally established for all that it sometimes shows and manifests itself even among the Gentiles, who are without any worship of God. How many philosophers have we heard of, read about, and even seen ourselves who were chaste, patient, modest, generous, temperate, kind, who rejected both the honors and pleasures of the world, and loved justice no less than knowledge?

Where, I ask, did people alienated from God receive these qualities that please God? And from where did they receive good qualities, unless from the goodness of nature?

When we see that the qualities I have mentioned are possessed either all together in one person or individually in different people, and when human nature is one, they show one another by their example that everything can exist in everyone—whether all qualities in one person or individual qualities in different people.

If even people without God show what they were made by God, consider what Christians can do, whose nature and life have been instructed for the better through Christ, and who are also aided by the assistance of divine grace.

### CHAPTER IV

Let us now come to the hidden places of our soul. Let each person look more attentively upon himself. Let us ask what our own thoughts feel about this matter. Let conscience itself pronounce judgment concerning the goodness of nature. Let us be instructed by the household teaching of the soul, and learn the goods of the mind from the mind itself more than from anywhere else.

What, I ask, is that which makes us either blush or fear at every sin, and makes us reveal the guilt of an act now by the redness of our face, now by pallor; which makes us, even in the smallest offenses, flee from a witness with a trembling spirit and suffer the bite of conscience—while, on the other hand, in every good deed we are joyful, steadfast, and fearless, and, if it is hidden, we even desire and wish it to become known?

It is because nature itself is its own witness. By the very fact that it is displeased by evil, it declares its goodness; and by trusting only in a good deed, it shows what alone is fitting for it.

This is why the torments of conscience often rage against the author of a crime like a hidden executioner, and secret punishment of the mind pursues the guilty person who lies concealed. After guilt there is no place for impunity, since guilt itself becomes punishment.

Conversely, an innocent person enjoys the security of conscience even amid torments, and, while fearing punishment, glories in innocence.

For there is, I say, in our souls a certain natural holiness, if I may put it so, which, presiding as if in the citadel of the soul, exercises judgment concerning good and evil. Just as it favors honorable and upright actions, so it condemns wrongful deeds; and, in accordance with the testimony of conscience, it distinguishes the two sides by a certain domestic law.

It deceives us in no way through any ingenuity or fabricated coloring of arguments; through our very thoughts—truly most faithful and unimpeachable witnesses—it either accuses or defends us.

The Apostle remembered this law when writing to the Romans. He testifies that it has been implanted in everyone, as if written on certain tablets of the heart: “When Gentiles, who do not have the Law, naturally do what belongs to the Law, although they do not have the Law, they are a law to themselves. They show the work of the Law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness to them, and their thoughts accusing or even defending them in turn” (Rom. 2:14–15).

All those whom Scripture records as having lived holily and pleased God between Adam and Moses made use of this law. Some of them must be set before you as examples, so that you may easily understand how great is the goodness of nature once you have proved that it taught righteousness in place of the Law.

### CHAPTER V

Abel was the first to follow this teacher. He so pleased the Lord that, when he offered him a sacrifice, his offering was so gratefully accepted by God that it stirred his brother to envy (Gen. 4:4–5).

The Lord himself recalled this just man in the Gospel (Matt. 23:35), briefly explaining his perfection. Every form of virtue is contained under the single name of justice.

We read that blessed Enoch pleased God so greatly that God snatched him from the midst of mortals and transferred him, perfected in the world, from the habitation of the world (Gen. 5:24; Ecclus. 44:16).

Noah is declared just in his generation and perfect (Gen. 6:9). His holiness is all the more admirable because, while the entire world had wholly turned away from justice, he alone was found just. He did not seek an example of holiness from another; he himself provided one.

Therefore, when shipwreck threatened the whole world, he alone among all deserved to hear: “Enter, you and your household, into the ark, because I have seen you to be just in this generation before me” (ibid. 7:1).

Before God, however, that person is proved just who is holy in body and in heart.

Melchizedek is read of as a priest of God. His merit can easily be understood from this: he prefigured long beforehand the future sacrament of the Lord; by the sacrifice of bread and wine he expressed the mystery of the body and blood; and by the type of his priesthood he represented Christ’s priesthood. To Christ the Father says: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (ibid. 14:18; Ps. 109:4; Heb. 7:1–22).

Moreover, in blessing Abraham, the chief of the patriarchs (Gen. 14:19)—the father of the Jews through circumcision and of the Gentiles through faith—he most clearly displayed the figure of the one who bestowed blessing upon Jews and Gentiles through faith.

Lot too, following the virtue of holy Noah, did not abandon justice amid so many examples of sinners (ibid. 19). Just as the example of the whole world did not overcome that man, so Lot, while the entire region in which he lived was sinning, maintained holiness against the vices of the multitude.

As the blessed apostle Peter says, he was “just in sight and hearing” (2 Pet. 2:8); placed among the worst of people, he turned away from their evils both with his eyes and with his ears. Therefore, in a similar example, just as Noah was rescued from the flood, so Lot was rescued from the fire.

What need is there to recall Abraham, the friend of God, or Isaac and Jacob? We can estimate how perfectly they fulfilled the Lord’s will from this alone: in a familiar and exceptional distinction, he wished to be named their God. “I am,” he says, “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. This is my name forever, and this is my memorial throughout generations of generations” (Exod. 3:15).

Joseph, the faithful servant of the Lord, is shown to have been righteous from boyhood amid great trials. First, he was sold into slavery to the Ishmaelites by his brothers, by those from whom he had seen himself receiving homage; then he was handed over to an Egyptian master. Yet he always preserved the dignity of a freeborn soul, and by his example taught both slaves and free people not to sin, and that condition harms no one, but the mind does.

Here, I ask you, pause for a little while and carefully consider the chaste soul, O virgin.

A woman, his mistress, desires the young man, but he is not enticed to desire her. She begs, and he flees. In this one matter she both flatters and pleads, though in all others she commanded.

The lover of God is not conquered by love of a woman. A chaste soul is moved neither by the age of youth [Col. 1103] nor by the authority of the woman who loves him.

After his mistress had often been rejected, she set closer snares for the young man. In private and without witnesses she shamelessly seized him by the hand and urged him toward crime with more brazen words. Even then he was not conquered; as word answered word, so deed answered deed.

For the man who had often refused her requests is now seized and held fast [Note: [Col. 1103] Another manuscript: *he fled*.]. And before the Gospel saying had been spoken, “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28), this man, provoked by the woman not merely through sight but almost through embrace itself, did not desire her.

Thus far you have marveled at the virtue of chastity; now consider his kindness.

Before the Prophet said, “Let no one remember the malice of his neighbor in his heart,” he returned love for hatred. When he saw his brothers—or rather, enemies who had come from his brothers—and wished to be recognized by them, he demonstrated the affection of love through holy grief. He kissed each one, and, bathing the necks of the frightened men with abundant tears, washed away his brothers’ hatred with tears of love. He loved them with genuine affection both while their father was alive and after his death.

He did not remember the pit into which they had thrown him to bring about his death; he did not think of brotherhood sold for a price. Rather, returning good for evil, he fulfilled the apostolic command under the still-existing law of nature (Gen. 37 and following).

### CHAPTER VI

What shall I say about blessed Job, that most famous athlete of God, who, after his wealth had been plundered and his possessions utterly destroyed, after the sudden death of his sons and daughters all together, finally fought against the devil with his own body?

Everything he possessed externally is taken away; foreign goods suddenly fall, so that what is truly his own may shine forth more brightly. He is stripped, as it were, of every garment, so that, naked, he may triumph more freely and more bravely, and conquer again by enduring sufferings the enemy whom he had previously overcome by bearing losses.

The Lord himself gives this testimony concerning him: “Have you considered my servant Job? For there is no one like him on earth, a blameless man, a true worshiper of God, abstaining from every evil” (Job 1:8; 2:3).

And not without reason. For, as he himself says, he always feared the Lord like waves swelling over him, and could not bear the weight of his presence (ibid. 31:23). He never dared to despise the one whom he believed always to be so present, and he said: “I am secure; for my heart has not reproached me throughout my life” (ibid. 27:6).

Before the Lord commanded that enemies be loved (Matt. 5:44), he could say: “If I rejoiced at the misfortune of my enemy; if I said in my heart, ‘It is well done’” (Job 31:29).

The Gospel saying had not yet sounded, “Give to everyone who asks you” (Luke 6:30), and already he was saying: “If I allowed the needy person to go out of my door with an empty purse” [Note: [Col. 1103] Another manuscript: “with an empty bosom”] (Job 31:16).

He had not yet read the Apostle’s command, “Masters, provide your slaves with what is just and fair” (Col. 4:1), and he cried out confidently to the Lord: “If I have harmed a slave, if I have injured a slave-girl, you know everything, Lord” (Job 31:13).

Before the same Apostle commanded the rich not to be high-minded or to place their hope in the uncertainty of riches (1 Tim. 6:17), Job possessed riches in such a way that he showed himself to be rich in another respect: “I did not trust in riches,” he says, “nor in a precious stone” (Job 31:24).

And he proved this not merely in words but also in deeds. When he lost everything, he did not grieve, but said with each loss: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord forever. Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall return there” (ibid. 1:21).

The affection with which we possess something is taught us when we lose it; and the pain of deprivation reveals the desire for enjoyment. If someone did not possess that desire in deprivation, how could he have possessed it in ownership?

O man evangelical before the Gospel, and apostolic before the apostolic commands; disciple of the Apostles! By revealing the hidden riches of nature and bringing them into the open, he showed from himself what all of us can do. He taught how great is that treasure of the soul which we possess without using, and that what we are unwilling to bring forth, we do not even believe we possess.

### CHAPTER VII

After saying many things about nature, we have also shown and proved its goodness through the examples of the saints. And lest, conversely, it be thought to be nature’s fault that some people have been wicked, I shall use the testimonies of Scripture, which everywhere burden sinners with the charge of will and do not excuse them on the grounds of nature’s necessity.

In Genesis we read: “Simeon and Levi, brothers, completed their wickedness by their own will” (Gen. 49:5–6).

The Lord spoke to Jerusalem: “For this reason they abandoned my way, which I set before them, and they did not heed my voice, but followed the desire of their evil heart” (Jer. 9:13–14).

Again the same prophet says: “You sinned against God and did not heed his voice, and you were unwilling to walk in his commandments, statutes, and testimonies.”

Through the prophet Isaiah also the Lord spoke: “If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land; but if you are unwilling and do not listen to me, the sword shall consume you” (Isa. 1:19–20).

And again: “You shall all fall by slaughter, because I called you and you did not answer; I spoke and you neglected me; you did evil before the sight of the Lord, and chose what I did not wish” (ibid. 65:12).

The Lord himself also says in the Gospel: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you! How often I wished to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you were unwilling” (Matt. 23:37).

Where we see willing and unwilling, choosing and rejecting, there we understand not the force of nature but the freedom of the will.

The volumes of both Testaments are full of testimonies of this kind, in which every good thing no less than every evil is always written to be voluntary. We omit them now for the sake of brevity, especially since we know that, devoted as you are to sacred reading, you drink more abundantly from that very fountain.

### CHAPTER VIII
Nor do we defend the goodness of nature in such a way as to say that it cannot do evil—for we openly profess that it is capable of both good and evil—but we defend it only from this injustice: that we should seem to be driven to evil by its fault, when we do neither good nor evil without the will, and when it is free for us always to do one of two things, since we are always capable of doing either. For why are some to judge and others to be judged, unless it is because within the same nature there is a different will, and because, although we are all capable of the same things, we do different things?

Accordingly, so that this very point may shine more clearly, further examples must be brought forward. Adam is cast out of paradise; Enoch is taken away from the world. In both cases the Lord demonstrates freedom of choice. For just as the one who sinned was able to please, so the one who pleased was able to sin. The just God would not have deservedly punished the one, nor chosen the other, unless each had been capable of both. The same is to be understood of the brothers Cain and Abel, and also of the twins Jacob and Esau; and it must be recognized that the sole cause why, in the same nature, merits are different is the will.

The just Noah rebuked the world extinguished by its sins in the Flood, and the holiness of Lot judged the crimes of Sodom. Nor is this a small argument for proving the goodness of nature: those first human beings lived for so many years without any admonition of the law—not, to be sure, because God had ever ceased to care for His creature, but because He knew that He had made human nature such that the law of nature itself would suffice for them to practice righteousness. Indeed, as long as the use of that more recent nature was still vigorous, and a long habit of sinning had not spread over human reason like a kind of darkness, nature was left without the law.

But when the Lord found it already buried beneath excessive vices and infected with a kind of rust of ignorance, He applied the file of the Law to it, so that it might be polished by this frequent admonition and be able to return to its own brightness. Nor is there any other reason why doing good is also difficult for us than the long habit of vices, which infected us from childhood and gradually corrupted us over many years. It afterwards binds and enslaves us so completely that it seems, in a certain sense, to possess the force of nature [Col. 1105]. All that time during which we were negligently instructed—that is, educated in vices—and during which we even took pains to be evil, when innocence was regarded as foolishness in comparison with the incentives to wickedness, now stands against us and comes to oppose us; the old habit attacks the new will.

And we wonder why, through idleness and sloth, without knowing anything, we seem almost to receive holiness from another, when we acquire no habit of goodness, although we learned evil for so long. Let these remarks about the goodness of nature be regarded as having been made hastily, as though in another’s work. We had to make them in order to clear a smoother path for you toward perfect righteousness, along which you may run more easily once you have learned that there is nothing rough or inaccessible in it.

For if, even before the Law—as we have said—and long before the coming of our Lord and Savior, certain people are reported to have lived justly and holily, how much more must we believe that we can do so after the illumination brought by His coming? We have been instructed through Christ’s grace and reborn as better human beings; cleansed and purified by His blood, and urged on by His example toward perfect righteousness, we ought to be better than those who lived before the Law, and better also than those who lived under the Law, since the Apostle says: “Sin will no longer rule over you; for you are not under the Law, but under grace” (Rom. VI, 14).

## CHAPTER IX

And since, as I think, we have spoken sufficiently about these matters, let us now form the perfect virgin, who, kindled always by both sources, should testify by the holiness of her conduct to the goodness both of nature and of grace.

The virgin’s first concern and first endeavor, therefore, should be to know the will of her Lord, and diligently to inquire what pleases Him and what displeases Him, so that, according to the Apostle, she may offer God a reasonable service (Rom. XII, 1), and may be able to order the whole course of her life according to His judgment. For it is impossible for anyone to please one whose pleasure she does not know; and it may happen that one who desires to obey gives offense because she has not first learned how she ought to obey. And just as it is greater to do the Lord’s will than to know it, so it is prior to know it than to do it. The former rightly precedes the latter in order.

Hence the prophet says: “And you, Israel, do not be ignorant.” And blessed Paul says: “But whoever is ignorant will be ignored” (I Cor. XIV, 38). Again, elsewhere: “Therefore do not become foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is” (Ephes. V, 17). The beginning of obedience is to desire to know what is commanded; and learning what you are to do is itself part of obedience.

Know, then, that in the divine Scriptures—through which alone you can understand the full will of God—some things are forbidden, some commanded, some permitted, and some advised. Evil things are forbidden, good things commanded, intermediate things permitted, and perfect things advised.

In the first two categories all sin is contained. In both, God’s command is present; for it belongs to the one who commands not only to order something but also to forbid it. For righteousness is generally commanded to all. The Savior, summing it up briefly but most completely in the Gospel, says: “Whatever you wish people to do for you, do the same for them” (Matt. VII, 12). That is, let us inflict no evil on others and render every good, because we wish both to be observed toward us by others.

This judgment binds everyone equally under the force of the command, and no one at all may transgress what has been commanded to all. It is an open contempt of God either to do what has been forbidden or not to do what has been commanded.

The two remaining matters, however—one of which is permitted and the other advised—have been left in our power, so that we may either use what is permitted with lesser glory, or, for the sake of a greater reward, reject even what has been allowed us. Marriage, the use of meat, and wine are indeed permitted; but abstinence from all these things is advised as the more perfect course.

The permission of marriage contributes to the honor of virginity, and the indulgence granted in foods makes the virtue of abstinence more distinguished. You have rejected marriage, virgin, although it was permitted to you before you rejected it. Burning with love for a greater reward, you vowed to God a virginity not commanded but praised; and, following the Apostle’s counsel, you made your law broader.

Entering the arena of the contest, you considered not so much the labor of the race as the prize of victory. You had read, I believe, that Gospel proclamation of perpetual chastity, and the Lord’s own saying had kindled you to love the preservation of virginity. He praised Peter’s judgment on this matter by the very greatness and difficulty of the undertaking, and, promising the kingdom of heaven to voluntary eunuchs, said: “Let the one who is able to receive it receive it” (Matt. XIX, 12).

I do not command or impose so great a matter; I offer it. Nor do I compel anyone to it, but I challenge them. Although the saying may appear to concern men alone, the palm of virginity is promised not only to men but equally to both sexes. And the Apostle says that he does not have a command from God concerning virgins, but gives advice (I Cor. VII, 25). Thus he says: “Do you seek proof of the one who speaks in me, namely Christ?” (II Cor. XIII, 3).

## CHAPTER X

Having therefore followed the counsel of perfection and undertaken the blessedness of a special calling, keep the general commandment. I have said it, and now repeat it: in the matter of righteousness, we all have one obligation. Virgin, widow, married woman, the highest, middle, and lowest rank—all are equally commanded to fulfill the precepts.

Nor is the one who proposes to do more than the Law released from the Law. On the contrary, no one ought more carefully to avoid what is unlawful than the one who rejects what was lawful. Nor does anyone promise to fulfill the commandments as fully as the one who ascends above the commandments through love of perfection. When she determines to do more than is commanded, she shows that what was commanded was less than she was able to do.

Moreover, if one professes such obedience that she willingly listens even to divine counsel, how should she not listen to a command? The former belongs to perfection [Note: Col. 1106. Another manuscript reads, “of choice” (electionis).]; the latter to necessity. Of virginity it is said: “Let the one who is able to receive it receive it.” Of righteousness it is not said, “Let the one who is able to do it do it,” but: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. III, 10; Luke III, 9).

Consider, I beg you, how far a command differs from counsel. There, some are excepted; here, all are included. There, a reward is proposed; here, a punishment. There, you are invited to do it; here, you are threatened unless you do it.

Distinguishing these matters, therefore, with the greatest care, observe what you offer and observe what you owe. Indeed, since you now owe both—the virginity that you freely offered to God and the righteousness that He Himself commanded—pay both in full.

That servant pleases his master who undertakes some task freely, yet also fulfills what has been commanded; who does not do one thing in place of another, but both; who does not exchange one service for another, but adds service to service.

Nor should you be deceived by those who applaud themselves for chastity alone and, in order to pursue their own pleasures [Note: Col. 1106. Another manuscript reads, “desires.”], cast aside the will of God. They wish to offer the good of perpetual chastity not together with righteousness but in place of righteousness; they count the reward of virginity as compensation for sins and ask immunity as their reward. Or, in still more shameless madness, they think that they themselves ought to be crowned and preferred to others in the kingdom of heaven, although by transgressing the commandments they have closed the way to heaven for themselves.

“Not everyone,” Christ says, “who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VII, 21).

Let them remember that the foolish virgins will be driven back from the bridegroom’s doors, and that it will be said to them: “I do not know you” (Matt. XXV, 12). Let them also remember that they belong with those of whom the Lord Himself says: “Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not cast out demons in your name, and in your name perform many mighty works?’ And then I will declare to them: ‘Truly I say to you, I do not know you; depart from me, all you workers of iniquity’” (Matt. VII, 22–23).

But your path must be entirely different. You wish, having trampled underfoot the love of the world and constantly pondering the things of God, to show yourself an apostolic virgin. You await the Lord’s coming, holy in spirit as well as in body; you continually pour the oil of holy works into the lamp of your soul; and, joined to the wise virgins, you prepare to go out to meet the bridegroom.

You must flee that broad road which the company of many who go to destruction wears down, and you must keep to the narrow path of that journey to eternal life which few find [Col. 1107].

You have already laid aside the greatest impediments, and everything that either delays or turns you back from the course of the spiritual life; you conquered these things at your first conversion. You rejected the pleasure of marriage, concern for offspring, the allurements of luxury, the pomp of the world, and the desire for riches, and with Paul you can say: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI, 14).

What should the perfection of such a beginning be? Bring me this virtue and this courage also in what remains. By the strength of mind with which you drove away the occasions of vice, now reject vice itself.

Let virginity be adorned with holiness of conduct, and let perfection of life follow upon the perfect calling. Certainly, if secular life had pleased you, you would have taken care that no one surpassed you in wealth, no one in bodily adornments, no one in abundance of possessions or honor. Now, since a different pursuit requires a different life, take care that no one surpass you in right living, no one excel you in holiness of conduct, and no one be preferred to you in virtues.

And in those matters we mentioned earlier, it was not within your power either to surpass everyone or to be surpassed by no one. All those things are sought from outside, and whatever is hoped for from elsewhere belongs to another. These things, however, are in your power and truly your own. They do not come from outside but are generated in the heart itself.

Those external goods are not found by everyone who seeks them, nor are they always retained by the one who finds them, since chance can grant them and also take them away. But these goods are found by everyone who seeks them, and whoever finds them never fears that they will be taken away. These alone are good things that we sometimes neither find without the will nor lose without it.

## CHAPTER XI

You therefore have here the means by which you may rightly be preferred to others—or rather, here especially. Bodily nobility and wealth are understood to belong to your family, not to you; but no one except yourself can confer spiritual riches upon you. In these, therefore, you are rightly to be praised and deservedly preferred to the others, since they cannot exist except from you and in you.

Is this the only life that has no contest for advancement, in which each person ought merely to remain what she began to be, without striving toward greater things through any desire for increase? When people are not satisfied with progress in any of the pursuits of the world, will it suffice here merely to have begun?

We are most fervent in earthly matters and most cold in heavenly ones. We display the greatest eagerness in small things and grow sluggish when greater things are at stake. It is shameful to consider how great is the fervor in the world, and with what care each human pursuit strives daily toward greater perfection.

The ardor for letters is extinguished at no age; rather, to use the judgment of a secular author, it is inflamed more strongly by age itself. The love of riches is insatiable; the desire for honors does not know how to be filled; things destined to have a swift end are sought without end.

We, however, neglect divine wisdom, heavenly riches, and immortal honors with a kind of sluggish indifference. We either do not touch spiritual riches at all, or, if we have tasted them lightly, immediately suppose that we are satisfied.

Divine Wisdom invites us differently to her feasts: “Those who eat me,” she says, “will hunger still, and those who drink me will thirst still” (Ecclus. XXIV, 29). No one is ever filled by such feasts, nor does anyone ever suffer disgust from satiety. Each person will be more capable, and more eager, the more he has drawn from them.

The Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be filled” (Matt. V, 6). He wishes us always to hunger and thirst for righteousness here, so that in the future we may be filled by the recompense of righteousness.

## CHAPTER XII

The force of the words themselves must be considered, and righteousness must be desired by us as food and drink are desired in hunger and thirst. This must be said generally to all who desire the rewards of immortal life.

It is now for you to estimate how much you ought to excel in spirit, since, moved by the desire for a greater reward, you have proposed to do more than others are required to do.

The Apostle, defining Christ’s virgin, set her far apart from the married woman and divided the merit of celibacy and marriage between different pursuits: “The unmarried woman and the virgin,” he says, “think about the things of the Lord, how she may please the Lord, so that she may be holy in body and spirit; but the married woman thinks about the things of the world, how she may please her husband” (I Cor. VII, 34).

The woman who is holy in body and spirit commits no offense either in her members or in her mind. But offending is possible not only in the matter of chastity, but also in any part of righteousness. For although a woman may be a virgin in body and a virgin in spirit, yet if she sins with her hands, eyes, ears, or tongue, how can she be called holy in body?

Moreover, if she is infected with hatred, envy, avarice, or anger, how does she possess holiness in spirit? And if the married woman, who thinks through love of marriage how she may please her husband and how much she may leave to her children, who is bound by various cares of the world and looks less often to the will of God, nevertheless cannot excuse herself from sins, what will the virgin do—she who, released and free from all the impediments of this world, has entered a kind of school of chastity?

## CHAPTER XIII

If, then, you wish your conduct to match the greatness of your calling, and to be joined to God in every respect; if you wish to make Christ’s easy and gentle yoke gentler and easier for yourself, devote yourself now, especially in the blessed life, to the greatest care. Strive now so that the new fervor of recent conversion may always kindle your still-warm faith, and so that, while you are still young, the practice of holy conduct may more easily take root.

Whatever you establish in yourself at the beginning will remain, and the rest of your life will run according to the rule of your beginnings. The end must be considered at the very outset: whatever kind of person you wish to reach that final day, strive now already to be such a person.

Habit is what nourishes either vices or virtues, and it has the greatest power when it has grown together with them from the beginning of life. The earliest years are best for forming conduct. They possess something pliant and yielding that can easily be shaped and drawn according to the will of the one who wishes; and in almost all matters whatever is tender becomes accustomed more quickly.

Young saplings, with scarcely established roots, are easy to bend in any direction while they still follow every shaping; when nature has usually bent them, they are quickly straightened according to the cultivator’s will. Young animals, still tender and in the first stage of life, are usually tamed without effort; and the sooner they are weaned from the freedom of wandering, the more easily they accustom either their necks to the yoke or their mouths to the bridle.

The studies of letters themselves are more effectively implanted in tender minds. Whatever first settles in the mind is accustomed to cling deeply to the senses.

The same is especially true in the way of living well. While age is still pliable and the mind easy to guide, the habit of goodness must be practiced and strengthened by continual meditation. The mind must be occupied with the best things, and the practice of holy conduct must be implanted more deeply.

Then the mind rises to the summit of perfection and benefits from long habit in its ability to live well. Admiring even its own virtues, it will in a certain sense think that what it is learning was born within itself.

## CHAPTER XIV

Consider, I beg you, how much holiness your grandmother and mother expect from you. They think that you have been born as a new and distinguished light for your family; now they have transferred all the care of their hearts to you alone and kindle the course of your calling with extraordinary devotion and favor.

Although they themselves formed you for honorable conduct from your earliest age, they now wish to be surpassed by you and think your victory their own praise. Their outstanding faith toward God shone forth especially in your profession. As soon as they learned that, although you had already been prepared for marriage, you wished something else, they immediately encouraged you, with remarkable speed of agreement, to pursue what you had chosen. They strengthened your decision, still hesitant because of your age, by the authority of their own will and made your vow their common vow.

Although they had seen many of their family attain the highest rank of dignity, they had never rejoiced over anyone as they rejoiced over you. They had seen nothing so great, nothing so illustrious, in anyone. You alone have provided your family with what it had not possessed for a long time in the past.

Although the male sex may have produced memorable consulships, and the illustrious standing of a family of the highest order may have frequently heard the names of distinguished men, nevertheless nothing in your family has ever been more outstanding than this honor of yours, which has been inserted not into a bodily register but into the book of immortal memory.

When theatrical applause has received those men throughout the world, and the delighted crowd has expressed the distinguished merits of the consuls through a remarkable harmony of acclamation [Col. 1109], nevertheless the glory of your honor is far greater, since it has produced joy in heaven and gladness among the angels.

Through you, it is not little prostitutes who are enriched but Christ’s virgins who are nourished; it is not a hunter or charioteer who is made wealthy but Christ’s poor who are supported. For their consulship, the various provinces of the whole world, to which the power of your house extends, sent exotic beasts and unknown animals, to stain the floor of the cruel arena with their own blood or that of human beings.

But to you the choicest virgins are sent, whom you may offer as a most precious gift to God and, by your example, summon to perpetual chastity—virgins who will serve not you but God together with you.

The glory of your profession has been spread among all by widespread report. The whole world rejoiced so greatly at your way of life that what people could scarcely yet believe out of immense joy seems to have been what they had always desired.

All are deeply moved by these beginnings and by the fragrance of your reputation; they desire to hear something extraordinary about you. Those who have learned the excellence of your profession now await the excellence of your way of life. Imagine that everyone’s mouths and eyes are now turned toward you, and that the whole world has taken its seat to watch the spectacle of your life.

Take care that through you the hearts of so many are not offended, and that they do not find less in you than they seek.

But why do I speak to you about human beings, and turn their expectations of you into an exhortation to you? God Himself, the ruler and Lord of all, watches your contest with the whole army of angels. As you fight against the devil, He prepares for you the crown of eternity and makes the heavenly reward an incentive to victory.

Consider what spirit and what virtue you ought to bring before so great a spectacle, and measure the greatness of the contest by the dignity of those who await your victory.

## CHAPTER XV

As you enter this contest, therefore, let this be your chief concern: in this first engagement, to conquer the war of destruction through virtue, and to swear allegiance to all the commandments of God against the camp of the devil—not merely to avoid what is forbidden but to fulfill what is commanded.

For it is not enough for you to be inactive with regard to evil if you are inactive with regard to good. The Law of God is distinguished by a twofold kind of commandments: it forbids evil and commands good, and it forbids contempt of itself on either side.

The servant who does what has been forbidden is not the only one who has despised his master; so has the one who has failed to do what was commanded. We stated shortly before: “Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. III, 10; VII, 19). Yet we flatter ourselves if we are not burdened with evil fruits, although we will be condemned if we remain barren of good ones!

According to this understanding, the Father will cut off every branch in the Son that does not bear fruit; and the one who hid the talent he had received in a cloth is condemned by the Lord as a useless and wicked servant. It is culpable not only to have diminished what was given but also not to have increased it.

Do not think that any commandments may be despised because they are lighter. The greatest and the smallest have alike been commanded by God, and contempt for any commandment is an insult to the one who commands.

Hence blessed Paul cries out and teaches: “Do everything without murmuring and hesitation, so that you may be blameless and sincere, as spotless children of God in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom you shine like lights in the world” (Philipp. II, 14–15).

## CHAPTER XVI

Let us linger here for a little while, virgin, and weigh, one by one, the most precious jewels with which Christ’s bride must be adorned, considering each word of the Apostle.

“Do everything,” he says. We must not choose some of God’s commandments according to our own judgment, as though they were optional, but fulfill them all without exception. Nor should we despise any of His precepts as cheap and insignificant gifts, but look in everything to the majesty of the one who commands.

No commandment of God can seem contemptible to us if we always consider its author.

“Without murmuring and hesitation.” We see lowly and ignoble masters openly despised by their little servants, who commonly resist them to their faces even in the smallest commands. But this is no longer tolerated with noble persons. The more powerful the masters, the more ready the servants are to obey [Col. 1110]; and when they give more difficult commands, they are obeyed more willingly.

Certainly, at a king’s command everyone is so prepared and stationed for obedience that they even desire to be ordered. They believe not only that they will deserve well if they do what is commanded, but, as though they had already deserved what they were ordered to do, they regard service as a benefit because of the dignity of the one who commands.

Yet God Himself—the eternal Majesty, the ineffable and immeasurable Power—sends us the sacred Scriptures and the truly worship-worthy letters of His commandments. We do not immediately receive them with joy and reverence, nor do we regard the command of so great and illustrious a Power as a great benefit, especially since what is sought is not the advantage of the one who commands but the welfare of the one who obeys.

Instead, with a wearied and sluggish spirit, in the manner of proud and wicked servants, we protest against the Lord and say: “It is hard; it is arduous; we cannot do it. We are human beings; we are enclosed in fragile flesh.”

O blind madness! O profane recklessness! With a double ignorance we accuse God of ignorance, so that He seems not to know what He made and not to know what He commanded. It is as though, forgetting the frailty of human beings—of which He Himself is the author—He had imposed on humanity commandments that it could not bear.

At the same time, what an abomination, we ascribe injustice to the just and cruelty to the compassionate. First we complain that He commanded something impossible; then we think that He ought to condemn a human being for what that person could not avoid. Thus, what it is sacrilegious even to suspect, God seems not to have sought our salvation so much as our punishment.

Therefore, the Apostle, knowing that the Lord of righteousness and majesty has commanded nothing impossible, removes from us the fault of murmuring. Murmuring ordinarily arises when what is commanded is unjust or when the person commanding is insufficiently worthy.

Why do we uselessly evade the matter and oppose the frailty of nature to the one who commands? No one knows the measure of our strength better than the one who gave us those very strengths. No one understands better how much we are able to do than the one who granted us the very power by which we are able.
