He who is just did not wish to command anything impossible, nor did the compassionate one intend to condemn a human being for something that person could not avoid.

## CHAPTER XVII

The Apostle continues: “So that you may be blameless and sincere.” This one word can suffice for all perfection of conduct; God also commands that it be sought when a bishop is being chosen. What life could be more circumspect, what life more holy, than one that incurs no reproach?

And who can be holier than the person who, holding fast to the virtue of true sincerity, never promises one thing in her heart while pretending another in her speech and expression?

“As spotless children of God.” No exhortation is more powerful than the one by which divine Scripture calls us children of God. Who would not blush and fear to do something unworthy of so great a Father, so that one who is called a child of God should become a servant of vice?

For this reason he adds: “So that we may be spotless.” It is not fitting for the children of God—since He Himself is the fountain of righteousness—to be found with the stain of sin.

“In the midst of a crooked and perverse generation.” This means: Although an infinite multitude of sinners surrounds you, and countless examples of vice are present, you must nevertheless remember your heavenly birth in such a way that, while living among the wicked, you overcome every evil.

“Among whom you shine,” he says, “like lights in the world.” And again we read in the Gospel: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. XIII, 43).

Life is compared with the reward, so that those who are to be granted the sun’s radiance in the future may already shine here with a similar brightness of righteousness and illuminate the blindness of unbelievers by works of holiness.

The meaning that the same Apostle discusses in his letter to the Corinthians should be applied to this passage: “There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory. So also is the resurrection of the dead” (I Cor. XV, 41–42).

The dwelling places in the kingdom of heaven differ according to the merits of each person. Differences in works produce differences in rewards; and to the degree that someone shines here in holiness, to that degree will he shine there in honor.

Therefore, direct the sharpness of your mind toward every perfection of conduct, and prepare a heavenly life for a heavenly reward. Let the holiness of the virgin shine before all like a most brilliant star [Col. 1111], and let the greatness of the future reward be displayed by the newness of her way of life.

Your course toward good is easier, since the habit of the evil-minded does not hold you back. We do not fear that vices will delay you from virtues or that the devil’s poisonous seeds will destroy Christ’s harvest.

For if even those who, through long practice of sinning, have in some sense buried the goodness of nature can be restored through repentance, extinguish one habit by another through a changed will to live, and become good even from being very bad, how much more can you overcome those by which you have not been overcome?

Your vices need not so much be expelled as rejected. It is certainly easier not to admit them than to put them away once admitted.

## CHAPTER XVIII

Nor are vices so sweet that we ought to prefer them to virtues, since not all of them contain an enticement of pleasure, and since most people reject even those that seem sweetest.

There are two vices above all that deceive human beings through the pleasure they provide: gluttony and lust. It is more difficult to lay them aside because it is sweeter to indulge in them. Yet we have seen many trample these vices—so troublesome and so dangerous through their very pleasure—underfoot, and remain virgins throughout their lives in the strictest abstinence.

I say nothing of those who, after a long indulgence in luxury and an entrenched habit of lust, have devoted themselves to chastity and temperance and exchanged both vices for the virtues opposed to them.

The case of other vices is altogether different. Although they contain no pleasure, they contain a great deal of bitterness; and although they are much easier to avoid, you rarely find anyone who avoids them.

What pleasure, I ask you, does envy provide to the envious person, whom jealousy itself tears apart with hidden claws of conscience and for whom another’s happiness becomes a torment?

What reward does the person who hates receive from hatred, except the dreadful darkness of the soul and the horror of a troubled mind? With a face and spirit always grieving, he tortures himself through the desire to harm another.

What does anger contribute to the angry person, when its fury, driven by the most savage goads, so casts him down from all judgment and reason that, while he is angry, he is believed to be insane?

Run through the individual vices in the same way, and you will find as many torments of the soul as there are vices. They can certainly be conquered more easily because they entice us with no pleasure.

How much more difficult, how much harsher it is—to say nothing of the labor of chastity—to abstain from wine and meat, even from oil itself; to take only cheap food, sometimes with difficulty, after two or even three days; to weaken one’s limbs through fasting and vigils; to reject the comforts of the bath; to deny the body what it needs; and to do violence, in a certain sense, to nature!

Show the same greatness of spirit in other matters, and see what you cannot accomplish. But we, shamefully, through a certain pleasure in sin, show the strength of our nature in some things while growing completely sluggish in others. We have rejected bodily pleasures for the love of virtues, yet again, through love of vices, we take on torments; and we yield so completely to our evils that we do not even think they can be laid aside.

What kind of judgment is this, I ask? What new way of living is this? I confidently undertake difficult matters full of labor, yet believe that easier things cannot be done. I conquer the greatest things, while being conquered by small ones; tirelessly I overcome lofty and arduous obstacles, yet fail when I come to level ground. I gladly flee what delights me, and refuse to avoid what torments me.

But this is characteristic of those who, having despised the will of God, seek only what more easily wins praise and quickly becomes famous, while neglecting the good qualities of conduct that are more hidden.

But you, who have trampled the world and its desires underfoot in order to make your trampling of it a kind of step by which you might ascend to heaven, must not seek the glory of the world. Strive only to please the one who is often displeased by what pleases human beings, and who will judge the very judgments of human beings.

Your abstinence and fasting are more pleasing to God when they are offered together with holy conduct, so that what in others are screens concealing vices may in you be ornaments of virtues.

## CHAPTER XIX
Consider, I beg you, that very dignity by which you have been illumined before God: through Baptism [Col. 1112] you were reborn as a daughter of God, and then, through the consecration of virginity, you began to be the bride of Christ. From both of these, let your honor here admonish you to care for your vocation. There ought to be no place for negligence where things so illustrious must be guarded. Every more precious garment is guarded with more anxious care against stains; a jewel acquired at great cost is possessed with greater vigilance; and, generally speaking, all great things are preserved with great care. Therefore, if you wish to guard yourself well, you must always consider your honor and your worth. For each person uses himself with proportionately greater negligence the cheaper he considers himself.

It is for no other reason that the name “children of God” is so frequently bestowed upon us in the divine Scriptures: “And I shall be a father to you, and you shall be sons to me, says the Lord Almighty” (Jerem. XXXI, 9, and II Cor. VI, 18). The Apostle likewise says, “Be imitators of God, as beloved children” (Ephes. V, 1). And blessed John says, “Beloved, we are now children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (I John III, 2); so that whoever has this hope in him sanctifies himself, just as he is holy.

He wishes frequently to impress upon us the dignity of the heavenly teaching with which we have been endowed, and to make our honor a source of shame at sin. Therefore the Lord himself, calling us to perfect kindness, says: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven.” Nothing makes people pleasing to God in such a way as the devotion and goodness of the mind; and these ought to be so abundant in a Christian that they overflow even toward the wicked, imitating the benevolence of God, who makes his sun rise upon good and evil and sends rain upon just and unjust alike (Matt. V, 44–45).

Let it therefore be far from you, above all, to harm anyone even by a word; strive to benefit everyone in every way you can; and, returning no evil in kind, repay evil with good, as the Apostle says (Rom. XII, 17, 20–21). Let no slander ever proceed from a virgin’s mouth. It is characteristic enough of base people, and of those who seek their own praise, to make others base, because they think that they are praised by another’s condemnation; and those who cannot please by their own merit wish to please in comparison with worse people.

I have said too little: not only must you yourself refrain from slander, but you must never even believe the slanderer. This is a most pernicious vice, which makes another person appear contemptible. Flee slander no less with your ears than with your tongue. Remember the Scripture, which says, “You shall not agree with those who disparage your neighbor, and you shall not receive sin against him.” And elsewhere: “Hedge your ears with thorns, and do not listen to a wicked tongue” (Eccli. XXVIII, 28). The listener is an accuser, for he makes the slanderer; but if he turns his ears away, contracts his face, and restrains his eyes by refusing assent, then, even while silent, he reproves the evil speaker, so that the speaker may learn not readily to say what he has learned is not readily heard.

Set a sufficiently watchful guard over your mouth. For there is nothing in us through which we can sin more easily than the tongue. Hence Saint James says that the perfect person is one who does not offend in speech (James III, 2); and Scripture says, “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Prov. XVIII, 21). Let your tongue know neither how to lie, nor to curse, nor to swear: “the mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. I, 11); and those who curse “shall not possess the kingdom of God,” according to the Apostle (Gal. V, 20–21). Christ himself prohibited swearing when he said, “But I say to you, do not swear at all”; and again, “Let your speech be ‘Yes, yes; No, no’; anything beyond this is from evil” (Matt. V, 34, 37).

The Apostle, briefly cutting away the vices of the mouth, says: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth, but only such as is good for building up in the faith, that it may give grace to those who hear” (Ephes. IV, 29). Let a virgin’s speech be prudent [Note: [Col. 1112] Another manuscript: “modest”], restrained, and infrequent; let it be precious not so much for eloquence as for modesty. Let everyone admire your modesty when you are silent, and your prudence when you speak. Let your speech always be adorned with gentleness and calm, with sweetness mingled with gravity, and wisdom with modesty. Let the manner of your silence and speech be deliberate, balanced, and exceedingly pleasing at the proper time. And let a virgin’s mouth never speak at all when it would be better to have remained silent. She must speak with great caution when she must avoid not only wicked speech but even idle speech.

## CHAPTER XX

Let it be your highest knowledge and fullest understanding to distinguish vices from virtues. Although these are always opposed to one another, some of them are joined by such a close resemblance that they can scarcely be distinguished at all. How many people regard pride as freedom, accept flattery in place of humility, embrace malice under the name of prudence, and give stupidity the name of simplicity! Deceived by this false and pernicious resemblance, they glory in vices as though they were virtues.

Although you must separate these things with the subtlest discernment, pursuing every virtue along its proper lines and never departing from them, flee especially counterfeit humility and pursue that which is genuine—the humility Christ taught, in which no pride is enclosed. Many follow the shadow of this virtue; few pursue its reality.

It is very easy for someone to wear a despised garment, offer a submissive greeting, kiss hands and knees, and, with head bowed toward the ground and eyes cast down, promise humility and gentleness; to break his words with a slow and faint voice, sigh frequently, and cry out at every word that he is a sinner and wretched; yet, if he is offended by even a slight remark, immediately to raise his eyebrows, lift his neck, and suddenly change that delicate tone of voice into a mad shout.

Christ taught us another kind of humility. He urges us to follow his example, saying, “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. XI, 29). “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten” (I Pet. II, 23). Blessed Peter makes this humility clear to us: “Be compassionate,” he says, “and humble, not returning evil for evil or abuse for abuse” (ibid. III, 8–9).

Let all verbal pretenses be removed; let feigned gestures cease; and let speech be calm before there is occasion for provocation. Patience under insult reveals the truly humble person. Therefore let there never be any place in your mind for any vice; let there be nothing proud in you, nothing arrogant, nothing, finally, disdainful. Before God there is nothing more exalted than humility. He speaks through the prophet: “Upon whom shall I look, if not upon the humble and peaceful person who trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI, 2).

And let your mind never blaze into anger, which is the seedbed of hatred. Let such fear of God fill your mind that you dare not become indignant at all, and let fear conquer anger. The blessed Apostle, cleansing our soul and preparing it as a dwelling place for God, cries out and says: “Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, shouting, and blasphemy be removed from you, together with all malice” (Ephes. IV, 31).

## CHAPTER XXI

Beware of flatterers as enemies: their words are smooth as oil, but they themselves are arrows. With feigned praises they corrupt shallow souls and inflict a soothing wound upon minds that readily believe. This vice has grown in our age and has reached its final limit; it can grow no further. We have all devoted ourselves to this school and discipline, so that we regard it as our duty to deceive others. What we ourselves gladly receive from others, we offer to others as a kind of gift; and, in the hope of receiving praise, we praise first those from whom we wish to be praised.

Often we resist the words of flatterers to their faces, while secretly favoring them in our minds; and we think we have gained the greatest reward if we are celebrated with even feigned praises. We do not consider what we ourselves are, but what we seem to be to others. Thus matters have reached the point where, neglecting the truth of merit, we care only about reputation, seeking testimony to our life not from our conscience but from public opinion.

Blessed is the mind that perfectly conquers this vice: that never flatters and never believes a flatterer; that neither deceives another nor is itself deceived; that neither does nor suffers this evil at all. Let there never be anything false or counterfeit in you. Regard your conscience—which certainly always lies open before God—as though you were living among a multitude of people. Never pretend one thing in your heart and another with your mouth. Whatever you are ashamed to say, be ashamed even to think.

It is already known and widely proclaimed how useful, and how necessary to this vocation, is the virtue of fasting and abstinence, especially in these years when the body contains greater heat. Not to eat meat or drink wine has been praised by the apostolic voice. Whatever can inflame the body, whatever supplies fuel to pleasure, must be avoided for love of chastity.

Yet we do not wish you to be burdened by this practice with such great labor that you immediately collapse beneath the weight. Many, lacking any reckoning of their strength because of excessive fervor of mind, have suddenly fallen; and they have attained from their vocation almost weakness before holiness. The best course in everything is moderation, and measure is praiseworthy everywhere. The body must not be broken but governed.

Let your holy fasts therefore be moderate and simple, practiced with complete humility of mind. Let them weaken the body without exalting the spirit, lest an act of humility produce pride and vices arise from virtue. “When they troubled me,” he says, “I clothed myself in sackcloth and humbled my soul with fasting” (Ps. XXXIV, 13). The despised garment, the lowly food, and the weariness of fasting ought to extinguish, not nourish, pride. Who would turn a remedy into a wound, and thereby injure the healthy parts through which the injured parts are to be healed? Or what hope of salvation will remain if the remedies of the soul themselves become poisons?

## CHAPTER XXII

Let works of mercy commend the labor of your fasting, and let your abstinence become more pleasing through feeding the poor. The Lord speaks through the prophet: “I desire mercy and not sacrifice” (Hos. VI, 6). In the Gospel of Christ we read the words, “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. V, 7).

But, I beg you, let your grandmother and mother undertake this care in your place; let them perform these duties for you, and let them raise your treasure to heaven. Let it be their task to feed the hungry, clothe the naked, visit the sick, receive strangers under their roof, and lend to Christ in the poor in hope of an eternal reward. He said, “Whatever you did for one of the least of these my brothers, you did for me” (ibid. XXV, 40).

But for you, especially while your mind is maturing in your vocation, it is necessary to withdraw from every occupation and devote all your effort and care to ordering your conduct. You must be so free for these things, and occupy your whole mind with them, that you do not consider yourself wealthy or a mistress. Remember your nobility for this one purpose: to strive, in the holiness of your conduct, to match the distinction of your lineage; to advance nobler in spirit than in bodily nobility; and to glory more in that nobility which makes people children of God and coheirs of Christ.

If you always look toward this nobility, then, while believing that you possess a greater joy, you cease to glory in what is lesser. Let all this dignity of illustrious birth, and the distinguished honor of Anician blood, be transferred to the soul. Let that person be illustrious, exalted, and noble; let that person think that he preserves his nobility intact if he disdains to serve vices and is not overcome by them. For whoever is overcome by something is its servant (II Pet. I, 19).

What is more unworthy of the soul than this slavery, or more shameful, than when hatred dominates it or envy reigns in it? What is more shameful than when greed possesses it, anger holds it captive, or the other vices claim it for themselves? No one should flatter himself about the nobility of his birth if, in the better part of himself, he becomes a servant. It is far more disgraceful to serve in mind than in body.

I think it unnecessary to advise you how sparingly and how rarely you should go out, since secular propriety has taught you this from childhood, and you readily understand that in this way of life it must be observed all the more, since it is especially suited to a woman living in seclusion. I do advise you to set a very definite limit even to the greetings that must be offered to you in your chamber. Let them not be excessive or daily, lest they seem to provide not so much courtesy as disturbance.

## CHAPTER XXIII

Although you ought to consecrate every moment of your life to divine work, and no hour at all should be empty of spiritual progress, since you must meditate upon the law of the Lord day and night (Ps. I, 2), there should nevertheless be a fixed and appointed number of hours in which you devote yourself more fully to God, and which, as though by a law, hold you to the greatest concentration of mind.

It is therefore best to assign the morning to this work—that is, the better part of the day—and, until the third hour, to exercise the soul daily as it contends in the heavenly struggle, as though in the gymnasium of a spiritual training ground.

During these hours each day, pray in the more secluded part of the house, with your chamber closed. Create solitude for yourself even in the City, withdraw for a little while from everyone, and draw closer to God; then, when you are returned to the view of your family, display the fruit of your reading and prayer.

For in this seclusion you should do nothing more than nourish your soul with divine utterances and satisfy it with this richer food, insofar as it can suffice for the whole day. Read the holy Scriptures in such a way that you always remember that they are the words of God, who commands that his law not merely be known but also fulfilled. It is of no benefit to learn what must be done and not do it.

You will use divine reading most effectively if you make it serve as a mirror, so that in it the soul may look upon itself as though at its own image, correcting whatever is foul and further adorning whatever is beautiful. Let prayer frequently interrupt your reading, and let the pleasing alternation of holy work continually kindle the soul that clings to God.

Now let the order of the heavenly history instruct you; now let holy David’s song delight you; now let Solomon’s wisdom teach you; now let the warnings of the prophets stir you to fear the Lord; now let the perfection of the Gospel and the Apostles unite you to Christ in complete holiness of conduct. Fix deeply in your memory what must be acquired, and preserve it through constant meditation. Frequently turn over what must be brought to maturity, so that this divine study and heavenly school may adorn both the conduct and the understanding of a virgin, and may hand over to you holiness together with wisdom.

Hence Scripture says: “Those who seek God find wisdom together with righteousness.” Let the reading itself be measured, and let counsel, not weariness, bring it to an end. For just as excessive fasts, the ardor of abstinence, and immense and disorderly vigils are condemned as intemperance—and by their very excess produce the result that afterward they cannot be practiced even moderately—so excessive devotion to reading falls under the charge of intemperance; and what is praiseworthy in its proper time becomes blameworthy through excess.

## CHAPTER XXIV

In general, briefly and concisely, this must be said: even in good things, whatever exceeds the proper measure is a vice. Great—very great, I say—is the discipline of a perfect life, and it requires great effort. It is the mark of consummate wisdom to know what to pursue, in what manner, and to place deliberation before every action, doing nothing that one will regret having done.

Within the space of a single hour one’s habit can be changed. To fast, abstain, sing psalms, and keep vigil require not so much effort as willingness. Anyone beginning these practices is perfect in them as soon as he wishes; indeed, those can do them more easily who bring the fresh strength of their bodies from the world into their vocation. But to change one’s conduct, to shape and perfect each virtue of the soul within oneself, requires great effort and long practice. Thus many of us grow old in this vocation without possessing the very things for which we came to it.

Your conduct, however, must be new: marked by remarkable gravity, patience, gentleness, and devotion. Whatever is holier and more perfect, whatever can commend you more to God and make you greater in heaven—always pursue and embrace it. Nothing should be more adorned than the bride of Christ. The greater the one whom you must please, the greater must be your zeal to please him.

The virgins of the world, who prepare themselves for marriage and prefer to follow the Apostle’s concession rather than his advice, embracing the remedy of incontinence more readily than the reward of continence, diligently strive to fashion themselves in wonderful ways so as to please their bridegrooms and inflame them more deeply with love for themselves. They enhance the natural beauty of their bodies with the art of adornment.

Their chief daily concern is to color their faces with becoming cosmetics, entwine their hair with gold [Col. 1116], and make glowing stones set in shells an honor for their heads; to hang fortunes from their ears, adorn their arms with necklaces and their sides with ornaments, and lower gems enclosed in gold from their necks onto their breasts.

Your bridegroom requires no less adornment. After he has purified the whole Church with the washing of saving water and presented her without spot or wrinkle (Ephes. V, 26–27), he desires daily that she become more beautiful, so that, once cleansed from vices and sins, she may always be adorned with the beauty of virtues.

And if he requires this from the whole Church, which includes widows and married women, how much do you think he expects from a virgin whom he seems to have chosen as a more august flower from that most beautiful meadow of the Church?

Assume, then, all the adornment by which you can please Christ. Consider your face sufficiently pleasing to God if you do not strive to appear beautiful to human beings. Preserve the adornment for your head that you acquired through the sacrament of chrism, when a kind of diadem of royal anointing was placed upon you as a sign of the mystery of the heavenly kingdom.

The best ornaments for the ears are the words of God. A virgin’s hearing should be ready for those alone, and should prefer them to the most precious stones. Let every limb be adorned with works of holiness, and let the whole beauty of the virgin soul shine like a jeweled necklace with the varied splendor of virtues.

Then the king will truly desire your beauty, and will say to you, “You are altogether beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (Song IV, 7). These ornaments of which I have spoken will also be the greatest defenses, able both to adorn you before God and to arm you against the devil. He sometimes enters the soul through some slight vice; and if the ramparts of the virtues do not resist him, he drives us from our own position and immediately becomes master instead of the enemy. Therefore Scripture exhorts us, saying: “If the spirit of one who has power rises against you, do not abandon your place” (Eccles. X, 4).

## CHAPTER XXV

From the time when you were first consecrated to the Lord through your profession of virginity, the adversary’s hatred toward you increased. He regards the gains of others as his own losses, and considers himself to have lost whatever he grieves to see you possessing. You need great vigilance and great care; and the enemy must be guarded against with all the more anxiety the richer you have begun to be in his eyes.

An empty and naked traveler does not fear a robber’s ambush. A poor man sleeps securely at night, even if he does not fortify his doors against thieves. But the rich always imagine that their wealth will bring the robber upon them, and their constant anxiety deprives them of sleep at night.

Thus your riches too—the heavenly treasure—need this caution and protection. The richer you are, the more vigilant you must be; for whoever possesses more must fear more lest he lose it.

The author of envy never ceases to envy. He who himself was once cast down by God is tormented by all the greater jealousy when he sees someone more honored by God. He envied Eve the paradise; how much more does he envy you the kingdom of heaven?

Believe me, he now goes about everywhere, as blessed Peter says, desiring to devour you (I Pet. V, 8). He comes like a roaring lion, or, like a crafty enemy, surveys everything and examines every entrance into your soul to see whether there is anything weak or insufficiently protected through which he might creep in. He now searches everything, testing each point, and looks for a place to wound.

You must carefully foresee his ambushes, so that you may not be ignorant, with Paul, of his devices (II Cor. II, 11). Although Paul describes the terrifying powers and principalities of the devil, he nevertheless urges us to battle and discloses the enemy’s strength in order to increase the soldiers’ vigilance. He does not want us to be fearful but prepared; finally, he does not recommend flight but supplies weapons.

“Therefore,” he says, “take up the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day and, having completed everything, to stand firm.” Then, handing over the individual instruments of spiritual battle, he adds: “Stand therefore, having girded your loins with truth, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, and having shod your feet in the preparation of the Gospel of peace; above all, taking up the shield of faith, with which you may extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one; and take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, with all prayer and supplication” (Ephes. VI, 11–18).

Since even women may triumph in this war, take up these weapons of Paul and confidently anticipate victory under the encouragement of so great a commander. If you possess all these instruments, you will proceed safely into spiritual battle and will not fear the devil with his entire army. “A thousand may fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand, but they shall not come near you” (Ps. XC, 7).

Blessed James too, that veteran soldier of Christ, promises us victory in this war with no less authority: “Submit yourselves to God,” he says; “but resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (James IV, 7). He shows how we must resist the devil: we must be subject to God, doing his will, so that we may also deserve divine grace and more easily resist the wicked spirit with the help of the Holy Spirit.

He does not fight against us in open battle, nor confront us openly and face to face. He conquers by deceit and fraud, and uses our own will against us. The adversary gains strength from our consent and, as the saying goes, slaughters us with our own sword. He is a weak enemy who cannot conquer anyone unwilling.

Let despair be far from us, and let all fear of our adversaries withdraw from the mind. Let us not assist our enemies but conquer them. They offer advice, certainly, but it is ours either to choose or reject what they suggest. They do not harm by compulsion but by persuasion; they do not extort our consent but seek it.

Hence it is said even to Ananias: “Why has Satan tempted your heart, so that you should lie to the Holy Spirit?” (Acts V, 3). The Apostle would never have charged him with this if the devil had done it without Ananias’s own will. Eve herself is condemned by the Lord for this reason: she was overcome by one whom she could have overcome. She would not have deserved to be punished by the Lord’s justice, though defeated, unless she herself had been able to conquer.

## CHAPTER XXVI

One of the first and most deceitful arts of this most wicked enemy is to weary inexperienced souls with thoughts, and sometimes to bring sorrow over the very vocation to minds newly committed to it, so that the soul may easily be deterred from pursuing something whose beginnings it has found bitter.

He therefore sometimes inserts such filthy and impious thoughts into the mind that the person being tempted, believing that what he thinks belongs to him, judges that he has been made worse by the unclean spirit in relation to his vocation; and he thinks that he possessed a much purer soul when he still loved worldly affairs.

For the most cunning enemy wishes, out of desperation for holiness, to make those whom he envies feel horror of their vocation, so that, while sadness besieges them, he may at least hold them back from progress, even if he does not turn them away from their vocation.

For this reason you must especially love the study of the holy Scriptures. The soul must be illumined by divine utterances, and the darkness of the devil must be driven away by the flashing light of God’s word. He quickly flees from the soul that divine speech illumines and that is always occupied with heavenly thoughts, in which the word of God is constantly present—a force that the wicked spirit cannot endure.

For this reason the blessed Apostle compared it to a sword among the other instruments of spiritual warfare (Ephes. VI, 17). It is safest and most perfect for the mind to become accustomed, through constant and vigilant watchfulness, to distinguish its thoughts; at the first movement of the soul, it must approve or reject what it thinks, nourishing good thoughts or immediately extinguishing bad ones.

Here is the source of good and the origin of sin. Every great offense begins in the heart with a thought, which paints each action beforehand, as though upon a tablet of the heart. Whether it is an act or a word, it is arranged beforehand before it is uttered or performed; and what is to happen is determined by the counsel of the thoughts.

You see how, sometimes in a very brief moment, a person thinks each of these things and carries out what he has thought. Nothing at all is done by the tongue, hand, or any other member unless thoughts have first commanded it. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “From the heart of man proceed evil thoughts, adultery, fornication, murders, thefts, false testimonies, greed, wickedness, deceit, immorality, an evil eye, blasphemy [Col. 1118], pride, folly. These are the things that defile a person” (Matt. XV, 19–20).

Let all your care and all your attention therefore be directed to guarding the heart. You must observe sin most carefully where it usually comes into being, and resist the first appearance of temptation, extinguishing evil before it grows. One must not wait for the increase of something that should be feared from its beginning, and which is conquered all the more easily the sooner it is resisted.

Therefore divine Scripture cries out: “Guard your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the issues of life” (Prov. IV, 23).

## CHAPTER XXVII

A distinction must be made between thoughts to which the will gives its favor and which it embraces with affection, and those thoughts that habitually fly across the mind like a faint shadow, merely showing themselves in passing—what the Greeks call τύποι (“forms” or “impressions”). A distinction must also be made between these and thoughts that are suggested to a resisting and unwilling mind, against which the mind struggles and resists with a certain horror, grieving when they are admitted and rejoicing when they are expelled.

In the thoughts that lightly display themselves to the mind and, as it were, reveal themselves while fleeing, there is neither sin nor struggle at all. But in those with which the soul wrestles for some time, and against which the will resists, there is an equal contest. Either we consent and are defeated, or we reject them and conquer, gaining victory through the struggle.

Sin therefore exists only in that thought which has given the mind’s consent to the suggestion, which fondly cherishes its evil, and eagerly desires to burst into action. Even if such a thought, prevented by some circumstance, does not fulfill its will, it is nevertheless condemned by the Lord as an act of crime. Thus we read in the Gospel: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V, 28).

Before God, to whom all things are known even before they happen, the complete will to do something is reckoned as the deed itself. For this reason—you must often hear me repeat what I always wish to be done—you must meditate upon the holy Scriptures without interruption, fill your mind with them, drive out evil thoughts, occupy your spirit with divine meanings, and show how much you love God by your love of his law.

Hence Scripture says: “Those who fear the Lord will seek what is pleasing to him, and those who love him will be filled with his law” (Eccli. II, 19). Then you will perceive how much wisdom assists you in loving him, how great is the help of the divine law within you, and you will sing joyfully with David to the Lord: “I have hidden your words in my heart, that I might not sin against you” (Ps. CXVIII, 11).

The spirit must always be aroused by spiritual goads and renewed each day with greater ardor. Perseverance in prayer, the illumination of reading, and the vigilance of watchfulness, by day and by night, are its incentives. For nothing is worse in this vocation than idleness, which not only acquires nothing new but also consumes what has already been gained.

The discipline of holy life rejoices and grows through progress; through cessation it becomes sluggish and declines. The mind must be restored by daily and fresh increases in virtue, and our path of life must be measured not by what has already passed but by what remains. As long as we are in this body, let us never believe that we have arrived at perfection; for thus one reaches it more effectively.

We do not fall back as long as we strive toward what lies ahead. But once we begin to stand still, we descend; for us, not to advance is already to turn back. Let all laziness cease, as well as the useless security derived from past labor. If we do not wish to return, we must run.

The blessed Apostle, living to God from day to day and always considering not what he had done before but what he ought to do, said: “Brothers, I do not consider myself to have grasped it. But forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue the goal, the prize of God’s heavenly calling” (Phil. III, 13–14).

If that blessed Paul, the chosen vessel, who was so clothed with Christ that he could say, “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. II, 20), nevertheless still stretches forward, still grows and makes progress, what ought we to do, whose hope must be that at our end we may be compared with Paul at his beginning?

Therefore imitate him who said, “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (I Cor. IV, 16). Forget everything past and consider yourself to be beginning each day, lest you charge the present day, on which you ought to serve God, with what belongs to the past. You will guard what you have acquired most effectively if you are always seeking; what has been secured will suffer loss if you cease to secure it.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

You may perhaps say, “The labor is great.” But consider what has been promised. Every task usually becomes easy when its value is considered, and hope of reward is a consolation for labor.

Thus the hardworking farmer rejoices that, with a forceful plow, he has split the field that long lay unplowed and the clods made more fertile by idleness; and, wonderfully made happy by the very difficulty of his work, he measures the hope of the harvest by his labor.

Thus the eager merchant disregards the seas, daring to look upon the foam of the waves and the fury of the winds. While he considers profit amid every labor and danger, he simultaneously forgets both weariness and fear.

Consider, I beg you, the greatness of your reward—if indeed anything immeasurable can be considered. After the soul’s departure, after the destruction of the flesh, after ashes and dust, you, a virgin, are to be restored to a better condition. Your body, committed to the earth, is to be raised into heaven, and your mortality is to be changed into the honor of immortality.

After this you are to be granted the fellowship of angels, to receive the kingdom of heaven, and to reign forever with Christ. What, then, will you repay the Lord for all that he has repaid you? (Ps. CXV, 12). What will you do that is worthy of so great a rewarder? Or what labor will you consider difficult when its rewards are so great?

Hence the blessed Apostle says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII, 18). For what worthy thing can we do or suffer in this brief time of our life, when it is to be compensated with immortality?

## CHAPTER XXIX

For this reason the same Apostle says: “The momentary and light burden of our present tribulation is producing for us, beyond all measure, an eternal weight of glory in sublimity” (II Cor. IV, 17).

Let honors be rejected, riches despised, and even our life itself be scorned for love of martyrdom. Even if all these things were not given in exchange for the reward of eternity, they would nevertheless someday perish. Those who always desire to possess them lose even this.

How many people does our memory retain who were established in the greatest honors and riches, only to fall suddenly from that lofty summit of power? And those who, lifted up by their pride, thought themselves something other than human beings, finally taught us by their end what they had been.

For what is stable in this world? What is firm? What, moreover, is not brief and uncertain, and subject to chance? What kind of good is that which you are always afraid of losing, which you fear may be taken away from you or know must be abandoned by you? For even if it is not taken away by any accident, it must certainly be lost through death.

And even if our life were extended for a thousand years, and we reached that final day of our entire lifetime amid daily delight and pleasure, how long, I ask, would this be, when its end destroys it? Or what fruit does that pleasure possess which, as soon as it has ceased, will seem to you never to have existed?

Come now, turn over in your mind the time of your life that has already passed. Will it not seem to you to have been a kind of shadow, now gone by, and will not everything that appears seem uncertain, like a fleeting dream? An old man in extreme age can feel this same thing, and it is fitting for him to say with the prophet: “My days have declined like a shadow, and I have withered like grass” (Ps. CI, 12).

## CHAPTER XXX
What, then, shall we say in the future, if we can say this even here, where this life, though brief, is highly valued because it is present? There, where the greater presence of eternity makes everything that has passed seem as nothing. Carefully turning these thoughts over within yourself, and despising the brevity of this life by contemplating eternity, despise even the contempt of the world with a greater strength of spirit, and prepare yourself for that day alone on which the world’s glory will come to an end—yes, for that day which the Savior compared with the Flood, and which, as the Apostle says, will overtake many deceived by a false sense of security, arriving secretly (I Thess. V, 2).

The blessed Peter also describes it, saying: “But the day of the Lord [Col. 1120] will come like a thief, in which the heavens will pass away with great force, while the elements will be dissolved by heat. Since, then, all these things are to be dissolved, what sort of people ought we to be in holy conduct and devotion, awaiting and hastening toward the coming of the day of the Lord, on which the burning heavens will be dissolved and the elements will melt in the heat of fire?” (II Pet. III, 10–12).

It is a recent event—and one that you yourself witnessed—that, at the sound of the shrill trumpet and the shouting of the Goths, Rome, mistress of the world, overcome by mournful fear, trembled. Where then was the order of nobility? Where were the fixed and distinct ranks of every dignity? Everything was mingled and confounded by fear; every household was filled with lamentation, and panic was equal among all. Slave and noble were one; the same image of death confronted everyone—except that those feared it more whose life had been more pleasant.

If we fear mortal enemies and the hand of man in this way, what shall we do when the terrifying trumpet begins to thunder from heaven, and at that voice of the Archangel, clearer than every trumpet, the whole world resounds in reply? When we see weapons not made by human hands shaken above us, and even the powers of heaven moved, as the prophet says: “When the Lord comes to make the world’s surface desolate and to destroy sinners from it”—what fear, what darkness, what gloom will then be ours, when that day finds us, though so often and repeatedly warned, nevertheless unprepared?

“Then,” he says, “all the tribes of the earth will lament over themselves, and they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty. Then they will say to the mountains, ‘Fall upon us,’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us,’ and to the rocks, ‘Open yourselves to us’” (Matt. XXIV, 30; Luke XXIII, 30).

But let these things belong to those who, held fast by the various cares of this world, do not think about the world’s end. You, however, for whom the coming of Christ is the meditation of days and nights, for whom the Lord’s presence is to be desired because of the purity of your conscience, and who await the consummation of the age as the fixed time of your reward—you will receive exultation from heaven, not fear.

For then you will fly up to meet the Bridegroom, mingling with the choirs of the saints and accompanied by holy virgins, and you will say: “I have found him whom my soul sought” (Song III). You will no longer fear separation at any time, since you are once and for all to be endowed with the glory of immortality and the splendor of incorruption, and you will be forever with Christ, as the Apostle says: “For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an Archangel, and with the trumpet of God; and the dead who are in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive, who remain, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with Christ” (I Thess. V, 15–16).

Let this, therefore, always be your concern; let this be your pursuit. Let these thoughts continually revolve in the heart of a virgin; let the labor of the whole day be occupied with them, and let the sleep of night be taken in them; let the soul awaken again to this. Indeed, no labor should seem hard, and no period of time long, by which the glory of eternity is acquired.

## Censure of the Louvain Theologians on the Two Letters That Follow

He was an unlearned impostor who fabricated the following letters concerning the death of Jerome under the names of Saint Augustine to Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, and of Cyril to Augustine. For it is established that Cyril died before Jerome. Hence Jerome writes in his *On Illustrious Men*: “Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, after being often driven from the Church and restored to it, finally held an undisturbed episcopate for eight years under the emperor Theodosius.”

Moreover, this false Cyril, in his reply, chapter 4, calls Sabinianus a pernicious heresiarch because he asserted two wills in Christ; and he adds that Jerome had published a letter for the destruction of this error. From this it follows that this author was both a heretic and an impostor. And these few points, though drawn from many, are sufficient against these letters.

**Of Saint Augustine (under a false title) to Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, concerning the splendid and admirable virtues of Saint Jerome.**

## LETTER XVIII

To the most venerable father Cyril: should one remain silent about the praises of the most glorious champion of the Christian faith, the cornerstone of holy Mother [Col. 1121] Church, upon which she stands most firmly established, the priest Jerome, formerly a shining star of God and now in heavenly glory? Or do you think that I, a man polluted in lips, will speak with the tongue of a stammering child?

“The heavens declare the glory of God,” and everything the Lord has made praises him in his saints. Should a rational creature be silent in God’s praise while irrational creation is not silent? Shall I be silent, or shall I speak, when, if I remain silent, I am commanded to cry out through stones? Certainly I shall speak, and I shall not be silent; with all my strength and effort I shall praise Jerome. Although I am an unworthy and inadequate praiser—for praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner—I shall nevertheless not cease from praising him.

Let our hand, then, be strengthened, and let our tongue not cleave to our palate, for this most holy man is truly great, admirable, and awesome above nearly all who are around us: great in the holiness of his most excellent life, great in the unfathomable depth of his wisdom, great in the extent of his greater glory now; admirable in his extraordinary wonders, and awesome because of the power entrusted to him by the Lord.

How great this most glorious Jerome was in the outstanding holiness of his life—how could my tongue make it known, when the tongues of all mortals would scarcely suffice to explain his excellence? Let him be called, then, in the holiness of his most excellent life, another Elijah, another Samuel, another John the Baptist.

Elijah and John the hermit mortified the flesh through great austerities of food and clothing. The most glorious Jerome was no lesser in his way of life: he too remained a hermit for four years in the wilderness, with wild beasts alone as his companions. For fifty years—as the letters of the venerable Eusebius, his disciple, which I received yesterday, more fully acknowledged, and as you yourself know even more certainly—he tasted neither wine nor strong drink in any measure. He so abstained from all eating of meat, and even of fish, that he scarcely wished to name them. He ate cooked food only twice, and then during his final illness. He mortified his flesh in a haircloth sack like an Ethiopian, covering himself above with the cheapest cloth; he never knew any bed other than the earth.

Once each day he ate only fruit, or leaves, or roots of plants. After Vespers he devoted himself to prayer and remained awake every day until the second hour of the night. Then, exhausted by sleep, he rested by sleeping on the ground until midnight. Rising immediately thereafter, he remained intent upon readings and holy writings, with which the whole Church shines like a collection of precious stones, until the hour of eating.

He wept over the lightest sins as though someone might have thought that he had killed a man. Three times a day he scourged his flesh with dreadful blows, so that streams of blood flowed from his body. He fled every idle word as though it were the greatest plague. He had no leisure for himself; he was always occupied either with sacred reading, writing, or teaching everyone.

What more should I say? If I searched through the lives of the individual saints, I think I would find no one greater than he. But since above we called him another Samuel, let us show that this Samuel was like him.

This indeed is the Samuel who, called away from empty literary studies by beatings, was assigned to the ministry of Sacred Scripture. In the radiance of whose face, as divine grace poured forth, we saw the light of both Testaments; and in the strength of whose arm the greater part of the heretics was scattered.

This man, transferring the glory of our virtue—that is, both Testaments—from the Hebrew language into Greek and Latin alike, and arranging them for posterity forever; explaining riddles and obscure matters, doubtful and knotty questions; preparing a sequence of offices for all the ministers of the Church—built up almost the whole Church. Hence he rightly appears great in the unfathomable depth of wisdom.

He knew the liberal arts so perfectly that, according to everyone’s report, no one like him has yet appeared. As for the sacred Scriptures, from the evidence of many of his letters that he sent to me, I have never known anyone equal to him.

He knew the languages and writings of the Hebrews, Greeks, Chaldaeans, Persians and Medes, Arabs, [Col. 1122] and nearly all nations as though he had been born and raised among them. What more shall I say? Whatever Jerome did not know in nature, no human being ever knew.

Do not think, venerable father, that I say these things because I imagine that you know Jerome’s life and virtues less well than I do, since you were his companion for so long. But I call God to witness that, because of the holiness of so ineffable a man, if I had wished to remain silent, I could not have done so.

Even the heavens themselves, in which he dwells forever in greatness, confess his holiness through his wondrous works. No one, therefore, should doubt that within the dwellings of the Father he possesses one of the greater and loftier seats. For since a person is rewarded there according to his works, and he lived a life almost more perfect than others, it is plainly evident that he will be one of the greater and loftier citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem.

To make this more fully and certainly credible to us, he appears in the world exceedingly admirable beyond all those whom our age remembers, through extraordinary signs and countless miracles, some of which the venerable Eusebius reported to me in his letters.

As for the other wonders that occur daily in remarkable ways, as I continually learn, and since I desire eagerly to hear more fully the reports of many people, I beg you, dearest father, not to refuse, as soon as opportunity permits, to send me in a brief volume whatever true and useful miracles concerning the devotion of that same most holy Jerome you are able to collect.

But so that the many merits of the most holy Jerome may not remain hidden, I shall relate what, by divine mercy, happened to me on the very day of his death.

On that same day and at that hour when the most holy Jerome, having cast off the garment of his flesh’s corruption and uncleanness, put on the clothing of perpetual immortality, immeasurable joy, and glory, I was resting in my little cell at Hippo, eagerly pondering the amount of glory and joy possessed by the souls of the blessed who rejoice with Christ. Wishing to compose a short treatise on this subject, at the urging of our Severus, formerly a venerable disciple of Martin, bishop of Tours, I took paper, pen, and tablet in my hands to write a brief letter to be sent to the most holy Jerome, so that he might reply with whatever he understood about these matters.

For I knew that in so difficult a question no other living person could teach me more fully or clearly. And when, already writing the beginning of the greeting, I had begun to address Jerome, suddenly an ineffable light, unseen in our times and impossible for our tongues to describe, entered the cell in which I stood, together with an ineffable and unheard-of fragrance of every kind of scent. It was already the hour of Compline.

When I saw it, I was overcome by astonishment and wonder, and suddenly lost the powers of both mind and body. For I did not then know that the wondrous right hand of God had exalted his servant, making his powers known among the peoples. I did not know that God had released his faithful servant from the uncleanness of the flesh by his ancient mercy and prepared for him so sublime a seat in heaven. I certainly did not know the unsearchable ways of the Lord; I did not know the treasures of God’s infinite wisdom and knowledge; I did not understand the secret and hidden judgments of God—for by his ineffable wisdom he brings those whom he wills to the knowledge of himself. Those whom he predestines, he calls, justifies, and glorifies, according as he determines to be fitting.

Thus, because my eyes had never before seen such a light and my sense of smell had never perceived such a fragrance, I was struck dumb with amazement at such novel and unheard-of marvels.

Meanwhile, while my thoughts resounded within me, wondering what this might be, a voice came forth from the light, saying:

“Augustine, Augustine, what are you seeking? Do you think you can put the whole sea into a small vessel? Enclose the entire globe of the earth in a small handful? Hold the heavens firm so that they do not perform their customary motions? Will your eye see what no human eye has been able to see? Will your ear hear what no ear has ever taken in through sound? Do you think you can understand what the human heart has in no way understood or even imagined?

“What end can there be to an infinite matter? By what measure will you measure the immeasurable? The whole sea might sooner be enclosed in the narrowest vessel; a tiny handful might sooner hold the globe of the earth; the heavens might sooner cease from their continual motion—than you could understand even the smallest part of the joys and [Col. 1123] glory in which the souls of the blessed possess themselves forever, unless, like me, you were taught by experience.

“Continue on through the brief span of time still remaining. Do not attempt to do the impossible until the course of your life is complete. Do not seek here what can be found elsewhere only—in the place toward which you are hastening so happily. Here, strive to perform such works that you may afterward possess forever there what you desire here, in however small a measure, to understand. Those who enter there never leave.”

At these words I was stunned with fear and almost out of my mind with astonishment at what I had not seen before, deprived of nearly all strength. Nevertheless, taking some courage, I said in a trembling voice:

“If only it were permitted me not to doubt, since you are so blessed, so glorious, and hastening with such honor toward those joys, and since you proclaim such sweet words to my throat!”

But she said:

“You seek my name? I am the soul of that priest Jerome to whom you have just begun writing the letter you intend to send. At this hour, in Bethlehem of Judaea, I have laid down the burden of the flesh. Accompanied by Christ and the whole heavenly host, adorned with every beauty, illumined by every splendor, clothed in that gilded garment of immortality, surrounded by every variety of good and joy, triumphant over all earthly things, crowned with every diadem, and enclosed by every blessedness and happiness, I no longer await any diminishment of glory, but only its increase.

“So gloriously and ineffably I proceed to the kingdoms of heaven, which will endure without end, until I am joined again to a body that will be glorified and will not die, but will possess the glory that I now possess alone, on the day, namely, of the resurrection of all flesh.”

Then, gathering greater strength of spirit within me, and unable to stop weeping for joy, I replied:

“If only I might deserve to become your distinguished attendant! But I beg you to remember your little servant—however worthless—whom you loved in the world with such great affection, so that through your intercessions I may be corrected from my sins; under your guidance may I proceed along the straight path with unhindered step; through your constant protection may I be shielded from the enemies who continually lie in wait for me; and under your holy direction may I reach the harbor of salvation.

“If it should please your will, answer me something that I ask!”

She replied: “Say what you desire, knowing that I shall answer according to all your wishes.”

“I should like to understand,” I said, “whether the souls of the blessed ever desire anything that they cannot obtain.”

She replied:

“Know this, Augustine: the souls of the saints are so established and strengthened in God in that eternal glory that they have no will other than God’s, and can desire nothing except what God wills. Therefore they can obtain whatever they desire. For whatever they desire, God also wills, and he fulfills it.

“None of us is cheated of his desires, because none of us desires anything apart from God. Since we always possess God as we wish, our desires are always fulfilled in the fullest possible measure.”

A long succession of words would be required, dearest father Cyril, if I were to write in this brief letter everything that that glorious soul revealed to me when I questioned her. For I hope, God permitting, to come to Bethlehem after not many cycles of years to visit such great relics. There you will then see clearly in writing what I heard and set down.

For several hours that most glorious soul remained there with me, revealing to my eager mind the unity of the most holy Trinity and the Trinity of the unity; the generation of the Son from the Father; the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son; the hierarchies and orders of the angels; the mysteries of those blessed spirits; the happy joys of the blessed souls; and other matters useful and weighty for human understanding. How subtly, clearly, wonderfully, and delightfully she disclosed these things to me—I could not explain in words even if I spoke with the tongues of all human beings.

Then that light disappeared from my eyes, but the sweetness of its ineffable fragrance remained for many days afterward.

How wondrous, then, is this man, who performs so many marvels and so many great and unfamiliar wonders among human beings! Let us therefore cry out to him with our mouths and rejoice, and let us give glory to his praise, for he is certainly worthy of all praise, and we are not sufficient to praise him.

He entered the house of the Lord, radiant and most beautiful, where without doubt he possesses one of the higher and more distinguished seats of glory.

[Col. 1124] To make the light of truth shine more clearly once again through more witnesses than one, I decided to add to my own vision what our aforementioned Severus, a man distinguished for learning and wisdom, saw with three others on the very day and hour of Jerome’s death in the city of Tours. He alone had been a witness to me of this, having come to me the day before.

God wished the sublime glory of Jerome not to remain hidden from the world, just as his sublime holiness—and almost the highest excellence among all living people—had not remained hidden. He did not wish those who delighted in following the footprints of that holiness to depart at some time from the path of holiness because they were ignorant of the reward to be received. He also wished others, seeing that so many and such great rewards were bestowed upon him, to cling to the footprints of that holiness and virtue—for hope of rewards lessens the burden of labor.

Therefore, on the day and at the hour when that glorious Jerome happily breathed his last, he revealed in the following manner the glory to be bestowed upon him to Severus and the three others standing with him.

At the hour of Compline, on that day, Severus was in his own house with three other Catholic men—two of whom had formerly been monks of the monastery of the venerable Martin—reading divine passages. Suddenly he heard throughout heaven, the air, and the earth countless voices singing a melody of the sweetest, unheard-of, ineffable, and incredible kind, together with the sounds of organs, drums, psalteries, the whole symphony, and instruments, by which heaven and earth and everything, as it seemed to him, resounded on every side. Their sweetness almost caused their souls to breathe forth from their bodies.

Immediately, all of them, astonished, raised their eyes and saw the whole heaven, the air, and everything contained within its circumference shining with a light seven times more brilliant than the light of the sun. From it arose the fragrances of every kind of spice.

When they saw these things, so astonishing, they entreated God in prayer that he not conceal from them why such events were occurring. A voice coming from heaven said to them:

“Let no astonishment move you, and do not find it strange if you see and hear such things. For today the King of kings and Lord of lords, Christ the Lord, has come in full festal procession to meet the soul of the most glorious priest Jerome, who dwelt in Bethlehem of Judaea, as it departs from this wicked age, so that he may lead it into his own kingdom with all the greater honor, excellence, and sublimity, in proportion as it shines above others through the merits of a more sublime and holy life.

“Today all the orders of angels, rejoicing and singing together in turn with such voices, are accompanying their fellow citizen. Today the gathering of all the Patriarchs and Prophets; today the choir of the Apostles and Disciples; today all the holy Martyrs; today the Confessors; today the glorious Mother of God, accompanied by all the holy Virgins; today the joyful and festive souls of all the blessed are going out to meet their compatriot and fellow citizen.”

After these words the voice fell silent; nevertheless, the light, singing, and fragrance continued for an hour before ceasing.

Thus it is plainly evident that he is to be one of the higher and greater citizens, and that he is great, admirable, and awesome above nearly all the saints because of the power entrusted to him.

Let no one doubt that, more than others, he can obtain whatever he wishes, just as his will is more closely united than theirs with the divine will.

But let no one think me so bold as to assert that he possesses greater glory than John the Baptist—of whom, according to the Savior himself, no greater has arisen among those born of women—or than Peter, Paul, and the other twelve Apostles, who were chosen and sanctified by Christ himself.

Although reason forbids anyone to dare affirm that Jerome possesses greater glory than they in the kingdom of heaven, nevertheless I see no reason why it should be wrong to say that Jerome will be their equal in glory, provided that he did not differ from them in the holiness of his life. For God is not a respecter of persons; he determines the merits of individuals and gives each person what he has deserved.

If someone thinks Jerome lesser than John and the Apostles, let him think him only slightly lesser in glory, since he can clearly see the merits of his holiness, the benefit of his labor, and the fruit of his writings and most truthful translation of both Testaments, as well as of his ordering of ecclesiastical offices, not only for those living now but also for those to come. [Col. 1125] I solemnly call God to witness that he will judge Jerome to differ from them in glory by very little, if at all.

Moreover, lest I seem to some to be laying a trap for ridicule by acknowledging that the most holy Jerome is equal to John and the Apostles in holiness and glory, I shall relate one thing that I saw in a vision less than four days afterward, so that the truth may not remain hidden.

And lest anyone think that I am repeating these praises either out of carnal affection—by which a human being strays most far from knowledge of the truth—or through the ignorance of a deranged mind, or for any other reason, let him know that I learned this not from a human being but through a revelation granted by almighty God, who exalts his saints and magnifies them by exalting them.

On the fourth night afterward, while I was eagerly considering what praise and due reverence for Jerome I might briefly set forth in a letter, he revealed the following to me.

As I was preparing, as I said, to write this letter to you and considering how to find suitable material for praise, when midnight arrived sleep overcame me. And behold, a very great multitude of angels appeared before me. Among them were two men who shone more brightly than the infinite sun. They were so alike and identical that no difference could be seen by which one could be distinguished from the other, except that one wore three wreaths on his head, made of gold and precious stones, while the other wore two.

They were clothed in brilliantly white tunics woven throughout with gold and gems, and were of such beauty that no one could imagine it. Both approached me and stood silently for a little while.

Then the one who wore three wreaths addressed me in these words:

“You are considering, Augustine, what praise you ought truthfully to proclaim concerning Jerome. Indeed, you have been thinking for a long time and still do not know; but we have both come here to reveal his glory to you.

“This companion of mine whom you see is Jerome himself. Just as he was my equal in holiness of life, so he is equal to me in every respect in glory. What I can do, he can do; what I will, he wills; and just as I see God, so he sees, knows, and understands him—in whom all our blessedness and glory, and that of all the saints, consists.

“No saint has greater or lesser glory than another except insofar as one contemplates or knows the divine appearance more or less fully.

“The third wreath that I wear beyond his is the little crown of martyrdom, by which my bodily life ended. Although he endured many labors, hardships, afflictions, blows, insults, human reproaches, mockery, and other very severe things in the world so peacefully and joyfully for God that he exulted in his infirmities and proved a true martyr, and although he did not lose the rewards of martyrdom, nevertheless, because he did not end his life by the sword, he does not possess the little crown given as the sign of martyrdom.

“The other two wreaths that we possess are the little crowns given only to virgins and teachers, so that they may be distinguished from others.”

At this I replied, as it seemed to me:

“Who are you, my lord?”

He answered: “I am John the Baptist, who have descended here to you to announce Jerome’s glory, so that you may announce it to the nations.

“Know this: the honor and reverence shown to each of the saints are shown to all the others. Do not think that there is any envy in heaven as there is in the world. Just as in the world every human being would rather preside over others than be subject to them, so in heaven, because of the ineffable love by which the blessed souls love one another, every saint rejoices in another’s glory as in his own.

“Indeed, each greater saint would wish every lesser saint to be his equal, and almost greater, because the other’s glory would be his own. Thus the lesser rejoices in the glory of the greater as though he possessed it himself; nor would he wish to possess it if the other did not possess it—rather, if it were permitted, he would share his own with him.

“Therefore the glory of each is the glory of all, and the glory of all is the glory of each.”

After these words the whole company departed.

When I awoke from sleep, I immediately felt in myself such flames of love as I had never before felt. From that time until now there has never been in me any desire or thought of envy, pride, or arrogance.

For God is my witness—he who knows everything before it happens—that afterward such fervor of love arose within me that I rejoice more in another’s good than in my own, and desire more to be subject to everyone than to be above everyone.

[Col. 1126] I have said these things not to acquire the reputation of human praise, but so that no one may think these were empty dreams by which our minds are often deceived. For God often discloses hidden and very great things through dreams.

Let us therefore magnify the Lord in his saint; let us magnify his works, for they are perfect, and there is no iniquity in them.

Let us confidently magnify the holy Jerome of the Lord, who reigns with God, since he acted magnificently in his life and received magnificent things at his death. Therefore he is great in our midst, holy and exalted in the outstanding holiness of his life; great, holy, and exalted in the unfathomable depth of his wisdom; great, holy, and supremely exalted in the extent of his greater glory now; admirable, praiseworthy, and glorious in wonders unseen, unheard, and extraordinary; awesome, honored, and venerated because of the power, honor, and everlasting glory entrusted to him by the Lord.

Let us therefore, I beg you, magnify him; let us not be silent, for he is greater than all praise. Let us make known among the peoples the praises of his glory.

Let no one be surprised that we praise the man whom God magnified and honored; let no one be reluctant to venerate and honor the man whom God honored and venerated.

Let no one think that, by equating Jerome with John and the Apostles in glory and holiness, we do an injury to John and the Apostles. For if they could, they would wish him to surpass them in both glory and holiness. His glory and blessedness are their glory, and their blessedness is his. The honor, praise, and reverence that we offer to Jerome are offered to each of them, and what is offered individually to them is offered to Jerome.

If, then, you wish to venerate John the Baptist and the Apostles, venerate him together with them, for in every respect he is their equal.

Therefore, with a secure mind and with all fear cast aside, let us confess with complete devotion and reverence that John the Baptist is Jerome’s equal, not his superior—for no greater has arisen than John. For if we make Jerome lesser, we detract from John’s glory and do him greater injury under the guise of praise.

Although this work of my unskilled speech has been completed inadequately, most poorly, and as nothing, I nevertheless send it to you, venerable father, with devotion and reverence, with a pure heart and great affection of devoted spirit. I beg you to read with due charity and equanimity the little words of my youthful effort, which, from the poverty of my ignorance, I have offered in praise of the distinguished Jerome—not mocking them, but bearing with them patiently.

Whatever I have said that was less than was due to the praise of so great a man, attribute it to my ignorance, to the brevity of the letter, and to the immeasurable greatness of his praises. For certainly, even if the tongues of all mortals alone set forth his praises, the result would still be less than was due.

Remember me, a sinner, venerable father, so that when you stand in the place where the sacred body of the distinguished Jerome rests, you may commend me through his intercessions. For no one doubts that Jerome can immediately obtain whatever he desires. He is in no way deprived of his desire.

**Of Blessed Cyril (under a false title) to Saint Augustine, concerning the miracles performed after the death of Blessed Jerome the priest.**

## LETTER XIX

To the venerable and distinguished bishop Augustine, prelate of Hippo, Cyril, pontiff of Jerusalem and the least of all priests, sends greetings, desiring to follow the footsteps of him whose holiness does not cease to shine on earth.

## CHAPTER I

—That glorious Jerome, whose memory is blessed forever and ever, whose greatness you likewise know well, since you especially enjoyed his conversation and instruction—about him I consider it almost audacious for me, though rejected and unworthy in every respect, to undertake a discourse.

Nevertheless, because your affection compels me to write something to you about the extraordinary signs unfamiliar to human beings that the Lord performed through him in our days, in order to make him famous in the world and glorious before all people, I shall undertake the task, trusting in your prayers as your devotion requires, and shall touch briefly upon a few [Col. 1127] matters out of many.

I do not doubt that you know of the glorious death of this man, my vision, and the marvelous events that occurred at that time. For the reverend Eusebius of Cremona, his disciple—in whom the holiness and learning of his teacher shone forth, and whose wisdom, integrity, and excellence you know—was taken from the misery of our mortality two years later and followed his most beloved teacher Jerome into the heavenly homeland, as his frequent miracles show. I shall speak of some of these below.

At that time he reported the entire sequence of Jerome’s death by letter to the venerable father Damasus, bishop of Porto; to Theodonius, a Roman senator; to his brother Severus, a most upright man; to Eustochium, a most holy woman; to you; and to many others whom there is no need to name individually.

To repeat what you already know would therefore be superfluous and would obstruct what must be said. Omitting these matters, then, let our pen turn, as your devotion demands, to the miracles of this same man that continually and ceaselessly shine forth.

And first let it take its beginning from Eusebius, the most holy man and disciple of that same most holy Jerome.

## CHAPTER II
After the death of the glorious Jerome, a certain heresy—that is, a sect—arose among the Greeks and reached even the Latins. By its wicked arguments it strove to prove that the souls of the blessed would be deprived, until the day of the universal judgment, when they would again be joined to their bodies, of the vision and knowledge of God in which the whole blessedness of the saints consists; and that the souls of the damned likewise would suffer no punishments until that day. Their argument was as follows: just as the soul merited reward or punishment with the body, so with the body it would receive rewards or punishments. The most wicked men of that sect also asserted that there was no place of purgatory where souls that had not yet completed full repentance in this world for their sins might be purified.

As this pestilential sect grew more widespread, such grief fell upon us that we became weary even of living. Therefore, after summoning all my suffragan bishops and other Catholic men, I imposed fasts and prayers upon them, so that divine goodness might not permit His Church to be so disturbed.

A wondrous thing—and perhaps nothing like it had ever been seen. When three days of fasting and prayer had been completed, on the following night the glorious Jerome visibly appeared to his most beloved son Eusebius, who was engaged in prayer. He comforted him with kindly words and said to him:

“Have no fear at all of this pestilential sect, since its end must now be imposed. ”

Eusebius looked upon him, shining with such brilliance that human eyes could not endure to gaze at him. As though awakening from a deep sleep, he poured sweet tears from his eyes and, scarcely able to form his voice, began to cry out as loudly as he could:

“Are you my father Jerome? Why do you reject my companionship? Surely I have hold of you, and I will not let you go; nor will you depart without your son, whom you loved.”

The glorious Jerome answered him:
