“I shall not abandon you, my dearest son. Take courage, for on the twentieth day you will follow me, and together we shall remain in joy without end. But tell Cyril and all the brothers that tomorrow they are all to assemble together beside the Lord’s manger, where my body rests, both Catholics and the men of that sect. You are also to have the unburied corpses of the three men who died in this city tonight carried to the place where my body has been buried. Place upon them the sack that I used; immediately restored to their former life, they will utterly uproot this heresy.”

After bidding him farewell, the glorious Jerome disappeared.

When morning came, the venerable Eusebius came to me—I was then at Bethlehem—and recounted everything he had seen. On hearing this, I gave boundless thanks to the Creator and had the bodies of the dead men brought together with everyone assembled at the aforesaid place, where the Savior was born for us from the undefiled Virgin and where the most sacred body of Jerome had also been buried.

O wondrous dispensation of God’s mercy toward humanity! In how many ways he knows how to help those who hope in him! With how many and what great honors he exalts his saints!

[Col. 1128]

Meanwhile the adherents of that sect were mocking us, believing that the hand of the Lord had been emptied of power. Let the whole assembly of the faithful, therefore, rejoice, and let them sing psalms to God with a voice of exultation, for “we have received the mercy of the Lord in the midst of his temple.”

The venerable Eusebius approached each of the corpses, knelt, stretched out his hands toward heaven, and prayed in the hearing of all:

“God, for whom nothing is impossible and nothing burdensome, of unconquered strength and power, who alone performs great wonders and despises none who hopes in you: hear now the prayers of your faithful. And so that your undefiled and inviolate faith, which you have given, may remain throughout the ages, and so that their error may be revealed through the merits and intercessions of your beloved glorious Jerome, introduce into these corpses the souls that you willed to depart from them.”

When this prayer had ended, he touched each corpse with the sack that the glorious Jerome had worn upon his flesh, and immediately he introduced into them the breath of life. With their eyes opened and every sign of life displayed, those men were perfectly restored to life. They began, in a clear voice, to make known to all the glory of the blessed souls and the punishments of sinners, both in purgatory and in hell.

For, as they later told me when I questioned them, blessed Jerome had taken them with him into paradise, purgatory, and hell, so that they might reveal to everyone what was being done there. He had told them that they must return to their bodies and do penance there for the sins they had committed; and that on the day and at the hour when the venerable Eusebius was to depart, they too would die again, and, if they did penance well, would attain glory with him. And so it happened, as I shall explain below.

When these things had been accomplished, the very great multitude of people—both the faithful and the defenders of that sect—who had gathered for so great a spectacle, so certain an indication of error and demonstration of truth, and who had witnessed the outstanding merits of blessed Jerome, gave boundless praise in loud voices to the Creator, who does not abandon those who hope in him.

And so, dearest Augustine, the merciful Lord permits the little boat of his most holy faith to be tossed upon the sea of this world by the waves raised by wicked men, but he does not permit it to be wrecked. Therefore, I beg you, be strong in spirit and act manfully. Do not fear to fight courageously against the persecutors of the faith beneath the protection of the wings of so merciful a Father, who does not allow the prayers of his faithful to be ineffective, provided that they are made with complete hope and a pure heart.

For our prayers cannot otherwise be heard unless either our hope is not fully placed in God, or we ask for things that ought not to be requested. Let us therefore cry out to the Lord not only with our mouths but with our whole hearts while we are afflicted; and he who rules in his might and daily regards us with the eye of his mercy will not permit us to be tempted beyond what we can bear.

But lest I now stray too far from my subject, I return to what I began: first completing the account of the death of the venerable Eusebius, and writing likewise of the departure of those three men whom you know were restored to life—since they were taken from this world and from the valley of misery at the same hour and on the same day as Eusebius—and then introducing some miracles of Jerome, a few out of many.

## CHAPTER III

When the day arrived on which the venerable Eusebius knew from the vision mentioned above that he would depart from this life through blessed Jerome, and with the third day approaching, he was violently shaken by the weakness of fever. Remembering his master, he had himself carried naked upon the ground by the brothers. He kissed each of the brothers, comforted them with kindly consolation, and admonished them to remain steadfast in their holy purpose.

Then he had the sack in which the glorious Jerome had clothed himself brought in, ordered it to be placed over him, and arranged that he should be buried naked, in the manner of his glorious master, in the church where the body of Saint Jerome lay.

After this, fortifying himself with communion of the most sacred body of Jesus Christ, he commended himself to the Lord and to blessed Jerome. For three days he lay deprived of speech and bodily sight, while the brothers around him took turns continuously reading the Psalter, the Passion of the Lord, and other sacred texts.

A harsh and terrifying thing happened, as I relate, to all who live rightly in this world. On the day on which he was to die, two hours before the departure of his blessed soul, the venerable Eusebius began to perform such dreadful actions that the monks standing around him, terrified with fear, lay upon the ground as though mad.

At times he would look sideways, clasp his hands together, wear a dreadful expression, and cry out in a terrible voice, as though seated:

“I will not do it, I will not do it! You are lying, you are lying!”

After this, returning to the ground, he pressed his face against it and cried out as loudly as he could:

“Help me, brothers, lest I perish!”

When the monks saw this, they questioned him amid tears and trembling:

“What is wrong, father?”

He answered them:

“Do you not see the armies of demons that wish to overcome me?”

They asked:

“What did they want you to do when you said, ‘I will not do it, I will not do it’?”

He replied:

“They are trying to make me appear a blasphemer of the divine name; and for that reason I cried out that I would not do it.”

They asked:

“Why, father, were you hiding your face in the ground?”

He answered:

“So that I would not see them. Their appearance is so foul and terrifying that, in comparison with it, almost all the fears that exist in the world are nothing.”

Repeating his earlier actions amid these words, he continued in this state until his final hour. The brothers who stood there, terrified by fear and grief, stood as though dead, not knowing what to do.

Glorious is God in his saints, wondrous in his majesty, kind and merciful to those who love him: he does not abandon his saints in a time of need.

When the venerable Eusebius reached his final hour, the glorious Jerome appeared to him and comforted him kindly. At his arrival, that whole, seemingly innumerable crowd of demons, terrified by fear of him, vanished from his presence like smoke. Many monks testify to this, saying that by divine dispensation they saw it with their own eyes.

But this is confirmed still more clearly: all those standing around heard Eusebius say:

“Where are you coming from, father? Why have you delayed so long? I beg you, do not abandon your son.”

Immediately, in the hearing of all, another voice answered:

“Wait, my son; do not fear, for I shall not abandon you, whom I love so greatly.”

When this voice had been heard, after a short interval had passed, the venerable Eusebius expired.

At that same hour the three men who had been restored to life also departed, and, as I think, reached eternal joys with Eusebius. For during all those twenty days after they had been restored to life, as you know, they gave themselves to such great penance that without doubt they now possess eternal blessedness.

I do not think I should pass over in silence what I learned from those same three men during the days in which they lived. Throughout that entire period I continually wished to investigate with one or another of them the secrets of that life which we await after this brief and momentary life, spending the day from the third hour until evening.

Although I learned many things from them, for the sake of brevity I shall relate only a few at present; the rest I shall omit, intending to tell them on another occasion.

On one occasion it happened that I went to one of them. I found him weeping bitterly and admitting no consolation from my words, so I began to ask him the cause of such weeping. After I had questioned him about this several times, without his answering my questions, at last, compelled by my persistence, he replied:

“If you knew what I experienced yesterday, you would always have cause to weep.”

I answered him:

“I beg you to explain what you saw.”

Then, remaining silent for a little while, he said:

“What punishments and torments do you think are prepared not only for the damned but also for those who are in purgatory?”

I answered him:

“What true judgment can be pronounced concerning things that are uncertain? For, as I think, they cannot be compared with the punishments we suffer here.”

He replied:

“If all the punishments, torments, and afflictions that could be imagined in this world were compared with the lesser punishment and torment found there, they would be consolations. If any living person knew those punishments by experience, he would prefer to be tormented without remedy until the end of the world by all the punishments and torments that appear here, which all human beings from Adam down to the present have endured individually, rather than to be tortured for a single day in hell or in purgatory by the lesser punishment found there.

“And therefore, if you ask the cause of my weeping, it is fear of the punishments that are justly inflicted upon sinners. For I know that I have sinned against my God, and I have no doubt that he is just. Therefore do not wonder that I weep; rather, if I did not weep, you ought to wonder greatly.

“But wonder instead why human beings, who do not doubt that they will die—at least from the experience of others—live here with such security and do not think about escaping such great punishments.”

Struck inwardly by grief, so that I could scarcely form words, I said:

“Alas, what am I hearing? But I beg you to tell me in what way the punishments of hell differ from those that are in purgatory.”

He answered:

“They do not differ from one another, because the punishments of purgatory and of hell are equal in magnitude. But there is one respect in which they may differ: the punishments of hell do not await an end but an increase—namely, on the day of the universal judgment, when the bodies there will be tormented together with their souls. The punishments of purgatory, however, have an end. For after completing their penance, those who are released from there will enjoy the most blessed joys.”

I asked:

“Are the torments equal for all who are in purgatory, or are they different?”

He replied:

“They are certainly different: greater in some and lighter in others, according to the magnitude of their sins. For in the homeland of the blessed, all the glorious souls contemplate the divine appearance, in which all glory consists. Although each of them has as much joy as it is able to desire or conceive, they are nevertheless not equal in their joys: one possesses greater joys, another lesser, according to the works they performed.

“But if this should give you cause for wonder—how there can be a diversity of joys among the saints when their cause is God alone, in whom there could never be any diversity—the answer is sufficiently clear. Since divine contemplation and knowledge, or understanding, is the whole reward and glory, it may be lesser in one of the saints and greater in another. Therefore, although all the souls together see and know God as he is, one sees and understands less, and thus has a lesser glory; another sees more clearly and understands more subtly, and thus possesses greater glory.

“The same can be said of the punishments of those wretched damned souls. Although all the souls of the damned are situated in one place of punishment, they are nevertheless tormented by different punishments according to the kinds of their vices.

“There is such a difference between the punishments of Christians who are tormented there and those of pagans that, in comparison with what false Christians and sinners endure, the torments of the pagans are almost nothing—although these torments are unspeakable and cannot adequately be imagined by the living. For those others received the grace of God in vain and did not wish to be corrected from their sins while they lived, despite the sacred Scriptures continually crying out, Scriptures that they regarded as worthless.”

Then I said:

“What you say is horrible. If only it would take firm hold of the minds of mortals, so that, even if they did not cease from evil out of love for glory, they might cease from it at least through fear of such punishments! But I beg you, briefly make known what happened to you when your soul departed yesterday.”

He answered:

“When the hour of my death arrived, such a multitude of wicked spirits came to the place where I lay awaiting my departure that they could not possibly be counted because of their number. Their appearance was such that nothing more painful or more horrible could be imagined. Any human being would rather expose himself to be burned by blazing flames than to have his eyes struck for a moment by the sight of those forms.

“They came to me and recalled to my memory every deed I had committed against God, persuading me not to hope any longer for the divine mercy whom I had offended so grievously. And you should know that, unless divine mercy had helped me, I would not have been able to resist them.

“For when, deprived of all strength of spirit, I began to yield somewhat to their words, the glorious Jerome appeared, surrounded by a great host of angels, seven times brighter than the sun, and comforted me. When he saw those unclean spirits harshly tormenting me, he was greatly angered against them and said to them in a terrible voice:

“‘Why have you come to this man, spirits of wickedness and of every curse? Did you not know that he was to be protected by my aid? Leave him immediately, and keep your wickedness far from him, as far as the east is from the west.’

“At this, that company of accursed spirits, terrified, departed from the threshold of the place where I lay amid dreadful howls and cries. Then the glorious Jerome commanded certain angels not to leave me but to wait until he returned, and he hastened away with the other angels.

“When he had gone, the angels who had remained to guard me began to comfort me, promising me gentle and sweet things if I persevered courageously. While these consoling conversations were taking place, about an hour having passed, blessed Jerome came a second time and, standing at the threshold, said:

“‘Come quickly.’

“Then suddenly the soul left the body with such severity and anguish that the human mind could not comprehend how great the pressures and sufferings were, unless, as I did, it had learned them through experience. For even if all human understanding estimated whatever anguish and pain it wished in comparison with the soul’s dissolution from the body, it would nevertheless count that anguish as nothing.

“These and other matters no less difficult and greatly to be feared by mortals, which I shall not record in the present work because of its length, I heard him relate.”

The day was therefore beginning to close with the setting of the sun, and I was obliged to leave unfinished what had happened after death. But because I was especially eager to know that, on the following day I summoned the other two men together with him and returned to the sequence of his account, wishing to hear it fully from those other two as well, so that I might be instructed more firmly by the testimony of three witnesses.

When they had begun to dictate, I replied:

“Although these things are useful, and although I should not grow weary of hearing them repeated, nevertheless, leaving aside what I have already heard, I beg you to pour out upon my gaping mind what happened to you after the dissolution of your bodies.”

The man who had told me the things you have heard on the previous day replied:

“What you ask, Cyril, cannot be fully related, because spiritual things cannot at all be comprehended by our senses. You know, indeed, that you will not be lifeless; yet you do not know what a soul is or of what nature it is.

“You certainly know that God is the beginning and end of all things, from whom all things begin and toward whom they tend. Yet, while you bear the heaviest burden of this corruptible flesh, you do not understand what God is or of what nature he is, except, of course, through a mirror and in an enigma. The same is evident concerning angels and the other incorporeal beings.

“Since, because of the weakness of our small understanding, we cannot comprehend many things that are well known in nature, how shall we understand heavenly and spiritual realities that are wholly alien to the knowledge of nature?”

“As you say,” I answered, “so it is; but please tell me as best you can.”

He replied:

“I shall speak indirectly about what you desire and shall say somewhat less than I am able to say. Those who experienced with me what I related yesterday will testify whether it is so.

“Yesterday my soul, dissolved from the body by the pressures and pains I described above, was suddenly, in the blink of an eye, carried ineffably before the presence of God the Judge. But by whom and how, I do not know. Nor is this surprising: now I am weighed down by the mass of the flesh, whereas then the soul was without flesh.

“The souls of these others were also there, fearing with unimaginable terror what the Judge would do. Alas! Why do mortals not know what will happen to them as it happened to us then? Certainly, if they were not ignorant of it, they would not sin so often.

“None of the sins we had committed throughout our lives could be hidden from the Judge; indeed, everything we had done was clear to all who stood present, as though it were actually occurring, so that even the least of our thoughts appeared exactly as it had been.

“Consider by what and how many terrors we were agitated. On one side stood a multitude of demons, bearing witness to the evils we had committed and declaring their places, circumstances, and times. On the other, we ourselves were wholly unable to contradict the charges brought against us, both because we recognized the Judge as knowing all things and because each of us acknowledged him to be perfectly just.

“Alas, what shall I say? What sentence shall we await? At the memory of it I now tremble. From every side our evil deeds cried out for vengeance to the Judge, and scarcely any good appeared by which we might hope for mercy. From every side all who were present cried out that we were worthy of punishment.

“When nothing remained except for the sentence that was deservedly to be imposed upon sinners to be proclaimed, behold, the glorious Jerome, more radiant than all the stars, accompanied by blessed John the Baptist, the supreme prince of the Apostles, Peter, and a great multitude of angels, came to the throne of the presiding Judge. He obtained that our sentence be suspended for a short time and that we be given to him, both out of reverence and devotion that we had shown him and because of the necessity of destroying the error.

“Then, taking us with him and surrounded by all that blessed company, he showed us the place where the souls of the faithful enjoy immeasurable glory forever, so that we might report what was being done there. After this, he led us to purgatory and hell, showing us not only what was there but also making us undergo the experience of the punishments.

“When all these things had been accomplished, at the hour when the venerable Eusebius touched our corpses with the sack used by blessed Jerome, that same glorious Jerome ordered us to return to our bodies. He commanded us to testify concerning what we had seen, and promised us that on the twentieth day, if we practiced the penance due for the sins we had committed, we would attain, together with the blessed Eusebius, who was then about to depart from this world, glory without end.

“And so our souls were joined to our bodies.”

Many things that are greatly to be feared, dearest Augustine, I learned clearly from them—things that, if impressed upon the minds of mortals, would, as I think, utterly uproot from them the love and vigilant concern for all earthly things by which so many people go astray. If I were to set these things down in these pages, the work would proceed at greater length than you might imagine, and I would not be able to fulfill what I have already promised.

Therefore, since I expect you soon to come to visit the relics of the glorious Jerome, as your letter, which I received yesterday, stated, I shall explain then whatever else I am able to recall to mind.

I shall close all these matters here, touching upon the burial of the venerable Eusebius, so that I may return to narrating the miracles that I promised above to relate. In the preceding sections I inserted, as briefly as I could, the account of the death of the venerable Eusebius and of the three men mentioned above, adding, as I think, certain remarks prompted by affection.

The account of the burials of those men is as follows.

After the death of the venerable Eusebius, several miracles were seen by all, bearing witness to the holiness of his former life. Of these I shall presently relate only two. A certain monk of the same monastery had been deprived of the bodily light of his eyes through tears and vigils. As soon as he touched the venerable body of Eusebius with his face, he immediately received the grace of his former sight. A certain demoniac, meanwhile, encountered the sacred body as we were carrying it to the church and was immediately delivered.

Near the church in which the most holy body of the glorious Jerome had been buried, we buried the body of the venerable Eusebius with the honor due to it, in the manner of his master. In the same cemetery the bodies of those three men, who had died at the same hour, were also laid to rest.

With these words concerning the venerable Eusebius, let all be silent, so that the great and ineffable wonders of the outstanding blessed Jerome, which I have already promised, may now take their place.

## CHAPTER IV

Having therefore entered the pleasant and most delightful meadow of the wondrous deeds of the most holy Jerome, I shall gather, as though making a garland, the chief and beautiful flowers of his miracles, insofar as I am able, for the adornment of this little work and for the benefit of our salvation and that of our descendants.

First I shall relate what happened yesterday concerning Sabinianus, the pestilential heresiarch whom you know.

Sabinianus, the heresiarch and supporter of heretics, asserted that there were two wills in Christ and, what is worse, that they were sometimes in conflict with one another. To support this wholly unexpected falsehood, he introduced what Christ said in the Gospel: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39). From this he drew extremely grave and almost insoluble arguments, claiming that Christ had wished by one will to avoid the Passion, while by another he had been compelled to undergo that same Passion. From this he said that Christ wished many things that he was unable to obtain. By this he brought such grief upon us that we cannot explain its magnitude.

That same pestilential serpent, that ravening wolf clothed in sheep’s clothing, was corrupting the flock entrusted to us. To exercise the savagery of his cruel heart more effectively, he had compiled a certain little work, proving by false arguments that this was so. To make us believe this little work, he had given it the name of the glorious Jerome, the mirror of all truth.

When I learned of this falsehood, knowing that the glorious Jerome had not long before his death issued a letter to you concerning the destruction of this error, I invited the aforesaid heresiarch, together with his disciples and the ministers of his wickedness, to the church of Jerusalem on a certain Sunday, to debate and establish his most wicked error.

On that day, when all my suffragan bishops and many other orthodox men, as well as the heresiarch himself with his wicked disciples, had assembled in the aforesaid church, the disputation began at the ninth hour and continued until evening.

When the same heresiarch cited against us the little work he had composed—falsely entitled with the name of the glorious Jerome—the archbishop of the holy church of Nazareth, Silvanus, a man of good memory, unable to endure such and so many insults against blessed Jerome, immediately rose against the heresiarch and harshly rebuked him for having committed so many and such great wickednesses.

Silvanus revered blessed Jerome with such affection of spirit and devotion that, whenever he did anything, he would invoke the divine name and that of blessed Jerome first; hence he was almost universally called Jerome.

When a long dispute arose between them, and each hurled insults at the other as best he could, at last they both agreed upon this condition: if blessed Jerome clearly showed, by the ninth hour of the following day, that the work had been falsely composed, the aforesaid heresiarch would be put to death; otherwise, the archbishop would be executed.

When these matters had been settled, each returned to his own place.

Throughout the whole night, each of us devoted himself to prayer, praying that the Lord, who had never rejected anyone who hoped in him, might come to our aid in our need. “Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised, and of his wisdom there is no number” (Psalm 144:3).

When the appointed day and hour arrived, the heresiarch came joyfully into the church with the sons of his wickedness. Running here and there, he searched for the servant and son of God like a roaring lion ready to devour him, as though God were unaware and did not hear the prayers of his servants.

But the more firmly the fool thought he stood, the more miserably he fell.

The whole assembly of the faithful stood in the church, each one calling upon the name of Saint Jerome. The glorious Jerome had in fact closed his ears, pretending to sleep and not attending to the prayers of the supplicants, so that he might appear more wondrous.

But I, wholly drenched in tears, was astonished and amazed at why Jerome was absent in this way and waited to see what would happen next.

At last, when no miracle appeared, the heresiarch began to rage with the madness of a dog, so that Silvanus might now fulfill what he had promised.

The most holy Silvanus came to the place where he was to be beheaded, joyful and unafraid as though coming to a wedding. He comforted the bishops and all the other Catholics who had gathered for this event with these words:

“Rejoice with me, dearest ones; be glad and do not grieve, for God does not abandon those who hope in him. If I am not heard, I have deserved this through my sins already committed.”

After this he knelt and said:

“Saint Jerome, be present to me, if it pleases you. Although I am worthy of this punishment and of an even greater one, nevertheless, lest falsehood prevail, come to the aid of the truth. But if it is not lawful that I be helped, be merciful to me at the hour of death, lest I be deprived of glory without end.”

Having said this, he offered his neck to the executioner and asked him to strike. The executioner raised his sword, wishing to sever the venerable bishop’s head with a single blow.

Suddenly the glorious Jerome appeared. While all looked on, he held the sword with an outstretched hand and commanded Silvanus to rise. Then he rebuked the heresiarch, indicated that the writings had been falsely composed, and threatened him; after this he vanished from the sight of everyone.

Would that the same thing might happen to this man and to those like him!

As soon as the glorious Jerome disappeared, the heresiarch’s head fell to the ground, severed from his body, as though the executioner’s hand had cut it off with a single stroke of the sword.

When all who were present saw this most wondrous event, they were immediately astonished and gave thanks to God and to the glorious Jerome. The heresiarch’s disciples returned to the path of truth.

Behold how effective was the venerable bishop’s trust in the Lord and in blessed Jerome: he did not fear to die for the truth.

The venerable bishop became a model for all other Christians. For he is not a Christian who fears to die for the truth. If Christ laid down his soul for us, to redeem us from every form of slavery, then let us also not fear to lay down our souls for him when the time comes, because no one can obtain the crown of glory unless he strives lawfully.

## CHAPTER V
Because you know that something has been said about Silvanus, I shall relate another deed performed on his behalf, no less marvelous, I think. It had as many witnesses as the cities of Nazareth and Bethlehem contain—people who saw it with their own eyes.

That ancient serpent, the devil, cast down into the depths of hell because of his pride, envying the excessive holiness of the venerable bishop Silvanus, was violently stirred against him by his tricks, being more cunning than all living creatures. In order to disgrace the man of God, so that those who were uplifted toward the paths of upright conduct by his example of holiness might fall into worse things through his downfall, one night he assumed the appearance of the holy man and appeared to a most noble woman who was already resting in bed. Pretending to approach her illicitly, he demanded her consent to intercourse.

Terrified by this, the woman, not recognizing the man’s appearance, saw that she was alone with a man in her chamber and did not know what to do. She began to utter dreadful cries, so that by her continual shouting all the sleepers were awakened—not only those in that house but also the neighbors. They all rushed to the chamber of the woman mentioned above and asked the frightened woman what had happened.

Meanwhile the cunning serpent concealed himself beneath the bed. Those who had rushed in, hearing what had occurred, began searching everywhere to discover who the man was. After investigating for a long time, they finally came to the place where the deadly serpent was hiding and found there a man concealed under another’s appearance. When they looked at him by the light of candles, they believed him to be Archbishop Silvanus.

All who were present were astonished and seemed almost deranged, as though they did not know what to do or say, for they knew the reputation of his holiness. Since they saw something so detestable and unexpected, they asked him why he had committed such wickedness.

“What evil have I done?” he replied. “This woman invited me to such an affair.”

When the woman heard this, she answered through her tears that he was lying. Then, in order to provoke the people to still greater hatred against the man of God, so that they might spread his disgrace more quickly, he began to utter such foul and abhorrent words that no one could bear to hear them amid the confusion. Therefore they inflamed themselves against him with insults and abuse and forcibly drove him from the house.

When morning came, they recounted what had happened and shouted that Archbishop Silvanus was a hypocrite, deserving to be burned. Because of this, almost the whole city of Nazareth was stirred against the archbishop, so that anyone who heard his name blasphemed him.

What marvelous patience this man displayed, and what a great sign of holiness! The report of so great a crime flew to the ears of the innocent bishop, yet his mouth did not move in response to the insults. Amid all these adversities his heart remained unmoved, turning toward no impatience. Always giving thanks to the divine Name, he confessed that he had deserved these evils.

“Alas, what shall I say, Augustine? I not only flee from enduring insults and abuse as best I can, but am also broken by every little word. I desire rewards and care nothing for labors, although I know that no one reaches the kingdom of heaven except by the path of labors and afflictions. For what else ought I to judge, when I find myself discordant with the conduct and life of the saints, except that I shall also be found discordant with them in death and reward? Mournful and grievous things confront me when I recall the life of the saints and my own. People such as I marvel as they recount the deeds of the saints, and yet they themselves wish to accomplish nothing. Moreover, what I am about to say exposes my folly. I know that I have often heard from the mouth of that same Silvanus that he had never been so happy as when he saw himself despised and trampled underfoot by human beings.”

His infamy grew so greatly that his reputation was carried as far as Alexandria, Cyprus, and nearly all the neighboring cities, on almost everyone’s lips. Yet he did not dare set foot upon the threshold of the house of the innocent [Col. 1135] bishop.

For the Lord, remaining above as the spectator of all things, permits his holy ones to slip into the hardships of tribulations, so that he may make them faithful through patience; but when necessity demands it, he does not abandon them in their distress.

When a year had passed since the devil’s cunning had perpetrated such things against the man of God, the holy man secretly left the city of Nazareth, in order somewhat to lessen the scandal among those peoples. He came to the church in which the body of the glorious Jerome lay buried, as to a harbor of refuge, and placed himself at the tomb to pray.

After he had remained there for about two hours, a certain man inflamed by the spirit of wickedness entered the church. Finding the saint praying over the tomb, he ran toward him like a serpent, reproaching him for continually inciting women’s minds toward his own lustful pleasures.

The innocent lamb Silvanus, rejoicing to be despised, invited him with his customary humility and gentle conversation to say such things to him repeatedly. When that wicked robber heard this, he shamefully drew with his right hand the sword hanging at his side in its sheath and raised it in order to plunge it into the bishop Silvanus’s throat.

When the venerable bishop opposed him with the words, “Come to my aid, glorious Jerome,” the raised sword entered the man’s own throat, his right hand having turned backward. Thus, as was fitting, the most wicked man killed himself, falling into the pit he had dug.

This was marvelous, but what follows is no less marvelous. Another most wicked man happened to arrive and, seeing what had been accomplished by divine vengeance, immediately seized the sword. Believing that the man had been killed by the man of God, he tried to kill Silvanus. Not to prolong the account, what had happened at first happened to him also.

Before this second man had yet fallen to the ground, two other men entered the church. Seeing what had occurred, but ignorant of the divine judgment, they thought that the only crime committed was this deed by the man of God. One of them, taking it more seriously than the other, a robber inflamed everywhere by the fury of madness, began to shout as loudly as he could:

“How long will your wickedness continue? You force women into your lustful pleasures, and secretly murder men! Surely today will be the end of your wickedness!”

Suddenly he ran forward as fast as he could, his sword drawn and brandished, to destroy him. But when Silvanus, as usual, cried out, “Come to my aid, glorious Jerome,” that man, like the first two, killed himself with his own hand and sword.

The other man who had come with him, seeing this, ran trembling from the vision toward the church doors. Believing that it had been done by magic, he began shouting as loudly as he could:

“Come running here, everyone! Behold the sorcerer Silvanus the archbishop: he not only violates women but also kills men by his enchantments with all his might!”

When they heard this, a huge crowd of men and women gathered. They struck him violently and shouted that Silvanus the archbishop was an utterly wicked man deserving to be burned.

This reached my own ears. Sorrowful and weeping, I went toward so monstrous a sight. The lamb stood among the fiercest wolves, raging like dogs maddened by great hunger, yet he was utterly gentle and joyful, as though enjoying prosperity. He said nothing except:

“I suffer this justly, because I have sinned grievously against my God.”

The innocent man was beaten and seized by everyone, so that he might be led to punishment all the more joyfully the greater the penalty was. While I was signaling with my hand for the crowd to be silent, wishing to calm its excessive fury, I suggested this to them; but the people became still more inflamed with anger and rage.

When the captured Silvanus was already being led outside the church, the glorious Jerome suddenly appeared to everyone, as it seemed, rising from the place where he had been lying. He was surrounded by such a great light that the eyes of those looking at him were dazzled by its rays. He came to give assistance to his most devoted bishop. Taking the right hand of venerable Silvanus in his own right hand, he commanded in a terrifying voice those who were holding the captured bishop to release him.

This vision possessed such power that, before the command had been completed, such fear suddenly seized them all that, deprived of all bodily strength, they fell to the ground like dead men.

Meanwhile a woman [Col. 1136] overshadowed by an unclean spirit, bound in chains and shackled with iron fetters and handcuffs, was being carried to the church by the hands of several men in order to obtain her release. When the woman’s foot touched the threshold of the church, the devil did not cease to emit howls and terrible cries:

“Have mercy on me, glorious Jerome, for through you I am tormented before my time!”

The glorious Jerome said to him:

“Unclean spirit, come out from this handmaid of God, and unravel the deceits you devised against Silvanus, revealing yourself to everyone in Silvanus’s form.”

Then, as the glorious Jerome had commanded, the devil appeared in the form of Silvanus the bishop, as everyone had supposed him to be, and recounted what he had done in order to disgrace the servant of God. After saying this, the unclean spirit disappeared from the church amid dreadful cries and howls.

When this exceedingly marvelous deed had been accomplished, the glorious Jerome did not release the right hand of his bishop. In a gentle voice he said:

“What do you desire, dearest Silvanus? I shall do what pleases you.”

“My lord,” he replied, “that you not leave me here any longer.”

The glorious Jerome answered him:

“What you ask shall be done. Come quickly after me.”

Having said this, he vanished from the sight of all. After an interval of one hour, Archbishop Silvanus died.

All were overcome by unprecedented astonishment and amazement. A multitude of men and women, and also of children, gathered from every side. The earth was wet with the outpouring of tears; voices, lamentations, howls, groans, and sighs sounded in Rama. Each person cried out, asking pardon for whatever he had committed against Silvanus. Throughout the following night the multitude of the peoples did not leave the church.

When morning came, the clergy prepared the bishop’s funeral. His body was carried with due honor to the church of Nazareth, accompanied by a multitude of people from both that city and Bethlehem. In the church of Nazareth we buried that venerable body as was fitting.

The merits of the venerable bishop Silvanus would surely deserve a long and even marvelous account. But since a very large store of things to be said lies open before us, I shall bring the deeds of that venerable bishop to an end, intending to relate certain other matters no less great in a brief form of words.

## CHAPTER VI

I think I should relate something quite marvelous, which I learned partly from the report of truthful witnesses and partly by seeing it with my own eyes.

Two very noble men, wealthy in transitory possessions, although belonging to the Catholic faith and ignorant of the truth, were nevertheless quite good, as people born into a pagan custom may be. Hearing of the miracles of the glorious Jerome, they set out from the city of Alexandria, after gathering together great wealth, fervent in devotion to him, in order to visit the relics of the same glorious Jerome.

Once they had begun their journey, they strayed from the road and entered a forest where no tracks of human beings or horses could be seen. Invoking the name of blessed Jerome, they entrusted themselves to his protection.

In that same forest lived a certain bandit chief who had more than five hundred robbers under his command. He sent them here and there on various routes, so that they might kill travelers and bring the spoils back to him and to the others.

When this chief saw the travelers passing by, he summoned three robbers and ordered them to approach and kill them. Eager to fulfill their leader’s commands, they took up their weapons and rushed swiftly in the direction of the road along which the Alexandrians were walking.

Great indeed were the merits of the glorious Jerome, and greater still the wonders—perhaps, I think, such things had never before been seen by lesser saints.

The robbers hurried to slaughter the travelers. But when they drew near, those whom they had first seen as only two they soon perceived to be innumerable. Among them walked a man surrounded by such great light that it was scarcely permissible to look upon him.

Fear, astonishment, and amazement seized the robbers. They did not know what else to do except return to the other robbers. But when, turning back, they had gone some distance, they again saw only the two men, as before.

The robbers were greatly astonished. Thinking themselves deceived, they began to move back toward the travelers. When they drew near, they saw them as they had seen them earlier. The robbers became more and more terrified [Col. 1137]. Realizing that they had returned to nothing, they turned their backs and quickly went to their chief, who was waiting to hear what they had done.

The chief rebuked them, asking what had taken them so long. When he heard what had happened, he considered them foolish and stupid. He summoned twelve other robbers and himself set out with them toward the passing travelers.

From a distance they saw two men, but as they drew near, they saw them just as the first group had seen them. Immediately their legs trembled, their hearts quaked, and they became almost deranged, deprived of all strength of mind.

At last they came to themselves and followed the travelers secretly, wishing to learn what would happen next. The travelers, unaware of this, were troubled when they saw the men and eagerly asked one another who they might be.

Finally, as the day declined toward sunset, they did not know what they would do during the night. Thinking that the twelve robbers were travelers, they decided to turn aside to ask their advice. But when they set out on the road toward the robbers, they saw only two robbers.

Thus the robbers recovered their courage and immediately went to meet the travelers. They all came together and greeted one another.

Meanwhile the robbers asked who they were, where they came from, and where they were going.

“We are from Alexandria,” they replied. “Coming from there, we are making for Bethlehem in order to visit the relics of the glorious Jerome.”

Then the bandit chief asked:

“Who were the men who had been coming with you up to this point?”

The travelers were astonished that he should speak in this way. They said that, after entering the forest, they had neither seen nor heard anyone except the robbers themselves and the three others.

The chief then recounted what had happened and earnestly begged them to explain, if they knew, why this had occurred.

They replied that they thought it had happened for no other reason than that they had entrusted themselves to the protection of the glorious Jerome.

At this, the Holy Spirit, who breathes wherever he wills, suddenly inspired the robbers. They abandoned all the ferocity they had previously possessed, fell prostrate at the travelers’ feet [probably *coram pedibus*, “before their feet”], and begged pardon for the crimes they had devised. They led the travelers to the other robbers.

But what shall I say? An equally remarkable sight now became visible. At the first hour of the night they reached the robbers who were waiting. They explained what had happened and humbly begged them to abandon their customary crimes and go with them to visit the glorious body of Jerome.

These words provoked laughter among the other robbers. They promised their chief and the others that they would put them to a most cruel death if they dared to speak such things again.

But when the travelers did not cease repeating what they had said before, many of the robbers, raging like dogs maddened by rabies, rose against them with drawn swords. They were indeed able to raise their great swords, but while the travelers called for the assistance of the glorious Jerome, they were utterly unable to lower them. They remained unable to put down their swords for as long as those who were about to be killed appealed to Jerome.

O ineffable mercy of the Savior, who causes those whom he wishes to come to recognition of his name by so many means!

When the whole assembly of robbers suddenly saw this unprecedented event, they gave due praise in loud voices to God and to the glorious Jerome and vowed to visit his relics.

When morning came, more than three hundred men who were then present and who had committed such crimes left the forest with the Alexandrians and came to the tomb of the glorious Jerome, recounting to everyone these unprecedented wonders.

The Alexandrians, who had been pagans, were baptized. After trampling underfoot all the vanities of the world, they led a religious life in a certain monastery. Those robbers likewise, through divine grace and the merits of the glorious Jerome, reached the light of truth and a holy and praiseworthy life.

## CHAPTER VII

As I learned after a short time from letters sent to me specifically about this matter from Constantinople, a miracle almost like the one I have just related happened to two young Romans who were coming from the city of Rome to Bethlehem to visit the body of the glorious Jerome. I shall relate it as briefly as I can.

When the two young men were approaching a certain estate, almost twelve miles from Constantinople, [Col. 1138] two men had been killed on nearly the same road by which they were traveling, before they entered the estate from a distance of two miles.

When news of their deaths resounded through the estate, the men of that place gathered together and began to investigate vigorously who their killer had been. After making a careful search, they found no one present except the young men mentioned above, who had already drawn near. They immediately seized them, believing that the men had been killed by them.

The young men, unaware of what had happened, were astonished and protested with all their strength that they knew nothing of the matter. But the others paid no attention to their words and hurried to lead them, as prisoners, to the estate.

After this, since judgment over those men did not belong to the estate, the captured young men were sent with the accusations to the ruler of Constantinople. To avoid making the account too long: although they had not committed the deed, the young men were forced by the severity of torture to confess, and, as was customary, the sentence of beheading was added.

Alas! What heart could hear the lamentations of innocent men—men adorned by the greatest beauty of youth, extraordinary comeliness, and noble birth—and restrain itself from tears?

The young men wept, watering their pale faces with heavy tears, and did not cease uttering howls, groans, and sighs.

“Glorious Jerome,” they said, “is this the kind of reward you give to those who serve you? Is this what we have earned by the labor of our journey? Alas, Rome, which knows our birth—never did we believe that you would be ignorant of our end!”

The innocent young men were led to the place of such punishment, where a very great multitude of the people was already waiting.

O ineffable mercy of our God, with which heaven overflows and earth resounds, and which does not forget to show mercy to anyone who runs to it!

Kneeling at the place where they were to be punished, both young men raised their hands toward heaven and said in a loud voice:

“Glorious Jerome, harbor of our salvation and aid, most wholesome and life-giving anchor of our hope, at this critical hour incline your merciful ears to our unworthy supplications. If we did not commit the crime for which we are being punished, may we, through your accustomed compassion, experience the power of your deliverance. But if we committed it, let us be condemned as justice requires.”

When they had said this, they extended their necks to the executioners to be struck, saying nothing except:

“Come to our aid, come to our aid, glorious Jerome!”

What wonder is it that the merciful helper Jerome could not refrain from showing mercy amid so many tears of all who called upon him, when the hearts of all the bystanders and even of the executioners were moved to compassion?

The executioners raised their swords and struck the young men’s necks, but the necks received the marks of the blows as though they were porphyry stones. The executioners were astonished, believing that they had missed their blows. They again raised their swords as high as they could and struck, but the young men’s necks remained as insensible as before.

They struck again and again, but the swords, as though they were made of straw, never injured the young men. Amazement arose among the bystanders, and the greatest astonishment seized everyone. People gathered from every side to see this unprecedented sight.

The man who had pronounced the sentence also heard of it and hurried there. He ordered the executioners to strike again while he watched, but the young men’s necks remained entirely unharmed.

The judge grew more and more astonished. Ignorant of the miracle’s meaning, he could think of no explanation except magic. He therefore ordered his servants, without further delay, to hand the naked young men over to the flames of a pyre.

A great fire was immediately kindled around them. Oil and pitch were poured onto the wood so that their lives might be destroyed more quickly.

But is it surprising that the glorious Jerome, who had protected them from swords, could free from the flames the young men who called upon him with persistent cries?

The flames of the fire rose immeasurably upward, but the young men remained safely beneath the wings of the glorious Jerome, as though they were resting in a pleasant and delightful garden.

After this, the judge wished to determine more certainly whether the event should be attributed to miracles or to magic. He therefore decided that, if the young men remained alive for eight days while suspended, they should be released and allowed to go wherever they wished.

When they had been suspended, the presence of the glorious Jerome immediately came to their aid. Holding the soles of their feet in his hands, he miraculously preserved them unharmed and alive for the appointed days [Col. 1139].

On the eighth day the men of the entire city and of the surrounding villages came running, and the judge came as well. They clearly saw the glorious miracle, while those assigned to guard the young men revealed what they had witnessed.

Everyone was astonished and raised their voices in praise of the Creator and the glorious Jerome. The innocent young men were soon taken down from the apparatus [possibly the gallows or torture-frame] and honored by the entire people with the greatest ceremonial respect.

They had entered Constantinople as prisoners in the grip of the most bitter grief; they left free, honored, and filled with unspeakable joy. At last, with God’s consent, accompanied by many of the people of Constantinople, they reached Bethlehem and paid the proper reverence to the relics of the glorious Jerome.

Immediately abandoning all concern for worldly affairs, they entered the monastery in which the glorious Jerome had lived. Devoting themselves day and night to penance and prayer, they still remain in that monastery, leading a celibate life of evident holiness.

## CHAPTER VIII

The preceding miracle of the young men was a source of great astonishment, joy, and devotion; but the following one is known to have produced much fear, especially among those established in sacred orders.

In the Upper Thebaid, it is said, there was an excellent and wealthy monastery for women two years ago, adorned with every beauty and distinction. Nearly two hundred women of honorable life remained there under continuous religious enclosure and disciplined conduct.

Those who are present should pay close attention, lest what one ear has taken in be poured out by the other. No matter how sound and intact a ship may be, it is of little—or rather no—use if, while wishing to cut across the deep sea, it leaves a small hole in its bottom and thereby admits a dreadful shipwreck. The reason I have said this will be revealed by the story of the present account.

Although the monastery mentioned above abounded in many virtues, it retained one most wicked vice by which it would fall: the vice of simony. For, at the devil’s instigation, this abuse was observed among those women: if they wished to receive someone as a nun, they did so not so much with regard to charity, mercy, and the goodness of the person to be received as with regard to money. No woman could enter the monastery to remain there unless a specified amount of money accompanied her.

There was in this monastery a certain elderly nun who, from her childhood, had served God through fasts and prayers. Freed from every stain, she had lived for God, and she detested that vice intensely.

One night, while she was engaged in prayer as usual, the glorious Jerome appeared to her, illuminating the place with immense light. He commanded her to go in the morning to the abbess and the other nuns of that monastery and announce that, unless they withdrew their hands from the sin that had now become old, they should immediately expect divine vengeance.

Having said this, he disappeared.

Terrified by the unfamiliar vision, the nun spent the whole night awake, eagerly considering who the one giving such orders might have been.

At dawn she summoned all the nuns to the chapter house by ringing the bell. They were astonished and wondered why they had been called together with such urgency. The nun rose among them and revealed to everyone what she had seen and heard.

At once all the nuns laughed at her. They called her a fool and mocked her with many chattering jests, suggesting that she had perhaps dreamed this in a state of excessive drunkenness.

Having suffered their insult, she armed herself with the shield of patience. She grieved greatly over their obstinacy but rejoiced at her own humiliation. She returned to her customary prayers, continually asking that what she had heard might not happen to her fellow nuns.

After ten days had passed, while the nun was devoutly engaged in prayer at midnight on account of this matter, the glorious Jerome appeared to her again. In a kindly address he commanded her once more to announce fearlessly to the nuns what she had previously told them.

“Who are you, lord,” she asked, “who command me to say such things?”

“I am Jerome,” he replied.

Then he vanished from her sight.

Knowing their hardness, she did not know what she should do or say. At last, preferring to be considered insane and drunk by the nuns rather than oppose divine [Col. 1140] commands, she summoned them again and wished to tell them what she had seen and heard.

But when the wicked nuns saw her rise, unaware of the divine judgment that was soon to come upon them, they left the chapter house with loud bursts of laughter before she had even begun to speak.

Three days later, the glorious Jerome appeared again at midnight to the nun while she was sleeping, surrounded, as it seemed, by an ineffable company of angels. He woke her and immediately commanded her to leave that monastery and not await the sentence that was soon to come.

When she begged him with many tears that this should not happen, the glorious Jerome said:

“Go to the abbess and the others without delay and tell them that, unless they repent, they will experience divine vengeance this very night. But if they remain in their obstinacy, leave immediately and do not remain any longer in the monastery.”

Having finished speaking, he departed.

When the nun heard this, full of anxiety and grief, she went to the chapter house and began ringing the bell violently so that the nuns would come there. The abbess awoke from sleep and, recognizing that this nun had rung the bell, hurried to the chapter house in anger.

When she saw her, she rebuked her with dreadful threats and refused to hear a word, promising that, unless she stopped doing this, she would no longer remain with her in the monastery.

“Please,” said the nun, “do not delay in doing what you promise. You should know that I certainly shall not remain here any longer. The glorious Jerome appeared to me and revealed that judgment would immediately come upon this monastery.”

When the abbess heard this, she began to laugh, thinking that the nun was speaking with an unbalanced mind. She summoned the portress and ordered her to drive the nun immediately from the monastery, instructing her later to let her back in at some suitable hour, so that she might thereby cease from the activities she had begun.

The nun was happy because of this and left the monastery as quickly as she could, although she was covered with tears and filled with sorrow over what she knew was about to happen to the monastery.

For God is terrible, strong, and powerful—and who can resist him? Alas, why do human beings not fear him, knowing that they cannot in any way escape his hands, so that his great and unspeakable judgment may not overtake them? At least let these wretched people be terrified by such examples. Let those who trust in their riches hear what judgment was hurled from heaven against this monastery because God had turned his face away from it on account of money, and against those who by the dryness of their greed provoke the Most High Lord to anger.

The nun had scarcely crossed the threshold of the door when suddenly the whole monastery collapsed, crushing all the nuns, so that not one of them remained alive.

That nun, however, still lives in outstanding holiness in a venerable monastery for women situated in the Lower Thebaid.

## CHAPTER IX

I considered it appropriate to join to the miracles related above certain other manifestations of divine judgment against sinners, so that perhaps, through the multitude of such precedents, the stubborn hearts of sinners, more stony than stone, might be turned to flesh; and, seeing themselves to be beasts on account of their sins, might strive to attain reason and self-knowledge, so as to become human beings.

For when they cast away the reason by which they are human, they are reduced below brute animals.

One day a certain Greek heretic was publicly disputing with a priest in the church of Jerusalem. When the priest, defending his own side, cited an authority of the glorious Jerome in order to refute the Greek’s arguments, the pestilent Greek did not blush to say with reckless lips that Jerome, the light of all truth, had lied.

But the man who had perpetrated such wickedness with his voice thereafter formed no voice at all.

## CHAPTER X

Another pestilent heretic of the Arians, during a disputation, responded with reckless boldness to someone who cited the authority of the glorious Jerome against him:

“He lies!”

He was immediately struck by divine vengeance. Before he had finished the word aloud, he did not cease crying out throughout the entire day without interruption:

“Have mercy on me, glorious Jerome, for I am tormented by you with the harshest punishments!”

He continued shouting this as loudly as he could throughout the whole day and died miserably at the hour of Compline, in the sight of all who had run together to witness it. [Col. 1141]

## CHAPTER XI

Another heretic of the pestilent Arian heresy—may the merciful Lord bring it to an end before my death—saw an image of the glorious Jerome in the church of Zion and said:

“If only I had held you in my hands while you were alive! I would have slaughtered you with my sword.”

As soon as he had said this, he drew his sword and with all his strength thrust it into the throat of the image.

How great was this Jerome, who performed so many miracles, and to whom no one appears equal according to his deeds!

The heretic’s right hand could indeed thrust the sword into the throat of the image, weak though it was; but he was utterly unable to withdraw either the sword from the image or his hand from the sword until the matter became known.

Immediately a stream of living blood flowed from the place of the blow as though from the body of a living man, and it has never ceased flowing, even to the present, as a testimony to the miracle.

At the same hour in which this occurred, the same glorious Jerome appeared to the judge, who was standing in the atrium, with the sword fixed in his throat. He demanded that vengeance be exacted for this offense and recounted what had been done to him. Having said this, he departed.

The judge was astonished. He hurried to the church with the others who were standing nearby and found the heretic holding the sword that had been thrust into the image. As soon as they saw this, he was able to remove his hand from the sword.

The heretic was arrested. Remaining obstinate, he said that he regretted nothing except that he had not held Jerome alive. For this chatter he was slaughtered by the multitude of the people with stones, pieces of wood, swords, and spears.

## CHAPTER XII

My nephew John, whom you know, shining with every beauty and whom I adopted in place of a son, told you yesterday, I think, what happened to him. Nevertheless, so that it may be more firmly committed to memory, I shall not pass over it in silence.

Two years ago John was captured by the Persians and sold to the servants of the Persian king. Because of his remarkable beauty, he was assigned to perform services for the king.

After he had remained for a year at court with no little sorrow and weariness, on the same day in the following year he was serving the king at dinner and, overcome by grief, could not restrain his tears.

When the king saw this, he eagerly asked him the reason for his tears. After learning it, he had John confined in a certain fortress.

One night, while John was there, soaked on every side with bitter tears, the glorious Jerome came to him in a dream. He took John’s hand, as it seemed to him, and led him with him to the city of Jerusalem.

When he awoke in the morning, thinking that he was still being held by soldiers in the fortress, he found himself in the house where I live.

Overcome with astonishment and almost beside himself, he could not distinguish whether he was in the fortress or in my home. At last coming to himself, he raised his voice and awakened the sleeping household.

The servants then ran to me, announcing that John was present in the house with unspeakable joy. I hurried there in doubt, believing him to be bound among the Persians, and saw him standing before me.

When he recounted what had happened to him, the greatest praises were offered to God and to the glorious Jerome.

## CHAPTER XIII
A certain religious woman, almost the most beautiful of all women, youthful in age but very mature in the wisdom of her spirit, and most devoted to blessed Jerome, still lives, as I believe, with great holiness in a certain convent of women. It is said that the following happened to her.

Let this woman serve as an example to others who never cease running here and there through streets and alleys, ensnaring the souls of foolish men with their appearance. By no snare does the devil capture so many souls as by the most wicked snare of women. This religious woman, as the testimony of all the nuns confirms, never sets foot outside her cell unless the greatest necessity compels her. For she does nothing else except devote herself to prayer, become absorbed in reading and meditation, or restore her body through sleep.

The ancient serpent, the devil, envying these practices and wishing to recall her from her holy purpose, inflamed the mind of a certain most noble young man with such desire for this same religious woman that day and night [Col. 1142] he could think of nothing except how he might reach her. Blinded to the true light, he continually went about the monastery and could find no other remedy. He was so darkened by the cloud of ignorance that, often seeing himself disturbed by his destructive passions, he wished to cast himself into the waters and drown.

The foolish young man was bound day by day with the chain of foolish love, so that, out of regard for her chastity, he did not dare disclose this to the ears of the religious woman. Therefore, deprived of every other means of achieving his purpose, he found a certain magician practicing sorcery and the abominable enchantments of demons, and promised him a large sum of money if he obtained what he desired.

Then, by the incantations of his sorceries, the magician summoned a demon and sent it swiftly, in the middle of the night, to the holy nun for the purpose of deceiving her. The demon approached the cell, but, overcome by great fear of the image of Jerome painted in the cell, it could not cross the threshold.

A marvelous thing, Augustine, as numerous examples make clear: such fear of glorious Jerome is present in the devil that he does not dare appear even before his painted image. For if a precious image of him is shown to someone whose body is possessed by a demon, the devil is immediately driven away from that person.

Thus, despairing of carrying out the assigned wicked deed, the evil spirit returned to the one who had sent it and explained that, because of the image of glorious Jerome painted in the cell, entry to the nun had been denied it. The magician mocked it and dismissed it.

Immediately he summoned another demon and sent it as quickly as possible to complete such a task. The same thing happened a second time as had happened the first. But the second demon, after perhaps remaining there for an hour under compulsion, began to utter loud cries:

“If you allow me, Jerome, to depart from here, I shall not return here again.”

At this, the woman, who was absorbed in prayer in her little cell, was terrified and asked with great fear who was uttering those cries. Since the devil did not cease shouting in this way, the nuns of that convent awoke and, struck by great fear, ran trembling to the cell, with the Lord’s cross going before them.

When they learned that it was an evil spirit, they adjured it to declare why it had come. The devil then recounted the whole affair and, revealing itself through groans and howls, said that Jerome held it bound in chains of fire. It begged them to obtain for it, through their prayers, permission to depart.

When the nuns heard this, they gave praise to God and glorious Jerome, humbly asking that he drive this demon from the convent and never allow it to return. Scarcely had they finished their prayers when the devil departed from that place with great shrieks and went to the magician. Seizing him, it scourged him with such blows and torments that for many hours scarcely any sign of life appeared. It cried out terribly:

“You were the cause of my torments, sending me to that nun; certainly I shall avenge myself upon you with these same blows.”

Meanwhile, as the magician heard these dreadful words and saw himself almost at the point of destruction, he realized that his arts could offer him no help. As one already shipwrecked, he turned to glorious Jerome as the harbor of every refuge:

“Glorious Jerome,” he said, “come to the aid of this wretched man who hastens to your mercy, and do not deny him the great gifts of mercy that you customarily bestow. For I promise that, if at this hour, aided by your help, I do not succumb to so dreadful a destruction, I shall henceforth, stripped of every deception, never withdraw from your service.”

When he had finished speaking, the evil spirit vanished from him like smoke.

For a year the magician then lay afflicted by the beatings, so helpless in body that he could move only with another’s assistance. Soon, having received a penance, and before rising from his bed, he burned all the books by which he had practiced those most wicked arts. He sold everything he possessed and distributed the proceeds to the poor. After the year had been completed, he shut himself into a certain cave to perform his penance. In the desert where glorious Jerome had stood for four years, he now flourishes in great holiness of life and severity of penance.

Let all young men hasten here, I beg, and learn from the example of this insane young man, lest they later grieve that what happened to him has happened to them.

The insane young man, thus bound with so many snares of lust, saw that he was altogether frustrated in the most wicked desire for his miserable pleasure [Col. 1143]. One night he hanged himself with a noose, and thus the wretched man deprived himself of temporal life—and rather, of eternal life as well.

Behold how clearly the most shameful vice of lust is the cause of so many evils. I consider no crime so readily destructive alike of soul and body as this most wicked one. From it arise murders, drunkenness, quarrels, and almost every evil, as countless examples of the Old and New Testaments show; continual and evident experience also makes this clear.

To provide young men with greater prudence for protecting themselves—for no condition is more dangerous than that of foolish youth—I have decided, though with great sorrow, to add another example involving my nephew Rufus, perhaps eighteen years of age.

## CHAPTER XIV

There is no doubt that what I am beginning to recount is recalled to my memory amid great tribulations. Nevertheless, as was said above, since it may serve as an example to everyone, and especially to young men, I cannot pass over it in silence.

A certain nephew of mine, named Rufus, deprived of both parents, came into my hands when he was one year old. Would that he had never emerged from his mother’s womb, so that what he now suffers might not have happened to him. I raised him with such care, despite his misfortune, that many people thought he had been born to me.

As the unhappy boy grew day by day, he increased in age but not in wisdom. He possessed great bodily beauty but none of the soul; he was adorned with grace and good manners, honesty, goodness, and the elegance of much wisdom. Yet, although his adornments were vain, everyone honored him with excessive affection.

In the eighteenth year of his age he died, weak and most wretched. On his account such mourning arose from everyone that it could scarcely come to an end for a month. But certainly mourning was insufficient for what had happened.

I, however, being deeply attached to him, repeatedly asked glorious Jerome to reveal to me what had happened to my nephew. Glorious Jerome granted my prayers, and I obtained what I had longed to know.

One day, while I was praying at the ninth hour, such a stench suddenly arose that I could not endure it in my nostrils. As I silently considered and wondered within myself where so great a stench could be coming from, I raised my eyes above my head and saw my unhappy nephew in a terrifying vision, so terrible that I did not dare fix my gaze upon him.

For he was bound round with chains of fire and belched forth the foulest flames like a furnace. At this vision such violent fear suddenly entered me that, although I repeatedly wished to speak, I was altogether unable to form a voice.

At last, coming somewhat to myself, I began to ask in a trembling voice whether he was my nephew. He answered amid howls and sighs:

“Would that I had never existed, so that I might not have been assigned to such dreadful torments! For know that I shall remain forever in the dwelling places of Tartarus.”

Alas, what shall I say? When he had spoken these words, such grief seized me that I have often wondered how life did not immediately depart from me.

After our long conversation had ended, I asked him why he had been so deprived of divine mercy, since in the world he had seemed to flourish in so many virtues.

“Know,” he replied, “that I have been condemned for no other reason than that I delighted especially in games. And because, after receiving penance at my death, I postponed confession through foolish ignorance, I did not deserve to obtain divine pardon.”

As he said this, he disappeared from my sight. Yet after he had gone, such a stench remained that no one has dared to enter that place to this day.

Behold how greatly the eyes of the divine majesty abhor the most shameful crime of gaming. Let us therefore fear lest such sudden death snatch us away defenseless, lest we fail to repent of our vices while there is still time, since afterward repentance would be useless.

Therefore, so that a Christian may flee far from the sacrilege of gaming and such great ruin—or rather, so that its memory may be erased altogether—I shall introduce a few other examples as briefly as I can.

## CHAPTER XV

In Samaria, before fifteen days had passed, a certain wretched man, while gambling and having apparently exhausted everything he possessed, began to blaspheme the name of glorious Jerome with reckless audacity. Scarcely had he finished uttering the abominable words of blasphemy when, while everyone watched in amazement, a thunderbolt came from heaven [Col. 1144] and killed him.

## CHAPTER XVI

The following happened to three other men who were gambling in Tyre. When they wished to begin their game, they said—as those who claim to have heard this from them and also to have seen the whole sequence of events themselves report:

“Exert whatever power you can, Jerome; for, in spite of you, we shall cheerfully finish this game.”

Having said this, they began their game. As soon as it had begun, almost in the space of a single instant, the earth opened and swallowed them alone, so that nothing more of them was ever seen.

## CHAPTER XVII

What is known by sight is confirmed by the most trustworthy testimony. Therefore, although what I say could be confirmed by many witnesses, I shall establish it through myself as witness, since I learned these things through my own vision.

Near my house, in which I live in Jerusalem, there was a certain most noble soldier, exceedingly wealthy in transitory possessions. He had one son, and, blinded by the same foolish love, he not only failed to correct him when he was wicked but even tried to instruct him himself in wickedness.

Foolish parents and those like this man, please turn the eyes of your minds here, so that you may not remain ignorant of the end that awaits. Many people have fallen into great ruin of soul and body because of the foolishness of wicked parents.

As the soldier’s son grew, deprived of every good habit, he reached the age of twelve. He spent all his time day after day in games, perjuries, blasphemies, and every kind of impurity, with his father encouraging him.

One evening, as he was engaged in his customary games with his father, and the game was not proceeding as he desired, he burst out first with these words:

“If that Jerome who forbids games has any power, let him now exert it; for, in spite of him, I shall not rise from here except as the victor.”

While he was continuing to speak in this way, an evil spirit in the form of a most hideous man, before everyone’s eyes, approached the place where he was playing with rapid steps and snatched away the unhappy boy. No one has ever learned where it carried him. But, as I think, it carried him into hell.

For at that same hour I happened by chance to be standing at a window of my house opposite the place where the father and son were staying and gambling. From there, with unmistakable clarity, I was compelled to see the entire course of that dreadful event.

Let young men therefore learn, during the time of youth—which is more excellent than other periods—to support themselves with desirable habits, lest a youthful mind shaped by worthless and fleeting ways be unable to change its condition in old age. What is written on a new tablet is not easily erased.

Let foolish parents also learn to educate their sons through correction and blows. Let them not allow the thorns of vices to put down roots that cannot easily be torn out, lest the consequences bring tears both here and in the future.

For, unless I am mistaken, the narrowest road to reaching the homeland of eternal joys—a road certainly known by very few—exists; whereas the way to destruction is broad and is filled with many—indeed, almost innumerable—paths.

Each mortal sin constructs its own path to destruction. It is therefore clear that the number of those who persist in manifold crimes is greater—not only among pagans but also among those washed by the water of holy Baptism. For there is no question that pagans are condemned. Among the baptized, scarcely any correction of such people is ever seen.

Indeed, speaking comparatively, when good and evil people alike are considered, “there is no one who does good, not even one”; rather, all walk after their shameful and worst pleasures. Consequently, it must be concluded that only the rarest people advance to the joys of eternal blessedness.

Countless—indeed, almost all—the authorities of sacred Scripture testify to this. We could clearly contemplate infinite examples sufficient to demonstrate this truth more fully.
