This single conclusion ought to be accepted from them all, and nothing can differ from it: no one can reach eternal joys in any way unless, after every vice has been eradicated—not merely in part but entirely—he hastens along the path of the virtues.

Having brought these matters to an end, and now approaching the conclusion of this work, I shall briefly introduce certain examples and marvels. I shall first recount two especially remarkable events that I learned from the venerable Nicholas, archbishop of the island of Crete.

## CHAPTER XVIII

The same venerable archbishop had come to Bethlehem shortly before, out of exceeding devotion to glorious Jerome, to visit his relics, which are to be honored by everyone. Since he was wholly fervent with charity, he refused to return until he had filled me with the greatest joys through his most welcome visit.

As an outstanding giver, and wishing according to his custom to bestow upon me most welcome gifts in great abundance, he was not content merely to visit me but graciously remained with me for several days. He is still here; would that his stay might last a long time. In Christ, dearest Augustine, this same venerable bishop greets you.

The venerable bishop often related to me, who eagerly listened to his words, that the following event had occurred in the city of Candia.

A certain priest, the custodian of his principal church, was shameless and devoted to lust and drunkenness. Before a year had been completed, he departed from this world. His body was buried in the common pit of the other priests, so that his punishment might become known to everyone as an example [Col. 1145].

On the following night there was such a tumult in the church and its cemeteries that the inhabitants of the city, awakened by the tremendous noise, ran to the church in great terror, as if beside themselves.

They all stood around the church, hearing violent disturbances and the ringing of bells. They entreated divine mercy to reveal why these things were happening, but they perceived no assistance in their prayers.

At dawn, when the disturbance ceased, they found everything in the church overturned and as though scorched on every side by flames of fire. Then the bishop mentioned above ordered prayers and instructed the people to wait and see what would happen the following night.

Not to dwell too long on words, the following night was followed by twice as much tumult and terror. The people, therefore, filled with bitterness and grief, saw that no help was coming to them from the Lord and remained as though they were wounded men cast down to sleep in tombs.

At daybreak, when everyone had gathered in the church for prayer, glorious Jerome suddenly entered the church, brighter than the sun, and proceeded to the altar before the eyes of all. He remained there almost silently for about an hour and then declared to the astonished people that this had happened because the wretched corpse of that priest had been buried unworthily in the holy places, as a terror to sinners.

He commanded them to disinter the miserable corpse, which after the resurrection of all would be assigned to the dwellings of Tartarus, and immediately consign it to the flames to be burned. Otherwise, he said, the plague that had begun would not depart.

Having said this, he vanished from the eyes of those who were watching. The people immediately carried out what he had ordered with joy, giving special praise to God and blessed Jerome. Thus the plague ceased.

Afterward, all the people unanimously began to honor the most blessed Jerome with the greatest devotion.

## CHAPTER XIX

In the same city there was also a certain extremely handsome young man named Titus, distinguished by honorable conduct, born of a family no less distinguished in the flesh, and exceedingly wealthy. He placed almost all his devotion and trust in blessed Jerome.

This young man, shining with virginal purity, persevered in the purpose of holy virginity with honorable conduct of life until his twentieth year. When that time had been completed, however, he was incited by the wicked counsel of his brother. He despised the most noble jewels of virginity, trampled underfoot the precious metal of gold, and turned violently toward the filth, mud, and stench of the flesh. He married a certain girl who shone with every bodily beauty.

He was so caught in the nets of his love for her that he could think of nothing except her, and day by day he began to forget divine services. But because the wretched man abandoned justice, he forgot God who nourished him; the Lord forgot to have mercy on him.

After the year had been completed during which the foolish young man had lived with the girl—not joined to her for the duties of marriage but for the fulfillment of lust—the young man’s brother, ensnared by love of the girl and for a long time eagerly [Col. 1146] seeking to enjoy her embraces, finally obtained what he had desired.

Let young men come here and learn through the example of this young man. What had happened became known to the girl’s husband. He kept silent, but eagerly considered how he might discover the truth of the matter. For several days he waited, pretending not to know.

Then one day he arranged to leave the city and travel abroad. He remained hidden in the city during the day, and in the middle of the night came to the house. The servant girl secretly unfastened the locks, as the two had previously arranged. He proceeded as far as the bedroom where his brother and his wife were in bed and asked that it be opened to him.

They were astonished and, terrified by great fear, neglected to open the door to the one who was knocking. At last, after the bedroom locks had been broken, the young man, burning everywhere with anger and immense fury like a blazing furnace, first drew his sword and killed his wife. Then, finding his own brother hiding beneath the bed, he killed him.

After this, he left the city and wandered here and there through the world for a long time. With certain others he began to rob travelers on the road and even to slaughter them.

After Titus had been involved in such activities for ten years, glorious Jerome appeared to him one day at dusk in the form of a merchant, so that Titus would not be deprived of the rewards of the devotion he had once possessed. Although he continually practiced so many and such great detestable vices, he still retained some devotion to blessed Jerome. Each day he commended himself to him and never failed to do something good in his honor.

When Titus saw the merchant, he summoned his wicked companions to their customary deeds of evil and quickly went with them, their spears brandished. He met Jerome, who appeared in the guise of a merchant. Rising against him, he ordered his companions to hold him until a sword could be thrust into his side.

Then he raised his hand, holding the sword with which he intended to kill him, so that he might complete so great a crime.

At this glorious Jerome said:

“For the love of Jerome, whom you cherish, grant me a brief opportunity to speak. Afterward, if you wish, do what you desire.”

Titus replied:

“For the love of the one you have named, you shall have the opportunity to speak and to live, as you request. Only set down the merchandise you are carrying.”

But glorious Jerome said:

“I myself am Jerome, who have come here for your liberation, so that the services you have rendered me might not pass away in vain. Let the many sins you have committed now bring you to repentance; return to yourself and do not be afraid. Know that until now, for the sake of your salvation in both soul and body, I have stood before the angry divine justice as your suppliant, lest it exercise upon you the vengeance you deserved.

“Hasten, therefore, as quickly as possible along the road of repentance and now lay down the burdens of your sins. Otherwise you shall no longer have me as your guardian and suppliant before God.”

After these words glorious Jerome disappeared from their sight.

Titus—and those who were with him—was so stunned by fear and amazement that he fell to the ground and could not rise for about an hour. Then suddenly the grace of the Holy Spirit was poured out upon Titus and his companions, and heavenly light illuminated them.

They were immediately changed into other, living men. Rejecting every impurity of vice, they returned to the path of repentance. Then they hastened to remote and unknown caves in the deserts and devoted themselves to great bodily austerities and a most holy life.

## CHAPTER XX

I have learned from the most trustworthy testimony of reliable witnesses that another miracle occurred in the upper regions of Egypt. I think it will be pleasing to add it to the preceding miracle as an example for people—and especially for young men, however chaste they may be—so that they may avoid the danger posed by women.

A certain young monk, handsome, distinguished by honesty and mature in conduct, was a venerable guardian of virginal purity and a mirror of holiness to all the monks of that monastery. He was a most devoted lover of glorious Jerome.

He had lived in the monastery for twelve years, continually devoting himself to prayer and to the study of Scripture. Because he feared for the sake of chastity that his heart might in any way be violated, he abhorred the sight of women [Col. 1147] beyond expression, so much so that he feared even their memory.

The ancient serpent, the devil and enemy of mankind, envied this purpose. He stirred up against the monk the schemes and arts of his long-practiced wickedness, and the worst tempter continually afflicted the young man with the goads of his thoughts. For two months he did not cease from tempting him day and night.

The prudent young man, however, commending himself to the victorious protection of the Lord and blessed Jerome, whose love burned within him, triumphed over the devil’s temptations through fasting and prayer.

Let young and old come here, I beg, and learn by this example how great is the peril of the deceptive beauty of women.

When the treacherous devil saw that the young man was overcoming him through harsh discipline, like a roaring lion he began to seek subtler arts of harm in order to devour him. A serious battle therefore arose between them.

On one side the worst enemy established his camp against the young man with his customary cunning; on the other, the young man’s prayers and the protection of glorious Jerome tore down the fortifications of that camp and despised its strength through a noble triumph.

Meanwhile, when his father fell gravely ill and was approaching death, the young man was compelled to leave the monastery and come into the city to his father’s house. His father repeatedly cried out that he would die of grief if he were deprived of seeing his son.

The monk grieved over this. Fearing that the sight of women might violate his pure heart, shining with virginal brightness, he would have preferred—had he not yielded to the entreaties of the brothers of his convent—to exercise cruelty toward his father for the sake of the Lord rather than withdraw from the monastery and show compassion to the sick man.

For he knew that nothing is more harmful, detestable, and deadly to a monk than to go about among villages, cities, and crowds of people. Certainly no tranquility of mind remains in a person entangled in the talk and empty chatter of many. To monks, silence accomplishes what water does for fish.

While the monk remained in his father’s house, he was afflicted for three days by such great weariness that he seemed to himself to have been handed over to a gloomy prison.

On the third day, as he and his sister—an extraordinarily beautiful girl—were rubbing their father’s legs together because of his illness, it happened that the sister’s right hand touched his right hand. At once, through the devil’s instigation, the monk’s heart was wounded by such terrible arrows of lust and such foolish and abominable desire for his sister that it almost invited him to unlawful acts, wholly abhorrent to mankind, had the fear of shame not intervened.

Alas, what shall I say? What vigilance of chastity will remain in those monks who continually enjoy the sight of women while conversing with them? A man remains chaste while constantly looking upon women’s faces no more than straw remains standing in fire.

Certainly the beauty of woman is a deceptive fall, extremely near to ruin, and an unavoidable danger.

The fear that the monk had feared came upon him, and what he had dreaded for so long happened to him. Yet this is not without a very great example for others: the command to obey parents does not apply where danger to the soul is feared.

The monk unwillingly left the monastery. But, with his heart inflamed by the heat of such wicked lust, he thought of nothing except seeing the face of his unsuspecting sister with the wicked gaze of his eyes, so that he scarcely remembered that he had ever had a monastery.

Meanwhile, his father recovered. But the monk invented excuses and delayed returning to the monastery from day to day. As he remained in his father’s house for three months, both the monks and his father were deeply astonished, and the entire household wondered why such a violent and unheard-of change had entered him.

They did not know the cause of the affair, and therefore they could not understand its effect.

At last he returned to the monastery with two monks sent to fetch him, reporting on his return the same weariness that he had brought with him when he departed.

Thus the monk’s body began to live in the monastery, but his heart did not in any way withdraw from his sister. His study of Scripture became a means by which he might attain the wicked thing he desired; his contemplation of divine matters became a means of finding how to accomplish his sin.

He was repeatedly struck [Col. 1148], alienated from himself, and continually led astray from knowledge of the truth by the devil, to whose most oppressive yoke he had submitted his feeble neck through the weapons of his new lust.

His days vanished like smoke; his bones were broken as though in a frying pan [the reading is uncertain], and his life weakened in pains. He became like an irrational animal.

He entirely forgot to implore divine mercy, spending the whole day thinking of what [uncertain reading: “nabilis”] method might present itself by which he could taste the cup of death.

Alas, how poor and wretched, deprived of every good and exiled, are those who distance themselves from the Lord! A man in sins becomes worse than brute animals, for God is separated from his soul by a greater distance than that by which heaven is separated from earth and east from west, than He is from them when the man is supported by divine grace.

Finally, while the monk was thinking—I do not know what way might be found of attaining the most abominable pleasure, horrible even to hear of—the devil, the sower of evil counsel, secretly insinuated the following plan into him through the vain thought of his heart:

In the dead of night, while everyone was asleep, he should remove his monastic clothing, put on secular dress, leave the monastery, and secretly approach his father’s dwelling. He should enter the house stealthily at nightfall and hide beneath his sister’s bed until she was asleep; then he should approach her and satisfy the lusts of his pleasure.

The ignorance of his insane mind approved the counsel that had been offered. He endeavored with all his power to put it into effect as quickly as possible.

When the middle of the following night arrived, he hurried silently to the doors of the monastery, holding the keys in his hands. But when he reached the entrances, he searched here and there throughout the entire night for the place where they had been put and could not find them.

Terrified by astonishment and amazement, and unable to understand why this was happening, he was compelled, as the hour approached when the monks kept vigil for the morning praises of the Lord, to return to his cell.

He remained in the cell, wondering, throughout that day. He proposed to do on the following night what he had not done. His feeble hand dared what it could not accomplish; the foolish beast hoped to gain the glory of triumph by fighting against the lion.

What do you think, senseless man? Do you suppose that a worthless beast can do what the most powerful lion, Jerome, opposes?

Cease bowing your knees before the image of glorious Jerome; cease honoring him any longer, and you will immediately be granted the power to fall into the pit you are digging and to suffer dreadful shipwrecks.

Services rendered to glorious Jerome can never, in whatever manner they are performed, be deprived of their reward.

That erring and wandering monk, enslaved to the devil’s dominion, kept in his cell an image of glorious Jerome painted on a panel. By ancient custom he bent his knees before it every day and repeatedly commended himself to him.

For this reason, so that Jerome’s remarkable mercy might become known to everyone, Jerome detained him on that day and prevented him from doing the evil he intended.

The monk, however, did not know this and went again to the monastery doors on the following night. But what had happened on the preceding night happened again on this one. Not to linger over the details, this continued to happen every night for almost a month.

When, as I think, the cycle of a month had been completed, blessed Jerome appeared in a dream by night to a certain most holy monk of that monastery as he rested in his bed. He revealed to him what this monk was doing and ordered him to explain to the erring monk how Jerome himself had guarded him because of the reverence shown to him, so that he could not see the doors and carry out the crime he had conceived.

He also ordered him to say that, unless the monk quickly corrected what he had begun, Jerome would withdraw his protection from him. Then he immediately departed.

When morning came, the monk told another monk what he had seen. But that monk, repeatedly protesting that he did not understand what this meant, began to say that the dream had occurred because of an emptiness in the monk’s brain.

The monk kept silent and withdrew.

The other monk, rejoicing, resolved that on the following night, showing Jerome no further customary reverence, he would open the monastery doors at will and carry out the wicked deed he had desired for so long.

To speak briefly: what the wretched man had long contemplated with eager desire—the power to perform his evil having been handed over to him by Jerome after he had been deprived of his customary honor [Col. 1149]—he accomplished as he wished. Yet in the end the mercy of glorious Jerome did not fail.

Leaving the monastery at night, concealed in another’s clothing, he came to his father’s house and spent the day moving around it secretly. When nightfall arrived, he entered the house and secretly approached the bed in which his virgin sister usually rested.

He hid beneath it for as long as he thought necessary to determine that his sister was asleep. Then he emerged, removed his clothing, and pressed himself against her right side.

His sister, sleeping lightly, awoke. Feeling a man beside her with her hand, she was exceedingly frightened and, uttering dreadful cries, summoned everyone to her.

Everyone ran with lights to the girl’s bedroom, and at last they found him lying in the bed. His parents were amazed and stunned; all who had run there saw what had happened and grieved.

The father asked his son the cause of so great a danger. The son confessed his guilt in silence.

As I have said, glorious Jerome wished the man to experience his own foolishness, so that afterward he might become more humble and prudent in taking precautions and defending himself in battle, and so that no one might thereafter trust or presume upon holiness because of his example.

For the greater the holiness present in a man while he sails in the stormy sea of this world, filled with armies of enemies, in the little boat of fragile flesh, the greater must be his fear and prudence in protecting himself.

That worst tempter, the devil, possesses countless arts of harming. The unwary man who proceeds is captured with the greatest ease. The one who fears in all things is feared here by all the devils.

Certainly nothing does more harm than to reject the counsel of others and walk according to one’s own will. Whoever trusts only his own will in everything he does will discover a hateful end.

Now that this great example has ended, a profound fear concerning our extreme fragility and the devil’s cunning and craft has been demonstrated to us all; but great hope of pardon for sinners has also been revealed.

When the monk saw that he had been cast down, deceived, and even held captive in such misery by the devil, he immediately sought the intercession of glorious Jerome, to whom he had always been devoted. Recognizing his misery and grave guilt with the utmost force, he returned to himself.

He left his father’s house and, abandoning every delay, hastened mourning and grieving to the fountain of repentance. Then, in his own monastery, he afflicted himself for two years with such severe abstinence that it would be beyond the capacity of a human heart to conceive it.

When the period of two years had been completed, he happily departed from this world only a few days ago.

## CHAPTER XXI

Having recently received letters from the venerable Damasus, bishop of Porto, I learned with eager attention certain things written in them. Out of reverence for him, I shall not omit them.

In Rome there was a certain cardinal named Caelestinus, a rival and detractor of glorious Jerome. One day, while he was present at a gathering of cardinals, he customarily burst forth with bold and reckless speech into words insulting Jerome.

Suddenly, driven by pain in his bowels, he hurried to the place reserved for nature. There all his entrails immediately poured out, and before he could leave that place, he died.

## CHAPTER XXII
Another cardinal presbyter, named Andreas, unlike the former but most devoted to and worshipful of the glorious Jerome, died on the preceding day in that same city of Rome, with many people standing around. When he was already in the church and the funeral rites had been prepared which are customarily performed for the bodies of the faithful to be buried, while the Supreme Pontiff stood by with almost the entire clergy and Roman people, who had gathered to honor the same Andreas, and while all were uttering wails and repeated groans, he suddenly rose from the bier in a miraculous manner, as though awakened from the sleep of slumber. All were astonished and rendered as if senseless. When he had been removed from the principal church of the blessed apostle Peter by the Roman Pontiff, and the entire people had been shut outside with the doors closed, he was questioned and spoke these words:

“While I stood to be judged at the divine tribunal, and was already being condemned to Tartarean torments because of the excessive abundance of the garments and foods I had used until then, someone suddenly arrived, brighter than the sun and whiter than snow. I understood—those standing by reported this to one another—that he was the glorious Jerome. Falling to his knees before the presiding judge, he obtained through his extended prayers that my soul be reunited to my body. When he had finished speaking these words, he withdrew from there in the blink of an eye, and my soul, as you see, has been joined to my body.”

At this the Supreme Pontiff and the others who heard him were astonished. These things became known to the people waiting outside the church; and when the church doors had been broken open, they immediately entered, all loudly praising God and the glorious Jerome.

## CHAPTER XXIII

Great distress of mind moves and saddens us when we learn that very many bishops, denying God and the Lord Jesus Christ, whose place they occupy, cling to the footsteps of earthly men “whose god is their belly.” From the stipends of the poor and the blood of Jesus Christ they fill the gluttony of their bellies with the most delicate dishes, together with actors and other rich men, to incite themselves to the filth of lust. They abuse clothing with ever-increasing excesses, and take no care for the poor, whose wages, snatched away by the hand of robbery, they devour, while the poor die of hunger and cold.

These men certainly ought to be called not bishops but devils. A bishop, however, is either most holy or diabolical. The episcopal office is certainly one of great dignity, but of infinite danger. The lightest sin, when charged against others, is charged against a bishop as the gravest. For the fault of a pontiff is spread among his subjects by example. The greater the things he receives, the greater his accountability grows. For however many of Christ’s sheep go astray into sins through the negligence or example of a bishop, for that many he must render an account to the Lord.

Alas! What shall I say, dearest Augustine? A heavy burden rests upon us, a heavy load. But since my shoulders are weak, what shall I carry? Certainly I am beset by anxieties that torment me on every side. And when I look upon the grave dangers ready for me, I am continually afflicted and saddened as the greatest fear increases.

It is safer to flee the episcopal office than to seek it. I certainly praise the episcopate as the vicariate of our Lord Jesus Christ; but I do not praise those who live in it as earthly soldiers, who seek the glory and pomp of the world. Rather, I advise them to flee it as far as they can. It would certainly have been better for them to live among earthly men as earthly men than, acting in this way at the summit of the pontificate, to descend to the lowest and deepest places, destined to be tormented more than others because they received more gifts than others.

For I understand that very many bishops bear the name rather than the reality; that they are ravenous wolves among Christ’s sheep rather than shepherds; destroyers of Christ’s Church rather than rulers. They plunder the alms of Christians and devour and consume the wages of the poor with wolfish jaws in the excesses of food and clothing. This is absurd, abominable, and lamentable.

I have said these things so that such an abomination may become known to all peoples, in order that, if they do not fear God, at least fear of men may hold them back somewhat from their abominations. Let such bishops hear, I beg, what we set forth in our account, and let them at least be terrified by the calamities of others.

## CHAPTER XXIV

In the upper regions of Egypt, in a certain desert uninhabitable by men because of the hardships of life, there lived a monk named Elias, very old and radiant with great holiness of life. While the most blessed Jerome was alive, Elias was very close to him; and the most blessed Jerome repeatedly related that he possessed the spirit of prophecy.

One day—as several monks, venerable for their lives and worthy of belief, testified to me, saying that they had often heard it from the mouth of that holy man—as he was occupied in his customary prayers, he fell into a brief sleep when sudden slumber overtook him. And behold, in a vision—by which means almighty God often reveals great and hidden mysteries to his faithful—he found himself, as it seemed to him, in a palace of wondrous beauty, ineffable and never seen by mortals.

As he walked through that palace for about an hour, admiring its extraordinary beauty here and there, he saw a tribunal being prepared by certain young men of surpassing beauty. Carpets and garments decorated with gold, gems, and a great variety of workmanship had been spread around, enclosing the wall.

Afterward a great and handsome king came, accompanied by a company of men brighter than the sun. His appearance possessed such sweetness that one who desires great things would wish for nothing else. He took his place to exercise judgment.

Meanwhile the soul of a certain man—whom Elias later understood from some who were present there to have been the bishop of Ancona—was brought before the royal majesty by an evil spirit, bound with chains and fiery bonds, bursting forth sulfurous flames like a furnace. Before it was questioned about anything, it began to proclaim in dreadful voices that it was entirely deserving of the dwellings of hell, assigning as the principal reason among others that it had been devoted to empty pomp and had delighted in banquets, clothing, and such foolishness.

When these words had been completed, the judge pronounced sentence that it should be handed over to infernal punishments to be tormented until, reunited with its body, it should endure double punishments forever. Immediately the whole crowd of evil spirits carried it away with them and departed from there with dreadful cries.

Then the soul of another man—whom Elias likewise understood to have been Theodonius the senator, brother of the aforementioned venerable Damasus, bishop of Porto—was presented before the royal majesty, with many evil spirits standing around and accusing it most severely.

While the devils prolonged their accusation and no one answered on the other side, a certain man seven times brighter than the sun, and, as it seemed to Elias, almost taller than the others standing there, rose to his feet while seated at the king’s right hand. When he rose, the king himself commanded silence from everyone with his hand.

Then the man who had stood, opposing all the accusers, declared that Theodonius had been most faithful and devoted to him and had continually shown him special reverence. At once he deprived them of the boldness to speak and imposed silence upon them.

Afterward he bent his knees before the king and obtained, by his customary piety and infinite mercy, that this most faithful servant be most mercifully granted pardon and eternal rest—yet in such a way that he would be purified in purgatory for the crimes committed in the world. Then the whole multitude of wicked spirits, groaning and howling, immediately withdrew from that place.

After an interval of one hour, a very handsome young man came swiftly through the palace. Approaching the one who had risen so eminent and glorious to help the senator Theodonius, he said that he had been sent by Peter, the Roman patrician most devoted to him, so that, hearing his prayers, he might deign to obtain a son for him from the Lord.

At this the king said: “What Peter asks of my son Jerome shall certainly be done.”

When all these things had been completed, the monk Elias immediately awoke from his sleep, rendering immense praises to God and to the glorious Jerome. Marking down the day on which he had seen such wonders, he later learned that on that very day the bishop of Ancona and the senator Theodonius had departed from this world. From this it is plainly evident that these were not empty dreams.

## CHAPTER XXV

You thought, dearest Augustine, that you would cause some people great astonishment, as though proposing something new and unheard-of to them, when in your earlier letters, which I received, you proved by unquestionably effective arguments and marvelous visions that the most holy Jerome was equal in holiness and glory to John the Baptist and the other Apostles.

Certainly there is no real ambiguity: these things are most true and entirely worthy of faith and devotion. Nor do I think that anyone who is not ignorant of his most holy life and of such extraordinary miracles performed by him among men would be astonished by them.

But since your arguments for declaring this truth were of such a kind that it would not be proper for me now to set my very slight and inexperienced arguments against them, I shall omit everything else and briefly introduce a marvelous vision which the venerable Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, affirmed in letters sent to me many days ago that he had seen.

After one full year had passed since the glorious death of the blessed Jerome, on the day of the birth of the most glorious John, the Lord’s precursor, after the morning praises had been completed, the pontiff mentioned above was, as usual, alone in the church before the altar of that glorious precursor of the Lord. Kneeling, he was contemplating his glory and excellence with great sweetness of spirit when he briefly fell asleep in a sudden slumber.

And behold, as it very clearly seemed to him, a vast multitude of exceedingly beautiful men entered the church in pairs, singing alternately with the sweetest chants, beyond human estimation, in wondrous order. Then, proceeding in pairs to the altar and kneeling there, they each took their places to sit.

When the church had become very full of these men, two men more eminent than the others, entirely alike and equal, infinitely brighter than the sun, entered the church together after all the rest. They were clothed in a most radiant and dazzlingly white stole, glittering everywhere ineffably with gold and gems.

At their entrance all those seated in the church immediately fell to their knees and paid them the highest reverence. Then, after the reverence had been shown to them before the altar, those two men sat down together in two golden chairs, marvelously and most beautifully decorated with a variety of precious stones and prepared for them by certain very handsome young men. They remained silent for a little while.

Meanwhile, after silence had arisen among them, one of the two began urging the other to speak. When a long dispute arose between them about which should begin preaching first, all began to cry out loudly that Jerome should expound the praises and magnificence of John, whose solemnity it was that day.

Then one of them immediately began his speech. He composed praises of the most blessed precursor of the Lord with such sweetness of speech, such adornment of words, and such profundity of meaning that it would not be possible for human language to express them.

When that speech was finished, the other—whom all who were present called John the Baptist—gave him repeated thanks and spoke the following words in his honor and glory:

“My dearest companion Jerome, equal to me in glory and also equal in holiness, has thus far pursued the sequence of my praises. Therefore it is fitting that I now devote myself to his praises.

“He truly is the light of the Church, driving away the darkness of errors and illuminating all blind men with the brightness of truth. He is the fountain of the water of saving wisdom, at which the thirsty, when they approach, are most abundantly satisfied.

“He is the tallest tree, whose crown rises to heaven; beneath the foliage of his teaching, from the sweet fruit of his mouth, the birds of heaven—that is, men of great understanding—and the beasts of the earth—that is, men of little understanding—are richly nourished.

“He was an ascetic with me in the world, and certainly no less than I macerated his flesh with abstinences. He was a shining and pure virgin with me. He was enlightened with me by the prophetic spirit. He was a teacher of truth with me.

“I left bodily life for the sake of justice and truth. Although he did not likewise lose his bodily life for the truth of his justice and most perceptive teaching, he nevertheless spent his entire time in the world amid martyrdom, afflictions, and pain.

“I was the messenger who went before the Christian faith and invited the nations; he, coming afterward, became the supporter of that same faith and its defender against the heretics who tore it apart.

“I touched Christ once with my own hands in baptism in the Jordan. He not only held him many times with his own hands at the altar, but also ate him with his own mouth.

“In holiness he was altogether equal to me. Now both of us rejoice together in the equal reward of eternal life.”

As the blessed John continued with these and many other words—which the same blessed Cyril was unable to commit entirely to memory—the first hour of the day had already arrived. The church’s custodian entered and, seeing the bishop asleep, woke him with his hands.

The pontiff awoke greatly filled with astonishment, wonder, and joy, and recounted with tears to the custodian what he had seen. Then, celebrating Mass most solemnly that day, he declared the marvelous vision to all the people.

## CHAPTER XXVI

There are infinitely more true and useful miracles that could be recounted than those written in this brief work. But so that the length of the work may not produce any weariness in its readers, one single miracle, performed at Bethlehem less than a month ago, will bring this work to its proper conclusion.

On the Sunday after the octave of Pentecost, when all my suffragan bishops and a very great multitude of men and women had gathered together in the church where the most sacred body of Jerome rests, with due honor and equally due and devout veneration, I myself, first putting on the sacred vestments, approached the place of the pit in which the venerable body lay. I began to excavate the earth of the burial place so that, after that most sacred body had been removed, it might afterward be placed in a marble tomb, decorated on every side with wondrous beauty, which had been constructed for this purpose.

When the pit had already been emptied, the most holy body remained intact in the middle of the pit, as though suspended in the air and touching the earth nowhere, as everyone watched; it had not been violated by any corruption.

Lifting it from there amid such a powerful and sweet fragrance as the human sense of smell had never experienced, we placed it upon the altar so that the people might see the most holy relics.

I would in no way be able to explain how many glorious miracles were performed that day while I and all who were present stood by. Sixteen blind people touched those relics with their faces and immediately recovered their sight.

Three men especially, possessed by demons and bound with chains, who had been carried into that church by the hands of many people, were immediately freed.

A poor little widow’s young child, her only son, was suffocated in the church by the crowd of people. When the mother found him dead, grieving and mourning, she immediately carried the child’s corpse in her arms to the pit in which the body of the glorious Jerome had been buried, threw him into the pit, and spoke these words:

“Glorious Saint Jerome, I shall not leave this place until you restore to me my only son, whom I have lost.”

Truly God is wondrous in his saints, performing extraordinary miracles. As soon as the earth touched the body of the dead child, his soul was reunited to him.

A certain man removed the body of one of his sons from the burial place in which it had lain for three days, immediately brought it to that pit, and threw it into the pit. The young man was at once restored to his former life.

There would be almost countless miracles to recount, performed from morning until evening, during which time the glorious corpse of Jerome, disinterred from the pit, remained placed upon the altar. But I shall not proceed further with miracles of this sort. I shall not remain silent about one that occurred on the following night.

## CHAPTER XXVII

Accordingly, in the evening hour we placed that most sacred body in the monument that we had prepared. But in the morning the monument was found empty, and we found the most holy body restored to its former pit.

When I was greatly astonished by this, the blessed Jerome appeared to me in a vision on the following night while I slept and revealed many great things to me. Among them he spoke these words to me:

“Know, Cyril, that my body will in no way be removed from the pit in which it lies until the city of Jerusalem is captured by the unbelievers. At that time it will be carried to Rome, where it will rest for a long period.”

After this I awoke and recounted to all the bishops and other Catholic men what I had seen. I do not otherwise know what these things mean or when they will occur.

If I have said anything useful or good in this letter, let it be attributed not to my merits but to those of the most glorious Jerome. But if anything superfluous, useless, or not good has been said, let everyone judge that this happened solely because of my foolishness and negligence.

Remember me, dearest Augustine, in your prayers.

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING DISPUTATION

In earlier editions this spurious Disputation occupied the place of Letter 178, although the work itself betrays its nature through both certain and manifest indications.

Augustine does indeed relate in the letter that is now numbered 238 that he debated the faith face-to-face with Pascentius. Yet in that dispute he could not obtain from his opponent that notaries record what was said. The proceedings of this Disputation, however, are reported as though everything had been taken down word for word by notaries.

That dispute was held at Carthage, according to Possidius, chapter 17; this one is prefaced in its title as having been conducted at Hippo. A certain judge named Laurentius is falsely represented as presiding over it. At the beginning, Laurentius indicates that some violent altercation had previously occurred between the parties. But in that Carthaginian dispute no judge presided; only several honored men were present, destined to be witnesses of what happened. Nor had Augustine held any conversation with Pascentius before that day, as is understood from the same Letter 238, section 8.

It therefore remains to say that this is another Disputation held later. Yet Possidius recognizes only one conference with Pascentius. He recorded its outcome, as well as the letters subsequently written back and forth on that occasion, with the greatest care. He would certainly not have passed over in silence a second and more solemn conference before a judge, had it been known to him—especially one in which the judge pronounced a decision in Augustine’s favor.

Moreover, this conference is not mentioned in the books of the *Revisions*, although Augustine elsewhere reviews whatever conferences had been left in writing. Nor can it be doubted that he published the *Revisions* somewhat after the time when, as is said here and in Letter 238, section 1, he regarded Pascentius as his superior by reason of age and dignity.

Furthermore, when you read through the proceedings of this Disputation, you might initially think that several days had elapsed between the first encounter and this second one. For what you read here as spoken by Laurentius—“if, after all that one party previously hurled against the other, person against person, insult,” and so forth—you would undoubtedly refer to what is recounted of the first encounter in Letter 238.

Certainly some intervening period must be admitted between the two encounters, during which both parties would have traveled from Carthage to Hippo and would have sent each other the letters that clearly were written before the later encounter.

Yet Pascentius is immediately introduced as speaking about the earlier encounter as though it had taken place the day before:

“And since yesterday,” he says, “when I commendably named the holy man Auxentius, a man of marvelous knowledge, and when brother Augustine was investigating more scrupulously which of the two that man had followed, Arius or Eunomius, I did not hesitate immediately to pronounce an anathema upon the aforesaid Arius and Eunomius, demanding that he too anathematize *homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον, ‘of the same substance’), because it is not found written in the Lord’s books,” and so forth.

This had in fact occurred in the first conference, according to Letter 238, section 4, except that it was not Augustine himself but Alypius who asked about Auxentius. Nor, we think, will anyone suppose that this happened again on the day immediately preceding the second Disputation.

For who could persuade himself that Pascentius raised the same complaint against *homoousion* a second time, and descended into a formal contest before Laurentius as presiding judge in order to advance once again, and for a third time, the single point that the word was not found written in the Lord’s books—after Augustine had so excellently refuted him in the first contest concerning the word *ingenitus* (“unbegotten”), which Pascentius had used of God the Father, as Letter 238 relates?

Furthermore, the matter is handled here very coldly by both sides, so that they scarcely answer one another except when Laurentius intervenes and presses them. And indeed this pseudo-Pascentius does not represent the Arian companion described by Possidius, who violently and continually attacked the Catholic faith and harassed and disturbed very many priests of God living according to a simpler faith with his insolence and influence; finally, after the first conference, becoming increasingly angry and raging, he uttered many falsehoods on behalf of his false faith.

Nor does the other man play Augustine’s role more successfully. He produces a few things opportunely, many things without learning, and everything in a confused and undigested manner; he shows none of that ability in disputation by which Augustine used to excel in other debates.

If we now turn our attention to the diction, it is very far from Augustine’s style, as can immediately be seen in such expressions as these:

“O most noble man of faith presiding.”

“Clothed around with the robe of true flesh.”

“That truthful interpreter of divine secrets, John.”

“As though they did not perceive the beam’s enormity.”

“Where the Lord’s flesh itself wished to be born from the Virgin.”

“By which he declares and intimates God’s secrets to mortals.”

What more is there to say? All the characters have the same manner of speech, one mode of expression throughout the entire Disputation; evidently one hand and one style composed it.

It is also surprising that the words found in Letter 238, section 9—“For the faith which you owe to the Republic, you do not fear the curses of provincials; for the faith which you owe to Christ, you fear the slanders of bishops”—were transferred here in this fashion, as though Augustine had said:

“Pascentius, owing loyalty to the Republic, may he also deign to state the name of the faith which he owes to Christ.”

What could be less appropriate to the matter? Moreover, the same source, the letter, supplied what is added immediately afterward concerning Pascentius’s authority and age, along with several other details.

Finally, it must by no means be passed over in silence that Augustine’s letters to Pascentius are contained in sixteen of our manuscripts, yet not one of those codices includes the appended Disputation. We were able to find it separately only in three manuscripts, namely those of Laon, Arnulf, and Corbie, all of which lack the aforementioned letters.

Since this is so, learned reader, you now understand that we were led by many serious reasons to count this kind of little work among spurious writings.

Finally, there is also a substantial conjecture concerning its true author, Vigilius, bishop of Thapsus. When the Vandals were spreading the Arian heresy in Africa, and it was not permitted him to oppose them openly by disputing on behalf of the Catholic faith, he released among the public certain works against the Arians under the names of distinguished doctors of the Church—Athanasius, Ambrose, and Augustine. Among these was a book against Felicianus falsely attributed to Augustine in earlier editions, volume VI, as well as this very Disputation under consideration, as we suspect from the similarity and affinity between it and Vigilius’s other works.

For example, just as in the *Disputation of Athanasius with Arius* he presents Probus as assessor and judge, initially helping Arius’s party but finally pronouncing judgment in favor of Athanasius, so here, in sections 5 and 7, Laurentius the assessor and judge shows some favor toward Pascentius, to such an extent that the pseudo-Augustine threatens the same judge with divine judgment. In the end Laurentius awards the palm of the contest to the pseudo-Augustine.

In that work Arius presents his arguments briefly, so that Athanasius may refute them at length. In this one Pascentius scarcely says anything except what provides material for the pseudo-Augustine to dispute.

Moreover, parallel expressions occur in both Disputations. In the former Probus says:

“Mark clearly, he says, by a suitable presentation what you believe.”

And somewhat later:

“Let Athanasius likewise indicate this in his presentation.”

But here Laurentius, section 5, says:

“Do you perceive . . . what he indicates in his presentation?” and so forth.

Thus the method, style, and arguments point to one and the same author, Vigilius. He wrote toward the end of the fifth century.

It is therefore not at all surprising that the Disputation with Pascentius should have been cited under Augustine’s name by earlier writers. It is cited not only in Bede’s familiar collection on 1 Corinthians 16 and Philippians 2—a collection that has been shown in volume I of the *Veterum Analecta* to belong to Florus, deacon of Lyons, who flourished in the middle of the ninth century—but also in the work attributed there to Bede, hitherto unpublished, namely the collection on 1 Corinthians 16.

Consult Bernard Vinding, a theologian of the Augustinian family, who before us judged this work to be spurious in the *Augustinianus Criticus* on volumes II and VI. In the latter place he lists fifteen little works that, in his opinion, proceeded from one and the same author. Most of these are now attributed by scholars to Vigilius of Thapsus.

## LETTER XX  
[Note: Letter 178 in other numbering.]

Or, as the Corbie manuscript and other manuscripts title it:

**The Conference of Blessed Augustine with Pascentius the Arian, held in the house of Anicius at Hippo Regius, in the presence of Laurentius, a judge chosen by Pascentius, a man of distinction.**

(C, G, S)

### 1

Laurentius, a man of the highest distinction, said, after the parties and persons had been brought into close proximity:

“The matter of God must be examined, and the perfection of his nature, in which most men fall into error, must be investigated. After all that one party previously inflicted upon the other, person upon person, in the way of insult, if tranquility of mind now remains in both of you, venerable Augustine and most noble Pascentius, deign to declare it.

“For a mind disputing about God ought to be found more serene, because, when the darkness of hostility has been driven away, God more readily offers himself to the pure mind for understanding the greatness of his nature.

“I therefore wish first to recognize your faith from your professions of belief, and then to inquire whether, besides the words of the divine Scriptures, it is permissible, by the legitimate necessity of defending a position, to affirm anything.”

### 2

Bishop Augustine said:

“There are certain things necessary to the faith that were established by the Fathers, which sound differently in the words of different languages while inwardly containing another meaning in secret. Thus the very flesh of Christ, God and man, outwardly displayed the weakness of complete humanity, while inwardly bearing the power of divinity.

“Since, however, Pascentius, a man of distinction, owes a faith to the Republic and was himself the challenger, may he also, on account of the faith he owes to Christ—that is, concerning the person of Christ [Note: The editions omit the words ‘that is, concerning the person of Christ’; they were restored from the Corbie manuscript]—by which he believes that his own soul is governed, deign to state his name. The order of his authority, age, and challenge most justly demands this.

“For my part, I am pleased that you preside as judge in this proceeding, and it is most clearly evident that this too has pleased him.”

### 3

Laurentius, a man of the highest distinction, said:

“It is sufficiently clear that, owing to your excellence, most noble Pascentius, we have obeyed you to a very great extent. For I preside as assessor, trembling in the matter of so great a concern and fearing that I might incur guilt by believing something otherwise concerning the nature of such omnipotence.

“I remember that I bound my mind and soul by a solemn oath not to feel out your intentions by any means [Note: Bad., Am., and Er. read: ‘and not to restrain your intentions . . . by any means.’ The manuscripts of Arnulf and Corbie likewise read this way; those two codices continue: ‘Nor to restrain them by anything far removed from justice.’], nor to restrain anything that is farther from justice.

“Because of your election, I appear to preside as judge in the examination of the faith between the two parties. Therefore, since the request of the party standing opposite, for whom the most serious man Augustine has shown that he will provide words of defense, is not without reason, deign to put it into effect, and at the same time state the name of your own religion.”

### 4

Pascentius, a man of distinction [Note: Here and throughout the Disputation, the editions read ‘Pascentius, a man of the highest distinction.’ The manuscripts consistently have ‘a man of distinction.’], said:

“Nor can the most prudent bishop Augustine, who is present, deny that I am a Christian. I profess that I believe in the Father unbegotten, in the Son begotten, and in the Holy Spirit; but not in one and equal substance or nature.

“And since yesterday, when I commendably named the holy man Auxentius, a man of marvelous knowledge, and when brother Augustine was investigating more scrupulously which of the two that man had followed, Arius or Eunomius, I did not hesitate immediately to pronounce an anathema upon the aforementioned Arius and Eunomius, demanding that he too anathematize *homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον, ‘of the same substance’), because it is not found written in the Lord’s books.

“He altogether refused to do this [Note: The manuscripts read ‘conceded’], and thus clearly revealed himself as a *homoousian*. You yourself plainly perceive how serious it is, trampling upon the authority of the Scriptures, to establish something that the same Scripture has not said. For if anything is established apart from the authority of the divine Books, it is judged to be empty.”

### 5

Laurentius, a man of the highest distinction, said:

“Do you perceive, honorable Augustine, what he indicates in his presentation, or with what complete manner of presentation the distinguished Pascentius confirms his opinion?”

### 6

Bishop Augustine said:

“I answer in this presentation as a Catholic believer in *homoousion* within the Holy Trinity. Let the response of the same distinguished Pascentius be upheld, provided that none of us ought or dares, in defending the faith, to apply or name anything except what has been written.

“For either it will be permissible, and it will be denied to no one—especially not to the Greeks, among whom the faith arose—or it will not be permissible, and the slander will most justly be rejected.

“Afterward, however, the Greek word *homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον), which indicates unity, will be explained: what it contains, what it possesses, and what remains.”

### 7

Laurentius, a man of the highest distinction, said:

“Augustine, an honorable man, has also answered most correctly. Either, as he himself has presented the matter, it is permissible to establish something unwritten for the legitimate purpose of defending the faith, and it must therefore be established lawfully; or it is not permissible, and both possibilities must be entirely and absolutely rejected.

“Therefore, once the term that expresses the profession has been recognized, there is no need to inquire further—unless venerable Augustine, the bishop of his religion, shows us the word *homoousion* itself written in the Law.”

### 8

Bishop Augustine replied:

“Since you hold the perfectly straight line of justice, O most noble man of faith who presides, acknowledge the matter and weigh the reason. For not only will other very wise men judge according to your judgment, but the truest God, who is the judge of all judges, will judge it more fully.

“For the judgment of God, who is different [from human judges], must not be scorned; sometimes even in the present life a judge rises as an avenger.

“Therefore deign now to investigate the reasoning of our faith, and command each of us to recite before all, into your ears, the creed by which faith is in some manner established [Note: The Corbie manuscript, corrected by a second hand, reads: ‘the faith of both parties.’].”

### 9

Laurentius, a man of the highest distinction, said:

“Since this in no way departs from justice, deign, Pascentius, most distinguished man, as the petitioner, to recite with reverence the creed of your faith.”

### 10

Then Pascentius recited the creed in a clearer voice, saying that he believed in God the Father almighty, invisible, unbegotten, and incapable of suffering, and in Jesus Christ, his Son, God born before the ages, through whom all things were made, and in the Holy Spirit.

### 11

Bishop Augustine replied:

“I do not doubt, presiding assessor, that your high dignity remembers our presentation in the matter of God, because the distinguished Pascentius asserted that nothing should be established in the reasoning of the faith except what the Scriptures contain.

“Although, following his authorities, he strives to oppose the word *homoousion* of the Catholic faith as a stain upon the name, we rightly defend from what he established—or rather prohibited—that the word *homoousion*, established by the Greek priests, ought all the more to be spoken in the assertion of the faith. We now approve that certain things unwritten were rashly established or spoken by them instead.”

12. The most distinguished Laurentius said: “As I see it, the honorable Augustine is hastily declaring that he has obtained the conclusion of the present case, and, asserting that he will prove it, is maintaining that the authors of the faith you follow, most distinguished Pascentius, have placed in it certain things that are not written. If he proves that these were not set down in the Law, but were rightly inserted by you through your own assumption of authority in matters of faith, it will now be necessary to ask—since it will by then be clear that this is permitted—what the word *ὁμοούσιον* contains in its depths, what it concerns, and to what matter this word is rightly judged applicable; and the very completeness of the faith will justly confirm whether it was properly discovered or inserted.”

13. The eminent Pascentius said: “It is not fitting for us to insert anything without the authority of the divine Scriptures. Yet, setting aside the artifice of calumny, what is it that our brother Augustine says or proposes while defending the opposite position? Let him publicly declare what, without the authority of the Law, he claims that we have inserted or said anywhere. And if he proves it, I too shall publicly proclaim that *ὁμοούσιον* was not unjustly inserted by them, and I shall immediately become a partner in their communion.”

14. The most distinguished Laurentius said: “Nothing is so good, nor so consonant with liberty, faith, and the soul, as to abandon promptly the long evasion which folly has been able to nourish, to repel the stubborn cloud of hostility by which injury is done to God, and to disclose in clearer light what is hidden in various tongues. But lest prolonged speech draw out a case whose victory has now nearly been accomplished, you, most distinguished Augustine, should deign to publish what you deny was inserted without the authority of the Law by the most distinguished Pascentius or by his authors.”

15. Bishop Augustine replied: “In his confession of faith he called the Father ‘unbegotten’ and ‘incapable’ (*ingenitum et incapabilem*), although Scripture nowhere testifies that the Father is either unbegotten or incapable. Although the Father is unbegotten—for this very point we both equally confess—nevertheless no text of either the Old or the New Scripture contains it. He is unbegotten because he was begotten by no one; but this is what ‘unbegotten begotten’ means, namely, God from God.

“For Adam is not a man simply because he is acknowledged to be unbegotten, nor is Abel not a man because he was begotten from him. [Note: [Col. 1158] Thus the manuscripts. But the editions read: “He who is begotten by no one; but that which is begotten is unbegotten.” Less well.] The unbegotten man begot a man; God, being what he is, begot one of the same substance and the same essence, begotten without time and coeternal with himself. Before him there is nothing, and he does not receive the measure of time. The Father, then, is unbegotten because, as has been said, he was begotten by no one; but he is coeternal with the begotten one. Thus fire, in its substance—in which it was created by the Creator—is indeed unbegotten, but the radiance begotten from it is consubstantial and coeternal with it.

“The Greeks preferred briefly to embrace this substance of the divine Trinity in the single word *ὁμοούσιον*. For this is not merely a name, but a fearful reality sounding forth in such a word. The Son himself openly declares what the word means when he says: ‘I and the Father are one’ (John 10:30). In this ‘one’ there subsists one substance; for, because it is one, both he himself and the Son remain in it. Hence, also clothed about with the robe of true flesh, he says: ‘No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him’ (Matthew 11:27).

“Behold, the Son too is shown to be invisible in himself. What, then, is the meaning of what they try to insert into the confession of faith as though with greater caution—‘incapable’? They neither read this nor defend it rightly. For how is the Father incapable, when the Son contains him wholly, the Son himself saying: ‘I am in the Father, and the Father is in me’ (John 14:10)? Of this the apostle Paul also says: ‘Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized’ (Philippians 2:6). Whoever fulfills the form of God possesses nothing less than God. How, then, is the Father called incapable, when he is wholly contained by the Son?

“Behold, you rashly insert into the creed things nowhere written in the Law, where nothing ought to be inserted otherwise than as the manner of truthful Scripture contains it. Why have you thought fit to stir up hostility against the Catholic faith on account of the word *ὁμοούσιον*, when, by simply believing that God has one substance, it received this word from the Greek fathers as something to be defended in the confession of faith? In the pledge—that is, in the creed which stands between our souls and God—what moved certain men to insert things not found written in the Law? For nowhere is the Father called either unbegotten or incapable.

“When we praise God, we customarily say in our prayers, admiring his greatness: ‘He who contains all things, whom no one contains’—but this refers to human beings. For the Son wholly contains him whose form he fulfills, in the secret of one unchangeable nature. Therefore, it is not the Father alone who is invisible; the Son too is invisible. [Note: [Col. 1159] Bad., Am., Er., and the Corbie manuscript read: “in which he remains.”] As the Father is invisible to human beings, so the Son is invisible to human beings according to that hidden reality in which he remains in the Father. Thus it was not rightly inserted into the creed that the Father alone is invisible, but that the whole Trinity, God, is invisible—except for the flesh assumed by the Son—of whom the Apostle says: ‘To the invisible God alone be honor and glory for ever and ever’ (1 Timothy 1:17).

“The Father therefore dwells wholly in the Son, whose form the same Son fulfills not partially but completely. Some, wrongly pronouncing and wrongly understanding the apostle Paul’s statement—which reveals and communicates God’s secrets to mortals, ‘Although he was in the form of God’—affirm that the Son did not dare to be equal through equality, but became equal to God the Father by seizure. This is an unjust interpretation. For if he had said, ‘Although he was God, he did not regard being equal to God as a seizure,’ anyone might have found, within the narrow confines of his faith, some sort of weak opening from which he could at once be excluded. But because he said, ‘Although he was in the form of God,’ he closed every avenue of unjust contrivance. Where there is the form, nature possesses absolutely nothing less.

“For the same Apostle says: ‘God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself’ (2 Corinthians 5:19). How could the lesser receive the greater, unless it recognized itself as equal in one nature? For this form of God is not extended by bodily outlines and spaces of limbs, as though the Father received the Son dwelling in him, or the Son displayed the Father remaining in him, as he himself says: ‘The Father, remaining in me, performs my works’ (John 14:10). Nor is it emptied when the Father and the Son bring forth their Holy Spirit, enlightening all their creation.

“How can it not be conceived, how can it not be explained, that what is one with itself, according to the wholly unchangeable substance which is God in the Trinity, cannot be conceived or explained? [Note: [Col. 1159] Lov.: “to be one.” But the other editions and the Corbie manuscript: “is one.”]

“Behold what *ὁμοούσιον* means, the word unjustly reproached. It is not merely a word, but the reality within the word; not merely speech sounding in the ears, but one substance of God to be believed in the mind. If the whole God is to be believed to dwell in a human being who believes in him, how can the Father not be believed to receive the whole Son into himself, or the Son the Father? Accordingly, he himself remains in the Father, and the Father in him; and the Holy Spirit must be believed to have proceeded not only from the Father and the Son [Note: [Col. 1160] Corbie manuscript: “or the Son.”] but always to proceed from them for the accomplishment of the works of the Trinity, just as the same Trinity deigned to visit its friend Abraham in the unity of its name (Genesis 18:1).

“What is the reason for their calumnies concerning the Greek word *ὁμοούσιον*, because it is not found written in the Law? Why do they not see their own fault? Why are they not displeased with themselves, when they insert into the creed words or names which are not set forth anywhere in Scripture? Whoever intends to accuse should not do what he seeks to accuse another of doing. They look at a simple word full of the meaning of faith as though at a speck in their brother’s eye, while, by inserting beyond Scripture what they believe, they fail to see their own wounded eye as though it were a massive beam.

“Behold, we rightly approve *ὁμοούσιον* as inserted and spoken by the Greek fathers in the confession of faith by which Catholics believe the unity of the Trinity. What if a Greek himself should object that it is more permissible for him—not for a Latin or a barbarian, but for himself—to disseminate words pertaining to the faith? For it must be understood that *Amen* and *alleluia*, which neither a Latin nor a barbarian is permitted to translate into his own language, are sung by all nations in a Hebrew word.

“For it was not in Africa or throughout all Barbaria, but in Syria or Greece—where the Lord’s very flesh chose to be born of a virgin—that it was fitting or necessary to establish the words of the faith in concise form. Finally, that venerable Moses, the Prophets, the Apostles, and the Evangelists themselves established the divine Scriptures not in Latin or barbarian style, but in Hebrew or Greek speech; and afterward approved and eloquent men, highly skilled in every language, laboriously rendered them first from Hebrew into Greek and from Greek into Latin.

“*Ὁμοούσιος*, therefore, is explained as ‘the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit of one substance.’ Let no one, then, bring a calumny against the word because, although what it contains inwardly or expresses is not written, it reveals that reality—not through some other substance, but through the one substance [Note: [Col. 1160] Elsewhere: “of one substance.”] of divinity in which the Son says to the Father: ‘All that is mine is yours, and what is yours is mine’ (John 17:10).

“Let them now consider for themselves how they dared to arrange in the creed names or words not written in the Law, desiring only to demonstrate that the Son is separated from the power of the Father as unbegotten and incapable. For God the Father begot from his own substance a Son equal to himself. That truthful interpreter of divine secrets, John, teaches this. ‘For this reason,’ he says, ‘the Jews sought to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God’ (John 5:18).

“The Father therefore begot a Son consubstantial with himself, because he did not receive, as a needy creature, something from which he might beget; in the fullness of what he himself is, he begot what he is. He begot him perfect, because the one who begot and the one begotten exist without time. If a human being begets what he is, could God not beget what he is? A human being received from God himself, and yet, although he received, he begets what he received. Could God the Father, receiving from no one, not beget what he is?

“The Greek expression *ὁμοουγία* reveals this equality of substance—nothing harsh, but something excellent and sweet—and introduces it into human hearts as something to be believed. Although the word itself is not found written in the Law, the reality itself is found there, because the Son’s equality with the Father is first confirmed through blessed John and afterward through Paul: John stated the equality; Paul fulfilled the form.

“For Scripture says: ‘On the testimony of two or three witnesses every word shall stand’ (Deuteronomy 17:6; Matthew 18:16). Through two most truthful witnesses we have already proved that the Father and the Son are of one substance and equal. Let us add a third: that disciple Thomas, who, after doubting, confessed the Lord and God more firmly—the one whom he had not believed to have risen after being crucified: ‘My Lord,’ he said, ‘and my God’ (John 20:28). The Son approves the statement because he knows that his creature has most justly proclaimed him God and Lord. He is coeternal with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

“*Ὁμοούσιον* is indeed a Greek word, and Christ is a Greek name. Whoever unjustly attacks the faith on account of a word he does not understand should not accept a name on account of its language. In Greek, the word *ὁμοούσιον* signifies one and the same substance—not some weak being, but the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

“Let no one, then, disapprove of it as though it were merely a Greek word; rather, let whoever can—and no one can—openly separate the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit from *ὁμοούσιον*. Let the dispute be directed against what the Greek word possesses, contains, and teaches, not against the word itself, which resounds in the ears articulated in syllables [Note: [Col. 1161] Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions read: “retained.”]; let the dispute be directed against the riches and equality of nature that the Greek word itself possesses, not against its outward shell, as though one who claims to dare this could prevail.

“Far be it from us Catholics, who remain throughout the world, to be ashamed that, on account of the true faith in one and the same substance, some who do not understand the Greek word call us *Homousians*, since we rejoice to be called Christians from the Greek name of Christ. The Greek word must not be accepted in one part and rejected in another. Let no one use Christ’s name because it is a Greek term; let him be ashamed to be called a Christian because the name is Greek.

“Nor should Paul be accepted, who, writing to the Romans, says: ‘In which we cry, Abba, Father’ (Romans 8:15), for in one name he uses two languages. He says *Abba*, calling “Father” by a Greek term, and again names the Father in Latin. [Note: [Col. 1161] Far be it thought that Augustine possessed such ignorance.] Let that same Apostle Paul be despised in the final part of his First Epistle to the Corinthians, where, reproving the people, he uses both a Greek and a Syrian word: ‘If anyone does not love the Lord, let him be accursed: Maranatha’ (1 Corinthians 16:22). In Greek speech he said *anathema*, ‘condemned’; he defined *maranatha* as ‘until the Lord returns.’

“Let no one, then, call the oil with which the faithful are anointed by the Greek name *chrisma*, while *ὁμοούσιον*, which expresses the one and the same nature of the Trinity, is rejected. For what else did the most blessed Paul mean when he said, ‘If anyone does not love the Lord,’ except ‘If anyone humiliates God’? [Note: [Col. 1161] Corbie manuscript: “is humbled before God.” Bad., Am., and Er.: “humbles himself before God.”]

“Therefore the one who dares to separate the one substance of God and Lord does not rightly claim to love the Lord, of whom it is said in the Law: ‘Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God’ (Deuteronomy 6:4). The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not extended as a body with bodily outlines, but are perfect in one divinity.

“Many things defined by Greek words are indeed found in the Law; but I believe these few examples suffice for the wise. If there were no equality, the inferior would not dare say to the superior: ‘All that is mine is yours, and what is yours is mine.’ Nor would he dare say: ‘I desire that where I am, they too may be with me’ (John 17:10, 24). He would not, I say, say ‘I desire,’ but, as one petitioning, ‘I ask.’

“It is therefore not absurd that in the councils of the fathers the one substance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit was affirmed by a Greek word, since, first of all, a diversity of tongues was poured out upon the Apostles by the Holy Spirit’s own generosity. For we read in the Acts of the Apostles: ‘We hear them speaking in our own languages the mighty works of God’ (Acts 2:11). The mighty works are surely not those of gods, but of God: that the one substance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit be believed in the Greek language.

“Thus the charge against the Lord was written by Pilate in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin above the Lord’s cross (Luke 23:38). If it was permitted—or rather, if the Lord himself allowed—the charge of his death to be written in Greek, why should it be abhorrent that the substance in which he is God, equal with the Father, should be approved and displayed by a Greek term?

“If it is altogether impermissible to express in the Greek language the one substance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, then neither should it be fitting for God to be praised in barbarian speech. For just as in Greek the word *ὁμοούσιον* signifies, or is believed by the faithful to signify, the one substance of the Trinity, so the one nature of the one God is asked by all Latins and barbarians to have mercy, so that even the barbarian tongue may in no way be alien from the praises of the one God.

“For in Latin it is said: ‘Lord, have mercy.’ Should this one mercy, then, be requested from the one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit only in Hebrew or Greek, or finally in Latin, but not in barbarian speech? If it is permitted to say—not only to barbarians in their own tongue but also to Romans—*Sihora armen*, which means ‘Lord, have mercy,’ why should it not be permitted in the councils of the fathers, in the very land of the Greeks from which the faith was sent everywhere, to confess in their own language *ὁμοούσιον*, namely, the one substance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit?

“[Note: Manuscript Arnulf has *Shroia armen*. The Corbie manuscript has *Kuroia armes*, with *Kuroi eleimen* written in the margin. Finally, an old manuscript seen by Nicolaus Rigaltius offers *Rhroti armes*. Consult the Glossary published by C. du Fresne and D. du Cange, where he observes that Stephanus Stephanius, in his notes on Saxo Grammaticus, p. 219, seems to think that the reading should be *Hething forbarme* (“Lord, have mercy”), in the Gothic language, which is here called barbarian. The Corbie marginal reading *Kuroi eleimen* likewise means “Lord, have mercy.” For Erasmus noted on this passage that this language was learned after the capture of Rome.]

“We also most truly confess that the Son’s subordination to the Father was assumed from the weakness of the flesh; in this weakness, because it is just, we confess him not only as subject but most clearly as a servant, since he himself says in prophecy to the Father: ‘O Lord, I am your servant; I am your servant and the son of your handmaid’ (Psalm 115:16). It is therefore evident in what respect the Son is equal to the Father, and in what respect he is not only subject or inferior but also the most humble servant. He himself, I say, shows in what respect he is humble, in what respect equal; whence he is almighty, whence weak, whence despised, whence beautiful, whence rich, and whence subject to poverty.”

16. The most distinguished Laurentius said: “It has become entirely clear that the most distinguished Augustine has fortified the affirmations of his faith by a correct defense, and that your authors, most distinguished Pascentius, have inserted many more things rashly and without Scripture; and that *ὁμοούσιον* is not the name of the faith, but rather the equality of the Trinity itself. But if the words that have been rejected are found in the Law, deign, most noble sir, to answer, so that you may certainly be able to proceed on equal terms. For without doubt you see that the present Augustine goes far beyond the assertions put forward by you. In your presence, most noble sir, I choose rather to incur the guilt of an enduring charge before God.”

17. The eminent Pascentius replied: “The writings I put forward are indeed not in the Law; but they are rightly defended as things that ought to be asserted for the honor of the Father.”

18. The most distinguished Laurentius said: “Then likewise, although *ὁμοούσιον*, which you proposed as a matter of doubt, is not written, the reality hidden in the word is nevertheless true. Let unity be believed in honor, lest injury be rashly done to the Trinity.”

## Notice

In a very ancient manuscript of the Abbey of Saint Peter at Chartres there survives a letter of Saint Augustine to Saint Bibianus, bishop of the city of Saintes, under this salutation:

“To the truly holy Bibianus, adorned with the palm of triumph and crowned with pontifical office, orthodox; Augustine, servant of the servants of God: greetings in the Lord.”

It begins as follows: “I have learned that you wrote to us through your deacon, our most beloved son Trojanus, concerning the letter of your Apostolate; and when your good health had been confirmed to us by the document, etc.” In this letter the subject is the rite of divine worship to be performed in the church of Hippo throughout the entire course of the year. But no one who has spent even a little time reading Augustine will fail to judge that this letter must be rejected as Augustine’s, beginning with its very title. For this reason we did not wish to burden our edition with such an unworthy offspring.

## Addenda to the Appendix of Volume II

### A Consolatory Letter of Saint Augustine to Proba

[Note: In an old codex of the Abbey of Monte Cassino this letter bears this heading; but its style clearly shows that it is not Augustine’s. The Benedictine Fathers and GG. improperly relegated it to the end of the tenth volume. M.]

**1.** I have received the writings of your affection, in which I learned that your heart had been moved to grief by the death of your daughter. What I chiefly admired was that the virtue of a Christian heart had been displayed in you, so that you bent your mind toward grief. I am astonished that the wall of faith should have been pierced by the wounds of bereavement—a wall that the hope of resurrection and of the heavenly kingdom ought to have lulled to rest. Hope never agrees with grief, nor will faith ever feel any kind of loss. We believe that our loved ones will rise again, and yet we mourn! What would we do if God had commanded us only to die, without resurrection? Surely his will would be sufficient for consolation, since we know that no affection ought to be placed above it. He who created took away what he had given: who else was there to mourn? What you had received for a time, he had lent so that you might possess it for however long he wished, and might take it back again when he wished. He took away nothing that was yours when he deigned to reclaim what was his; and it was fitting that the creditor should reclaim his own loan, and that the borrower should nevertheless give thanks to his creditor.

[Note: [Col. 1175] Perhaps, “who cares for what belongs to another.”]

[Col. 1176] We read in Job a most devout utterance, one that we ought to follow: “The Lord gave,” he says, “and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21).

**2.** Therefore the father’s only consolation was not that no one ought to weep over a gain when he has returned what belonged to another, since it was not lawful for what had been necessary to its master to be retained by someone else. Another provision of consolation is added, one that might meet the darts of bereavement. We ought to envy those departing from the world if we felt the world’s hostile enmities. We mourn the Lord’s gifts, though he knows how to give our weakness what benefits it. Did you still wish to see the wretched woman laboring? Why do you suppose that a Christian and faithful soul should long remain within the prison of the world—for whom the whole world is a shipwreck, and who has escaped so many and such great attacks of the devil, so many battles of the body, and so many disasters of the age? You pour out tears as though you did not know what you yourself suffer every day. Your tears contend against hers, and your love has no equal in weeping to her love. She did not abandon him, but went before him; and, lest she should grieve for her departing father, she hastened to receive him.

[Col. 1175] **END OF VOLUME TWO.**
